## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with numerous manuscripts, corrected with the greatest care; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all the works completed after the very extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material below; expanded by works that are doubtful or apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in what places of their works. An exceedingly accurate edition, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes—uniformly similar throughout the entire work—the modest price, and above all this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Complete Courses* in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Augustine of Hippo

[Column 0009]

## Preface to Volume Nine

Although Augustine endured extremely arduous labors in refuting the Manichaeans and Arians, as may be sufficiently understood from the little works of the preceding volume, nevertheless, if these are compared with the writings that follow, which he likewise published against the Donatists, those earlier struggles will easily seem like mere playful skirmishes and shadowy battles. For among the Donatists there were far more violent passions, a more hardened obstinacy, and an untamed cruelty, to which the armed hand of the soldiers supplied courage and fury. Against these the most holy Doctor opposed no other weapons than charity, gentleness, and unbroken patience, with which he fortified his disputations and conferences with those schismatics, whether conducted in writing or in conversation.

To read these works profitably, readers’ minds should first be prepared by a brief account of events relating to the history of the Donatists. Thus, in accordance with this purpose, the learned may briefly review what they already know, while those less familiar with the subject may approach this reading properly equipped.

The schism of the Donatists arose in Africa approximately forty-three years before Augustine’s birth, after the end of the persecution of Diocletian. In the year of Christ 303 he first promulgated an edict against the Christians, in March, if we follow Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 8, chapter 2), or in April, according to the *Acts of the Martyrs of Palestine*. By that edict, “the churches were ordered to be demolished to their very foundations, and the sacred books to be consumed by fire.”

The edict was carried out with the utmost severity in Africa under Anulinus, the proconsul, and Florus, prefect of Numidia, where those Christians who resisted the edict were cruelly persecuted. Some of them voluntarily exposed themselves to punishment, openly declaring that they would never hand over the sacred books in their possession. Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, disapproved of this excessive zeal and forbade those who had brought martyrdom upon themselves in this way to be regarded as martyrs, following the example of Cyprian (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*, third day, chapter 13; Cyprian, letter 83, or 81). The Council of Elvira had previously provided the same rule concerning those who had destroyed idols for this purpose (Council of Elvira, canon 60).

Others, however, fell into the opposite extreme through weakness and abjectness of spirit, handing the sacred books over to profane hands. For this reason they were called *Traditores*, “Traditors”—a notorious designation that furnished the Donatist schism with both its occasion and its pretext. Mensurius, the predecessor of Caecilianus, was accused by them of this crime; still more especially Felix of Aptunga, Caecilianus’s ordainer, whom they declared in their council at Carthage to be the source of all evils. But this accusation lacked legitimate proof, and afterward it was more justly turned back upon the accusers themselves (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, third day, chapter 13; letter 88, section 3; and *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 60).

Indeed, after the persecution concerning the surrender of the books, at the Council of Cirta—which was held in 305 by eleven or twelve bishops of Numidia for the purpose of ordaining a bishop in place of Paul—Bishop Secundus of Tigisis, superior to the others by virtue of his seniority, wished first of all to establish that every bishop individually and collectively in that assembly was free from the crime. Yet, during the investigation itself, he was forced to halt, showing indulgence to his colleagues, who were considered guilty of the commonly alleged Traditorship, lest he himself become liable to the same accusation (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapters 26–27).

Accordingly, while the purgation remained pending, Silvanus was placed in charge of the Church of Cirta, not without the protest of the people, who shouted that Silvanus was a Traditor and demanded another in his place (*Proceedings before Zenophilus the Consular*, in the Appendix to this volume).

Six years later, through these men, the Donatist schism was formed. Donatus, bishop of the Church of the Black Houses in Numidia, had already prepared the way for it by disturbing the Church of Carthage at the time when Caecilianus was its deacon (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*, third day, chapter 12). Yet no division of unity occurred until the death of Mensurius and the substitution of Caecilianus, which took place in 311, when Maxentius granted the Christians freedom (Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, chapter 16, section 29).

At that time three classes of men rose up against Caecilianus: “the impious, the thieves, and the proud” (Augustine, *Psalm Against the Party of Donatus*). Botrus and Caelestius belonged to the last class; as aspirants to the Carthaginian see, they begrudged it to Caecilianus. The middle class consisted of the senior faithful members of the Carthaginian people, who refused to return to the successor the money of that church which Mensurius had deposited with them when he departed for the imperial court. For this reason they were called “thieves of ecclesiastical silver” (Optatus, book 1; Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 1, chapter 3, section 5).

Finally, the leader of the first class was Lucilla, an extremely wealthy and factious woman who was hostile to Caecilianus because, when he was a deacon, he had rebuked her. Before “spiritual food and drink,” Optatus says, she was said “to kiss a bone of some martyr—if indeed of a martyr” (Optatus, book 1).

All these people conspired against Caecilianus and appealed to Secundus of Tigisis and the other bishops of Numidia, summoning them to Carthage for a new election and alleging that Caecilianus’s ordination was defective because it had been performed by Felix of Aptunga, whom they claimed was implicated in the crime of Traditorship.

Accordingly, approximately seventy bishops assembled at Carthage [Column 0011] (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, third day, chapter 14). Among them were those Traditors of the Council of Cirta, whom Secundus had forgiven after they confessed their Traditorship, together with Silvanus, likewise a Traditor, whom they had appointed bishop of that same city of Cirta (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 27). All were received as guests by the aforesaid factionalists, not by the Catholics, at whose request Caecilianus had been ordained (Optatus, book 1).

Caecilianus was summoned to judgment but refused to appear, since he knew that those who had convened were not true judges but enemies and corrupt men. Indeed, the whole Church supported Caecilianus so that he would not hand himself over to brigands. Therefore those seditious bishops condemned him in his absence and against his will, on the ground that he had been ordained by Traditors and because, when he was a deacon, he was said to have forbidden food to be brought to martyrs held in custody (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, third day, chapter 14). In his place they installed Majorinus, a member of Lucilla’s household, who had been a lector in Caecilianus’s diaconate (Optatus, book 1).

From this ordination the whole of Africa was split into two parties, with two bishops established in most churches, one for each side, while other provinces of the Christian world remained entirely in communion with Caecilianus.

Moreover, from the beginning the emperor Constantine favored Caecilianus. When he ordered distributions from the treasury to be made in Africa to the ministers of the Catholic religion, he ordered them to be made through Caecilianus himself. He also honored him with a letter in which he declared that he did not approve of “certain men of insufficiently balanced mind”—that is, the Donatists—“who were corrupting the people of the most holy and Catholic Church by criminal and adulterous falsehood” (Constantine’s letter to Caecilianus, in the Appendix to this volume).

The Emperor also clearly supported Caecilianus in a letter to Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, concerning the immunity of the clergy. In his report to Constantine, Anulinus wrote that he had communicated the Emperor’s sacred letter to Caecilianus and to others “who acted under him,” whom he had urged to restore the unity of the Church (Anulinus’s report, in the same Appendix). He also stated that two petitions had been handed to him by Caecilianus’s opponents for him to forward to the Emperor.

One of these petitions was entitled: “Petition of the Catholic Church concerning the Crimes of Caecilianus, Submitted by the Party of Majorinus.” This was the name first used by those schismatics, before they adopted the designation derived from the faction of Donatus. The second petition was probably the supplication of the Donatists, submitted on 15 April 313, in which they asked the Emperor for judges from Gaul who were free from the charge of Traditorship.

Constantine granted their requests. Three bishops from Gaul were appointed as judges: Maternus from the city of Cologne, Reticius from Autun, and Marinus of Arles (Optatus, book 1). At the Emperor’s command they traveled to Rome. Together with fifteen Italian bishops, they assembled in the house of Fausta in the Lateran under the consulship of Constantine III and Licinius III, on the sixth day before the Nones of October—a Friday, that is, in the year 313. Miltiades presided, to whom the Emperor’s sacred letter had entrusted the task of judging this case with the greatest care and bringing it to an end according to the prescriptions of justice (Constantine’s letter to Miltiades, in the Appendix to this volume).

Caecilianus likewise appeared as ordered before the council with ten bishops from his communion. An equal number appeared from the opposing faction, among them Donatus of the Black Houses, the leader of the schismatics. After the case had been debated and examined in three sessions, Caecilianus was acquitted, while Donatus himself was condemned as the author and instigator of the entire faction, “and individual sentences were pronounced against him because he confessed that he had rebaptized and had laid hands upon fallen bishops, which is foreign to the Church” (Optatus, book 1).

As for the other bishops of the same party, so that their weakness might be treated with greater leniency and healed within the Church, it was decreed that if they wished to return to communion with the Church, they should be received in their offices, even if they had been ordained outside the Church (Augustine, letter 185, chapter 10, section 47; and letter 43, chapter 5, section 16).

“At the same time,” says Optatus—whether after the Roman council or after the Council of Arles, about which we shall speak shortly—“that same Donatus” requested permission to return to Africa on the condition that he not approach Carthage. At the same time, it was suggested to the Emperor “that, for the sake of peace, Caecilianus should be detained at Brescia, and this was done.”

Two bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, were additionally sent to Carthage. They reported that the Catholic Church was the one spread throughout the whole world and joined in communion with Caecilianus, and that Caecilianus had finally been acquitted by the judgment of the nineteen bishops of the Roman council, which could not be dissolved (Optatus, book 1). See the Appendix to this volume, in the extracts relating to the history of the Donatists, the section entitled: “Bishops Eunomius and Olympius Sent to Africa,” etc.

This decision appeared sufficient to suppress the schism and restore peace. But the Donatists, hardened in their obstinacy, complained to the Emperor that the case had not been judged correctly, “because their entire case had not been heard; rather, those same bishops had shut themselves up in a certain place and judged as it suited them” (Constantine’s letter to Ablavius, in the Appendix to this volume).

They added that the number of bishops at that Roman assembly had been too small to bring such a great controversy to an end, and that another episcopal judgment was therefore necessary for them. Their protest, however, focused especially on Felix of Aptunga, the bishop through whom, they argued, Caecilianus could not have been ordained properly and legitimately, since Felix was a Traditor (Constantine’s letter to Chrestus, in the same Appendix).

Although their demands were utterly unjust, Constantine assented to them in order to close every path and opportunity by which the schismatics might stir up disturbances. He allowed the accusation against Felix to be examined in a public African court before Aelianus the proconsul. Felix was declared innocent of the charge brought against him.

The Emperor also convoked a synod at Arles so that the entire case of Caecilianus might be brought under examination again, apparently in the year after the Roman council. [Column 0013] After the matter had been weighed more carefully, Caecilianus’s case once again emerged superior from that celebrated council.

Yet even then the obstinacy of the Donatists was not broken. They lodged an appeal to the Emperor and challenged his supreme judgment. Constantine accepted this appeal with no little irritation and indignation, but with the intention that, if they continued thereafter to provoke quarrels and disputes, the gravest punishments would be inflicted upon them.

Both parties were therefore summoned to Milan. After the parties had been heard and the weight of the arguments on both sides had been assessed, the Emperor declared Caecilianus “endowed with complete innocence,” as is established by his own letter written to Eumalius on 19 November 316.

But when even this most solemn judgment failed to satisfy those utterly obstinate men, “the same Augustus,” if we believe Parmenianus, “ordered them to be led to the field—that is, to punishment—with the Spaniard Hosius,” as Parmenianus maliciously says, “giving the suggestion” (Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 1, chapter 8).

Certainly Constantine “issued a very severe law; he enacted many measures against the error; he ordered their basilicas to be taken away,” and commanded “that the places of their assemblies be claimed for the treasury” (Augustine, letter 105, section 9; *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 92; and letter 88, section 3). It is also understood from the fact that Constantine, in 321, “sent a letter concerning the ending of their exile and the abandonment of their fury to God the avenger,” that exile had been decreed against some of them (Augustine, *After the Conference, One Book to the Donatists*, chapter 33).

Thus the schism of the Donatists was transformed into a heresy—not only because Augustine calls “an established schism” a “heresy” (Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 69), while “schism” is “a recent disagreement within an assembly arising from some diversity of opinions” (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 2, chapter 7), but also because, after violating the unity of the Church, they fell into false doctrines as well.

For once they had established this as a defense of their obstinacy—namely, that one incurred the guilt and liability of those with whom one associated—they then inferred that the Catholic Church had remained intact only in the party of Donatus, while it had perished everywhere else in the world, “as though extinguished by the contagion of communion,” namely, “on account of the crimes of Caecilianus” (Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 69), with whom the other churches had communicated.

In addition, they asserted that the efficacy of the sacraments depended upon the virtue of the ministers, and therefore that baptism outside the fellowship of Donatus was null and invalid. Consequently, they did not hesitate to baptize again Catholics who crossed over to their party.

Nevertheless, Tichonius—himself a Donatist—testifies, according to Augustine, that at a council of 270 bishops of his sect held at Carthage it had been decreed that “if the Traditors did not wish to be baptized, they should be received into communion as unimpaired” (Augustine, letter 93, section 93). This decree, however, does not appear to have been observed.

Finally, Donatus—not Donatus of the Black Houses, but the Carthaginian bishop after Majorinus—did not hold the Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity, as Augustine gathers from his writings. The holy Doctor adds, however, that the Donatists did not deliberately embrace this error of that Donatus, and that scarcely anyone among them could be found who knew that he had held such a view. Nevertheless, his eloquence and authority had such influence among his own people that many thought the Donatists had derived their name from him.

Optatus discusses this Donatus at length, precisely because he was held in exceptional esteem among his own people, and he notes the frivolity and fury of his spirit, but especially his intolerable pride. For “his heart was so exalted,” he says, “that he now seemed to himself to be not a man but a god; and he demanded so much from the bishops that all revered him with no less fear than God” (Optatus, book 3).

The flattery of his disciples touched and encouraged the man’s swelling pride. “With the clearest voices,” Augustine says, “these words are said to have been sung to Donatus: ‘Well done, well done, good leader, illustrious leader.’ Yet he did not say, ‘Let those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” immediately turn away and be ashamed’; nor did he wish to correct them so that they would say to Christ, ‘Good leader, illustrious leader’” (Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 69, section 5).

Perhaps Optatus exaggerated Donatus’s pride. Nevertheless, its immoderate character is demonstrated by the fact that he so despised the communion of other churches that he willingly and gladly withdrew from them, as though he would be polluted by their fellowship or lose the grace of holiness.

It is highly probable that in his time the Donatists began to have a bishop in the city of Rome. For when Optatus was writing—he had Parmenianus as his contemporary, the immediate successor of Donatus—Claudianus was already the sixth bishop of that sect in the City. He was not there to be joined in communion with “the Roman Church, in which the primacy of the apostolic see has always flourished” (Augustine, letter 43, chapter 3, section 7), but to retain in their defection those of his own people who had migrated to Rome.

There they “enclosed a certain cave outside the city with wickerwork, where at that time they could hold their little assembly in place of a basilica. Hence they were called Montenses and Cutzupitani” (Optatus, book 2. See the Appendix to this volume, in the extracts relating to the history of the Donatists, the section entitled: “The Donatist Strangers Living in Rome Have … a Cave Outside the City Instead of a Basilica”).

With the same purpose and intention the Donatists sent one of their bishops to Spain to manage the house and estates of a certain noble matron, and another to some unknown place outside Africa—namely, to prevent their followers from abandoning the schism (Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 108; and *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 63).

It is not certainly known when that Donatus succeeded Majorinus. His followers themselves maintained that it occurred before Constantine’s final judgment; in writings composed after the Conference at Carthage they wished to commend him in such a way “that they said that, before the Emperor Constantine’s tribunal, he himself had both accused and convicted Caecilianus” (Augustine, *After the Conference, One Book to the Donatists*, chapter 16).

Jerome’s *Chronicle* records that this same Donatus became known in 328 and was expelled from Carthage in 355. Optatus reports that he boldly resisted the prefect Gregory and also Paul and Macarius (Optatus, book 3).

The same author clearly and systematically records the three celebrated persecutions which the Donatists boasted had been stirred up against them by the Catholics. From Ezekiel’s prophecy he assigns them the names of storm, rain, and stones.

“There was first a storm,” he says, “under Ursacius: the wall was shaken, but did not fall, so that the rain might have a place in which to work. Rain followed under Gregory: the wall was wetted, but did not become soaked, so that the stones might have a place in which to work. After the rain, stones followed under the Workers of Unity: the wall was scattered, but restored itself again upon its foundations” (Appendix to this volume, at the end of the section entitled “The Persecution of Paul and Macarius”).

The first persecution of Ursacius may be assigned to the year 320. For the proceedings before Zenophilus the consular, after which Silvanus of Cirta—called a Traditor by them—was sent into exile “through the persecution of Zenophilus and Ursacius” (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 30), were, according to Cresconius, written in that same year.

Optatus often joins Leontius with Ursacius, a person entirely unknown among the writers of that age. This gives rise to the suspicion that the Donatists may have invented the name of Leontius, as well as those of Ursacius and Taurinus, in order to arouse hatred against the imperial ministers who had been employed to repress them.

Gregory, to whom Donatus sent such atrocious letters, calling him “the stain of the senate and the disgrace of the prefects” (Optatus, book 3; see the Appendix, the section on the persecution of Paul and Macarius), held the office of prefect toward the end of Constantine’s reign, according to the Theodosian Code (*Theodosian Code*, law 3, *On Grain Supply and Taxes*, and law 2, *On Contracts of Sale*), that is, in the years 336 and 337.

Finally, the Workers of Unity—namely Paul and Macarius—were sent into Africa by the Emperor Constans after his father’s death, both to distribute alms from the treasury among the populace and to promote the cause of unity.

Donatus of Carthage resisted them stubbornly and shamelessly, maintaining that “the Emperor had nothing to do with the Church” (Optatus, book 3). Indeed, Donatus, bishop of Bagai, stirred up against them a mob of frenzied men, namely the Circumcellions. Because of their profession of continence, the Donatists set them against the monks of the Catholic Church.

Augustine briefly describes their character and says that they were “a rustic class of men of notorious boldness, perpetrating monstrous crimes not only against others, but also not sparing themselves in the same insane savagery” (*On Heresies*, section 69). They considered it glorious and close to martyrdom to kill themselves by throwing themselves from precipices, by fire, or by drowning.

Their fury toward every kind of crime became so inflamed shortly before the undertaking of unity began that their bishops were compelled to write to Count Taurinus so that he might restrain their ungovernable madness (Optatus, book 3). But when soldiers sent by the Count wounded some of them and even killed others, their companions nevertheless began to regard those men as martyrs and Taurinus as one of their persecutors.

Donatus therefore led a frenzied mob from there. To meet its fury, Paul and Macarius requested soldiers from Count Silvester. The Donatist ministers attacked them first, although they attributed the entire cause of this tragedy to Macarius.

Donatus and Marculus perished amid mutual slaughter on both sides. Augustine writes that it is uncertain whether they threw themselves to their deaths, especially since Roman laws did not prescribe such punishments, although Optatus does not deny that many harsh actions were carried out by the Workers of Unity.

The Donatists nevertheless attributed their deaths to the Catholics, whom they called the authors of the “Macarian” persecution. They arranged for those two factionalists to be recognized as martyrs and for accounts of their deeds to be written. Through ignorance, this resulted in their being included in certain of our martyrologies.

Although the men who announced unity used only exhortations, most of the schismatic bishops, seized by empty fear together with their clergy, fled. Those who wished to appear more vigorous and courageous were captured and sent into distant exile (ibid.). It is reasonable to believe that Donatus of Carthage was among the latter; Petilianus calls him a man of martyrial glory in the Conference at Carthage (Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, second day, chapter 10).

The peace and unity of the African Church, restored for a time through the care of Constans by Paul and Macarius, endured for approximately fourteen years. It began to be restored around 347, and indeed before the Council of Carthage under Gratus, at which this peace is praised, as is also the Council of Sardica held in that same year, 347. Certainly it occurred before 350, when the Augustus Constans died. It remained complete and inviolate until 361, when Julian was elevated to the imperial power after the death of Constantius.

At that time the Donatist bishops asked him for permission to return from exile. Rogatianus, Pontius, Cassianus, and the other bishops and clergy of the party of Donatus joined in the supplication. In the letter presented to the Emperor, they carried impious flattery so far as to say that justice alone had a place with him (Augustine, *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 97, section 224; Optatus, book 2; Appendix to this volume, in the extracts relating to the history of the Donatists; see the section entitled “The Horrible Crimes of the Donatist Bishops”).

Julian granted their flattering petitions. Thus those flatterers returned from exile, among them Parmenianus, the third bishop of the party of Donatus at Carthage and the successor of Donatus.

From this followed countless massacres, sacrileges, and horrible crimes, which Julian tolerated and which could not be suppressed immediately under the succeeding emperors (Optatus, ibid.). After Julian’s death on 26 June 363, the reign of his successor Jovian was too brief for him to remedy such evils.

After Jovian’s death, which occurred in February of the following year, Valentinian issued laws against the Donatists, including one directed from the city of Trier to Julian, proconsul of Africa, on 20 February 373. Nor did the commander Romanus favor those same schismatics. He commanded the Roman forces from the time of Jovian until the year 373 and was himself regarded by the Donatists as one of their persecutors, together with Taurinus and Macarius.

Gratian Augustus dealt no more gently with them. Indeed, by a severe law addressed to Flavianus, vicar of Africa, he decreed that they should at last withdraw from their errors and restore to the Catholic Church the churches they were retaining contrary to the faith.

Finally, the law of Theodosius the Elder, addressed to Tatianus, prefect of the praetorium, on 15 June 392, imposed a fine of ten pounds of gold on any clergy who ordained or were ordained in heresy. Thereafter no group was more strongly affected by this law than the Donatists.

Yet nothing suppressed this disastrous sect and finally brought it to destruction so much as the internal dissensions among its followers. Hence, as Augustine testifies, it happened that “many fragments were made throughout Africa from that fragment” (Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 1, chapter 4, section 9)—a fitting and just instance of divine retribution, so that, just as Donatus had attempted to divide Christ, he himself might be divided daily by his own people (Augustine, *On the Christian Struggle*, chapter 29).

First of all, Tichonius, famous for his writings and especially for his *Book of Rules*, published for the understanding of Sacred Scripture, turned his pen against the doctrines of the Donatists and caused Parmenianus much trouble. From Tichonius Augustine received this celebrated saying against them: “What we want is holy” (Augustine, letter 93, section 43).

The Urbanenses also stirred up disturbances among their own adherents in a certain part of Numidia (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 4, chapter 60).

Likewise there were the Rogatists, or Rogatenses, so called from Rogatus, a Moor by nationality and apparently bishop of Cartennum. They were, Augustine says, “a very small fragment cut off from the larger fragment” (Augustine, letter 93, chapter 8). The persecution of the Donatists, under the leadership of Firmus, the tyrant who rebelled against the Romans in 372, made them somewhat more prominent and better known.

The Claudianists also split off within the sect of Donatus; this division united with Primianus before the schism of the Maximianists (Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 36, section 20).

This Primianus, the fourth Donatist bishop at Carthage, succeeded Parmenianus around the year 391, the year in which Augustine became a presbyter of Hippo. In the second year after Primianus’s accession to the episcopate, he found the Maximianists intensely hostile to him.

For when he had removed Maximianus, a deacon of his church, from communion in sacred matters, Maximianus, unable to endure the injury done to him, convened two assemblies of schismatics against Primianus: one at Carthage, consisting of forty-three bishops; the other at Cabarsussis in the province of Byzacena in 393, composed of one hundred or more bishops. These removed Primianus and substituted Maximianus in his place.

On the other hand, in the following year Primianus assembled a larger council of 310 bishops at the town of Bagai. At that council Primianus was acquitted, while the Maximianists were condemned.

From these dissensions, and especially from the very case of the Maximianists, the Catholic Church derived great advantage—not only because the Donatist schism was thereby greatly weakened, or because sound arguments were drawn from the disputes of the opposing parties for exposing and refuting their secession from the Catholic Church, but also because their solemn decree—that guilt is incurred through association with those with whom one communicates; that Baptism outside their assembly is null and invalid and must therefore be repeated; and, finally, that their complaints about the diligence of Christian rulers and their officials, which they themselves called persecution, were employed for their conversion—all these claims utterly collapsed in view of the manner in which the Donatists themselves acted toward the Maximianists. “For,” as Augustine reports, “they received some of them, together with those whom they had baptized outside their Church, into their offices without any repetition of Baptism whatsoever; nor did they cease to act against them through the public authorities in order to correct them; nor did they fear to contaminate their communion by the crimes which had been vehemently aggravated by the judgment of their council” (ibid., *On Heresies*, no. 69).

Primian’s party was especially assisted by Optatus, surnamed Gildonianus, or Gildo’s henchman, who employed against the Maximianists the authority and power of that count who commanded the Roman forces in Africa from 386 to 397. This Optatus was bishop of Thamugadi, a man of notorious reputation and hated by everyone because of his crimes; nevertheless, the other Donatists maintained communion with him and even accepted the Baptism he administered. This was once again a strikingly useful example for Catholics in refuting the Donatist doctrines.

Augustine vigorously employed these weapons against them; divine and all-powerful providence had destined him to defeat them. It is astonishing how powerful this sect had become in Africa when the holy man attacked it. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the great number of bishops present both at the council of Bagai and at that of Cabarsussis, which, as we have just seen, numbered more than four hundred. “With the party of Donatus rebaptizing the greater multitude of Africans,” Possidius says, “Africa lay seduced and oppressed” (*Life of Augustine*, chapter 7). But as soon as Augustine began to wield his stylus and pen, together with his voice, for its restoration, the Catholic Church, with the Lord’s help, began to raise her head. His opponents, although greatly superior in both number and power, were unable even to endure his presence and conversation—not because, as they wished people to believe, they distrusted their own cause, but because they fled from the craftiness of their dialectical opponent. Accordingly, they gave no written answer to his writings; or, if they did give one, they did so with such caution that it was obvious to everyone that they feared an encounter with their distinguished adversary and greatly dreaded that their replies might fall into his hands. The holy Doctor reproaches the Donatists themselves for this in these words:

“For if they wish themselves to be understood as wise men, scribes, and prophets, while we are supposedly persecutors of the wise and the prophets, why do they refuse to speak with us, since they were sent to us? Finally, if we press the man who wrote that letter to which we are now replying, asking him to acknowledge by subscribing in his own hand that it is his, perhaps he will not do so: so greatly do they fear that we may retain any of their words.”

Thus, when he was searching for the letter of Petilianus to which he had begun to reply, he could scarcely find a complete copy even after a year or two, because, he says, “no one from whom it was requested was willing to give it, after they learned that we were replying to the part of it which had reached us” (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 1, chapter 19, no. 21). Finally, they so avoided the pen and conversation of the unconquerable Doctor that they considered it preferable to remove him from their midst than to refute him with an appropriate reply (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 9).

When he had become a presbyter of Hippo in 391, as we have already said, and a bishop four years later, he published his first work against the Donatists during his presbyterate. He entitled it *The Psalm against the Party of Donatus*, an acrostic work adapted to the understanding of the less educated populace and intended to be sung. In it he set forth the entire history of the schism, apparently taken from Optatus, together with a brief refutation, in clear and simple words. In the *Retractions* he places this work after another, *On Faith and the Creed*, which he composed at the Council of Hippo in 393. That council contains a decree concerning the reception of Donatist clergy. Although at first Catholics had received them with their offices, this was later prohibited, perhaps in 392, at the Synod of Capua. The Council of Hippo confirms the prohibition, except in the case of those who were shown not to have rebaptized, or who wished to pass into Catholic communion together with their congregations (Appendix to this volume, *On Donatist Clergy*, etc.). The same was decreed at the Council of Carthage in 397.

Shortly afterward, on 16 June 401, the Fathers of another Carthaginian synod decided that Pope Anastasius and Venerius, bishop of Milan, should be approached so that they might agree that those who had received Baptism among the Donatists from childhood could be promoted to the clergy; the others, however, they judged should be left to their more careful consideration (ibid., *On Reconciliating the Donatists*, etc.). In another council convened on 13 September of the same year, it was determined that all could be admitted with their offices, if this seemed beneficial to the Catholic Church.

The Donatists, for their part, also held their own little councils, one at Constantina and another in the city of Milevis; their acts have perished (Augustine, letter 34, no. 5). This loss, however, is far more tolerable than the loss of the books which Augustine, then a presbyter, composed against the *Letter of Donatus*, namely the Carthaginian Donatus, in which he sought to establish that the Baptism of Christ existed only in communion with himself (ibid., *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 21). The holy Doctor afterward held conferences with the Donatists: one in 397 or the following year at Tubursicum with the Donatist Fortunius, bishop of that city, and several other Donatists (ibid., letter 44). Another took place by letter with another bishop of the same sect, named Honoratus, and with Clarentius, likewise a bishop. The same would have been done with Crispinus of Calama, celebrated among his own people for his age and reputation, had he not himself prevented it (ibid., letters 49, 70, 51).

Around the same year, 400, he composed two books which we still regret having lost, entitled *Against the Party of Donatus*. At about the same time he refuted in three books the letter written by Parmenianus against Tichonius. In them he treated and resolved the celebrated question of whether, within unity and communion in the same Sacraments, the wicked contaminate the good. Then, in seven books *On Baptism*, he demonstrated that the arguments of the schismatics for repeating Baptism were worthless, and that Cyprian was so far from favoring them that, on the contrary, nothing was so effective for refuting the Donatists and completely silencing them as Cyprian’s letters and conduct. Another work from the same period has perished, entitled *Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists*.

Not long afterward, Petilianus of Cirta—or, which is the same thing, the bishop of Constantin—, among the schismatics perhaps the most celebrated of all, wrote a letter to his clergy against the Catholic Church. Although the Donatists guarded it very carefully in secret, the holy man nevertheless intercepted it and attacked it in two successive works: partly in the year 400, when he did not yet possess it in full, and entirely in 402. Petilianus answered the first book with nothing but insults; this supplied the subject and occasion for Augustine’s third book, truly an admirable work. Nor should the *Letter to the Catholics*, commonly called *The Book on the Unity of the Church*, be passed over in silence. It was written on the same occasion, as is stated at its beginning.

Meanwhile, the emperor Honorius enacted a law prescribing capital punishment for violators of churches and sacred ministers; this law clearly applied to the Donatists as well. They alone were certainly affected by another edict of the same emperor in the year 400, ordering that throughout the public streets there should be posted “the rescript which the Donatists were said to have obtained from the emperor Julian,” concerning their recall from exile, together with the records in which such a claim had been inserted. Honorius issued this order so that everyone might recognize their desperation and disguised treachery.

On 25 August 403, a general assembly of the Catholic bishops of Africa was summoned at Carthage. Its decree was that the Donatists should be formally challenged, in a public conference, to give an account of their defection (ibid., *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 45). They rejected this condition in an unworthy manner by common agreement. Augustine therefore wrote a letter to the laypeople of the same sect (ibid., letter 76), so that from the withdrawal of their bishops they might finally learn to regard the justice of their cause with suspicion.

But the Donatists’ insolence did not stop there. For Crispinus, bishop of Calama, attacked Possidius, the Catholic bishop of that same city, so violently that Possidius could scarcely preserve his life except by flight (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 46; and Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12). For this and other crimes Crispinus was summoned to court and treated as a heretic. When a fine of ten pounds of gold had been imposed on him under the terms of Theodosian law of 392, he pleaded his case before the proconsul and attempted to remove the charge of heresy from himself. Possidius proved in a public disputation that the sentence imposed on him under that designation was just and lawful. Nevertheless, at Possidius’s request the fine was remitted. Crispinus appealed to the emperor, who imposed the same fine upon him and upon the other Donatist clergy.

While these events were taking place, the Circumcellions attacked Maximianus, bishop of Bagai, and others with such atrocious violence (Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 43) that on 26 June 404 the Fathers of the Council of Carthage decided that the emperor should be approached to restrain such monstrous behavior by law. Augustine, however, added the condition that the laws should contain more moderation than severity (Appendix to this volume, among the excerpts relating to the history of the Donatists; see the section entitled “The Embassy of the Council of Carthage to the Emperor Honorius against the Donatists”). Yet the cruelty of these madmen toward Maximianus extorted the strictest laws from Honorius.

At this time Cresconius, a grammarian from the Donatist party, attempted to defend Petilianus’s letter against Augustine’s first book. The holy Doctor defeated the man’s futile effort in four books, which were composed only after the laws promulgated by Honorius. Not long afterward, three other Augustinian works appeared which have not survived: a book entitled *Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists*; another, *Against Some Donatist or Other*; and a third entitled *Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists* (Augustine, *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 27 and following). In addition, another work by Petilianus, *On the One Baptism*, occasioned a new refutation by Augustine bearing the same title. That work survives, but the treatise which followed it, *Against the Donatists concerning the Maximianists*, has perished. In it he once again showed more carefully that their error against the Church was utterly overturned by the case of the Maximianists alone.

On 30 January 406, Maximinus, bishop of Siniti, and several other Donatists requested a hearing in a public assembly at Ravenna before the prefect of the praetorium, where they debated their case with the Catholics. Maximinus, however, returned to a sounder mind and deserved to enter into communion with the Catholic Church (ibid., *Brief Summary of the Conference with the Donatists*, day 3, chapter 141; letter 88, no. 10; and letter 105, no. 4).

In 407 there were again new decrees by the African Fathers and new laws by Honorius. On 13 June certain canons were enacted at a council of Carthage concerning the churches of the Donatists who were returning to communion with the Church. On 15 and 24 November Honorius issued new laws for restraining the Donatists.

After Stilicho was killed on 23 August 408, new disturbances were stirred up by the Donatists, as though his death had released them from the laws. To give their audacity some appearance of justification, they invented a pardon supposedly granted by Honorius. But the laws enacted by the emperor against them in that same year and the next immediately dispelled the fiction. As the governors pressed upon them with the strict execution of these laws, Augustine attempted to remove the punishment of bloodshed from the schismatic rebels.

Yet the laws of rulers are fickle. Around the middle of 409, Honorius granted heretics freedom to practice their religion. But at the request of the legates of the Council of Carthage held the following year, he revoked that freedom in August of the same year by a letter addressed to Heraclianus, the count of Africa.

Finally, on 14 October of that same year, 410, the emperor Honorius summoned a solemn conference between the two parties. It was held at Carthage on 1, 3, and 8 June 411, under the presidency of the tribune Marcellinus. In this conference the Donatists were defeated, though not convicted. For they immediately appealed to the emperor, who, by a new edict issued against them on 30 January 412, finally brought it about that many embraced communion with the Church.

Because the records of this conference, with their great length, wearied readers, Augustine abridged them and called the work the *Brief Summary of the Conference*. But because the Donatists attempted to corrupt and falsify the records of the same conference with various lies in order to retain the loyalty of their followers, the most energetic Athlete opposed their calumnies by publishing a book for the lay Donatists entitled *After the Conference, to the Donatists*. Shortly afterward the same author produced another work on the same subject, arising from the Council of Cirta held on 14 June 412.

After that great conference which we have just mentioned, the Donatists pursued the tribune Marcellinus, who had presided over it, with deadly hatred, especially because he pressed the execution of the imperial laws against them in Africa (Augustine, letter 141). They therefore defamed him before Count Marinus by evil arts and secret intrigues, so that by Marinus’s order the tribune was beheaded on 13 September 413 (ibid., letter 151). Yet the Donatists were treated no more mildly. Against them Honorius enacted, on 29 June of the following year, the strictest of all the laws, and at the end of August he sent letters declaring that the death of Marcellinus had in no way diminished the authority of the Carthaginian conference over which he had presided. Nor did the Donatists fare better in their importunate appeal to Count Boniface. Rejecting the slanders of those most mendacious men, he preferred Augustine’s advice, as set forth for him in that outstanding book or letter entitled *On the Correction of the Donatists* (ibid., letter 185).

[Col. 0023] In 418, on 1 May, the Fathers of the universal Council of Carthage enacted new decrees for extinguishing the remnants of the most obstinate sect. In the following September, while Augustine was staying at Caesarea in Mauretania, Emeritus was brought with great difficulty from his hiding place to enter into a disputation with the holy Doctor. His presence, however, so weakened and broke his spirit that he did not dare even to mutter or utter a sound. Somewhat earlier Augustine had published a book entitled *To Emeritus, the Donatist Bishop, after the Conference*, which briefly gathered together the matters by which Emeritus was defeated, or shown to have been defeated (ibid., *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 46).

Around the same year, 418 or 419, a meeting of the Donatists was held, attended by Petilianus and more than thirty other bishops. They decreed that those who had communicated with Catholics should be eligible for pardon and be received in their offices as bishops or presbyters, provided only that they had not offered sacrifice or addressed the people (ibid., *Against Gaudentius*, chapter 37).

Meanwhile Dulcitius, the executor of the imperial commands against the Donatists, urged Gaudentius, a bishop of that sect, by letter to return to unity. He dissuaded him from the burning by which Gaudentius threatened to consume himself and his followers together with the church in which he was. Gaudentius replied to Dulcitius’s letters. At Dulcitius’s request Augustine answered Gaudentius in a published book, to which he added another book replying to Gaudentius’s response.

These are the final works of the holy Doctor against the Donatists. Their numbers declining day by day, they finally allowed the unconquerable writer to rest. Nevertheless, the pestilential sect was not then so extinguished that remnants of it did not survive long after Augustine’s time, like the image of a dying body hastening toward destruction, or like ash or smoke left behind by a great fire.

For the rest, at the end of these works we have placed a sermon which seemed doubtful to us, attributed to Augustine and entitled *On Rusticianus, a Subdeacon Rebaptized by the Donatists and Ordained a Deacon*. After this sermon we have added an index of the holy Doctor’s works against the Donatists published piecemeal in the preceding volumes, together with a list and summaries of the letters written on the same occasion.

We also thought it worthwhile to publish in the Appendix, after the spurious book *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*, various writings and documents relating to the history of the Donatists—some complete, others in fragments. In particular, from the Carthaginian Conference: the opening of each proceeding; the emperor’s order for holding the conference; Marcellinus’s first and second edicts; the Donatists’ formal notice responding to the edict; the Catholics’ mandate in which the whole case was summarized; the second formal notice of the Donatists; the Donatists’ letter against the Catholics’ mandate; and finally the judge’s sentence. Nothing has been omitted that Augustine said in the same conference.

For the happy and successful outcome of this conference must be credited above all to Augustine’s care and industry. “Therefore,” says Possidius, who himself took part in the conference as one of the seven bishops appointed to debate, “whoever wishes to know more fully the diligence and labor of Augustine, of blessed memory, on behalf of the condition of God’s Church, should also read through those records.” For “that entire good work was both begun and completed through that holy man, with the agreement and joint efforts of our bishops” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapters 14, 13).

## ON THE PSALM AGAINST THE PARTY OF DONATUS

See book 1, chapter 20 of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 617, from the words “Also wishing” through the words “It is a hypopsalm,” where Augustine speaks of a certain prologue to the case. The Benedictine Fathers say that this is plainly different from the hypopsalm and that it is still missing. M.

[Col. 0023]

## THE PSALM AGAINST THE PARTY OF DONATUS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO

[Note: [Col. 0023] Written around the end of the year of Christ 393, since in the *Retractions* it is placed second, after the book *On Faith and the Creed*, composed at the Council of Hippo in that same year.]

[Note: [Col. 0023] The acrostic Psalm against the party of Donatus has been checked anew against the older editions of Johann Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the theologians of Louvain, as well as against the variant readings of the old Belgian manuscripts of Cambron and Endove.]

[Note: [Col. 0023] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, S)

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

[Col. 0024] The abundance of sins usually troubles the brothers:

For this reason our Lord wished to warn us beforehand,

[Col. 0025] Comparing the kingdom of heaven to a net cast into the sea,

Gathering [Note: [Col. 0025] Amerbach and Erasmus: “gathered.”] many fish, every kind, from both sides.

When they had drawn them to the shore, then they began to separate them:

They put the good into vessels; the remaining bad ones into the sea.

Whoever knows the Gospel, let him recognize it with fear.

He sees the net as the Church; he sees this age as the sea.

The mixed kind of fish, moreover, is the righteous together with the sinner.

The shore is the end of the age: then is the time for separating.

When the nets broke, they greatly loved the sea.

The vessels are the seats of the saints, where the wicked cannot [Note: [Col. 0025] Here Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts add “the wicked.”] arrive (Matthew 13:47–50).

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

The good listener perhaps asks: Who broke the net?

Very proud men, who say that they themselves are righteous.

Thus they made a rift, and altar against altar.

They handed themselves over to the devil when they quarrel over the handing over,

And the crime which they committed they wish to transfer to others:

They themselves handed over the Books, and dare to accuse us,

So that they may commit a worse crime than they had committed before.

They could excuse the case of the Books on the ground of fear,

Because Peter denied Christ (ibid. 26:70) when he was terrified of death.

But now how will they excuse the deed of altar against altar?

And, with Christ’s peace torn apart, place their hope in a human being?

What persecution [Note: [Col. 0025] The manuscripts read thus. The printed editions have “persecutor.”] did not do, they themselves did in a time of peace.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Our guardian, great God, you can deliver us

From these false prophets, who seek to devour us.

They cover an accursed wolfish heart with a sheep’s fleece [Note: [Col. 0025] Something appears to be missing here in most printed editions. For the other stanzas of this Psalm contain twelve verses, whereas this one contains only ten. Erasmus and Lyons add: “The name of the righteous is a sheep’s fleece; schism is in the wolfish heart,” but this is insufficient, since the number is still not properly completed. M.]:

Those who do not know the Scriptures, they are accustomed to deceive.

For they hear of the traditores and do not know what happened before.

If I say to them, “Prove it,” they have nothing to answer.

They say they have believed their own people; I say that they have lied:

For we too believe our own people, who say that they handed them over.

Do you wish to know who speaks falsely? Those who are not in unity.

Long ago the case was finished, because you do not stand in peace.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

[Col. 0026] Our elders spoke, and made books about it,

Those who at that time investigated the case, so that they could prove what was recent.

There were certain traditores of the Books of the holy law,

Bishops from Numidia, and not just anyone from the common people.

When they had come to Carthage to ordain a bishop,

They found Caecilianus already ordained in his own seat.

They were angry because they themselves had been unable to ordain him.

There were Botrus and Caelestius [Note: [Col. 0026] Optatus names him “Celesius” in book 1 *Against Parmenianus*.], very hostile to Caecilianus,

Impious, thieves, proud men—too much would be required to recount them—

All joined together to heap the accusation upon him.

They said that the man who ordained him had handed over the holy Books.

Thus they broke the nets of peace and now wander through the sea.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is, brothers, to dwell together as one (Psalm 133:1).

Hear the voice of the Prophet, so that you may be in unity.

Who proved to us [Note: [Col. 0026] One edition has “to you.”] the ancient charge concerning the handing over?

Who brought an accusation in court? Who sat as judges?

By what witnesses did he convict? Who dared to make the assertion?

But they gladly invented this, because they knew that they themselves had done it:

For rumor was already speaking of the handing over of the Books;

But those who had done it were hiding in that destruction.

Then they defamed others so that they themselves might conceal themselves.

Because of them the other leaders of that party went astray:

For they thought it shameful for them not to believe their colleagues.

Now, brothers, let the error end [Note: [Col. 0026] Perhaps “let the error be ended.”], and let us be in unity.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

They did what they wished in that blindness at the time:

No judges sat, no priests in the customary manner,

Who, gathered together in important cases, are accustomed to judge.

The accuser and the accused did not stand in an inquiry;

There were no witnesses, no document by which they could prove the crime:

Only fury, deceit, and tumult, which reign in falsehood.

Let the records that are customary in a council be brought before us;

Let us see what compelled the making of altar against altar.

If the priest was evil, he should first have been deposed:

If he could not be deposed, he should have been tolerated within the net,

Just as now you openly tolerate so many evil men;

And you who endure many for the sake of fury should have endured one for the sake of peace.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

It would have been a great joy for us if you had not wished to go astray then;

But if the truth was not seen then, now, from experience, behold it [Note: [Col. 0026] Amerbach and Erasmus: “if it has now been experienced.” Louvain: “on the part”—a faulty reading.].

You now have many wicked men who greatly displease you:

[Col. 0027] Yet you do not separate them from your communion.

I do not speak of those sins which you can also deny:

I speak of clubs, fires, and deaths, which your people commit in broad daylight.

Yet you tolerate them, either through error or fear.

How slight a thing it would have been for your fathers to endure one for the sake of unity,

If the tumult was so great that they could not degrade him?

I add that he was innocent, and they could prove nothing.

But lest the crime be investigated where they saw themselves implicated,

They pretended to be exceedingly righteous while wishing to disturb everything.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Whoever seeks empty honors does not wish to reign with Christ,

Like the leader of this evil party, whose side they are called.

For when Donatus wished to possess all Africa,

He requested overseas judges from the emperor.

But this unjust request did not arise from charity.

The truth itself cries out, which I now wish to report.

For the emperor agreed and sent men to sit at Rome—

Priests who could then hear Caecilianus together with him.

The case was heard; nothing was proved. He even dared to appeal,

And, after the judgment of his colleagues, to seek a hearing from the emperor.

Here this request is shown not to have arisen from charity.

Then, defeated everywhere, he began to rebaptize Christians.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

If you wish to follow justice, consider the whole case.

Why was what he did afterward not done earlier?

The priests were divided throughout the whole African region;

Overseas priests could have judged the matter.

Why do you rush into schism and altar against altar?

So that you could no longer hear what was judged afterward,

And might be compelled to appeal from your own judges,

While you wished by any means to confirm the reign of error.

And now you too do not know the whole matter, and pretend not to know it;

When the truth presses you, you say that your fathers erred,

As though anyone now prevented you from withdrawing from error.

But pride has bound you to the seat of pestilence.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Whoever possesses the charity of Christ cannot hate peace.

You too, peoples, listen now and agree with us [Note: [Col. 0027] The printed editions read “remember”; less suitably.],

You who do not hold the seat for which you unjustly fight.

If your bishops from some one region

Had a dispute among themselves, whom would you want to judge them except men from other regions, who were not involved in that dispute,

[Col. 0028] But who, after examining the case, would pronounce for one side?

You would never communicate with those who refused to agree with them.

Why, then, did you agree with those who previously did this?

For they themselves did not agree with the judgment of the overseas bishops,

Who judged on our behalf; they are joined to us today.

If Christ the Judge says this, what will you have to answer?

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

If the light of the heart is in you, you can see the truth.

There are Donatus’s petitions and the records: prove by them what was said.

If you do not wish to believe these, bring forward some documents of your own;

If we do not believe them either, there will be strife without end.

Let us therefore embrace peace [Note: [Col. 0028] Amerbach and Erasmus: “the peace of Christ.”]: what is it to us what happened before?

You accuse us of handing over; we reply that you did it.

You cry out against Macarius, and we against the Circumcellions.

Our matter has now been settled; your people have not ceased to this day.

Let your threshing floor have its chaff; this alone is what you wish to be:

For you do not want peace; they threaten with the club.

And would that they merely threatened, and did not beat people down [Note: [Col. 0028] Amerbach and Erasmus: “were ashamed”; this makes no sense.] every day.

If these men drive them out, your people have no one through whom to reign.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

If Macarius exceeded the bounds written in Christian law,

Or invoked the king’s law so that he might fight for unity,

I do not say that he committed no sin, but that your people are worse.

For who commanded them to rage in this way throughout Africa?

It is not proved that Christ or the emperor permitted this—

Clubs, private fires, and madness without law.

Because it is written, “Put away the sword” (Matthew 26:52), they do not consider a crime to use the club.

Not so that a man may die,

But so that he may be badly crushed

And afterward die, with his strength exhausted by suffering.

Yet even if they show mercy, they kill with a single club.

They call the clubs “Israels,” saying this with honor,

So that they may ravage the name itself more than the body which they strike with them.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Do not now, brothers, charge us with the time of Macarius.

If those men were cruel, and greatly displeased us,

And if false things are said about them, God can judge.

Let us love the peace of Christ and rejoice in unity.

If there are wicked people in the Church, they can do us no harm.

If they cannot be with us, let them be excluded, with peace preserved;

If they cannot be excluded, let them at least be excluded from the heart.

Holy Ezekiel said that certain people were marked,

Those who groaned over the sins of their brothers and did not separate themselves from them (Ezekiel 9:4).

Thus, because of wicked brothers, let us not separate ourselves from the mother.

That is what the impious did then, setting up an altar outside,

So that now they might have worse men than those whom they pretend to have fled.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Everyone who reads the Scriptures knows what I wish to reveal.

John the Baptist then openly said to the Jews

That Christ could winnow them as his threshing floor (Matthew 3:12).

He sent workers, his disciples, to preach in the harvest (ibid. 9:37):

Through them the threshing floor was gathered and winnowed by the cross.

Then the righteous, like grain, filled the Churches in purity,

Selling what they possessed and saying farewell to the world.

They were like seed scattered throughout the whole world,

So that another harvest might arise, to be winnowed at the end.

This harvest grows among weeds, because heresies exist everywhere:

Its chaff consists of the unjust, who are not in unity (ibid. 13:24–30, 37–43).

If Macarius was among them, why do you wish to rebaptize us?

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Place two threshing floors in your heart, so that you can see what I say [Note: [Col. 0029] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts: “see in your heart.”].

Certainly the earlier people too had saints, as the Scriptures show.

For God said that he had left seven thousand men (1 Kings 19:18; Romans 11:4).

And in the law there are many righteous priests and kings.

There you have so many prophets; you have many also from the common people.

Tell me: which of the righteous then separated an altar for himself?

That wicked people committed many crimes:

Sacrifice was offered to idols, and so many [Note: [Col. 0029] The printed editions of Amerbach and Erasmus lack “so many.”] prophets were killed.

Yet none of the righteous withdrew from unity.

The righteous endured the unrighteous, awaiting the coming winnower.

They were mingled in one temple, but were not mixed in heart.

They spoke so much against them, yet had one altar.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

What do you think of these things? The second harvest is the Church,

Which grows throughout the whole world and must endure more.

For it has the Lord’s example, even in Judas the traitor (Matthew 10:4).

He bore that man among the good and sent him also to preach.

The wicked servant preached, but Christ was the object of faith.

For those who believed the Judge did not concern themselves with the herald.

When he gave the holy supper, he did not exclude him even then (ibid. 26:25);

[Col. 0030] And he could have been betrayed through him even if he had departed beforehand.

But an example was given to us: to tolerate wicked brothers,

So that, when they cannot be excluded, we may separate ourselves in heart alone [Note: [Col. 0030] The printed editions read “let them be separated in heart alone.” The manuscripts more suitably read “let us separate ourselves in heart alone.”].

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

I ask you: answer us—why do you wish to rebaptize?

You expel your fallen priests from communion,

Yet no one afterward dared to rebaptize;

And all whom they baptized communicate with you today.

What did they receive from them, if they had nothing to give?

Read how adulterers are punished in the holy law.

For they cannot say that they sinned out of fear.

If only the holy baptize, rebaptize those who came after them.

Why do you accuse us because we are in unity,

We who had not yet been born during that persecution?

It is written that the sins of fathers do not belong to their children (Deuteronomy 24:16).

But no one bears good fruit if cut off from the vine.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

You know what “Catholic” means, and what has been cut off from—
avoid:

If there are any prudent among you, let them come and live in the root;

Before they dry out too much, let them already be freed from the fire.

Therefore we do not rebaptize, because there is one sign in the faith—

Not because we see you as holy, but because you possess only the form.

For the branch cut off from the vine has that very form.

But what benefit is the form to it if it does not live from the root?

Come, brothers, if you wish to be grafted into the vine.

It is painful when we see you lying there, cut off in this way.

Count the priests, beginning from the very seat of Peter,

And see in that succession of fathers who succeeded whom:

That is the rock which the proud gates of hell do not overcome (Matthew XVI, 18).

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

If someone such as this comes to you [Note: [Col. 0030] Er. Lugd. Ven., “If such a person should come.” M.],

Full of the Catholic faith, such as all of us are accustomed to hear those holy men described—

And if he says to you, “Brother, why do you wish to rebaptize me?

I do not know what happened before; now, however, I am in the faith of Christ.

If what I do not know defiles me, show me what sort of person you now are.

Behold, I look at your face; I do not know what is in your heart.

If what I do not know defiles me, perhaps you are defiling me.

And if I believe you to be holy, look at those with whom you share communion.

If what we do not know defiles us, you can no longer be holy,

Since so many sins, which your people secretly commit, defile you.

But if you do not care about what you do not know, neither do I care about what was done before.

And yet you dare to rebaptize such a Christian.”

[Col. 0031]

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Woe to you, who contend so unjustly for your sees!

You proclaim that you alone are holy, but say something else in your heart;

For you too see that many wicked people abound everywhere.

Can you say, “We are mixed together within the net”?

You are answered: you have already torn that net apart.

Nor can you say, “We tolerate the chaff”:

For we answer again, “You would have done this before as well.” [Note: [Col. 0031] The Lov. edition has, “You have done this.” It is corrected from the other books.]

For those people were not worse than that traitor Judas,

With whom the Apostles received the first sacrament of the supper (Matthew XXVI, 25; and John XIII, 26),

Even though they already knew among themselves that he was guilty of so great a crime;

Yet the filth in another’s heart did not defile them.

And yet you dare to rebaptize Christian brothers.

All who rejoice in peace, now judge truly.

Listen, brothers, to what I say, and do not be angry with me:

For what you hear is not false; you can also consider it.

What if the Church herself should now address you in peace

And say, “O my children, why do you complain about your mother?

Why did you abandon me? I now wish to hear from you.

You accuse your brothers, and I am grievously torn apart.

When the nations oppressed me, I endured much pain;

Many abandoned me, but they did so out of fear.

You, however, were compelled by no one to rebel against me in this way.

[Col. 0032]

You say that you are with me, but you see that this is false.

I am called Catholic, while you belong to Donatus’s party.

The Apostle commanded me to pray for the kings of the world (1 Timothy II, 1–2);

You envy those who are now kings in the Christian faith.

If you are children, why do you envy the fact that my prayers have been heard?

For when they sent gifts, you refused to accept them.

And you have forgotten the Prophets, who foretold this beforehand:

That the great kings of the nations would send gifts to the Church (Psalm LXXI, 10).

When you rejected those gifts, you showed that you were not [of the Church];

And you forced Macarius to avenge his grief [Note: [Col. 0032] See Optatus, book 3.].

But what have I done to you, your mother throughout the whole world?

I expel the wicked whom I can; those whom I cannot, I am compelled to endure.

I endure them until they are healed or separated at the end.

Why have you abandoned me, while I am tormented by your death?

If you hate the wicked so greatly, look at the sort of people you have.

If you too tolerate the wicked, why not remain in unity,

Where no one rebaptizes and there is no altar against altar?

You tolerate so many wicked people, but without any good reward,

Because what you ought to endure for Christ, you wish to endure for Donatus.

We sing peace to you, brothers, if you are willing to listen.

Our Judge will come; we give, and he demands.

[AGAINST THE LETTER OF PARMENIANUS.]

[Col. 0031]

NOTICE ON THE BOOKS AGAINST THE LETTER OF PARMENIANUS.

There follows the work Against the Letter of Parmenianus. At the beginning of this work Augustine says that he had previously discussed many matters against the Donatists, partly in written treatises and partly in addresses or sermons delivered to the people. Indeed, he had already written several letters against their schism: namely, Letter 23, to Maximinus; Letter 33, to Proculeianus; Letters 34 and 35, to Eusebius; Letters 43 and 44, to Glorius, Eleusius, and Felix; Letter 49, to Honoratus; and certain others issued before the year of Christ 400, which are presented in the second volume. He had also published several books: one against the Letter of Donatus, the schismatic bishop of Carthage, and two others against the Party of Donatus. The book which he calls Against the Letter of Donatus belonged approximately to the year of Christ 393, since in the first book of the *Retractions* he places it immediately after the Psalm against the Party of Donatus and testifies that it was composed during the same period of his presbyterate. The two books against the Party of Donatus, however, which he assigned a place in the second book of the *Retractions*, where he lists the works composed during his episcopate, between the books *On Christian Doctrine* and the books of the *Confessions*, are to be assigned approximately to the year of Christ 398. Leaving aside these two little works, which are still missing, the three books Against the Letter of Parmenianus appear here; they are earlier than the other extant books of Augustine directed against the Donatists.

Parmenianus, the Donatist bishop at Carthage, predecessor of Primianus and successor of Donatus, is known from his contemporary, Optatus, the Catholic bishop of Milevis, who published a substantial work against Parmenianus. Yet in Optatus’s work there is no mention of the letter which Augustine undertakes to refute in the books that follow. Parmenianus had written this letter to the Donatist Tichonius in order to restrain a member of his own communion who was incorporating into his writings certain distinguished testimonies and arguments from Scripture on behalf of the Catholic Church. Hence Augustine writes to Vincentius the Rogatist in Letter 93, no. 44:

“That is Tichonius,” he says, “whom Parmenianus restrains by writing to him and deters from writing such things. He does not, however, refute the very things that Tichonius writes; rather, as I said above, he presses him on one point: although Tichonius spoke in this way about the Church spread throughout the whole world, and although the sins of others did not defile anyone within its unity, Tichonius nevertheless separated himself, as it were, from the contagion of the Africans whom he regarded as traditors, and he was in Donatus’s party.”

And in Letter 249 he urges Restitutus to read Tichonius, who “seems to have vigorously treated and resolved the question of how, in the Church of God, if we are perhaps unable to correct or eradicate some perverse or even criminal persons, they must be tolerated while the bond of unity remains intact.”

Augustine attacks Parmenianus’s letter in three books. In the first, he responds to the accusations and unjust complaints that Parmenianus poured out against the Catholics. In the second and third, he examines the testimonies of Scripture which Parmenianus, by applying them wrongly in an attempt to deceive the unlearned and persuade them to separate from the wicked, was endeavoring to use, and he restores them to their proper meaning.

These books should probably be assigned to near the year of Christ 400. For in the *Retractions* they are placed beneath the work *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, which we assigned to approximately the year 400. Moreover, whenever Augustine speaks here of Optatus Gildonianus—namely, in Book 2, chapters 1, 4, 9, and 15—he sufficiently indicates that Optatus was already dead; and in the same second book Against Parmenianus, chapter 2, where he calls him “the ten-year groan of all Africa, Optatus Gildonianus,” he indicates that his tyranny had been brought to an end. This occurred in the year of Christ 398, as we shall later see from Book 2 Against the Letter of Petilianus, chapter 92. Finally, in Book 1, chapter 9, he says that “the images of the gods were ordered to be overturned and shattered by recent laws.” No one is unaware that these laws were issued by Honorius no earlier than the year 399.

In this same work he promises that he will treat the question of Baptism more fully elsewhere. That he promptly fulfilled this promise is easily understood from the sequence of the *Retractions*, where he arranged for the books composed on Baptism to follow immediately after this work.

[Col. 0033]

[Note: [Col. 0033] For the subsequent Books Against the Letter of Parmenianus, see Book 2, chapter 17, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 637, from the words “In three books” to the words “Against the Donatists.” M.]

**THE THREE BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE LETTER OF PARMENIANUS** [Note: [Col. 0033] Written approximately in the year of Christ 400.] [Note: [Col. 0033] We have corrected the books Against the Letter of Parmenianus with the help of two Vatican manuscripts, four Gallican manuscripts, and the Casalinian, Benignian, Michaelinian, and Pratellian manuscripts, as well as four different readings from Belgian manuscripts cited by Lov., and by collating the earlier editions of Am., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0033] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

He responds to the accusations and unjust complaints of Parmenianus against the Catholics, and shows that Christian rulers rightly establish penalties, in accordance with their office and authority, to restrain heretics and schismatics.

### CHAPTER I

**1.** I have indeed discussed many matters against the Donatists elsewhere, to the extent of the strength God supplies, partly by writing and partly also by delivering addresses.
