But now, since a certain letter of Parmenianus, formerly their bishop, has fallen into our hands—a letter written to Tichonius, a man endowed both with a keen intellect and with abundant eloquence, but nevertheless a Donatist, since Parmenianus thought that he was mistaken in confessing under compulsion what was true—the brothers asked, indeed commanded, me to answer this same letter of Parmenianus, especially because he accepts certain testimonies from Scripture otherwise than they ought to be understood.

For Tichonius, surrounded on every side by the voices of all the sacred writings [Note: [Col. 0033] The Lov. edition has “of all the sacred writings.”], awoke [Note: [Col. 0033] In the manuscripts, *circumtunsus*.] and saw the Church of God spread throughout the whole world, just as long before it had been foreseen and foretold concerning her through the hearts and mouths [Col. 0034] of the saints. Having perceived this, he undertook to demonstrate and assert against his own people that no human being’s sin, however wicked and monstrous, can override the promises of God; nor can any impiety committed by any persons within the Church bring it about that the faithfulness of God concerning the future Church, destined to be spread to the ends of the earth—preserved in the promises to the fathers and now made manifest—should be nullified [Note: [Col. 0034] The printed editions, after “and now made manifest,” have *would be nullified*. The manuscripts more correctly have *is nullified*.].

While Tichonius was arguing this forcefully and at length, and was closing the mouths of his opponents with many great and clear testimonies from the sacred Scriptures, he failed to see what should have followed from this: namely, that those Christians in Africa belong to the Church spread throughout the whole world who are connected, through communion, not with these people separated from the communion and unity of that same world, but with the world itself.

Parmenianus and the other Donatists, however, saw that this followed, and preferred to adopt the most obstinate attitude against the manifest truth asserted by Tichonius rather than, after conceding it, be defeated by the African Churches which enjoyed communion in the unity asserted by Tichonius, from which these people had separated themselves. Parmenianus at first thought that Tichonius should be corrected by means of a letter; afterward, however, he reports that Tichonius was condemned by their council.

We have therefore decided to answer, in this work, Parmenianus’s letter to Tichonius, in which he rebuked him for proclaiming that the Church was spread throughout the whole world and warned him not to dare to do so.

### CHAPTER II

**2.** Let us therefore first examine what sort of statement this is: he says that “the Gauls and Spaniards and Italians and their associates”—by which he evidently wishes the whole world to be understood—“are like the African traditors in the commerce of crimes and fellowship in wickedness.”

To a man producing so many and such weighty proofs from the sacred Scriptures, Parmenianus himself speaks without proofs and wants to be believed without proving anything, inviting Tichonius, as it were, to imitate him, since Parmenianus too believed certain of his fellow bishops, against so many Churches established throughout the vast extent of all the lands, merely because they spoke. What could be found more reckless than such credulity?

For he says that “certain men who had served as envoys,” as he himself asserts, “came to those same provinces as thoroughly trustworthy witnesses”; then, “by the repeated arrival of the most holy priests of the Lord,” as he himself says, “the charges were made public clearly, more fully, and more truthfully”—a man who thinks that he ought to be believed more than God.

Tichonius produces the thunderclaps of the divine Testament: what was accomplished in the promise to Abraham and in the promise to Isaac and Jacob, whose God he declares himself to be, saying, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (Exodus III, 6, 15). But Parmenianus sets against this the reports of his fellow priests.

What was said to Abraham? “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII, 18).

What was said to Isaac? “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because Abraham your father heard my voice” (ibid. XXVI, 4–5). [Note: [Col. 0035] In the manuscripts, “because of which.”]

What was said to Jacob? “I am the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac; do not be afraid. For the land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed; and your seed shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall be spread toward the sea, toward the southwest, toward the north, and toward the east; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your seed” (ibid. XXVIII, 13–14).

But lest they think that this was said about the Jews, let the Apostle explain what the seed of Abraham is, in which it was said that all nations would be blessed. “The promises,” he says, “were made to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians III, 16).

Therefore, that all nations would possess blessing in Christ was promised with such authority and fulfilled with such truth—and yet those who wish to be called Christians contradict it! And what do they set against this?

“Certain most trustworthy witnesses,” he says, “came as envoys to those same provinces; then, through the repeated arrival of the most holy priests of the Lord, the matter was made public clearly, more fully, and more truthfully.”

What, I ask you, what was made public through those faithful witnesses whom you wish to be more trustworthy than God? Was it that, through the African traditors, the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, was not permitted to reach all nations, and that where it had reached, it dried up?

Now declare that your colleagues must be believed more than the Testament of God; and in saying this, you boast that you have preserved that very Testament from the flames, although you are trying to destroy it with your tongue.

**3.** But let each person choose what he prefers; and if earthly smoke of falsehood has any power against the heavenly thunderbolts, let it abandon heaven and vanish into the winds.

For if Parmenianus did not favor his own see, he would choose to believe the Scripture of God rather than his colleagues. For God says to Jacob, “I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you” (Genesis XXVIII, 15).

It is far more credible, however, that those men had already been rejected by a just judgment and were not admitted to communion with those parts where God was already fulfilling what he had promised to the fathers; and that, for this reason, they had made such claims about the holy priests of God, by whom they had not deserved to be received, in order to agitate the weak minds of the peoples whom they had deceived with false rumors and, by the pride of their name, to ensnare minds that were rashly credulous and tear them away from the peace of the whole world.

What could be found more insane than this folly—or rather, madness?

Among the many nations of the world, God has fulfilled, and is still fulfilling, for the greater part, what he promised, until it reaches them all—he who said, “I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you.”

And these people now believe those who report that what God promised has not been fulfilled; and therefore they believe that, from those parts of the earth where it had already been fulfilled, the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, has perished, and that God’s promises have been nullified because they themselves were not admitted to communion with those among whom the world already possessed this fulfillment.

And no one says to them, “God is truthful, but every human being is a liar” (Romans III, 4). Instead, you say this about your own people: “The one who speaks falsehood speaks from himself” (John VIII, 44). Therefore you lie as human beings, because, as human beings, you are angry.

This is not said to them; instead, they are believed when they say that Christ has perished from the world which he had already begun to possess. And those who believe this, while shamelessly saying, “We are Christians,” dare also to say, “We alone are.”

### CHAPTER III

**4.** Parmenianus also says that from this it is proved that the whole world was implicated in the crimes of traditio and other sacrileges: although many such crimes were committed during the time of persecution, no separation of the peoples was therefore made in those provinces.

As though it could not have happened that some wicked persons remained hidden and were not accused, so that they could not be condemned without recklessness; while others were exposed and condemned, and, since they were not charged with manifest offenses, refrained from disturbing and dividing the Churches.

Thus it may have happened that, while some people were not accused and certain uncertain crimes were entrusted to God for the sake of genuine peace [Note: [Col. 0037] Am. and most manuscripts have “certain crimes.”], some crimes, once exposed and proved, were condemned in such a way that no condemned person could deceive the people by simulated innocence, and the bond of unity was not broken.

For this monstrous evil of division would not have occurred even in Africa unless the faction of those who fabricated false accusations had prevailed over the true reasoning of those who established guilt.

**5.** Let those who wish read what the venerable Optatus, bishop of Milevis and of the Catholic communion, relates and by what proofs he establishes so many points (*Against Parmenianus*, Book 1): whether concerning Lucilla, at that time a very wealthy and highly factious woman, whom the holy Caecilianus, while still a deacon, had offended on account of ecclesiastical discipline; or concerning the other associates of her faction—whether thieves of ecclesiastical silver, or men grieving that they had not attained the episcopate and pursuing Caecilianus, who had been preferred to them, with whatever plots they could devise; or concerning the Numidian bishops whom this faction had summoned for Caecilianus’s ruin, so that, after Caecilianus’s deposition, another might be ordained for them.

When these men came with their primate, Secundus of Tigisis, and with the others whose confessed crimes of traditio Secundus himself had pardoned, supposedly concerned for peace, as the ecclesiastical Acts testify, they judged the absent Caecilianus to be a traditor without any delay for a more careful inquiry and without allowing him any opportunity to respond.

Thus the crimes of traditio merely alleged against Caecilianus, who was absent, were made to harm him, while they had pardoned among themselves, in one another’s presence, crimes that had been confessed.

Accordingly, in opposition to the one seated in the see with which the entire Christian world—through the Christian Churches overseas and in distant lands, as well as through the stronger African Churches better able to resist such deceptions—was in communion [Note: [Col. 0037] Perhaps, “was in communion.”], they ordained another bishop [Note: [Col. 0037] Majorinus.], so that by their action they might contradict the promises of God, preventing all nations from being blessed in the seed of Abraham; and so that they might even call those parts of the world polluted by African traditors which had never heard Caecilianus’s name.

Moreover, against the whole world, which said, “What you charge against your fellow citizens I was unable to learn, nor ought I to condemn what was unknown to me” (or at least, whatever his life was like—which these men nevertheless convicted him of no crime—the man would have heard this as an innocent), they produce the testimony of the Apostle: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans I, 32).

Was it not enough for them to condemn so many and such great Christian peoples without a hearing, unless they also dared to bring forward against the Apostle himself his words, but not his meaning?

For if “to consent to those who do evil” means being with them in the Church, then the Apostle himself consented to the false brothers among whom he testified that he was in danger (2 Corinthians XI, 26); and he permitted those who preached the Gospel not chastely but out of envy and without love to preach nevertheless (Philippians I, 15, 17–18).

[Col. 0038]

But if consenting to those who do evil means nothing other than approving and praising their evil deeds, then, following the Apostle’s example, the whole world would not consent to the crimes of the Africans, even if it knew of them and tolerated them for the sake of the Church’s peace. Yet these people do not prove that the world knew of those crimes, even if they could have proved that the crimes were true.

### CHAPTER IV

**6.** Parmenianus therefore says in vain that the traditors condemned in Africa were received by the overseas provinces into the fellowship of condemnation.

For this is what we must not believe, lest, through sacrilegious recklessness, we condemn the whole world founded in the unity of Christ on the basis of their false accusation, rather than love it on the basis of the true promise of God.

What should be believed more: what God said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” or what these people say, “In the seed of the African traditors all nations are cursed”—so that what iniquity committed should prevail over what truth promised?

Why then do we not rather believe that those who were received into communion by the overseas provinces were either innocent and could not be oppressed by their accusers, a view that can be supported by many proofs; or, if they were wicked, could not be convicted and were received as people believed to be innocent, without any contamination of those who received them?

And what if, even through wicked brothers of the sort whom the Apostle tolerated within the unity of the Church, and whom the martyr Cyprian laments in his Letter on the Lapsed—even if through such brothers, appointed among the judges, some matter had been handled with such perversity that the traditors could not be excluded and convicted, and the Christian world had been deceived by their feigned innocence, it would in no way have lost its own innocence.

**7.** As for what they say about Hosius, formerly the Catholic bishop of Cordoba, they must be compelled to prove not only that he was such as they say, but also that it was manifest to those with whom they assert that he shared communion that he was such.

Unless they prove this, they say in vain that they knew what sort of person he was. For he could not harm those who did not know, and these people, by separating themselves from the innocent, cannot themselves be innocent because of the sacrilegious injustice of that separation.

For this is more credible—if indeed Hosius was condemned by the Spaniards and acquitted by the Gauls—that it could have happened in this way: the Spaniards, surrounded by false accusations and deceived by the clever fraud of plots, pronounced a sentence against an innocent man; afterward, in Christian humility and peace, they submitted to the judgment of their colleagues by whom his innocence had been established, lest, by defending their earlier decisions with obstinate and impassioned perversity, they rush blindly into the sacrilege of schism, which surpasses all crimes.

This is what these wretched men did; and even now, after being divided and cut apart so many times, they do not at last recognize what they have done.

**8.** They therefore make it abundantly clear from what cause they have become incurable: namely, lest they be compelled to condemn their own sentences, rashly pronounced against the absent Caecilianus, if they submitted, in consideration of truth and peace, to the overseas judgment in which they had been defeated by Caecilianus when he was present.

They would have won a greater victory if, after the judgment, they had overcome human hostility than if they had overcome a human being in the judgment itself. For that victory is loftier and more complete in its triumph when it is won not merely over one defeated man but over an entire subjugated city, as Scripture says: “The one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city” (Proverbs XVI, 32).

They wished to conquer a man, though anger was conquering them. And because they could not conquer the man, they were defeated both by the man and by anger: by the man, because they were defeated in the judgment; by anger, because even after their defeat they did not grow quiet, hearing or reading with their most perverse hearts the Apostle’s judgment: “For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Galatians II, 18).

If the Apostle himself had understood these words with such a hostile disposition, he would have become neither a Christian nor an apostle, and he would not have built up as a preacher the Churches that he had previously destroyed as a persecutor.

Nowhere, therefore, did these people reveal so openly why they refused to be corrected even after being defeated as when they detest the Spaniards because, after their own sentences had been pronounced, the Spaniards submitted to the later examination and judgment of their colleagues.

The former action was one of Christian gentleness, just as the latter was one of diabolical contention. It is therefore no wonder that peace was preserved by the former humility and shattered by the latter arrogance.

Accordingly, what they did is rightly returned to them, for they taught such conduct to their descendants. The Maximianists too refused, for no other reason, to submit to the judgment of their three hundred and ten colleagues, by whom Primianus [Note: [Col. 0039] Primianus, successor of Parmenianus as the Donatist bishop of Carthage, was first condemned by one hundred bishops at the Donatist council of Cabarsussum; afterward he was judged innocent by three hundred and ten bishops at the council of Bagai. See also the *Exposition on Psalm 36*, sermon 2, no. 19, and elsewhere.], whom they themselves had first condemned, was judged innocent, except by opposing to the unlearned the apostolic sentence in support of their declared [Note: [Col. 0039] Perhaps “manifest,” that is, “open.”] obstinacy and saying, “For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor.”

For one hundred colleagues had destroyed Primianus, and therefore refused to rebuild him together with the three hundred. Thus, while pretending to take care not to rebuild the man whom they had destroyed, they destroyed themselves by the evil of sacrilegious schism [Note: [Col. 0039] The Vatican manuscripts have, “they destroyed themselves by the greater evil of sacrilegious schism.”].

**9.** Yet if Parmenianus were alive, he would no longer dare to rebuke the Spaniards and call them transgressors because they turned from their own sentence to the sentence of their colleagues. Otherwise he would offend his own colleagues, many of whom, after having condemned Primianus, later corrected themselves for the better and passed over to the council of three hundred, choosing to act against their own previous sentences rather than against the peace of unity, even within Donatus’s party.

Parmenianus would especially spare Praetextatus of Assuri and Felicianus of Musti. Although they too had been condemned by their three hundred and ten fellow bishops, they returned, out of zeal for concord, to those very people by whom they had been condemned; and, with the same zeal, they were received by their condemners without any loss of honor, for the sake of peace.

No one thought that those who had been baptized by them outside, in schism, needed to be rebaptized.

Or perhaps, because Parmenianus greatly dislikes those who correct their own judgments, and because, without understanding whom the Apostle calls transgressors, he would detest these men for preferring to return inside rather than remain outside, he might have created additional Parmenianists by joining to himself certain similar associates—just as many fragments have already been made throughout Africa from this fragment [Note: [Col. 0040] Some manuscripts have, “have been broken.”].

Yes, yes: those who placed the swelling of their hostility above the most holy bond of Catholic peace must necessarily perish, cut up and divided into ever smaller pieces.

For we should not fear so much what Parmenianus threatens as attend to what he admits.

### CHAPTER V

**10.** For when he said that, through the assistance provided by Hosius the Spaniard to Caecilianus, the number of holy and unblemished persons was being forced into their communion, and that the faith of God’s servants had remained unbroken against this impiety, he admitted without compulsion that his own people had also approached Constantine and that, by his decision, their case had been heard by episcopal judges presided over by Miltiades [Note: [Col. 0040] In ancient manuscripts the name appears in various forms: rarely *Melchiades*, more frequently *Miltiades* or *Meltiades*, and also *Meletiades*.], bishop of the city of Rome.

In that judgment, as the ecclesiastical Acts testify, because these people were defeated and Caecilianus was found innocent, they accuse that same Miltiades of the crime of traditio.

How, I ask, did they discover this?

If they knew it before the judgment, they ought not to have prejudiced their own case by beginning proceedings before such a judge and, even at the command of the Emperor whom they themselves had approached, submitting to such a judgment [Note: [Col. 0040] The printed editions have, “even at the command of the Emperor whom they had approached, they underwent such a judgment.” The manuscripts more smoothly have, “submit to such a judgment.” But instead of *even*, *and even* seems to be required.].

But if they claim that they learned that he was a traditor after the case had been heard and the sentence pronounced, are these people so insane that, against the judges before whom they were defeated, they believe the defeated litigants [Note: [Col. 0040] This is how one of the Vatican manuscripts reads. Lov. has, “that the two hundred judges before whom they were defeated should be considered inferior to the defeated litigants.” Other printed editions and manuscripts, although they omit “should be considered inferior,” nevertheless have “two hundred” or “two hundred judges,” incorrectly. The matter concerns the Roman judgment in which, as is clear from Optatus’s first book, only eighteen bishops besides Miltiades were present.]?

And yet, in all these matters—although with great recklessness they accuse the Italians, Gauls, and Spaniards, leaving aside so many other provinces and peoples from whom they have separated themselves by their unspeakable sacrilege, and whose interests could not be harmed by the crimes of the Italians, Spaniards, and Gauls even if the accusations were true—they now accuse the other lands in blind fashion, or rather in madness, and are angry with them.

For, they say, when there were two parties in Africa, one of traditors and the other of the innocent, they preferred to associate with themselves the traditors rather than the innocent.

This single accusation is refuted very briefly and very truthfully in this way: when they heard that there were two parties in Africa, one of traditors and the other of the innocent, they believed that party to be innocent which had prevailed in its case before neighboring ecclesiastical judges.

Therefore those always remained innocent who, without knowing how these matters had been conducted in Africa, nevertheless believed what they ought to have believed peacefully and religiously. Separation from those innocent people could in no way itself be innocent.

### CHAPTER VI

**11.** Parmenianus also admits that the town of Arles, the episcopal judges, and the parties from Africa had gathered—namely, Caecilianus and the Donatists. There he believed everything his own people told him, since, having been defeated, they could do nothing except complain about the judges [Note: [Col. 0041] This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “who, having been defeated, were able to complain about the judges,” omitting “except.”].

Yet he does not deny that they came to Constantine again; and because they were also defeated there in the final judgment, he accuses Constantine himself of having been corrupted by bribery.

When all these matters are considered, let anyone who judges without partisan bias choose whom to believe: whether the judges who pronounced the sentences, or the litigants against whom the sentences were pronounced and who refused to bring the suit to an end.

Certainly, the whole world believed the judges.

Those, however, who agree with and defend the Donatists admit that they believe people who, whatever their case may have been, were nevertheless unable to prevail in so many hearings overseas, and they credulously accept the murmurs and accusations that those people directed against the judges.

If they call themselves innocent in this matter, and if they know that the others were defeated, how much more innocent are those who refuse rashly to believe anything evil about the judges themselves, since it is necessary that those who were defeated should complain about them?

For not only does the person who has lost a good case complain about an unjust, slow, or negligent judge; even the person who has been defeated with complete justice murmurs against an innocent judge with the same blindness with which he litigated against an innocent opponent.

Therefore these people are not wicked because they refuse rashly to believe something about everyone who has been defeated. They are wicked because, in the madness of schism, they cut themselves off from those innocent people who, with much greater reason, refuse to believe anything of this sort about those judges.

## CHAPTER VII

**12.** Let there exist, then, some most illustrious Church of those regions in the name of Christ, one of those seven—and, if you please, especially Philadelphia (Rev. 3:7), which through the Greek language conveys fraternal love by its mystical name. Let us therefore hear her voice; and let it not be the voice of her chaff, but of her grain.

If, then, she were to say to these people:

“What do you accuse in me, brothers? What do you charge me with? You have been able partly to know and partly to hear how far I am removed from Africa in earthly location. What the traditors, or the accusers or condemners of traditors, or the slanderers or oppressors of the innocent, did there at that time, I altogether do not know. But our Lord, who purchased the whole world at the price of his blood, whose holy commerce the prophet proclaimed so long beforehand, saying, ‘They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones. They themselves considered and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment they cast lots’—he did not establish empty and barren spaces between us and you for Christians. He filled all these places with the sanctification of his name.

“For in that very psalm of the Passion, not only how many he purchased but also how much he purchased is declared. For shortly afterward it says: ‘All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; for the kingdom is his, and he shall rule the nations’ (Ps. 21:17–19, 28–29).

“I might perhaps then be compelled to judge your case if I were either nearby or so remote that no other Christians, marked with the same name and reconciled in the same unity, lived between us and you. Many nations lie between us, purchased together with me by the blood of him before whom they worship together with me. Through them news of you has reached me; they were able, because of their proximity, to examine your case. If this was not done, you neglected it; for if you had been neglected by the others, you would surely not have reached even us. But if something was judged, pardon me: I do not dare rashly to believe you, who have been defeated, and to condemn your judges with the same rashness.

“Moreover, there is another matter that greatly moves me. If you had been innocently oppressed, you would at least have loved us, your brothers, who did you no harm. Yet when you attempt to tear apart with curses and bitter hatred us, who are fully conscious of our innocence and who know that your case was entrusted by the proper law of the Church to your neighboring bishops, who know before God how they judged—when you attack us nevertheless, and even attempt to rebaptize us, as though because of you Christ had lost his inheritance among us—what good opinion can we form of your case?

“For when you do not hesitate to condemn brothers living far away by rash suspicions, you show how justly you were condemned by your neighbors. Why should I not believe that one who has been heard could rightly be condemned by a neighboring judge, when he does not hesitate to condemn me, a brother living so far away, without hearing me? He charges me with this as the greatest crime: that, since I could not be present, I believed the judges to whom the case was brought rather than the litigants who were defeated.

“If I had not believed those judges, even if the men who were defeated had been innocent, I could not have been innocent. We would have been implicated in a great offense if, since we could not see human hearts and did not maintain ecclesiastical discipline, we refused to believe those who judged, beyond whom the case could proceed no further and through whom news of it could reach us.

“You tear yourself away from these innocent people by an impious robbery and call yourself innocent. If you truly were innocent, when you saw in the holy Scriptures that the harvest of your Lord cannot be separated from the weeds and chaff before the final separation and winnowing (Matt. 3:12; 13:27–43), you would choose rather to be strong in tolerating the wicked than impious in abandoning the good.

“For why should we not think that these are the Churches scattered throughout the world, and those most just words that I represented as spoken by Philadelphia?”

[Note: Lov. reads “What do you accuse me of?” omitting the particle *in*.]

[Note: In the printed editions, the text reads *fuisse dicamus* (“we say that it was entrusted”); *dicamus* is absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VIII

**13.** Parmenianus even dares to complain that Constantine ordered those men to be led to the *campus*, that is, to punishment, who, after being defeated before ecclesiastical judges, could not prove what they alleged even before Constantine himself, and who still persisted in sacrilegious fury in the severance of the holy Church. He accuses Constantine of having given this order with savage cruelty at the prompting of the Spaniard Hosius—condemning, as usual, men unheard on the basis of his own suspicions.

As though someone else might not have believed, more humanely and more plausibly, that Hosius, acting as a bishop, had rather suggested this so that the emperor might be moved toward a milder punishment, even though the crime was exceedingly grave—namely, the sacrilegious schism.

For what do these people not justly suffer, when they suffer by the judgment of God, who presides from on high and warns them through such scourges to avoid the eternal fire, and when they suffer both according to the desert of their crimes and according to the order of the authorities? Let them first prove that they are not heretics or schismatics; then let them utter their livid complaint about their undeserved punishments; then let them dare, when they suffer something evil, to call themselves martyrs of the truth.

Otherwise, if everyone who pays a penalty from the emperor or from judges sent by him is immediately a martyr, all prisons are full of martyrs, all judicial chains drag martyrs along, martyrs languish in every mine, martyrs are deported to every island, martyrs are struck down by the legal sword in every place of punishment, martyrs are thrown before every beast, or are burned alive by order of judges.

But if, as the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God, and he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil, and he does not carry the sword without reason. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13:1–4)—then whatever the good person suffers, praise comes to him from the authority that inflicts it; but the wicked person, who suffers deservedly for his wrongdoing, should not attribute it to the cruelty of the authority.

**14.** And yet what do these people suffer that is comparable to what they themselves do, except that the multitude of human beings has a heart not in its heart but in its eyes? If blood flows from mortal flesh, whoever sees it shudders. But when souls cut off and separated from the peace of Christ die in the sacrilege of heresy or schism, because it is not seen, it is not mourned. Indeed, a death more dreadful and more grievous—and, to speak plainly, more real—is mocked by force of habit, while the perpetrators of such great deaths publicly insult us and do not even deign to confer with us for the sake of making the truth known.

And if they suffer some temporal hardship through the most certain and most righteous order of the authorities, although they themselves everywhere and daily commit much graver acts through private bands of madmen, without any royal or ecclesiastical law, they call us persecutors of bodies but do not call themselves murderers of souls, even though by private license they spare not even bodies.

But because, through Christian gentleness, an eye torn out in a quarrel is judged much more severely than a mind blinded in schism, they both speak against us and speak with us; and when truth compels them to fall silent, iniquity does not permit them to be silent.

[Note: Am. reads “if peace”; Lov. “if on behalf of peace.” The manuscripts’ “if cut off from peace” is preferable.]

[Note: In the printed editions, *semper* (“always”) is added before “through Christian gentleness.” The manuscripts do not contain it.]

## CHAPTER IX

**15.** Or perhaps it is unlawful for the emperor, or for those whom the emperor sends, to say anything concerning religion? Why, then, did your delegates come to the emperor? Why did they make him judge of their case, if they were not going to follow what he judged?

But why is this being said? Even if they succeed in establishing that it does not belong to the emperor to impose any penalty upon those who follow a perverse religion, will they therefore be martyrs if he kills or punishes them? This argument would open the same claim to all heretics, against whom, by the hidden authority of God operating through the visible authority of human beings, many severe measures have been established for their restraint—and not merely against heretics, even those who have at least been whitened by the Christian name in some fashion, but also against pagans themselves.

For they too are impious in a false religion; their images have been ordered by recent laws to be overturned and smashed, and their sacrifices to be prohibited under threat of capital punishment. If one of them is condemned for such a crime, is he to be regarded as a martyr because he suffers the penalty prescribed by the laws for a superstition that he believed to be a pious religion? Certainly no one who is in any way a Christian dares to say this.

Therefore not everyone who is punished by the emperor in some religious matter becomes a martyr. Those who think such things do not see that they are advancing to the point of claiming that even the demons themselves can lay claim to the glory of martyrs, because they suffer this persecution through Christian emperors: throughout nearly the whole world their temples are overturned, their idols smashed, their sacrifices removed, and those who honor them punished if they are discovered.

But if it is utterly insane to say this, then justice is not established by suffering; rather, suffering is glorious because of justice. Therefore the Lord, lest anyone cast a fog over this matter for the unlearned and seek the praise of martyrdom in the condemnation of his own merits, did not say generally, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” but added a great distinction by which true piety is separated from sacrilege: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice” (Matt. 5:10).

But those who have divided Christ’s Church, and who, under the appearance of justice, attempt to separate it prematurely from its chaff while attacking its grain with false accusations, suffer in no way for justice. Rather, like the lightest chaff, they have been separated from it by various gusts of rumor.

But they say: “We have not done these things.” Let them therefore first free themselves from this charge, and then let them dare, if they suffer any troubles or punishments from Christian emperors, either to bring them forward in complaint or to claim them as glory. Concerning this matter—that is, the question of the schism itself—if I said nothing else, what has already been said above would suffice.

[Note: Mss. read “so that he might not present a fog to the unlearned.” See Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.82.]

[Note: Am. and the manuscripts read *vere* (“truly”); the printed editions have *vera* (“true”).]

[Note: The printed editions read “and while, under the appearance of justice, they attempt to separate themselves prematurely from the chaff and attack its grain with false accusations, while they themselves are rather separated from it.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER X

**16.** Or perhaps they will say that, even if they are convicted of sacrilegious dissent, so that if they suffer anything for that madness they are not martyrs, nevertheless such things ought not to belong to the authority of emperors to restrain or punish.

Here I ask what they will say. Is it because such authorities should take no concern for a corrupt or false religion? But we have already said much about pagans and about the demons themselves, and about the persecutions they suffer from emperors. Does this also displease them? Why, then, do they themselves, wherever they can, overthrow temples and persist in doing or avenging such things through the violence of the Circumcellions? Is private violence more just than royal diligence?

But I set this aside. I ask this: since the Apostle plainly lists the works of the flesh—“fornications, impurities, contentions, rivalries, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these” (Gal. 5:19)—what do they think? Do they believe that the crime of idolatry is rightly punished by emperors? Or, if they do not wish even this, why do they admit that the force of the laws is rightly exercised against poisoners, but refuse to admit it against heretics and impious dissensions, when these too are numbered by apostolic authority among the fruits of iniquity?

Or perhaps these human authorities are not permitted to concern themselves with such matters of human institution? Why, then, does he who is called God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against those who do evil, carry the sword?

Unless perhaps, as some of their most ignorant men are accustomed to understand it, this was said about ecclesiastical honors, so that the sword is understood as spiritual vengeance, which works excommunication. But the most provident Apostle makes sufficiently clear what he is speaking about in the continuation of the passage. For there he adds: “For this reason you also pay taxes”; and then he continues: “Render to all their due: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue, honor to whom honor, fear to whom fear” (Rom. 13:1–7).

It remains, then, for them by these arguments to forbid Christians to pay taxes, even though the Lord, when confronted with Pharisees who held such opinions—and whom these people imitate—looked at the coin and said: “Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

But these people, disobedient and impious in both matters, render neither Christian love to God nor human fear to kings. They are so blind and insane that, when they themselves expelled their schismatics, the Maximianists, from the basilicas through authorities sent by Catholic emperors, and compelled them to withdraw by the great force of imperial orders and assistance, they accuse the Catholic Church if Catholic rulers order something similar to be done on its behalf.

Let those same Maximianists remember what savage and bitter suffering that Rogatus the Moor endured at the hands of the barbarian king Firmus before they became Maximianists—that is, while they still belonged together in the single fellowship of the Donatists. Let them be silent and not dare to complain if they suffer anything of this kind either from the Primianists because of their schism or together with the Primianists because of the Donatists—not for sacred religion, but for sacrilegious hostility.

[Note: Concerning Firmus the tyrant, whom Theodosius, the father of the elder Theodosius, sent by Valentinian the Elder into Africa and defeated in battle, Paul the Deacon writes in book 12.]

[Note: The printed editions read “because of the Donatists.” The manuscripts read “because of the Donatists’”—with *schism* understood.]

## CHAPTER XI

**17.** Perhaps they say that they have suffered more grievously at the hands of Catholic emperors than the Rogatists suffered through barbarian kings, or the Maximianists through judges of Catholic emperors, or than they themselves inflict through the fury of the Circumcellions upon everyone they can reach.

As though the question were whether they suffer more grievously than they inflict. I would by no means concede that. For many of their most savage acts are recounted—or rather, cannot be counted—which, if they were fewer or afflicted those against whom they are committed less severely, would for that very reason certainly be more grievous: they are not ordered by duly constituted authorities but are committed in extraordinary fits of madness.

The measures they carried out against the Maximianists through judges established by human authority are not so numerous. Let them include in that category, if they wish, the actions they carried out against Rogatus the Moor through the barbarian Firmus, even if they count him among the lawful authorities, although he was a most savage enemy of the Romans. But these acts are not as numerous as the many things they do every day through furious bands of drunken young men, whom they appoint as leaders. At first these men were armed only with clubs; now they have begun to arm themselves with swords. They roam throughout Africa under the very well-known name of Circumcellions and commit savage acts against every order of laws and authorities.

When their crimes are reported to the Donatists, they pretend to be unaware that such a class of men exists, or they assert with utterly shameless lips that it does not concern them at all. Yet they do not even accept this declaration from the whole world—a declaration much more plausible and true—that the world does not know what has happened in Africa, whether on the side of Donatus or against it. This is much more credible than that the bishops of the Donatists in Africa itself either do not know what the Circumcellions have done or say that it does not concern them.

**18.** But, as I had begun to say, the question now is not whether they suffer more grievous things than they inflict, but whether such things may rightly be done against heretics and schismatics.

If they say that it is not lawful, why do they themselves do it? But if they admit that it is lawful, let them also show—something they cannot do in any way—that they suffer more grievously from Catholic emperors than they themselves inflicted upon their schismatics through their judges or through the barbarian king, or than they inflict upon every kind of person through the madness of the Circumcellions.

Nor is it surprising if rulers can do more than judges sent by rulers; if Roman emperors can do more than barbarian kings; and if a robber deservedly suffers more severely under the laws than the wrongs he himself commits against the laws. Hence, by just enactments, the handlers of the Circumcellions deservedly suffer more severe penalties than the Circumcellions inflict. And yet Christian gentleness is so great that their crimes are incomparably surpassed by the moderation of their punishments.

But behold: three hundred and ten Donatist bishops condemned the Maximianists in their council at Bagai. The Maximianists, however, stubborn in their perversity, refused to withdraw from their basilicas. Judges were brought in; their council was introduced into the proconsular records. Then it was ordered that those who had been condemned by so great a number of bishops should withdraw from the places. Those who withdrew readily suffered little. But those who attempted to resist—who does not know how they were afflicted?

Yet if the ferocity of the resisters had been so great that it reached the point of attacking the judges, would they not have suffered much harsher penalties under Roman law?

So also, when, after the conclusion of the case in which these people had severed themselves from the Catholic Church, proceedings consequently began so that they would no longer occupy the basilicas—and they continued to occupy them by resisting imperial orders—so that the notorious force of the Circumcellions prevailed, with the additional circumstance that Paul and Macarius, traveling through Africa with the Church’s gifts sent by the emperor, were harassed by the most turbulent and savage seditions, laws were issued against them so severe that they were not even allowed to retain the basilicas that did not belong to the unity but had been built by those who had separated and remained in their schism.

In this matter the royal authority had already avenged its own injuries. For what can the enemies of justice justly possess?

[Note: The Bagai council.]

[Note: Am. and most manuscripts read “they were added”; the printed editions have “they were brought in.”]

[Note: So the Vatican manuscripts. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “it seemed.”]

[Note: The printed editions read “and they withdrew readily, and suffered little.” The Vatican manuscripts more appropriately read “those who withdrew readily suffered little.”]

[Note: Vatican manuscripts read “through judges of human condition.”]

[Note: The printed editions read *quam quae* (“than which”); the reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: Vatican manuscripts read “whom they appoint as leaders,” referring back to *they do* in the preceding clause.]

[Note: The old Dijon codex reads *municipes* (“townsmen”) rather than *mancipes* (“handlers” or “managers”).]

[Note: The name *Bagaitanum* refers to the council at Bagai.]

## CHAPTER XII

**19.** No one is found to have issued any decree on their behalf except the apostate Julian, who disliked Christian peace and unity exceedingly, since he also disliked the religion from which he had impiously fallen.

These Donatists, as the records of the judges testify—the records to which they appealed in support of what they had obtained—petitioned him in such words that some people may perhaps have consented to the worship of idols through fear more mildly than these madmen praised him.

For they said that with him alone justice had a place. What else, then, are they found to have said except that Christian holiness was not justice, since it had no place with him, or that the honor paid to demons was justice?

Who is unaware of the other emperors’ laws that were issued with great force against them? One general provision against all who wish to be called Christians but do not communicate with the Catholic Church and gather separately in their own conventicles contains this: “Whether the one who ordains a cleric or the one who has been ordained, each shall be fined ten pounds of gold; and the place where the impious separation gathers shall be confiscated.”

There are also other general orders by which they are deprived either of the ability to make wills or to transfer anything by donations, or of the ability to receive anything through donations or wills.

For in one case, when a nobleman had petitioned the emperors because his sister, who had belonged to the party of Donatus, had at her death transferred many possessions to certain members of her communion, especially to a certain Augustine, one of their bishops, it was ordered under that general law that everything be restored to the brother. The Circumcellions were also mentioned there: if they violently resisted in their customary manner, instructions were given concerning the type of assistance and support by which they were to be repelled.

They were so notorious and so well tested in many battles that a petition concerning them was made to the emperor, and the emperor could not remain silent.

[Note: Am. and most manuscripts read *solum* (“only,” neuter), which is incorrect, as is clear from *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 36, sermon 2, §18; see also Letters 93.12, 105.9, and *Against the Letters of Petilianus* 2.203, 224.]

## CHAPTER XIII

**20.** Although these things are so, and although they are condemned by both divine and human laws, Christian gentleness is nevertheless so great that they not only occupy the basilicas they built after their separation, but have not even returned all those that the unity had held from the beginning.

And although they themselves, through judges sent by Catholic emperors, vigorously expelled the Maximianists from basilicas belonging to the party of Donatus, nevertheless they are not excluded by the laws of those same Catholic emperors from many places that the Catholic unity previously held.

Finally, if something was at some time done against them with excessive severity, beyond Christian leniency, this displeases all the grains of the Lord’s harvest—that is, Christians praiseworthy in Christ, who grow throughout the Catholic Church in the whole world, bearing fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold.

## CHAPTER XIV

**21.** Therefore let them accuse with us, as abundantly as they wish, the weeds or chaff of the Catholic field; but let them not refuse to bear them with us with the utmost patience.

For the Lord did not wish the weeds to be uprooted before the proper time and separated from the mingling with the grain. “Let both grow,” he said, “until the harvest.” And when he explained the meaning of that same parable to the disciples who asked him, he did not say, “The field is Africa,” but said, “The field is this world.”

Therefore this crop has been sown throughout the whole world; throughout the whole world the weeds have been sown over it; throughout the whole world both grow until the harvest.

Was Donatus a greater reaper? Or had the time of harvest arrived when these people separated themselves from the whole world? The same Lord, so that no one might interpret the matter according to his own wishes, said most plainly: “The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels” (Matt. 13:23–30, 36–43).

Such reapers cannot err, either by gathering grain in place of weeds or by putting weeds in place of grain.

But when these people flee as though they were weeds, they show that they themselves are weeds, publicly preaching in the clearest sacrilege against the Lord’s sentence. For while he says, “Let both grow until the harvest,” they contend that throughout so great a field—that is, throughout the whole world—the weeds grow, while the grain has diminished and remained only in Africa. In this way they inflict a sacrilegious injury upon Christ our king and ruler.

For it is written: “In the multitude of the people is the glory of a king, but in the diminution of the people is the ruin of a ruler” (Prov. 14:28).

But now, as I think, it is time to attend carefully to the very testimonies of Scripture by which they deceive the unlearned through false interpretation, and, insofar as the Lord grants it, to open them according to the understanding of Catholic truth.

[Note: Lov. reads *religent* (“tie up again”). Am. and the manuscripts more appropriately read *redigant* (“put away”), with “into the barn” understood.]

[Note: The edition of Am. adds *geminata* (“doubled”); Lov. has *germinata* (“sprouted”). Neither word appears in the manuscripts.]

[Note: Vatican manuscripts read “that is, the whole world only.”]

# BOOK TWO

The testimonies of Scripture are examined, whose perverse interpretation the Donatists used in attempting to deceive the unlearned.

[Col. 0049]

## CHAPTER I

**1.** What force except blindness and vanity of mind compels a person, as the saying goes, with closed eyes to throw something at another, when it immediately returns upon the one who threw it and strikes him with a reciprocal blow, leaving untouched the person whom he wished to wound—just as these Donatists do with nearly all the testimonies of Scripture?

When they imagine that they are producing these passages against us, they seem rather to be warning us what sort of people Scripture itself proves them to be.

For what else is Parmenianus doing, whether he thinks the following passage is on his side or against us: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make light darkness and darkness light, who make what is bitter sweet and what is sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20)?

O most foolish blindness! For what is so good and so pleasant as “for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1)? Those who separated themselves from all their brothers call that evil and make it bitter, because they were unwilling either not to stir up their vain suspicions—or, I should say, their factious slanders—or to remove them once they had been stirred up.

If they truly hated the chaff, and were not themselves chaff, they would not separate themselves because of it from the Lord’s wheat, sown and growing throughout the whole field—that is, the world.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts read “truly.”]

[Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “they ought to have separated themselves.”]

**2.** Let them therefore cry out as loudly as they can: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.” We reply briefly: This is true. And we add something else: “Woe to those who have lost endurance, who make light darkness and darkness light” (Sirach 2:16).

For what is brighter than the promises of God, who in our own times has brought to fulfillment what he foretold thousands of years ago: that in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, all nations would have blessing (Gen. 22:18)?

And what is darker than the presumptions of human beings, who, because of charges rashly brought forward and never proved against traditors—charges which, even if true, could never prejudice God so as to prevent him from fulfilling what he promised—say that the Christian name has perished from all the nations throughout the world and remained only in Africa?

They call this presumption of theirs light; but they strive to cover the promises of God, already illumined by the very fulfillment of events, with the darkness of lies.

Moreover, they shout their own deeds against us, saying: “Woe to those who make light darkness and darkness light.” Was Optatus light when he called the whole world darkness? Or did all Africa rather perceive him to be darkness, while these people called him light—these people who make light darkness and darkness light?

“But he was displeasing,” they say, “to all the good people in our communion.” Then you were not calling him light, and yet you communicated with him.

Choose, therefore, whichever alternative you wish: either that darkness does not harm light within one communion, but that it is enough for light to disapprove of darkness and, if it cannot drive it out, to tolerate it for the sake of unity; and thus there was no reason for you to separate yourselves by the dark sacrilege of schism from innocent brothers whom you certainly could not prove to be wicked, even if you claim to have known them.

Or, if it is not enough for light to disapprove of darkness that it cannot expel—that is, if it is not enough for the good to disapprove of the wicked whom they cannot exclude or correct—then the one Optatus, so notorious and manifest in the party of Donatus in one Africa, stained it more easily than any African traditor—accused, if I may not say on false charges, yet unknown, as is most shamelessly denied—could stain all the nations throughout the world.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts read “and when he called all Africa darkness.” Other manuscripts read “when he called the whole of Africa darkness.” A little earlier Lov. reads “they shout against us by their deeds”; Lugd. and Ven. agree with Lov.]

[Note: Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read “who do not make.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts read “by whom you could not prove them to be wicked.”]

**3.** Therefore, when they receive the Scriptures with a perverse mind—the manuscripts read “in the wrong order”—they do not make them harmful to us but to themselves, when they think that this was written for the purpose that the grain should not tolerate the chaff among itself until the time of winnowing: so that, when they misunderstand “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil,” there may be fulfilled in them, “Woe to those who have lost endurance.”

But if they understand that this was said against those who, thinking that evil is good, commit evil deeds, or against those who consent to such people by praising and approving them, they will understand correctly and will not be disturbed when wicked people are found among them—except that they tolerate for the party of Donatus those whom they ought to have tolerated for the unity of Christ.

Through this obstinacy of their hostility, the wretched are forced in their schism to bear with those whom they know, while accusing throughout the world those whom they do not know.

Whoever, therefore, corrects by reproving what he can correct; excludes, while preserving the bond of peace, what he cannot correct; or, when he cannot exclude it while preserving the bond of peace, disapproves it with equity and bears it with steadfastness—such a person is peaceful.

He is wholly free, entirely secure, and completely separate from the curse that Scripture pronounces: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make light darkness and darkness light, who make what is bitter sweet and what is sweet bitter.”

[Note: In the printed editions, after “and completely separate from that curse,” the word *immunis* (“free from it”) is added, but it is superfluous.]

[Editorial apparatus omitted above:]

[Note, Ch. VIII: One edition reads *praecisionem* (“severance”).]

[Note, Ch. VIII: The printed editions read “bands commit many graver acts”; the manuscripts read “commit much graver acts through bands.”]

[Note, Ch. IX: Am. reads “and therefore”; Lov. “or therefore.” The particles added before “therefore” are redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]

[Note, Ch. IX: The manuscripts read *obtenderet imperitis* (“might spread before the unlearned”); compare Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.82.]

[Note, Ch. X: Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read: “I ask this which the Apostle plainly enumerates, saying . . . what do they think?”]

[Note, Ch. X: Vatican codices read *utrum* (“whether”).]

[Note, Ch. X: Lov. reads “and schismatics in impious dissent”; the manuscripts read “impious dissensions,” omitting “schismatics.”]

[Note, Ch. X: Some codices read “these authorities of human constitution are permitted to concern themselves [with such matters].”]

[Note, Ch. X: Vatican manuscripts read “which works excommunication.”]

[Note, Ch. XI: The manuscripts read “or say that their deeds do not concern them”; the printed editions read “say that their words do not concern them.”]

[Note, Ch. XI: Paul and Macarius; see Optatus, book 3.]

[Note, Ch. XII: The manuscripts read “the laws which were issued very vigorously against them”; the printed editions read “the emperors’ justice and laws which were vigorous against them.”]

[Note, Book II, Ch. I: All manuscripts read “men with closed eyes.”]

[Note, Book II, Ch. I: The manuscripts read “or against those who commit evil”; the printed editions omit *vel* (“or”).]

[Note, Book II, Ch. I: The printed editions read, “those whom they know to have been accused and condemned by the world”; the manuscript reading is “those whom they know, while accusing throughout the world those whom they do not know.”]

## CHAPTER II

**4.** Again, with their customary blindness, they raise a similar objection. “Concerning you,” they say, “Scripture declares: ‘He who judges the just man unjust, and the unjust man just, is accursed before God’” (Prov. XVII, 15). Why does this curse not rather fall upon those who have dared to condemn the entire Christian world, in which, among so vast a multitude of people, there certainly were and are many innocent of their crimes, without any doubt? In this way, then, they judged what was just to be unjust, when they honored and retained in communion Optatus Gildonianus,[^c0006-1] while he was a priest and their colleague, although all Africa had groaned under him for ten years.

Or, if they disapproved of him in their hearts but tolerated him for the sake of peace, let them learn that the patience of no peacemaker who does not consent to evil can be stained by any evil people. Let them therefore understand in what destruction those lie who, because of the Africans’ crimes—whether false or true (for that is not the issue now)—do not preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace with the whole world. If they were to say,[^c0006-2] “We do not know whether good Christians exist among so many transmarine peoples,” they would be speaking with the utmost impudence. For God bears witness to his wheat, which has been sown throughout the whole field, even though mixed with the weeds sown over it by the devil; nevertheless, he foretold that both would grow until the harvest. Thus, even if we know the people themselves less well, we nevertheless know that they exist, because with the most certain faith we hold that God cannot have lied.

When, therefore, with sacrilegious impudence they said,[^c0006-3] “We do not know whether good Christians exist in the rest of the world,” let them see with what madness they dare to say—and do not hesitate to say every day—“We know that there are no Christians there.” It is one thing to say, “We do not know whether they exist,” and another to say, “We know that they do not exist.” Both statements are unbelieving and impious. But if the person who says, “I do not know whether God spoke the truth,” is detestable, what shall we say of the person who says, “I know that God did not speak the truth”?

**5.** Surely I think I ought to offend none of them if I place God before Donatus. However much they may love Donatus, they fear God more. Finally, however much they themselves may love Donatus, we know that “God alone is true, and every human being is a liar” (Rom. III, 4).

Christ, therefore, who is God blessed above all forever (ibid. IX, 5), and who most truthfully said of himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6)—when his servants asked him whether he wished them to go and gather up the weeds—said, “Let both grow until the harvest.” Donatus, however, says that the weeds grew, but that the wheat was diminished. Let these people choose whom they will believe.

Christ, that is, the Truth, says, “This field is the world.” Donatus, however, says that God’s field remained only in Africa. Let them choose whom they will believe.

Christ, that is, the Truth, says, “At the time of the harvest I will say to the reapers, ‘Gather the weeds first,’” and he explains, saying, “The harvest is the end of the age.” Donatus, however, says that the weeds were separated from the wheat before the harvest by the cutting off of his party. Let them choose whom they will believe.

Christ, that is, the Truth, says, “The reapers are angels” (Matt. XIII, 24–30, 36–43). Donatus, however, says that he and his colleagues did before the harvest what Christ said the angels would do at the harvest. Let them choose whom they will believe.

Certainly they call themselves Christians. We place Christ and Donatus before them. If they give their words to Christ but their hearts to Donatus, let them consider what they are.[^c0006-4] I spare them; I do not attack them; I suppress my grief more than I express it. But if they say that they give their hearts to Christ, then let them believe Christ, who says that throughout the whole world both the children of the kingdom and the children of the evil one grow—not Donatus, who says that throughout the whole world only the children of the evil one have grown, while the good children have been reduced to Africa alone.

If they believe Christ, we shall no longer say that they should be at peace with the churches of the world, but that they should be at peace with the Gospel itself—although they boast that they preserved it from the fire, something which they do not prove by their actions.[^c0006-5]

## CHAPTER III

**6.** What bearing, then, has that passage which the same Parmenianus thought should be brought against us from the prophet Isaiah?

“Is the hand of the Lord not strong enough to save, or has he made his ear heavy so that he does not hear? But your sins separate you from your God, and because of your sins he has turned his face from you, so that he does not have mercy. For your hands are stained with blood, and your fingers with sins; your lips have spoken iniquity, and your tongue meditates injustice. No one speaks what is just; there is no true judgment. They trust in vain things and speak vain things,[^c0006-6] because they conceive pain and give birth to iniquity. They have burst forth asps’ eggs,[^c0006-7] and they weave a spider’s web.[^c0006-8] Whoever was going to eat from those eggs finds something foul when he crushes it, and in it a basilisk. Their web, therefore, will not serve for clothing, nor will they cover themselves with their works. For their works are works of iniquity; their feet run toward wickedness, swift to shed blood; and their thoughts are the thoughts of fools. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Isa. LIX, 1–8).

Wherever those whom Scripture describes in this passage may be found among the good, they do not harm the good, just as chaff does not harm the wheat until the lord of the threshing floor comes, carrying a winnowing fan in his hand, to cleanse his threshing floor, gather the wheat into his granary, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. III, 12).

In the same way, that great multitude of wicked people did not harm the good who, through the prophet Ezekiel, are said to have been those who groaned and mourned over the crimes of the people committed in their midst (Ezek. IX, 4). Since they could not correct those people, nor in any way ought they to separate themselves from the unity of God’s people,[^c0006-9] they deserved, on account of the merit of their utterly innocent endurance, to be marked and delivered amid the devastation and destruction of those condemned people.

Yet these people who bring such charges against Catholics—why do they not look at themselves? Their gangs of frenzied men fly here and there armed with iron and clubs. Although they can never be satisfied by the frequent massacres they carry out wherever they can, amid the tombs of their corpses such drunkenness rages with women—who roam about indiscriminately with them day and night, contrary to the order of divine and human things—that from it they conceive the daily madness not only of attacking others but also of throwing themselves headlong into destruction.

Do their feet not run toward evil,[^c0006-10] and are they not swift to shed blood? Does judgment not depart from those who arrogate to themselves even the most unjust licenses of disordered power? Do darkness not come upon these people when they cannot endure the light in their false martyrdom? Do they not walk in the midst of the day as though in the middle of the night, since the Apostle says, “Those who get drunk are drunk at night” (I Thess. V, 7)? Do they not grope at midday as though in the middle of the night (Job V, 14)?

This, indeed, is characteristic of all heretics: they cannot see what has been established in the light of all the nations, though it is perfectly manifest. Whatever they do outside its unity, even if it appears to be carried out with great skill and diligence, nevertheless does them no good against the wrath of God; for even spiders’ webs cannot protect them from the cold.

**7.** What, then, do they find in this prophetic chapter that cannot be turned back against themselves—unless perhaps it is the asps’ eggs, of which the drafter of that decree of the plenary council of three hundred and ten, assembled with all the provinces of Africa, had spoken long before?[^c0006-11]

Certainly, if Parmenianus were alive, he would not say this, nor would he cite against us from the prophet Isaiah, “They have burst forth asps’ eggs.” For he would look at Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri, who had been joined to his own fellowship. Though they had been numbered among the condemned, they were received again as though sound, supposedly for the sake of peace—not the peace of Christ, however, but that of Donatus. They had indeed been asps’ eggs, and they had burst forth.

For the three hundred and ten members of the full council describe them in this way, “with truthful mouth,” as the records cited from their own proconsular proceedings also testify.[^c0006-12] These are certainly the words of their council:

“For although the womb of a poisonous belly had for a long time concealed the harmful offspring of viperous seed, and the moist clots of conceived crime had slowly been warmed into the limbs of asps by lingering heat, nevertheless the conceived poison could not be hidden when its covering veil vanished. For, though late, the teeming vows of crimes gave birth to their public crime and parricide.”[^c0006-13]

These asps’ eggs had burst forth, and, already horrible and foul-smelling with their poisonous offspring, they had been cast out from their fellowship. But Optatus the basilisk was inside, and with a certain royal nod—for he is said to excel among serpents—he recalled even the asps that had been cast out.[^c0006-14]

Or, if these things do not harm them for the sake of peace, why do they bring accusations against Catholics whom they were unable to convict, when they themselves have received those whom they had condemned with their own mouths?

If these things do not harm them for the peace of Christ, they nevertheless harm them for the peace of Donatus, to whom great favor is shown in injury to the peace of Christ. For this sacrilege, whatever bodily sufferings they endure are a warning from God that they must beware eternal condemnation.

For they truly shed blood—not only bodily, through the madness of the Circumcellions, but also spiritually, since they attempt, if they can, to rebaptize the whole world.

Or, if only the person who wounds or kills mortal flesh sheds blood, while the person who kills deceived souls through the sacrilege of schism does not shed blood, why did they say such things about their own schismatics, the Maximianists, in the same judgment of their full council?

“Swift are their feet to shed blood,” they said, although it is clear that none of them was killed or wounded bodily. Indeed, it is clear that they suffered many things at the hands of these people when they were expelled from the basilicas by judicial authorities—things which, before the separation of the Maximianists, when they were all together as one, they had done in great number to those who had previously created schisms on the side of Donatus.[^c0006-15]

For what schismatic of theirs have they ever spared, when they themselves shamelessly wish to be spared by the whole world, of which they are the schismatics? Yet schisms are most justly punished by that one true unity itself—if such things are to be punished in that manner.

## CHAPTER IV

**8.** As for what is written, “According to the ruler of the people, so are his ministers; and as is the ruler of the city, so are its inhabitants” (Ecclus. X, 2), if they understood where this applies, they would not bring it against us,[^c0006-16] nor would they themselves boast arrogantly in empty vaunting.

We, however, so that we may not place human hope—which is safe and rightly secure only in God—in human beings, remember that it is written, “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. XVII, 5). We do not understand the ruler of the people and the governor of the city in this passage to signify a bishop.

This is not because we cannot point to innumerable holy bishops in the Catholic faith, but so that, as I said, no one’s hope may be placed in a human being. Otherwise, if someone happened to live in a city where there was not a good bishop, he might suppose that he could become evil with impunity, using this Scripture—so perversely understood by them—as his defense, and saying that he could not be good because “according to the ruler of the people, so are his ministers; and as is the governor of the city, so are its inhabitants.”

The Truth’s own voice contradicts this error when it says, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matt. XXIII, 3).

Therefore, when peoples have such bishops—men who say good things from the chair of Moses but, because of their own wickedness, do not do what they say—if those peoples do the good things that their bishops say and do not do the evil things that the bishops do, as the Lord commands, do they not make it sufficiently clear that the ruler of the people and the governor of the city should not be understood in the way these people understand them?

There can be good peoples where there are evil bishops, just as there could be an evil people where Moses was a good ruler and governor.

Because they wander in the words of the holy Scriptures and, as the Apostle says, do not understand either what they say or about what they make assertions (I Tim. I, 7), they themselves suffer the greater distress from the perversity of their interpretation when they are told: “Then whatever Optatus was, so also was the people of Thamugadi. And if, as you say, those who disapprove of evil deeds are contaminated by communion in the sacraments, as are also those who tolerate such deeds for the peace of unity, then so are all of you, who shared communion both with that colleague and with that people, while all Africa openly declared, with manifest groaning, that he was a satellite of Gildo.”[^c0006-17]

I mention him so often because he was so notorious that, wherever his name is mentioned, no one can reply that he was unknown.

**9.** Let them themselves look back and remember how many similar people they have among them—people whose wickedness is equal, though their notoriety is unequal. Let them eventually arrive at the true meaning of these words and understand that there is one ruler of the people: our Lord Jesus Christ, whose ministers are the good.

He is also the governor of that city, Jerusalem, which is our mother in heaven, eternal. Its inhabitants correspond to the dignity of its governor—not by equality, but according to their measure, because it was said to them, “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. XIX, 2). This is according to a certain likeness of the image into which we are transformed “from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18), through the gift of him who makes us conform to the image of his Son (Rom. VIII, 29).

There is also another ruler of an evil people: the devil, and he is governor of that city which is mystically called Babylon. The Apostle Paul calls him “the ruler and governor of these darknesses”—that is, of sins—and calls his angels the same (Eph. VI, 12). His ministers are like him, because they transform themselves into ministers of righteousness, just as he transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. XI, 15, 14), and the inhabitants correspond in similar deeds to their most wicked ruler.

The separation of these peoples and cities will be open when this harvest has been winnowed. Until that happens, the love of the wheat endures everything, lest, while the grains prematurely flee the chaff, they impiously separate themselves from their fellow grains.

## CHAPTER V

**10.** What bearing, then, does it now have upon the case that these people bring against us the fact that the Lord says through Isaiah concerning wicked sacrificers:

“The criminal who sacrifices to me a calf is like one who kills a dog; and he who offers fine flour is like one who offers swine’s blood; and he who offers incense in remembrance is like a blasphemer” (Isa. LXVI, 3)?[^c0006-18]

These words apply much more fittingly to those who, against the Church of God spread throughout the whole world as it was promised, have erected the altar of their schism. This sacrilege involves all of them, and whoever, wherever he may be, offers a sacrifice with such a heart or in such deeds brings destruction upon himself by deserving to hear these words—not upon those good people who receive the same sacraments from them,[^c0006-19] who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, groan and mourn over the sins committed in their midst (Ezek. IX, 4), although they do not separate themselves from them bodily.

For God assigns to each person according to his heart.

If wicked priests did not harm good colleagues in former times—as Zacharias was (Luke I, 5)—or good people among the populace—as Nathanael was, in whom there was no deceit (John I, 47)—how much less does an evil bishop harm good fellow bishops or laypeople within Christian unity, now that that priest according to the order of Melchizedek, our high priest, sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us (Heb. VII, 17, 25), he who was handed over on account of our sins and raised for our justification (Rom. IV, 25)?

Nor does what is most truly said—“The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 23)—harm the good; it harms those who offer them. For he did not say, “The Most High does not approve the gifts of those who tolerate the wicked for the sake of peace.”

Yet these people could not themselves prove what they alleged at the time when they created their schism. Otherwise, once those people had been excluded, the inheritance of Christ, spread throughout the whole world, would have retained these people in Catholic communion.

## CHAPTER VI
