**11.** “The sacrifices of the wicked,” they say, “are an abomination to the Lord, for they offer them wickedly” (Prov. XXI, 27).

The answer has already been given: Christ is not wicked. He offered himself for us and is our mediator in heaven. While he governs his Church, the wicked do not harm the good—whether the wicked are unknown or tolerated for the sake of peace—until he comes and separates the weeds from the harvest, having first sent the reapers, and separates the chaff from the wheat with his winnowing fan.

Although these people—as must often be said—have brought forward false accusations, even if those accusations were true they would not harm the charity of the good, who tolerate everything within unity for the sake of unity, provided that the accusations could not perhaps even after becoming known persuade ecclesiastical judges.

The sacrifices of the wicked, then, harm those who offer them wickedly. For one and the same sacrifice, because of the name of the Lord that is invoked,[^c0006-20] is always holy, and it becomes for each person what the heart of the person approaching to receive it makes it. “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI, 29). He does not say, “Upon others,” but “upon himself.”

Therefore, whoever eats and drinks worthily eats and drinks grace for himself. Let them see, then, whether they eat worthily—those who have divided by wicked schism so many parents and children, husbands and wives, and, most conspicuously, so many heirs of God and coheirs with Christ spread throughout the whole world. If they were good and truly rebuked the wicked, they could tolerate them fruitfully for the peace of Christ, whereas they tolerate them disastrously for the peace of Donatus.[^c0006-21]

## CHAPTER VII

**12.** “In Exodus,” they say, “it is written: ‘The priests who approach the Lord God shall be sanctified, lest perhaps the Lord abandon them’” (Exod. XIX, 22). And again: “When the ministers approach the altar, they shall not bring sin upon themselves, lest they die” (ibid. XXX, 20–21). And in Leviticus: “A man who has a blemish or defect shall not approach to offer gifts to God” (Lev. XXII, 21).

They rightly bring forward these testimonies from the ancient Books. Let them tell me, then: who, established either among the priests or among the people, was harmed in spiritual salvation by an evil or blemished priest?

Where Moses and Aaron were, there were sacrilegious grumblers whom God continually threatened to destroy from his presence. Where Caiaphas and others like him were, there was Zacharias; there was Simeon and the other good people. Where Saul was, there was David; where Jeremiah, Isaiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel were, there were evil priests and evil peoples. But each person bore his own burden.

**13.** I will pass over the matter of how criminally arrogant they are when they say that none among their colleagues—or among themselves—has any blemish or defect, not of the limbs but, what is worse, of character.

When we begin to deal with them about this, they will reply that it matters what kind of blemish and what kind of defect it is—as though Scripture made a distinction when it says, “A man who has a blemish or defect shall not approach to offer gifts to God.”

Did Optatus have no blemish or defect—not to mention Parmenianus, but Donatus himself? Yet these people are so blinded by their love of human beings, and in their impure hearts do not hesitate to make adulterers equal to the one legitimate husband, that they insist that what could be said only of the Lord Jesus Christ was also perfected in Donatus.

“Who will give my eyes a fountain of tears?” (Jer. IX, 1). What lamentation appropriate to this crime can be drawn from a shaken breast?

But for the moment, let them consider whether Optatus at least had any blemish or defect. They are not so blind as to claim that his life was entirely spotless and free from every defect. Why, then, did he approach to offer gifts to God, and why did the others receive from him with joined hands what a blemished and defective man had offered?

Let them consider their other colleagues and ask whether drunkenness is no blemish. But first let them read to which wicked people the Apostle joined drunkards. Is greed no blemish, when the same Apostle so detests it that he compares it with the service of idols (Eph. V, 5)?

**14.** Those who think most correctly understand that any human being—although, on account of participation in human society, it may not improperly be said that he lives most justly—nevertheless cannot be without some defect so long as “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17).

It is also written, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (I John III, 9), and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (ibid. I, 8).

Although, insofar as we have been born of God, we do not sin, there still remains in us what we have inherited from Adam, because “death has not yet been swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. XV, 54). That victory is also promised in the resurrection of bodies, so that we may be altogether blessed, spotless, and incorruptible. We are already sons of God according to faith, but according to appearance it has not yet been revealed what we shall be (I John III, 2).

For we have not yet been saved in reality, but in hope. “Hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.” And while we await with patience the redemption of our bodies (Rom. VIII, 23–25), let us not dare to say that we are free from every defect, lest pride itself be the most monstrous defect.

Let us therefore wake up at last and see that, in the priests of that time, when bodily defects were avoided, the one who was prefigured was he who, although he was God, became human for us: the one true spotless lamb and priest without defect.

For that reason also, at that time the priest alone entered the Holy of Holies, while the people stood outside. So now that priest, after his resurrection, has entered the secret places of heaven to intercede for us at the right hand of the Father.

But the people of whom he is priest still groan outside. For while the bishop alone is inside, the people both pray with him[^c0006-22] and, as though subscribing to his words, answer, “Amen.”

At that time, then, when bodies were sought because the souls of the priests could not be without any blemish or defect, the one priest alone was being prefigured—not these proud and impious men, who do not show zeal for the fornicating soul on behalf of her bridegroom, but dare to present themselves as the bridegroom.

## CHAPTER VIII

**15.** “In the Gospel,” they say, “it is written: ‘God does not hear sinners; but if anyone worships God and does his will, him he hears’” (John IX, 31).

This is certainly an unqualified statement. If two people pray together, one a sinner and the other one who worships God and does his will, does he surely hear the one and not hear the other?

What, then, does this testimony mean, or how do they suppose that it should be cited on their behalf, when these words especially reassure the good who are among the wicked, and when no bodily separation is called for, so that people should separate even from the good through an impious schism? After all, the wicked can also be heard among the good on account of their faith.

God, who examines the heart, does not err, so as to hear or reject one person in place of another.

Or do they say this so that it may be understood that an evil bishop is not heard when he prays for the people? Even if that were so, the people, provided they are good and faithful, should not therefore be anxious. Scripture makes them secure when it says:

“Brothers, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II, 1–2).

Let them hear how truly and devoutly humbly this was said, if they have ears with which to hear.

John said, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin.” If he had then continued by saying, “And if anyone sins, you have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for your sins,” he would seem to have separated himself from sinners, as though he no longer needed the propitiation made through the Mediator who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us (Rom. VIII, 34).

That would have been not only arrogant but also false.

If, however, he had said, “I have written these things to you so that you may not sin; and if anyone sins, you have me as mediator with the Father, and I plead for your sins”—just as Parmenianus in one passage made the bishop a mediator between the people and God—what faithful and good Christian could have tolerated him? Who would regard him as an apostle of Christ rather than as an antichrist?

And yet the cracked cisterns endure the smoky water of these people’s arrogance,[^c0006-23] but they cannot contain the Holy Spirit, so as to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3), and in all their prayers to be secure in the one Mediator.

**16.** All Christians, after all, commend one another to one another in their prayers. But the one for whom no one intercedes, and who himself intercedes for all, is the one true Mediator.

Since his type was prefigured in the priest of the Old Testament, no one there is found to have prayed for the priest.

The Apostle Paul, although he was a principal member under the head, nevertheless, because he was a member of Christ’s body and knew that the greatest and truest priest had entered for us—not figuratively through the interior of the veil into the Holy of Holies (Heb. IX, 12), but through the manifest and accomplished reality[^c0006-24] into the interior of heaven, into holiness not imaginary but eternal—also commends himself to the prayers of the Church.[^c0006-25]

He does not make himself a mediator between the people and God; rather, he asks that all the members of Christ’s body pray for one another. For the members are concerned for one another: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice together” (I Cor. XII, 25–26).

Thus the prayer of all the members who still labor on earth for one another ascends to the head who has gone before into heaven, in whom there is propitiation for our sins.

For if Paul were a mediator, then his fellow apostles would also be mediators, and there would thus be many mediators. Nor would the reasoning of Paul himself remain consistent when he said, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (I Tim. II, 5).

In him we too are one, if we preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. We must not abandon the good because of the wicked; rather, for the sake of the good we must endure the wicked, lest, while wishing to defend what we rashly presumed to leave, we be compelled by a greater crime to condemn people whom we have not heard.

**17.** It is also certain that God hears sinners; and this is indeed found in Scripture.

The prophet Balaam, who was not from the people of Israel but a foreigner, was hired by an enemy[^c0006-26] to curse God’s people, yet he was turned by the Lord to bless them (Num. XXIV). We hear and read all his words as the words of one blessing well. Although he had something else in mind, the words of the one praying are nevertheless good, and they are heard by the Lord on behalf of the people.

Therefore it is not surprising that good words spoken in prayers for the people—even when spoken by evil bishops—are nevertheless heard, not because of the perversity of the leaders but because of the devotion of the peoples.

Nevertheless, what is written in the Gospel—“God does not hear sinners; but if anyone worships God and does his will, he hears that person”—was not spoken by the Lord, but by the man whose bodily eyes had already been restored, while the eyes of his heart had not yet been opened. For this reason he still thought that the Lord was a prophet. Later, once he had recognized him as the Son of God, he worshiped him.

The Lord himself, however, when a Pharisee and a tax collector were praying in one temple, says that the tax collector who confessed his sins was justified more than the Pharisee who boasted of his merits (Luke XVIII, 10–14). These people resemble the Pharisee.

Although the justified man ceased to be a sinner, he had prayed as a sinner in order to be justified; he confessed as a sinner, and, having been heard, he was justified so that he might cease to be a sinner. He certainly would not have ceased to be a sinner unless the sinner had first been heard.

Therefore, the Truth itself bears witness that not every sinner is heard, but that nevertheless not every sinner is not heard.

---

But if they were to say…” The manuscripts correct the text.

The Vatican manuscripts read, “they falsely boast, because…” The reference is to the persecution under Diocletian, during which Christians were compelled to surrender their sacred books and throw them into the fire. The Donatists accused Caecilian and other Catholics of committing this offense.

[^c0006-21]: The Vatican manuscripts read, “for the peace of Donatus’s party.”

## CHAPTER IX

### 18

They also object to what is said in the Psalm:

> “But to the sinner God said: ‘Why do you recite my justifications and take up my covenant in your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue contrived deceit. Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block’” (Ps. 49:16–20).

*[Note: [Col. 0061] Thus in the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “and with adulterers you placed your portion”; yet in those same editions, later, when Augustine turns that statement against his opponents, the reading was “and with adulterers you placed a portion,” etc.]*

*[Note: This verse, “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue contrived deceit,” is absent from the manuscripts, nor does Augustine repeat anything from it in his response. He usually reads, “and your tongue embraced deceitfulness.”]*

But let them at last open the ears of their hearts and cease to be people who understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7). They attend to the words addressed to the sinner, “Why do you recite my justifications and take up my covenant in your mouth?” but they do not understand that this was said so that he might know that the words he utters with his mouth profit him nothing if he does not himself do what he says; nevertheless, those same words benefit others, who hear and do them even when they come through evil men. The Lord himself teaches this in the Gospel, when he says of the Pharisees:

> “They sit on the chair of Moses. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they preach, but do not practice” (Matt. 23:2–3).

### 19

Would that they wished, in these words which they have recalled from the Psalm, to behold themselves as though in a mirror. How do they not cast God’s words behind them, when they proclaim peace to the peoples but do not love peace? How do they not hate discipline, when they dare to condemn the whole world unheard, and, because according to their deserts—or rather, far less than their deserts, considering the audacity of so great a frenzy—they suffer temporal troubles according to the discipline of divine mercy, do not confess that their sins are being punished, but boast that their merits are being crowned?

I will not say that they have run with the thief, for the plunderer is worse than the thief—a fact that Optatus loudly proclaimed everywhere.

*[Note: The African manuscripts and some others read, “I say that they have run with the thief,” omitting “not.”]*

Do they not place their portion with adulterers who shamefully allow the drunken bands of their nuns to wander day and night mixed together with the drunken bands of the Circumcellions? Do they not, sitting, slander their brothers, who, because they have been unable to convict certain persons, contend throughout the inheritance of Christ, spread across the whole earth, that they are not Christians?

And so, against the son of their mother—that is, against one still a child in faith and needing to be nourished on the milk of the sacraments—they place a most destructive stumbling block, since the one who does not yet know how to follow God the Father, because he is weak, follows a human being; and, enticed by a counterfeit and shadowy appearance of truth, he is torn away by cruel laceration from the bond of unity.

*[Note: The manuscripts read, “they place a destructive stumbling block.”]*

*[Note: [Col. 0062] Several manuscripts read, “a weak man, enticed by a counterfeit and shadowy appearance of truth,” omitting the words “follows a human being.”]*

*[Note: The better manuscripts read “in the common sacrilege of schism.” Others read “in the communion of sacrilegious schism”; the printed editions, “in the crime of sacrilegious schism.”]*

But if those who do not commit evil are displeased by the evil deeds of others in the same party, and do not believe that the crimes of others harm them, while they groan and grieve over crimes committed in their midst, why do they perniciously tolerate in the common sacrilege of schism those whom they could fruitfully tolerate within the integrity of unity?

For they can say—if, awakened at last by the facts themselves, they ever become alert—that the evil of individuals does not harm the others who neither approve nor commit such things. Yet they can very easily be proved, though with the greatest difficulty persuaded to confess, that the sacrilege of schism is not the evil of individuals but belongs to all who do not share in Catholic unity.

For the reason why the crimes of others do not belong to those who share their communion is precisely the reason why schism is the crime of all: since, when they now say that they cannot be stained among themselves by the crimes of others, they must at the same time admit that they had no reason to depart from unity, where the crimes of others cannot stain them. And therefore, by the most manifest crime of schism, they are bound together as by one deadly bond.

## CHAPTER X

### 20

“But Jeremiah prophesied.” What did Jeremiah prophesy? They say that those who abandon God do not possess true Baptism. For he says:

> “The heavens were astonished at this, and shuddered with utter horror, says the Lord, because this people has committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:12–13).

And again:

> “[Col. 0063] She has become for me,” he says, “like deceitful water, which has no faith” (Jer. 15:18).

*[Note: The printed editions add “my people” here. It is absent from the manuscripts, is not found at this point in Jeremiah, and had not been added by Parmenianus, as Augustine’s reply below, section 22, shows.]*

And that passage which is written,

> “He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit?” (Sir. 34:30).

*[Note: The edition of Amerbach restored here the words from Ecclesiasticus that had been omitted, namely, “and again he touches him.” All the manuscripts lack these words. Although they are necessary to the case against the Donatists, Augustine regularly passes over them, because, as he observes in *Retractions* 1.21.3, Ecclesiasticus itself did not contain them in many African manuscripts. Cyprian likewise omits them in his letter to Quintus and in the Council of Carthage held under his presidency.]*

And that passage in the Psalm:

> “But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5).

And again elsewhere:

> “Dead flies ruin the sweetness of the oil” (Eccl. 10:1).

And elsewhere:

> “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1:5).

If all these passages are to be understood in the way they understand them, the reasoning of truth agrees neither with us nor with them. But if I show that they are to be understood in another way, they alone are thrown into confusion. Yet, so that they may not be confused, let them take refuge in the Catholic understanding, since, entangled in the crime of schism, they find no way out in their reply.

For they too certainly have among themselves—I will not say, “such people,” but I will say what they either confess or most insanely deny—they too, then, have people who abandon God, who is the fountain of living water: namely, those who live wickedly.

*[Note: The manuscripts read, “I will not say, ‘such people,’ but I will say what they either confess or most insanely deny: they too have those who abandon God,” whereas the printed text is less complete.]* For God is abandoned not with the feet but with the heart.

They also have deceitful people, without faith, professing one thing and living otherwise. They also have the dead. For if the Apostle does not allow even the more delicate and weaker sex to indulge in pleasures, saying, “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6), let them ask whether no men among them—and, what is more, no leaders or ministers—live in pleasure. If they dare to do so, let them declare that they have no dead among them and that they are better than that Church whose angel, under the figure of its leaders or souls, is told not to be living but dead; and yet that Church is numbered among the seven Churches, nor is it divided from the structure of Christ’s body, but, persevering in unity, receives instructions for life (Rev. 3:1–6).

*[Note: The printed editions, instead of “nor is it divided,” read “acting differently” or “acting in division.” “Acting” is absent from the manuscripts.]*

*[Note: The Gallican manuscripts read, “are given later.” The Vatican manuscripts read, “are given additionally.”]*

I pass over what they said in their council against the Maximianists:

> “The shores are filled with the funerals of those perishing, after the example of the Egyptians” (Exod. 14:31).

Felicianus, who is now within their ranks, belongs to the number of those dead; he still baptizes while dead. Or, if he has already come back to life, he has with him those whom, while dead in schism, he baptized.

They certainly have sinners. For if any of those who seem great to themselves among them are questioned, they do not deny that they themselves are sinners. They do not, after all, beat their breasts—or, when they do so, do they do it hypocritically? If that is the case, then at least they sin wretchedly, deceiving their peoples by simulated humility. Or else they do not say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

*[Note: [Col. 0064] Amerbach and all the manuscripts read “or else they do not say”; Louvain reads “or when they say.”]*

That petition certainly does not concern those sins which were forgiven in the regeneration of Baptism, but those which human weakness contracts daily from the bitterest fruits of the world. For the curing of these, the remedies of almsgiving, fasting, and prayer are applied, so that in prayer one says what is enacted in almsgiving. To forgive another the sin he has committed against you, so that God may also forgive you, is a great work of mercy.

But if they say this deceitfully and not truthfully in prayer, thinking that they have nothing for which God should forgive them, that very thing is an unforgivable sacrilege; that very impious and insane pride is certainly an enormous sin.

*[Note: The printed editions read, “But if people say this deceitfully and not truthfully.” The manuscripts read, “But if they say this deceitfully and not truthfully in prayer”: namely, if the Donatists say, “Forgive us our debts.” This is better, especially if what was said above is read: “Or else they do not say.”]*

What should I say about dying flies, when we have shown that among them there are found in many ways not merely flies that are still dying but ones already dead—whether they confess this or are proved to be so? Let them consider, in light of what was said above, how many deceitful people who are fleeing from the Holy Spirit of discipline and living ruinously without understanding they have among themselves.

For even those wicked people who lie hidden there—this is certain because they are often exposed, convicted, and condemned, not merely for recent acts but also for an old habit of crimes, since they were able to be concealed for a long time through their most foolish deception—are all the more deceitful because, by pretending to be good, they deceive themselves.

*[Note: All the manuscripts affirm the reading, “since they were able to be concealed for a long time,” omitting “not.”]*

### 21

If, then, these passages are to be understood as they understand them, how can their reasoning stand concerning those who abandon God by living wickedly, whether they are hidden or known? Why have they not been broken cisterns, unable to hold water?

And if the sacrament of Baptism is to be understood in this passage, why are their deceitful and faithless ministers believed either to give or to possess not deceitful water but truthful water? Why does the washing of those baptized by their dead produce any benefit?

*[Note: The manuscripts read: “Why, when their deceitful and faithless ministers are believed either to give or to possess not truthful water but deceitful water, does the washing of those baptized by their dead profit them?”]*

Why do sinners fatten the heads of others with oil? What have dying or dead flies deserved from you, that they should not ruin the sweetness of the oil? By what privilege are all those who are deceitful there—that is, who cover a wolf with the skin of righteousness—protected so that the Holy Spirit of discipline does not flee from them? Or, if the Holy Spirit flees from them, how is he given through them to those who are baptized?

Here they cannot say what they habitually say with utter foolishness and shamelessness:

> “Someone can be baptized by an evil person only if the evil of the baptizer is hidden.”

*[Note: The manuscripts read, “what they habitually say most ignorantly,” rather than “with utter foolishness and shamelessness.”]*

But the one who is deceitful is all the more deceitful the more deeply he is hidden. Since, then, the Holy Spirit withdraws from him, what hope will the baptized person have if the merit of the baptizing human being is to be considered in that grace of God?

Here they find absolutely nothing to answer—those who deny that they have openly evil people among them, a denial in which they are most clearly convicted. But what is that to us? For the necessary point in our case it is enough that they cannot deny that they have deceitful good people among them, that is, hidden evil people.

[Col. 0065] They are refuted by the many who, while living among them with depraved and wicked conduct and having long remained hidden through that very deception, were eventually exposed and expelled. Let us believe, then, that if they do not wish any such people still to be among them, those who were expelled certainly were such while they lay hidden in the same deception and while the Holy Spirit fled from them, of whom it is written, “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from a hypocrite” (Wis. 1:5). How, then, could they baptize?

*[Note: The manuscripts read “Let us say, then … how could they baptize?” The Louvain edition reads “Let us say, then, if … how can they baptize?”]*

Why do they not at least list those who are alive, so that they may receive the Baptism which, evidently, they could not have received from the deceitful people whom the Holy Spirit was abandoning?

*[Note: The Casalinus manuscript reads: “Why are not at least those who received from them listed, so that they may receive Baptism?” Some others read: “Why do they not at least list them so that they may receive Baptism from Catholics?”]*

But if they say, “The Holy Spirit was absent from the deceitful men who were giving Baptism and justifying, but he was present with those who received it and believed, cleansing them through the ineffable efficacy of his power”—being able to do both, to flee from the former and cherish the latter, to condemn the former and cleanse the latter—let them see that, by solving this question on their own behalf, they have simultaneously solved it on ours.

### 22

What is understood in this statement of Holy Scripture—which they themselves, certainly not understanding it, and proposing it as though it supported their side, bring forward to convict themselves—we remind them should be understood in nearly all such questions: namely, that all the sacraments, although harmful to those who handle them unworthily, nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through their ministry, just as the word of God does.

*[Note: The printed editions read, “as the word of God also testifies.” “Testifies” is absent from the manuscripts. The implied sense is that the word of God, like the sacraments, harms those who handle it unworthily but nevertheless benefits those who worthily receive it through their ministry.]*

Hence it was said:

> “Do and observe whatever they tell you; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3).

For who prevents me from understanding the digging of broken cisterns, which cannot hold water, in this way: namely, as turning toward an earthly desire and being unable to contain the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the name of “water” in the Gospel—something no Christian, in whatever manner, can be unaware of?

*[Note: Several manuscripts read “earthly pleasure” rather than “earthly desire.”]*

Likewise, “deceitful water that has no faith” can be understood not as a false baptism but as a deceitful and faithless people, excluding those who are truthful and faithful and including only those who are deceitful and faithless.

For let them read in the Apocalypse that peoples are sometimes signified by the term “waters,” and let them first bring their accusations against themselves rather than against us. For this is what is said to John:

> “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and crowds and nations and languages” (Rev. 17:15).

*[Note: The printed editions read, “peoples and tribes.” The manuscripts read, “peoples and crowds.” The Greek is καὶ ὄχλοι (*kai ochloi*), “and crowds.”]*

And that passage which is written, “He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit?” (Sir. 34:30)—leaving aside for the moment a more careful investigation of these words—

*[Note: See Book 2 of *Against Cresconius*, chapters 24 and following.]*

—I most safely accept as indicating the baptisms of pagans, because they worship human beings who are dead both to righteousness and to this life, and they are baptized in their name.

[Col. 0066] Although their priests too may be called dead because of their impiety, the passage is not understood in this way because of them, but because of their dead gods, in whose significance it is said, “Our God is the living God” (Jer. 10:10).

Therefore, even if among Christians there are some leaders or ministers who are dead through their impiety and wickedness,

*[Note: Some manuscripts read “because of their impiety.”]*

the one of whom it is said in the Gospel, “This is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33), nevertheless lives. For, as the Apostle says:

> “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9).

But the Psalm makes perfectly clear how “the oil of the sinner” should be understood. It says:

> “The righteous shall correct me in mercy and shall rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5).

From this it is evident that “the oil of the sinner” signifies the flatteries of a sycophant. Rejecting and detesting these, he chooses to be corrected and rebuked by the righteous, because when the righteous does this—not with the deceptive gentleness of flattery but with the truthful harshness of reproof—he does it all the more mercifully.

Hence there is also the passage in the Apocalypse:

> “Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline” (Rev. 3:19).

And the passage in Solomon:

> “The wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6).

Many passages of this kind are also found.

But “the oil of sweetness,” that is, a good fragrance or the good reputation of Christians, is ruined by those who intend to live wickedly and return to the death of their sins, rushing forward in great numbers so that their sins may be forgiven through Baptism and so that they may return to those sins again.

For this reason, I believe, they are compared with flies (Eccl. 10:1), on account of their numbers. But they ruin the oil of sweetness who regard not the grace of God itself but human conduct; and because, just as grains are not seen among chaff, so those who live devoutly do not easily appear among crowds of wicked people, they are offended in a carnal way and are either held back from receiving eternal salvation or turn away from it altogether.

*[Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read “are either drawn away.”]*

That the good fragrance consists in the good reputation of Christians who live rightly, the Apostle teaches when he says:

> “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15).

*[Note: The word “for God” is absent from the manuscripts.]*

On the other hand, those to whom it is said, “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Rom. 2:24), certainly ruin the oil of sweetness.

Thus these passages possess other, more sound interpretations; if they follow them, they too are released from the difficulties of these questions. But if their interpretations are not confirmed by us, they entangle them alone; if they are confirmed by us, they entangle both them and us.

## CHAPTER XI

### 23

What need is there now to examine more? Unless perhaps they will be disturbed by the fact that, when Parmenianus wished to prove that carnal people cannot beget spiritual children, he added a testimony from the Gospel:

> “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6).

[Col. 0067] As though we were saying that any human being, by himself, generates spiritual children, and not through the Gospel; in whose proclamation the Holy Spirit works to beget spiritual children in Baptism, even when he flees from a deceitful minister, as we said above.

*[Note: We restore the negative particle, which the Louvain editors rejected. It appeared in the edition of Amerbach and in our manuscripts and seems entirely necessary to the sense.]*

And so, when the Apostle was speaking to such children, if he had said, “I begot you,” and had not added, “in Christ Jesus through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15), no believer would in any way religiously acknowledge that he had been born from him.

But even the thief Judas preached the Gospel without harm to believers. And although they themselves concede that spiritual children are begotten through their deceitful people—that is, through hidden evil men—from whom the Holy Spirit flees, nevertheless they assert that this occurs through their ministry.

For who could endure such madness that, while he calls the married man who begets children carnal, he should call the adulterer spiritual?

“God forbid,” he says, “that I should think this.”

How, then, could a hidden adulterer, while he was a leader among them, beget spiritual children if carnal people cannot do so? Or perhaps Christ, or the Holy Spirit, or perhaps an angel baptized through his hands at that time?

If, then, a human being baptizes when the baptizer is openly good, but when the baptizer is a hidden evil man God or an angel baptizes, and each person is spiritually born according to the character of the one by whom he is baptized, let those who desire Baptism hope that the human beings through whom they are baptized will not be openly good but secretly evil, so that, with God or an angel baptizing, they may deserve to be reborn more holy.

If they consider how to avoid this absurdity, let them acknowledge that whenever someone is baptized with Christ’s Baptism through any human being, Christ is the one who baptizes; for of him alone it was said:

> “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

*[Note: The printed editions read, “If they think they can avoid this absurdity in this way, through any human being, so that when someone …” The manuscripts correct this reading.]*

### 24

For that passage from the Gospel,

> “As the Father sent me, so I send you,”

when he had said this, he breathed on them and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:21–23),

would be against us, so that we would be compelled to admit that this is done by human beings, not through human beings, if, after saying, “So I send you,” he had immediately added, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; and if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained.”

But since the words intervene, “When he had said this, he breathed on them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’” and only afterward follows the statement that forgiveness or retention of sins takes place through them, it is sufficiently shown that they themselves do not accomplish this, but that the Holy Spirit certainly does it through them, just as he says elsewhere:

> “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit who is in you” (Matt. 10:20).

The Holy Spirit is present in a leader or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not deceitful, the Spirit works through him for his reward unto eternal salvation

*[Note: [Col. 0068] The printed editions read “and for his reward”; “for” is absent from the manuscripts.]* and for the regeneration or edification of those who through him are either consecrated or evangelized.

But if he is deceitful, since it is most truly written, “The holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” he is absent from his salvation, withdrawing from thoughts that are without understanding; nevertheless, he does not abandon his ministry, through which he works the salvation of others.

For this reason the Apostle says:

> “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:17);

that is, it benefits those to whom I administer it, not me, who am deceitful.

For the one who acts unwillingly because of carnal advantages and pleasures—which, if he could possess them in another way, he would abandon that ministry—is himself deceitful. Therefore he does not say, “If I act unwillingly, I benefit nothing those for whom I act”; rather, he excludes himself from the reward of salvation, but not them, to whom even an evil servant supplies the Lord’s food.

*[Note: The manuscripts read, “and therefore he does not say, ‘If I act unwillingly, I benefit those for whom I act, but exclude myself only from the reward of salvation, and do not deprive those to whom I supply food,’” whereas the printed editions have a somewhat different wording.]*

But the Apostle was not such a man; rather, he was such that he acted willingly—that is, he dispensed gratuitous grace with the devotion of a pure heart. Through him the Holy Spirit also worked out his reward, which, as he himself says, the Lord, the righteous judge, will repay him on that day (2 Tim. 4:8).

*[Note: Only the printed editions read “the reward of others.”]*

But concerning those who proclaimed the Gospel not purely—who proclaimed nothing other than the truth, that is, Christ, yet not with the truthfulness of their own good heart but for the sake of their own advantages

*[Note: The manuscripts read “of their own heart,” rather than “of a good heart.”]*—he says:

> “Let these people proclaim.”

And he rejoices, not in them, certainly, but in those who were being saved through them, holding to the command:

> “Do and observe whatever they tell you; but do not do what they do, for they preach but do not practice” (Matt. 23:3).

The Apostle also speaks of them to the Philippians:

> “Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from goodwill. Some do so from love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel; but others proclaim Christ out of contentiousness, not purely, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains. What then? Provided that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and I will continue to rejoice” (Phil. 1:15–18).

Would he permit them to preach Christ when they were not preaching the truth of the Gospel with the sincere purity of their hearts? Would he rejoice in the preaching of such people unless he knew that, although it was harmful to them to proclaim a pure matter impurely, it was beneficial to those who, hearing good and true things through them, were advancing toward salvation?

But where not Christ, who is the truth, but falsehood and lying are preached, he most clearly forbids it, saying to the Galatians:

> “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9).

Likewise, he says to Timothy:

> “As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain in Ephesus, so that you might instruct certain people not to teach otherwise” (1 Tim. 1:3).

But those envious, contentious, obstinate, impure people, seeking an opportunity to carry out their evil will, were such that the Holy Spirit fled from their deceit without abandoning their ministry, through which Christ was preached. He not only permits them to act, but also rejoices that they act.

*[Note: The printed editions read “does not permit”; “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]*

[Col. 0069]

## 25

We present these testimonies from the Holy Scriptures so that it may easily appear that nothing is more serious than the sacrilege of schism. There is no just necessity for cutting off unity, since good people tolerate the wicked—who cannot spiritually harm them—precisely so that they may not be spiritually separated from the good. Consideration for preserving peace restrains or postpones the severity of discipline; yet security exercises that severity when it becomes clear that something can be punished by ecclesiastical judgment for wholesome correction without wounding schism.

For we say that the name of the Lord belongs more to those who fear him, although they are mixed among crowds of those who do not fear him;

*[Note: The manuscripts read “that the name of the Lord belongs more to those who fear him.” The printed editions read “that the great name of the Lord is with those who fear him.”]* and we affirm what the Apostle says:

> “The Lord knows those who are his, and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from injustice” (2 Tim. 2:19).

For if, for the sake of the good of peace, lest the wheat be uprooted together with the weeds before the proper time, someone is compelled to remain among the unjust, let him depart from injustice and safely call upon the name of the Lord.

*[Note: The Louvain edition reads, “let him call upon the name of the Lord.” It is corrected from the manuscripts. The same edition, together with Amerbach, soon after reads “Likewise therefore”; the manuscripts correct this reading.]*

For in this way he both withdraws from the unjust and departs and separates himself from them meanwhile in heart, so that at the end he may deserve to be separated from such people in body as well.

## CHAPTER XII

### 26

There is also what is written:

> “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

Certainly, in the mouth of the faithful it is beautiful. Yet each person has a mouth of his own, and no one is wounded by another’s mouth without the assent of his own heart.

But when the sinner’s preaching proceeds from his mouth,

*[Note: The Vatican manuscripts read “prayer.”]*

we must ask what sort of sinner Scripture intended to signify in this passage. For the Publican, who was justified more than that Pharisee, was certainly a sinner (Luke 18:14). If his sins were not real, his confession of sins was false; but if his confession was true—and because of it he deserved even to be justified—then undoubtedly his sins were real.

I would say the same most truly about the prayer of the holy Daniel,

*[Note: The Gallican manuscripts read “about the mouth.”]* who plainly says truthfully:

> “When I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people” (Dan. 9:20).

In whose mouth, then, is praise not beautiful, unless especially in the mouth of a liar and a deceitful person, from whom the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee?

Yet when he speaks the truth,

*[Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “The Spirit of discipline flees from him. Whom, then, does it flee from, when he nevertheless speaks the truth?”]*

praise is not beautiful in his mouth, because it is not attributed to one who does not share in it. Thus prophecy was not beautiful in the mouth of Caiaphas, the high priest of the priests, who did not know what he said, but, because he was high priest, prophesied (John 11:51). Nevertheless, through him the praise of God was beautiful in the ears of those who heard and in the hearts of those who believed.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 27

Moreover, by misusing a statement of the Apostle, Parmenianus dares, as though in mockery, to address those whom he denies possess Baptism and therefore says cannot give it. For, he says:

> “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

To pass over where and why the Apostle says this, which is made clear by the context of his Letter: if he wants this understood of Baptism,

[Col. 0070] and if one who does not possess it cannot give it, while the one who does not possess it is the one who did not receive it—so that what is written, “What do you have that you did not receive?” may somehow support him—I ask whether he does not possess what he received among them.

If they say, “He possesses it,” I ask whether he loses it if he departs from them. If they say, “He loses it,” then he must be baptized again if he returns, so that what he lost may be restored to him.

But if this does not happen, and no one says that it should happen, then he had not lost it. Furthermore, if he received it and was not deprived of it, then he certainly possesses what he received. And therefore, according to their interpretation, one cannot say to him, “What do you have that you did not receive?”

Now turn your attention to the very origin of the schism. However they may regard Caecilianus—we believe him innocent—he was undoubtedly baptized in unity, for this division had not yet occurred. Let us suppose, as they wish, that he himself departed from unity: he certainly did not lose what he had received, for if he returned he would not be baptized again in order to recover what he had lost.

Furthermore, if he had not been deprived of what he had received, he certainly possessed it. If, then, even to him it could not be said, according to their perverse interpretation, “What do you have that you did not receive?”, much less can this be said to one who received from the Lord through Caecilianus.

For why could a person who was not joined to you receive through one who had not lost it when he departed from you?

*[Note: The manuscripts, with great agreement, read, “who was not convicted by you,” rather than “who was not joined to you.”]*

How much more recklessly, then, is it said to the whole world, “What do you have that you did not receive?” From the whole world the continuity of that sacrament came into Africa, and no crime of any traditor could deprive it of God’s promise, which was made with the clearest assurance to Abraham:

> “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18),

even if these people had been not impious slanderers of their brothers but genuine investigators of crimes.

*[Note: In the printed editions, “in the unity of faith” is read. “Of faith” is absent from the manuscripts.]*

### 28

As for the statement which some of them, overcome by the truth, have begun to make:

> “One who departs from the Church does not lose Baptism, but nevertheless loses the right to give it,”

it appears in many ways to be said uselessly and emptily.

First, no reason is shown why one who cannot lose Baptism itself can lose the right to give it. For both are sacraments, and each is given to a person through a kind of consecration: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained. Therefore, in the Catholic Church, neither may be repeated.

For whenever leaders who came over from that very party were received for the sake of peace after correcting the error of schism, and it seemed necessary that they should perform the same offices they had performed, they were not ordained again. Rather, just as Baptism remained whole in them, so Ordination remained whole, because the fault had been in the separation, which was corrected by the peace of unity, not in the sacraments, which wherever they exist are themselves.

*[Note: The printed editions read, “which wherever they exist are themselves true.” “True” is absent from the manuscripts.]*

[Col. 0071] And when it is judged beneficial to the Church that their leaders, upon coming to Catholic fellowship, should not administer their honors there, the sacraments of Ordination themselves are not taken away from them; they remain upon them. Therefore hands are not laid upon them in the presence of the people, lest injury be done not to the person but to the sacrament itself.

And if this is done unknowingly, and the act is not defended stubbornly but corrected devoutly once it is recognized, pardon is easily obtained. For our God is not a God of dissension but of peace (1 Cor. 14:33). Nor are the sacraments of his Church the enemies of those who have departed from the Church; the enemies are the people themselves who have departed.

Just as they possess in Baptism what can be given through them, so in Ordination they possess the right to give it. Both, indeed, are to their own destruction so long as they do not possess the charity of unity.

Yet it is one thing not to possess something, another to possess it perniciously, and another to possess it beneficially. Whatever is not possessed must be given when there is need for it to be given. But what is possessed perniciously must be dealt with by removing the danger, so that it may be possessed beneficially.

29. Although even if some layman, compelled by necessity, should give to one who is perishing [Note: [Col. 0071] Amerbach and Vatican manuscripts: “should give to one perishing, compelled by some necessity.”], what he had learned how to give when he himself received it [Note: [Col. 0071] Printed editions: “had learned that it ought to be given,” omitting “how,” which we have restored here from the Vatican codices. Other manuscripts read: “had learned what ought to be given.”], I do not know whether anyone could piously say that it ought to be repeated. For if it is done without any compelling necessity, it is an usurpation of another’s office; but if necessity presses, it is either no offense or a venial one. Yet even if it is usurped without necessity, and what was given is given by anyone to anyone, what has been given cannot be called not given, although it can rightly be called illicitly given. The illicit usurpation, however, is corrected by the disposition of one who remembers and repents [Note: [Col. 0071] Amerbach and the manuscripts: “Therefore the illicit usurpation is corrected.”]. If he does not correct it, what was given will remain for the punishment of the usurper, or of the one who illicitly gave it, or of the one who illicitly received it; nevertheless, it will not be regarded as though it had not been given. Nor will the royal insignia be violated in any way by a loyal soldier because it was usurped by private persons.

For if some people, secretly and outside the prescribed order, should stamp gold, silver, or bronze in the public mints [Note: [Col. 0071] So the Gallican codices. The printed editions, however, read: “and extraordinarily, should stamp not gold or silver in the public mints, but bronze.”], when the matter had been discovered, would not the recognized royal mark be gathered into the royal treasuries, after those men had been punished or released by clemency [Note: [Col. 0071] Lovaniensis: “would be compelled to be brought in.” The word “brought in” is absent from the other books; and instead of “would be compelled,” the Vatican manuscripts read “would be gathered”?]

Or if someone—whether a deserter or one who had never served in the army at all—should mark a private person with a military stamp, would not, when the matter had been discovered, the one so marked be punished as a deserter, and all the more severely in proportion as it could be proved that he had never served at all, with the most audacious marker punished along with him if he had denounced him? Or if that man, not being a soldier, should fearfully shrink from the military mark on his body and flee to the Emperor’s clemency, and, after pouring out his plea and obtaining pardon [Note: [Col. 0071] The Gallican manuscripts read: “and after peace had been made.”], should then begin military service, would that mark be taken away once the man had been freed and corrected, rather than recognized and approved? [Col. 0072]

Or do Christian Sacraments adhere less firmly than this bodily mark, when we see that even apostates are not without Baptism—which, when they return through repentance, is certainly not restored to them, and for that reason is judged incapable of being lost? Or was the comparison with military service inappropriate, when the Apostle too cries out concerning athletic contests and plainly says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him” (2 Timothy 2:4)?

30. But this is another question: whether Baptism can also be given by those who have never been Christians [Note: [Col. 0072] See Book 7, chapter 53, On Baptism against the Donatists.]. Nothing should be rashly asserted about this without the authority of so great a council as is sufficient for so great a matter. Regarding those who have been separated from the unity of the Church [Note: [Col. 0072] The Vatican manuscripts: “from the unity of the Catholic Church.”], however, there is no longer any question that they both possess it and can give it, and that they possess it harmfully and transmit it harmfully outside the bond of peace. For this has already been examined, considered, settled, and established within the unity of the whole world itself [Note: [Col. 0072] The same, Book 1, chapter 7, and Book 2, chapters 4 and 9.].

But if we are doing wrong, let them explain how the Sacrament of the baptized cannot be lost, while the Sacrament of the ordained can be lost; for they say: “One who withdraws from the Church does not lose Baptism, but loses the right to give it.” If both are Sacraments, as no one doubts, why is one not lost while the other is lost? Neither Sacrament ought to be wronged. If holy things flee from the wicked, let both flee; if holy things remain inviolably in the wicked, let both remain.

If they should say, “Baptism is rightly given only in the true Church,” the answer is made to them: “Baptism is rightly possessed only in the true Church.” Why cannot it be given where it is not rightly given, when it can be possessed where it is not rightly possessed? Is it because not possessing something is one thing, and not possessing it rightly another? Likewise, is not giving something one thing, and not giving it rightly another?

Just as the one who departs from unity does not possess Baptism rightly, yet does possess it, and therefore it is not given back to him when he returns, so also the one who departs from unity does not give it rightly, yet does give it; and therefore what he received from him is not repeated when he comes to unity. They, however, maintain that what is not rightly given has not been given. But if someone else should maintain that what is not rightly possessed cannot be possessed, would we not protest against both [Note: [Col. 0072] The printed editions read: “But if they should maintain that something which is not rightly possessed cannot be possessed, we protest against both sides.” The manuscripts correct the wording.], and say that the one who has departed from unity does possess it, but does not possess it rightly?

Therefore, if they want that person to hear what we protest together, let them themselves hear us protesting that the one who has departed from unity does give it, but does not give it rightly. Consequently, just as what he possessed outside is not given back to the one who returns, so what he also received outside is not to be repeated for the one who comes to unity.

From this it follows that the perversity of human beings must be corrected, but the holiness of the Sacraments must in no way be violated in any perverse person. For it is established that this holiness remains undefiled and inviolable in perverse and wicked people, whether they are inside or outside. And because evil people are said to pollute it, they are said to do so only insofar as it lies within their power, while it nevertheless remains undefiled; in the good it remains for reward, and in the wicked it remains for judgment.

For even concerning the Spirit, who cannot in any way be extinguished, it was nevertheless said, “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) [Note: [Col. 0073] The Vatican manuscripts: “the Holy Spirit.”]—that is, insofar as it lies within you, do not act as though you were trying to extinguish the Spirit, or regard the Spirit as extinguished. And the name of God cannot in any way be polluted, yet it was said: “Father and son entered the same girl, to profane the name of their God” (Amos 2:7).

31. Nor can these men in any way extricate themselves when they are asked why the holiness of the Sacrament can both be possessed and given by one whom God has already condemned as wicked while he is inside, but begins to be unable to give it only when he has been condemned by human beings, although even then he cannot lose that holiness [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions read: “nor can he then lose it.” The manuscripts more suitably read “it,” namely, the holiness of the Sacrament.].

Finally, why did Felicianus, whom three hundred and ten men condemned along with Maximianus, and who, as they themselves declared in their council [Note: [Col. 0073] The council at Bagai.], remained for a long time outside in sacrilege as a schismatic [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions read: “who also remained for a long time outside in sacrilege . . . a schismatic.” The manuscripts omit “who” and have “of schism” instead of “a schismatic.”], not lose either Baptism itself or the right to give it? For he was received in his former rank, just as he had gone out, together with all those whom, while outside, he had baptized, and none of them was rebaptized. If they had judged that any of those whom he had baptized outside ought to be rebaptized, they would have judged that he had lost the right to give Baptism while he was outside; and consequently, if they rebaptized those people, they would also have had to ordain him again.

But when they are recalled to the peace of Christ, they are slanderers; when they take measures for the peace of Donatus, they are dissemblers. What else is this than what their Tichonius [Note: [Col. 0073] The printed editions read “their teacher Tichonius.” “Teacher” is absent from the manuscripts.] says about them: “What we want is holy”?

CHAPTER XIV

32. Why, then, does Parmenianus exult in empty boasting and say: “The judgment of divine law will never permit a dead man to give life to anyone, a wounded man to heal, a blind man to enlighten, a naked man to clothe, or a polluted man to cleanse”?

The Lord raises the dead; the Lord heals the wounded; the Lord enlightens the blind; the Lord clothes the naked; the Lord cleanses the polluted. Why does he claim for himself what does not belong to man? Are those who do not sin so alive among them that they are even said to be able to give life, although they cannot give increase? “I planted,” says the Apostle, “Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). When can the one who cannot give increase give life to the dead?

“For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). Are they so healthy among them that they can even heal those who are not healthy [Note: [Col. 0073] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads: “so that they can heal those who are not healthy among them,” omitting “even.”]? What else are these men doing than setting themselves up as those who bless in place of the Lord? But they cannot deceive those who, hoping not in man but in God, sing:

“Bless the Lord, my soul,  
and do not forget all his rewards;  
he who forgives all your iniquities,  
who heals all your diseases” (Psalm 102:2–3) [Note: [Col. 0074] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “your infirmities”; and below, “ought to heal,” instead of “claims to heal.”].

If he himself heals all diseases, he leaves none for Parmenianus to claim that he heals. Are their lights so great that they can even enlighten? John the Evangelist does not grant this even to John the Baptist, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, concerning whom he says: “He was not that Light, but came to bear witness to the Light. He was the true Light, which enlightens every person who comes into this world.”

If that Light enlightens every person, it leaves none for Parmenianus to claim that he enlightens. For although holy people are called “lights” in a certain sense, the illuminated lights are one thing, and the Light that illuminates is another—the Light of which that same John the Baptist says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:8–9, 16).

And who clothes the naked except the one who says, “Bring out the first robe for him” (Luke 15:22), and the one who will clothe this corruptible with incorruption and this mortal with immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53)? Is anyone said to clothe another with divine clothing when it is a great thing if he himself deserves to be clothed [Note: [Col. 0074] The Vatican and some Gallican manuscripts: “And is any human being said to clothe another?”]?

Furthermore, let him dare to say that he cleanses the polluted, if he first dares to say that he himself is not polluted. We have been cleansed through the grace of God; but even then we shall not cleanse anyone when our cleansing has been perfected—how much less now, when “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15)! For “who can boast of having a pure heart,” or “who can boast of being clean from sin” (Proverbs 20:9, according to the Septuagint)?

To cleanse and to heal, in spiritual matters, amount to the same thing. And just as we have been saved in hope, so we have been cleansed in hope, awaiting perfect salvation and perfect purity [Note: [Col. 0074] Perhaps: “in imperfect salvation and imperfect purity.” See Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 146–147. M.]. How, then, can we already heal and cleanse, when we shall not be able to do so even then, when we have been entirely saved and made pure?

“But God,” he says, “does this through a human being.” Certainly he does; but he also did it through Judas, whom he sent with the others to preach the Gospel (Matthew 10:1–8). He also did it through the Pharisees, in those who themselves practiced the good things they heard through them, while the Pharisees did not practice what they said.

Finally, why do their wicked and criminal men—whether they are hiding or are tolerated for the sake of the peace of Donatus [Note: [Col. 0074] Amerbach and the manuscripts: “for the Donatist cause.”—]—give life, heal, enlighten, and cleanse? Are they not themselves dead, wounded, blind, and polluted? Or do the blind not therefore fall together into the pit with the blind leading the blind (Matthew 15:14), because the latter follow not the men themselves but the God whom those men preach, by hearing and obeying him?

Yes, that is so—but they preach God only if they gather with Christ. Whoever does not gather with him scatters (Matthew 12:30): by preaching Donatus rather than God, the blind follow the blind and fall together into the pit.

But, with the Lord’s help, we shall treat the question of Baptism more fully elsewhere (Book 1, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 1), when we have answered Parmenianus concerning all the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that he thought ought to be brought against us [Note: [Col. 0075] The manuscripts read: “we shall answer.” The Vatican manuscripts continue as follows: “Whom he truly matches in the overthrow nearest to him,” and so forth.]. For he truly matches those nearest to him in the overthrow produced by his iniquity: he has poured into them such a pernicious error that, not for peace but for division and separation, he himself not only speaks, but also persuades them that the divine Books speak.

CHAPTER XV

33. Among many other things, I am astonished that, while arguing that Baptism cannot be possessed unless it has been received, and cannot be received without someone giving it, he introduced this testimony from the Gospel: “No one,” he says, “can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27).

For someone ignorant of those words might have thought, when he began to say, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him,” but before he added “from heaven,” that he was going to say “from Donatus,” or “from Parmenianus,” or “from someone belonging to the Donatist party,” or from the Donatist party itself.

I recognize the Gospel, and I acknowledge that it is written: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” But is Donatus heaven? Is Parmenianus heaven? Is the Donatist party itself heaven? It is not heaven; it is not in heaven.

For the one who said, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven,” would never have said, “unless it has been given to him from the sun, or from the moon, or from the stars,” although these are in heaven. How much less would he have said, “unless it has been given to him from the Donatist party,” which is not only not heaven and not in heaven, but does not even wish to be in the kingdom of heaven.

Nor, surely, would he have said, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from the Church,” for the Church itself receives from heaven. But if he had said, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him by a righteous person,” these brazen men would certainly rush forward and proclaim themselves righteous, so that anyone who wished to receive might receive from them.

Nor would we raise the question whether they were righteous or not; but we could easily show that hidden unrighteous people were among them from the evidence of certain men who had been exposed and expelled. Yet we would not reject them, nor would we say that what had been given and received from such people had not been given or received [Note: [Col. 0075] Some Gallican manuscripts: “yet we would not approve of them as such.”].

But this too would falsely be said: “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him by a righteous person.” For I ask from whom the righteous person, from whom the other receives, received it. If he too received it from a righteous person, and I ask the same question about that person, continuing until I reach the very head of the human order, someone who did not receive it from a human being, then I demonstrate that it is false that no one can receive anything unless it has been given to him by a human being.

34. What are these men doing, then, by means of this evangelical testimony, in their ignorance [Col. 0076] [Note: [Col. 0076] The printed editions read: “in ignorance of the evangelical testimony,” omitting “by means of,” which we restore from the manuscripts.] except warning people at last to awaken and understand that, when a person desires to receive something holy, he must truly look not to human beings but only to the one who gives from heaven to humanity? For “no one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.”

If they should say, “He receives it from heaven, not from a human being, but through a human being,” I ask: through what kind of person? If through a righteous person only, then those who received among them through the most wicked men hiding among them do not possess it. If also through an unrighteous person, what reason is there for rebaptizing anyone?

If through an unrighteous person only when he is hidden, they do not possess it who were baptized by Optatus, the notorious henchman of Gildo, when he was openly known. If also through an unrighteous person who is openly known, provided he has not yet been condemned and expelled from the Church’s communion, then those whom Felicianus of Musti baptized in the schism of Maximianus, while he was outside their communion, do not possess it—yet now, when they have returned with him, no one rebaptizes them.

Finally, if a human being, although the gift is from heaven, can receive nothing except through a human being, I ask through what human being John the Baptist himself, who said this, had received what he had certainly received from heaven. No such person is found [Note: [Col. 0076] In the printed editions, the words immediately following “and no such person is found” were: “Yet a human being can receive something divinely without the intervention of a human being.” Then followed: “and thus, by the testimonies he himself had brought forward,” and so on. We restore the passage from the Vatican manuscripts.]. Thus his case is convicted as bad by the testimonies he himself has produced.

For although the Son says that he received from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit receives from what belongs to the Son—not as though this occurred by stages, but as he himself explained when he said, “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said, He will take from what is mine” (John 16:15)—John himself testifies by his own example that a human being can receive something divinely without the intervention of a human being.

So did the many saints before the Son of God became human; and after he rose and ascended into heaven, one hundred and twenty people were gathered together, whom the Holy Spirit, coming from heaven, filled without any human being on earth laying hands upon them (Acts 1:15; 2:1–4). And after the order of the Church had already been established, Peter himself was astonished that the centurion Cornelius, before Baptism and before the laying on of hands, was filled with the same Holy Spirit, together with those who were with him (Acts 10:44).

Therefore no one receives without someone giving. But as far as the holiness of Baptism is concerned, God is present as the giver and a human being as the receiver—whether God gives directly, or through an angel, or through a holy human being, as through Peter or through John, or through an unrighteous human being, as through so many hidden or openly known people whom the household servants of the father are forbidden to gather from the harvest before the proper time. The Lord’s grain, meanwhile separating them from itself in heart as chaff, does not rashly abandon them bodily, but bears them with spiritual piety until the time of winnowing.

CHAPTER XVI

35. “The one who has believed wrongly,” he says, “cannot obtain the Sacrament of Baptism, because it is written, ‘You cannot adorn what is perverse’” (Ecclesiastes 1:15, according to the Septuagint).

What, then, if someone among them had been baptized who had thought, for example, that Christ began to exist only when he was born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary? Later, having been instructed by the word of truth and having learned that he was the one of whom John said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and of whom he subsequently said, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14), suppose that he confessed his former error to them and anxiously acknowledged that he had held it when he was baptized. Would they order him to be baptized again?

They certainly would never do so. Rather, they would rejoice that the ignorant simplicity of the man, previously corrupted by a carnal opinion [Note: [Col. 0077] The manuscripts read: “a corrupt opinion.”], had been corrected by the reasoning of truth. Or, if such perversity seemed to him something that he ought stubbornly to defend, and if, after long resistance, he remained uncorrected and was even expelled from the Church, and later came to recognize the truth, they would judge that he ought to be healed by repentance, not wounded by a repetition of Baptism—although he confessed that he had held this belief in his heart even at the time when he had been baptized among them.

“You cannot adorn what is perverse,” therefore, because the Sacrament he had received would not benefit him as an ornament if he persisted in perverse faith, but rather as a punishment. Yet the Sacrament itself would remain intact in its own nature, even in the perverse person whom it did not adorn but judged. Therefore the holiness of that Sacrament must in no way be violated, even while the perversity of that person must be corrected.

CHAPTER XVII

36. Parmenianus also dares to set before us divine examples by which he thinks he can show that a holy person must be sought from whom the Sacrament ought to be received.

“He himself,” he says, “the Son of God himself, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, from whom the beginning of spiritual Baptism arose, when he was to be baptized according to the Father’s will, is he shown to have gone to the treacherous and profane Pharisees, or to the most holy John?”

But if this example invites us to receive Baptism, we ought to seek someone inferior to us from whom we may be baptized, since the Lord was baptized by one who had declared that he himself ought to be baptized by the Lord, and who testified that he was unworthy to loosen the strap of his footwear (Matthew 3:14, 11).

Indeed, to set aside for the moment a more careful inquiry into why our Savior himself wished to be baptized—for he certainly wished it for some reason—perhaps he wished this because, although he could baptize himself, and could also baptize the one who baptized him, the Lord desired to be baptized by a servant, and the one through whom all things were made by one who was made among all things. In this way he both taught humility and showed that it makes no difference who baptizes whom, provided that the person is baptized with the Baptism with which he ought to be baptized.

Nor would he disdain to be baptized by the Pharisees if they had a baptism of the kind with which he wished to be baptized for the sake of the grace of that Sacrament. And when he was to be circumcised, was John sought out? This was already customarily done by the Jews. And when a legal sacrifice was to be offered for him, was that temple avoided which he calls a den of robbers (Matthew 21:13)? Certainly both good and evil people entered it, and the evil did not harm the good. For the Lord, who says, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:45), makes his holy people dwell inviolably among the wicked so that they may preserve the holiness they receive [Note: [Col. 0078] So the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read: “so long as they preserve it.”].

In the same way, the Lord Jesus was not polluted by any contagion of wickedness among the Jewish people, neither when he received those first Sacraments under the Law according to the perfect way of humility, nor when he later lived with his chosen disciples, including his betrayer, up to the final kiss.

By his example—not merely of avoiding evil but also of refusing consent to any wickedness [Note: [Col. 0078] The printed editions read: “not doing evil but also not consenting.” The manuscripts correct the wording.]—the grain is safe among the chaff, because the good neither do such things nor consent to those who do them, even if, in the same field until the harvest, on the same threshing floor until the winnowing, and in the same nets until the separation that will take place on the shore, the good tolerate the wicked (Matthew 3:12; 13:37–45, 47–50).

But these men are truly blind guides of the blind: they see so many wicked people among their own number, yet do not see the way of peace. And they persuade people to follow them, not in bearing with one another for the sake of the bond of unity, but in separating from one another through the sacrilege of schism.

CHAPTER XVIII

37. “But,” it is said, “the prophet said to King Jehoshaphat: ‘O King Jehoshaphat, if you help a sinner, or love one whom the Lord hates, for this reason the Lord’s anger was upon you.’”

Which of us says that a sinner should be helped for the very purpose in which he wishes to sin? That is what Ahab was doing when Jehoshaphat helped him by going with him into battle, while Ahab was disregarding the truthful words of the prophet Micaiah [Note: [Col. 0078] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “when he helped him.”].

Yet even in this way Ahab’s wickedness did not harm the innocence of King Jehoshaphat. For the Lord rescued Jehoshaphat, who cried out to him, from the danger of battle, but allowed that sacrilegious contemptor to fall into the hands of the enemy (1 Kings 22). And if Jehoshaphat suffered any danger, which the Prophet indicates came from God’s anger, he had not deserved it because of another’s sin but because of his own, since he had helped a sinner, as was said to him. Nevertheless, his other good deeds prevailed before God.

For this is what was said to him: “You have helped a sinner and have been a friend to one who is against the Lord, and for this the Lord’s anger is upon you. Nevertheless, good things have been found in you before God, because you removed the sacred groves from the land and prepared your heart to seek God” (2 Chronicles 19:2–3).

The person who lives in God’s Church, where there are also those who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, who preach Christ through envy and rivalry, not sincerely—and where it is said, “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice and will continue to rejoice” (Philippians 2:21; 1:15–18)—remains undefiled and whole among them, because he does not consent to them in seeking their own interests, while he censures and reproves this.
