Rather, he helps them not toward sinning but toward the wider proclamation of Christ, so that those who hear and practice the good things proclaimed by people who do not practice what they say may believe in Christ, hope in Christ, and love Christ.

For the same Apostle commands such people: “Do not be joined with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? What fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? What agreement does the temple of God have with idols? For you are the temple of the living God” [Note: [Col. 0079] In the manuscripts here and below: “you are temples of the living God.”]. He says: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore come out from among them, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be your father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty” (2 Corinthians 6:14–18).

These men, understanding those words carnally, cut themselves into pieces through so many divisions, fragment by fragment, within Africa itself. They do not understand that no one is joined with unbelievers except the one who commits the sins of pagans [Note: [Col. 0079] The printed editions read: “the sin of pagans.” The Vatican manuscripts read: “the sins of pagans.”], or favors those who commit such sins; nor does anyone become a partner in iniquity except the one who either commits or approves iniquity.

Who has fellowship with darkness except the one who, through the darkness of his consent, abandons Christ and follows Belial? Who assigns himself a portion with unbelievers except the one who becomes a participant in their unbelief? In this way he ceases to be the temple of God, and he does not otherwise join himself to idols.

But those who are the temple of the living God and who appear “as lights in the world in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, holding the word of life” (Philippians 2:15)—nothing that they tolerate for the sake of unity defiles them. Nor are they distressed, because God dwells and walks among them. They come out from the midst of the wicked and are meanwhile separated from them in heart, lest, when they wish to do this through the sedition of schism, they separate themselves spiritually from the good before they separate themselves bodily from the wicked.

CHAPTER XIX

38. What is written—that God said, “Those who glorify me I will glorify, and those who despise me shall be despised” (1 Samuel 2:30)—they especially refuse to consider.

For how do they glorify God, when they say that his promises cannot be fulfilled throughout the world—promises he made to our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and which, having foretold them long beforehand through the Prophets, he fulfilled through his only Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:2–3), so that in him, that is, in the seed of Abraham, all nations might be blessed?

They say that the Son of God himself spoke in vain when he said, “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matthew 13:30), as though he had been false or had deceived himself, when only weeds grew throughout the world, while the grain had failed everywhere on earth except in the Donatist party.

How do they glorify God while it is written, “In the multitude of a nation is the glory of a king, but in the diminution of a people is the ruin of a prince” (Proverbs 14:28)?

Or how do they not despise God, when with incredible impiety and rashness they blow away his Baptism in those whose case they have not heard and concerning whom they could in no way judge? They dare to claim for themselves what belongs to God. They receive into their full honors those whom they have condemned, for the sake of Donatist peace, while they abominate those whom they have not heard, against the peace of the Lord. They maintain that the Baptism transmitted by the Apostles in those regions of the world has perished, yet they admit that the Baptism transmitted by Felicianus among the Maximianists has not perished [Note: [Col. 0080] The printed editions read “they maintain.” The manuscripts more correctly read “they admit.”].

But how do Catholics fail to glorify God, when they trust that his promises cannot be hindered from being fulfilled by any human crimes? They show that they honor his Sacraments with due reverence, so that even when those Sacraments have been administered by the unworthy, and the unworthy have been condemned for their perversity, the Sacraments themselves remain untouched in holiness [Note: [Col. 0080] The printed text has an apparent OCR error, “al indignis”; read “ab indignis,” “by the unworthy.”].

CHAPTER XX

39. “Again,” they say, “it is written: ‘Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them. For it is shameful even to mention what they do secretly’” (Ephesians 5:11–12).

We have already explained how these words themselves are to be understood: not to participate means not to consent. But for the discipline of the Church that is not enough unless they are also rebuked, so that they may be corrected. These things, however, must be done while preserving peace, and insofar as the duty of preserving unity permits, lest the wheat also be uprooted at the same time.

CHAPTER XXI

40. “Again, the same Apostle says to Timothy: ‘Do not participate in the sins of others; keep yourself pure’” (1 Timothy 5:22).

He consequently taught how what he had said earlier was to be understood. For the one who keeps himself pure does not participate in the sins of others. If he participates, he consents; if he consents, he is corrupted; if he is corrupted, he does not keep himself pure.

But at last Parmenianus did awaken and paid attention to what Tichonius had said—yet in vain. Immediately, out of love for his own opinion, he closed his eyes against the truth. He says:

“My dearest brother, do the sins of others not pollute other people? And is this what it means not to participate in the crimes of criminals: that, although you associate with them, you do not commit their deeds?”

Yet he did not say everything. It is not enough not to commit their deeds unless one disapproves of them; it is not enough to disapprove of them unless they are rebuked. Not doing something is one thing; not participating in it—that is, not consenting to those who do it—is another; and rebuking it is still another.

Why, then, when he had begun to see this, did he immediately turn away, refuse to reach the end, and scarcely set down a third of the whole? Was it as they did with the people, and did he think that the judgment of truth ought to be cut short?

We say that the person who neither does evil, nor consents to the one who does it, and who rebukes the one doing it, lives firmly and wholly among the wicked, like grain among chaff. He, however, merely says, “not to commit their deeds.” Let us see, nevertheless, how he refutes a third part of the whole statement.

41. “That this is contrary to divine law,” he says, “no one who reveres the law is ignorant.”

So far these words can be said in common by both sides. For another person could say: “That this is in accordance with divine law, no one who reveres the law is ignorant.” But it is necessary to prove the point, not merely to state it.

Let us therefore consider how he proves it. “For what benefit is there,” he says, “in having preserved innocence, if he is mixed with the guilty and the condemned?”

Certainly, if this is so, preserving innocence is of no benefit [Note: [Col. 0081] Perhaps: “there is no benefit in not preserving innocence.”]; but then innocence has not been preserved. No one can rightly be said to be mixed with the guilty and condemned except through the consent of a conscience stained by them.

But the one who fulfills what is written—“Nothing wicked pleases the righteous” (Proverbs 12:21, according to the Septuagint)—cannot be mixed with iniquity, wherever necessity compels him to live among it.

“Or how,” he says, “will you be able to remain uncorrupted if you associate with the corrupt?”

Quite so, if he associates with them—that is, if he commits some evil together with them or favors those who commit it. But if he does neither, he does not associate with them in any way.

Furthermore, if he adds a third action, so that he is not sluggish in administering correction, but either, as a righteous man, rebukes and reproves with mercy, or, if he holds that office and the reason of preserving peace permits it, rebukes sinners publicly so that the others may fear, and even removes them either from some rank of honor or from communion in the Sacraments—and does all this with love for correction, not with hatred for persecution [Note: [Col. 0081] Supply: “he does.”]—then he has fulfilled the fullest duty not only of the most chaste innocence but also of the most diligent severity [Note: [Col. 0081] Several manuscripts read “severity”; supply: “of the most diligent innocence.”].

Where other measures are obstructed, those two things, always retained, preserve him incorrupt and pure: that he neither does evil nor approves what has been done.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 42. Yet let us see where he learned what he asserts. “Since it is written,” he says, “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). Parmenian said this and moved on; nor can it now be pointed out to him that in the party of Donatus there was not merely a little leaven, but a great deal of poison, issuing from those ruptured eggs of vipers—men already powerful serpents—who had been condemned on Primian’s account and then recalled again to Primian [Note: Some editions and several manuscripts read: “and recalled for a third time to Primian.”].

“But they have been corrected,” he says. Thanks be to God. If this is true, I do not begrudge it, and would that it might be brought to completion. For if returning from the Maximianists to the party of Donatus is some degree of correction [Note: The printed editions read, “is some measure of correction.” But our Gallican manuscripts, together with the Vatican manuscripts, have, “is some degree.” This reading, noted in the margin of the Amerbach edition, was judged preferable by Henry Gravius, provided that it existed in the manuscripts.], how much truer and more perfect is the correction of returning from the party of Donatus itself to Catholic unity?

Tichonius, indeed, said many things which show that in those times—as he knew inwardly—they were unwilling to admit that their entire lump had been corrupted not by a little but by a great deal of leaven, while they accused the whole world of having been leavened by the sins of the Africans. But I am astonished at these men, if they still wish to understand these apostolic words in this way, and if they want to defend Optatus of Gildonia so zealously that they will not concede even that he was a little leaven [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read, “that they contend.”].

If they concede even this, how large do they think their lump is, that it could not have been wholly corrupted? Or, if it was wholly corrupted only among those who approve of Optatus, let them learn by experience to understand what they read. The whole lump consists of those to whom the word “whole” applies, whether for good or for evil: it consists of those who consent; it does not consist at all of those who do not consent. Therefore ecclesiastical discipline must be exercised [Note: The printed editions read, “and therefore it must be exercised in ecclesiastical discipline.” The word “in” is absent from the manuscripts.], lest the evil spread to many through persuasion. Whenever the requirements of peace permit this and it is not done, that very negligence incurs guilt and, through the slothfulness of correction, becomes a participation in the danger of consent.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 43. From this rule we must also understand what he next brings forward, saying that it is written: “Let it be a perpetual ordinance for you throughout your generations: to distinguish between holy things and profane things, and between the clean and the unclean” (Lev. 10:9–10) [Note: The printed editions read, “it must be considered”; this is erroneous.].

For each person fulfills this better in proportion as he makes progress in the Church. When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared. And although the household servants already distinguished and separated the two by their master’s knowledge, they were nevertheless ordered to let them grow until the harvest (Matt. 13:26–30).

But enough of this for now. What remains must be examined and treated somewhat more carefully from another beginning.

# BOOK THREE

The remaining passages of Scripture that Parmenian had brought forward are treated.

[Col. 0081]

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Since every godly principle and every method of ecclesiastical discipline ought above all to keep in view the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, which the Apostle commands us to preserve by bearing with one another (Eph. 4:3, 2), and since, when this is not preserved, the remedy of vengeance is not merely superfluous but harmful—and therefore is shown no longer to be a remedy at all—those evil sons who do not act from hatred of others’ iniquities but from zeal for their own quarrels, and who seek either to drag along whole weak congregations ensnared by the vaunting of their own name or at least to divide them, swollen with pride, mad with obstinacy, treacherous in their accusations, and turbulent in their seditions, lest they appear to lack the light of truth, hold out the shadow of rigid severity.

They seize upon passages of the Holy Scriptures which, with sincere love preserved and the unity of peace maintained, prescribe that fraternal faults be corrected with a sharper [Note: The printed editions read, “more moderate.” The manuscripts more appropriately have, “sharper.” The reference is to those passages of Scripture prescribing a more severe correction of faults, which the Donatists abused to persuade people to separate from the wicked.] treatment, and use them for the sacrilege of schism and as an occasion for cutting people off, saying: “Behold, the Apostle says, ‘Remove the evil from among yourselves.’ Surely,” they say, “if such evil did not harm the sound and whole, it would not be ordered to be removed.”

### 2. In the meantime, let us see whether the Apostle did not say this for good reason. He did not say, “Remove evil people from your congregation,” but, “Remove the evil from yourselves.” For when someone is prevented from separating wicked people from the Church’s congregation, if he removes the evil from himself, he does not mingle with them in his heart [Note: H. Retractations, chapter 17.]; and thus spiritually he is not only joined to the good but also separated from the wicked.

So, in the passage addressed to Timothy, after saying, “Do not share in the sins of others,” as though Timothy had said that it might be impossible for him to separate certain wicked people from the Church’s congregation and that he was therefore compelled to tolerate them, the Apostle gives him advice on how not to share in their sins: “Keep yourself chaste,” he says (1 Tim. 5:22). For an evil person can mingle with evil people [Note: All the manuscripts read: “For no one except an evil person can mingle with evil people.”], but a good person cannot do so in any way, even though he lives among them in one congregation.

So also here, in the passage to the Corinthians, after saying, “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Are you not to judge those who are inside?”—lest they be disturbed by the large number of wicked people, mixed in with the wheat in such a way that they could not be gathered and separated without harming it—he says, “Remove the evil from yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:12–13). Thus, if they could not remove the wicked from their congregation, by removing the evil from themselves—that is, by not sinning with them and by neither consenting nor showing favor to their sin—they could live among them wholly sound and incorrupt.

For each person consents to the wicked through his own evil. But if he removes the evil from himself, he has no means of consenting to another’s evil.

Therefore, whoever disregards the discipline of the Church of God, so that he ceases to admonish, correct, and rebuke wicked people with whom he does not sin and to whom he gives no support—and, if he holds such an office and the peace of the Church permits it, ceases even to exclude them from participation in the Sacraments [Note: The manuscripts have this form. The printed editions read: “if he even holds such an office and the peace of the Church permits someone to exclude him from participation in the Sacraments.”]—sins not through another’s evil but through his own.

For negligence in so serious a matter is itself a grave evil. Therefore, as the Apostle teaches, if he removes the evil from himself, he will remove not only the audacity to commit evil and the contagion of consent, but also the laziness of correcting and the negligence of punishing, exercising prudence and obedience in what the Lord commands: that the wheat not be harmed (Matt. 13:29).

Whoever tolerates weeds among the wheat for this purpose, removing the evil from himself, does not share in their evil. In the meantime he distinguishes and judges them, reserving judgment until the appointed day; for he does not know what tomorrow will bring. Therefore, while preserving love, whatever necessary severity compels one to punish must be punished, not without hope of correction [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read: “whatever necessary severity requires to be corrected or punished.”].

To make this sufficiently clear, let us examine the whole passage of the apostolic Epistle more carefully.

### 3. “What do you want?” he says. “Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” Here it is already evident that he is speaking of punishment, since he uses the rod as its symbol. Yet is the rod without love, because he has set the words together in this way: “Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love”? But what follows—“with a spirit of gentleness”—makes us understand that the rod too possesses love.

One kind of love belongs to severity, another to gentleness. It is one love, certainly, but it operates differently in different circumstances.

“It is actually reported,” he says, “that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife.” Let us see how he commands them to act harshly concerning such a monstrous deed.

“And you,” he says, “are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who did this deed might be removed from among you.” Why “mourned” rather than “become angry,” except because “if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26)? And not “mourned because he was removed,” but “mourned so that he might be removed”—that is, so that the grief of those who mourned might rise to God, and that God himself might remove this deed from among them as he knew best, lest perhaps through human ignorance they uproot the wheat as well.

Therefore, when necessity compels such punishment, the humility of those who mourn ought to obtain the mercy that the pride of those who rage drives away [Note: The word “those who rage” is restored from the Vatican manuscripts. Some other manuscripts read, “the proud mind.” See below, chapter 2, section 5, where the humility of those who mourn is again contrasted with the pride of those who rage.]. Nor should the salvation of the very one who is removed from the midst of his brothers be neglected. Everything must be done so that such punishment may benefit him; and if he cannot be corrected by rebukes, it must be done with vows and prayers.

Accordingly, he continues: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are assembled, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:21–5:5).

What, then, was the Apostle doing except providing for spiritual salvation through the destruction of the flesh? This might occur either through some bodily punishment or death, as when Ananias and his wife fell dead at the feet of the Apostle Peter (Acts 5:5, 10), or through repentance, since the man had been handed over to Satan, so that the sinful desire of the flesh might be destroyed in him.

For he also says, “Put to death therefore your members that are upon the earth,” among which he mentions fornication (Col. 3:5). And again: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:13).

Yet he does not separate from brotherly love the one whom he commands to be separated from the brotherly congregation [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read, “he does not separate heavenly love from the one whom he commands to be separated from the heavenly congregation.”].

He says this more clearly to the Thessalonians: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed; and do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.” Let these men listen at last and understand how apostolic love strives “to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” by bearing with one another (Eph. 4:2–3).

For here too, after saying, “Do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother,” as though showing why he had said this, he immediately added: “May the God of peace himself give you peace always in every good thing” (2 Thess. 3:14–16).

So also, concerning the man who had his father’s wife, he commands mourning rather than anger and everywhere commends peaceful love. He says of himself: “I fear that when I come again, my God may humble me before you, and that I may mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and fornication that they practiced.” And shortly afterward he says: “I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them” (2 Cor. 12:21; 13:2).

Therefore he judged with mourning, so that God’s mercy, without destroying the bond of peace in which salvation wholly consists, might crush and correct sinners—as he is understood to have done concerning this very man who had committed fornication with his father’s wife.

For there is no indication that he means anyone else in the second Epistle to the same Corinthians when he says: “Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not to make you sorrowful, but to let you know the love that I have abundantly for you. But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part—not to burden all of you. This punishment by the majority is sufficient for such a person, so that, on the contrary, you should forgive and comfort him, lest such a one be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Therefore I urge you to confirm your love for him. For this is why I wrote: to test whether you are obedient in everything. Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have done it for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:4–11).

What could be done or said with greater moderation, greater care, or greater fullness of devout concern and paternal and maternal love? Just as he applies correction to the sinner, so he wishes consolation to be restored to the one who has been corrected and who, by crushing and humbling his heart in repentance, is grieving, lest, he says, he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow [Note: The printed editions read, “he applies condemnation, and so to the one corrected and crushed … he wishes to offer consolation.” The Vatican manuscripts more appropriately read, “he applies correction.” The other manuscripts, together with them, have, “and to the one who is crushed … he wishes consolation to be restored,” except for one Divion manuscript, which prefers, “and to the one who is converted.”].

But what does he mean by concluding this statement with the words, “so that we may not be outwitted by Satan”? “For,” he says, “we are not ignorant of his designs.” He is the one who, under the appearance of just severity, persuades people to cruel savagery, seeking nothing else through his most poisonous cunning than to corrupt and rupture the bond of peace and love. When that bond is preserved among Christians, all his power to do harm is weakened, the traps of his ambushes are crushed, and his plans for destruction vanish.

## CHAPTER II

### 4. Even if the Apostle was speaking of someone else in the second Epistle to the Corinthians, he nevertheless showed there with what love ecclesiastical punishment ought to proceed against anyone.

This is the principal matter that these men, failing to understand it, habitually exploit amid their accusations: “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5).

But since these men have not learned how to correct in mercy, they pursued Caecilian’s innocence with savage suspicions and anointed the power of Optatus of Gildonia with the deceptive oil of flattery.

For if, out of concern for the bond of peace, they had tolerated the iniquity of Optatus with groaning and mourning, they would certainly not have ruptured Christian and Catholic peace throughout the world and holy unity [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “they would not have ruptured holy unity throughout the world.”]. Or at least, if their ancestors had impiously ruptured it through blindness, they would have grieved over this in such a way that, having learned from their own experience how many wicked people they had to bear for the sake of Donatus’s peace, they would extinguish their restless accusations by the peace of their correction.

### 5. But let us return to what follows in that First Epistle to the Corinthians. After the Apostle had said, “to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus,” repeatedly commending that this should be done with the humility of those who mourn, not with the pride of those who rage, he immediately added: “Your boasting is not good”—or, by way of reproachful assertion, “Your boasting is good.” For some manuscripts, especially Latin ones, have this wording, while the meaning is the same in either case.

There is no need to fear that anyone will understand him to have praised them by saying, “Your boasting is good,” since above he had said, “You are puffed up, and have not rather mourned,” and here immediately adds, “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (1 Cor. 5:6). This can more appropriately be referred to the corruption of their empty boasting [Note: The Vatican manuscripts have this wording. The printed editions read, “what can be referred to the corruption itself …?” which is less correct.].

Pride, deriving from the oldness of the first man—who fell through pride—makes those whose minds are, as it were, fermented and corrupted, and who agree with one another in the vanity of similar boasting, swell into one lump.

To boast not of one’s own sins but over another’s sins, as though by comparison with one’s own innocence, seems to be a little leaven; for to boast even of one’s own iniquities is much leaven. Yet that little leaven also corrupts the whole lump.

The proud person falls because of his pride and begins, by defending his sins, to wish to boast of them as well. Foreseeing this, the same Apostle says: “Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

And again: “If anyone is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:1–2).

What is the law of Christ except, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34)? What is the law of Christ except, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27)?

What he says here—“Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ”—he says elsewhere in this form: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

There also appeared to be a little leaven in that Pharisee, because he not only did not grieve over the sinner but exalted himself over the other’s sins on account of his own merits. But the other man went down justified because he confessed his sins, more justified than the Pharisee who boasted of his merits; for “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:10–14).

The Apostle continues: “Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.” What does “so that you may be,” and what does “as you are,” mean, except that some of them were already such, while others were not, and that he urged the latter to become such by the example of the former?

Yet he addresses all of them as one, as though they were the same, so that those who were already such would not despair of those who were not yet such or judge them not to belong to the structure of their body. He addresses them all together when he says, “so that you may be as you are.”

Those who were already such knew—and, at the Apostle’s urging, ought to have known increasingly—that they should bear with those who were not yet such, so that by bearing with one another in love they might preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace and, by bearing one another’s burdens, fulfill the law of Christ. By that law our Lord Jesus Christ, to teach the way of humility, humbled himself even to death on a cross (Phil. 2:8), and, like a physician with the sick, bore sinners with love. Of them he had said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12).

He immediately set forth the principal example, saying: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed,” so that by the example of such great humility they might learn to cleanse out the old leaven—that is, whatever pride remained in them from the old person.

“Therefore,” he says, “let us keep the feast”—not merely one day, but the whole of life—not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Malice and wickedness consist in boasting, as though over another’s sin, as if one ought to rejoice in one’s own righteousness only when one has not seen another to be righteous.

Sincerity and truth consist in remembering what one has been, even when one is making progress, and showing all the more pity to those who have fallen—since the person who stands upright was himself raised from his fall by Christ’s mercy, Christ having humbled himself for sinners despite having no sin of his own [Note: Several manuscripts read, “he humbled himself to sinners.”].

### 6. But lest the sins of others be perniciously left alone and neglected under a pretense of indifference—for this is no less cruel than that pride—the Apostle continues: “I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the robbers, or the idolaters; for then you would need to go out of the world.” Your task in this world is to win sinners for Christ unto salvation. This cannot happen if you avoid their conversation and companionship.

“But now,” he says, “I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother and is a fornicator, or an idolater, or a greedy person, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber.” With such a one do not even eat. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Are you not to judge those who are inside? God will judge those who are outside. Remove the evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:7–12).

### 7. See how the Apostle arrived at this statement, whose final clause Parmenian thought fit to cite, saying that it is written: “Remove the evil from yourselves.” “Surely,” he says, “if it did not harm the good and the sound, it would not be ordered to be removed.”

But he omitted what had been said earlier, by which he reached this point—material that could have helped him persuade people that a bodily separation from the wicked ought to be made, since the Apostle says, “With such a one do not even eat.”

Why, then, did he not mention what seemed most capable of supporting his intention? Since he presses so forcefully to persuade people that a bodily separation must be made from those who live wickedly, why does he not cite the Apostle’s testimony: “If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or a greedy person, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat”?

Why else, except that he saw that if he said this, he could be answered: “Do you yourselves either not have fornicators and idolaters, or are you unaware of them? Do you see and know no greedy person, reviler, drunkard, or robber among you? Why, then, contrary to the Apostle’s command, do you not merely eat with such people at your tables but also share the Lord’s table with them?”

Parmenian therefore, I believe, tried to avoid this objection, and so did not include what would have seemed most strongly to support his case. For if this passage of the apostolic Epistle had escaped him [Note: This is the reading of the more excellent manuscripts. Some others have, “if it had been with him.” The printed editions read, “if he had consulted it.”], and had not occurred to him, he would not have cited its final clause: “Remove the evil from yourselves.”

### 8. But now that we have said this, perhaps these men will dare to deny that there are greedy people, revilers, drunkards, or robbers among them. Perhaps they will even try to defend Optatus himself, who was known throughout all Africa and whom they tolerated as long as they feared him.

Let them say, if they can, that they now possess a better and more purified Church than the unity that existed in the days of the blessed Cyprian. Cyprian did not separate himself bodily from his colleagues, yet without naming any of them individually, and wisely and soberly applying a remedy of salutary sharpness [Note: The manuscripts and some printed editions have this reading. Many more printed editions have “inserting.”], he gravely rebuked them in these words: they wanted to possess abundant silver while their brothers in the Church were hungry; they seized estates through treacherous frauds; and they increased their profits through multiplying usuries.

To show most clearly that he was speaking of people with whom he lived in communion in one Church, he added: “What would we not deserve to suffer for such sins?” (Cyprian, Sermon on the Lapsed).

For he did not say, “What would they deserve,” but “What would we deserve”—something he would never have said, since he himself was certainly not such a person, unless he wished to make clear that he was mourning over the deeds of people who were joined to him not only by the unity of the Church [Note: The printed editions read, “not only in the unity of the Church.” The manuscripts do not have the word “in.”] but also by fellowship in the college of bishops, although he differed from them in life, character, heart, and purpose.

Let these men, then, say that their Church is now better and that they do not have people such as Cyprian had within that unity. Let those who wish believe them, and let them close their eyes against the evils alleged concerning their character [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read: “Let them close their eyes against those things concerning their character that strike the face of those who dissimulate.” Some other manuscripts, together with Amerbach, read: “that strike the face of those who pretend.” The Benignian manuscript reads: “that are reported concerning the character of those who pretend; let them close their eyes.” Perhaps the reading should be: “that strike the face of those who dissimulate; let them close their eyes.”].

I, however, shall call them back to those very earlier times of unity and ask them whether, when that great bishop of the Church of Carthage, Cyprian, lamented over such a wicked body of colleagues in testimony of his free voice, even in writings that would benefit posterity, the Church of Christ existed or did not exist.

If it existed, how did Cyprian and the others like him fulfill what the Apostle commanded: “If anyone bears the name of brother and is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even eat”—when they ate the Lord’s bread and drank the Lord’s cup with those greedy and rapacious men who wanted to possess abundant silver while their brothers in the Church were hungry, seized estates through treacherous frauds, and increased their profits through multiplying usuries?

### 9. Or are these crimes perhaps insignificant and to be considered trivial? These men are also accustomed to saying this, weighing such offenses not on the just scales of the divine Scriptures but on the crooked scales of their own customs.

Whatever crime and iniquity intoxicates a multitude loses the truth of judgment. But for this reason the declarations of the heavenly Scriptures are set before human beings like a perfectly clear mirror, so that each person may see there how serious any sin is—even one that is perhaps great but, through the blind custom of those who live wickedly, is despised.

Could greed have been accused more gravely in the divine words than by being shown to be equal to idolatry and called by its name, when the Apostle says, “and greed, which is idolatry” (Col. 3:5)?

Could it have been judged worthy of a greater punishment than by being placed among those crimes whose practitioners, being enslaved to them, will not possess the kingdom of God?

Let the eyes of the heart be opened, lest the eyes of the body be open in vain, and let them read the free preacher of truth writing in that same First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

How, then, did Cyprian and other such wheat of the Lord in that Church of unity at that time eat the Lord’s bread and drink the Lord’s cup with the greedy and rapacious—with those who will not possess the kingdom of God—not merely with laypeople or with just any clergy, but even with the bishops themselves—when the same Apostle commands that they not associate with such people and cries out, “With such a one do not even eat”?

Or, since they could not separate themselves bodily from them without uprooting the wheat at the same time, was it enough for them to separate themselves from such people in heart, to distinguish themselves from them in life and conduct, for the sake of preserving peace and unity, and for the salvation of the weak and, as it were, of the infant wheat, lest the members of Christ’s body be torn apart by sacrilegious schisms?

### 10. But behold, I am not forcing any of them to understand it in this way. Let them explain how that Church at that time could have been glorious, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), when there were people who wanted to possess abundant silver while their brothers in the Church were hungry, who seized estates through treacherous frauds, who increased their profits through multiplying usuries, and who were so entangled in iniquities that they would not possess the kingdom of God.

But if the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle was counted as consisting only of those who mourned and lamented over the iniquities committed in their midst, and if, according to the prophecy of the holy Ezekiel, they thereby deserved to be marked with their own sign, so that they might escape utterly secure from the devastation and destruction of the wicked [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read, “indeed also.”], let them stop slandering the good—those who do not commit evil through diseased desire but tolerate it for the sake of peaceful love. To them it was said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

For this reason the Holy Spirit, through the prophet Ezekiel just mentioned, used such language to designate the wicked whom the good tolerate within unity: he said that they were situated “in the midst” of the good. If he had said that the good were in the midst of the wicked, they would seem to be, as it were, outside and external.

“They groan,” he says, “and lament over the iniquities of my people that are committed in their midst” (Ezek. 9:4), so that we might understand that those wicked people were not merely excluded but included.

### 11. But if the Church did not exist even then, because Cyprian and all who knew those greedy and rapacious people with him—people unlike themselves—although they accused them with the gravest groans and most illustrious words, nevertheless entered the same church with them and administered the same Sacraments in one congregation, then through such communion they became partners in the same lot.

For they did not obey the Apostle’s command that they should not even eat with such people, nor his command, “Remove the evil from yourselves.” Why, then, do we still labor? Why do they boast that they possess any Church, if the Church ceased to exist already in those times?

Let them say where Majorinus or Donatus arose, so that through them Parmenian and Primian might arise [Note: Majorinus, Donatus, Parmenian, and Primian were, in succession, Carthaginian bishops of the Donatists.].

What benefit is it to them to pretend that they either do not now have greedy and rapacious people in their congregation, with whom the Apostle forbids eating, or that such people are unknown to them, when there were such people in that Church of unity from which they boast that they arose, while attempting to persuade people that the Church remained only in their own fellowship—that is, in the communion of Donatus?

If they say that the Church perishes through communion with such people, why do they not say that it perished in Cyprian’s time? And, since they cannot discover from where they themselves arose, let them stop saying that the Church remained among them—the Church which, according to their own claim, perished entirely in earlier times.

But if the Church always remained, remains, and will remain in those good people who dislike such things, let these men learn at last not to understand the Apostle’s words, “Remove the evil from yourselves,” in such a way that, by attempting through schisms to gather the weeds, they uproot the wheat at the same time.

We argue all this so that those who read or hear it may remember that they have never been able to demonstrate—whether at that time, when the heresy was still very recent, or now, when the whole world is joined in Christian peace within the Catholic Church with a much firmer consciousness of innocence—that Caecilian or those who remained harmoniously attached to him were weeds.

But so that each person may remain secure within the unity of the holy Church, and so that those who desert that unity may not follow them and perish with them, this is what we say: if those people had been weeds, they ought rather to have been tolerated until the harvest than separated by uprooting the wheat through the destruction of schism.

### 12

But someone may say: How shall we be able to obey the Apostle when he commands us not even to take food together with such a person? For if he were commanding that separation from them be made only in the heart, he would not say, “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators”—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, that is, with those who are not Christians, concerning whom he later says, “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are inside that you judge? God will judge those who are outside.” Since, therefore, he commands a separation of this kind—not from those evil people who are not Christians, but from those who are Christians—while separation in the heart must be made from all evil people, and consequently we must also be separated in heart from those evil people who are not Christians, what remains except that we understand the Apostle to command us not to mingle with whatever Christians are evil [Note: Vatican manuscripts read “with certain Christians” (*ut quibusdam*)], of the sort he himself identifies, by the kind of association through which we mingle with pagans in the ordinary society of human life?

For this reason he says elsewhere: “If an unbeliever invites you, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions” (1 Cor. 10:27). But here he does not even permit us to take food with such a person. With unbelievers—that is, with those who have not yet believed in Christ—he says that we should eat whatever they set before us; concerning them, since they are outside, God will judge. But with those who are inside—that is, if someone is called a brother and is a fornicator, or serves idols, or is greedy, or abusive, or drunk, or rapacious—he forbids even taking food. Thus he appears to persuade us to separate the weeds from the wheat before the harvest. But if we are unwilling to do this, because the Lord forbids it, we must tolerate them and persist in separation from them only in will and heart—and consequently also take food with such people, which the Apostle indeed forbids.

### 13

In this apparent difficulty of the question I shall not say anything new or unusual, but only what the sound practice of the Church observes: when one of the brothers—that is, one of the Christians established within the fellowship of the Church—is found in some such sin that he is considered worthy of excommunication, this should be done where there is no danger of schism, and it should be done with that love concerning which the Apostle himself gives instruction elsewhere, saying, “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:15). It is not for uprooting, but for correction. [Note: Printed editions read, “For you are not.” Several manuscripts lack the word *estis* (“are”).]

If he does not acknowledge his fault and correct himself through repentance, he will go out of his own accord and, by his own will, be cut off from communion with the Church. [Note: Thus all manuscripts. Printed editions read, “will be cut off from the unity of the Church.”] For the Lord himself, when the servants wished to gather the weeds, first gave the reason, saying, “Let both grow until the harvest,” and, “Lest while you wish to gather the weeds, you uproot the wheat together with them” (Matt. 13:30, 29).

Here he sufficiently shows that when this fear is absent, and complete certainty remains concerning the firm stability of the wheat—that is, when someone’s crime is so well known and appears so hateful to everyone that he has either no defenders at all or no defenders through whom schism could arise—the severity of discipline should not fall asleep. Correction of depravity is all the more effective the more diligently charity is preserved. [Note: Printed copies read *confirmatio* (“confirmation”); all manuscripts read *conservatio* (“preservation”).]

This can then be done without staining peace and unity and without harming the wheat, when the multitude of the Church’s congregation is alien from the crime for which the person is excommunicated. Then it assists the superior who is correcting rather than the guilty person who is resisting; then it healthfully refrains from association with him, so that no one takes food with him—not in hostile rage, but in brotherly restraint. Then that person is both struck by fear and healed by shame, when he sees himself excommunicated by the whole Church and cannot find a companion crowd with whom he may rejoice in his wrongdoing and insult the good.

### 14

For this reason the Apostle himself says, “If anyone is called a brother.” In what he says, “If anyone,” he seems to have intended nothing else than to signify that a person can be healthfully corrected in this manner when he sins among those who are unlike him—that is, among those whom the plague of similar sins has not corrupted. But by saying “is called,” he clearly intended it to be understood that it is not enough for someone to be such a person unless he is also so called—that is, unless he is publicly known—so that the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him may appear fully justified to everyone.

In this way he is corrected while peace is preserved, and he is not struck as though to destroy him, but burned as a means of healing. Therefore he also said concerning the man whom he wished to heal by such treatment: “This punishment by the majority is sufficient for him.” For correction by the majority cannot be salutary unless the person being corrected does not have a multitude accompanying him. But when the same disease has seized many, nothing remains for the good except sorrow and lamentation, so that by that sign revealed to the holy Ezekiel they may deserve to escape unharmed from the devastation of those people (Ezek. 9:4).

They cry out to the one who cannot err: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood” (Ps. 25:9). Let them not, while wishing to gather the weeds, uproot the wheat together with them; let them not cleanse the Lord’s field through excessive zeal, but rather be counted themselves among the refuse through rashness.

Accordingly, when the same Apostle had discovered that many had been defiled by unclean lust and fornications, he wrote to those same Corinthians in his Second Epistle and did not likewise command them not to take food with such people. There were many of them, and it could not be said of them, “If anyone is called a brother who is a fornicator, or serves idols, or is greedy, or anything of that kind, with such a person do not even take food.” Rather, he says: “Lest, when I come again, God humble me before you, and I mourn over many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness, lust, and fornication that they committed”—threatening that through his mourning they would instead be restrained by a divine scourging, rather than through that correction which would make the others refrain from association with them. [Note: Manuscripts read *minatur* (“he threatens”); printed editions read *minans* (“threatening”).]

He then appropriately says: “Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you: ‘Every matter shall be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.’ I have already told you, and I now tell you in advance, as I did when present the second time and now while absent, to those who sinned before and to all the others, that if I come again I will not spare them, since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me” (2 Cor. 12:21–13:3).

What else did he mean here by “I will not spare,” except what he said above, “and I mourn over many”? His mourning would obtain from the Lord a scourging by which those people might be corrected—people who, because of their numbers, could no longer be corrected in such a way that the others would refrain from association with them and make them feel shame, as should happen if a brother is publicly identified as guilty of some offense unlike that of the others.

And truly, if the contagion of sinning has invaded the multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For schemes of separation are both futile and pernicious, indeed sacrilegious; they become impious and proud. [Note: Printed editions read “For just as” (*sicut enim*); following the manuscripts, *enim* (“for”) is omitted.] and they disturb weak good people more than they correct bold evil people.

As that most faithful witness concerning the greed of his colleagues—when he attributed the tribulations and evils that the Church was suffering at that time to divine judgment and discipline—said after recalling the worst conduct of bishops whom he knew: they wanted to possess abundant silver while their brothers were hungry, seized estates by treacherous frauds, and increased their interest-bearing loans through multiplying usury. “What,” he said, “would we not deserve to suffer for such sins?” He then adds testimony from the Psalms, saying that divine judgment had long ago warned and declared (Cyprian, *Sermon on the Lapsed*):

> “If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not observe my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:31–34).

### 15

Therefore let a person correct mercifully what he can; what he cannot correct, let him bear patiently, and let him groan and mourn with love [Note: The American and Erasmian editions and several manuscripts read “and with love”], until either God from above amends and corrects it, or postpones uprooting the weeds and winnowing the chaff until the harvest. Yet Christians of good hope, secure concerning their salvation, should live in unity among the despairing whom they cannot correct: let them “remove the evil from among themselves,” that is, let there not be found in themselves what displeases them in the conduct of others.

For when the Apostle had said, “For what have I to do with those who are outside? Is it not those who are inside that you judge? God will judge those who are outside” (1 Cor. 5:12), they might have replied to him: “What are we to do when we are so oppressed by the multitude of the wicked that we cannot exercise our judgment in any form of discipline?” He answers: “Remove the evil from among yourselves”—that is, if you cannot remove the evil people from your midst, remove the evil itself from yourselves. [Note: See *Retractations* II, chapter 17.]

If someone wishes to understand the statement, “Remove the evil from among yourselves,” in the sense that every evil person must be removed from the congregation of the brothers through corrective separation, no one will doubt that this must nevertheless be done with the intention of healing, not with hatred aimed at destruction. We have discussed what procedure should be used and what times should be observed, so that the peace of the Church may not be violated—for in this matter the wheat must especially be spared, lest it be uprooted together with the weeds. Whoever considers these matters carefully neither neglects the severity of discipline in preserving unity nor, through immoderate coercion, breaks the bond of fellowship.

### 16

For this very command of the Apostle—“With such a person do not even take food together”—how many good Christians do not hesitate to carry out, concerning those for whom they exercise more particular care, so that they can separate themselves from the companionship of those whom they believe can be corrected by such correction, or of those whom they despair can be corrected at all, lest they corrupt others through the contagion of evil conversations? [Note: Printed editions add *faciunt* (“do”) after “many good Christians”; the word is superfluous.]

A person does this well—that is, with humble love and kindly severity—when he presides over the brothers in such a way that he remembers himself to be their servant, just as the Lord’s command and example require (Matt. 20:26–28). It is then done without the arrogance of self-exaltation toward the person, and with mourning supplication before God. [Note: Printed edition of the American recension reads *typo* (“arrogance”); the note’s main text has *typho*.]

But just as easily as any individual is removed by a bishop from the rank of the clergy, or from the number of the poor whom the Church feeds, or from the congregation of the laity—whether by the bishop, the clergy, or any superior possessing the authority—so that no one who is permitted to receive this command takes food with such a person, the multitude of evil people in any order of the Church cannot so easily be excluded and expelled from commingling with the good.

For in their own households all faithful people likewise regulate and govern the discipline of their dependents, so that there too they obey the Apostle’s command, “With such a person do not even take food,” when they do this, or order it to be done, concerning their own children and their household of peace. [Note: The word *pacis* (“of peace”) is absent from the Casalino manuscript.] They do so when they see their dependents living in such a way that the love they bear them itself suggests that this must be done.

But when there is an opportunity among the people to deliver a public address, the crowd of wicked people should be struck by a general rebuke, especially if some scourge of the Lord from above has provided the occasion and opportunity, making it apparent that they are suffering blows according to their merits. Then the calamity of the hearers lends humble ears to a sermon of correction, and afflicted hearts are more easily driven to groaning confession than to resistant murmuring. Thus blessed Cyprian might not have spoken those words about his colleagues at that time unless divine severity from above had aided him.

At that time he spoke them under such distress, calamity, and mourning that they not only dared not be angry with him, but even felt that they could scarcely obtain pardon from those who were angry. Nevertheless, even if no calamity of tribulation is pressing, when the opportunity is given, a multitude may usefully be rebuked in the midst of the multitude. For just as it is accustomed to rage when separated, so in the congregation itself it is accustomed to groan when rebuked.

Therefore the Apostle’s command must in no way be neglected when it can be carried out without danger of violating peace, because he himself did not wish the evil person to be separated from the congregation of the good in any other way. At the same time, his other instruction must be observed above all: “Bearing with one another, let us strive to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

Likewise, we must obey the Lord in the Gospel where he says, “If he refuses even to hear the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:17), and where he forbids the weeds to be gathered, lest the wheat also be uprooted (ibid. 13:29). Both commands can be observed by those to whom it was said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (ibid. 5:9).

## CHAPTER III

### 17

But now let us examine the other testimonies that Parmenianus has set forth. Among all the passages in which their sacrilegious arrogance appears [Note: The Casalino codex reads “in which the arrogance of sacrilege appears”], he revealed himself nowhere more clearly than in daring to include even that passage from the prophet Jeremiah, by which he sought to persuade other people that the communion of the Donatists is not only the true Church [Note: Two manuscripts read “the old Church”], but already at this present time such as the holy Church will be after the final winnowing. I do not know what could be added to this sacrilegious presumption and abominable arrogance.

In many passages of their writings they appear to do nothing other than presume such things; yet sometimes they do feel shame, when the truth begins to press them, especially when they are asked whether they themselves are not sinners. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “when someone begins to press them.”] Nevertheless, in this prophetic testimony they most openly exposed their impious vanity and excessive perversity.

For when the holy Jeremiah wished to show that, even though the good and the evil may for a time belong to one fellowship of the congregation, the conditions of their conduct and the end of their merits are nevertheless very different, he said: “What has straw in common with wheat?” (Jer. 23:28).

But Parmenianus, wishing to refute Tichonius, who said that the evil must meanwhile be tolerated together with the good within unity for the sake of peace and separated at the end of the final judgment, introduced this testimony from Jeremiah. In his perversity and error he inflames the perverse and erring to the most turbulent and criminal seditions, so that anyone who, with an inflated mind, seems to himself to be something when he is nothing (Gal. 6:3), regarding himself and those like him as thoroughly purified grains, refuses to approach the congregation of the Church. In that congregation, those who belong to eternal life must necessarily tolerate, like wheat tolerating its straw, those who belong to eternal fire until the appointed end.

No other puff of wind has shaken the lightest straw from Christ’s threshing floor before the time of winnowing; no other sacrilegious presumption has produced whatever schisms exist, wherever they exist. [Note: Printed editions read *praesumptione* (“by presumption”); the manuscripts’ *praesumptio* (“presumption”) is better.]

### 18

“The most holy Jeremiah,” he says, “admonishes us that the fruitless and barren crowds of sinners are to be distinguished from the honored produce of the righteous, saying: ‘What has straw in common with wheat?’”

O trumpet of fury! O accursed voice of pestilence! Has the human race perhaps fallen into such error that it does not recognize Parmenianus as the winnower? Or does he too give place to Donatus and boast that he has come to the mass purified by him? For I do not know whether that man considers Majorinus worthy of recognition.

Or were these three, like the three horns of some winnowing-fork in the Lord’s hand, the means by which the harvest of the whole world was to be cleansed? Was Africa chosen as the place where the purified mass would remain, while all the rest of the earth would be covered by separated straw?

Where, then, do such great bands of Circumcellions come from? Where do such enormous crowds of drunken banqueters come from, and the innumerable debaucheries of women who are unmarried but not undefiled? Where does such a multitude of kidnappers, greedy men, and usurers come from? Where do so many men come from who are notorious in their respective regions, wanting as much as Optatus did, though unable to achieve as much as he did?

What will they answer to these things? Do such people not exist? Or will they say, “This too is wheat”? Woe to the most shameless denial if they say that such people do not exist among them; woe to the most criminal perversity if they answer that they are wheat.

Finally, after such an authoritative triad—that is, Majorinus, Donatus, and Parmenianus—Primianus again dared to winnow the mass of purified wheat, separating the Maximianists from his communion. Or did he perhaps throw out wheat? What, then, is he himself, together with his followers, who threw such people out? Or was this wheat purified in such a way that they do not recognize one another and, by condemning one another, try to winnow one another?

Could straw baptize wheat? If it could, why do they say, “What has straw in common with wheat?” But if it could not, why, when Felicianus flew out from among the straw of the Maximianists, did all those whom he baptized return with him to that most purified mass, and why do they now all keep them inside and not say to themselves, “What has straw in common with wheat?” [Col. 0097]

### 19

Let them therefore wake up at last and understand how the Prophet said, “What has straw in common with wheat?” Let them consider where it is said, if they possess any human understanding at all.

Can it be said in the field, “What has straw in common with wheat,” when both are sustained by the same root? Can it be said on the threshing floor, where both are threshed together? But certainly in the granary it is said: “What has straw in common with wheat?” For the master of the household will come carrying a winnowing-fork in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the straw with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12).

In another parable, all the wheat is signified by the name of sheep, and all the straw by the name of goats; these two kinds of animals are meanwhile pastured together under one shepherd. But he says: “The Son of man will come with his angels, and all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left. Then he will say to those who are at his right: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ But to those at his left he will say: ‘Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’” (ibid. 25:31–41).

Then, therefore, the prophecy “What has straw in common with wheat?” is fulfilled, when the goats and sheep can no longer share a common pasture.

If good fish can say to bad fish within that net [Note: Printed editions read “good fish with bad fish”; the word “with” corrupts the sense and is absent from the manuscripts] of which the Lord said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” “Depart from us,” or “We shall depart from you until all are brought out onto the shore, and the good are placed by the angels into vessels while the bad are thrown outside” (ibid. 13:47–48), then what is said—“What has straw in common with wheat?”—can be fulfilled at the present time.

But those who now think their congregation is purified wheat have flown away from the commingling of wheat and straw like pure straw. Those who do not acknowledge that they are still pastured under one shepherd together with the goats have been separated from the Lord’s flock by the snares of wolves. Those who do not think they have been gathered together with bad fish are not merely bad fish themselves; they have also broken the nets of unity.

But if we understand the words of Jeremiah—“What has straw in common with wheat?”—as already being fulfilled at the present time, we can rightly understand them in no other way than this: the wheat and straw are indeed in one congregation until, at the end of the winnowing, they are also separated bodily; yet the heart of the wheat is above, while that of the straw is below. For the straw seeks what is its own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21); but the wheat stores up treasure in heaven, and where its treasure is, there also is its heart (Matt. 6:20–21).

## CHAPTER IV

### 20

The words of the blessed Isaiah must likewise be understood in this way. [Note: Gallican manuscripts read, “Thus also the words of the blessed Isaiah.”] Parmenianus, failing to understand them similarly, attempts to twist them toward the same conclusion of his error.

What, then, does Isaiah say? “Depart, depart; go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean. Go out from the midst of it, and separate yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11).

Does this need to be repeated every time the manner of separation in the heart from evil people is discussed? [Note: The manuscripts, except the Casalino manuscript, read “as often as the manner in which separation is made”; printed editions omit “the manner in which.”] For the person who consents to no one’s sin does not touch what is unclean. He goes out from there so that his case before God may remain sound, if he does not neglect, while preserving peace, the discipline of correcting and reproving.

For the person who wishes bodily to abandon those who are openly evil abandons spiritually those who are secretly good: he is compelled to accuse people whom he has neither tested nor known, while attempting to defend his separation.

### 21

But let them answer this: If Felicianus is clean, why did he go out from their midst? If he is unclean, why does he now touch what is clean? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “why do they now touch what is unclean?” The note that follows begins, “But if …”]

But if he was unclean when he was outside, those whom he baptized there are unclean, because they touched an unclean person. Or were they all cleansed when they returned with him? Thus those baptized outside can be cleansed, even though they were not baptized in their communion? [Note: Printed editions read, “those baptized outside can baptize the cleansed”; the manuscripts correct this reading.]

Why, then, do they rebaptize others? Or is it perhaps considered some great privilege to be condemned by the three hundred and ten who sat at Bagai? [Note: The American and Erasmian editions and some manuscripts read, “perhaps they deserved some privilege.”] And for that reason anyone from the whole world who comes to them is rebaptized, because the whole world did not deserve this privilege—to be condemned by the council of Bagai?

What, then? [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons, Venetian, and Louvain editions omit “what.”] Are those baptized by Maximianus and his other associates rebaptized when they do not return to Primianus’s communion? [Note: Several manuscripts read, “to Primianus’s fellowship.”] Or are they spared?

If they are rebaptized, the privilege of Bagai is violated, for the baptizers of these people were also condemned there. But if they are spared, these men should be asked to assemble again at the town of Bagai. And if that number of three hundred and ten has perhaps now been consecrated, let an equal number assemble and pronounce a sentence against the whole world, just as they pronounced one against the Maximianists. Then, whenever they wish to rebaptize someone coming from some part of the world, let him defend himself with an equal privilege, asserting that he ought to be spared in the same way as the person whom a Maximianist baptizes is spared. For by then not only the Maximianists but also the whole world will have deserved to be condemned by the council of Bagai.

Then they will free themselves from so great an accusation. [Note: Printed editions add, “from so great and so marvelous a death”; these words are absent from the manuscripts. Two manuscripts instead read, “Then, as they fall into such great marvels, when they begin …”; the Louvain editors read “may free themselves” rather than “will free themselves.”] When they begin no longer to rebaptize those baptized in the Church established throughout all lands, if anyone asks them why they no longer do what they previously did, let them answer:

> When we did these things, we had not yet condemned the whole world by the council of Bagai. But now, yielding mercifully to their request, we have granted that we should condemn them by such a council as that by which we condemned the Maximianists, whose Baptism we do not repeat.

What great or difficult thing is it, then, to grant all nations such a great privilege of condemnation? [Note: Several manuscripts read, “so great a privilege,” omitting the word “of condemnation.”] Is it permissible to repeat the baptism of the whole world, but not permissible to repeat the condemnation of the whole world?

Let them be confident about this also: we shall not find any council by which they condemned so many nations and provinces. They condemned a few people in Africa, and by the judgment of the whole world they were defeated by those opponents. [Note: This judgment of the whole world, by which the Donatist litigants were defeated by their opponents, was none other than the judgment at Arles.] Nor did they afterward dare to condemn the judges before whom they had been defeated—for what would have been more shameless, what more insane?

Much less were they able to condemn those established in the other regions of the earth, who preferred to believe such ecclesiastical judges rather than defeated litigants. Yet the Baptism of the Maximianists, whom three hundred and ten Donatists condemned at the council of Bagai, is acknowledged, accepted, and admitted. But the Baptism of the whole world—through which Christ’s inheritance has been displayed as it was promised, and in which they themselves were present a few years ago, though they could condemn it by no legal right and did condemn it by no council, however perverse—is rejected, repudiated, and repeated.

O holy condemnation, which the Maximianists deserved! And what laborious innocence on the part of the nations, which lost the Christian name among them merely because it could not find a place for such condemnation!

### 22

But if only those coming from the Maximianists are not rebaptized who return together with their baptizers, as did those who returned with Praetextatus and Felicianus, let them first observe how they equally affirm the Baptism of the same schism, given outside their communion, in some people and repudiate it in others—honoring it in one case and violating it in another.

For wherever they violate it, they are guilty. [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “there they become guilty.”] But wherever they affirm it, they are found to have witnesses against their own guilt. If afterward they affirmed it in such a way that they ceased violating it, this would be called correction, not inconsistency. But when they reject in some people what they approve in others, they are accused in the former and give testimony against themselves in the latter.

For I ask why you do not rebaptize those whom Felicianus baptized in the schism of Maximianus. Is it because they received Christ’s Baptism, or because they received Felicianus’s? If because they received Felicianus’s, he gave it among the Maximianists after he had been condemned; he gave it outside, beyond your communion. This is that Baptism which was also given by Salvius of Membressa and others of that sort.

But if because they received Christ’s, then Felicianus among the people of Musti has more value in your eyes on behalf of Christ’s Baptism than Christ himself throughout all the lands. In your eyes, the person sitting at your side and condemned by you has more value on behalf of Christ’s Baptism than the one sitting at the Father’s right hand and crucified for you.

Christ’s Baptism is spared in a very few people, lest Felicianus be offended; and it is not spared lest Christ himself be repudiated among so many thousands of nations?

### 23

But the blindness of these people is incredible. I cannot understand how such perversity could be believed to exist in human beings unless their own words and deeds made it evident that they keep the eyes of their hearts so tightly closed that, when they cite testimonies from Holy Scripture, they do not observe in the deeds of the Prophets how the words of the Prophets are to be understood.

Jeremiah said, “What has straw in common with wheat?”—not so that he himself would withdraw from the straw of his people, against whom he spoke all those true things. [Note: We have added the negative particle from the Casalino manuscript. If it is preferred to delete it, the particle *ut* (“so that”) should apparently also be deleted, or *at* (“but”) should be read in its place. Shortly afterward the same Casalino manuscript reads, “against whom he spoke such a great denunciation.”]

Isaiah said, “Depart, depart; go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean.” Why, then, did he touch within that people, in one congregation together with them, the uncleanness that he so severely denounced? Let them read how much and how vehemently and truthfully he spoke against the evil among his people, from whom he nevertheless did not separate himself by any bodily division. [Note: The American edition and the manuscripts read *direptione* (“seizure”); as above, Book 1, no. 8, the intended reading is evidently *diremptione* (“separation”).]

David said: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter with evildoers. I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. 25:4–5).

Let them read what sort of people he himself tolerated in that people during his own time. He showed such honor to the mystical sacrament of anointing that he did not despise it even in the most criminal Saul; indeed, he revered it so greatly that he could honor it no more.

If we were to set their words against their deeds, would they not answer us: “Certainly, we had no fellowship in our hearts with such people, nor did we touch what is unclean where contact can defile; that is, by the consent and decision of our conscience we withdrew from them and went out from them. We not only did not do such things ourselves, but we did not remain silent before those who did them”?

But these seditious and insane people, who seek a defense for their separation from the oracles of the Prophets, have only to go so far in their mad impiety as to accuse the conduct of the Prophets on the basis of the Prophets’ words.

Will they say that in those times the righteous were not permitted to withdraw from the evil people, whereas in these times they are permitted to do so? What could be said more perversely: that at that time the good could not separate bodily from the evil, when many sacraments appeared to be observed bodily, but that bodily separation is now necessary, when those same things are already observed spiritually?

24. Woe to the blind who lead and to the blind who follow! Do they not fear saying such things, lest perhaps, throughout the vast breadth of the world in which Christ’s faith and name have been spread, before these men separated themselves, the righteous had already done this in some region most remote from the African lands, while these men were still living in contact with the uncleanness from which those others had fled? For who protects them [Note: So the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions have, “who protects them” with the pronoun in a different form], who makes them secure, if this kind of separation from the wicked must be made, that before it was made by these men it had never been made so far away that Africa knew nothing of it [Note: The printed editions have, “so that they did not know Africa at all.” One should read either, with the Vatican manuscripts, “so that Africa knew nothing of it,” or “so that the Africans knew nothing of it,” as we suspect was written in most other manuscripts. But because the vowel *i* lacked its mark, *Africani* began to be read incorrectly as *Africam*]? This is just as, in the farthest regions of those lands [Col. 0101], the party of Donatus is entirely unknown.

Perhaps they will say that what they did not know could not harm them.
