Then, likewise, what was done in Africa cannot harm those lands, which know nothing of it—even if what these men say about the crimes of the Africans were true. But if they say that such a thing could not have remained hidden from them had it occurred, let them now say throughout all the regions of the earth where a schism has taken place. I ask too much: let the Carthaginian Donatists themselves, or whoever are in the city of Carthage, say in Africa itself how many divisions of that very party of Donatus have arisen throughout Numidia and Mauretania, the causes of all of which they certainly ought to know. Perhaps some righteous people in those regions avoided the fellowship and assembly of their wicked neighbors and departed from there, lest they touch the unclean, lest they enter in with criminals; perhaps, some years ago, in some corner of Numidia or Mauretania, when the wheat separated itself, the chaff remained behind, and these men do not know it [Note: The Casalinus manuscript reads, “and the Carthaginian Donatists do not know it, and they communicate with them, and this does not harm them. But whence…”].

But whence are they secure, unless because they are certain that those who separated themselves from the communion of Donatus—which is spread throughout all Africa—could not have been good? For if they endured some wicked people in their vicinity whom they could not point out to the others, they ought rather to have tolerated them than to separate themselves from so many innocent people [Note: The word “innocent” is absent from the manuscripts], who could not be persuaded that another’s sins were theirs, even if they themselves knew those sins perfectly well.

Why, then, is this innocence not attributed to the whole world, amid such a multitude of nations, wherever Christ’s inheritance extends, so that it may be certain and assured that those who call themselves good and separate themselves from the unity of the whole earth thereby demonstrate what they are? They appear righteous to themselves and despise the rest; and therefore they do not sing the new song, because they are lifted up by the pride of the old man. For they separate themselves from the communion to which it was said: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95:1). If they were truly righteous, they would be humble; but if they were humble, even if they endured genuinely wicked people in the assembly of their neighborhood whom they could not expel from Christ’s unity, they would lovingly tolerate them through Christ’s charity.

How, moreover, can they render a just judgment concerning those very people whom they accuse of wickedness in their own vicinity, when in reckless blindness they bring charges against people placed so far away and entirely unknown to them? Whether they know the citizens or neighbors whom they accuse to be wicked is uncertain to the whole world. But that they separate themselves, through reckless blindness, from those whose lives they cannot know because they are far away is certain to the whole world. And it is certain to the whole world that the wicked are tolerated with the praise of patience, lest the unknown good be condemned. Therefore the whole world judges securely that those who separate themselves from the whole world, in whatever region of the earth they may be, are not good.

25. Finally, if the Prophets warned their successors to separate themselves bodily from the chaff before the time of the final winnowing [Col. 0102], and by such separation to beware of touching the unclean and of entering in with criminals, why did the apostle Paul not do this? Were those who proclaimed Christ not from truth but from envy not chaff? Were those who did not preach the Gospel purely not unclean—those whom Scripture testifies to have existed in the Church of that time (Philippians 1:15, 17), and whose surpassing charity, enduring all things, later generations also imitated? Is greed not uncleanness [Note: The printed editions read: “Is uncleanness? Or even greed?” The manuscripts correct this to the present reading], which Cyprian did not touch in his heart, yet among greedy colleagues lived in the greatest peace?

Apparently he had become deaf to the words of the Psalms, so that he sat in the assembly of vanity and entered in with criminals, did not hate the gathering of the wicked, and sat with the impious [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “did not sit.” The word “not” is absent from the Vatican manuscripts]. Was there not an assembly of vanity among those who, while their brothers in the Church were hungry, desired to shine through their abundant silver? Were they not criminals who seized estates through treacherous fraud? Were those who increased their capital through multiplying interest not utterly wicked?

But he washed his hands with the innocent and went around the altar of the Lord. For this reason he tolerated the guilty: lest he abandon the innocent with whom he washed his hands, because he loved the beauty of the house of the Lord, and that beauty existed in the honorable vessels [Note: See Cyprian, *Sermon on the Lapsed*]. In a great house, however, there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels. Some are for honor, others for dishonor. “He cleansed himself from such things, so that he might be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20–21). Yet he did not separate himself from the great house because of the vessels that were for dishonor; rather, while reproving them within the unity of that house, he tolerated those from whom he kept himself clean by not imitating them [Note: Ambrosius, Erasmus, and certain manuscripts read, “by not imitating them he preserved himself.”].

CHAPTER V

26. Parmenian knows how to set forth the words of the Prophet:

“I have not sat with the council of vanity, and with criminals I will not enter in; I have hated the assembly of the wicked. I will wash my hands with the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord, to hear the voice of praise and to declare all your wonders. Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory. Do not destroy my soul together with sinners, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are crimes and whose right hands are filled with gifts” (Psalm 25:4–10).

Parmenian knows how to set this forth, but he does not care to notice how one can serve these words without any sacrilegious act of division. The beauty of the house and the place of God’s glorious dwelling are, as I have said, in the vessels—not in all the vessels that are nevertheless in one great house, but in those that are sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, and always prepared for every good work.

Whoever among these has loved the beauty of God’s house and the place of his glorious dwelling tolerates those that are for dishonor, and does not leave the house because of them, lest he himself become not a vessel for dishonor—which is nevertheless tolerated in the house—but refuse that is thrown out of the house. And because of that temporal [Note: Many manuscripts have “such”] gathering with the wicked in one house, he prays, saying:

“Do not destroy my soul together with sinners, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are crimes and whose right hands are filled with gifts.”

He certainly prays this: that he may not perish together with those with whom Christ’s charity—which endures all things—urges him to live together. He has already offered the sacrifice of this prayer, saying: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of your glorious dwelling.” Because I have loved the beauty of your house, and because of that love I tolerate the vessels that are for dishonor—because charity endures all things—do not destroy my soul together with them [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have: “Praying this, that he may not perish together with those with whom the charity that endures all things compels him to live together: does it not appear in these words…” Almost all omit the six intervening verses, from “he has already offered the sacrifice…” through “my soul.”].

Does it not appear in these words the voice of those who were foretold through Ezekiel, mourning and grieving over the iniquities of the people that were being committed in their midst? Because they were vessels for honor, they deserved to receive their own sign, so that when all the others began to be devastated and destroyed, God would not destroy their souls together with the sinners (Ezekiel 9:4).

But these men are wretched: they presume that they have been purified from every assembly of the wicked as wheat from chaff. Through this vanity they have prejudiced themselves, so that in the peoples over whom they preside they do not dare to rebuke the most unjust and disgraceful crowds so that they may be corrected. Otherwise they would be forced to confess that they are wicked, and it would be said to them: “Certainly you speak as purified wheat; why, by these words, do you admit that there is such a mixture?” [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “that such a quantity of chaff is mixed.”]

And therefore, because they are not righteous, they do not correct and reprove them with mercy; rather, they fatten their heads with the oil of flattery (Psalm 140:5)—the very heads they wish to be—because they refuse to exist under the one head that is in heaven, within the unity of the body that extends throughout the whole earth. Thus it is rightly said to their peoples: “Those who call you happy lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet” (Isaiah 3:12).

27. Therefore, whoever does not wish to sit in the council of vanity [Note: The manuscripts have “in the assembly of vanity”] must not be puffed up with the pride by which he seeks assemblies of the righteous separated from the unity of the whole world—assemblies he cannot find.

The righteous are throughout the universal city that cannot be hidden, because it has been established upon a mountain (Matthew 5:14). I mean that mountain of Daniel on which the stone cut without hands grew and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35) [Note: The word “cut” is absent from many manuscripts].

Throughout this city, therefore, spread across the whole world, the righteous groan and mourn over the iniquities committed in their midst. Let no one seek righteous people who are separated; rather, let him groan harmoniously with them amid the temporal mixture of the wicked.

For he will not sit in the assembly of vanity, because he will sit where he has his citizenship. But he will hear the Apostle saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). There he will not be with criminals; there he will not endure the assembly of the wicked; there he will not sit with the impious. Let him dwell in such hope [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “he will dwell”], so that he may one day deserve to reach the reality for which he hopes.

We have not yet risen as Christ did, nor do we yet sit with him in the heavenly places. Yet because he has given us such hope, and through that hope we already dwell there in a certain manner, the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Think on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:1–3).

In that life of ours which is hidden with Christ in God, we do not sit in the assembly of vanity, because, as the Apostle says, “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6)—in hope, not yet in reality. “But hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

This patience the wretched men have lost. Hastening to separate themselves before the proper time as though from chaff, they have shown themselves to be the lightest chaff, carried away by the wind from the threshing floor.

Let us therefore hold fast what Wisdom says: “Whoever listens to me will dwell in hope and will be silent without fear of every evil” (Proverbs 1:33). While we dwell in hope, considering not what we are but what we shall be—for we are indeed children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared; when it appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2)—while we dwell in such hope, because this dwelling [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have “this dwelling of thought”] contains no wicked people, we neither tolerate assemblies of vanity, criminals, iniquitous people, nor the impious.

Yet we tolerate them in the Catholic congregation spread throughout the whole world, in the hope that is not seen [Note: The Vatican manuscripts have “in the hope that is seen,” omitting “not”], until iniquity passes away, until the weeds are gathered at harvest time (Matthew 13:30), until at the final winnowing the chaff is separated from the wheat (Matthew 3:12), until the good fish are selected on the shore from among the bad fish with which they were gathered in the same nets (Matthew 13:48), until the goats are separated at the end to the left from the sheep with which they have for so long grazed under one shepherd in the same pastures (Matthew 25:33).

28. There is therefore no security for unity except from the promises of God concerning the Church [Note: Many manuscripts have “of the Church”], which, as has been said, has been established upon a mountain and cannot be hidden; and therefore it must be known in every region of the earth.

Let us therefore hold firmly and unshakably [Note: The manuscripts have “firmly and unshakably,” omitting “therefore”] that no good people can separate themselves from it. That is, no good people, even if they endure wicked people known to them wherever they may be, can on their account separate themselves through the reckless sacrilege of schism from good people far away and unknown to them.

Thus, wherever these things have occurred, are occurring, or will occur, while the other regions of the earth—far away, ignorant whether these things occurred or why they occurred—nevertheless remain with the whole world in the bond of unity, there is this very firm security: that such an act could have been committed only by people driven mad by swelling pride, deranged by the envy of resentment, corrupted by worldly advantage, or perverted by carnal fear.

All these causes result either in good people being branded with false accusations, or in false things being rashly believed about good people, or even in wicked people—who, when tolerated for the sake of the bond of unity, do no harm to the good—being wickedly fled from, while the peace of the good is shattered. Thus people usurp for themselves before the harvest what the angels will do at the harvest, and spare no thought for the distress of the wheat.

CHAPTER VI

29. Since these things are so, even sacrilegious schisms and impious heresies dare, whenever they are chastised so that they may be corrected, to count the punishments of their madness among martyrdoms.

Parmenian, thinking this as well, at the end of his letter exhorts Tichonius to remain in the party of Donatus and to endure persecutions. He says that he ought not voluntarily to join those with whom he was not joined under compulsion of persecution. He also adduces the testimony of Scripture, which says:

“Woe to those who have lost endurance and turned aside into crooked paths. And what will they do when the Lord begins to inspect them?” (Ecclesiasticus 2:16–17).

As is his custom, he sets forth everything from the divine Books against himself [Note: The printed editions have “setting forth”; the Divionensis manuscript has “he sets forth,” namely, Parmenian].

For who have lost endurance except those who were unable to convict the people whom they accused of crimes, because they refused to tolerate them for the sake of Christ’s peace? Later, when they realized that their own party must not be divided into many fragments, they again tolerated, for the sake of the false peace of Donatus, the manifestly sacrilegious people whom they themselves had condemned.

Let them finally understand and correct what they wickedly did, having learned it at least from what they suffered at the hands of Maximian. But, of course, they are ashamed to be corrected by such manifest arguments [Note: The printed editions have, “But, if it is permitted, let them be ashamed.” The Vatican manuscripts correct this to the present reading], because they resisted the commands of the emperors, lest, once corrected, they should appear to have lost what they complain they suffered—as though it were not better for them to lose those things than to perish themselves.

For if they possess some shadow, however false and deceptive, nevertheless some image of courage, in refusing to yield to an emperor who commands, what enticement of merely human praise is there in openly contradicting the truth?

Why, with their eyes closed, do they produce so many testimonies from Scripture which, once understood and brought forward against them, they reject? If these testimonies are accepted according to their understanding, they nevertheless convict them of their perversity.

Is it not written: “Do not contradict the truth in any way” (Ecclesiasticus 4:30)? And whom does one contradict rather than the truth, when one resists even a king who commands something according to the truth?

But a human king who threatens or exacts punishment is troublesome only for a time. It is not so with that King who is also called Truth, who now too cries out to them through the Prophet: “In vain I struck your children; they did not accept correction” (Jeremiah 2:30).

For this reason he now mercifully admonishes them through human authorities, lest at the end he punish them in such a way that the proud cannot boast even of their own condemnation. Under the punishment of kings, human obstinacy may wish to be praised falsely under the name of courage; but to be burned in eternal fires will neither be nor be called courage.

On that day there will not be those who anoint their heads with the oil of flattery, or who, deceived by various [Note: The Vatican manuscripts have “empty”] deceptions, dream that the condemned have been crowned, saying, “Well done, well done!” They will not swear by the gray hairs of those who did not have a sound head, nor by the joints [Note: Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 18–20, argues that one should read *compagos*, meaning the episcopal leggings] of those who did not know the way of peace.

These men dare to offer the temporary punishments of their schism to the sufferings of martyrs, while turning such crowds away from Christ’s unity and wishing to convert them to their own name, so that the anniversaries of their punishments may be celebrated with a great gathering of frenzied people. Among these are those who, even when no one persecutes them, voluntarily hurl themselves from the crags of mountains, so that they may end a bad life by a worse death.

On that day there will not be foolish peoples to whom they can say, “We are righteous because we suffer persecution,” nor will there be blind people to whom a rejected stone is sold as a precious gem—that is, carnal hardness as spiritual endurance.

There will not be those who recite at the altars the names of the leaders of their madness, whether of those who separated them from Christ’s unity or of those whom they raised up in opposition under the name of Christ [Note: Ambrosius, the Vatican manuscripts, and most Gallican manuscripts have “whom they raised up against the Church.” Because the word “Church” was absent from the Belgian manuscripts, the Louvain editors removed it, saying, “so that the meaning is ‘whom they raised up in opposition.’”].

These are the prices they seek to receive. While wishing to have something to sell, they provoke the severity of the authorities against themselves through their defiant perversity, lest those who are led astray by them and therefore think them righteous because they pay the penalties of iniquity should come to their senses and consider why they suffer the things in which they boast.

How little would it have taken for them to notice that Parmenian says to Tichonius, concerning the endurance of persecutions and the glory of tolerance, the same things that all heretics say, against whom similar royal commands are issued for purposes of restraint or punishment! Surely Salvius says similar things to his own people of Membresa, by whom he suffered such blows and insults at Abitina, and through whom these men deserved that he be expelled from the Church [Note: Ambrosius and Erasmus have “that they be expelled.” Although the manuscripts support the ancient editions, the Louvain editors corrected this to “that he be expelled,” because only Salvius’s expulsion is at issue. The Membresitans are said to have deserved this through the Abitinans. Thus, in *Against Cresconius*, book 4, no. 59, he says: “through which city nearby”—that is, Abitina—“your people deserved to fulfill the judgment,” namely, so that Salvius might be expelled from his see], so that they even tied the corpses of dead dogs around his neck, and finally danced with him to obscene voices and songs.

What speech do we think he had afterward, once he had suffered such things, with his followers, whom he had miserably deceived into building another basilica for themselves? How much did he say about the justice for which he deserved to suffer such things: persuading himself that he was holy because he suffered, and that they were utterly wicked because they had done it?

The ancient cruelty of the Etruscan tyrants is recorded: they joined dead bodies to living bodies, human bodies to human bodies (Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.484–487). But whether anyone ever recalls hearing or reading of dogs joined to human beings, and these to episcopal limbs, I do not know.

Everyone knows that bishops are accustomed to restrain foolish and disgraceful dances. Who has ever remembered that people whom they had summoned to the aid of a bishop danced together with the bishop? Or perhaps Salvius was not a bishop at that time, because his condemnation is recited in the sentence of the council of Bagai? What if he was a bishop only later, after being reconciled to Primianus, just as Felicianus was reconciled, although he had been condemned by the “truthful mouth of that plenary council,” as their words are recited there?

Or perhaps he would no longer have been admitted because the sacrilege of schism that had defiled him could be cleansed, as in the case of Felicianus, whereas one whom dead dogs suspended from his neck had made unclean could not be purified?

I should like to know what they say to these things—so clear, so public, so recent—who bring their ancient accusations against us as though they were our crimes. Whoever among them thinks that I am making false claims: what great or difficult thing would it be, if he cared for his soul, to go to Membresa, inquire whether these things occurred, and defend them if he can?

If he says that such things were rightly done to schismatics whom the three hundred and ten Donatist bishops condemned, let them not complain whenever they suffer something, even though we prove by the authority not of three hundred and ten but of the whole world that they committed schism against Christ’s unity [Note: This refers to the first Council of Arles, which above, section 21, is said to represent the judgment of the whole world].

But if he says that what Salvius suffered was trivial, I ask whether, if the emperor compelled one of the Donatist bishops to dance and threatened beasts and fires if he refused, he would not prefer to suffer those things rather than submit to that act; and, once he had suffered them, whether these men would not list him among the holy martyrs.

Salvius, therefore, suffered something more severe when people danced with him than if he had been burned alive. For if these two alternatives were proposed to any one of them—whether he would prefer not to dance himself, but to have people dance with him, rather than be burned alive—what would they say he would choose?

But if he says that the Primianists obtained nothing else from the proconsul except that Salvius be expelled from the basilica through the Abitinans, while the Abitinans themselves voluntarily did everything they later did so cruelly and disgracefully, why does he not say to himself that Catholics too can ask the emperors for nothing else except that these men be expelled from the basilicas they retain under a sacrilegious name, while the emperors, of their own accord and while preserving royal authority and dignity, might punish them as sacrilegious people much more mildly than the Abitinans, without any imperial law or judicial command, punished Salvius of Membresa [Note: The printed editions have “they punished.” The Vatican manuscripts more elegantly have “to have punished.”]?

Considering these matters, let them first observe what they do and afterward what they suffer, lest, while they close their eyes to their deeds and open their eyes to their punishments, they suffer temporal troubles here in vain and, at the final judgment of God, be punished with eternal punishment for this very reason: that God warned them through such troubles in vain, so that they might be corrected.

I am not rehearsing ancient matters, in which they deceive as many as they can. Briefly, I speak of the present; I thrust it before them; I point to it with my finger.

Condemned Maximianists are received; unknown peoples are accused. The Baptism of the Maximianists is accepted; the Baptism of the whole world is blown away.

Here are the Assuritans; here the Mustitans; here Praetextatus, who died not long ago; here Felicianus, still alive; here the names of those cited among the condemned in the acts of the council of Bagai. Such recent and present deeds sufficiently show what sort of people they have been from the beginning.

If they suffer anything for such perversities [Note: So all the manuscripts. The printed editions have “for such adversities”] and iniquities, if they do not wish to be corrected, let them at least not dare to boast.

[Col. 0107]

[Note: Concerning the following seven books, see Book 2, chapter 18, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 637, from the words “Against the Donatists” through column 638, ending with “Against the Letter of Parmenianus.” M.]

THE SEVEN BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON BAPTISM AGAINST THE DONATISTS [Note: Written around the year of Christ 400; concerning this matter, see above the *Introduction* to the books against the Letter of Parmenianus.]

[Note: The seven books *On Baptism against the Donatists* have been collated against ancient manuscripts: the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, Floriacensis, Beccensis, Pratellensis, and Michaelinus; the book of the Church of Laon; the Georgianus, that is, the manuscript named after the illustrious Lord de Saint-Georges, nominated archbishop of Tours; one manuscript of the Bernardine College in Paris; one of the Augustinians of the larger convent; one of the Dominicans on the Rue Saint-Jacques; two Vatican manuscripts; and finally the editions of Ambrosius, Erasmus, and Louvain, together with the variant readings collected through the work of the Louvain editors from three Belgian manuscripts.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

BOOK ONE

It proves that Baptism can be given outside Catholic communion by heretics or schismatics, but that it should not nevertheless be received from them, nor profit anyone in heresy or schism.

[Col. 0107]

CHAPTER ONE

1. In the books that we wrote against the Letter of Parmenianus, which he gave to Tichonius [*Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 2, chapter 14], we promised that we would treat the question of Baptism more carefully [Col. 0108]. Even if we had not made that promise there, we nevertheless remember and acknowledge that the brothers who ask it of us have a claim upon us.

Therefore, in this work, with the Lord’s help, we have undertaken not only to refute what the Donatists are accustomed to bring against us concerning this matter, but also to say what the Lord grants us concerning the authority of the most blessed martyr Cyprian, from which they try to prop up their perversity lest it collapse under the force of truth. In this way all who judge without being blinded by partisan zeal may understand that Cyprian’s authority not only does not help them, but is especially what convicts and overthrows them.

2. It has already been said in the books mentioned above that Baptism can exist outside Catholic communion in the same way that it can be possessed outside it. None of them denies that apostates also possess Baptism; when they return and are converted through repentance, it is judged that they could not have lost what is not restored to them.

Likewise, those who withdraw from the Church’s communion through the sacrilege of schism certainly possess the Baptism they received before they withdrew. For when they return, it is not given to them again; and thus they are shown not to have been able to lose, by separating themselves, what they received while in unity [Note: The printed editions add “from unity,” which is absent from the manuscripts].

If it can be possessed outside, why can it not also be given outside? If you say, “It is not rightly given outside,” we reply: just as it is not rightly possessed outside, and yet it is possessed, so it is not rightly given outside, but nevertheless it is given.

As, through reconciliation in unity, what was uselessly possessed outside unity begins to be possessed beneficially, so through the same reconciliation what was uselessly given outside it begins to be beneficial. Nevertheless, it is not right to say that what was given was not given, or for anyone to slander the giver by denying that he gave what he acknowledges he had received.

For the sacrament of Baptism is what the baptized person possesses; and the sacrament of conferring Baptism is what the ordained person possesses. Just as a baptized person does not lose the sacrament of Baptism if he withdraws from unity, so an ordained person does not lose the sacrament of conferring Baptism if he withdraws from unity.

No sacrament may be wronged. If a person departs from the wicked, both depart; if he remains among the wicked, both remain. Therefore, just as the Baptism that the person who withdrew from unity could not lose is accepted, so the Baptism given by the person who had not lost the sacrament of conferring it when he withdrew must be accepted.

For just as those who return, having been baptized before they withdrew, are not rebaptized, so those who return, having been ordained before they withdrew, are not ordained again. They either administer what they had administered, if the Church’s usefulness requires it, or, if they do not administer it, they nevertheless retain the sacrament of their ordination; and therefore hands are not imposed upon them among the laity.

For neither the sacrament of Baptism nor the sacrament of conferring Baptism was lost by Felicianus when he withdrew from them with Maximianus. For now they have him with them, together with those very people whom, while he was outside, he baptized in the schism of Maximianus.

Therefore others were able to receive from them, although they had not joined our fellowship, what those men had not lost when they withdrew from our fellowship.

These matters show both that those who attempt to rebaptize the unity of the whole world act wickedly, and that we act rightly when we do not dare to condemn God’s sacraments even in the schism itself. In what they agree with us, they are also with us; but they have withdrawn from us in what they disagree with us.

For this approach and withdrawal must not be measured by bodily movements rather than spiritual ones. Just as the joining of bodies occurs through the continuity of places, so there is a kind of contact between souls through the agreement of wills.

If, then, the person who has withdrawn from unity wishes to do something other than what he received in unity, in that respect he withdraws and is separated. But if he wishes to act as it is done in unity, where he received and learned this, in that respect he remains and is joined.

### Chapter III

**4.** There are also two things that we say: that Baptism exists in the Catholic Church, and that it is rightly received only there. The Donatists deny both of these. Again, we say two other things: that Baptism exists among the Donatists, but that it is not rightly received there. Of these two points they strongly affirm one—namely, that Baptism exists there—but they refuse to admit that it is not received validly there.

Of these four propositions, three are ours alone, while one we both affirm. For we alone say that Baptism exists in the Catholic Church, that it is rightly received there, and that it is not rightly received among the Donatists; but that Baptism exists also among the Donatists, they assert and we concede.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be baptized, and is already certain that for his Christian salvation he must choose our Church [Note: [Col. 0111] The printed editions read *diligendam*, “to be cherished.” In the judgment of the Louvain editors, *deligendam*, “to be chosen,” is better; so also does our old Remigianus manuscript read.], and that the Baptism of Christ is beneficial only in it, even if it has been received elsewhere—but nevertheless wishes to be baptized in the party of Donatus because we both say that Baptism exists there—let him consider the other three points.

For if he has chosen to follow us in those matters in which they do not agree with us, while preferring the points on which we both agree to those which we alone affirm, it is enough for us that he prefers what they do not affirm, and what we alone affirm, to what they alone affirm.

We say that Baptism exists in the Catholic Church; they do not. We say that Baptism is rightly received in the Catholic Church; they do not. We say that Baptism is not rightly received in the party of Donatus; they do not. Therefore, just as he believes more readily what we alone say ought to be believed, so let him do more readily what we alone say ought to be done.

But what we both say ought to be believed, let him believe more firmly—if he thinks it so—than what we alone say. For he will believe more firmly that the Baptism of Christ exists in the party of Donatus, which both of us affirm, than that Baptism exists in the Catholic Church, which only Catholics affirm.

But again, he will believe more readily that the Baptism of Christ exists also among us, which we alone affirm, than that it does not exist among us, which they alone affirm. For he has already decided, and is certain, that in the matters on which we disagree, we must be preferred to them.

Thus he will believe more readily that what we alone say is rightly received among us than that it is not rightly received among us, since the latter is affirmed only by them. By the same rule, he will believe more readily that what we alone say is not rightly received among them than what they alone affirm—namely, that it is rightly received among them.

It is therefore useless for him to think himself secure in receiving there what we both say exists there, but what we do not both say ought to be received there. Yet he himself has chosen to adhere to us in what we do not both affirm. Let him therefore receive securely where he is certain both that Baptism exists and that it is validly received; but let him not receive there what they say exists there, while they do not say that it ought to be received there—the very people whose position he has decided to choose.

Even if he were in doubt whether what he was certain was validly received in the Catholic Church might be received validly there, he would nevertheless sin gravely in matters pertaining to the salvation of the soul, if only because he preferred uncertain things to certain ones.

For he is certain that a person is rightly baptized in the Catholic Church precisely because, although baptized elsewhere, he has decided to transfer to it. Let him at least hold as uncertain that a person is rightly baptized among the Donatists, since those whose position he is certain must be preferred to the Donatists say that it is not so. By preferring certainties to uncertainties, let him be baptized here, where he is certain that it is rightly done because, even when he had been thinking of doing it elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0112] The printed editions read “doing otherwise elsewhere.” *Otherwise* is absent from the manuscripts.], he had decided that he ought to transfer here.

### Chapter IV

**5.** If someone does not understand how it can be that we confess something to exist there but say that it is not validly administered there, let him observe that we do not even say that it rightly exists there in those whom they themselves say depart from their communion.

Let him also consider the analogy of a military mark, which can be both possessed and received outside the army by deserters; nevertheless, outside the army it ought neither to be possessed nor received, and once a person has been restored or brought into the army, it should neither be changed nor repeated.

Yet the case of those who imprudently fall among these heretics, thinking that they themselves are the Church of Christ, is one thing; the case of those who know that the Catholic Church is none other than the Church which, as it was promised, is spread and extended throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, is another.

This Church, growing amid the weeds and longing for the future rest while wearied by scandals, says in the Psalms: “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you; when my soul was weary, you raised me upon a rock.” The rock was Christ; in him, the Apostle says, we have already been raised and seated in heaven (Ephesians 2:6)—not yet in reality, but in hope.

Therefore the Psalm continues and says: “You led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60:3–4). From his promises, established like weapons and arrows in a most strongly fortified tower, the enemy is not merely guarded against but also defeated—the enemy who clothes his wolves in sheep’s skins (Matthew 7:15), so that they may say, “Look, here is Christ; look, there” (Matthew 24:23), and separate many from the universal city established upon a mountain, drawing them away into the small plots of their ambushes and slaughtering them.

Although they know this, they choose to receive the Baptism of Christ outside the communion of the unity of Christ’s body, intending afterward to transfer to that same communion with the Baptism they received elsewhere.

They will therefore have, knowingly, the Baptism of Christ against the Church of Christ on the very day on which they receive it. If this is a wicked act, who would say, “Let me be permitted to commit wickedness for one day”? For if he is going to transfer to the Catholic Church, I ask the reason. What else will he answer except that it is evil to be in the party of Donatus and not to be in Catholic unity?

Therefore, for however many days you commit this evil, you will commit an evil lasting that many days. It can be said that a greater evil is committed over many days and a lesser one over fewer; but it cannot be said that no evil is committed at all. Why, then, is it necessary to commit this utterly detestable evil for even one day or one hour?

The person who wants this to be permitted him could ask the Church, or God himself, to allow him to apostatize for one day. For there is no reason why he should fear being an apostate for one day but not fear being a schismatic or heretic for one day.

### Chapter V

**6.** “There,” he says, “I preferred to receive it, where both parties agree that Baptism exists.”

But those to whom you are going to transfer say that it is not rightly received there; those from whom you are going to transfer say that it is rightly received there. Therefore, what those whom you yourself place second say, while contradicting those whom you yourself place first, is either false or, to put it more mildly, uncertain.

Prefer, then, true things to false ones, or certain things to uncertain ones. For you yourself confess that in the place to which you are going to transfer, after having received Baptism elsewhere, what you desire can rightly be received—not only those to whom you are going to transfer, but you yourself, who are going to transfer, confess this.

If you doubted whether it could be rightly received there, you would also doubt whether you ought to transfer there. If it is uncertain whether receiving Baptism in the party of Donatus is a sin, who could doubt that it is certainly a sin not rather to receive it where it is certain that there is no sin?

Those who, through ignorance, are baptized there, thinking that it is itself the Church of Christ, sin less in comparison with these others; nevertheless they are wounded by the sacrilege of schism. They do not therefore sin gravely merely because others sin more gravely. When it was said to some, “It will be more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew 11:24), this was not said because the people of Sodom would not be punished, but because those others would be punished more severely.

**7.** Perhaps this matter was once hidden and uncertain. But from the very point at which those who take notice and correct themselves are healed, those who, when they are no longer permitted to remain ignorant, stubbornly rage to their own destruction are burdened.

The condemnation of the Maximianists, and the reception of those who had been condemned—together with those whom, as their council loudly declares, they had baptized in schism as sacrilegiously outside their communion [Note: [Col. 0113] The Bagai council]—has settled the entire question and removed all controversy.

Nothing at all has been left between us and those Donatists who are in communion with Primian from which it could be doubted that the Baptism of Christ can not only be possessed but also administered by those who are separated from the Church.

For just as they themselves are compelled to confess that those whom Felicianus baptized in schism received true Baptism, because they now have them with themselves in the very Baptism which they received in schism, so we say that the Baptism of Christ exists even outside Catholic communion, administered by those who have been cut off from that communion, because when they were cut off they did not lose it.

And what they themselves think they bestowed upon those whom Felicianus baptized in schism when they reconciled them to themselves—that is, not that they should receive something they did not have, but that what they had received and possessed uselessly in schism should become beneficial to them—this God truly confers and grants through Catholic communion upon those who come from some heresy or schism where they received the Baptism of Christ.

That is, they do not begin to possess the sacrament of Baptism, which they did not have; rather, what they possessed begins to benefit them [Note: [Col. 0113] Erasmus and the Louvain editors read: “what they had uselessly.”].

### Chapter VI

**8.** Therefore, between us and the principal Donatists themselves, whose bishop at Carthage is Primianus, there is now no controversy on this matter. God wished to bring it to an end through the Maximianists, so that they might confess, compelled by their own example, what they had been unwilling to admit when urged by charity.

But we continue to discuss the matter lest those who do not even communicate with these people should think that they have anything to say—those who claim that the Donatists who have remained among them are the purer because they are fewer.

Even if they alone were Maximianists, we ought not to disregard their salvation. How much more, then, since that same party of Donatus has been split into many tiny fragments, all of which reproach this one much larger part, in which Primianus is found, for having received the Baptism of the Maximianists; and each of them strives to assert that true Baptism has remained only with itself, and that it exists nowhere else—not throughout the whole world where the Catholic Church is spread, nor in the larger party of Donatus, nor in any of the other tiny parties besides itself.

If all these little parties were willing to heed the voice not of a human being but of the most manifest truth itself, and to tame the passionate spirit of their perversity, they would certainly return—not to the larger party of Donatus from which they were cut off, and from which those parties were cut off in turn, but to the very living greenness of the Catholic root, leaving behind their own dryness.

For all these people, wherever they are not against us, are for us; but wherever they do not gather with us, they scatter.

### Chapter VII

**9.** I do not want it to seem that I am pursuing this matter by human arguments. The obscurity of this question compelled great men and bishops, fathers endowed with great charity, in the earlier periods of the Church, before the schism of Donatus, to debate and waver among themselves while preserving peace. For a long time the differing decrees of councils in their respective regions remained unsettled, until what was most salutary was confirmed, with all doubts removed, by a plenary council of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0114] See below, Book 2, chapter 9.].

Therefore, I bring forward certain proofs from the Gospel, by which, with the Lord’s help, I demonstrate how rightly and truly according to God it was judged that, in the case of a schismatic or heretic, that part should be healed by ecclesiastical medicine in which the wound of separation lay [Note: [Col. 0114] Several manuscripts read: “in which he was wounded.”]; but that which remained sound should rather be recognized and approved than, by being disapproved, be wounded.

Certainly the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Yet when the disciples reported to him that they had seen someone casting out demons in his name and had prevented him because he was not following them, he said: “Do not prevent him. Whoever is not against you is for you. For no one can do something in my name and then speak evil of me” (Mark 9:38–39; Luke 9:49–50).

If nothing in that man needed correction, then let anyone who gathers in Christ’s name outside the communion of the Church, separated from Christian fellowship, be secure; and the statement “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” will be false.

But if what the Lord’s disciples wished to do through ignorance needed correction, and the Lord said, “Do not prevent him,” why did he himself forbid that he be prevented? And how will the statement “Whoever is not against you is for you” be true?

In that action he was not against them but for them, since he was performing healings through the name of Christ. Therefore, for both statements to be true, as they are—the one in which he says, “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters,” and the one in which he says, “Do not prevent him; for whoever is not against you is for you”—what remains to be understood except this?

That man had to be strengthened in his reverence for so great a name, because he was not against the Church but for the Church; yet he had to be reproved for that separation in which, if he gathered, he would scatter. And if he should come to the Church, he would not receive there what he already had, but would be corrected in the matter in which he had gone astray.

### Chapter VIII

**10.** Nor were the prayers of Cornelius, a gentile, unheard, nor his alms unaccepted. Indeed, he was deemed worthy both to have an angel sent to him and to see the one who was sent, through whom he could certainly have learned everything necessary without the intervention of any human being.

But because whatever good he possessed in his prayers and alms could not benefit him unless he were incorporated into the Church through the bond of Christian fellowship and peace, he was commanded to send for Peter; through him he learned about Christ; and through him, after being baptized, he was joined also by the fellowship of communion to the Christian people, with whom he had been joined only by a likeness in good works (Acts 10).

For he would have dangerously despised the good which he did not yet possess, while taking pride in what he did possess.

Similarly, those who separate themselves from the fellowship of the others, violating charity and breaking the bond of unity, if they do none of the things they received in that fellowship, are separated from it in every respect. Therefore, if someone whom they have joined to themselves wishes to come to the Church, he ought to receive everything he did not receive.

But if they do some of the same things, they have not separated themselves from us in those matters; in that respect they remain held within the structure of the fabric, although in other respects they are torn away.

Therefore, if they have joined someone to themselves, he is connected to the Church in that respect in which they too are not separated. Thus, if he wishes to come to the Church, he is healed in the matter in which he was wounded by error; but where he was connected in health, he is not healed but recognized, lest, when we try to heal what is sound, we should instead wound it.

Thus, those whom they baptize are healed of the wound of idolatry or unbelief, but they inflict upon them the more serious wound of schism. The sword killed idolaters among the people of God (Exodus 32), whereas a chasm in the earth swallowed up schismatics (Numbers 16).

And the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.”

**11.** If someone were brought to a physician with a serious wound in some necessary part of his body, and the physician said, “Unless it is treated, he will die from it,” I do not think that those who brought him would be so foolish that, after examining and counting his other healthy limbs, they would answer the physician: “What? Are all these healthy limbs unable to preserve his life, while that one wounded limb is able to cause his death?”

They would certainly not say this, but would offer him for treatment. Yet because they offer him for treatment, they would not ask the physician to treat even those parts which are healthy; rather, they would ask him to apply medicine urgently to that one place from which death threatens even the healthy parts and will arrive unless it is healed.

What, then, does sound faith benefit a person—or perhaps the one sound element of faith, the sacrament—when the health of charity has been destroyed by the deadly wound of schism, and through the destruction of charity alone even those sound elements are dragged into death?

To prevent this, God’s mercy does not cease to act through the unity of his holy Church, so that they may come and be healed by the medicine of reconciliation and the bond of peace.

Let them not therefore think themselves healthy merely because we say that they possess something sound. Nor, again, should they think that what is sound must therefore be healed because we show that something has been wounded.

Thus, in the soundness of the sacrament, because they are not against us, they are for us; but in the wound of schism, because they do not gather with Christ, they scatter.

Let them not exalt themselves because of what they possess. Why do they turn proud eyes so intently toward their sound elements? Let them humbly consent to look upon their wound, and attend not only to what is present but also to what is absent.

### Chapter IX

**12.** Let them see how many and how great things are of no benefit if one thing is lacking, and let them see what that one thing is. They should not listen to me on this point, but to the Apostle:

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” [Note: [Col. 0116] The printed editions read “I have become like sounding bronze.” “Like” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]. “And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

What benefit is it to them if they possess an angelic tongue in the sacred mysteries, and prophecy like Caiaphas (John 11:51) and Saul (1 Samuel 18:10), so that they sometimes prophesy, although Holy Scripture testifies that they were condemned?

What benefit is it if they not only know the sacraments but also possess them, as Simon Magus possessed them (Acts 8:13)? What benefit is it if they have faith, as the demons confessed Christ? For they certainly did believe when they said, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? We know who you are” (Mark 1:24).

What benefit is it if they distribute even their own property among the poor, as many do—not only in the Catholic Church but also in various heresies? What benefit is it if, when persecution arises, they hand over their bodies to the flames with us for the faith which they confess together with us?

Nevertheless, because they do these things while separated, neither bearing with one another in love nor striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:2–3), since they do not have charity, they cannot attain eternal salvation with all those things that are of no benefit to them.

### Chapter X

**13.** But they seem to ask with great subtlety “whether the Baptism of Christ generates children in the party of Donatus or does not generate them.”

If we agree that it does generate them, they assert that their Church is the mother, since it was able to generate children from the Baptism of Christ; and because there ought to be one Church, they then accuse us of not being the Church.

But if we say that it does not generate them, they ask: “Why, then, are those who pass from us to you not reborn through Baptism, if they were baptized among us, since they have not yet been born?”

**14.** As though it generated them from what separates it, rather than from what unites it. It is separated from the bond of charity and peace, but it is united in the one Baptism.

Thus there is one Church, which alone is called Catholic; and whatever it possesses as its own in the communions of those separated from its unity, it is itself, through what it possesses as its own in them, that generates—not those communions.

For their separation does not generate them; what they retained from this Church does. If they abandon that as well, they generate nothing at all.

This Church therefore generates in all places wherever her sacraments are retained, from which such a thing can be generated anywhere, although not all whom she generates belong to her unity—the unity that will save those who persevere to the end.

For not only those who are manifest through the open sacrilege of separation do not belong to her; those also do not belong to her who are bodily mixed within her unity but are separated from it by a most evil life.

Indeed, the Church herself had given birth through Baptism even to Simon Magus, yet he was told that he had no share in the inheritance of Christ (Acts 8:13, 21). Did he lack Baptism? Did he lack the Gospel? Did he lack the sacraments? But because he lacked charity, he was born in vain, and perhaps it would have been better for him not to be born.

Were those to whom the Apostle says, “As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food,” not born? Yet he calls them back from the sacrilege of schism, into which they were rushing because they were carnal:

“As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to receive it. Indeed, you are still not able, for you are still carnal. Since there are jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways? For when one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I belong to Apollos,’ are you not human?” (1 Corinthians 3:1–4).

Of these people he had already said above:

“I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you.

I say this because each of you says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:10–13).

If these people had remained in this obstinacy and perversity, they would certainly have been born, and yet they would not belong through the bond of peace and unity to the very Church from which they had been born.

Therefore, it is the Church herself that generates, both through her own womb and through the wombs of her servant women, from the same sacraments as from the seed of her husband. For the Apostle does not say in vain that all those things happened figuratively (1 Corinthians 10:11).

But those who grow proud and do not join themselves to their lawful mother are like Ishmael, of whom it was said: “Cast out the servant woman and her son; for the son of the servant woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Genesis 21:10).

Those who peacefully love the lawful wife of their father, through whose lawful right they were born, are like the sons of Jacob, although born of servant women, yet receiving the same inheritance (Genesis 30:3).

But those who are born within the unity from the womb of that mother herself and neglect the grace they have received are like Esau, son of Isaac, who was rejected, with God bearing witness and saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” although both were conceived from one intercourse and born from one womb (Malachi 1:2–3; Genesis 25:24).

### Chapter XI

**15.** They also ask whether sins are forgiven through Baptism in the party of Donatus. If we say that they are forgiven, they reply: “Then the Holy Spirit is there,” because, after the Lord breathed upon the disciples and gave him to them, he then continued and said: “Baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19); and, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

“And if this is so,” they say, “our communion is the Church of Christ; for the Holy Spirit does not effect the forgiveness of sins outside the Church. And if our communion is the Church of Christ, your communion is not the Church of Christ. For there is one Church, whatever she may be, of whom it was said, ‘My dove is one, the one belonging to her mother’ (Song of Songs 6:8); and there cannot be as many Churches as there are schisms.”

But if we say that sins are not forgiven there, they reply: “Then Baptism is not truly there; and therefore you ought to baptize those whom you receive from us. Since you do not do this, you admit that you are not in the Church of Christ.”

**16.** We resist these arguments according to the Scriptures, questioning them so that they themselves may answer what they ask of us.

For I ask them to say whether sins are forgiven where there is no charity. Sins are the darkness of souls. We hear John say: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:11). No one would create schisms if he were not blinded by hatred of his brother.

If, then, we say that sins are not forgiven there, how is the person who is baptized among them reborn? For what is it to be reborn through Baptism except to be renewed from one’s old condition? But how is someone renewed from his old condition if his past sins are not forgiven?

If he has not been reborn, neither has he put on Christ, and so it would follow that he must be baptized again. For the Apostle says: “As many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). If he has not put him on, he must not be considered baptized in Christ.

But because we say that he has been baptized in Christ, we confess that he has put on Christ; and if we confess this, we confess that he has been reborn. If this is so, then his sins have also been forgiven.

How, then, does John say, “Whoever hates his brother remains in darkness until now,” if forgiveness of sins has already taken place? Is there not hatred of brothers in schism? Who could say so, when the origin and persistence of schism have no other cause than hatred of one’s brother?

**17.** They seem to solve this question for themselves when they say: “Then there is no forgiveness of sins in schism, and therefore no rebirth of the new person, and consequently no Baptism of Christ.”

But because we confess that the Baptism of Christ exists there, we put this question to them for solution: Was that magician, Simon, truly baptized with the Baptism of Christ? They will answer, “Yes,” because they are compelled by the authority of Holy Scripture.

I therefore ask whether they admit that his sins were forgiven. They will certainly admit it. Again I ask why Peter told him that he had no share in the lot of the saints. “Because,” they say, “he sinned afterward, wishing to purchase with money the gift of God, thinking that the Apostles were its sellers.”

### Chapter XII

**18.** What if he approached Baptism with deceit? Were his sins forgiven or were they not forgiven? Let them choose whichever they wish; either choice is sufficient for us.

If they say that they were forgiven, how then will the Holy Spirit, who flees deceit, flee the deceiver (Wisdom 1:5), if he worked the forgiveness of sins in this deceiver?

If they say that they were not forgiven, I ask: if afterward, with a contrite heart and true sorrow, he confessed his deceit, would he be judged in need of baptism again?

Since it is utterly foolish to say this, let them admit that a person can be baptized with the Baptism of Christ and yet, while his heart persists in wickedness or sacrilege, prevent the abolition of his sins from taking place.

In this way, let them understand that people can be baptized in communions separated from the Church, where the Baptism of Christ is administered and received in the same celebration of the sacrament. Yet it benefits them for the forgiveness of sins only when, having been reconciled to unity, they cast off the sacrilege of dissension by which their sins were held and prevented from being forgiven.

For just as the person who approached deceitfully is not baptized again but is cleansed by the pious correction and truthful confession itself—a cleansing that could not take place without Baptism—so that what had previously been given then begins to become effective for salvation when the deceit has departed through truthful confession, so also the person who received the Baptism of Christ in some heresy or schism—though those who separated themselves did not lose it—while being an enemy of the charity and peace of Christ, and whose sins were not forgiven because of that sacrilegious crime, is not to be baptized again when he has corrected himself and come to the fellowship and unity of the Church.

For through that reconciliation and peace he is granted this: that the sacrament which he received in schism, and which could not benefit him there, may now begin to benefit him in unity for the forgiveness of his sins.

**19.** But if they say that, in the person who approached deceitfully, his sins were indeed forgiven through the holy power of so great a sacrament at that very moment, but immediately returned because of his deceit—so that the Holy Spirit was present with the baptized person in order to make the sins depart, yet fled his continuing deceit so that they returned; so that both statements are true, “As many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ,” and “The Holy Spirit flees deceit”—that is, so that the holiness of Baptism clothes him with Christ, while the ruin of deceit strips him of Christ, just as someone passes from darkness through light into darkness, with his eyes continually directed toward the darkness, although the light cannot help but pour over him as he passes—

if they say this, let them understand that the same thing occurs in those who are baptized outside the communion of the Church but with the Baptism of the Church, which, wherever it exists, is holy in itself. For this reason it does not belong to those who separate themselves, but to the one from whom they separate themselves.

Nevertheless, it has this effect among them: that through its light they pass into the darkness of their dissension, with the sins returning immediately which the holiness of Baptism had forgiven at that moment—just as the darkness returns when the light that had dispelled it in passing returns to obscurity.

**20.** The Lord teaches most clearly that forgiven sins return where fraternal charity is absent, in the case of the servant who, when found to owe ten thousand talents, begged for mercy and had everything forgiven him.

But when he failed to show mercy to his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, his master ordered him to repay what he had forgiven him. The time at which forgiveness is received through Baptism is therefore like the time of settling accounts, so that all debts which are found may be forgiven.

Yet that servant had not afterward lent money to his fellow servant which the latter was unable to repay and for which he then failed to show mercy. Rather, his fellow servant already owed him when he himself, rendering an account to his master, was released from such an enormous debt. He had not forgiven his fellow servant what the man owed him, and so he approached his master in order that his master might forgive him.

This is indicated by the words of the fellow servant: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you” [Note: [Col. 0120] The printed editions read: “and I will repay you everything.” “Everything” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Otherwise he would have said: “You had already forgiven me this; why are you asking for it again?”

The Lord’s own words make the point even clearer. He says: “But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii” (Matthew 18:23–35). He did not say, “To whom he had already forgiven the debt of one hundred denarii.” For if he had forgiven it, the man would not have owed him.

Since he says that the man owed him, it is clear that he had not forgiven him. It would certainly have been better, and more fitting for one who was about to render an account concerning such a great debt and was awaiting his master’s mercy, if he himself had first forgiven his fellow servant what was owed to him and then approached to render his account, where he was to implore his master’s mercy.

Nevertheless, the fact that he had not yet forgiven his fellow servant did not prevent his master, at the time of settling accounts, from forgiving him everything he owed. But what did it profit him, since, because of his persistence in hatred, everything was immediately charged against him again?

In the same way, the grace of Baptism is not prevented from forgiving all sins, even if hatred of one’s brother persists in the mind of the person whose sins are forgiven. Yesterday is canceled, and everything before it is canceled as well [Note: [Col. 0120] Ammianus and Erasmus read “everything that remains.” The reading of the Louvain editors and the manuscripts, “everything before it,” is better; that is, before yesterday.], including the very hour and moment before Baptism and in Baptism [Note: [Col. 0120] The Vatican codices read: “Even the hour of the moment which is before Baptism is canceled, in Baptism.”].

Afterward, however, he immediately begins to be liable not only for the days, hours, and moments that follow, but also for those of the past, when everything that had been forgiven returns [Note: [Col. 0120] Ammianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “when all the sins that had been forgiven return.” The same manuscripts later add: “and this often happens in the Church.”]. And these things often happen in the Church.

### Chapter XIII

**21.** It often happens that a person has an enemy whom he hates most unjustly, although we are commanded to love even unjust enemies and to pray for them.

Then, suddenly endangered by the threat of death, he begins to be troubled and asks for Baptism. He receives it in such haste that the time of danger scarcely permits the necessary interrogation of a few words—how much less a lengthy discourse—so that the hatred may be driven from his heart, even if the person baptizing him knows of it.

Certainly such cases do not cease to occur among them any more than among us. What, then, do we say? Are this man’s sins forgiven or are they not forgiven? Let them choose whichever answer they wish.

For if they are forgiven, they immediately return: the Gospel speaks; truth cries out. Therefore, whether they are forgiven or not forgiven, medicine is afterward necessary. Yet if he lives, learns that this must be corrected, and corrects it, he is not baptized again, whether among them or among us.

In the same way, whatever schismatics or heretics possess and practice in the same way as the true Church, when they come to us we do not correct but rather approve. For in those matters in which they do not dissent from us, they are not separated from us.

Nevertheless, because these things benefit them nothing so long as they are schismatics or heretics, on account of the other matters in which they dissent from the truth and on account of the very grievous crime of separation—whether the sins have remained in them or were immediately forgiven and then returned—we exhort them to come to the health of peace [Note: [Col. 0121] The older editions of Ammianus and Erasmus, and all the manuscripts, read “to the salvation of peace.”] and charity.

We exhort them not merely so that they may possess something they did not possess, but so that what they possessed may also begin to benefit them.

## CHAPTER XIV

**22.** In vain, therefore, they say to us: “If you accept our Baptism, what do we lack, that you should think it necessary for us to seek your communion?” We reply: We do not accept your Baptism, because that Baptism is not the Baptism of schismatics or heretics, but of God and of the Church, wherever it is found and to whomever it is transferred. What is yours, however, is only what you wrongly believe, sacrilegiously practice, and impiously separate yourselves from. For even if you either believe or possess all the other things truly [Note: Some manuscripts: “all the other things, whether you possess or believe them”], yet persist in that same separation against the bond of fraternal peace, against the unity of all the brethren who throughout the whole world have been presented just as they were promised—whose cases and hearts you could never in any way know or examine, so as to condemn them justly—and who cannot therefore be guilty because they believed ecclesiastical judges rather than litigants: this alone you lack, namely, what the one who does not have charity lacks.

Why, then, should we recapitulate the matter? Look for yourselves in the Apostle and see how much you lack. What difference does it make, for one who does not have charity, whether he flies outside, carried away by some wind of temptation, or remains inside, only to be separated in the final winnowing from the Lord’s harvest? And yet, if such people have once been born through Baptism, they ought not to be born again.

## CHAPTER XV

**23.** The Church indeed gives birth to all through Baptism, whether within herself—that is, from her own womb—or outside herself, from the seed of her husband; whether from herself or from the slave-woman [Note: The words “whether from herself or from the slave-woman,” absent from the manuscripts, seem to have migrated from the margin into the text].

But Esau too was born from a wife and, because of fraternal discord, was separated from the people of God. Asher, although born through the authority of a wife, was born from a slave-woman and, because of fraternal concord, received the promised land. Thus, for Ishmael also, it was not his slave-woman mother that prevented his being separated from the people of God, but fraternal discord; nor did the authority of the wife benefit him, although he was more properly her son, since through her marital rights he had been begotten in the slave-woman and received from the slave-woman.

So among these people all who are born are born by the Church’s right, which is present in Baptism. But if they are in concord with their brethren, they come to the promised land through the unity of peace—not to be cast out again from the mother’s womb, but to be recognized in the father’s seed. If, however, they persist in discord, they will belong to Ishmael’s cord.

Ishmael came first, Isaac afterward; Esau first, Jacob afterward—not because heresy gave birth before the Church, or because the Church herself first produced the carnal or animal and afterward the spiritual, but because, in the condition of mortality that is ours, from the time we are born of Adam, what comes first is not the spiritual but the animal, and afterward the spiritual (1 Cor. 15:46). From this animal understanding, because the animal person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit (ibid. 2:14), all dissensions and schisms arise. The Apostle says that those who persist in this understanding belong to the Old Testament (Gal. 4), that is, to the desire for earthly promises, in which spiritual realities are indeed represented, but the animal person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit.

**24.** Therefore, at whatever point in this life such people begin to exist—people already imbued with the divine Sacraments according to the distribution of the ages, yet still thinking carnally [Note: Erasmus, the Erfurt edition, and many manuscripts omit the particle *ut* (“so that”) here; but below, after “imbued with the sacraments,” they add it and continue, “if they still…”] and hoping for and desiring carnal things from God, whether in this life or after it—they are animal.

The Church, however, which is the people of God, is an ancient reality even during the pilgrimage of this life. In some people she has an animal portion, in others a spiritual one. The Old Testament belongs to the animal, the New to the spiritual. Yet in the earliest times both were hidden, from Adam until Moses. From Moses onward the Old Testament was made manifest [Note: Earlier manuscripts: “was manifest”], and within that very Old Testament the New was concealed, because it was signified secretly. Afterward, when the Lord came in the flesh, the New was revealed; the Sacraments of the Old Testament ceased, but such desires did not cease.

They are found in those whom the Apostle says, although already born through the Sacrament of the New Testament, are still animal and unable to perceive the things of God’s Spirit. For just as, under the Sacraments of the Old Testament, certain spiritual people lived who secretly belonged to the New Testament, which was then hidden, so now, under the Sacrament of the New Testament, which has already been revealed, many live as animals.

If they do not wish to advance toward perceiving the things of God’s Spirit, to which the apostolic word exhorts them, they will belong to the Old Testament. But if they advance, then, even before they understand, by that very progress and approach they belong to the New Testament. And if they are snatched from this life before becoming spiritual, they are kept safe by the holiness of the Sacrament and are counted among the land of the living, where our hope and portion is the Lord.

Nor do I find any truer understanding of what is written, “Your eyes saw my unformed substance,” than this, since what follows is, “And in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 138:16).

## CHAPTER XVI

**25.** The one who gave birth to Abel, Enoch, Noah, and Abraham gave birth also to Moses and the Prophets who came later, before the Lord’s advent; and the one who gave birth to these gave birth also to the Apostles, our martyrs, and all good Christians. For all appeared as born at different times, but they are contained within the fellowship of one people. They are citizens of the same city, have experienced the labors of this pilgrimage—and some are experiencing them now—and the rest will experience them to the end.

Likewise, the one who gave birth to Cain, Ham, Ishmael, and Esau gave birth also to Dathan and others like him in the same people; and the one who gave birth to these gave birth also to Judas the pseudo-apostle, Simon Magus, and all the pseudo-Christians down to the present day who are obstinately hardened in an animal disposition, whether they are mingled within the unity or openly dissent in separation.

But when such people are evangelized and imbued with the Sacraments by spiritual persons, Rebecca herself seems to give birth to them, as she did to Esau. When, however, such people are generated within the people of God through those who proclaim the Gospel not sincerely (Phil. 1:17), it is Sarah—but through Hagar.

Likewise, when good spiritual people are generated by carnal persons who evangelize or baptize, Leah or Rachel indeed gives birth to them by marital right, but through the womb of the slave-women [Note: Erasmus and many manuscripts: “through the slave-woman’s womb”]. But when good believers are generated through spiritual persons in the Gospel—those who either advance into the disposition of spiritual maturity, or do not cease striving toward it, or fail to do so because they cannot—they are born, as Isaac from Sarah’s womb or Jacob from Rebecca’s, into new life and the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XVII

**26.** Therefore, whether they appear to remain inside or are openly outside, what is flesh is flesh; whether they persist in their sterility within the threshing-floor or, on the occasion of temptation, are lifted outside like chaff by the wind, what is chaff is chaff.

Anyone who is divided from the unity of that Church which is without stain or wrinkle [Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 18], even if he is mixed with the congregation [Note: Printed editions: “in the congregation.” The manuscripts correct this] of the saints in carnal obstinacy, is nevertheless divided from it.

Yet no one is to be despaired of, whether he appears to be such while inside or more openly resists outside. Spiritual people, and those who are advancing toward this very condition through devout effort, do not go outside.
