For even when they appear to be expelled by some perversity or necessity of human beings, they are tested more truly there than if they remained inside while in no way rising up against the Church; rather, they are rooted in the solid rock of unity [Note: Vatican manuscripts: “in the solid rock of unity”] by the strongest strength of charity.

To this belongs what is said in Abraham’s sacrifice: “But he did not divide the birds” (Gen. 15:10).

## CHAPTER XVIII

**27.** I have now, I think, discussed the question of Baptism sufficiently. Since the schism now called by the name of the Donatists is so manifest, it remains for us devoutly to believe concerning Baptism what the whole Church, removed from the sacrilege of schism, preserves.

Yet if, within that Church, some still held one opinion and others another about this question, while peace was preserved, until a universal council established one clarified and sound judgment, the charity of unity would cover the error of human weakness, as it is written: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). For the same charity, in whose absence other things are possessed in vain, makes certain deficiencies pardonable when it is present.

**28.** There are great testimonies in the writings of the blessed martyr Cyprian; let me now turn to him, whose authority these people flatter themselves with carnally, while they are spiritually destroyed by his charity.

For in those times, before the consensus of the whole Church had confirmed by the decision of a plenary council what ought to be followed in this matter, it seemed right to him and nearly eighty of his fellow bishops from the African Churches [Note: See below, Book 2, chapter 9] that anyone baptized outside the communion of the Catholic Church ought to be baptized again when coming to the Church.

The Lord doubtless did not reveal to so great a man that this was not rightly done, so that his devout humility and charity in beneficially preserving the Church’s peace might be made evident, and that this might be marked out—not only for the Christians of that time but also for posterity—as a medicinal, so to speak, lesson.

When a bishop of such merit, of so great a Church, of such a heart, such a voice, and such virtue held a different opinion about Baptism from what more carefully investigated truth would later establish; and when many of his colleagues, although the matter had not yet been clearly manifested, nevertheless held what both the Church’s earlier practice and afterward the entire Catholic world embraced, he still did not separate himself from those who held a different view by withdrawing from their communion. He also did not cease persuading the others to bear with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:2–3).

Thus, while the structure of the body remained intact, if something in certain members was weakened, it might rather recover through their health than, being killed by separation, refuse every possibility of healing.

And if he had separated himself, how many would have followed him? How great a name would he have made for himself among human beings? How much more widely would they have been called Cyprianists than Donatists?

But he was not a son of perdition, of the sort concerning whom it is said, “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). He was a son of the Church’s peace. Endowed with such illumination of heart, he failed to see one thing so that through him something more excellent might be seen.

“And still,” says the Apostle, “I show you a more excellent way: if I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 12:31–13:1).

He therefore penetrated less deeply, so as to perceive the hidden secret of the Sacrament; but if, knowing all the Sacraments, he had not had charity, he would have been nothing. Since, while perceiving that matter less fully, he nevertheless guarded charity humbly, faithfully, and courageously, he deserved to reach the crown of martyrdom. Thus, if some cloud arising from human condition had entered his luminous mind, it was driven away by the glorious brightness of his shining blood.

For the Lord Jesus Christ himself did not speak without purpose when he called himself the vine and his followers branches on the vine, and said that branches should be cut off and removed from the vine as useless branches that did not bear fruit. What is the fruit, except that new growth of which he also says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34)?

That is the charity without which other things are of no benefit. The Apostle also says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. 5:22–23). All these begin with charity and, through the rest of their joining together, form something like a marvelous cluster [Note: Manuscripts: “and through the rest of their joining together form a cluster,” omitting “like”].

Nor did the same Lord add without purpose: “But the branches in me that bear fruit, my Father cleanses, so that they may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–5). For even those who excel in the fruit of charity can still have something requiring cleansing, which the farmer does not leave uncultivated.

Thus, the fact that this holy man, holding a different opinion about Baptism from what the matter actually was—something later examined and established by the most careful consideration—remained within Catholic unity was compensated by the abundance of charity and cleansed by the sickle of his passion.

## CHAPTER XIX

**29.** But lest I seem to say these things in praise of the most blessed Martyr merely to avoid the force of the evidence—although the praise belongs not to him but to the one by whose grace he became such—let us now produce testimonies from his writings by which the mouths of the Donatists may be especially silenced.

For they bring forward his authority before the uninstructed, in order to appear to be acting rightly when they rebaptize the faithful who come to them. They are exceedingly wretched—and, unless they correct themselves, wholly condemned by themselves—because in so great a man they choose to imitate what did him no harm precisely because he walked with the most persevering steps to the end in that peace from which they have strayed, they who have not known the way of peace (Ps. 13:3).

It is indeed true that Christ’s Baptism is holy everywhere; and although it may be among heretics or schismatics, it is nevertheless not the Baptism of that heresy or schism. Therefore those who come from there to the Catholic Church ought not to be baptized again. But it is another matter to judge that those who deviate from Catholic peace and have been hurled into the wicked pit of separation should additionally be rebaptized.

The blemish in that holy soul’s brightness was covered by the abundance of charity; but the soot in these people’s hellish ugliness is displayed by their hostile expression.

But the matters that we shall next treat concerning the authority of blessed Cyprian we shall take up from another beginning.

# BOOK TWO

In this book Augustine proves that the authority of Cyprian, bishop and martyr, is futilely brought forward by the Donatists, since it is more opposed to them than to Catholics. For Cyprian did not think that the opinion of his predecessor Agrippinus concerning the baptism of heretics in the Catholic Church, when they come to it, should be retained, except on the condition that peace with those who held another opinion always be preserved and that the Church’s unity never be broken by any schism.

[Col. 0125]

## CHAPTER I

**1.** I have undertaken, with the Lord’s help, to demonstrate how much the things brought forward by the party of Donatus against us, as though from the authority of the blessed Cyprian, contribute to our cause—that is, to Catholic peace—and how much they oppose those who bring them forward.

If, then, the necessity of replying should compel me to recall things that I have already set forth in other books—although I shall do so briefly—this should not be burdensome to those who have already read and retained them. For things necessary to instruction ought often to be impressed upon the heart; and when the same matters are handled and treated in many different ways, they also help those endowed with greater understanding both toward ease of learning and toward abundance in discussion.

I also know how it can sadden a reader when, from the book he has in his hands, upon encountering some difficult point in a question, he is sent to another book where he must seek its solution—one which perhaps he does not possess. Therefore, if the necessity of the present questions compels me briefly to repeat anything already said in other books, let those who know it pardon me, so that those who do not know it may not be offended. It is better to offer something to one who has it than to postpone it for one who does not.

**2.** What, then, do these people say when they are strangled by the force of the truth, to which they refuse to assent?

“Cyprian,” they say, “whose great merit and great teaching we know, established in council, together with many of his fellow bishops who were exchanging their own opinions, that heretics or schismatics—that is, all who are outside the communion of the one Church—do not possess Baptism; and therefore anyone baptized by them who comes to the Church must be baptized within the Church.”

Cyprian’s authority does not terrify me, because Cyprian’s humility refreshes me. We certainly know the great merit of Cyprian, bishop and martyr; but was it greater than that of the apostle and martyr Peter?

Concerning Peter, Cyprian himself speaks in his letter to Quintus as follows:

“For neither did Peter,” he says, “whom the Lord first chose and upon whom he built his Church (Matt. 16:18), when Paul afterward disputed with him concerning circumcision, arrogantly claim anything for himself or presumptuously assume anything, saying that he held primacy and that obedience ought rather to be given to him by those who were recent and later; nor did he despise Paul because he had previously been a persecutor of the Church. Rather, he accepted the counsel of truth and readily agreed to the legitimate reasoning that Paul was asserting, thereby giving us an example both of concord and of patience, so that we should not stubbornly love our own opinions, but should instead regard as our own those things that are at times usefully and beneficially suggested by our brethren and colleagues, if they are true and legitimate” (Epistle 71, to Quintus).

Here Cyprian recalls what we too have learned in the holy Scriptures: that the apostle Peter, in whom the primacy of the Apostles stands out with such eminent grace, was accustomed to act concerning circumcision in a way other than truth required and was corrected by the later apostle Paul.

If Peter, then, could fail to proceed correctly in some matter concerning the truth of the Gospel, so that he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize—as Paul writes in the letter in which he attested before God that he was not lying, saying, “What I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20)—and after this holy and terrible attestation before God narrated all these things, saying, “When I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (ibid. 2:11–14),

if Peter, I say, could compel the Gentiles to Judaize against the rule of truth that the Church afterward held, why could Cyprian not compel heretics or schismatics to be baptized again against the rule of truth that the whole Church afterward held?

I think that, without any insult to Cyprian, Bishop Cyprian may be compared with the apostle Peter insofar as concerns the crown of martyrdom. But I must be more careful lest I insult Peter. For who does not know that the primacy of the Apostolate is to be preferred to any episcopate? [Note: Belgian manuscripts at Louvain read: “the primacy of anyone.”] Yet even if the grace of the sees differs [Note: The word “grace” is absent from the Laon manuscript], the glory of the martyrs is one.

And even if the hearts of confessors who die for the true faith in the unity of charity perhaps surpass one another in some respect, the Lord knows. By his hidden and wondrous distribution of graces, the thief hanging on the cross confesses him once and is sent into paradise that very day (Luke 23:40–43), while Peter, following the Lord, denies him three times (Matt. 26:69–75) and is delayed from the crown [Note: Erasmus and many manuscripts: “and is delayed from the crown,” omitting “from”]. It is rash for us to judge from this.

Nevertheless, if someone now compelled another to be circumcised according to Jewish custom and then to be baptized, the human race would detest this much more than if someone were compelled to be rebaptized.

Therefore, when Peter is corrected by Paul, who came later, for doing that, and is advanced toward martyrdom while being preserved in the bond of peace and unity [Note: Vatican manuscripts: “with the bond of peace and unity preserved.” Certain later Gallican and Belgian manuscripts have “is advanced” instead of “is promoted”], how much more readily and firmly must what has been established by the statutes of the universal Church be preferred either to the authority of one bishop or to the council of one province?

Cyprian himself said what he thought in such a way that he wished to remain in the unity of peace even with those who held a different opinion on this matter. This is indicated by his opening speech at the beginning of the same council that these people bring forward. It runs as follows:

## CHAPTER II

**3.** “When many bishops from the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and Mauritania had gathered at Carthage on the first of September, together with presbyters and deacons, with a very large part of the people also present, and when the letter of Jubaianus to Cyprian had been read, as well as Cyprian’s reply to Jubaianus concerning the baptism of heretics, and what Jubaianus afterward wrote back to Cyprian, Cyprian said:

‘You have heard, most beloved colleagues, what our fellow bishop Jubaianus wrote to me, consulting my modest judgment concerning the unlawful and profane Baptism of heretics, and what I replied to him—namely, judging as we have judged once, twice, and often, that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with the Church’s Baptism.

Likewise, other letters of Jubaianus have been read to you, in which, replying to our letter with sincere and religious devotion, he not only agreed but also gave thanks that he had been instructed.

It remains for each of us to state what he thinks about this matter, judging no one and removing no one who holds a different opinion from the right of communion. For none of us has constituted himself bishop of bishops or compelled his colleagues by tyrannical terror to obey, since every bishop has, in accordance with the freedom and power granted to him, his own judgment, and can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another. But let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and uniquely has the power both to place us over the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct.’”

## CHAPTER III

**4.** Now let the proud and swollen necks of heretics, if they dare, rise up against the holy humility of this speech.

Insane Donatists—whom we desire and wish to return to the peace and unity of the holy Church and to be healed within it—what do you say to this?

You are accustomed to bring forward Cyprian’s letters, Cyprian’s opinion, and Cyprian’s council against us. Why do you claim Cyprian’s authority for your schism but reject his example for the Church’s peace?

Who does not know that the holy canonical Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its definite limits, and is placed before all later letters of bishops in such a way that there can be no doubt or dispute whatsoever about whether something is true or right, once it has been established that it is written there?

But the letters of bishops that were or are written after the canon was confirmed may be criticized—if anything in them has perhaps deviated from the truth—by the more learned speech of anyone more skilled in that matter, by the greater authority and more learned prudence of other bishops [Note: Erasmus, with some manuscripts, reads “and more learned”; the Maurist edition reads “and of more learned men”], and by councils.

And the councils held in individual regions or provinces must yield without any equivocation to the authority of plenary councils held from the whole Christian world. Even plenary councils themselves may often be corrected by later ones, when some experience of events reveals what had been closed and makes known what had been hidden.

All this must be done without any insolent pride of sacrilege, without any swollen neck of arrogance, without any contentiousness of envious hostility, but with holy humility, with Catholic peace, and with Christian charity.

## CHAPTER IV

**5.** Therefore holy Cyprian, made so much greater by being so much more humble, loved Peter’s example so greatly that he said:

“Giving us, plainly, an example both of concord and of patience, so that we should not stubbornly love our own opinions, but should rather regard as our own those things that are at times usefully and beneficially suggested by our brethren and colleagues, if they are true and legitimate.”

He thus sufficiently showed that he would very readily have corrected his own opinion if someone had demonstrated to him that Christ’s Baptism could be given by those who had gone outside in the same way that it could not be lost when they went outside. We have already said much on this subject.

Nor would we ourselves dare to assert such a thing unless supported by the unanimous authority of the whole Church. Cyprian himself would undoubtedly have yielded to it if, in his time, the truth of this question had been clarified and established by a plenary council.

For if he praises and proclaims that Peter was corrected patiently and harmoniously by one later colleague, how much sooner would he himself, together with his provincial council, have yielded to the authority of the whole world once the truth had been revealed? Surely so holy and peaceful a soul could very readily agree even with one person who spoke and demonstrated the truth.

Perhaps this actually happened [Note: Bede asserts that it did happen in Book 8, question 5], but we do not know. For not everything that took place among the bishops at that time could be committed to memory and writing, nor do we know everything that was committed to writing.

How could this matter, wrapped in such dense clouds of controversy, have been brought to the splendid illumination and confirmation of a plenary council unless it had first been examined and established over a long period throughout the regions of the world, through many discussions and exchanges among bishops on both sides?

This is what the health of peace accomplishes: when obscure matters are investigated for a long time and, because they are difficult to discover, produce differing opinions in fraternal discussion, the bond of unity remains until the clear truth is reached [Note: The Louvain edition reads “or clear truth”; *or* is absent from the Amsterdam, Erasmus, and most manuscript witnesses], lest an incurable wound of error remain in a severed part.

## CHAPTER V

**6.** For this reason, something is often revealed less fully to the more learned, so that their patient and humble charity—in which there is greater fruit—may be tested, either in how they preserve unity while holding differing opinions about obscure matters, or in how they receive the truth when they learn that it has been declared contrary to what they had thought.

Of these two things, we clearly possess one example in the blessed Cyprian: namely, how he preserved unity with those from whom he differed. For he says:

“Judging no one, and removing no one who held a different opinion from the right of communion.”

The other matter—how he might have received the truth when it was discovered to be contrary to what he thought—though the letters are silent, his merits cry out; if the letter is not found, the crown bears witness; if the council does not indicate it, the fellowship of angels indicates it.

For it is no small testimony to a most peaceful soul that he deserved martyrdom within that unity from which, while holding a different opinion, he refused to separate himself.

We are human beings. To think differently from the way a matter actually is is a human temptation. But to love one’s own opinion excessively, or to envy those who are better, and to proceed as far as the sacrilege of severing communion and creating a schism or heresy, is a diabolical presumption.

To think in no respect differently from the way a matter actually is is angelic perfection.

Therefore, since we are human beings but are angels in hope—since in the resurrection we shall be equal to the angels (Matt. 22:30)—as long as we do not possess angelic perfection, let us not possess the devil’s presumption.

Thus the Apostle says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13). It is therefore human to think differently about something. For this reason he says elsewhere: “Let those of us who are perfect think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you.”

To whom, whenever he wills, whether in this life or after this life, does he reveal these things except to those who walk in the way of peace and turn aside into no separation? Not to people such as these, who have not known the way of peace (Ps. 13:3) and who broke the bond of unity for no other reason.

Therefore, after the Apostle had said, “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you,” lest they suppose that what they thought differently could be revealed to them outside the way of peace, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, in what we have attained, let us walk” (Phil. 3:15–16).

Walking in this way, Cyprian, through the most persevering endurance—not with blood un-shed, but with blood shed in unity [Note: We restore here the negative particle that Erasmus and the Louvain edition had removed]—reached, through his martyr’s confession, the light of the angels. Thus, if it had not been revealed earlier, he certainly recognized there that, although he had held a different opinion, he had not placed that opinion before the bond of unity.

## CHAPTER VI

**7.** What, then, do you say to this, Donatists?

If our opinion concerning Baptism is true, then all those who held a different opinion in Cyprian’s time were not separated from the Church’s unity until God revealed to them what they thought differently. Why, then, did you break the bond of peace through sacrilegious separation?

But if your opinion concerning Baptism is true, Cyprian and the others with whom you claim he held such a council remained in unity with those who held a different opinion. Why, then, did you break the bond of peace?

Whichever of these alternatives you choose, you are compelled to hear a judgment against your separation.

Answer: Why did you separate yourselves? Why did you erect an altar against the whole world? Why do you not communicate with the Churches to which you possess and read the apostolic Letters, and according to which you say that you live?

Answer: Why did you separate yourselves?

Certainly it was so that you would not perish through communion with the wicked. How, then, did Cyprian and all his colleagues not perish?

Although they believed that heretics and schismatics did not possess Baptism, they nevertheless preferred to communicate with those received without Baptism—even while believing that their sins were so monstrous and sacrilegious that they stood upon them [Note: Erasmus and many manuscripts: “believing that they remained upon them.” Other manuscripts, with the Louvain edition, have “stood upon them,” as again below, no. 11; Book 5, no. 1; and Book 6, no. 23]—rather than separate themselves from unity. Cyprian said:

“Judging no one, and removing no one who held a different opinion from the right of communion.”

**8.** If the righteous perish through such communion with the wicked, then the Church had already perished in Cyprian’s time.

From where, then, did Donatus originate? Where was he catechized, where baptized, where ordained, when the contagion of communion had already extinguished the Church?

But if the Church existed, the wicked could not harm the good within one communion.

Why did you separate yourselves?

Look: in unity I see Cyprian and his other colleagues, who, after holding a council, judged that all who had been baptized outside the Church’s communion did not possess Baptism, and therefore that it should be given to them when they came.

But look again: in that same unity I see some who held a different opinion about this matter and who, recognizing Christ’s Baptism in those who came from heretics or schismatics, did not dare to baptize them again.

Catholic unity embraces all these within her maternal bosom, bearing one another’s burdens and striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:2–3), until the Lord should reveal to some of them, if they held a different opinion, what they had thought differently.

If these people held the truth, were the others not contaminated by them—or were they? If the others held the truth, were these people not contaminated by them—or were they?

Choose whichever answer you wish.

If they were contaminated, then the Church did not exist at that time. Answer: From where did you come here?

But if the Church continued to exist, the good are in no way contaminated by the wicked through such communion. Answer: Why did you break the bond?

9. Or do schismatics received without Baptism not defile, while traditors of the holy Books do? That your people were traditors is testified by the clearest record of events. And if at that time you were speaking truth against them, you would have persuaded the unity of the whole world of your case, so that, while you were retained, they would be excluded. But if you attempted this and did not prevail, the whole world is innocent, since it believed ecclesiastical judges rather than defeated litigants; if, however, you were unwilling to prosecute your case, the whole world is innocent, since it could not condemn those who had not been heard. Why, then, did you separate yourselves from the innocent? You cannot defend the sacrilege of your schism.

But I pass over this. I say this: if traditors could defile you—men who were not convicted by you and by whom you were defeated—then, according to your own judgment, the sacrileges of schismatics and heretics received without Baptism could much more have defiled Cyprian. Yet he did not separate himself. And since the Church remained, it is clear that he could not be defiled [Note: Er. and Lov. read *in Ecclesia*, “in the Church”; the preposition *in* was added incorrectly, since it is absent from Am. and the manuscripts.]. Why, then, did you separate yourselves—not, I will not say, from the innocent, which is proved, but from those very traditors, which is not proved? Or, as I began to say, are the crimes of traditors more serious than those of schismatics?

Let us not bring forward deceitful scales on which we weigh whatever we want, and in whatever manner we want, declaring at our own discretion, “This is serious; this is light.” Rather, let us bring the divine scale from the holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasuries, and weigh on it what is more serious; or rather, let us not weigh it ourselves, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord.

At the time when the Lord showed, through fresh examples of punishment, that earlier offenses were to be avoided, idolatry was punished by the sword when an idol was fashioned and worshiped (Exod. 32); the burning of the prophetic book by military slaughter and foreign captivity (Jer. 36); and schism by the earth’s opening, with its authors buried alive and the rest consumed by heavenly fire (Num. 16). Who, then, would doubt that the offense committed was more wicked which was more severely punished?

If those coming from such sacrilegious persons [Note: Am. and most manuscripts read “from such sacrileges” (*sacrilegiis*)], without Baptism—as you say—did not defile Cyprian, how could you be defiled by traditors who were not convicted [Note: Some Gallican manuscripts read “not joined together” (*non conjuncti*)], but fabricated [Note: *conficti*]—traditors who, if they had not handed over the Books to be burned but had burned them with their own hands, would certainly have been guilty of a lesser crime than if they had committed schism? For the former was punished more mildly, the latter more severely—not by human judgment, but by divine judgment.

## CHAPTER VII

10. Why, then, did you separate yourselves? If you have any understanding, you certainly see that you cannot find an answer. “Things have not failed so completely,” they say, “that we cannot answer: We will have it so” [Note: Am., Er., and some manuscripts read “If we will it,” which is less correct, as is clear from what immediately follows and from §15, where these same words are repeated.].

“Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Rom. 14:4).

They do not understand that this was said against those who wanted to judge, not manifest deeds, but the hearts of others. For how, then, does he himself speak at such length about the crimes of schisms and heresies? Or how is it sung in the Psalms: “If indeed you love justice, judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. 57:2)? Why, moreover, does the Lord himself say, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:24), if it is not permitted to judge anyone? Finally, concerning those traditors about whom they made a false judgment, why did they judge at all concerning another’s servants? Before their own master they stood or fell.

Why, finally, did they not hesitate to pronounce, with what they call the truthful voice of the plenary council, such a judgment concerning the recent Maximianists that they compared them with those earlier schismatics whom the earth swallowed alive? Yet, as they cannot deny, they either condemned some of them while innocent or received them again when guilty.

But when the truth is spoken and they cannot answer, they gnaw at rough mutterings [Note: Some manuscripts read, “they gnaw with leprous mouths”: *rodunt murmur ora leprosa*]: “We will have it so.”

“Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls.”

But when a weak sheep is seen in the wilderness, where the shepherd who might cry out appears absent, they bare their teeth and tear the feeble throat: “You would be a good man if you were not a traditor. Consider your soul; be a Christian.”

O shameless madness! When it is said to a Christian, “Be a Christian,” what else is being taught except that he should deny that he is a Christian [Note: Am., Er., and many manuscripts read: “What else is said except, ‘Deny yourself to be a Christian’?”]? Was there anything else that those persecutors of Christians wished to teach, against whom those who resisted became martyrs? Or is what is committed under the threat of the sword considered less serious than what is committed by a tongue lying in ambush?

11. Answer these things, ravening wolves who, desiring to be clothed in sheep’s skins (Matt. 7:15), imagine that the letters of blessed Cyprian support you. Did the sacrilege of schismatics defile Cyprian, or did it not defile him? If it defiled him, then the Church perished at that time; there was no Church from which you could have sprung. But if it did not defile him, by what offense of another can the innocent be defiled within unity, if they cannot be defiled by the sacrilege of schism? Why, then, did you separate yourselves? Why, while fleeing the lesser things that you invent, did you commit the very sacrilege of schism, which is the gravest of all?

Or perhaps you now prefer to admit that those who had been baptized outside the communion of the Church, whether in some schism or in some heresy, were no longer schismatics or heretics, because, by passing over to the Church and anathematizing their former errors, they had ceased to be what they were? How, then, had their offenses not remained upon them without Baptism? Or was it the Baptism of Christ, but it could not benefit them outside the communion of the Church; and when they came, anathematized their former error, and were received into the peace of the Church by the laying on of hands, did it then begin to benefit them—once they had been rooted and founded in love, without which the other things are fruitless—for the remission of sins and the sanctification of life, although they had carried it outside without fruit?

12. Do not, then, bring against us Cyprian’s authority for the repetition of Baptism. Rather, hold with us Cyprian’s example for the preservation of unity. For the question of Baptism had not yet been carefully investigated, yet the Church maintained a most salutary practice: among schismatics and heretics alike, to correct what is wrong, not to repeat what has been given; to heal what has been wounded, not to treat what is sound.

I believe that this practice came down from apostolic tradition—as did many things which [Note: Am., Er., and most manuscripts omit *quae* (“which”).] are not found in the writings of the apostles or in later councils, yet, because they are observed throughout the universal Church, are believed to have been handed down and commended by the apostles themselves. Blessed Cyprian therefore says that this most salutary practice began to be corrected, as it were, through Agrippinus, his predecessor.

But as the truth, more diligently investigated, later taught—a truth brought, after great waves of doubt, to confirmation by a plenary council—it is more correctly believed that through Agrippinus it began to be corrupted, not corrected. Thus, when so great a question burst upon the Church, and it was difficult to give a rational account of whether the remission of sins and the spiritual regeneration of a human being could take place among heretics or schismatics, while the authority of Agrippinus and of certain others who had agreed with him—men who had failed in this question—preceded them, they preferred to devise something new rather than hold to a practice whose defense they did not understand. Plausible arguments then rushed upon the eyes of their minds and blocked the path to the careful investigation of truth.

## CHAPTER VIII

13. Nor do I think that blessed Cyprian freely expressed an opinion contrary to the practice for any other reason, or that he was the first to state it, except so that, if someone should perhaps arise to whom the matter had been more fully revealed, he might receive him with the greatest gratitude, and show that not only diligence in teaching but also modesty in learning ought to be imitated.

If no such person should arise—someone who could bring forward anything by which all those plausible arguments that moved him might be refuted—he would remain in the same opinion, with a good conscience, neither concealing what was thought to be the truth nor abandoning the unity that he loved.

For he also understood in this way what the Apostle says: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine; but if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (1 Cor. 14:29). “In this passage,” he says, “he taught and showed that many things are revealed to individuals for the better, and that each person ought not obstinately to contend on behalf of what he had once absorbed and retained; but, if something better and more useful should appear, to embrace it willingly” (*Epistle* 71, to Quintus).

By these words he not only admonished those who did not see anything better to agree with him, but also urged them, if any could bring forward something by which the earlier practice might rather be shown to be worth preserving, to do so—so that, if what they brought forward could not be refuted, he himself might demonstrate how truthfully he had said that “each person ought not obstinately to contend on behalf of what he had once absorbed and retained, but, if something better and more useful should appear, to embrace it willingly.”

But since at that time no one arose except those who opposed the practice to him, while the defenses of the practice were not presented in a form capable of moving such a mind, that most serious man was unwilling to yield his arguments—although they were not true, a fact hidden from him, yet not defeated—to a practice that was true, though not yet established. Yet unless Agrippinus first, and some of his fellow bishops throughout Africa, had attempted to abandon that practice even by conciliar decision, this man would not have dared to reason against it.

Rather, disturbed in so obscure a question and everywhere observing the universal and powerful practice, he would have constrained himself, through prayer and the intention of his mind, toward God, so that he might discern and teach that what was later determined by a plenary council was true. But when he inherited the authority of the preceding council held through Agrippinus, already wearied, he preferred to defend what he regarded as the discovery of his predecessors rather than labor further in investigation [Note: The manuscripts read, “rather than labor further in seeking.”]. At the end of his letter to Quintus he shows the couch of authority on which, as though weary, he found rest.

## CHAPTER IX

14. “This,” he says, “was also established by Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, together with his fellow bishops who at that time governed the Church of the Lord in the province of Africa and Numidia, and was confirmed after the balanced examination of a common council. We too have followed their religious, legitimate, and salutary judgment, one consonant with the faith and the Catholic Church” [Note: Some manuscripts read, “consonant with the faith because of the Church”; others, “consonant with the faith of the Church.”].

By this testimony he sufficiently shows that he would have mentioned it all the more if any overseas or universal council concerning this matter had been held. But none had yet been held, because the whole world was held by the strength of custom; and this alone was opposed to those who wanted to introduce novelty, because they were unable to grasp the truth.

Later, however, while the matter was discussed and investigated among many on both sides, the truth was not only discovered but also brought to the authority and strength of a plenary council—after Cyprian’s martyrdom, indeed, but before we were born [Note: This plenary council, on whose authority the author repeatedly relies throughout this work, is either the Council of Arles or the Council of Nicaea: the latter was held in 325, the former in the year 314 of Christ, and thus both before Augustine was born. He commends the judgment of this same council in *Against Parmenianus*, Book II, chapter 13, §30; in *On Heresies*, heresy 69; and in Letter 43 to Glorius and Eleusius, chapter 7, §19. For the view that the Council of Arles is always intended, it is useful to indicate several passages omitted in the excellent dissertation that Joannes Launoius published on this subject. In these passages Augustine attributes to an episcopal judgment, by which the Donatists were defeated after their case had been heard and decided, the authority of the whole world. In *Against Parmenianus*, Book III, chapter 4, §21, he says: “They condemned a few in Africa, but by the judgment of the whole world they were defeated”; and he adds that Catholics preferred to believe such ecclesiastical judges rather than defeated litigants. In the same work, chapter 6, §30, he says that the Donatists, because “they made a schism from the unity of Christ,” were convicted not by “three hundred and ten” African bishops, “but by the authority of the whole world.” Moreover, in Book I against the same opponent, chapter 6, he reports that, after the judgment at Arles, they came again to Constantine and were defeated there by the “final judgment”—that is, at Milan, according to Letter 43 to Glorius and Eleusius, chapter 7, §20, in the year of Christ 316, as is understood from *After the Conference*, chapter 33.].

That this was the practice of the Church, later confirmed by a plenary council after many complications had been examined and the truth recognized, is sufficiently shown also by the words of blessed Cyprian himself in the same letter to Jubaianus, which is recorded as having been read at the council. For he says:

“But someone says, ‘What, then, will become of those who in former times, coming from heresy to the Church, were admitted without Baptism?’”

Here he certainly shows sufficiently what used to be done, even if he did not wish it to be done; and by the very fact that he mentions the council of Agrippinus, he plainly indicates that another practice of the Church existed. For there would have been no need to wish to establish this by a council if it were already maintained by custom. Moreover, some statements in that very council plainly declare that they decreed against the practice of the Church what they judged ought to be decreed.

Therefore, let these men consider one point that is evident to all: if Cyprian’s authority is to be followed, it ought to be followed more in preserving unity than in changing the practice of the Church. But if attention is given to his council, a later council of the universal Church must be preferred to it—a council of which he rejoiced to be a member and repeatedly urged the others to imitate him in remaining within the structure of the whole body.

For later councils are rightly preferred to earlier ones [Note: Vatican manuscripts read, “are to be preferred”], and the whole is always, by the best right, preferred to its parts.

[Col. 0136] ## CHAPTER X

15. What do these men do when it is shown that, although holy Cyprian did not admit those baptized in heresy or schism, he nevertheless remained in communion with those who did admit them? He made this entirely clear when he said: “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion” (in the Council of Carthage mentioned above, chapter 2).

If he was stained by communion with such people, why do they follow his authority when discussing Baptism? But if he was not stained by communion with such people, why do they not imitate his example in preserving unity? Is anything left except for them to say, “We will have it so”?

What else do all the wicked and criminal—lustful men, drunkards, adulterers, and people shameless in every way; thieves, robbers, murderers, bandits, sorcerers, idolaters—answer when truth reproves them, except, “This is what I want; this pleases me”? And if they are marked with the Christian name, they also say, “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14:4).

Yet these men are more modest in this respect: when, under divine and human laws, they suffer some punishment for their ruined morals and deeds, they do not call themselves martyrs. These men, however, want at once to possess both the life of sacrilegious people and the reputation of the innocent; both freedom from punishment for criminal deeds and the glory of martyrs amid just punishments.

It is as though God’s mercy and patience toward them were not greater precisely because, correcting them in part, he gives room for repentance (Wis. 12:10), and in this life does not cease to multiply the scourges, so that, considering what they suffer and why they suffer it, they may eventually come to their senses.

Those who have already accepted the Baptism of the Maximianists for the unity of Donatus should instead embrace the Baptism of the whole world for the peace of Christ; let them be restored to the root, reconciled to unity, and see that nothing remains for them to say, though something still remains for them to do: they must offer, to the God whom they offended by their wicked crime, the sacrifice of love for their past deeds. They broke his unity by an unspeakable crime and inflicted such long-lasting injuries upon his sacraments.

“For the Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in mercy and truth” (Ps. 102:8). Let them embrace in the present life the merciful and patient Lord, and fear the truthful Lord in the life to come. For he does not desire the death of the wicked so much as that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 33:11), because he turns his judgment away from the injuries inflicted.

This is our exhortation.

## CHAPTER XI

16. For this reason they regard us as enemies: because we speak the truth; because we fear to remain silent; because we dread ceasing from such persistence as we can maintain; because we obey the Apostle, who says, “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4:2).

But, as the Gospel says, they “loved the glory of men more than the glory of God” (John 12:45), and, while they fear being reproved for a time [Note: The manuscripts read “and to be reproved,” omitting *while*], they do not fear being condemned forever. They themselves see what evil they are doing; they see that they have no answer at all. Yet they cast clouds before the inexperienced, while they themselves are swallowed alive—that is, they perish knowingly and with full recognition.

They saw people shudder and detest deeply the fact that they themselves had divided into many schisms, especially in the chief city of Africa, the famous city of Carthage [Note: He refers to that great schism among the Donatists which occurred when Maximian was ordained bishop of Carthage against Primianus.]. They tried to patch the disgrace of their own rags. Thinking that they could remove the Maximianists, they pressed the matter vigorously and with great effort through Optatus Gildonianus, inflicting many evils and savage persecutions upon them.

From among these they received some, thinking that all might be converted by the same terror. But with those whom they received they were unwilling to commit the injustice of baptizing again those who had been baptized by them in schism—or rather, of having them rebaptized inside by those very people by whom they had been baptized outside—and in this way they set aside their own wicked custom.

They perceive how criminally they now act when, having received the Baptism of the Maximianists, they violate the Baptism of the whole world. But they fear their own rebaptized members, lest those members perhaps not spare them if they themselves spare the others, and lest they demand their lives from them if they cease slaughtering the souls of others.

## CHAPTER XII

17. They cannot find what answer to give concerning the Maximianists they received. If they say, “We received innocent men,” the answer is made to them: “Then you had condemned innocent men.” If they say, “We did not know,” the answer is: “Then you judged rashly”—just as they also pronounced a rash judgment concerning the traditors—and you spoke falsely when you said, “Know that they were condemned by the truthful voice of the plenary council” (in the decision of the Council of Bagai).

For innocent men could not have been condemned by a truthful voice. If they say, “We did not condemn them,” the council is read aloud; the names of both the bishops and the cities are read aloud. If they say, “That is not our council,” the proconsular records are read, where they repeatedly cited the same council in order to exclude those same Maximianists from the basilicas and drive them away amid the uproar of legal proceedings and the force of official assistance.

If they say that Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri, whom they later received, were not with Maximianus, the records are read in which they demanded from the public courts that these men be excluded from the basilicas on the basis of their own council, which they had held against the Maximianists.

If they say, “They were received for the sake of peace,” the answer is: “Why, then, do you not recognize true and complete peace? Who drove you, who compelled you, to receive for the sake of Donatus’s peace a condemned schismatic, while condemning the world, which had not been heard, in opposition to the peace of Christ?”

Truth presses them from every side [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read “indeed” (*utique*)]. They see that they have no answer and think that they have nothing to do [Note: The printed editions read “think that they have something to do” (*se habere*); this should not be adopted unless all our manuscripts, with strong agreement, did not here prefer *se non habere* (“they have nothing”).]; they cannot find what to say. They are not permitted to remain silent. They prefer to resist the truth with perverse voices rather than, by acknowledging their errors, be restored to peace.

## CHAPTER XIII

18. Who, then, does not understand what they can say in their hearts? “What, then,” they say, “are we to do about those whom we have already rebaptized?”

The answer is: Return with them to the Church. Offer, through the medicine of peace, those whom you wounded to be healed; offer, through the life of love, those whom you killed to be raised up. Fraternal concord has great power to appease God.

“If two of you,” says the Lord, “agree on earth, whatever you endure will be done for you” (Matt. 18:19). If this is true of two human beings, how much more of two peoples? Let us prostrate ourselves together before the Lord. Share unity with us; let us share sorrow with you; and let love cover the multitude of sins.

Seek counsel from blessed Cyprian himself. Consider how much he presumed upon the good of unity, and how he did not break away from those who held a different opinion. Although he thought that those who were baptized outside the communion of the Church did not possess Baptism, nevertheless, because of the bond of unity itself, he believed that those simply admitted into the Church could attain forgiveness [Note: The printed editions read here only “reach forgiveness” (*ad veniam pervenire*), but in the immediately following chapter they agree with the manuscripts in reading “attain forgiveness” (*ad veniam pertinere*).].

For he resolves the question that he himself posed when he wrote to Jubaianus:

“But someone says, ‘What, then, will become of those who in former times, coming from heresy to the Church, were admitted without Baptism?’ The Lord is able in his mercy to grant forgiveness and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, having been simply admitted into the Church, fell asleep in the Church” (*Epistle* 73, to Jubaianus).

## CHAPTER XIV

19. It is difficult to judge which is more harmful: not being baptized at all or being rebaptized. I certainly see what people detest and dread more. Nevertheless, returning to that lordly scale in which the weight of things is measured not by human feeling but by divine authority, I find the Lord’s judgment concerning both matters.

For he said to Peter, “The one who has been washed has no need to wash again” (John 13:10); and to Nicodemus, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). What God’s more secret judgment may contain is perhaps difficult for people such as ourselves to know. Yet, as far as the words themselves are concerned, it is clear to anyone how great the difference is between “has no need to wash” and “will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Finally, the Church itself maintains the tradition in such a way that it cannot admit a person without Baptism to the altar at all. But since a rebaptized person may be admitted after repentance, what else is shown except that he is not without Baptism?

If, then, Cyprian presumed that those whom he considered to be without Baptism could nevertheless attain forgiveness because of the bond of unity, the Lord is able, through that same bond of unity and peace, to be reconciled with those who have been rebaptized; through that very compensation of peace, to become merciful toward those by whom they were rebaptized; and to forgive all the offenses they committed in their error, when they offer the sacrifice of love, which covers a multitude of sins.

Thus he may regard not how many were wounded by their departure, but how many more were liberated by their return. Within the bond of peace in which Cyprian believed that, through the mercy of God, those whom he thought had been admitted into the Church without Baptism could not be separated from the gifts of the Church, we believe that, through the same mercy of God, those who have been rebaptized can attain forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XV

20. For the Catholic Church, both in the time of blessed Cyprian and in the period before him, held within the embrace of unity either those who had been rebaptized or those who did not possess Baptism. Either the former or the latter attained salvation only through the merit of that unity itself.

For if those who came from heretics did not possess Baptism, as Cyprian asserts, they were not rightly admitted; yet he himself did not despair of their forgiveness through the Lord’s mercy, on account of the unity of the Church. If, therefore, they did possess Baptism, they were not rightly rebaptized. What, then, helped them except that same love of unity, so that, through divine mercy, God did not count against those who loved peace what human weakness had concealed in its treatment of the sacrament?

Why, then, when you fear your own rebaptized members, do you begrudge both them and yourselves the means of salvation? There was once doubt concerning Baptism; those who held different opinions remained in unity. As time passed, that doubt was removed when the truth was recognized. The question, not yet settled, did not deter Cyprian from withdrawing; once settled, it invites you to return.

Come to the Catholic Church in agreement, which Cyprian did not abandon while it was wavering. Or, if Cyprian’s example now displeases you—he who remained in communion with those who received people baptized by heretics, openly saying, “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion”—where are you going, wretched people? What are you doing? Flee from yourselves as well, because you have proceeded from the place where he remained.

But if, because of the abundance of his love, his affection for the brethren, and the bond of peace, neither his own sins nor the sins of others could harm him, return here, where what your people have fabricated will harm both us and you far less.

# BOOK THREE

This book undertakes to refute those points in Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus that seem to prove that Christ’s Baptism cannot be conferred through heretics.

[Col. 0139]

## CHAPTER I

1. I think it can now be clear to everyone that the authority of blessed Cyprian ought to be invoked on our side rather than on the side of the Donatists, in order to retain the bond of peace and in no way violate the Church’s most salutary love of unity.

For if they wish to use Cyprian’s example to rebaptize Catholics, because he judged that heretics ought to be baptized in the Catholic Church, we instead use his example by which he most plainly established that one must not withdraw through separation from Catholic communion—that is, from Christians spread throughout the whole world—even when bad and sacrilegious people have been admitted. For he did not wish to remove from the right of communion even those who, as it seemed to him, were admitting into Catholic communion sacrilegious people who had not been baptized, saying: “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion.”

## CHAPTER II

2. Yet I see what can still be asked of me: namely, that I answer those plausible arguments by which either Agrippinus, or Cyprian himself, or those in Africa who agreed with them, or perhaps some people from overseas and distant lands—moved not by any plenary or even regional council, but by an exchange of letters—came to think that this ought to be done.

The earlier practice of the Church had not held this, and later the Catholic world rejected it with the strongest firmness of agreement. What had begun to creep into certain minds through such disputations, the more powerful truth arising from salvation through unity, the universal remedy, healed.

Let them see, then, how confidently I undertake this discussion. If I cannot attain and show how the things they affirm from Cyprian’s council or letters are to be refuted—namely, that Christ’s Baptism cannot be conferred through heretics—I shall remain secure in the Church, in whose communion Cyprian himself remained with those who did not agree with him.

3. But if they say that the Catholic Church existed at that time for this reason: because there were there a few people—or, if they think so, even many—who rejected Baptism given among heretics and baptized those who came from them, then what follows?

Before Agrippinus, through whom this supposed new theory began, contending against the practice, was there not a Church? And afterward, when, unless there had been a return to the earlier practice, it would not have been necessary for Cyprian to convene another council, was there not a Church? For at that time the practice was maintained everywhere that Christ’s Baptism was regarded as nothing other than Christ’s Baptism, even if it was proved to have been given among heretics or schismatics.

If the Church existed even then, and Christ’s inheritance had not been destroyed by interruption but remained, increasing among all nations, the safest course is to remain in that same practice, which at that time embraced good and bad together.

But if the Church did not exist then because sacrilegious heretics were received without Baptism and this was maintained by universal practice, where did Donatus appear? From what land did he spring? From what sea did he emerge? From what heaven did he fall?

We, then, as I began to say, are secure in the communion of that Church throughout whose extent what is now being done was likewise done before Agrippinus and between Agrippinus and Cyprian. And neither Agrippinus, nor Cyprian, nor those who agreed with them abandoned the Church’s universality, although they thought differently from the others; rather, together with those from whom they differed, they remained in the same communion of unity.

Let these people themselves consider where they are. They cannot say from where they sprang, if the Church had already been lost at that time through the contagion of communion with heretics and schismatics received without Baptism. Nor do they agree with Cyprian himself. For he professed that he remained in communion with those who received heretics and schismatics, and therefore also with those who had been received. These people, however, because of the traditors whom they disgraced in Africa but did not convict in an overseas judgment, separated themselves from the communion of the whole world.

Even if they had brought true charges against them, the crimes of heresies and schisms would have been far greater—crimes from which, according to Cyprian’s own view, people came without Baptism and were received into Catholic communion without Baptism, yet could not defile Cyprian.

Nor, in the very matter in which they claim to imitate Cyprian, do they find an answer concerning the Baptism of the Maximianists that they received. They recalled into their communion, in that same episcopate in which they had condemned them, those whom they had persecuted both after condemning them in their plenary council and by the judgment of earthly authorities.

Therefore, if the communion of the wicked destroyed the Church in Cyprian’s time, these people have no origin for their own communion. But if it did not destroy the Church, they have no defense for their separation. Moreover, they follow neither Cyprian’s example [Note: B. reads *sectantes* (“following”); Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read *secuti sumus* (“we have followed”).], since they broke the bond of unity; nor his council, since they received the Baptism of the Maximianists.

## CHAPTER III

4. Let us, then, remaining within Cyprian’s example, consider also Cyprian’s council. What does Cyprian say?

“You have heard,” he says, “most beloved colleagues, what our fellow bishop Jubaianus wrote to me, consulting our mediocrity about the unlawful and profane Baptism of heretics; and what I replied to him—namely, affirming what we have affirmed once, twice, and often: that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with the Church’s Baptism.

“Likewise, other letters of Jubaianus were read to you. In them, replying to our letter with sincere and religious devotion, he not only agreed but also gave thanks that he had been instructed.”

From these words of blessed Cyprian we understand that Jubaianus consulted him, what he answered the one consulting him, and that Jubaianus gave thanks because he had been instructed.

Are we to be considered obstinate if we wish to examine that very letter by which Jubaianus was persuaded? For until we too are persuaded—if this can be established by true arguments—Cyprian himself makes us secure in the right of Catholic communion.

5. For he continues and says: “It remains, then, that each of us should state what we think about this matter, judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion if he should think differently.” Therefore he grants me not only the right to continue seeking the truth while retaining the right of communion, but also to think differently. “For,” he says, “none of us has constituted himself bishop of bishops, or by tyrannical terror compelled his colleagues to the necessity of obeying.” What could be gentler? What more humble? Certainly no authority deters us from seeking what is true. “For every bishop,” he says, “has, by virtue of the freedom and power granted to him, his own proper judgment, and he can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another”—I take this, of course, to refer to questions that have not yet been examined with fully clarified precision. For he knew how deeply the whole Church was then engaged in disputation concerning the sacrament, and he left the freedom of inquiry open, so that the truth, once examined, might be disclosed.

For he was not lying, nor was he attempting to catch his simpler colleagues through the wording [Note: [Col. 0142] The Louvain edition alone reads “he wished.”], so that, when they had revealed that they thought differently, he might then decide that they should be excommunicated, contrary to what he had promised. Far be such criminal treachery from so holy a soul. Those who attribute this to such a man, ostensibly to his praise, merely confess that they themselves are such. I could in no way believe that Cyprian—a catholic bishop, a catholic martyr, and, the greater he was, the more he humbled himself in all things so as to find grace before God (Ecclesiasticus 3:20)—had uttered with his lips in the holy council of his colleagues anything other than what he held in his heart, especially since he adds and says:

“But let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and uniquely has the power both to appoint us to the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct” (from the Council of Carthage).

Under such a solemn recollection of judgment, while awaiting the truth and hearing it from his colleagues, would he first have offered them an example of lying? May God avert such madness from any Christian, and all the more from Cyprian! We therefore have the freedom to inquire, granted to us by Cyprian himself in language most gentle and truthful.

## CHAPTER IV

6. His colleagues are now beginning to state their own opinions; but they had heard the letter addressed to Jubaianus. For it was read aloud, as was recalled at the beginning. Let it therefore be read aloud to us as well, so that we too may investigate from it what we ought to think, insofar as the Lord assists us.

Perhaps someone will say: “What, then? Are you now saying what Cyprian wrote to Jubaianus?” I admit that I have already read it, and I certainly would have adopted the same opinion, had not the great authority of others recalled me to more careful consideration—others whom the Church, spread throughout the whole world among Latin, Greek, barbarian, and even Hebrew peoples—a Church which had brought forth them too—was able to produce, some equal in the grace of learning, and perhaps others even more learned, who could not possibly have wished to maintain this opinion without good reason. This is not because it could not happen that, in a very obscure question, one or a few might have a truer opinion than the many; but because a judgment should not readily be delivered in favor of one or a few against countless men of the same religion and unity, endowed with great intelligence and abundant learning, unless the matter has been examined and understood to the extent of one’s ability.

Accordingly, as I investigated more carefully, how much even Cyprian’s own letters suggested to me in support of the opinion now held by the catholic Church—that Christ’s Baptism should be recognized and approved not on the merit of those through whom it is administered, but on that of the one of whom it was said, “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33)—the matter itself will show in the course of our discussion.

Let us therefore suppose that the letter sent by that same man to Jubaianus has already been read to us, just as it was read in the council [Note: [Col. 0143] “Of Carthage.”]. Let the person who is going to read what I am about to say first read it, lest he should think that I have withheld something necessary. It would be too long, and it does not pertain to the explanation of the matter undertaken, for us now to recall every word of this letter.

## CHAPTER V

7. But if anyone asks what position I hold in the meantime, while I examine these matters, I reply that Cyprian’s letters first suggested to me what I should hold, until I could see the character of what was subsequently argued. For Cyprian himself says:

“But someone says: ‘What, then, will become of those who in former times, coming from heresy to the Church, were admitted without Baptism?’” (Epistle 73, to Jubaianus).

Whether these people truly were without Baptism, or whether they were admitted because those who admitted them understood them to possess Baptism, we shall soon consider. Nevertheless, Cyprian himself sufficiently shows what the custom of the Church had been, when he says that those coming from heresy to the Church had formerly been admitted without Baptism.

8. Castus of Sicca also says in the council itself:

“Whoever, disregarding the truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward the brethren to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.”

Whether the truth had been revealed we shall soon inquire; nevertheless, even he confessed that the custom of the Church had once been different.

## CHAPTER VI

9. Libosus of Vaga likewise says:

“In the Gospel the Lord says, ‘I am the truth’” (John 14:6); “he did not say, ‘I am custom.’ Therefore, when the truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth.”

Who, plainly, would doubt that custom ought to yield to manifest truth? But we shall soon see about the manifest truth; for the present, this man too makes clear that the custom had once been different.

## CHAPTER VII

10. Likewise Zosimus of Tharassa said:

“When the truth has been revealed, error must yield to truth; for Peter too, who formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul when Paul preached the truth.”

This man did not wish to say “custom,” but “error.” Nevertheless, when he says, “For Peter too, who formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul when Paul preached the truth,” he sufficiently indicates that another practice concerning Baptism had also been customary. At the same time, he reminds us that it was not impossible for Cyprian to have thought differently about Baptism from what the truth required—a truth that the Church retained both before and after him—just as Peter too could have thought differently from what the truth held, as we learned from the apostle Paul, his teacher (Galatians 2:11–14) [Note: [Col. 0143] Several other books read: “from what the truth did not hold.”].

[Col. 0144]

## CHAPTER VIII

11. Likewise Felix of Buslacena said [Note: [Col. 0144] The printed editions read “of Buslacena”; the manuscripts read “of Buslaceni,” as in Cyprian, or “of Buslacceni.” Thus also the very ancient Corbie manuscript and the manuscript of Fleury.]:

“When heretics are admitted without the Baptism of the Church, let no one place custom above reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom.”

If reason and truth require this, very well; but we shall soon see. In the meantime, the words of this man too show that the custom had once been different.

## CHAPTER IX

12. Likewise Honoratus of Tucca said:

“Since Christ is the truth, we ought to follow truth rather than custom.”

All these opinions make clear that we have not been placed outside the communion of the Church, until the truth which, they say, must be preferred to this custom has clearly come to light. But if the truth has shown that what that custom prescribed ought to be retained, it will be evident both that the custom was not instituted and strengthened without reason, and that, after these debates, the most salutary observance of so great a sacrament could not have been changed in the catholic Church, but was rather confirmed with the greater authority of councils and most religiously preserved.

## CHAPTER X

13. Cyprian therefore writes to Jubaianus concerning the Baptism of heretics. In his view, those who are placed outside and established beyond the Church claim for themselves something that is neither their right nor within their power. “We,” he says, “cannot regard it as valid or legitimate, since it is clearly unlawful among them.”

We do not deny that someone baptized among heretics or in some schism outside the communion of the Church does not benefit from it insofar as he consents to the perversity of heretics and schismatics. Nor do we deny that those who baptize, although they truly confer the true sacrament of Baptism itself, nevertheless do not act rightly in gathering people outside the Church and thinking contrary to the Church. But it is one thing not to possess something, and another not to possess it lawfully or to usurp it unlawfully.

Therefore the Sacraments of Christ and of the Church are not for that reason nonexistent, because not only heretics but also all wicked and ungodly people use them unlawfully. They, however, must be corrected or punished; the sacraments must be recognized and revered.

14. He does indeed say that not one but two or more councils were held concerning this matter, though they were African councils. For he also recalls that in one of them there were seventy-one bishops, but we do not hesitate, with the peace of Cyprian himself, to place above the authority of all those bishops the authority of the universal Church, spread throughout the world with far more bishops—of that universal Church in whose indissoluble member he rejoiced to be.

15. The water over which the name of God is invoked is not profane and adulterous, even if it is invoked by profane and adulterous people, because neither the creature itself nor the name itself is adulterous. Baptism, however, consecrated by the evangelical words of Christ, is holy both when administered by adulterers and when received among adulterers, although they are shameless and unclean. For its holiness itself cannot be polluted, and divine power attends its sacrament, whether for the salvation of those who use it well or for the destruction of those who use it badly.

Or does the light of the sun or even of a lamp, when it is spread through filthy places, contract no defilement from them, while Christ’s Baptism can be polluted by anyone’s crimes? For if we turn our attention to the visible things through which the Sacraments are administered, who does not know that they are corruptible? But if we attend to what is accomplished through them, who does not see that it cannot be corrupted, even though the people through whom it is accomplished either receive rewards or suffer punishments according to their character?

## CHAPTER XI

16. Cyprian was right not to be influenced by what Jubaianus wrote: that the Novatianists rebaptized those who came to them from the Catholic Church. For not everything that heretics perversely imitate is therefore something Catholics ought not to do merely because they do the same thing. But the reason why heretics ought not to rebaptize is one thing, and the reason why the Catholic Church ought not to do so is another.

Heretics ought not to do it even if it ought to be done in the Catholic Church, because they say that Catholics do not possess what they themselves received while they were there and took away when they departed. The Catholic Church, however, ought not to repeat the Baptism given among heretics, lest she seem to judge that what belongs to Christ belongs to them, or lest she seem to say that they do not possess what they received within and cannot lose by going outside.

For Cyprian himself, together with the others, established that those who had been baptized in the Church, if they returned from heresy to the Church, were to be received not through Baptism again but through repentance. Hence it is clear that they cannot lose by departing what they do not receive again when they return.

But just as their heresy is theirs, and their error is theirs, and the sacrilege of their dissension is theirs, so the Baptism that belongs to Christ must not be called theirs. Therefore, when those evils of theirs are corrected upon their return, what is not theirs must be recognized as belonging to the one to whom it belongs.

## CHAPTER XII

17. Blessed Cyprian shows that he had not established something new or sudden by saying that this practice had already begun under Agrippinus.

“It is many years,” he says, “and a long period of time, since, under Agrippinus of blessed memory, many bishops assembled and established this.”

Accordingly, a new practice was introduced by Agrippinus himself. But I do not see how he can say:

“And from that time to the present day, so many thousands of heretics in our provinces who have been converted to the Church have neither rejected nor hesitated, but have rather embraced, reasonably and willingly, the grace of the life-giving and saving Baptismal washing” (Epistle 73, to Jubaianus),

unless perhaps by “from that time to the present day” he means that, since they were baptized in the Church through the council of Agrippinus, no question of excommunication concerning them has arisen.

Otherwise, if the custom of baptizing those coming from heresy continued from Agrippinus to Cyprian, why were councils held by Cyprian concerning this matter? Why does he say to Jubaianus that he is not introducing something new or sudden, but something established by Agrippinus [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions read “instituted.”]? Why would Jubaianus have been disturbed by the novelty, so that he needed to be reassured by the authority of Agrippinus, if the Church had maintained this practice from Agrippinus to Cyprian? Finally, why did so many of his colleagues say in the council that reason and truth must be preferred to custom, instead of saying that those who wished to do otherwise would act both contrary to truth and contrary to custom?

## CHAPTER XIII

18. Concerning the remission of sins—whether it takes place through Baptism among heretics—I have written what I thought in another volume (above, Book 1, chapters 11 and following); but I shall briefly recall it here as well.

If the remission of debts takes place there through the holiness of Baptism, then the debts return again through persistence in heresy or schism. Therefore such people must come to catholic peace, so that they may cease to be heretics and schismatics and may, through the charity operative in the bond of unity, merit purification from the sins that had returned upon them.

But if, although Christ’s Baptism is the same among heretics or schismatics, it nevertheless does not work the remission of sins there because of the same foulness of discord and wickedness of dissension, then that same Baptism begins to avail for the forgiveness of sins when they come to the peace of the Church—not [Note: [Col. 0146] The negative particle is omitted in the Ambrosian edition. It is also absent from several manuscripts, which subsequently read “not as that one” in place of “nor as that one.”] as though sins already truly forgiven were not retained, nor as though that Baptism were rejected as foreign or different and another were to be conferred, but so that the very same Baptism, which outside had worked death because of discord, might inside work salvation because of peace.

For it was the same fragrance of which the Apostle says, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” [Note: [Col. 0146] The printed editions read, “We are God’s fragrance in every place.” The word “God’s” is absent from the manuscripts and is usually omitted by Augustine.]; and yet he says, “both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one, a fragrance of life unto life; to the other, a fragrance of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). Although he said this about another matter, I have applied it here so that it may be understood that something good can produce not only life for those who use it well, but also death for those who use it badly.

## CHAPTER XIV

19. When the integrity and holiness of the sacrament are under discussion, it does not matter what the recipient believes or with what kind of faith he has been formed. It matters greatly, certainly, for the way of salvation, but it has no bearing on the question of the sacrament.

For it can happen that a person possesses the sacrament intact while holding a perverse faith, just as it can happen that he retains the words of the Creed intact and nevertheless does not believe correctly—whether concerning the Trinity itself, or the resurrection, or something else. It is no small matter to possess within the Catholic Church an intact faith, so that one believes nothing concerning any creature, but concerning God himself, differently from what the truth holds.
