If, then, someone baptized in the Catholic Church should later, through reading, hearing, and peaceful discussion, come to know, with the Lord revealing it, that he previously believed differently from what he ought, must he be baptized again? What fleshly and natural person does not wander through the phantasms [Note: [Col. 0146] Thus the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions and our manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads, “Who, then, unless he is a fleshly and natural person, wanders through phantasms,” and so forth.] of his heart and fashion for himself a god such as pleases him according to his carnal understanding, and thus believe about God in a way as far different from what God is as vanity differs from truth?

The Apostle, full of the light of truth, stated a most truthful judgment:

“The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

And yet he said this about people whom he himself plainly shows had already been baptized. For he says to them:

“Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

These people therefore possessed the sacrament of Baptism; yet, thinking carnally, what could they believe about God except according to the perception of their flesh, where the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God?

To such people he says:

“I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly people. As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. Indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still fleshly” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

Such people too are carried about by every wind of doctrine, of whom he says [Note: [Col. 0147] The manuscripts read, “of whom he says.”]:

“So that we may no longer be infants, tossed and carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14).

If, then, these people should progress to the spiritual maturity of the inner person and, through sincere understanding, recognize how differently they had believed about God through the deception of their phantasms from what the truth required, must they be baptized again?

Likewise, it can happen that a catholic catechumen comes upon a book by some heretic and, not knowing how to distinguish error from the truth, believes something contrary to the catholic faith, although the words of the Creed do not contradict that error. For innumerable heretical errors have arisen under those same words.

Suppose, then, that this person, thinking the book belongs to some great and learned Catholic, is baptized in the Catholic Church while believing such things, and later, through more careful study, learns how he ought to believe and, having embraced the catholic faith, rejects that former belief from his heart. If he confesses this, must he be baptized again?

Or if, before he learns and makes this confession, he is found to hold this opinion, is taught what he ought to reject and what he ought to believe, and it becomes clear that he was baptized while holding that false belief, must he be baptized again? Why not? Because the holiness of the sacrament, consecrated by the evangelical words, remained intact in him, just as he had received it when it was administered, although, while established in the vanity of a carnal mind, he believed at his baptism something other than what he ought to have believed.

Therefore it is clear that the sacrament of Baptism can remain intact in someone whose faith is not intact; and for that reason the things said about the variety of different heretics do not pertain to this question. In each person, what must be corrected is what the one correcting him has recognized to be wrong. What is sick must be healed; what is lacking must be given—and above all, the charity of peace, without which the other things cannot benefit. Yet when these things are present, they are not to be conferred as though they were absent; rather, action must be taken so that they may be possessed fruitfully and not harmfully through the bond of peace and the excellence of charity.

## CHAPTER XV

20. Therefore, if Marcion consecrated Baptism with the evangelical words, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), the sacrament was intact, although his faith—since under those same words he held an opinion different from what catholic truth teaches—was not intact, but polluted by fabulous falsehoods [Note: [Col. 0148] Compare the First Council of Arles, canon 8.].

For under those same words, namely, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” there might be found not only Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, or Eunomius, but also the fleshly infants of the Church themselves—those to whom the Apostle said, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly people.” If each of them could be carefully questioned, perhaps as many different opinions as people would be counted. For “the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.”

Do they therefore fail to receive the sacrament intact? Or, if they progress and correct the vanity of their carnal opinions, must what they received be administered to them again?

Each person receives according to his faith, but only as much as he grasps under the guidance of that mercy of God [Note: [Col. 0148] The Louvain edition reads “him”; our manuscripts, together with the Ambrosian and Erasmian editions, read “that mercy.”], relying upon which the same Apostle says:

“If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you” (Philippians 3:15).

Nevertheless, the snares of heretics and schismatics are exceedingly harmful to the fleshly because their progress itself is obstructed: their vain judgment is confirmed against catholic truth, and the obstinacy of their dissension is confirmed against catholic peace.

Yet if the Sacraments are the same, they are intact everywhere, even if they are wrongly understood and administered amid discord, just as the text of the Gospel itself, if it is the same, is intact everywhere, even if it is asserted amid an innumerable variety of false opinions.

For if Jeremiah’s words, “Why do those who distress me prevail? My wound is solid; how shall I be healed? In becoming so, it has become for me like deceitful water that has no faith” (Jeremiah 15:18), were set down figuratively and allegorically, and nowhere in prophetic speech did “water” signify anything except Baptism, we would struggle to discover what Jeremiah’s words meant. But since in the Apocalypse waters are most plainly explained as representing peoples (Revelation 17:15), why should I not understand deceitful and faithless water as a deceitful and faithless people? I do not know.

## CHAPTER XVI

21. Our predecessors wished the statement that the Holy Spirit is given only in the Catholic Church through the laying on of hands to be understood in accordance with what the Apostle says:

“Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

This is the very love that those who have been cut off from communion with the catholic Church do not possess. Consequently, even if they speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, if they know all the mysteries and possess all knowledge, and if they have all prophecy and all faith so as to move mountains, and distribute all their possessions to the poor, and hand over their bodies to be burned, it profits them nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

Those who do not love the unity of the Church do not possess the love of God; consequently, it is rightly understood that the Holy Spirit is received only in the Catholic Church.

For the Holy Spirit is not now given through the laying on of hands with the temporal and perceptible miracles that once attested it, as it was formerly given to commend the beginning of the faith and to enlarge the Church at its origins. Who now expects that those upon whom hands are laid for the reception of the Holy Spirit will suddenly begin to speak in tongues? Rather, it is understood to be inspired invisibly and secretly in their hearts, on account of the bond of peace, so that they may say:

“Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

There are, however, many works of the Holy Spirit. When the same Apostle had recalled as many of them in one place as he thought sufficient, he concluded:

“But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing them individually to each person as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

Since, therefore, one thing is the sacrament which Simon Magus too could possess (Acts 8:13), another is the operation of the Spirit, which often occurs even in wicked people, as Saul possessed prophecy (1 Samuel 10:6, 10), and another is the operation of that same Spirit which only the good can possess, such as “the fulfillment of the commandment: love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5), whatever heretics and schismatics may receive, the love that covers a multitude of sins is the proper gift of catholic unity and peace—and not of all within it, since not all belong to it, as we shall see in its place.

Nevertheless, that love cannot exist apart from it; without that love, the other things, even if they can be recognized and approved, cannot benefit or set free.

The laying on of hands, however, unlike Baptism, can be repeated. For what is it other than prayer over a person? [Note: [Col. 0149] Such is the laying on of hands of which below, in Book 5, chapter 23, it is said: “But if the laying on of hands were not administered to one coming from heresy, he would be judged to be free from every fault.”]

## CHAPTER XVII

22. Since the Lord, as a figure of unity, gave Peter the power that what he loosed on earth should be loosed, it is clear that this unity was also called the one perfect dove. Do all the greedy people, then, about whom that same Cyprian lamented grievously within the Catholic Church, belong to the same dove? For, in my opinion, robbers may be called not doves but hawks.

How, then, did those people baptize who seized estates through treacherous frauds and increased their interest through multiplying usury (Book or Letter on the Lapsed), if that dove alone—that is, that unity which can be understood only in the good, as simple, chaste, and perfect—baptizes?

Or perhaps, through the prayers of the spiritual saints who are in the Church, as through the dove’s most persistent lament, a great sacramental work is accomplished, and God’s mercy is secretly administered, so that even the sins of those who are baptized not by the dove but by the hawk may be forgiven if they approach that sacrament in the peace of catholic unity.

But if this is so, why then are the sins of anyone coming from heresy or schism to catholic peace not forgiven through their prayers?

The integrity of the sacrament is recognized everywhere, but outside the unity of the Church it will not avail for that irrevocable remission of sins. Nor can the prayers of the saints—that is, the lament of that one dove—help someone established in heresy or schism, just as they cannot help someone placed within if he himself, through a most wicked life, retains the debts of his sins against himself, whether he is baptized by a hawk or even through the pious ministry of the dove itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII

23. “As the Father sent me,” he says, “so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said:

“Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

Therefore, if they represented the person of the Church, and this was said to them as though it were said to the Church herself, the peace of the Church forgives sins, and alienation from the peace of the Church retains sins—not according to human judgment, but according to the judgment of God and the prayers of the spiritual saints, who judge all things but are themselves judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2:15).

The rock retains; the rock forgives. The dove retains; the dove forgives. Unity retains; unity forgives.

The peace of this unity, however, exists only in the good—whether those already spiritual or those progressing toward spiritual things through harmonious obedience. It does not exist in the wicked, whether they rage outside or are endured inside amid lamentation, baptizing and being baptized.

Just as those who are endured inside amid lamentation, although they do not belong to the same unity of the dove or to that glorious Church without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind (Ephesians 5:27) [Note: [Col. 0150] See Two Books of Retractations, chapter 18], nevertheless, if they are corrected and confess that they approached Baptism in a most wicked state, are not rebaptized but begin to belong to the dove, through whose lamentation sins are forgiven, whereas those alienated from its peace were held fast in their sins [Note: [Col. 0150] The Louvain edition reads, “those alienated were held fast”; less well], so also those who are more openly outside, if they have received the same Sacraments, when corrected and coming to the unity of the Church, are freed not through Baptism repeated but through the same law of charity and bond of unity.

For if it is permissible to baptize only for those placed in authority within the Church and founded upon the evangelical law and the Lord’s ordinance, were those who seized estates through treacherous frauds and increased interest through multiplying usury such people? I suppose that those are founded upon the Lord’s ordinance to whom the Apostle gave this rule:

“Not greedy, not given to sordid gain” (Titus 1:7) [Note: [Col. 0150] Two editions, the Ambrosian and Erasmian, read “the Lord’s prayer”; incorrectly. The Vulgate has “desiring sordid gain,” as do certain editions; but the manuscripts, and Augustine himself elsewhere, have “given to sordid gain.” M.]

Yet such people baptized in the times of Cyprian himself. He confesses with great lamentation that they were his fellow bishops, and endures them with the great reward of patience. Nevertheless, they did not grant the remission of sins, which is given through the prayers of the saints—that is, through the lamentation of the dove—whoever the baptizer may be, if those to whom it is given belong to the dove’s peace.

For the Lord would not say to robbers and usurers, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they will be retained.” Outside, nothing can be bound or loosed where there is no one who can bind or loose; but the person is loosed who makes peace with the dove, and the person is bound who has no peace with the dove, whether he is openly outside or appears to be inside.

24. We know that Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, who attempted to usurp for themselves the right to sacrifice against the unity of God’s people, and Aaron’s sons, who placed strange fire upon the altar, did not do so with impunity (Numbers 16; Leviticus 10:1–2). Nor do we say that such crimes remain unpunished unless those people correct themselves, if God’s patience, leading them to repentance (Romans 2:4), grants time for correction.

## CHAPTER XIX

25. Those who say that Baptism should not be repeated because only hands were laid upon those whom the deacon Philip had baptized (Acts 8:5–17) are making an argument irrelevant to the matter. Far be it from us, when seeking the truth, to use such arguments.

Therefore we yield even less to heretics [Note: [Col. 0151] For Cyprian subsequently writes in his letter to Jubaianus: “Therefore, dearest brother, we ought not to think that we should yield to heretics, so as to suppose that the Baptism given to the one and only Church should be betrayed.”] if we say that what they possess from the Church of Christ does not belong to them, and if, because of the crimes of those who have deserted the Emperor, we do not refuse to recognize his insignia.

Rather, because the Lord our God is a jealous God (Deuteronomy 4:24), whatever of his we recognize in someone, we should in no way allow that person to regard it as his own possession. That jealous God himself reproaches the woman who fornicates against him, in the figure of the transgressing people, and says that she gave her lovers what belonged to him, and again received from them things that were not theirs but his.

Among the adulterous woman and her adulterous lovers, God, like a jealous man in anger, nevertheless recognizes his own gifts. And we call the Baptism consecrated by the evangelical words the Baptism of heretics, moved by their deeds to attribute to them even things that belong to God, as though they could have contaminated them, or as though they could make God’s things their own simply because they themselves refused to belong to God?

### 26

What is that adulterous woman whom the prophet Hosea depicts, saying: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my garments and my linens, and everything that is suitable for me” (Hos. 2:1–13)? Certainly this may also be understood of the treacherous people of the Jews. But whom do the pseudo-Christians—for all heretics and schismatics are such—imitate, if not the pseudo-Israelites? For there were also true Israelites, as the Lord himself bears witness to Nathanael, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

But who are the true Christians except those of whom the same Lord says: “He who loves me keeps my commandments” (John 14:21)? What is it to keep his commandments except to persist in love? Hence he also says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”; and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:34–35). Who could doubt that these words were spoken not only to those who then heard the words of the one present in the flesh, but also to those who now learn through the Gospel the words of the one seated in heaven? For he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17). “The fulfillment of the Law is love” [Col. 0152] (Rom. 13:10).

Cyprian abounded greatly in this love: although he held a different opinion concerning Baptism, he nevertheless did not abandon unity, and was a fruitful branch rooted in the Lord’s vine, which the heavenly farmer would also cleanse with the knife of suffering, so that it might bear greater fruit (John 15:1–5). The enemies of this fraternal love, whether they are openly outside or seem to be within, are pseudo-Christians and antichrists. When they find opportunities, they go out, as it is written: “He who wishes to separate seeks opportunities” (Prov. 18:1). But even if opportunities are lacking, when they seem to be within, they are separated from that invisible bond of love. Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19). He does not say that they became alien by going out; rather, he declared that they went out because they were alien.

The apostle Paul also speaks of certain people who had wandered from the truth and were overturning the faith of some, whose speech was spreading like gangrene. Although he said that they were to be avoided, he nevertheless indicates that they had been in one great house, but as vessels for dishonor. I believe that they had not yet gone out. Or, if they had already gone out, how does he say that they were in the same great house with the honorable vessels, unless perhaps, because of the Sacraments—which remain unchanged even in the separated gatherings of heretics—he says that all belong to one great house, but with different merits: some to honor, others to dishonor?

For this is how he writes to Timothy:

> “Avoid profane novelties of words; for they will advance greatly toward impiety, and their speech will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have wandered from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overturn the faith of some. But the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’; and, ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.’ But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; and some indeed are for honor, while others are for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from such things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Tim. 2:16–21).

What is it to cleanse oneself from such people except to do what he said shortly before: “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness”? And lest anyone suppose that, as though in one great house, he could perish together with such people, he very carefully declared beforehand: “The Lord knows those who are his”—namely, those who, by departing from iniquity, cleanse themselves from vessels made for dishonor, so that they may not perish together with those whom they are compelled to tolerate in the great house.

### 27

Thus the wicked and criminal—carnal, animal, and devilish people—believe that the things which are exclusively God’s gifts, whether Sacraments or certain spiritual operations concerning the present salvation, are given to them by their deceivers. But these people do not possess love for God; rather, they are preoccupied with those whose pride deceives them. They are compared with the adulterous woman whom the prophet mentions as saying: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my garments [Col. 0153] and my linens and my oil, and everything that is suitable for me.”

Thus heresies and schisms arise, when the carnal people, who are not founded upon the love of God, say: “I will go after my lovers”—with whom they disgracefully commit fornication, whether through the corruption of faith or through the exaltation of pride.

But for the sake of those who, having suffered the difficulties, hardships, and blockages of the empty reasoning of those by whom they are deceived [Note: [Col. 0153] Am. and Er.: “in various reasonings”; several manuscripts: “in vain reasonings.”], are pierced by fear and return to the way of peace in order to seek God sincerely, the passage continues and says:

> “Therefore, behold, I will hedge up her way with stakes, and I will build thorns across her path, and she will not find her track. She will pursue her lovers, but will not overtake them; she will seek them, but will not find them. And she will say, ‘I will go and return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than now.’”

[Note: [Col. 0153] In the manuscripts: “and they return to the way of peace and seek God sincerely.”]

Then, lest the things which the deceivers possess intact and which come from the doctrine of truth—through which they deceive people into the falsehoods of their doctrines and dissensions—be thought to belong to them, he immediately added:

> “And she did not know that I had given her grain and wine and oil, and had multiplied money for her; but she made vessels of gold and silver for Baal” (Hos. 2:5–8).

For earlier she had said: “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread,” and so forth, not understanding that all these things belonged to God, not to human beings—even when the deceivers hold what is intact and legitimate. They would not claim these things for themselves and, as though they were their own, assert ownership over them, unless they in turn were deceived by the deceived peoples, when they are believed and such honors are paid to them that through these they acquire the power to say and claim such things for themselves—so that their error is called truth and their crime is considered righteousness, on account of the Sacraments and Scriptures which they possess for appearance, not for salvation.

Therefore, through Ezekiel also, the same adulterous woman is addressed:

> “And you took from the vessels of your glory, from my gold and my silver, which I had given you; and you made for yourself male images, and committed fornication with them. And you took my multicolored garment and covered your idols with it; and you placed my oil and my incense before your idols; and my bread, which I had given you, and fine flour and honey and oil, with which I had fed you, you placed before your idols as a pleasing fragrance. And you completed these things” (Ezek. 16:17–19).

For she turns all the Sacraments and the words of the holy Books toward the images of her fantasies, with which the carnal soul delights to wallow. [Col. 0154] Yet because those images are false and are doctrines of demons, spoken in the hypocrisy of liars (1 Tim. 4:1–2), the Sacraments and divine utterances must not on their account be so dishonored that they are considered to belong to those images. The Lord says that they are his: “My gold and my silver and my multicolored garment, my oil and incense and bread,” and the rest.

Or, because those wandering people think that these things belong to the ones by whom they are deceived, should we therefore fail to recognize whose they are, when he himself says: “And she did not know that I had given her grain, wine, and oil, and had multiplied silver for her”? For he did not say that she had not possessed these things because she was an adulterous woman; rather, she is said both to have possessed them and not to have possessed them as her own or as belonging to her lovers, but as belonging to God, whose alone they are.

Therefore, although she possessed her fornication, the things with which she adorned that same fornication, whether deceived or deceiving, were not hers but God’s.

If these things were figuratively represented by the Jewish people, among whom the scribes and Pharisees rejected God’s commandment in order to establish their own traditions, and thus in a certain way committed fornication with the people that was abandoning God, nevertheless the fornication of that people at that time—which the Lord exposed by his rebuke—did not make their Sacraments belong to them, since those Sacraments were not theirs but God’s. He speaks to the adulterous woman and declares that all those things are his. Hence the Lord himself sent even those whom he had cleansed of leprosy to the same Sacraments, so that they might offer a sacrifice for themselves to the priests, because the sacrifice which he later willed to be celebrated in the Church for all those people had not yet replaced them; for he himself was foretold through all those things.

How much more, then, should we, when we find the Sacraments of the New Testament among whatever heretics or schismatics, neither attribute them to those people nor reject them as though they were unrecognized? Rather, just as one may recognize the gifts of a legitimate husband in an adulterous woman and correct, by the word of truth, the fornication that belongs to the shameless woman, without condemning the gifts that belong to the Lord who shows mercy, so should we act here.

### 28

In consideration of these and similar matters, our fathers—not only before Cyprian or Agrippinus, but also afterward—maintained the most salutary custom of approving rather than denying whatever divine and legitimate element they found intact in any heresy or schism; but whatever was alien and properly characteristic of that error or dissension, they truthfully reproved and healed.

However, the matters that remain to be considered from the letter written to Jubaianus must, because of the length of this volume, be taken up and treated from another beginning, as I think.

## BOOK FOUR

In this book he treats what follows in the same letter of Cyprian to Jubaianus.

[Col. 0153]

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1

The comparison of the Church with paradise (Cyprian, Letter 73, to Jubaianus) indicates to us that people can indeed receive its Baptism even outside it, but that no one can either attain or retain outside it the salvation of blessedness. For the rivers from the spring of paradise, as Scripture testifies, also flowed out abundantly beyond it. They are specifically mentioned, including the lands through which they flow; and it is known to everyone that they were established outside paradise (Gen. 2:8–14). Yet in Mesopotamia or Egypt, wherever those rivers reached, there is not the happiness of life that is mentioned as existing in paradise.

Thus it happens that although the water of paradise is outside paradise, blessedness is nevertheless found only within paradise. In the same way, the Baptism of the Church can exist outside the Church, but the gift of blessed life is found only within the Church. She is also founded upon the rock and has received the keys of binding and loosing (Matt. 16:18–19). She alone holds and possesses all the authority of her bridegroom and Lord. Through this marital authority she can also bear children from servant women; if they do not become proud, they will be called to the share of the inheritance, but if they become proud, they will remain outside.

### CHAPTER TWO

#### 2

Since, then, we are fighting for the honor and unity of the Church, let us not attribute to heretics whatever element of the Church we recognize among them. Rather, while reproving them, let us teach them that what they possess from unity is of no value for salvation unless they come to that same unity.

The water of the Church is faithful, salutary, and holy for those who use it rightly. No one can use it rightly outside the Church. For those who use it wrongly, whether outside or within, it is borne toward punishment, not granted as a support toward reward.

Therefore Baptism cannot be corrupted or adulterated, even if it is possessed by corrupt and adulterous people—just as the Church herself is incorrupt, chaste, and pure. For this reason avaricious people, robbers, and usurers do not belong to her. Yet Cyprian himself testifies in many passages of his writings that such people are found not only outside but also within; nevertheless, they are baptized and baptize without a change of heart.

#### 3

For in one of his letters he says this as well (Letter 11, to the Clergy), writing to the clergy about praying to God and, like the holy Daniel, taking upon himself the sins of his people. Among the many evils that he mentions, he also says:

> “They renounce the world in words only and not in deeds,”

as the Apostle says of certain people:

> “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

Thus blessed Cyprian accuses of remaining within the Church those who are baptized without a change of heart, since they renounce the world in words but not in deeds. Yet the apostle Peter says:

> “Baptism now saves you in a corresponding way—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience” (1 Pet. 3:21).

They certainly did not possess such a conscience, of whom it is said: “They renounce the world in words only and not in deeds.” Nevertheless, by rebuking and reproving them he seeks to bring them eventually to walk in the way of Christ and to prefer to be his friends rather than friends of the world.

### CHAPTER THREE

If they had obeyed him and had already begun to live rightly—not as pseudo-Christians but as true Christians—would he command them to be baptized again? Certainly not. Rather, their true conversion would accomplish this for them: the Sacrament, which when they were unchanged was effective for destruction, would begin, once they had changed, to be effective for salvation.

#### 4

Those who seem to be within and live against Christ—that is, who act against Christ’s commandments—are not devoted to the Church (Cyprian, Letter 73, to Jubaianus). Nor should they at all be judged to belong to that Church which he himself cleanses with the washing of water in the word, so that he may present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind (Eph. 5:26–27).

If they are not in this Church, and do not belong to her members, they are not in the Church of which it is said: “My dove is one, she is the only one of her mother” (Song 6:8). For she is without spot and wrinkle. Let whoever can assert that those who renounce the world in words but not in deeds are members of this dove.

For the present, we see something [Note: [Col. 0156] Am., Er., and the manuscripts: “toward which we see.”], from which I believe the saying is derived: “He who observes the day, observes it for the Lord” (Rom. 14:6), for God judges every day.

According to the foreknowledge of God, who knows those whom he predestined before the foundation of the world to be conformed to the image of his Son [Note: [Col. 0156] The printed editions have “to become conformed to the image.” “To become” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.], many who are openly outside and are called heretics are better than many good Catholics. What they are today, we see; what they will be tomorrow, we do not know. Before God, indeed, with whom future things are present, what they will be is already the case. But we, according to what each person is at present, ask whether they should today be counted among those members of the Church called the one dove and the bride of Christ, without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0156] Second Book of Retractions, chapter 18].

Of such people Cyprian says in the letter I mentioned that they do not hold the way of the Lord or keep the heavenly commandments given to them for salvation, and that they do not do the Lord’s will:

> “They devote themselves to wealth and profit, pursue pride, occupy themselves with rivalry and dissension, neglect simplicity and faith, renounce the world in words only and not in deeds, each one pleasing himself and displeasing everyone” (Letter 11, to the Clergy).

If that dove does not recognize them among her members, and if the Lord will say to such people, should they persist in the same perversity, “I do not know you; depart from me, you who practice iniquity” (Matt. 7:23), they seem to be in the Church, but they are not; indeed, they act against the Church.

How, then, can they baptize with the Baptism of the Church (Letter 73, to Jubaianus)—a Baptism that benefits neither themselves nor those who receive it, unless they are changed inwardly through true conversion, so that the very Sacrament which did not benefit them when they renounced the world in words but not in deeds begins to benefit them once they also begin to renounce it in deeds?

So too with those whose separation is open: neither these nor those are today among the members of that dove, although some of them may perhaps become so in the future.

### CHAPTER FOUR

#### 5

We do not, then, accept the Baptism of heretics when we do not baptize those who come after them. Rather, because we recognize what belongs to Christ even in evil people—whether openly outside or secretly separated within—we receive it with the reverence due to it, after correcting them in the matter in which they had gone astray.

But just as I seem to be pressed when someone says to me, “Then does a heretic forgive sins?” so I press the matter in turn when I say: “Then does one who does not keep the heavenly commandments—an avaricious person, robber, usurer, envious person, one who renounces the world in words but not in deeds—forgive sins?”

If it is through the power of God’s Sacrament, then the one as well as the other does so; if through his own merit, neither the one nor the other. For that Sacrament is recognized as belonging to Christ even in evil people. But neither the one nor the other is found in the body of the one dove, incorrupt, holy, pure, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27) [Note: [Col. 0157] Second Book of Retractions, chapter 18].

And just as Baptism does not benefit the person who renounces the world in words but not in deeds, so it does not benefit the person baptized in heresy or schism. Yet once either has been corrected, what previously did not benefit him begins to benefit him, although it was already present.

#### 6

Therefore, someone baptized in heresy does not become a temple of God. But is he for that reason not to be regarded as baptized? An avaricious person baptized within the Church likewise does not become a temple of God if he has not departed from avarice. For those who become the temple of God certainly possess the kingdom of God. But the Apostle says, among other things:

> “Neither the avaricious nor the robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

In another passage the same Apostle compares avarice with the service of idols:

> “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5).

Cyprian developed this interpretation in his letter to Antonianus to such an extent that he did not hesitate to compare avaricious people with those whose sin consisted in professing, during the time of persecution, that they would offer incense by means of certificates [Note: [Col. 0157] Several manuscripts: “the sins of those who … he did not hesitate to compare with the avaricious.”] (Cyprian, Letter 55, to Antonianus).

Thus, someone baptized in heresy in the name of the Holy Trinity nevertheless does not become a temple of God if he does not depart from heresy, just as one baptized in the same name while living in avarice does not become a temple of God if he does not depart from avarice, which is the service of idols. The same Apostle also says:

> “What agreement does the temple of God have with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:16).

Let us not, then, be asked whose temple the person becomes when we say that he does not become a temple of God. Yet he is not for that reason unbaptized, nor does his impure error make the holy Sacrament which he received, consecrated by evangelical words, cease to be holy. In the same way, the avarice of the other—an avarice that is the service of idols and a great impurity—cannot make the holy Baptism which he receives cease to be holy, even if he is baptized by another avaricious person through the same evangelical words.

### CHAPTER FIVE

#### 7

“Therefore,” he says, “some people who are defeated by argument bring custom against us in vain, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters we ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit.”

This is certainly true, because reason and truth are to be preferred to custom. But when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly. Then he continues and says:

> “For simple error can be forgiven, as the apostle Paul says of himself: ‘Although I was previously a blasphemer and a persecutor and an insolent man, I received mercy because I acted ignorantly’” (1 Tim. 1:13).

> “But after inspiration and revelation have been given, a person who knowingly and deliberately persists in what he had erred in sins without the excuse of ignorance. For he relies upon a kind of presumption and obstinacy when he is defeated by reason.”

This is entirely true: the sin of the person who sins knowingly is much more serious than that of the person who sins unknowingly.

And therefore, since the holy man Cyprian was not only learned [Col. 0158] but also teachable—understanding this as something to be praised in a bishop, as the Apostle indicates (2 Tim. 2:24), so that he said that it should be valued in a bishop not only that he teach knowingly but also that he learn patiently (Letter 64, to Pompeius)—I have no doubt that if he had discussed this question, which had long and extensively been debated in the Church, with the most holy and learned men through whom it later came about that the ancient custom was confirmed by a plenary council, he would have shown without hesitation not only how learned he was in the matters he had grasped with the firmest truth, but also how teachable he was in matters to which he had paid less attention.

And yet, since it is perfectly clear that the person who sins knowingly sins much more seriously than the one who sins unknowingly, I should like someone to tell me: if one person falls into heresy without knowing how great an evil it is, while another does not depart from avarice while knowing how great an evil it is, which of them is worse?

I can also put the question this way: if one person unknowingly rushes into heresy, while another knowingly does not depart from idolatry—since the Apostle says, “Avarice, which is the service of idols”—and Cyprian himself understood the same statement in no other way, as I said, when writing to Antonianus, where he says (Letter 55, to Antonianus):

> “Let heretics not flatter themselves in this matter, saying that they do not share with idolaters, when among them too there are adulterers and fraudulent people who are held under the charge of idolatry. ‘For know this with understanding: no fornicator, or impure person, or fraudulent person, who is an idolater, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God’ (Eph. 5:5). And again: ‘Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols’ (Col. 3:5).”

I ask, then, who sins more seriously: the person who unknowingly falls into heresy, or the person who knowingly does not depart from avarice, that is, from idolatry?

According to the rule by which the sins of those who know are placed above the sins of those who are ignorant, the avaricious person, with knowledge, surpasses the other in wickedness. But lest perhaps the magnitude of the crime itself have the same effect in the case of heresy as knowingly committing avarice does in the case of avarice, let the ignorant heretic be equated with the knowing avaricious person.

Nevertheless, the testimony which Cyprian himself quoted does not seem to show this. For what do we detest in heretics except blasphemies? But, wishing to demonstrate that ignorance pertains to the ease of receiving forgiveness for sin [Note: [Col. 0158] Am. and Er. and certain manuscripts: “that the sins of the ignorant pertain to forgiveness.”], he quoted the Apostle’s testimony in which he says:

> “Although I was previously a blasphemer and a persecutor and an insolent man, I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (1 Tim. 1:13).

But if, as I said, the sins of both can be weighed equally—the blasphemy of the ignorant person and the idolatry of the knowledgeable person—and judged by the same sentence, then why is the Baptism and evangelical language of the person who, while seeking Christ, falls into a plausible statement of falsehood rejected, while those of the person who knowingly resists Christ speaking through the Apostle are approved?

The Apostle says:

> “Every fornicator, or impure person, or avaricious person, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.”

Both are found to be alien from the members of the dove. Is it because the first is an openly contentious person outside, who is not to be admitted, while the second is a crafty flatterer within, who is not to be cast outside?

### CHAPTER SIX

#### 8

As for his statement, “Let no one say, ‘What we received from the Apostles, that is what we follow,’” since the Apostles handed down only one Church and one Baptism, which was established only in that same Church, this does not move me so much that I would dare reject the Baptism of Christ even when it is found among heretics—just as, when I find the Gospel itself among them, I must approve it, although I detest their error—as it reminds me that in the time of holy Cyprian there were certain people who said that the custom opposed by the African councils, about which he himself had shortly before said, “Some who are defeated by argument bring custom against us in vain,” had been handed down by the Apostles.

I cannot see why he found this custom—which after Cyprian was also confirmed by a plenary council of the whole world—so firmly established even before his time that, when a man of such learning sought an authority for changing it which he could follow, he found only the council of Agrippinus, held in Africa alone a few years before him.

When he saw that this was insufficient against the custom of the whole world, he adopted the arguments that we, now considering them more carefully because of the antiquity of the custom itself and the authority of the plenary council subsequently established, find to be plausible rather than true. They seemed true to him as he struggled with an exceedingly obscure question and was uncertain whether the remission of sins can fail to occur in the Baptism of Christ, and whether it can occur among heretics.

If something was revealed to him less fully, so that the greatness of his love—which did not abandon unity—might be demonstrated, no one should therefore dare to place himself above him because, admonished by the firmness of the universal council, he sees something that Cyprian did not see, since the Church did not yet possess a plenary council concerning this matter.

Nor is anyone so insane as to place himself above the merits of the apostle Peter because, instructed by the writings of the apostle Paul and strengthened by the now-established custom of the Church, he does not compel the Gentiles to Judaize, although Peter once did compel them to do so (Gal. 2:14).

#### 9

We do not, then, find that any person who had been baptized among heretics was admitted by the Apostles in that same Baptism and entered into communion. Nor do we find that anyone coming from the heretics who had been baptized among them was baptized again by the Apostles.

But that custom—which even then people looking upward did not see to have been instituted by those who came later—is rightly believed to have been handed down by the Apostles. There are many such examples, but it would take too long to repeat them.

Therefore, if those people were saying something significant when Cyprian, wishing to persuade him of what seemed right to him, said, “Let no one say, ‘What we received from the Apostles, that is what we follow,’” how much more firmly do we now say:

> “What the custom of the Church has always maintained, what this disputation could not dissuade, and what the plenary council confirmed—that is what we follow.”

Moreover, after carefully considering the arguments on both sides of the dispute and the testimonies of Scripture, it may also be said:

> “What truth has made clear—that is what we follow.”

### CHAPTER SEVEN

#### 10

For in truth, the statement that certain people opposed to Cyprian’s arguments—“Nevertheless, in every way, whether through opportunity or through truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:18)—is correctly refuted by Cyprian, who shows that it does not pertain to the case of the heretics.

The Apostle was speaking of people who, with malicious envy and seeking their own interests, were living within the Church. They proclaimed Christ as the truth requires, the truth by which we believe in Christ, but not with the spirit in which he was proclaimed by the good evangelists, the sons of that dove.

“Nor was Paul speaking,” he says, “of heretics or of their Baptism in his letter, so that he could be shown to have said anything relevant to this matter. He was speaking of brothers who either walked disorderly and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline or who preserved evangelical truth with the fear of God.”

Of these people, he says that some spoke the word of God consistently and fearlessly, while others were occupied with envy and dissension; some preserved kindly love toward him, while others possessed malicious disagreement. Nevertheless, he patiently endured everything, provided that, whether in truth or through opportunity, the name of Christ which Paul preached might reach the knowledge of many, and that the propagation of the new and still unformed message might grow through the preaching of those who spoke.

Moreover, it is one thing for those who are within the Church to speak in the name of Christ, and another for those who are outside and act against the Church to baptize in the name of Christ (Letter 73, to Jubaianus).

These words of Cyprian seem to admonish us to distinguish between those who are evil outside and those who are evil within. He says that those of whom the Apostle states that they proclaimed the Gospel impurely and out of envy were within, and he says this truly.

Yet I think I may say this without rashness: if no one outside can possess anything that belongs to Christ, then no one inside can possess anything that belongs to the devil. If that enclosed garden could contain the thorns of the devil, why could the spring of Christ not also flow outside the garden? But if it could not, how could there have been, among those who were within even in the time of the apostle Paul himself, such a great evil as envy and malicious dissension?

These are Cyprian’s words. Or is envy and malicious dissension perhaps a small evil? How, then, were these people in unity when they were not in peace? For the voice was not mine or that of any human being, but the voice of the Lord himself; and it sounded not through human beings but through angels when Christ was born:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

This angelic proclamation would certainly not have sounded at the earthly birth of Christ unless God intended it to be understood that those who are in the peace of Christ are in the unity of the body of Christ, and that those who are of good will are in the peace of Christ.

Just as good will exists in benevolence, so evil will exists in malevolence.

### CHAPTER EIGHT

#### 11

But how great an evil is envy itself, which cannot exist except as malevolence? [Col. 0161] Let us not seek other witnesses: Cyprian himself is sufficient for us. Through him the Lord thundered so many most truthful warnings about jealousy and envy and gave such salutary commands.

Let us therefore read Cyprian’s letter on jealousy and envy and see how great an evil it is to envy those who are better—a fault whose origin he memorably teaches to have arisen from the devil himself:

> “To be jealous of what you see to be good and to envy those who are better seems to some people, dearly beloved brothers, to be a light and minor offense.”

Then, shortly afterward, when he was seeking the head and origin of this evil, he says:

> “From this the devil, at the very beginning of the world, both perished first and brought destruction.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What a great evil it is, dearly beloved brothers, by which an angel fell; by which that lofty and excellent sublimity could be deceived and overthrown; by which the very one who deceived was himself deceived!”

From that time envy spreads through the earth, while the one destined to perish through envy obeys the teacher of perdition, while he imitates the devil who is jealous, as it is written:

> “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world; and those who belong to his faction imitate him” (Wis. 2:24–25).

We recognize how true and powerful these words of Cyprian are in the letter known among the peoples. It was fitting that Cyprian should both gravely rebuke and warn against jealousy and envy, since the great abundance of his love proved that his heart was wholly alien to so deadly an evil.

While he guarded this love most vigilantly, he remained in the unity of communion with his colleagues who held a different opinion about Baptism without malice. He himself held another view not through malicious contention but through human temptation, and God would later reveal to him, as he persevered in love, what others held [Note: [Col. 0161] Manuscripts: “what”; Am. and Er.: “what, as they”; Lov.: uncertain reading.], when he willed it (Phil. 3:15). He openly said:

> “We judge no one, nor do we remove anyone from the right of communion if he holds a different opinion. For none of us has constituted himself bishop of bishops, nor does he compel his colleagues to the necessity of obedience through tyrannical terror” (At the Council of Carthage).

And at the end of this letter:

> “This brief reply,” he says, “is all that, in accordance with our limited ability, we have written to you, dearest brother, prescribing or prejudging nothing, so that each bishop may do what he thinks, possessing the free authority of his own judgment. As far as lies within us, we do not contend with our colleagues and fellow bishops on account of the heretics, since with them we maintain divine harmony and the peace of the Lord—especially since the Apostle says: ‘If anyone thinks he should be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God’ (1 Cor. 11:16). The love of the heart, the honor of our fellowship, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood are preserved by us with patience and gentleness.

> “For this reason we have now also composed a little book on the Good of Patience, to the extent that our limited ability permitted, with the Lord allowing and inspiring us; and we have sent it to you as an expression of our mutual affection” (Letter 73, to Jubaianus).

[Note: [Col. 0161] Am., Er., and the manuscripts: “in brief.” Only the Lov. edition has “briefly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0161] The Lov. edition omits “now.” It is found in Am. and in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER IX

**12.** With this charitable patience he endured not only good colleagues who, in an obscure question, held a different opinion without ill will—as he himself was tolerated [Col. 0162] until, in the course of time, when God willed it, a most salutary custom was confirmed by a plenary council after the truth had also been made clear—but also manifestly wicked men, personally well known to him, who did not hold a different view because of the obscurity of the question, but whose depraved way of life led them to do the opposite of what they preached, as the Apostle says of them: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2:21).

Concerning such men, this same bishop of that time says in his letter to his colleagues and to those who remained in communion with him: “To be willing to possess abundant silver while brothers in the Church are hungry; to seize estates by deceitful frauds; to increase interest by multiplying usury” (*Sermon on the Lapsed*). Here there is no obscurity of the question: Scripture openly cries out, “Neither the greedy nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10); and, “Who has given his money at interest” [Note: [Col. 0162] Erasm. Lyons, Venice: “Who has not given his money at interest.” Louvain and its manuscripts: “Who gives his money at interest.” M.] (Ps. 14:5); and, “Every fornicator and unclean person and greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5).

Therefore, he would not have reproved such greedy men—men who not only eagerly stored up their own possessions but also fraudulently seized those of others—such idolaters, as he himself understands and proves them to be, unless he knew them. For he would not have borne false witness against his fellow bishops. Yet, for the sake of Christ, who died for the weak, lest the wheat also be uprooted at the same time as the weeds before the proper time (Matt. 13:29), he endured them with the tenderness of paternal and maternal love. He thus imitated the Apostle Paul, who endured those who were ill-disposed and envious toward him with the same love toward the Church (Phil. 1:15–18).

**13.** Yet, since through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him—not in what was created by God, but in what they have perversely made themselves, as Cyprian himself recalls—for the devil too, before he became the devil, was an angel and was good: how, then, are those who belong to the devil’s party within the unity of Christ? Without doubt [Note: Some Belgian manuscripts read: “whence those who are of the devil’s party are not in the unity of Christ; without doubt”], as the Lord himself says, “An enemy has done this; he sowed weeds over it” (Matt. 13:28, 25). Therefore, just as what belongs to the devil must be reproved within, so what belongs to Christ must be recognized outside.

Does Christ have none of his own outside the unity of the Church, while the devil has his own within the unity of the Church? Perhaps this may be said of human beings, so that God has none of his own outside the Church’s communion, just as the devil has none of his own among the holy angels. But in this Church, which still bears the mortality of the flesh while it journeys far from the Lord, the devil has been permitted to mix weeds—that is, wicked people—with the Church; and this has been permitted for the sake of the Church’s pilgrimage, so that the rest of that homeland in which the holy angels rejoice might be desired more ardently.

But this cannot be said concerning the Sacraments. For just as such people can possess and administer them—not for their salvation but for their destruction, since their inner weeds are destined for the fire—so too can the outward weeds [Col. 0163] possess what they received from those who departed from within, because when those people departed they did not lose it. This is certainly made clear when it is not restored to those who return, whenever some of those who had departed happen to come back.

Nor should anyone say, “What wheat do the weeds have?” For if this is so, the condition is the same both within and outside—only to this extent, at least. For grains of wheat are not absent among the outward weeds while they are present among the inward ones. When the question concerns the Sacrament, however, the question is not whether the weeds possess something of wheat, but whether they possess something of heaven. For upon both the outward and inward weeds, together with the wheat itself, falls the same rain, which is heavenly and sweet in itself, even if the weeds grow fruitlessly from it. So too Christ’s evangelical Sacrament is divine and sweet, and it must not be condemned because of the barrenness of those whom it also waters outside.

## CHAPTER X

**14.** Someone may say that the inward weeds are more easily converted into wheat. I grant that this is so; but what does it have to do with repeating Baptism? Suppose someone converted from the heretics, at the time and with the ease of his conversion, should get ahead of someone who is more slowly corrected and changed from wickedness while remaining within: is Baptism not to be repeated for him, while it is to be repeated for the one who was anticipated by the person coming from the heretics, because he was corrected more slowly?

Therefore, it is irrelevant to the question now before us who is converted sooner or later from his own perversity to uprightness of faith, hope, or love. For although the wicked within may more easily become good, sometimes certain people from among those outside precede certain people within by their conversion; and, while the latter remain barren, those who have been reconciled to unity bear fruit with perseverance—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold (Matt. 13:23; Luke 8:15).

Or, if only those weeds are to be called weeds that persist in wicked error to the end, then there are many wheat-grains outside and many weeds within.

**15.** But are the wicked outside worse than the wicked within? It is indeed a great question whether Nicolaus, already outside (Rev. 2:6), was worse than Simon, still within (Acts 8:9–24), since the former was a heretic and the latter a magician. If the very separation itself, because it is the clearest indication of violated love, is considered the more serious evil, I grant that this is so.

But many who have lost love do not go outside because they are held by secular advantages; seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), they do not wish to depart from the unity of Christ, but rather from their own advantages. Hence it is said in praise of love, “It does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5).

**16.** The question, then, is how people who belong to the devil’s party could belong to the Church “without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Eph. 5:27) [Note: *Retractations* II, chap. 18], of which it was also said, “My dove is one” (Song 6:8). If they cannot, it is evident that she groans amid strangers, both those plotting within and those barking from without.

Yet even within, such people both receive Baptism, possess it, and administer it [Col. 0164]—holy in itself—and it is not violated in any way by their wickedness, in which they persist to the end. Accordingly, blessed Cyprian teaches us that Baptism itself must be considered as consecrated by evangelical words, just as the Church received it, without any perversity or wickedness of either those receiving or those administering being added or mixed into it.

For he himself reminds us of both facts: that there were some within who did not preserve benevolent love but lived in envy and malicious dissension, concerning whom the Apostle Paul spoke; and that the envious belong to the devil’s party, as he testifies in the clearest terms in the letter he wrote concerning jealousy and envy.

Therefore, since it is clear that the Sacrament can be holy among those who belong to the devil’s party—not for their salvation but for their judgment—not only when they become perverse after receiving Baptism but also when they receive it as such, as Cyprian likewise shows when they renounce the world in words alone and not in deeds (*Letter 11, to the Clergy*)—and since, if they are later corrected, what they received while perverse is not for that reason to be repeated, it is, in my judgment, already clear and evident that in this question concerning Baptism we must consider not who gives it but what he gives; not who receives it but what he receives; not who possesses it but what he possesses.

For if people who belong to the devil’s party, and therefore in no way belong to the one dove, can nevertheless receive, possess, and give the holiness of Baptism—which their perversity in no way violates, as we are reminded by Cyprian’s own letters—why do we attribute to heretics what belongs to another? Why do we say that what belongs to Christ is theirs, rather than recognizing in them the signs of our Emperor and correcting the deeds of deserters?

Accordingly, it is one thing, as Saint Cyprian says, for those who are within the Church to speak in Christ’s name; it is another for those who are outside and act against the Church to baptize in Christ’s name (*Letter 73, to Jubaianus*). Yet many who are within act against the Church by living wickedly and leading weak souls into their own way of life; and some who are outside speak in Christ’s name and are prohibited, not from doing what belongs to Christ, but from remaining outside, when we correct, rebuke, or exhort them so that they may be healed.

The man who did not follow Christ with the disciples was also outside, yet he drove out demons in Christ’s name; the Lord warned that he should not be prohibited from doing so (Luke 9:49–50). Nevertheless, he certainly needed to be healed of the condition in which he was wounded by those words of the Lord: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30).

Thus some things are also done outside in Christ’s name, but not against the Church; and within there are people belonging to the devil’s party who act against the Church.

## CHAPTER XI

**17.** Moreover, a careful observer discovers something remarkable that can occur: some people, while preserving love, teach something useless—as Peter compelled the Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2:14), and as Cyprian himself taught that heretics should be baptized again. To such good members, rooted in love but not walking rightly in some respect, the Apostle says, “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that to you also” (Phil. 3:15).

[Col. 0165] Others, in turn, teach something beneficial without love. Concerning such people the Lord says, “They sit on Moses’ seat. Do what they say; but do not do what they do, for they speak but do not act” (Matt. 23:2–3). Hence the Apostle also says concerning those envious and malicious people who nevertheless proclaimed Christian salvation, “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:15).

Therefore human perversity must be corrected both within and outside, while divine Sacraments and divine words must not be attributed to human beings. This does not therefore support the heretics, since it does not attribute to them what, although it exists among them, it recognizes nevertheless as not belonging to them.

We do not grant Baptism to the heretic; rather, wherever we find the Baptism of the one of whom it was said, “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33), we recognize it. But if an unbelieving and blasphemous person persists in unbelief and blasphemy, he receives remission of sins neither outside nor within the Church. Or, if he receives it for a moment because of the power of the Sacrament, that same power operates both outside and within, just as the power of Christ’s name also operated outside in the expulsion of demons.

## CHAPTER XII

**18.** But, someone may say, we find the Apostles in all their letters cursing and detesting the sacrilegious perversity of heretics, so that they say that their word spreads like cancer [Note: Only the Louvain edition has “like a cancerous growth”].

What of those who said, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”? Does not Paul reveal that they were corrupters of good morals through evil conversations, immediately adding, “Bad conversations corrupt good morals”? And yet he indicates that they were within when he says, “How do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Cor. 15:32–33, 12).

Where does he not detest the greedy? Or could anything stronger have been said than that greed should be called the service of idols, as the same Apostle stated (Eph. 5:5)? Cyprian understood this no differently and inserted it where necessary in his writings. Yet he admits that in his own time there were in the Church not merely ordinary greedy people, but robbers and usurers—and not just any men, but bishops.

I would like to understand those of whom the Apostle says, “Their word spreads like cancer,” as having been outside; but Cyprian himself does not allow me to do so. For when, writing to Antonianus, he showed that before the time of the final separation of the righteous and the wicked one must in no way withdraw from the Church’s unity because of the mixture of the wicked—and when he declared how holy he was and how worthy of the glory he had earned through martyrdom—he said:

“What a swelling of arrogance, what a forgetfulness of humility and gentleness, what a display of one’s arrogance, for anyone to dare or think that he can do what the Lord did not grant even to the Apostles: that he can distinguish the weeds from the wheat; or, as though it had been granted to him publicly to carry away the harvest and purge the threshing floor, to attempt to separate the chaff from the wheat! Yet when the Apostle says, ‘In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also vessels of wood and earthenware,’ he seems to choose the vessels of gold and silver but to despise, reject, and condemn those of wood and earthenware, although the wooden vessels are to be consumed only on the day of the Lord in the fire of divine ardor, and the earthen vessels [Col. 0166] are broken by him to whom an iron rod has been given (Ps. 2:9)” (*Letter 55*).

Thus, in reproving those who, as though avoiding fellowship with the wicked, had torn themselves away from unity, Cyprian shows that the great house mentioned by the Apostle—where there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also vessels of wood and earthenware—was understood by him as nothing other than the Church, in which the good and the wicked exist until the end, when she will be purified like gold after being winnowed.

If this is so, then within that very Church—that is, within that very great house—there were vessels destined for dishonor, whose word spread like cancer. For when the Apostle spoke of them, he taught this:

“Their word spreads like cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overturn the faith of some. But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his,’ and, ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’ But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also vessels of wood and earthenware” (2 Tim. 2:17–20).

If, then, these people—whose word spread like cancer—were in the great house as vessels destined for dishonor, and if Cyprian understands that great house as the unity of the Church itself, did their cancer violate Christ’s Baptism?

Thus, neither outside nor within can anyone who belongs to the devil’s party defile, either in himself or in anyone else, the Sacrament that belongs to Christ. Therefore, the word that spreads like cancer into the ears of those who hear does not grant the remission of sins (*Letter 73, to Jubaianus*). But when Baptism is given with evangelical words, however perversely the person through whom it is given or the person to whom it is given may understand them, it is holy in itself because of the one to whom it belongs.

And if someone receives it through a perverse human minister, yet does not receive the minister’s perversity but only the holiness of the mystery, and is joined to the unity of the Church in good faith, hope, and love, he receives remission of sins—not through words that spread like cancer, but through evangelical Sacraments flowing from the heavenly source.

If, however, the person who receives it is himself perverse, what is given does not benefit him for salvation; nevertheless, what is received remains holy in him, and if he is corrected, it is not repeated for him.

## CHAPTER XIII

**19.** There is therefore no participation between righteousness and iniquity—not only between what is outside but also between what is within. For “the Lord knows those who are his,” and “let everyone who invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

There is likewise no communion between light and darkness (2 Cor. 6:14)—not only between those outside but also between those within. For, as John says, “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:9).

Certainly those who hated Paul were the people who, proclaiming Christ out of envy and malicious dissension [Note: Am. Er. and some manuscripts read “the malice of envy and dissension”; certain other manuscripts read “envy, and malice, and dissension”], thought that they would stir up tribulation against his chains (Phil. 1:15, 17). Yet Cyprian himself understands that they were within.

Since, then, darkness cannot illumine and iniquity cannot justify, as he himself says, I ask how these people [Col. 0167] could baptize within the Church itself. I ask how those vessels that the great house contains—not for honor but for dishonor—could within that same great house administer what is holy for the sanctification of human beings, unless it is because the holiness of the Sacrament cannot be polluted by the unclean, whether it is given through them or received by those who are not changed for the better in heart and life?

Concerning such people placed within, he himself says, “Renouncing the world in words alone and not in deeds” (*Letter 11, to the Clergy*).

**20.** There are therefore enemies of God even within, people whose breasts the spirit of Antichrist has occupied; yet they administer spiritual and divine things (*Letter 73, to Jubaianus*). These things cannot benefit them for salvation so long as they remain such, nor can they themselves defile them by their uncleanness.

What he says—that those who scatter [Note: Am. Er. and several manuscripts read “despising” for “scattering”; other manuscripts, with the editions of Cyprian, have “scattering.” Some good manuscripts read “unto salvation” for “unto ecclesiastical and saving grace”] and attack Christ’s Church, being adversaries of Christ himself and antichrists of his Apostles, are permitted nothing pertaining to ecclesiastical and saving grace—is to be understood in this way: such people are found both outside and within.

Nevertheless, the separation of those who are within from the perfection and unity of that dove is known by God in some cases and by human beings in others. When people see their manifestly wicked and confirmed depravity, and compare it with the rules of the divine commandments, they understand how many weeds and how much chaff, placed either outside or within, the Lord will at the end most openly separate, saying, “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:23), and, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

## CHAPTER XIV

**21.** As for conversion, no one should be despaired of, whether situated outside or within, so long as God’s patience is leading him to repentance (Rom. 2:4), and he visits their crimes with a rod and their sins with scourges. In this way he does not withdraw his mercy from them (Ps. 88:33–34), provided that they too eventually have mercy on their own souls and thereby please God (Sir. 30:24).

For just as “the good person who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13), so the wicked person, whether outside or within, who perseveres to the end will not be saved.

We do not say that those who are baptized anywhere and in any manner obtain the grace of Baptism, if by the grace of Baptism one understands the salvation conferred through the celebration of the Sacrament. Many do not obtain this salvation even within, although it is evident that they possess the Sacrament, which is holy in itself.

Therefore the Lord rightly warns us in the Gospel not to consent to those who give evil counsel, though they walk under Christ’s name (Mark 13:21). Such people are found both within and outside, because they do not go outside unless they were first wicked within.

The Apostle was speaking of vessels placed in the great house when he said, “If anyone cleanses himself from such things, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.” He showed somewhat earlier how [Col. 0168] each person should cleanse himself from such people, saying, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Tim. 2:21, 19), lest at the end he hear, together with the chaff—whether the chaff that has already flown from the threshing floor or that which will be separated at the end—“Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:23).

Accordingly, it is indeed evident, as Cyprian says, that we must not immediately accept and take up whatever is proclaimed in Christ’s name, but what is done in Christ’s truth.

Yet it is certainly not done in Christ’s truth to seize estates by deceitful frauds, to increase interest by multiplying usury (*Sermon on the Lapsed*), or to renounce the world in words alone (*Letter 11, to the Clergy*). That all these things are also done within is sufficiently declared by this highly reliable witness himself.

## CHAPTER XV

**22.** As for what he develops at length—that those who blaspheme Christ’s Father cannot be baptized in Christ (*Letter 73, to Jubaianus*)—it is clear that they blaspheme through error. For no one who approaches Christ’s Baptism openly blasphemes Christ’s Father; rather, a person is shown to blaspheme by holding a view about Christ’s Father different from what the truth teaches.

We have already shown sufficiently that, with respect to Baptism consecrated by evangelical words, the error of either the giver or the recipient—whether concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—does not matter, even if that person thinks differently from what heavenly doctrine teaches.

For many carnal and natural people are also baptized within, although the Apostle plainly says, “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14); and after they have already received Baptism he says that they are still natural (1 Cor. 3:2).

According to a carnal understanding, a soul devoted to bodily senses can think of God only in a carnal manner. Hence many people who make progress after Baptism—and especially those baptized as infants or children—when their understanding becomes clearer and more illuminated, as the inner person is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16), reject their former opinions about God, which they held while being deluded by their fantasies, laughing at them, detesting them, confessing them, and casting them away.

Yet they are not therefore thought not to have received Baptism, nor are they said to have received a Baptism of the same character as their error. Rather, in them the integrity of the Sacrament is honored and the vanity of the mind is corrected—even if that vanity had become firmly established and perhaps been defended through many disputes.

Therefore even a heretic who is plainly outside, if he received evangelical Baptism there, did not receive a Baptism corresponding to the error by which he is blinded. Consequently, if he comes to his senses and sees that what he had wrongly held must be abandoned, he must not at the same time abandon the good that he had received. Nor, because his error must be condemned, is Christ’s Baptism in him to be rejected.

For from those whom it happens to find within, baptized while holding false opinions about God, it is sufficiently evident that the truth of the Sacrament must be distinguished from the error of the one who believes wrongly, although both may be found operative in one person.

Therefore, when someone established outside in some error has nevertheless been baptized with the true Sacrament, and is restored to the Church’s unity, just as true faith succeeds false faith, true Baptism cannot likewise succeed true Baptism, because the very same thing cannot succeed itself [Col. 0169]; nor can it depart.

Heretics therefore come to the Catholic Church so that what is evil in them may be corrected, not so that what belongs to God and is good may be repeated.

## CHAPTER XVI

**23.** Someone may say: “Then does it make no difference if two people are established in equal error and wickedness, with neither their life nor their heart changed, and one of them is baptized outside while the other is baptized within?”

I admit that it makes a difference. The one who is baptized outside is worse—not because he is baptized, but because he is outside. For the division itself is neither a negligible nor a small evil.

This is so, however, only if the one baptized within wished to remain within not for some earthly or temporal advantage, but because he preferred the unity of the Church, spread throughout the whole world, to the fragmentation of schisms. Otherwise he too must be counted among those who are outside.

Let us therefore posit two people of this kind: one, for example, who holds concerning Christ what Photinus held and is baptized in his heresy outside the communion of the Catholic Church; and another who holds the same view but is baptized in the Catholic Church, believing that this is the Catholic faith.
