I do not yet call the latter a heretic, unless, after the Catholic doctrine of faith has been made known to him, he chooses to resist it and to retain what he had held. Before that happens, it is clear that the person baptized outside is worse [Note: The word “baptized” is absent from some manuscripts].

Thus, in the latter, only the false opinion must be corrected; in the former, the division itself must also be corrected. But in neither of them must the truth of the Sacrament be repeated.

If someone holds the same opinion as the former person and knows that it is a heresy separated from Catholic unity, where that opinion is taught and learned, but wishes to be baptized within the Catholic unity for the sake of some secular advantage, or, having been baptized within it, does not wish to leave it for that reason, he must be regarded not only as separated but as guilty of a much greater crime, insofar as he adds the deceit of simulation to heretical error and division from unity.

Therefore, the perversity of each person must be corrected with greater urgency and effort in proportion as it is more dangerous and more twisted. Nevertheless, if that person possesses something whole and sound—especially if it is not his but God’s—it must not, because of his perversity, be considered nonexistent, condemned in the same manner, or attributed to his perversity rather than to the generosity of the one who, even to a soul fornicating against him and pursuing her lovers, gave his bread, his wine, his oil, and other foods or ornaments that came neither from the soul itself nor from its lovers, but from him who, in his mercy toward her, wished everywhere to remind her to return to him (Hos. 2:5–7).

## CHAPTER XVII

**24.** “Can the power of Baptism,” he says, “be greater or more effective than confession? Than martyrdom? That someone should confess Christ before human beings and be baptized in his own blood? And yet,” he says, “even this Baptism does not benefit the heretic, although he confessed Christ and was killed outside the Church.”

This is entirely true. For one who is killed outside the Church is shown not to have had love, concerning which the Apostle says, “If I deliver my body to be burned but have not [Col. 0170] love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

If martyrdom profits nothing because love is lacking, then it does not profit those whom Paul says live within in envy and malice without love; Cyprian explains this. Yet they can both receive and administer true Baptism.

“There is no salvation,” he says, “outside the Church.” Who denies it? Therefore whatever belongs to the Church, if possessed outside the Church, does not avail for salvation. But it is one thing not to possess something and another not to possess it beneficially. Whoever does not possess it must be baptized so that he may possess it; whoever does not possess it beneficially must be corrected so that he may possess it beneficially.

Nor is the water in the Baptism of heretics adulterous. For neither is the creature that God made evil, nor are the evangelical words to be condemned among people who are in error; rather, their error is adulterous, in which the soul is adulterous, even if it possesses the ornament of the Sacrament from its legitimate husband.

Baptism can therefore be shared by us and by heretics, just as [Note: Corbie manuscript: “I think”] the Gospel can be shared by us and by them, although their error differs from our faith—whether they hold something different from the truth concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or, having been cut off from unity, fail to gather with Christ but scatter (Matt. 12:30).

For if we are the Lord’s wheat, we can also share within with the greedy, the robbers, the drunkards, and other such plagues, of whom it is said, “They will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10), both the Sacrament of Baptism and yet not the vices by which they are separated from the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**25.** For the Apostle does not say only concerning heresies, “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.” But let us not hesitate to observe briefly the things he enumerates together:

“The works of the flesh are manifest,” he says, “which are fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, angers, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

Let us therefore posit someone who is chaste, continent, not greedy, not serving idols, hospitable, ministering to the needy, no one’s enemy, not quarrelsome, patient, peaceable, rivaling no one, envying no one, sober, temperate—but a heretic. No one can doubt that, for this one reason, namely that he is a heretic, he will not possess the kingdom of God.

Let us posit another who is a fornicator, unclean, licentious, greedy, or even more openly devoted to idols; a sorcerer, quarrelsome, contentious, jealous, angry, seditious, envious, drunk, and a carouser—but a Catholic. Will he possess the kingdom of God merely because he is a Catholic, while doing the things concerning which the Apostle concludes, “I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God”?

If we say this, we deceive ourselves. For God’s word does not deceive us: it neither remains silent nor spares us, nor does it deceive us through any flattery. That is why it also says elsewhere, “Know this with certainty: [Col. 0171] no fornicator or unclean person or greedy person, which is the service of idols, has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words” (Eph. 5:5–6).

There is therefore no reason for us to complain about God’s word. It says plainly, openly, and freely that those who live wickedly do not belong to the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER XIX

**26.** Since the Catholic is surrounded by all these vices, let us not flatter him; and because he is a Christian Catholic, let us not dare promise him the impunity that divine Scripture does not promise. Nor, if he possesses only one of the things just mentioned, should we promise him fellowship in that heavenly homeland.

For in writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle lists them individually, with the implication in each case that such people will not possess the kingdom of God:

“Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

He does not say, “Those who have all these vices together will not possess the kingdom of God,” but, “Neither these nor those,” so that you should understand in each individual case that none of them will possess the kingdom of God.

Therefore, just as heretics will not possess the kingdom of God, so the greedy will not possess the kingdom of God.

It must indeed not be doubted that the very punishments by which those who will not possess the kingdom of God will be tormented differ according to the diversity of their crimes, some being more severe than others, so that in the same eternal fire there may be different torments of punishment corresponding to the unequal weight of sins.

For the Lord himself does not say without reason, “It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for you on the day of judgment” (Matt. 11:24). Nevertheless, with respect to not possessing the kingdom of God, choosing the milder of those vices has as much force as choosing several of them, or one that you recognize to be more serious.

And because those will possess the kingdom of God whom that judge will place at his right hand, while nothing other than the left remains for those who will not deserve to be placed at the right, there is no remaining declaration except that which they will hear as goats from the shepherd’s mouth: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:32–33, 41). Yet, as I have said, different punishments may be assigned within that fire according to the diversity of their crimes.

## CHAPTER XX

**27.** But whether we ought to prefer a Catholic of the worst morals to some heretic in whose life, apart from the fact that he is a heretic, people find nothing to criticize, I do not dare to decide hastily. If someone says that, because he is a heretic, this alone cannot be the case without other consequences—for he is carnal and animal, and therefore must also be contentious, hot-tempered, envious, and hostile to truth itself and dissenting from it—let him understand that, among those other evils also, whichever he has chosen as the milder cannot exist alone in anyone, for the very reason that he is carnal and animal. Consider drunkenness, for example, which they have now grown accustomed not only to mention without horror but even to praise before an amused public: can it exist alone in someone who possesses it? For what drunkard is not also quarrelsome, hot-tempered, envious, dissenting from the soundness of the precepts, and bitterly hostile to those who rebuke him? [Col. 0172] Indeed, it is difficult for him not also to be a fornicator and adulterer; yet such a man can be no heretic, just as a heretic can be neither a drunkard, nor an adulterer or fornicator, nor a profligate, nor a lover of money, nor a sorcerer—and he may be none of these things at the same time. [Note: Col. 0172. This is the consistent manuscript reading. But the printed editions, after “it is difficult,” read: “But it does not follow. For a drunkard can be and not be a heretic; just as a heretic can be and not be a drunkard, nor an adulterer or fornicator, etc.”]

For no single vice necessarily brings all the others with it. Let us therefore place before us two people: one a Catholic with all these vices, the other a heretic without those things that may be absent from a heretic. Although neither of them disputes against the faith, both nevertheless live against the faith, both are deceived by a vain hope, and both dissent from spiritual charity; for this reason both are alien from the body of that one dove. Why, then, do we recognize Christ’s Sacrament in one of them but refuse to recognize it in the other, as though it belonged either to this person or to that, when it is the same in both, belongs to God alone, and remains good even in the worst people?

And if, among those who possess it, one person is worse than another, the thing they possess is not therefore worse in the former than in the latter. For even among two wicked Catholics, if one is worse than the other, he does not bear a worse Baptism; nor, if one is good and the other wicked, is Baptism wicked in the wicked person and good in the good person. It is good in both—just as sunlight, or even lamplight, is not worse in inferior eyes than in better eyes, but is the same in both, although it may either gladden or torment them differently according to their differing condition.

## CHAPTER XXI

**28.** As for the objection made to Cyprian concerning catechumens—that those who were apprehended in martyrdom and killed for Christ’s name were crowned even without Baptism—I do not sufficiently understand what relevance it has, unless perhaps they were saying that heretics possessing Christ’s Baptism could much more readily be admitted to his kingdom, into which catechumens were admitted, even though Christ himself said: [Note: Col. 0172. Erasmus reads “than”; M reads “into which.”] “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

In this matter I too have no doubt that I would prefer a Catholic catechumen burning with divine charity to a baptized heretic. But even within the Catholic Church itself we prefer a good catechumen to a wicked baptized person. Yet we do not thereby insult the sacrament of Baptism, with which the latter has already been imbued while the former has not; nor do we think that the sacrament of the catechumen should be preferred to the sacrament of Baptism, when we recognize that a particular catechumen is more faithful and better than someone who has been baptized. [Note: Col. 0172. Am., Er., and fewer manuscripts read, “nor do we think that the sacrament of Baptism should be preferred to the catechumen.” Someone had wrongly emended the text thus, supposing that the catechumen’s sacrament was nothing other than Baptism. But Augustine recognizes this sacrament proper to the catechumen—called the sacrament of salt in the First Council of Carthage—in On Instructing Beginners, no. 50, and in book 2 of On the Merits of Sins, no. 42.]

The centurion Cornelius, though not yet baptized, was better than the baptized Simon. The former was filled with the Holy Spirit even before Baptism (Acts 10), whereas the latter, after Baptism, was puffed up with an unclean spirit (Acts 8:13, 18–19). Nevertheless, if Cornelius, after already receiving the Holy Spirit [Col. 0173], had refused to be baptized, he would have become guilty of despising so great a sacrament. When he was baptized, however, he did not receive a better sacrament than Simon; rather, differing human merits were distinguished under the equal holiness of the same sacrament. Thus a person’s good or bad merit neither increases nor diminishes the holiness or goodness of Baptism.

Just as a good catechumen lacks Baptism in order to obtain the kingdom of heaven, so a wicked baptized person lacks true conversion. For the one who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” also said, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20). The former statement was made so that the catechumen’s righteousness would not be secure without Baptism; the latter was made so that the baptized person’s wickedness would not be secure merely because he had received Baptism. [Note: Col. 0173. Most manuscripts omit “of the baptized.”] Either one without the other is insufficient; together they make a person heir to that possession.

Accordingly, just as we ought not to reject a person’s righteousness merely because it began before he was joined to the Church—for Cornelius’s righteousness began before he himself belonged to the Christian people—so, if it had been rejected, the angel would not have said to him, “Your almsgiving has been accepted and your prayers have been heard” [Note: Col. 0173. The manuscripts read “have been accepted.”], nor would he have been instructed to send to Peter if that righteousness had been sufficient for obtaining the kingdom of heaven (Acts 10:4, 31, 5). In the same way, the evangelical sacrament of Baptism must not be rejected even when it has been received outside the Church. Yet because it does not contribute to salvation unless the one who possesses the integrity of Baptism, with his perversity corrected as well, is incorporated into the Church, we should correct the error of heretics in such a way that we recognize in them what belongs not to them but to Christ.

## CHAPTER XXII

**29.** The blessed Cyprian also adduces as significant evidence that suffering can sometimes take the place of Baptism the case of the robber to whom, although he had not been baptized, it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). But on considering this more and more carefully, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what was lacking from Baptism; faith and conversion of heart can do so as well, if, perhaps because of the pressure of circumstances, it is impossible to administer the mystery of Baptism. [Note: Col. 0173. Retractations II, chapter 18.]

For that robber was not crucified for Christ’s name but for the merits of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed—rather, while suffering, he came to believe. Thus it was demonstrated in him how powerful, even without the visible sacrament of Baptism, is what the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). It is fulfilled invisibly, however, when the ministry of Baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by the urgency of necessity.

Indeed, it could have seemed much more superfluous for Cornelius and his companions than for that robber [Col. 0174] to be washed also with water, since the gift of the Holy Spirit had already appeared in them—and Holy Scripture testifies that no others except the baptized had received it—through a definite sign also suited to those times, when they spoke in tongues. Yet they were baptized, and in this act apostolic authority stands forth.

Therefore no one, whatever progress he may perhaps have made in the inward person, if before Baptism he has advanced with a devout heart even to spiritual understanding, ought to despise the sacrament that is physically administered through the work of ministers; through it God accomplishes the person’s consecration spiritually.

I believe that John was given the ministry of baptizing, so that it would be called John’s baptism, for no other reason than that the Lord himself, who had granted it, by accepting the baptism of a servant did not disdain to receive it (Matthew 3:6, 13). In this way he dedicated the path of humility and made absolutely clear, by such an act, how highly his own Baptism—the Baptism with which he himself was going to baptize—ought to be esteemed.

For, like a highly skilled physician of eternal salvation, he saw that there would not be lacking certain people’s arrogance. Having advanced so far in understanding the truth and in commendable morals that they would not hesitate to place themselves above many baptized people in life and teaching, they might think it unnecessary for them to be baptized, once they felt that they had reached that disposition of mind toward which many baptized people were still striving to ascend.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**30.** What the sanctification of the sacrament, physically administered to a person, accomplishes and what effect it has in him is difficult to say. Yet that robber was not without it, since it was not that he lacked the will to receive it, but that necessity prevented his receiving it. If it did not have great power, the Lord would not have accepted the baptism of a servant.

But because it must be considered in itself, apart from the salvation of the person for whose perfection it is administered, its character is sufficiently indicated by the fact that it remains intact both in wicked people and in those who renounce the world in words but not in deeds, even though they cannot possess salvation unless they are corrected.

Just as the robber possessed perfect salvation because the sacrament was physically absent through necessity but spiritually present through devotion, so, when the sacrament itself is present, salvation is perfected if what was present in the robber is lacking through necessity.

This is the tradition held by the universal Church when infants are baptized. They certainly cannot yet believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation, as the robber was able to do. Indeed, while the mystery is being celebrated in them, by weeping and wailing they drown out the mystic utterances with their own cries; yet no Christian would say that they are baptized in vain.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**31.** If anyone seeks divine authority on this matter, although what the whole Church maintains—not instituted by councils but always retained—is rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority, we can nevertheless infer truthfully what the sacrament of Baptism accomplishes in infants from the circumcision of the flesh, which the earlier people received, and which Abraham received after he had already been justified.

Cornelius too was enriched with the gift of the Holy Spirit before he was baptized. [Col. 0175] Yet the Apostle says of Abraham himself: “He received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith,” which he had already believed in his heart and which had been reckoned to him as righteousness (Romans 4:11, 3).

Why, then, was he commanded thereafter to circumcise every male infant on the eighth day (Genesis 17:9, 14), when the infant could not yet believe with the heart so that it might be reckoned as righteousness, unless the sacrament itself also had great power? This was manifested in the son of Moses through an angel. While the child was still being carried uncircumcised by his mother, circumcision was demanded in an immediate and evident danger (Exodus 4:24); and when it had been performed, the calamity was averted.

Thus, just as in Abraham the righteousness of faith preceded and circumcision was added as the seal of the righteousness of faith, so in Cornelius spiritual sanctification in the gift of the Holy Spirit preceded, and the sacrament of regeneration in the washing of Baptism was added.

And just as in Isaac, who was circumcised on the eighth day of his birth, the seal of the righteousness of faith preceded, and, because he imitated his father’s faith, that same righteousness followed as he grew—the seal of which had preceded in infancy—so in baptized infants the sacrament of regeneration precedes. If they preserve Christian devotion, conversion of heart will also follow, whose mystery preceded in the body.

And just as in the robber the goodness of the Almighty completed what was lacking from the sacrament of Baptism, because it was lacking not through pride or contempt but through necessity, so in infants who die after being baptized we must believe that the same grace of the Almighty completes what is lacking—not through impious unwillingness but through the incapacity of their age. They can neither believe with the heart unto righteousness nor confess with the mouth unto salvation.

Therefore, when others answer on their behalf so that the celebration of the sacrament may be completed for them, it certainly contributes to their consecration, since they cannot answer for themselves. But if someone else answers on behalf of one who can answer, it does not have the same effect. From this rule comes the saying in the Gospel that naturally moves everyone when it is read: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 9:21). [Col. 0176]

## CHAPTER XXV

**32.** All these considerations show that the sacrament of Baptism is one thing and conversion of heart another, but that human salvation is completed through both. If one of them is absent, we must not therefore conclude that the other is absent as well, since the one can exist without the other in an infant, and the other could exist without the one in the robber, with God completing in either case what was lacking not through the will. When, however, one of these is lacking through the will, the person becomes entangled in guilt.

Baptism can exist where conversion of heart is absent; conversion of heart can exist without Baptism having been received, but it cannot exist where Baptism has been despised. For conversion of heart toward God cannot in any way be said to exist when God’s sacrament is despised.

We therefore rightly rebuke, anathematize, detest, and abominate the perversity of the heretics’ hearts. Nevertheless, they do possess the evangelical sacrament; they do not possess it in the way that is beneficial. Accordingly, when they come to the faith and the truth and, doing penance, ask that their sins be forgiven, we neither deceive nor mislead them when, having corrected and reformed them in what was depraved and perverse, we instruct them in the heavenly disciplines for the kingdom of heaven. In doing so, we do not violate in any way what remains intact in them, nor, because of a human defect, do we say that what belongs to God in a person is either nonexistent or defective.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**33.** Only a few matters remain from the letter to Jubaianus. But since they discuss both the former custom of the Church and John’s baptism—a matter that often greatly troubles people who pay too little attention to what is evident, because the Apostle commanded those who had received John’s baptism to be baptized in Christ (Acts 19:3–5)—they must not be treated carelessly, but deferred to another volume, lest this one become disproportionate in length.

# BOOK FIVE

The final part examines Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus, as well as his letter to Quintus, his synodical letter to the bishops of Numidia, and his letter to Pompeius.

[Col. 0175]

## CHAPTER I

**1.** We have the testimony of the blessed Cyprian that the ancient custom of the Catholic Church is now maintained: when people come from heretics or schismatics, if they have received Baptism consecrated with the evangelical words, they are not baptized again.

He himself raised the question from the mouths of brothers—whether they were seeking the truth or contending on behalf of the truth. In the course of his arguments, by which he wished to show that heretics ought to be baptized again, arguments we discussed sufficiently in the preceding books, he says:

“But someone says: What, then, will become of those who in former times, coming from heresy to the Church, were admitted without Baptism?” (Letter 73, to Jubaianus).

Here the entire cause of the Donatists, with whom we are in conflict [Col. 0176] over this question, has been utterly shipwrecked. [Note: Col. 0176. The manuscripts read “if indeed”; the printed editions read “but if.”] For if those who came from the heretics and were received in this way truly did not have Baptism, and their sins remained upon them, then, when communion was extended to such people either by those who lived before Cyprian or by Cyprian himself, one of two conclusions must be stated: either the Church had already perished, being polluted by communion with such people, or the foreign sins of others do not harm anyone who remains within unity.

Since they cannot say that the Church then perished through communion with those who, as Cyprian says, were admitted to it without Baptism—for otherwise they will be unable to assert their own origin if the Church then perished—because more than forty years elapsed between Cyprian’s martyrdom and the burning of the sacred books, from which, as the order of the consuls shows, these people, casting out the smoke of their accusations, found the opportunity to create their schism [Note: Col. 0177. See below, book 7, chapter 2.], it remains for them to admit that the unity of Christ is not contaminated by communion with any wicked people, even when their wickedness is known.

When they admit this, they will find no reason why they should claim that they ought to have separated themselves from the Churches throughout the world, which we likewise read were established through the Apostles. For neither could those Churches perish through the mixture of any wicked people, nor could these people, who would not have perished had they remained with them in unity, avoid perishing in schism when they separated themselves from them and broke the bond of peace.

The sacrilege of schism is therefore clearly exposed if there was no cause for separation. That there was no cause for separation becomes apparent if even known wicked people do not stain the good within unity.

We teach [Note: Col. 0177. Some manuscripts read, “We are taught.”] that the good are not stained within unity even by known wicked people, with Cyprian as our witness. He says that those who formerly came from heresy to the Church were admitted without Baptism. Yet their wicked sacrileges, which remained upon them because they had not been remitted through Baptism, could not pollute and destroy the holiness of the Church; therefore the Church cannot perish through any contagion of the wicked.

Accordingly, if they agree that Cyprian spoke the truth, his testimony defeats them in the crime of schism. [Note: Col. 0177. The printed editions read, “his testimony proves them to be guilty of the crime of schism.” The manuscripts, omitting “to be,” read “defeats them.”] If they contend that Cyprian spoke falsely, they should not use his testimony in the question of Baptism.

## CHAPTER II

**2.** But let us continue the conversation we have begun with the blessed Cyprian, a peaceful man. [Col. 0178] When he had put before himself the objection that he knew was made by the brothers—“What, then, will become of those who in former times came to the Church from heresy and were admitted without Baptism?”—he says:

“The Lord in his mercy is able to grant forgiveness, and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, having been simply admitted to the Church, fell asleep within the Church.”

He rightly presumed that the charity of unity could cover a multitude of sins. If they did possess Baptism, and those who judged that they ought to be baptized again were mistaken, the charity of unity covered that error, so long as what existed was not a diabolical disagreement but a human temptation—until, as the Apostle says, the Lord should reveal to them if they thought otherwise (Philippians 3:15).

Woe, therefore, to those who, by sacrilegious separation, have torn themselves away from unity and rebaptize people if Baptism exists both among us and among them, but do not baptize them if it exists only in the Catholic Church. Whether they rebaptize or do not baptize, they are not within the bond of peace. Let them apply medicine to whichever of these wounds they please.

But if we admit people to the Church without Baptism, we belong to the number of those [Note: Col. 0177. Most manuscripts read, “and we belong to their number.”] whom Cyprian presumed could be forgiven for the sake of preserving unity.

If, however—as I believe is now clear from what we said in the preceding books—the integrity of Christian Baptism can exist even amid the perversity of heretics, then if people at that time baptized again but nevertheless did not withdraw from the bond of unity, they too could belong to forgiveness through the same love of peace by which Cyprian testifies that those admitted without Baptism could not be separated from the gifts of the Church.

Furthermore, if it is true that the Baptism of Christ does not exist among heretics and schismatics, how much less would the sins of others harm those who remained within unity, if the sins of those who came to unity and were admitted without Baptism were forgiven along with their own! For if, according to Cyprian, the bond of unity has such power, how could those who refused to withdraw from unity be harmed by the sins of others, if even the unbaptized who wished to come to it from heresy were not destroyed by their own sins?

## CHAPTER III

**3.** As for what Cyprian adds when he says, “Yet it is not because an error was once made that we must always err. Rather, it is more fitting for the wise and God-fearing to obey willingly and without hesitation a truth that has been disclosed and understood than stubbornly and obstinately to resist the brothers and fellow priests on behalf of heretics”: he speaks most truly, and the person who resists the clearest truth is opposing no one more than himself.

But through all that we have already said at such length, it is, as I believe, plainly apparent and certain that the Baptism of Christ cannot be violated by the perversity of heretics when it is given and received among them.

Even if this is not yet certain, whoever, despite resistance, considers what has been said admits at least that the matter remains doubtful. We therefore do not resist the clearest truth; either we are contending for manifest truth, as I believe, or else, as those who think this question has not yet been resolved may suppose, we are still seeking the truth.

Accordingly, if the matter is otherwise than we say, we receive those baptized among the heretics with the same simplicity with which those people [Note: Col. 0178. The manuscripts read “received”; the printed editions read “were received.”] received them whom Cyprian presumed could be forgiven for the sake of unity.

But if the Baptism of Christ, as the many things already said indicate, can remain intact even in a life or faith that is not whole [Note: Col. 0178. The printed editions read “and not whole,” omitting the particle “in,” which occurs in the manuscripts]—whether in those who appear to be within the Church but do not belong to the members of that one dove, or in those who do not belong to it in such a way that they are also openly outside—then those who repeated Baptism in those times deserved the same forgiveness through the charity of unity which Cyprian believed was deserved, through that same kind of charity, by those whom he supposed had been admitted without Baptism.

Those, therefore, who, without any cause—since, as Cyprian himself demonstrates, the wicked cannot harm the good within unity—cut themselves off from the charity of that same unity have forfeited every place of forgiveness. They would have perished through the crime of schism itself even if, after becoming Catholic, they had not rebaptized; how much punishment, then, do they deserve when they either attempt to give to Catholics what Cyprian asserts they do not possess, or, as the facts themselves reveal, accuse the Catholic Church of not possessing what they themselves possess?

## CHAPTER IV

**4.** [Col. 0179] But since, as I had begun to say, we have undertaken to converse with Cyprian’s writings, I do not think that he himself, had he been present, would have regarded me as stubbornly and obstinately resisting the brothers and fellow priests on behalf of heretics, if he accepted the many considerations that move us to believe that even among heretics, perversely established in their wicked error, the Baptism of Christ can nevertheless be holy and most revered in itself.

Since he himself also bears witness—and his testimony carries great weight—that such people were formerly admitted in this way, anyone moved by his words to have no doubt that heretics ought to be baptized again should regard those who have not yet been persuaded by the many arguments against this view as being like those who formerly admitted people baptized in heresy, once their personal error had simply been corrected, and who could be saved with them through the bond of unity.

But whoever understands, from the former custom of the Church, from the later authority of the plenary council, from so many and such great testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, from Cyprian’s own many proofs, and from the evident arguments of truth, that Baptism consecrated by evangelical words is not made corrupt by the perversity of any person, should understand through that same bond of unity that those people could have been saved for whom something else seemed right at that time while charity remained intact.

And consequently such a person must understand at the same time that those whom no weeds and no chaff could have stained within the fellowship of the Church spread throughout the whole world, if they themselves had wished to be wheat, and who therefore, without any cause for separation [Note: Col. 0179. The word “separation” is absent from manuscripts of good quality], broke the same bond of unity—whichever of the two alternatives is true, whether what Cyprian then thought or what the universal Catholic Church, from which he did not withdraw, maintained—are plainly established outside and cannot be saved in the manifest sacrilege of schism. Everything they possess from the divine sacraments and from the generosity of the one legitimate husband, so long as they remain such, serves rather for their shame than for their salvation.

## CHAPTER V

**5.** Therefore, even if heretics truly wished to come to the Church after correcting their error because they thought they did not possess Baptism unless they received it in the Catholic Church, we still ought not consent to their repeating Baptism. Rather, they should be taught that the integrity of Baptism does not benefit their perversity if they refuse to be corrected; that their perversity did not violate the integrity of Baptism so long as they refused correction; and that, because they now wish to be corrected, Baptism does not become better in them. Instead, they themselves are beginning to depart from wickedness, and what was previously present for their destruction is beginning to benefit them for salvation.

When they learn these things, they will desire salvation within Catholic unity; they will not suppose that what belongs to Christ belongs to them; and they will not mingle the sacrament of truth, although placed within them, with their own error.

**6.** This is reinforced by the fact that people, through some hidden inspiration of God—I scarcely know how—detest the idea of receiving Baptism again after having received it anywhere already. Thus, when the heretics themselves discuss the matter, they rub their foreheads in embarrassment; nearly all their laypeople who have grown old among them and developed an impassioned obstinacy against the Catholic Church admit that this is the one thing they dislike in their community.

Many who wish to cross over to them in order to obtain some secular advantage or avoid some disadvantage secretly strive to have this particular and private benefit granted to them: that they should not be rebaptized. And some, although they believe the rest of their empty errors and false accusations against the Catholic Church, are held back by this one consideration from wishing to join them, lest they be compelled to be rebaptized.

Fearing this attitude, which occupies the hearts of absolutely everyone, the Donatists preferred to accept the Baptism given among the Maximianists whom they had condemned, and in this way to cut off their own tongues and close their mouths, rather than rebaptize so many people from the communities of Mustitana [Note: Col. 0180. The printed editions had “Musticanae” in place of “Mustitanae,” and below “Praetexatus” in place of “Praetextatus.” These have been corrected from the manuscripts] and Assuritana and the other communities whom, together with Felicianus, Praetextatus, and the others whom they had condemned and who later returned to them, they received.

## CHAPTER VI

**7.** When this happens rarely among individuals, across long intervals of place and time, the horror of the deed is not felt so strongly. But if those whom the aforementioned Maximianists had baptized over such a long period—whether under the pressure of dangers threatening death or during the Paschal solemnities—were suddenly assembled and told to be baptized again because what they had received in the sacrilege of schism was nothing, they would indeed be made to say what the obstinacy of their error would compel them to say, so that they could cover the rigidity and icy hardness of their position with whatever false appearance of steadfastness they could muster.

But because the Maximianists themselves could not endure this, and because even those who would carry it out could not tolerate what would happen to so many people—especially since the very people who had already baptized them in the party of Maximian would rebaptize them in the party of Primian—their Baptism was received and the arrogance of these people was thwarted.

They would never have chosen to let this happen unless they judged that the horror people felt at being dipped again would oppose them more strongly than reflection on their lost defense.

I do not say this because we ought to be deterred by human feeling if truth compelled those coming from heretics to be baptized again. Rather, because Saint Cyprian says that heretics could thereby have been driven more forcefully to the necessity of coming over if they were baptized again in the Catholic Church, I wished to mention how deeply this deed is almost universally dreaded in people’s minds. I believe that this horror was divinely infused so that, against whatever arguments the weak are unable to answer, the Church might be fortified by the horror itself.

## CHAPTER VII

**8.** [Col. 0181] When I consider Cyprian’s own words, I am reminded that certain matters must be said to settle this question. He says:

“If they see that, by our judgment and decision, it is decreed and established that the Baptism with which they are baptized there is considered just and legitimate, they will think that they also justly and legitimately possess the Church and the other gifts of the Church.”

He does not say, “They will think that they possess the gifts of the Church,” but, “that they justly and legitimately possess them.”

We grant that they do not possess Baptism justly and legitimately; but we cannot say that they do not possess it, since we recognize the Lord’s sacrament in the evangelical words.

They therefore possess legitimate Baptism, but do not possess it legitimately. Whoever possesses it both within Catholic unity and while living worthily of it possesses it both legitimately and legitimately in practice. Whoever possesses it either within the Catholic Church as chaff mixed with wheat, or outside it as chaff blown away by the wind, possesses legitimate Baptism, but not legitimately.

For one possesses it according to the way one uses it. But whoever uses it contrary to the law does not use it legitimately; and everyone who, whether inside or outside, lives wickedly after being baptized does this.

## CHAPTER VIII

**9.** Therefore, just as the Apostle said concerning the law, “The law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 2:8), so we can rightly say concerning Baptism: “Baptism is good, if one uses it lawfully.”

And just as those who did not use the good law lawfully did not thereby make the law cease to be good or make it altogether nonexistent, so no one makes Baptism cease to be good or cease to be Baptism altogether by failing to use it lawfully, whether because he lives in heresy or because he lives in the worst morals.

Accordingly, when a person turns either to Catholic unity or to a life worthy of so great a sacrament, he does not begin to possess another legitimate Baptism; rather, he begins to possess that same Baptism legitimately.

The remission of sins that cannot be repeated does not follow Baptism unless it is possessed not only legitimately in itself but also legitimately in practice. Yet even if it is not possessed legitimately, and sins are either not remitted or, though remitted, are imputed again, the sacrament of Baptism in the baptized person is not thereby evil or nonexistent.

Just as Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel, gave the devil a place in himself not by receiving something evil but by receiving something good evilly (John 13:27), so no one who takes the Lord’s sacrament unworthily makes it evil because he himself is evil, or makes it nothing because he does not receive it for salvation.

For it was nevertheless the body of the Lord and the blood of the Lord even for those of whom the Apostle said: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Therefore, heretics should not seek in the Catholic Church what they already possess, but what they do not possess: the end of the commandment, without which many holy things may be possessed but cannot benefit anyone.

The end of the commandment is “charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

As for the sacrament of the font, if they have already been washed with it—even in heresy—they should not hurry to Catholic unity and truth in order to possess the sacrament, but in order to possess it beneficially for salvation.

## CHAPTER IX

**10.** We must now consider what is said about John’s baptism. [Col. 0182] In the Acts of the Apostles we read that Paul baptized those who had already been baptized with John’s baptism (Acts 19:3–5). The reason was only that John’s baptism was not Christ’s Baptism, but had been granted by Christ to John, so that it could properly be called John’s, just as John himself says: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27).

And lest it perhaps seem that he received this from God the Father in such a way that he did not receive it from the Son, speaking again of Christ himself he says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16).

John received this ministry as part of a definite dispensation. It was not to last long, but only long enough to prepare the way for the Lord, whose forerunner he was required to be.

Since Christ was to enter that way humbly and lead those who followed him humbly to excellence, just as he washed the feet of servants (John 13:4–5), so he wished to be washed with the baptism of a servant (Matthew 3:13).

For just as he subjected himself to the feet of those whom he himself directed, so he subjected himself to the ministry of John, which he himself had granted. In this way everyone could understand how great a sacrilegious act of pride it would be to despise the Baptism one ought to receive from the Lord, when the Lord himself had received what he had provided to his servant so that the servant might give it as his own.

And although John—than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women (Matthew 11:11)—bore such witness to Christ that he confessed himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (John 1:27), Christ was found to be most humble among human beings by accepting John’s baptism; and God most high was believed, by taking away the place of John’s baptism [Note: Col. 0182. Erasmus reads “by offering”; the Lyons and Venice editions, “by bringing forward”], to be at once the teacher of humility and the giver of exaltation. [Note: Col. 0182. The Louvain edition alone reads “that is.”]

11. For we read that no prophet, indeed no human being at all, was granted in the divine Scriptures the privilege of baptizing with the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, which was granted to John. By this wondrous grace he held the hearts of the peoples suspended upon himself, so that he might prepare within them the way for the One whom he proclaimed to be so much greater than himself.

But the Lord Jesus Christ cleanses the Church with a baptism such that, once it has been received, no other is required. John, however, administered a preliminary baptism such that, once it had been received, the Lord’s baptism would still be necessary—not so that that baptism should be repeated, but so that those who had received John’s baptism might also be given Christ’s baptism, for which he was preparing the way.

For if Christ’s humility did not need to be commended, John’s baptism would not have been necessary. Again, if John were the endpoint, Christ’s baptism would not have been necessary after John’s baptism. But because “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4), the one to whom we should proceed was demonstrated by John; when we have reached this one, we should remain with him [Note: [Col. 0182] Am. Er. and several manuscripts read *permanetur* (“one remains”) instead.].

Thus John proclaimed both the Lord’s exalted status, when he placed him far above himself, and his humility, when he baptized him as though he were the least. But if John had baptized Christ alone, John would have been thought to be the administrator of a better baptism—one with which Christ himself alone was baptized—than Christ’s baptism, with which Christians are baptized. Again, if everyone had to be baptized first with John’s baptism and then with Christ’s, Christ’s baptism would rightly appear less complete and less perfect, since it would not suffice for salvation.

Therefore the Lord was baptized with John’s baptism, so that he might bend the proud necks of human beings toward his saving baptism. Nor was he alone baptized with that baptism, lest this very fact demonstrate that the earlier baptism was superior, since he alone had been deemed worthy to be baptized with it. Nor did he allow anyone to continue beyond it, lest that one baptism with which he baptizes should appear to require another beforehand.

## CHAPTER X

12. I ask, then: if sins were forgiven through John’s baptism, what more could Christ’s baptism provide for those whom the apostle Paul wished to baptize with Christ’s baptism after John’s baptism? But if sins were not forgiven through John’s baptism, were the people in Cyprian’s time better than John—those of whom he says that they seized estates through deceitful schemes and increased interest through multiplying usury (*Sermon on the Lapsed*)—and yet, when such men baptized, remission of sins took place? Or was it because the unity of the Church held them?

What, then? Was John not in the unity of the Church—that friend of the bridegroom, preparer of the Lord’s way, and baptizer of the Lord himself? Who, except a madman, would say this?

Accordingly, although I believe that John baptized with water for repentance unto the remission of sins in such a way that sins were forgiven in hope to those baptized by him, but in reality this took place in the Lord’s baptism—as the resurrection expected at the end has already taken place in us in hope, as the Apostle says, “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6), and again, “For we were saved in hope” (Romans 8:24)—for John himself says, “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, unto the remission of sins” [Note: [Col. 0183] Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions have “in water of repentance.”] (Matthew 3:11), and, seeing the Lord, says, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29): nevertheless, so that no one may argue that sins were also forgiven in John’s baptism, but that some greater sanctification was conferred through Christ’s baptism upon those whom Paul ordered to be baptized again (Acts 19:3–5), I will not argue obstinately.

## CHAPTER XI

13. For what chiefly concerns the present matter must be considered—however John’s baptism may stand, since it is clear that he belonged to Christ’s unity: what reason caused people to need to be baptized after holy John, but not after avaricious bishops?

No one denies that in the Lord’s field John was wheat, and, if nothing greater can be said, wheat yielding a hundredfold. Likewise, no one doubts that avarice, which is the worship of idols, is counted among the chaff in the Lord’s harvest.

Why, then, is one baptized after the wheat but not after the chaff? If Paul baptized after John because he was better than John, why did Cyprian not baptize after his fellow bishops who practiced usury, when he was incomparably better than they? If Cyprian did not baptize after such colleagues because they were in unity with him, Paul ought not to have baptized after John either, because John was held within that same unity [Note: [Col. 0183] Am. and the manuscripts read *continebantur* (“they were held within”) instead.].

Or perhaps fraudsters and robbers belong to the members of that one dove, while the one upon whom the power of the Lord Jesus Christ was displayed when the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove does not belong to it (Matthew 3:16; John 1:33)? On the contrary, he belongs to it most intimately; whereas those others do not belong to it at all, whether they are to be separated from the wheat on account of some scandal or at the final winnowing. Yet people were baptized after John, but are not baptized after those others.

What, then, is the reason, unless it is that the baptism which Paul ordered those people to receive was not the baptism given through John? And therefore, within that same unity of the Church, if Christ’s baptism is administered by a usurer, it cannot be repeated. But those who received John’s baptism—even from John himself—had afterward to be baptized with Christ’s baptism.

## CHAPTER XII

14. I too, therefore, can use the words of the blessed Cyprian himself to turn the hearts of my hearers toward consideration of a certain astonishing matter, if I say:

That John, considered greater than the prophets; that John, filled with divine grace while still in his mother’s womb; that John, strengthened by the spirit and power of Elijah, who was not the Lord’s adversary but his forerunner and herald; who foretold the Lord not only in words but also displayed him to human eyes; who baptized Christ himself, through whom the others are baptized—he was not worthy to baptize in such a way that those baptized by him should not be baptized afterward. And after avaricious men, fraudsters, robbers, and usurers, will no one think that anyone should be baptized in the Church?

When I make this provocative outcry, will I not be answered: “Why do you consider this improper, as though John had been dishonored or the avaricious man honored?” But John’s baptism should not be repeated, for John himself says of Christ, “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). Through whatever minister it is given, it is the baptism of the one of whom it was said, “This is he who baptizes.”

Yet John’s own baptism was not repeated when the apostle Paul ordered those baptized by John to be baptized in Christ. What they had not received from the friend of the bridegroom, they had to receive from the bridegroom himself, of whom that friend had said, “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XIII

15. For if he had wished, the Lord Jesus could have given the authority of his baptism to one or several of his more distinguished servants, whom he had already made his friends, such as those to whom he said, “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). Then, just as Aaron was shown to be a priest by means of the flowering staff (Numbers 17:8), so in his Church, where many greater miracles have occurred, ministers and administrators of the mysteries of superior holiness might have been identified by some sign, and only they would have been required to baptize.

But if this had happened, although their baptism would have been bestowed upon them by the Lord, it would already have been called their baptism, just as John’s was John’s baptism. For this reason Paul gives thanks to God that he baptized none of them, since, as though they had forgotten in whose name they had been baptized, they were dividing themselves according to the names of human beings (1 Corinthians 1:12–15).

For just as baptism given through a contemptible human being has the same efficacy as baptism given through an apostle, so it is recognized as belonging neither to the one nor to the other, but to Christ. John testifies that he learned this from the Lord himself through the form of the dove. For I plainly do not see in what other sense he could have said, “And I did not know him.”

If he had not known him at all, he would not have said to him, when he came to his baptism, “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matthew 3:14). What, then, does he mean when he says:

“For I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him. And I did not know him. But he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John 1:32–33)?

The dove had certainly descended upon the one who was baptized. Yet, when he came to be baptized, John had already said to him, “I ought to be baptized by you.” Therefore John already knew him.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”—since this occurred after Jesus had been baptized—unless John knew him in one respect but still did not know him in another?

He knew him, evidently, as the bridegroom, the Son of God, from whose fullness everyone would receive. But he did not know whether Christ would give the authority to baptize to others in such a way that it would be called their baptism, or whether he would possess his own baptism in such a way that, through whomever it was given—whether through a minister of greater grace or of lesser grace, whether through a person bearing a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold fruit, whether through wheat or through chaff—it would nonetheless be recognized as belonging to that one alone. This he learned through the Spirit, descending like a dove and remaining upon him.

## CHAPTER XIV

16. Thus we find the apostles saying, “my glory” (1 Corinthians 9:15), although certainly glory in the Lord; “my ministry” (Romans 11:13); “my understanding” (Ephesians 3:4); and “my Gospel” (2 Timothy 2:8), although these were certainly bestowed and given by the Lord. But none of them ever said, “my baptism” [Note: [Col. 0185] The printed editions read “said by the Apostle”; the manuscripts read “said by the apostles.”].

For not everyone possesses equal glory, nor do all minister equally, nor are all endowed with equal understanding. In preaching the Gospel, one works better than another, and therefore one may be called more learned than another in that very saving instruction [Note: [Col. 0185] The manuscripts read “and in that saving instruction.” Several have “spiritual.”]. But no one can be called more or less baptized than another, whether baptized by an inferior or by a superior minister.

Since, therefore, the works of the flesh are manifest—“fornications, impurities, debauchery, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these” (Galatians 5:19–21)—if it is astonishingly said, “People were baptized after John, but are not baptized after heretics,” why is it not astonishingly said, “People were baptized after John, but are not baptized after the envious,” when Cyprian himself testifies in his Letter on Jealousy and Envy that the envious belong to the devil’s party, and, as we have already shown, Cyprian himself demonstrates from the apostle Paul that there were envious proclaimers of Christ in the Church during the apostolic age (Letter 73, to Jubaianus)?

[Col. 0186] ## CHAPTER XV

17. Since, then, John’s baptism was not the same as Christ’s baptism, I think this has been sufficiently demonstrated. Therefore nothing can be brought forward from John’s baptism as evidence that people ought to be baptized after heretics merely because they were baptized after John. John was not a heretic, and he could possess a baptism which, although granted by Christ, was not Christ’s own baptism, since he possessed the charity of Christ. A heretic, however, can possess Christ’s baptism and the perversity of the devil, just as someone within the Church can possess Christ’s baptism and the envy of the devil.

18. “But surely one ought all the more to be baptized after a heretic, because John was not a heretic, and yet people were baptized after him.”

So, someone might say, one ought all the more to be baptized after a drunkard, because John was sober, and yet people were baptized after him. We will have no answer to give him except this: to those baptized by John, who did not possess Christ’s baptism, Christ’s baptism was subsequently given; but in those who possess Christ’s baptism, no perversity of theirs can possibly cause Christ’s baptism not to be present in them.

19. A heretic therefore did not obtain the right to baptize because he baptized first, but because he did not baptize with his own baptism. And even if he did not possess the right to baptize, what he gave belongs to Christ, and the one who received it belongs to Christ.

Many things are given contrary to legal right, but they are not for that reason said either not to have been given or not to exist. For even the person who renounces the world in words alone and not in deeds does not legally receive baptism; nevertheless, he receives it. Cyprian himself reports that there were such people in the Church in his time, and we encounter them and lament them.

20. It is astonishing how it can be said that Baptism and the Church cannot in any way be separated from one another [Note: [Col. 0186] The Lov. edition omits “from one another” (*a se*), which is found here in the other books and in Cyprian.]. If baptism remains inseparably in the baptized person, how can the baptized person be separated from the Church while baptism cannot be separated?

That baptism remains inseparably in the baptized person is clear. For however deep the abyss of evils or however dreadful the gulf of sins into which a baptized person may plunge—even into apostasy—he does not lose baptism. Therefore it is not given back to him when he returns through repentance, because he is judged never to have been able to be without it.

But who could doubt that a baptized person can be separated from the Church? From the Church all the heresies have gone out, deceiving people under the Christian name.

## CHAPTER XVI

Since, therefore, it is clear that baptism is present in a baptized person when that baptized person is separated from the Church, the baptism that is in him is necessarily separated from the Church together with him. Thus not everyone who possesses baptism possesses the Church, just as not everyone who possesses the Church also possesses eternal life.

Or if we say that only those possess the Church who keep the divine commandments, we must already acknowledge that many possess baptism without possessing the Church.

21. A heretic therefore does not preempt baptism when he has received it from the Church. Nor could he lose it when he withdrew, since we say that he no longer possesses the Church and yet concede that he possesses baptism.

No one diminishes his own primacy and grants it to a heretic merely by saying that the heretic took away with him something which he did not lawfully give, though he did give something legitimate, and no longer lawfully possesses it, though he possesses something legitimate.

Primacy exists only in holy conduct and a good life. To this belong all those members of the bride who has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), and of that dove who groans amid the wickedness of many ravens [Note: [Col. 0187] *Second Book of Revisions*, chapter 18.]. Unless perhaps, since Esau lost his primacy through his desire for lentil stew (Genesis 25:29–34), fraudsters, robbers, usurers, the envious, drunkards, and others of this kind—people over whom Cyprian also lamented in writing in the Church of his time—are to be considered holders of primacy.

Therefore either possessing the Church is not the same as possessing primacy in divine matters; or, if everyone who possesses the Church also possesses primacy, then all those wicked people do not possess the Church, although they are visibly within it and, as none of us denies, both give and receive baptism. For who would say that such people possess primacy in divine matters, unless he understands nothing divine?

## CHAPTER XVII

22. We have now reached Cyprian’s peaceful words—that is, the end of the letter—after considering and examining everything. When I read and reread them, they do not satisfy me: such delight in fraternal love breathes from them, and such sweetness of charity overflows.

He says:

“We have written this brief reply to you, dearest brother, according to our limited ability, prescribing or prejudging nothing for anyone, so that each bishop may do what he thinks right, possessing the free exercise of his own judgment. For our part, insofar as we are able, we do not quarrel with our colleagues and fellow bishops on account of the heretics; we maintain concord and the peace of the Lord with them, especially since the Apostle also says, ‘But if anyone thinks that he is contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God’ (1 Corinthians 11:16) [Note: [Col. 0187] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read “if anyone has thought”; Lov. has “if anyone is thought.”]. We preserve patiently and gently the charity of the spirit, the honor of the college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood. For this reason also, as far as our limited ability allowed, with the Lord permitting and inspiring us, we composed the treatise *On the Good of Patience*, which we have sent to you out of mutual affection.”

23. These words contain much that should be considered, and in this man—who loved the beauty of the Lord’s house and the place where his dwelling was established (Psalm 25:8)—the splendor of Christian charity shines brightly.

First, he did not keep silent about what he believed. Second, he expressed it so gently and peacefully. Third, he maintained ecclesiastical peace with those who held a different opinion. Fourth, he understood that there is such great benefit in the bond of unity. Fifth, he loved and soberly guarded that unity. Sixth, he saw and understood that even those who held different opinions could hold them without forfeiting charity.

For he would not have said that he maintained divine concord and the Lord’s peace with wicked people, since a good person can have peace toward the wicked but cannot maintain peace with them when they themselves do not maintain it.

Finally, because he prescribed nothing for anyone and prejudged no one, but allowed each bishop to do what he thought right, possessing the free exercise of his own judgment, he also gave people such as us an opportunity to discuss these matters peacefully with him.

He is present not only through his letters but also through that charity which flourished in him above all and could never die. Desiring, therefore, to cling and be joined to him—unless the incongruity of my sins prevents me, with the help of his prayers—I will learn, if I can, through his letters, with what peace the Lord governed his Church through him and with what consolation. Clothed in bowels of humility through the affection of his words, if I perceive something more truly in agreement with the whole world, I will not set my own heart above it—not even on the very point on which, though he held a different view, he was nevertheless not separated from the whole world.

For greater strength of virtue shone forth in him when this question still wavered, not yet having been resolved: although he held a different opinion from many of his colleagues, he exercised such moderation that he did not cut off the holy fellowship of the Church of God through any stain of schism. This was greater than if he had held not only the true opinion but also the same opinion as everyone else, without possessing this virtue.

I would not please him if I desired to place his intellectual ability, his eloquence, and the abundance of his teaching above the holy council of all nations, in which he was certainly present through the unity of the Spirit. This is especially so now that he has been placed in such a light of truth that he sees with complete certainty what he was seeking here so peacefully.

From that abundance he laughs at these words of ours, which appear like the rudiments of children. There he sees by what rule of piety he acted here, so that nothing in the Church was dearer to him than unity. There too, with ineffable delight, he beholds by what provident and merciful dispensation the Lord chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, in order to heal our swellings [Note: [Col. 0188] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “God chose the weak things of the world to heal our swellings; he chose the weak things of the world to confound the wise.”], and so beneficially arranged everything in the ranks of the members of his Church that people chosen for the aid of the Gospel could not claim to have been chosen on account of their intellectual ability or literary learning—abilities whose possession they still did not know was due to his gift—and thus become dangerously inflated with pride.

O how Cyprian rejoices! How much more serenely he beholds in that light why it was done for the salvation of the human race that something should be found which may rightly be criticized, even in the Christian and devout writings of orators, while nothing of the kind is found in the writings of fishermen!

Regarding this joy [Note: [Col. 0188] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read *ergo* (“therefore”). M.] of that holy soul I am entirely confident. Nevertheless, I do not dare either to think or to say that my writings are free from every error. Nor do I place my opinion above his judgment in which he thought that those coming from the heretics should be received differently from the way they had previously been received, as he himself testifies, or from the way they are now received, according to the reasonable custom confirmed by the full council of the Christian world.

Rather, I place above it the judgment of the holy Catholic Church, which he loved and loves so greatly, in which he produced such abundant fruit through his endurance. He was not the totality of that Church, but remained within its totality. He never abandoned its root, but in that root, so that he might be fruitful, he was pruned by the heavenly farmer and made more fruitful. For the peace and salvation of the Church—so that the wheat might not be uprooted together with the weeds—he both rebuked, with the freedom of truth, the great evils of people established with him in unity, and endured them through the strength of charity.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0189] In the following two chapters he examines Cyprian’s Letter 72, to Quintus.]

24. For this same Cyprian also admonishes us at great length that many people, dead in their offenses and sins, although they do not belong to the fellowship of Christ or to the members of that one innocent and simple dove—if she alone baptized, such people would certainly not baptize—nevertheless appear to be inside the Church, and are both baptized and baptize.

Although they are dead, Christ’s baptism lives in them, for Christ does not die, and death will no longer rule over him. Since, then, there are dead people inside the Church, and not merely hidden ones—for Cyprian would not have said so much about them—who either do not belong to that living dove or do not yet belong to it, and since there are dead people outside who more evidently either do not belong to it or do not yet belong to it; and since it is true that one who himself does not live cannot give life to another, it is clear that those baptized inside by such people are given life by the one whose baptism it is, if they approach with a true conversion of heart.

But if such people renounce the world in words and not in deeds, as Cyprian testifies that there are people inside the Church who do this, they themselves are not given life unless they convert. Nevertheless, they truly possess baptism, even if they do not convert.

It is likewise clear that those dead people outside the Church, although they neither live nor give life, nevertheless possess the living baptism, which will benefit them unto life if they convert to peace.

## CHAPTER XIX

25. Those who at that time came from the heresies were received in the same baptism of Christ which they had received outside the Church, and they said that they were following the ancient custom, just as the Church receives them now. It was therefore pointless to argue against them that among the ancient heresies and schisms [Note: [Col. 0189] Perhaps: “heresy and schisms.”] there had first been beginnings, so that those people had been members of the Church who withdrew from it, and had previously been baptized there; consequently, when they returned to the Church and did penance, they did not need to be baptized.

For as soon as any heresy arose and departed from the fellowship of Catholic communion, it could baptize those who rushed into it—not on some later day, but on that very day. Therefore, if this was the ancient custom, that such people should be received in this way—which even those who argued against it could not deny—no one who pays closer attention can doubt that those who had been baptized outside in the heresies were also received in this way.

26. I do not see what reason there is for someone not yet to be called a wandering sheep when, while seeking Christian salvation, he falls into the error of the heretics and happens to be baptized among them, while someone inside the Catholic Church is called a sheep once he has become one, though he has renounced the world in words alone and not in deeds and received baptism with that falsity of heart.

Or if such a person does not become a sheep until he has turned to God with a truthful heart, then just as this person is not baptized when he becomes a sheep, if he had already been baptized, but was not yet a sheep, so the person who comes from the heretics in order to become a sheep should not then be baptized if he had already been baptized among them with the same baptism, even though he was not yet a sheep.

Therefore, since all the wicked people inside the Church—avaricious people, the envious, drunkards, and those living contrary to Christian discipline—may rightly be called liars, people of darkness, dead people, and antichrists, do they nevertheless fail to baptize because nothing can be shared by falsehood and truth, darkness and light, death and immortality, Antichrist and Christ?

27. It is therefore not merely on the basis of custom but also on the basis of truth’s reasoning that someone relies when he says that God’s sacrament cannot be made perverse by the perversity of any human being, since it is shown to exist even in perverse people.

The apostle John certainly says most plainly, “The one who hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:9), and again, “The one who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Why, then, do such people baptize inside the Church, when Cyprian himself records that they were characterized by malicious envy (Letter 73, to Jubaianus)?

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0190] In the next three chapters he answers Cyprian’s Letter 70, written from the Council of Carthage to Saturninus, Maximus, and others.]

How does a murderer cleanse and sanctify water? How do people of darkness bless oil? But if God is present with his sacraments and words, regardless of the people through whom they are administered, then God’s sacraments are everywhere valid, while wicked people, for whom they are of no benefit, are wicked everywhere.

28. What sense does it make to suppose that a heretic does not possess baptism because he does not possess the Church? And yet, when he is baptized, he is also questioned about the holy Church. Is it as though the person who renounces the world inside the Church in words but not in deeds is not questioned about this in baptism?

Therefore, just as this person’s false response does not make the baptism he receives cease to be baptism, so the other person’s false response concerning the holy Church does not make the baptism he receives cease to be baptism. And just as, if the first person later fulfills truthfully what he had answered falsely, baptism is not repeated for him but his life is corrected, so, if the other person later comes to the Church about which he had falsely answered when questioned—because he thought he possessed it although he did not—the Church he did not possess is given to him; what he had received is not repeated.

But why should God be able to sanctify oil through words proceeding from the mouth of a murderer, while he cannot do so upon an altar established by heretics? I do not know, unless perhaps the deceitfully turned heart of a human being, which does not impede God’s presence within, is less obstructive than a piece of wood deceitfully placed outside, preventing God from deigning to be present with his sacraments—God whom no human falsity can impede.

If, then, the Gospel’s statement, “God does not hear a sinner” (John 9:31), means that sacraments are not celebrated through a sinner, how does God hear a murderer praying over baptismal water, or over oil, or over the Eucharist, or over the heads of those upon whom hands are imposed?

Yet all these things are both performed and effective even through murderers—that is, through those who hate their brothers, even inside the Church itself. Since no one can give what he does not possess, how does a murderer give the Holy Spirit? And yet that same murderer also baptizes inside the Church. Therefore God gives the Holy Spirit even when that murderer is the one baptizing.

## CHAPTER XXI

29. But when he says that the person who comes to the Church must be baptized and renewed so that he may be sanctified inside through holy people, what will he do if inside the Church he also encounters people who are not holy? Is a murderer perhaps holy?

And if such a person is baptized in the Church so that he may also renounce this very thing—that when he came to God while seeking a priest, he fell through a deceitful error into a sacrilegious person—where will he later renounce it if, while seeking a man of God inside the Church itself, he falls through a deceitful error into a murderer?

If nothing in a human being can be empty while something else prevails, why can a holy sacrament exist in a murderer while a holy heart does not? If anyone who cannot give the Holy Spirit cannot baptize either, why does a murderer baptize inside the Church? Or how does a murderer possess the Holy Spirit, when everyone who possesses the Holy Spirit has been enlightened, while the one who hates his brother is still in darkness?

If, because there is one baptism and one Spirit, those who do not possess one Spirit cannot possess one baptism, why do the innocent person and the murderer inside the Church possess one baptism while they do not possess one Spirit?

Thus it follows that in each person we must acknowledge what he possesses and give him what he does not possess. If nothing that is done by those whom the Lord calls his enemies and adversaries can be valid and firm before the Lord, why is the baptism administered by murderers valid? Do we not call murderers the enemies and adversaries of the Lord? “The one who hates his brother is a murderer.”

How, then, did those who hated Paul, the servant of Christ Jesus, baptize? By hating Paul they also hated Jesus, since Jesus himself said to Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), when Saul was persecuting Christ’s servants. And at the end the Lord himself will say, “What you did not do to one of the least of mine, you did not do to me” (Matthew 25:45).

Therefore all who go out from us are not of us, but not all who are with us are of us. When the threshing floor is being threshed, whatever flies away from it is not wheat; but not everything that is there is wheat. Hence John also says, “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

Therefore God gives the sacrament of grace even through wicked people, but he gives grace itself only through himself or through his holy ones. Thus he effects the remission of sins either through himself or through the members of that dove to whom he says, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:23).
