As for baptism, which is the sacrament of the remission of sins, no one doubts that even murderers can possess it—people who are still in darkness because brotherly hatred has not been excluded from their hearts. Whether none of their sins have been forgiven, if they were baptized without a change of heart for the better, or whether the sins immediately forgiven returned, we recognize that baptism is holy because it belongs to God himself. Whether such people administer or receive it, their perversity does not violate it, either inside or outside the Church.

## CHAPTER XXII

30. Accordingly, we agree with Cyprian that heretics cannot grant remission of sins, but can grant baptism. Baptism can indeed be harmful to both those who give it and those who receive it, when they misuse so great a gift of God. The same is true of the wicked and envious, whom Cyprian himself testifies to be present inside the Church: they cannot grant remission of sins, although we all acknowledge that they can give baptism.

For if it was said concerning those who have sinned against us, “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:15), how much more impossible is it for sins to be forgiven by those who hate the brothers by whom they are loved and are baptized in that very hatred? Yet when such people are later corrected, baptism is not given to them again; rather, in their true conversion the forgiveness which they were not worthy to receive at that time is granted to them.

Therefore neither what Cyprian writes to Quintus nor what he writes with his colleagues Liberalis, Caldonius, Junius, and the others to Saturninus, Maximus, and others should, after careful consideration, be brought forward against the consensus of the whole Catholic Church. They rejoiced to be members of that Church, and they neither cut themselves off from it nor allowed those who held different opinions to be cut off from it. At last, through the Lord’s will, in a full council—although only after many years—what was more correct became clear, not through the establishment of some novelty but through the strengthening of antiquity.

## CHAPTER XXIII

31. [Note: [Col. 0192] In this and the following chapters he refutes Cyprian’s Letter 74, to Pompeius.]

Cyprian also writes to Pompeius about this same matter. There he plainly indicates that Stephen, whom we have learned was at that time bishop of the Roman Church, not only did not agree with him in these matters but also wrote and instructed against him.

Stephen certainly did not communicate with the heretics for this reason: that he dared not condemn Christ’s baptism, which he recognized as remaining intact amid their perversity. For if those who hold erroneous views about God do not possess baptism, it has already, as I think, been sufficiently argued that this can also occur inside the Church.

The apostles, however, issued no command concerning this matter. But the custom that was set against Cyprian should be believed to have originated in their tradition, just as there are many practices held by the whole Church which are rightly believed to have been commanded by the apostles for that reason, although they are not found in writing [Note: [Col. 0192] Only three manuscripts read, “and for this reason [by] the Apostles.”].

32. “But it is written concerning heretics that they are condemned by themselves” (Titus 3:11).

What, then? Were those others not also condemned by themselves, to whom it was said, “For in judging another you condemn yourself”? To them the Apostle also says, “You who preach that one should not steal, do you steal?” (Romans 2:1, 21), and so forth.

Those people were surely like this: although they were bishops and stood with Cyprian in Catholic unity, they seized estates through deceitful frauds, while preaching to the people the Apostle’s words, “Nor will robbers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

33. Therefore, I shall not hesitate to review briefly, according to the same principles, the remaining statements of the letter written to Pompeius. By what authority of the holy Scriptures is it shown to be contrary to God’s command that those who come from the heretics, if they have already received Christ’s Baptism there, should not be baptized again? Yet it is plainly shown that many false Christians, although they do not possess the same charity as the saints—without which whatever holy things they may have been able to possess are of no benefit—nevertheless possess Baptism in common with the saints. This has already been demonstrated sufficiently and abundantly.

He says that the Church, the Spirit, and Baptism cannot be separated from one another, and therefore wishes it to be understood that those separated from the Church and from the Holy Spirit are also separated from Baptism. But if this is so, when someone has received Baptism in the Catholic Church, he remains in it for as long as he himself remains in the Church; if he departs from there, he departs from Baptism. Yet this is not so. For this reason Baptism is not given back to one who returns: when he departed, he did not lose it.

Just as the wicked sons do not possess the Holy Spirit as the beloved sons possess him, and yet they possess Baptism, so heretics do not possess the Church as Catholics possess it, and yet they possess Baptism. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5), yet Baptism will not flee from it. Thus, just as Baptism can exist where the Holy Spirit withdraws, so Baptism can exist where the Church is not.

The laying on of hands, however, if it were not administered to one coming from heresy, would be judged to leave him entirely free of guilt. But because of the bond of charity—which is the greatest gift of the Holy Spirit, without which whatever other holy things may be in a person have no power to save—hands are laid upon heretics when they have been corrected.

## CHAPTER XXIV

34. I remember having already discussed sufficiently the temple of God and how the words “As many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27) are to be understood. For the greedy are not the temple of God, since it is written, “What partnership has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Cyprian has adopted Paul’s testimony that greed is idolatry. [Note: Col. 0193. Er., Lugd., Ven. read *assumpsit* (“adopted”); M. has *assumpserit* (“has adopted”).]

People put on Christ sometimes only as far as receiving the sacrament, and sometimes also as far as the sanctification of life. The former can be common to both the good and the wicked; the latter belongs properly to the good and devout. Therefore, if Baptism cannot exist without the Spirit, heretics also possess the Spirit—but for destruction, not for salvation, just as Saul possessed him (1 Samuel 19:23). For demons are cast out through the name of Christ in the Holy Spirit, and even the man who was outside the Church could do this; the disciples reported this to the Lord (Mark 9:37).

So too the greedy possess the Spirit, although they are not the temple of God: “What partnership has the temple of God with idols?” [Col. 0194] But if the greedy do not possess the Spirit of God and nevertheless possess Baptism, Baptism can exist without the Spirit.

35. If heresy cannot beget children for God through Christ because it is not Christ’s bride, neither can that crowd of wicked people established within the Church, because it too is not Christ’s bride. For Christ’s bride is designated as being “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27) [Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 18]. Therefore, either not all who have been baptized are children of God, or even one who is not the bride can beget children of God.

And just as it is asked whether the person who received Christ’s Baptism among the heretics has been born spiritually, so it can be asked whether the person who received Christ’s Baptism in the Catholic Church without turning to God with a truthful heart has been born spiritually—yet for that reason he did not fail to receive Baptism.

## CHAPTER XXV

36. I do not wish to retract what he poured forth in anger against Stephen, since there is no need. The same things are said there that have already been sufficiently examined, and it is better to pass over those matters that involved the danger of a destructive dissension.

Stephen, however, had thought that those who attempted to overturn the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be shunned. This man, moved by the difficulty of the question itself and endowed most abundantly with the holy affections of charity, maintained that one should remain in unity with those who held different opinions. Thus, although he expressed his indignation with some agitation, he nevertheless did so fraternally. The peace of Christ prevailed in their hearts, so that no evil schism arose among them in such a dispute.

Heresies and schisms did not therefore grow more abundantly from this, because what belongs to Christ in them is approved, while what belongs to them is rejected. Indeed, those who maintained this law of rebaptizing were cut into more numerous fragments.

## CHAPTER XXVI

37. Moreover, when he says, “A bishop must be teachable” (2 Timothy 2:24), and adds, “A teachable person is one who is patient and gentle in learning—for a bishop must not only teach but also learn, since the one who grows and advances daily by learning better things also teaches better,” by these words the holy man, endowed with devout charity, clearly indicates that we need not fear reading his letters in such a way that, if something is later discovered through more numerous and prolonged investigations and confirmed by the Church, we should not hesitate to accept it.

For just as the learned Cyprian had many things to teach, so there was also something that the teachable Cyprian could learn. His admonition that we should return to the fountain—that is, to apostolic tradition—and from there direct a channel into our own times is excellent and must undoubtedly be followed.

It was therefore handed down to us, as he himself recalls, from the Apostles, that there is one God, one Christ, one hope, one faith, one Church, and one Baptism (Ephesians 4:4–5). Since, then, in the very times of the Apostles we find that there were some who did not have one hope but did have one Baptism, truth is conveyed from that fountain to us in such a way that it becomes clear how it can happen that, although there is one Church, just as there is one hope and one Baptism, those who do not have one Church nevertheless possess one Baptism—just as even in those times it could happen that those who did not have one hope possessed one Baptism.

For how did those who said, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Corinthians 15:32), have one hope with the saints and righteous, since they said that there was no resurrection of the dead? And yet they were among those to whom the same Apostle says, “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (ibid. 1:13). To them he writes most openly, saying, “How can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (ibid. 15:12).

## CHAPTER XXVII

38. The Church is described in the Song of Songs as “a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apple trees” (Song of Songs 4:12–13). I dare understand this only of the saints and righteous, not of the greedy, fraudulent, robbers, usurers, drunkards, and envious—although from Cyprian’s own writings, as I have often recalled, we learn and teach more abundantly that these people shared Baptism with the righteous, though they certainly did not share charity with them.

Let someone tell me how those whom Cyprian testifies to have renounced the world with words alone and not in deeds, and yet to have been within the Church, slipped into the enclosed garden and sealed fountain. For if they too are there, and they too are Christ’s bride, is that bride truly “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27) [Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 18], and is that beautiful dove disfigured by such a part of its members? Or are these the thorns, among which stands the lily mentioned in the same Song: “Like a lily among thorns” (Song of Songs 2:2)?

Therefore, to the extent that it is a lily, to that extent it is also an enclosed garden and a sealed fountain: namely, in those righteous who are Jews inwardly, by circumcision of the heart (Romans 2:29)—“all the beauty of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14)—in whom there is the fixed number of saints predestined before the foundation of the world.

That multitude of thorns, whether by hidden or open separations, lies outwardly beyond the number. “I proclaimed and spoke,” he says; “they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39:6). Therefore, that number of the righteous who have been called according to God’s purpose (Romans 8:28), of whom it is said, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19), is itself the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, the well of living water, and the paradise with the fruit of apple trees.

Some of this number live spiritually and walk along the surpassing way of charity. When they instruct someone who has been overtaken in any offense, in a spirit of gentleness, they take care lest they themselves be tempted (Galatians 6:1). And when they themselves happen to be overtaken, the affection of charity is somewhat restrained in them, but it is not extinguished; rising again and burning anew, it is restored to its former course. For they know how to say, “My soul slumbered from weariness; strengthen me according to your words” (Psalm 118:28).

When they think differently about something, God will also reveal that to them, provided they remain fervent in charity and do not break the bond of peace (Philippians 3:15).

Others, however, still carnal and animal, diligently exercise themselves in their progress. To make themselves capable of spiritual food, they are nourished with the milk of the holy mysteries. They avoid in the fear of God those things that are manifest even by popular judgment in their depraved conduct. They strive with the utmost vigilance to take less and less delight in earthly and temporal things. They hold firmly to the rule of faith, carefully investigated; and if they deviate from it in any respect, they are quickly corrected by Catholic authority, although in their understanding of its words, according to a carnal sense, they still fluctuate amid various collisions of imaginings.

There are also some of this number who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the Gentiles; yet even there the Lord knows those who are his. For in God’s ineffable foreknowledge, many who appear to be outside are within, and many who appear to be within are outside.

From all these, then, who are, so to speak, within inwardly and secretly, that enclosed garden, sealed fountain, well of living water, and paradise with the fruit of apple trees is constituted. Of their gifts granted by God, some are proper to them, such as unfailing charity in the present age and eternal life in the age to come; others, however, are shared with the wicked and perverse, such as all the remaining things among which are the most sacred mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

39. From this point, therefore, consideration of that ark becomes easier and more straightforward—the ark whose builder and helmsman Noah was (Genesis 6–7). Peter says:

“In Noah’s ark a few, that is, eight human souls, were saved through water; and Baptism, in a corresponding form, now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but an appeal of a good conscience” (1 Peter 3:20–21).

[Note: Col. 0196. Am. reads, “as people appear … to be baptized”; Er. likewise, though below it reads “to be baptized” for “baptized.” Most manuscripts read, “as they appear to people … baptized.”] Therefore, if people appear to human beings to have been baptized within Catholic unity, although they renounce the world with words alone and not in deeds, how do they belong to the mystery of this ark, in whom there is no appeal of a good conscience? Or how are those saved through water who, making evil use of holy Baptism, appear to be within but persevere to the end of life in disgraceful and destructive conduct? Or how were those not saved through water whom Cyprian himself recalls as having previously been admitted simply into the Church together with the Baptism they had received in heresy?

The unity of the same ark saved them, and no one was saved in it except through water. For he himself says: “The Lord in his mercy is able to grant pardon and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, having been simply admitted into the Church, fell asleep in the Church” (*Letter* 73, to Jubaianus).

If not through water, how were they in the ark? If not in the ark, how were they in the Church? But if they were in the Church, then certainly they were in the ark; and if in the ark, certainly through water.

It can therefore happen that some baptized outside are, by God’s foreknowledge, more truly reckoned baptized within, because there the water begins to benefit them for salvation. For they cannot otherwise be said to have been saved in the ark except through water.

And again, some who appeared to have been baptized within are, by that same foreknowledge of God, more truly reckoned baptized outside. For by making evil use of Baptism, they die through water; and at that time this happened to no one except one who was outside the ark.

Certainly it is clear that what is meant by being within and outside the Church must be understood as referring to the heart, not the body. All who are within in heart are saved in the unity of the ark through the same water; through that same water all who are outside in heart—whether or not they are also outside in body—die as adversaries of unity.

Therefore, just as the same water, not a different one, saved those who were in the ark and destroyed those who were outside the ark, so the same Baptism, not another, saves good Catholics and destroys wicked Catholics or heretics.

As for what the most blessed Cyprian thought about the Catholic Church, and how heretics are utterly crushed by his authority, although I have said much, I have nevertheless decided, if it pleases the Lord, to speak separately, at somewhat greater length and with greater clarity, after I have first said what I think is owed concerning his council. I shall undertake that in the following volume, according to God’s will.

# BOOK SIX

In this book the Council of Carthage, held concerning the Baptism of heretics through Cyprian’s care and authority, is examined.

[Column 0197]

## CHAPTER I

1. Perhaps what has already been said might be sufficient: through arguments repeated so many times and discussed and examined in so many ways, with the testimonies of the divine Scriptures also added, and with so many testimonies of Cyprian himself supporting it, even those who are slow of heart now understand, as I think, that Christ’s Baptism cannot be violated by any perversity of the person who gives it or of the person who receives it.

In those times, when this question was being debated against the ancient custom [Note: Col. 0197. Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “against the useful custom”], while the disputants nevertheless preserved charity and unity, certain distinguished bishops of Christ—among whom the blessed Cyprian especially stood out—thought that Christ’s Baptism could not exist among heretics or schismatics for no other reason than that the sacrament was not distinguished from the effect or use of the sacrament.

Because its effect and use—release from sins and uprightness of heart—were not found among heretics, it was thought that the sacrament itself was not there either. But when attention was turned to the multitude of the inward chaff, and it became apparent that those who are perverse and live destructively within the very unity cannot either grant or possess remission of sins—since it was said not to wicked but to good sons, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:23)—it nevertheless became sufficiently clear to the pastors of the Catholic Church spread throughout the world that wicked people possess, give, and receive the sacrament of Baptism.

Later, the original custom was confirmed by the authority of a plenary council: the sheep that wandered outside, and that had received the Lord’s mark outside from its deceitful plunderers, when it comes to the salvation of Christian unity, is corrected from error, freed from captivity, and healed from its wound; yet the Lord’s mark is recognized in it rather than rejected.

For many wolves—even wolves themselves—imprint that same mark upon wolves. Though they appear to be within, they are shown by the fruits of their conduct not to belong to that sheep which, though drawn from many, is one, because they persist in those ways to the end. For according to God’s foreknowledge, just as many sheep wander outside, so many wolves lurk within. Yet among them the Lord knows those who are his. They hear no voice except that of the shepherd, even when he cries out through men like the Pharisees, of whom it was said, “What they say, do” (Matthew 23:3).

2. Just as the spiritual person who possesses the goal of the commandment—that is, charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1:5)—may, because of something in the body that is still subject to corruption and weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), perceive something less clearly and think differently about it, and God will reveal it to him when he wills, provided he remains in the same charity (Philippians 3:15), so in a carnal and perverse person some good and useful thing may be found that comes from elsewhere, not from the person himself.

For just as something in a fruitful vine-shoot may be found that needs pruning so that it may bear greater fruit, so a grape may hang even on a barren, dry, or bound reed. And therefore, just as it is foolish to cherish the refuse of a fruitful vine-shoot, while the person acts wisely who does not reject sweet fruit wherever it hangs, so whoever has been cut off from unity rebaptizes because Cyprian thought that those coming from heretics ought to be baptized again: he rejects what should be praised in so great a man, pursues what should be corrected, and does not attain even what he pursues.

Cyprian, in his grave zeal for God, detested those who had separated themselves from unity and consequently thought that they were also separated from Baptism itself. These people, however, thinking it a small crime that they themselves are separated from Christ’s unity, insist that his Baptism is not there either, but has gone out with them. They are therefore so far from Cyprian’s fruitfulness that they do not even equal his refuse.

## CHAPTER II

3. Likewise, whoever lacks charity and walks along the destructive paths of the worst conduct appears to be within although he is outside, and does not repeat Christ’s Baptism among the heretics. Nothing helps his barrenness, since it is not fertilized by his own fruit but burdened with another’s.

It can happen that someone flourishes in the root of charity and thinks most rightly about the matter on which Cyprian thought differently, while nevertheless more fruitful things are found in Cyprian than in that person, and more things requiring pruning are found in that person than in Cyprian.

We therefore do not merely refrain from comparing wicked Catholics with him; we do not even easily place good Catholics on an equal footing with the blessed Cyprian, whom the devout mother Church numbers among the rare and few men of outstanding grace.

This is so even though these people recognize Christ’s Baptism among heretics, while Cyprian thought otherwise. Through him, who saw somewhat less clearly while remaining most firmly in unity, it was demonstrated more plainly to heretics by what sacrilegious crime the bond of peace would be broken.

For the blind Pharisees, although they sometimes said what ought to be done, were not to be compared with the Apostle Peter, although he sometimes said what ought not to be done. Nor should the barrenness of these people be compared with Cyprian’s freshness; nor should the fruit of others be equated with his abundance.

No one now compels the Gentiles to Judaize, yet no one who has made whatever progress in the Church can therefore be compared with the Apostle Peter.

Therefore, while rendering the reverence that is due and paying, as far as I can, the honor worthy of the peaceful bishop and glorious martyr Cyprian, I nevertheless dare to say that he thought differently about baptizing schismatics or heretics from what the truth later revealed—not on my own authority, but according to the judgment of the universal Church, strengthened and confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.

In the same way, while venerating Peter, the first of the Apostles and the most eminent of the martyrs, according to his merit, I nevertheless dare to say that he did not act rightly in compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. I say this too not on my own authority, but according to the salutary teaching of the Apostle Paul, retained and preserved throughout the universal Church (Galatians 2:14).

4. Therefore, discussing Cyprian’s opinion, though far beneath Cyprian’s merits, I say that both the good and the wicked can possess, give, and receive the sacrament of Baptism. The good do so beneficially and savingly; the wicked, destructively and as a penalty. Yet the sacrament itself remains equally whole in both. Its equal integrity is unaffected by how wickedly someone possesses it among the wicked, just as it is unaffected by how well someone possesses it among the good.

Accordingly, it makes no difference how wickedly someone administers it, just as it makes no difference how well someone administers it; and it makes no difference how wickedly someone receives it, just as it makes no difference how well someone receives it. For in itself, both in those who are not equally righteous and in those who are not equally wicked, it is equally holy.

## CHAPTER III

5. That the wicked, without being changed for the better, possess, administer, and receive Baptism, we have demonstrated sufficiently, as I think, both from the canonical Scriptures and from Cyprian’s own letters.

That they do not belong to the holy Church of God, although they appear to be within, is most clearly evident from the fact that they are greedy, robbers, usurers, envious, malicious, and so forth. The Church, however, is that one dove (Song of Songs 6:8), modest and chaste, the bride without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27) [Note: *Retractations* II, chapter 18], the enclosed garden, sealed fountain, and paradise with the fruit of apple trees (Song of Songs 4:12–13), along with the other things similarly said about her.

This is understood only of the good, holy, and righteous: not merely according to the operations of God’s gifts that are shared by the good and wicked, but also according to the inward and surpassing charity of those who possess the Holy Spirit. To them the Lord says, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; and if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:23).

## CHAPTER IV

6. Accordingly, no adequate reason can be given why the wicked person who is able to possess Baptism cannot also administer it—just as he possesses it destructively, so he can administer it destructively—not because he administers something of that kind, nor because someone of that kind administers it, but because he administers it to someone of that kind [Note: The Louvain editors, against all published books and manuscripts, corrected the text to read: “not because he administers to someone of that kind, but because someone of that kind administers it.”].

When the wicked person administers it to the good person—that is, to one changed by a truthful conversion within the bond of unity—the wickedness of the minister does not separate the good sacrament that is administered from the good believer to whom it is administered [Note: The Ambrosian edition reads, “the wickedness is separated.” Erasmus and all manuscripts read, “the wickedness is overcome,” with the negative particle omitted].

And when sins are forgiven for one who has truly turned to God, they are forgiven by those to whom he is joined by that true conversion. For the same Holy Spirit forgives them—the Spirit who has been given to all the saints joined to one another in charity, whether or not they know one another bodily.

Similarly, when someone’s sins are retained, they are retained by those from whom the person whose sins are retained separates himself through dissimilarity of life and aversion of heart, whether or not they know him bodily.

## CHAPTER V

7. Therefore all the wicked are spiritually separated from the good. If they are also separated bodily by open dissent, they become worse. But, as has been said, it makes no difference to the holiness of Baptism how wickedly someone possesses it or how wickedly he administers it. A person separated from unity can administer it, just as he can possess it; but he possesses it as destructively as he administers it.

The person to whom he administers it can receive it beneficially if he himself receives it without being separated. This happened, for example, to many who, with a Catholic mind and a heart not alienated from the unity of peace, were driven by the necessity of impending death to enter the presence of some heretic. They received Christ’s Baptism from him without sharing his perversity; and whether they died or were freed, they did not remain with those to whom they had never passed over in heart.

But if the recipient himself was separated when he received it, he receives it more destructively in proportion to the greatness of the good that he receives improperly [Note: At “greater good” (*majus bonum*), Am. and the manuscripts read *magis* (“more”)]; and it contributes more to his destruction while separated in proportion to how much it could contribute to his salvation while joined to unity.

Therefore, if he is corrected from that perversity and turns away from separation and comes to Catholic peace, his sins are forgiven under the same Baptism that he had received. Under that Baptism his sins had been retained because of the sacrilege of division; through the bond of charity they are now forgiven. For in both the just person and the unjust person, that which is always holy is neither increased by anyone’s righteousness nor diminished by anyone’s wickedness.

8. Since these things are so, what harm to this truth, so clear and evident, is caused by the fact that many of Cyprian’s fellow bishops agreed with him in that opinion and brought forward their own views in agreement with it? Nothing, except that the charity of that man toward Christ’s unity becomes increasingly known.

If he alone had held this opinion and remained without anyone’s agreement, it might have seemed that he had recoiled from the crime of schism merely because he found no companions in error. But with so many agreeing with him, and while remaining in unity with those who held different opinions from the others, he preserved the most holy bond of Catholic universality—not through fear of solitude, but through love of peace.

It might therefore now seem superfluous to review separately the individual opinions of the other bishops of that council. But since those who are slow of heart do not think that a response has been given if one responds to a particular passage of someone’s speech not there but elsewhere, even though the response could also be applied to that passage, it is much better that they be worn down by extensive reading so that they may be sharpened than that, through understanding too little, they complain and thereby be refuted.

## CHAPTER VI

9. First, then, let us recall again Cyprian’s consultation, which reveals a peaceful soul overflowing with abundant charity and with which the consultation itself begins:

“You have heard, beloved colleagues,” he says, “what our fellow bishop Jubaianus wrote to me, consulting our humble judgment about the illicit and profane Baptism of heretics, and what I wrote back to him—namely, expressing the opinion that we have expressed once, twice, and often: that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with the Church’s Baptism.

“Other letters of Jubaianus were also read to you. In them, responding to our letter with sincere and devout dedication, he not only agreed but also gave thanks that he had been instructed. It remains for each of us to state what we think about this matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he has a different opinion.

“For none of us has constituted himself bishop of bishops, or compelled his colleagues by tyrannical terror to obey, since every bishop has, according to the liberty and power of his own judgment, the freedom to decide for himself, and he cannot be judged by another any more than he himself can judge another. Let us all await the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone has the power both to appoint us over the governance of his Church and to judge our conduct” (at the Council of Carthage).

## CHAPTER VII

10. In the preceding books, as far as I think sufficient and as far as we were able, we have discussed not only the letter he wrote to Jubaianus, but also the one he sent to Quintus, the one he wrote with certain colleagues to certain other colleagues, and the one he wrote to Pompeius, in support of the universal Catholic consensus and of the council in whose unity these men remained as devout members.

It therefore now seems appropriate to consider individually what the others also thought, with the freedom that Cyprian himself did not take away from us when he said, “Judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he has a different opinion.”

That he did not say this in order to seize the secret thoughts of his colleagues—as though he had drawn them out of hiding under such a guarantee of safety—but because he truly loved peace and unity is very easy to see from other similar passages, where he wrote to individuals, as he did to Jubaianus. [Note: Col. 0201. The printed editions add *puto* (“I think”) here; it is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts.]

“We have written this to you,” he says, “very briefly according to our humble capacity, dearest brother, prescribing or prejudging nothing, so that each bishop may do what he thinks, possessing free authority over his own judgment.”

And lest anyone appear to be expelled from the fellowship of the others if he held a different opinion under this same freedom, he continues:

“As far as lies in us, we do not contend with our colleagues and fellow bishops on account of the heretics, since with them we maintain divine concord and the Lord’s peace.”

A little later he says:

“We preserve patiently and gently the charity of spirit among our colleagues, their honor, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood” (*Letter* 73).

Likewise, in the letter he wrote to Magnus, when the question concerned Baptism by immersion and by pouring and whether there was any difference, he says:

“In this matter our modesty and restraint prejudge no one, so that each person may think what he considers right and do what he has thought” (*Letter* 69).

From these statements of his it is sufficiently clear that these matters were being discussed at a time when they were not yet being drawn from a clearly declared truth without ambiguity, but were still being sought with great effort, as though enclosed.

We, therefore, holding the custom of the universal Church—everywhere to be recognized in the simplicity of Baptism [Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions read, “everywhere for recognizing it.” Several manuscripts read, “the simplicity to be recognized everywhere,” which is not unsuitable if joined with “simplicity”]—a custom also strengthened by universal councils, and having received greater confidence from Cyprian’s words, by which even then I was permitted to hold a different opinion without violating the right of communion, while preferring and praising the unity that the blessed Cyprian and his colleagues who held that council maintained with those who thought differently, driving away and overturning the seditious calumnies of heretics and schismatics in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who speaks through his Apostle:

“Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3);

and through him also says:

“If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that to you also” (Philippians 3:15),

we now undertake to consider and examine the opinions of the holy bishops, while preserving with them the bond of unity and peace. In retaining this bond, we imitate them as far as the Lord himself assists us.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. Caecilius of Bilta said:

“I know of one Baptism in the Church alone, and none outside the Church. This one will be where there is true hope and certain faith. For it is written: ‘One faith, one hope, one Baptism’ (Ephesians 4:4–5).

“Not among heretics, where there is no hope and false faith, where everything is done through falsehood, where a demon-possessed person performs an exorcism, where the sacrament is questioned by one whose mouth and words pour forth cancer, where an unbeliever gives faith, a criminal grants remission of sins, and an antichrist baptizes in the name of Christ; where one cursed by God blesses, a dead man promises life, one without peace gives peace, a blasphemer invokes God, a profane person administers the priesthood, and a sacrilegious person sets up an altar.

“To all these things there is added that evil: that the bishop of the devil dares to make the Eucharist. Let those who stand with them say that all these things are false concerning the heretics [Note: The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts omit *omnia*, ‘all these things’].

“See what the Church is forced to agree to, and compelled to share in without Baptism and without remission of sins [Col. 0203]. We must flee and avoid this, brothers, separate ourselves from so great a crime, and hold the one Baptism that has been granted to the Church alone.”

12. To this I reply: whoever, even while within, professes to know God but denies him by his deeds—such as the greedy and the envious, and those who, because of hatred toward a brother, are called murderers not on my testimony but that of the holy apostle John (1 John 3:15)—has no hope, because he bears an evil conscience; is faithless, because he does not do what he vowed to God; a liar, because he professes what is false; demonic, because in his heart he makes room for the devil and his angels; and his words produce corruption, when through evil conversations they corrupt good morals. He is faithless, because he mocks what God threatens to such people; wicked, because he lives impiously; an antichrist, because his conduct opposes Christ; accursed by God, because Holy Scripture everywhere curses such people; dead, because he lacks the life of righteousness; without peace, because by contrary deeds he contends against the word of God; blasphemous, because through his ruined actions the Christian name is dishonored; profane, because he has been spiritually excluded from that inner sanctuary of God; sacrilegious, because by living badly he corrupts the temple of God within himself; and a bishop of the devil, because he serves fraud and greed, which is idolatry.

Yet both the apostle Paul and Bishop Cyprian testify that some—indeed very many—such people are also within. Why, then, do these men baptize? Why are some who renounce the world with words and not deeds baptized by people of this kind without having been changed from such behavior, and, when they do change, are not rebaptized?

Moreover, when he becomes indignant and says, “Behold to what things the Church is compelled to consent, and is forced to communicate without Baptism and remission of sins,” unless there were other bishops compelling the others to do these things, he would certainly not say this. From this it is also shown that those who did not depart from the former practice—which was later confirmed by the agreement of the whole council—at that time held the more truthful view.

But what does he add when he says, “This, brothers, we must flee and avoid, and separate ourselves from so great a crime”? If he says this in the sense that he neither does nor approves these things, that is one matter. But if he says it in order to condemn and exclude those who think differently, he is resisting Cyprian’s earlier [Note: [Col. 0203] In the manuscripts, “earlier.”] words, in which he says: “Judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion if he has held a different opinion.”

## CHAPTER IX

13. Felix, first, of Migirpa, said:

“I judge that everyone coming from heresy ought to be baptized. For he supposes in vain that he has been baptized there, since there is no Baptism except the one true Baptism in the Church; for there is one Lord, one faith, and one Church, in which there exist the one Baptism, holiness, and the rest. For the things performed outside have no effect toward salvation.”

[Note: [Col. 0203] “Felix, first, of Migirpa said,” together with Felix’s statement that follows, is entirely absent from the Amerbach edition and from all the manuscripts. In those codices, when the preceding chapter ends with the word “removing,” the following words are immediately appended: “To the things Felix of Migirpa said, we reply as follows.” The Louvain editors therefore think that Felix’s words were added by Erasmus [Col. 0204] from Cyprian; from the same source, they believe, the name “first” was transferred here, since it was entirely absent from Augustine. Cyprian, without Felix’s name, has: “First, of Misgirpa, said.”]

[Col. 0204] 14. To what Felix of Migirpa said, we reply as follows:

“If there were no one true Baptism except in the Church, it would certainly not exist among those who depart from unity. Yet it does exist among them; for those who return do not receive it again, for no other reason than that those who departed had not lost it.

“As for his statement, ‘For the things performed outside have no effect toward salvation,’ I agree, and I believe it to be entirely true. For it is one thing not to be there, and another thing to have no effect toward salvation. When people come to catholic peace, the things that existed outside begin to benefit them, although they had not previously benefited them.”

## CHAPTER X

15. To Polycarp of Hadrumetum, who said, “Those who approve the Baptism of heretics annul our own,” we reply:

“If the Baptism given through heretics belongs to heretics, then the Baptism given within by greedy and murderous people belongs to the greedy and murderous. But if the latter does not belong to them, neither does the former belong to those others. Therefore, whoever possesses it, it belongs to Christ.”

## CHAPTER XI

16. Novatus of Thamugade said:

“Although we know that all Scripture bears witness to saving Baptism, we must nevertheless express our faith. Heretics and schismatics who come to the Church, and who appear to have been falsely baptized, ought to be baptized in the perennial font. Therefore, according to the testimony of the Scriptures and according to the decree of our most holy fellow bishops [Note: Cyprian has “men of most holy memory,” namely those who had previously held a council with Agrippinus concerning this matter], all schismatics and heretics who have been converted to the Church ought to be baptized; and all who appeared to have been ordained ought to be received among the laity.”

[Note: So it appears in Erasmus and Cyprian. The Louvain editors point out that, although unsupported by manuscript copies, it has been emended to “I baptized,” and below, “I received among the laity,” presumably because Augustine answers accordingly: “Novatus of Thamugade said what he did.”]

[Note: The whole of Novatus’s statement is omitted by Amerbach and the manuscripts.]

17. Novatus of Thamugade said what he did, but he brought forward nothing by which he might show that he ought to have done what he did. For he mentioned the testimony of the Scriptures and the decree of his fellow bishops, but he produced nothing from them that we could examine.

## CHAPTER XII

18. Nemesianus of Tubunis said:

“That the Baptism given by heretics and schismatics is not true is declared everywhere in the Holy Scriptures, because their leaders are false Christs and false prophets. The Lord says through Solomon:

> ‘Whoever trusts in false things feeds the winds; he himself also pursues flying birds’ (Prov. 10:4). For he abandons the paths of his vineyard and has gone astray from the paths of his field. He enters deserted and dry places and land appointed for thirst, and with his hands he grasps fruitless things.’

[Note: Some of Nemesianus’s words here, which did not fit sufficiently well with Augustine’s reply in Erasmus’s edition, were altered by the Louvain editors and corrected according to Cyprian’s text. The Louvain editors add: “Moreover, this entire statement, as though cited from Solomon, is found today neither in Hebrew, nor Greek, nor Latin copies. Its first part, ‘whoever trusts … flying birds,’ occurs in Proverbs 10, but is marked with an obelus. Hence there is a suspicion that the following words, too, were once read there in African copies.” M.]

“And again: [Col. 0205]

> ‘Abstain from foreign water, and do not drink from a foreign fountain, so that you may live a long time and years of life may be added to you.’

“And in the Gospel our Lord Jesus Christ spoke with his own voice, saying:

> ‘Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (John 3:3).

“This is the Spirit who in the beginning was borne over the water (Gen. 1:2). For the Spirit cannot work without water, nor water without the Spirit. Therefore some wrongly interpret the matter when they say that they receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and are thus received; since it is manifest that they must be reborn in the Catholic Church through both sacraments.

“Then they will be able to be sons of God, as the Apostle says:

> ‘Taking care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, one God’ (Eph. 4:3–5).

“All these things the Catholic Church proclaims. And again in the Gospel he says:

> ‘What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit’ (John 3:6), because the Spirit is God and is born of God (ibid. 4:24).

“Therefore all heretics and schismatics, whatever they do, do carnally. The Apostle says:

> ‘For the works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleanness, incest, idolatries, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousy, anger, dissensions, heresies, and things like these; concerning them I forewarn you, as I have forewarned you, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God’ (Gal. 5:19–21).

“The Apostle condemns along with all evils those who create division—that is, schismatics and heretics. Unless, therefore, they receive saving Baptism in the one Catholic Church, they cannot be saved, but will be condemned with the carnal at the judgment of the Lord.”

[Note: This entire statement of Nemesianus is absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.]

19. Nemesianus of Tubunis [Note: The old Corbie manuscript has: “But Nemesianus of Tubunis.” The word “but” also occurs in other manuscripts and in Amerbach.] brought forward many testimonies from Scripture; but he said many things in support of the Catholic position which we have undertaken to explain and defend.

Unless, perhaps, we should think that the one who trusts in false things is not the person who trusts in the hope of temporal goods, as do all the greedy and robbers, and those who renounce the world not by deeds but by words—although Cyprian testifies that such people are also within, and both baptize and are baptized (Letter 13, To the Clergy). They too pursue flying birds (Prov. 10:4), because they do not grasp the things they desire.

But he abandons the paths of his vineyard and goes astray from the path of his field; he enters deserted and dry places and land appointed for thirst, and with his hands grasps fruitless things—not only the heretic, but everyone who lives badly; for all righteousness is fruitful, and all iniquity is fruitless.

Those who drink foreign water from a foreign fountain are not only heretics, but all who do not live according to what God teaches and live according to what the devil teaches. For if he were speaking about Baptism, he would not say, “Nor shall you drink from a foreign fountain,” but, “You shall not wash yourself in a foreign fountain.”

Now, as for what the Lord says, “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot [Col. 0206] enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), I do not see at all how this helps the position he holds. For it is one thing to say: “Everyone who will enter the kingdom of heaven is first reborn of water and the Spirit, because unless he is reborn of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven”—which the Lord said, and which is true. It is another thing to say: “Everyone who is born of water and the Spirit will enter the kingdom of heaven”—which is certainly false.

For that magician Simon had also been born of water and the Spirit (Acts 8:13), and yet he did not enter the kingdom of heaven. The same thing, therefore, can happen even to heretics.

Or, if no one is born of the Spirit except one who is changed by genuine conversion, then all who renounce the world with words and not deeds are born not of the Spirit but of water alone—yet such people are also within, as Cyprian testifies.

One of two things must necessarily be granted: either those who falsely renounce the world are born of the Spirit, though for destruction rather than salvation, and so heretics can be born of the Spirit as well; or, if the statement “For the Holy Spirit will flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5) also applies here, so that those who falsely renounce the world are not born of the Spirit, then someone can be baptized with water without being born of the Spirit, and Nemesianus’s statement is pointless: “Neither can the Spirit work without water, nor water without the Spirit.”

Moreover, it has often been explained elsewhere how those who do not have one Church can nevertheless share one Baptism; just as within the Church itself those who are righteous and those who are impure through greed may not possess one Holy Spirit, and yet possess one Baptism. For the text says “one body,” that is, the Church, just as it says “one Spirit” and “one Baptism.”

The rest of what he said, however, supports our position more than his. For he cited from the Gospel: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), because the Spirit is God and is born of God (ibid. 4:24). He then added: “Therefore all heretics and schismatics, whatever they do, are carnal,” citing the Apostle: “For the works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleanness,” and the other things that the Apostle lists there, where he also mentioned heresies. Nemesianus continued: “For those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

Then he added and said: “The Apostle therefore condemns along with all evils those who create division, that is, schismatics and heretics.” It is good that, when enumerating the works of the flesh, among which he finds heresies, he recognized that the Apostle condemned all these together.

Let him therefore ask the holy Cyprian himself, and hear from him how many people within the Church live according to the evil works of the flesh, which the Apostle condemns together with heresies, and yet baptize and are baptized. Why, then, are heretics alone said to be unable to possess the Baptism possessed by their companions in condemnation?

## CHAPTER XIII

20. Januarius of Lambaese [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain have “Lambese.” Our older manuscripts, as in Cyprian, have “Lambaese.”] said:

“On the authority of the Holy Scriptures, I decree that all heretics must be baptized and thus admitted to the holy Church.”

[Col. 0207] 21. To him the reply is made:

“On the authority of the Holy Scriptures, the Catholic council of the whole world has decreed that the Baptism of Christ found even among heretics is not to be rejected. If he were to produce testimonies from Scripture, we would demonstrate either that they are not against us or that they are even in our favor, as in the case of the one who follows him.”

## CHAPTER XIV

22. Lucius of Castra Galba said:

“When the Lord said in his Gospel, ‘You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by people’ (Matt. 5:13); and again, after his resurrection, when sending his Apostles he commanded them, saying, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (ibid. 28:18–19): since it is therefore clear that heretics, that is, enemies of Christ, do not possess the complete confession of the sacrament, and that likewise schismatics cannot season with spiritual wisdom, since by departing from the one Church they have become insipid and hostile, let it happen as it is written:

> ‘The houses of those opposed to the law require cleansing’ (Prov. 14:9, according to the Septuagint).

“And consequently those who have been baptized by the opposed and thereby polluted must first be cleansed, and only then baptized.”

[Note: Erasmus’s edition and later books added Lucius’s words here; they were previously absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.]

23. Lucius of Castra Galba [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and seven manuscripts have “of Castra Galba.” The old Corbie manuscript has “of Castra Galbae.”] brought forward a testimony from the Gospel, where the Lord says, “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by people”—as though we were saying that the people themselves, once thrown outside, are of some value either for their own salvation or for that of others.

But those who appear to be such within are not only spiritually outside; at the end they will also be separated bodily. For all such people are good for nothing, and yet the sacrament of Baptism that is in them is not therefore nothing.

Indeed, in those who are thrown outside, if they come to their senses and return, the salvation that had departed returns to them; but Baptism, because it had not departed, does not return.

Nor did the Lord’s statement, “Go therefore and teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” permit only good people to baptize. For he would not say to the wicked, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:23).

How, then, do wicked people within baptize, when they cannot forgive sins? How do they also baptize wicked people who have not been changed, whose sins still remain upon them, as John says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:9)?

But if their sins are forgiven when they join themselves in inward love to the good and righteous, through whom sins are forgiven in the Church, even though they have been baptized by wicked people, then the same applies to those who come from outside and approach that same joining of the body of Christ through the inward bond of peace.

Nevertheless, the Baptism of Christ must be recognized in both groups and rejected in none—whether before they are converted, although it benefits them nothing, or when they are converted, so that it may benefit them.

“Since by departing from the one Church,” he says, “they have become insipid and hostile [Col. 0208], let it happen as it is written: ‘The houses of those opposed to the law require cleansing.’ And consequently,” he says, “those who have been baptized by the opposed and polluted must first be cleansed, and only then baptized.”

What, then? Are robbers and murderers not opposed to the law that says, “You shall not kill; you shall not steal” (Exod. 20:13, 15)? They require cleansing—who would deny this? Yet not only are those baptized within by such people not rebaptized, but even those who are baptized by people of this kind without having been changed, although they still require cleansing in order to be changed, are not baptized again once they have been changed.

Such is the force of the sacrament of simple Baptism that, while we acknowledge that someone who has been baptized and continues to live wickedly must be cleansed, we nevertheless forbid him to be baptized again.

## CHAPTER XV

24. Crescens of Cirta said:

“In this great assembly of most holy fellow priests, after the letters of our dearest Cyprian to Jubaianus, and likewise to Stephanus, have been read—letters containing so many most holy testimonies descending from the divine Scriptures [Note: Older manuscripts omit “descending testimonies.” Several others have “testimonies,” but, together with Amerbach and Erasmus, lack the word “descending.”] that we ought rightly, by God’s grace, all to agree in unity—I judge that all heretics or schismatics who wish to come to the Catholic Church should not enter before they have been exorcised and baptized, except, certainly, those who were previously baptized in the Catholic Church, provided that they are reconciled to the Church through the laying on of hands in penance.”

25. Here we are again prompted to ask why he said, “except, certainly, those who were previously baptized in the Catholic Church.” Was it because they had not lost what they had received within? Then why could they not also confer outside what they were able to possess outside? Or is it illicitly conferred outside? But it is also not lawfully possessed outside, and yet it is possessed; thus it is illicitly given outside, and yet it is given.

What is granted to the person returning who had received it within is granted to the person coming who had received it outside: namely, that he may lawfully possess within what he had unlawfully possessed outside.

Someone may perhaps ask what the blessed Cyprian’s letter to Stephanus said about this matter [Note: [Col. 0208] Some manuscripts have “what the letter of blessed Cyprian has to say about this matter,” omitting “later, said.” Other manuscripts have neither “has” nor “said.”], since that letter is mentioned in this statement, although it was not mentioned at the beginning of the council. I believe this was because it was not thought necessary.

For he also said that the letter itself had been read in this assembly of fellow priests. I have no doubt that this was done, as I suppose is customary, so that the bishops already gathered might together learn something even about the matter contained in that letter.

For it has absolutely no bearing on the present question. I am more surprised that he wanted to mention it than that its mention was omitted at the beginning of the council.

If anyone thinks that I was unwilling to bring forward something contained in it that is necessary to the present case, let him read it and learn that what I say is true; or, if he finds something else, let him refute me. For that letter says nothing at all about Baptism given among heretics or schismatics, which is the matter under discussion here.

[Note: Two letters of Cyprian to Stephanus are extant: one concerns the removal of Marcianus, bishop of Arles, and is now numbered 68; the other is synodical and deals entirely with the question at issue, namely, the baptism of heretics and schismatics. Augustine had seen only the former, not the latter.]

[Col. 0209] ## CHAPTER XVI

26. Nicomedes of Segermis [Note: The Corbie manuscript has “of Segermes.”] said:

“My opinion is that heretics who come to the Church should be baptized, since outside, among sinners, they obtain no remission of sins.”

27. To him the reply is made:

“This is the judgment of the whole Catholic Church: that heretics, even though they have already been baptized with Christ’s Baptism in heresy, are not to be baptized when they come to the Church.

“For if there is no remission of sins among sinners, then sinners within the Church do not forgive sins either; and yet those baptized by them are not rebaptized.”

## CHAPTER XVII

28. Monnulus of Girba said:

“The truth of the Catholic Church, our mother, has always remained and remains among us, brothers, especially in the Trinity of Baptism, since our Lord says:

> ‘Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19).

“Since, therefore,” he says, “we plainly know that heretics possess neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, those who come to the Church, our mother, must truly be reborn and baptized, so that what they had as corruption [cancer], the wrath of condemnation, and the poison of error [offectura; note the variants below], may be sanctified through the holy and heavenly washing.”

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have “offocatum,” “choked.” Some manuscripts have “offensa,” “injury” or “offense,” but most have “offectura.” Cyprian has “effectura.”]

29. To him we reply:

“All who are baptized with Baptism consecrated by evangelical words possess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit at least in the sacrament. But in heart and life even those who live ruinously and abominably within do not possess them.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

30. Secundinus of Cedias [Note: The old Corbie manuscript and one Vatican manuscript have “of Cezas.” Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts have “of Chezas.”] said:

“When our Lord Christ says, ‘Whoever is not with me is against me’ (ibid. 12:30), and the apostle John calls those who go out from the Church antichrists (1 John 2:18), without doubt the enemies of Christ and all those called antichrists cannot administer the grace of saving Baptism. Therefore I judge that those who flee from the snares of heretics to the Church ought to be baptized by us, who by his favor have been called friends of God.”

[Note: The word “God” is absent from Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts.]

31. To him the reply is made:

“All are adversaries of Christ to whom he will say—although they say, ‘Lord, did we not perform many mighty works in your name?’ and other things mentioned there—at the end, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’ (Matt. 7:22–23).

“All this chaff, if it perseveres in wickedness to the very end, is destined for the fire, whether some of it flies outside before its separation or appears to remain within.

“If, therefore, heretics who come to the Church must be baptized for the reason that they are baptized by friends of God, are the greedy, robbers, and murderers friends of God? Or must those whom they have baptized be baptized again?”

## CHAPTER XIX

32. Felix of Bagai [Note: Several manuscripts have “of Baga.” The old Corbie manuscript has “of Vagai.”] said:

“Just as [Col. 0210] a blind man leading a blind man, both fall into a pit (Matt. 15:14), so a heretic baptizing a heretic falls with him into death.”

33. This is true, but what he adds is not true for that reason:

“Therefore,” he says, “the heretic must be baptized and given life, lest we, being alive, communicate with the dead.”

Were those who said, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15:32), not dead? They did not believe in the resurrection of the dead. Therefore, were those who were corrupted by their evil conversations and followed them not falling into the pit together with them?

Yet among those people were the very ones to whom the Apostle was writing, already baptized and nevertheless not rebaptized if they were corrected.

Does not the same Apostle say, “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6)? Certainly the greedy, deceivers, and robbers had their minds set on the flesh; Cyprian himself was lamenting among them.

What harm, then, did the dead do to those living in unity? Or who could say that the Baptism of Christ which such people possessed or administered had been violated by their iniquities?

## CHAPTER XX

34. Polianus of Mileum [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and all our manuscripts have “Pollianus.” Some of these have “of Mileu,” and one has “of Mileii.” Amerbach and Erasmus have “of Milen.”] said:

“It is right that a heretic be baptized in the holy Church.”

[Note: This is how it appears in the ancient manuscripts and in Cyprian. In the printed editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, however, it reads “in the Church of Christ.”]

35. Nothing could indeed have been said more briefly. But I think this is also brief:

“It is right that the Baptism of Christ not be blown upon in the Church of Christ.”

## CHAPTER XXI

36. Theogenes of Hippo Regius said:

“According to the sacrament of God’s heavenly grace which we have received, we believe that there is one Baptism, which is in the holy Church.”

[Note: The word “God,” which Erasmus and Louvain had removed, has been restored from the manuscripts and Amerbach.]

37. This could also be my opinion. For it is so carefully balanced that it contains nothing contrary to the truth. We too believe that there is one Baptism which is in the holy Church.

But if he had said, “We believe that there is one Baptism which is in the holy Church alone,” the reply would have had to be made as to the others. But because he said, “We believe that there is one Baptism which is in the holy Church,” so that he says that it is indeed in the holy Church but does not deny that it exists elsewhere as well, whatever he may have intended, there is no need to argue against these words.

For if I were asked separately whether there is one Baptism, I would answer that there is one. Then, if I were asked whether this Baptism is in the holy Church, I would answer that it is. Third, if I were asked whether I believed this Baptism, I would answer that I did believe it; and thus I would answer that I believe in one Baptism which is in the holy Church.

But if I were asked whether it exists in the holy Church alone, and not among heretics or schismatics, I would answer, together with the whole Church, that I do not believe this.

But since he did not put this in his statement, I think it would be improper for me to add words to him against which I might argue, although I did not find them there.

For if he were to say, “There is one water of the Euphrates River which is in paradise,” he would certainly be speaking truly. But if he were asked whether that water existed in paradise alone, and said that it did, he would be speaking falsely. [Col. 0211] For it also exists outside paradise, in the lands through which it flows from that source.

But who would be so rash as to say that this is what he would have answered—the false statement—when he might perhaps have answered what is true?

Therefore the words of this statement ought not to be contradicted, because they do not obstruct the truth.

## CHAPTER XXII

38. Dativus of Badis said:

“As far as lies within us, we do not communicate with a heretic unless he has been baptized in the Church and has received remission of sins.”

39. The reply is made:

“If you want him to be baptized because he has not received remission of sins, and if you find within the Church someone who, while holding hatred against his brother, was baptized in this way, will you order him, once corrected, to be baptized again, since the Lord cannot lie when he says, ‘If you do not forgive, you will not be forgiven’ (Matt. 6:15)? Certainly not. Therefore, neither should you rebaptize the heretic.

“Still, we must not pass over the fact that this man did not say briefly, ‘We do not communicate with a heretic,’ but added, ‘as far as lies within us.’ He saw that many agreed with this opinion, yet he could not separate himself from their fellowship without violating unity. Therefore he added, ‘as far as lies within us,’ clearly showing that he did not willingly communicate with those whom he believed not to possess Baptism, but that, for the sake of the good of peace and unity, all things had nevertheless to be tolerated.

“This was also done by those who thought that these men were acting wrongly, but held to what the truth, later more clearly explained, taught, and what an older custom, confirmed by a later council, established more firmly. Yet while preserving charity and holding different opinions, they tolerated one another with conscientious devotion, striving to preserve ‘the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace’ (Eph. 4:2–3), until God should reveal that also to whichever of them held some different view (Phil. 3:15).

“Let those who attack unity through this council hear this—a council through which it is shown how greatly unity ought to be loved.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

40. Successus of Abbir Germaniciana [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have “of Birgermaniciana,” incorrectly.] said:

“Heretics either can do nothing or can do everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit. But if they cannot give the Holy Spirit because they do not have the Holy Spirit, neither can they baptize spiritually. Therefore we judge that heretics must be baptized.”

[Note: The Lyon and Venice editions have: “Therefore we judge that heretics ought to be baptized.” Erasmus likewise has “we judged” instead of “we judge.” M.]

41. To him one may reply in almost the same words:

“Murderers either can do nothing or can do everything. If they can baptize, they can also give the Holy Spirit. But if they cannot give the Holy Spirit because they do not have the Holy Spirit, neither can they baptize spiritually. Therefore we judge that those baptized by murderers—or murderers who have been baptized and have not been changed for the better—should be baptized when they have corrected themselves.”

But this is not true. For whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). Cyprian knew that such people were within, and they [Col. 0212] certainly baptized. Therefore such arguments concerning the baptism of heretics have been made in vain.

## CHAPTER XXIV

42. Fortunatus of Thuccabor said:

“Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, the Son of God the Father and Creator, built the Church upon the rock [Note: The manuscripts have “upon Peter”], not upon heresy; and he gave the power of baptizing to bishops, not to heretics. Therefore those who are outside the Church and stand against Christ, scattering his sheep and flock, cannot baptize outside.”

[Note: This is how it appears in most manuscripts and in Louvain and Cyprian. Amerbach and Erasmus, however, have: “Why? Because they are outside,” and so forth.]

43. He added “outside” so that a brief [Col. 0212] reply could no longer be made to him. For one could answer him in almost the same words:

“Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, the Son of God the Father and Creator, built the Church upon the rock, not upon iniquity; and he gave the power of baptizing to bishops, not to the wicked. Therefore those who do not belong to the rock upon which those who hear and do the words of God build, but live against Christ by hearing his words and not doing them, and thus build upon sand, corrupt his sheep and flock by the example of their depraved conduct; they cannot baptize.”

Could this not plausibly be said? Yet it would be false. For the wicked do baptize, since the robbers whom Cyprian rebuked as placed with him in unity are wicked (Sermon on the Lapsed).

“But for that reason,” he says [Note: Erasmus and Louvain have “I say.” Amerbach and the manuscripts have “he says”; understand “the Donatist.”], “he added ‘outside.’”

Why, then, can these people not baptize outside? Is it because they are worse by the very fact that they are outside? But it makes no difference to the integrity of Baptism when the one who administers it is worse. For the difference between a bad person and a worse person is not as great as the difference between a good person and a bad person; yet when a bad person baptizes, he gives nothing different from what a good person gives.

Therefore, when a worse person baptizes, he too gives nothing different from the one who is less bad.

Or perhaps it belongs not to the merit of the human being but to the sacrament of Baptism itself that it cannot be given outside? If this were so, it could not be possessed outside either, and it would be necessary for everyone to be baptized as many times as he departed from the Church and returned again to the Church.

44. Now, if we inquire more carefully into what “outside” means—especially since he himself mentioned the rock upon which [Note: Several manuscripts have “Peter upon whom”; this is incorrect, as is clear from what follows] the Church is built—are not those in the Church who are on the rock, while those who are not on the rock are not in the Church?

Let us therefore see whether those who hear Christ’s words and do not do them establish their building upon the rock. The Lord himself contradicts them, saying:

> “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon the rock.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon the sand” (Matt. 7:24, 26).

If, then, the Church is on the rock, those who are upon the sand, because they are outside the rock, are plainly outside the Church.

Let us therefore remember how many [Col. 0213] people Cyprian mentions as though placed within who build upon sand—that is, who hear Christ’s words and do not do them. And because they are upon the sand, they are shown to be outside the rock, which is to be outside the Church.

Nevertheless, as long as they remain in that condition and are not—or never are—changed for the better, they baptize and are baptized; and the Baptism they possess remains intact, although they are destined for condemnation.

45. Nor can it be said here [Note: [Col. 0213] On this passage the Louvain editors, *Annotations*, p. 47: “He therefore understands all the things contained in the Lord’s discourse on the mount to be precepts.”]: For who does all the words of the Lord that are written in that very Gospel discourse, which he concludes by saying that those who hear these words and do them build upon the rock, whereas those who hear them and do not do them build upon the sand? For even if some things are not fulfilled by certain people, he nevertheless placed the remedy in that same discourse, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And after the Lord’s Prayer, which he recalled and recorded in that same discourse, he says: “For I tell you, if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. 6:14–15). Hence Peter also says [Note: [Col. 0213] The older manuscripts read, “John said.” “Peter said,” however, is more accurate.]: “Because love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Those people certainly did not possess this love; consequently, they were building upon the sand. Of them the same Cyprian says that within the Church, even in apostolic times, they were living in malicious envy without love (*Letter* 73, to Jubaianus). And therefore, although they seemed to be inside, they were outside, because they were not upon that rock by which the Church is signified.

## CHAPTER XXV

46. Sedatus of Tuburbo [Note: [Col. 0213] Am. Er. and several manuscripts read, “of Tuborbo.”] said: “To the extent that water sanctified in the Church by the priest’s prayer washes away sins, to that same extent, infected as though by a cancer through a heretic’s words [Note: [Col. 0213] Thus Am., Er., and the manuscripts here and in Cyprian; Louvain reads *cancer*.], it heaps up sins. Therefore, we must strive with every peaceful effort to prevent anyone infected and tainted by heretical error from refusing [*detrectet*; Note: [Col. 0213] Am. and most manuscripts read, *retractet*; Er., *detractet*.] to receive the one true Baptism, by which anyone who has not been baptized will be made an alien from the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0213] This is the reading of the manuscripts and of Cyprian. Louvain, however, reads: “The Church will be made alien from the kingdom of heaven.”].

47. He is answered as follows: If water is not sanctified when someone praying pours out words containing some error through ignorance, then many not only wicked but also good brethren in the Church itself do not sanctify the water. For the prayers of many people are corrected every day when they are recited before more learned persons, and many things are found in them contrary to the Catholic faith. Surely, if it were revealed that some people had been baptized when those prayers had been spoken over the water, would they be ordered to be baptized again [Note: [Col. 0213] Almost the only reading in the Louvain edition is: “If some baptized persons were revealed, … would they be ordered to be baptized again?”]? Why is that? Because often the disposition of the one praying overcomes the defect of the prayer itself. And the certain Gospel words without which Baptism cannot be consecrated are so powerful that through them whatever is said in a defective prayer contrary to the rule of faith is nullified, just as a demon is expelled by the name of Christ.

For if a heretic brings a defective prayer, and does not possess the good disposition of love by which that ignorance could be overcome, then he is like anyone in the Catholic Church who is envious and ill disposed, such as Cyprian censures there. Suppose he also brings—as commonly happens—a prayer in which he speaks against the rule of faith. Many people rush into prayers composed not only by ignorant and talkative persons but also by heretics, and, through the simplicity of ignorance, use them because they are unable to distinguish them, thinking that they are good. Yet whatever is perverse in them does not nullify what is correct there; rather, it is itself nullified by those correct elements. So it is with a person of good hope and commendable faith, but still merely a human being: if he thinks something differently, the things he thinks correctly are not thereby nullified, until God reveals to him what he thinks incorrectly as well (Phil. 3:15).

But if the person himself is evil and perverse, and recites an entire prayer that is in no respect contrary to the Catholic faith, he is not thereby himself made upright because the prayer is upright. And if he brings a prayer that is perverse in some respects, God is present with his Gospel words, without which Christ’s Baptism cannot be consecrated.
