He himself sanctifies his Sacrament, so that for a person who genuinely turns to him—whether before being baptized, while being baptized, or at some later time—the same Sacrament may contribute to salvation, whereas it would have contributed to destruction had he not turned.

Moreover, who does not know that it is not Christ’s Baptism if the Gospel words that constitute the Creed are absent? Yet heretics who do not baptize at all are more easily found than those who do not baptize with those words. Therefore, we say that it is not every baptism—for people are said to be baptized in many sacrilegious rites of idols—but Christ’s Baptism, consecrated by the Gospel words, that is everywhere one and the same, and that it is not invalidated by the perversity of any people whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0214] See above, Book 3, chapters 14 and 15.].

48. Certainly, in this statement too, we must not carelessly omit what he inserted and said here: “Therefore, we must strive with every peaceful effort to prevent anyone infected by heretical error,” and so forth. For he had in mind those words of blessed Cyprian: “Judging no one, nor removing anyone from the right of communion if he thinks differently” (at the beginning of the Council).

See how powerful love of unity and peace is among the good sons of the Church. Those whom they called sacrilegious and profane, whom they thought had been admitted without Baptism, they chose to tolerate rather than, if they could not correct them as far as they believed necessary, break that holy bond because of them—lest the wheat should also be uprooted together with the weeds (Matt. 13:29). They allowed, as far as lay within them, just as in that most famous judgment of Solomon, the infant’s body to be nourished by the false mother rather than cut in pieces (1 Kings 3:26). This, however, was done both by those who had the more accurate view of the Sacrament of Baptism and by those to whom, because of such great love, God was later to reveal that they were thinking wrongly.

## CHAPTER XXVI

49. Privatianus of Sufetula [Note: [Col. 0215] Am. and Er. read, “of Suficula.”] said: “Whoever says that heretics have the power to baptize must first say who founded heresy. For if heresy is from God, it may possess divine indulgence; but if it is not from God, how can it either possess or confer God’s grace upon anyone?”

50. He can be answered in exactly the same words: Whoever says that the malicious and envious have the power to baptize must first say who founded malice and envy. For if malice and envy are from God, they may possess divine indulgence; but if they are not from God, how can they either possess or confer God’s grace upon anyone?

But just as these statements, expressed in the same way, are manifestly false, so too are the statements made in order to refute them. The wicked and envious do baptize, as Cyprian himself concedes, since he also testifies that they are inside. Heretics, therefore, can likewise baptize, because Baptism is Christ’s Sacrament. Envy and heresy, however, are works of the devil; and whoever possesses them does not thereby cause the Sacrament of Christ, if he possesses it, to be counted among the works of the devil.

## CHAPTER XXVII

51. Privatus of Sufes said: “Those who approve the Baptism of heretics—what else are they doing than communicating with heretics?”

52. He is answered: It is not the baptism of heretics that we approve in heretics, just as it is not the baptism of the greedy, the treacherous, the fraudulent, the rapacious, or the envious that we approve in them. All such people are unrighteous; but Christ is righteous, and by their unrighteousness they do not violate in themselves the Sacrament that belongs to him, insofar as it pertains to him.

Otherwise someone could say: “Those who approve the baptism of the unrighteous—what else are they doing than communicating with the unrighteous?” If anyone made this objection to the Catholic Church herself, the answer given to him would be the one just given here.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

53. Hortensianus of Laribus said: “Let the presumers or supporters of heretics determine how many baptisms there are. We claim for the Church the one Baptism, which we know exists nowhere except in the Church. Or how can those people baptize anyone in the name of Christ whom Christ himself says are his adversaries?”

54. We answer him in a similar sequence of words: Let the presumers or supporters of the unrighteous determine the matter. We claim the one Baptism, which we know exists nowhere except in the Church, and wherever we find it, whenever we can, we recall it to the Church.

Or how can those people baptize anyone in the name of Christ whom Christ himself says are his adversaries? For he says to all the unrighteous: “I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:23). Yet when they baptize, it is not they who baptize, but the one of whom John says: “He is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

## CHAPTER XXIX

55. Cassius of Macomades said: “Since there cannot be two Baptisms, whoever grants Baptism to heretics takes it away from himself. Therefore, I judge that the wretched and diseased heretics must be baptized when they begin to come to the Church, and that, washed with the sacred [Note: [Col. 0216] Am. and the older manuscripts read, “so that they may be sacred.”] and divine washing and illumined with the light of life, they should be received into the Church—not as enemies but as people at peace; not as aliens but as members of the household of the Lord’s faith; not as adulterers [Note: [Col. 0216] The new edition of Cyprian reads, “adulterine.” But all our books consistently read, “adulterers.” Cassius alludes to Hebrews 12:8: “Then you are adulterers and not sons.”], but as sons of God; not made children of error but of salvation. This excludes those who, though faithful of the Church, had been led astray and passed over into the darkness of heresy [Note: [Col. 0216] Louvain reads, “in the Church.” But Am., Er., and the better manuscripts, as in Cyprian, read, “from the Church”; nevertheless, below Augustine’s response reads, “in the Church.”]; but they are to be restored through the laying on of hands.”

56. Someone else could say: “Since there cannot be two Baptisms of Christ, whoever grants Baptism to the unrighteous takes it away from himself.” But those people too would resist us and say: “We grant Baptism to the unrighteous; it does not come from them, as iniquity does, but from Christ, whose righteousness it is, and whose Sacrament is not unrighteous even among the unrighteous.”

Whatever they would say to us concerning the unrighteous, let them say to themselves concerning the heretics. Therefore, what follows should rather have been stated in this way: “I judge that the wretched and diseased heretics, if they already possess Christ’s Baptism, should not be baptized when they begin to come to the Church, but should be corrected from their perversity.”

The same can also be said concerning the unrighteous, of whom heretics are a part: “I judge that the wretched and diseased unrighteous, if they have already been baptized, should not be baptized when they begin to come to the Church—that is, to that rock outside which are all who hear Christ’s words and do not do them—but that, already washed with the sacred and divine washing, they should then be illumined with the light of life. They should be received not as enemies but as people at peace, for the unrighteous have no peace; not as aliens but as members of the household of the Lord’s faith, for it was said to the unrighteous: ‘How have you turned into bitterness, an alien vine?’ (Jer. 2:21); not as adulterers but as sons of God, for the unrighteous are sons of the devil; not made children of error but of salvation, for iniquity does not save.”

They are to be received into the Church—that is, onto that rock, into that dove, into that enclosed garden and sealed fountain, which is recognized only in the wheat and not in the chaff, whether the chaff is separated from it far away by the wind or appears mixed with the grain until the final winnowing.

Cassius therefore added his final clause in vain: “Excluding those who, having been deceived while faithful in the Church, passed over into the darkness of heresy.” For if they had lost Baptism by withdrawing from the Church, let it be restored to them also; but if they had not lost it, then let what was given through them be recognized.

## CHAPTER XXX

57. Another Januarius, of the village of Caesar, said: “If error does not obey truth, much less does truth consent to error. Therefore, we stand with the Church over which we preside, claiming its Baptism for it alone, so that we may baptize those whom the Church did not baptize.”

58. The answer is: Those whom the Church baptizes are certainly baptized by that rock outside which are all who hear Christ’s words and do not do them. Let all who have been baptized by such people therefore be baptized again. But if this is not done, then, in the case of these people just as in the case of heretics, Christ’s Baptism must be recognized and approved, while their iniquity and perversity are condemned or corrected.

## CHAPTER XXXI

59. Another Secundinus, of Carpis, said: “Are heretics Christians or not? If they are Christians, why are they not in the Church of God? If they are not Christians, let them become so. Or to what will the Lord’s saying refer: ‘Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters’ (Matt. 12:30)? Hence it is clear that the Holy Spirit cannot descend upon alien sons and offspring of Antichrist merely through the laying on of hands, since it is manifest that heretics do not possess Baptism.”

60. He is answered: Are the unrighteous Christians or not? If they are Christians, why are they not upon that rock upon which the Church is built? For they hear Christ’s words and do not do them. If they are not Christians, let them become so. Or to what will the Lord’s saying refer: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters”?

For those who lead his sheep, through perverse imitation, into the corruption of their own morals scatter them. Hence it is clear that the Holy Spirit cannot descend merely through the laying on of hands upon alien sons—by which all the unrighteous are designated—and offspring of Antichrist—by which all who oppose Christ are designated—if a true conversion of heart is not present. For it is manifest that the unrighteous, so long as they remain unrighteous, can possess Baptism, but cannot possess the salvation of which Baptism is the Sacrament.

Let us see whether heretics are described in that psalm where it says of alien sons:

“Lord, deliver me from the hand of alien sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity; whose sons are like young plants, firmly established [Note: [Col. 0217] Here *eorum* (‘their’) is added from the manuscripts.], and whose daughters are adorned like the likeness of a temple. Their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing to another; their sheep are fertile, multiplying in their offspring; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no exit, and no cry in their streets. They called the people who possess these things blessed; blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:7–15).

If, then, these are the alien sons—those who place blessedness in temporal things and the abundance of earthly prosperity, and who despise the divine commandments—let us see whether they are not the very people of whom Cyprian speaks in the following passage, transforming them into his own person so that he shows himself to be speaking about those with whom he shared the Sacraments:

“While we do not keep the Lord’s way,” he says, “nor observe the heavenly commandments given to us for salvation: our Lord did the Father’s will, but we do not do the Lord’s will, pursuing wealth and profit, following pride, and so forth” (*Letter* 11, to the Clergy).

But if these people were able both to possess and to transmit Baptism, why is it denied that Baptism can exist among alien sons? Yet he urges them, by observing the heavenly commandments sent to them through the only Son, to merit becoming his brothers and sons of God.

## CHAPTER XXXII

61. Victoricus of Thabraca said: “If heretics are permitted to baptize and to grant the remission of sins, why do we defame them by calling them heretics?”

62. What if someone else were to say: “If the unrighteous are permitted to baptize and to grant the remission of sins, why do we defame them by calling them unrighteous?” What would be answered to this person concerning the unrighteous should also be answered to the other concerning heretics: namely, that the Baptism with which they baptize is not theirs, and that it does not follow that whoever possesses Christ’s Baptism is thereby secure concerning the remission of sins. If he possesses it only in the Sacrament and has not been converted through a truthful turning of heart, so that he may be forgiven by the one who forgives [Note: [Col. 0218] Several manuscripts read, “confession,” instead of “conversion.”], then it does not benefit him.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

63. Another Felix of Uthina [Note: [Col. 0218] The old Floriacensis codex reads, “of Tubina.” Several other manuscripts read, “of Unita.”] said: “There is no doubt, most holy fellow priests, that human presumption cannot prevail to the extent of the worshipful and venerable majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, mindful of the danger, we must not only observe this ourselves but also establish it among all of us: that all heretics who hasten to the bosom of Mother Church should be baptized, so that the heretical mind, polluted by long-standing corruption, may be cleansed by the sanctification of the washing and reformed for the better” [Note: [Col. 0218] Er. and several manuscripts read, “cannot prevail so greatly.”].

64. Perhaps this man, who made the long-standing corruption to be cleansed the reason why heretics ought to be baptized, would spare those who had rushed into some heresy, remained there only a short time, and then quickly corrected themselves and passed over from it to the Catholic Church.

Moreover, he himself paid too little attention to the fact that the statement could be made in this way: All the unrighteous who hasten to that rock in which the Church is signified should be baptized, so that the unrighteous mind that was building outside the rock upon the sand—hearing Christ’s words and not doing them—may be cleansed by the sanctification of the washing and reformed for the better. Yet this is not done if they have already been baptized, even if they are proved to have been such when they were baptized; that is, if they renounced the world in words but not in deeds.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

65. Quietus of Buruch said: “We who live by faith must, with believing observance [Note: [Col. 0218] The Cambronensis codex and Cyprian’s edition read *sedula*, ‘diligent,’ rather than *credula*, ‘believing.’], obey the things previously set forth for our instruction. For it is written in Solomon: ‘What benefit is there in the washing of one who is baptized by a dead person?’ [Note: [Col. 0218] Am. Er. and Cyprian add, “and again touches a dead person,” incorrectly; with this addition the passage has no relevance to the issue.] (Sirach 34:30). This plainly speaks of those who are baptized by heretics and of those who perform the baptizing. For if those who are baptized among them attain eternal life through the remission of sins, why do they come to the Church? But if nothing pertaining to salvation is received from a dead person, and for that reason, once their former error has been recognized, they return with repentance to the truth, then they ought to be sanctified by the one life-giving Baptism that exists in the Catholic Church.”

66. What it means to be baptized by a dead person, without prejudging a more careful consideration of that Scripture, we have already said elsewhere (*Against Parmenianus*, Book 2, chapter 10).

But I ask why they want only heretics to be understood as dead, when the Apostle Paul spoke generally about sin: “The wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23); and again: “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6). And since he calls the widow who lives in pleasure dead (1 Tim. 5:6), how can those not be dead who renounce the world in words but not in deeds?

What benefit, then, is there in the washing of one who is baptized by such people? Only this: if he himself is such a person, he possesses the washing, but it does not benefit him for salvation. But if the person by whom he is baptized is such, while he himself turns to God with a sincere heart, then he is not baptized by that dead person, but by the living one of whom it was said, “He is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33), regardless of who performs the bodily act of baptizing.

As for what he said concerning heretics—“For if those who are baptized among them attain eternal life through the remission of sins, why do they come to the Church?”—the answer is this: They come because, even if they have received Christ’s Baptism insofar as the Sacrament is celebrated, they nevertheless do not attain eternal life except through the love of unity. The same is true of those malicious and envious people whose sins would not be forgiven even if they retained hatred against those from whom they suffered injury, because the Truth said: “If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. 6:15). How much more is this true when they hated those to whom they repaid evil for good (Ps. 35:12)?

Yet if these people, who renounced the world only in words and not in deeds, were later corrected, they would not be baptized again; they would be sanctified by the one life-giving Baptism. This Baptism is indeed in the Catholic Church, but not in the Catholic Church alone, just as it is not found only among the saints who have been built upon the rock and from whom that one dove is perfected (Song 6:8).

## CHAPTER XXXV

67. Castus of Sicca said: “Whoever, despising the truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward the brethren to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.”

68. If he had convicted those who held a different opinion and maintained it—which the whole world later obtained after it was confirmed by a Christian council—of following custom in such a way that they despised the truth, we ought to fear these words. But since that custom is found to have been propagated by the truth and strengthened by the truth, we have no fear in this judgment.

Yet if those people were envious and malicious toward their brethren, or ungrateful toward God, see with whom they communicated; see what kind of people they were who, as Cyprian stated beforehand, they did not remove from the right of communion even though they held a different opinion; see from whom they were not contaminated in the preservation of unity [Note: [Col. 0219] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *in conversatione unitatis*, ‘in the conduct of unity.’]; see how greatly the bond of peace must be loved; see what those should consider who slander us because of the council of our predecessor bishops [Note: [Col. 0219] The manuscripts read, “preceding bishops.”], whose love they do not imitate and by whose example, rightly considered, they are condemned.

If it was the custom, as this statement bears witness, for heretics who came to the Church to be received with the Baptism they possessed, then either this was rightly done, or the wicked do not contaminate the good within unity. If it was rightly done, why do they accuse the whole world because heretics are received in this way? But if the wicked do not contaminate the good within unity, how do they excuse themselves from the crime of sacrilegious separation?

[Col. 0220]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

69. Eucratius of Thenis said: “God and our Lord Jesus Christ, teaching the Apostles with his own mouth, completed our faith, the grace of Baptism, and the rule of ecclesiastical law, saying: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19).

“Therefore, the false and unrighteous Baptism of heretics must be driven away by us and rejected with every protest [Note: [Col. 0220] In Cyprian, “detestation.” A little later he also reads, “from the presumption of their blasphemy.”]. From their mouths comes poison, not life; not heavenly grace, but blasphemy against the Trinity. And therefore it is clear that heretics who come to the Church must be baptized with complete and Catholic Baptism, so that, purified from the blasphemy of their presumption, they may be reformed by the grace of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0220] Our manuscripts read, “reformed in glory.”].

70. Certainly, if Baptism is not consecrated in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let it be attributed to the heretics and rejected by us with every protest; but if we recognize that name in it, we distinguish the Gospel words more effectively from the error of the heretics, approving what is sound in them and correcting what is defective [Note: [Col. 0220] The manuscripts read, “unrighteous” (*iniquum*, neuter). But the Louvain editors prefer, as in the earlier editions, the masculine *iniquus*, because Augustine’s response has *baptismus* (masculine), not *baptisma* (neuter).].

## CHAPTER XXXVII

71. Libosus of Vaga [Note: [Col. 0220] Am. and Er., with some manuscripts, read “of Agra.” The same editions, however, more accurately read above, Book 3, no. 9, “Libosus of Vaga.”] said: “In the Gospel the Lord says, ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6); he did not say, ‘I am custom.’ Therefore, once the truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth, so that even if someone formerly did not baptize heretics in the Church, he may now begin to baptize them.”

72. Here he made no attempt to show how the truth is constituted to which he says that custom ought to yield [Note: [Col. 0220] In the printed editions the word “made manifest” is unnecessarily added here.]. Nevertheless, what helps us more against those who have divided themselves from unity is that he admits that this was the custom than the fact that he thinks it ought to yield to a truth he has not demonstrated.

For this is the custom: if it admitted sacrilegious people to Christ’s altar without the cleansing of Baptism and did not contaminate any of the good within unity, then all who separated themselves from that same unity—in which they could not be contaminated by the infection of any wicked people—committed the manifest sacrilege of schism without cause.

But if all were polluted and perished through that custom, from what cave do these people emerge, without the original truth and with the cunning of slander? If, on the other hand, it was a correct custom by which heretics were received in this way, let them abandon their fury and confess their error. Let them come to the Catholic Church, not to be baptized again with the Sacrament of Baptism, but to be healed of the wound of their division.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

73. Lucius of Thebeste [Note: [Col. 0220] The Corbeiensis codex and other older manuscripts read, “Lovicius of Theveste.” Several others read, “Leucius.” Am. and Er. read, “Leutius of Thabeste.”] said: “I judge that heretics, blasphemers, and the unrighteous, who tear apart the holy and venerable words of Scripture with various expressions, must be cursed; and therefore they must be exorcized and baptized.”

74. I too judge that they must be cursed, but not therefore exorcized and baptized. What I curse is their fabrication; what I venerate is Christ’s Sacrament.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

75. Eugenius of Ammedera said: “I too hold the same opinion: heretics must be baptized.”

76. He is answered: But this is not the opinion of the Church, to which God has now revealed, even through a plenary council, what at that time you still thought differently about (Phil. 3:15). Yet because love was preserved among you, you remained in unity.

## CHAPTER XL

77. Another Felix of Amaccura [Note: [Col. 0221] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “of Ammacura.” The Floriacensis reads, “of Ammacurra.” Several others, with Am. and Er., read “of Accura,” or “of Acurra,” or “of Accurra.”] said: “Following the authority of the divine Scriptures, I too judge that heretics must be baptized, and also those who insist that they were baptized among schismatics.

“For if, according to Christ’s injunction, our fountain is private, let all the adversaries of our Church understand that it cannot belong to another [Note: [Col. 0221] Am. and Er. read, “cannot belong to others.” Cyprian’s edition reads, “they are alien.”], nor can the one who is shepherd of a single flock grant the water of salvation to two peoples. Therefore, it is clear that neither heretics nor schismatics receive anything heavenly, since they dare to receive it from sinful people and from those who are strangers to the Church. When there is no place for the giver, it surely does not benefit the recipient either.”

78. He is answered: The divine Scriptures nowhere commanded that heretics baptized among heretics should be baptized again. But in many passages they have shown that all who are not upon the rock and do not belong to the members of that dove are strangers to the Church, and yet that they both baptize and are baptized, possessing the Sacrament of salvation without salvation.

As for our fountain, which resembles the fountain of paradise because, like that one, it also flows outside paradise, enough has already been said (above, chapter 21). I grant and agree that the one who is shepherd of a single flock cannot grant the water of salvation to two peoples, that is, to his own and to an alien people. But is it the case that, because the water is not salutary for strangers, it therefore does not exist?

The water of the Flood was salutary for those inside the ark, but deadly for those outside the ark; nevertheless, it was the same water. And many strangers—that is, the envious, whom Cyprian says and demonstrates from the Scriptures to be on the devil’s side—seem to be inside, yet unless they were outside the ark, they would not die through the water.

When such people misuse it, Baptism kills them, just as the Apostle says of those people: “It was the good odor of Christ unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16).

Why, then, do schismatics or heretics not receive something heavenly, just as thorns or weeds receive the rain, and just as those who were outside the ark did indeed receive the water descending from the cataracts of heaven, but to destruction rather than salvation?

Therefore, I make no effort to refute his final statement: “When there is no place for the giver, it surely does not benefit the recipient either.” For we too say that it does not benefit those who receive it when they receive it in heresy while consenting to heretics. That is why they come to Catholic peace and unity [Note: [Col. 0222] Several manuscripts read, “truth.”], not to receive Baptism, but so that what they had received may begin to benefit them.

## CHAPTER XLI

79. Another Januarius of Muzulis said: “I am astonished that, although everyone confesses that there is one Baptism, not everyone understands the unity of that same Baptism. The Church and heresy are two different things. If heretics possess Baptism, we do not; but if we do not possess it, heretics cannot possess it. There is no doubt that the Church alone possesses Christ’s Baptism, since it alone possesses Christ’s grace and truth.”

80. Someone else could say something similar and, similarly, say something untrue: “I am astonished that, although everyone confesses that there is one Baptism, not everyone understands the unity of that same Baptism. Justice and iniquity are two different things. If the unrighteous possess Baptism, the righteous do not; but if the righteous possess it, the unrighteous cannot possess it. There is no doubt that only the righteous possess Christ’s Baptism, since they alone possess Christ’s grace and truth.”

This is certainly false, as those people themselves also acknowledge. For those envious people who belong to the devil’s party, who are placed inside, as Cyprian says, and who were well known to the Apostle Paul, possessed Baptism [Note: [Col. 0222] Some books read, “and the Apostle Paul, the Baptism that was well known.”]. Yet they did not belong to the members of that dove which is secure upon the rock.

## CHAPTER XLII

81. Adelphius of Thasbalte [Note: [Col. 0222] Am. and Er. read, “Adelphus of Thasbalte.” Louvain and the manuscripts read, “Adelphius,” or “Adelfius.” Later, the older codices have “of Thasvalte.”] said: “Without cause, they attack the truth with a false and envious expression, saying that we rebaptize, when the Church does not rebaptize heretics but baptizes them.”

82. On the contrary, it does not rebaptize them now, because it does not baptize anyone except those who have not been baptized. This earlier custom was later more carefully confirmed by the perfected truth, also through a subsequent council.

## CHAPTER XLIII

83. Demetrius of Lepti-minus [Note: [Col. 0222] Am. and Er. read, “of Aleptuninus,” incorrectly, instead of “of Lepti-minus,” which is a city of the province of Byzacena; besides this city there was also Leptis Magna of Tripolitana. More is said about it below, Book 7, no. 92.] said: “We preserve one Baptism because we claim its own possession for the Catholic Church alone. But those who say that heretics truly and legitimately baptize are the ones who make not two [Note: [Col. 0222] This is the reading of Am., Er., and all the manuscripts here. Louvain and Cyprian read, “not one.”] but many baptisms. For since there are many heresies, the baptisms will be counted according to their number.”

84. He is answered: If this is so, then let as many baptisms be counted as there are works of the flesh, concerning which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21). Heresies are counted among these works, and so many of their works are tolerated within, as though among the chaff [Note: [Col. 0222] The printed editions read, “these works themselves”; the manuscripts, “of their works.”]; yet there is one Baptism for them all, which no work of iniquity violates.

[Col. 0223]

## CHAPTER XLIV

85. Vincentius of Thibaris said: “We know that heretics are worse than the pagans. If they wish to turn to God and come, they certainly possess the rule of truth that the Lord entrusted by divine command to the Apostles, saying: ‘Go, in my name lay hands upon them and drive out demons’ (Mark 16:17). And elsewhere: ‘Go and teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 28:19). Therefore, first through the laying on of hands in exorcism, and second through the regeneration of Baptism, they can come to Christ’s promise; otherwise, I judge that it ought not to be done” [Note: [Col. 0223] The word “judge” is absent from the manuscripts.].

### 86

I do not know from what rule he says that heretics are worse than pagans, since the Lord says, “If he refuses even to hear the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (ibid. 18:17). Or is a heretic even worse than such a person? I offer no resistance; nevertheless, because the person himself is worse than a pagan—that is, than a Gentile and pagan—it does not follow that Christ’s sacrament, if he possesses it, is mixed with and destroyed by his vices and behavior.

For those who depart from the Church and become not merely followers but also founders of heresies, if they depart already baptized, nevertheless possess Baptism, since, when corrected, they do not receive it again; and if they had lost it, they would certainly receive it. It can therefore happen that someone is worse than a pagan and yet that Christ’s sacrament not only exists in him but is not worse than it is in a holy and righteous person. For although, so far as that person is concerned, he did not preserve it but violated it in mind and will, nevertheless, so far as the sacrament itself is concerned, it remained whole and inviolate even with its despiser and repudiator.

Were not the Sodomites pagans—that is, Gentiles? The Jews, therefore, were worse, to whom the Lord says, “It will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you” (ibid. 11:24), and to whom the prophet says, “You justified Sodom” (Ezek. 16:51)—that is, in comparison with you, Sodom was made righteous [Note: [Col. 0223] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition read, “Sodom was justified.” M.]. Yet were the divine sacraments that [Col. 0224] existed among the Jews therefore like the Jews themselves—those sacraments which the Lord himself also received, and for the observance of which he sent the lepers whom he had cleansed (Luke 17:14), and while an angel stood beside Zechariah as he ministered, announced that he had been heard while sacrificing in the temple (ibid. 1:11, 13)? These same sacraments existed both among the good people of that time and among the wicked, who were worse than pagans, since they were preferred to the Sodomites in wickedness; and yet those sacraments were whole and divine in both groups.

### 87

Even if the Gentiles were able to possess something divine and sound in their teachings, our holy men did not reject it, although the Gentiles, because of their superstitions, idolatry, pride, and other depraved practices, were to be detested and, unless corrected, punished by divine judgment. Thus the apostle Paul, when speaking about God among the Athenians, testified that some of them had said something of the kind (Acts 17:28)—something which, if they came to Christ, would be recognized in them, not rejected.

Saint Cyprian too uses such people as witnesses against those same pagans. For when he was speaking of the magi, he says: “Their chief, Hostanes, nevertheless both denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels stand beside his throne. In this Plato also agrees in like manner; while preserving belief in one God, he calls the other beings angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus likewise speaks of one God and confesses him to be incomprehensible and beyond estimation” (*On the Vanity of Idols*).

If these people had come to receive Christian salvation, they would certainly not have been told, “You possess this evil,” or, “You possess this falsehood.” Rather, it would properly have been said: “Although this belief of yours is whole and true, it would nevertheless profit you nothing unless you came to Christ’s grace.” If, therefore, something divine can be found and rightly approved even among pagans, although salvation must still be granted to them by Christ, we ought not to be so disturbed—even if heretics are worse—that we wish to correct what is evil in them but refuse to acknowledge what is Christ’s and good in them.

We shall now undertake an examination of the remaining opinions of this council, beginning elsewhere.

## BOOK SEVEN

### In which the remaining opinions of the Council of Carthage are examined

[Col. 0223]

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1

Let us not trouble our readers if we discuss the same matters in different ways and repeatedly. Although the holy Catholic Church, existing among all nations, is fortified by the authority of ancient custom and of a plenary council against those who cast some obscurity over the question whether the same Baptism can exist among heretics and schismatics as exists in the Catholic Church, nevertheless, because certain men whose opinions deserve respect—and especially Cyprian—at one time judged otherwise within that same unity, and because those who are far removed from his charity attempt to use his authority against us, we are therefore compelled, in order to examine and consider [Col. 0224] everything we have discovered on this matter in his council and writings, to handle this same question somewhat longer, as though turning it over in our hands.

We must show how much more truly it has pleased the whole Catholic Church that heretics or schismatics who received Christ’s Baptism in the place from which they come should be admitted into Catholic communion with that Baptism, once corrected from their error and rooted and grounded in charity, so that, as regards the sacrament of Baptism, what was lacking should not be supplied, but what was present should be of benefit.

Blessed Cyprian, now that his corruptible body no longer weighs down his soul and his earthly dwelling no longer depresses his [Col. 0225] thinking mind (Wis. 9:15), sees the truth more clearly and serenely than before, having deserved to attain it through charity. Let him therefore assist us by his prayers while we labor in the mortality of this flesh, as though in a dark cloud, so that, by the Lord’s gift, we may imitate his good qualities as far as we can.

But if he judged otherwise and persuaded certain brothers and fellow bishops of that view—something which he now sees, with the one whom he loved revealing it, though we are far inferior to him in merit—we, following according to our weakness the authority of the Catholic Church, of which he himself is an outstanding and distinguished [Note: [Col. 0225] Several manuscripts read, “dearly loved.”] member, disentangle the matter against heretics and schismatics. They have been cut off from the unity which he maintained, withering away from the charity in which he flourished, and slipping away from the humility in which he stood. He condemns and rejects them all the more strongly because he knows that they wish to scrutinize what he wrote in order to lay ambushes, while refusing to imitate what he did in order to make peace.

In the same way, those who call themselves Christian Nazarenes and, following Jewish custom, circumcise their fleshly foreskins—heretics born from that error into which Peter deviated and from which Paul recalled him (Gal. 2:11)—still persist [Note: [Col. 0225] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition read, “persist in this to the present.”]. Thus, just as those people remained separated from the Church in their perversity after Peter, crowned with the glory of martyrdom in his primacy among the apostles, so these people, after Cyprian was received into the company of the saints through the abundance of his charity and the glory of his passion, acknowledge themselves exiles from unity and, in support of their accusations, set a citizen of unity against the homeland of unity.

Let us now examine the remaining opinions of that council according to the same method.

### CHAPTER TWO

#### 2

Marcus of Mactari [Note: [Col. 0225] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “of Mattari.”] said:

“It is not surprising if heretics, enemies and adversaries of the truth, claim for themselves what belongs to another’s power and dignity. What is surprising is that certain of our own transgressors against the truth support heretics and oppose Christians. Therefore we decree that heretics must be baptized.”

#### 3

We reply: Rather, it is more surprising—and worthy of being proclaimed with great praise—that these men loved unity so greatly that, while remaining in unity with those whom they considered transgressors against the truth, they were not afraid of being polluted by them.

For when this man said, “What is surprising is that certain of our own transgressors against the truth support heretics and oppose Christians,” he appeared likely to say, “Therefore we decree that communion with them must not be maintained.” He did not say this, however, but said, “Therefore we decree that heretics must be baptized,” preserving what the peaceable Cyprian had previously established when he said, “Judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion.”

Since the Donatists therefore slander us and call us traditors, if some Jew or pagan, after reading this council, were to call both them and us, according to their rules, transgressors against the truth, I should like to know how we ought to conduct our common case in order to refute and dispel so serious a charge.

They call those men traditors whom they were unable either at any time to convict [Col. 0226] or now to identify, and they are rather shown to be involved in the same crime themselves. But what does that matter to us? What shall we say, certainly, about those transgressors?

If we are called traditors, although falsely, because they accuse us of succeeding traditors within the same communion, then we have all succeeded those transgressors, since the party of Donatus had not yet separated itself from unity in the time of blessed Cyprian. For it was after his passion, forty years and more having passed, that the handing over of the books took place, from which time they began to be called traditors.

If, therefore, we are traditors because, as they think or invent, we arose from traditors, then both groups derive their origin from those transgressors. There is no basis for saying that these men did not share communion with them, since they call them their own; and the council says—something they themselves especially bring forward [Note: [Col. 0226] The manuscripts read thus; the printed editions have “put forward.”]—“Certain of our own transgressors against the truth support heretics.”

Cyprian’s testimony also contributes to this, sufficiently demonstrating that he remained in their communion when he said, “Judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion.” For those who held a different opinion were the very people whom this speaker calls transgressors, since they supported heretics by receiving them into the Church without Baptism.

That it was also the custom for them to be received in this manner is made clear by Cyprian himself in many passages and by several bishops in this council. Hence it appears that, if heretics do not possess Baptism, the Church of those times was full of transgressors who supported them by receiving them in this way.

Let the common case therefore be brought against the crime of transgression, which they cannot deny; and there our case against the crime of traditorship, which they have been unable to prove, will also be brought forward [Note: [Col. 0226] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “which they will not have been able to prove.”].

But let us act as though they had proved it. Whatever we would answer those who accuse us of the transgression of our ancestors, we shall answer these people who accuse us of the traditorship of our ancestors.

For just as, through the traditorship of our ancestors—the very reason for which these people separated themselves from us—we are dead, so through the transgression of our ancestors, who were both their parents and ours, both we and they are dead. But because they say that they are alive, they believe that that transgression does not pertain to them; therefore that traditorship does not pertain to us either.

According to their own position, that transgression is certain. According to ours, however, neither is the earlier transgression true, since we say that heretics can possess Christ’s Baptism, nor is the later traditorship true, since they themselves were defeated in that matter.

These people therefore have no reason to separate themselves from us by the wicked crime of schism. If our ancestors were not traditors, as we say, there is no reason why it should pertain to us at all. But if they were traditors, as these people say, then it does not pertain to us, just as those transgressors pertain neither to us nor to them.

Accordingly, since no guilt of ours arises from the iniquity of our ancestors, their guilt arising from their own schism is certain.

[Col. 0227]

### CHAPTER THREE

#### 4

Satius of Sicilibba [Note: [Col. 0227] Am. and Erasmus read, “of Sicilippa.”] said:

“If sins are forgiven heretics in their Baptism, they come to the Church without cause. For since it is sins that are punished on the day of judgment, heretics have nothing to fear from Christ’s judgment if they have obtained the forgiveness of sins.”

#### 5

This too could have been our opinion; let its author consider with what intention it was spoken. Its wording, however, has been so qualified that I do not hesitate to agree and subscribe to it in the sense that I too hold: heretics may indeed possess Christ’s Baptism, but they do not possess the forgiveness of sins.

He does not say, “If heretics baptize or are baptized,” but says, “If sins are forgiven heretics in their Baptism, they come to the Church without cause.” For if, instead of heretics, we understand those whom Cyprian knew in the Church—those who renounced the world in words alone and not in deeds—we too can state this opinion with complete truth in exactly the same words: “If sins are forgiven those who have turned hypocritically in their Baptism, they are afterward brought to true conversion without cause.”

For since it is sins that are punished on the day of judgment, those who renounced the world in words alone and not in deeds have nothing to fear from Christ’s judgment if they have obtained the forgiveness of sins.

But this reasoning is completed by adding the following: “They ought nevertheless to fear Christ’s judgment and at some point turn with a sincere heart.” When they have done so, they certainly do not need to be baptized again.

They were therefore able to receive Baptism without receiving the forgiveness of sins, or, after their sins had been forgiven, to become burdened with them again immediately. The same is therefore true of heretics.

### CHAPTER FOUR

#### 6

Victor of Gor said:

“Since sins are forgiven only in the Church’s Baptism, whoever admits a heretic to communion without Baptism does both things contrary to reason: he neither cleanses heretics nor pollutes Christians.”

#### 7

We reply that the Church’s Baptism exists among heretics, although they themselves are not in the Church, just as the water of paradise exists in the land of Egypt, although Egypt itself is not paradise.

We therefore do not admit heretics to communion without Baptism; and because they come corrected from their perversity, we receive not their sins but Christ’s sacraments. Concerning the forgiveness of sins, we say here what we said above.

As for the final point he made, saying that “he does both things contrary to reason: he neither cleanses heretics nor pollutes Christians,” Cyprian himself and the colleagues who agreed with him initially and most emphatically reject it. For he did not believe himself polluted when he decided that communion should be maintained with such people for the sake of the bond of peace, saying, “Judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion.”

Or, if heretics admitted to communion are polluting because they are not baptized [Note: [Col. 0227] Erasmus and the manuscripts read, “since they are not baptized.”], then the whole Church was polluted by the custom mentioned here so many times.

And just as these people call us traditors because of our ancestors, [Col. 0228] although they have been unable to prove anything of the kind against us, if each person becomes what the person with whom he communicates is, then everyone became a heretic.

But if anyone says this, he is out of his mind. The statement, “Whoever admits a heretic to communion without Baptism neither cleanses heretics nor pollutes Christians,” is false.

Or, if it is true, they were not admitted without Baptism; rather, they possessed Christ’s Baptism, although it had been given and received among heretics. According to the custom which these people themselves acknowledge, they were admitted in this way. Consequently, they are rightly admitted in the same manner even now.

### CHAPTER FIVE

#### 8

Aurelius of Utica said:

“Since the Apostle says that we must not share in the sins of others (1 Tim. 5:22), what else does the person share in but the sins of others who shares communion with heretics without the Church’s Baptism? Therefore I decree that heretics must be baptized, so that they may receive the forgiveness of sins, and communion may then be maintained with them.”

#### 9

Cyprian, then, and all these men shared in the sins of others when they remained in communion with such people, since they removed no one who held a different opinion from the right of communion. Where, then, is the Church?

Furthermore, leaving heretics aside, since the words of this opinion can also be applied to other sinners—such as those whom Cyprian saw, groaned over, rebuked, and tolerated within the Church [Note: [Col. 0228] The Vatican manuscripts read, “struck.”]—where is the Church, which according to these words was already thought to have perished through the contagion of sins?

But if, as the most firmly established truth maintains, the Church remained and remains, the sharing in sins which the Apostle forbids must be understood only as agreement with them.

Let heretics be baptized again, then, so that they may receive the forgiveness of sins, if perverse and envious people are baptized again—those who renounced the world in words and not in deeds and were able to receive Baptism but did not obtain the forgiveness of sins, since the Lord says, “If you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. 6:15).

### CHAPTER SIX

#### 10

Jambus of Germaniciana said:

“Those who approve the Baptism of heretics reject ours, since they deny that those baptized outside the Church—not merely washed but defiled—ought to be baptized in the Church.”

#### 11

We reply that none of us approves the Baptism of heretics, but Christ’s Baptism, although it exists among heretics as among external chaff, just as it exists among other wicked people as among internal chaff.

For if those who are baptized outside the Church are not washed but defiled, then surely those who are baptized outside the rock upon which the Church is built are not washed but defiled. All who hear Christ’s words and do not do them are outside that same rock.

Or, if they are indeed washed by Baptism but remain defiled in their sins, from which they have refused to change for the better, the same is true of heretics.

### CHAPTER SEVEN

#### 12

Lucianus of Rucuma [Note: [Col. 0228] Am. and Erasmus read, “of Rucumma.”] said:

“It is written, ‘And God saw the light, that it was good, and he divided between the light and the darkness’ (Gen. 1:4). If light and darkness can have something in common, then we can have something in common with heretics. Therefore I decree that heretics must be baptized.”

[Col. 0229]

#### 13

We reply: If light and darkness can have something in common, then the just and the unjust can have something in common. Let him therefore decree that those unjust people whom Cyprian rebuked within the Church be baptized again. Or, if those who renounce the world in words and not in deeds are not unjust, let anyone who can say so say it.

### CHAPTER EIGHT

#### 14

Pelegianus of Luperciana said:

“It is written, ‘Either the Lord is God, or Baal is God’ (1 Kings 18:21). So now too, either the Church is the Church, or heresy is the Church. Moreover, if heresy is not the Church, how can the Church’s Baptism exist among heretics?”

#### 15

We can answer him as follows: Either paradise is paradise, or Egypt is paradise. Moreover, if Egypt is not paradise, how can the water of paradise exist in Egypt? But we will be told: “It reached there also by coming out.” So too, therefore, with Baptism among heretics.

We say likewise: Either the rock is the Church, or the sand is the Church. But since the sand is not the Church, how can Baptism exist among those who build upon sand by hearing Christ’s words and not doing them (Matt. 7:24–27)? [Note: [Col. 0229] Louvain reads, “how can the Church’s Baptism exist?” Am. and the manuscripts omit “of the Church” here.] Yet it does exist. So too, therefore, among heretics.

### CHAPTER NINE

#### 16

Jader of Midila said:

“We know that there is only one Baptism in the Catholic Church; therefore we must not admit a heretic unless he has been baptized among us, lest he think that he has been baptized outside the Catholic Church.”

#### 17

We reply that if this were said about those wicked people who are outside the rock, it would certainly be said falsely. The same is therefore true when it is said about heretics.

### CHAPTER TEN

#### 18

Another Felix of Marazana [Note: [Col. 0229] The word “another” is absent from Am., Erasmus, and the manuscripts. Am. and Erasmus subsequently read, “Felix of Mazrazana.” The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “of Maranzana.” Cyprian’s edition reads, “of Marrazana.”] also said:

“One faith, one Baptism (Eph. 4:5), but that of the Catholic Church, which alone has the right to baptize.”

#### 19

What if someone else were to say: “One faith, one Baptism, but only that of the righteous, who alone have the right to baptize”? Just as those words would be refuted, so let this opinion be refuted.

Or do the unjust, who have not been changed even in Baptism while renouncing the world in words alone and not in deeds, belong to the members of the Church? Let them see whether that is the rock, whether that is the dove, whether that is the bride without spot or wrinkle (ibid. 5:27) [Note: [Col. 0229] See *Retractations* 2.18.].

### CHAPTER ELEVEN

#### 20

Paulus of Bobba [Note: [Col. 0229] Am. and Erasmus read, “Paulus of Obba.”] said:

“It does not trouble me if someone does not defend the faith and truth of the Church, since the Apostle says: ‘What then? If some of them fell away from the faith, does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true, and every human being a liar’ (Rom. 3:3–4). But if God is true, how can the truth of Baptism exist among heretics, among whom God is not?”

#### 21

We reply: What? Is God among the greedy? And yet Baptism exists there; so too among heretics.

[Col. 0230] For among those with whom God is present, they are the temple of God. But what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols (2 Cor. 6:16)? Paul understands greed as idolatry, and Cyprian agrees with him; yet Cyprian himself remains, in the company of plundering colleagues who nevertheless baptize, earning the great reward of forbearance.

### CHAPTER TWELVE

#### 22

Pomponius of Dionysiana [Note: [Col. 0230] Am. and Erasmus read, “Pomponius of Josiniana.”] said:

“It is clear that heretics cannot baptize or grant the forgiveness of sins, since they do not possess the power to loose or bind anything on earth.”

#### 23

We reply that murderers do not possess this power either—that is, those who hate their brothers. For it was not to such people that it was said, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:23). Yet they baptize, and Paul tolerates them in the same communion of Baptism, while Cyprian acknowledges them.

### CHAPTER THIRTEEN

#### 24

Venantius of Tinisa [Note: [Col. 0230] Louvain reads, “of Thimisa.” Am., Erasmus, our older manuscripts, and Cyprian’s new edition read, “of Tinisa.”] said:

“If a husband, departing abroad, entrusted his wife to a friend to guard, would that friend not preserve the woman entrusted to him with the greatest possible diligence, lest her chastity and holiness be violated by anyone? Christ the Lord and our God, departing to the Father, entrusted his bride to us. Do we preserve her undefiled and inviolate, or do we betray her integrity and chastity to adulterers and corrupters? Whoever makes the Church’s Baptism common with heretics betrays Christ’s bride to adulterers.”

#### 25

We reply: What about those who, when they are baptized, turn to the Lord with their lips and not with their hearts? Do they not harbor an adulterous mind? Are they not lovers of the world, which they renounced not in deeds but in words, and therefore corrupt good morals through evil conversations, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Cor. 15:33, 32)?

Was the apostolic statement not also watchful against such people when it says, “But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may somehow be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3)?

Since Cyprian therefore held Christ’s Baptism in common with such people, was he for that reason betraying Christ’s bride to adulterers, rather than recognizing the bridegroom’s necklace even in an adulteress?

### CHAPTER FOURTEEN

#### 26

Aymnius of Ausuaga [Note: [Col. 0230] Am. and Erasmus read, “Aymnius of Ausuagiga.” Some manuscripts read, “Hymmius of Ausuagida.” The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “Aymmus of Ausaugiga.” The Georgian manuscript reads, “Aymnius of Ausuagiga.”] said:

“We have received one Baptism, and we administer that same Baptism [Note: [Col. 0230] Erasmus and Louvain add, “and hold it.”]. Whoever says that heretics too have the right to baptize makes two Baptisms.”

#### 27

We reply: Why does the person who says that the wicked too baptize not likewise make two Baptisms? Since the righteous and the wicked are opposed to one another, the Baptism given by the righteous—such as Paul, or even Cyprian—is not opposed to the Baptism given by those wicked people who hated Paul, whom Cyprian understands to be not heretics but bad Catholics.

[Col. 0231] And although continence, which was found in Cyprian, and greed, which was found in Cyprian’s colleagues, are opposed to one another, the Baptism which Cyprian gave was not opposed to the Baptism which they gave, but was one and the same, because it is he who baptizes of whom it was said, “He is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

### CHAPTER FIFTEEN

[Col. 0231]

#### 28

Saturninus of Victoriana said:

“If heretics have the right to baptize, those who do unlawful things are excused and defended. Nor do I see why Christ would call them his adversaries, or the Apostle call them antichrists.”

#### 29

We reply: We say that heretics do not have the right to baptize in the same way that we say that swindlers do not have the right to baptize.

For God says not only to heretics but to the sinner, “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your lips?” To this person he certainly said, “When you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Ps. 49:16, 18).

How much worse, then, were those who did not run with thieves but themselves seized estates through deceitful schemes? Yet Cyprian did not run with them, although he tolerated them in the Catholic field, lest the wheat also be uprooted at the same time.

And nevertheless, the Baptism which they gave was also the very same Baptism, because it was not theirs but Christ’s.

Thus, although Christ’s Baptism is recognized among these people, they are nevertheless not excused or defended when they do unlawful things. Christ rightly calls them his adversaries, because those who persist in such practices will hear, “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:23). They are also called antichrists because they are opposed to Christ, living contrary to what he commands. The same is true of heretics.

### CHAPTER SIXTEEN

#### 30

Another Saturninus of Tucca said:

“Although the Gentiles worship idols, they nevertheless acknowledge and confess the supreme God, the Father and Creator. Marcion blasphemes against him, and some are not ashamed to approve Marcion’s Baptism [Note: [Col. 0231] He is speaking of Pope Stephen, concerning whom Cyprian writes in Letter 74 to Pompeius: “Why has the obstinacy of our brother Stephen burst forth with such harshness that he even contends concerning Marcion’s Baptism … and that of the others who blaspheme against God the Father, that children are born to God?”]. How do such priests either preserve or defend God’s priesthood, when they do not baptize God’s enemies and thus communicate with them?”

#### 31

We reply: Clearly, in saying such things they exceed the proper measure and fail to consider that they too shared communion with such people, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion.

Yet this very opinion of his contains something from which he could be admonished, if he paid attention: whatever is wrong in a person must be corrected, while whatever is right must be approved. For he says that “although the Gentiles worship idols, they nevertheless acknowledge and confess the supreme God, the Father and Creator.”

If such a Gentile therefore came to God, would he wish to correct and change in him the fact that he confessed and knew God as Father and Creator? I do not think so [Note: [Col. 0231] “I do not think so” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Rather, he would correct the idolatry that he possessed as an evil; he would pass on the Christian sacraments that he did not possess; whatever sound knowledge he found in him, he would approve; whatever perverse thing he found, he would correct; [Col. 0232] and whatever was lacking, he would supply.

So too, in a Marcionite heretic he would recognize the integrity of Baptism, correct his perversity, and teach Catholic truth.

### CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

#### 32

Marcellus of Zama [Note: [Col. 0232] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “of Dama.”] said:

“Since sins are forgiven only in the Church’s Baptism, whoever does not baptize a heretic shares communion with a sinner.”

#### 33

What about the person who shares communion with one who does this? Does he not share communion with a sinner? What else were all those people doing when they judged no one or removed from the right of communion anyone who held a different opinion?

Where, then, is the Church? Or do these things not harm those who patiently tolerate the weeds so that the wheat may not be uprooted (Matt. 13:29)?

Let these people, who have committed the sacrilege of schism by separating themselves pointlessly from the whole world, say why they have Cyprian’s opinion in their mouths when they do not have Cyprian’s patience in their hearts.

Marcellus can be answered from what was said above concerning Baptism and the forgiveness of sins: how Baptism can exist in a person even though the forgiveness of sins does not exist in him.

### CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

#### 34

Irenaeus of Ululis [Note: [Col. 0232] The Louvain editors corrected this to “of Usulis,” since in *Against Cresconius* 3.22 we read of “Theodorus of Usula.”] said:

“If the Church does not baptize a heretic because he is said already to have been baptized, heresy is the greater power.”

#### 35

We reply: In this way one could say, “If the Church does not baptize a greedy person because he is said already to have been baptized, greed is the greater power.” But this is false; therefore the other statement is false as well.

### CHAPTER NINETEEN

#### 36

Donatus of Cibaliana said:

“I know one Church and its one Baptism. If anyone says that the grace of Baptism exists among heretics, let him first show and prove that the Church exists there.”

#### 37

We reply: If by the grace of Baptism you mean what Baptism is, then it exists among heretics. But if Baptism is the sacrament of grace, while grace itself is the abolition of sins, then the grace of Baptism does not exist among heretics.

There is one Baptism and one Church in the same way that there is one hope. Therefore, just as the good and the wicked, although they do not possess one hope, can nevertheless possess one Baptism, so Baptism can be shared by those who do not share one Church.

### CHAPTER TWENTY

#### 38

Zozimus of Tharassa said:

“When the truth has been revealed, error must yield to truth, since Peter too, who previously practiced circumcision, yielded to Paul, who preached the truth (Gal. 2:11).”

#### 39

This statement could also be ours, and this is what happened in the question concerning Baptism. For when the truth was afterward revealed more clearly, error yielded to truth, once that most salutary custom had also been confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.

It is nevertheless good that they so often remember that even Peter, the first of the apostles, could have held an opinion different from what the truth required. We believe that this also happened to Cyprian, without any insult to him—we who love Cyprian—for he must not be loved with a greater charity than Peter.

[Col. 0233]

### CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

#### 40

Julianus of Telepte said:

“It is written, ‘No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven’ (John 3:27). If heresy is from heaven, it can give Baptism.”

#### 41

Let him also hear someone else say: “If greed is from heaven, it can give Baptism.” Yet the greedy do give it; so too, therefore, do heretics.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO

#### 42

Faustus of Timida Regia said:

“Let those who protect heretics not flatter themselves. Whoever intervenes on behalf of heretics for ecclesiastical Baptism makes them Christians and us heretics.”

#### 43

We reply: If someone were to say that a person who, while receiving Baptism, retained hatred of his brother in his heart had not received the forgiveness of sins, but that when he dismissed that hatred from his heart he should not be baptized again, would he thereby be intervening through ecclesiastical Baptism on behalf of murderers, or make them righteous and us murderers? Let him understand the same thing concerning heretics.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE

#### 44

Geminius [Note: [Col. 0233] Am. and Erasmus read, “Geminus.” The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “of Fornis.”] of Furni said:

“Some of our colleagues may place heretics before themselves; they cannot place them before us. Therefore we hold to what we once decreed: that we baptize those who come from heretics.”

#### 45

Here too he most openly admits that some of his colleagues held a different opinion. This confirms again and again their love of unity: they were not separated from one another by any schism until God should reveal to the others, if they held any different view (Phil. 3:15).

But we reply to him that his colleagues did not place heretics before themselves. Rather, they recognized Christ’s Baptism in heretics, just as it is recognized in the greedy, swindlers, plunderers, and murderers.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR

#### 46

Rogatianus of Nova said:

“Christ established the Church; the devil established heresy. How can the synagogue of Satan possess Christ’s Baptism?”

#### 47

We reply: Since Christ established the devout and the devil the envious, does it follow that the group shown to belong to the devil through its envy cannot possess Christ’s Baptism?

### CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE

#### 48

Therapius of Bulla said:

“Whoever grants heretics the Church’s Baptism and betrays it—what else is he than Judas, the betrayer of Christ’s bride?”

49. O great exposure of the schismatics, who by wicked sacrilege have separated themselves from the inheritance of Christ spread throughout the whole world! If Cyprian communicated with men of the sort that Judas the traitor was, and yet was not defiled by them; or if he was defiled, then all became Judases—therefore now also all are Judases; or if they are not, then they do not belong to the later crimes of their predecessors, although they were propagated from the same communion [Note: [Col. 0233] Ambrose and the manuscripts: “to their descendants” (*ad posteros*).]. Why, then, do they accuse us of being traitors, whom they have not convicted, and not accuse Judas, with whom Cyprian and his colleagues communicated?

Here is the council of which they are accustomed to boast. We indeed say that the man who recognizes Christ’s Baptism even among heretics does not thereby betray the Church’s Baptism to heretics, just as the man who recognizes Christ’s Baptism even among murderers does not thereby betray the Church’s Baptism to murderers. But since these men strive to prescribe to us, on the authority of this council, what we ought to think, let them themselves first agree with it.

Here men are compared with Judas the traitor—those who said that heretics, even though baptized in heresy, ought not to be baptized again. Yet Cyprian communicated with such men, for he said: “Judging no one, nor removing from the right of communion anyone who held a different opinion” [at the beginning of the Council of Carthage]. That such men had previously existed in the Church is also plainly shown by the statement: “But someone says, ‘What, then, will become of those who in the past were admitted into the Church without Baptism?’” [Letter 73, to Jubaianus]. Those who convened this council themselves frequently recall that this had been the custom of the Church.

Therefore, if whoever does this is nothing other than a Judas to Christ’s bride, as this judgment has declared—and Judas, as the Gospel teaches, was a traitor—then all who at that time were saying these things communicated with traitors; indeed, before they said these things, all had become traitors through that custom which the Church then maintained. Therefore all of us—that is, both we and those who have been propagated from that unity—are traitors.

But we are defended in two ways: first, because we do not agree with this council, where this was decreed, while preserving the right of unity, just as Cyprian himself had previously declared; and second, because we judge that the wicked do no harm to the good within catholic unity, until at the end the chaff is separated from the wheat.

But these men, because they both produce this council as supporting their cause and insist that the good perish through communion with the wicked, as though by contagion, cannot find a way to say either that the earlier Christians from whom they derive were not traitors—for they are convicted by this council—or that the crimes of their predecessors do not belong to them—for they accuse us of the actions of our ancestors.

### CHAPTER XXVI

50. Likewise another Lucius, from Membresa [Note: [Col. 0234] Ambrose, Erasmus, and several manuscripts, with double *s*, *Membressa*.], said: “It is written, ‘God does not hear a sinner’” (John 9:31). How, then, can one who is a sinner be heard in Baptism?

51. We answer: How are the covetous, the robber, the usurer, and the murderer heard? Are these not sinners? Yet Cyprian rebukes and tolerates them within the Catholic Church.

### CHAPTER XXVII

52. Likewise another Felix, from Buslacena [Note: [Col. 0234] Ambrose and Erasmus, *ab Uslaccenis*. Cyprian’s edition, *a Buslaceni*, or *a Buslacene*.], said: “When those who are heretics are admitted without the Church’s Baptism, let no one place custom above reason and truth; for reason and truth always exclude custom.”

53. To him it is answered: You do not demonstrate the truth; you acknowledge the force of custom. We would therefore rightly hold to a custom confirmed by a later plenary council, even if the truth were still hidden—though we believe that it has now been made manifest.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

54. Another Saturninus, from Abitina [Note: [Col. 0234] Ambrose and Erasmus, *ab Itinis*. Cyprian, *Avitinis*.], said: “If the Antichrist can give someone the grace of Christ, then heretics too can baptize, since they have been called antichrists.”

55. What if someone else were to say: “If a murderer can give someone the grace of Christ, then those who hate their brothers can baptize, since they have been called murderers”? Surely this would seem to be saying something true—and yet they can. So, then, can heretics as well.

### CHAPTER XXIX

56. Quintus, from Aggya [Note: [Col. 0235] The Remigianus manuscript, together with Ambrose and Erasmus, *ab Aggiva*. Several other manuscripts, *ab Anguia*. The Corbie manuscript, Florus, and Georgianus, *ab Agguia*.], said: “One who has something can give something; but what can heretics give, when it is clear that they have nothing?”

57. To him it is answered: If, then, one who has something can give something, it is clear that heretics can give Baptism, because when they withdraw from the Church they retain the sacrament of the washing which they had received there. For when they return, they do not receive it again, because they had not lost it when they withdrew.

### CHAPTER XXX

58. Another Julianus, from Marcelliana [Note: [Col. 0235] Ambrose, Erasmus, and certain manuscripts, *a Marcellina*.], said: “If a person can serve two masters, God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24), “then Baptism too can serve two masters, the Christian and the heretic.”

59. Rather, if it can serve the continent and the covetous, the sober and the drunken, the devout and the murderer, why not also the Christian and the heretic? In truth, it does not serve them; rather, it is administered to them, or by them, for salvation when used well, and for judgment when used badly.

### CHAPTER XXXI

60. Tenax, from the Horrea of Caelia, said: “There is one Baptism, but it belongs to the Church. Where the Church is not, Baptism cannot be there.”

61. We answer him: Why, then, can it be where the rock is not but sand is, since the Church is on the rock, not on the sand?

### CHAPTER XXXII

62. Another Victor, from Assuras, said: “It is written, ‘Because there is one God and one Christ, one Church and one Baptism’” (Ephesians 4:4). How can anyone be baptized there, where God and Christ and the Church are not [Note: [Col. 0235] In Cyprian, “where one Church is not.”]?

63. How can it be in that sand, where there is neither the Church—for it is on the rock—nor God and Christ, because the temple of God and Christ is not there?

### CHAPTER XXXIII

64. Donatulus, from Capsa, said: “I too have always held this view: that heretics, who have obtained nothing outside, should be baptized when they turn to the Church.”

65. To this it is answered: They have indeed obtained nothing outside—but nothing for salvation, not nothing with respect to the sacrament. Salvation belongs properly to the good; the sacraments, however, are common to both the good and the wicked.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

66. Verulus, from Rusiccade, said: “A heretical person cannot give what he does not have; still less can a schismatic, who has lost what he possessed.”

67. We have already shown that they possess it, because they do not lose it when they withdraw. For they do not receive it again when they return. Therefore, if they seemed unable to give it because they were thought not to possess it, let it now be understood that they can give it, because it is understood that they possess it.

### CHAPTER XXXV

68. Pudentianus, from Cuiculi, said: “The newness of my episcopate, dearest brothers, caused me to wait for the judgment of my predecessors. For it is manifest that heresies possess nothing and can do nothing; and accordingly it has been most justly decreed that if any come from them, they should be baptized.”

69. Just as the answer was given to those whom he was waiting to see what they would judge, so let it be understood that an answer has also been given to him.

### CHAPTER XXXVI

70. Petrus, from Hippo Diarrhytus [Note: [Col. 0236] Ambrose, Erasmus, and our manuscripts, *ab Hippone Zarito*.], said: “Since there is one Baptism in the Catholic Church, it is clear that baptism cannot take place outside the Church. Therefore I judge that those baptized in heresy or in schism ought to be baptized when they come to the Church.”

71. Baptism is one in the Catholic Church in such a way that when some depart from it, two baptisms do not arise in those who depart, but the same one remains. Therefore, what is recognized in those who return is also present in those who received it from those who departed—what they did not lose when they departed.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

72. Likewise another Lucius, from Ausafa [Note: [Col. 0236] Ambrose and Erasmus, *ab Avasafa*.], said: “According to the movement of my mind and of the Holy Spirit, since there is one God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one Christ, and one hope, one Spirit, one Church, there ought to be one Baptism. Therefore I say that if anything has been performed or administered among heretics [Note: [Col. 0236] In Cyprian’s edition, *ab haereticis motum*, ‘performed by heretics’.], it ought to be annulled, and that those who come from there ought to be baptized in the Church.”

73. Then let what those baptize who hear the words of God and do not practice them be annulled, when they begin to migrate from wickedness to righteousness—that is, from sand to the rock. But if this is not done because what belonged to Christ in them was not violated by their wickedness, let this also be understood of heretics. For they do not have the same hope while they are on the sand as those have who are upon the rock; nevertheless, the same Baptism exists in both, although Baptism is called one just as hope is one.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

74. Felix, from Gurgites, said: “I judge that, according to the precepts of the holy Scriptures, those who were illicitly baptized by heretics outside the Church should obtain the grace of Baptism, where it is lawfully administered, if they wish to take refuge in the Church.”

75. It is answered: Rather, let them lawfully begin to possess for salvation what they unlawfully possessed for destruction. For under the same Baptism a person is justified when he turns to God with a truthful heart, under which he was judged when, upon receiving it, he had renounced the world in words only and not in deeds.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

76. Pusillus, from Lamasba [Note: [Col. 0236] In Cyprian, *a Lambesâ*.], said: “I believe that saving Baptism exists only in the Catholic Church. Whatever exists apart from the Catholic Church is pretense.”

77. This is indeed true: saving Baptism exists only in the Catholic Church. For it can itself exist outside the Catholic Church, but it is not saving there, because there it does not effect salvation—just as that good odor of Christ is certainly not saving among those who perish (2 Corinthians 2:15), not because of any fault in the odor itself, but because of theirs.

Whatever exists outside the Catholic Church is pretense, insofar as it is not catholic. Yet something catholic can exist outside the Catholic Church, just as the name of Christ could exist outside Christ’s congregation, in that name by which the man who did not follow with the disciples drove out demons (Mark 9:38). For pretense can also exist within the Catholic Church, namely in those who renounce the world in words and not in deeds; yet such pretense is not catholic. Therefore, just as there is within the Catholic Church something that is not catholic, so something catholic can exist outside the Catholic Church.

### CHAPTER XL

78. Salvianus, from Gazaufala, said: “It is clear that heretics have nothing; therefore they come to us so that they may receive what they did not have.”

79. We answer: Then those who founded the heresies were not themselves heretics, because they withdrew from the Church and certainly possessed what they had received there. But if it is absurd to say that those through whom the others become heretics are not themselves heretics, it can happen that a heretic possesses something by whose bad use he perishes.

### CHAPTER XLI
