80. Honoratus, from Tucca, said: “Since Christ is the truth, we ought to follow the truth rather than custom, so that we may sanctify with the Church’s Baptism those heretics who come to us because they were unable to receive anything outside.”

81. This man too bears witness to custom, where it greatly helps us, whatever else he may seem to say against us. Heretics do not come to us because they received nothing outside; rather, they come so that what they received may begin to be useful to them. For outside, it cannot be useful in any way.

### CHAPTER XLII

82. Victor, from Octavum [Note: [Col. 0237] The old Corbie manuscript, of excellent quality, *ab Octavavo*.], said: “As you yourselves know, I was appointed bishop only recently, and for that reason I was waiting for the counsel of my predecessors. I therefore hold that all who come from heresy should unquestionably be baptized.”

83. Let the answer given to those whom he was waiting for be understood as having been given to him also.

### CHAPTER XLIII

84. Clarus, from Mascula, said: “The judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ is clear: he sent out his Apostles and entrusted to them alone the authority given him by the Father. We have succeeded them, governing the Lord’s Church with the same authority and baptizing the faith of believers. Therefore heretics, who possess neither authority outside nor the Church of Christ, cannot baptize anyone with his Baptism.”

85. Did impious murderers also succeed the Apostles? Why, then, do they baptize? Is it because they are not outside? But they are outside the rock, to which the Lord gave the keys and upon which he said he would build his Church (Matthew 16:18–19).

### CHAPTER XLIV

86. Secundianus, from Thambeae [Note: [Col. 0237] The same Corbie manuscript, *a Satambeis*. Ambrose and Erasmus, *a Tabeis*.], said: “We ought not, through our presumption, to deceive heretics, so that when the day of judgment comes they may charge us with the fact that, having not been baptized in the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ and consequently not having obtained the remission of sins, they were not baptized through us and did not obtain the pardon of divine grace. Therefore, since there is one Church and one Baptism, when they turn to us let them obtain the Church and the Church’s Baptism together.”

87. Rather, once transferred to the rock and joined to the dove, let them receive the remission of sins, which they could not possess outside the rock and outside the dove—whether openly outside, as heretics are, or apparently within, as lost Catholics are. Yet it is clear that such people both possess and give Baptism without the remission of sins, since even from them such persons receive it who, without changing for the better, honor God with their lips while their heart is far from him (Isaiah 29:13).

Nevertheless, Baptism is one in the same way that the dove is one, even though those who are not in the dove may commonly possess Baptism.

### CHAPTER XLV

88. Likewise another Aurelius, from Chullabi [Note: [Col. 0238] The Corbie manuscript and several others, *a Cillavi*. Others, *a Cillabi*. Ambrose and Erasmus, *a Cillani*.], said: “The Apostle John wrote in his Epistle: ‘If anyone comes to you and does not have the teaching of Christ, do not receive him into your house, and do not say “Hail” to him. For whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil deeds’” (2 John 10–11). How can such people be rashly admitted into the house of God, when they are forbidden to be admitted into our private house? Or how can we communicate with them without the Church’s Baptism, when, if we merely say “Hail” to them, we share in their evil deeds?

89. There is no need to discuss John’s testimony at greater length, since it has absolutely nothing to do with the question of Baptism that we are now treating. For he says: “If anyone comes to you and does not have the teaching of Christ.” Heretics, however, abandon the teaching of their error and turn to Christ’s teaching, so that they may be incorporated into the Church and begin to belong to that dove whose sacrament they possessed. Therefore what they did not possess is given to them—that is, peace and charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1:5).

What they did possess is recognized and received without any insult, just as God recognizes his gifts in the adulteress even when she follows her lovers; for when, after her fornication has been corrected [Note: [Col. 0238] The printed editions read *corrupta*, “corrupted”: a mistake.], she turns to chastity, the gifts themselves are not condemned, but she herself is corrected (Hosea 2).

Just as Cyprian could defend himself if John’s testimony were brought against him, since he communicated with such people, so let those against whom this testimony is cited defend themselves. For, as I said, it has absolutely nothing to do with this question.

John says that “Hail” must not be said to people of another doctrine; but the Apostle Paul says still more forcefully: “If anyone called a brother among you is either covetous, or a drunkard, etc., not even to eat together with such a one” (1 Corinthians 5:11). Yet Cyprian had a common table—not a private table, but God’s altar—with colleagues who were usurers, schemers, fraudsters, and robbers. How this can be defended has already been sufficiently stated in other books.

### CHAPTER XLVI

90. Litteus [Note: [Col. 0239] Ambrose and Erasmus, *Licteus*.], from Gemellae, said: “If the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14). Since it is therefore clear that heretics, being blind, cannot enlighten anyone, their Baptism is of no value.

91. Nor do we say that it is effective for salvation as long as they remain heretics, just as it is not effective for those murderers as long as they hate their brothers. For they too are in darkness, and if anyone follows them, both fall into the pit. Yet this does not mean that they either do not possess Baptism or do not transmit it.

### CHAPTER XLVII

92. Natalis, from Oea [Note: [Col. 0239] Ambrose, Erasmus, and certain manuscripts, *Nalis a Boea*; or *ab Oea*.], said: “Both I, who am present, and Pompeius of Sabrata, and Dioga of Leptis Magna, who have sent me their instructions—absent in body but present in spirit—hold the same view as our colleagues: that heretics cannot have communion with us unless they have been baptized with ecclesiastical Baptism.”

93. I believe he means the communion that belongs to association with the dove. For they certainly communicated in the participation of the sacraments, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion.

But whatever he meant, these words need not be refuted at length. Certainly, a heretic does not communicate unless he has been baptized with ecclesiastical Baptism. Yet it is established that Baptism consecrated among heretics with evangelical words is also ecclesiastical, just as the Gospel itself is ecclesiastical. It does not belong to their perversity; rather, it retains its own sanctity [Note: [Col. 0239] Several manuscripts read *sanitatem*, “soundness.”].

### CHAPTER XLVIII

94. Junius, from Neapolis, said: “I do not depart from what we once judged: that we should baptize heretics who come to the Church.”

95. Since he has offered neither reason nor testimony from the Scriptures, this need not hold us for long.

### CHAPTER XLIX

96. Cyprian, from Carthage, said: “My position is expressed most fully in the letter written to our colleague Jubaianus: that heretics, according to evangelical and apostolic testimony, have been called adversaries of Christ and antichrists; and that when they come to the Church they ought to be baptized with the Church’s one Baptism, so that they may become friends instead of adversaries, and Christians instead of antichrists.”

97. What more is there to discuss here, when we have treated with as much diligence as we could the very letter to Jubaianus that he mentioned?

And let us remember that what he has said here can be said of all the wicked, whom he himself attests to be within the Catholic Church and to possess and give Baptism—something none of us doubts.

Those who come to the Church are those who pass from the devil’s portion to Christ, build upon the rock, are incorporated into the dove, and are protected in the enclosed garden and sealed fountain. Not all who live contrary to Christ’s commands are there, wherever they may seem to be.

For in the letter he wrote to Magnus, when he was dealing with this very matter, he gave us a sufficiently clear warning about the sort of communion in which the Church ought to be understood. Speaking of a certain person, he says: “Let him be alien and profane, an enemy of the Lord’s peace and the Lord’s unity [Note: [Col. 0240] In Cyprian, “and divine unity”], not dwelling in the house of God—that is, in the Church of Christ, in which only those who are harmonious and of one mind dwell” (Letter 69).

Let those who wish to prescribe Cyprian to us pay a little attention to what we are saying here. If only those who are harmonious and of one mind dwell in the Church of Christ, then certainly those who proclaimed Christ out of envy and rivalry without charity did not dwell in the Church of Christ, although they appeared to be within it. Paul the Apostle mentions them not as heretics or schismatics, but as false brothers living inwardly alongside him (Philippians 1:15, 17).

They certainly ought not to have baptized, because they did not dwell in the Church, in which Cyprian says that only the harmonious and like-minded dwell—unless perhaps someone is so estranged from the truth as to say that the envious and ill-disposed, the quarrelsome and uncharitable, were harmonious and of one mind. Yet they baptized, and their detestable perversity did not in any way diminish or violate the sacrament of Christ, which was handled and administered through them.

### CHAPTER L

98. It is certainly worthwhile to examine the entire passage placed in the same letter to Magnus, which he composed as follows:

“Not dwelling in the house of God,” he says, “that is, in the Church of Christ, in which only those who are harmonious and of one mind dwell, the Holy Spirit speaking in the Psalms and saying, ‘God makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house’” (Psalm 67:7).

Finally, the very sacrifices of the Lord declare that Christians are joined to one another by firm and inseparable charity. For when the Lord calls his body bread (John 6:52), formed from the union of many grains gathered together, he indicates our people, whom he was bearing, as united. And when he calls his blood wine (Matthew 26:26–29), pressed from many clusters and grapes and brought together into one, he likewise signifies our flock, joined by the mingling of a united multitude.

These words of blessed Cyprian show that he both understood and loved the beauty of God’s house. He affirmed that this house consists of those who are of one mind and in harmony, and he taught this by prophetic testimony and by the symbolism of the sacraments. Yet those envious and uncharitable ill-wishers who baptized were certainly not in that house.

From this it is evident that the sacrament of Christ can exist in those who are not in the Church of Christ, and can be given by those who are not in the Church of Christ, although Cyprian himself testifies that only those who are of one mind and in harmony dwell in that Church.

Nor can it even be said that they were able to baptize only when they remained hidden, since those whom Paul the Apostle did not fail to notice were not hidden from him. In his Epistle, that most truthful witness marks them out and says that he rejoices because they too were proclaiming Christ. Of them he says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice” (Philippians 1:18).

### CHAPTER LI

99. Considering all these matters, I think I may say without rashness that some are in the house of God in such a way that they themselves are also that same house of God—the house said to be built upon the rock (Matthew 16:18), called the one dove (Song of Songs 6:8), the beautiful bride without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0241] 2nd *Retractions*, chapter 18] (Ephesians 5:27), the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, the well of living water, and the paradise with the fruit of trees (Song of Songs 4:12–13). This house also received the keys and the power of binding and loosing (Matthew 16:19).

If anyone despises this house when it reproves and corrects him, it says: “Let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matthew 18:17).

Of this house it is said: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8); and, “He makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house” (Psalm 67:7); and, “I rejoiced in those things which they said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Psalm 122:1); and, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 84:5); and countless similar passages.

This house is also called wheat, producing fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold with perseverance (Matthew 13:23; Luke 8:15). This house consists of vessels of gold and silver (2 Timothy 2:20), precious stones, and imperishable wood. To this house it is said: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3); and, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

This house exists among good believers and holy servants of God scattered everywhere and bound together by spiritual unity in the same communion of the sacraments, whether they know one another face-to-face or do not know one another.

Others, however, are said to be in the house in such a way that they do not belong to the structure of the house or to the fellowship of fruitful and peaceful righteousness, but are like chaff said to be among the wheat. For we cannot deny that these too are in the house, since the Apostle says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor” (2 Timothy 2:20) [Note: [Col. 0241] 2nd *Retractions*, chapter 18].

From this innumerable group arise not only the crowd within, pressing upon the small number of the saints in comparison with so great a multitude, but also heresies and schisms, when the nets are torn. Such people are more properly said to be from the house than in the house, and of them it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

Those who have been separated even bodily are more completely separated than those who live inwardly in a carnal and animal manner but are spiritually separated.

### CHAPTER LII

100. Of all these groups, the first—those who are in God’s house in such a way that they themselves are God’s house, whether they are already spiritual or are still little ones nourished with milk but are progressing toward spiritual maturity with an attentive heart—certainly possess Baptism beneficially and transmit it beneficially to those who imitate them.

But the insincere, from whom the Holy Spirit flees, receive it without benefit, even though those through whom they receive it transmit it beneficially, insofar as lies in them; for they do not imitate them.

Those who are in the great house as vessels for dishonor possess Baptism without benefit and transmit it without benefit to those who imitate them. But those who are joined not to them in heart and conduct but to the holy house receive it from them beneficially.

Those who are more completely separated—who are not so much in the house as from the house—neither possess it beneficially nor can it be beneficially received from them, unless perhaps the necessity of receiving it presses urgently and the mind of the recipient does not withdraw from the bond of unity.

Nevertheless, they do possess it, though they possess it without benefit; and it is received from them, even when it is without benefit to those who receive it. For it to become beneficial, one must withdraw from heresy or schism and adhere to that house. This must be done not only by heretics and schismatics, but also by those who are in the house through communion in the sacraments while remaining outside the house through the diversity of their conduct. Thus the sacrament also begins to be useful to them, although otherwise it is useless.

### CHAPTER LIII

101. It is also customary to ask whether Baptism should be approved when it is received from someone who did not receive it himself, if perhaps he learned by some sort of curiosity [Note: [Col. 0242] Lov. reads *si forte curiositate aliqua*, omitting *hoc*, which Ambrose and the better Gallican manuscripts contain.] how it should be administered; and whether it makes no difference with what disposition the person to whom it is given receives it—whether with pretense or without pretense.

If with pretense, one may ask whether he is deceiving, as in the Church or in what is thought to be the Church, or whether he is joking, as in a mime. One may also ask which is more wicked: to receive it deceitfully in the Church, or without deceit in heresy or schism—that is, with an unfeigned disposition; and whether it is worse to receive it deceitfully in heresy or with faith in a mime, if someone, while acting, should suddenly be moved by piety.

Even if we compare such a person with one who deceitfully receives Baptism within the Catholic Church itself, it would be astonishing if there were any doubt about which should be preferred to the other. For I do not see how the sincere disposition of the giver can benefit a deceitful recipient.

But let us suppose that someone gives it deceitfully, when both the giver and the recipient act deceitfully within Catholic unity itself. Is that Baptism more acceptable, or is the Baptism given in a mime more acceptable if someone receives it faithfully after being suddenly moved? Or, as far as the people themselves are concerned, is there a great difference between one who believes in the mime and one who mocks in the Church, while as far as the integrity of the sacrament itself is concerned there is no difference?

For if, with respect to the integrity of the sacrament within the Catholic Church itself, it makes no difference whether some perform it deceitfully or truthfully, provided that both perform the same thing, I do not see why it should make a difference outside, when the recipient has been changed not by a covering of pretense but by religious conviction.

Or do those who are truthful among whom the sacrament is performed have greater power to confirm it than the deceitful have to frustrate it—those by whom it is performed and in whom it is performed? Yet if the deceit is later exposed, no one repeats the Baptism; rather, the pretense is punished by excommunication or healed through repentance.

102. But it is safe for us not to advance with any rash judgment into matters that have neither been begun in a catholic regional council nor concluded in a plenary council. We may confidently assert what has been strengthened by the universal agreement of the Church under the governance of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ.

Nevertheless, if someone should press me, seated in a council where a question of this kind was being discussed, to say what I myself thought, without those whose opinions I would prefer to follow having spoken first—if I were in the frame of mind I had when I composed these words—I would have no doubt that those possess Baptism who, wherever and from whomever, have received it consecrated with evangelical words, without their own pretense and with some faith.

Although it would not benefit them for spiritual salvation if they lacked the charity by which they would be incorporated into the Catholic Church. For he says: “If I have faith so as to remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

Just as, in accordance with the established judgments of our predecessors, I do not doubt that those also possess Baptism who receive it deceitfully, provided that they receive it in the Church—or in what is thought to be the Church—among those in whose fellowship it is received, of whom it has been said: “They went out from us” (1 John 2:19).

But where there were neither any fellowship of believers of this kind nor anyone who received it there with such belief, but everything was performed playfully, theatrically, and as a joke, I would judge that we ought to seek divine judgment concerning whether Baptism so given should be approved, through the oracle of some revelation, with united prayer and the groans of earnest devotion.

I would certainly wait humbly for those who were going to express their judgments after me, so that they might bring nothing already tested and known. How much more, then, should I now be understood to have said this without prejudice to more careful inquiry or greater authority?

### CHAPTER LIV

103. But now, as I think, it is time to bring these books on the question of Baptism to their proper conclusion.

Here our Lord God has shown us, through the peace-loving bishop Cyprian and those who agreed with him, how greatly catholic unity ought to be loved: they tolerated those who thought differently, until God should also reveal this matter to them (Philippians 3:15), rather than separating themselves from them by wicked schism.

Here the mouths of the Donatists are completely closed, even if we say nothing about the Maximianists. For if the wicked contaminate the good within unity, Cyprian himself found no Church with which he could associate. But if the wicked do not stain the good within unity, the sacrilegious Donatist has no cause for separation.

If so many others who perform works of the flesh possess and transmit Baptism—works of the sort whose practitioners will not possess the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19–21)—then heretics also possess and transmit it, since they are numbered among those works. They did not lose it by withdrawing, and by retaining it they were able to transmit it. But such people transmit it to people like themselves as fruitlessly and uselessly as those other equals of theirs, because they will not possess the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0244] In the old Corbie manuscript and almost all other manuscripts, *patres eorum*, “their fathers,” instead of *pares eorum*, “their equals.”].

And just as, when those others are corrected, Baptism does not begin to exist in them as something previously absent, but begins to benefit them as something already present, so it is also with heretics.

Therefore Cyprian and those who shared his view could not prescribe their opinion against the Catholic Church, which they refused to cut off. We do not shrink from the fact that they thought differently, because with them we venerate Peter as well. But we rejoice that they did not withdraw from unity, because with them we are built upon the rock.

## [AGAINST THE LETTERS OF PETILIAN]

[Col. 0243]

### ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS

After the books on Baptism, the next book in the series of the *Retractations* is entitled *Against What Centurius Brought Forward from the Donatists*. If that book still existed, its proper place here would be before the minor works against Petilian.

Petilian, a bishop in the party of Donatus, had previously been a courtroom advocate. In that capacity he boasted that he had earned the name “Paraclete,” as Augustine testifies in Book 3, chapter 16, of this work.

Augustine likewise says, in his sermon *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, and here in Book 2, chapter 104, that Petilian was born at Cirta—or Constantina, which was the same city in Numidia—to Catholic parents, while they were Catholics, and that he was abducted by the Donatists and forcibly baptized by them, and ordained against his will.

Petilian later became the most vigorous defender of the party of Donatus and was one of the seven bishops selected to debate against an equal number of Catholic bishops at the Conference of Carthage.

He wrote, long before that same conference, the letter addressed to the Donatist presbyters and deacons against the Catholics, which is refuted in the three books that follow. In the first book Augustine attacks the first part of Petilian’s letter, which had been handed to him while he was in the church at Constantina, in the presence of Absentio, as the beginning of the book states, and of Fortunatus, bishop of that church. In place of *Absentio*, *Alypio* may perhaps be the correct reading, so that this would refer to the very occasion on which the same bishops—Fortunatus, Alypius, and Augustine—were together. On that very occasion the same bishops—Fortunatus, Alypius, and Augustine—jointly wrote Letter 53 among Augustine’s letters to Generosus, which is assigned to about the year 400; that letter also mentions, in chapter 1, the letter of the Donatist bishop of Constantina. Augustine wrote the second book, in which he subsequently refutes Petilian’s entire surviving letter, while Anastasius was seated at Rome, as is clear from chapter 51—or at least before he had learned of Anastasius’s death, which occurred on April 27, 402. Finally, after seeing Petilian’s reply, or second letter, he composed the third book to overthrow it.

[Col. 0245] Baronius noted Augustine’s statement here, in book 2, chapter 20: “I do not recall any law having been given by the emperors that you should be killed,” and concluded that these books were composed before the law of Honorius dated April 25, in the year which he thinks was 398, by which capital punishment was decreed against those who inflicted injury upon persons and sacred places. Augustine, however, indicates fairly clearly in book 1, chapter 9, that he was writing after the death of Optatus Gildonianus, which occurred toward the end of 398; and in book 2, chapter 92, §210, he explicitly mentions another law of Honorius, from the year 399, concerning the removal of idols. He therefore did not recall that earlier law of 398—perhaps because he had never seen it enforced in Africa against the Donatists. Besides, it is not sufficiently clear whether that law concerned the Donatists or was promulgated in 398. In any event, it is reasonable to think that Augustine did not assign these books a place in the *Retractions* arbitrarily, after certain of his shorter works that he composed in 400 or 401.

[Col. 0245]

[Note: [Col. 0245] For the books that follow, see also book 2, chapter 25, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 640, from the words “Before I finished” through the words “Your letter,” col. 641. M.]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE LETTERS OF PETILIAN, DONATIST BISHOP OF CIRTA: THREE BOOKS. [Note: [Col. 0245] We compared the books *Against the Letters of Petilian* with four Gallican manuscripts—the Floriacensis, Beccensis, Pratellensis, and Cygirannensis, or Saint-Cygirannus manuscripts—and with the printed editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain. We also consulted the variant readings of the Belgian codices collected by the Louvain editors.] [Note: [Col. 0245] We further compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0245] Written about the year of Christ 400.]

Written in the form of a letter addressed to the Catholics, in which the first portions of Petilian’s letter, which he himself had written to his own people, are refuted.

[Col. 0245] AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord to his most beloved brothers who are entrusted with the care of our administration.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

You know that we have often wished to bring the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics into public knowledge and expose it—not so much from our own words as from their own mouths [Note: [Col. 0245] The printed editions read “by our work.” The older codices, however, read “from their mouth,” which is better.]—and to refute it. For this reason we also sent letters to some of their leading men: not letters of communion, since by dissenting from the Catholic Church they had already made themselves unworthy of such letters; nor yet insulting letters, but peaceful ones. We wished that, after the question that had torn them away from the holy communion of the whole world had been examined with us, and the truth considered, they might consent to be corrected and might not defend the stubborn perversity of their ancestors with still more foolish obstinacy, but might be restored to the root of the Catholic Church for the fruit of charity.

But since it is written, “With those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Psalm 119:7), they rejected my letters just as they hated the peace for which those letters sought to provide. Now, while I was in the church at Constantina, in the presence of Absentio [Note: [Col. 0246] Perhaps Alypius.] and of my colleague Fortunatus, its bishop, some brothers brought me a letter which they said the bishop of that same schism had given to his presbyters, as the heading of the letter itself also indicated. When I had read it, I was so astonished that in its opening words he had cut away the whole communion of his party at the roots that I was unwilling to believe it was the letter of a man whom popular reputation usually praises as surpassing all the others among them in learning and eloquence. But since, while I was reading, certain men were present who knew the refinement and ornament of his speech, they began to persuade me that the eloquence was entirely his. Nevertheless, whoever had written it, I considered that it had to be refuted, lest whoever wrote it should appear, in the eyes of the inexperienced, to have written something to his own advantage against the Catholics.

### 2

This, then, is what he first set down in his letter. He said that we accuse them of baptizing twice, although under the name of baptism we have polluted our souls with a guilty washing. But why should we go through all his insulting words? Since it is one thing to establish proofs and another to deal with insults by refuting them, let us attend rather to the way in which he wished to demonstrate that we do not possess baptism, and therefore that he is not repeating what already existed but giving what did not exist.

For he says: “The conscience of the giver is considered, for he cleanses the conscience of the recipient.” But what if the giver’s conscience is hidden and perhaps stained? How will he be able to cleanse the conscience of the recipient, if—as he says—the giver’s conscience is considered, since it is he who cleanses the recipient’s conscience? If he should say that whatever evil is hidden in the giver’s conscience does not concern the recipient, that ignorance may perhaps suffice to prevent the recipient from being unknowingly stained by the conscience of the one who baptizes him. Let it therefore be enough that another person’s stained conscience, when it is unknown, does not stain someone; but can it also cleanse him?

## CHAPTER II

### 3

From what, then, is the recipient of baptism to be cleansed when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the recipient is unaware of it? Especially since he adds and says: “For whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt.”

Behold, a faithless man stands ready to baptize, while the one who is to be baptized is unaware of his faithlessness. What do you suppose that person will receive: faith or guilt? If you say “faith,” you will concede that it can happen that someone receives faith from a faithless person and not guilt; and the statement “Whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt” will be false. For we find that someone can receive faith even from a faithless person if he is unaware of the giver’s faithlessness.

He did not say, “Whoever receives faith from an openly or knownly faithless person,” but said: “Whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt.” This is certainly false when someone is baptized by a hidden faithless person. But if he should say, “Even when the faithless baptizer is hidden, the recipient receives from him not faith but guilt,” then let them rebaptize those whom it is established were baptized by men who remained criminally hidden among them for a long time and were later exposed, convicted, and condemned.

## CHAPTER III

For while they remained hidden, all those whom they baptized could not have received faith from them but guilt, if it is true that “whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt.” Therefore let them be baptized by good men, so that they may receive faith and not guilt.

### 4

But how will they be secure even concerning these good men [Note: [Col. 0247] Supply “good men.”], if the conscience of the giver is considered, while it remains hidden from the eyes of the recipient? Thus, according to their opinion, that spiritual salvation becomes uncertain, contrary to the holy Scriptures, which say, “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Psalm 117:8), and, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5). They take away from the Lord God the hope of those who are to be baptized and persuade them that it must be placed in man.

The result is that salvation is not merely uncertain but entirely nonexistent, because “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3:9), and “Vain is the salvation of man” (Psalm 59:13). Therefore whoever has placed his hope in a human being, even one whom he knows to be just and innocent, is cursed. Hence the apostle Paul also rebukes those who said that they belonged to Paul, and says: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

## CHAPTER IV

### 5

Therefore, if those who wished to belong to Paul were in error and would perish unless they were corrected, what hope can there be for those who seek to belong to Donatus? These men are trying to make the origin, root, and head of the baptized person none other than the one by whom he is baptized. Thus, since it is often uncertain what sort of person the baptizer is, the entire hope is also uncertain—its origin uncertain, its root uncertain, and its head uncertain [Note: [Col. 0248] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “the hope of man.”].

And since the giver’s conscience may be criminal and stained, while the recipient is unaware of this, it follows that, with a criminal origin, a criminal root, and a criminal head, the baptized person’s hope is also vain and empty. For in his letter this man says: “Everything consists in its origin and root, and if something has no head, it is nothing.” Since he wishes the origin, root, and head of the baptized person to be understood as the human being by whom he is baptized, what benefit does it bring the wretched baptized person that he is unaware of how evil his baptizer is? He does not know that he has an evil head, or indeed that he is entirely without a head.

Yet what hope is there for someone whose head is utterly wicked or nonexistent, whether he knows it or not? Does ignorance itself become a head for him when his baptizer is either an evil head or no head at all? Whoever thinks this is truly without a head.

## CHAPTER V

### 6

We therefore ask this, since he said, “Whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt,” and immediately connected this with the statement, “Everything consists in its origin and root, and if something has no head, it is nothing.” We ask, then: when that faithless baptizer is hidden, does the one whom he baptizes receive faith and not guilt? If at that time his baptizer is not his origin, root, and head, from whom does he receive faith? Where is the origin from which he arises? Where is the root from which he sprouts? Where is the head from which he begins?

Or perhaps, when the person being baptized is unaware that the one baptizing him is faithless, Christ then gives faith; Christ is then the origin, root, and head? O human rashness and pride! Why do you not rather allow Christ always to give faith, making a Christian by giving faith? Why do you not allow Christ always to be the Christian’s origin, for the Christian to plant his root in Christ, and for Christ to be the Christian’s head?

For even when spiritual grace is imparted to believers through a holy and faithful steward, is it the steward himself who justifies, and not that one of whom it was said that he “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5)? Or is the apostle Paul the head and origin of those whom he planted, or is Apollo their root, because he watered them, rather than the one who gave them faith when they believed? Yet Paul himself says: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

Paul himself was not their root; rather, it was the one who said, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5). How could he be their head when he says that we, though many, are one body in Christ, and in many passages proclaims most openly that Christ himself is the head of the whole body?

## CHAPTER VI

### 7

Therefore, whether someone receives the sacrament of baptism from a faithful or a faithless steward, let his entire hope be in Christ, lest he be cursed who places his hope in man.

Otherwise, if each person is spiritually reborn according to the character of the one by whom he is baptized, so that when the baptizer is openly a good man he himself gives faith and is the origin, root, and head of the one being born, but when the faithless baptizer is hidden the recipient receives faith from Christ, derives his origin from Christ, is rooted in Christ, and glories in Christ as his head, then everyone who is baptized should wish to have faithless baptizers and remain unaware of them. For however good their baptizers may be, Christ is incomparably better; and Christ will be the baptized person’s head precisely when the faithless baptizer is hidden.

## CHAPTER VII

### 8

But if it is utterly foolish to believe this—for Christ always justifies the ungodly, making a Christian out of the ungodly; faith is always received from Christ; Christ is always the origin of those who are reborn and the head of the Church—what weight can those words have, which foolish readers do not consider in their inner meaning but only notice how they sound?

A person who does not receive words with the ears alone, but also examines their meaning with the mind, will respond when he hears, “The conscience of the giver is considered, for he cleanses the conscience of the recipient”: “Human conscience is often unknown to me, but I am certain of Christ’s mercy.”

When he hears, “Whoever receives faith from a faithless person does not receive faith but guilt,” he will respond: “Christ, from whom I receive faith and not guilt, is not faithless.”

When he hears, “Everything consists in its origin and root, and if something has no head, it is nothing,” he will respond: “Christ is my origin; Christ is my root; Christ is my head.”

When he hears, “Nothing regenerates well unless it is regenerated by good seed,” he will respond: “The seed by which I am regenerated is the word of God. I have been instructed to hear it obediently, even if the one through whom I hear does not himself do what he tells me, since the Lord says and makes me secure: ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they preach but do not practice’” (Matthew 23:3).

When he hears, “What perversity can there be in one who is guilty of his own crimes making another innocent?” he will respond: “No one makes me innocent except the one who died for our sins and rose for our justification. I do not believe in the minister through whom I am baptized, but in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that faith may be credited to me as righteousness” (Romans 4:25, 5).

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9

When he hears, “A good tree produces good fruits; an evil tree produces evil fruits. Do they gather grapes from thorns?” (Matthew 7:17, 16), and, “Every good person brings good things out of the treasure of his heart, while an evil person brings evil things out of the treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35), he will respond:

“Then this is the good fruit: that I should be a good tree—that is, a good person—and produce good fruit, that is, good works. This will not be given to me by the one who plants or the one who waters, but by God who gives the growth.

“For if a good tree is a good baptizer, so that the person whom he baptizes is his good fruit, then whoever has been baptized by an evil person, even one who is not openly evil, cannot be good, for he has arisen from an evil tree. A good tree is one thing; a hidden tree, though still evil, is another.

“Or if, when the evil tree is hidden, whoever is baptized by it is born not from that tree but from Christ, then those who are baptized by hidden evil men are justified more holily than those who are baptized by openly good men” [Note: [Col. 0250] See below, book 2, §12.].

## CHAPTER IX

### 10

Likewise, when he hears, “He who is baptized by the dead receives no benefit from his washing” (Sirach 34:30), he will respond:

“Christ lives; he no longer dies, and death no longer rules over him” (Romans 6:9). Of him it was said, “He is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

Those are baptized by the dead who are baptized in temples of idols. They do not consider themselves to receive from their priests the sanctification they imagine, but from the gods. Since those gods were human beings and died in such a way [Note: [Col. 0250] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “and are now such.” In book 2, *Against Cresconius*, §30, the sentence is repeated as follows: “and died in such a way that they live neither upon the earth nor in the rest of the saints.”] that they live neither upon the earth nor in the repose of heaven, they are truly baptized by the dead—if, indeed, the words of Holy Scripture can be sought truthfully, examined profitably, and understood in some other way.

For if in this passage I understand “the dead” to mean a sinful baptizer, the same absurdity follows: whoever has been baptized by a hidden ungodly man has been washed in vain, as though baptized by a dead person. For he does not say, “Whoever is baptized by an openly dead person,” but simply says, “by a dead person.”

If they think that someone is dead only when they know him to be a sinner, but alive even when a criminal is most cleverly hiding within their communion, then first they arrogate to themselves, with execrable pride, more than they attribute to God: when a sinner is known to them, he is called dead; when he is known to God, he is considered alive.

Further, if that sinner is to be called dead who is known to human beings, what will they say about Optatus, whom they feared to condemn even though they had known him to be criminal for a long time? Why are those who were baptized by him not said to have been baptized by a dead man? Or was he alive because faith accompanied him [Note: [Col. 0250] Perhaps the reading should be “because God accompanied him,” as likewise below, book 2, §§53, 88, and 237.]?

They themselves are accustomed to boast and praise this saying, which was cleverly and elegantly uttered by some prominent colleague of theirs, without understanding that, in the outcome of the most arrogant Goliath [Note: [Col. 0250] Thus the old codex. The printed editions read “the outcome.”], his head was cut off by his own sword (1 Samuel 17:51).

[Col. 0251]

## CHAPTER X

### 11

Finally, if they do not wish to call either a hidden criminal or an openly known one who has not yet been condemned by them “dead,” but only someone both openly known and condemned, so that whoever is baptized by him is baptized by the dead and gains no benefit from his washing, what will they say about those whom, in the truthful pronouncement of their plenary council [Note: [Col. 0251] The council of Bagai.] they condemned together with Maximianus and the others who ordained him?

I mean Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras, about whom I am speaking for the moment. They are numbered among the twelve who ordained Maximianus and erected an altar against the altar over which Primianus presides.

These men are certainly reckoned by them among the dead. The witness is the celebrated judgment of that council of theirs. When it was once recited among them for decision, they acclaimed it with mouths opened wide [Note: [Col. 0251] Only the Louvain edition reads “with joyful mouths,” as again in book 4, *Against Cresconius*, §48.]; but now, if it happens to be recited to them by us, they fall silent. They ought rather first to have rejoiced that it was eloquent, lest later they lament that it had been published abroad.

For there they speak in this way about the Maximianists excluded from communion with them:

“Because the members of some shipwrecked vessel have been cast by the truthful wave upon harsh rocks, and, after the manner of the Egyptians, the shores are filled with the funerals of the perishing, whose punishment in death is made worse by this: after their life has been wrested from them by the avenging waters, they do not even find burial.”

Thus these men insult their own schismatics, calling them both dead and unburied. Yet they ought certainly to have wished them to be buried, lest Optatus Gildonianus, walking among the multitude of corpses lying unburied on the shore with a military troop, like a rushing wave [Note: [Col. 0251] The manuscripts read “like a raging wave.” So also Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition.], surging farther forward, should later swallow Felicianus and Praetextatus back inside.

## CHAPTER XI

### 12

I ask them, then: when they returned by crossing over to their sea, did they come back to life, or do they still remain dead there? If they are still corpses, the washing does not benefit those who are baptized by these dead men. But if they came back to life, how does the washing benefit those whom they baptized outside while they were lying lifeless, if the statement “He who is baptized by a dead person—what benefit does his washing bring him?” is to be understood in the way they think?

Those whom Praetextatus and Felicianus baptized while they still shared communion with Maximianus, these men now keep within their communion, together with the same baptizers—Felicianus and Praetextatus—without rebaptizing them. If, on this account, they were not fostering the supremacy of their own obstinacy but were considering how certain the destruction of their spiritual salvation was, they ought surely to awaken, recover soundness of mind, and draw breath in Catholic peace.

They should set aside the swelling of pride and overcome the fury of stubbornness, and should consider with what monstrous sacrilege the baptism of the churches overseas is rejected—churches which we have learned from the holy books were established from the beginning—while the baptism of the Maximianists, whom they themselves condemned with their own mouths, is accepted.

[Col. 0252]

## CHAPTER XII

### 13

But our brothers themselves, the sons of those churches just mentioned, neither knew then nor know now what happened in Africa so many years ago. Therefore the crimes that members of their party charged against the Africans could not contaminate them, even if those crimes were true, since the brothers were unaware of them.

These men, however, openly separated and divided, are said to have taken part in Primianus’s ordination; they condemned Primianus, ordained another bishop against Primianus, baptized outside communion with Primianus, rebaptized after returning to Primianus, and returned to Primianus with those whom they had baptized outside, as well as with those whom no one had rebaptized inside.

If such a close association with the Maximianists does not stain the Donatists, how could the reputation of Africans have stained foreigners? If lips that condemned one another come together in the kiss of peace without guilt, why is someone condemned by them across the sea in churches very far removed from their judgment not kissed as a faithful Catholic but driven away with a breath as an impious pagan?

But if they made peace with the Maximianists whom they received for the sake of their unity, behold, we do not criticize them—except that by their own judgment they cut their own throats. For, when they gather up again those whom they themselves had cut off for the sake of the unity of their divided party, they refuse to repair that division itself into true unity.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 14

If, for the unity of Donatus’s party, no one rebaptizes those baptized in the nefarious schism; if those guilty of so great a crime that they compared them in their council with those ancient authors of the schism whom the earth swallowed alive (Numbers 16:31–35) are either not punished when separated or are restored in full when condemned, why is the true and complete law of that inheritance not recognized for the unity of Christ, which is spread throughout the whole world?

It was foretold of this inheritance that “he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8); and what was foretold is seen and shown to be coming to fulfillment. Why, then, is this not recognized for that true unity—the complete law of that inheritance—which resounds from the common books: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8)?

For the unity of Donatus they are not compelled to reclaim what they scattered, but are admonished to hear what the Scriptures proclaim. Why do they not understand that God’s mercy has dealt with them in this way: since they were accusing the Catholic Church with false charges and did not wish their excessive holiness to be contaminated by what they called contagion, they were compelled, under the rule of Optatus Gildonianus, to receive again and associate with themselves the true and greatest crimes condemned, as they say, by the truthful voice of their plenary council?

Let them finally perceive how they are filled with the true crimes of their own people, they who invent false accusations against their brothers. Even if they had spoken the truth, they ought by now to understand how much must be endured for the sake of peace, and, for the peace of Christ, to return to the Church, which did not condemn what it did not know—if, for the peace of Donatus, they were willing to recall those whom they had condemned.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 15

Therefore, brothers, let this single matter—the action taken among them concerning the Maximianists—be sufficient to admonish and correct them. We do not examine ancient archives [Note: [Col. 0253] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions incorrectly read “secrets.”]; we do not rummage through old chests; we do not send our proof to distant lands. We set aside all the documents of our ancestors and postpone [Note: [Col. 0253] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “we bring forward,” incorrectly.] the testimonies that cry out throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER XV

### 16

Behold the cities of Musti and Assuras. [Note: [Col. 0253] In the Erasmus, Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions: “Behold, the cities of Musticana (Louvain: Mustitata) and Assuritata still remain to others.” M.] There are still alive in this life and in this province those who separated themselves and those from whom they separated; those who erected an altar and those against whom they erected it; those who condemned and those who were condemned; those who received and those who were received; those who were baptized outside and were not rebaptized inside.

If these things stain them for the sake of unity, let the stained silence their voices. If these things do not stain them for the sake of unity, let those who have been corrected remove the dispute.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 17

Let the very man who wrote his letter now laugh at its words—the man who, by incompetently and falsely appropriating a testimony in which he recalls the statement, “He who is baptized by a dead person—what benefit does his washing bring him?”, tries to show us the extent to which a traditor is considered dead in life.

He adds, saying: “The one who did not deserve to be born through true baptism is dead; likewise, the one who was born through just baptism but was mixed with a traditor is dead.”

If the Maximianists are not dead, why do they say in their plenary council that the shores are filled with the funerals of those who are perishing? But if they are dead, from where did the baptism they gave acquire life? Further, if Maximianus is not dead, why is anyone rebaptized after him? But if he is dead, why did Felicianus of Musti, the man who ordained him, not die with him, while an overseas colleague was able to die with some African traditor whom I do not know?

Or if he too is dead, how do those whom he baptized outside—without being rebaptized—live inside with him among you?

## CHAPTER XVII

### 18

Next he added: “Neither of the two possesses the life of baptism: neither the one who never possessed it at all nor the one who possessed it and lost it.”

Therefore the person whom the Maximianists Felicianus or Praetextatus baptized outside never possessed it; but they themselves lost what they had possessed. When, then, these men were received together with their followers, who gave to those whom they had baptized what they did not possess? And who restored to the men themselves what they had lost?

But if they carried away with them the form of baptism while they lost the very power of baptism through their evil schism [Note: [Col. 0253] The printed editions read “did not lose.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.], why do you reject that form—which is always and everywhere holy—in the Catholics whom you have not heard, while embracing it in the Maximianists whom you punished?

### 19

Whatever he seemed to wish to say accusingly about Judas the traditor, what does it concern us? We are neither proved by them to be traditors, nor would the traditio of some of those who died in our communion before our time, even if it were proved, contaminate us in any respect by being itself condemned and displeasing to us [Note: [Col. 0253] Thus Amerbach and the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “nor would that itself contaminate us.”].

For if they themselves are not contaminated by crimes they condemned and by people whom they received again, how much less can we be contaminated by persons whom you merely accuse and reject? However fiercely he attacks the traditores, let him count them as being accused by me in exactly the same words. But I make a distinction: he accuses someone already long dead whom my own knowledge never judged; I point out one who clung to the side of a man whom he had condemned—or at least from whom he had separated in sacrilegious schism—and whom he nevertheless received without diminishing his honor in any way.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 20

“The most wicked traditor,” he says, “you became our persecutor and executioner while we were keeping the law.”

If the Maximianists kept the law when they separated from you, then you too should be a keeper of the law when you are separated from the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world.

But if you are speaking of persecutions [Note: [Col. 0254] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “if you are speaking of our persecutions.” The Louvain editors corrected this from book 3, *Against Cresconius*, §45, to “if you are speaking of persecutions.”], I answer at once: if you have suffered anything unjustly, it does not concern those who, although they disapprove of people who do such things, nevertheless commendably endure them for the peace of unity [Note: [Col. 0254] Perhaps the reading should be “although they do so wickedly.” Compare book 3, *Against Cresconius*, §45.].

Therefore you have no reason to reproach the Lord’s wheat for enduring its chaff until the final winnowing. You would never have withdrawn from that wheat unless, being lighter chaff, you had flown away in the wind of temptation before the arrival of the winnower.

But I will not depart from this one example, which the Lord has cast back into their faces in order to silence them, correct them if they have sense, and confound them if they remain in their perversity. If those who suffer persecution are more righteous than those who inflict it, then the Maximianists are more righteous: their basilica was utterly demolished, they were severely harassed by the military escort of Optatus, and the proconsul’s orders to exclude all of them from the basilicas were openly obtained by the Primianists.

Therefore, if they dared to do so much against the Maximianists while the emperors detested the Maximianists’ communion, what would they have done if, through communion with kings, they had been able to accomplish something against them?

But if they did these things in order to correct the wicked, why are they surprised when Catholic emperors decree that those who attempt to rebaptize the entire Christian world should be pressed and corrected by greater authority, since they have no legitimate cause for dissent? After all, they themselves testify that even if the wicked brought true charges, the wicked must nevertheless be endured for the sake of peace, since they received those whom they had condemned together with their honors and with the baptism they had administered outside.

Let them consider at last what they deserve to suffer [Note: [Col. 0254] The word “suffer” is absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.] at the hands of the Christian authorities of the world, as enemies of Christian unity spread throughout the whole world.

Now, if correction is slow to come, at least let shame appear, lest these same men, when they begin to read what they have written, be overcome by laughter because they do not recognize in themselves what they wish to be seen in others, and do not recognize in themselves [Note: [Col. 0254] Thus Amerbach and the manuscripts. Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “and do recognize in themselves.”] what they charge against others.

## CHAPTER XIX

### 21

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that this man in his letter represented the Lord as saying to the Jews: “Therefore I am sending you prophets, wise men, and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will flog” (Matthew 23:34)?

For if they wish themselves to be understood as the wise men, scribes, and prophets, and us as persecutors of the wise and the prophets, why do they refuse to speak with us, since they have been sent to us?

Finally, if we press this man who wrote the letter to which we are now replying to acknowledge, by signing it with his own hand, that it is his, he may perhaps refuse to do so. They are so afraid that we may retain any of their words. For when we wished in some way to obtain the latter part of that same letter, since those from whom it had been given to us could not copy it in full, no one from whom it was requested was willing to provide it after they learned that we were replying to the portion we had obtained.

Thus, when they read how the Lord says to the prophet, “Cry out vehemently; do not spare, and write their sins with my stylus” (Isaiah 58:1), these prophetic men who have been sent to us fear nothing so much as that their cry should be heard by us. Certainly, if they were speaking the truth about us, they would not fear this. Not without reason, as it is written in the Psalm, “The mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped” (Psalm 62:12).

For if they refuse to accept our baptism because we are “a brood of vipers,” as this man wrote in his letter, why did they accept the baptism of the Maximianists, about whom their council speaks as follows?

“That the belly of a poisonous womb had long concealed the harmful offspring of viperous seed, and the moist coagulations of conceived crime had slowly been warmed by heat into the limbs of asps.”

Was it not also said of these same people in that council, in continuation: “The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Psalm 13:3)?

Yet they now keep even these men inside, with their full honors, and with those whom they baptized outside now received within.

## CHAPTER XX

### 22

Therefore, if these men truly wished to speak about the brood of vipers, the poison of asps under their lips, and the other things that were said against those who did not know the way of peace, they themselves would rather be the people described. For the sake of Donatus’s peace they received the baptism of those against whom they had made these statements by the judgment of their council, while for the sake of the sacrilegious injury done to the peace of Christ they reject the baptism of Christ’s Church, which is spread throughout the whole world and from which that very peace came into Africa.

Who, then, are the false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves? Are they those who either do not know that there are wicked people in the Catholic Church and innocently share communion with them, or who cannot separate from the Lord’s threshing floor those whom they tolerate for the sake of the peace of unity before the winnower arrives?

Or are they those who do in their schism the very things that they criticize in the Catholic Church, who pretend to flee in unity what must be tolerated there, even though it is uncertain, but receive in their own separation things that are manifest and condemned by themselves?

## CHAPTER XXI

**23.** Finally, it is said in this way—and he himself also recalled it: [Col. 0256] “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:15–16). Let us therefore consider the fruits. You bring forward the charge of delivering up the Scriptures; we bring this very charge against them with much greater probability. And, not to run through many examples, in that same city of Constantina your ancestors, at the very beginning of their schism, ordained Silvanus as bishop. While he was still a subdeacon, he was exposed as an unmistakable traditor in the municipal records.

If you produce some documents against our ancestors, equal treatment is required, so that we believe either both sets to be true or both to be false. If both are true, you are unquestionably guilty of schism, since you pretended to flee crimes in the communion of the whole world which you possessed within your own little fragment of separation. But if both are false, you are unquestionably guilty of schism, since you are stained by the monstrous crime of separation on account of false charges against traditores. If, however, we produce some evidence and you none, or if ours is true and yours false, there is no need to investigate how completely your mouths should be closed.

[Note: [Col. 0256] Lov. reads, “there is no need to investigate except thoroughly.” But other printed editions and our manuscripts read, “there is no need to investigate how thoroughly.” The same is found below, Book 3, no. 70.]

## CHAPTER XXII

**24.** What if the holy and true Church of Christ were to convict and defeat you, even if we possessed no documents—or only false ones—concerning the tradition, while you possessed some that were true? What would remain for you except that, if you are willing, you should love peace; and if you are unwilling, at least fall silent?

[Note: [Col. 0256] Thus the printed editions; perhaps *obmutescatis*, “become silent.” M.]

For whatever evidence you might now produce, I would most easily and most truthfully say this: you ought then to have proved it against the full and catholic unity of the Church, already spread and firmly established

[Note: [Col. 0256] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read, “ought to have established.”]

among so many peoples, so that you would be inside, while those whom you convicted would be driven outside. If you tried to do this, you plainly could not prove it; and, defeated or enraged, you separated yourselves from innocent people who could not condemn uncertain matters, committing a monstrous sacrilege.

But if you did not even try to do this, then, offended by a few weeds in Africa, you cut yourselves off in an exceedingly detestable and impious blindness from Christ’s wheat, which grows throughout the whole field—that is, throughout the whole world—until the end.

[Note: See below, Book 2, chapter 16; Book 3, nos. 69–70; and Against Cresconius, Book 3, no. 33, and Book 4, no. 66.]

## CHAPTER XXIII

**25.** Finally, a testament is said to have been handed over to the flames by certain people during the time of persecution. Let it now be produced from wherever it has been found and read aloud. Certainly, at the beginning of the testator’s promises, this is found to have been said to Abraham: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). What this means, the truthful Apostle explains: “In your offspring,” he says, “which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

No one’s handing over of the Scriptures nullified the faithfulness of God. Enter into communion with all nations—and then boast that you preserved the testament from the destruction of the flames. But if you are unwilling, which side should more reasonably be believed to have persisted in burning the testament, except the side unwilling to agree with the testament once it was produced? For how much more certainly, without any sacrilegious rashness, should the one be judged to have succeeded the traditores who now persecutes with his tongue the testament [Col. 0257] which those men are said to have persecuted with fire?

You bring forward persecution. The Lord’s wheat answers you: “It was done justly, or our chaff did it.” What do you say to this? You object that we do not possess Baptism. The same Lord’s wheat answers you that the form of the sacrament can benefit nothing even certain people inside, just as it benefited Simon Magus nothing when he had been baptized; and much less can it benefit those who are outside. Nevertheless, it is proved to be present in them when they depart from this life, because it is not restored to those who return.

Therefore, you will never be able to shout against this wheat except with the utmost shamelessness, saying that they are false prophets dressed in sheep’s skins but inwardly ravenous wolves, since they either do not know the wicked within Catholic unity or, for the sake of unity, tolerate those whom they do know.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0257]

**26.** But if we consider your fruits, I say nothing of your tyrannical domination in the cities and especially over other people’s estates; I say nothing of the madness of the Circumcellions,

[Note: In the manuscripts, here and below in this book, *Circellionum* is found; alternatively, *Cercellionum* or *Cercicellionum*.]

nor of the sacrilegious and profane cults of the corpses of those who voluntarily cast themselves to their deaths, nor of drunken revelries, nor of the ten-year groaning of all Africa under one Gildonian Optatus. I pass over these things because among you there are some who loudly proclaim that they disapprove of them and have always disapproved of them; but they say that, because they cannot suppress them, they tolerate them for the sake of peace. In this they condemn themselves by their own judgment, because if they loved peace, they would not tear apart unity.

For what greater madness could there be than to wish to abandon peace within peace itself and to wish to retain it in dissension? Therefore, on account of those who pretend not to see the evils of the same party of Donatus—evils which everyone sees and condemns—to such an extent that they even say of Optatus himself, “What did he do? Who accused him? Who convicted him? I do not know; I did not see; I did not hear”—on account of these people who pretend not to know what is manifest, the Maximianists arose, so that their eyes might be opened and their mouths closed.

They openly separate themselves; openly they set up altar against altar; openly, in the council [Note: At Bagai], they are called sacrilegious men and vipers, swift to shed blood, and are compared with Dathan, Abiram, and Korah; openly they are condemned and denounced in harsh words; and openly they are again received into their former honors, together with those whom they baptized.

These are their fruits: for the peace of Donatus they do such things as to conceal themselves under sheep’s skins, while refusing the peace of Christ throughout the whole world, so that inwardly they may be ravenous wolves.

## CHAPTER XXV

**27.** Finally, I do not think I have passed over anything that this man included in his letter, at least anything I was able to find in the portion to which we have now come. Let them produce the remainder as well, lest perhaps there be something there that cannot be refuted.

As for what, with the Lord’s help, we have answered, I urge Your Charity not merely to give it to those who ask, but also to press it upon those who do not ask. Let them respond if they wish; and if they do not wish to respond to us, let them at least send letters to their own people—

[Note: [Col. 0257] It would be better read *quas tamen*, according to Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 232–233. M.]

provided they do not order those letters to be hidden from us. If they do so, they most clearly display their fruits: they are shown to be [Col. 0258] ravenous wolves in sheep’s clothing, secretly lying in wait for our sheep and openly afraid to answer the shepherds.

We charge them only with the crime of schism, in which they are all wholly entangled—not with the crimes of certain individuals among them, which some of them may answer that they themselves disapprove of. If they do not bring against us the crimes of others, they have nothing to bring against us. Therefore, they absolutely cannot defend themselves from the crime of schism, because—whether on account of false crimes fabricated by them, or even on account of true crimes that nevertheless belong to the chaff—they separated themselves by a wicked division from the Lord’s threshing floor and from the innocence of the wheat growing throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0258]

**28.** Unless perhaps you expect me also to refute what he inserted concerning Manichaeus. In this matter, the only thing we find displeasing is that he blamed the most pestilential and destructive error—that is, the Manichaean heresy—with an altogether trivial and nearly nonexistent criticism, whereas the Catholic Church attacks it with the strongest proofs of truth.

[Note: Printed editions read, “whom Catholic truth attacks with the strongest proofs.” But the manuscripts read, “the Catholic Church attacks him with the strongest proofs of truth,” with “Church” understood.]

For Christ’s inheritance, established among all nations, is safe against all the disinherited heresies. But just as the Lord says, “How can Satan cast out Satan?” (Mark 3:23), so how can the error of the Donatists overthrow the error of the Manichaeans?

[Note: See below, Book 2, nos. 40–41.]

## CHAPTER XXVII

**29.** Therefore, dearest brothers, although this error has been overcome and defeated in many ways, and although it dares to resist the truth not by any sort of reason but only by shameless obstinacy,

[Note: [Col. 0258] One Belgian manuscript and another, a French manuscript from Fleury, read: “and by no errors of any sort of reasoning.”] nevertheless, lest the multitude of proofs burden your memory, hold fast to this one deed of the Maximianists. Drive it into their forehead; force it into their mouths to silence their deceitful tongues; with it, as though with a three-pronged weapon, slaughter their three-headed accusation.

They object to the handing over of the Scriptures; they object to persecution; they object to false Baptism. Answer everything from the case of the Maximianists alone.

They think it is hidden that their ancestors handed the holy books over to the flames. But when they received back into their former honors those defiled with the sacrilege of schism, they certainly could not conceal this.

Likewise, they think that the most violent persecutions which they inflict wherever they can are hidden. But since spiritual persecution surpasses bodily persecution, they received back into their former honors the Maximianists whom they themselves had persecuted bodily and of whom they themselves had said, “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. 13:3). This, certainly, they cannot conceal.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Finally, they think that the question of Baptism, by which they deceive the wretched, is hidden. But when they say that all who are baptized outside the communion of the one Church do not possess Baptism, they nevertheless received back into their former honors the Maximianists together with those whom they themselves baptized in schism outside their communion. This, certainly, they cannot conceal.

[Col. 0259] **30.** “But these things,” they say, “do not defile us for the sake of peace; and it is good to bend the rigor of severity toward mercy, so that the broken branches may be grafted in again.”

Thus the whole case is brought to its conclusion: defeated in their case, undefeated on ours. For if the name of peace is assumed as a defense of any kind for tolerating wicked people in schism, then undoubtedly, with a terrible crime and without any defense, true peace itself is violated through the unity of the whole world.

## CHAPTER XXIX

**31.** Hold fast to these things, brothers, as things to be done and proclaimed with tireless gentleness: love the people, kill the errors; confidently uphold the truth without pride; fight for the truth without cruelty.

Pray for those whom you rebuke and convict. For such people the prophet entreats God, saying: “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:17).

The Lord has already done this, so that the disgrace of the Maximianists might most plainly fill their faces. It remains for them to learn to blush to their healing. For in this way they will be able to seek the name of the Lord, from whom they have most destructively turned away while exalting their own name in his place.

May you live and persevere in Christ, and multiply and abound in the love of God, among yourselves, and toward all, dearest brothers.

# BOOK TWO

[Note: Written around the beginning of the year 402.]

In this book Augustine responds to all and each of the words of Petilian’s letter as though he were conversing with his opponent in person.

[Col. 0259]

## CHAPTER I

**1.** Those who were able to read or hear the first portions of Petilian’s letter—the only portions we had found—remember that we responded to them sufficiently. But afterward the entire letter was found by the brothers, copied, and sent to us so that we might answer it as a whole. We therefore could not avoid this task of our pen—not because he says anything new, since he has already been answered in many ways and often, but for the sake of the slower brothers, who cannot apply what they may have read somewhere to all similar cases.

I shall therefore accommodate those who compel me to respond to every point, as though we were discussing the matter in one another’s presence through alternating speeches. I shall place the words from his letter under his name and give the response under my own name, as though they had been recorded by notaries while we were conducting the dispute.

Thus no one will have grounds to complain that I passed over anything or that, because of the indistinct arrangement of the persons, he was unable to understand. At the same time, the Donatists themselves, who refuse to discuss the matter with us face to face, will not escape the truth responding to each of their points through the letters they have published for their own people—as though they were conversing with us face to face.

**2.** At the very beginning of his letter PETILIAN said:

“Petilian, bishop, to his dearest brothers, fellow presbyters and deacons serving throughout the diocese with us in the holy Gospel: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

**3.** AUGUSTINE replied:

I recognize the apostolic greeting. You seem to know whom you are quoting; consider, nevertheless, from whom you learned what you are saying. Paul greets the Romans in this way, the Corinthians in this way, the Galatians in this way, and likewise the Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, and Thessalonians.

What madness, then, is it to refuse to share the greeting of peace with those Churches in whose letters you learned a peaceful greeting?

## CHAPTER II

**4.** PETILIAN said:

“Twice they bring Baptism as an accusation against us—those who, under the name of Baptism, polluted their souls with a guilty washing. For them, indeed, every obscenity and all filth are cleaner than those whom their perverse purity has happened to defile with its water.”

[Col. 0260]

**5.** AUGUSTINE replied:

We are not defiled by our water, nor are we cleansed by yours. But when the water of Baptism is given to someone in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, it is neither ours nor yours. It belongs to the one of whom it was said to John: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

## CHAPTER III

**6.** PETILIAN said:

“For the conscience of the giver is taken into account, since he cleanses the conscience of the recipient.”

[Note: Lov. reads *quae* here; but the manuscripts consistently read *qui*.]

**7.** AUGUSTINE replied:

Then we are secure because of the conscience of Christ. For if you put forward any human being, the cleansing of the recipient will be uncertain, because the conscience of the one cleansing is uncertain.

## CHAPTER IV

**8.** PETILIAN said:

“For whoever receives faith from an unfaithful person does not receive faith but guilt.”

**9.** AUGUSTINE replied:

Christ is not unfaithful. From him the faithful person receives faith, not guilt. For he believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness (Rom. 4:5).

## CHAPTER V

**10.** PETILIAN said:

“For every matter depends upon its origin and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing. Nor does anything regenerate well unless it is regenerated from good seed.”

**11.** AUGUSTINE replied:

Why do you wish to set yourself against Christ, beneath whom you do not wish to place yourself? He is the origin, the root, and the head of the one being born. We do not fear in his case, as we do in the case of any human being, lest he perhaps be false and evil, and lest we arise from an evil origin, spring from an evil root, or be conformed to an evil head.

For what human being can be secure concerning another human being, since it is written: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5)?
