The seed by which we are regenerated is the word of God, that is, the Gospel. Hence the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15). Yet he permits even those who proclaim the Gospel not chastely to proclaim it, and rejoices in this (Phil. 1:17–18), because although they did not proclaim it chastely, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), what they proclaimed was nevertheless chaste.

And the Lord had said concerning certain such people: “Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3).

If, therefore, what is chaste is proclaimed chastely, the proclaimer himself also, because he is joined to the word, begets the believer in the same family. But even if he himself is not regenerated, what he proclaims remains chaste; and the believer is born not from the barrenness of the minister but from the fruitfulness of the truth.

[Col. 0261]

## CHAPTER VI

**12.** PETILIAN said:

“Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can there be in one who is guilty through his own crimes making another innocent, when the Lord Jesus Christ says: ‘A good tree produces good fruits, and a bad tree produces bad fruits; surely they do not gather grapes from thorns’ (Matt. 7:17, 16)? And again: ‘Every good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and every evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure’ (Matt. 12:35)?”

**13.** AUGUSTINE replied:

Every person, even if he is not guilty through his own crimes, does not make another innocent, because he is not God. Otherwise, if the innocence of the baptizer is expected to produce the innocence of the baptized, each person will be more innocent according to how innocent a person he finds to baptize him; and he himself will be less innocent according to how less innocent the person is by whom he is baptized.

And if the one who baptizes happens to hold hatred against someone, this too will be charged against the one who is baptized. Why, then, does the wretched man hasten to Baptism? Is it so that his sins may be forgiven, or so that the sins of others may be imposed upon him? Is it like a merchant’s ship, which puts down some cargo and takes on other cargo?

We customarily understand the good tree and its good fruit, and the bad tree and its bad fruit, as human beings and their works, as is shown in the words that follow and which you too recalled: “The good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure.”

But when he preaches the word of God and administers the sacrament of God, if he is evil he does not preach or administer from what is his own. Rather, he will be counted among those of whom it was said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.” For they say what belongs to God but do what belongs to themselves.

If, then, what you say is true—that is, if the fruits of the baptizers are reckoned to the baptized—then you announce a great evil for Africa, since as many offspring of Optatus have sprung up as Optatus baptized.

## CHAPTER VII

**14.** PETILIAN said:

“And again: ‘The washing of one baptized by a dead person does not benefit him’ (Ecclus. 34:30). He did not assert that the baptizer was a dead person—a lifeless body or a corpse laid out—but one who does not possess the Spirit of God and is compared with a dead person, as the Gospel, bearing witness, makes clear to the disciple in another passage.

His disciple said to him: ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Follow me, and let the dead bury their dead’ (Matt. 8:21–22).

The disciple’s father was not baptized; a pagan committed a pagan to the pagans. Unless he was speaking of unbelievers, he said, ‘A dead person cannot bury a dead person.’ The dead person, therefore, was not struck by some other death,

[Col. 0262]

[Note: The manuscripts read, “What is it? Not by some other death.”]

but by his own life. For one who lives in such a way as to be guilty is tormented by a dead life.

To be baptized by a dead person, therefore, is to receive death, not life. We must act and speak so as to establish to what extent a traditor is considered dead in life. He is dead who was not worthy to be born through true Baptism; likewise, he is dead who, having been born through a just Baptism, was joined to a traditor. Both lack the life of Baptism: the one who never possessed it at all and the one who possessed it and lost it.

For the Lord Jesus Christ says: ‘Seven spirits worse than himself will come into him, and that person will become worse than before’ (Matt. 12:45).”

**15.** AUGUSTINE replied:

Examine more carefully how the testimony you have quoted from Scripture was spoken and how it should be understood. It is clear that all the wicked are customarily called dead in a spiritual sense. But Christ, whose Baptism is true, though you call it false because of human vices, lives seated at the right hand of the Father; he will no longer die even through the weakness of the flesh, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9).

The person baptized with Christ’s Baptism is not baptized by a dead person. Even if deceitful ministers, seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, are called dead on account of their sins—

[Note: [Col. 0262] Am. and Er. read, “workers of the devil.” Lov. and the manuscripts read, *operaris dolosi*. Augustine alludes to 2 Cor. 11:13: “For such pseudo-apostles are deceitful workers.”]

ministers who do not proclaim the Gospel chastely and preach Christ through rivalry and envy—the sacrament of the living God does not die even in a dead person.

That Simon, who was baptized by Philip in Samaria and wanted to purchase the gift of God with money, was dead (Acts 8:13, 18–19); nevertheless, the Baptism he possessed remained alive for his condemnation.

**16.** But how false is what you say—“Both lack the life of Baptism: the one who never possessed it at all and the one who possessed it and lost it”—you may recognize from this: those who apostatize after being baptized and return through repentance are not given Baptism again. If they had lost it, it would be restored to them.

But according to your understanding, how do your dead people baptize? Are drunkards not dead—to say nothing else and to mention what is known and experienced by everyone every day—when the Apostle says of the widow, “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6)?

Furthermore, at that council of yours in which you condemned Maximianus together with his supporters or ministers, have you forgotten how eloquently you said, in the manner of the Egyptians: “The shores are filled with the funerals of the perishing; and in death itself their punishment is greater, because after their life had been torn from them by avenging waters, they did not even find burial”?

And yet, whether one of them, Felicianus, came back to life, you may decide for yourselves. Nevertheless, he has with him inside your communion those whom, while dead, he baptized outside it.

Therefore, just as the one who is clothed with the Baptism of the living Christ is baptized by the living one, so the one who is enveloped in the Baptism of the dead Saturn—or of any other—has been baptized by a dead person. For the moment, let us state briefly how the words you have quoted can be understood without causing difficulty for either of us. As you interpret them, you are striving not to explain them but to entangle us together with yourselves.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0263]

**17.** PETILIAN said:

“As I have said, we must act and speak so as to establish to what extent the treacherous traditor is considered dead in life.

Judas was an Apostle when he betrayed Christ. After losing the honor of an apostle, he died spiritually; afterward he was to die by his own noose, as it is written: ‘I am sorry,’ he said, ‘because I betrayed righteous blood’; and he went away and hanged himself (Matt. 27:4–5).

The traditor perished by a noose and left a noose for such people. Concerning this the Lord Christ cried out to the Father: ‘Father, those whom you gave me, I have kept them all; and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled’ (John 17:12).

Long ago David had pronounced this sentence concerning the one who would betray Christ to the treacherous: ‘Let another take his bishopric; let his wife be a widow and his children orphans’ (Ps. 108:8–9).

Behold how great is the spirit of the prophets, that he saw all future events as present, so that a traditor who was to be born many centuries later might be condemned in advance.

Finally, so that the sentence might be fulfilled, the holy Matthias, after the apostle had been lost, received his bishopric. Let no foolish or treacherous person argue about this. Matthias brought back a triumph, not an injury, for from the victory of the Lord Christ he brought back the betrayer’s spoils.

Why, then, do you claim the bishopric for yourself, heir of a more wicked traditor? Judas betrayed Christ carnally; you, raging spiritually,

[Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “he betrayed the carnal one, and you the spiritual one.”]

handed the holy Gospel over to sacrilegious flames.

Judas betrayed the Lawgiver to the treacherous; you, as though handing over his relics, delivered the law of God to human beings to be destroyed. If you loved the Law, as the young Maccabees did, you would have been killed for the laws of God—if one may call it death for human beings whom dying for the Lord perfects into immortality.

One of those brothers, for example, answered the sacrilegious tyrant with this declaration of faith: ‘You, wicked and impious man, destroy us from the present life; but the King of the world, who reigns eternally and whose kingdom shall have no end, will raise us up, who die for his holy laws, into the preservation of eternal life’ (2 Macc. 7:3).

[Note: [Col. 0263] The manuscripts read *conversationem* (“way of life”) instead of *conservationem* (“preservation”).]

If you were to burn the testament of a dead person in the flames, would you not be punished as a forger? What, then, will happen to you, who burned the most holy law of God the Judge?

Judas repented of his deed even in death. You not only do not repent; you, the most wicked traditor, have become a persecutor and executioner of us who preserve the Law.”

**18.** AUGUSTINE replied:

See the difference between your slanderous words and our truthful assertions. Pay attention for a moment.

You have magnified the crime of tradition and, in the most inflammatory words, like a crafty inventor, compared us with Judas the betrayer.

[Note: [Col. 0263] The manuscripts read, “like an abundant inventor, compared us with Judas the lost one.”] When I answer you very briefly, “I did not do what you say; I did not hand anything over; you bring false accusations; you will never prove it”—does not all that smoke of enormous words suddenly disperse?

Or perhaps you will try to prove it? You should do this first, and then rise up against us as though we had been convicted, with whatever mass of invective you wished. Here is one vanity; hear another.

[Col. 0264]

**19.** When you were speaking of the condemnation of Judas mentioned above, you said: “Behold how great is the spirit of the prophets, that he saw all future events as present, so that a traditor who was to be born many centuries later might be condemned.” Yet you did not see that in the same prophecy, with its stable, certain, and unshaken truth, it was foretold not only that one disciple would betray Christ but also that the whole world would believe in Christ.

Why did you pay attention in the prophecy to the man who betrayed Christ, but not there to the world for which Christ was betrayed? Who betrayed Christ? Judas. To whom did he betray him? To the Jews. What did the Jews do to him? “They pierced,” he says, “my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They looked and stared at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

How great, then, is what was purchased at so great a price? Read a little further on in the same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21:17–19, 28–29).

Who could be sufficient to recall all the other innumerable prophetic testimonies concerning the world that would believe? But you praise the prophecy because you see in it the man who sold Christ; you do not see in it the possession which Christ, having been sold, purchased.

Here is another vanity; hear a third.

**20.** Among the many words of your invective, you said: “If you were to burn the testament of a dead person in the flames, would you not be punished as a forger? What, then, will happen to you, who burned the most holy law of God the Judge?”

In saying this, you did not consider what ought certainly to have moved you: how could we have burned the testament while standing in the inheritance written in that testament? Yet you are remarkable for having preserved the testament while losing the inheritance.

Is it not written in that testament: “Ask me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8)? Enter into communion with this inheritance, and bring against me whatever charge you wish from the testament.

What madness it is, then, to say that you did not wish to hand the testament over to the flames, while disputing against the words of the testator?

But although we have in our hands ecclesiastical and municipal records in which we read that those who ordained another bishop against Caecilianus—

[Note: Majorinus.]

were more likely to have been traditores of the divine books, we do not insult you, we do not attack you, we do not lament the ashes of the sacred pages in your hands, nor do we turn against you the flaming tortures of the Maccabees, saying, “You would hand over your own limbs to the flames rather than the words of God.”

[Note: Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read, “the swelling of your fear.”]

For we do not wish to be foolish and stir up empty noise against you over offenses committed by others, which you either do not know or disapprove of.

But when we see that you have separated yourselves from the communion of the whole world—a crime that is both the greatest, manifest, and shared by all of you—if I wished to magnify it, time would run out before my words.

And if you wish to defend this, you will bring against the whole world charges which, if they ought to be brought, show you where you may be accused more fully; but if they ought not to be brought, you will not have defended yourself.

[Col. 0265]

Why, then, do you swell up against me over a tradition which is neither mine nor yours, if that agreement remains by which we are not to bring against one another what belongs to others? But if it does not remain, the tradition belongs to you rather than to me.

Although, even if that agreement remains, I think I am entirely justified in saying that the one should be judged a companion of him who betrayed Christ who did not surrender himself to Christ together with the whole world.

Thus, says the Apostle, “You are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:29). And again he says: “If children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17).

He also demonstrates that this offspring of Abraham belongs to all nations from what was said to Abraham: “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

Therefore, I think it just that I ask us to pay some attention to God’s testament, which was opened long ago, and that we judge the person whom we do not find a fellow heir of the one who was handed over to be the heir of the traditor. Let the one who denies that Christ is the purchaser of the world belong to the seller of Christ.

For when, after his resurrection, he showed himself to the disciples and offered his limbs to be touched by those who doubted, he said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

Behold from what inheritance you alienate yourselves; behold which heir you resist. Would one who contradicts Christ seated in heaven really spare him when he walked on earth? Do you still not understand that whatever you bring against us, you bring against his words?

The Christian world is promised, and it is believed. It is fulfilled, and you contradict it. Consider, I beg you, what you ought to have suffered for such impiety. Yet if you have suffered anything, I do not know; I did not see; I did not do it.

You who today do not suffer the force of my persecution, give me an account of your separation. But again and often you will say things which, if you do not prove them, concern no one; and if you prove them, do not concern me.

## CHAPTER IX

**21.** PETILIAN said:

“Surrounded, then, by these crimes, you cannot be a true bishop.”

**22.** AUGUSTINE replied:

What crimes? What have you taught? What have you shown? And even if you had shown crimes belonging to certain unknown people, what would that have to do with Abraham’s offspring, in whom all nations are blessed?

## CHAPTER X

**23.** PETILIAN said:

“If the Apostles persecuted anyone, or if Christ betrayed anyone—”

**24.** AUGUSTINE replied:

I could indeed say that Satan himself is worse than all wicked people, and yet the Apostle handed a man over to him for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus (1 Cor. 5:5). Likewise, he speaks of others: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

And the Lord Christ drove wicked merchants from the temple after scourging them; there too the testimony of Scripture is joined in which it says, “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (John 2:15–17).

Behold, we find an Apostle who handed someone over and Christ who persecuted. I could say these things,

[Col. 0266]

and cast you into no small turmoil, so that you would be compelled to inquire not into the complaints of those who suffer but into the disposition of those who act.

But do not trouble yourself over this. I am not saying these things. Rather, I say that whatever was wrongly done to you does not belong to Abraham’s offspring, which is found among all nations—perhaps it belongs to the chaff of the Lord’s harvest, which nevertheless is also found among all nations.

You, therefore, give an account of your separation. But first consider what kind of people you have among yourselves, whom you do not wish to have brought against you. See how unjustly you act when you bring against us the deeds of others, even if you could prove the things you allege.

Thus there will be no justification for your separation.

## CHAPTER XI

**25.** PETILIAN said:

“But someone may say, ‘We are not the sons of a traditor.’ A person is the son of the one whose deeds he follows. For these are certainly sons, and like their parents—not begotten by flesh and blood but made like their parents by their morals and deeds.”

26. AUGUSTINE replied: A little earlier you were saying nothing against us; now you have even begun to say something on our behalf. For your proposition binds you to this: if you do not today convict us, with whom you are dealing, of being traitors and murderers—and of whatever else you accuse us—then whatever such thing you may show in those who preceded us in time cannot possibly harm us at all. For we cannot be the sons of those whose deeds we do not share. And see into what a predicament you have thrust yourself: if you should perhaps convict even some man of our own age, living among us, of some such crime, this in no way prejudices all the nations who are blessed in the seed of Abraham, from whom you are found to have separated yourself sacrilegiously.

Thus—something that cannot happen—unless you know all who are everywhere, and have not merely learned but also demonstrated that the conduct and deeds of all of them are as evil as you say, you have no reason to bring charges against the whole world, which is in the saints, on account of certain parents whose likeness to them you prove. Nor will it help you if you are even able to demonstrate that those who are not such people receive the common Sacraments together with those who are such. First, you ought to look to yourselves, with whom you celebrate these things, to whom you give them, and from whom you receive them, while refusing to have such people brought up against you. Further, if those who imitate his deeds are sons of Judas, who was the devil among the Apostles, why should we not call those sons of the Apostles who share not their deeds with such people but the Lord’s Sacraments, just as the Apostles took the Lord’s Supper together with that traitor?

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0266] The printed editions read, “to us.” The manuscripts read better, “to you.”] you are far unlike us: you bring against people who preserve unity what you yourselves do after tearing unity apart.

## CHAPTER XII

27. PETILIAN said: Concerning himself the Lord Christ says to the Jews, “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me” (John 10:37).

28. AUGUSTINE replied: I have already answered above: this is both true and is in our favor against you.

## CHAPTER XIII

29. PETILIAN said: Thus, again and again, he rebukes false speakers and liars: “You are sons of the devil; for he was an accuser from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth.”

[Col. 0267] 30. AUGUSTINE replied: We do not usually read, “He was an accuser,” but, “He was a murderer” (John 8:44). We ask, however, in what sense the devil was a murderer from the beginning, and we find that he killed the first man—not by drawing a sword or inflicting any bodily violence, but by persuading him to sin [Note: [Col. 0267] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “inflicting.”] and casting him down from the happiness of paradise. What paradise was then, the Church is now. Therefore those are sons of the devil who, by leading human beings away from the Church, kill them.

Just as we know from the words of God where paradise was planted, so from the words of Christ we have learned where the Church is: “Throughout all nations,” he says, “beginning from Jerusalem.” Whoever separates a person from this whole body and attaches him to any particular part is proved to be a son and murderer of the devil.

But even the word you yourself used concerning the devil—“He was an accuser, and he did not stand in the truth”—consider to whom it applies. You accuse the whole world on the basis of the crimes of others, whom you have been able to accuse rather than convict; and you have not stood in the truth of Christ. For he says that the Church begins from Jerusalem and extends throughout all nations, whereas you say, “In the party of Donatus.”

## CHAPTER XIV

31. PETILIAN said: Thirdly, in a similar way he calls the madness of persecutors by this name: “Brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? Therefore I send you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify and scourge in your synagogues, until all the righteous blood that you have shed upon the earth comes upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:33–35).

Are they truly bodily sons of vipers, and not rather serpents in mind, with three-tongued malice, a deadly touch, and blazing with a spirit of poison [Note: [Col. 0267] The printed editions read: “Are they truly carnal . . . and tongues of malice . . . and scourging with a spirit of poison.” The readings have been corrected according to the ancient codices.]? They have truly become vipers, vomiting death through their bites upon innocent peoples.

32. AUGUSTINE replied: If I say that these words were spoken concerning people such as you are, you will answer, “Prove it.” What then? Have you proved it? Or if you think that the statement is proved merely by being uttered, there is no need to repeat the same words. Recite those very words to yourself and from us against you [Note: [Col. 0267] The printed editions read, “and from you against you.” The manuscripts read more suitably, “and from us against you.”]. Behold, I too have proved it, if this is what proving means.

Yet learn what it is to prove. I do not seek external evidence in order to prove you vipers. Behold, the very fact of not having the support of truth in your mouth, but the poison of cursing, is viper-like, as it is written: “The poison of asps is under their lips.” And because anyone might say this indiscriminately about anyone else, as though the question were, “Whose?” he immediately added, “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Psalm 13:3).

Since, then, you say such things about people scattered throughout the whole world, whom you entirely do not know—and many of whom have heard neither the name of Caecilianus nor that of Donatus—and do not hear them replying in silence, “Whatever you are saying does not concern us; we have not seen it; we have not done it; we have absolutely no idea what you are talking about”—you, who want nothing other than to say what you cannot prove at all, what else is your mouth than full of cursing and bitterness?

Now see whether you can show that you are not vipers unless you show that all Christians of every nation are traitors and murderers, and are not Christians. Indeed, even if you can know and demonstrate the lives and deeds of individual people scattered throughout the entire world, nevertheless, before you do so, when you recklessly hurl such charges, your mouth is viper-like; your mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.

Show us now, if you can, which prophet, which wise man, which scribe we have killed and crucified and scourged in our synagogues. Consider how much effort you have expended, yet have in no way proved [Note: [Col. 0268] The manuscripts read, “that you are about to prove.”] that Donatus and Marculus were prophets, or wise men, or scribes—because they were not. Even if you could prove this, what could you do to show that they were killed by us, whom we ourselves do not even know? How much less could the whole world know them, when you curse it with your poisonous mouth [Note: [Col. 0268] See below, section 46, and Against Cresconius, book 3, section 54.]?

Or how can you show that we possess a disposition like that of the killers of people whom you cannot even show to have been killed by anyone? Consider all these matters; see whether you can prove any of them either about the whole world or to the whole world [Note: [Col. 0268] Here we have added from the manuscripts, “or to the whole world.”]. Yet because you do not cease to curse the whole world, you show in yourselves the things that you falsely hurl against it.

33. Moreover, if we wished to prove that you are killers of prophets, it would take far too long to collect, place by place, the massacres that your mad leaders, the Circumcellions, and the very bands of drunkards and madmen have perpetrated not only from the beginning of your schism, but have by no means ceased to perpetrate [Note: [Col. 0268] In the edition of Amerbach this was corruptly read, “to such an extent.” In Erasmus and Lovaniensis, “of young men.” The error is corrected from the manuscripts.].

I am dealing with what is close at hand [Note: [Col. 0268] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “and have by no means ceased to perpetrate massacres in the nearby field. Let the records be brought forward,” etc.]: let the divine utterances that are in the hands of both us and you be brought forward. Let us regard as killers of the prophets those whom we find contradicting the prophets’ words with their tongues. What could be said more learnedly? What could be demonstrated more quickly? You would act more mildly by driving a sword through the entrails of the prophets than by trying to kill the prophets’ words with your tongue.

The Prophet says: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 21:28). Behold, it is taking place; behold, it is being fulfilled. Yet you not only close unbelieving ears against what is said, but also thrust out furious tongues against what is already happening.

Abraham heard it said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18); and he believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Romans 4:3). You see the fulfillment and protest against it; and you do not want what would rightly be reckoned to you as unrighteousness to be reckoned to you [Note: [Col. 0268] In the printed editions, here and in the next passage, “as righteousness”: incorrectly.], even if you had not believed something that had not yet happened but had merely been said. Indeed, you not only do not want it reckoned to you as unrighteousness, but even if you suffer anything for this impiety, you want it reckoned to you as righteousness.

Or, if these are not persecutions of the prophets because they are carried out not by the sword but by words, why was it divinely said: “The sons of men— their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5)?

But when shall I collect from all the prophets all the testimonies concerning the Church spread throughout the whole world—testimonies that you attempt to kill and extinguish by contradicting them all? But you are bound, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

Nevertheless, I shall recall one testimony from the mouth of the Lord, who is the witness of witnesses: “It was necessary,” he says, “that all things should be fulfilled that are written in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me.” Let him himself indicate what these things are: “Then he opened their understanding,” he says, “that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them, For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:44, 47).

Behold what is written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning the Lord. Behold what the Lord himself opened concerning himself and concerning the Church, showing himself and promising her.

But when you resist such clear testimonies [Note: [Col. 0269] In Amerbach, “this” was corruptly printed instead of “such.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis did not correct it properly, reading “steadfastly.”], and, because you cannot erase them, attempt to corrupt them, what would you do if you found the limbs of the prophets, seeing that you rage against the prophets’ words so violently that you do not even listen to the Lord who fulfills, reveals, and interprets the prophets? For insofar as you can, you even strike him himself, since you do not yield even to him [Note: [Col. 0269] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “since you do not believe even in him.”].

## CHAPTER XV

34. PETILIAN said: “Concerning you also, David says this to persecutors [Note: [Col. 0269] The manuscripts read, “persecutors.”]: ‘Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes. Will they not know, all who work iniquity, who devour my people as though eating bread?’” (Psalm 13:3–4).

35. AUGUSTINE replied: “Their throat is an open tomb,” from which the deaths of lies exhale. For “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

But if nothing is truer than what Christ said—that he established his Church throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem—then nothing is more false than what you say, “In the party of Donatus.”

Their tongues are deceitful who, although they know their own deeds, not only claim to be righteous men but even claim to be justifiers of men—referring to what was said of one person, “who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5), and to the one who is both just and justifying (ibid. 3:26). We have said enough about the poison of asps and the mouth full of cursing and bitterness.

But you have also said that the Maximianists have swift feet for shedding blood: witness the judgment of your plenary council, cited so often in the proconsular and municipal records. Yet, as far as we hear, they killed no one bodily. You have therefore understood that blood can also be shed through the spiritual slaughter of souls, by the sword of the schism that you condemned in Maximianus.

See, then, whether your feet are not swift to shed blood when you cut people off from the unity of the whole world—if you rightly said this of the Maximianists because they cut some people off from the party of Donatus.

Did we not know the way of peace, we who strive to preserve “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”? And do you know it, who resist the speech of Christ to his disciples after the resurrection—a speech so peaceful that he began with the words, “Peace be with you” (John 20:19, 21)—in such a way that you are convicted of saying nothing other than this to him: “What you said about the unity of all nations is false; what we say about the crime of all nations is true”?

Would those who said such things have the fear of God before their eyes? See, therefore, whether by saying these things daily you do not try to finish with your teeth, as though it were bread, the people of God spread throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER XVI

36. PETILIAN said: “The Lord Christ also warns us: ‘Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing [Note: [Col. 0270] The manuscripts omit “who”; they read, “they will come to you in sheep’s clothing.” Petilianus may perhaps have cited it in this form.], but inwardly are ravenous wolves: you will know them by their fruits’” (Matthew 7:15).

37. AUGUSTINE replied: If I ask you by what fruits you recognize us as ravenous wolves, you will cite the crimes of others, which have never been proved to belong to those whom they are said to belong to. But if you ask me by what fruits we recognize you rather as ravenous wolves, I bring against you the crime of schism, which you will deny but which I shall immediately prove: for you do not share communion with all nations or with those Churches founded through apostolic labor.

Here you will say, “I do not share communion with traitors and murderers.” The seed of Abraham answers you: “These crimes are either not true or are not mine.” But for the moment I set these matters aside. You show us the Church.

Then that voice will resound in my ears which the Lord warned us to avoid in false prophets who point out particular sections and try to alienate people from the whole: “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there.” Do you really think that the true sheep of Christ, to whom it was said, “Do not believe” (ibid. 24:23), are so lacking in understanding that they will listen to a wolf saying, “Behold, here is Christ,” but will not listen to the Shepherd saying, “Throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem”?

## CHAPTER XVII

38. PETILIAN said: Thus, thus, wicked persecutor, whatever veil of goodness you cover yourself with, whatever name of peace you use while waging war with kisses, by whatever word of unity you lure the human race—you who have continued to deceive and mislead—truly you are a son of the devil, since your conduct reveals your father.

39. AUGUSTINE replied: Consider these words as having been spoken by us against you; and, so that you may know to whom they apply more suitably, recall what I said above.

[Col. 0271] ## CHAPTER XVIII

40. PETILIAN said: Nor is it so surprising that you unlawfully assume the name of bishop. This is the devil’s true habit: to deceive only after claiming for himself the title of holiness, as the Apostle declares: “It is no wonder,” he says, “if Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light, and his ministers as ministers of righteousness” (2 Corinthians 11:14–15).

It is therefore no wonder that you falsely call yourself a bishop. For those fallen angels too, lovers of worldly virgins, who were corrupted by corrupting the flesh, although stripped of their divine powers and having ceased to be angels, nevertheless retain the name of angels and always consider themselves angels—those who, released from divine service, passed over in likeness into the army of the devil—while the great God cries out, “My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3).

To these guilty ones and to you the Lord Christ will say: “Go into the everlasting fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). If the angels were not evil, the devil would not have angels. The holy Apostle says that these will be condemned by holy human beings at that judgment of resurrection: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3). If they were true angels, human beings would not have the judgment of God’s angels.

So also the sixty apostles who, after the Twelve had been left with the Lord Christ, withdrew as apostates from the faith are still regarded by wretched people as apostles to such an extent that from among them Manichaeus and the others in many diabolical sects entangle many souls—souls whom they destroyed in order to capture them [Note: [Col. 0271] Perhaps the text should read, “who perished.”].

For surely the lost Manichaeus, if indeed he existed, should not be placed among those sixty, if his name as an apostle is included among the Twelve, or if he was appointed by the voice of Christ in place of Judas the traitor, with Paul as the thirteenth [Note: [Col. 0271] The printed editions read: “if indeed he was not among those sixty . . . he was ordained as the thirteenth Paul.” The manuscripts read, “if indeed he existed”; then the Cygirannensis codex, omitting “not,” continues: “He should be placed among those seventy, if the name of his Apostle is included among the Twelve.” But “in the place,” etc. The Floriacensis, better preserving the particle “not,” reads “or in the place,” etc., but adds the particle “as” after “was ordained”; the Endoviensis codex of the Louvain edition adds it as well.]—Paul who recalls himself as the last of the Apostles, so that no one might think that some later apostle existed. For he said: “For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (ibid. 15:9).

Nor should you flatter yourselves on this point: a Jew had done these things, although you too, like pagans, bring destruction upon us. For you unlawfully wage war against those whom it is not lawful to resist. You desire to live with us dead; for us, however, victory consists in fleeing or being killed.

[Note: [Col. 0271] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “we wage war.”]

41. AUGUSTINE replied: You may see how you have deployed the testimonies of Scripture, or how you have understood them; they have nothing to do with the matter now under discussion. You said all these things, certainly, in order to prove that there are false bishops, just as there are false angels and false apostles.

We too know that there are false angels, false apostles, and false bishops, and, as the true Apostle says, false brothers (2 Corinthians 11:26). But since such accusations can be hurled by either side against the other, it is necessary to prove something, not to speak emptily. Recall, however, against whom the charge of deceit applies; remember what we said above, and you will find it—so that we do not weary our readers by repeating the same things too often.

And yet what does any of this have to do with the Church spread throughout the whole world—whether with what you may say about its chaff, which is with it throughout the whole world, or with what you said about Manichaeus and the other diabolical sects? For if whatever is said even about the chaff that is still with the wheat does not pertain to the wheat, how much less do ancient and openly separated monstrosities pertain to the members of Christ spread throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0272] Up to this point Augustine had answered the first book of Petilianus’s Letter, as he himself testifies below, book 3, section 61.]?

## CHAPTER XIX

42. PETILIAN said: The Lord Christ commands us: “When people persecute you in this city, flee into another; and if they persecute you in that one, flee into another. Truly I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (Matthew 10:23).

If he warns us concerning Jews and pagans, then you, who claim to be a Christian, ought not to imitate the dreadful deeds of the Gentiles. Is this how you serve God, that we should be killed by your hands? You are mistaken, you are mistaken, wretched men, if you believe this. God does not have executioner-priests.

43. AUGUSTINE replied: Fleeing from city to city in the face of persecution was neither commanded nor permitted to heretics or schismatics, which is what you are, but to preachers of the Gospel, which you resist.

To prove this easily: at present you are certainly in your cities, and no one is persecuting you. Therefore you must come forward and give an account of your separation. For just as the weakness of the flesh is excused when it yields to the violence of persecution, so truth ought not to yield to falsehood.

Accordingly, if you are suffering persecution, why do you not leave the cities in which you are, so as to fulfill what you have recalled from the Gospel? But if you are not suffering persecution, why do you refuse to answer us? Or if perhaps you are afraid that, once you answer, you will suffer persecution, how then do you imitate those preachers to whom it was said, “Behold, I am sending you as sheep in the midst of wolves”? To whom it was also said, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (ibid. 10:16, 28).

And how are you not acting against the command of the Apostle Peter, who says: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you about your faith and hope” (1 Peter 3:15)?

Finally, why are you voluntarily wicked toward Catholic Churches through extremely violent mobs, wherever you have been able [Note: [Col. 0272] Amerbach reads, “wherever you have been able to observe that.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “wherever you will be able to observe that.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “wherever you have been able,” without the verb “to observe.”]? The matter itself demonstrates this through innumerable examples.

But you say that you are defending your places, and you resist with clubs and every kind of violence as far as you are able. Why did you not hear there the voice of the Lord saying, “But I say to you, do not resist evil” (Matthew 5:39)?

Or, if it is possible sometimes to resist violent people rightly by bodily force, without thereby violating the command we hear from the Lord, “But I say to you, do not resist evil,” why is it not also possible for a pious person to expel an impious person, and a just person an unjust person, from places unlawfully usurped or retained to the injury of God, through duly constituted and legitimate authorities?

For the false prophets did not suffer persecution from Elijah in the same way that Elijah did from the most wicked king (1 Kings 18). Nor, because the Lord was scourged by persecutors, should those whom he himself drove from the temple after scourging them be compared with his sufferings.

It remains, therefore, that you must admit that nothing else need be investigated except whether you separated yourselves from communion with the whole world justly or impiously. For if it is found that you acted impiously in doing this, do not be surprised if God has ministers through whom you are scourged, because you suffer persecution not from us but, as it is written, from your own deeds (Wisdom 11:21).

## CHAPTER XX

44. PETILIAN said: Again the Lord Christ cries from heaven to Paul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:4–5). Saul was then his name, so that afterward Baptism might transform his name.

For you, then, is it not hard to persecute Christ so many times in his priests [Note: [Col. 0273] The printed editions read, “who are in his priests.” “Who are” has been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.], while the Lord himself cries, “Do not touch my christs” (Psalm 104:15)? Count the many deaths of the saints, and you have killed the living Christ so many times. Finally, if you are not sacrilegious, you cannot be a holy murderer.

45. AUGUSTINE replied: Defend yourselves against the persecution that you suffered from your own people who separated themselves from you with Maximianus; there you will find our defense. If you say that you did not do this, we shall read the proconsular and municipal records. If you say that you rightly acted against them, why do you yourselves not want to suffer such things? If you say, “But we did not make a schism,” then let this be investigated; and before it is established whether this is so, let no one accuse the persecutors.

If you say that schismatics ought not to have suffered persecution either, I ask whether they ought not also to be expelled by duly constituted authorities from the basilicas in which they lie in wait to lead astray the weak. If you say that they ought not even to be expelled from these, first return the basilicas to the Maximianists, and then deal with us.

If you say that they ought to be expelled, then ask what they ought to suffer from the constituted authorities when, by resisting them, they resist the ordinance of God. Hence the Apostle clearly says: “For he does not bear the sword without cause; for he is an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Romans 13:2, 4).

But if, after the truth has been examined with complete care, it should be found that schismatics ought not to suffer anything even through public judgments, nor be driven from the places of their ambushes and deceits, and if you say that you disapprove of the fact that the Maximianists suffered these things at the hands of some of your people, why do the grains of the entire field of the Lord—that is, of the whole world—not cry out more freely [Note: [Col. 0273] Amerbach and the manuscripts read, “more abundantly.”]: “What the tares or what our chaff does does not concern us, because we disapprove of it”?

If you confess that it is sufficient for your purification that whatever evil is done by your people displeases you, why, then, did you separate yourselves? Your own defense accuses you on this point. For if you do not separate yourselves from the wicked among the party of Donatus [Note: [Col. 0273] The printed editions read, “from the wicked parties of Donatus.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.] for the reason that each person bears his own burden, why did you separate yourselves from the wicked throughout the world, whom you either believe or pretend to exist? Was it so that all of you might bear the burden of schism together?

[Col. 0274] 46. And when we ask you which of your people you can prove were killed by ours, I recall no law issued by the emperors ordering you to be killed. As for those about whom you are accustomed to arouse the greatest indignation—Marculus and Donatus—to put the matter more moderately, it is uncertain whether they threw themselves down, as your teaching does not cease to display through daily examples, or whether they were thrown down by order of some authority.

For if it is incredible that the teachers of the Circumcellions were accustomed to inflict unusual deaths upon themselves, how much more incredible can it be that Roman authorities were able to order unusual punishments? Thus, concerning this matter, which you consider extremely damaging to our reputation, if what you say is true, what does it have to do with the Lord’s wheat?

Let the chaff that has flown outside accuse the chaff that has remained inside; for the whole of it cannot be separated except by the final winnowing fan. But if it is false, what wonder is there if the chaff, blown away by the light breath of dissension, also attacks the Lord’s wheat with false accusations?

Therefore, concerning all such damaging charges, this wheat of Christ—which was commanded to grow throughout the field, that is, throughout the whole world, together with the tares—answers you in a free and confident voice: “If you do not prove what you say, it concerns no one; but if you prove it, it does not concern me.”

Hence it follows that whoever separated himself from this unity of the wheat on account of the crimes of the tares or the chaff cannot, on account of the very evil of dissension and schism, defend himself even from the charge of murder, since Scripture says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

## CHAPTER XXI

47. PETILIAN said: Therefore, as we have said, the Lord Christ cried out to Paul, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.” Paul then said, “Who are you, Lord?” And the answer was given to him: “I am Christ the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.” And trembling and astonished, he said, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” And the Lord said to him: “Rise, and enter the city, and it will be told you what you must do.”

And afterward: “Saul rose from the ground, and when his eyes had been opened, he saw nothing.”

O blindness that avenges fury, which obscures the persecutor’s light of the eyes, destined to depart only through Baptism! Let us see, then, what he did in the city. “Ananias entered,” he says, “to Saul, and after laying his hands upon him, said: Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight, and he arose and was baptized” (Acts 9:4–18).

Since, therefore, Paul, freed from the crime of persecution by Baptism, received innocent eyes, why do you, a blind persecutor and traitor with a false baptism, not want to be baptized by those whom you persecute?

48. AUGUSTINE replied: You do not prove that he is either a persecutor or a traitor, whom you want to baptize again. And even if you prove this of someone, a persecutor and traitor is nevertheless not to be baptized again if he has already been baptized with the Baptism of Christ.

Paul had to be baptized for the reason that he had never been immersed in such a baptism. Therefore, what you wanted to introduce concerning Paul has nothing resembling the case you are arguing with us.

But if you had not introduced this, you would not have found a place for your childish declamation, where you said, “O blindness that avenges fury, destined to depart only through Baptism!” How much more forcefully must we cry out against you: “O blindness that avenges fury, which, compared not with Paul but with Simon, does not depart from you even after Baptism has been received!”

For if persecutors are to be baptized by those whom they persecute, let Primianus be baptized by the Maximianists, whom he persecuted with the greatest zeal.

## CHAPTER XXII

49. PETILIAN said: But you constantly object that Christ said to the Apostles: “The one who has been washed once has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.”

If you examine these words fully, you are overcome by what follows. For he spoke in this way, saying: “The one who has been washed once has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean. And you are clean, but not all.” He said this on account of Judas, who was going to betray him (John 13:10–11).

Therefore, whoever has become a traitor has lost Baptism. Finally, after that traitor himself had been condemned, Christ more fully confirmed the eleven Apostles in this way: “Now you are clean, because of the word that I have spoken to you. Remain in me, and I in you” (ibid. 15:3–4).

And again he said to these eleven: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (ibid. 14:27). Since these things, then, were said—as we have stated—to the eleven Apostles after the traitor had been condemned, you too, as traitors, likewise have neither peace nor Baptism.

50. AUGUSTINE replied: If, then, a traitor lost Baptism, let anyone baptized by you who later becomes a traitor be baptized again if he wishes to return to you. If you do not do this, you yourselves sufficiently judge that the statement, “Whoever has become a traitor has lost Baptism,” is false.

For if he lost it, let him return and receive it; but if he returns and does not receive it, he had not lost it.

Further, if the words “Now you are clean” and “I give you my peace” were said to the Apostles because the traitor had already departed, then that supper of so great a Sacrament was not clean and peaceful when he gave it to all before the traitor went out [Note: [Col. 0275] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “since before”; and below, instead of “we cry out,” they read, “now we cry out.”].

If you dare to say this with closed eyes, what can we do except cry out instead: “O blindness that avenges fury in those who want to be teachers of the Law,” as the Apostle says, “understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions” (1 Timothy 1:7)?

Unless the blindness of stubbornness prevented it, the meaning would not be difficult: you would see that the Lord did not say, while Judas was present, “You are not yet clean,” but “Now you are clean.” He added, “but not all,” because one who was not clean was there.

Yet if his presence polluted the others, he would not have said to them, “Now you are clean”; rather, as I said, he would have said, “You are not yet clean.” But after that man departed, he said to them, “Now you are clean,” and did not add, “but not all,” because the one whose presence had occasioned the qualification “clean, but not all,” since one unclean man was there, had now departed.

Therefore, by these words the Lord more clearly declared that, within one assembly of people receiving the same Sacraments, the uncleanness of some cannot harm the clean.

Certainly, if you think that there are people like Judas among us, say these words to us: “You are clean, but not all.” You do not say this, however; rather, on account of certain unclean people you say, “You are all unclean.”

The Lord did not say this to the disciples while Judas was present. Therefore the person who says it has not learned from the good Teacher what he says.

## CHAPTER XXIII

51. PETILIAN said: But if you say that we perform Baptism twice, you do so yourselves, since you kill those who have been baptized—not because you baptize them do we say this, but because, whenever you kill someone, you cause him to be baptized in his own blood.

For the baptism of water or of the Spirit, when the martyr’s blood has been shed, is as though made twofold. Thus the Savior himself, first baptized by John, declared that he was to be baptized a second time—not now with water or with the Spirit, but with the baptism of blood, through the cross of his passion—as it is written:

“Two disciples, the sons of Zebedee, approached him, saying: Lord, when you come into your kingdom, grant that we may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left. Jesus answered them: You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized? They said to him: We can. And he said to them: You can indeed drink the cup that I am going to drink, and you will be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized” (Mark 10:35–38), and so forth.

If these are two baptisms, your persecution praises us, we confess it. For when you kill our bodies, we receive Baptism twice; but we are baptized with our baptism and with blood, as Christ was.

Be ashamed; be ashamed, persecutors: you make martyrs like Christ, whom, after the water of true Baptism, the blood of the Baptizer drenches with baptism.

## 52

**AUGUSTINE replied:** First, we answer briefly: we do not kill you; rather, you kill yourselves with a true death when you cut yourselves off from the living root of unity.

Next, if all who are killed are baptized in their own blood, then all robbers, wicked men, ungodly men, and criminals who are struck down under sentence must be regarded as martyrs, because they are baptized in their own blood. But if no one is baptized in his own blood except those who are killed for righteousness’ sake—for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:10)—then you should first have investigated why you suffer, and only afterward what you suffer.

Why, then, are your cheeks puffed up before your deeds have been defended? Why does your tongue make such a clamor before your life has been put to the test? If you have made a schism, you are ungodly; if you are ungodly, you die as a sacrilegious person when you are punished for your ungodliness; if you die as a sacrilegious person, how are you baptized in your own blood? Or do you say, “I have not made a schism”? Let us therefore investigate this: why do you shout before you prove it?

## 53

Or do you say, “Even if I am sacrilegious, I ought not to be killed by you”? That is one question: the atrocity of my deed, which you never truly demonstrate. The baptism of your blood is another question, about which you boast falsely. For you neither prove that I killed you, nor that you were killed by anyone. Even if you should prove it, whoever killed you is no concern of mine, whether he acted justly according to the authority legitimately given by the Lord, or whether, like chaff from the Lord’s harvest, he committed a crime out of some evil desire.

Just as it is no concern of yours who, in recent times, with intolerable power and even with soldiers accompanying him—not because he feared anyone, but so that he might be feared by all—oppressed widows, overthrew orphans, betrayed other people’s estates, broke up other people’s marriages, arranged for the property of innocent people to be sold, and divided the proceeds of the sales with the owners, who were weeping. I may seem to be saying these things on my own authority, unless it is recognized, without my naming him, whom I mean [**Note: [Col. 0277] He means Optatus the Gildonian.**].

If these things are true, then just as these matters do not concern you, so nothing you say concerns us, even if you were speaking truthfully. But if false rumor has lied about that just and innocent colleague of yours, then in no way should we believe rumor, which has been spread about innocent men as though they were betrayers of the books, or as though they were murderers.

Furthermore, I am speaking of one who lived among you, whose anniversary you attended with such great celebration, to whom you joined the kiss of peace amid the Sacraments, into whose hands you placed the Eucharist, to whom you in turn extended your hands when he distributed it, whose ears you feared offending openly amid Africa’s great groaning. I do not know which of you, because he touched him with the utmost urbanity, even if only indirectly, when he said that he had God as his Comes [**Note: [Col. 0277] Gildo.**], was carried about with immense praise.

Yet you throw those other men in our faces—men with whom we did not live, whose faces we never saw, and in whose time we were children or perhaps had not yet been born. What is this great injustice and perversity: that you wish to impose upon us the burdens of strangers, while you refuse to carry the burdens of friends?

Holy Scripture cries out: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Ps. 49:18). If the man whom you saw did not defile you, why do you reproach me with one whom I could not see? Or do you say, “I did not run with him, because his deeds displeased me”? But surely you approached the altar with him.

Come, then: defend yourself. Distinguish these matters, and say that running together into sin is one thing—as the two elders ran together when they plotted against Susanna’s chastity—and that receiving the Lord’s Sacrament with a thief is another thing, as the Apostles received that first supper even with Judas. I favor your defense. But why do you not consider how much more easily, by this defense of yours, you absolve the nations and the ends of the earth over which Christ’s inheritance is spread?

For if you were able to see a thief and communicate in the Sacraments with a thief whom you had seen, yet not communicate in his sin, how much less could the most remote nations have shared in the evil deeds of African betrayers or persecutors—even if what you say were true and you demonstrated it—although they shared the Sacraments with them?

Or do you say, “I saw that bishop, but I did not see that thief”? Say what you wish; I even favor this defense. By it the whole world is absolved from your accusations. For if you were permitted not to know the life of a man you knew, why is the whole world not permitted not to know those whom it did not know? Unless, perhaps, Donatists are permitted not to know what they refuse to know, while the nations are not permitted not to know what they cannot know.

## 54

Or do you say, “Theft is one thing, and betrayal or persecution is another”? I grant that they are different; nor is it necessary now to labor to show the distinction. Consider the short answer. If that man did not make you a thief because you did not approve of theft, who can make betrayers or murderers of those who disapprove either of betrayal or of murder?

First, then, confess that you are whatever evil Optatus was—the man whom you knew—and only then reproach me with whatever evil those men were whom I did not know.

Do not say to me, “But those things were great, whereas these are small.” You must first confess that those small things apply to you—not so that I too may confess them, but so that I may at least permit you to allege who knows what great things against me.

Did Optatus, whom you knew, make you a thief because he was your colleague and you used to approach the altar with him while he was committing these acts, or did he not? Answer one of these two alternatives.

If you say, “He did not,” I ask why he did not. Was it because he himself was not a thief? Or because you do not know? Or because you disapproved?

If it was because he himself was not a thief, then all the more must we refuse to believe that those about whom you accused us were what you say they were. For if we should not believe what Christians, pagans, and Jews—finally, both our people and yours—say about Optatus, how much less should we believe what you say about anyone else?

If it was because you do not know, all the nations answer you: “Much more do we not know whatever you allege against those men.”

If it was because you disapproved, they answer you in the same words: “Although you never proved such things, we too disapprove of them.”

But if you say, “That Optatus whom I knew made me a thief because he was my colleague, and I used to approach the altar with him while he was committing these acts; but I do not care, because the sin is slight. You, however, were made betrayers and murderers by those men,” I answer: I do not concede that I too have been made a betrayer and murderer by another person’s sins, because you confessed that you were made a thief by another person’s sin. You became a thief not by our judgment but by your own mouth.

For we say that each person carries his own burden, as the Apostle testifies (Gal. 6:5). But you, not because you committed theft or consented to theft, but because you considered another person’s deed to concern you, voluntarily placed your shoulders beneath Optatus’s burden.

For, as the Apostle says when speaking about foods: “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him; but to the one who considers something to be common, to him it is common” (Rom. 14:14). By the same rule it may be said that other people’s sins do not concern those who disapprove of them; but if anyone considers them to concern him, they do concern him.

Therefore, you do not convict us of being betrayers or murderers, even if you prove something of that sort concerning those who communicate the Sacraments with us. But you, even if you disapprove of whatever Optatus did, we hold to be a thief—not through our slander, but through your own sentence.

And lest you think this a slight matter, read the Apostle’s words: “Neither will thieves possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Those who will not possess the kingdom of God will certainly not be on the right hand, among those to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” If they will not be there, where will they be except on the left? They will therefore be among those to whom it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

You therefore make yourself secure in vain by considering slight the sin that separates one from the kingdom of God and sends one into eternal fire. How much better you would flee to a true confession and say: “Each one of us will carry his own burden,” and the final winnowing fan will separate the chaff from the wheat.

## 55

But evidently you fear that someone may immediately say to you: “Why, then, while you try to impose other people’s burdens upon others, have you dared to separate yourselves, before the final winnowing, from the Lord’s harvest of the whole world?”

Thus you, who disapprove of the deeds of your own people, while taking care lest the schism that you all committed be charged against you, involve yourselves even in sins that you did not commit. And while the eloquent Petilian fears that I may be permitted to say that I am not such as he thinks Caecilian was, he himself is forced to say that he is such as he knows Optatus to have been.

Are you not such as all Africa loudly proclaims him to have been? Neither, then, are we such as those whom you bring against us, whether your error suspects them to have been such, your fury defames them, or truth proves them to have been such. Much less are the Lord’s grains throughout all the nations such as these men, whose very name they have never heard.

There is therefore no reason why you should perish through so great a crime of separation and sacrilege of schism. Yet if, because of such great ungodliness, you suffer something under divine judgment, you even say that you are baptized in your own blood—so that it is not enough that you are not grieved at being divided [**Note: [Col. 0279] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *dimissi*; Amerbach reads *divisim*. The manuscripts more correctly read *divisi*.**], unless you also glory in being punished.

# CHAPTER XXIV

## 56

**PETILIAN said:** Yet you persist in the same point: “The one who has been washed once has no need except to wash his feet” (John 13:10). That which has an author is once; that which truth confirms is once.

## 57

**AUGUSTINE replied:** Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit has Christ as its author (Matt. 28:19), not just any human being. And Christ is the truth, not just any human being.

# CHAPTER XXV

## 58

**PETILIAN said:** For when you commit false things as a guilty man, I do not perform Baptism twice, which you yourself do not perform once.

## 59

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You do not prove us guilty. And if a guilty person baptizes with a false baptism, all who are baptized by them—including those who among you are already not only manifest but also hidden offenders—do not have true Baptism.

For if the one who gives Baptism gives God’s possession, how can he give God’s possession when he is already guilty before God? If a guilty person does not give true Baptism, how can he give God’s possession? But you are waiting for him to be guilty in your eyes as well, as though what he is going to give belonged to you [**Note: [Col. 0279] Amerbach reads *si enim*; the manuscripts read *sic enim*.**].

# CHAPTER XXVI

## 60

**PETILIAN said:** For if you mix false things with true ones, falsity often imitates truth in the very same tracks. Thus, thus the depiction of nature simulates a real human being, expressing false faces of truth in colors. Thus, thus the brightness of the mirror seizes the face, so as to draw back the eyes of the one looking; thus, thus it presents its own faces to those who approach, so that the face of the approaching person meets itself face to face. And so powerful is the clean deception [**Note: [Col. 0279] The printed editions read *immunda fallacia*, “unclean deception.” The manuscripts read *munda*—that is, “the deception of a clean mirror.”**] that the very eyes which perceive them recognize themselves, as it were, in another.

The shadow itself, when it stands still, doubles the images, dividing unity for the most part by means of a falsehood. Is it therefore true because the image lies?

But painting a human being is one thing, and generating one is another. For who fashions false infants for a father longing for children? Or who would expect real heirs from the falsehood of a painting? Surely it is the mind of a madman that, having abandoned what is true, loves a picture.

## 61

**AUGUSTINE replied:** Are you not ashamed to call Christ’s Baptism false, even if it were found in a most deceitful person? Far be it from us to believe that the Lord’s wheat—which was commanded to grow throughout the whole field, that is, this world, among the weeds until the harvest, that is, until the end of the age (Matt. 13:24–30, 36–43)—has perished through your curses.

Nevertheless, even among the weeds, which were commanded not to be gathered but to be tolerated until the end, and in the very chaff, which will be entirely separated only by the final winnowing fan (ibid. 3:12), does anyone dare to say that the Baptism given and received in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is false?

Those of your colleagues or presbyters whom you depose from office after they have been convicted by the testimony of pregnant women [**Note: [Col. 0280] Thus in the manuscripts; the editions read *gravidarum*, “of women.”**]—since such examples are not lacking everywhere—I ask whether, before they were convicted, they were deceitful or truthful. You will certainly answer, “Deceitful.”

Why, then, did they both possess and give true Baptism? Why did human deceit not corrupt the divine truth in them? Is it not most truly written: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1:5)?

Since the Holy Spirit fled from these deceitful men, why was the truth of Baptism present among them, unless it was because the Holy Spirit fled from the deceitfulness of the human being, not from the truth of the Sacrament?

Moreover, if deceitful men also possess true Baptism, possessing what truthful men possess [**Note: [Col. 0280] The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “possessing what truthful men possess.” The Cygirannensis reads, “possessing what untruthful men possess.”**], you must realize that your speech is instead colored with childish pigments. And therefore the person who, neglecting the living word [**Note: [Col. 0280] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read *verbo vero*, “the true word.”**], delights in such cosmetics, loves a picture instead of the truth.

# CHAPTER XXVII

## 62

**PETILIAN said:** But the Apostle Paul says: “One God, one faith, one Baptism” (Eph. 4:5). We profess one; for it is certain that those who think there are two are insane.

## 63

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You say these things against yourselves, but in your insanity you do not know it. Those say that there are two Baptisms who think that the just possess one and the wicked another, whereas it belongs neither to the one nor to the other, but is Christ’s one Baptism in both. They themselves are not one, however: the one group possesses what is one for salvation, the other for destruction.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

## 64

**PETILIAN said:** But, to compare one thing with another, a double sun appears to madmen, even though a blue cloud may often pass across it, and its discolored surface, struck by the radiance and reflecting the sun’s rays, may seem to send out rays of its own. Thus, thus, in the faith of Baptism, seeking images is one thing, and recognizing the truth is another.

## 65

**AUGUSTINE replied:** What are you saying, I ask? When a blue cloud, struck by the sun’s rays, reflects them, does it appear as two suns only to madmen, and not to everyone who looks? But when it appears so to madmen, it appears so to them alone. Yet, if my admonition is not troublesome, consider instead whether it may be madness to say and speak in this way.

Still, you apparently wished to say that the just possess the truth of Baptism, while the unjust possess an image. If that is so, I dare to say that there was an image in your Optatus [**Note: [Col. 0281] Optatus.**], for whom God was not God, but a certain Comes [**Note: [Col. 0281] Gildo.**]. The truth, however, was either in you or in the man who elegantly uttered this against him when he said, “He has God as his Comes.”

Now distinguish those whom both men baptized. In some approve the true Baptism; from others exclude the image and introduce the truth.

# CHAPTER XXIX

## 66

**PETILIAN said:** But, to pass over these lesser matters, does one who is not a magistrate of the court administer justice? Or is what he has said law, when a private person disturbs public laws? Is he not rather not only useless as a guilty man, but, together with what he produces, regarded as a forger [**Note: [Col. 0281] Thus in the manuscripts; the editions read *obtinet*, “obtains.”**]?

## 67

**AUGUSTINE replied:** What if this private person and forger gives someone the emperor’s law? When that person compares it with those who possess the law and discovers it to be the same, does he not attend to whom he received it from, but to what he received?

For when a forger gives something from his own forgery, it is false. But when something true belonging to another is given by someone—even if it is given by a forger—although the giver himself is not truthful, what is given is nevertheless true.

# CHAPTER XXX

## 68

**PETILIAN said:** Or if someone knows the hymns of a priest by heart, is he therefore a priest because he proclaims a priest’s hymn with a sacrilegious mouth?

## 69

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You say this as though we were now asking who is a true priest, and not what is true Baptism.

For in order for someone to be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the Sacrament but also with righteousness, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131:9).

But one who is a priest by the Sacrament alone—such as the high priest Caiaphas, the persecutor of the one and supremely true Priest—even though he himself is not truthful, nevertheless gives something true if he does not give what is his own but what belongs to God. Thus it was said of Caiaphas himself: “He did not say this from himself; but, since he was high priest, he prophesied” (John 11:49–51; 18:14).

And yet, to use the very comparison that you yourself proposed: if you hear from some profane person a prayer of a priest, formed according to evangelical words and mysteries [**Note: [Col. 0281] The editions read *confirmatam*, “confirmed”; the manuscripts read *conformatam*, “formed according to.”**], can you say to him, “It is not true,” although he is not only not a true priest but is not a priest at all?

The Apostle Paul called a certain testimony true—the testimony of some prophet of the Cretans who was not counted among God’s prophets. For he says: “One of themselves, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true” (Titus 1:12–13).

If, then, the Apostle, because he found the testimony of some foreigner to be true, himself also affirmed it, why do we not distinguish, whenever we find what belongs to Christ and is true in someone, between the fault that the person possesses and the truth that he possesses—not as his own, but as God’s—and say, “This Sacrament is true,” just as the Apostle said, “This testimony is true”?

Do we therefore say, “That man himself is truthful,” because we say, “This Sacrament is true”? And did the Apostle therefore count that prophet among God’s prophets because he affirmed as true what he found to be true in him?

Similarly, when the same Apostle was at Athens, among the altars of demons he noticed an altar on which it was written, “To an unknown god.” He took this testimony and used it to build them up in Christ, so that he mentioned it in his speech and added: “What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.”

Because he found that altar erected either among idols’ altars or by sacrilegious people, did he therefore condemn or reject what was true in it? Or, because he had read something true upon it, did he persuade them to follow the sacrileges of the pagans?

And consequently, when he wished to make the Lord himself—unknown to them but known to him—known to them also, insofar as he judged it appropriate, he said among other things: “Indeed, he is not far from each one of us; for in him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said” (Acts 17:23, 27–28).

Because he found testimonies of truth among sacrilegious people, did he therefore approve those people because of those testimonies? Or did he condemn those testimonies because of those people?

But you must always go astray so long as, because of human faults, you violate God’s Sacraments, or think that, because of God’s Sacraments—which we do not wish to violate in you—we must also assume the sacrilege of your schism.

# CHAPTER XXXI

## 70

**PETILIAN said:** “For every authority is from God” (Rom. 13:1), not authority in a human being [**Note: [Col. 0282] The Floriacensis manuscript reads *nomine*, “in the name.”**]. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ answered Pontius Pilate: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11). And again John says: “A human being can receive nothing unless it has been given to him from heaven” (ibid. 3:27).

Teach us, then, betrayer, when you received authority to counterfeit the mysteries.

## 71

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You teach us instead when the whole world—over which Christ’s inheritance has been spread, and that multitude of nations where the Apostles founded Churches—lost the authority to baptize.

You will never teach this.
