Not only because, while accusing them, you do not prove them to be betrayers, but also because, even if you did prove it, the crime of any evil people—whether unknown, deceitful, or to be tolerated like weeds or chaff—cannot overturn God’s promises, so that all the nations would not be blessed in the seed of Abraham.

You make yourselves strangers to these promises by refusing to maintain communion of unity with all the nations.

# CHAPTER XXXII

## 72

**PETILIAN said:** Although Baptism is one, it has nevertheless been consecrated in three stages. John gave water without the name of the Trinity, as he himself confessed, saying: “I baptize you in the water of repentance; another will come who is mightier than I, whose sandal I am not worthy to carry; he baptizes you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11).

Christ gave the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “He breathed upon their face and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:12).

And the fire itself, the Paraclete, blazing with crackling flames, came upon the Apostles. O true divinity, which appeared to set them alight without burning, as it is written: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as though a mighty wind were being carried along, and it filled the whole house where the Apostles were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and it rested upon each one of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:2–4).

But you, persecutor, do not even possess the water of repentance, since you retain not the authority of the slain John but of his murderer Herod. You therefore, betrayer, do not possess the Holy Spirit of Christ; for Christ was handed over to death, not did Christ hand over to death.

For you, there is a fire alive in spirit among the inhabitants of the underworld, which, burning with its meager letters, may be able to scorch your limbs throughout the age but not bring them to an end, as it is written concerning the punishment of the guilty in hell: “Their fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24).

## 73

**AUGUSTINE replied:** You are that abusive reviler, not a truthful disputant. Will you never cease saying such things—things which, if you do not prove them, concern no one, and which, if you do prove them, concern not at all the unity of the whole world, which exists in the holy as in the wheat?

If it pleased us to return curses for curses, we too might perhaps revile eloquently. We too might say, “With crackling flames.” But what is said ineptly does not sound eloquent to me at all. We too might say, “Burning with meager letters.” But we do not want the letters of our writings, when read by a sane person, to be judged meager in the juice of seriousness, with the reader himself laboring in a pointless fast because he is not nourished by any useful thoughts in them.

Look: I say that your Circumcellions burn, not with crackling flames, but with the flames of madness that hurl them headlong. If you answer, “What does that have to do with us?” why, when you have brought forward whomever you wished, should you not in turn hear, “We do not know either”?

If you answer, “You do not prove it,” why should the whole world not answer you in turn, “Nor do you prove it”?

Let us therefore agree, if you wish, that you should neither bring against us the evil men whom you suppose to be ours, nor should we bring yours against you. In this way you will see that, by so just an agreement, firmly established, you have nothing to bring against the seed of Abraham among all the nations.

And yet I find something great to bring against you: Why, then, have you impiously separated yourselves from the seed of Abraham, which exists among all the nations? Certainly, you have no way to defend this.

For we both clear ourselves of the crimes of others. But the fact that you do not communicate with all the nations that are blessed in the seed of Abraham is a great crime—not of some of you, but of all of you.

## 74

And yet you know, and you recall, that the Holy Spirit came in such a way that those whom he then filled spoke in every tongue. What did that sign and portent mean? Why is the Holy Spirit now given in such a way that no one to whom he is given can speak in every tongue, unless that miracle then foretold that all the nations would believe, and that the Gospel would thereby be present in every language?

This was also foretold long beforehand in the Psalm: “There are no tongues or languages whose voices are not heard.” This was said concerning those who, after receiving the Holy Spirit, were going to speak in every tongue.

But because it signified that the Gospel would in the future be present among all nations and in all languages, and that the body of Christ would resound throughout the whole world in every language, the Psalm continues: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Hence it comes about that no one is unaware of the true Church. Thus there is that saying which he himself gives in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14).

Therefore, in the same Psalm it is joined to this: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun”—that is, in manifestation—as we read in the Books of Kings: “What you did in secret, you will suffer in the sun” (2 Kings 12:12).

And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, “rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” “His going forth is from the summit of heaven”: there you have the Lord’s coming in the flesh. “And his course reaches to its summit”: there you have the resurrection and ascension. “And there is no one who hides himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:4–7): there you have the coming of the Holy Spirit, whom he sent in fiery tongues in order to display the fervor of love. Indeed, the person who does not maintain unity of spirit in the bond of peace with the Church that exists in every language does not possess that love.

## 75

As for your statement that Baptism is one (Eph. 4:5), but nevertheless consecrated in three stages, and your distribution of those three stages among individual persons in such a way that you assign water to John, the Holy Spirit to the Lord Jesus Christ, and the third element, fire, to the Paraclete sent from above, consider for a moment how great your error is.

You were led to think this because John says: “I indeed baptize in water; but the one who comes after me is greater than I; he himself baptizes you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11).

You did not wish to consider that the three elements are not individually matched with three persons—water with John, the Spirit with Christ, and fire with the Paraclete—but that these three belong rather to two: one to John and the other two to the Lord.

For it was not said: “I indeed baptize you in water; but the one who comes after me is greater than I, whose sandal I am not worthy to carry, he himself baptizes you in the Holy Spirit; but the Paraclete who will come after him baptizes you in fire.” Rather: “I indeed,” he says, “in water; but the one who comes after me, in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11).

He assigns one element to himself and two to the other. You see, then, how the number deceived you.

Consider further. You said that Baptism is one, consecrated in three stages—water, the Holy Spirit, and fire—and you assigned three persons to the individual stages: John to water, Christ to the Spirit, and the Paraclete to fire.

If, then, John’s water belongs to the same Baptism whose unity is being commended, those whom the Apostle Paul found had been baptized by John ought not to have been baptized at his command. They already possessed water belonging, as you say, to the same Baptism; it remained for them to receive the Spirit and fire, which John lacked, so that Baptism might be completed in the three stages in which you assert that it was consecrated.

But when they were ordered to be baptized by apostolic authority, it was clearly demonstrated that John’s water did not belong to Christ’s Baptism, but had belonged to another dispensation, necessary for its particular time.

## 76

Finally, what did you intend when, wishing to prove that the Holy Spirit was given by Christ, you brought forward the Gospel testimony that, after rising from the dead, he breathed upon the face of the disciples, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:12), and, wishing to identify that final fire which was named together with Baptism with the fiery tongues manifested at the coming of the Paraclete, you said, “And the fire itself, the Paraclete, blazing with crackling flames, came upon the Apostles” [**Note: [Col. 0285] The editions read: “wishing to show that final fire, which was named together with Baptism, in the fiery tongues that were manifested when the Paraclete came? For you said, ‘And the fire itself,’ etc.” The manuscripts do not differ. But the sense requires that *ad* be changed to *atque*, followed by corrected punctuation and the deletion of *enim*, so that it reads: “wishing to show this, you said, ‘And the fire itself …’”**].

You spoke as though there were one Holy Spirit whom he gave by breathing upon the face of the disciples, and another who came upon the Apostles after his ascension. Are there therefore two Holy Spirits? Who, except the most insane person, would say this? [**Note: [Col. 0285] The editions read, “Who would say this unless he were utterly insane?” The Lovanienses observe that *nisi* was added unnecessarily in that form; it is likewise absent from our manuscripts.**]

Christ himself therefore gave the same Holy Spirit, whether by breathing upon the face of the disciples or by sending him from above on the day of Pentecost through a definite manifestation of the Sacrament [**Note: [Col. 0285] Amerbach reads *circa sacramenti commendationem*, “around the manifestation of the Sacrament”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *citra sacramenti commendationem*. The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.**].

Accordingly, it was not that Christ gave the Holy Spirit and the Paraclete gave fire, as though the statement “in the Holy Spirit and fire” were thereby fulfilled. Rather, Christ himself gave the Holy Spirit, whom, while he was situated on earth, he manifested through his breath, and, while he was situated in heaven, manifested through fiery tongues.

To make clear that the statement “He himself baptizes you in the Holy Spirit” was not fulfilled at the time when he breathed upon their face, so that they might appear to be baptized no longer in the Spirit but in fire when the Paraclete was to come, recall the very clear Scripture and see what he said to them when the Lord himself ascended into heaven: “John indeed baptized with water; but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit, whom you are going to receive not many days from now, at Pentecost” (Acts 1:5).

What testimony could be clearer? According to your interpretation, he ought to have said: “John indeed baptized with water; but you were baptized in the Holy Spirit when I breathed upon your face, and from now on you will be baptized in the fire which you are going to receive not many days from now”—so that, evidently, the three stages might be completed in which you say that one Baptism was consecrated.

It follows that you still do not know what is meant by the statement, “He himself baptizes you in the Holy Spirit and fire,” and that you rashly wish to teach what you do not know.

# CHAPTER XXXIII

## 77

**PETILIAN said:** But, wishing to discuss fully the Baptism of the Trinity, the Lord Christ said to his Apostles: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep everything that I command you” (Matt. 28:19–20).

Whom do you teach, betrayer? Whom do you condemn? Whom do you teach, betrayer? Whom do you kill? Finally, whom do you teach? Someone whom you have made a murderer?

How, then, do you baptize in the name of the Trinity? You cannot call God your Father. For when the Lord Christ said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (ibid. 5:9), you, who do not possess peace of heart, do not possess God as Father.

How, moreover, do you baptize in the name of the Son, when you betray him, and do not imitate the Son of God in any sufferings or crosses?

How do you baptize in the name of the Holy Spirit, when the Holy Spirit came upon those Apostles who had not been betrayers?

Since, then, God is not your begetter, you are not truly born from the water of Baptism [**Note: [Col. 0286] The Floriacensis manuscript reads *vera nascimini*, “you are truly born”; the Cygirannensis reads *vera nascamini*, “you will truly be born.”**]. None of you has been born at all; you have neither father nor mother, you ungodly men.

Therefore, I ought not to baptize people such as you, even if, like the Jews who baptize the flesh, you were to wash yourselves a thousand times.

78. AUGUSTINE replied: Certainly you had proposed to examine the Trinity’s Baptism fully, and you had held our attention greatly; but, as is plainly what comes most easily to you, how quickly you turned to your customary curses. This you indeed do abundantly. You set before yourself whomever you wish, against whom you may rail as much as you please; but in the great breadth of your speech you are compressed by the one very short word, “Prove,” into the narrowest straits. For this is what the seed of Abraham says to you: in it all nations are blessed, and they do not care when they are cursed by you.

Nevertheless, since you are discussing Baptism, which you think is true when it is in a righteous person but false when it is in an unrighteous person, look: if I too examine the Trinity’s Baptism according to your rule, I shall be able, I think, to say more fully that it does not have God as Father, whose Count is God [Note: [Col. 0286] See above, n. 53]; nor does it believe in its Christ except for the one on whose behalf he suffered; nor does it have the Holy Spirit, who, in a far different manner, set pitiable Africa ablaze with fiery tongues.

How, then, do they have Baptism, or how do they give it [Note: [Col. 0286] In the manuscripts, “he gives”; yet in the other part of the sentence one reads, “they have Baptism”] in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit? Surely you now perceive that Baptism can exist in an unrighteous person, or be given by an unrighteous person, without itself being unrighteous, but righteous and true—not because it belongs to that person, but because it belongs to God.

And I make no false accusation against you concerning this, as you never cease doing against people throughout the world, and, what is more intolerable, you do not prove anything against them either. But I do not know how that can be tolerated which you bring forward: you not only make accusations against holy people on account of unrighteous people, but you also attribute guilt, arising from the contagion of human sins, to holy Baptism itself, which must necessarily be holy in any unrighteous person. Thus you say that Baptism is such as the person is by whom it is possessed, given, or received.

Furthermore, if a person is such as the one with whom he approaches the sacred rites, and if the Sacraments themselves become such as the people in whom they are, then it is enough consolation for holy people that, together with holy Baptism, they commonly hear from you the false charge. But consider how you are condemned by your own mouth, if your sober people become drunkards through the contagion of your drunkards, your merciful people become robbers through the contagion of your robbers, and everyone who is not what the evil people among you are is nevertheless forced to be what they are; and if Baptism itself is unclean in all your unclean people, and varies according to the diversity of that uncleanness, if it is forced to be such as the one by whom it is possessed and given.

These things are certainly false, and therefore they do us no harm when you say them against us without looking at yourselves. But they harm you, because when you say these false things, they do not fall upon us; rather, because you think them true, they rebound upon you.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

79. PETILIAN said: Now, if the Apostles were permitted to baptize those whom John had washed with the baptism of repentance, will I not be permitted to baptize you sacrilegious people?

80. AUGUSTINE replied: Where, then, is what you said above—that John’s Baptism was not one baptism and Christ’s another, but one Baptism consecrated in three stages, of which John gave the water, Christ the Spirit, and the Paraclete the fire? Why, then, did the Apostles repeat the water for those to whom John had already given water belonging to one Baptism consecrated in three stages? You plainly see how necessary it is for each person to know what he is saying.

## CHAPTER XXXV

81. PETILIAN said: For the Holy Spirit cannot be infused into anyone by the laying-on of the bishop’s hands unless the generative water of a pure conscience has first preceded it.

82. AUGUSTINE replied: In these few words of yours there are two errors. One of them does not greatly concern the question being examined between us, but it exposes your ignorance. For the Holy Spirit came upon the one hundred and twenty without anyone’s laying on of hands; and upon Cornelius the Centurion and those who were with him, even before they were baptized (Acts I, 15; II, 4; and X, 44).

But the other error in these words of yours completely destroys your whole case. You say that the water of a pure conscience must precede, so that the Holy Spirit may follow. Therefore either all water consecrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is the water of a pure conscience—not on account of those by whom it is administered or received, but on account of the one who instituted this Baptism undefiled—or, if water is made the water of a pure conscience only by the pure conscience both of the ministering person and of the recipient, what will you do with those whom you find baptized by people who, before they were exposed, carried a stained conscience?

What especially will you do if among these baptized people there is someone who admits that, when he was baptized, he had a bad conscience, perhaps because he intended by that very opportunity to advance toward some disgraceful act? When it has been made clear to you that neither the one who administered Baptism nor the one who received it had a pure conscience, will you judge that he must be baptized again? You will neither say nor do this.

The purity of Baptism, therefore, is altogether distinct from the purity or uncleanness of the conscience, whether of the giver or of the recipient. Come, then, dare to say that the fraudulent man, the robber, the oppressor of orphans and widows, the destroyer of marriages, the betrayer, seller, and divider of other people’s patrimonies had a pure conscience [Note: [Col. 0288] Optatus the Gildonian].

Dare also to say that those people had pure consciences whose absence in such times would be difficult to find: people who perhaps sought baptism not for Christ or eternal life, but to gain earthly friendships and satisfy earthly desires. If you do not dare to say that these people had pure consciences, then, if you find any of them baptized, give them the water of a pure conscience, which they did not receive. If you do not do this, stop boasting against us about what you do not know, lest you be forced to answer us concerning what you do know.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

83. PETILIAN said: The Holy Spirit certainly could not come upon you, whom not even the baptism of repentance washed, but whom the polluted water of the betrayer has polluted—which is something to be repented of, as is true.

84. AUGUSTINE replied: You not only fail to prove that we are betrayers; your fathers could not prove that our fathers were betrayers either. If they had been proved so, they certainly would not have been our fathers, according to your earlier assertion, since we would not have followed their deeds. Yet on their account we would not be torn away from communion in unity or from the seed of Abraham, in which all nations are blessed (Genesis XXII, 18).

Nevertheless, if Christ’s water is one thing and the betrayer’s water another because Christ was not a betrayer, why should Christ’s water not be one thing and the robber’s water another, since Christ certainly was not a robber either? You baptize, then, after your robber, and I shall baptize after a betrayer who is neither mine nor yours—or, if documents produced are to be believed, both mine and yours. But if the communion of the whole world is to be trusted more than the party of Donatus, he is not mine but yours.

According to the better and sounder judgment, however, since, in the apostolic words, “Each of us will bear his own burden” (Galatians VI, 5), that robber is not yours if you are not robbers, and no betrayer is either ours or yours if we are not betrayers. Therefore we are Catholics, because according to this judgment we do not abandon unity; but you are heretics, because on account of the crimes of certain people, whether true or false, you do not wish to maintain charity with the seed of Abraham.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

85. PETILIAN said: But so that these acts performed by the Apostles may shine before us, we are instructed by their deeds, as it is written:

“Now it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus. And when he found certain disciples, he said to them, ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said, ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ And Paul said, ‘In what, then, were you baptized?’ And they replied, saying, ‘In John’s Baptism.’ But Paul said, ‘John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in the Lord Jesus Christ.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them. They spoke in various tongues and prophesied. There were about twelve men in all” (Acts XIX, 1–7).

If, then, those people were baptized so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, why do you not, if you wish to receive the Holy Spirit, after your lies receive true renewal? If we do wrong in this, why do you seek us? Or, if it is a crime, first condemn Paul, who washed away what had already existed, whereas we baptize in you what does not yet exist. For, as we have often said, you do not baptize yourselves with true Baptism; rather, under an empty name, you defame yourselves with false baptism.

86. AUGUSTINE replied: We do not accuse Paul, who gave Christ’s Baptism to people because they did not have Christ’s Baptism, but John’s Baptism, according to their own answer. When they were asked in what they had been baptized, they replied, “In John’s Baptism.” That Baptism does not belong to Christ’s Baptism, nor is it any part or stage of it. Otherwise either the water of Christ’s Baptism was being repeated at that time, or, if Christ’s Baptism was then completed through two waters, it is less complete now because the water given through John is not given. To think either of these things is impious and sacrilegious.

Paul therefore gave Christ’s Baptism to those who did not have Christ’s Baptism, but John’s.

87. Why John’s baptism was necessary at that time, though it is no longer necessary now, we have explained elsewhere; and it does not pertain to the matter being treated between us now, except insofar as it demonstrates that John’s baptism was one thing and Christ’s another. The same is true of that other baptism in which the Apostle says that our fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, when they crossed the Red Sea through Moses (1 Corinthians X, 1–2).

For the Law and the Prophets had Sacraments that foretold what was to come until John the Baptist; the Sacraments of our time testify that what those foretold has come. John, therefore, was the nearest herald of Christ among all those who preceded him.

Since all the righteous and prophets of earlier times desired to see accomplished what, through the Spirit’s revelation, they perceived would come—for the Lord himself says, “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matthew XIII, 17)—John was therefore called more than a prophet, and no greater was found among those born of women. To the earlier righteous it was granted only to foretell Christ; to John it was granted both to foretell him while absent and to see him present. Thus it is found that what they desired was opened to him [Note: [Col. 0290] In the manuscripts, “so that it may be found that he was able to do this from here”].

For this reason his baptismal sacrament still belongs to the foretelling of Christ, but plainly to its final stage, since until him there were only predictions of the Lord’s first coming; now there are proclamations of that coming, no longer predictions. Yet the Lord, teaching the way of humility, deigned to receive the sacraments of his own foretelling that he found here—not to assist in his own purification, but as an example of our devotion. He thereby showed us with what devotion we ought to receive the things that testify that he has already come, since he did not disdain to receive the things that symbolized that he would come.

Thus John, although he was the nearest predecessor and was his contemporary by less than a year, nevertheless went before Christ when he baptized those who came to him. For this reason it was said of him, “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way.” And he himself preached, saying, “After me comes one stronger than I” (Malachi III, 1; and Mark I, 2, 7).

In the same way, circumcision on the eighth day, which was given to the fathers, foretold our justification through the stripping away of carnal desires by the Lord’s resurrection. That resurrection took place after the seventh day—that is, the Sabbath—on the eighth day, that is, the Lord’s day, which is the third day after his burial. Yet Christ as an infant received that same circumcision of the flesh which was prophetic.

And just as the Passover celebrated by the Jews in the slaughter of the lamb foretold the Lord’s passion and his passage from this world to the Father—and yet the Lord himself celebrated that very Passover, which was contained in the same prophecy, with his disciples when they suggested to him, saying, “Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” (Matthew XXVI, 17)—so he also received John’s baptism, which belonged to the immediate foretelling of him.

But just as the Jews’ circumcision of the flesh is one thing and what we celebrate on the eighth day of those baptized is another; and just as the Passover which they still celebrate from a sheep is one thing [Note: [Col. 0290] He thought that the Jews dispersed throughout the world still celebrated Passover by sacrificing sheep, as in *Retractions* I.10; but the Law plainly forbade this in Deuteronomy XVI, 6, so that Passover might not be sacrificed in places other than Jerusalem], while that which we receive in the body and blood of the Lord is another, so John’s baptism was one thing and Christ’s Baptism is another.

For those former rites foretold that these things would come; these latter proclaim that those things have been fulfilled. And although Christ received those former rites, they are not necessary for us, because we have received the very one who was announced through them. But at the Lord’s recent coming, whoever had received those former rites needed also to be imbued with these; whoever, however, had been imbued with these did not need to be compelled backward into those former rites.

88. Therefore do not create darkness concerning John’s baptism. Whether its cause and rationale is the one I have explained or whether some other, better and more certain explanation is given, this nevertheless remains clear: John’s baptism was one thing and Christ’s another. That it was called John’s baptism is shown both by the reply of those whom you mentioned and by the Lord’s own statement, when he said to the Jews, “John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from human beings?” (Matthew XXI, 25).

This Baptism, however, is not called Caecilian’s, Donatus’s, Augustine’s, or Petilian’s, but Christ’s Baptism. For if you think us shameless because, after us, we want no one to be baptized, even though we see that after John people were baptized—and he is incomparably greater than we are—are John and Optatus perhaps equals? It seems ridiculous; yet I think you believe that Optatus is not their equal but greater.

After John, an Apostle baptized; you dare not baptize anyone after Optatus. Is it because Optatus was in your unity? I do not know by what frame of mind this can now be endured. If a friend of the Count [Note: [Col. 0291] Gildo’s. See above, n. 53], whose companion was God, is said to have been in unity, and the friend of the bridegroom outside unity, the matter is extraordinary indeed.

But if John was especially in unity, and was far more excellent and greater than not only Optatus but all of us and all of you, and yet the Apostle Paul baptized after him, why do you not baptize after Optatus? Unless your blindness compresses you into this dilemma, so that you say that Optatus could give the Holy Spirit, but John could not.

If you do not say this—lest even the insane themselves laugh at your insanity—what will you answer when asked why people had to be baptized after John, but no one is to be baptized after Optatus? Is it not because those people had been baptized with John’s baptism? Whoever is baptized with Christ’s Baptism, whether he is baptized through Paul or through Optatus, has a Baptism no different from theirs, although Paul and Optatus differ so greatly.

Return, then, transgressors, to your senses (Isaiah XLVI, 8), and do not measure divine Sacraments by the character and deeds of human beings. They are holy through the one to whom they belong [Note: [Col. 0291] Printed editions read, “they have been made”; corrected from the manuscripts]. When handled worthily, they bring a reward; when handled unworthily, they bring judgment. And although those who handle God’s Sacrament worthily and those who handle it unworthily are not one, the Sacrament itself is one, whether it is handled worthily or unworthily—not so that it becomes better or worse, but for the life or death of those who handle it.

As for what you said—that in those whom Paul baptized after John he washed away what had already existed—you certainly would not have said it if you had considered for a little while what you were saying. If John’s baptism had to be washed away, it was unquestionably filthy. What more, then, should I press upon you? Recall or read, and see from whom John received this; you will discover upon whom you have poured this blasphemy. When you have discovered it, let your breast at least be struck, if your tongue is not restrained.

89. As for what you now think you say so cleverly to us—“If we do wrong in this, why do you seek us?”—do you not sometimes remember that only those who have perished are sought? Or does failing even to see this belong to perdition itself?

That sheep, too, could absurdly say to its shepherd, “If I am doing wrong by wandering from the flock, why do you seek me?” It would not understand that the reason it thinks it should not be sought is precisely the one reason why it is being sought.

Who, then, seeks you—whether through his Scriptures, through Catholic and peaceful tongues, or through the scourges of temporal tribulations—except the one who dispenses this mercy to you in all things? We seek you, therefore, in order to find you. We love you so much that you may live, just as we hate your error so that the one who is destroying you may perish, so long as he himself does not perish.

Would that we sought you in such a way that we might also find you, and joyfully say of each one of you, “He was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 32)!

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

90. PETILIAN said: If you say that you hold the Catholic Church, “Catholic” is what in Greek is called “the unique” or “the whole.” Look: you are not in the whole, because you have withdrawn into a part.

91. AUGUSTINE replied: I have acquired very little knowledge of the Greek language—almost none. Nevertheless, I say without shame that I know that ὅλον (*holon*) does not mean “one,” but “whole,” and καθ’ ὅλον (*kath’ holon*) means “according to the whole.” From this the name “Catholic” has been derived, as the Lord himself says:

“It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth” (Acts I, 7–8).

There you have the reason it is called Catholic. But with eyes so tightly shut you stumble against the mountain which, according to Daniel’s prophecy, grew from a small stone and filled the whole earth (Daniel II, 35), so that you tell us that we have withdrawn into a part and are not in the whole, although our communion is spread throughout the entire world.

Yet if you were to tell me that I am Petilian, I would not find a way to refute you except either by laughing at you as a joker or grieving for you as a madman. I see that I must do the same now. But since I do not believe you are joking, you see what remains.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

92. PETILIAN said: But a part of darkness does not belong with light, nor a part of bitterness with honey; life has no part with death, innocence no part with guilt, water no part with blood. Nor does dregs have a part with oil, although there is a muddy kinship between them; but everything reprehensible will flow away. This is the cesspool of vices, as John says:

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II, 19).

Gold is not found with its filth; all precious things are purified. For it is written:

“Just as the furnace tests gold, so tribulation tests the righteous” (Wisdom III, 6).

Cruelty cannot be a part of gentleness, nor sacrilege of religion; nor can Macarius in any way be a part of us [Note: [Col. 0292] The Floriacensis codex omits “be our part.” Below, it reads *maculat* (“defiles”), whereas the Cygirannensis manuscript has *maculant* (“they defile”)], because he defiles the appearance of our rite.

For an enemy force is not a part of us when it fulfills the name of an enemy. If it is truly called a part, it will incur Solomon’s fitting sentence:

“Let their portion perish from the earth” (Proverbs II, 22).

93. AUGUSTINE replied: What is it to boast of these words and prove nothing, except to rave? You observe the weeds throughout the world, but do not observe the wheat, although both have been commanded to grow throughout the whole world. You observe the seed of the evil one, which will be separated at harvest time (Matthew XIII, 24–30, 36–43), but you do not observe the seed of Abraham, in which all nations are blessed (Genesis XXII, 18).

As though you were already a purified mass, pure honey, clarified oil, pure gold, or even the appearance of a whitened wall [Note: [Col. 0293] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “nor even the appearance,” less correctly]. To say nothing of the other vices, do drunkards form part of the sober, or are the greedy counted among the wise? If gentle people possess the name of light, where will the fury of the Circumcellions be counted except among darkness?

Why, then, does Baptism given among you have validity through such people, while the same Baptism of Christ has no validity through anyone whatsoever throughout the world? You plainly see that you have separated yourselves from the communion of the whole world to such an extent that, although not all of you are drunkards, nor all greedy, nor all violent, you are all heretics, and therefore all impious and all sacrilegious.

94. But who with a sound mind would call the whole world rejoicing in Christian fellowship a part of Macarius? Yet because we say that you belong to the party of Donatus, you seek someone whose party you can say we belong to; and, in your great straits, you name some person who may perhaps be known in Africa but is unknown in the other regions of the world.

Therefore the whole seed of Abraham throughout the whole earth answers you: “We do not know this Macarius, whose party you say we belong to, at all.” In turn, answer that you do not know Donatus. But even if we say that you belong to the party of Optatus, which of you can say that he does not know Optatus—unless perhaps you mean that you do not know him by sight, just as you do not know Donatus by sight?

But you evidently rejoice in the name of Donatus. Do you also rejoice in the name of Optatus? What benefit, then, is Donatus to you, when Optatus has polluted all of you? What benefit is Donatus’s sobriety to you, when you are defiled by the drunkenness of the Circumcellions? What benefit, according to your opinion, is Donatus’s innocence to you, when you are stained by Optatus’s rapacity?

For this is your error: you think that a person’s iniquity has greater power to contaminate another than a person’s righteousness has to purify another. Thus, if two people share the divine Sacraments together, one righteous and the other unrighteous, but in such a way that neither imitates the other’s character—the one not imitating the other’s iniquity, nor the other this one’s righteousness—you do not say that both thereby become righteous, but that both become unrighteous. You say that even the holy thing which they receive together becomes unclean and loses its own holiness.

Where has iniquity found such advocates, that, through their ravings, it is thought victorious? Why, then, do you applaud yourselves over the name of Donatus amid such a great error of perversity, where it is not Petilian who deserves to be Donatus, but Donatus himself is forced to be what Optatus is?

Let the house of Israel say, “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm LXXII, 26); let the seed of Abraham among all nations say, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm XV, 5). For it knows how to say this in the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God.

You too, through the sacrament that is in you, prophesy unknowingly, like Caiaphas, the persecutor of the Lord (John XI, 51). For what is called Μακάριος (*Makarios*) in Greek is *Beatus* (“Blessed”) in Latin.

So, plainly, we are of the party of Macarius. For what is more blessed than Christ, to whom we belong, of whom all the ends of the earth are mindful and are converted, and in whose presence all the peoples of the nations worship?

Therefore this Macarius’s—that is, this blessed one’s—party does not fear your final curse, perversely taken from Solomon, lest it perish from the earth. For when Solomon said, “Let their portion perish from the earth” (Proverbs II, 22), he was speaking of the impious. You attempt to turn this against Christ’s inheritance and insist that this has happened to it.

When you say that the promises “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II, 8) and “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm XXI, 28) have now perished from the earth, you want to apply to Christ’s inheritance what was spoken concerning the lot of the impious. But while Christ’s inheritance remains and grows, you perish as you say these things.

You do not everywhere prophesy through God’s sacrament, since here, through your madness, you utter evil wishes. But the prediction of the Prophets is stronger than the curse of false prophets.

## CHAPTER XL

95. PETILIAN said: The Apostle Paul also cries out:

“Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?” (2 Corinthians VI, 14–15).

96. AUGUSTINE replied: I recognize the Apostle’s words, but I do not see at all how they help you. For which of us says that there is a partnership between righteousness and iniquity, even if a righteous and an unrighteous person, like Judas and Peter, share the Sacraments together?

From one and the same holy thing Judas received judgment for himself, while Peter received salvation. So it was with you, if you were unlike Optatus when you received the Sacrament with him and were not a robber as he was. Or is robbery not iniquity? Who could be so mad as to say this? What partnership, then, was there between your righteousness and his iniquity when you approached the one altar together?

## CHAPTER XLI

97. PETILIAN said: Again he taught that schisms should not arise:

“I say this to you, that each one of you says, ‘I indeed belong to Paul’; ‘but I to Apollos’; ‘but I to Cephas’; ‘but I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians I, 12–13).

98. AUGUSTINE replied: Remember, you who read this: Petilian is quoting these words from the Apostle. When would you ever believe that he would thus speak against himself on our behalf?

## CHAPTER XLII

99. PETILIAN said: If Paul said this to the unlearned and the righteous, I say this to you unrighteous people: Is Christ divided, so that you have cut yourselves off from the Church?

100. AUGUSTINE replied: I fear that someone may think the scribe has made a mistake in this work of mine and has written “Petilian said” where he should have written “Augustine replied.” But I see what you have done: you wanted to forestall us, as though to prevent us from saying these things. But what have you done except cause them to be said twice?

If, then, you enjoy hearing things that are directed against you, so long as they are spoken, hear them from me, Petilian: Is Christ divided, so that you have cut yourselves off from the Church?

## CHAPTER XLIII

101. PETILIAN said: Did Judas the betrayer die by his own noose for you, or are you baptized into his ways, whose deeds you imitate by seizing the Church’s treasures and selling us, the heirs of Christ, to the powers of this age?

102. AUGUSTINE replied: Judas did not die for us; Christ died for us. To him the Church, spread throughout the whole world, says:

“I will answer those who reproach me with a word, for I have hoped in your words” (Psalm CXVIII, 42).

When, therefore, I hear the Lord saying, “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth” (Acts I, 8), and the prophet saying, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII, 5), the bodily mixture of evil people does not disturb me at all, if I know how to say, “Receive your servant for good; let the proud not slander me” (Psalm CXVIII, 122) [Note: [Col. 0295] The manuscripts read *si* (“if”); the printed editions, *sed* (“but”)].

I therefore do not care about an empty slanderer, because I hold fast to a trustworthy promiser.

But if you complain about the ecclesiastical properties or places that you held and no longer hold, the Jews too could call themselves righteous and charge us with iniquity because Christians now possess the place where they once ruled impiously. What, then, is disgraceful if Catholics possess, in accordance with the Lord’s equal will, what heretics once held?

For the Lord’s statement applies to all who are similar—that is, to all the impious and unrighteous:

“The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing righteousness” (Matthew XXI, 43).

Or was it written without reason, “The labors of the impious the righteous will eat” (Psalm CIV, 44)?

Therefore you ought to wonder more that you still retain anything than that you have lost anything. But do not wonder even at this: the whitened wall is gradually falling.

Consider, nevertheless, the Maximianists: what places they held, and by what people acting and attacking from there they were expelled. If enduring such things is justice and doing them is iniquity, dare to speak, if you can.

First, because you did these things, while they suffered them. Second, because according to this rule of justice you are found inferior. They were expelled from their ancient places by judges acting under Catholic emperors; you, however, are not expelled from the basilicas of unity even by the commands of those same emperors. Why is this, unless you are of lesser merit—not only than your other colleagues, but even than those very people whom, in the voice of your plenary council, you condemned as sacrilegious?

## CHAPTER XLIV

103. PETILIAN said: For we, as it is written, put on Christ who was betrayed through our Baptism (Galatians III, 27), whereas through your contagion you put on Judas the betrayer.

104. AUGUSTINE replied: I too could say that through your contagion you put on Optatus, the betrayer, robber, oppressor, and separatist. But far be it from me to let the desire to return a curse provoke me into any falsehood. You do not put on him, nor do we put on this one.

Therefore, if someone coming to us answers that he was baptized in the name of Optatus, he will be baptized in the name of Christ. And you, all of you who baptized people coming from us, if they said that they had been baptized in the name of Judas the betrayer, we do not criticize what you did. But if they had been baptized in the name of Christ, do you not see with what great error you suppose that divine Sacraments are altered by the variety of human vices, or polluted by anyone’s filth of life [Note: [Col. 0296] The printed editions read, “or in you”; corrected from the manuscripts]?

## CHAPTER XLV

105. PETILIAN said: But if these are the parties, the names of those sharing a party do not prejudice us. For there are two ways: one is narrow, along which we proceed; the other belongs to the impious, along which they will perish. Yet the equality of the name is widely distinguished, so that the way of righteousness is not polluted by sharing a name.

106. AUGUSTINE replied: You feared the multitude of the whole world when compared with the multitude of your own people, and you wanted to compare yourself with the few who walk along the narrow way, as though in praise of your small number.

Would that you had compared yourself not with the praise of that number but with the way itself! You would surely have perceived that this same small number exists in the Church of all nations, and that people are called few righteous in comparison with the many unrighteous. In the same way, in comparison with the chaff, a few grains can be called abundant in a very rich harvest; yet, gathered by themselves into the heap, they fill the granary.

For just as in the tribulations involving the loss of places, so also in smallness—if you think justice consists in these things—the Maximianists themselves will surpass you.

## CHAPTER XLVI

107. PETILIAN said: In the first psalm David separates the blessed from the impious—not by making parties, of course, but by separating holiness from all the impious:

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the impious, and has not stood in the way of sinners.”

Let the one who had gone astray return to the way of righteousness, lest he perish.

“And has not sat upon the seat of pestilence.”

Since he admonishes you in this way, wretched people, why do you sit?

“But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night. And he will be like a tree planted beside channels of water, which will give its fruit in its season. Its leaf will not fall, and everything he does will prosper. Not so the impious, not so; but like dust which the wind drives away from the face of the earth.”

It fills the eyes in order to blind [them].

“Therefore the impious will not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. For the Lord knows the ways of the righteous, but the path of the impious will perish” (Psalm I).

108. AUGUSTINE replied: Who does not distinguish these two kinds of people in the Scriptures? But you who curse attribute the crimes of the chaff even to the wheat; and although you are nothing but chaff, you boast that you alone are wheat [Note: [Col. 0296] The printed editions read *maledicti* (“cursed”); this is corrupt.].

But the truthful prophets say that both kinds, before the winnowing which will take place on the day of judgment, are mixed throughout the whole world—that is, throughout the whole field of the Lord.

Nevertheless, I advise you to read this first psalm in Greek. Then you will not dare to charge the whole world with belonging to Macarius as a crime, because perhaps you will understand whose party Macarius belongs to among all the saints who are blessed throughout all nations in the seed of Abraham.

For where the Latin has “Blessed is the man,” the Greek has Μακάριος ἀνήρ (*Makarios anēr*), “Blessed is the man.”

But that Macarius who displeases you, if he was evil, belongs neither to this lot nor does he harm this lot. If he was good, let him prove his own work, so that he may have glory in himself and not in another (Galatians VI, 4).

## CHAPTER XLVII

**109. PETILIANUS said:** The same psalmist also sang the praises of our Baptism:

> “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me. He has led me beside the water of refreshment; he has restored my soul. He has led me along the paths of justice for his name’s sake. For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death”—if, he says, my persecutor kills me—“I shall fear no evil, because you are with me, O Lord. Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me.”

Thus, clad in the oil of chrism, the soul defeated Goliath:

> “You have prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me. You have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, intoxicating, is exceedingly excellent. And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Psalm 22).

**110. AUGUSTINE replied:** This psalm speaks of those who receive Baptism rightly and use the holy thing in a holy manner. For these words do not also apply to Simon Magus, who nevertheless received the same holy Baptism. Because he was unwilling to use it in a holy manner, he did not thereby defile it, nor did he teach that it should be repeated for people of his kind.

But since you mentioned Goliath, consider that psalm concerning Goliath himself, and see that in the new song he is depicted as defeated [Note: [Col. 0297] In Ambrose and the manuscripts: “he has been defeated.”]: for there it says, “O God, I will sing a new song to you; on the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Psalm 143:9). And see whether the one who does not share in the whole world belongs to this song.

For elsewhere it says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95:1). Therefore all the earth, in whose unity you do not stand, sings the new song. And these words also belong to all the earth: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing,” and so forth.

These are not the words of weeds, although the weeds are tolerated in the same field until the harvest; they are not the words of straw, but of wheat, although they are nourished together by the same rain and threshed together on the same threshing floor [Note: [Col. 0297] In the manuscripts: “tormented.”], until at the final winnowing they are separated from one another. These two groups certainly possess one Baptism in common, although they are not one.

But even if your party were the Church of God, surely you would admit that this psalm does not belong there to the frenzied bands of the Circumcellions. Or if they too are led along the paths of justice, why do you deny that they are your companions when they are brought against you, although often the smallness of your cut-off faction is comforted not by God’s rod and staff but by their clubs, by which you imagine yourselves protected against the Roman laws? To run into these men—what is it other than to walk in the midst of the shadow of death?

Yet the one with whom the Lord is does not fear evil. Still, you will certainly not dare to say that even these frenzied men speak the words sung in this psalm. And yet you not only confess that they possess Baptism, but openly profess it.

Therefore these words are spoken only by those who are refreshed by holy water, like all God’s righteous people—not by those who are overturned through misusing it, like that magician baptized by Philip. Yet the water itself is one and holy in both.

These words are spoken only by those who will belong on the right—not by all those who graze in the same pasture under one shepherd, both sheep and goats, until they are separated to receive what is due them.

These words are spoken only by those who receive life from the Lord’s table, like Peter—not judgment, like Judas. Yet the table itself was one for both, although it did not benefit both unto the same end, because they themselves were not one.

These words are spoken only by those who are blessed in spirit by holy oil, like David—not by those who are consecrated only in the body, like Saul. Yet although both received one and the same thing, the sacrament was not unequal for them; their merit was unequal.

These words are spoken only by those who receive the Lord’s cup with a changed mind unto eternal life—not by those who eat and drink judgment upon themselves, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 11:29). Yet that one cup is one for both, though they are not one: it intoxicates martyrs for the attaining of heavenly things, but the Circumcellions for the destruction of themselves in fatal precipices.

Remember, then, that the conduct of wicked people does nothing against God’s sacraments, so as to make them either not exist at all or be less holy. It harms the wicked people themselves, so that they possess the sacraments as testimony to their condemnation, not as assistance toward their healing.

At least you should have considered the final words of this psalm and understood, concerning those who apostatize after receiving Baptism, that not everyone who receives holy Baptism can say, “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.” Yet whether they remain or fall away, while they themselves are not one, Baptism is one; and although neither group is holy in both cases, Baptism is holy in both. For if apostates return, they are not baptized as though they had lost Baptism; rather, they are humbled because they have wronged what remains in them.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**111. PETILIANUS said:** But so that you may not call yourselves holy, I assert first that whoever is not innocent does not possess holiness.

**112. AUGUSTINE replied:** Show us the tribunal on which you sat, so that the whole world might stand before you; and tell us with what eyes—not to mention the consciences of all people—you inspected and examined even their actions, so that you could judge that the world had lost its innocence.

The man who was caught up to the third heaven says, “Nor do I judge myself” (1 Corinthians 4:3); and you dare to pronounce judgment upon the whole earth, across which Christ’s inheritance is spreading!

Furthermore, if what you said seems sufficiently decisive to you—“Whoever is not innocent does not possess holiness”—I ask: if Saul did not possess the holiness of the sacrament, what was David venerating in him? But if he possessed innocence, why did he persecute an innocent man?

For because of the sacred anointing David both honored him while he was alive and avenged him after he was killed. And because he had cut off even a small piece from Saul’s garment, he trembled with a stricken heart.

There you have it: Saul did not possess innocence, and yet he possessed holiness—not the holiness of his life, for no one can have that without innocence, but the holiness of God’s sacrament, which is holy even in wicked people.

## CHAPTER XLIX

**113. PETILIANUS said:** For if you faithless people know the Law, let me say this without insulting the Law itself: even the devil knows it. For when the Lord God was dealing with the righteous Job, he answered concerning the Law as though he were righteous, just as it is written:

> “The Lord said to the devil, ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a man without wickedness, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil and persevering in integrity? But you asked that I should destroy all that he has without cause.’ And the devil answered and said to the Lord, ‘Skin for skin, and whatever a man has he will give for his life’” (Job 2:3–4).

There he speaks legally—the one who strives against the Law. And again he dared to test the Lord Christ with his words, as it is written:

> “The devil took Jesus into the holy city, set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, ‘Throw yourself down; for it is written, “He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may lift you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”’ Jesus said, ‘Again it is written, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God”’” (Matthew 4:5–7).

You know the Law, I say, like the devil, who is defeated in his attempts and confounded in his deeds.

**114. AUGUSTINE replied:** I could indeed ask you in what Law the words spoken by the devil when he accused the holy man Job before God are written—if my purpose were to show that, although you say the devil knows the Law, you yourself do not know it. But since that is not the issue between us, I pass it over.

You tried to demonstrate that the devil was learned in the Law, as though we were saying that everyone who knows the words of the Law is righteous. I therefore do not see how your wish to mention the devil helps you, unless perhaps it was so that we might remember how you imitate the devil himself.

For just as he brought forward the words of the Law against the giver of the Law, so you accuse people whom you do not know by means of the words of the Law, in order to resist the promises of God written in that same Law.

Furthermore, I would like you to tell me, when those Confessors of yours hurl themselves to their deaths, for whom do they claim martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0299] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “for whom do they say they suffer martyrdom.” Ambrose and the manuscripts read, “for whom do they claim martyrdom.” The phrase is frequent in Augustine elsewhere in ancient manuscripts.]? For Christ, who drove away the devil when he suggested such things, or rather for the devil himself, who suggested that Christ do such things?

There are two especially disgraceful and common deaths among those who kill themselves: the noose and the precipice. You yourself said at the beginning of this letter, “The betrayer perished by the noose; he left the noose for such men.” That has nothing whatever to do with us. For we do not honor as martyrs those who tied a rope around their own necks.

How much more plausibly may we say against you: the devil, the teacher of the betrayer, wished to persuade Christ to throw himself from the precipice, but was repelled. What, then, should those be called who were persuaded by him and obeyed? What but enemies of Christ and friends of the devil; disciples of the seducer and fellow disciples of the betrayer?

For both groups learned voluntary deaths from one teacher: he taught the noose, these the precipice.

[Col. 0300]

## CHAPTER L

**115. PETILIANUS said:** But in order to destroy your individual arguments: if you call yourselves priests, God the Lord said through the prophet, “The Lord’s vengeance is upon false priests.”

**116. AUGUSTINE replied:** Seek rather what you can say truthfully, not where you can curse; and what you can teach, not what you can accuse.

## CHAPTER LI

**117. PETILIANUS said:** If, as we said above, you wretched men claim the chair for yourselves, you certainly possess the chair that the prophet and psalmist David declared to be the chair of pestilence (Psalm 1:1). It has justly been left to you, because the holy cannot sit upon it.

**118. AUGUSTINE replied:** Do you not see that these are not arguments but empty insults? This is what I said shortly before: you speak the words of the Law, but do not consider against whom you speak them—just as the devil spoke the words of the Law but did not recognize to whom he was speaking.

The devil wished to cast down our Head, who was to ascend on high, whereas you wish to reduce the body of that same Head, which is spread throughout the whole earth, to a tiny part.

Shortly before, you yourself said that we know the Law and speak legally, but blush in our deeds. You say these things without proving anything; but even if you proved them against some people, you would not thereby establish them against the rest.

Nevertheless, if everyone throughout the world were such as you most foolishly accuse them of being, what has the Chair of the Church of Rome done to you, in which Peter sat and in which Anastasius now sits? Or what has the Church of Jerusalem done to you, in which James sat and in which John now sits? We are joined to these churches in catholic unity, while you have separated yourselves from them by criminal frenzy.

Why do you call the apostolic Chair the chair of pestilence? If it is because of people whom you think speak the Law but do not practice it, did the Lord Jesus Christ, because of the Pharisees of whom he said, “They speak and do not act,” do any injury to the chair on which they sat?

Did he not commend the chair of Moses and rebuke them while preserving the honor of the chair? For he said:

> “The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ chair. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they speak and do not act” (Matthew 23:2–3).

If you considered these things, you would not blaspheme, on account of the people whom you defame, the apostolic Chair with which you do not share communion. But what else is this than not knowing what to say and yet being unable to do anything except curse?

## CHAPTER LII

**119. PETILIANUS said:** If you judge that you perform sacrifices, God himself says this concerning you, the most wicked of men:

> “The criminal who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog; and whoever offers fine flour is like one who pours out swine’s blood” (Isaiah 66:3).

Know what your sacrifice is, you who have already shed human blood. And again:

> “Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning; everyone who eats of it will be defiled” (Hosea 9:4).

**120. AUGUSTINE replied:** We say that each person’s sacrifice is such as is the person who approaches to offer it and such as is the person who approaches to receive it; and that those people eat from the sacrifices of such persons who approach them in the same condition as those who offer them.

Thus, if a wicked person offers to God and a good person receives from it, it is such for each person as each one has been; for it is also written, “All things are clean for the clean” (Titus 1:15).

By this true and catholic principle, you too were not defiled by Optatus’s sacrifice, if you disapproved of his deeds. Certainly, the bread of the one beneath whose wickedness the whole of Africa was mourning was bread of mourning. But it is the evil of schism, common to all of you, that makes the bread of mourning common to all of you [Note: [Col. 0301] In the manuscripts: “But the bread of mourning, common to all of you, is made the fault of all of you by the evil of schism.”].

For according to the judgment of your council, Felicianus of Musti shed human blood. For when you condemned them, you said at the Council of Bagai, “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Psalm 13:3).

See, then, what sort of sacrifice the man offers whom you have as a priest, when you have condemned him as a sacrilegious person. And if you think that this does you no harm, I ask you: what harm will the emptiness of your accusations do to the whole world?

## CHAPTER LIII

**121. PETILIANUS said:** If you offer a prayer to the Lord or pour out an entreaty, it benefits you nothing at all. Your feeble prayers are emptied of their force by your bloodstained conscience, because the Lord God hears a pure conscience more readily than prayers, as the Lord Christ says:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

God’s will is certainly good; for that reason we ask in the sacred Prayer, “Your will be done in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 6:11), so that, because his will is good, he may grant us what is good. You therefore do not do God’s will, because you perpetrate evil every day.

**122. AUGUSTINE replied:** If we said all these things against you, would not anyone who heard us—provided he himself were sane—judge us to be mad litigants rather than Christian disputants?

We therefore do not return curse for curse. “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, correcting those who think differently with modesty” (2 Timothy 2:24–25).

If we were to bring forward those who commit evil among you every day, we would be arguing foolishly, accusing some people on the basis of others. But if we admonish you that, just as you do not want those things brought against you, so you should not bring the deeds of others against us, then we correct you with modesty—if you ever come to your senses [Note: [Col. 0301] The printed editions read, “if anyone ever comes to his senses”; the particle “but” has been omitted.].

## CHAPTER LIV

**123. PETILIANUS said:** Even if, perhaps—which I do not know—you drive out demons, this will not benefit you. For the demons yield neither to your faith nor to your merits; they are driven out in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

**124. AUGUSTINE replied:** Thanks be to God, because at last you have confessed that the invoked name of Christ can be effective for the salvation of others, even when it is invoked by sinners.

Understand from this, then, that when Christ’s name is invoked, the sins of others do not harm another person’s salvation. As for how we invoke Christ’s name, we do not need your judgment, but that of the one whom we invoke. For he alone can know with what heart he is invoked.

Yet from his words we are certain that he is invoked for salvation by all the nations that are blessed in the seed of Abraham.

[Col. 0302]

## CHAPTER LV

**125. PETILIANUS said:** Even if you perform miracles and wonders in every respect, because of your wickedness the Lord does not know you—not even then, as the Lord himself says:

> “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ Then I will say to them, ‘I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

**126. AUGUSTINE replied:** We acknowledge the Lord’s words. Hence the Apostle also says, “If I have faith so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

The question, then, is who possesses love. You will find that it is none but those who love unity. As for the expulsion of demons and the power of miracles—since many who do not perform such things nevertheless belong to the kingdom of God, while many who do perform them do not belong to it—neither our people nor yours should glory if some happen to possess these abilities.

For the Lord did not even wish the Apostles, who truly could perform such things in a saving and beneficial manner, to rejoice in them, when he said to them, “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Therefore I could say these things that you have taken from the Gospel to you, if I saw you performing miraculous works; and you could say them to me, if you saw me doing such things. Let us not say to one another what can equally be said against the other side.

And, setting aside evasions, since we are seeking where Christ’s Church is, let us hear the one who redeemed it with his blood saying, “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and even to the whole earth” (Acts 1:8).

When you hear whose words these are, you can see from whom the person who does not share communion with this Church—which is spread throughout the whole earth—has separated.

What, then, is more foolish than to share in the Lord’s sacraments and not share in the Lord’s words? Such people will surely say, “In your name we ate and drank,” and will hear, “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:22): they eat and drink his body and blood in the sacrament, but do not acknowledge in the Gospel his members, spread throughout the whole world, and therefore at the judgment they are not counted among them [Note: [Col. 0302] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “with them”; Ambrose and the manuscripts read, “among them.”].

## CHAPTER LVI

**127. PETILIANUS said:** Even if, as you yourselves think, you follow the Lord’s Law purely, let us dispute legally from that most holy Law itself. The Apostle Paul says:

> “The Law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 1:8).

What, then, does the Law say?

> “You shall not kill.”

What Cain the murderer did once, you have often done to your brothers.

**128. AUGUSTINE replied:** We do not wish to be like you. For there is no lack of things that can be said, just as you say these things; nor of things that can be known, although you do not know these; nor of things that can be demonstrated, although you do not demonstrate these.

## CHAPTER LVII

**129. PETILIANUS said:** It was said, “You shall not commit adultery.” If each of you is chaste in the flesh, he is an adulterer in spirit, because he adulterates holiness.

**130. AUGUSTINE replied:** These things can truthfully be said of some people, both ours and yours. If they are displeasing to both of us, they belong neither to our side nor to yours.

But what you say of some, and do not prove even in their case, you want accepted as though you had proved it—not merely of some who degenerate from the seed of Abraham, but of all the nations that are blessed in the seed of Abraham.

## CHAPTER LVIII

**131. PETILIANUS said:** It was said, “You shall not bear false witness.” When you falsely claim that we hold what belongs to you before the kings of this world [Note: [Col. 0303] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “you hold”; manuscript reading.], are you not fabricating falsehoods?

**132. AUGUSTINE replied:** If what you hold is not ours [Note: [Col. 0303] The printed editions read “yours.” Corrected from the manuscripts.], then what you received from the Maximianists was not theirs either.

But if those possessions were yours because the Maximianists had committed sacrilegious schism by refusing communion with Donatus’s party, consider what places you hold and with whose inheritance you refuse communion. Think about what you can answer—not to the kings of this world, but to Christ the King.

Of him it was said, “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8). What river, indeed, except the place where he was baptized and where the dove descended upon him—a great sign of love and unity?

You do not share communion with this unity, yet you continue to hold the places belonging to unity. And you bring against us the charge of association with the kings of this world, although by the decrees of proconsuls you expelled your own schismatics from the places belonging to Donatus’s party.

These are not words flying idly through the air. People are alive; cities bear witness; proconsular and municipal records are read aloud. Let the slanderous voice finally fall silent—the voice that accuses the whole earth of association with the kings of this world, through whose proconsuls the severed faction could not spare the faction that had been severed.

Therefore, when we say that you hold what is ours, we are not shown to be bearing false witness unless you show that we are not in Christ’s Church. You never cease to say this, but you will never be able to demonstrate it. Indeed, when you say this, you bring the charge of false testimony not against us now, but against Christ himself.

For we are in the Church that was foretold by his own testimony, where he testified through his witnesses, saying, “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and even to the whole earth.”

We show that you are false witnesses not only because you resist this truth, but also in the very judgment by which you contended against the Maximianist schism.

For if you were acting according to the Law of Christ, how much more appropriately may some Christian emperors establish judgments according to that Law, if pagan proconsuls are able to judge according to it?

But if you thought that the laws of earthly authority should also be employed for assistance, we do not criticize you. Paul did this when, against those who were injuring him, he declared that he was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25).

But I ask: by what earthly laws was it decreed that the Maximianists should be expelled from their places? You will find none at all. Rather, you wanted to expel them by the laws enacted against heretics, including laws enacted against you yourselves. Against the weak, you prevailed as though you were the stronger.

Since they could do nothing, they call themselves innocent—as a wolf under a lion [Col. 0304]. Yet surely you would not use laws enacted against you against others except by bearing false witness.

For if those laws are true, you too should yield the places you hold. But if they are false, why did you use them to exclude others? What is more, they are true, and you could not have expelled others by them except deceitfully.

For the judges wished to serve those laws by expelling heretics; consequently, they ought to have expelled you first. But you declared yourselves Catholics so that the laws by which you oppressed others would spare you.

You may see what you appear to yourselves in your own eyes; yet according to those laws you are not Catholics. Why, then, did you either deceive those laws by false testimony if they were true, or use them to oppress others if they were false?

## CHAPTER LIX

**133. PETILIANUS said:** It was said, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exodus 20:13–17). You plunder what belongs to us so that you may possess it as your own.

**134. AUGUSTINE replied:** Whatever unity possessed belongs to us, since we remain in unity not according to human accusations but according to the words of Christ, in whom all the nations of the whole earth are blessed.

Nor do we separate ourselves from the fellowship of the wheat because of the wicked whom we cannot separate from the Lord’s wheat before the winnowing of the judgment.

And if you began to possess places that had already been cut off, because the Lord gave us what had been taken from us, we do not therefore covet what belongs to another: by the command of the one to whom all things belong, they became ours, and justly ours. You used them for separation; we use them for unity.

Otherwise, even the first people of God could have been accused by those from whom they were expelled, by divine power, because they were using that land wickedly, of coveting what belonged to another.

The Jews themselves, from whom the kingdom was taken and given, according to the Lord’s words, “to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43), could accuse the Church of Christ of coveting what belonged to another, because the Church possesses the places where Christ’s persecutors once ruled.

And finally, when it is said to you yourselves, “You covet what belongs to another, because you expelled the Maximianists from the basilicas,” you cannot find an answer.

## CHAPTER LX

**135. PETILIANUS said:** By what law, then, do you show yourselves to be Christians, when you act contrary to the Law?

**136. AUGUSTINE replied:** You wish to quarrel, not to debate.

## CHAPTER LXI

**137. PETILIANUS said:** The Lord Christ says, “Whoever does and teaches in this way shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” But he condemns you wretched men in this way: “Whoever annuls one of these commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.”

**138. AUGUSTINE replied:** When you perhaps state the testimonies of Scripture differently from the way they stand, and when they do not pertain to the matter under discussion between us, I do not greatly concern myself with it. But when they obstruct what we are treating, unless they are quoted truthfully, I do not think you ought to be angry if I remind you how it is written.

Look: what you have just quoted is not written that way. It is written rather:

> “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

And immediately he continued:

> “For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19–20).

Elsewhere he shows and reproves the Pharisees because they speak and do not act. He signified them here also when he said, “Whoever breaks and teaches in this way”—that is, teaches in words what he has broken in deeds.

He commanded that our righteousness exceed theirs, so that we should do and likewise teach. Yet even because of those Pharisees, to whom you compare us not through prudence but through malice, the Lord did not command that the chair of Moses be abandoned, which certainly prefigured his own.

For while saying that they sit on Moses’ chair and speak but do not act, he nevertheless urged the people to do what they say and not to do what they do (Matthew 23:2–3), so that the holiness of the chair would not be abandoned and the unity of the flock would not be divided because of wicked shepherds.

## CHAPTER LXII

**139. PETILIANUS said:** And again: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come.”

**140. AUGUSTINE replied:** This too is not written that way, and see how greatly you have been misled.

The Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18).

But this is one thing, and something else is what the Lord said in the Gospel:

> “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:31–32).

You began with a sentence from the Apostle and ended it as though it were one sentence from the Gospel. I do not believe you did this through fraud, but through error.
