Neither passage pertains to the matter at hand, and I do not see at all why you said these things or in what manner you said them—unless perhaps, because you had said above that those who annul one of the commandments were condemned by the Lord, you considered how many people you have who annul not one commandment but many.

To prevent this from being brought against you, you wished in passing to introduce a distinction among sins: that it is one thing to break some commandment, from which forgiveness can readily be obtained, and another thing to sin against the Holy Spirit, which will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

Fearing, then, the contagion of sins, you did not want to leave this unmentioned [Note: [Col. 0305] The manuscripts read thus. The printed editions read, “you wanted to leave this unmentioned,” and shortly afterward “this again,” instead of “this in passing”; the latter is less satisfactory.]. And again, fearing the depth of the question, which exceeded your strength, you wanted to touch upon it hurriedly, with such agitation that—just as people who are hurrying in confusion sometimes dress or put on their shoes incorrectly—you did not attend either to what belonged where or to where and how it was written.

But you are so ignorant of the nature of that sin which will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come that, although you believe us to be guilty of it, you nevertheless promise us its remission through your Baptism.

How can this happen if it is such a sin that it will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come?

[Col. 0306]

## CHAPTER LXIII

**141. PETILIANUS said:** By what means, then, do you fulfill the divine commandments? The Lord Christ says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” You exhale the riches of your persecuting madness.

**142. AUGUSTINE replied:** Say these things rather to your Circumcellions.

## CHAPTER LXIV

**143. PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” You, therefore, the unmeek, have lost both earth and heaven.

**144. AUGUSTINE replied:** Hear the Lord saying again and again, “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and even to the whole earth” (Acts 1:8).

Why, then, did those not lose earth and heaven who, so as not to share communion with the whole earth, despise the words of the one seated in heaven?

As for your meekness, let not your voices but the clubs of the Circumcellions be questioned. You will say, “What does that have to do with us?” As though we were mentioning these things for any other reason than that you should give this answer.

Your schism does concern you precisely because you do not want the sin of others to concern you. Yet you separated yourselves from us for no other reason than that you brought another person’s crime against us.

## CHAPTER LXV

**145. PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” You, our executioners, make us mourn, but you do not mourn.

**146. AUGUSTINE replied:** Consider for a moment how many people, and how great a mourning, your armed men’s cry, “Praises to God,” has caused [Note: [Col. 0306] The printed editions read, “how much and how great a mourning the praises of your devotees have brought to God” (or “therefore the praises of your devotees”). Corrected from the manuscripts. Erasmus alone has “therefore the praises,” incorrectly. For “Praises to God” was the cry of the Circumcellions: “People fear them more than the roar of a lion—‘Praises to God,’” Augustine says, *Exposition on Psalm 132*, no. 6. Likewise in the same work: “Your ‘Praises to God’ make people weep.”].

Say again, “What does that have to do with us?” And I will again ask: what does what you say—“What does that have to do with us?”—have to do with the whole world? What does it have to do with those who praise the Lord’s name from the rising of the sun to its setting? What does it have to do with the whole earth that sings the new song? What does it have to do with the seed of Abraham, in which all nations are blessed (Genesis 22:18)?

Therefore the sacrilege of your schism does concern you, because you say that the deeds of your people do not concern you [Note: [Col. 0306] The printed editions read, “because they do not concern us.” The manuscripts are more accurate.]. From this you understand that the deeds of those on account of whom you separated yourselves from the whole world would not concern the whole world either—even if you approved of them.

## CHAPTER LXVI

**147. PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” For you, righteousness consists in thirsting for our blood.

**148. AUGUSTINE replied:** What can I say to you, except that you are slanderous? The unity of Christ indeed hungers and thirsts for you. May it consume you, so that you will not be heretics!

## CHAPTER LXVII

**149. PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” When should I call you merciful, since you inflict punishments upon the righteous? Or should I call your communion most wicked, since you defile souls? [Note: [Col. 0306] The manuscripts read: “When should I call you merciful, since you inflict punishments upon the righteous? Or should I call you to the most wicked communion, since you defile souls?”]

[Col. 0307]

**150. AUGUSTINE replied:** You do not prove yourselves righteous, nor do you prove that we inflict punishments even upon the unrighteous. Yet just as deceptive flattery is often cruel, so correction is always merciful when it is just.

For what is the meaning of the words you do not understand: “Let the righteous correct me in mercy, and rebuke me”? After speaking of the severity of merciful correction, he immediately added something about the gentleness of harmful flattery and said, “But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Psalm 140:5).

You, then, consider the place to which you are called and from which you are called back. For how do you know with what disposition toward you is the person whom you consider savage?

Whatever that disposition may be, each person carries his own burden, both among us and among you. But cast away the burden of schism, which all of you carry, so that you may carry your good burdens in unity; and those who carry evil burdens, if you can, correct mercifully, and if you cannot, tolerate peacefully.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

**151. PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” When will you see God, you who carry the blindness of an unclean wickedness in your hearts?

**152. AUGUSTINE replied:** Why do you say this? Perhaps we bring against all nations things that people say without knowing them, while we refuse to understand plainly what God foretold concerning all nations?

This is great blindness of heart. And if you do not recognize it in yourselves, that is an even greater blindness of heart.

**153. [Note: [Col. 0307] Here the printed editions, Ambrose, and Erasmus mark chapter 69; afterward they agree with Lovaniensis in placing the material under chapter 70, beginning with the words “PETILIANUS said: He says to you,” etc.] PETILIANUS said:** “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:3–9). You fabricate peace through crime and seek unity through war.

154. **AUGUSTINE replied:** We do not fabricate peace through crime; rather, we proclaim the peace of the Gospel. If you are at peace with the Gospel, you will also be at peace with us. When the Lord rose again and offered himself to his disciples not merely to be seen with their eyes but also to be touched with their hands, he began from this point: “Peace be with you,” he said. And he disclosed in the words that followed how that peace itself was to be maintained. For there he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem” (Luke 24:36, 45–47). Be at peace with these words, and you will not dissent from us.

For if we seek unity through war, our war could not have been praised more splendidly, since it is written, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 5:43). And again it is written, “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29). Yet “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). If no one hates his own flesh, and yet he desires against his own flesh, behold: unity is sought through war, so that the chastised body may be subjected to servitude.

But what the spirit does against the flesh, warring not out of hatred but out of love, this spiritual people do against the carnal, so that what they do toward themselves they may also do toward them, because they love their neighbors as neighbors. The war of spiritual people is that correction carried out in love; their sword is the word of God. It is for such a war that they are summoned by the apostolic trumpet, sounding with great force: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2). Behold, we do not act with iron, but with the word.

You, however, neither answer with truth nor accuse truthfully; you do not correct your own faults but bring forward those of others. Christ gives true testimony concerning the whole world; you give false testimony against the whole world in opposition to Christ. If we believed you rather than Christ, we would be peacemakers; because we believe Christ rather than you, we fabricate peace through crime. And while you say and do these things, you dare moreover to invoke the words, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”

### CHAPTER LXIX

155. **PETILIAN said:** When the apostle Paul says: “I beseech you, brethren—I, a prisoner in the Lord—that you walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, earnestly striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:1–3).

156. **AUGUSTINE replied:** If you not only said these things but also listened to them, you would bear known evils for the sake of peace, rather than inventing unknown ones on account of dissension—or because you later learned to bear, for the sake of Donatus’s unity, the evils of Optatus, which were notorious and widely known. What madness is this? Known men are tolerated lest the division be divided again; unknown men are defamed lest one remain within that very integrity.

### CHAPTER LXX

157. **PETILIAN said:** The prophet says to you: “Peace, peace—and where is there peace?” (Jer. 8:11).

158. **AUGUSTINE replied:** You are saying this to us, not the prophet. We therefore answer you: If you seek where peace is, open your eyes and see of whom it was said, “He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 45:10). If you seek where peace is, open your eyes toward that city which cannot be hidden, established upon a mountain. Open your eyes also toward the mountain itself, and let Daniel show it to you growing from a small stone and filling the whole earth (Dan. 2:35).

But when the prophet says to you, “Peace, peace—and where is there peace?” what will you point out? The party of Donatus, unknown to countless nations among whom Christ is known? It is not the city that cannot be hidden. And why is it not, except that it has not been established upon that mountain? For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14)—not Donatus, who made one into two.

### CHAPTER LXXI

159. **PETILIAN said:** “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). You are not blessed, but you make martyrs blessed—martyrs whose souls, of course, fill heaven and whose bodily memorials have made the earth flourish. You therefore do not venerate them; rather, you make those whom we are to venerate.

160. **AUGUSTINE replied:** Certainly, if it had not been said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” but instead had been said, “Blessed are those who throw themselves headlong,” your martyrs would fill heaven. Indeed, we see many flowers of the earth arising from their bodies, but, as the saying goes, the flower is ashes.

### CHAPTER LXXII

161. **PETILIAN said:** Since, then, you are not blessed because you falsify the commandments, the Lord Christ condemns you by divine pronouncements:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people: for you yourselves do not enter, and you do not allow those entering to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you traverse sea and dry land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law, judgment and mercy and faith. These things ought to have been done, and those not omitted. Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:13, 15, 23–28).

162. **AUGUSTINE replied:** Tell me whether you have said anything that could not similarly be said against you, in a cursing and abusive voice. Yet from what I have said above, anyone who wishes will find that these things can be said against you not through empty insults but through true testimonies.

Nevertheless, since the occasion has arisen, something must not be passed over. Certainly the ancient people of God regarded circumcision as corresponding to Baptism. I therefore ask: if those Pharisees against whom so much is said had made someone a proselyte—someone who, if he imitated them, would have been, as it is said, twice as much a son of Gehenna as they were—if that person were corrected and wished to imitate Simeon, Zachariah, and Nathanael, would he then be judged by them to require circumcision again?

If it is ridiculous to say this, although by your customary manner and empty rhetoric you compare us with such people, why do you baptize after us? And if you are such people, how much more truly and properly do we not baptize after you, just as those whom I have named ought not to have been circumcised after the worst Pharisees?

Furthermore, since such men sat in Moses’ seat, to which the Lord preserved its honor, why do you blaspheme the Apostolic Chair on account of those whom you compare, rightly or wrongly, with these men?

### CHAPTER LXXIII

163. **PETILIAN said:** But such things do not frighten us Christians. For what you are about to do wickedly, we have as a command beforehand from Christ the Lord: “Behold,” he says, “I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10:16). You embody wolfish rage, for you lay or prepare snares for the churches no differently than wolves greedily eye sheepfolds, ever breathing destruction and, with throats suffused with blood, exhaling their wrath.

[Note: [Col. 0309] The printed editions have *suspirant* (“they sigh” or “breathe out”); the manuscripts have the better reading *respirant* (“they exhale” or “breathe out”).]

164. **AUGUSTINE replied:** I would gladly apply that saying to you, but I would not use those words: they are exceedingly foolish, or rather insane. What was necessary was for you to show by some definite proofs—not by the emptiest curses—that we are wolves and you are sheep.

For when I say in turn, “We are sheep, but you are wolves,” do you really think that it makes any difference because you express it in swollen language? But observe how I prove what I say. Surely you know that the Lord says in the Gospel, whether you wish it or not: “My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

There are many voices of the Lord concerning different matters. To give an example: if someone were doubtful whether the same Lord had risen bodily, and his words were recited in which he said, “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have”; if, even after hearing these words, he refused to assent to belief in his risen body, he would certainly not be reckoned among the Lord’s sheep, because he did not follow his voice after hearing it.

So now, since the question between us is where the Church is, when we recite the words from that very Gospel passage in which, after his resurrection, he also offered his body to be touched by those who doubted, we recite the words that follow, in which he demonstrated the future extent of the Church, saying: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem” (Luke 24:39, 46–47).

[Note: [Col. 0310] The printed editions read “we recite the following words to those disputing”; *disputantibus* (“to those disputing”) is absent from the manuscripts.]

And you refuse to share communion with all the nations among whom these things have been fulfilled. How, then, are you the sheep of this shepherd, whose voice you hear but not only do not obey—you even oppose it?

We demonstrate from this that you are not sheep. But that you are wolves, hear how we demonstrate it. Since it is already evident from his own words where the Church is, it is clear where Christ’s sheepfold is. Therefore, from this sheepfold, demonstrated and defined by the Lord’s most certain words, whoever separates sheep—not, I do not say, through false accusations, but through the uncertain accusations of human beings, as is plainly the case—and kills those who have been snatched away and alienated from the life of unity and love, are they not themselves ravenous wolves?

But they too praise and preach the Lord Christ. These, therefore, are the ones of whom he himself says: “They are clothed in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:15–16). The sheep’s skin is found in their praises of Christ; the wolf’s fruit is found in their cursing teeth.

### CHAPTER LXXIV

165. **PETILIAN said:** O wretched traditors! It was indeed fitting that Scripture should be fulfilled in this way; but this is what I grieve about in you: that you deserved to fulfill the part of wickedness.

166. **AUGUSTINE replied:** I could more appropriately say, “O wretched traditors!” if I wished—or rather, if justice counseled me—to charge all of you with the deeds of some among your number. As for what applies to all of you, “O wretched heretics!”—I would say the rest of your words myself. For it is written: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

“Therefore, it was necessary that Scripture should be fulfilled in this way; but this is what I grieve about in you: that you deserved to fulfill the part of wickedness.”

[Col. 0311]

### CHAPTER LXXV

167. **PETILIAN said:** But the Lord Christ commanded us, in opposition to your deadly deeds, to practice simple patience and innocence. For what does he say? “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you”; and, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35).

168. **AUGUSTINE replied:** Unless you transferred these words, so remote from your conduct, onto the surface of your speech, how would you cover yourselves with sheep’s clothing?

### CHAPTER LXXVI

169. **PETILIAN said:** The apostle Paul also, when he suffered immense persecutions from all nations and endured still greater ones from false brothers, as he himself testifies after being frequently afflicted, says: “In dangers from nations, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from false brothers” (2 Cor. 11:26). And again he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16). Since, then, you attack us as false brothers,

[Note: [Col. 0311] So the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: “you call us false brothers.”]

we imitate the patience of Paul our teacher amid our dangers.

[Note: [Col. 0311] Two manuscripts have: “amid your dangers,” that is, “the dangers we suffer from you.”]

170. **AUGUSTINE replied:** Certainly these are the false brothers about whom the same apostle complains elsewhere, while commending Timothy’s genuine sincerity: “I have no one of like mind who will be genuinely concerned for you. For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:20–21).

He was speaking, of course, about those who were with him at the time when he wrote that Epistle. He was not saying that all Christians everywhere sought their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ. As I have said, he lamented those whom he had with him at the time when he wrote these words.

Whom else does he mean when he says elsewhere, “Outside were battles, inside fears” (2 Cor. 7:5), except those whom he feared all the more intensely because he feared them inwardly? If, then, you wished to imitate Paul inwardly, you would be one who tolerated false brothers, not one who slandered innocent people outside.

### CHAPTER LXXVII

171. **PETILIAN said:** For what sort of faith is there in you that does not possess love? Paul himself says:

“If I speak in the languages of human beings and have the knowledge of angels, but do not have love, I am like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. Or if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

172. **AUGUSTINE replied:** This is what I said shortly before: you wish to cover yourself with sheep’s skin, so that, if possible, the sheep may feel you biting it before it senses your approach.

Is this not a praise of love that habitually refutes your slander with the clearest truth? Or will these weapons of ours not be weapons because you are trying to seize them first? These are indeed living arrows: wherever they are thrown, they are recognized by those whom they kill.

[Note: [Col. 0311] The older codices read *agnoscunt* (“they recognize”) rather than *agnoscuntur* (“they are recognized”).]

If they are sent by us, they will remain lodged in you; if they are sent by you, they are turned back against you. By these apostolic words, which commend the excellence of love, we customarily show you how it profits people nothing, even when the sacraments or faith are present in them, if love is absent. Thus, when you come to Catholic unity, you may understand what is conferred upon you and how much you lacked.

For Christian love cannot be preserved except in the unity of the Church. In this way you may see that without it you are nothing, even if you retain Baptism and faith and, through it, could move mountains.

If this is also your judgment, let us not, in you, detest and repudiate either the sacraments of God, which we recognize, or faith itself; rather, let us hold fast to love, without which we are nothing both with the sacraments and with faith.

[Note: [Col. 0312] Erasmus and the Cygirannensis manuscript read “not in us.”]

We hold fast to love if we embrace unity; and we embrace unity if we recognize it not by fabricating it in our own part through our words, but through Christ’s words in unity.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII

173. **PETILIAN said:** And again: “For love is magnanimous and kind; love is not jealous, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests. You seek what belongs to others. It is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, endures all things; love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:1–8).

This is to say briefly: Love does not persecute; love does not inflame emperors against other souls; love does not seize what belongs to others; love does not even kill the people whom it has stripped.

174. **AUGUSTINE replied:** How many times must I say to you: if you do not prove these things, they apply to no one; but if you do prove them, they do not apply to us—just as those things do not apply to you which your own people daily commit through the crimes of the furious, the debaucheries of the drunken, the blindness of those who rush headlong, and the tyranny of robbers.

Who does not see that what I proclaim is true? But now, if love were in you, you would rejoice with the truth. How elegantly the words “Love bears all things, endures all things” are spoken beneath sheep’s skin! But when the investigation begins, the wolf’s teeth cannot be covered.

For when love, because of what was said—“bearing with one another in love, earnestly striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3)—would compel you, even if you knew of certain evils within, not to consent to them but nevertheless, if you could not prevent them, to endure them, lest, because of the wicked who are to be separated at the final winnowing, you should now break the bond of peace with the society of the good, you are shaken outside by the wind of frivolity, and you charge the wheat with the crime of the chaff. What you invent about the wicked, you assert to have force through contagion even against the good.

And when the Lord said, “The field is this world,” and, after speaking about the wheat and the weeds, said, “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13:38–39, 30), you labor through your words to make people believe that the wheat has already failed throughout the whole field and remains only in your tiny portion—while you wish Christ to be considered a liar and yourself truthful.

Indeed, you speak against your own conscience. No one who looks in any way at the Gospel would dare say in his heart that, among so many nations where “Amen” is answered with almost one voice and “Alleluia” is sung, there are no Christians.

And yet, lest the party of Donatus, which does not share communion with the whole world, appear to be in error, if an angel from heaven who could behold the entire world were to tell you that nowhere outside your communion are there innocent and good people, you would undoubtedly rejoice over the iniquity of the human race and boast that you had spoken the truth before you knew it.

How, then, is love in you, when it does not rejoice over iniquity? But do not be deceived: throughout the field—that is, throughout the world—the Lord’s wheat is growing until the end of the age. Christ said this; Christ is the truth. Let love be in you, and let it rejoice with the truth. Even if an angel from heaven should preach against the Gospel, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8).

### CHAPTER LXXIX

175. **PETILIAN said:** Finally, what is the justification for persecution? I ask you, wretches: perhaps you think you are committing sin with some authority from the law.

176. **AUGUSTINE replied:** Whoever sins does not sin by the authority of the law but against the authority of the law. Since you ask what the justification for persecution is, I in turn ask you whose voice it is in the Psalm that says, “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. 100:5).

Therefore, inquire into either the cause or the manner of persecution, and do not, with such great ignorance, condemn persecutors of the wicked in general.

### CHAPTER LXXX

177. **PETILIAN said:** I, on the contrary, answer that Jesus Christ persecuted no one. And when certain sects displeased the Apostles, who brought the matter to him—for he had come to establish the faith in such a way that he did not compel people but rather invited them—the Apostles said to him: “Many lay hands in your name, and they are not with us.” Jesus said: “Leave them; if they are not against you, they are for you.”

178. **AUGUSTINE replied:** You speak the truth, that you will bring forth much more abundantly from your own resources things that are not found in the Scriptures. For if you wish to produce testimonies from the Holy Scriptures, will you produce things that you have not found?

The extent of your lies is in your own power. Where, indeed, is what you have stated written? When was it suggested to the Lord, or when was that answer given by the Lord? “Many lay hands in your name, and they are not with us”—no disciple ever said this to the Son of God. Therefore he could not have answered, “Leave them; if they are not against you, they are for you.”

There is, however, something similar that we really do read in the Gospel as having been reported to the Lord: someone was casting out demons in his name, but was not following him with the disciples. There the Lord says, “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Luke 9:49–50).

But this has absolutely nothing to do with demonstrating sects that the Lord supposedly spared. If some similarity of wording deceived you, it is not a lie but a human error. But if you wished to cast a fog of falsehood over those inexperienced in the Holy Scriptures, may you be pierced with remorse, confounded, and corrected.

There is nevertheless something for us to discuss concerning the very matter reported to the Lord. Just as at that time the holiness of Christ’s name had great efficacy apart from communion with the disciples, so the holiness of the sacrament has efficacy apart from communion with the Church.

For Baptism is consecrated only in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. What utterly insane person would say that, apart from communion with the Church, the name of the Son has efficacy but the names of the Father and the Holy Spirit do not? Or that it has efficacy in healing a person but not in consecrating Baptism?

[Note: [Col. 0314] The printed editions omit the words “but the names of the Father and the Holy Spirit do not”; after “the name of the Son has efficacy” they continue: “For what can have efficacy in healing a person?” The reading is corrected with the help of the Floriacensis manuscript.]

But plainly, apart from communion with the Church, the most holy bond of unity, and the supremely excellent gift of love, neither the one from whom a demon is expelled nor the one who is baptized attains eternal life—just as neither do those who appear to be inside through communion in the sacraments but are understood to be outside through the wickedness of their conduct.

We have already stated above that Christ also persecuted people physically when he drove them from the temple by scourging them.

### CHAPTER LXXXI

179. **PETILIAN said:** But the holy apostle Paul says this: “However Christ is proclaimed.”

180. **AUGUSTINE replied:** You speak against yourself; yet because you speak for the truth, if you love it, what you say may be for you. For I ask you: of whom did the apostle Paul say this? Let us recall the passage briefly, if you please.

“Some,” he says, “proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. Some do so out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel; but others proclaim Christ out of contentiousness, not sincerely, thinking that they can stir up affliction in my chains. What then? So long as Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether by pretense or in truth, I rejoice in this, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. 1:15–18).

We see that these people proclaimed something holy, pure, and true, but did not proclaim it purely; rather, they did so out of envy and rivalry, without love and without purity. Shortly before, you seemed to speak against us in praise of love, on the testimony of the Apostle, because where love is absent, whatever exists is of no benefit. Behold, these people lacked love, and yet the preaching of Christ was present—concerning which the Apostle says that he rejoiced.

For he did not rejoice in their evil but in the good of Christ’s name. Love was in him, for love “does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth” (1 Cor. 13:6). The envy that was in them, on the other hand, is a diabolical evil; through it the devil both fell and caused others to fall.

Where, then, were these people who were so wicked, whom the Apostle rebuked, but in whom there was so great a good that the Apostle rejoiced over it—inwardly or outwardly? Choose whichever you wish.

If they were inwardly present, behold: Paul knew them, and yet they did not defile him. In the same way, those about whom you say either true things or fabricate false ones would not defile you within the unity of the whole world. Why, then, did you separate yourselves? Why did you destroy yourselves through the sacrilege of criminal schism?

But if they were outside, behold: even in those who are outside—and who certainly cannot belong to eternal life because they lack love and do not hold unity—the holiness of Christ’s name is nevertheless present. On account of that very holiness of the name, the Apostle confirms their preaching with rejoicing, although he detests them.

Therefore, when those who were outside come to us, we do not wrong the name itself; rather, we correct the people and honor the name. You, then, must see how wickedly, in those whose deeds you apparently condemn, you also reject the sacrament of Christ’s name, which is holy in them.

You, for your part, judge that those whom the Apostle mentioned were outside the Church, as your words indicate. Thus, while you fear suffering persecution from Catholics—about which, by your speaking, you seek to arouse hatred against us—you have confirmed the name of Christ in heretics, against which you commit an offense by rebaptizing them.

[Note: [Col. 0315] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *baptizando* (“by baptizing”). Ambr. and the manuscripts have the better reading *rebaptizando* (“by rebaptizing”).]

### CHAPTER LXXXII

181. **PETILIAN said:** If, then, the great power of faith did not oppose some people, by what right do you persecute them, so as to force people to be defiled?

182. **AUGUSTINE replied:** We do not persecute you except in the way truth persecutes falsehood. Nor are we responsible if someone else has persecuted you in another way, just as you are not responsible for whatever your own people do in the same manner. Nor do we compel you to be defiled; we urge you to be healed.

[Note: [Col. 0315] The printed editions have *nostri* (“our people”) and below *si suademus* (“if we urge”); these have been corrected from the manuscripts to *vestri* (“your people”) and *sed suademus* (“but we urge”).]

### CHAPTER LXXXIII

183. **PETILIAN said:** If it had been lawful to compel someone by law even toward good things, then you yourselves, wretches, ought to have been compelled by us toward the purest faith. But far be it, far be it from our conscience, that we should compel anyone to our faith.

184. **AUGUSTINE replied:** No one is to be compelled to faith against his will. Yet through the severity—or rather, through the mercy—of God, unbelief is customarily punished by the scourges of tribulation. Surely, because the best conduct is chosen by freedom of will, it does not follow that the worst conduct is not punished by the integrity of the law.

Nevertheless, discipline that avenges evil living is out of order unless the preceding instruction in good living has been despised. Therefore, if laws have been enacted against you, you are not compelled by them to do good; you are prohibited from doing evil.

[Note: [Col. 0315] See below, no. 217, and *Against Gaudentius*, Book 1, nos. 28–54.]

For no one can do good unless he has chosen it, unless he has loved what lies within free will. But fear of punishment, even if it does not yet possess the delight of a good conscience, at least restrains evil desire within the confines of thought.

Who, then, enacted the laws that restrain your audacity? Were they not the very people of whom the Apostle says that they do not bear the sword without reason, “for they are God’s ministers, avengers for wrath against the one who does evil” (Rom. 13:4)?

The whole question, therefore, is whether you are not doing evil, when the whole world charges you with the sacrilege of so great a schism. Neglecting to examine this question, you speak of irrelevant matters; and while you live like robbers, you boast that you die like martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0315] See Letter 88, no. 8.]

And because you fear either the laws themselves, or public resentment, or your inability to resist—not, I say, so many people, but so many Catholic nations—you even glory in your gentleness, claiming that you compel no one to join your party.

In this way a kite, when frightened and unable to snatch the chicks, might call itself a dove. For where were you able to act, and did not act? From this you show how much more you would do if you could.

When Julian, hostile to the peace of Christ, restored to you the basilicas belonging to the unity, who could adequately recount the slaughter you carried out when your temples stood open and even demons exulted with you? Let Mauritania Caesariensis itself inquire what Rogatus the Moor endured from you in the Firmian war.

[Note: [Col. 0316] Concerning Rogatus the Moor, bishop of Carthennus in Mauritania Caesariensis, from whom the Rogatists—a schism among the Donatists—took their name, Augustine speaks in Letter 93 to Vincentius. The Rogatists called the other Donatists “Firmians” because they had suffered many grievous things from them through the tyrant Firmus; see Letter 87 to Emeritus, no. 10.]

During the time of Gildo, since one of your colleagues was his intimate and familiar friend, let the Maximianists see what they experienced.

[Note: [Col. 0316] Optatus of Thamugadi was a friend of Gildo.]

[Note: [Col. 0316] In the earlier editions this passage reads: “Who could adequately recount what Rogatus the Moor endured from you in the Firmian war? Let Mauritania Caesariensis itself inquire (Lov.), and the times of Gildo (Am.; ‘and during the time of Gildo,’ Er.; ‘and the times of Gildo’), since one of your colleagues was his most intimate friend. Let the Maximianists see (Am., ‘they saw’) what they experienced,” etc. The older books correct the errors and unsuitable punctuation.] 

For if one were permitted to summon Felicianus himself, who is now with you, to swear whether Optatus did not compel him to return unwillingly to your communion, he would not dare to move his lips—especially if the people of Musti were looking upon his face, since they witnessed what happened then.

But let these people, as I said, see what they suffered from those with whom they had done such things to Rogatus. The Catholic Church, consolidated under Catholic rulers who governed by land and sea, was savagely and hostilely attacked by Optatus with armed crowds.

That event was what first caused that law concerning ten pounds of gold to be brought against you before the deputy Seranus—a law which none of you has yet paid—and yet you accuse us of cruelty! What could be gentler than that such great crimes of yours should be punished by fines?

Who could recount all the things that, without any friendship—

[Note: [Col. 0316] Perhaps “without any authority.”]

—of judges or of any officials, each of you commits in your own places through your own domination, wherever you can? Who among us, in our own communities, has not either learned of some such thing from those who came before, or experienced it personally?

[Note: [Col. 0316] The printed editions have: “Who among you, in your own communities.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

At Hippo, where I am, are there not people who remember that during the time of his rule your Faustinian ordered that, because Catholics were few there, no one should bake bread for them? Thus the tenant-baker of one of our deacons threw away uncooked bread from his master’s house,

[Note: [Col. 0316] The printed editions have “his master’s house.” The manuscripts have *domnaedii sui*, “his lord’s house.” This word has already been restored elsewhere, in *Expositions on the Psalms* 38, no. 21.]

and denied him communion not only in the Roman city—

[Note: [Col. 0316] Augustine also indicates in Letter 35 to Eusebius, no. 3, that Hippo had been ennobled by the legal status of a Roman city.]

—but also in his own homeland, and not only in his homeland but even in his own house, although he had been condemned under no law of exile?

And what of the recent event—which I still mourn? Did not your Crispinus of Calama, after purchasing a property, and one under an emphyteutic lease at that, hesitate to submerge nearly eighty souls on the estate of Catholic emperors, whose laws ordered you not even to exist in their cities, by rebaptizing them in a single assault of terror, while they muttered amid pitiable groans?

[Note: [Col. 0317] Augustine complains about this matter to Crispinus himself in Letter 66.]

And for what reason, except because of such deeds, did you force even the laws about which you complain to be enacted—laws certainly far below the deserts of your crime, but laws nonetheless? Or would we not be driven from the fields on every side by the violent raids of your Circumcellions, who under your leadership serve in frenzied bands, unless we held you as hostages in the cities, so that, whether through fear or at least through shame, you might be unwilling to endure the public gaze and the reproach of honorable people?

Do not, therefore, say, “Far be it, far be it from our conscience that we should compel anyone to our faith.” You do so wherever you can; where you do not, you cannot—whether because you fear the laws, public resentment, or the multitude of those who resist you.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV

185. **PETILIAN said:** For the Lord Christ says, “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44). Why, then, do you not allow each person to follow free will, since the Lord God himself gave human beings free will, while showing the way of righteousness so that perhaps no one might perish through ignorance?

For he said: “I have set good and evil before you; I have set fire and water before you. Choose what you will.” By this freedom of choice, wretches, you have chosen for yourselves not water but fire. “Yet,” he says, “choose the good, so that you may live” (Sirach 15:17–18). You have condemned yourself as unwilling to live because you do not wish to choose the good.

[Note: [Col. 0317] The Cygirannensis manuscript has *clamasti* (“you cried out”) only here.]

186. AUGUSTINE replied: If I were to put to you the question of how God the Father draws people to the Son when he has left them to their free will, perhaps you would find it difficult to answer. For how does he draw them, if he leaves each person free to choose what he wishes? Yet both are true; few are able to penetrate this by understanding. Therefore, just as it is possible for the Father to draw to the Son those whom he has left to their free will, so it is possible for the coercive measures of laws, when they admonish people, not to take away free will.

Whatever hard and distressing thing a person suffers admonishes him to consider why he suffers it: so that, if he sees that he is suffering for justice, he may choose that good itself—to endure such things for justice; but if he sees that it is for iniquity that he suffers, then, considering that he is laboring and being tormented most fruitlessly, he may change his will for the better and at the same time be free both from sterile distress and from the iniquity itself, which would otherwise harm him much more gravely and destructively.

And when rulers establish something against you, believe that you are being admonished to consider why you suffer these things. If it is on account of justice, then they truly are your persecutors; but you, blessed because you have suffered persecution for justice, will possess the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:10; 1 Pet. 2:20). If, however, it is on account of the iniquity of your schism, what are they except your correctors? And you, like the other people guilty of various crimes who pay penalties imposed by the laws, are surely unhappy both in this age and in the age to come.

No one, then, takes away your free will. But attend carefully to what you choose instead: whether, corrected, to live in peace, or, persevering in wickedness, to endure true punishments under the name of a false martyrdom. I address you as though you were suffering something deserved by your iniquity, although you commit so many unworthy acts and reign amid such great impunity: so frenzied that through praises of God you terrify people more than with a war trumpet; so slanderous that you even attribute the voluntary plunges of your own people to our persecutions.

187. He also speaks as a most kindly teacher: “You who do not wish to choose the good have condemned yourself to be unwilling to live.” Indeed, if we believed your accusations, we would live well [Note: The old Floriacensis manuscript has “we would live well.”]; but because we believe God’s promises, we condemn ourselves to be unwilling to live.

You surely remember well what the apostles said to the Jews when they were forbidden to preach Christ. We therefore say the same, so that you may answer us whether one ought to obey God more than human beings (Acts 5:29). “Traitors,” “those who offer incense,” and “persecutors”—these are the words of human beings against human beings.

Christ has remained in Donatus’s faction alone, they say, in “love” [Note: Perhaps “dominion.”]. These are the words of people who exalt human glory under the name of Christ, so that Christ’s own glory may be diminished. For it is written, “In a populous nation is the glory of a king; but in the diminution of the people is the ruin of the ruler” (Prov. 14:28). These, then, are human words.

But the words in the Gospel—“It was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47)—are the words of Christ, commending the glory that he received from the Father in the breadth of his kingdom.

Having heard both, we choose this communion of the Church instead, and we place Christ’s words above human words. I ask: who is there who says that we have chosen evil, except one who says that Christ taught evil?

CHAPTER LXXXV

188. PETILIAN said: Did God, then, command that even schismatics be put to death? If he had commanded this altogether, you ought to be killed by some Scythians or barbarians, but not by Christians.

189. AUGUSTINE replied: Let your Circumcellions keep quiet, and do not frighten us with barbarians [Note: Perhaps, “and do not frighten us away from the barbarians.”]. But whether we or you are the schismatics, let neither you nor I be consulted; let Christ be consulted, so that he may identify [Note: The printed editions read “judge.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.] his Church.

Read the Gospel, then, and it answers you: “In Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Whoever, therefore, is not found in the Church should no longer be questioned, but should either be corrected and converted, or, when reproved, should not complain.

CHAPTER LXXXVI

190. PETILIAN said: For the Lord God has never rejoiced in human blood, since he wished the murderer of his brother Cain to remain alive as a living executioner [Note: The American and Erasmian editions read, “to remain alive as an executioner.” The Louvain editors correctly emended this from the manuscripts to “as a living executioner.” Yet afterward they themselves followed the error of the earlier editors in Augustine’s reply, printing “but to leave life to the executioner”; this has been corrected according to the old manuscripts, because they consistently join “executioner” adjectivally to “life.” [Col. 0319] So again below, together with the printed editions, they have “may they be tormented by an executioner’s life.”].

[Col. 0319] 191. AUGUSTINE replied: If God did not wish death to be inflicted on the murderer of his brother, but wished an executioner’s life to be left to him, see whether this may perhaps be the meaning: although the king’s heart is in God’s hand, and from that hand he has himself established many laws to admonish and correct you, no royal law has nevertheless commanded you to be killed. Perhaps this is because those among you who persist in the stubborn breath of sacrilegious madness are to be tormented with the punishment of Cain the parricide, by an executioner’s life [Note: The printed editions read “and by an executioner’s life.” The conjunction “and” is absent from the manuscripts.].

For we read that many were mercifully killed by Moses, the servant of God. In the fact that, on account of their abominable sacrilege, he pleaded with the Lord in such a way as to say, “Lord, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of your book” (Exod. 32:28, 31), his indescribable love and mercy are sufficiently apparent. Did he suddenly become cruel, then, when he descended from the mountain and ordered so many thousands to be killed?

Consider, therefore, whether perhaps, through the many laws enacted against you, you have been killed by no emperor because of God’s greater anger. Or do you not think that you should be compared with those fratricides?

Hear the Lord speaking through the prophet: “From the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense shall be brought to my name, and a pure offering. Great is my name among the nations, says the Lord almighty” (Mal. 1:11).

By your slanders you show that you begrudge this fraternal sacrifice, upon which God looks. And whenever you hear that the Lord’s name is praised from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. 112:3)—which is the living sacrifice of which it is said, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14)—your face falls like that of the murderer.

But because you cannot destroy the whole world, you are held by hatred of the thing itself, since John says, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). And would that an innocent brother were slaughtered by the weapons of your Circumcellions rather than fall into your tongue to be rebaptized! [Note: The American and Erasmian editions read “into your water,” with the manuscripts disagreeing.]

CHAPTER LXXXVII

192. PETILIAN said: We therefore admonish you, if you are willing to listen; and if you do not willingly accept it, we admonish you nonetheless, because the Lord Christ established for Christians not a model of killing but of dying. For if he so loved us while we resisted, he would not have wished to be killed for us.

193. AUGUSTINE replied: Would that your martyrs followed his example! They should not throw themselves down, which he did not do when the devil suggested it (Matt. 4:6–7). But when you persecute even our elders after their death with false testimony, where did you learn this example? When you try to stain us with the crimes of unknown people, while refusing to let the notorious evil deeds of your own people count against you, where did you learn this example?

But we are excessively proud if we grow angry with you on our own account, when we see you bearing false witness against the Lord himself. For he both promised and manifested his Church among all nations, and you contradict him.

You did not receive this example even from the Jews themselves, your persecutors. They persecuted the flesh of one walking on earth; you persecute the Gospel of one seated in heaven. The Gospel endured the flames of raging kings more mildly than it endures your tongues. When those kings set it on fire, unity remained; when you speak, unity cannot remain.

Those who wanted the Lord’s words destroyed by fire did not believe that what had been read could be despised. They would not therefore have exercised their flames against the Gospel if you had allowed your tongues to act against the Gospel.

In that persecution, Christ’s Gospel was sought out by some who raged, betrayed by others who were afraid, burned by still others who raged, and hidden by others who loved it. It was attacked by none who contradicted it. After the persecution of the nations had passed, you preserved for yourselves the more criminal parts of persecution.

Those who persecuted Christ’s name came to believe in Christ; those who are honored on account of Christ’s name contradict Christ.

CHAPTER LXXXVIII

194. PETILIAN said: Here you have the fullest proof that it is not lawful for a Christian to be involved in another’s destruction. The beginning of this discipline was established with Peter, as it is written: “Peter struck the ear of the servant of the Jewish high priest and cut it off. Jesus said to him, ‘Peter, put your sword back into its sheath. For whoever uses the sword will die by the sword’” (Matt. 26:51–52).

195. AUGUSTINE replied: Why, then, do you not restrain the weapons of the Circumcellions with a similar saying? Or would you think that you were speaking outside the Gospel if you said, “Whoever uses a club will die by a club”?

Grant us pardon, then, because our elders were unable to restrain those from whom you complain that Marculus was thrown down. For it is not written in the Gospel, “Whoever throws someone down will die by being thrown down.”

And would that, just as those acts were either false or belonged to the past, these men’s wooden weapons might also cease [Note: The printed editions read, “that their tongue might cease.” The manuscripts support the present correction.].

Perhaps you are angry because we strip your legions of their weapons—if not by laws, at least by words—by saying that they rage only with clubs. This was indeed their old wickedness, but now they have advanced excessively. Amid drunken banquets, and with women who have no husbands, they have learned to turn not only clubs but also to brandish iron and swing slings, enjoying free license to accompany, wander, jest, drink, and spend the night.

But why should I not say to them—may God know with what spirit I say it, and with what spirit they receive it—“Madmen, Peter’s sword, although still moved by a carnal impulse of mind, was drawn for Christ’s body against the body of the persecutor. Your weapons, however, are divided against Christ. The body of which he is the head, namely his Church, is throughout all nations.”

He said this himself and ascended into heaven, where the fury of the Jews could not follow him. Your fury attacks his members in the body that, by ascending, he commended to us.

Those who, in the Catholic Church, are still of weak faith and possess the spirit Peter then possessed, when he drew the sword for Christ’s name, rage against you and resist you on behalf of these members. But there is a great difference between your persecution [Col. 0321] and theirs.

You are like the servant of the Jewish priest, because, serving your rulers, you arm yourselves against the Catholic Church, that is, against Christ’s body. They, however, are like Peter was then, who fought even bodily for Christ’s body, that is, for the Church.

But if they are told to keep quiet, as Peter was told then, how much more must you be told to lay aside your heretical madness [Note: The American and Erasmian editions read “error”] and belong to those members for which they fight in this way.

Yet because we too are harmed by such people, you hate us; and, as though you had lost your right ears, you do not hear Christ seated at the Father’s right hand.

But to whom shall I speak, or when shall I speak to those whom I cannot find even for an hour, belching wine in the morning—whether already drunk or still [Note: After “or still,” the Louvain editors added “drinking,” based solely on Erasmus’s conjecture, who had noted its absence in the margin of the book. But at this point the noun “drunk” is understood: “whether already drunk or still [so],” indicating not the beginning but the continuation of drunkenness.]?

Indeed, they threaten us—not only those men, but even their bishops threaten us on their behalf, prepared to deny that what they have done belongs to them.

May the Lord grant us a Song of Ascents, so that we may say, “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause” (Ps. 119:7).

For this is said by Christ’s body, which throughout the whole earth is attacked by heretics—by some here, by others elsewhere, and by all the others in the various places where they are [Note: See Book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 67, and Book 4, chapters 60–61.].

CHAPTER LXXXIX

196. PETILIAN said: Therefore, I say, he established that death must be undergone for the faith, which must be inflicted on no one for the sake of communion [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain editions read, “which must be inflicted on each person for the sake of communion.” The corrupt passage, according to the judgment of the Louvain editors, is restored with the aid of Gallican manuscripts.]. For Christianity advances through deaths. No one, however faithful [Note: Two old manuscripts, the Endoviensis and Floriacensis, read “most faithful.”], would live if the faithful feared death.

For the Lord Christ says: “If a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, does not die, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much fruit” (John 12:24–25).

197. AUGUSTINE replied: I should like to know who among your party first threw himself down. That grain was exceedingly fertile, from which such a harvest of corpses of those who had thrown themselves down sprouted.

Certainly, when you remember the Lord’s words—that he said the grain would die and produce much fruit—why do you begrudge the fruit itself, which has most truly [Note: According to Morel, “most fruitfully.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 114 M.] grown throughout the whole world? And why do you charge it with the crimes of weeds or chaff, whether those you have heard or those you have invented?

CHAPTER XC

198. PETILIAN said: But you scatter thorns and weeds, not seeds, and it is fitting that you be burned with them at the final judgment. We do not curse; but every thorny conscience is held by God’s sentence in this way.

199. AUGUSTINE replied: At least, when you remembered the weeds, the wheat would also have come to mind, since both were commanded to grow throughout the field until the harvest. But you fix the eye of malevolence sharply upon the weeds and maintain, contrary to Christ’s sentence, that they alone have grown throughout the world, except Africa.

CHAPTER XCI

200. PETILIAN said: Where is what the Lord Christ says: “If you receive a slap, prepare the other cheek as well” (Matt. 5:39)? Where is the one who endured spittle on his face—the one who opened the eyes of the blind with his most holy spittle? Where is what the apostle Paul says: “If anyone strikes you in the face”? Where is what he says again: “In wounds beyond measure, in frequent deaths, in prisons more abundantly” (2 Cor. 11:20, 23)? He recounts what he endured, not what he did. It was enough for the Christian faith that these things were done by the Jews. Why do you wretched men perpetrate them?

201. AUGUSTINE replied: Do you really offer the other cheek when you have received a slap? Your frenzied bands, wandering everywhere through all Africa with terrifying disgrace, have certainly not acquired such a reputation for you.

Would that people made peace with you so that, at least according to the old Law, you might ask for an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Deut. 19:21), rather than raising clubs over words that you have heard.

CHAPTER XCII

202. PETILIAN said: What have you to do with the kings of this world, whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile? To make the point briefly: a king persecuted the Maccabean brothers (2 Macc. 7). A king also, although he himself was sacrilegious, unknowingly delivered three boys to religious flames (Dan. 3). A king sought the life of the boy Savior (Matt. 11:16). A king cast the most just Daniel to the bites of beasts, as he supposed (Dan. 6). And the most wicked judge of a king killed the Lord Christ himself (Matt. 27:26).

That is why the Apostle cries out: “We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this world, which is being brought to nothing; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, which was hidden, which God ordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this world knew. For if they had known it, they would certainly not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:6–8).

But let this have been said about the ancient pagan kings. You, however, rulers of this age, because you desire to be Christians, do not allow Christians to be Christians. With the disguise and fog of your falsehood, you lead those same people, believing with good intentions, wholly into your iniquity, so that, prepared with their weapons against the enemies of the state, they attack Christians and think that, if they kill us whom you hate, they are performing a service for God at your persuasion. For the Lord Christ says, “The time will come when whoever kills you will think that he is performing a service for God” (John 16:2).

Thus it makes no difference to you, who teach evil, whether the kings of the world desire to be pagans—which God forbid—or Christians, since you do not cease arming them against Christ’s household.

But do you not know—or rather, have you not read—that the crime of the person who kills a human being is less than the crime of the person who persuades him? Jezebel had stirred up her husband the king to kill a just or poor man, yet both husband and wife perished under the same punishment (1 Kings 21).

You drive kings on in no other way than by the subtle feminine persuasion by which the woman drove the king into guilt. For through her daughter Herod’s wife obtained and secured that John’s head be brought on a platter to the table (Matt. 14:8–9).

The Jews compelled Pontius Pilate in such a way that he crucified Christ the Lord, whose avenging blood they wished to remain always upon themselves and their descendants (Matt. 27:24–26). So you heap up guilt against yourselves by sinning through our blood. For even if a judge strikes us, it is your slanders that have struck us more truly. The prophet David says from the person of the Lord Christ:

“Why did the nations rage,
and the peoples meditate on empty things?
The kings of the earth stood forth,
and the rulers gathered together
against the Lord and against his Christ.
Let us break their bonds
and cast their yoke from us.
He who dwells in heaven will mock them,
and the Lord will deride them.
Then he will speak to them in his anger,
and in his fury he will trouble them.
But I have been appointed king by him
over Zion, his holy mountain,
proclaiming his command.
The Lord said to me:
‘You are my Son;
today I have begotten you.
Ask of me, and I will give you the nations
as your inheritance,
and your possession to the ends of the earth.
You will rule them with an iron rod,
and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them.’”

He warned those same people—that is, kings—not to desire to persecute Christians as though they were ignorant or unaware, and he gave them these commands so that they might not perish. Since they do not know those commands, would that we might teach them—or at least, you would certainly show them to them if you wanted them to live—or, what is the third possibility, your wickedness would allow them to read them for themselves.

The first Davidic psalm would urge them altogether to live and reign as Christians. You have badly deceived them by entrusting themselves to you. For you fabricate for them what is evil and conceal what is good.

Let them read this at last, even if late, which they ought to have read long ago. For what does it say?

“And now, kings, understand;
be instructed, you who judge the earth.
Serve the Lord in fear,
and rejoice before him with trembling.
Embrace discipline,
lest the Lord become angry,
and you perish from the righteous way.
When his anger is quickly kindled against you,
blessed are all who trust in him” (Ps. 2).

I say that you oppress the emperors with your persuasion, as the Jews oppressed Pilate, although he cried out while publicly washing his hands, “I am innocent of the blood of this just man” (Matt. 27:24). Yet how can the one who carried it out be free from guilt?

But, leaving ancient examples aside, consider in your own examples how many emperors and judges of yours have perished by making persecution against us. I shall leave aside Nero, who was the first to persecute Christians; likewise Domitian, who was in many respects another Nero; Trajan; Geta [Note: The editions of the American and Erasmus substitute “Varius” for “Geta.” He was Aurelius Antoninus Heliogabalus, or Alagabalus, who received the name Varius because he was thought to have been conceived from various and uncertain parentage, as Lampridius relates. But the manuscripts consistently prefer “Geta,” the name of the other son of Severus, the brother of Antoninus Caracalla.]; Decius; Valerian; and Diocletian. Maximian also perished.

While they were proclaiming incense-offerings, after the Lord’s books had been burned, Marcellinus, the first bishop of the Romans, and also Mensurius of Carthage and Caecilianus remained as though they were mere sparks or ashes from those sacrilegious flames. The guilt of the incense-offering entangled all of you who consented to Mensurius.

Macarius perished; Ursacius perished [Note: Optatus defends Macarius’s case at length in Book 3 against Parmenian. There too, concerning Ursacius, he says: “The times of I know not what Leontius, Ursacius, Macarius, and the rest displease you.” Augustine also, below in Book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 20, reports on behalf of the Donatists the objection concerning Silvanus, bishop of Cirta: “But after he had refused to communicate with Ursacius and Zenophilus while they were persecuting, he was driven into exile.” Usuardus, deceived by some false history fabricated by the Donatists, records in his Martyrology, on the Kalends of March, the pseudo-martyr Donatus as having suffered under Ursacius and the tribune Marcellinus, in these words: “On the same day, Saint Donatus, martyr, who suffered under Ursacius, judge (or commander), and Marcellinus, tribune.”] [Col. 0324] and all your Counts likewise perished by God’s vengeance. For Ursacius, struck down in battle against the barbarians, was torn apart by the savage claws of birds and the hungry teeth of dogs.

Is not the one who, at your instigation, kills a just and poor man—as King Ahab, whom we mentioned, was persuaded by a woman to do—also a murderer (1 Kings 21)? In the same way you do not cease to slaughter us, who are also just and poor—poor, I mean, with respect to worldly assistance, for we are not poor in God’s grace [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “worldly,” feminine, rather than “worldly assistance.”].

For even if you do not do it by hand, you slaughter a human being with an executioner’s tongue. For it is written, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). Therefore, whoever has been killed, you who persuaded the killing have killed. The executioner’s hand does not grow hot unless your tongue does, and that cruel heat of the heart is kindled by your words against another’s blood—the just blood that will avenge its shedder.

203. AUGUSTINE replied: Since you have so copiously enlarged upon and arranged this passage, in which you speak spitefully against us about the kings of this world, I fear that, if I answer suitably and worthily, you will accuse me also of wishing to stir up the anger of kings against you.

Yet since, following your custom, you direct the force of this attack universally against all Catholics, you certainly do not pass over me either. I shall nevertheless try to show, if I can, that by saying such things you have done this more than I have by answering them.

First, observe how you contradict yourself. You certainly began this passage in the following way: “What have you to do with the kings of this world, whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile?” By these words you forbid us, surely, to approach the kings of this world.

Yet shortly afterward you say: “He warned those same people, that is, kings, not to desire to persecute Christians as though they were ignorant or unaware, by these commands, so that they might not perish. Since they do not know those commands, would that we might teach them—or at least, you would certainly show them to them if you wanted them to live.”

How, then, do you want us to be teachers of kings?

As for our people, if they have some friendship with Christian kings and use it well, they commit no sin. But if some are thereby exalted, they sin much less than you do. For what did you have to do with the pagan king—and, what is more serious, the apostate Julian, the enemy of the Christian name—from whom you begged that your basilicas be restored to you, and in whose praise you placed the claim that justice alone had standing with him?

By these words—for I believe you understand Latin—Julian’s idolatry and apostasy were called justice. The petition submitted by your elders is preserved; the decree that they obtained [Note: The American and Erasmian editions read, “the decree which they gave to Constantius.” But there is no place for the emperor Constantius in this Donatist history, nor was anything requested or obtained from him in the name of the Donatists. Therefore the Louvain editors restored “the decree,” a reading also found in the Gallican manuscripts.]; and the official records in which they presented their case are preserved [Col. 0325].

Wake up and pay attention: to the enemy of Christ, the apostate, the adversary of Christians, the servant of demons, that Pontius of yours—that Pontius, I say, your own Pontius—pleaded in such words.

Go now and say to us, “What have you to do with the kings of this world?” Thus, like the deaf reading to deaf peoples what they themselves refuse to hear, you read: “You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam in your own eye” (Matt. 7:3).

204. “What,” you say, “have you to do with the kings of this world, whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile?” After saying this, you tried to enumerate the kings whom the just had experienced as enemies. You did not consider that many more could be enumerated whom they had as friends.

The father Abraham was both treated as a friend and received a gift from a king divinely admonished not to touch his wife (Gen. 20). His son Isaac likewise experienced a king as a very close friend (Gen. 26:11). Jacob was honorably received into Egypt by a king, whom he even blessed (Gen. 47).

What shall I say about his son Joseph, who, after the tribulation of prison—in which his chastity was tested like gold by fire—was raised by him to great honors (Gen. 39 and 41), and even swore by Pharaoh’s life (Gen. 42:15), not lifted up by arrogance but showing gratitude for goodwill?

The daughter of the king adopted Moses (Exod. 2:10). David, compelled by the injustice of the king of Israel, fled to a foreigner (1 Sam. 27). Elijah ran before the chariot of the worst king, not at that king’s command but in obedience to his own duty (1 Kings 18:44–46). Elisha even thought that he should voluntarily offer a hospitable woman whatever she might perhaps wish to have granted her by the king through his intercession (2 Kings 4:13).

But let me now come to those very times when God’s people were held captive, where—if I may speak more mildly—a remarkable forgetfulness slipped over you. For, wishing to prove that Christianity has never experienced kings except as hostile, you recalled the three boys and Daniel, and what they suffered from persecuting kings. Yet you could have been admonished by the circumstances themselves—not by merely neighboring events, but plainly by the very events you mentioned—what kind of king that king became after the miracle of the innocent flames, whether in praising and proclaiming God or in honoring the boys themselves.

You could also have seen what kind of Daniel the king had, and with what honors he adorned Daniel, who did not refuse them, when Daniel, rendering the honor due to royal power—as is sufficiently apparent from his words, since he indicated the gift of God with which he was endowed—did not withhold from the king the interpretation of his dream.

Thus, when the king was unwillingly compelled by the envious men, who slandered the holy man with sacrilegious madness, to throw him into the lions’ den, although he did so sadly, he nevertheless presumed that Daniel would be saved through the aid of his God.

And so, when Daniel lived unharmed because God had restrained the lions’ rage, after the king himself had sent his anxious and friendly greeting ahead of him, Daniel also answered from the den with a blessing: “O king, live forever!” (Dan. 3–6).

Why, when your speech was concerned with kings in that very place, and when you yourself were recalling examples of these servants of God in whom these things occurred, did you either not see these friendships between kings and the holy, or did you not wish to see them—or, what I do not know how you can excuse, did you see and know them but remain silent about them?

If a zeal for establishing falsehood had not hindered you, as it hinders the defender of a very bad cause, and had not turned you, unwillingly or unknowingly [Note: The manuscripts read, “willingly or unknowingly.”], away from the light of truth, you would surely have recalled without difficulty that some kings were good and others bad, and that some were friends of the saints and others their enemies.

And we wonder that your Circumcellions throw themselves down in this way. Who was running after you, I ask? What Macarius, what soldier, was pursuing you? Surely none of us pushed you into this precipice of falsehood.

Why, then, do you rush headlong with your eyes closed, so that, after saying, “What have you to do with the kings of this world?” you did not add, “whom Christianity has often experienced as hostile,” but did not hesitate to say, “whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile”?

Did you really not think for yourself—or did you suppose that those who read your writings would not think—of so many examples of kings crying out against you, “He does not know what he is saying”?

205. Or do you think that the kings I mentioned have no bearing on your argument because they belonged to ancient times? For you did not say, “whom justice has never experienced except as hostile,” but said, “whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile,” perhaps intending “from the time when they began to be called Christians,” and wishing to imply that kings had been hostile to the just from that time onward.

What, then, are the examples from ancient times doing here, by which you wished—still more foolishly—to teach what you had said foolishly? Did not the Maccabeans, the three boys, and Daniel all act or suffer those things before Christ was born on earth?

Furthermore, why, as I mentioned shortly before, did you plead with Julian, who was hostile to Christianity? Why did you ask him for basilicas? Why did you say that justice alone had standing with him? If one hostile to Christianity hears these things, from whom does he hear them?

But Constantine, in no way hostile to the Christian name, but plainly glorious in the Christian name, mindful of the hope he carried in Christ and judging most justly for Christ’s unity, deserved to be accepted by you even when you did not appeal to him.

Both lived already in Christian times, but both were not Christians. If both were hostile to Christianity, why did you appeal in this way to one of them and plead in this way with the other? [Note: The printed editions continued after “plead in this way with the other” with the following: “But if what is true is that, when your elders petitioned, …,” and repeated the same words below. With the aid of the old manuscripts, these repetitions have been corrected here.]

When your elders petitioned, Constantine granted an episcopal judgment, both at Rome and at Arles. You accused the first before him and appealed from the second to him.

If, as is true, one of them had believed in Christ while the other had apostatized from Christ, why is the Christian who supported unity despised, while the apostate who favored division is praised?

Constantine ordered your basilicas to be taken away; Julian ordered them to be restored. Do you wish to know which of these actions accords with Christian peace? The one who believed in Christ did the first; the one who had abandoned Christ did the second.

How you would like to say, “It was wrong to plead with Julian in that way—but what does that have to do with us?” If you said this, then in these words of yours the Catholic Church would indeed prevail, since it matters far less to the saints spread throughout the whole world what you say about whomever you wish and in whatever way you wish.

But you cannot say that it was wrong to plead with Julian in that way. Domestic authority blocks your throat and constrains your tongue. Pontius did it; Pontius pleaded; Pontius called the apostate “most just”; Pontius proclaimed before the apostate that justice alone had standing.

In that same rescript Julian himself explicitly stated, by name and without ambiguity, that Pontius had pleaded with him in these words. Your petitions still exist. Public records, not uncertain rumor, testify to this.

Or perhaps, because the apostate granted something to your petition against Christ’s unity, you think it true that justice alone had standing with him; but because Christian emperors establish measures against your will when they believe those measures serve Christ’s unity, you call them hostile to Christianity?

May all heretics reason as foolishly as this—and recover their senses, so that they may no longer be heretics.

206. “And where,” you will say, “was what the Lord says fulfilled: ‘The hour is coming when whoever kills you will think that he is offering a service to God’ (John 16:2)?” For this could not have been said of the pagans, who persecuted Christians not for God’s sake but for the sake of idols. Do you not see that, if this had been said of those emperors who rejoiced in the Christian name, they would certainly above all have ordered you killed? Yet they never ordered this at all. But your people, resisting the laws in a hostile manner, suffer the punishments they deserve; and, while they regard their voluntary deaths as bringing us reproach, they do not regard them as destructive to themselves.
