But if they think that this was said by the Lord about kings who honor the name of Christ, let them ask what the Catholic Church endured in the East when Valens, an Arian, was emperor. There, surely, I would have something by which to understand as fulfilled what the Lord says: “The hour is coming when whoever kills you will think that he is offering a service to God”—so that heretics might not claim for the glory of their reputation that Catholic emperors had ordered anything against their error.

Nevertheless, we remember that this hour was fulfilled after the Lord’s ascension; Holy Scripture, which is known to all, bears witness to this. The Jews thought they were offering a service to God when they were killing the Apostles. Among those who thought they were rendering service to God was our Saul—ours not yet—so much so that he counts this among his former deeds, which he now wished to forget: “A Hebrew of Hebrews,” he says, “as to the law a Pharisee, as to zeal persecuting the Church” (Philippians 3:5–6). Behold the man who thought he was offering a service to God when he was doing what he himself soon afterward suffered.

For forty Jews had conspired to kill him. He made this known to the tribune, so that, surrounded by armed soldiers, he might escape their ambush (Acts 23:12–33). But there was not yet anyone to say to him, “What have you to do—not with kings, but with tribunes and royal arms?” There was not yet anyone to say to him, “Do you dare seek protection through soldiers, when your Lord was led by them to his passion?” Such ravings had not yet appeared; but examples were already being prepared then against these future ravings.

[Col. 0328] **207.** You even dared to put forward and say with terrible emphasis: “But, to say nothing of the rest, observe in your own examples how very many of your emperors and judges have perished by persecuting us.”

When I read this in your letter, I waited with the greatest attention to hear what you would say and whom you would enumerate. Then, as though merely passing them over, you began to mention Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Geta [Note: The printed editions again have *Varius* in this place, whereas the old manuscripts consistently read *Geta*.], Decius, Valerian, Diocletian, and Maximian.

I admit that there were many more; but you have completely forgotten against whom you are speaking. Were all these men not pagans, and did they not universally persecute the Christian name on behalf of their idols? Wake up, then: they did not belong to our communion. They persecuted the entire unity itself, from which either we have gone out, as you suppose, or you have gone out, as Christ teaches.[Note: Some printed editions read *existitis* (“you exist”); the manuscripts read more correctly *existis* (“you have gone out”), from *exeo*.]

But you had proposed to show that our emperors and judges had perished by persecuting you. Or do you not require us to count these men either [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “and do you require us”?], since, after passing them over, you mentioned them by saying, “To leave Nero aside,” and under this act of leaving him aside you ran through the rest [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and the other manuscripts have *caeteros cucurristi* (“you ran through the rest”), omitting the particle *per*.]? What need was there, then, to mention people irrelevant to the matter? But what is that to me? I now leave these men to you along with the others. Let those many men whom you promised at least now come forward—unless perhaps they cannot be found because you said that they had perished.

**208.** You proceed now and name bishops whom you customarily accuse concerning the handing over of the codices. Concerning them we also customarily reply: either you do not prove it, in which case it concerns no one; or you prove it, in which case it does not concern us. They carried their own burden, whether good or bad—and we believe it was good; but whatever it was, it was their own. So too your wicked men carried neither your burden nor you theirs; rather, the common and worst burden of all of you is schism. We have said this often enough.

Produce, then, not the names of bishops, but of our emperors and judges who perished by persecuting you. This is what you proposed; this is what you promised; this is what you had made us await with such attention.

“Listen,” you say: “Macarius perished, Ursacius perished, and all your Counts likewise perished by God’s vengeance.” You mentioned only two, neither of whom was an emperor. Who could approve this, I ask you? Do you not yourself displease yourself? You promise to mention very many of our emperors and judges who perished by persecuting you, and, while saying nothing about emperors, you name two judges or Counts.

For what you add—“And all your Counts likewise perished by God’s vengeance”—does not pertain to the matter. In this way you could already have ended the whole passage earlier, without naming anyone at all. Why, then, did you not mention our emperors, that is, those of our communion? Did you fear being accused of treason? Where is the Circumcellionist [Note: The old Floriacensis manuscript has *Cercicellionica*.] courage?

Moreover, what do you say [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “what do you make?”] of those whom you named above in such numbers, who can more appropriately say to you, “Why were you looking for us? For they contributed nothing to your case, and yet they were named”? And what sort of person are you, who fear to name those whom you mention as having perished? At least you could have named more of the judges or Counts whom you evidently did not fear.

You have remained with Macarius and Ursacius. Are “very many” two? Or do you have the wisdom we learned as children? For if you ask me what number two is—singular or plural—what could I answer except “plural”? But even now I am not without something to say [Note: The manuscripts read, “But even for this”; the printed editions read, not improperly, “But even now.” They subsequently read less well, “there is not lacking what I may say.” “I see Macarius from two”: corrected from the manuscripts.]. I remove Macarius from the count, for you did not say how he perished. Or perhaps whoever persecutes you, unless he is immortal in this world, will be considered to have died because of you when he dies?

What if Constantine had not lived through so long a reign and such prolonged prosperity—he who was the first to enact many measures against your error? And what if Julian had not been so quickly taken from this life—he who gave you basilicas [Note: Constantine held the imperial power for nearly thirty-two years, according to Eusebius in his *Life of Constantine*. Julian, after the death of his cousin Constantius, died in battle against the Persians after about one year and seven months of his reign, at the age of thirty-one.]? When would you put an end to this babbling [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and all the manuscripts read *garrire taceretis* (“you would cease babbling”); the printed editions have *garriendi finem faceretis*.], since even now you do not want to be silent?

Yet we do not say that Julian died quickly for this reason: because he gave you basilicas. We could indeed be equally copious in these matters, but we do not wish to be equally vain.

Therefore, as I had begun to say, I set Macarius apart from those two [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions corruptly read *cerno Macarium* (“I distinguish Macarius”).]. For when you had proposed the two—Macarius and Ursacius—you repeated Ursacius’s name in order to show us what death he deserved, and said: “For Ursacius, struck down in a barbarian battle, was torn apart by the savage claws of birds and the greedy teeth of dogs.”

From this it is sufficiently clear that, since you customarily arouse much greater odium against Macarius—so that we are called “Macarians,” not “Ursacians”—you would have said much more about him if you had been able to say anything of that sort about his death.

Of these two, then, once Macarius is separated, the proper name remaining is Ursacius, a singular number. Where, therefore, is that threatening and terrifying promise of “so many” men [Note: Erasmus and Lovanius have *quam plurium* (“of very many”) in place of *tam plurium*.]?

**209.** Those who know how to speak in any fashion at all, I think, understand how ridiculous this is: after saying, “Macarius perished, Ursacius perished, and all your Counts likewise perished by God’s vengeance,” as though we were demanding proof—for certainly no listener or reader would demand anything else—you immediately joined to it a great demonstration by which you would prove that all our Counts had likewise perished by God’s vengeance.

“For Ursacius,” you say, “struck down in a barbarian battle, was torn apart by the savage claws of birds and the greedy teeth of dogs.”

In this same way someone else, equally ignorant of what he was saying, could say that all your bishops had wasted away in prison by God’s vengeance; and when asked by what evidence he proved this, could immediately add: “For Optatus, accused of belonging to Gildo’s retinue, was killed by that kind of death.”

We are compelled to hear, examine, and refute such nonsense. We are concerned only for the weak, lest, being slower to understand, they quickly run into your snares.

As for this Ursacius, however, if he lived well and truly died in this way, he will be comforted by God’s promise: “I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast” (Genesis 9:5).

**210.** As for your accusation that we incite the kings of this world against you to anger, by not teaching them divine Scripture but instead suggesting our military power to them: I do not think you are so deaf to the very words of the holy books that you would not rather fear that they know those words.

Whether you wish it or not, they enter the Church; and if we are silent, they lend their ears to the readers. To say nothing of the rest, they listen with the greatest attention to the very psalm that you mentioned. For you said that we do not teach them, nor willingly allow them to know what is written:

“And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry,” and so forth.

Believe that this too is sung and that they hear it. But they certainly also hear the earlier passage in the same psalm, which, unless I am mistaken, you did not want to pass over [Note: The printed editions have *voluisti* (“you wanted”); the manuscripts more correctly read *noluisti* (“you did not want”), as is clear above from section 202.], lest you be understood to have feared it.

They therefore also hear this:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2).

When they hear this, they are surely astonished that there are people who oppose this inheritance of Christ and attempt to reduce it to a small portion of the earth. Perhaps, in their astonishment, they ask—because of what they hear later, “Serve the Lord in fear”—how they can serve him insofar as they are kings.

All human beings must serve God: in one way according to the common condition by which they are human beings, and in another way through different gifts, since one person carries out one task in human affairs and another a different task. A private individual could not order idols to be removed from the earth, something foretold so long beforehand (Isaiah 2:18; Zechariah 13:2). Kings therefore have, in addition to the fellowship of the human race, and precisely insofar as they are kings, a way to serve the Lord such as those who are not kings cannot have.

**211.** While they consider these things [Note: The manuscripts read *Ista ergo cum cogitent* (“While they therefore consider these things”); the printed editions have *cogitant* (“they consider”).], they also hear what you yourself mentioned concerning the three young men, and they hear it with remarkable solemnity. For the same Scripture is sung in the Church especially when that festival makes even those who are more sluggish during the rest of the year more fervent.

What disposition, then, do you think Christian emperors have when they hear that three young men were thrown into a furnace of blazing fire because they refused to consent to the king’s wicked demand that they worship the image [Note: The printed editions have *simulacra* (“images”); the manuscripts more correctly have *simulacri* (“of the image”), that is, the statue of Nebuchadnezzar, from Daniel chapter 3.]? Surely they think that the pious freedom of the saints can be overcome neither by royal power nor by the enormity of punishment. And they rejoice that they are not among those kings who punished contempt for idols as sacrilege.

Then, when they hear in what follows that the same king—terrified by so great a miracle, not only on account of the young men but also on account of the flames serving God—himself began to serve God in fear, to rejoice with trembling, and to embrace discipline, do they not understand that these things were written and are recited with such great solemnity so that examples might be set before both God’s servants, that they might not yield to kings in sacrilege, and kings themselves, that they might believe in God for the sake of religion?

Therefore, wishing also, in response to the admonition of that psalm—which you too inserted into your writings—to understand, to be instructed, to serve the Lord in fear, to rejoice with trembling, and to embrace discipline, these men listen attentively to what that king later said.

For he said that he would issue a decree to all the peoples over whom he ruled: whoever spoke blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego would be put to death, and his house would be destroyed. When they recognize that he issued this decree so that the God who controls the fires and liberated the three young men would not be blasphemed, they surely consider what they ought to decree in their own kingdom, so that among his faithful that same God—the forgiver of sins and now the liberator of the whole world—will not be scornfully rejected.

**212.** Consider, then, when Christian kings establish something against you for the sake of Catholic unity, whether perhaps you accuse them on your lips as ignorant of the divine Scriptures while inwardly grieving that they are sufficiently instructed.

Who could tolerate this sacrilegious and hateful deception of yours: in the single case of Daniel, to accuse kings because he was thrown into the lions’ den, while not praising kings because he was honorably exalted? Even when he was thrown into it, the king himself believed that he would be saved rather than killed, and, anxious about him, did not eat dinner.

Then you dare say to Christians, “What have you to do with the kings of this world?” because Daniel suffered persecution from a king; yet you do not consider that same Daniel faithfully interpreting dreams for kings, calling the ruler “lord king,” and receiving gifts and honors.

Likewise, in the case of the same three young men, you stir up the flames of envy against kings because they were thrown into the fire when they refused to worship the statue, while you keep silent about and conceal the fact that they were praised and honored in this way by the king.

Suppose the king was a persecutor when he threw Daniel to the lions. What about when, rejoicing and giving thanks after receiving Daniel back safe, he sent his enemies to be torn apart and consumed by those same lions (Daniel 2–6)? Was he a persecutor then, or was he not? I want you to answer.

For if he was, why did Daniel himself not resist him, especially since he could easily have done so with such great intimacy? And you tell us to restrain kings from persecuting human beings.

But if he was not a persecutor for this reason—that he most justly avenged the crime committed against a holy man—how should kings avenge the fact that the Sacraments of Christ are insulted, if the members of a prophet, because they had been placed in danger, deserved to be avenged in this way?

Likewise, I concede—and it is evident—that the king was a persecutor when he sent the three young men into the flames because they refused to worship the image. But I ask whether he was a persecutor when he issued the decree that those who blasphemed the one true God should be put to death and their houses destroyed.

For if he was a persecutor, why do you answer the words of the persecutor, “Amen” [Note: Augustine refers to this in Letter 105 to the Donatists, section 7: “Do you not know that these are the words of the king: ‘The signs and wonders that the most high God has done for me have seemed good to me to announce in my presence, how great and powerful his kingdom is, an eternal kingdom, and his power throughout all generations’? When you hear this, do you not answer, ‘Amen’; and, having said this in a loud voice, do you not sign yourselves at the king’s edict during the holy solemnity?” In the Gothic liturgy these words were said on Holy Saturday, and the response was “Amen.”]?

But if he was not a persecutor, why do you call those persecutors who deter you from the madness of blasphemy?

If they compel you to worship an idol, they are like the impious king, and you are like the three young men. But if they forbid you to resist Christ, you are impious if you do so. As for what those rulers are, if they forbid this with terrifying force, I will not say; you find something else to call them, if you do not wish to call pious emperors.

**213.** If I had brought forward these examples of Daniel and the three young men, perhaps you would have resisted and loudly declared that examples from those times ought not to be applied to our own age. Thanks be to God that you yourself introduced them, for the purpose you intended, but you see that they have served rather for the purpose you did not intend.

Is this not your deception, but merely human error? Would that it were so. Correct yourself, then; do not be afraid—you will not thereby become lesser. Indeed, it is a sign of greater intelligence to extinguish the flames of resentment by confessing them than to avoid the mists of falsehood by understanding them.

## CHAPTER XCIII

**214. PETILIAN said:** Where is God’s law, where is your Christianity, if you inflict and order slaughter and deaths?

**215. AUGUSTINE replied:** For this, see what the co-heirs of Christ throughout the whole world say. We neither inflict nor order slaughter and deaths. And you rage far more wickedly against those who do such things, because you commit these acts against the minds of human beings, against eternal life.

## CHAPTER XCIV

**216. PETILIAN said:** If you want us to be friends, why do you draw us against our will? But if you pretend that we are enemies, why do you kill your enemies?

**217. AUGUSTINE replied:** We neither draw the unwilling nor kill enemies. Whatever we do with you, although we do it against your will, we do from charity, so that you may correct yourselves willingly and, once corrected, live. For no one lives unwillingly. Yet a boy is beaten unwillingly so that he may learn this willingly, and this is often done by someone who loves him dearly [Note: Perhaps one should read: “For no one wills unwillingly, and yet a boy, that he may learn willingly, etc.,” deleting *hoc* (“this”), which is absent from the old Floriacensis manuscript.].

Indeed, kings would say these things to you if they struck you; for their power has been divinely ordered for this purpose. But since even they do not strike you, you cry out.

## CHAPTER XCV

**218. PETILIAN said:** What reason, or what inconsistency of vanity, is there in this: although you falsely call us heretics, you greatly desire our communion?

[Col. 0333] **219. AUGUSTINE replied:** If we greatly desired the communion of heretics, we would not want you to be corrected from heretical error. But since we are dealing with you so that you may not be heretics, how can we greatly desire the communion of heretics?

Dissent and division make you heretics; peace and unity make people Catholic. Therefore, when you come from there to here, you cease to be what we hate and begin to be what we love.

## CHAPTER XCVI

**220. PETILIAN said:** At last, choose one of two alternatives and say which you mean [Note: The Lovanius edition alone has *quod dicatis* (“what you should say”).]. If you have innocence, why do you pursue us with the sword? Or if you call us guilty, why do you seek us as innocent?

**221. AUGUSTINE replied:** O most acute dilemma—or rather, most foolish verbosity! Is it not customary to propose a choice between two alternatives where both cannot be chosen? If you proposed that I choose one of two things to say—whether we are innocent or guilty, or likewise one of two others, whether from those or from these—I could choose only one thing to say.

But now you propose these two alternatives: whether we are innocent or you are guilty, and you want me to choose one of them as my answer. I do not want to say only one, because I say both: we are innocent, and you are guilty.

We say that we are innocent of your false and slanderous accusations—at least all of us in the Catholic Church who can say with a clear conscience that we have neither handed over the holy books, nor consented to petitions on behalf of idols, nor killed anyone, nor committed any other evil that you customarily bring against us.

And if some people perhaps did these things—which, indeed, you have not proved even concerning those individuals—they have not closed the kingdom of heaven against us, but against themselves, because each person carries his own burden (Galatians 6:5). There is your first alternative.

As for the second, we say that all of you are guilty and criminal—not because of the crimes of some among you, which are committed by some and condemned by others, but because of the crime of schism. No one among you can say that he is exempt from this monstrous sacrilege so long as he does not share in the unity of all nations, unless he is forced to say that Christ lied about the Church that is spread throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). There is your second alternative.

Behold, I have given you the two alternatives of which you wanted us to say only one. You ought certainly to have recognized that we could say both; and at least, if this was what you wanted, you should have asked us to say one when you saw that we could say both.

**222.** “But if you have innocence,” you say, “why do you pursue us with the sword?”

Look for a moment at your own bands, which are not armed, as were their ancestors in ancient times, only with clubs, but have added axes, lances, and swords. Recognize whose voice ought rather to be saying, “Why do you pursue us with the sword?”

“Or if you call us guilty,” you say, “why do you seek us as innocent?”

Here is my brief answer: you are sought as guilty by the innocent so that you may cease to be guilty and begin to be innocent.

Behold, I have chosen both of our alternatives and answered both of yours. Now you choose one of two: Are you innocent or guilty? You cannot say both—but say both, if that pleases you. Certainly you cannot be innocent and guilty in the same matter.

If you are innocent, do not be surprised that brothers seek you for peace. But if you are guilty, do not be surprised that kings seek you for punishment.

Since, however, you claim one of these alternatives for yourselves and hear the other from us—you claim innocence for yourselves, while you hear from us that you live impiously—listen again to what I say about both.

If you are innocent, why do you contradict Christ’s testimony? But if you are guilty, why do you not flee to his mercy? For his testimony concerns the unity of the world, and his mercy is found in brotherly charity.

## CHAPTER XCVII

**223. PETILIAN said:** Finally, as we have often said already, what presumption is yours, that you presume upon kings, when David says: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Psalm 117:8–9)?

**224. AUGUSTINE replied:** We do not hope in man; rather, insofar as we can, we admonish human beings to hope in the Lord. Nor do we hope in princes; rather, insofar as we can, we admonish princes to hope in the Lord. And if we ask something from princes for the benefit of the Church, we nevertheless do not place our hope in them.

For the Apostle did not hope in that tribune as in a prince when he secured the provision of armed escorts for himself; nor did he hope in those armed men as human beings, by whose multitude he escaped the ambush of the wicked (Acts 23:12–33).

Nor do we accuse you yourselves because you asked the Emperor to have the basilicas restored to you, as though you had hoped in Julian as a prince. Rather, we accuse you because you despaired of Christ’s testimony, from whose unity you separated those very basilicas.

You received them at the command of Christ’s enemy, so that within them you might despise Christ’s commands, while regarding as valid and true what Julian decreed, saying:

“Moreover, in response to the petitions of Rogatianus, Pontius, Cassianus, and the other bishops, as well as the clergy, this further provision is added: that, once the things improperly done against them without a rescript have been annulled, everything should be restored to its former condition.”

But you regard as invalid and false what Christ decreed when he said: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

We implore you: correct yourselves. Return to this most evident unity of the whole world, so that everything improperly done may be restored to its former condition—not by the words of the apostate Julian, but by the words of Christ the Savior.

Have mercy on your souls. We are no longer comparing Constantine and Julian in order to demonstrate how unequal they were. We are not saying: “If you did not hope in man and in a prince when you said to a pagan and apostate emperor that justice alone had a place with him, in the petitions and rescript recorded there, as the records of the proceedings of your allegation testify—when the party of Donatus made universal use of these—then you should much less accuse us as hoping in man and in a prince if we asked something from Constantine or from the other Christian emperors without any sacrilegious flattery; or if they, without our asking, remembered the account they must render to the Lord, under whose words they tremble when they hear those that you yourself mentioned, ‘And now, O kings, understand,’ and many others, and voluntarily establish measures for the unity of the Catholic Church.”

But I say nothing about Constantine. We set Christ and Julian before you. I say too little: God and man, the Son of God and the son of Gehenna, the Savior of our souls and the destroyer of his own soul.

Why do you hold Julian’s rescript for possessing the basilicas, but do not hold Christ’s Gospel for embracing the peace of the Church?

We too cry out: “Everything improperly done should be restored to its former condition.” The Gospel of Christ is older than Julian’s rescript; the unity of Christ is older than the party of Donatus; the prayers of the Church to the Lord for the unity of Christ are older than the prayers of Rogatianus, Pontius, and Cassianus to Julian for the party of Donatus.

Is it improperly done when kings forbid division, but not improperly done when bishops divide unity? Is it improperly done when kings serve Christ’s testimony in order to defend the Church, but not improperly done when bishops contradict Christ’s testimony in order to deny the Church?

We therefore implore you: let even the words of Julian himself, to whom you petitioned in this way, be heard not against the Gospel but according to the Gospel; and let everything improperly done be restored to its former condition.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

**225. PETILIAN said:** I appeal to you—you, miserable people—who, terrified by fear of persecution, seek your riches rather than your souls. You do not so much love the treacherous faith of the traditors as the protection you have procured for yourselves against their wickedness.

You are like shipwrecked people who meet the waves that are about to crash down upon them in the midst of the waves, and, in the great danger of life, seek what they fear. Just as tyrannical fury, so as not to fear anyone, wants to be feared even at its own peril, so, so you flee to the stronghold of wickedness in order to watch the losses or punishments of the innocent without fear for yourselves [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and the printed editions have *arcem* (“stronghold”); Erasmus and the Erfurt edition have *artem* (“artifice”).].

If this is to avoid danger, it is to flee beneath a collapse. Moreover, to keep faith with a robber is also a damnable fidelity. Finally, it is the bargain of a madman to lose your souls so that you may not lose your riches.

For the Lord Christ says: “If you gain the whole world and lose your soul, what will you give in exchange for your soul?” (Matthew 16:26).

**226. AUGUSTINE replied:** I admit that this exhortation would be useful if anyone were using it in a good cause. You have thoroughly warned people not to prefer riches to their souls.

But you who have heard these words, listen to us for a little while. We say the same thing, but observe how we say it.

If kings threaten to take away your riches because you are not Jews according to the flesh, or because you do not worship idols or demons, or because you are not transferred into any heresy but remain in Catholic unity, choose rather to let your riches perish so that you yourselves may not perish. Do not prefer anything else—not even this temporal life—to the eternal salvation that is in Christ.

But if kings threaten you with losses or condemnation because you are heretics, they terrify you not cruelly but mercifully. You, however, do not fear them courageously but obstinately.

Hear Peter, then, saying: “What credit is there if, when you sin, you endure punishment?” (1 Peter 2:20). Otherwise you will have neither earthly consolations here nor eternal life in the age to come, but here the hardships of the unhappy and there the Gehenna of heretics.

You see, then, brother—for it is with you that I am now dealing—that you ought first to show whether you hold the truth, and then exhort people to be prepared, for the sake of holding it, to do without all the things they possess temporarily.

Since you cannot show this—not because you lack intelligence, but because your cause is bad—why do you hasten by your exhortations to make people both beggars [Note: The printed editions have *mendaces* (“liars”); the manuscripts’ *mendicos* (“beggars”) should be restored.], ignorant, needy and wandering, ragged and contentious, hungry and heretical—losing temporal goods in this world and finding eternal evils at Christ’s judgment?

The prudent son, who, fearing his father’s rod, withdraws from the serpent’s lair, is neither beaten nor destroyed. But the one who, because of his destructive will, despises the pains of discipline is both beaten and destroyed.

Do you still not understand, eloquent man, that whoever gives up all earthly things for the peace of Christ has God, while whoever loses even a few coins for the party of Donatus has no heart [Note: The Venetian edition has *cur non habet?* (“why does he not have a heart?”).].

## CHAPTER XCIX

**227. PETILIAN said:** We, however, are poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3). We do not fear riches [Note: All the manuscripts have *non divitiis metuimus* (“we do not fear riches”); the printed editions have *non divitias amamus* (“we do not love riches”).], but we dread riches. Having nothing and possessing everything (2 Corinthians 6:10), we regard the soul as our wealth, and with our punishments and blood we purchase the eternal riches of heaven.

Thus the same Lord says: “Whoever has lost his substance will receive it a hundredfold.” [Note: This is Petilian’s wording in the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “Just as the same [Lord].” According to Morel’s *Elementa Critica*, p. 87, it should read, “may we merit heaven,” since, etc.]

**228. AUGUSTINE replied:** It is relevant to remind you how the passage is written. When nothing obstructs my purpose, I care nothing whether, in matters of Scripture, you deceive or are deceived.

It is not written, then, “Whoever has lost his substance,” but “Whoever has lost his soul for my sake” (Matthew 16:25). Concerning substance, it is not written, “Whoever has lost,” but “Whoever has left” (Matthew 19:29)—and not merely money, but many other things as well.

For the moment, however, you have not lost your substance. Whether you have left it, since you boast so much about your poverty, I do not know. Perhaps my colleague Fortunatus knows, since you are in the same city; he has never told me, because I have never asked.

Nevertheless, even if you have done this, you yourself have cited against yourself in this very letter the apostolic testimony: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and deliver my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

If you had charity, you would not hurl at the world—which is ignorant of you and unknown to you—even the proven crimes of Africans [Note: The printed editions corruptly read *fratrum* (“of the brothers”) instead of *Afrorum* (“of the Africans”).].

If you had charity, you would not fabricate accusations in your calumnies; rather, you would recognize the unity most clearly expressed in the Lord’s words, “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

But if you have not done this, why do you boast as though you had? Do you really fear riches so much that, having nothing, you possess everything?

Say this to your colleague Crispinus, who recently bought an estate near our Hippo, where he might plunge people into the deep [Note: See above, chapter 83.]. I know this extremely well; perhaps you do not, and therefore you cry out confidently, “We dread riches.”

That is why I am astonished that this voice of yours, in reaching us, passed over him. Between Constantina, where you are, and Hippo, where I am, lies Calama, where he is—indeed closer to us, though situated between us.

I am therefore amazed that he did not first intercept this voice and echo it back so that it could not reach us, and that he did not recite against you, at much greater length, praises of riches. For he not only does not dread riches but loves them.

At any rate, before you publish such things in the future, recite them to him first. If he does not correct them, we will answer. But if it is true that you are poor, there you have my brother Fortunatus. You will more easily please that colleague of mine there than this one of yours.

## CHAPTER C

**229. PETILIAN said:** We, who live by the fear of God, do not fear the punishments and deaths that you inflict with the sword. But in the end we flee only this: that by your most wicked communion you slaughter souls, as the Lord himself says:

“Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who has power to cast body and soul into the Gehenna of fire” (Matthew 10:28) [Note: In the manuscripts Petilian quotes *habet in potestatem* (“has power over”); the printed editions have *habet potestatem* (“has power”).].

**230. AUGUSTINE replied:** What you say you do, not with the visible sword, but with the sword of which it is said: “The teeth of the sons of men are their weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm 56:5).

With this sword, as accusers and slanderers of a world unknown to you, you slaughter the souls of the ignorant.

But if you accuse us of the most wicked communion, then, behold, by your own mouth—not mine—whether you ascend, descend, enter, remain, or evade: you are such as Optatus was. But if you return to your heart and discover that you are not such—not because he did not share the Sacraments with you, but because you disliked him—you will absolve the whole world from the crimes of others and will discover that you are entangled in the crime of schism.

### CHAPTER CI

**231. PETILIAN said:** You, then, who wish to be washed by a most false baptism rather than born anew, not only do not put away your own sins, but load your souls with the crimes of the guilty. For just as the water of the guilty has been emptied of the Holy Spirit, so plainly it has been filled with the crimes of the Traditors. Whoever, then, unhappy man, is baptized by such people—if you wish to be free from falsehood—you are drenched with falsity. If you wished to exclude sins of the flesh, with the conscience of the guilty intervening you will receive guilt as well. If you wished to extinguish the flame of avarice, you are drenched with fraud, drenched with wickedness, drenched also with rage. Finally, if you believe that faith belongs to the one who receives as well as to the one who gives, you are drenched with the blood of your brother by one who kills a human being. Thus it happens that the one who came innocent to Baptism returns from Baptism a murderer of his brother.

**[Note: [Col. 0337]** An old Florentine manuscript reads *accendente* instead of *accedente*.]

**232. AUGUSTINE replied:** I wish I could converse with those who, after reading or hearing these words, shouted their approval. Such people do not have ears in their hearts, but hearts in their ears. Nevertheless, let them read again and again, reflect, and understand what these words mean—not merely what they sound like.

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** The manuscripts read *sentiant*; the printed editions read *sentient*.]

First, let me examine this final point: “Thus,” you say, “it happens that the one who came innocent to Baptism returns from Baptism a murderer of his brother.” First answer this: who comes innocent to Baptism, except the one who does not come to be baptized in order that his iniquity may be washed away, but in order that humility might be commended to us through him? For what can be forgiven to an innocent person? Or are you so eloquent that you can show us some kind of sinful innocence?

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read: “Or are you not so eloquent.”]

Do you not hear Scripture saying, “No one is pure from sin in your sight, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job 14, according to the Septuagint)? For why, then, do people run to the remission of sins even with infants? Do you not hear another passage: “I was conceived in iniquity” (Psalm 50:7)? Further, if the one who came without murder returns a murderer because a murderer baptizes him, then all who were baptized by Optatus returned as Optatus’s followers. Go on, then, and accuse us of stirring up the anger of kings against you. Are you not afraid that as many followers of Gildo will be sought from among you as there may have been people baptized by Optatus?

Do you see at last how this opinion of yours, like a bladder, has burst—not only with an empty sound, but also over your own head?

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** This is the reading of the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “this opinion of yours, not merely a bladder.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** The manuscripts read *veniat* (“comes”); the printed editions read *venerat* (“had come”).]

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** The manuscripts and the Ambrosian edition read: “Or are you not so eloquent.”]

**233.** As for all the earlier points that we have now undertaken to refute, they are of such a character that anyone baptized by such a person is said to return exactly like the person by whom he was baptized. But God forbid that those whom you baptize should return from you as mad as you are in saying these things.

How beautifully your phrase sounded: “You are drenched with fraud, drenched with wickedness, drenched also with rage!”

**[Note: [Col. 0338]** Earlier editions read *bene* (“well”) instead of *belle* (“beautifully”).] Yet unless you had been drenched—not merely filled—with rage, you would not have poured out such words. Is it really the case, to pass over everything else, that all who come to your avaricious colleagues or your presbyters without being avaricious return avaricious? And that all who soberly hurry to those wine-pits to be baptized return drunk?

While thinking and teaching such things, you even dare to cite against us what you stated shortly before: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in a human being; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Psalm 117:8–9). What else, I ask, do you teach except that one should hope not in the Lord but in a human being, when you say that a baptized person becomes whatever the baptizer was? And because you assume for yourselves the leadership of baptizing, let people believe you; and those who were hoping in the Lord should hope in princes?

Rather, let them not listen to you, but instead to those testimonies that you set forth against us.

**[Note: [Col. 0339]** An old manuscript from Cygirannum reads *vos* (“you”) rather than the transmitted wording.]

And let them hear something even more terrifying: not merely, “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in a human being,” but also, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17:5).

### CHAPTER CII

**234. PETILIAN said:** At least imitate the Prophets, who feared that their sacred souls might be deceived by false baptism. For Jeremiah first said that among impious people there is deceitful water. “Water,” he says, “that lies has no faithfulness.”

**235. AUGUSTINE replied:** Anyone ignorant of the Scriptures who hears this, and who does not believe either that you are so mistaken that you do not know what you are saying, or so deceptive that the person deceived by you does not know what he is saying, will suppose that the prophet Jeremiah, when he wished to be baptized, took precautions against being baptized by impious people and spoke these words for that reason.

For what else does your statement mean, made immediately before you introduced this testimony—“At least imitate the Prophets, who feared that their sacred souls might be deceived by false baptism”—than that, as though in Jeremiah’s time anyone were cleansed by the sacrament of Baptism? The Pharisees, except insofar as they repeatedly washed themselves in those purifications that the Lord rebuked, washed couches, cups, and dishes almost at every moment, as we read in the Gospel (Matthew 23:25).

How, then, could Jeremiah have said these things as though he desired baptism and wished to avoid being baptized by impious people? He said this when the subject was an unfaithful people, whose wicked conduct afflicted him, although he did not mingle himself with their deeds. Yet he did not physically separate himself from that people, nor did he seek other sacraments than those which that people, according to the order of the Law appropriate to that time, observed.

He therefore called this badly living people a wound by which the heart of the righteous was grievously struck—whether he was speaking about himself or portraying in himself what he foresaw would happen. For he says:

“Lord, remember me and visit me, and make me innocent of those who persecute me, not in your longsuffering. Know how I have received reproach from those who despise your words. Bring them to an end, and your word will be joy and gladness to my heart, because your name has been called upon me, Lord Almighty. I did not sit in the assembly of those who rejoice, but I feared before the face of your hand; I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness. Why do those who grieve me prevail against me? My wound is severe; from where shall I be healed? It has become for me like deceitful water that has no faithfulness” (Jeremiah 15:15–18).

In all this it is evident what the Prophet wished to be understood—though it is evident only to those who do not wish to twist what they read in order to support their perverse cause. Jeremiah said that his wound had become for him deceitful water without faithfulness. By his wound he wished those people to be understood who grieved him by living wickedly.

Thus the Apostle also says, “Outside are conflicts, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5); and again, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

And because he despaired that they could be corrected, he therefore said, “From where shall I be healed?”—as though he would always have to endure pain as long as such people remained among whom he was compelled to live.

That a people is customarily signified by the word “water” is made clear in the Apocalypse, where we learn by an interpretation stated there explicitly—not by our own conjecture—that the many waters signify many peoples (Revelation 17:15).

**[Note: [Col. 0340]** The manuscripts read *nostra* (“our”); the printed editions read *vestra* (“your”).]

Do not, then, through a perverse interpretation—or rather through error—blaspheme the sacrament of Baptism, even when it has been received by a most depraved person. For even in Simon the liar, the water of Baptism that he received was not deceitful (Acts 8:13), nor do all your liars give deceitful water when they baptize in the name of the Trinity. They do not first become liars when their crimes are exposed and proved and they confess them; rather, they were already liars when, although adulterous and wicked, they pretended to be chaste and innocent.

### CHAPTER CIII

**236. PETILIAN said:** David also said, “Let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.” Whom, then, does he call a sinner: me, who suffer your crimes, or you, who persecute an innocent man?

**237. AUGUSTINE replied:** I answer in the person of the body of Christ, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth, spread throughout the whole world because of the Gospel preached, as the Apostle says, “in every creature that is under heaven” (Colossians 1:23). I answer in the person of the whole world, of which the same David—whose words you do not understand—says, “He established the world, and it shall not be moved” (Psalm 92:1), while you insist that, because of the sins of others, it has not merely been shaken but has utterly perished.

In the person of that world, then, I reply: I do not persecute an innocent man.

David said “the oil of the sinner”; he did not say “of the Traditor,” nor “of the incense-bearer,” nor “of the persecutor,” but “of the sinner.” What, then, will you do according to your interpretation? First consider whether you yourself are not a sinner.

Do not tell me, “I am not a Traditor, I am not an incense-bearer, I am not a persecutor.” Nor am I, God willing, any of these things; nor is the world, which shall not be moved. But say, if you dare, “I am not a sinner.” For he said, “the oil of the sinner.” Whatever slight sin is found in you—how will you show that it does not belong to what is meant by “the oil of the sinner”?

**[Note: [Col. 0340]** In the printed editions the negative particle was wrongly transposed: “how will you not show it to belong?” The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.]

I ask whether you pray the Lord’s Prayer. If you do not pray with the prayer by which the Lord taught his disciples to pray, from where did you learn another prayer that surpasses, because of your greater merits, the merits of the Apostles? But if you pray as that Teacher graciously instructed, how do you say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”? For we do not ask forgiveness in those sins that were forgiven to us in Baptism.

Therefore, these words of the prayer either prevent you from being a petitioner before God or reveal you as a sinner. Go on, then, and let those who were baptized by you kiss your head—their heads having perished through your oil. But you must consider what you are, or what you think of yourself.

Was Optatus—whom pagans, Jews, Christians, our people and yours throughout all Africa loudly proclaim to be a thief, robber, Traditor, oppressor, separatist, and the satellite, not friend or client, of Gildo, whom one of your own called “Count God”—not at least some kind of sinner?

**[Note: [Col. 0340]** The reference is to Gildo.]

What, then, will become of those whose heads a defendant in a capital crime has anointed? Do they not also kiss your heads, although through this interpretation you judge so wickedly concerning their heads?

**[Note: [Col. 0341]** The manuscripts read “through their interpretation.”]

At least expose those people and warn them to be healed. Or is it rather your own head that needs healing, since you rave in this way?

“What, then,” you will say, “did David mean?” Why do you ask me? Ask him himself; he answers you in the preceding verse: “The righteous,” he says, “will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Psalm 140:5).

What could be clearer? What more evident? “I would rather,” he says, “be healed by a merciful rebuke than be deceived and perverted by flattering words, as though my head were being anointed.”

The same meaning is expressed elsewhere in Scripture in different words: “The wounds of a friend are better than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

### CHAPTER CIV

**238. PETILIAN said:** He praises the ointment of concord among brothers in this way:

“Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. It is like ointment upon the head, descending upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, descending upon the edge of his garment; like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion. For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever” (Psalm 132).

Thus, he says, unity is anointed, just as the priests were anointed.

**239. AUGUSTINE replied:** You speak truly. That priesthood, as a figure of the body of Christ, possessed an anointing by which it is saved through the bond of unity. Christ himself is also named from chrism, that is, from anointing. The Hebrews call him *Messiah*, a word resembling a term in the Punic language, as do many other Hebrew words and almost all of them.

**[Note: [Col. 0341]** On this subject, see *Tractates on the Gospel of John* 15.27: “Messiah, he says, means ‘anointed’; in Greek, the anointed one is *Christus*, in Hebrew *Messiah*. Hence in Punic, *Messe* is said for ‘anoint.’ For these languages—the Hebrew, Punic, and Syrian—are related and neighboring.”]

What, then, in that priesthood are the head, the beard, and the edge of the garment? Insofar as the Lord grants me understanding, the head is the Savior himself, the head of the body, concerning whom the Apostle says, “He himself is the head of the body, the Church” (Colossians 1:18).

The beard may appropriately be understood as strength. Therefore, upon those who are strong in his Church and cling to his mouth, so that they may proclaim the truth without fear, holy ointment descends from Christ himself as from the head—that is, spiritual sanctification.

**[Note: [Col. 0341]** The Erfurt, Lyon, and Venice editions read *orae ejus* (“to his edge”) instead of *ori ejus* (“to his mouth”).]

The edge of the garment may be understood as the part of the garment at the head, through which the head of the one wearing it enters. By this are signified the perfect faithful in the Church. For perfection is found in the edge. Surely you remember that it was said to a certain rich man, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” He departed sorrowfully, neglecting perfection and choosing defection (Matthew 19:21–22).

But did that mean that there were no others upon whom the ointment of unity would descend from the head, through the renunciation of earthly possessions that made them perfect, as upon the edge of the garment? For, apart from the Apostles and those who were appointed with them as leaders and teachers—whom we understand as the more eminent and stronger members signified by the beard—read in the Acts of the Apostles and see who placed the proceeds from the sale of their possessions at the Apostles’ feet. No one claimed anything as his own; everything was held in common; and distribution was made to each according to his need. They had one soul and one heart directed toward God (Acts 4:32–35).

You recognize that this is how it is written. Recognize, then, the good and pleasant dwelling of brothers together. Recognize Aaron’s beard. Recognize the edge of the spiritual garment.

Ask Scripture itself where these things began to occur: you will find them in Jerusalem. From this edge of the garment the whole unity is woven throughout all nations. The head entered the garment so that Christ might be clothed with the varied colors of the whole world, because in this edge of the garment the variety of languages itself appeared.

Why, then, do you resist the very head from which that ointment of unity—the fragrance of spiritual love—descends, while it testifies and says, “Repentance and remission of sins will be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47)?

And in this ointment you wish to interpret the sacrament of Chrism.

**[Note: [Col. 0342]** The Ambrosian and Erfurt editions and the manuscripts read *vult* (“he wishes”).]

Certainly, as a visible sign, it is holy, just as Baptism is. Yet it can exist even among the worst people, among those who consume their life in works of the flesh and will not possess the kingdom of heaven. For that reason they belong neither to Aaron’s beard, nor to the edge of his garment, nor to any woven part of the priestly garment.

Where will you place the works of the flesh that the Apostle lists? “The works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:19–21).

I will set aside fornications committed secretly. Interpret uncleanness however you wish; I will set that aside as well. Let us place sorcery there, since no one openly prepares and distributes poisons. I will also set aside heresies, since that is what you want. Should I set aside service to idols? The Apostle places avarice there, and avarice rages openly.

After setting these things aside, are there no licentious people among you, no avaricious people, no one who stubbornly practices enmity, no quarrelsome people, no jealous or hot-tempered people, no one devoted to dissension, no envious people, no drunkards, no people given to revelry? Are no such people anointed among you, and do none of them die inwardly known and outwardly manifest?

If you say that there are none, then, since you plainly lie out of a spirit of contention, take care that you are not yourself one of them. But if you are free from such people—not by physical separation but by a difference of life—and you see such crowds around your altars, groaning, what shall we say? They have been anointed with holy oil, yet, as the Apostle confirms with unmistakable truth, they will not possess the kingdom of God. Must Aaron’s beard and the edge of his garment therefore be subjected to sacrilegious insult, so that we should suppose such people belong there? God forbid.

Distinguish, then, the visible holy sacrament, which can exist both among the good and among the wicked—bringing reward to the former and judgment to the latter—from the invisible anointing of love, which belongs properly to the good.

Distinguish these things; distinguish them. May God distinguish you from the party of Donatus and restore you to the Catholic Church, from which they seized you as a catechumen and bound you with the deadly chain of an honor that brings death.

As for the dew of Hermon upon the mountains of Zion, however you understand it, you are not on the mountains of Zion, because you are not in the city established upon a mountain, which has this unmistakable sign: it cannot be hidden. It is known to all nations, whereas the party of Donatus is unknown to many nations. Therefore, that party is not the Church.

### CHAPTER CV

**240. PETILIAN said:** Woe, then, to you, who, by violating what is holy, sever unity, as the Prophet says:

“If the people have sinned, the priest will pray for them; but if the priest has sinned, who will pray for him?”

**241. AUGUSTINE replied:** A little earlier, when we were discussing the oil of the sinner, I seemed to be anointing your forehead so that you might dare to say whether you yourself were not a sinner. There—you have said it. What a crime! What a monstrosity!

Since you claim to be a priest, what else did you say through this prophetic testimony than that you are entirely without sin? For if you have sin, who will pray for you according to your interpretation?

This is how you sell yourselves to miserable congregations. You cite the Prophet: “If the people have sinned, the priest will pray for them; but if the priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25), so that they may believe you to be without sin and entrust their sins to be cleansed by your prayers.

What great men you are—exalted, heavenly, divine, no longer human but angels! You pray for the congregations, but you do not want the congregations to pray for you.

Are you more righteous than Paul? Are you more perfect than that great Apostle, who commended himself to the prayers of those whom he taught? “Devote yourselves to prayer,” he says, “keeping watch in it with thanksgiving, praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also imprisoned, so that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak” (Colossians 4:2–4).

There: prayer is offered for the Apostle, something you do not want done for a bishop. Do you see how diabolical this pride is? Prayer is offered for the Apostle, that he may proclaim the mystery of Christ as he ought to speak. Therefore, if you had devout congregations, you ought to have urged them to pray for you, so that you would not speak as you ought not.

Are you more righteous than the evangelist John, who says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

Finally, are you more righteous than Daniel, whom you yourself mentioned in this very letter, saying that “the king exposed the most righteous Daniel to the bites of wild beasts, as he thought”?

Daniel had not thought that this would happen. Indeed, with the affection of a friend, as the context of the reading proves, the king said to Daniel himself, “Your God, whom you serve continually, will deliver you” (Daniel 6:16).

But we have already said much about this. What concerns us now is that Daniel was most righteous—not merely on the testimony you give, although that is sufficient for the case I am pursuing with you, but on the testimony of the Spirit of God, speaking also through Ezekiel. There he named three outstandingly righteous men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—and said that they alone could be delivered from a particularly fierce anger of God that was about to fall upon the others (Ezekiel 14:14).

That most righteous man, one of the three renowned figures, prays and says, “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people before the Lord my God” (Daniel 9:20).

Yet you say that you are without sin because you are a priest, and that if the people sin you pray for them, but if you sin, who will pray for you?

Truly, through the impiety of such enormous arrogance, you make yourself unworthy of having that priest intercede for you whom the Prophet intended to signify by these words that you do not understand.

I shall now explain, insofar as the Lord grants it, so that no one may ask why this was said. God was preparing the minds of human beings through the Prophet to desire such a priest that no one could pray for him. He was foreshadowed in the period of the first people and the first temple, where everything was a figure of our reality.

For this reason the high priest alone entered the holy of holies to pray for the people; the people did not enter those inner sanctuaries with the priest (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). So also that priest entered the hidden places of heaven, into the truer holy of holies, while we are still here, for whom he intercedes.

Therefore the Prophet said, “If the people have sinned, the priest will pray for them; but if the priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” That is: Desire such a priest who cannot sin, so that he will not need anyone to pray for him.

And therefore the peoples pray for the Apostles (Acts 14:22), but no one prays for that priest who is the teacher and Lord of the Apostles.

Hear John confessing this and saying: “Brothers, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; he himself is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

“We have,” he said. “Our sins,” he said.

Learn humility, lest you fall—or rather, so that eventually you may rise. For you would not have said these things unless you had fallen.

### CHAPTER CVI

**242. PETILIAN said:** And lest a layman absolve himself of guilt, he is bound by this injunction: “Do not share in the sins of others.”

**[Note: [Col. 0344]** The manuscripts read *Ac ne* (“and lest”); the printed editions read *At ne* (“but lest”).]

**243. AUGUSTINE replied:** Through pride you are mistaken, as the saying goes, by the whole extent of heaven, because you do not wish to share in the world through humility.

For this was not said to a layman, and you do not know how it was said. When the Apostle wrote to Timothy, he was giving this warning to Timothy himself. Elsewhere he says to him, “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1 Timothy 4:14).

**[Note: [Col. 0344]** The printed editions read *presbyteri* (“of a presbyter”); the manuscripts, followed here, read *presbyterii* (“of the presbytery”).]

Many other indications also show that he was not a layman. When he says, “Do not share in the sins of others,” he intended this to be understood as consent and approval. Hence, immediately adding how Timothy should do this, he says, “Keep yourself pure” (1 Timothy 5:22).

Paul himself certainly did not share in the sins of others merely because he tolerated in bodily unity false brothers over whom he grieved. Nor did the Apostles who preceded Judas share in his theft and wickedness merely because they shared the sacred supper with him, when he was already the Lord’s betrayer and had been identified by the Lord.

### CHAPTER CVII

**244. PETILIAN said:** Again, through this statement the Apostle compares the associates of an evil conscience:

“Those who do such things,” he says, “and those who approve of those who do them are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32).

**[Note: [Col. 0345]** The manuscripts read *Hac itemque sententia* (“through this same statement”).]

**245. AUGUSTINE replied:** However you may have said these things, I do not care. They are true, and this is what the Catholic Church teaches: that there is a great difference between those who approve of such things because they are pleased by them and those who tolerate people by whom such things are displeasing.

The former become chaff, as the chaff follows barrenness; the latter are wheat. Let them wait until they are separated by Christ the winnower.

**[Note: [Col. 0345]** The manuscripts read: “They are wheat, waiting until they are separated.” The Lovaniensis edition reads: “They are wheat, while they wait to be separated by Christ the winnower.”]

### CHAPTER CVIII

**246. PETILIAN said:** Come, then, peoples, to the Church, and flee the Traditors, if you do not wish to perish with them. For, so that you may easily recognize that, although they themselves are guilty, they can judge our faith very well, I baptize those whom they have defiled; they, God forbid, receive mine as baptized. They certainly would not do this if they had recognized any faults in our Baptism. See, then, what we give, and how holy it is that the sacrilegious enemy fears to destroy.

**247. AUGUSTINE replied:** We have already said much against this error, both in this work and elsewhere. But because you imagine that this statement is such a great foundation of your vanity that you thought you should end your letter with it, so that it might remain more freshly in the minds of readers, I shall answer briefly.

We approve Baptism among heretics—not the baptism of heretics, but the Baptism of Christ—in the same way that among fornicators, unclean persons, the licentious, idolaters, sorcerers, those who harbor enmities, quarrelsome people, the jealous, the hot-tempered, those devoted to dissension, the envious, drunkards, revellers, and people like them, we approve Baptism—not theirs, but Christ’s.

For all these people, including the heretics who are placed among them, will not possess the kingdom of God, as the Apostle says (Galatians 5:19–21); and therefore they will belong on the left hand with the devil. Yet they are not to be considered part of the body of Christ, which is the Church, merely because they participate bodily in his sacraments.

For the sacraments are holy even in such people, and, when handled and received by them unworthily, they will contribute to their greater judgment. But they themselves are not within that structure of the Church which grows through connection and contact among the members of Christ, for the increase of God.

That Church is founded upon the rock, as the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). But they build upon sand, as the same Lord says: “Everyone who hears my words and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who builds his house upon sand” (Matthew 7:26).

But do not suppose that the Church founded upon the rock exists in only one part of the world and is not spread to the ends of the earth. Hear her voice from the Psalm, groaning amid the evils of her pilgrimage. For she says, “From the ends of the earth I have cried to you; when my heart was distressed, you raised me upon a rock; you led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy” (Psalm 60:3–4).

See how she cries from the ends of the earth. Therefore she is not confined to Africa alone, nor to Africans alone, with a bishop being sent to Rome for a few Montenses and from Africa to Spain to the household of a single woman.

**[Note: [Col. 0346]** Augustine observed that the Donatists in Rome were called Montenses in *On Heresies*, chapter 69, and in Letter 53. Before him, Optatus also mentioned them in Book 2. We learn from Letter 53 and from *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3, that they were also called Cutzupitani or Cutzupitae.]

**[Note: [Col. 0346]** The woman was Lucilla.]

See how she is raised upon the rock. Therefore not everyone who builds upon sand is to be counted as belonging to her—that is, those who hear Christ’s words and do not do them, although among both us and you they possess and administer the sacrament of Baptism.

See how her hope is God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—not Peter, not Paul, and still less Donatus or Petilian.

What we fear to destroy, then, is not yours but Christ’s; and it remains holy in itself even among sacrilegious people. For when people come to us from you, we cannot receive them unless we destroy what is yours.

We destroy the infidelity of the deserter; we do not destroy the emperor’s mark.

Therefore consider carefully what you yourself have said and destroy it: “I baptize,” you say, “those whom they have defiled; they, God forbid, receive mine as baptized.”

You do not baptize those who have been defiled; rather, by the fraud of your error, you rebaptize them. We do not receive your baptized people; we destroy your error, from which they are yours, and receive the Baptism of Christ, through which they have been baptized.

Thus, quite appropriately, you placed the words “God forbid” in the middle of your statement: “They, God forbid, receive mine as baptized.” For while you intended “God forbid” to mean that we should not receive your people, I take you—without your knowing it—to have said, “Mine, God forbid.”

Indeed, God forbid that those who now pass over to the Catholic Church should be yours. Nor do they pass over in such a way as to become our baptized people; they become our companions. But as those baptized with Christ, they are with us.

### BOOK THREE

Augustine refutes the second letter that Petilian wrote against him after seeing the first of the preceding books. The letter was full of abuse. Setting aside his own defense, Augustine shows that Petilian has failed in his case and has been unable to answer the matter under discussion.

**[Note: [Col. 0345]** Possidius identifies this third book in his *Index*, chapter 3, with the words: “Against the second letter of the same man, one book.”]

**[Col. 0345]**

### CHAPTER ONE

**1.** Petilian, I read your letter when I was able to read it. In it you made sufficiently clear that you were opposed to the Catholic Church on behalf of the party of Donatus, that you were neither able to say anything adequate nor permitted to remain silent.

What agitation you suffered! Through what storms of heart did you toss when you read the things to which I replied, with as much brevity and clarity as I could, concerning that part of your letter which had then come into my hands?

For you saw that the truth which we hold and defend was strengthened by such firmness and illuminated by such light that you could not find anything to say against it by which it might be convicted and refuted.

You also observed that the expectation of many who had read it had turned toward you. They wanted to know what you would say, what you would do, how you would escape, and by what route you would break out of the great straits with which the word of God had surrounded you.

At that point, instead of disregarding the opinion of foolish people and proceeding toward a true and sound judgment, you did what Scripture had foretold concerning such people: “You loved wickedness more than goodness, iniquity rather than speaking righteousness” (Psalm 51:5).

Accordingly, if I wished to repay your abuse with abuse, what else would we be than two abusers? Those who read us would either reject us both with healthy seriousness, as objects of disgust, or else eagerly absorb our maliciousness with a perverse pleasure.

**[Note: [Col. 0347]** The manuscripts read *malivola voluptate* (“malicious pleasure”) rather than *malevola voluntate* (“malicious inclination”).]

Whenever I answer anyone, whether by speaking or writing, even when provoked by insulting accusations, I restrain and crush, insofar as the Lord grants me strength, the barbs of empty indignation. Concerned for the hearer or reader, I do not act so as to become superior to a man by reviling him, but more beneficial by refuting his error.

**2.** If those who consider what you have written possess any kind of heart, what benefit did it bring your case—the case being debated between us concerning Catholic communion or the party of Donatus—that, abandoning a matter of public concern, you attacked the life of one man with private hostility and insulting abuse, as though that man were the issue under investigation?

You thought so poorly—not merely of Christians, but of the human race itself—that you did not believe your writings could fall into the hands of prudent people who would rise above our persons and instead investigate the question at issue between us. They would attend not to what kind of people we were, but to what we said for the truth or against error.

You ought to have respected the judgment of such people and guarded against their criticism, lest they think that you had found nothing to say except by setting before yourself someone whom you could abuse in any way.

But evidently you also acted for the sake of certain people’s frivolity and vanity—people who gladly listen to quarrels among eloquent disputants, so that, when they attend to how eloquently you revile, they do not notice how truthfully you are refuted.

**[Note: [Col. 0347]** The printed editions read *nugantium* (“those who jest”); the manuscripts read *jurgantium* (“those who quarrel”).]

I think you also intended that, while occupied with defending myself, I would abandon the case I had undertaken, and that, with people’s attention turned not to the words of disputants but to the words of litigants, the truth—which you fear may shine forth and become known—would be obscured.

What, then, can I do against such a plan except, setting aside my own defense, hold fast to the matter from which no accuser of mine can divert my purpose?

I shall exalt the house of my God, whose beauty I have loved, by the proclamation of a serving voice; but I shall humble and abase myself. For I have chosen to be despised in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of heretics (Psalm 83:11).

Therefore, Petilian, I shall turn my speech away from you for a little while and address those whom you have tried to turn away from me by your abuse—as though I were trying to turn people toward myself, rather than toward God together with me.

## CHAPTER II

### 3

Hear, then, all of you who have read the curses which Petilianus, more enraged than thoughtful, has spewed out against me. First I shall address you in the words of the Apostle; and these words are certainly true, whatever I myself may be. “Let a man regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, what is sought among stewards is that one be found faithful. But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you or by a human tribunal; indeed, I do not even judge myself.”

Now, although I do not dare to apply what follows to myself and say confidently, “For I am conscious of nothing” [Note: [Col. 0348] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “faithfully.”], nevertheless I say in the sight of God: I am conscious of none of the things with which Petilianus has accused the period of my life after I was baptized in Christ; yet I am not thereby justified. “It is the Lord who judges me. Therefore do not judge anything before the time [Note: [Col. 0348] The printed editions have, “judge anyone.” The manuscripts have, “judge anything.” In Greek: *ti krinete* (‘what do you judge?’).], until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness, and will disclose the purposes of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God.” But these things, brothers, “I have transferred to myself,” so that “no one may be puffed up on behalf of one against another beyond what is written” (1 Corinthians 4:1–6).

Therefore, “let no one glory in a human being. For all things are yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (ibid. 3:21–23). Again I say: let no one glory in a human being. I repeat it more often: let no one glory in a human being. If you discern anything praiseworthy in us, refer it to the praise of the one from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift”; for it comes down from above, from the Father of lights, “with whom there is no change or shadow due to alteration” (James 1:17). For what do we have that we did not receive? And if we received it, why should we glory as though we had not received it? (1 Corinthians 4:7).

And in all these matters, whatever good you know to be in us, “be imitators of us, if indeed we are of Christ” [Note: [Col. 0348] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “as we are of Christ.”] (ibid. 11:1). But if you suspect, believe, or see any evils in us, hold fast to that saying of the Lord by which you may safely avoid abandoning his Church on account of the evils of human beings: “What we say, do; but whatever evils you think or know that we do, do not do” (Matthew 23:3).

For now is not the time for me to clear myself before you, since, setting aside my own case, I have undertaken to commend to you something beneficial: that no one should glory in a human being. “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17:5). If this command of the Lord and of the Apostle is retained and observed, then even if I should fail and be crushed in my own case, as the enemy wishes me to be regarded, the cause which I serve will be victorious.

For if you hold most firmly what I exhort and strive to impress upon you—that everyone who places his hope in a human being is accursed, and that no one should glory in a human being—you will in no way abandon the Lord’s threshing floor on account of the chaff which either now, struck by the wind of pride, flies away, or will be separated at the final winnowing (Matthew 3:12). Nor will you flee from the great house on account of vessels made for dishonor (2 Timothy 2:20). Nor, because of the bad fish to be separated on the shore, will you go out through the torn nets (Matthew 13:47–48). Nor, because of the goats who will be placed on the left by the shepherd when he divides them, will you leave the good pastures of unity (ibid. 25:32–33). Nor, because of the weeds mingled with the wheat, will you separate yourselves by an impious division from the fellowship of the wheat, whose head is that grain which, having died, multiplied, and which grows together throughout the world until the harvest [Note: [Col. 0349] Perhaps, “they grow.”]. For the field is the world, not Africa; and the harvest is the end of the age (ibid. 13:24–40), not the time of Donatus.

## CHAPTER III

### 4

You certainly recognize why these Gospel likenesses were given: for no other reason than that no one should glory in a human being, and that no one should be puffed up on behalf of one against another and say, “I belong to Paul,” since Paul was not crucified for you, and you were not baptized in the name of Paul—much less in the name of Caecilianus or of any one of us (1 Corinthians 1:12–13).

You were given these examples so that you might learn, while the chaff is threshed together with the grain, and while the bad fish swim together with the good within the Lord’s nets, to endure the mixture of the wicked for the sake of the good until the time of the winnowing, rather than violate the love of the good on account of the wicked.

This mixture is not eternal but temporary; nor is it spiritual but bodily. The angels will not err in it when they gather the wicked from among the righteous and cast them into the furnace of burning fire [Note: [Col. 0349] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain have, “and cast them into it.”]. For “the Lord knows those who are his.” And although one cannot at present withdraw bodily from the wicked, nevertheless everyone who names the name of the Lord should withdraw from iniquity itself (2 Timothy 2:19).
