It is possible meanwhile to be separated and withdrawn from the wicked in life, conduct, heart, and will; and this separation must always be maintained. But bodily separation should be awaited confidently, patiently, and courageously until the end of the age. With reference to this expectation it is said: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26:14).

For the greatest crown of endurance is not to disturb, by any tumultuous and rash dissension, the love of those who do not seek their own but the things of Jesus Christ, among false brothers who have slipped in and seek their own rather than the things of Jesus Christ; nor proudly and impiously to tear apart the unity of the Lord’s net, which gathers fish of every kind while it is being drawn to the shore—that is, to the end of the age.

Yet each person thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, and so deceives himself; and he wishes his own judgment, or that of his own people [Note: [Col. 0349] The manuscripts, together with the Amsterdam and Erasmus editions, have, “or their judgment.”], to suffice for separating Christian peoples. These people openly claim to know that certain wicked persons are unworthy of communion in the sacraments of the Christian religion. Yet whatever they claim to know, they cannot persuade the universal Church, which, as foretold, is spread among all nations.

When they shun communion with those whom they suppose they know, they abandon unity. Rather, if they possessed that love which bears all things, they ought not to separate themselves from the good whom they could not teach about the evils of others in all nations; instead, they ought themselves to tolerate in one nation what they knew.

Accordingly, even without an investigation of the case—a case in which they are convicted by the most serious evidence of having calumniated the innocent—they are more plausibly believed to have fabricated false charges of betrayal, since they did not hesitate to commit the far more wicked crime of impious division.

For even if everything they have proclaimed concerning the betrayal were true, they still ought in no way to have abandoned the fellowship of Christians whom divine Scripture commends to the ends of the earth, merely because they themselves knew something while the others did not.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5

I have not said this in order that ecclesiastical discipline should be neglected, or that each person should be permitted to do whatever he wishes without any correction, medicinal punishment, fearful gentleness, or severity arising from charity. For where then would be the Apostle’s command: “Correct the restless, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone” (1 Thessalonians 5:14–15)?

When he added, “See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone,” he clearly showed that correcting the restless is not repaying evil for evil, even though the punishment of correction is imposed for the fault of restlessness. The punishment of correction, therefore, is not itself evil, although the fault is evil. For the iron belongs not to an enemy who wounds but to a physician who cuts.

These things take place in the Church, and that inward spirit of gentleness burns with zeal for God, lest the chaste virgin betrothed to one husband, Christ, should in some of her members be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ, just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

Nevertheless, far be it from the servants of the master of the household to forget the command of their Lord and, inflamed against the multitude of weeds, burn with the fervor of holy indignation so that, when they wish to gather them before the proper time, the wheat too may be uprooted together with them.

They would be guilty of this sin even if they demonstrated that the true crimes they charged against those whom they accused had actually been committed. For they were separated by impious presumption not only from the wicked, whose fellowship they appeared to avoid, but also from the faithful good established among all nations, to whom they could not prove what they claimed to know. They also dragged many people—those over whom they had some authority and who were less able to understand that the unity of the Church spread throughout the whole world must not be abandoned on account of the sins of others—into the same destruction.

Thus, even if they knew that they were charging certain people with genuine crimes, the weak person would perish through their knowledge, for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11), since, offended by the evils of others, he was destroying within himself the good of peace that he had with good brothers—some of whom had not heard such things, some of whom feared rashly to believe matters neither investigated nor proved, and some of whom had humbly left the whole case, whatever it might be, to the ecclesiastical judges before whom it had been brought across the sea [Note: [Col. 0350] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “however great they might be.”].

## CHAPTER V

### 6

You, therefore, holy offspring of the one Catholic mother, subject to the Lord, guard yourselves against an example of this kind of crime and error with all the vigilance you can.

However brightly anyone may shine with the light of learning and reputation, and however much he may boast that he is a precious stone, if he wishes to draw you after himself, remember that the strong woman, that one woman beloved by her one husband, whom Holy Scripture describes at the end of Proverbs, is more precious than precious stones.

Let no one say, “I shall follow him, because he made me a Christian,” or, “I shall follow him, because he baptized me.” “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16).

No one, even while proclaiming the name of Christ and bearing and administering Christ’s sacrament, should be followed against the unity of Christ. Let each person test his own work; and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. For “each will carry his own burden” (Galatians 6:4–5)—namely, the burden of rendering an account, because each one of us will render an account for himself.

Therefore, “let us no longer judge one another” (Romans 14:12–13). But as regards the burdens of mutual love, “bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” For “whoever thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Galatians 6:2–3).

Let us therefore bear with one another in love, making every effort to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:2). Outside this unity, whoever gathers does not gather with Christ; and whoever does not gather with Christ scatters (Matthew 12:30).

## CHAPTER VI

### 7

Therefore, whether the matter concerns Christ, his Church, or anything else pertaining to your faith and life [Note: [Col. 0351] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “our faith and life.”], I will not speak of ourselves—for we cannot possibly be compared with the one who said, “Even if we”—but I will speak altogether of what he added next: “If an angel from heaven should announce to you anything beyond what you have received in the lawful and evangelical Scriptures, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).

As we continually affirm these things with you and with all whom we desire to win for Christ, and as, among other things, we proclaim the holy Church which we read to have been promised in God’s Scriptures and which we see being fulfilled among all nations just as it was promised, we have earned from those whom we desire to draw into her peaceful embrace the flames of hatred—as though we had bound them to that side concerning which they can find nothing to say, or as though we had commanded the Prophets and Apostles, long beforehand, to place no testimonies in their books by which the part of Donatus might be taught to be the Church of Christ.

And indeed, dearest brothers, when we hear false accusations from those whom we offend by proclaiming the words of truth and refuting the empty talk of error, we have, as you know, abundant consolation.

For if, in those matters with which they accuse me, the testimony of my conscience does not stand against me in the sight of God, to which no mortal eye is directed, then I ought not merely not to grieve; I ought also to rejoice and exult, because my reward is great in heaven.

Nor should we consider how bitter what I hear is, but how false it is; how truthful is the one for whose name I hear it; and to whom it is said, “Your name is oil poured out” (Song of Songs 1:2). Rightly, therefore, his name is fragrant among all nations, while those who curse us attempt to confine its fragrance within one small part of Africa.

Why, then, should we indignantly endure the fact that they defame us, when they thus detract from Christ’s glory—those whose party and contentiousness are opposed to what was foretold so long beforehand concerning his ascent into heaven and the pouring out of his name like ointment: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Psalm 56:12)?

## CHAPTER VII

### 8

As we produce these and similar divine testimonies against human empty talk, we endure bitter insults from the enemies of Christ’s glory. Let them say whatever they wish, while he exhorts us, saying:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they persecute you, curse you, and speak every evil against you falsely on my account.”

What he said above, “for righteousness’ sake,” he repeated when he later said, “on my account,” because “he became for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption,” so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Since he says, “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew 5:10–12), if I hold in a good conscience what was said, “for righteousness’ sake” and “on my account,” then whoever deliberately detracts from my reputation unwillingly adds to my reward.

For he did not merely teach me this by his word; he also confirmed it by his example. Follow the faith of the Holy Scriptures, and you will find that Christ rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Follow the accusations of his enemies, and you will now suppose that he was stolen from the tomb by his disciples.

What else, then, should we expect, insofar as he grants it, when we defend his household against his enemies? “If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (Matthew 10:25).

If, therefore, we endure, we shall also reign with him. But if the anger of the accuser strikes not merely one ear but also bites the conscience with the truth of the accusation, what does it profit me if the whole world raises me up with continual praise? Thus neither does the praise of the one who praises heal a bad conscience, nor does the reproach of the one who insults wound a good one.

Nevertheless, your hope, which is in the Lord, is not deceived, even if perhaps in secret we are such as the enemy wishes us to be thought, because you have not placed that hope in us, nor have you ever heard this from us.

You are therefore secure, whatever we may be, since you have learned to say, “With the Lord as my hope, I shall not be moved” [Note: [Col. 0352] The printed editions have, “I shall not be weakened.” But the old Floriacensis codex has, “I shall not be moved.” Augustine likewise has this reading in his exposition of the same Psalm 25.] (Psalm 25:1), and, “In God I shall hope; I shall not fear what a human being can do to me” (Psalm 56:12).

And to those who attempt to seduce you toward the earthly heights of proud human beings, you know how to reply: “I trust in the Lord. How can you say to my soul, ‘Flee like a sparrow to your mountain’?” (Psalm 11:2).

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9

Not only are you secure—you in whom the very truth of Christ pleases, however much and wherever it is proclaimed through us, and who, because you gladly hear it through the small service of our tongue, also think well and kindly of us—whatever we may be, because your hope is in him whom we proclaim to you through his mercy toward you.

You too are secure, whoever among you has received the sacrament of holy Baptism through our ministry; indeed, rejoice with that same security, because you were baptized not in us but in Christ.

You did not therefore put on us but Christ. Nor did I ask you whether you were turning to me, but to the living God; nor whether you believed in me, but in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

And if you answered with a truthful heart, it was not the removal of dirt from the flesh but “the appeal of a good conscience” that saved you (1 Peter 3:21)—not a fellow servant but the Lord, not a herald but the judge.

For it is not true, as Petilianus inconsiderately said, that “the conscience of the giver,” or, as he added, “the conscience of the holy giver,” is regarded as cleansing the conscience of the recipient. When what belongs to God is given, even an unholy conscience gives something holy.

Whether that conscience is holy or unholy, the recipient certainly cannot inspect it. But what is given can plainly be received with complete security, since it is known to him who is always holy, regardless of the sort of minister through whom it is received.

If the holy words had not been spoken from the chair of Moses, Truth would not have said, “Do whatever they say.” But if those who spoke the holy words had themselves been holy, he would not have said, “Do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:3).

For in no way is a grape found among thorns, since it never grows from the roots of thorns. But when a vine branch has become entangled among thorny hedges, the fruit hanging there is not for that reason rejected; the thorn is avoided, and the grape is plucked.

## CHAPTER IX

### 10

Therefore, as I have often said and emphatically insist, whatever we may be, you are secure, since you have God as Father and his Church as mother.

Although goats may graze together with sheep, they will not stand at the right hand. Although chaff may be threshed together with wheat, it will not enter the granary. Although bad fish may swim together with good fish within the Lord’s nets, they will not be placed in vessels.

Let no one glory—not even in a good human being. Let no one flee from God’s good gifts—not even because of a wicked human being.

## CHAPTER X

### 11

These things, dearest Christian Catholic brothers, should suffice for you concerning the present matter. If you retain them with Catholic love, since you are one flock secure under one shepherd, I am not greatly concerned about whatever enemy insults either me, or your fellow member, or certainly your dog—provided that he compels me to bark more for your defense than for my own.

If my own defense were necessary for the case, I would use one that was very brief and easy: I would condemn and detest before everyone the whole period of my life before I received Christ’s Baptism, insofar as it concerned my desires and errors, lest I should appear to seek my own glory in defending that period rather than the glory of the one who, by his grace, freed me even from myself.

Accordingly, when I hear that my former life is being blamed, whatever the motive of the person who does this, I am not so ungrateful as to grieve. For in proportion as he accuses my vice, I praise my physician.

Why, then, should I now labor to defend those past and abolished evils of mine, about which Petilianus said many things that were false, but did not say more things that were true? As for the period of my life after Baptism, I speak needlessly to all of you who know me about matters that can be known by human beings.

But those who do not know me ought not to be so unjust toward me as to believe Petilianus about me more than they believe you. For if one should not believe a friend who praises, neither should one believe an enemy who attacks.

There remain those things which are hidden within a human being, where conscience alone is witness [Note: [Col. 0354] The printed editions have, “where such a conscience is witness.” The manuscript reading, “where conscience itself is witness,” is better.], though it cannot be a witness before human beings.

In these matters Petilianus says that I am a Manichaean, speaking about another person’s conscience; I say that I am not one, speaking about my own conscience. Choose whom you will believe.

Nevertheless, since even this brief and easy defense of mine is not needed here, where the question concerns not the merit of some individual human being but the truth of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0354] Erasmus and Louvain have, “the unity.” Amsterdam and the manuscripts have, “the truth.” The latter is supported by the passage below, section 28, “concerning the truth of the Church or of Baptism,” and also by *On the Single Baptism*, section 22, “those walking in the truth of the Church.”], I must say more to you—all of you in the party of Donatus who have read the curses Petilianus wrote against me. He would not have uttered them against me if he had disregarded your destruction; but then he would not have had the inward compassion of Christian charity.

## CHAPTER XI

### 12

What wonder, then, if, when I drag the grains from the Lord’s threshing floor inward together with earth and chaff, I suffer the injury of the rebounding dust; or if, when I diligently seek out the lost sheep of my Lord, I am torn by the brambles of thorny tongues?

I beg you: lay aside for a little while your partisan zeal, and judge between Petilianus and me with some fairness. I want you to understand that I am pleading the Church’s case; he wants you to understand that I am pleading my own. Why else would this be, except that he does not dare to say of my witnesses, whom I consistently bring forward in the Church’s case, “Do not believe them”? For they are the Prophets and Apostles, and Christ himself, the Lord of the Prophets and Apostles.

But whatever he wishes to say about me—one human being against another, and your fellow member against an outsider—you readily believe. And if I should produce any witnesses to my life, how difficult would it be for him to say that they should not be believed and quickly persuade you of this? Especially since anyone who says a single word on my behalf will immediately be regarded as an enemy of the party of Donatus and therefore as your enemy.

Petilianus therefore reigns. Whenever he hurls any insults against me, you all applaud and cheer him. He has found a winning case—but with you as judges. He will require neither witness nor argument, since his only task is to prove what he says, and he proves it by cursing most abundantly the person whom you hate most.

Since the testimonies of divine Scripture, when they are recited so densely and clearly on behalf of the Catholic Church, leave him mute while you grieve, he has chosen a subject on which he can speak while you favor him. Though defeated, he pretends to maintain his position [Note: [Col. 0354] The manuscripts have, “pretending to maintain his position.” One of them, the Cygirannensis, has *statim* (“immediately”) instead of *statum* (“position”).], and says such things against me, or even more wicked ones.

It is enough for the matter I am now handling [Note: [Col. 0354] According to Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 326–328, the passage would be better read: “on which he can speak while you favor him, and though defeated—if he should say such things against me a thousand times over, or even more wicked ones—it is enough for me.”], that, whatever my condition in it, the Church on whose behalf I speak is nevertheless unconquered.

## CHAPTER XII

### 13

For I am a human being from Christ’s threshing floor: chaff if I am wicked, grain if I am good. Petilianus’s tongue is not the winnowing shovel of this threshing floor; and therefore, whatever evil he may truly say even against its chaff, in no way prejudices its wheat.

Whatever curses and slanders he may hurl against the wheat itself exercise its faith on earth and increase its reward in heaven.

For the holy servants of God, who serve God in holiness, do not wage war against Petilianus and flesh and blood of this kind, but “against principalities and powers and rulers of such darkness” (Ephesians 6:12), all of whom are adversaries of the truth. Would that we might say to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (ibid. 5:8).

Whatever criminal insults are spoken against the servants of God who wage this warfare—insults which create a bad reputation among the malicious and the rashly credulous—are left-hand weapons. Even by these the devil is conquered.

For when we are tested by a good reputation as to whether we are not lifted up into pride, and by a bad reputation as to whether we love the very enemies who invent these things against us, we conquer the devil by “the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left” [Note: [Col. 0355] The printed editions have, “with the right hand and with the left.” The manuscripts provide the corrected reading.] (2 Corinthians 6:7).

When the Apostle had mentioned these weapons, saying, “the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,” he immediately explained what he meant: “through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute” (ibid. 6:8), and other things of this kind. He counted glory and good repute among the weapons of the right hand, and dishonor and ill repute among those of the left.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 14

If, then, I am God’s servant and a soldier not rejected, however eloquent an insulter Petilianus may be, should I be distressed because the most skillful craftsman of weapons of the left hand has been prepared for me [Note: [Col. 0355] The manuscripts have, “has been procured.”]?

It is necessary that, with the help of my Lord, I fight with the utmost skill [Note: [Col. 0355] The Louvain edition alone has, “with the utmost openness.”] using these weapons, and strike with them the one against whom I fight invisibly—the one who, with a most perverse and ancient cunning, deliberately contrives and works so that I may hate Petilianus on account of these things, and thus be unable to fulfill Christ’s command: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35).

May the mercy of the one who loved me and gave himself for me turn this away from me, so that, hanging on the cross, he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid. 23:34), and taught me to say concerning Petilianus and such enemies of mine: “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are saying.”

## CHAPTER XIV

### 15

Therefore, if I obtain from you, as I have intended, that, with all partisan zeal removed from your minds, you judge fairly between Petilianus and me, I shall show you that he did not answer my writings. Then you will understand that, compelled by a lack of truth, he abandoned the case and was able to hurl whatever insults he could against the human being who handled the case in such a way that he could not reply.

Although what I am going to say is so plainly evident that, even if partisan zeal and hatred of me alienate your minds from me, provided only that you read both writings, you will certainly admit within your own hearts that I have spoken the truth.

### 16

In my reply to the first part of his writings, which had then come into my hands, I passed over his insulting and sacrilegious verbosity, where he says:

“Twice-baptism is brought up against us by those who, under the name of Baptism, have polluted their souls with a guilty washing; to whom all filth is cleaner than they are; whom a perverse cleanliness has managed to defile with its water.”

I retained for examination and refutation what follows: “For the conscience of the giver is regarded, which cleanses the conscience of the recipient.” And I asked from what the recipient is to be cleansed when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the person who is to receive it is unaware of this (above, book 1, chapter 1).

## CHAPTER XV

### 17

Now read his most abundant curses, which, puffed up and angry, he poured out against me. See whether he answered me when I asked from what the recipient is to be cleansed if the giver’s conscience is polluted and the recipient is unaware of this.

I beg you: search carefully. Examine all the pages, count all the lines, turn over all the words, analyze every syllable, and tell me whether you find where he answered: when the giver’s conscience is polluted, from what is the conscience of the person who is to receive this to be cleansed, if he is unaware of it?

### 18

For what relevance did it have that he added the word which he claimed I had omitted, and insisted that he had written it this way: “For the conscience of the holy giver is regarded, which cleanses the conscience of the recipient”?

To make clear that I had not omitted it, the addition in no way hinders my inquiry, nor does it relieve his failure. I ask again about the very words and inquire whether he answered [Note: [Col. 0356] Louvain has, “and I ask again.”]:

“If the conscience of the holy giver is regarded, which cleanses the conscience of the recipient, from what is the recipient’s conscience cleansed when the giver’s conscience is stained and the person who is to receive it is unaware of this?”

Insist that he answer this. Do not allow anyone to abandon the case and turn away abusively:

“If the conscience of the holy giver is regarded”—see that I did not say, “the conscience of the giver,” but added, “of the holy giver.” If, I say, “the conscience of the holy giver is regarded, which cleanses the conscience of the recipient,” then from what is the one who receives Baptism to be cleansed when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the person who is to receive it is unaware of this?

## CHAPTER XVI

### 19

Let him now go on and, with gasping lungs and swollen throat, accuse me as though I were a dialectician. Indeed, let him summon dialectic itself before the public tribunal as an artificer of lying, and, with the most thunderous uproar, stretch out the mouth of a courtroom advocate in its defense.

Let him say whatever he wishes before the unlearned—enough to irritate the learned and deceive the ignorant. Let him stigmatize me on account of rhetoric by invoking the name of Tertullus the orator, by whom Paul was accused (Acts 24:1). Let him assume for himself, on account of the advocacy in which he once boasted of his power, the name of Paraclete, and, because of this, deliriously claim that he is not, but once was, a namesake of the Holy Spirit.

Let him eagerly exaggerate the impurities of the Manichaeans, and, by barking, attempt to twist them against me. Let him recite the deeds of condemned persons unknown and known to me, and turn into a charge of a crime supposedly already prejudged the fact that, in defense of himself, a former friend of mine named me in my absence more than he named himself—by some new right of his own, I do not know what.

Let him read the titles of my letters, inscribed by himself or by his followers as they pleased, and take delight as though he had caught me in them. Let him brand the eulogies of bread, given simply and cheerfully, with the ridiculous name of poisonous obscenity and madness. Let him think so badly of your hearts [Note: [Col. 0357] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “our hearts.”] that he presumes he can make you believe that love-magic was given to a woman with her husband not only aware of it but even approving [Note: [Col. 0357] The word “approving” is absent from all the manuscripts and from the editions of Amsterdam and Erasmus. Erasmus placed it in the margin of his book, noting that something similar seemed to be missing.].

Let him try to use against me what the man who was later to ordain me bishop wrote about me in anger while I was still a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0357] Megalius, bishop of Calama and primate of Numidia, ordained Augustine, according to Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 8. Augustine responds again to the same accusation, arising from the letter of Megalius the primate, in *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 80, section 92, and book 4, chapter 64, sections 78–79.].

But what he sought and obtained from the holy council—a pardon for having sinned against us in this way—he does not want to count in my favor. He is so ignorant of, or forgetful of, Christian gentleness and the Gospel command that he even treats as a crime the fact that what was mercifully forgiven a brother who humbly asked to be forgiven, as he himself wished to be forgiven, was in fact forgiven.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 20

Let him also proceed in a prolix but plainly empty speech concerning matters he entirely fails to understand, or in which he rather abuses the ignorance of the majority.

From the confession of a certain woman—who said that she was a catechumen of the Manichaeans, although she had been a nun in the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0357] Louvain has, “and.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have, “in”; “Church” is understood.]—let him say and write whatever he pleases about their baptism, not knowing, or pretending not to know, that those people are not called catechumens there [Note: [Col. 0357] The printed editions have, “illicitly”; and below, “as though Baptism.” Moreover, at “owed,” the Amsterdam and Erasmus editions have, “removed.” The manuscripts provide the readings followed here.] as though Baptism were at some time owed to them, but are called this because they are also called “Hearers” (*Auditores*): namely, because they are thought unable to observe the better and greater precepts observed by those whom they distinguish and honor under the name of the Elect.

With astonishing recklessness, whether falsely or deceptively, let him insist that I too was a Manichaean when I was a presbyter. Let him propose and attack the words of the third book of my *Confessions* [Note: [Col. 0357] All the manuscripts read, “of the fourth book.”], although they are perfectly clear to readers in themselves and in light of the many things said before and after them, according to whatever interpretation seems appropriate to him.

Finally, let him exult as a victor, as though he had exposed me as a thief of his words because I allegedly removed two of them.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 21

In all these matters, as you will be able to learn or relearn by reading, he certainly exercised the force of his tongue with whatever breadth of boasting he wished. Yet nowhere did he say from what the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware that the giver’s conscience is stained.

But amid or after his great uproar—so great, and, as he himself thinks, so terrifying—I slowly, as the saying goes, and gently [Note: [Col. 0358] According to Morel, “and softly” is better. See *Elementa Critica*, pp. 110, 141.] repeat this very question and demand that you answer it [Note: [Col. 0358] Perhaps, “that he answer it.”]:

“If the conscience of the holy giver is regarded, which cleanses the recipient’s conscience, from what is the one who is unaware of the giver’s stained conscience to be cleansed?”

Throughout his entire letter I find nothing said in response to this.

## CHAPTER XIX

**22.** For perhaps one of you will say to me: “Everything he said against you was intended to disfigure you, and through you to discredit those with whom you share communion, so that neither they themselves nor those whom you try to bring over to your communion may any longer regard you as being of any importance. But from the moment he set out the words of your letter, one must consider whether he responded to them at all.” Let us therefore proceed in this way: let us examine what he wrote at that very point.

Accordingly, apart from the preface with which I wished to prepare the reader’s mind, and from passing over a few of his first words, which were more insulting than relevant to the matter [Note: Col. 0358. The printed editions read *praevia*; the manuscripts read *prima*.], he says—I repeat: “For the conscience of the giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient.”

But what if the giver’s conscience is hidden, and is perhaps polluted? How will it be able to cleanse the recipient’s conscience, if, as he says, the giver’s conscience is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient? If he should say that whatever evil is hidden in the giver’s conscience does not concern the recipient, that ignorance may perhaps suffice to ensure that the person baptized cannot unknowingly be defiled by the conscience of his baptizer. Let it therefore be enough that another person’s polluted conscience, when it is unknown, does not defile him. But can it also cleanse him?

Whence, then, is the person cleansed who receives Baptism, when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the one who is about to receive it is unaware of this—especially since he adds and says: “For whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt” (above, Book I, chapter 1, §§2–3)?

## CHAPTER XX

**23.** Petilianus proposed all these words from my writings for refutation. Let us therefore see whether he refuted them, whether he answered them at all. For I shall add the words which he falsely accuses me of having omitted, and repeat the same point in a still shorter form. By adding these two words, he himself has greatly assisted me in making the proposition brief.

“If the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient, and if whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt, whence is the recipient’s conscience cleansed, when he is unaware of the giver’s polluted conscience, and when, unknowingly, he receives faith from a faithless man? I ask: whence is he cleansed? Let him tell us. Let him not turn to something else; let him not throw up clouds before the inexperienced.

Finally, after inserting and completing at least many circuits and winding evasions, let him tell us at last whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when the polluted conscience of the faithless baptizer is hidden, if the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient, and if whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt.

For unknowingly he receives it from a faithless man who does not possess the conscience of a holy giver, but one that is polluted and hidden [Col. 0359] [Note: [Col. 0360] [The note appears at the foot of column 360, but its callout number was not printed in the text.] Lov. writes in the margin: ‘Perhaps, *viam*.’]. Whence, then, is he cleansed? Whence, then, does he receive faith? For if he is neither cleansed then nor receives faith then, when the faithless and polluted baptizer is hidden, why, once that man has later been exposed and condemned, is he not baptized again, so that he may be cleansed and receive faith?

But if, while that faithless and polluted man is hidden, the recipient is cleansed and receives faith, whence is he cleansed, whence does he receive it, when the conscience of the holy giver, which cleanses the recipient, is not present? Let him say this; let him answer this: whence is he cleansed, whence does he receive it, if the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient—and this conscience is not present when the polluted and faithless baptizer lies hidden?”

There is absolutely no answer to this [Note: The manuscripts of Amerbach and Erasmus, as well as our manuscripts, read *respondendum* (“to be answered”); the printed editions read *responsum* (“answer”).].

## CHAPTER XXI

**24.** But behold: cornered in the case, he again launches against me an obscure and windy attack, so that the serenity of truth may be clouded; and he becomes copious in utter poverty—not by speaking truth, but by uttering empty abusive words without correcting them [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *non emendando* (“by not correcting”), less correctly.].

Hold firmly and with the greatest attention to what he ought to answer [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read *debeatis* (“you ought”); Lovaniensis, *habeatis* (“you should have”); the Gallican manuscripts, *debeat* (“he ought”).]: namely, whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when the giver’s polluted conscience is hidden. Otherwise, perhaps, his blast will snatch this from your hands, and you yourselves will be swept away by the dark storm of his confused speech, so that you will have no idea either where you have departed from or where you must return.

And observe how the man wanders wherever he can, since he cannot stand his ground in the matter he has undertaken. Observe how much he says, having nothing to say. He says that I slip like something slippery, yet remain held fast; that I neither destroy nor establish what I bring forward; that I devise uncertainties as certainties; that I do not allow readers to believe what is true, but make them suspect more deeply what is doubtful.

He says that I possess the condemnable Academic genius of Carneades [Note: On Carneades’ genius, see Lactantius, Book V, chapter 14. He records that Carneades was sent to Rome as an envoy by the Athenians and there spoke first in favor of justice and on the following day against justice, being accustomed to argue on both sides in such a way that he could refute anyone asserting anything whatsoever.].

He also attempts to suggest what the Academics think about the falsity or deceptiveness of the human senses, although he has no idea at all what he is talking about. He claims that they say snow is black when it is white, and silver black; that a tower appears round or smooth when it is angular [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “when it is long.” Below they likewise read “a round tower” instead of “a long one.”]; and that an oar appears broken in water when it is whole.

And all this merely because, after he had said, “The conscience of the giver, or of the holy giver, is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient,” I replied, “What if the giver’s conscience is hidden and perhaps polluted?” These are his black snows, his black silver, his round tower instead of an angular one, and his broken oar instead of a whole one! For I said something that might be supposed, though it might not be the case: that the giver’s conscience might be hidden and perhaps polluted.

**25.** He continues and cries out: “What does ‘What if’ mean? What does ‘Perhaps’ mean? Is it not the uncertain and inconsistent hesitation of one who doubts, about which your own poet says:

> ‘What if I now return to those who say,  
> “What if the sky should now collapse?”’”

(Terence, *Heautontimorumenos*, Act IV, scene 3, line 41.) [Note: Terence does not have *nunc* (“now”), and rightly so, according to the manuscripts.] [Col. 0360]

Is what I said—“What if the giver’s conscience is hidden and perhaps polluted”—the same as if I had said, “What if the sky should now collapse”? Certainly the phrase “What if” was used because it is possible that the conscience is hidden, and possible that it is not hidden. For when it is unknown what he is thinking or what he has done, the giver’s conscience is certainly hidden from the recipient; but when his sin is revealed, it is no longer hidden.

And I said “perhaps it is polluted” because it is possible that it is hidden and clean, and again possible that it is hidden and polluted. That is why “What if”; that is why “Perhaps.” Is this anything like “What if the sky should now collapse”?

How often have men been both convicted and confessed to having polluted and adulterous consciences when, unknown to those receiving it, they baptized them—afterward being degraded once their crime was exposed—yet the sky did not collapse!

What has Pilo and Furius to do here [Note: Compare *The City of God*, Book II, chapter 21, where Ludovicus Vives makes one man out of Pilo and Furius.]—men who defended injustice against justice? What has the atheist Diagoras to do here [Note: In the manuscripts, here and below, the name is *Protagoras* instead of *Diagoras*. Both were atheists, according to Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Lactantius, Book I, chapter 1.]—who denied that God exists, so that the prophet appears to have foretold him: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1)?

What do these men have to do here? Why have they been named, except to intervene on behalf of a man who has nothing to say, so that, while something is said about them without reason, the case may appear to be argued, and what has not been answered may be thought to have been answered?

## CHAPTER XXII

**26.** Finally, if these two or three words—“What if” and “Perhaps”—are so intolerable that on their account the Academics of old, Carneades, Pilo, Furius, and Diagoras, together with black snows, the collapse of the sky, and other similarly insane and absurd things, are aroused from sleep, let them be removed from the discussion. For what we mean can indeed be said without them.

Behold, what was written shortly afterward and inserted by Petilianus himself from my writings is sufficient: “Whence, then, is the person to be cleansed who receives Baptism, when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the one who is about to receive it is unaware of this?” (above, Book I, chapter 2, §3).

Here there is neither “What if” nor “Perhaps.” Let him answer, then. Take care lest perhaps he answer this in what follows.

“But I,” he says, “bind you, as a quibbler, to the faith that must be believed, so that you may not wander any farther. Why do you turn life away by foolish arguments and errors? Why do you confuse the rational basis of faith with irrational matters? With this one word I hold and convict you.”

These are Petilianus’s words, not mine. They are taken from Petilianus’s letter [Note: The manuscripts read “but to whose words”; the printed editions, “but merely words.”]. But to them I added the two words which he accuses me of having removed, and nevertheless showed that the point of my inquiry—which he does not answer—stood much more briefly and clearly.

Certainly these are the two words: “holy” and “knowingly.” Thus it is not simply the conscience of the giver, but the conscience of the holy giver; and it is not simply one who has received faith from a faithless man, but one who has knowingly received faith from a faithless man.

I had not removed these words; I had not found them in the copy that had been given to me. It is possible, however, that the copy was faulty. For it is not unbelievable that even from this circumstance Academic suspicion might be stirred up against me, and that what I said—that the copy was faulty—might be declared to be like saying that snow is black.

Why should I repay his rash suspicion by saying that he himself later added the words, when he falsely alleged that I had removed them? The copy, which does not take offense, can bear this mark of corruption without my malicious rashness.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**27.** The first of these two words—“of the holy giver”—does not in the least obstruct my inquiry, by which he is strongly pressed: whether I should say, “If the giver’s conscience is taken into account,” or rather, “If the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient, whence, then, is the person cleansed who receives Baptism, if the giver’s conscience is polluted and the one who is about to receive it is unaware of this?”

As for the other word that is added—“knowingly”—so that the statement is not, “Whoever receives faith from a faithless man,” but, “Whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt”: I confess that, as though it were absent, I said certain things which I readily tolerate losing, since they impeded the speed of my argument more than they assisted its force.

For how much more efficiently, plainly, and briefly do I ask this: “If the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient, and if whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt, whence is the person cleansed who is unaware of the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver, and whence does the one who is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man receive true faith?

Let the answer be given—whence? There the whole matter of Baptism will become clear; there everything being sought will shine forth. But let the answer be given, rather than time being brought to an end by slander.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

**28.** Whatever, therefore, he either maliciously criticizes concerning these two words as omitted or boasts about as having been added, you plainly see that it does not obstruct my question. Finding nothing to answer it, yet unwilling to remain silent, he repeatedly rushes against my person; I would say that he withdraws from the case, if he had ever approached the case at all.

As though the matter concerned me, and not the truth of the Church or of Baptism [Note: The printed editions read “of the Church”; the manuscripts, more aptly, “of the Church’s,” namely, truth.], he says that I argued by removing those two words so that it might appear that my own conscience was not harmed by my ignorance, as he puts it, of the sacrilegious conscience of my defiler.

If this were so, the word “knowingly,” once added, would rather benefit me, while its removal would harm me. For if I had wished to defend myself in such a way that it would be thought I had been unaware of the conscience of my baptizer, I would have taken Petilianus as speaking on my behalf when he said—not simply, “Whoever has received faith from a faithless man,” but, “Whoever has knowingly received faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt.”

Thus I could boast that I had received not guilt but faith, since I could say: “I did not knowingly receive it from a faithless man; I was unaware of the conscience of the other man, the giver.”

See, therefore, and count, if you can, how much superfluous talk he devotes to the single word “I was unaware,” which he claims that I said, although I did not say it at all. The matter did not concern me, so that I should say it; nor had any crime appeared in the man who baptized me, so that I would be compelled to say, in my own defense, that I had been unaware of his conscience.

## CHAPTER XXV

**29.** Yet, in order not to answer what I said, he sets before himself something I did not say. He diverts people from attention to his obligation, so that what ought to be answered [Note: The printed editions read *responsum* (“answer”); the manuscripts read *respondendum* (“to be answered”).] will not be demanded. He repeatedly interjects, “I was unaware,” he says; and he replies, “But if you were unaware.” He acts as though he had proved that I may not say, “I was unaware.”

He mentions Mensurius, Caecilianus, Macarius, Taurinus, and Romanus, and asserts that they acted against the Church of God—things, he says, which I could not have been unaware of, since I am an African and by now almost an old man.

Yet, as I hear, Mensurius died in communion with the Church before the party of Donatus separated itself. As for the case of Caecilianus, I have read that they brought it before Constantine, and that he was acquitted by the bishops whom that emperor appointed as judges—once, twice, and, when they appealed to the emperor from those bishops, even a third time by the emperor himself [Note: The printed editions had omitted the conjunction *et*, which is restored from the manuscripts. Thus the preceding phrase, “once and twice,” refers to the episcopal judges by whom Caecilianus was acquitted first at Rome and afterward at the Council of Arles.].

As for Macarius, Taurinus, and Romanus, whatever they did against the obstinate fury of those men by judicial or executive authority on behalf of unity, it is clear that they acted according to the laws. The Donatists themselves forced those laws to be brought and applied against them when they referred Caecilianus’s case to the emperor’s judgment.

**30.** Among many things entirely irrelevant to the matter, he also says that I was struck down by the judgment of the proconsul Messianus, so that I fled Africa. Because of this falsehood—which, if he did not invent it himself, he certainly maliciously believed those who invented it out of malice—he did not hesitate, with astonishing rashness, to say and even write many other falsehoods in consequence.

For I came to Milan before the consulship of Bauton, and on the Kalends of January recited a panegyric to that consul, before a great gathering and in the sight of many people, in accordance with my profession at that time as a rhetorician. From that journey I returned to Africa only after the death of the usurper Maximus. But the proconsul Messianus heard the Manichaeans after Bauton’s consulship, as the date of the proceedings inserted by Petilianus himself shows.

If it were necessary to prove these things to those who doubt or contradict them [Note: The printed editions read “to those who contradict”; the manuscripts read “to those who doubt.”], I could produce many prominent men of the world as highly reliable witnesses to the whole course of my life during that period.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**31.** But why do we pursue these matters? Why do we endure and create such needless delays? Shall we find here the source from which the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware of the giver’s polluted conscience, or the source from which he receives faith when he is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man?

Petilianus had proposed this to himself from my letter as though he were going to answer it, but he spoke about whatever he wished rather than about what the case demanded. How often did he say, “If you were unaware,” as though I had said what I never said—that I was unaware of the conscience of my baptizer?

He appears to have done nothing else with his slanderous mouth than to try to convict me of not having been unaware of the evils of those among whom I was baptized and with whose communion I was associated—clearly understanding well enough that ignorance would not make me guilty.

Well then: if I had been unaware, as he so often repeated, I would undoubtedly be innocent of all those evils. Whence, then, would I be cleansed, since, being unaware of the conscience of a non-holy giver, I could not in the least be hindered by his crimes? Whence would I receive faith, since I would be unknowingly baptized by a faithless man?

For he did not repeatedly say, “If you were unaware,” without reason, except to prevent me from being thought innocent. He evidently judged that no one’s innocence is violated if, without knowing it, he receives faith from a faithless man and is unaware of the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver.

Let him therefore say whence such persons are cleansed, whence they receive faith and not guilt. But do not let him deceive you: let him answer. Let him not say nothing by saying many things, or rather say many things by saying nothing.

Furthermore, something has occurred to me which must not be passed over. If I am guilty for this reason—that I was not unaware, to speak according to him—and if I was not unaware because I am an African and already almost an old man, then at least the children elsewhere throughout the whole world cannot be guilty. They could not have known these charges of yours, whether true or false, either by nationality or by age [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “our”; Amerbach and the manuscripts, more correctly, read “your.”]. Yet, if they should fall among you, they are rebaptized without any consideration.

## CHAPTER XXVII

**32.** But we are not asking about these matters now. Let him answer this instead—which he avoids answering by wandering at great length into irrelevant matters [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis substituted *altercatur* (“he quarrels”). But the manuscripts, together with Amerbach’s edition, read *alienatur*, meaning that he wanders into foreign territory outside the case. This is the sense of the passage above (§18): “Do not allow anyone, after abandoning the case, to wander away into abuse.”—] namely, whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware of the giver’s polluted conscience, if the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient; and whence the one who is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man receives faith, if whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt.

Leaving aside his curses, which he hurled against me without any sound consideration, let us still see whether perhaps he says in what follows what we demand.

It is amusing to observe how he presented these matters as though he could easily tear them apart and overthrow them. “But let us return,” he says, “to that argument of your phantom, by which you seemed to yourself to paint for us in words whatever person you baptize. For it was appropriate for you to imagine plausible things, since you do not see the truth.”

Petilianus spoke these words before presenting my words. He then added: “Behold, you say, a faithless man stands ready to baptize, but the person who is to be baptized is unaware of his faithlessness” (above, Book I, chapter 2, §3).

He did not state my entire proposition and question. Immediately he himself began to question me, saying: “Who is this man, or from where has he sprung, whom you propose? Why do you seem to yourself to see the man whom you invent, so that you may not see the man whom you ought most diligently to see, investigate, and test?”

But since I understand that you are ignorant of the order of the Sacrament, I tell you this briefly: “You ought both to have investigated the baptizer and to have been investigated by him.”

What were we expecting? That he would say whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware of the non-holy giver’s polluted conscience, and whence he receives faith rather than guilt when, without knowing it, he receives Baptism from a faithless man?

Behold, we have heard that the baptizer must be most carefully investigated by the person who wishes to receive faith and not guilt, so that he may find the conscience of a holy giver, which cleanses the recipient. For anyone who has not investigated him and has unknowingly received Baptism from a faithless man had, precisely because he did not investigate him and was unaware of the giver’s polluted conscience, no source from which to receive faith rather than guilt [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “but guilt.”].

What, then, did the addition of the word “knowingly”—which he maliciously accused me of removing—accomplish? When he refused to say, “Whoever has received faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt,” he seemed to leave some hope for the person who was unaware.

But now, when he is asked whence the one who is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man receives faith, he replies that the person ought to have investigated the baptizer. Clearly he does not even allow the wretched person to remain unaware, since he finds no source from which he can receive faith unless he has placed his hope in the human baptizer.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**33.** This is what we dread in you; this is what divine judgment condemns, crying out most truly and plainly: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5).

This is what holy humility and apostolic charity most openly prohibit, when Paul cries out: “Let no one glory in man” (1 Corinthians 3:21).

This is why the attack of empty accusations and the sharpest curses against us grows ever more intense: so that, once the man has supposedly been overthrown, no hope may remain for those to whom, according to the stewardship entrusted to us, we minister the word of God and the Sacrament.

We answer them: “How long will you add to man?” The venerable Catholic fellowship answers them: “Is not my soul subject to God? For from him comes my salvation. Indeed, he is my God and my protector; I shall not be moved” (Psalm 62:1–2).

For what other reason did these people depart from the house of God except that they pretended they could not endure vessels made for dishonor, without which that house will not exist until the day of judgment? Yet the records and written documents of those events then show that they themselves were more guilty of this and falsely charged it against others [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *appareat* (“it may appear”). Amerbach and the manuscripts, more suitably, read *appareant* (“they may appear”).].

Concerning these vessels made for dishonor, lest anyone, disturbed by them, should depart from the great house [Note: In uncorrected editions, “the house of God.” The word “of God” is absent from the manuscripts.], which belongs as one household to the great master of the house, the servant of God—and the good and faithful person who is about to receive faith in Baptism—says what I quoted shortly before: “Is not my soul subject to God?” To God, certainly, not to man. “For from him comes my salvation,” not from man.

Yet this man will not even then allow God to cleanse and purify the person when the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver is hidden and whoever receives from a faithless man does so unknowingly. “This,” he says, “I tell you briefly: you ought both to investigate the baptizer and to be investigated by him.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

**34.** I beg you, give your attention here [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis read “give your attention here” with a different adverb; the manuscripts have the reading translated above.].

I ask whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware of the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver, if the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient; and whence the person receives faith who is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man, if whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt.

He answers me that both the baptizer and the person being baptized must be investigated.

To prove this—although there is no question about it—he introduces the example of John: that those who asked him who he said he was investigated him (John 1:22); and that John himself also investigated those to whom he said, “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3:7).

What has this to do with the matter? What has this to do with the case? God had borne witness to John’s outstanding holiness by a most illustrious prophecy that preceded both his conception and his birth. Those people, already believing him to be holy, were asking whom among the saints he said he was, or whether he himself was the Holy of Holies, that is, Christ Jesus.

Such great grace [Note: The excellent Floriacensis manuscript lacks the word *gratia* (“grace”); perhaps *fides* (“faith”) should be read in its place.] was attributed to him that whatever he said about himself would immediately be believed.

But if this example is used to assert that every baptizer today must be investigated, then whatever each person says about himself must be believed. Yet what impostor is there whom the Holy Spirit certainly avoids, as it is written (Wisdom 1:5), who would not want to be believed about himself in the best possible way and do everything he could through words to achieve this?

When, then, he is asked who he is and replies that he is a faithful steward of God and that he possesses a conscience undefiled by anyone’s crime, will this be the whole investigation? Or must his conduct and life also be examined more carefully?

Certainly they must. But it is not written that those who questioned John in the desert beside the Jordan did this [Note: The printed editions read, “Certainly, not this”; they omit *sed* (“but”).].

## CHAPTER XXX

**35.** Therefore this example has absolutely no bearing on the matter under discussion. Rather, that apostolic injunction sufficiently imposes this responsibility: “Let them first be tested, and then let them serve, being without accusation” (1 Timothy 3:10).

When this is done diligently and in the customary manner almost everywhere by everyone, whence have so many rejected men been discovered after the administration of this office? Is it not because human diligence is often deceived, and because some who were initially good are changed for the worse?

Since such things occur so frequently that they permit no one either to ignore them or forget them, what is the point of Petilianus’s insulting brief instruction—that the baptizer must be investigated by the person being baptized—when we are asking whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed if he is unaware of the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver, when the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient?

“Since I understand,” he says, “that you are ignorant of the order of the Sacrament, I tell you this briefly: you ought both to investigate the baptizer and to be investigated by him.”

O, answer me! A great multitude of people surrounds him in so many places, people baptized by men who, although previously regarded as just and chaste, were afterward convicted and cast out when their crimes were exposed. And he thinks he can evade the force of this question by saying simply that the baptizer ought to have been investigated, while we ask whence the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when he is unaware of the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver, if the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read, “O, answer me!” Lovaniensis reads, “Answer me this: for he is surrounded in so many places,” and so forth. The manuscripts correct the wording.].

Nothing is more wretched than refusing to assent to the truth, by which a person is so hemmed in that he cannot find a way out.

We ask from whom the person receives faith who is unknowingly baptized by a faithless man. The answer is: “He ought to have investigated his baptizer.”

Then, because he did not investigate him and unknowingly received Baptism from a faithless man, does he therefore receive not faith but guilt? Why, then, are those not baptized again who are shown to have been baptized by men who, while their crimes were still hidden, were later exposed and convicted?

## CHAPTER XXXI

**36.** “And where is the word I added,” he says, “‘knowingly,’ so that I did not say, ‘Whoever has received faith from a faithless man,’ but, ‘Whoever has knowingly received faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt’?”

Then the person who unknowingly received it from a faithless man received faith and not guilt. That is why I ask whence he received it.

When cornered, he answers: “He ought to have investigated him.”

Granted: he ought to have. He did not, or was unable to. What do you judge concerning him? Has he been cleansed, or not?

If he has been cleansed, I ask whence. For the polluted conscience of the non-holy giver, of which he was unaware, could not cleanse him.

But if he has not been cleansed, order him to be cleansed. You do not order it. Therefore he has been cleansed.

Say whence. At least you say what he did not say. I present the same words to which he was unable to respond:

“Behold, a faithless man stands ready to baptize, but the person who is to be baptized is unaware of his faithlessness. What do you suppose he will receive: faith or guilt?” (above, Book I, chapter 2, §2).

What has been proposed up to this point is sufficient [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “what has been proposed so far.”]. Answer, or carefully investigate what he answered.

You will find even the accusations refuted [Note: The manuscripts read, “You will find his accusations refuted.”]. For, as though mocking me, he blames me for proposing plausible things while not seeing the truth.

He also repeats my words, though with the sentence cut in half: “You say,” he says, “Behold, a faithless man stands ready to baptize, but the person who is to be baptized is unaware of his faithlessness.”

Then he adds: “Who is this man, or from where has he sprung?” As though there were only one or two such men, and not everything everywhere full of people of this kind.

Why does he ask me who this man is or from where he has sprung, rather than look around and see that there are few churches, whether in cities or in the countryside, that do not contain men exposed in their crimes and expelled from the clergy?

While their crimes were hidden, they wanted to appear good when they were evil and to be considered chaste when they were adulterers. They were certainly impostors; certainly the Holy Spirit, as it is written, was fleeing from them.

From the crowd of such men still lying hidden came the faithless man I proposed. Why does he ask me from where he sprang, closing his eyes to such a great crowd? Even if one considers only those who have been exposed and expelled, the sound of them is enough for the blind.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**37.** What of the fact that he himself wrote in his letter that Quodvultdeus, convicted among you of two adulteries and expelled, was received by our people [Note: The Council of Carthage, on September 13, 401, dealt with the reception of Donatist clergy while preserving each one’s rank.]?

What, then—let me say this without prejudice to his case, which he either proved or persuaded others was good—what is received from such men among you who have not yet been exposed when they baptize: faith or guilt?

Certainly not faith, because they do not possess the conscience of a holy giver, which cleanses the recipient.

But neither guilt, because of that added word: “For whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith, but guilt.”

When people were baptized by these men, they certainly did not know what sort of men they were. Therefore, since they did not receive faith from them—for they did not possess the conscience of a holy giver—and since they likewise did not receive guilt, because they were baptized not knowingly but unknowingly of their crimes, they remained without faith and without guilt.

They are therefore not counted among such criminals. But neither can they be counted among the faithful, since they could no more receive faith from them than they could receive guilt.

Yet we see you count them among the faithful. None of you judges that they should be baptized, but you regard their baptism as valid [Note: The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read “but guilt,” plainly an error.].

They therefore received faith, though they did not receive it from those men, who did not possess the conscience of a holy giver that would cleanse the recipient. Whence, then, did they receive it?

This is what I am laboring over; this is what I urgently ask; this is what I most forcefully demand should be answered.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**38.** Now observe Petilianus, lest he wander uselessly through our insults, accusing and proving nothing, so that he may avoid answering this—or lest he appear to have been exposed as unable to answer it. And wherever he perhaps attempts to resist the case as though fighting vigorously, he is everywhere easily overcome.

Yet on this one point he answers absolutely nothing: “If the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, which cleanses the recipient, whence is the person cleansed who receives Baptism when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the one who is about to receive it is unaware of this?”

After recalling these words from my letter, he presented me as asking the question and showed himself answering nothing.

For after he had said what I have already recalled—and in which I showed that he had not answered what I asked—and after, being pressed by great difficulties, he had been forced to say that the baptizer must be investigated by the person being baptized and the person being baptized by the baptizer—and after he had attempted to establish this by the example of John, in case he happened to find extremely negligent or ignorant hearers—he introduced other testimonies from Scripture that have nothing to do with the matter.

He cited the words of the eunuch to Philip: “Behold, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36), because, he says, the eunuch knew that the lost were forbidden to be baptized; and he said that Philip did not prevent him from being baptized because he had tested him to see how he believed in Christ—as though Philip had forbidden Simon Magus.

He also cited the fact that the prophets feared being deceived by a false baptism, and therefore Isaiah said, “Deceitful water, having no faith” (Jeremiah 15:18), as though this showed that among faithless men the water itself is deceitful. Yet it was not Isaiah but Jeremiah who said this about deceitful men, figuratively calling the people water, as is demonstrated most clearly in the Apocalypse (Revelation 17:15).

He also cited David’s words, “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head,” although David said this about the flattery of a sycophant who deceives by false praise, so that the head of the praised person may swell with pride.

The preceding words in the same psalm make this interpretation clear. For he says:

> “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and reprove me;  
> but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head”  
> (Psalm 141:5).

What could be clearer than this judgment? What more evident? He prefers to be corrected by the righteous through harsh correction that mercifully heals him, rather than to be anointed with the gentle flatteries of a sycophant so that he may be puffed up [Note: The manuscripts read, “so that he may not be puffed up.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**39.** Petilianus also recalls that the apostle John warned us not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1). He acts as though this diligence is prescribed so that the wheat may now, before the proper time, be separated from the chaff, rather than so that the wheat may not be deceived by the chaff.

Or does it follow that, if a lying spirit has said something true, it must therefore be denied because a detestable spirit said it? Whoever thinks this is so is so insane that he might even contend that Peter ought not to have said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), because the demons had already said something similar (Matthew 8:29; Mark 1:24; Luke 8:28).

Therefore, whether administered by an unjust or by a just man, the Baptism of Christ is nothing other than the Baptism of Christ. A cautious and good faithful person must avoid the man’s iniquity, but must not condemn God’s Sacraments.

40. In all these matters Petilian does not answer this question: if the conscience of the one who gives the sacrament in holiness is taken into account, so that it cleanses the recipient, from what source is the recipient to be cleansed when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the one who is to receive it does not know this?

A certain Cyprian, his colleague from Thubursicubure, was caught in a brothel with a most disgraceful woman, and was brought before Primian of Carthage and condemned. When he was baptizing [Note: [Col. 0368] The printed editions read *quanquam* (“although”); the manuscripts more correctly read *quando* (“when”).]—before he was exposed and expelled—he certainly did not possess the conscience of one who gives the sacrament in holiness, a conscience that could cleanse the recipient. From what source, then, were those cleansed who are not baptized again today, now that he has been condemned? I would not have named the man unless to prevent Petilian from saying again: “Who is this man, or from where did he spring?” [Note: [Col. 0368] The printed editions read, “unless Petilian should say again”; they omit *ne*, which is restored from the manuscripts.]

Why did your people not investigate this baptizer, just as—according to Petilian’s view—John was investigated by Petilian? Or did they investigate him as far as human beings could investigate a human being, but fail for a long time to find him because he was hiding through an artful deception?

### CHAPTER XXXV

Was this man’s water not deceitful, or is the fornicator’s oil not the sinner’s oil? Or was it, as the Catholic Church says—and this is true—that neither that water nor that oil belonged to the one by whom it was administered, but to the one whose name was invoked there?

Why were those baptized by this fictitious and hidden man not to “test the spirit,” since it was not from God? For “the Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit” (Wisdom 1:5). Or did the Spirit flee him too, yet not abandon its own sacraments, although they were administered through him?

Finally, since you do not deny that those whom you do not take care to baptize again after his condemnation were cleansed, consider whether, amid all these clouds and layers of obscurity, Petilian answers anywhere from what source these people were cleansed—if the conscience of the one who gives the sacrament in holiness is taken into account, so that it cleanses the recipient, although the hidden unclean man could not possess such a conscience.

41. Since he gives no answer at all to this question, which is pressed upon him so insistently, he next secures for himself further room to speak, saying:

“Since both the Prophets and the Apostle cautiously feared these things, with what face do you say that, for those who believe rightly, the sinner’s Baptism is holy?”

As though I, or any Catholic, said that the Baptism is the sinner’s which is administered or received when a sinner administers it, rather than belonging to the one in whose name the believer is baptized.

From this point he launches into Judas the betrayer and says against him everything he can, adducing prophetic testimonies that had been set forth about him long beforehand—as though he could pour the impiety of Judas the betrayer over the Church of Christ spread throughout the whole world, the Church whose cause is at issue here. He does not consider that from this very fact he ought to have been warned that there should be no more doubt that the Church which is extended among all nations is the Church of Christ than there is doubt that Christ had to be betrayed by one of the disciples, since this too was foretold in the same way.

### CHAPTER XXXVI

42. But after this, when Petilian comes to the objection we made—that they accepted the Baptism of the Maximianists whom they had condemned (above, Book 2, chapter 10, sections 11–12)—although in presenting this question he preferred to use his own words rather than mine—for we do not say that the Baptism of sinners ought to benefit us; indeed, we say that it is not the Baptism of sinners, nor of any human beings at all, because we recognize it as Christ’s—this is how he formulated the matter:

“But you stubbornly insist,” he says, “that the Baptism of sinners ought to benefit you, because we too, as you have said, preserve the Baptism of those guilty persons whom we justly condemned.”

When he reached this question, as I have said, all his struggle—even his feigned struggle—failed him. He found no place to go, no way out, no entrance to examine or construct by which he might escape secretly or break out by force. He did not find one.

“Although I shall demonstrate in the second book,” he says, “how great the difference is between our people and yours, whom you call innocent, for the present first rescue yourselves from the crimes of your colleagues, which you know, and then demand an account concerning those whom we cast out.” [Note: [Col. 0369] The printed editions read *objicimus* (“we bring charges”); the Louvain editors consider *objicitis* (“you bring charges”) preferable. The Gallican manuscripts read *abjicimus* (“we cast out”).]

Could any human being answer in this way—could anyone answer in this way—except one who opposes the truth, against which he cannot find an answer?

[Note: [Col. 0369] The manuscripts read: “Could anyone, could any human being answer in this way, except one who opposes the truth, against which he cannot find an answer?” The printed editions read: “Could any human being answer in this way—could anyone answer in this way—except one who opposes the truth, against whom he cannot find what to answer?” We have preferred the reading of the Cygirannian manuscript. Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 355–356, supports the manuscripts, changing the phrasing and punctuation as follows: “Could anyone answer in this way? What human being would answer in this way, except one who opposes the truth, against which he cannot find an answer?” M.]

If, then, we also use the same words—“First rescue yourselves from the crimes of your colleagues, which you know, and then bring against us any charge concerning those whom you think are bad among us”—have we both won, or have we both been defeated?

No indeed: he has won for his Church and in his Church who taught us in his Scripture that no one should glory in a human being, and that “the one who glories should glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 3:21; 1:31).

For here we are, saying in agreement with the language of truth that the believer is not justified by the human being by whom he is baptized, but by the one of whom it is written: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Since we do not glory in a human being, and since, when we glory, we strive to glory in the Lord through his gift, how secure we are, whatever error or crime he may be able to prove concerning certain members of our communion!

Among us, any evil persons who are completely hidden, or who are known to some but unknown to the good among whom they cannot be convicted, are tolerated for the sake of the bond of unity and peace, lest the wheat be uprooted together with the weeds. They bear the burden of their own wickedness in such a way that no one shares in it except those who take pleasure in their iniquity.

For we do not fear that those whom they baptize cannot be justified, since those people believe in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that their faith may be reckoned as righteousness (ibid., 5).

### CHAPTER XXXVII

43. Accordingly, among us neither the man whom he said was cast out by us [Note: [Col. 0370] The printed editions read “by you”; a little later they also read “the man whom he mentions as penitent among us.” In both places we follow the old Gallican codices.] on account of the crime of the Sodomites, with another appointed in his place and then restored again to our own college—he does not know what he is saying—nor the man whom he mentions as having been penitent among you, prejudices the Church of God in any way, whether their cases can be defended or cannot be defended.
