The Church is spread among all nations and grows in the world until the harvest. If those whom you accuse really are evil, they are no longer in the Church itself but in its chaff; but if they are good, while you defame them with unjust accusations, they are tested like gold, while you burn like chaff.

Nevertheless, the Church is not stained by the sins of others. According to the most faithful prophecies, it has been enlarged throughout the whole world and awaits the end of the age as a shore, where, once brought to its destination, it will be rid of the bad fish with which, within the same nets of the Lord, it had to remain for as long as it could innocently endure the inconvenience of nature, since they could not impatiently be separated from it before the proper time.

Yet ecclesiastical discipline is not thereby neglected by Christ’s steadfast, diligent, and prudent stewards when crimes are so manifest that they cannot be defended by any plausible argument. Countless examples exist among those who were bishops or clerics of some other such rank and who have now been degraded, or have gone away to other lands out of shame, or have passed over to you or to other heresies, or are known in their own regions [uncertain reading]. Their number is so great, scattered throughout the world, that if Petilian would restrain for a little while his reckless eagerness to curse and reflect upon it, he would never fall into that plainly false and empty assertion by which he thought he should say to us: “None of you is innocent, where no guilty person is condemned.”

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

44. To omit others living in different lands—for scarcely anywhere is this kind of person absent, by which it is shown that wicked leaders and ministers are also accustomed to be condemned in the Catholic Church—he could have observed Honorius of Milevis close at hand.

As for Splendonius, whom he condemned as a deacon in the Catholic Church and made a presbyter after rebaptizing him, our colleague Fortunatus proposed that his condemnation in Gaul, sent to us by the brothers, be publicly read there at Constantina. Petilian later cast him out after experiencing his dreadful plots. How, then, could Petilian fail to be reminded by this Splendonius of the way in which evil men are degraded even in the Catholic Church?

I wonder what precipice of rashness his heart occupied when he dictated these words, daring to say: “None of you is innocent, where no guilty person is condemned.”

Therefore, the evil in the Catholic Church—physically mingled together but spiritually separated—whether they are unknown because of human circumstances or condemned after disciplinary investigation, bear their own burdens. Consequently, all who are baptized through them with Christ’s Baptism are secure, provided that they do not share in their sins by imitation or consent. For even if they were baptized by the very best people, they would still be justified only by the one who justifies the ungodly. Indeed, faith is reckoned as righteousness for those who believe in the one who justifies the ungodly.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

45. But when the Maximianists are brought up against you—condemned by the judgment of a council of three hundred and ten [Note: [Col. 0371] The council of Bagai.], attacked, with that same council cited against them, by so many proconsuls and so many municipal records [Note: [Col. 0371] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read this passage as follows: “Attacked at that same council, with so many proconsular authorities and so many municipal records cited against them.” M.], driven from the basilicas they occupied by the orders of judges and with the assistance of the cities [Note: [Col. 0371] The editions read *perturbati*, “disturbed”; the manuscripts support the correction *proturbati*, “driven out.”]—and then received and honored again by you, together with those whom they had baptized outside your communion, without any question concerning Baptism, you find no answer.

You are defeated by your own judgment—not by a true judgment, but by the one you yourselves maintain: that within the same communion of the sacraments, some perish through the crimes of others, and that each person is such as the human being is by whom he was baptized—if guilty, guilty; if innocent, innocent.

If this is true, then, leaving aside countless others, the Maximianists certainly have destroyed you. At a council of such size, you magnified their crime until it resembled the crime of those whom the earth swallowed alive. But if the crimes of the Maximianists did not destroy you, then your opinion is false; and still less could some unproved crimes of Africans destroy the whole world.

Thus, as the Apostle writes, “Each person will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5); and no one’s Baptism belongs to anyone but Christ. Petilian therefore makes a vain promise when he says that he will discuss in the second book what we are raising concerning the Maximianists. He has too poor an opinion of human hearts, as though they did not understand that he has nothing to say.

### CHAPTER XL

46. For if the Baptism which Praetextatus and Felicianus administered within the communion of Maximian belonged to them, why was it accepted by you as Christ’s Baptism in the case of those whom they baptized?

But if it truly is Christ’s—as it is—and if it could not benefit even them, because they possessed it while committing the crime of schism, what do you say that you were able to provide for those whom you received together with that same Baptism? Was it anything other than this: that, once the crime of their wicked division had been removed through the bond of peace, they were not compelled to receive the sacrament of the holy washing as though they did not have it, but that what had previously been harmful to them should now begin to benefit them, since they possessed it?

Or, if this was not provided for them in your communion because it could not be provided for schismatics among schismatics, nevertheless it is provided for you in the Catholic communion—not so that you receive Baptism as though you lacked it, but so that the Baptism you received may benefit you.

For all Christ’s sacraments, without the charity of Christ’s unity, are held not for salvation but for judgment. But since it is not a true judgment, but your own, that Christ’s Baptism perished from the whole world through the Baptism of certain unknown traditors [Note: [Col. 0372] The manuscripts read: “through the Baptism of I know not which traditors.” The printed editions read: “through the Baptism of I know not whose traditors.”], you rightly find no answer concerning the Baptism of the Maximianists that was received.

47. Observe, then, and remember with the greatest vigilance how Petilian did not answer even those questions which he himself sets out in such a way as to appear to say something.

He abandoned that matter altogether long ago and did not wish to address it to us—for certainly he could not—nor will he ever address it before the end of his book: namely, the point which he recalled from the first parts of my letter as though it had to be refuted.

For although he added two words, which he proudly claimed I had omitted as though they were his strongest defenses, he nevertheless lies there unprotected, finding no answer when he is asked:

“If the conscience of the one who gives the sacrament in holiness is taken into account, so that it cleanses the recipient, from what source is the conscience of the recipient cleansed when he does not know that the one who gives it does so with a polluted conscience? And if someone knowingly receives faith from an unfaithful person, he receives not faith but guilt; from what source, then, will the person who is baptized unknowingly by an unfaithful person receive faith rather than guilt?”

It has long been clear, ever since he began speaking, that he has given no answer to this.

48. Next, with a cursing mouth, he proceeded to criticize monasteries and monks, even reproving me because, he claimed, this way of life had been instituted by me [Note: [Col. 0372] See Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapters 5 and 11.]. He does not know at all what this way of life is—or rather, although it is known throughout the whole world, he pretends not to know.

Then, asserting that I had said Christ is the baptizer, he added certain words from my letter, as though I had said from my own position what I had said from yours and his. He launched into an exceedingly violent attack, as though against me for having said this, although the opinion he criticizes is not mine but his and yours. I shall demonstrate this clearly, as far as I am able, a little later [Note: [Col. 0372] See below, chapter 45, section 54.].

Next he tried to teach us, in many superfluous words, that it is not Christ who baptizes, but that people are baptized in his name and at the same time in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Concerning that Trinity he said either what he wished or what he was able to say: that Christ is the middle of the Trinity.

Then he thrust upon us whatever insults he pleased concerning the names of the magicians Simon and Bar-Jesus [Note: [Col. 0373] We have not hesitated to restore the name *Bar-Jesus*. In the ancient manuscripts, through an obvious scribal error, we found written *Variae suae* in its place. The printed editions have *Variae*, omitting *suae*.].

Then, suspending the case of Optatus of Thamugadi step by step, lest he be covered by the disgrace attaching to him, he said that neither he nor his people had been able to judge him; and in this very matter he accused us, claiming that Optatus had been pressured by my suggestions.

### CHAPTER XLI

49. Finally, he concluded his letter by exhorting and warning his own people not to be deceived by us, while lamenting that we had made our people worse than they had been.

After these points have been carefully considered and examined, it is sufficiently clear from the very letter he wrote that Petilian did not answer at all the question I first raised in my letter: if, as he says, the conscience of the giver—or rather, to add what he considers a great reinforcement, if the conscience of the one who gives the sacrament in holiness—is taken into account, so that it cleanses the recipient, from what source is the person who receives Baptism to be cleansed when he does not know that the giver’s conscience is polluted?

It is therefore no wonder that a man resisting on behalf of falsehood, pressed by the narrow confines of the truth confronting him, breathed forth mad insults rather than walk with the truth, which cannot be defeated.

50. Now, I beg you, pay attention for a little while, so that I may clearly show you what he feared and why he did not answer this question, and bring into the light what he tried to obscure.

When we asked from what source the recipient is to be cleansed when the giver’s conscience is polluted and the recipient does not know this, he could very easily have answered: “From the Lord God.” He could have said with complete confidence: “God most certainly cleanses the recipient’s conscience when the recipient is unaware that the giver’s conscience is stained and the sacrament is not administered in holiness.”

But this man, who had already been compelled by the purpose of your sect to place the recipient’s cleansing in the giver’s conscience—for he had said, “The conscience of the giver, or of the one who gives in holiness, is taken into account, so that it cleanses the recipient”—feared that it might appear better for a person to be baptized by a hidden evil man than by a manifestly good man. For then the recipient would be cleansed not by the conscience of a human being who gives the sacrament in holiness, but by the most excellent holiness of God himself.

Fearing this, lest such absurdity—or rather, such madness—should follow him that he would not know how to escape it, he refused to say from what source the recipient’s conscience is cleansed when the recipient is unaware that the giver’s conscience is stained and that the sacrament is not administered in holiness.

Instead, he preferred to conceal through contentious noise what was being asked of him rather than answer the questioner with the answer that would immediately have strangled his argument. He never imagined, however, that people of sound judgment could read our writings, or that those who had read mine could read his, in which he pretended to answer them.

### CHAPTER XLII

51. For what I have just said is set out most clearly in that very letter of mine, to which he said nothing by writing against it. Please pay attention for a little while to what he did there. Although you favor him and hate us, tolerate it, if you can, with an impartial mind.

In his earlier letter, the first parts of which alone had then reached our hands and to which I first replied, he had placed the hope of the baptized person in the human being who baptizes, saying: “For every matter consists in its origin and root, and if something has no head, it is nothing” (above, Book 1, chapter 4, section 5 and following; and Book 2, chapter 5, sections 10–11).

Since Petilian had said this, intending the origin, root, and head of the baptized person to be understood as nothing other than the human being by whom he was baptized, I added and said:

“We therefore ask: when that faithless baptizer is hidden, if the one whom he baptizes then receives faith and not guilt, and if the baptizer is not then his origin, root, and head, from whom does he receive faith? Where is the origin from which he is born? Where is the root from which he sprouts? Where is the head from which he begins?

“Or perhaps, when the one being baptized is unaware that the baptizer is faithless, then Christ gives faith; then Christ is the origin, the root, and the head?

“This, then, I say and cry out now, just as I cried out there: O human rashness and pride! Why do you not rather allow Christ always to give faith, making a person a Christian by giving him faith? Why do you not allow Christ always to be the origin of the Christian, so that the Christian fastens his root in Christ and Christ is the Christian’s head?

“For even when spiritual grace is bestowed upon believers through a holy and faithful steward, it is not the steward himself who justifies, but the one alone of whom it is said that he ‘justifies the ungodly’ (Romans 4:5).

“Was the Apostle Paul the head and origin of those whom he planted, or was Apollo the root of those whom he watered? Was it not rather the one who gave them growth? The same Paul says: ‘I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

“Paul himself was not their root; rather, it was the one who said: ‘I am the vine, you are the branches’ (John 15:5).

“How could Paul be their head, when he says that we, many though we are, are one body in Christ, and in many passages most openly proclaims Christ himself to be the head of the whole body?

“Therefore, whether a person receives the sacrament of Baptism from a faithful or a faithless steward, let all his hope be in Christ, lest he be accursed who places his hope in a human being” (above, Book 1, chapter 5, sections 6–7).

### CHAPTER XLIII

52. I think I set these points out in my earlier letter, when I was replying to Petilian, both clearly and truthfully. I have recalled them now as well, indicating and commending this principle: our hope must not be in a human being at all, but we must believe that God, Christ, is the cleanser and justifier of human beings, and that the faith of those who believe in him who justifies the ungodly is reckoned as righteousness—whether the person who administers Baptism is holy, or ungodly and deceitful, whom the Holy Spirit flees.

Then I added that, if the matter were otherwise, great absurdity would follow, and I said what I say now:

“Otherwise, if each person is reborn in spiritual grace in accordance with the character of the one by whom he is baptized, and when the one who baptizes is manifestly a good man, he himself gives faith and is himself the origin, root, and head of the one being born; but when the faithless baptizer is hidden, then each person receives faith from Christ, derives his origin from Christ, is rooted in Christ, and glories in Christ as his head—then all who are baptized ought to wish to have faithless baptizers and remain unaware of them.

“For however good the baptizers they have may be, Christ is incomparably better. He will be the head of the baptized person if the faithless baptizer is hidden.

“But if it is utterly mad to believe this—for Christ always justifies the ungodly, making a Christian out of the ungodly; faith is always received from Christ; Christ is always the origin of the regenerate and the head of the Church—what weight do those words have, when shallow readers do not attend to what they contain within but only to how they sound?” (above, Book 1, chapter 6, sections 6–7).

This is what I said then; this is what was written in that letter of mine.

### CHAPTER XLIV

53. A little later, since he had said:

“Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can there be, that one who is guilty through his own crimes should make another innocent, when the Lord Jesus Christ says: ‘A good tree produces good fruits, and an evil tree produces evil fruits; surely they do not gather grapes from thorns?’ (Matthew 7:17, 16). And again: ‘Every good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and every evil person brings evil things out of his treasure’” (ibid., 12:35),

by these words Petilian showed plainly enough that the human being who baptizes is to be understood as the tree, and the person who is baptized as its fruit.

I replied to this:

“If the good tree is the good baptizer, so that the person whom he baptizes is his good fruit, then whoever is baptized by an evil man, even one who is not manifestly evil, cannot be good: he has arisen from an evil tree.

“For a good tree is one thing, and a hidden but nevertheless evil tree is another.

“What else did I intend to be understood by these words except what I had set out a little earlier: that the tree and its fruit are not to be understood as the one who baptizes and the one who is baptized, but that the human being is to be understood as the tree and his work and life as its fruit—a life which the good person always has as good and the evil person as evil?

“Otherwise the following absurdity would result: that a person baptized even by a hidden evil man would be evil, as the fruit of a tree that is hidden but nevertheless evil.”

To this he gave absolutely no answer.

### CHAPTER XLV

54. But lest he—or any of you—should say that when the baptizer is secretly evil, the one whom he baptizes is not his fruit but Christ’s fruit, I immediately added what insane error would follow even from this opinion. I repeated, in different words, what I had said shortly before:

“If, when the tree is secretly evil, whoever is baptized by it is born not from it but from Christ, then those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men” (above, Book 1, chapters 7–8, sections 8–9).

Thus Petilian, pressed by such severe difficulties, suppressed the preceding statements on which these words depended and recalled the absurd conclusions that follow from his error in his reply as though I had stated them as my own opinion. They had been said so that he might notice how much evil followed from his position and be compelled to change it.

Having therefore perpetrated this fraud upon his hearers or readers, and despairing altogether that what we had written could be read, he began to attack me gravely and insolently, as though I had believed that all who are baptized ought to wish to have faithless baptizers and remain unaware of them, because however good their baptizers might be, Christ is incomparably better, and Christ will be the baptized person’s head if the faithless baptizer is hidden.

Likewise, he acted as though I had believed that those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men.

Yet I mentioned this remarkable insanity precisely because it necessarily follows those who agree with Petilian that the baptized person relates to his baptizer as fruit relates to the tree from which it is born—good from a good tree, evil from an evil tree.

When we ask such people to answer whose fruit they consider the baptized person to be when he is baptized by a hidden evil man—for they do not dare to baptize him again—they are compelled to answer that he is then not the fruit of that hidden evil man but the fruit of Christ.

Thus what they do not want follows from their position, and what it is madness to believe: if the human being is the fruit of his human baptizer when he is baptized by a manifestly good man, but when he is baptized by a hidden evil man he is not that man’s fruit but Christ’s, then those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men.

### CHAPTER XLVI

55. By attributing this to me, as though I had held this opinion, Petilian attacks me with sufficient gravity and force. Yet through that very vehement attack he himself demonstrates how wicked it is to hold such an opinion. Thus, whatever he wished to appear to have said against me because of this position, he is found to have said against himself, since he is shown to hold such views.

There he demonstrates how powerfully he has been overcome by the force of truth, since he finds no other escape than to pretend that I held what he himself holds.

It would be as though those whom the Apostle rebukes because they said that there is no resurrection of the dead wished to accuse the same Apostle because he said: “Neither has Christ been raised,” and that the preaching of the Apostles is empty, the faith of believers is empty, and witnesses against God are found to be false because they had said that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise.

Petilian tried to do this to me, despairing that what I had written could be read, because he could not answer it, yet eagerly desiring to be thought to have answered it.

But if someone had done this to the Apostle, and the entire passage from his letter had been read aloud, with the preceding words from which any reader could understand that these statements depended, the whole calumnious criticism would have rebounded upon the forehead of those making the accusation. So, when the preceding passages of my letter are restored, Petilian’s accusation rebounds with greater force upon his own face, from which he tried to remove them.

56. In fact, the Apostle, refuting those who denied the resurrection of the dead, corrects them through the absurdity that necessarily follows against their will when they hold such an opinion, so that, while they recoil from what it is wicked to say, they may correct what they dared to believe.

Accordingly, he says:

“If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty and your faith is vain. We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise” (1 Corinthians 15:13–15).

While they fear saying that Christ has not been raised, along with the other evil and wicked consequences that follow, they correct the foolish and faithless assertion they had made—that there is no resurrection of the dead.

If, then, you remove what is placed at the head of this reasoning—“If there is no resurrection of the dead”—the remaining statements are badly expressed and must be attributed to the Apostle. But if you restore the premise on which they depend and place at the beginning, “There is no resurrection of the dead,” then the consequences properly follow: “Neither has Christ been raised,” “Our preaching is empty,” “Your faith is empty,” and the rest connected with these statements.

All this was said well and wisely by the Apostle, because whatever evil these statements contain must be attributed to those who denied the resurrection of the dead.

The same applies to my letter. Remove what is written there:

“If each person is reborn in spiritual grace in accordance with the character of the one by whom he is baptized, and when the one who baptizes is manifestly a good man, he himself gives faith and is himself the origin, root, and head of the one being born; but when the faithless baptizer is hidden, then each person receives faith from Christ, derives his origin from Christ, is rooted in Christ, and glories in Christ as his head”—

remove this, on which the following statement depends, and the statement is very wickedly expressed and must be attributed to me:

“It is to be wished by all who are baptized that they have faithless baptizers and remain unaware of them. For however good their baptizers may be, Christ is incomparably better, and he will be the baptized person’s head if the faithless baptizer is hidden” (above, Book 1, chapter 6, section 7).

But restore the statements you make; then what depends on them and follows from them as a connected conclusion will be found not to be my opinion, and whatever evil it contains [Note: [Col. 0377] In the Amiens and Erasmus editions and in the manuscripts, the reading is *habent* (“they contain”), which is unsuitable unless referred to “the statements you make.”] will rebound upon your position.

Likewise, remove what is written:

“If the good tree is the good baptizer, so that the one whom he baptizes is his good fruit; and if, when the tree is secretly evil, whoever is baptized by it is born not from it but from Christ”—

remove these statements, which you are compelled to confess both from your own sect and from Petilian’s letter, and the insane statement that follows will be mine and must be attributed to me:

“Those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men” (ibid., chapter 8, section 9).

But restore the statements on which this depends, and you will immediately see both that I rightly set this out in order to correct you and that everything in this position which rightly displeases you has rebounded upon your own face.

### CHAPTER XLVII

57. Therefore, just as those who denied the resurrection of the dead could in no way defend themselves against the many evils which the Apostle connected in order to refute them—saying, “Neither has Christ been raised,” and similarly the other wicked consequences—unless they changed their opinion and confessed that there is a resurrection of the dead, so too, if you do not want to be held responsible for what we say to convict and correct you—namely, that those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men—change your opinion and do not place the hope of those who are baptized in a human being.

For if you do place it there, consider what I say, lest someone once again suppress it and claim that I held the opinion which I recall in order to refute and correct you.

Consider what I say, and what the statement I am about to make depends upon:

“If you place the hope of those who are to be baptized in the human being by whom they are baptized; if, as Petilian wrote, you make the human baptizer the origin, root, and head of the person who is baptized; if you understand the good tree to be the good human being who baptizes, and his fruit to be the good person who has been baptized by him, then you compel us to ask you from what origin the person born from a secretly evil baptizer comes, from what root he sprouts, to what head he is attached, and from what tree he is born.

“To this inquiry also belongs the question which I have repeatedly emphasized that Petilian did not answer: From what source is the person who receives Baptism cleansed when he is unaware that the giver’s conscience is stained and that the sacrament is not given in holiness?

“For he wants this conscience of the giver, or of the one who gives in holiness, to be the origin, root, head, seed, and tree from which the baptized person’s sanctification comes forth, is propagated, begins, sprouts, and is born.”

[Note: [Col. 0378] All the books read *hanc etiam*, “this also.” The Louvain editors thought *hanc enim*, “for this,” should be read.]

### CHAPTER XLVIII

58. When, then, we ask from what source the person has been cleansed whom you do not rebaptize in your communion, even when it has been established that he was baptized by someone who, because of hidden wickedness, no longer possessed the conscience of one who gives the sacrament in holiness, what will you answer except “by Christ” or “by God,” although Christ too is God, “who is blessed forever” (Romans 9:5); or “by the Holy Spirit,” since he too is God, because this Trinity is one God [Note: [Col. 0378] The manuscripts read: “because this Trinity is the unity God.”]?

Thus, when Peter had said to the man, “You dared to lie to the Holy Spirit,” he immediately continued by explaining what the Holy Spirit was and said: “You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

Finally, even if you say that the person is cleansed and purified by an angel when he is unaware of the polluted conscience of the one who does not give the sacrament in holiness, observe that holy human beings, when they rise to eternal life, are then said to be “equal to the angels of God” (Matthew 22:30).

Whoever, therefore, is cleansed even by an angel is cleansed more holily than if he were cleansed by the conscience of any human being [Note: [Col. 0378] The manuscripts read: “of any kind of human being.”].

Why, then, do you not allow it to be said to you: If a human being cleanses when he is manifestly good, but when the human being is secretly evil, because he does not possess the conscience of one who gives in holiness, it is no longer he but God or an angel who cleanses, then those who are baptized by hidden evil men are more holily justified than those who are baptized by manifestly good men?

If this opinion displeases you—as indeed it ought to displease everyone—remove the premises from which it arises; correct the premises from which it is connected. If those do not come first, this conclusion will not follow.

## CHAPTER XLIX

**59.** Therefore do not say, “The conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, and it is this that cleanses the recipient,” lest it be said to you: “When the polluted conscience of the one who administers is hidden, who cleanses the conscience of the recipient?” And when you answer, “Either God or an angel” (since you have no other answer to give), let the consequence follow that will put you to shame: “Those who are baptized by hidden evil persons are justified more holily, so that they may be cleansed either by God or by an angel, than those who are baptized by manifestly good persons, who cannot be compared with God or angels.”

But say what the Truth and the Catholic Church say: not only when the minister of Baptism is evil, but even when he is holy and good, hope must not be placed in a human being, but in the one who justifies the ungodly, and to those who believe in him faith is reckoned for righteousness (Rom. 4:5). For when we say, “Christ baptizes,” we do not mean this of a visible ministry, as Petilianus thinks—or wants it thought—that we mean; we mean it of a hidden grace, a hidden power in the Holy Spirit, as John the Baptist said of him: “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

Nor, as Petilianus says, has he now ceased to baptize; rather, he still does it—not through the ministry of the body, but through the invisible operation of his majesty. For when we say, “He himself baptizes,” we do not mean, “He himself holds and dips the bodies of believers in the water,” but, “He himself invisibly cleanses,” and this he does throughout the whole Church. For we must believe the apostle Paul, who said of him: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Eph. 5:25–26). [Note: Col. 0379. The printed editions read “in the word of life”; *life* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.]

Behold that Christ sanctifies; behold that Christ also, by the very washing of water in the word, where ministers are visibly seen to perform the work, himself washes and himself cleanses. Let no one, therefore, claim for himself what belongs to God. Thus human beings’ hope is secure when it is fixed in the one who cannot deceive, since “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5), and “Blessed is the one whose Lord God is his hope” (Ps. 39:5). [Note: Col. 0379. The printed editions read, “if the sure hope of human beings is fixed with him”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

For the faithful steward will receive the reward of eternal life. But as for the unfaithful steward, when he distributes the Lord’s provisions to his fellow servants, far be it from him to make those provisions useless through his unfaithfulness. For Scripture says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3). This command was given against evil stewards so that God’s good gifts might be received through them, while their evil life might be avoided by distinguishing it from those gifts.

## CHAPTER L

**60.** Since it is manifest that Petilianus did not respond to those opening words of my letter, and that where he attempted to respond he showed even more clearly that he had been unable to do so, what shall I say of those parts of my writings to which he did not even attempt to respond, which he did not touch at all? Yet if anyone wishes to review what those passages are like—anyone who possesses both my writings and his—I think he will understand with what strength they have been fortified.

To show this to you briefly, recall, or reread, the very testimonies drawn from the Holy Scriptures which he set forth as though they were against us, and those which I too set forth in my response against you. Observe how I showed that the passages he cited were directed not against us but rather against you; while he entirely ignored those which I cited and which were of the greatest importance. [Col. 0380] In that one passage of the Apostle which he attempted to interpret as though it supported his case, you will see how completely he found no way out.

**61.** The first part of the letter which he wrote to his own people—from its beginning to the place where he says, “The Lord commands us: ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another; and if they persecute you in that one also, flee into another’” (Matt. 10:23)—first came into our hands. We responded to it. When our response also came into his hands, he wrote the reply against it which we are now refuting and showing that he did not answer ours.

In that first part of his writings, to which we first responded, these are the testimonies of Scripture which he thought were against us:

> “A good tree produces good fruits, and an evil tree produces evil fruits. Surely grapes are not gathered from thorns?” (Matt. 7:17, 16)

And again:

> “Every good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and every evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12:35).

And again:

> “The washing of one who is baptized by a dead person does not benefit him” (Sir. 34:30).

By these testimonies he wished to show that the person who is baptized becomes such as the one by whom he is baptized. I showed, in response, how these testimonies ought to be understood and that they contributed nothing to his position. As for the remaining statements he quoted against evil and wicked people, I sufficiently demonstrated that they were not directed against the Lord’s wheat, which has been spread throughout the whole world in accordance with the predictions and promises, and that they could rather be brought by us against you. Read them again, and you will find this.

**62.** But the passages I cited in support of the Catholic Church were these. With regard to Baptism, so that what we are regenerated, cleansed, and justified by God’s grace might not be attributed to the human administrator:

> “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in a human being” (Ps. 117:8);

and:

> “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5);

and:

> “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3:9);

and:

> “Human salvation is futile” (Ps. 59:13);

and:

> “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7);

and because the one in whom people believe justifies the ungodly, so that his faith may be reckoned for righteousness (Rom. 4:5).

In support of the unity of that very Church, which is extending among all nations and with which you do not share communion, I cited these testimonies as predictions concerning Christ:

> “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8);

and:

> “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

I also cited the fact that God’s covenant made with Abraham is recited on behalf of our communion—that is, the Catholic communion—where it is written:

> “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:18),

which the Apostle interprets when he says:

> “And to your seed, which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

Hence it is evident that in Christ not merely Africans or Africa, but all nations, were to have the blessing promised so long beforehand, in accordance with which the Catholic Church is extended. [Note: Col. 0380. The printed editions read “promised”; the manuscripts read *promissam*, agreeing with *benedictionem* (“blessing”).]

I also cited the fact that the chaff remains with the wheat until the final winnowing, so that no one may excuse the sacrilege of his separation by accusations concerning the crimes of others, claiming that he has abandoned or deserted the communion of all nations. [Col. 0381]

And so that the Christian fellowship might not be divided on account of evil stewards—that is, leaders—I also cited this testimony:

> “Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3).

These testimonies from the Holy Scriptures, which I had cited, he neither showed how they should be understood differently, so as to demonstrate that they were neither for us nor against you, nor did he wish to touch them at all. [Note: Col. 0381. This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions have “against us,” less correctly.] Rather, he busied himself with the tumult of his insults, so that, if possible, no one who wished to read his letter after reading mine would even remember that I had said these things.

## CHAPTER LI

**63.** As for the passage from the writings of the apostle Paul which I cited and which he attempted to interpret as supporting his case, pay attention for a moment to what it is like.

“You said,” he writes, “that the Apostle Paul rebukes those who said they belonged to the apostle Paul, and says: ‘Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?’” (1 Cor. 1:13). “Therefore, if those people were in error and would perish unless they were corrected—those who wanted to belong to Paul—what hope is there for those who wanted to belong to Donatus? For these people are doing precisely this: making the origin, root, and head of the baptized person none other than the one by whom he is baptized” (above, Book 1, chapters 3–4, §§4–5).

He recalled these words and this testimony of the Apostle from my letter and set them before himself for refutation. Therefore observe whether he responded to the point. He says:

> “This statement is empty, inflated, childish, and foolish, and utterly remote from the principle of our faith. You would rightly say this if we said, ‘We were baptized in the name of Donatus,’ or, ‘Donatus was crucified for us,’ or, ‘We were baptized in our own name.’ But since we neither have said nor do say these things, because we follow the form of the divine Trinity, it is certain that you, who make such charges against us, are insane. Or, if you think that we were baptized in the name of Donatus or in our own name, you are disastrously mistaken; and at the same time you sacrilegiously confess concerning yourselves that you pollute wretched people in the name of Caecilianus.” [Note: Col. 0381. Here too the printed editions incorrectly read “concerning us”; corrected from the manuscripts.]

This was Petilianus’s response to what I had said. He did not grasp—or rather, by his clamorous interruption he prevented anyone else from grasping—that he had not responded at all to anything relevant to the issue under discussion.

For who does not see that we cited this testimony of the Apostle all the more appropriately precisely because you do not say that you were baptized in the name of Donatus, nor that Donatus was crucified for you, and yet, on account of Donatus’s party, you separate yourselves from communion with the Catholic Church? The people whom Paul was rebuking likewise did not say that they had been baptized in Paul’s name or that Paul had been crucified for them, and yet they were creating a schism in Paul’s name.

Thus, just as it was said more fittingly to those for whom Christ, not Paul, was crucified, and who had been baptized in Christ’s name, not Paul’s, but who nevertheless said, “I belong to Paul”:

> “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

so that they might cling to the one who was crucified for them and in whose name they had been baptized, and might not divide themselves in the name of Paul; so it is said even more appropriately to you, because you do not say, “We were baptized in the name of Donatus,” and yet you wish to belong to Donatus’s party:

> “Was Donatus crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Donatus?”

You know that Christ was crucified for you and that you were baptized in Christ’s name, yet on account of the name and party of Donatus you resist with such obstinacy the unity of Christ, who was crucified for you and in whose name you were baptized.

## CHAPTER LII

**64.** Since Petilianus’s writings aimed to make the origin, root, and head of the baptized person none other than the one by whom he is baptized, and since I did not say this point emptily, childishly, or foolishly, review the opening passages of his letter to which I then responded. Indeed, pay close attention as I recall them carefully.

“The conscience,” he says, “of the holy giver is taken into account, and it cleanses the recipient; for whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless person receives not faith but guilt.”

And as though he were asked, “How do you prove this?” he says:

> “Everything consists in its origin and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing; nor does anything generate well unless it is generated from good seed.” [Note: Col. 0382. The manuscripts here and below consistently read “is generated” (*generetur*) rather than “is regenerated.”]

Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can there be in this: that one who is guilty through his own crimes should make another innocent? The Lord Jesus Christ says:

> “A good tree produces good fruits; surely grapes are not gathered from thorns?”

And again:

> “Every good person brings good things out of the treasure of his heart, and every evil person brings evil things out of the treasure of his heart.”

And again:

> “The washing of one who is baptized by a dead person does not benefit him.”

You see what all this is intended to mean: namely, that the conscience of the holy giver—so that no one who receives faith from a faithless person may receive not faith but guilt—is itself the origin, root, head, and seed of the baptized person.

For he wanted to prove that the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account and cleanses the recipient, and that whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless person receives not faith but guilt. Immediately he added:

> “Everything consists in its origin and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing; nor does anything generate well unless it is generated from good seed.” [Note: Col. 0382. The manuscripts here and below consistently read *generetur* (“is generated”) rather than “is regenerated.”]

And lest anyone be so slow as still not to understand that he was speaking of the person by whom someone is baptized, he explains this in what follows and says:

> “Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can there be in this: that one who is guilty through his own crimes should make another innocent? The Lord Jesus Christ says: ‘A good tree produces good fruits; surely grapes are not gathered from thorns?’”

And lest a listener or reader still blind with incredible dullness of heart fail to see that he was speaking of the person who baptizes, he adds another passage in which he also names the human being: [Note: Col. 0382. The manuscripts read the variant spelling *obtunsitate*.]

> “And again,” he says, “every good person brings good things out of the treasure of his heart, and every evil person brings evil things out of the treasure of his heart; and again, the washing of one who is baptized by a dead person does not benefit him.”

Surely it is now clear; surely it no longer needs an interpreter, disputant, or demonstrator: these people are trying to make the origin, root, and head of the baptized person none other than the one by whom he is baptized.

Yet, overcome by the force of truth and as though he had forgotten what he had said, Petilianus later concedes to me that Christ is the origin and root of the regenerate and the head of the Church, not some human administrator or minister of Baptism.

For after saying that the Apostles baptized in Christ’s name and laid Christ as the foundation in order to make Christians, and after attempting to prove this by testimonies and examples from the Holy Scriptures—as though we denied it—he says:

> “Where now is that voice with which, rattling on in petty and frequent little questions, you spoke at length—wrapped in much talk about Christ, for Christ, and in Christ—against human rashness and pride, maliciously and arrogantly?” [Col. 0383; Note: the manuscripts read “trembling” (*trepidans*) for “rattling on” (*crepitans*).]

“Behold,” he says, “Christ is the origin of the Christian; Christ is the head; Christ is the root.”

After hearing this, what should I do but give thanks to Christ himself, who compelled the man to confess?

Those statements, therefore, which he made at the beginning of his letter are false, when he wished to persuade us that the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account and cleanses the recipient, and that whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless person receives not faith but guilt.

For, wishing as it were to show how much depends upon the person who baptizes, he had offered these supposed great proofs, saying:

> “Everything consists in its origin and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing.”

But later, when he says what we also say—“Behold, Christ is the origin of the Christian; Christ is the head; Christ is the root”—he erases what he had said earlier: that the conscience of the holy giver is the origin, root, and head of the recipient.

Truth has therefore prevailed, so that the person who desires Christ’s Baptism may place his hope not in the human minister, but may approach Christ himself with confidence as the origin that does not change, the root that is not uprooted, and the head that is not cast down.

## CHAPTER LIII

**65.** Finally, who would not notice the inflated vein from which the following statement proceeds? When he seemed to be explaining the Apostle’s sentence, he said:

> “When he said, ‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth,’ what else did he say but, ‘I made a human being a catechumen in Christ; Apollos baptized him; God confirmed what we had done’?”

Why, then, did Petilianus not add what the Apostle added, and what I especially emphasized, so that he might explain this to us as well:

> “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6–7)?

If he wishes to explain it according to what he stated above, it necessarily follows that neither the one who baptizes is anything, but God who gives the growth. [Note: Col. 0383. The manuscripts read “the one who is baptized” rather than “the one who baptizes.”]

For what relevance does it now have how the words “I planted, Apollos watered” should be understood? Should they really be taken as though he had said, “I made a catechumen; Apollos baptized”? Or is there another, truer and more appropriate interpretation?

For the moment, according to his own interpretation, neither the one who makes a catechumen nor the one who baptizes is anything, but God who gives the growth.

There is a great difference, however, between confirming what another does and doing it. The one who gives the growth does not confirm a tree or vine; he creates it. By that growth, the planted wood produces and fixes its root; by that growth, the seed that has been cast forth sends out a shoot.

But why discuss this at greater length? It is enough that, according to Petilianus himself, neither the one who makes a catechumen nor the one who baptizes is anything, but God who gives the growth.

When would Petilianus ever say this, so that we might understand him to be saying, “Neither Donatus of Carthage is anything, nor Januarius, nor Petilianus”? [Col. 0384; Note: the manuscripts read *Januarianus*.] When would that swollen pride tolerate it—the pride by which a human being thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, and deceives himself (Gal. 6:3)?

## CHAPTER LIV

**66.** Moreover, shortly afterward, when he began and undertook as though once again to review the Apostle’s words which we had brought against him, he did not wish to include the words I had cited, but chose others in which human inflation could somehow breathe.

“For,” he says, “let us repeat the Apostle’s words which you brought against us.” [Note: Col. 0384. Lovaniensis reads “for, that we may repeat them”; the manuscripts, with some earlier editions, read “for, that we may repeat his [the Apostle’s] words.”] He then said:

> “What, after all, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of the one in whom you believed” (1 Cor. 3:4–5).

“What else,” he says, “does this say to all our people but: ‘What is Donatus of Carthage, what is Januarius, what is Petilianus, except ministers of the one in whom you believed?’”

I did not cite this testimony of the Apostle. I cited the passage he did not wish to mention:

> “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

Petilianus, however, wanted to insert those words of the Apostle in which he asks what Paul or Apollos is and answers, “Ministers of the one in whom you believed.” The entire neck of heretical pride could somehow endure this. But it could not endure the passage in which he did not ask and answer what they were, but said that they were nothing.

Now I wish to ask whether a minister of Christ is not anything. Who could say that? How, then, is it true that “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth,” unless it is because he is something for one purpose and is nothing for another?

For ministering and administering the word and the Sacrament, he is something. But for cleansing and justifying, he is nothing, because this is not accomplished in the inner person except by the one through whom the whole human being was created, and who, remaining God, became human—namely, the one of whom it was said:

> “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9),

and:

> “The one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly” (Rom. 4:5).

Petilianus wished to place this testimony in my words, but in his own words he neither discussed nor touched it.

## CHAPTER LV

**67.** The minister, therefore—that is, the steward of the evangelical word and Sacrament—if he is good, becomes a partner in the Gospel; but if he is evil, he is not for that reason no longer a steward of the Gospel.

If he is good, he does this willingly. If he is evil—that is, if he seeks his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ—he does this unwillingly, on account of the other things he seeks.

Yet consider what the same Apostle said:

> “If I do this willingly,” he says, “I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:17).

It is as though he were saying: “If, being good, I announce what is good, I myself also attain the goal; but if I am evil, I still announce what is good.” Did he say, “If I do it unwillingly, I will not be a steward”?

Peter and the other good men proclaimed the Gospel; Judas proclaimed it unwillingly, yet he proclaimed it with them after being sent with them. They have a reward; to him a stewardship was entrusted.

Those who received the Gospel while all these men were proclaiming it could be cleansed and justified not by the planter or the waterer, but by the one who gives the growth.

Nor can we say that Judas did not baptize while he was still among the disciples, when what is written was taking place:

> “Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples” (John 4:2).

Or, because he had not yet betrayed Christ—the man who kept the money box and took away what was put into it (John 12:6), and who could not remain innocent as keeper of the money—was he nevertheless a steward of grace without harm to those who received it?

Or, if he did not baptize, surely you admit that he evangelized. If you regard this as something minor and insignificant, consider what you think of the apostle Paul himself, who said:

> “Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize” (1 Cor. 1:17).

Furthermore, Apollos, who watered by baptizing, would begin to be superior to Paul, who planted by evangelizing, even though Paul claims for himself the role of a father toward the Corinthians on this very account and does not grant that title to those who came to them after him.

For he says:

> “Even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15).

He says to them, “I begot you,” although elsewhere he says:

> “I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, and the household of Stephanas” (1 Cor. 1:14). [Col. 0385; Note: Lovaniensis, with the Vulgate, reads *Caius*; Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read *Gaius*; Greek: *Gaion*.]

He had therefore begotten them—not through himself, but through the Gospel.

Even if he were seeking his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, and did this unwillingly and without receiving his reward, he would nevertheless be administering the Lord’s money. Although evil, he would not make that money evil or useless to those who received it properly.

## CHAPTER LVI

**68.** If this is rightly said of the Gospel, how much more must it be said of Baptism, which belongs to the Gospel so fully that without it no one reaches the kingdom of heaven—provided that he approaches the Sacrament with righteousness?

For the one who said:

> “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5),

also said:

> “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

The form of the Sacrament is given through Baptism; the form of righteousness through the Gospel. Neither one without the other leads to the kingdom of heaven.

Nevertheless, even the less learned can baptize perfectly, whereas to evangelize perfectly is a much more difficult and rarer task. [Note: Col. 0385. The printed editions read “and when we read”; the manuscripts read “and yet we read.”] Therefore the teacher of the nations, preeminent among many, was sent to evangelize, not to baptize, because the former could be carried out by many, while the latter could be carried out by few, among whom he excelled.

And yet we read that in certain places he said:

> “My Gospel” (2 Tim. 2:8).

But he never said “my Baptism,” nor did any other person say this of the Baptism administered by him. For only the Baptism given by John is called “John’s Baptism” (Acts 19:3). That man received this special function in his ministry: that the sacrament preceding the washing should also be called the baptism of the one through whom it was administered.

But the Baptism administered by Christ’s disciples was called the baptism of none of them, so that it might be understood to belong to the one of whom it was said:

> “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Eph. 5:25–26).

If, then, the Gospel is so truly Christ’s that even its minister, on account of the duty of administration, can call it his, and if a person can receive it without danger even through an evil steward, doing what that steward says but not doing what he does, how much more can anyone who approaches Christ with good faith receive Christ’s Baptism without contamination from an evil minister, since none of the Apostles administered it in such a way that he dared to call it his own?

## CHAPTER LVII

**69.** Therefore, since Petilianus, after I had demonstrated that the testimonies from Scripture which he cited were not directed against us, entirely ignored some of the testimonies I cited, while in the case of those he wished to discuss he showed that he could do nothing other than fail to escape from them, you do not need to be urged or admonished for long to see what you ought to hold and what you ought to avoid.

But perhaps he appeared to be such in the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, while in those proceedings conducted among human beings concerning the schism itself he achieved something? On the contrary, even there—although after the divine testimonies such matters are sought in vain—what did he recall or prove?

Although he had bitterly attacked the traditors and had loudly produced many testimonies against them even from the Holy Books, he nevertheless said nothing by which he could show that they were traditors. [Note: Col. 0386. The Cygirannensis manuscript reads “by which he could show *us* to be traditors.”] I, however, recalled that Silvanus of Cirta—whom he himself succeeded after several intervening persons, while he was still a subdeacon—had been explicitly identified as a traditor in the municipal records.

Against this he did not dare even to mutter. And surely you see how great was the necessity compelling him to respond: he should have shown that his predecessor—and not merely his associate but, so to speak, even his fellow occupant of the same cathedra—was innocent of the crime of traditio, especially since you establish your entire case by calling traditors those whom you either pretend or suppose to have succeeded traditors through the chain of communion.

If, therefore, the necessity of your own case required him to defend anyone from your party—whether from Rusiccade, Calama, or any other city—whom I said had been demonstrated by municipal records to be a traditor, he would have been compelled by every means to defend him. Yet he kept silent about his own predecessor.

Why was this, unless it was because here he found no darkness with which to obscure the matter, and therefore no means even of deceiving people who were especially slow-minded and sleepy?

For what could he say except that these charges against Silvanus were false? But we cite the records, both of when it took place and of when it was also brought before Zenophilus, the consular official. [Note: Col. 0386. See Book 3 against Cresconius, chapters 27–28, §§30, 32.] How could he resist these records, surrounded on every side by the excellent case of the Catholic Church and the very bad case of your party?

For this reason I recall these words from my letter, to which he wished to appear to have responded through the letter I am now refuting, so that you may see how irrefutably the point was made, against which he could find no safer defense than silence. [Col. 0387]

## CHAPTER LVIII

**70.** When he had produced from the Gospel what he thought was a testimony against us, where the Lord says:

> “They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits,”

I responded and said, “Then let us consider the fruits.” Immediately I continued and added:

> “You bring against us the charge of traditio; we bring this very charge against you with much greater probability.”

And, not to prolong the matter, I said that in that same city of Constantina your elders, at the very beginning of your schism, ordained Silvanus bishop. While he was still a subdeacon, he had been clearly identified as a traditor in the municipal records.

If you produce against our elders any documents, equity demands that we believe either both sets to be true or both to be false. If both are true, you are unquestionably guilty of schism, since you pretended to flee in the communion of the whole world from crimes which you possessed within your own little section of division.

But if both are false, you are unquestionably guilty of schism, since you are stained by the enormous crime of separation on account of the false crimes of traditors.

If we produce some documents and you none, or if ours are true and yours false, it is unnecessary to discuss how thoroughly your mouths are closed.

What if the holy and true Church of Christ were to convict and overcome you, even if we possessed no documents or false documents while you possessed some true documents concerning traditio? What would remain for you except, if you wish, to love peace, and if you do not wish this, at least to fall silent?

For whatever you might now bring forward, I could most easily and truly say that you ought first to have proved these charges to the full and Catholic unity of the Church, already spread and established among so many nations, so that you might be inside while those whom you convicted were expelled.

If you attempted to do this, you certainly could not prove it; and, defeated—or enraged—you separated yourselves from innocent people, who could not condemn what was uncertain, by an enormous sacrilege.

But if you did not even attempt to do this, then with excessively detestable and impious blindness you cut yourselves off from Christ’s wheat, which grows throughout the entire field—that is, the world—until the end, because you were offended by a few weeds in Africa (above, Book 1, chapters 21–22, §§23–24).

To these points, which I recalled from my earlier letter, Petilianus made no response whatsoever. And surely you see that in these few words the whole case being argued between us is contained. What could he attempt to say, when he would be defeated by whatever position he chose?

**71.** For when documents concerning traditors are produced both by us against your people and by you against ours—if indeed you produce any, of which to this day we know absolutely nothing—for Petilianus would certainly not have failed to insert them in his letter, since he took such care to recall and insert the portions of the records relevant to the case against me; [Col. 0388] nevertheless, as I had already begun to say, if such documents are produced both by us and by you, although to this day we know nothing whatever of yours, then surely either both are true, or both are false, or ours are true and yours false, or ours are false and yours true. No further alternative can be found.

## CHAPTER LIX

But in all four of these possibilities, the truth supports communion with the Catholic Church.

For if both are true, you ought not on account of people such as you also had to abandon the communion of the whole world.

If both are false, then, on account of no crimes of traditio, you ought to have avoided the most atrocious crime of division.

If ours are true and yours false, you have no longer anything to say.

If yours are true and ours false, we may have been deceived, together with the whole world, concerning the wickedness of human beings, but not concerning the truth of the faith.

For the seed of Abraham, spread throughout every nation, ought not to attend to what you claimed to know, but to what you proved before judges.

How do we know what those whom your elders accused actually did—even if the charges against them were true—when either the judges of the case, or at least the Church spread everywhere, which ought to attend only to the judgments of judges, considered those charges not true but false? [Note: Col. 0388. The manuscripts read “when either the judges”; the Amerbach and Erasmus editions read “or when the judges,” omitting *when*.]

God does not thereby acquit whatever crime human beings cannot know to have been committed, simply because they are human beings. Nevertheless, I do not think that anyone is rightly judged guilty if he believes a person not proved guilty to be innocent.

How, then, is the whole world guilty if it could not know—even perhaps the true crime of the Africans? It could not know either because no one brought the matter before it, or because, in what was brought before it, it trusted the judges who examined the case rather than the complaints of the defeated.

For this reason Petilianus deserves praise: seeing that this point was completely unanswerable, he passed over it in silence. He certainly does not deserve praise for having similarly attempted to cover the other unanswerable points—which he nevertheless thought could be obscured—with clouds of words, and for having made me the subject of the case when he had failed in the case itself. Concerning me personally he said nothing except what was either entirely false, or not blameworthy, or no longer relevant to me.

Meanwhile, you whom I have placed as judges between him and me: do you possess enough understanding to distinguish true from false, inflated from solid, turbid from calm, swollen from healthy, divine predictions from human presumptions, proofs from accusations, documents from fabrications, the prosecution of a case from the evasion of a case?

If you possess such understanding, well and rightly. But if you do not, we shall not regret having cared for you, because even if your hearts are not turned toward peace, our peace will nevertheless return to us.

# ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0389]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Only one handwritten copy of this book from Belgium was available to the Louvain scholars: the Endovian copy. We also had only one from Gaul: the Floriacian copy.

In the Endovian copy the title is: *On Petilianus’s Letter to the Catholics concerning the Sect of the Donatists*. In the Floriacian copy it is: *Aurelius Augustine’s Letter to the Catholics concerning the Sect of the Donatists*. At the end of the book, the same Floriacian copy reads: “Here ends the Letter of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, to the Catholic brothers.”

When this latter title is compared with Possidius’s Index, we are readily led to believe that this is the very book which is listed in the third chapter of that Index as follows: “One book, a letter against those mentioned above”—that is, against the Donatists—“to the Catholic brothers.”

At the fifth general council, in Conference 5, words from the third chapter are cited in this form: “From the same Augustine’s Letter to the Catholics.”

In the Amerbach edition it is entitled *One Book against the Letter of Petilianus the Donatist*. In later editions, *On the Unity of the Church* was added in the upper margin. This title certainly suits this work no less than the other short writings against the Donatists.

The work appears to belong approximately to the year 402 and to have been published before the third book against Petilianus. For at the beginning of the work Petilianus is challenged either to respond to this very work or to the first two books of Augustine against his letter. The second letter of Petilianus, which is refuted in Augustine’s third book, had therefore not yet been seen. In that letter Petilianus attempts to respond to Augustine’s first book, but nevertheless does not address Augustine’s second book, which appeared around the aforementioned year 402.

This very substantial work is not mentioned at all in the *Retractations*; perhaps because, as the Louvain editors observe, it is properly an epistle, not a book. Nor should it be troubling that a work much shorter than this one, and likewise written in epistolary form, is there listed as the first book against Petilianus: for that first book is wholly connected with the second and third, and for that reason has always necessarily been reckoned among the books.

There are, nevertheless, other features here which, we do not deny, cause us concern. First, the greeting formula, “The salvation which is in Christ,” etc., is new and unusual for Augustine. Next, the transitions, figures, and expressions are frequently inelegant and improper. For example, chapter 6, no. 11, when he turns to the testimonies of Scripture: “O Donatists, read Genesis.” Chapter 8, no. 21: “Who is so deviant and absurd from the divine utterances?” Chapter 15, no. 38: “So that even in those admirable holy [men]…” In the same place: “But by sight and hearing, the righteous one dwelling in a righteous soul was tormenting [it] through the wicked factions of others.” Chapter 24, no. 69: “So that I may diminish our case considerably.” In the same place: “You who evade [the question of] how you may be received.” Chapter 25, no. 73: “When [he is acting] against men who have been maliciously insinuated against themselves by their colleagues.”

It is also troubling that the very man who, in *Epistle* 23, no. 4, and in book 1 against Cresconius, chapter 31, nos. 36–37, explicitly teaches that the Samaritans are a heresy—or heretics—of the Jews, should in chapter 13, no. 33, of this work be unwilling to have that portion of the people which was severed from the kingdom of Judah regarded as a heresy. He relies especially on this argument: that it was separated at God’s command; yet God never commands a heresy to arise, and he commanded the kingdom to be divided, not the religion. At this point the Louvain editors endeavor to defend Augustine against the reproach, as they say, of a man who was not unlearned.

We further observe that the passages of Scripture are here cited not according to the customary version. Thus, in chapter 11, no. 29, from Acts 1:14: “All these were serving unanimously in prayer.” In the same place, no. 30, from Acts 9:15: “That he may magnify my name before the nations, and kings, and the children of Israel.” In the same place, from Acts 10:11: “Like a clear linen cloth.” Chapter 16, no. 42, from Ezekiel 28:3: “Are you better than Daniel?” where one usually reads “wiser,” as can be seen in *Epistle* 111, no. 4. Finally, although at the beginning of the book he establishes that, leaving aside ambiguous matters, something clear should be sought by which the Church may be manifested, he nevertheless employs, in chapter 7, no. 19; chapter 24, no. 70; and chapter 25, no. 75, an unusual interpretation of the statement from Isaiah 62:4, “Your land is the inhabited world” (and we do not recall his ever using this expression elsewhere against the Donatists).

Furthermore, in chapter 24, no. 68, when the water flowing from the Lord’s side is alleged to signify Baptism, he replies that this may perhaps still require more careful investigation, although he is accustomed to present and insist upon precisely this as an established fact—for example, in *Tractate* 9 and *Tractate* 120 on John, and in Sermon 218, *On the Passion of the Lord*, no. 14. Finally, what is read near the end of the book—that the man who does evil works which exclude him from the kingdom of God has not yet been cut off from the root, provided that he does not also resist the most evident truth on account of those very works—presents some difficulty when compared with book 2 against Cresconius, chapter 21.

[Col. 0391]

# TO THE CATHOLICS: AN EPISTLE AGAINST THE DONATISTS, COMMONLY CALLED *THE BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH*, ONE BOOK

[Note: [Col. 0391] The *Book on the Unity of the Church*, formerly corrected by the Louvain editors through collation with the Endovian manuscript, has now been corrected again by us on the basis of the readings of the old Floriacensis manuscript and of the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0391] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, G, S)*

The question having been proposed—whether Christ’s Church is among the Catholics or among the Donatists, a matter which here must be determined solely from certain and clear passages of sacred Scripture—first, very many testimonies are brought forward from the Old and New Instrument, by which it is shown clearly and certainly that the true Church of Christ is the one spread throughout the whole world. Then, those few passages from the same canonical Scriptures which the schismatics ordinarily object on behalf of Donatus are shown to be ambiguous and uncertain, and, since they can be explained in the contrary sense, to possess no force for defending their case. The Donatists’ other accusations against the Catholics—concerning the handing over of the sacred books, persecution, and related matters—are also refuted as occasion permits.

[Col. 0391] Augustine, bishop, to his most beloved brothers entrusted with the care of our administration: May the salvation that is in Christ, and the peace of his unity and charity, be with you; and may your spirit, soul, and body be preserved whole for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

# CHAPTER ONE

**1.** You remember, brothers, that a very small portion of the letter of Petilianus, bishop of the Donatists at Constantina, once came into our hands, and that I wrote to Your Charity what answer I had made to that fragment. But afterward, when the whole and complete letter was sent to us by the brothers who are there, it pleased me to answer it from the beginning, as though we were dealing with its author in person. You know that we have always wished to deal with them in this way, so that, through a discussion conducted before all, it might become clear what is said either by them or by us, without the contentious zeal of partisanship.

For we have learned that this letter is in the hands of many people, who also retain much of it by memory, thinking that he has said something true against us. But now, if they are willing to read what we have answered, they will certainly understand what they ought to reject and what they ought to retain. For these are not our own words, as they themselves can see if they are willing to judge without partisan zeal: everything has been brought forward and proved from the holy Scriptures in such a way that no one can deny it unless he professes himself an enemy of those Scriptures.

But I see what the most stubborn defenders of so bad a cause may say about that work of ours: namely, that I answered an absent man’s letter, in a place where he could not hear my words and immediately reply to them. Let him therefore defend the words of his own letter and, if he can, show that they were not refuted and convicted by my replies. Or, if he does not wish to do this, let him do to this letter of mine what I did to his own letter, to which I have already replied. For he wrote that letter to his own people, just as I have written this one to you; let him also answer it, if he wishes.

# CHAPTER TWO

**2.** Certainly the question between us concerns where the Church is: whether among us or among them. It is one Church, which our ancestors called *Catholic*, so that by the very name they might show that it is “according to the whole.” For “according to the whole” is said in Greek as καθ’ ὅλον (*kath’ holon*). This Church, moreover, is the body of Christ, as the Apostle says: “For the body of him, which is the Church” (Colossians 1:24). From this it is plainly evident that one who is not among the members of Christ cannot possess Christian salvation.

The members of Christ, however, are joined to one another by the charity of unity, and through that same charity they cleave to their head, which is Christ Jesus. Everything, therefore, that is proclaimed about Christ consists of head and body. The head is Jesus Christ himself, the only-begotten Son of the living God, himself “the Savior of the body” (Ephesians 5:23), who died because of our sins and rose again for our justification (Romans 4:25). His body is the Church, of which it is said: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27).

The question between us and the Donatists, then, is where this body is—that is, where the Church is. What are we to do, therefore? Are we to seek her in our own words, or in the words of her head, our Lord Jesus Christ? I think that we ought rather to seek her in the words of him who is the truth and who knows his own body perfectly. “For the Lord knows who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

**3.** Pay attention to what our words are—the words in which the Church ought not to be sought—and observe also what difference there is there between our words and theirs. Yet we do not wish the Church to be sought in our words.

Whatever we accuse one another of—the handing over of the divine books, the burning of incense, the persecutions—these are our words. In such matters, indeed, we adopt this position: either both sets of accusations are to be considered true, whether those made by us or those made by them; or both false; or ours true and theirs false; or ours false and theirs true. In all these cases we show that no crime attaches to the Christian world with which we are in communion.

For if the accusations made by us against them and by them against us are true, let us do what the Apostle says: “Forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave us” (Ephesians 4:32). In this way, wicked men—whether those who perhaps were or are among us, or those who were or are among them—will not obstruct our concord and the bond of peace. Let the one crime of those people be corrected: that they have separated themselves uselessly from the unity of the whole world, even though they had such people among them.

But if both accusations are false—whether those which we make against them or those which they make against us concerning the handing over of the sacred books or the persecution of the innocent—I see no cause for the dispute except that there is a reason why they should correct themselves, since they separated themselves without cause.
