If, however, what we say is true, since we support the Acts which we produce with written imperial documents addressed to the emperor to whom they first wrote and later appealed, and with the communion of the whole world; while what they say is shown to be false because, at the very time when the same question was being debated, they were completely unable to prevail in their case—then there appears in them a greater fury of sacrilegious hostility and a greater persecution of innocent souls than if they were held guilty only of the crime of schism.

And let them attribute those accusations, not to all their people, but to whomever they wish among them; nevertheless, schism is the crime of them all. But if they wish the charges of handing over the sacred books and persecution to be true—the charges which they bring against us—and those brought against them by us to be false, even so they are not cleared of the crime of schism. Those charges may indeed pertain to certain individuals, not to the whole Christian world.

If they think that the whole world has perished through contamination, I shall say nothing of how many evils known to the saints, for the sake of the good of peace, have been tolerated in human communities. I shall say this: let them show how those were not destroyed by the contamination of people whom they either do not now know, or once did not know, to be sacrilegious violators of the consecrated chastity of women, hiding or having hidden among them.

They will certainly say that they were not contaminated precisely because they did not know. How, then, has the world been contaminated, when it does not yet know whether these things that are being said are true? Let us suppose that these matters have now been proved and demonstrated to us. What shall we do about all those nations? They are abandoned in ignorance, and therefore innocent people are abandoned. Since their ignorance is no crime at all, our action begins to be a most heinous crime.

Are we to run and inform them of what we know? Why? So that they may be innocent? They are innocent even while they do not know. We preserve innocence not by knowing the evil deeds of human beings, but by refusing to consent to what we know and by not rashly judging what we do not know.

Accordingly, as I have said, the whole world is innocent, because it is ignorant of the crimes which these men allege against certain persons—even if those crimes are true. But those who separated themselves from these innocent people have lost their innocence through that very crime of separation and schism. And now they teach us that they speak the truth about certain individuals, so that we may separate ourselves from people against whom they have no true accusation.

[Note: [Col. 0393] The printed editions read *dicunt*, “they say.” The Floriacensis manuscript has the better reading, *dicant*, “they may say.”]

[Note: [Col. 0393] Likewise, in *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 1, chapters 21–22, nos. 23–24, and book 3, chapters 58–59, nos. 70–71.]

**4.** For the whole world says this to them—a statement very brief in words, but most powerful in truth.

The African bishops were in conflict among themselves. If they could not bring the dispute that had arisen among them to an end—whether by settling it through agreement, or by degrading those who were wrongly contending, so that those who had the good cause might remain in communion with the whole world through the bond of unity—then it nevertheless remained for the overseas bishops, since the greater part of the Catholic Church was spread among them, to judge the disputes of their African colleagues. This was especially so because those who accused others of the crime of an improper ordination were pressing the matter.

[Note: [Col. 0394] The Floriacensis manuscript has *stantibus*.]

If this was not done, the fault belongs to those by whom it ought to have been done, not to the whole world, which did not know what had not been brought before it. But if it was done, what fault did the ecclesiastical judges commit? Even if the accusations were true and brought before them, they could not in any way condemn them unless the accusations had been proved to them. Could evil people contaminate judges when those people could not be made manifest to them?

But if the accused were made known to them, and through some negligence or connivance they refused to remove such people from communion, and even pronounced judgments in their favor through a perverse decision, what fault did the whole world commit?

[Note: [Col. 0394] In the printed editions, as commonly in ancient books, *cohibentia* is written for *conniventia*.] It did not know that those men had bad judges and did not believe that they had judged badly.

[Note: [Col. 0394] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “believed that they had judged well.”]

For just as the crime of the accused, if it escaped the notice of the judges, certainly did not contaminate them, so also the crime of the judges, if there was any, because it escaped the notice of the whole world, could certainly not contaminate the world.

Thus we innocently share communion with these innocent people.

[Note: [Col. 0394] The Floriacensis manuscript has *communicamus*, “we share communion.” The editions of Erasmus and others have *communicabimus*, “we shall share communion”; Amerbach and Louvain have *communicavimus*, “we shared communion.”]

Even today we do not know what was then done. Therefore, even if today we learn that the accusations they make against certain people are true, there is no reason for us to withdraw from innocent people who do not know these things and pass over to those who, because they did what they urge us to do, have all become implicated in the crime of schism: they urge us not, following the example of the Apostles, to tolerate the wicked, but, following the example of heretics, to abandon the good.

But let us suppose—something that cannot happen—that the whole world today could come to know with complete certainty that the crimes of certain people whom they accuse are true. Could it thereby become more innocent than it was before it knew? For just as unknown evils could not contaminate them, even if those people were still alive in this world, so those who have already departed this life cannot be contaminated even by evils that have become known.

If, then, our case concerning the crimes of certain individuals—the accusations which we make against one another—is so invincible that it remains so even if what we say against some of their people is false and what they say against some of ours is true, let us today consider what answer they have. Whether what we say is rather true and what they say false; whether both are false; or whether both are true—how can they fail to be defeated at the very point which they desire above all else to have believed?

# CHAPTER THREE

**5.** But, as I had begun to say, let us not listen to “You say this, I say that”; let us listen instead to “Thus says the Lord.”

There are certainly the Lord’s books, whose authority we both accept, to which we both submit, and which we both serve.

[Note: [Col. 0394] The printed editions read *credimus*, “we believe.”]

Let us seek the Church there; there let us examine our case.

At this point they may perhaps say: “What are you seeking in books which you handed over to the flames?” To this I reply: “Why are you afraid that these books should be read, if you protected them from the flames?” Surely the one who handed them over ought to be regarded as the person who, after reading them, is proved not to agree with them.

Or if these books perhaps identify their betrayer in the same way that the Lord identified Judas, let them read in those books, by name and explicitly, that either Caecilianus or those who ordained him were destined to be betrayers of those same books; and if I do not anathematize them, let me myself be judged, along with them, to have handed them over.

But neither do we find in those books that the ordainers of Majorinus are designated as betrayers, although we may cite such things from elsewhere. Let those matters, therefore, be removed from the dispute—matters which we cite against one another not from the divine canonical books but from other sources.

If they refuse to have them removed, let them see that, even if both sets of accusations are true, there was no reason for their separation, so that they might flee from people whom they had among them. If both are false, there was no reason for their separation, so that they might flee from people in whom they found no crime. If our accusations are true and theirs false, there was no reason for their separation, because they ought rather to have corrected themselves and remained in unity. If our accusations are false and theirs true, there was no reason for their separation, because they ought not to have abandoned the innocent whole world, to which they either refused or were unable to demonstrate these matters.

**6.** Someone may perhaps ask me: “Why, then, do you wish these matters removed from the dispute, when your communion remains invincible even if they are brought forward?”

Because I do not wish the holy Church to be demonstrated by human documents but by divine oracles.

For if the holy Scriptures designated the Church only in Africa, and among a few Romans at Cutzupita—or among the Montenses—and in the house or estate of one Spanish woman,

[Note: [Col. 0395] Lucilla. See above, *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 108, no. 246.]

then, whatever may be produced from other documents to the contrary, only the Donatists possess the Church.

If holy Scripture determines that the Church is among a few Moors of the province of Caesarea, then we must pass over to the Rogatists. If it is among a few Tripolitans, Byzacenians, and Provincials, the Maximianists have reached it. If it is among the Easterners alone, it must be sought among the Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians, and among any others who are there.

But who could enumerate all the individual heresies of the individual nations?

If, however, the Church of Christ is designated by the divine and most certain testimonies of the canonical Scriptures among all nations, then, whatever those people may bring forward, and from whatever source they may quote who say, “Here is Christ,” or “There,” let us rather listen—if we are his sheep—to the voice of our Shepherd saying, “Do not believe it” (Matthew 24:23).

Those individual groups are not found in the many nations where this Church is found; but this Church, which is everywhere, is also found wherever those groups are. Therefore let us seek it in the canonical holy Scriptures.

# CHAPTER FOUR

**7.** The whole Christ consists of head and body. The head is the only-begotten Son of God,

[Note: [Col. 0395] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “God the Son.”]

and his body is the Church: bridegroom and bride, “the two shall be one flesh” (Ephesians 5:23, 30–31).

Whoever disagrees with the holy Scriptures concerning that head, even if they are found in all the places in which the Church is designated, are not in the Church.

And again, whoever agrees with the holy Scriptures concerning that head but does not share in the unity of the Church is not in the Church, because concerning Christ’s body, which is the Church, he disagrees with Christ’s own testimony.

For example, those who do not believe that Christ came in the flesh from the virgin Mary, from the seed of David, as the Scripture of God most clearly declares; or who do not believe that he rose again in that very body in which he was crucified and buried—even if they are found throughout all the lands in which the Church exists, they are certainly not in the Church. For they do not hold the very head of the Church, which is Christ Jesus; nor are they misled by any obscurity in the divine Scriptures, but they contradict their most familiar and clearest testimonies.

Likewise, whoever does believe that Christ Jesus came in the flesh as has been said, and rose again in the same flesh in which he was born and suffered; and believes that he is the Son of God, God with God, one with the Father, and the immutable Word of the Father,

[Note: [Col. 0396] The same manuscript reads: “and the immutable one Word of the Father.”]

through whom all things were made; but nevertheless disagrees with his body, which is the Church, to such an extent that their communion is not with the whole Church wherever it is spread, but is found in some separated part—then it is clear that they are not in the Catholic Church.

Therefore, since our dispute with the Donatists concerns not the head but the body—that is, not Jesus Christ the Savior himself but his Church—let the head himself, concerning whom we agree, show us his body, concerning which we disagree, so that through his words we may cease to disagree.

He is the only-begotten Son and Word of God. For this reason the holy prophets could not have spoken truly unless the very Truth, which is the Word of God, had revealed to them what they should say and commanded them to say it.

Accordingly, in earlier times the Word of God sounded forth through the prophets; afterward through himself, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14); and then through the Apostles, whom he sent to preach him

[Note: [Col. 0396] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “to preach,” omitting “himself.”]

so that salvation might reach the ends of the earth (Matthew 28:19–20). In all these sources, therefore, the Church must be sought.

# CHAPTER FIVE

**8.** Since, however, malicious people often turn against whomever they wish and to whomever they wish things said about others or for another purpose; and since many things have also been set down figuratively and obscurely, for the exercise of rational minds, in the images of riddling figures or in the twofold sense of ambiguity, and are sometimes thought to agree and correspond with a deceptive interpretation—I therefore announce and propose this as well: let us choose whatever is open and evident.

If such things were not found in the holy Scriptures, there would be no means at all by which closed matters could be opened and obscure matters illumined.

For example, see how easy it would be for us to say against them, or for them to say against us, what the Lord said to the Pharisees: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every kind of impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matthew 23:27–28).

Whether these words are spoken by us against them or by them against us, unless it is first proved by the clearest evidence who those people are who, although unjust, pretend to be just, who of even moderate sanity does not understand that such words are spoken more by abusive frivolity than by truth that proves?

For the Lord spoke those words against the Pharisees in a different manner, as Lord—that is, as knower of the heart and both witness and judge of all human secrets. We, however, must first discover and demonstrate what we are accusing, lest we ourselves rather be accused of the most serious crime of insane rashness.

Certainly, if they first prove that we are such people, we should by no means refuse to be reproved and crushed by such words of the holy Scriptures. Likewise, if we prove that they are such people, it will similarly lie within our power to strike those who have already been exposed and convicted with the Lord’s denunciations.

**9.** So too, for the moment, we must set aside those matters which are obscurely stated, wrapped in veils of figures, and capable of being interpreted either according to our view or according to theirs.

It is indeed the task of keen-minded people

[Note: [Col. 0397] The manuscripts read *cautorum*, “of cautious people.”]

to judge and distinguish who interprets them more plausibly. But we do not wish to entrust our discussion, in a case which holds entire peoples, to these contests of intellect.

None of us doubts that, without violating the historical truth of what happened, the Church was also represented by Noah’s ark, in which the house of the righteous was saved from the flood when sinners had been destroyed. Yet this might seem a conjecture of human ingenuity, unless the Apostle Peter said it in his letter (1 Peter 3:20–21).

But if one of us should say something which Peter did not say there—namely, that all the kinds of animals were present there because the future Church among all nations was being foretold—this might perhaps seem otherwise to the Donatists, and they might wish to interpret it differently.

Likewise, if they interpret some obscure and ambiguous passage according to their own view, and it should occur to us to say from it something else that sounds in our favor,

[Note: [Col. 0397] Elsewhere: *placeat*, “should please.” M.]

what end will there be?

One of their bishops, when he was preaching to the people here at Hippo, as we have heard, said that Noah’s ark had been coated with pitch on the inside so that it would not let its own water out, and on the outside so that it would not admit foreign water.

He wished this interpretation to serve the purpose of preventing anyone from believing either that Baptism can go out beyond the Church or that Baptism given outside the Church can be accepted.

He appeared to have said something, and those who willingly listened applauded, without carefully considering what they had heard. If they had done so, they would easily have noticed that it could not happen that the framework of the wood should admit water from outside if it did not let water out from within. But if it lets water out through the side that is inside, it follows that it must also admit water through the side that is outside.

But even if what he said about joined wood were true, who would prevent me, concerning an ark coated with pitch on both sides, from saying something else, so that it would be uncertain which of these meanings—or perhaps some third meaning—the matter signified?

For it is not absurd, and indeed it may be much more plausible, to say that the pitch signifies charity, since pitch is a powerful adhesive and a very hot substance. Why else is it said in the Psalm, “My soul has been glued to you” (Psalm 62:9), except by the most ardent charity?

And because it is commanded that charity should exist among us and toward all, the ark was therefore coated with pitch both inside and outside.

Or certainly, because it is written, “Charity endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7), the very power of endurance that preserves unity was signified by the pitch. For this reason the ark was smeared inside and outside: because evil people must be endured both inside and outside, lest the framework of peace be broken.

In this discussion of ours, therefore, let us spare such interpretations and seek something clear by which the Church may be manifested.

**10.** It is written in the Book of Judges:

“Gideon said to the Lord: ‘Since you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, behold, I shall place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor; and if there is dew on the fleece, while there is dryness over all the earth, I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.’

And it happened so. Gideon rose early on the following day and squeezed the fleece, and he poured out from the fleece a basin full of water.

And Gideon said to the Lord: ‘Let not your anger be kindled against me, Lord, and I shall speak once more and test once more with the fleece. Let there be dryness on the fleece alone, but let there be dew over all the earth.’

And God did so that night: there was dryness on the fleece alone, but there was dew over all the earth” (Judges 6:36–40).

I do not see what else is represented and foretold here except that we should understand the threshing floor as the whole world and the place of the fleece as the people of Israel.

For we know that that former nation was once drenched, as it were, by the grace of the divine sacrament, like heavenly dew. Among all the surrounding nations, which lacked that gift, there was, as it were, dryness.

Among that people the gift was present in the fleece—that is, under a veil and, as it were, in a cloud of secrecy,

[Note: [Col. 0398] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “and as it were a cloud of secrecy.”]

because it had not yet been revealed.

Now, however, we see the whole world being nourished by the dew already revealed through the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was then represented under that covering. But that nation, having lost the priesthood which it possessed because it does not understand Christ in the Scriptures, has remained, as it were, like a dry fleece.

Nevertheless, even in such figures of things, although I do not see what else could be understood here, I do not wish us to seek the Church. Let us set aside for the moment all matters that require any such interpretation—not because the things which are unraveled in this way by interpreting such coverings are false, but because they either require an interpreter, and I do not wish our intellectual abilities to be compared in them.

Rather, let evident truth cry out, shine forth, break into deaf ears, strike the eyes of those who dissemble; let no one seek in these hiding places a position for his false opinion; let it confound every effort at contradiction and crush the brow of every shameless person.

# CHAPTER SIX

**11.** O Donatists, read Genesis.

“By myself I have sworn,” says the Lord, “because you have done this thing and have not spared your beloved son for my sake, unless I bless you indeed and greatly multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand which is beside the seashore; and your seed shall possess by inheritance the cities of your enemies.

“And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because you obeyed my voice” (Genesis 22:16–18).

[Note: [Col. 0399] The editions read *adversariorum tuorum* (“of your enemies”); *tuorum* is absent from the Floriacensis manuscript and the Greek Septuagint.]

What do you say to this? Are you contending with us in the perversity of the Jews, so that you say that the seed of Abraham must be understood as only the people born from Abraham’s flesh?

But the Jews do not read the Apostle Paul in their synagogues, whereas you read him in your gatherings. Let us hear, then, what the Apostle says.

For we are now asking how the seed of Abraham is to be understood.

“Brothers,” he says, “I speak in human terms: even a humanly confirmed covenant no one annuls or adds conditions to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3:15–16).

There is the seed in which all nations are blessed. There is the covenant of God. Open your ears.

“No one,” he says, “annuls or adds conditions to a humanly confirmed covenant.” Why do you annul God’s covenant by saying that it has not been fulfilled among all nations, and that the seed of Abraham has already perished from the nations among which it existed?

Why do you add conditions by saying that Christ remains heir in no lands except where he could have Donatus as a co-heir?

We begrudge no one. Read this to us from the Law, from the Prophets, from the Psalms, from the Gospel itself, and from the apostolic Letters. Read it, and we shall believe it—just as we read to you from Genesis and from the Apostle that all nations are blessed in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ.

**12.** Hear this same covenant addressed also to Isaac, Abraham’s son:

“There was a famine in the land, besides the former famine which had occurred in the time of Abraham. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines,

[Note: [Col. 0399] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “Palestinians.”]

at Gerar. The Lord appeared to him and said: ‘Do not go down into Egypt, but dwell in the land which I shall tell you. Dwell in this land, and I shall be with you and bless you. For I shall give you and your seed all this land, and I shall establish with you the oath which I swore to your father Abraham. I shall multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I shall give you and your seed all this land. And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my commandments, my ordinances, and my statutes’” (Genesis 26:1–5).

Respond to this. The seed of Abraham is the same seed as the seed of Isaac, namely Christ. For who, in any manner whatsoever, who is a Christian, is ignorant of how Christ came from the tribe of Judah in the flesh through a virgin?

**13.** Hear this same covenant addressed to Jacob:

“Jacob departed from the Well of the Oath and went toward Charran. He came to a certain place and slept there, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, put it at his head, and slept in that place.

“And he saw a vision, and behold, a ladder was set upon the earth, whose top reached to heaven; and the angels of God were ascending and descending upon it. And the Lord was leaning upon it, and said: ‘I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. Do not be afraid. The land upon which you are sleeping, I shall give it to you and to your seed. And your seed shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall be multiplied over the sea, and toward the southwest, and toward the north, and toward the east. And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your seed.

“And behold, I am with you, guarding you on every road wherever you go, and I shall bring you back to this land, because I shall not abandon you until I have done everything that I have spoken to you” (Genesis 28:10–15).

There is the promise which you resist; there is the covenant which you render void, although it is so firm.

God says, “I shall not abandon you until I have done everything that I have spoken to you.” Yet you contradict him, saying that we should instead believe whatever accusations you bring against a world that is ignorant and unaware, while we should not believe God when he says, “I shall not abandon you until I have done it.”

14. Read to us from the canonical Scriptures that they delivered those divine books which you specifically accuse; read passages as clear as those which we have read to you from Genesis. We are not asking you what that stone signifies which Jacob placed beneath his head when he slept; what the ladder fixed upon the earth signifies, whose top reached to heaven; or what the angels of God ascending and descending upon it signify. Let those who are more prudent and learned inquire into these matters and explain them among a peaceful people, where malicious contradiction does not interrupt them by arming its shamelessness with the obscurity of a sacrament and the riddle of a passage.

There are faithful hearts whom the Lord recalls from the Gospel, where he says—when he had seen an Israelite in whom there was no deceit—that Jacob, who saw these ladders, was himself called Israel. There are therefore people whom the Lord himself recalls from that passage; for there he says, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:47, 51), that is, upon the seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations are blessed.

But I am not pressing these points upon those who refuse them. Hear this: “Your seed shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall multiply over the sea, and toward the southwest, and toward the north, and toward the east; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your seed.” Give me this Church, if it exists among you; show that you share fellowship with all the nations whom we already see being blessed in this seed. Give it to me, or, laying aside your rage, accept it—not from me, but from the very one in whom all the nations are blessed. It will be enough to have recalled these matters from the first book of the Law; more will become clear to readers without impious contention and with devout love.

## CHAPTER VII

15. What numerous and manifest testimonies there are in the Prophets to the Church spread throughout all the nations and over the entire world! I shall recall a few, leaving more to the leisure of diligent readers who read with the fear of God. Let us receive the divine answers through the mouth of the holy Isaiah, and question his lips as though they were the oracles of God. Let the spirited and destructive battles of human controversies be silent; let us incline our ear to the word of God. [Col. 0401]

Let Isaiah say where, by God’s revelation, he foresaw the holy Church, so that in the words of one declaring future things we may already see what is present. “The whole earth,” he says, “has been filled so that it may know the Lord, as abundant water covers the sea. And on that day there shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isaiah 11:9–10).

No Christian, in any manner whatsoever, is ignorant that Christ is the Root of Jesse, born according to the flesh from the seed of David. If anyone is contentious, let him contend with the Apostle, who uses this testimony in his writings (Romans 15:12).

Again he says: “Israel shall sprout and blossom, and the whole world shall be filled with its fruit” (Isaiah 27:6). Israel, of course, was the son of Isaac and the grandson of Abraham, to whom it was promised that all nations would be blessed in his seed; the Apostle interprets that seed as Christ. Christ came from the seed of Abraham through Isaac and through Israel, and thereafter through the generations pertaining to Christ’s birth, as the Evangelist has set them out (Matthew 1).

Therefore, whoever wishes to argue against this should contradict the Gospel and deny that Christ came from the seed of Israel, so that he may deny what Isaiah says: “Israel shall sprout and blossom, and the whole world shall be filled with its fruit.”

Again he says: “I am God, the first, and I am he among the things that are to come. The nations saw and feared, and the ends of the earth were afraid” (Isaiah 41:4–5). This is what Scripture says elsewhere: “The first and the last” (Revelation 22:13), so that there may be an alpha and an omega, the letters in the sign of Christ known to all. For in place of “the last,” which appears there, this passage has, “I am he among the things that are to come.”

Those who refuse to believe—or rather, who refuse now to see fulfilled—what follows contradict this manifestation: “The nations saw, and the ends of the earth were afraid.”

Again, a little later:

“Jacob is my servant; I shall receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul has accepted him. I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor cease, nor shall his voice be heard outside. He shall not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax, but in truth he shall bring forth judgment. He shall shine forth and shall not be broken, until he establishes judgment upon the earth; and in his name the nations shall hope” (Isaiah 42:1–4).

This testimony is to be understood of Christ, and it has also been placed in the Gospel. Let anyone who dares contradict it do so; but whoever does not dare should hope in him together with the nations and not withdraw from the unity of the nations hoping in him—or, if he has withdrawn, let him return, lest he perish.

16. Again Isaiah says:

“And now thus says the Lord: He who formed me in the womb as a servant for himself, that I might gather Jacob and Israel to him; I shall draw him near, and I shall be honored before the Lord [Note: In the Floriacensis manuscript: ‘and Israel. I shall draw near to him, and I shall be honored before the Lord.’ In the Greek Septuagint: συναχθήσομαι καὶ δοξασθήσομαι ἐναντίον Κυρίου (*sunachthēsomai kai doxasthēsomai enantion Kyriou*), ‘I shall be gathered together and glorified before the Lord.’]; and my God shall be my strength. And he said to me: It will be a very great thing for you to be called my child, so that you may establish the tribes of Jacob and convert the offspring of Israel. And I have placed you as a covenant of the race, as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth.”

And a little later he adds:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: At the most acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you.”

When the Apostle Paul recalled these words, he showed them to be fulfilled only in Christians [Col. 0402]. For he connected them by saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Let us therefore hear what Isaiah adds:

“I have given you as a covenant of the nations, so that you may inhabit the earth and possess the inheritance of the wilderness.”

Then, after inserting other material, he continues and says:

“Behold, these shall come from afar; some from the north and the sea; others from the land of the Persians. Rejoice, heaven, and be glad, earth; let the mountains send forth joy, because God has had mercy on his people and has addressed the humble of his people.

“But Zion said: ‘The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me.’ Can a woman forget her child, or can it happen that she does not have compassion on the child of her womb? Now behold, even if forgetfulness should possess her, I nevertheless shall in no way forget you, says the Lord. Behold, I have engraved your walls upon my hands; you are also continually before my sight, and soon you shall be built by those by whom you were overthrown.”

Since the apostolic voice does not permit us to understand this of the Jewish people but of Christians, what are we to understand in what Isaiah says here—“Soon you shall be built by those by whom you were overthrown”—except that the kings of the earth who first persecuted the Church were afterward to assist it, as was foretold so long beforehand?

But because many of them were destined to die in their own iniquities, he adds:

“And those who laid you waste shall depart from you.”

Then, because all the nations would be joined to the Church, he continues:

“Look around with your eyes on every side, and see them all. As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these and arrange them as a bride’s ornament, because the places in you that were desolate, ruined, and fallen shall now be greatly confined because of those who dwell there; those who devoured you shall be made far from you” [Note: The printed editions read, “those who dwell there. These shall be made far from you, who will devour you.” The reading has been corrected according to the Floriacensis manuscript.].

“For your sons whom you had lost shall say in your ears: ‘This place is too narrow for us; make room for us here also, so that we may dwell.’

“But you shall say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me, since I know that I am childless and a widow? Who, then, has raised these for me? For I was left alone; where were these?’”

Thus says the Lord:

“Behold, I shall raise my hands toward the nations, and I shall set up my signal among the islands; and they shall bring your sons in their bosom, and your daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders. Kings shall be your guardians, and their chief women your nurses. They shall bow their faces to the earth and plead with you, and they shall lick the traces of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and you shall not be ashamed” (Isaiah 49:5–23).

And a little later he adds and says:

“Listen to me; listen, my people; kings also, give heed to me; for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall be a light to the nations. My righteousness draws near quickly, and my salvation shall go forth, and by my arm the nations are saved” (Isaiah 51:4–5).

Let us consult the apostolic Scriptures concerning this arm. When the Apostle Paul had brought forward the testimony of the same prophet concerning the unbelief of the Jews, showing that Christ had not been revealed to them, he cited this:

“Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been [Col. 0403] revealed?” (Romans 10:16; Isaiah 53:1).

Then, in what follows, Isaiah adds and says:

[Col. 0403] “Let the desolate places of Jerusalem break forth together in joy” [Note: The printed editions read *erumpat*, “let it break forth”; but the Floriacensis codex has *erumpant*, “let them break forth,” referring to *deserta*, “the desolate places.” The Greek has τὰ ἐρῆμα, “the desolate places.”], “because he has had mercy on her and has redeemed Jerusalem; and the Lord shall reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the nations shall see, even to the ends of the earth, the salvation that comes from God” (Isaiah 52:9–10) [Note: The Floriacensis codex reads *intima terrae*, “the innermost parts of the earth.”].

Who is so deaf, who so insane, who so blind in mind, that he would oppose such evident testimonies? [Note: The Amiatinus and Floriacensis codices lack the particle *ut*, “that”: its absence does no harm here. But below, after the word *obloquatur*, “would oppose,” the printed editions had wrongly added *nisi qui nescit quid loquatur*, “unless he is one who does not know what he is saying”; this is absent from the Floriacensis manuscript.]

17. But let us come to more manifest matters. Certainly we know of the most sacred marriage in the Scriptures: the bridegroom and the bride, Christ and the Church. Isaiah describes both, lest we happen to err regarding either one—for whoever errs in one loses both. Since it was said sacramentally of this marriage, as the Apostle testifies, “The two shall become one flesh” (Ephesians 5:31).

Thus the bridegroom himself is described first. After many things Isaiah says about him—things that even the Jews themselves fall silent before; let it not be too long to recall them all—pay attention briefly to this:

“And he himself shall bear their sins; therefore he shall possess many as an inheritance, and he shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because his soul was delivered to death, and he was numbered among the wicked. He himself bore the sins of many, and for our iniquities he was delivered up” (Isaiah 53:11–12).

You confess that these things were foretold and prophesied so long beforehand concerning our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: So reads the Floriacensis codex. The printed editions have *fatemur*, “we confess.”].

Why, then, was this bridegroom delivered to death? Why was he numbered among the wicked, in such profound humiliation of his exalted dignity? What did he accomplish; what did he acquire? Who is so deaf as not to hear these things? Who so dull as not to understand? Who so blind as not to see?

“Therefore,” he says, “he himself shall possess many as an inheritance, and he shall divide the spoils of the mighty, because his soul was delivered to death, and he was numbered among the wicked.”

What is it, heretics, that you boast about your small number, if the Lord Jesus Christ was delivered to death for this reason: that he might possess many as an inheritance? And who are these many, or how widely do they occupy the earth? Let us hear what follows.

18. Having foretold and clearly expressed the bridegroom, let the bride now come forward in Isaiah’s words. Let us read her in the truth of the sacred pages and recognize her throughout the world. The Apostle Paul also cited this testimony as having been foretold concerning the holy Church. Contentious heretical evasion has nowhere to flee.

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Galatians 4:27).

Where, I ask, is your boast about your small number? Are these not the many of whom it was said shortly before, “Therefore he himself shall possess many as an inheritance”? For what is his inheritance except his Church?

“Many,” he says, “are the children of the deserted woman, more than those of her who has a husband” [Col. 0404]—meaning that the synagogue of the Jews is the one who has a husband, since it had received the Law.

From this what we are saying can now be judged. Let them compare their multitude established among the Africans or in Africa with the multitude of Jews dispersed throughout all the lands, wherever they are scattered, and let them see how very few they are in comparison with the Jews. How, then, will they apply to themselves the words, “Many are the children of the deserted woman, more than those of her who has a husband”?

Again, let them compare the multitude of Christians throughout all the nations with whom they do not share fellowship, and let them see how few all the Jews are in comparison. At last let them understand that in the Catholic Church spread throughout the world this prophecy has been fulfilled: “Many are the children of the deserted woman, more than those of her who has a husband.”

But who is the one with a husband whom this deserted woman has surpassed in the multitude of her children may remain obscure and enigmatic. Nevertheless, that this is the Church of Christ, of which it was said, “Many are the children of the deserted woman, more than those of her who has a husband,” whoever contradicts does not contradict me but the Apostle.

19. And concerning where she would have many children, he consequently adds and says:

“For the Lord has said: ‘Enlarge the place of your tent and your curtains’” [Note: The Lovanienses added here *pelles*, “skins,” although it is not found in the manuscripts; and in place of *aularum*, “curtains,” they think *aulaearum* or *aulaeorum* should be read. The Greek has τῶν αὐλαίων (*tōn aulaiōn*). See *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 29.], “fix them firmly; do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes; extend still farther to the right and to the left. Your seed shall possess the nations, and you shall inhabit deserted cities. Do not fear, for you shall prevail; do not be afraid that you have been despised. You shall forget eternal confusion and shall not remember the shame of your widowhood, because I am the Lord who makes you; the Lord is his name,” and he who redeemed you shall be called the God of Israel, of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:1–5).

Behold how far she was commanded to extend her cords: until her God, the God of Israel, is called the God of the whole earth.

For concerning her he also says elsewhere through the same prophet:

“For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until my righteousness goes forth like light and my salvation burns like a torch. And all the nations shall see your righteousness, and kings your honor; and he shall call you by your new name, which the Lord has named. You shall be a crown of beauty in the sight of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Deserted. For you shall be called ‘My Will,’ and your land ‘The Whole World’” (Isaiah 62:1–4).

What could be demanded that is still more clearly stated? Behold how many and how plain are the passages from one prophet alone! Yet they resist and contradict—not any human being, but the Spirit of God and the most evident truth.

And still those who wish to glory in the Christian name begrudge glory to Christ himself, lest people believe that what was foretold about him so long beforehand is being fulfilled, when it is no longer merely foretold but displayed, seen, and possessed.

Now, if I wished to gather into this one Epistle testimonies from all the Prophets concerning the Church prefigured beforehand, which we read about and see, I fear that I myself would seem to judge them few, although they are so numerous that, even if I wished to assemble everything from this one Isaiah alone, I would exceed the proper measure of a discourse [Col. 0405].

## CHAPTER VIII

20. Let us now hear a few things from the Psalms, sung so long beforehand, and let us see with great joy that they are now being fulfilled. First, let them hear and judge with what face Petilianus placed this very passage in his Epistle [Note: Perhaps, “why he placed it.”]:

“The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth’” (Psalm 2:7–8).

For what Christian has ever doubted that this was foretold concerning Christ, or understood that this inheritance was anything other than the Church?

And because it was to contain good and wicked people within the same nets of the sacraments, he says: “You shall rule them with an iron rod; like a potter’s vessel you shall crush them.” For by the same firm and inflexible justice the good are ruled and the wicked are crushed.

21. Who is so far astray from and so absurdly opposed to the divine utterances that he does not recognize the Gospel itself when that psalm is sung in which it is written:

“They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves considered and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my garment they cast lots” (Psalm 21:17–19; Matthew 27:30; John 19:24)?

When the Evangelist narrated that this had happened, he too remembered this testimony.

But what was acquired by the price of this cross, by such exalted greatness in such profound humiliation, by that most innocent and divine blood, except what is said there in what follows?

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:28–29).

Did the Apostle not explain that this was spoken of the preachers of the New Testament: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10:18; Psalm 18:5)?

Of whom else but Christ is this understood?

“The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor” (Psalm 49:1–2).

Whose voice is it but Christ’s?

“I slept in agitation.”

And why was he agitated? The passage continues:

“The sons of men—whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword”—whose, except those who cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23:21)?

Why was all this done? For whose benefit, for whose gain? Hear what follows:

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Psalm 56:5–6).

Behold: you have Christ sleeping in his Passion and ascending above the heavens in his resurrection. And whence is his glory over all the earth, except because his Church is throughout all the earth?

In these two very brief statements I ask you heretics about the whole matter at issue between us:

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.”

Why do you preach that the Lord Christ has been exalted above the heavens, yet do not share in his glory over all the earth?

[Col. 0406] 22. The seventy-first Psalm bears the title “For Solomon.” But because the things said there cannot fit that temporal king, who afterward sinned grievously, they are defended with absolute certainty—even against the Jews themselves—as having been foretold concerning Christ. No Christian denies this. For statements are made there of such a kind that there can be no doubt that they pertain to Christ.

There also it speaks in such a way that the Church spread throughout the whole world may be recognized, with all kings likewise subjected to Christ [Note: See *The City of God*, book 17, chapter 8]:

“And he shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.”

The river, of course, is the place where the Holy Spirit manifested him in the form of a dove and the voice from heaven revealed him.

Then it continues:

“Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents. And all kings shall worship him” [Note: The printed editions add *terrae*, “of the earth”; this is absent from the Floriacensis manuscript and from the Greek Septuagint.], “all nations shall serve him.”

And a little later:

“And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. And blessed is the name of his glory forever and unto ages of ages. And his glory shall fill the whole earth. Amen, amen.”

Go now, Donatists, and cry out: “Let it not be; let it not be.” The word of God has defeated you, saying: “Let it be; let it be.”

Behold, the Church spread throughout the whole world has been manifested in the Psalms, and the glory of its king rests upon her.

Therefore she herself is also his queen and bride, concerning whom it is said to him in the forty-fourth Psalm:

“The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold and surrounded with variety.”

And immediately the divine word is directed to her to exhort her:

“Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty, for he is your God.”

Notice where divine prophecy began to address the bride of Christ:

“Hear,” it says, “daughter, and see.”

But you neither wish to hear these things foretold nor to see them fulfilled; nevertheless, unwillingly, you both hear and see them.

Hear, then, what is said to her a little later; hear from the divine page how it is foretold, and see throughout the whole earth how it is fulfilled:

“In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them as princes over the whole earth.”

How many testimonies of Scripture concerning this matter I pass over is known to those who read, and I too know it; but I do not wish to burden an Epistle to which I demand a response.

## CHAPTER IX

23. What will they say to these things that I have recalled from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning the Church of Christ, which is spread throughout the whole world, and against which the perverse prefer to fight rather than, once corrected, to share fellowship?

What, I ask, will they say: that these things are false, or obscure?

They do not dare to say that they are false, for they are crushed beneath the weight of such great authority. Since, therefore, they admit that these things are true, they contend that they cannot be fulfilled—as though it were something other than accusing the prophecy of falsehood to say that what it foretold cannot be fulfilled. For this is to say that it is not prophecy but false prophecy.

And when you ask them why these things cannot be fulfilled [Col. 0407], they answer: “Because people do not wish it.”

“For,” they say, “human beings were created with free choice, and if someone wishes, he believes in Christ; if he does not wish, he does not believe. If he wishes, he perseveres in what he believes; if he does not wish, he does not persevere. For people become Christians by free choice. And therefore, when the Church had begun to grow throughout the world, people did not wish to persevere, and the Christian religion failed among all the nations except the party of Donatus.”

As though the Spirit of God did not know the future choices of human beings! Who could say such a mad thing? Why, then, did he not rather foretell what he knew would result from human choices?

In the manner in which these people think such things were foretold, anyone who wished could be a prophet. When the things he had predicted had not been fulfilled, he could answer: “People did not wish it; Christians have free choice.”

In this way someone could have prophesied that Christ would not suffer on a cross but would die by the sword; and when it happened otherwise, he could reply: “What could I do? Human beings, placed under free choice, did not wish to do to him what I had foretold, and they did what they themselves wished.”

Who would not see how many things could be prophesied in this way—or even can be prophesied by any human beings?

Who has ever doubted that Judas, if he had wished [Note: The Floriacensis codex here and below reads *si noluisset*, “if he had not wished,” instead of *si voluisset*, “if he had wished”], would certainly not have betrayed Christ, and that Peter, if he had wished, would not have denied the Lord three times?

But the prediction concerning these matters was certain because God also foresees future choices.

## CHAPTER X

24. Nevertheless, although these things are clear even to slow hearts, let us hear from here the voice of the Word himself, expressed by the mouth of his own flesh.

Certainly, after the resurrection, when he offered himself to be touched and handled by the hands of his doubting disciples, and when he had received and eaten before them what they had offered him, he said to them:

“These are the words that I spoke to you when I was still with you: that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled.”

Of whom else could the things we too have recalled from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms have been written, as I have demonstrated point by point?

Since he himself, who is the Truth (John 14:6), says, “Everything had to be fulfilled,” how do they deny this except because they are enemies of the truth?

But if they still say that these things are obscure, let us also hear from this very head, the truest interpreter of his body.

When he had said, “Everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled,” as though we might ask whether, in what he said—“about me”—the Church was also to be understood, on account of what is written, “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), so that we might possess certain divine oracles not only concerning the head but also concerning the body, the Evangelist continues and says:

“Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: ‘Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.’”

Here the head itself is shown—the very one who also offered himself to be handled by the disciples’ hands [Col. 0408].

See how he adds what concerns the body, which is the Church, so that he does not permit us to err either concerning the bridegroom or concerning the bride:

“And that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:44–47).

What voice is more truthful, more divine, more manifest than this? I am reluctant to commend it in my own words, yet the heretics are not ashamed to attack it in theirs.

25. Let them say that the testimonies I have cited from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms are obscure and expressed figuratively, and that they can also be understood in other ways—although I have done as much as I could to prevent them from daring to say even this. But let them say it.

Is this also obscure, or shaded by the veil of an enigma, which Christ himself said?

“Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

If “I slept in agitation” is obscure, is this also obscure: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer”?

If “Be exalted above the heavens, O God” is obscure, is this also obscure: “and to rise on the third day”?

If “Your glory is over all the earth” (Psalm 56:5–6) is obscure, is this also obscure: “and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations”?

If “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” is obscure, is this also obscure: “and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations”?

For the earth was summoned from the rising of the sun to its setting in the same way that he himself said: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13).

If “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor” (Psalm 49:1–2) is obscure, is this also obscure: “beginning from Jerusalem”?

For that is Zion which is Jerusalem.

But what is this to me? Let them say that the things I have cited from the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms do not pertain to these words of the Lord that are read in the Gospel. I do not care, and I do not resist.

Nevertheless, unless these things had been foretold in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—whether in the testimonies I have cited or in others—the Lord would certainly not have said:

“Everything that is written in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms about me must be fulfilled.”

And then, after opening their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, he would not have taught them those very things written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, in the manner in which he said:

“Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

I may not have been able to recognize that these things were written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; nevertheless, the one who is the Truth says that they are written there.

But even if he had not said that these things were written there, it would undoubtedly have been sufficient for Christians that Christ himself had said that repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

Yet, although his disciples had seen and handled his body, he wished to confirm them in their uncertainty by the greater testimony of the Scriptures rather than merely by presenting himself visibly and tangibly to mortal senses [Col. 0409]. [Note: In Am. and Er., chapter 10.]

Let us therefore hold fast to the Church designated by the Lord’s own mouth: where it would begin and how far it would extend—namely, beginning from Jerusalem and reaching to all the nations.

26. At this point, whoever says that “Jerusalem” should not be understood as that visible city but as a figurative designation, so that it is to be understood spiritually as the whole eternal Church in heaven and, in part, as the pilgrim Church on earth, may also say that the statement, “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day,” was expressed figuratively.

Whoever says this is in no way to be regarded as a Christian.

Therefore, just as the former expression is used literally, so too is what has been added concerning the Church of all nations beginning from Jerusalem.

For the Lord explained that these things had been spoken about himself in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; and this explanation itself could not have been figurative, otherwise it would not have been an explanation.

Moreover, if Jerusalem, taken figuratively and understood spiritually, signifies the universal Church, how does the universal Church begin from the universal Church—as though Jerusalem were to begin from Jerusalem?

It is therefore clear that the reference is literally to that city from which the Church is also proved to have begun. The Lord himself repeatedly made this clear, leaving no hiding place for heretical cunning.

For the passage continues:

“And you are witnesses of these things; and behold, I send my promise upon you. But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

In which city did he command them to remain until they were clothed with power from on high—that is, with the Holy Spirit, whom he had promised to send? He foretold that the Church would begin from that city.

But if they do not think that city was Jerusalem, let them hear what follows:

“He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them. And it happened that while he blessed them, he departed from them. And they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple, praising God” (Luke 24:48–53).

Behold where that city is shown in which he commanded them to remain until they were clothed with power from on high.

## CHAPTER XI [Note: There is no such division in Am. and Er.]

27. The number of days he was with them after he had shown himself alive to their eyes and hands following his Passion is omitted here; it is not, however, passed over in silence in the Acts of the Apostles. There, by the same presentation of the Lord’s words, the future Church throughout the world is again foretold.

No one is permitted to doubt—unless he doubts the faith of the sacred Scriptures—that this was the visible city of Jerusalem, from which the Church began after the resurrection and ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ; nor that he wished to indicate anything other than the places on this earth from which he would give it its beginning and the manner in which he would spread it from there throughout all things.

For this is what is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“I composed the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach until the day on which he chose the Apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the Gospel. To them he also showed himself alive after his Passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking [Col. 0410] about the kingdom of God.

“And while he was staying with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem but to await his promise, which you have heard from my mouth—for John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will also receive not many days from now.

“So when they had come together, they asked him, saying: ‘Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?’ But he replied to them: ‘It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority’” [Note: The Floriacensis codex omits *vel momenta*, “or moments,” as manuscripts sometimes omit it elsewhere.], “but you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the whole earth” (Acts 1:1–8).

Behold, here too it has been made clear where the Church would begin and how far it would extend.

### 28.

What do those who boast most arrogantly that they are Christians, and who most openly contradict Christ, say to this? We hold to this Church and admit no human accusations against these divine utterances. For we are deeply moved by the fact that our Lord—whom it is sacrilegious and impious not to believe—left these salutary and final instructions to the primitive Church in the last words he spoke while on earth. Immediately after saying these things, he ascended into heaven. He wished to fortify our ears against those whom he had foretold would arise in the course of time and say, “Look, here is the Christ; look, there” (Matt. 24:23). He warned us not to believe them.

Nor will we have any excuse if we believe contrary to the voice of the shepherd—a voice so clear, open, and manifest that no one, however dull or slow of heart, can say, “I did not understand.” For who could fail to understand: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem”? Who could fail to understand: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth”? After saying these things, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him, and they saw him going into heaven.

What does this mean, I ask? When the last words of a dying man are heard—of one who is about to go to the underworld—no one calls him a liar, and an heir is judged impious if he should perhaps disregard those words. How, then, shall we escape the wrath of God if we reject, whether by refusing to believe or by despising them, the last words of the only Son of God, our Lord and Savior, who was about to go into heaven, from there to observe who neglects them and who keeps them, and from there to come to judge all things?

I have the clearest possible voice of my shepherd, commending the Church to me and expressing it without any ambiguity. I shall blame myself if I wish to be deceived and led astray from his flock—which is the Church herself—by human words, especially since he warned me, saying, “My sheep hear my voice and follow me” (John 10:27). Behold, his voice is clear and open. Once it has been heard, how will anyone who does not follow him dare to call himself one of his sheep?

Let no one say to me, “Oh, what Donatus said! Oh, what Parmenianus said! Or Pontius, or any of the others!” For even Catholic bishops must not be followed wherever they happen to be mistaken and hold an opinion contrary to the canonical Scriptures of God. But if, while preserving [Note: [Col. 0411] Lovaniensis has *sed qui custodito*, “but if, with the bond of unity and charity preserved.”] the bond of unity and charity, they fall into this error, what the Apostle says will be fulfilled in them: “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:15).

But these divine utterances concerning the universal Church are so clear that only heretics, in their obstinate perversity and blind fury, can bark against them.

### 29.

We have therefore shown that the Church foretold in the word of God—her bridegroom—whether through the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, or through his own mouth, was to begin from Jerusalem and reach to the ends of the earth. But how she began from Jerusalem and, spreading from there among all nations, bears fruit is also shown in that same word of God through the Apostles, just as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Lord is recorded—as I have already mentioned—as saying: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth.”

Then it continues:

> When he had said this, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And as they were looking into heaven while he was going, behold, two men stood beside them in white clothing. They also said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”  
> 
> Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. And when they had entered, they went up into the upper room, where Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James were staying. All these persevered with one accord in prayer, together with the women and Mary, who was the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.  
> 
> In those days Peter rose in the midst of the disciples—it was a crowd of about one hundred and twenty persons—and spoke.

Then it is related, while Peter was delivering his speech, how Matthias was appointed in the place of Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. After his appointment the Scripture continues:

> When the days of Pentecost had been fulfilled, they were all together in one place [Note: [Col. 0411] The printed editions have *in eodem loco*, “in the same place.” But the Floriacensis codex has *in unum*. The Greek is *epi to auto*.]. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent wind rushing along, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire; it rested upon each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance.  
> 
> Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men [Note: [Col. 0411] The Floriacensis codex has *Judaei viri et religiosi*, “Jews, both men and devout.”], from every nation under heaven. And when this sound had occurred, the multitude gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. They were astonished and wondered, saying to one another: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we each hear our own language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites; those who dwell in Mesopotamia; Jews from Judaea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene; and visitors from Rome, both Jews and foreigners; Cretans and Arabs”—they heard them speaking in their own languages of the mighty works of God.  
> 
> They were all astonished and perplexed, saying to one another: “What can this mean?” But others mocked them, saying: “These men are full of new wine.”  
> 
> But Peter, standing with the eleven disciples, raised his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judaea, and all of you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you,” and so forth, as he exhorted them to faith.

When he had finished, the Scripture continues its account as follows:

> When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the Apostles: “What shall we do, brothers? Tell us.” Peter said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children, and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God will call.”  
> 
> And with many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.”  
> 
> Those who received his word believed, and they were baptized. And about three thousand persons were added on that day (Acts 1–2).

Behold how the Church began from Jerusalem and from there was to proceed through all languages. This too was prefigured in those who, having received the Holy Spirit there, spoke in every language.

### 30.

Let us now see how she proceeded among other nations, as Peter himself had foretold when he said, “The promise is for you and for your children, and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God will call.” For what happened then in Jerusalem is subsequently narrated, up to the martyrdom of Stephen the deacon; Saul is also mentioned as consenting to his killing.

After this had taken place, the account continues:

> On that day a great persecution arose against the Church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the Apostles, who remained in Jerusalem.

See how what the Lord had said in order is subsequently fulfilled: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth.” What had been said concerning Jerusalem had already taken place; what followed concerned Judaea and Samaria, since they were scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria.

For this is immediately said of them:

> Those who had been scattered went from place to place through the towns and villages, preaching the word of God.

The Apostles too had gone forth. When they heard that Samaria had received the word of God and that its people had received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of their hands, this is said concerning Peter and John:

> Peter and John, having testified to the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in many Samaritan villages as they went.

Then the account is given of the eunuch who, returning from Jerusalem, was baptized by Philip. Concerning Philip himself it is said:

> The angel of the Lord snatched Philip away from him, and the eunuch no longer saw him. He went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found to have come to Azotus. From there he returned, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea (Acts 8).

Thus the gospel is found to have been preached in the towns of both Judaea and Samaria.

It remained, then, that in due order it should also be preached among all nations, as the Lord had said, “to the very ends of the earth.” Saul is therefore called from heaven, and from persecutor becomes a preacher. The Lord says concerning him to Ananias:

> Go, for he is a chosen instrument for me, to carry my name before the nations, and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.

We therefore already possess the Church in Jerusalem, throughout Judaea, and in Samaria. Shortly afterward it is said most explicitly:

> The Churches throughout all Judaea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace, being built up and strengthened in the fear of the Lord; and they were filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit (Acts 9).

After a short interval the narrative reaches the place where Cornelius the centurion believed and was baptized with his household; all of them were uncircumcised Gentiles.

Before this happened, Peter saw, while praying in an ecstatic state, heaven opened and a vessel, like a clean linen cloth, fastened at its four corners, in which was every kind of four-footed animal, wild beast, and bird of the air. And a voice came: “Peter, rise, kill, and eat.” Peter replied: “Lord, I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” And the voice came to him again: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.”

There is no need for us to conjecture that this vision signified the nations who were to believe; the Apostle himself explains it in the vessel shown to him [Note: [Col. 0413] Lovaniensis has *in illa voce*, “in that voice,” referring, of course, to the voice mentioned shortly afterward: “Thus he explained that voice.”]. For when he entered the house where Cornelius was, and many had gathered, he said to them:

> You yourselves know how abhorrent it is for a Jewish man to join himself to or associate with a foreigner. But God has shown me that I should call no person common or unclean (Acts 10).

Thus he explained the voice he had heard concerning the animals displayed in the linen cloth: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.”

Now who cannot see that the vessel signified the whole world, together with all its nations? It was fastened at its four corners because of the four well-known regions: east and west, south and north, which Scripture very frequently commends.

As for Paul, who was sent to the nations, the places through which he traveled spreading the word of God and strengthening the Churches that had been founded, it would take too long to enumerate them. When the Jews opposed him at Antioch, he and Barnabas said to them:

> It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you [Note: [Col. 0413] The Floriacensis codex has *sermonem Dei*, “the discourse of God.”]. But since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations. For so the Lord has commanded us: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be for salvation to the very ends of the earth.”

And the account continues:

> When the nations heard this, they received the word of God, and all who had been appointed for eternal life believed (Acts 13:46–48).

Here too the testimony from the prophet Isaiah is recalled, the same testimony we cited: “that there may be salvation to the very ends of the earth” (Isa. 49:6).

### CHAPTER XII  
[Note: [Col. 0413] There is no chapter heading in the manuscripts of Am. and Er.]

### 31.

Without, then, mentioning the nations that believed after the time of the Apostles and joined the Church, let these men tell us how those Churches alone which we find in the sacred Scriptures—in the Acts, in the Epistles of the Apostles, and in the Apocalypse of John—which we both embrace and to which we both submit, perished through an African quarrel [Note: [Col. 0414] See Book 2 against Cresconius, chapter 37.].

For we received these Churches not from councils of disputing bishops, not from recent controversies, not from legal or municipal records, but from the canonical sacred Scriptures.

How could the Church of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26), have perished through the crimes of Africans? How could so violent an African storm have scattered so far away a pestilence whose originators, or those among whom the evil arose, could not even have been known by name—in Athens, Iconium, or Lystra? Who destroyed the Churches founded through apostolic labor?

At the end of his Epistle to the Romans the same Apostle, the teacher of the nations, says:

> I have written to you somewhat boldly, as reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus among the nations, consecrating the gospel of God, so that the offering of the nations may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit. I therefore have my glory in Christ Jesus before God. For I will not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem and its surrounding region as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of Christ (Rom. 15:15–19).

Donatists, if you do not know, inquire. Count, along the land routes from Jerusalem through the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum, how many stages there are. If we count that many Churches, tell us how they could have perished through African disputes.

To the Corinthians, Ephesians, Philippians, Thessalonians, and Colossians, you read only the Apostles’ Epistles; we retain both the Epistles in reading and faith, and the Churches themselves in communion.

Galatia, moreover, is not a single Church, but there are innumerable Churches in that region. Consider how he greeted the Corinthians:

> Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the Church of God that is in Corinth, together with all the saints who are throughout Achaia (2 Cor. 1:1).

How many Churches do you think there are throughout all Achaia? Perhaps you do not know where Achaia is, and in such blindness you pass judgment on a province so unknown that you say it perished through the crimes of Africans.

Are not all the places Peter named—Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia—filled with flourishing Churches (1 Pet. 1:1)? What of the places to which John wrote: Smyrna, Pergamum, Sardis, Thyatira, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, which are Churches (Rev. 1:11)? We have already mentioned Ephesus.

Let one of you tell me where these places are and how far they are from one another. Perhaps you are now seeking to learn this, whether by reading or by hearing. [Note: [Col. 0414] Formerly in Am. and Er., chapter 11.] Learn, then, how far they are removed from Africa, and tell us why, with such sacrilegious recklessness, you accuse Churches entirely unknown to you yet plainly revealed in the Apostolic Letters, and say in such madness that they perished through African crimes.
