Finally, I know what is written about them in the holy canonical books; what you say about them, I do not know. Certainly, just as we read them as Churches of Christ in the codices that you too venerate, so read to us from the codices that we too venerate how they perished.

Or does it please you that, against Churches which are members of the one Church spread throughout the whole world, Churches whom the Holy Spirit commended and entrusted to us through the Scriptures, we should believe every curse uttered by any people anywhere? That pleases you, but it does not please us. You yourselves can see which side has the stronger claim to approval; but overcome by obstinacy, you refuse to be overcome by truth.

Behold the Scriptures of God; behold the Churches in them, both designated and expressed in the name of the universal whole world and individually. Your ancestors did not know what they had charged against their colleagues; they did not know what sort of judges that case had; how, then, did those Churches perish?

Here are the Scriptures in which I believe; here are the Churches with which I share communion. Where you read me their names, read me their crimes there as well.

### 32.

But if you shout or recite something from elsewhere, then, after the voice of our shepherd—made perfectly clear to us through the mouths of the Prophets, through his own mouth, and through the mouths of the Evangelists—we admit, believe, and accept none of your voices.

“My sheep,” says the heavenly shepherd, “hear my voice and follow me” (John 10:27). His voice concerning the Church is not obscure. Whoever does not wish to stray from his flock should hear him and follow him.

His most faithful steward, the teacher of the nations, speaking in faith and truth—for Christ himself was speaking in him—says:

> I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you in the grace of Christ to another gospel—which is not another gospel at all, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:6–9).

The Church that was to come into being throughout the whole world was preached to us in advance. The Lord himself testified that this had been foretold in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. He predicted that she would begin from Jerusalem and continue among all nations, and, when he was already ascending into heaven, foretold that they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth [Note: [Col. 0415] Er., Lugdunensis, and Venetus have *permansuram*, “would remain,” instead of *permanaturam*.].

The events that followed fulfilled these words. How she began from Jerusalem, then advanced into Judaea and Samaria, until she reached the whole world—where the Church is still growing—and from there will extend to the remaining nations until the end, wherever she does not yet exist, is shown successively by the testimony of the holy Scriptures. Whoever preaches anything else, let him be accursed.

### CHAPTER XIII  
[Note: [Col. 0415] In Am. and Er., chapter 12.]

To preach something else is to say that the Church has perished from the rest of the world and has remained only in Africa, in the party of Donatus. Therefore, let him be accursed. Or let him read this to me in the holy Scriptures, and let him not be accursed.

### 33.

“I do read it,” they say. “For among all human beings, Enoch alone pleased God, and he was taken away” (Gen. 5:24). And afterward, when the whole world had been destroyed by the floodwaters, Noah alone, with his wife, his sons, and his daughters-in-law, deserved to be saved in the ark (Gen. 7:1).

They also add the case of Lot, who alone was rescued from Sodom with his daughters (Gen. 19:12). They mention Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as well, saying that few pleased God in a land devoted to idols and demons [Note: [Col. 0416] Thus the Floriacensis codex reads. The printed editions have: “few pleased God, while the rest were devoted to idols and demons.”].

Finally, after the people of Israel had multiplied, during the period of the kings in the Promised Land—which had been distributed among all twelve tribes—they point out that ten tribes were divided off and handed over to the servant of Solomon, while two remained with Solomon’s son for the kingdom that was Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:11–13).

“So now also,” they say, “the whole world has apostatized, while we, like those two tribes, have remained in the temple of God, that is, in the Church.”

They also say that when the Lord Jesus Christ was followed by a great number of disciples, and seventy-two apostatized, only the twelve remained with him.

By such examples and others of the same kind, heretics attempt to commend their small number and do not cease to blaspheme the multitude of the holy Church spread throughout the whole world.

But I ask them: if—God forbid—I did not wish to believe that these very examples they cite were true, how would they convince me? Would it not be from the holy Scriptures, where they are recorded with such clarity that anyone who accepts those writings in faith cannot help but confess that these things are most true?

But if I were compelled to believe that these examples are true because they are written there, where I could not say that what is written is false, why do they themselves not believe, through those same Scriptures, in the Church spread throughout the whole world?

Behold, we believe all those things. Let them also believe what the Lord says: that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. Let them believe what he said finally as he was about to ascend into heaven: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth” (Luke 24:44–51; Acts 1:8–9).

Let both those things and these things be believed to be true, and no dispute will remain between us, because those true things do not hinder these, nor do these true things hinder those.

“But we believe these things,” they say, “and we confess that they have been fulfilled. But afterward the whole world apostatized, and only the communion of Donatus remained.”

Let them read this to us, just as they read about Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; about those two tribes that remained after the ten were separated; and about the twelve Apostles who remained when the others apostatized. Let them read this in the same way, and we will offer no resistance.

But if they do not read these things from the holy Scriptures and instead try to persuade us through their own disputes, I believe what is read in the holy Scriptures; I do not believe what vain heretics say.

But since they think they should be compared with those two tribes that remained with Solomon’s son, let them read, and they will regret having chosen this comparison [Note: [Col. 0417] The printed editions have *legisse*, “having read.” The Floriacensis manuscript more appropriately has *elegisse*, “having chosen.”].

For the Scriptures refer to those two peoples in this way: the portion that belonged to Jerusalem is called Judah; the other portion, which was separated with Solomon’s servant in greater number, is called Israel.

Let them read what the Prophets say about each, and how they call Judah worse than Israel, to the point of saying that the apostate Israel was justified in comparison with the transgressing Judah (Ezek. 16:51)—that is, that Judah’s sins were so grave that, in comparison with her, Israel had to be called righteous.

Yet the sins of neither Judah nor Israel harmed the righteous who are found to have lived in both. For even in that portion which they put forward as an example of destruction—that is, in Israel—there were holy prophets. There was the celebrated Elijah, to say nothing of others, to whom it was also said: “I have left to myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 19:18).

Therefore that portion of the people must by no means be regarded as having been a heresy. God had commanded those same tribes to be separated, not so that their religion would be divided, but so that the kingdom would be divided, and in this way vengeance might be taken upon the kingdom of Judah.

But God never commands schism or heresy. Nor, because kingdoms are often divided throughout the world, is Christian unity therefore divided, since the Catholic Church is found in both portions.

### 34.

I have thought it necessary to mention this concerning Judah and Israel, especially so that these people may be warned that it does not harm the righteous who are situated among the wicked, whatever is said about those peoples because of the multitude of the wicked. Let them cease gathering together whatever testimonies they find spoken—whether through the Prophets, through the mouth of the Lord, or through the Evangelists—about the weeds or chaff of the whole world.

For the divine word often rebukes the wicked crowds within the Church, who are not even counted as belonging to the Church, yet who share with the holy the sacraments they possess in common. Because they have in themselves a certain form of piety, while denying its power, as the Apostle says, “Having the form of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5), Scripture rebukes them as though all were of this kind and no good person at all had remained.

From this we are warned that they are all said to belong to a certain number of their own: that is, to the number of all the children of Gehenna, to which God foreknew that they belonged.

These people, therefore, acting either ignorantly or deceitfully, gather from the Scriptures passages that are found to have been spoken either about the wicked mixed with the good until the end, or about the devastation of the former Jewish people. They wish to twist these passages against the Church of God, so that she may appear to have failed and perished from the whole world.

Let them therefore cease producing such arguments if they wish to reply to this letter. For we do not say that the Church is spread throughout the whole world in such a way that only the good are present in her sacraments and not also the wicked—indeed, the wicked are much more numerous, so that the good are few in comparison with them, although the wicked themselves constitute an enormous number.

### CHAPTER XIV  
[Note: [Col. 0417] In Am. and Er., chapter 13.]

### 35.

We have innumerable testimonies both to the mingling of the wicked with the good in the same communion of the sacrament—for Judas, wicked from the beginning, lived among the other eleven—and to the small number of the good in comparison with the greater number of the wicked, and again to the multitude of the good considered in itself.

To avoid making this lengthy, I shall mention a few of these testimonies.

In the Song of Songs there is a passage that every Christian recognizes as spoken about the holy Church:

> As a lily among thorns, so is my neighbor among the daughters (Song 2:2).

Why does he call them thorns, except because of the wickedness of their conduct? And why does he call the same people daughters, except because of their communion in the sacraments?

Ezekiel too sees certain people marked so that they would not perish together with the wicked. Concerning them he is told:

> Those who groan and mourn over the sins and iniquities of my people that are committed in their midst (Ezek. 9:4).

He would not call them his people—people whom he immediately orders to perish while those marked are unharmed—unless they were the people who bore his sacraments.

The Lord also speaks of the weeds that were sown over the field:

> Let both grow until the harvest;

that is, both the wheat and the weeds. He himself interprets the harvest as the end of the age and the field where both were sown as the world. Both, therefore, must grow throughout the world until the end of the age.

From this these people are no longer permitted to conjecture or assert what they say: that all the good have failed from the world and remained only in the party of Donatus. For they are trying to argue against the Lord’s most explicit statement: “The field is this world”; “Let both grow until the harvest”; and “The harvest is the end of the age.”

There is another exceedingly clear parable about the mingling of the wicked and the good within the same communion and bond of the sacraments, which the Lord himself both presents and explains:

> The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it ashore, and sitting down they selected the good into their vessels, but threw the bad outside. So it will be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and they will cast them into the furnace [Note: [Col. 0418] The Floriacensis codex has *in fornacem*, “into the furnace.”] of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 13:24–50).

Therefore no mingling of the wicked frightens the good, so that they wish for this reason to tear the nets, as it were, and leave the assembly of unity, lest people who do not belong to the kingdom of heaven be endured in fellowship with the sacraments. For when the shore is reached—that is, the end of the age—the proper separation will take place, not through human rashness but through divine judgment.

### 36.

Concerning the small number of the good, the Lord himself says most clearly:

> Enter through the narrow gate. For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who go along it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it (Matt. 7:13–14)!

The Donatists think that they are these few, and therefore say that the whole world has perished while they themselves have remained in this small number praised by the Lord.

When they are compared with others, we point out to them the far fewer Rogatists or Maximianists who separated from them—if they think that they should boast on the basis of their small number.

Nevertheless, let them read and see that Scripture has commended this small number in comparison with the multitude of the wicked, but has not been silent about the multitude of the good when considered in itself; they will find very many testimonies.

Why is the seed of Abraham promised to be like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea (Gen. 15:5; 22:17), except because of its countless multitude? The Apostle says that this is why it was said, “In Isaac your offspring shall be called,” because it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are counted as offspring (Rom. 9:7).

Why, “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1)? Why, “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matt. 8:11–12)—that is, the impious Jews?

Why does the Apostle say that Christ gave himself “to cleanse for himself a people of abundance, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14)? Why does the Apocalypse say that there are “thousands of thousands” of the saints, the children of the Church (Rev. 5:11)?

Behold, the same people are called both many and few. Why, except that they are many when considered in themselves, but few in comparison with the wicked?

### CHAPTER XV

### 37.

They say that this was spoken about us: “The first will be those who were last” (Matt. 20:16). The gospel came to Africa later, they say; and therefore it is nowhere written in the Apostolic Letters that Africa believed. But concerning the eastern peoples and the other nations mentioned in the holy books as having received the Christian faith, it was said, “The last will be those who were first,” because they were going to depart from the faith [Note: [Col. 0419] The Floriacensis manuscript has *recesserunt*, “departed.”].

Is this not the cunning of heretics, who wish to turn the words of God away from the truth for which they were spoken and toward the perversity in which they themselves exist?

Why should we not rather understand this concerning the Jews, who became last although they had been first, and concerning Christians from the nations, who became first although they had been last?

Even if I could not establish this interpretation by some more certain proof, it ought to have been sufficient for a sound-minded hearer that I had found a way out in these words which shows that these people have brought forward nothing certain on their own behalf, such that there could be no doubt.

For even if there were no Jews and nations concerning whom I could understand this saying, some barbarian nations believed after Africa. It is therefore certain that Africa was not last in the order of those who came to faith.

Moreover, the Lord himself explained of whom he was speaking and closed the mouths of his slanderers. Speaking to the Jews, who would say to him, “You taught in our streets,” he says:

> When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the Prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being cast outside, and people coming from the east and the west, from the north and the south, and reclining in the kingdom of God, then behold, there are last who were first, and there are first who were last (Luke 13:26–30).

Here certainly no contradiction can be found.

### 38

Again, they say that the following words of the Lord refer to the apostasy of the whole world: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8). We understand this either as referring to the perfection of faith itself, which is so difficult among human beings that even in [Col. 0420] admirable saints—such as Moses himself (Deut. 32:51)—there is found something in which they have trembled or could have trembled; or as referring to the abundance of the wicked and the scarcity of the good, about which we have said enough.

For this reason the Lord spoke as though he were doubting. He did not say, “When the Son of Man comes, he will not find faith on the earth,” but, “Do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?” Yet it is not fitting for him who knows and foreknows all things to doubt about anything. Rather, his doubt represented our doubt, because, on account of the many scandals that would spring up around the end of the age, human weakness would at some point speak in this way.

Hence it is said in the Psalms: “My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me with your words” (Ps. 118:28). Why does he say, “My soul has slumbered from weariness,” except because of what the Lord says: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold”? And why does he say, “Strengthen me with your words,” except because of what follows: “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13)?

There are therefore, throughout the whole world, people in whom, because iniquity abounds, the love of many will grow cold. And again, throughout the whole world there are those who will be saved by persevering to the end, because he says: “Let both grow together until the harvest”; and, “The harvest is the end of the age, while the field is the world” (Matt. 13:30, 39, 38).

That human weakness also has this voice: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed, for truths have diminished among the children of men.” Yet among these there is one heart and one soul of the faithful crying out to God, “Save me, Lord.” Since this one person who says, “Save me, Lord,” consists of many, a little later in the same psalm it says: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord.” And again, shortly afterward, in the plural number: “But you, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever” (Ps. 11:2, 6, 8).

What generation is meant except the one of which it was said above, “The holy one has failed, and truths have diminished among the children of men”? Yet both kinds exist throughout the whole world until the end, because he says: “Let both grow together until the harvest”; and, “The field is the world, and the harvest is the end of the age.”

That one person himself, who is the body of Christ composed of many, will be transferred like Enoch, pleasing God (Gen. 5:24), and will be delivered like Lot from Sodom (Gen. 19:12), and like Noah from the flood (Gen. 7:1). In him there is “the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor,” because his soul slumbers from weariness when he asks to be strengthened by the words of God.

In that psalm he says what causes this weariness: “Weariness,” he says, “has seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (Ps. 118:53). That same person cries out when his heart is oppressed by the same weariness; but let them see from where he cries out: “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you when my heart was distressed” (Ps. 60:3).

He truly suffers persecution for righteousness, not only if he suffers bodily torments—for that does not always happen—but in what he suffers always, as long as iniquity continues: namely, the anguish of his heart, when weariness seizes him because of sinners who abandon the law of God.

For Lot was certainly suffering persecution in Sodom, where, although he lived there, no one troubled him with bodily punishments. Yet, as a righteous man living among them, “by seeing and hearing, he tortured his righteous soul with the lawless deeds of others” (2 Pet. 2:7).

Of this the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution.” But concerning those who abandon the law of God—the same body of Christ says of them, “I saw the senseless and was wasting away” (Ps. 118:158)—he says: “But evil people and impostors will advance toward worse, deceiving and being deceived” (2 Tim. 3:12–13).

Yet both kinds exist throughout the whole world until the end, because he says: “Let both grow together until the harvest”; “The field is the world, and the harvest is the end of the age.”

### 39

Nevertheless, I am astonished that they do not consider what they are saying when, as though citing something in their own support, they recall the Lord’s words, “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?”—as though Africa were not earth.

For if he said this as though he would find faith in absolutely no one, or if he spoke about some particular land and it is uncertain which one he meant, or if he spoke about the whole earth, they cannot explain how he did not speak about Africa as well.

Indeed, let them beware lest the words that follow have touched upon people such as they are. For when he had said, “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on the earth?”, I believe that this vain and inflated thought could have entered the hearts of certain proud heretics who had separated themselves, in some part of the earth, from the unity of the world: that they themselves were righteous while the remaining nations, through which the communion of the Church is extended, were failing and perishing in faith.

Immediately afterward the Evangelist says: “But he also spoke this parable to certain people who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others.” Then follows the account of the two men praying in the Temple, the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:8–14). In these two are represented the proud boasting of good works and the humble confession of sins.

Therefore, if they are prepared to answer this Letter, let them stop recalling those testimonies which, when we ourselves recall them, we apply either to the destruction of the Jews, or to the weeds, or to the chaff, or to the bad fish of the whole world.

And just as we have established, by the clearest testimonies, that the Church is spread throughout the whole world, so let them themselves bring forward something equally clear by which they may show that it was foretold that, while the other nations were perishing from faith in Christ, Africa alone would remain, and that bishops would be sent from Africa wherever they wished.

[Note: The Louvain editors, in their Annotations, suspect that *nic* should be read instead of *et quocumque*. But the author seems to have written *et quocumque*, that is, “and those places of the Donatists to which they themselves would send bishops from Africa.” They sent them to Rome, to their own Cutzupitani or Montenses, and to Spain, to Lucilla’s household, as he said above, chapter 3, section 6.]

## Chapter XVI

[Note: In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 14.]

### 40

“It is written,” they say, “in the Song of Songs, with the bride—that is, the Church—speaking to the bridegroom: ‘Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.’”

This is the one testimony which they imagine resounds in their favor, on the grounds that Africa is situated in the southern part of the world.

First, therefore, I ask how the Church can ask Christ to tell her where the Church is. There are not two Churches, but one. Or let them explain—since they do not [Col. 0422] deny that these words are spoken by the Church to Christ—which Church is asking and which Church she is asking about.

For she asks where she may come to her bridegroom, and says to him: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” This Church, then, is still the one speaking and asking where the Church is at midday.

She does not ask, “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down?” and receive the answer, “At midday,” as though the bridegroom were replying, “At midday I pasture; at midday I lie down.” Rather, all these words belong to the question: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday?”

[Note: See Sermon 46, *On Shepherds*, section 35, and Sermon 438, section 9.]

For she herself continues: “Lest I become like one who is veiled among the flocks of your companions.” Then he replies: “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women” (Song 1:6–7), and so forth.

These words, therefore, do not show that the Church exists only in the southern region. Rather, established in other parts of the world, she perhaps asks what belongs to her communion at midday—that is, where her bridegroom pastures and lies down at midday, because he pastures his own and lies down among his own.

For some of her members—that is, good believers—from overseas regions come to Africa. When they hear that the party of Donatus is here, they fear falling into the hands of some rebaptizer, and they invoke Christ in prayer, saying: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday”—that is, who are those of the south where you pasture and lie down: those who possess charity and do not divide unity.

And see what they add: “Lest I become like one who is veiled over the flocks of your companions.” That is: lest, as though hidden, unknown, and unrevealed—for this is what “veiled” means—I become not over your flock, but over the flocks of your companions, who, although they were at first with you, wished to gather outside you, not your flock but their own flocks; and they did not heed you when you said, “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30), nor what you said to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), not your own.

But this Church is not veiled, because she is not under a bushel but on a lampstand, so that she may shine for all who are in the house. Of her it was said: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:15, 14).

Yet to the Donatists she is as though veiled, although they hear such bright and manifest testimonies that demonstrate her throughout the whole world. They prefer, with closed eyes, to stumble against the mountain rather than climb it—though it was a stone cut from the mountain without hands, grew, became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth (Dan. 2:34–35).

### 41

The words “where you pasture, where you lie down at midday” may also be understood in another way. For in the Psalms they are his words, spoken in the person of Moses, the servant of God: “Make your right hand known to me, and instruct those who are learned in heart in wisdom” (Ps. 89:12).

“Midday” is spoken of in relation to such people because of the immense light of wisdom and the immense ardor of charity. Hence, when the Spirit of God exhorts someone to good works through the Prophet, he also promises him this: “Your darkness will be like midday” (Isa. 58:10).

But even if a particular place in the world were to be understood by the words “at midday,” nevertheless the words themselves, as I have said, all of which [Col. 0423] form a single question, would in no way allow anyone to twist this statement to suit his own interpretation.

And if, as an answer to the one asking where he pastured and where he lay down, a terrestrial place were given—“At midday”—we ought not immediately to understand Africa. Africa is indeed in the southern part of the world, but toward the southwest, not toward the south, where midday truly is. For there the sun makes the middle of the day; under that region of the sky Egypt is more properly situated.

Therefore, if the bridegroom, questioned by the bride about a place especially beloved and about a certain secret resting place of his, were to answer that he was at midday, the Catholic Church would much more plausibly recognize this in those of her members who are in Egypt: in the thousands of servants of God who live in holy fellowship in the desert and strive to maintain the perfection of the evangelical commandment, according to which it was said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

For how much more appropriately could the Son of God be said to pasture and lie down there more secretly—that is, to rest—than amid the restless crowds of the frenzied Circumcellions, an evil peculiar to Africa?

[Note: In the Floriacensis manuscript, *Cercicellionum*. You may understand from Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 132, section 3, that they were commonly called *Circelliones*.]

For Isaiah prophesies concerning Egypt in this way: “On that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the land of the Egyptians, and a monument at their borders to the Lord; and it will be an everlasting sign to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians. For they will cry out to the Lord against those who oppress them, and the Lord will send them a man who will save them; judging, he will preserve them. And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will fear the Lord on that day. They will offer sacrifices, make vows to the Lord, and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike the Egyptians with a plague and heal them in his mercy; they will turn to the Lord, and he will hear them and heal them” (Isa. 19:19–22).

What do they say to this? Why do they not share communion with the Church of the Egyptians that was foretold? Or, if Egypt signifies the world through prophetic prefiguration, why do they not share communion with the Church of the whole world?

### 42

Therefore, let them examine the Scriptures and, against the many testimonies by which it is shown that the Church of Christ is spread throughout the whole world, let them produce a single testimony as certain and as manifest as those are, by which they may demonstrate that the Church of Christ has perished from the other nations and remained in Africa alone—as though it were to be propagated from another beginning, not from Jerusalem but from Carthage, where they first raised up bishop against bishop.

[Note: Instead of *tanquam ab alio initio*, “as though from another beginning,” one might perhaps read *propagandam ab alio initio*, “that it was to be propagated from another beginning.”]

But if we wish to understand Donatus as the prince of Tyre, because Carthage was called Tyre, what is prophesied concerning him through Ezekiel?

[Note: In the Floriacensis manuscript, *Tyria*, only here. Carthage was a colony of the Tyrians, just as Tyre was of the Sidonians. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.12–13: “There was an ancient city, Tyrian colonists held it, Carthage.” From this Carthage is called Tyrian and the Carthaginians Tyrians. Moreover, in Isaiah, chapter 23, where the destruction of Tyre is foretold, the Septuagint translated, “Howl, ships of Carthage.” Compare Optatus, book 3 *Against Parmenian*, who similarly twists Ezekiel’s prophecy against the Donatists and understands Donatus as the prince of Tyre.]

There he identifies him especially by saying: “I will show you that you are a man and [Col. 0424] not God.” For they boast more in the name of this man than in the name of God.

Since God alone is without sin, together with that priest who intercedes for us—for it was also said of him, “who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5)—these imitators of Donatus wish to appear so free from sin that they even claim to be the justifiers of human beings and to possess their own oil, which is not “the oil of the sinner” (Ps. 140:5).

It is rightly said to the prince of Tyre: “You said, ‘I am God’; yet you are a man and not God.” He is also asked: “Are you better than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:2–9). Daniel confesses his own sins and the sins of his people (Dan. 9:20); but these people, who belong to the prince of Tyre, say that they are heard when they pray for the sins of the people because they themselves are without sin.

It is rightly said to the prince of Tyre: “Are you better than Daniel?”

Behold, we can find something peculiar to them, and this very great evil arising from the head of Africa, that is, from Carthage. People know how appropriately Tyre can be understood as Carthage; yet we do not insist on such interpretations, for perhaps Tyre signifies something else. How much less, then, should we insist on “midday,” since the very words compel another interpretation?

### 43

But how little they are even permitted to seek something by which they might prove that it was foretold that, when the other nations had fallen away from the Christian faith, the Church would remain in Africa alone—let them consider what I have often recalled: that both are to grow until the harvest, and that the field is the world, while the harvest is the end of the age (Matt. 13:30, 38–39), not according to our interpretation but according to the Lord himself, who interpreted his parable.

There is also another most evident point that entirely removes from them the labor of seeking how they might prove that, after the world had perished, the Church had been reduced to the Africans alone. Something may exist without being found; but something cannot be found if it does not exist.

Let them therefore stop seeking what they will not be able to find—not because it is hidden, but because it does not exist.

There are still some nations among whom the Gospel has not yet been preached. Yet everything that was foretold about Christ and the Church must be fulfilled; therefore it must also be preached among those nations.

[Note: After *in eis praedicari*, “be preached among them,” the editions added: “When this has been fulfilled, then the end will come.” These words are absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter XVII

[Note: Formerly chapter 15.]

How, then, do they say that what the Lord said has already been fulfilled—namely, that “repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47)—but that afterward, when the others had fallen away, Africa alone remained for Christ, when this still has to be fulfilled and has not yet been fulfilled?

When it has been fulfilled, the end will come. For the Lord says: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

How, then, when the faith of all nations had supposedly been completed, did the destruction of the nations—with Africa excepted—follow? The faith of all nations has not yet been completed.

### 44

Unless perhaps this remains for human madness: that they should say the preaching of the Gospel among all nations is not to be fulfilled through those Churches founded by the labors of the Apostles [Col. 0425], but that, after those Churches have perished, their restoration will come from Africa through the party of Donatus, together with the acquisition of the remaining nations.

I think they themselves laugh when they hear this. Yet unless they say what they would be ashamed to say, they have absolutely nothing to say.

[Note: The words *si dicant*, “if they say it,” are absent from the manuscripts.]

But what does this matter to us? We envy no one. Let them read this to us from the Holy Scriptures, and we will believe it. Let them, I say, read from the canon of the divine books that so many cities—which to this day have retained the Baptism entrusted to them through the Apostles—have perished from the faith of Christ because of crimes unknown to the Africans; that they must be baptized again by the party of Donatus; and that from there the Gospel must be preached to the remaining nations that have not yet heard it.

Let them read this to us. Why do they delay? Why do they evade the issue? Why do they impede the salvation of the nations? Let them read it, and together with that reading let them send new apostles to rebaptize so many nations and to baptize the remaining ones.

### 45

But let them consider, when they come to the Colossians, how they will read or hear there the Epistle addressed to them, in which the Apostle says:

“We give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, since we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. You heard of this beforehand in the word of truth, the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it is bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, as it is among you also, from the day when you heard and came to know the grace of God in truth” (Col. 1:3–6).

These words agree with the Gospel, where it was said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man sowing good seed in his field.” Later it is explained that the field is this world.

For just as it was foretold that what had been sown would grow until the harvest, so the Apostle says that it is “bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, as it is among you also, from the day when you heard.”

It grows until the end, because it grows until the harvest. For the harvest is the end of the age (Matt. 13:24, 30, 38–39).

Not only the Colossians, to whom this Epistle was addressed, but also all the others among whom it is read—where it is established through the apostolic Letters that the good seed was sown and had already begun to grow and bear fruit—will therefore say:

“What new thing are you bringing us? Must the good seed be sown again, when, from the time it was sown, it grows until the harvest?”

If you say that what was sown through the Apostles perished in those places and therefore must again be sown from Africa, the answer will be: “Read this to us from the divine utterances.” But you cannot read it unless you first show that what is written is false: that the seed previously sown there grows until the harvest.

And because the divine words in no way contradict one another, you will find in them no passage that you can recite against this truth so clearly stated.

It remains, therefore, that you say these things not from the divine books but from yourselves. Accordingly, the most appropriate answer will be: “Let you be accursed.”

For the Churches founded through apostolic labor hold fast to the warning given them with such care: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel besides what you received, [Col. 0426] let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9).

## Chapter XVIII

[Note: Formerly chapter 16.]

### 46

Since, then, the Church is clearly recognized in the Holy Scriptures as beginning from Jerusalem and growing through the other nations until it embraces them all to the end of the age—and since not only its wheat but also its refuse is mentioned—first, after you have been corrected, share communion with the wheat; then you will see what you ought to say about the weeds or the chaff.

Otherwise, you are compelled by detestable error both to adorn the wicked with the praises of the good and to accuse the good with the crimes of the wicked.

Indeed, we carry in our hands documents by which we can prove that your ancestors, whose schism you follow, handed over the Holy Books to the flames in municipal records and that, in ecclesiastical records, they could not deny having done so. We can also prove that those same men were among the judges who at Carthage issued sentences against Caecilian and his absent colleagues.

Indeed, the same men are read about in both municipal and ecclesiastical records as traditors, yet afterward you present them as condemners of absent traditors.

Indeed, Nundinarius, your deacon of that period, disclosed all Lucilla’s dealings before Zenophilus the governor. She had purchased Caecilian’s condemnation from the bishops because he had become her enemy by preaching the truth.

Indeed, afterward those same men sent letters to the emperor Constantine. When he appointed, as they had requested, bishops to hear the case, they refused to accept their judgment; afterward they accused those same bishops before him as unjust judges; and, after other judges had been appointed for them at Arles, they appealed to the emperor himself. When he heard the parties, they were found and condemned as false accusers, yet they persisted in the same madness.

Indeed, you yourselves say that Christian holiness was utterly destroyed from all those nations among which the Apostles had firmly established it, because those nations shared communion with men whom your ancestors had condemned at the Council of Carthage of seventy bishops.

But do you not now share communion with those whom you condemned, together with Maximian, at the Council of Bagai, consisting of three hundred and ten bishops?

Do you not read that Praetextatus of Assuri was condemned in that very council, accused and attacked by you in the proconsular records, and yet received with honor in the very status in which he had been condemned and died in your communion?

Do you not read that Felicianus of Musti was condemned by the bishops in the same way, in the same case, and in the same council; accused before the judges; afterward received by you; and now lives among you as a bishop?

Do not those who were baptized by men condemned by you now share communion with you in the same Baptism?

But apparently all those transmarine Churches founded through apostolic labor lose salvation and the Christian religion if they share the sacraments with men whom they themselves did not condemn even when accused before them, but whom they heard had later been cleared and acquitted by others.

Meanwhile, the party of Donatus both condemns whom it wishes and magnifies the sacrileges of schism in that very condemnation to such an extent that it does not hesitate to compare [Col. 0427] those men with people whom the earth swallowed alive; yet, whenever it wishes, it receives them again in the same honor, shares communion with them, and remains holy and undefiled!

O rule of Numidian law! O privileges of Bagai!

[Note: For *Bagaitana*, “of Bagai.”]

And the Baptism of Christ is repudiated in those who received it in the apostolic Churches; but in those whom the condemned sacrilegious men Praetextatus and Felicianus baptized—as it is written in the Council of Bagai—the Baptism of Christ is spared. It is not spared because it is Christ’s Baptism, but because it was given through men who deserved to depart from their own condemners as bishops and to return to their own condemners as bishops.

[Note: Amerbach and the Floriacensis manuscript read *episcopi*, “as bishops.” Erasmus and Louvain read *episcopis*, “from the bishops.”]

[Note: See book 3 *Against the Epistle of Parmenianus*, sections 21–22, and book 4 *Against Cresconius*, section 32.]

### 47

All these matters, which I have now been recalling for a long time, are recited as having occurred in imperial letters and in ecclesiastical, municipal, and proconsular records.

Nevertheless, Donatists, if you possessed the Church spread throughout the whole world, which is designated and expressed by the clearest testimonies of the canonical Scriptures, none of these things ought to have any force against you. The crimes of the chaff would not prejudice you if you were the wheat in it; nor, if you were the chaff and the crimes belonged to you, would you prejudice the wheat of the Lord’s harvest in any way. That wheat has been sown in the Lord’s field so that it may grow until the harvest—that is, it has been sown in the world so that it may grow until the end of the age.

Accordingly, if in the same way you possessed documents—something you have never yet proved to us—against our chaff, while we had none of the many documents I have mentioned against you, even then nothing you said—however true, however manifest, however well established—against the chaff among our wheat would prejudice our wheat spread throughout the whole world.

Therefore, let all these delaying evasions be removed.

Whatever false accusation is made concerning human sins should not be brought forward; let conscience be addressed instead.

Whatever true accusation is made concerning human sins but cannot be proved, or could not be proved when it ought to have been proved, should not be brought forward.

Whatever true and proven accusation is made concerning human sins, but does not concern the wheat hidden among the chaff and instead concerns the chaff itself, which will be separated at the end, should not be brought forward.

For we too could bring forward such matters in much greater abundance and with greater plausibility—not with the foolishness of making our case depend on them, but to show them that we refuse to rely on such things not because we cannot find such things to say, but so that we do not waste time useful for necessary matters on matters that are unnecessary.

They do this because they cannot find strong and firm documents supported by truth with which to defend their case. They wish to seem to be saying something while they are ashamed to remain silent, and they are not ashamed to speak empty words.

Therefore, after all such matters have been removed, let them demonstrate their Church, if they can—not in the speeches and rumors of Africans; not in the councils of their bishops; not in the letters of any disputants, whoever they may be; not in false signs and wonders, since [Col. 0428] we have been prepared and made cautious against these also by the Lord’s word—but in the law as prescribed, in the prophecies of the Prophets, in the songs of the Psalms, in the words of the one Shepherd himself, and in the preaching and labors of the Evangelists; that is, in all the authoritative canonical writings of the holy Books.

Nor should they do this by collecting and recalling passages that are obscure, ambiguous, or figurative, which each person interprets according to his own meaning. Such passages cannot rightly be understood and explained unless those things that have been stated most openly are first held with firm faith.

### 48

Therefore, whoever is preparing to answer this Letter, I warn him in advance not to say to me:

“They handed the Lord’s books over to the flames; they sacrificed to the idols of the nations; they inflicted the most unjust persecution upon us—and you agreed with them in everything.”

I answer briefly, as I have often answered: Either you are speaking falsely; or, if these things are true, what you say belongs not to the wheat of Christ but to their chaff.

The Church does not perish on this account. At the final judgment she will be winnowed and cleansed by the separation of all these things.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read *optimo judicio*, “by the best judgment,” but this is erroneous.]

I am seeking the Church herself: where is she who, hearing Christ’s words and doing them, builds upon the rock; and who, by hearing and doing, tolerates those who, hearing but not doing, build upon sand (Matt. 7:24–27)?

Where is the wheat that grows among the weeds until the harvest (Matt. 13:30), not what the weeds themselves have done or are doing?

Where is the beloved of Christ, in the midst of wicked daughters, like a lily among thorns (Song 2:2), not what the thorns themselves have done or are doing?

Where are the good fish that, until they reach the shore, tolerate being caught in the same net with the bad fish (Matt. 13:47–48), not what the bad fish themselves have done or are doing?

## Chapter XIX

[Note: Formerly there was no division at this point.]

### 49

Therefore, setting aside these delaying tricks, let them show that the Church is to be retained in Africa alone, after so many nations have perished, or that she is to be restored and completed from Africa among all the nations.

And let them show this without saying: “It is true because I say it,” or “because that colleague of mine said it,” or “because those colleagues of mine said it,” or “because those bishops, clerics, or laypeople of ours said it.”

Nor should they say: “It is true because Donatus or Pontius, or someone else, performed this or that miracle”; or because people pray at the memorials of our dead and are heard; or because this or that happens there; or because this brother of ours saw such a vision while awake, or that sister of ours dreamed such a vision while asleep.

[Note: Compare Tractate 13 on John, section 17.]

Let these things be removed, whether they are fabrications of lying human beings or portents of deceptive spirits.

For either the things being reported are not true, or, if some miraculous deeds have been performed among heretics, we ought to be even more cautious. When the Lord had said that certain deceivers would arise who, by performing various signs, would deceive even the elect, if that were possible, he added with great emphasis: “See, I have told you beforehand” (Matt. 24:25).

Hence the Apostle also warns: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, giving attention to [Col. 0429] deceitful spirits and teachings of demons” (1 Tim. 4:1).

Moreover, if someone who prays at the memorials of heretics is heard, he receives either good or evil not because of the merit of the place but because of the merit of his desire.

For “the Spirit of the Lord,” as it is written, “has filled the world,” and “the ear of jealousy hears everything” (Wis. 1:7, 10).

Many are heard even by an angry God. Of such people the Apostle says: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. 1:24).

And to many people God, in his mercy, does not grant what they want, so that he may grant what is useful.

Thus the same Apostle speaks of the thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan, which he says was given to him to strike him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations: “For this I pleaded with the Lord three times, that it might depart from me. And he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

Do we not read that some people were heard by the Lord God himself on the high places of the mountains of Judea, although those high places were so displeasing to God that kings who did not destroy them were blamed, while those who destroyed them were praised?

From this it is understood that the disposition of the one asking has greater force than the place of the petition.

As for deceptive visions, let them read what has been written: that Satan himself “transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14), and that “many have been led astray by their dreams” (Sir. 34:7).

Let them also listen to what the pagans tell about things miraculously done or seen in their temples and in relation to their gods. Yet “the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5).

Many people, therefore, are heard in many ways—not only Catholic Christians, but also pagans, Jews, and heretics devoted to various errors and superstitions.

They are heard either by deceptive spirits—which nevertheless do nothing unless permitted by God, who in his lofty and ineffable judgment determines what should be granted to each—or by God himself, whether as punishment for wickedness, consolation in misery, or admonition to seek eternal salvation.

But no one reaches salvation itself and eternal life unless he has Christ as his head.

No one can have Christ as his head unless he is in his body, which is the Church. And we must recognize this Church, like Christ her head, in the canonical Holy Scriptures; we must not seek her in the various rumors, opinions, deeds, words, and visions of human beings.

### 50

Let no one, then, who is prepared to answer me, raise these objections against me: for neither do I say that one ought to believe me on the grounds that the communion of Donatus is not the Church of Christ because certain men who were bishops among them are proved by ecclesiastical, municipal, and judicial records to have handed over the divine Scriptures to the flames; or because they did not prevail in the case they had requested before the bishops’ tribunal; or because, when they appealed to the Emperor himself, they received from him a judgment contrary to their own; or because such men are leaders among their Circumcellions; or because the Circumcellions commit such great crimes; or because among them there are men who throw themselves down precipices, or cast themselves into fires which they themselves have kindled, or frighten people—even unwilling people—into exacting their own slaughter, and, by terrifying even unwilling people, extort their own slaughter from them, and seek so many voluntary and frenzied deaths in order to be worshiped by others; [Col. 0430] or because, around their tombs, drunken bands of vagrant men and women, in mingled wickedness, bury themselves in wine day and night and corrupt themselves with shameful acts.

Let all that crowd be their chaff; it should not prejudice the grain, if they themselves possess the Church. But whether they possess the Church, let them demonstrate only from the canonical books of the divine Scriptures. For neither do we say that we ought to be believed on the grounds that we are in the Church of Christ because Optatus of Milevis, or Ambrose of Milan, or countless other bishops of our communion commended the Church we hold; or because it was proclaimed in the councils of our colleagues; or because throughout the world, in the holy places frequented by our communion, such great miracles occur—whether of answered prayers or of healings—that the bodies of martyrs hidden for so many years [Note: Protasius and Gervasius. See *The City of God* 22.8, and *Confessions* 9.7, etc.] were revealed to Ambrose, as many who ask can hear, and that at those very bodies a man blind for many years, well known to the city of Milan, received back his eyes and his sight; or because one man saw a dream, and another, taken up in spirit, heard something—whether so that he would not go over to the party of Donatus, or so that he would withdraw from the party of Donatus.

Whatever such things occur in the Catholic Church, they are to be approved because they occur in the Catholic Church; the Catholic Church is not thereby demonstrated because such things occur in it. When the Lord Jesus had risen from the dead and was offering his body to the eyes of the disciples to be seen and to their hands to be touched, nevertheless, lest they should suppose that they were suffering some deception, he judged that they ought rather to be confirmed by the testimonies of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, showing that those things concerning him had been fulfilled which had been foretold so long beforehand.

In the same way he commended his Church, saying that repentance and the forgiveness of sins were to be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. He himself testified that this was written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44–47). We hold this commendation given by his own mouth. These are the proofs of our case, these its foundations, these its supports [Note: All manuscripts read: “These are our case; these are the proofs.”].

### 51

We read that it was said of certain believers in the Acts of the Apostles that they searched the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). Which Scriptures, surely, except the canonical books of the Law and the Prophets? To these were added the Gospels, the apostolic Epistles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse of John.

Search through all these, and bring forth something clear by which you may demonstrate that the Church either remained in Africa alone, or was destined to come from Africa alone [Note: Thus the Floriacensis manuscript; the printed editions read: “was destined to be”], so that what the Lord says might be fulfilled: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14). But bring forth something that requires no interpreter, and by which you cannot be convicted of its having been spoken about another matter while you try to twist it to your own meaning.

You see how the one passage you are accustomed to produce—“Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?” (Song of Songs 1:6)—indicates, when all the words of that passage are examined, something quite different from what you think. [Col. 0431] And if it meant what you want, the Maximianists would defeat you in this matter. For Proconsular Province, Byzacium, and Tripolis, where those men are, whoever they are, are more truly “the south” than Numidia, where you are predominant.

Thus they themselves can boast of “the south” more genuinely and distinctly, so that you cannot exclude them from this interpretation unless you hold the true and Catholic meaning of those words. You must show that, according to the four corners of the world, the south is more properly from the south wind than from Africa; and that, according to the figurative expressions of Scripture, “noon” signifies the perfect illumination of the mind and the greatest ardor of charity. Hence it is written: “Your darkness shall be as noon” (Isaiah 58:10).

Bring forth, then, something which cannot more truly be interpreted against you, but which requires no interpreter at all. “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18) requires no interpreter, because the Apostle, not I, interprets Abraham’s seed as Christ (Galatians 3:16).

“Your name shall be called ‘My Will,’ and your land ‘the whole world’” (Isaiah 62:4) requires no interpreter, because it is said of her whom no Christian understands as anyone other than the Church of Christ.

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:28–29) requires no interpreter, because this occurs in the psalm where the Lord’s passion is also declared by the testimony of the Gospel (Matthew 27:35; John 19:24).

“This was necessary: that Christ should suffer, rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47) requires no interpreter.

“You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8) requires no interpreter. The fact that the Church began from Jerusalem and proceeded from there through Judea, Samaria, and the other nations is attested by the subsequent events, established by canonical evidence.

“This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” requires no interpreter. For when the Lord was asked about the end of this age, after he had mentioned certain beginnings of birth-pangs [Note: The Greek Gospel has *ōdinōn*, that is, “pangs,” as in childbirth.], he said: “But the end is not yet” (Matthew 24:14, 8, 6). He foretold that the end would come after the Gospel had been preached throughout the whole world among all nations.

“Let both grow until the harvest” requires no interpreter, because when an interpretation was needed, the Lord himself interpreted it. He himself explained it, and no one can contradict him, especially in that parable which he himself spoke: he said that the good seed was the children of the kingdom, the field was the world, and the harvest was the end of the age (Matthew 13:30, 38–39).

Bring forth even one such passage by which Africa may be most plainly declared either to have been left alone among the others [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “among the remnants”], or to have been preserved alone for the beginning of the world’s renewal and fulfillment. [Col. 0432] For it would not have been commended by so many testimonies if it were soon to perish, nor would it have been spoken of in this way if it alone were to be left, or if the whole world were to be restored and filled from it alone.

But if you cannot show what we so justly demand of you, yield to the truth [Note: Thus the Floriacensis manuscript. The printed editions read: “believe the truth.”], fall silent, fall asleep, and awaken from your fury to salvation.

### 52

Do you still say: “If the Church is with you, why do you compel us to its peace by persecuting us? Or if we are evil, why do you seek us? And if we are weeds, let us grow until the harvest”?

As though we were doing anything else, insofar as we are able, except preventing the wheat from being uprooted along with the weeds when the weeds are separated before the proper time. For whoever will be good for eternity, even if he is evil for a time [Note: The same Floriacensis manuscript omits “even if he is evil for a time.”], is not a weed but wheat in the foreknowledge of God.

You accuse us of seeking you, if you are evil, as though you had not perished in the very respect in which you are evil, and as though you ought not therefore to be sought because you have perished—so that, having been lost, you may be sought; [Col. 0432] having been sought, found; and having been found, brought back, like that sheep by the shepherd, that drachma by the woman, and that son who was dead and came to life again, who had been lost and was found (Luke 15).

He seeks you who dwells in the saints and commands that you be sought.

## CHAPTER XX [Note: Formerly chapter 17.]

### 53

Your complaint about persecution will be quieted if you first consider and understand that not every persecution is blameworthy. Otherwise it would not rightly be said: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 100:5).

For every day we see a son complain about his father as about his persecutor; a wife about her husband; a slave about his master; a tenant about his landowner; a defendant about his judge; and a soldier or provincial about his commander or king. Often, by their properly ordered authority, those in power restrain and prevent people subject to them from greater evils through fear of lesser punishments. At other times, however, they deter them from a good life and good deeds by threats and violence.

When they prohibit evil and unlawful conduct, they are correctors and advisers; but when they prohibit what is good and lawful, they are persecutors and oppressors. Even those who prohibit evil are blamed if the measure of their coercion exceeds the measure of the offense. Likewise, those who rush turbulently and disorderly to coerce people who are subject to no law of theirs are rightly blameworthy.

### 54

Accordingly, we rightly condemn the disorderly license and proud madness of your Circumcellions, even when they use violence against certain very wicked people. For it is not good to avenge unlawful acts unlawfully, or to deter people from unlawful acts unlawfully.

But when they persecute innocent people, either without knowing the case or out of the most unjust hostility, who would not shudder at their criminal brigandage?

As for your decision that the fury of the Maximianists should be restrained by public laws, so that, driven from the basilicas they occupied by the orders of judges, the enforcement of officials, and the assistance of the cities, you might force them to reflect upon their crime [Note: The printed editions read “convict them.” The manuscript reading has been restored.], we do not condemn you—except because in them you persecuted what you yourselves did, indeed far more mildly than you did it. [Col. 0433]

For they raised the altar of sacrilegious dissension against the party of Donatus; you raised it against the whole world and against the words of the one who commended his Church as beginning from Jerusalem and extending through all nations.

Moreover, if the Maximianists dared unlawfully and madly to resist the orders of judges obtained against them, would they not themselves bring judgment upon themselves? The Apostle says: “Whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil” (Romans 13:2–3).

When, therefore, their evil conduct existed—conduct which you were attempting to restrain through duly ordered authorities—if they wished, on account of that very evil conduct, to oppose the laws by an even worse act, would they suffer whatever evil came upon them from you rather than from themselves?

If someone had wished to blaspheme the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and, in accordance with the king’s edict, had been destroyed along with his household (Daniel 3:96), would he have suffered those deserved evils from the three men whom the king, moved by their rescue from the fire, had ordered this—or even from the king himself—or rather from himself?

If those forty Jews who had conspired to kill Paul had attacked the armed men who were escorting Paul under an orderly guard (Acts 23:12–33), would Paul have killed them, or would they have destroyed themselves by resisting the authorities?

### 55

Therefore, without agitation of spirit, without turbulent contention, and without the bitterness of hatred, carefully consider the measures that the kings of our communion establish against you, and for what reason you suffer them.

If you discover that you are in the Church of Christ, rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven (Matthew 5:12). You are crowned as martyrs, while they are judged as persecutors of martyrs.

But if holy and canonical Scripture proves that you have raised an altar against the Church of Christ; that you have been separated by sacrilegious schism from the Christian unity spread throughout the whole world; and that, by rebaptizing, blaspheming, and opposing as far as you can, you are enemies of the body of Christ, which is the Church spread throughout the world—then you are impious and sacrilegious. Those who decide that, for so great a crime, you should be restrained by warnings of penalties, or by deprivation of places, honors, or money, and so gently deterred and corrected that, reflecting upon why you suffer these things, you may recognize and abandon your sacrilege and be freed from eternal damnation—those people are to be regarded as most diligent governors and most devout advisers.

Christian Catholic emperors owe you this love: because of Christian gentleness, they should decree that your sacrileges not be punished according to their deserts; but because of Christian solicitude, they should not leave them entirely unpunished.

God is at work in them, yet you refuse to recognize his mercy even in these troubles about which you complain.

For our part, insofar as it lies with us, and insofar as the Lord grants and permits, we do not even invoke against you the laws of the mildest coercion except so that [Col. 0434] the Catholic Church may be kept free from your terrors, for the sake of the weakness of the vulnerable, so that they may be allowed without fear to choose what they should hold or follow.

Thus, if some of your people violently attack ours, you—whom we hold as hostages on estates and in cities—will not suffer what your people inflict, but, through duly ordered judgments and subject to the laws, you will be struck by monetary penalties.

If this seems grievous to you, let your people spare us and be quiet. But if those who are either under you or with you continue to rage against us, you have no grounds for complaining about us, since we have placed them under your authority or that of your people so that, even while following your heresy, they may suffer no losses, provided that the Catholic Church suffers no violence from you or yours.

If any violence does occur, against your will and while you are unable to restrain it, you are mercifully and justly admonished by those very losses about the sort of people you have, from whom you do not think yourselves contaminated. From this you are compelled to understand how empty are the accusations you bring against the Church of Christ spread throughout the whole world.

Do not now object to us that we persecute you. Blame your own people instead, if they prefer that we be harassed by their violence and that you be crushed by public laws rather than that they themselves be calmed in their customary fury.

If you suffer something hateful and harmful at the hands of our people who do not preserve the measure and purpose of Christian charity, I would not quickly call them ours. They will either become ours if they correct themselves, or be separated at the end if they persist in wickedness.

Nevertheless, neither do we break the nets because of the bad fish (Matthew 13:47), nor do we abandon the great house because of the vessels made for dishonor (2 Timothy 2:20).

If you likewise say that those from whom the Catholic Church suffers such things are not yours, according to the same rule, examine your disposition, correct your error, and embrace the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

For if neither those people contaminate you nor these people contaminate us, let us not reproach one another for the crimes of others. Let us grow together as wheat in one charity, and let us endure the chaff until the winnowing fan.

### 56

Therefore, if the testimonies of the canonical Scriptures which commend the Church as existing in the communion of the whole world require no interpreter; if from those same books you cannot find such support for your separation established in Africa; and if you do not justly complain about persecutions—which the Church itself endures more severely the more widely it spreads, tolerating everything in faith, hope, and charity—not merely the kinds of things that your Circumcellions and their like inflict upon its members wherever they can, but every scandal of various iniquities bursting forth throughout the whole world, concerning which the Lord cried, “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7): [Col. 0435] what more do you have to say?

For a son persecutes his father more severely by living wickedly than a father persecutes his son by correcting him. A slave-girl persecuted Sarah more severely through unjust pride than Sarah persecuted her through proper discipline (Genesis 16). Those on whose account it was said, “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68:10), persecuted the Lord more severely than he persecuted them when he overturned their tables and drove them from the temple with a whip (John 2:15).

## CHAPTER XXI [Note: Formerly chapter 18.]

### 57

Shall we now bring forward your final objection? “Look,” they say, “you possess the Church. How will you receive us if we wish to cross over to you?”

I answer briefly: We receive you as the Church receives you—the Church whom we find in the canonical holy books.

Once the contentious hostility has been laid aside, by which all who refuse to be conquered by God’s truth swell with pride and are conquered by their own perversity, you can easily understand that the divine sacraments may exist both among the good and among the wicked: among the good for salvation, among the wicked for condemnation.

Although there is such a great difference between those who administer these things worthily and unworthily, the things themselves nevertheless remain the same: for the one group they are effective unto reward, for the other unto judgment.

### 58

Therefore, when the Lord baptized more people than John, as it is written in the Gospel, where the Evangelist adds, “Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples” (John 4:1–2), although there was such a great difference between Peter and Judas, there was nevertheless no difference between the Baptism administered through Peter and that administered through Judas.

What was administered through them was one Baptism, although they themselves were not one: it belonged to Christ, while of the two, one belonged to the members of Christ and the other to the party of the devil.

But although John the Baptist and the Apostle Paul were one, since each was a friend of the Bridegroom, nevertheless, because the baptism administered by John and that administered by Paul were not one and the same baptism, Paul commanded those who had been baptized with John’s baptism to be baptized with the Baptism of Christ.

Thus it is called John’s baptism; but the baptism given through Paul is not called Paul’s baptism. Rather, he says, he commanded them to be baptized in Christ (Acts 19:4–5).

Behold: John and Paul are one, yet they do not give one baptism. Peter and Judas are not one, yet they give one Baptism. Peter and Paul are both one and give one Baptism.

Abraham and Cornelius, justified by faith, are one, yet they did not receive one sacrament. Likewise, Cornelius and Simon Magus are not one, yet they received one sacrament. But Cornelius and the eunuch whom Philip baptized on the road are both one and received one sacrament (Acts 10:48; 8:13, 38).

Therefore, when the sacrament is one, neither different administrators nor different recipients can make what is one cease to be one.

### 59

These people, however, while wishing to make what belongs to Christ belong to human beings, try to persuade others of propositions that are utterly false and absurd, so that there would be nearly as many baptisms as there are people through whom they are administered.

Thus they try to twist to this purpose what the Lord said about a person and his work: “A good tree produces good fruits, and a bad tree produces bad fruits” (Matthew 7:17)—as though someone baptized by a good person were good, and someone baptized by an evil person were evil.

It follows, whether they wish it or not, that someone baptized by a better person would be better, and someone baptized by an inferior person would be inferior. From this it would follow that those whom Jesus himself did not baptize before the Lord’s passion, but whom his disciples baptized, would have been born much more holily if he himself had baptized them.

For who could even imagine how great the difference was between him and the disciples by whom they were baptized? Did he begrudge them a holier birth, preferring that they be baptized by his disciples whom he had appointed for this purpose? Anyone who believes this is surely insane.

What, then, did the Lord deign to demonstrate by this except that what was given belonged to him, whoever might be the one through whom it was given; and that he baptizes—the one of whom that friend of the Bridegroom had said, “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33)—through the hands of whatever minister the person who believed in him might be baptized?

Paul also says: “I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name” (1 Corinthians 1:14–15).

By this reasoning, Paul too should be believed to have begrudged people a better sanctification, if those baptized by him could be baptized better in proportion to how much better he was.

On the contrary, the intention of that most careful and faithful steward was vigilant precisely so that no one would think he had been baptized more holily because he had been baptized by a holier minister, and so that he would attribute to the servant what belonged to the Lord.

### 60

Since, therefore, both good and evil people administer and receive the sacrament of Baptism, while only the good are spiritually regenerated and built into the body and members of Christ, that Church is certainly among the good to which it is said: “As a lily among thorns, so is my companion among the daughters” (Song of Songs 2:2).

For among these are those who build upon the rock—that is, those who hear Christ’s words and do them—for he also said to Peter, who confessed him as the Son of God: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

It is not among those who build upon the sand—that is, those who hear Christ’s words and do not do them. For he himself said: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon the rock.” And shortly afterward, in the same place: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon the sand” (Matthew 7:24, 26).

Those, therefore, who have been incorporated by the bond of charity into the building established upon the rock, and into the lily shining among thorns, will certainly possess the kingdom of God.

But who could doubt that those who build upon the sand or are counted among the thorns will not possess the kingdom of God? The sacrament of Baptism profits such people nothing. Yet no injury should thereby be done to the sacrament they possess merely because their foundation is unstable and their wickedness barren.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 61

Accordingly, in that passage from the Epistle of the Apostle Paul which he wrote to the Galatians, consider without any spirit of contention how rightly it is done that, when correcting a heretic’s error, if he possesses the sacrament which he ought to possess, he should receive what was lacking to him, while what was already present is neither condemned nor blasphemed.

“The works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:19–21). [Note: Formerly chapter 19 here, in the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus.]

None of these people, therefore, are in the lily or upon the rock. Heretics too are placed among them.
