Why, then—to leave aside everything else—do you not baptize after drunkards, the licentious, and the envious, who will not possess the kingdom of God and therefore are not upon the rock? And because they are not upon the rock, they plainly are not counted in the Church, since he says, “Upon this rock I will build my Church.”

Yet you want us to baptize after heretics, who are listed among the same thorns that will not possess the kingdom of God, and who likewise possess the sacraments, since the sacraments themselves are the same—but they do not benefit from them, because although the sacraments are right, the people themselves are perverse.

### 62

Considering and reflecting upon these matters without obstinacy, you can easily understand that in each person what is crooked must be corrected, while what is straight must be approved; that what is lacking must be given, while what is present must be acknowledged.

When a heretic comes to become Catholic, let him correct his own error, but not violate Christ’s sacrament. Let him receive the bond of peace which he did not have, without which the Baptism he did have could not profit him.

Both are necessary for attaining the kingdom of God: Baptism and righteousness. There cannot be righteousness in someone who despises Christ’s Baptism. Baptism, however, can exist in someone who does not possess righteousness, but it cannot benefit him.

For just as the Truth said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), so the same Truth said, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20).

Thus it is not Baptism alone, but righteousness also, that leads to the kingdom. Whoever lacks either both together or one of them cannot reach it.

Therefore, when heretics are told, “You lack righteousness”—which no one can possess without charity and the bond of peace—and when they themselves admit that many possess Baptism but not righteousness, or when they do not admit it, divine Scripture convicts them of it, I am amazed that they think we act as though we judged them to lack nothing when, although they possess not their own Baptism but Christ’s, we do not baptize them again.

Because Baptism is not given to them in the Catholic Church, though they are found to possess it, they suppose that they receive nothing there—although there they receive what is necessary, without which what they possess avails them for destruction, not salvation.

If they refuse to understand this, it is enough for us that we hold the Church which is demonstrated by the clearest testimonies of the holy and canonical Scriptures.

### 63

Let the heretic now say to me: “How will you receive me?”

I answer immediately: “As the Church receives you, the Church to which Christ bears witness.”

Can you know better how you ought to be received than our Savior, the physician of your wound?

Perhaps you say: “Then read to me how Christ commanded that those who wish to cross over from the heretics to the Church should be received.”

Neither I nor you reads this plainly and evidently. For if John had been a heretic and had baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, after whose baptism Paul commanded people to be baptized, you would have established your position, and I would have nothing to say against it.

Again, if Peter had been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the one to whom the Lord said, “The one who has bathed has no need to wash again” (John 13:10)—I would have established my position, and you would have nothing to say against it.

But now, since in the Scriptures we do not find that anyone came over to the Church from the heretics and was received either in the way I say or in the way you say, I think that if some wise person had existed, to whom the Lord Christ bore witness, and we had consulted him about this question, we ought in no way to doubt that we should do what he said. Otherwise we might be judged to be resisting not so much that person as the Lord Christ, by whose testimony he was commended [Note: Compare *Against Cresconius* 1.31 and 1.33.].

Christ, however, bears witness to his Church. Here is the Gospel; read where he says: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer, rise on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

Therefore, just as this Church, beginning from Jerusalem and extending throughout all nations, receives people—without any evasions or equivocations—so you must be received.

If you do not wish this, you are resisting, most destructively to your salvation, not me or any human being who wishes to receive you in this way, but the Savior himself. You refuse to believe that you ought to be received in the way that Church receives you—the Church commended by the testimony of the one whom you admit it would be wicked not to believe.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 64

“But Jeremiah said: ‘She has become for me like deceitful water, without faith.’”

He did not speak of the water you think he meant. Read carefully.

In prophetic fashion, he called the multitude of human beings a deceitful water, just as prophets customarily speak figuratively. Likewise, in the Apocalypse we know that peoples are called by the name “waters” (Revelation 17:15).

For Jeremiah says: “Why do those who grieve me prevail? My wound is severe; how shall I be healed? It has become for me like deceitful water, without faith” (Jeremiah 15:18).

He said that his wound had become for him like deceitful water. He called those who grieved him that same wound. What he says above—“those who grieve me”—he later expressed by “my wound”; and what he says above—“they prevail”—he later expressed by “it is severe.”

### 65

You act similarly in the passage where it is written: “Abstain from alien water, and do not drink from an alien fountain” (Proverbs 5:15).

You think this refers to the Baptism found among heretics, so that it is “alien water” because heretics will not possess the kingdom of God. But the same is true of drunkards, the envious, and others of this sort, of whom it is likewise said, “They will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10; Galatians 5:21).

Yet in all such people, if they have been baptized according to the Gospel, the Baptism is Christ’s, not theirs. Therefore that water is not alien, even though those people are alien—to them he will say, “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:23).

Why should I not instead understand “alien water” and “an alien fountain” as the teaching of the evil spirit, by which those alienated from God are deceived and led astray through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts? The Apostle expresses this more clearly: “The Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons” (1 Timothy 4:1).

This is the alien water and the alien fountain. For if water is understood in a good sense as the Holy Spirit, why should water not also be understood in an evil sense as the evil spirit?

Whenever Scripture mentions water, it does not always intend this visible sacrament of Baptism to be understood. Sometimes it means that, and sometimes something else.

The disciples of the Lord had already baptized others with visible Baptism before the Holy Spirit came upon them according to his promise. Yet Jesus himself says of that Spirit: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The Evangelist then follows and explains what this meant: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37–39).

Behold: he calls the Spirit “water,” although the Spirit had not yet been given, while that water of Baptism had already been given to many.

### 66

This is also why you fail to understand that other passage similarly: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells; let the spring of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you; and let your waters not overflow outside, and let your waters run through your streets” (Proverbs 5:15–17).

The passage commends not visible Baptism, which even outsiders can possess—that is, those who will not possess the kingdom of God—but the gift of the Holy Spirit, which belongs only to those who will reign with Christ forever.

For, as the Apostle says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

The breadth of heart which charity produces—which is why he says that it has been “poured out”—and of which he speaks to the Corinthians in these words, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11), is signified by the name “streets.”

67. What, then, we hear plainly—“Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). **Note:** The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “test the spirit that is from God.”—we hear figuratively in the words, “Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a foreign fountain.” And what we hear plainly—“The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us”—we hear figuratively in the words, “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you.” For strangers may possess many gifts of God—not only those they share with stones and trees, such as existence and growth, nor only those they share with animals, such as breathing and sensation, but also greater gifts proper to human beings, such as reason, speech, countless useful skills, and many other things.

Even of the gifts given to the household of God, strangers—that is, those who will not possess the kingdom of God—possess some. At the end they will be told, “I do not know you,” even though they will say, “In your name we prophesied and performed many mighty works.” For, as the Apostle says, “Even if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

This, then, is the particular gift of the Holy Spirit from which no stranger shares. It is lacking in all the wicked and the children of Gehenna, even if they are baptized with Christ’s Baptism, as Simon had been baptized. It is also lacking in heretics; they receive it when, having been corrected, they come and sincerely embrace the bond of unity. If they did not receive it, then, although they possessed Christ’s Baptism, they would not possess Christ’s kingdom, because they had not entered that proper fountain of waters running through the streets of the saints and not running out into the open—the fountain through which the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

Therefore stop recalling those testimonies which you either do not understand or understand as being against you and for us. If passages stated ambiguously could be interpreted both for us and for you, they would in no way assist your cause; for if we wished to use such passages, we could use countless ones that would likewise do nothing for our cause. But passages of this kind plainly sustain a bad cause, at least by causing delay.

## CHAPTER XXIV

68. “Look,” they say, “water flowed from the body of the Lord.” And how does this help you, heretic?

“Very much,” he says. “For it signifies that Baptism exists only in the body of the Lord, that is, in the Church.”

You would do better to say “from the body of the Lord,” that is, from the Church—even if it is already established (though perhaps this still needs more careful investigation) that that water signified Baptism. For we too say that the Baptism which you possess is from the body of the Lord, that is, from the Church, although you yourselves are not in it, just as are all who do not build upon the rock but upon the sand.

Why, however, do you not attend to the fact that the water which you say signified Baptism was not merely in the body of the Lord, but also went out from his body—and this through the wound inflicted by the persecutor? For neither heretics nor any of the wicked would have dragged the Sacraments outside with them if they had preserved the integrity of unity in the body of the Lord. But you also see how profound this is, and how hidden it is in the great depth of its mystery.

69. Enough now: stop dealing in such passages. Everything of this kind that you produce is either for us or—at most diminishing the strength of our case—it is uncertain for whom it is. But you willingly linger over obscure matters, so that you may not be compelled to acknowledge what is clear.

Look, I ask you: what are you suffering from the Church? Look at the Church, commended and expressed by so many perfectly clear testimonies of the holy Scriptures, foretold and demonstrated: “As we have heard, so have we seen” (Ps. 47:9). Why do you evade the question of how you are to be received? Why do you refuse to be received in the manner in which she receives—the one to whom testimony is given by him who could not lie?

Show from the canonical Scriptures that they plainly said that a person baptized among heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit must be baptized again in the Catholic Church. If you cannot show this, then show that some clear and manifest testimony from the canonical Scriptures is given to this communion of yours—that is, to the party of Donatus, where you learned this. Then I will admit that one must pass over to you and that heretics must be received otherwise than the Church in which you are receives them, because that Church has been established by such testimony.

Why are you agitated? Why are you disturbed? You do not find in the canonical Scriptures what we most justly demand of you. For as to what you are accustomed to say, “Where do you pasture, where do you lie at noon?” (Song 1:6), you see what kind of passage it is and how little it supports you. Do not seek such passages, then.

For even if the party of Donatus were in the northern regions, opposed to the southern regions, it would say that this had been spoken of itself: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. 47:3). The city of the great King is certainly none other than the Church; and this passage more certainly indicates the Church than does “Where do you pasture, where do you lie at noon?” But perhaps the heretic Marcion would use that testimony, since he is said to have been Pontic, and those regions lie toward the north.

Again, if the party of Donatus were in the west, it would say that this had been spoken of itself: “Make a way for him who ascends over the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67:5). For perhaps it would say that “he ascends over the setting sun” is more exalted than “he lies at noon.”

These things are mystical, hidden, and figurative. We demand from you something manifest, something that requires no interpreter.

70. I therefore receive you in the manner in which the seed of Abraham receives you, in whom all the nations are blessed (Gen. 22:18). This might be obscure unless Paul had disclosed that the seed of Abraham is Christ (Gal. 3:16).

I receive you in the manner in which that barren woman receives you—she whose children are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband. This would be obscure unless Paul had said that she is our mother, the Church: to her it was said, “The Lord who redeemed you, he himself shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:1, 5; Gal. 4:26–27); and to her it was said, “Your land shall be the whole world” (Isa. 62:4).

I receive you as that queen receives you, of whom it is said in the Psalms, “The queen stood at your right hand,” and to whom it is said, “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:10, 17).

Finally, not to recall many passages, I receive you as the Church receives you, beginning from Jerusalem and extending through all nations (Luke 24:47); as the Church receives you, which is Christ’s witness in Jerusalem, throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth (Acts 1:8). For he receives you who spoke this about her, who displayed her in such words so that no one might doubt her.

I receive you as the wheat sown in the field receives you, wheat that grows together with the weeds until the harvest. “These are the children of the kingdom; the field is the world, and the harvest is the end of the age” (Matt. 13:30, 38–39). The Lord explained this; it is the Gospel; they are the Lord’s words; they are clear.

I could say to you: I receive you in the manner in which you also received those whom Praetextatus and Felicianus, condemned by you, baptized outside your communion. You have absolutely no answer to this. But I shall say instead what most decisively prevails even against the Maximianists—those who completely defeated you in the two testimonies which, although you use them most foolishly, you use most frequently: the testimony concerning smallness and that concerning noon. What I shall say, then, will extinguish what all of you bring against us as though you were rising together against us.

We receive you, if you wish to be corrected, as the Church receives you—the Church which the Lord Jesus said would begin from Jerusalem, and which we read in the Acts of the Apostles did begin there; which would go through all nations, and which we read in the Acts of the Apostles went through many nations before it came to Africa, and which would go through all nations before the end comes. For the Lord himself says, “This Gospel will be preached among all nations, and then the end will come.”

Here are its refuse: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold.” Here is its grain: “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–14). Where is Africa named here as belonging to the party of Donatus?

Here again is its grain: “So that you may know,” the Apostle says, “how you ought to conduct yourself in the household of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. And without question, great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:15–16).

Here is its refuse: “The Spirit,” he says, “plainly declares that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons” (1 Tim. 4:1), and so forth. Where here too is Africa named as belonging to the party of Donatus, so that the pillar and foundation of the truth—or the mystery of piety, which continued to run its course to the end, so that it could say, “preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory”—remained in that party?

71. What more need I say? Whoever intends to answer this letter should search the Scriptures and either produce a clear testimony concerning Africa—whether that the party of Donatus exists only in Africa or proceeds only from Africa—or, if he seeks credulous followers of his suspicions, accusations, or slanders and wishes to turn them toward another Gospel, which is no Gospel, and to announce to us something beyond what we received, then, “even if an angel from heaven” were to do so, “let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

For the devil also fell from heaven because he did not stand in the truth. If he had been accursed by the man when he announced to him something beyond what he had received from the Lord God, our first parents would neither have fallen under the punishment of death nor departed from the place of blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXV

**Note:** Formerly chapter 20 in the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus.

72. Therefore, dearest brothers, to whom I am writing this letter, hold with the most faithful and steadfast heart the command of the Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep and now, glorified and exalted, sits at the right hand of God the Father. He says: “My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

You have heard his exceedingly clear voice, not only through his Law, Prophets, and Psalms, but also through his own mouth, commending the future of his Church. And as you read the Acts and Letters of the Apostles—which complete the canon of the divine Scriptures—you see how, in due order, the things he foretold came to pass.

The question is not obscure, nor can those whom the Lord himself foretold would come and say, “Look, here is the Christ; look, there”—“look, in the desert,” as though where there is no gathering of the multitude; “look, in the inner rooms” (Matt. 24:23, 26), as though in secret traditions and teachings—deceive you.

You have the Church spread everywhere and growing until the harvest. You have the city of which the one who founded it said, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). It is therefore the Church that is known everywhere, not merely in some region of the earth.

At times it suffers temporal storms even among its own grain, so that in certain places it is not recognized; nevertheless, even there it remains hidden. For the divine judgment cannot be deceived, since they grow until the harvest.

73. Thus, in other nations also, certain members of the Church have often been pressed down and overshadowed by the uprisings of heresies and schisms; nevertheless, because they were present, they soon afterward became evident to everyone without dispute.

The same happened in Africa after the seditious and turbulent council of Secundus of Tigisi at Carthage, where corruption brought about by the noblewoman Lucilla was later recorded in judicial Acts. **Note:** See above, chapter 18, no. 46.

After letters had been sent from that council through almost all Africa, where the Churches of Christ had already begun to sprout, the council’s letters were believed—as was only right. It therefore seemed as though the Lord’s grain had failed in some part of the field. Yet the grain that had truly been predestined and sown, and that was germinating fruitfully with a deep root, had in no way failed.

They had believed the council’s letters with a clear conscience. For no incredible thing was being said to them by people about other people, nor were they believing anything against the Gospel. But after those men had pursued their mad obstinacy with the most stubborn contention all the way to sacrilegious dissension against the entire Christian world, and after it became known to the good faithful people—whom false accusation had alienated from Caecilianus—that they had been deceived, they saw that, if they persisted in that communion, they would no longer be judging merely one man or several men wickedly, but the Church spread throughout the whole world.

They preferred to believe Christ’s Gospel rather than the council of their colleagues. Thus, leaving those men, many bishops, clergy, and people soon returned to Catholic peace. Even before they did so, they were counted among the wheat. For they were not acting as they did against the Church of God, which grows among all nations, but against men whom their colleagues had maliciously misrepresented to them. **Note:** Thus reads the Floriacensis manuscript; the printed editions read, “that contradiction was maintained.”

Thus, in Africa too, the wheat which the Son of Man had sown remained wheat. From that time until now it has grown and continues to grow, and henceforth it will bear fruit and grow until the harvest, just as it does throughout the whole world.

**Note:** The printed editions read *veraciter* (“truly”); the Floriacensis manuscript reads *feraciter* (“fruitfully”). The latter has been preferred.

74. Some people of good will, through carnal blindness, continued to wander for a longer time in that dissension even after the fury of the wicked against the Church of God had been confirmed—just as though tender wheat were still being trampled and the vitality of the living root were being crushed. Yet God knew even that wheat of his, although it needed to be admonished and rebuked so that it might revive.

For the words spoken to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16:23), were not spoken in the same way as the words spoken about Judas, “One of you is a devil” (John 6:71).

Some also contradicted the most evident truth with misguided zeal. Those people had been uprooted or cut off; but because they did not remain in unbelief, they were replanted by the divine hand or grafted in again, as the Apostle says concerning certain broken branches (Rom. 11:17–23).

A person is still fruitless and has not yet been cut from the root when, through evil desire, he performs the deeds of which it was said, “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21). But when, because of those deeds, he also begins to resist the most evident truth by which he is reproved, then he is cut off.

Many such people remain in communion with the Church in the Sacraments, and yet are no longer in the Church. Otherwise, if a person were cut off only when visibly excommunicated, it would follow that he was grafted in again when visibly restored to communion. What, then, if a false person approaches and carries a heart utterly hostile to the truth and to the Church, even though that solemn rite is performed upon him? Is he reconciled? Is he grafted in? Certainly not.

Therefore, just as someone who again receives communion has not yet been grafted in, so anyone who carries a hostile disposition toward the truth by which he is convicted and reproved has already been cut off, even before he is visibly excommunicated.

Thus both the good seed and the bad seed grow throughout the field until the harvest: that is, both the children of the kingdom and the children of the evil one grow throughout the world until the end of the age—the former bearing fruit with endurance, the latter becoming bitter through their barrenness.

75. Relying on all these perfectly clear testimonies of the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, the Lord himself, and the Apostles concerning the holy Church spread throughout the whole world, demand from these people that they produce some clear testimony from the canonical Books concerning Africa as it relates to the party of Donatus.

For, as I have already said, it could in no way happen that the Church—which, as they say, and God forbid, was so quickly to perish from so many nations—would be proclaimed by so many testimonies in such exalted and unmistakable terms, while silence was maintained concerning the Church of their choosing, which, as they claim, was destined to remain until the end.

Remember what was said to the rich man when he was being tormented in the underworld and wished someone from the dead to be sent to his brothers. “They have Moses and the Prophets there,” he said. And when he replied that they would not believe them unless someone went to them from the dead, the answer was: “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead” (Luke 16:29–31). **Note:** The remainder was lacking in the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. The Louvain editors restored it here from an old Endovian manuscript; it is also found in our Floriacensis manuscript.

Moses said that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. 22:18). The Prophets said, “You shall be called My Will, and your land shall be the whole world” (Isa. 62:4), and, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21:28).

Through these and similar perfectly clear predictions demonstrating the Church, these people refused to believe.

The Lord rose from the dead and said that repentance and the forgiveness of sins were to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). Those who had not believed Moses and the Prophets did not believe the Lord when he rose from the dead either. What remains except that they should receive the torments of that rich man?

While you are fleeing those torments, while there is still time, before you depart this life, cling steadfastly to the divine utterances, so that you may neither be troubled in this life nor fail to receive after this life what was promised to the seed of Abraham. Amen.

[Col. 0445]

**Note:** Concerning the books that follow, see Book 2, chapter 26 of the *Retractationes*, volume 1, column 641, from the words “The grammarian also” through the word “ignorant.” M.

**The Four Books of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against Cresconius the Grammarian of the Party of Donatus.** (C)

**Note:** Written around the year of Christ 406. For when Augustine wrote these four books, the emperor Honorius had already issued laws against the Donatists, as the holy Doctor himself testifies in Book 2, chapter 26 of the *Retractationes*. Augustine calls those laws of Honorius “the most recent laws” below, in Book 3, chapter 47, after he had expressly indicated in chapter 43 of the same Book 3 that he was speaking of the laws issued in the year 405 against the Donatists, following the killing of the Catholic bishop Maximianus. On that occasion, he says, “all the previous laws against them were revived, and new ones were enacted.”

Among these laws is law 38 of the Theodosian Code, “Concerning Heretics,” the edict of Honorius—which is called the Edict of Unity in the Council of Carthage of the year 407:

> “Let no one recall a Manichaean or a Donatist—who, as we have discovered, above all do not cease raging—to mind. Let there be one Catholic worship and one salvation; let the equal and harmonious holiness of the Trinity be sought. But if anyone should dare to involve himself in what has been forbidden and unlawful, and does not escape the snares of the countless former enactments and of the law recently issued by our clemency, and if crowds should perhaps assemble, let him not doubt that the sharp points of an intensified agitation will be deployed against the incitement to sedition. Issued on the day before the Ides of February [12 February 405], at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius.”

Likewise, in the Theodosian Code, law 4, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated”: 

> “The Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Hadrianus, Praetorian Prefect: ‘The adversaries of the Catholic faith,’” and so forth, as presented in its proper place in the Appendix to this volume.

Likewise, in the same title, law 5:

> “To Hadrianus, Praetorian Prefect: Lest the secret practices of the Donatists violate divine grace by repeated Baptism, and lest they retain an opportunity for deception, by the severity of this decree we abolish it, establishing that the appropriate penalty and the avenging force of the law shall pursue such people who have committed themselves to the Catholic religion with a perverse doctrine. We therefore order that if anyone henceforth is discovered to rebaptize, he be brought before the judge presiding over the province, so that, fined by the confiscation of all his property, he may undergo the penalty of poverty,” and so forth. Issued on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius.

Likewise, in the same Code, law 2, “Concerning Religion”:

> “The Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Diotimius, Procurator of Africa: We wish the edict which Our Clemency directed concerning unity throughout the African regions to be posted in various places, so that all may know that the one true Catholic faith of almighty God, which right belief confesses, must be retained. Issued on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March 405], at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius.”

Likewise, in the Theodosian Code, law 39, “Concerning Heretics”:

> “The Augusti to their Diotimius, greetings: We decree that the heretics of the Donatist superstition, wherever they are found, whether confessing or convicted, shall, with the force of the law observed, pay the penalty owed without delay. Issued on the sixth day before the Ides of December [8 December 405], at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius.”

By this enactment Honorius wished the Donatists to be treated as heretics wherever they were found and compelled to pay the penalty owed, namely a fine of ten pounds of gold, which had long before been established by the force of the law of Theodosius the Elder against all heretics.

How Honorius was prompted to issue that enactment, especially by the appeal of the Donatist bishop Crispinus to him, Augustine explains in Book 3, chapter 47 of this work. Possidius likewise relates the matter in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12, where he writes:

> “Crispinus was declared a heretic by a proconsular and libellary sentence. On his behalf, the Catholic bishop [Possidius, bishop of Calama] interceded before the cognitor, so that the gold fine might not be exacted, and this favor was obtained for him. When, therefore, in his ingratitude, he appealed to the most pious Emperor, a reply was given to the imperial report as required, and an order followed that Donatist heretics should in no place be permitted to exist and that everywhere they should be subject to all the laws enacted against heretics. Consequently the judge, his office, and Crispinus himself were ordered to pay ten pounds of gold into the treasury because it had not been exacted.”

See the embassy of the Council of Carthage of the year 404 below in the Appendix, and Augustine’s letters 88, no. 7, and 185, nos. 25–27.

**Note:** For the correction of the books against Cresconius, we used the most ancient Corbie manuscript, as well as the Michaelinus, Cygirannensis, Georgiana, and one manuscript of the Bernardine College of Paris. We also used the variant readings of five Belgian manuscripts published by the Louvain theologians, as well as the older and more authoritative editions, those of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.

**Note:** We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractationes* and the *Confessiones*, volume 1. M.

# BOOK ONE

Augustine begins to refute the letter of Cresconius, published in defense of Petilianus and addressed to Augustine himself. He proves that neither eloquence nor any kind of dialectic should be feared by defenders of the truth, lest they refute its adversaries by disputing with them; nor should a person be considered contentious who takes care to engage in verbal contest with stubborn and resistant people in order to refute them. He then shows that it does not follow that, if Baptism is granted to exist in the party of Donatus, it must also be granted that Baptism ought to be received there. For outside the Catholic Church it is possessed uselessly and perniciously, yet truly and completely.

[Col. 0445]

## CHAPTER I

1. Although I did not know when my writings might reach you, Cresconius, I did not at all despair that they would reach you eventually. For your writings also, although they came to me long after you had written them, nevertheless were at last able to reach me. You thought you ought to write them against what I had replied, as briefly as I could and in part, to Petilianus, your bishop of Cirta, who was attempting to establish the repetition of Baptism and was attacking our communion not by the weight of evidence but by the frivolity of insults.

At that time his entire letter had not come into my hands, but only a small part of its beginning. Why ask how this happened, since when the whole letter later reached us, I was not reluctant to answer the whole of it?

If I did not reply to these writings of yours, which you sent to me, you might perhaps consider me insulting you. But because I do reply, I am again afraid that you may consider me contentious. Yet when you found my writings—which had not been addressed to you—merely because they seemed to rebuke the bishop of the party of Donatus or the party of Donatus itself, you judged that it was your duty, since you were conscious of possessing some ability, to take up and express a contradiction, because you belong to that communion, although you are bound to the clerical office by no function.

How much less was I permitted, in fulfillment of the burden entrusted to me, to remain silent either against Petilianus or against you yourself, when he was attacking the Church for which I serve, while you, in a similar undertaking, expressly addressed, presented, and composed a discourse against me?

2. In the opening sections of your work you labored to make eloquence seem suspect to people. As though praising my manner of speaking, and again as though fearing that by this manner I might deceive you or anyone else by persuading falsely, you proceeded to accuse eloquence itself. You even brought against it a testimony from the holy Scriptures, where you suppose it is said, “From much eloquence you will not escape sin.” **Note:** The manuscripts read “you suppose” (*putes*); the printed editions, “you suppose” (*putas*).

**Note:** The printed editions add *totius* (“of the whole”), which is absent from the manuscripts.

But it does not say “from much eloquence”; it says “from much speaking” (Prov. 10:19). Much speaking is excessive speech, a fault of speaking contracted through love of talk.

Often those who love to speak do not know what they are saying or how they are saying it—whether in regard to the soundness of their thoughts or to the correct sound and order of words, which are learned through the grammatical art.

Eloquence, however, is the ability to speak, setting forth appropriately what we think. It should be used when we think rightly.

The heretics did not use it in this way. For if they had thought rightly, it would not merely have been no evil, but would even have been something good, that they could set forth eloquently.

Therefore you accused eloquence in vain by recalling these examples. A soldier is not for that reason to be disarmed in defense of his country because some have taken up arms against their country. Nor should good and learned physicians refrain from using surgical instruments for healing because ignorant and wicked people also misuse them for destruction.

For who does not know that, just as the things being sought are useful or useless according to whether they are useful or useless, so eloquence—that is, skill and ability in speaking—is useful or useless according to whether what is said is useful or useless? I do not think that even you are unaware of this.

**Note:** The printed editions read, “just as useful or useless things are”; we have preferred the reading of the older manuscripts, although the sentence remains somewhat perplexing.

## CHAPTER II

3. But, I suppose, when you saw that some people considered me eloquent, you thought eloquence should be accused so as to deter a reader’s or listener’s interest from me. Your intention was that whoever had been frightened by you, and who considered that he ought therefore to avoid and flee me as one speaking eloquently, would no longer attend to what I said.

Take care, then, lest what you did belong to that evil art which, as you recalled concerning Plato, some rightly judged ought to be expelled from the state and from human society.

This is not eloquence—if only it had come to me in accordance with my desire, for explaining what I think—but a certain sophistical and malicious profession which proposes to itself, not from sincerity but from contentiousness or advantage, to argue for everything and against everything.

Of this the holy Scripture says, “One who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Ecclus. 37:23). **Note:** All the manuscripts read “of this” (*de hoc*).

It seems to me that the Apostle Paul forbids Timothy’s youth this practice when he says, “Do not contend with words; for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear.” And lest he be thought to have prohibited the ability to speak rightly, he immediately added: “Take care to present yourself as a proven worker, not ashamed, handling the word of truth rightly” (2 Tim. 2:14–15).

Clearly, then, this disposition of mind slipped into you: through your zeal for contradiction—not because you thought so, but because you wished to turn away from us the attention of anyone wishing to learn—you called us eloquent and blamed eloquence.

For how can I believe that you did this sincerely, when I know how you are accustomed to praise the eloquence of Donatus, Parmenianus, and your other leaders? What could be more useful than that such eloquence should flow in so abundant a stream for the peace of Christ, for unity, and for truth and love?

But why should I speak of others? In your own case, did you not reveal that you were not sincerely, but contentiously, a critic of eloquence, since you attempted both to persuade through eloquence everything else that you wrote and to accuse that same eloquence eloquently?

## CHAPTER III

4. You say that you are unequal to us in the art of speaking and completely untrained in the examples of Christian teaching. What, I ask, is the relevance of this?

Did I compel you to reply to my writings? Is this the voice of someone refusing and making excuses? If, then, you are completely untrained, why do you not rather keep silent, or speak in such a way as to show that you desire to be instructed?

You say that I am always pressing and challenging you, so that your people may dispute with me in order to distinguish the question of truth. But you say that your people act more prudently and patiently: they teach the crowds in the Church only what has been commanded in the Law, and do not take care to answer us, knowing that if the divine law and so many proofs of the legal Scriptures cannot persuade us what is better and truer, no human authority will ever be able to recall us from our errors to the rule of truth once those errors have been exposed.

What, then, seemed right to you, that while they remained silent you should speak against us? If they are acting well, why do you not imitate them? If badly, why do you praise them?

5. You say that I believe, with intolerable arrogance, that I alone can settle what seemed inexplicable to others and was therefore left to the judgment of God. Yet shortly before you said that I wished to bring this matter to an end after so many years and after so many judges and arbiters, although it could not be settled before rulers when so many learned men, on behalf of the bishops of both sides, were disputing.

Certainly I alone am laboring over this; certainly I alone desire that this question be settled through discussion? I think that if you had wished to blame only our people for attempting this, you would not also admit that your people had attempted it.

Since, therefore, you can no longer criticize that attempt, that intention, and that persistence—at least on account of your own people—I do not wish to be a stranger to so good a work. What are you accusing? What are you criticizing? Are you envious? This should not rashly be believed of you.

It remains, then, that through the zeal of contention you blame me for what you are compelled to praise in your own people.

## CHAPTER IV

6. “But,” you say, “what was not settled among so many and such men can be settled by one person only if he presumes to do so with intolerable arrogance.”

Please do not think that this should be attributed to me alone. We are very many who insist that this be settled—or rather, that it be recognized as already settled.

They said that it had not been settled who refused to agree to the settlement itself and concealed it from you, so that, deceived by their authority, you too would believe that it had not been settled.

But our people, from the time it was settled, never ceased, whenever they were able to do so publicly or privately, to make the settlement known itself, lest anyone persisting in a most destructive error should complain at the final judgment that God’s ministers had been negligent toward him.

We do not therefore wish to reopen from the beginning a case settled long ago, but to demonstrate how it was settled, especially for those who do not know this. Thus, when the defenders of error are convicted, either they themselves may be corrected and freed, or, once they have been refuted and remain in open obstinacy, those who desire truth more than contention may see what they should follow.

## CHAPTER V

7. Nor is this without benefit, as you suppose. For if you could see how far and how widely this error had spread through Africa, and how few remnants of it remained that had not yet been corrected and passed over into Catholic peace, you would in no way consider the persistence of the defenders of Christian peace and unity fruitless or empty.

**Note:** The printed editions read *pervaserit* (“has spread”); the manuscripts, more correctly, read *pervaserat* (“had spread”).

Even if the diligence expended on this healing treatment benefits no one, it is sufficient for giving an account to God that it did not cease to be expended.

For just as the malicious persuader of sin, even if he has not persuaded anyone, will deservedly incur the punishment of a deceiver, so the faithful preacher of righteousness, even if rejected by human beings, must not be deprived before God of the reward due to his office.

A certain thing is therefore done for an uncertain result. By “uncertain” I mean not the reward of the one who acts, but the disposition of the hearer. We do not know whether the person to whom truth is preached will consent. But it is certain that truth ought to be preached even to such people; and it is certain that those who preach it faithfully will receive a worthy reward, whether it is accepted, rejected, or whether they consequently suffer any temporal adversity.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “When you enter, say, ‘Peace to this house.’ If those who are there are worthy, your peace will rest upon them; if not, it will return to you” (Matt. 10:12–13).

Did he make them certain that those to whom they preached peace would receive it? Yet he made them certain that they should preach it without hesitation.

## CHAPTER VI

**8.** The Apostle Paul also says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with restraint; in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance for recognizing the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, having been taken captive by him for his will” (2 Tim. 2:24–25). Notice how, although he did not want him to quarrel, he nevertheless wanted him to correct those who thought differently with restraint, lest the servant of God regard the prohibition of insolence as an opportunity for laziness.

But because many people—even when the correction is carried out moderately—bear it heavily and irritably, either because they favor their sins or because they cannot find what to answer and yet do not yield to the truth, they call those who earnestly deal with them and do not shrink from exposing their error quarrelsome and contentious. Falsehood, which fears being stripped bare and refuted, accuses the diligence of truth under the name of those vices that truth condemns.

Must one therefore desist from this persistence? Observe how the same Apostle binds Timothy, lest any sluggishness in preaching should steal upon him because the preaching of truth is disagreeable to some people. “I testify,” he says, “before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his manifestation and his kingdom: preach the word; persist in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching.” [Note: [Col. 0450] The preposition *per* is absent from all the manuscripts.] Who, hearing these words, if he faithfully serves God and is not a deceitful laborer, would rest from such diligence and persistence? Who would dare be sluggish under so solemn a testimony?

Therefore, let your eloquence not obstruct us in this matter. With the help of the Lord our God, we preach the usefulness, devotion, and holiness of Christian unity; we preach in season to those who are willing, and out of season to those who resist. With all the strength we possess, and by every means available to us, we show that this controversy between us and the party of Donatus has long been settled.

## CHAPTER VII

**9.** Let those recognize in themselves the name and guilt of contentious hostility who either, through obstinate cunning, provide a defense for falsehood, or, through envious boasting, supply publicity for truth. The Apostle Paul expressed both kinds of contentious people: the first in Alexander, of whom he says, “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You too avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words” (2 Tim. 4:1–2, 14–15); the second in those of whom he says: “Some indeed preach Christ from envy and contention, not purely, supposing that they can arouse affliction against my chains.”

They were undoubtedly preaching the very thing Paul preached, but not with the same mind, intention, or charity; rather, as he said, from envy and contention, wishing in their proud attitude to excel in that very proclamation and to place themselves above the Apostle Paul. He did not take this badly; indeed, he rejoiced that he saw them preaching what he wanted to become more widely known: “What then?” he says. “Provided only that Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether by pretext or in truth?” (Phil. 1:17–18).

They were not proclaiming him with the truth of their heart, since their intention was not sincere but competitive; nevertheless, they were proclaiming the truth—that is, Christ. Since you cannot be a judge of the inner movements of our heart, pay attention only to whether we resist the truth or seek to refute those who resist the truth.

For undoubtedly, if we persuade people of the truth and refute error—even if we do so not from a true personal intention, but while seeking the profit of this age and human glory—lovers of truth ought to rejoice, because even on this occasion truth is being proclaimed, just as the Apostle says: “And in this I will rejoice” (Phil. 1:18).

But if—as God knows most fully, and as you yourself could have known, insofar as human ability permits, had you lived with us—we are engaged in the labor of this administration through pious concern born of charity, I think our ministry can in no way rightly be blamed if, against whatever adversaries of truth, we contend for the truth with fervent spirit.

## CHAPTER VIII

**10.** For if among you anyone is regarded as contentious, passionate, and a maker of quarrels simply because he has taken care either to initiate a verbal dispute with someone or to answer one, consider what you think about the Lord Jesus himself and about his servants, the Prophets and Apostles.

The Lord himself, the Son of God—did he converse about the truth only with his disciples and with the crowds who believed in him, and not also with enemies who tested him, slandered him, questioned him, resisted him, and cursed him? Was he ashamed to dispute even with the one woman concerning a question about worship, against the opinion or heresy of the Samaritans?

“But,” you say, “he knew that she would believe.” What of all the things he said openly to the Jews, Pharisees, and Sadducees—people who not only would certainly not believe, but would also contradict and persecute him most violently? Did he not, whenever he wished, put questions to them voluntarily, in order to convict them by their own answer? When they sought to question him deceitfully and fell silent after being refuted, did he not answer them without any ambiguity?

Yet none of them is recorded as having been converted to follow him when he did these things. And certainly he knew—for he was prescient—that when he said these things to them, against them, or concerning them, he would accomplish nothing for their salvation. But perhaps he strengthened us by his example, since we cannot foresee the future faith or unbelief of human beings. He did this so that, if we have spoken to people excessively hard and perverse without fruit for their salvation, we might not grow faint or desist from the persistence of preaching when it has wearied us to labor in vain.

Moreover, although not only God but even human beings can no longer doubt that the devil himself will in no way be converted to righteousness [Note: [Col. 0452] All the manuscripts read *conversurum* (“will be converted”).], the Son of God nevertheless convicted him, when he was craftily testing him and setting traps from the holy Scriptures, by answering him from the holy Scriptures. Christ did not judge it unworthy to converse with Satan about divine utterances (Matt. 4:3–10). What did he foresee by this, except that what benefited neither the Jews nor the devil would benefit the Gentiles who would believe?

**11.** We also read that Prophets were sent to people so disobedient that God himself, who was sending the Prophets, foretold concerning those to whom he sent them that they would not obey their words. I omit the fact that, through the prophetic spirit by which they saw future events, they could certainly also have known that the people would despise their words—yet they did not cease to speak them with vehement persistence.

The Lord says most plainly to the prophet Ezekiel: “Go and enter the house of Israel, and speak my words to them; for you are not being sent to a people of an unknown language, to the house of Israel, nor to many peoples speaking languages different and difficult, whose words you could not understand. If I had sent you to such people, perhaps they would have listened to you. But the house of Israel will not listen to you, because they do not want to listen to me. For the whole house of Israel is of an unsettled and hardened heart. But I have made your face strong against their faces, and I will strengthen your struggle against their struggle” (Ezek. 3:4–8).

There you have it: God’s servant is sent and commanded to speak to those who would not listen to him, while the very Lord who sent him and commanded him to speak foretold that they would not listen. For what reason, to what purpose, with what benefit or result, is he sent to contend in proclaiming the truth against people who would contend and disobey?

Would anyone dare say that God’s holy Prophets fell under the reproach you cast at me when you said: “If you know that the matter under discussion cannot be settled by you, why do you undertake labor in vain? Why expend useless effort? Why contend pointlessly and without result? Is it not a great error to want to explain what you cannot explain?”—especially since the Law also warns, saying, “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you” (Ecclus. 3:22); and again, “An impetuous man prepares quarrels, and an angry man intensifies sin” (Ecclus. 28:11).

You certainly would not say these things to Ezekiel, who was sent with the word of God to engage in conflict with people who would not obey, who would think contrary to him, speak contrary to him, and act contrary to him. For if you did say them, he might answer you what the Apostles answered the Jews: “Whom ought one to obey—God or human beings?” (Acts 4:19; 5:29). I myself would answer you the same.

## CHAPTER IX

**12.** If at this point you demand that I show where God has also commanded me to do what you forbid, remember that the Apostolic Epistles were written not only to those who heard them at the time when they were written, but also to us; they are read in the Church for no other reason.

Consider also what the Apostle says: “Do you want to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Recall now not what Paul said, but what Christ spoke through him—the words I mentioned shortly before: “Preach the word; persist in season and out of season,” and so forth.

Consider also how, when explaining to Titus what sort of person a bishop ought to be, he said that he must also persevere according to the teaching of the faithful word: “so that he may be able,” he says, “both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict. For there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those from the circumcision; they must be refuted” (Titus 1:9–11).

He does not say that only those from the circumcision are such, but that they are especially such. Nevertheless, he established by an unmistakable command that empty talkers and deceivers of minds must be reproved and refuted by a bishop in sound doctrine.

From this I recognize that this too has been commanded to me. I do what I can; I persist in this work insofar as the one who gave the command assists me. Why do you obstruct me? Why do you oppose me? Why do you forbid it? Why do you criticize it? Must one obey you or God?

## CHAPTER X

**13.** Unless perhaps you think that the examples I have brought from the holy Scriptures should be understood in this way: the practice you praised among your people is that the things commanded in the Law are taught only in the Church. Perhaps you think that those who think differently should be corrected and convicted there, so that each teacher may amend the error of his own people merely by disputing and preaching.

But if anyone persists in doing anything of this kind with those who are outside, then, you say, he should be considered passionate, contentious, or quarrelsome. For Ezekiel himself, you say, and the other Prophets were sent with the words of God to their own people—Israelites, that is, to Israelites. [Note: [Col. 0453] The word *agere* (“to do”) is absent from some manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XI

**14.** I answer you on this point as well. I have already mentioned above that the Lord Jesus himself, who offered himself to his disciples as an example for imitation, did not disdain to affirm the truth and answer from the Law not only to Jews, but also to Pharisees, Sadducees, Samaritans, and even to the devil himself, the chief of all deceits and errors.

But lest you think that this was permitted to the Lord while not permitted to his servants, hear what is read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“A certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, came to Ephesus, a man powerful in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0453] The oldest Corbie manuscript and certain other manuscripts read “he had been instructed in the way,” omitting the word “of the Lord.” They again omit it shortly afterward before the words “and they explained the way to him more accurately.”] “and, fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught most accurately the things concerning Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John. He also began” [Note: [Col. 0454] The manuscripts read *coeperat* (“had begun”).] “to act boldly in the synagogue. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him, they took him in and explained the way of the Lord to him more accurately. When he wished to go to Achaia, the brothers wrote to the disciples, exhorting them to receive him. When he arrived, he greatly benefited those who had believed there; for he vigorously refuted the Jews publicly, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ” (Acts 18:24–28).

What do you say about this man? What do you think? Would you not perhaps accuse him of being contentious, passionate, and a promoter of quarrels, if you were not constrained by the authority of so great a sacred book?

## CHAPTER XII

**15.** Or, because he was a Jew who had believed in Christ, was he therefore obliged publicly to refute the Jews who resisted the Christian faith and denied that Jesus was the Christ, whereas we, because we have never belonged to the party of Donatus, are not obliged to refute the party of Donatus when it resists Christian unity?

Was the Apostle Paul ever a worshiper of idols, or was he ever in the heresy of the Epicureans or Stoics, with whom nevertheless he was neither ashamed nor reluctant to converse about the question of the living and true God? Hear what is written about this matter in the same book:

“While Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him when he saw that the city was devoted to idols. Therefore he disputed with the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0454] The printed editions read *cum Judaeis* (“with the Jews”). The preposition *cum* is absent here and below, in section 18, from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.] “in the synagogue, and with the Gentiles, and with those who worshiped, in the marketplace, every day, with those who happened to be there. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conversed with him. Some said, ‘What does this babbler wish to say?’ Others said, ‘He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign demons.’”

There you have the Apostle Paul refusing to avoid conversation with Stoics and Epicureans—sects different not only from him but also from one another, and opposed to one another—disputing with them not merely outside the Church but even outside the synagogue. Nor was he frightened by their insults or, as though avoiding quarrels and contentions, did he cease preaching Christian truth.

For observe what the holy Scripture next testifies: “They took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying: ‘May we know what this new teaching is that you are speaking? For you bring certain strange things to our ears; therefore we wish to know what these things mean.’ Now all the Athenians and the foreigners residing there spent their time in nothing else than either saying or hearing something new. But Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: ‘Men of Athens, I see that in all things you are very religious. For as I passed through and observed your objects of worship, I also found an altar on which was written, “To an unknown god.” What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you’” (Acts 17:19–23)—and the rest, which would take too long to recount in full.

But for the question we are now examining, pay attention, I beg you, to the Apostle of Christ, a Hebrew of Hebrews, standing and speaking not in a Jewish synagogue, nor in a Christian church, but in the Areopagus of the Athenians—that is, among Greeks who were especially contentious and impious.

For there the most talkative philosophical sects arose. Some of them, like the Stoics mentioned here, contend more about the opposition of words than about the opposition of things [Note: [Col. 0455] The Michaelinus manuscript reads “difference” (*diversitate*).]. This is what the Apostle forbade Timothy, saying that it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear (2 Tim. 2:14). Concerning such people, as you know, Cicero says: “For controversy about a word has long tormented the little Greeks, who are more desirous of contention than of truth” (*On the Orator*, book 1, chapter 11, §48).

Yet our Paul undertook to address and correct these people. He was not frightened by the name of the place, which echoes a name derived from Mars, whom they call the god of wars. There, fearless, he spoke peaceful words to those who would believe; there, girded with spiritual weapons, he attacked destructive errors. As the gentlest of men, he did not fear the contentious; as the simplest, he did not fear the dialecticians.

## CHAPTER XIII

**16.** For you know how greatly dialectic flourished among the Stoics. Even the Epicureans, whom ignorance of the liberal disciplines not only did not make ashamed but actually pleased, boasted that they themselves both possessed and taught certain rules of disputation by which no one who used them would be deceived.

For what else is dialectic than skill in disputation? I thought this needed to be made clear because you also wished to reproach me with dialectic, as though it were incompatible with Christian truth, and because your teachers judged that I, as a dialectical person, ought properly to be avoided and guarded against rather than refuted and defeated.

They did not persuade you of this—for you were not reluctant to dispute against us even in writing—yet you accused me of dialectic in order to deceive the ignorant and praise those who had been unwilling to engage me in disputation.

But surely you do not use dialectic when you write against us? Why, then, did you throw yourself into so great a danger of disputation when you do not know how to dispute? Or, if you do know, why does a dialectician accuse dialectic—being either so rash or so ungrateful that you do not restrain the ignorance by which you are defeated, or that you accuse the learning by which you are helped?

I examine your discourse, the very one you wrote to me. I see that you explain some things copiously and ornately—that is, eloquently—while you discuss other things subtly and acutely—that is, dialectically. Yet you criticize eloquence and dialectic.

If these things are harmful, why do you practice them? If they are not harmful, why do you accuse them? But let us not be tormented by a controversy about words. Since the matter itself is understood, there is no need to labor over what people have chosen to call it.

Therefore, if someone should be called eloquent who speaks not only copiously and ornately but also truthfully, and if someone should be called dialectical who argues not only subtly but also truthfully, then you are neither eloquent nor dialectical—not because your expression is barren and disordered, nor because your argument is dull and crude, but because you misuse eloquence and skill themselves in defense of falsehood.

If, however, eloquence or dialectic may properly be named even when someone argues or acts vigorously in support of a bad cause rather than in support of truth, then you are both eloquent and dialectical, because you speak vanities fluently and argue falsehoods acutely. But I shall leave you to yourself.

## CHAPTER XIV

**17.** The Stoics were certainly preeminently dialectical. Why did the Apostle Paul not avoid them with the greatest caution, lest they converse with him, while you praise your bishops because they do not wish to converse with us as though we were dialecticians?

Or, if Paul was a dialectician and therefore did not fear conversing with the Stoics because he argued not only acutely, as they did, but also truthfully, which they did not, be careful not to accuse anyone of dialectic as a crime when you admit that the Apostles used it.

When you make this accusation against me, I do not think you are being deceived through ignorance, but that you are deceiving others through cunning. The word “dialectic” is Greek. If usage permitted it, perhaps it might be called *disputatoria* in Latin, just as the most learned in both languages have called grammar *litteratura* in Latin.

For just as grammar takes its name from letters, since letters are called *grammata* in Greek, so dialectic takes its name from disputation, because disputation is called *dialogē* or *dialexis* in Greek.

Just as the ancients called a grammarian in Latin a *litteratus* (“learned in letters”) [Note: [Col. 0456] Lovaniensis and certain manuscripts read *litterator*.], so in Greek a dialectician is much more commonly and acceptably called in Latin a *disputator* (“one who disputes”).

I suppose that by now you will not deny that the Apostle was a disputant, even if you deny that he was a dialectician. Therefore, to disapprove in a Greek word what you are compelled to approve in Latin—what is this except to set a trap of deception for the unlearned and to do an injustice to the learned?

Or if you also deny that the Apostle was a disputant, although he disputed so constantly and so excellently, then you know neither Greek nor Latin—or, what is more believable, you deceive those who do not know Greek through the Greek word and those who do not even know Latin through the Latin one.

For what could be more deceptive—not merely more ignorant, since you do know these things—than to hear and read so many and such varied discourses of the Apostle asserting truth and convicting falsehood, yet deny that he was accustomed to dispute, when this cannot be done except by disputing?

**18.** If you admit that he did this because you are compelled to admit it by his writings, but nevertheless insist that these should be called not disputations but discourses or letters, why should I continue dealing with you in this way, so that those who do not know these things may approve whichever of us they wish and disapprove whichever they wish?

From the divine Scriptures themselves, to which you must yield, I demonstrate this. I bring forward the very words and the very terms used for the things themselves.

In the same testimony I recalled from the Acts of the Apostles, you have this written about Paul himself: “Therefore he disputed with the Jews in the synagogue, and with the Gentiles, and with those who worshiped in the marketplace.”

In another passage, although he was dealing with a Christian congregation, with the brothers gathered in the church, it is written: “A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window, overcome by deep sleep, while Paul was disputing” (Acts 20:9).

You also have in the Book of Psalms: “Let my disputation be pleasing to him” [Note: [Col. 0456] In Greek, *dialogē mou*.] (Ps. 103:34).

And in the prophet Isaiah: “Come, let us dispute” [Note: [Col. 0456] *Dielechthōmen*.], says the Lord (Isa. 1:18, according to the Septuagint).

Read in many other places in the divine Scriptures wherever you find this word, and examine the Greek manuscripts in those same testimonies of the holy Scriptures. You will see from where dialectic received its name. Do not, therefore, fail to imitate with wise devotion what all the righteous do even with God, to whom it is said, “Come, let us dispute,” and instead accuse it with senseless rashness.

## CHAPTER XV

**19.** For the person who disputes distinguishes truth from falsehood. Those who cannot do this, yet wish to appear dialecticians, seek the assent of the unwary through deceptive questions, so that from their answers they may draw conclusions from which they can either laugh at those whom they have deceived into open falsehood or persuade the deceived of a hidden falsehood—one which they themselves often also believe to be the truth.

But the true disputant—that is, one who distinguishes truth from falsehood—first performs this task within himself, lest, failing to distinguish correctly, he himself be deceived. He cannot accomplish this unless he is helped by God.

Then, when he brings before others for their instruction what he has worked out within himself, he first considers what they already know with certainty, so that from these things he may lead them to what they did not know or were unwilling to believe. He shows that these new things follow from what they already retained through knowledge or faith.

Thus, through truths concerning which they see themselves agreeing, they are compelled to approve other truths that they had denied. In this way what had previously been thought false is distinguished from falsehood when it is found to be consistent with the truth already held [Note: [Col. 0457] Am. and Er. read “the falsehood already held.” The word “falsehood” is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent.]

## CHAPTER XVI

**20.** When this true disputant proceeds broadly and expansively, he does so eloquently, and then he is considered and designated by another term: he is called a speaker rather than a disputant. Thus the Apostle expansively enlarges and unfolds that passage:

“In everything,” he says, “commending ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in hardships, in blows, in imprisonments, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering” [Note: [Col. 0457] Am. and Er. add *in goodness*. The Greek has no corresponding word except *en chrēstotēti*, which is sufficiently expressed by “in kindness.”], “in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet recognized; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6:4–10).

What could you easily find more abundant and ornate—that is, more eloquent—than this apostolic style? [Note: [Col. 0457] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. omit the word *facile* (“easily”). M.]

But when he proceeds concisely and compactly, people are accustomed to call him more a disputant than a speaker. Thus he treats of the circumcision and uncircumcision of Abraham the father, or of the distinction between law and grace. Some people, failing to understand him—or rather, slandering him—accused him of saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8).

Whether he is a speaker or a disputant, speech does not exist without disputation, since even in the breadth of eloquence truth is distinguished from falsehood. Nor can disputation exist without speech, since the compactness of an argument is necessarily expressed through words and language itself—whether he uses a continuous discourse or, by questioning the person with whom he is dealing, compels him to answer what is true and from this leads him to another truth that was being sought. It is especially in this latter activity that dialectic is said to reign.

## CHAPTER XVII

**21.** When someone is defeated by his own answers, if he answered badly, he has no one to blame but himself; and if he answered well, he is ashamed to resist any further—not the disputant, but himself.

When the Lord repeatedly dealt with the Jews in this manner and convicted them by trapping and confining them through their own answers, they had not learned it from you, nor had they learned from you to insult him. Indeed, they would perhaps have called him a dialectician more willingly and more spitefully than a Samaritan.

How twisted and confused do you think they were when, wishing to trap him in his words, they first asked whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar? They were setting a two-headed trap, so that whichever answer he chose, he would be caught. If he answered that it was lawful, he would seem guilty of acting against the people of God; but if he said that it was not lawful, he would be punished as an enemy of Caesar [Note: [Col. 0458] All the manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have *perimeretur* (“would be killed”).]

Then he asked that a coin be shown to him and asked whose image and inscription it bore. When they answered, “Caesar’s”—for manifest truth compelled them to answer this—the Lord immediately drew them along, bound and captured by their own response, saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

I ask you: were they the dialecticians, who attempted to overcome him by deceitfully and calumniously setting traps through their question, or was he the dialectician, who, by the wisdom of his questioning, drew from the very question they had asked a true answer from them and compelled them to confess the truth that they thought it dangerous for him to state?

## CHAPTER XVIII

**22.** If you say that they were dialecticians because, by questioning deceitfully, calumniously, and maliciously, they wished to trap him in his words—for you want us also to appear such—why, then, did the Lord answer them? Why did he lead them, by giving a reason, all the way to a confession of the truth? Why did he say to them, “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” (Matt. 22:15–21), and not add, “Dialecticians”?

Why did he insist that a coin be shown to him, so that he could express his true judgment even from the mouth of deceitful people? Why did he not instead say, “Go away; one ought not to speak with you, since you put forward deceptive questions and wish to deal with me dialectically”?

He said nothing of the kind. Against deceptive questioners and clever captors of our words, he did not set before us such an example. Rather, he taught us to compel even enemies of truth, through vigilant questioning and unconquerable reasoning, to bear witness to the truth.

Let your people do this to us if we are malicious and dialectical. Or do they reveal that they are afraid lest we do this to them instead?

But if you call Christ a dialectician, you will praise the dialectic that you had accused me of as a crime.

## CHAPTER XIX

**23.** To prevent you from doing this, I can see what you may perhaps say: neither they nor he did anything dialectically in that conversation.

If, then, neither those who speak craftily and deceitfully in order to deceive those with whom they are dealing in their words, nor those who convict such people by their answers, act dialectically, finally tell us what dialectic is. Teach us how much evil it contains, how much harm it does, and how greatly it ought to be avoided. You maliciously attach its name to the ignorant; show its crime to those who ask.

You do not wish to admit that the one who skillfully and correctly questions people turned away from the truth, leading them through their answers to the truth, acts dialectically, lest you admit that Christ also acted dialectically with the Jews.

Likewise, you do not wish to admit that those who set traps through deceptive questions and attempt to deceive the person answering act dialectically, lest it be shown that the Jews acted in this way with Christ. Yet Christ did not avoid them by remaining silent; rather, he overcame them by speaking. Thus you would be compelled to admit that your bishops, whom you regard as learned and wise, are wrong not to wish to converse even with dialecticians, so that they may teach invincible truth.

I see that you are suffering great distress over how to define a dialectician: he must be neither a skilled disputant, lest you be compelled to praise what you have criticized, nor a deceptive captor of words, lest it be said to you, “As Christ dealt with such people, so should a Christian deal with this man.”

Therefore, if you wish to be freed from this difficulty, define as a dialectician the person with whom the learned men of the party of Donatus do not wish to converse. What else should be suggested to you, when you accuse us of dialectic and therefore praise your bishops because they do not wish to converse with us?

**24.** Perhaps you can find something to say about the Jews, and—although they held out the traps of their questions craftily and cunningly—say that they were not dialecticians.

But certainly nothing of the sort can be said about the Stoics. They were not only dialecticians; they also surpassed the other philosophical schools in this art or ability.
