The Stoic Chrysippus, as you will recall with me, was the man of whom the Academic Carneades held this opinion: whenever he had to dispute with Chrysippus, his heart needed to be purged with hellebore; but after a meal he could easily overcome all the others [Note: [Col. 0459] See Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 7.]

If, then, the books of the Stoics taught us to dispute dialectically, let your bishops bring forward the teaching of Paul against us. Nevertheless, let them allow us to converse with them, just as Paul did not reject the Stoics when they wished to converse with him.

## CHAPTER XX

**25.** For Christian doctrine never fears this art called dialectic, which teaches nothing other than how to demonstrate consequences—whether true consequences from truths or false consequences from falsehoods. The Apostle did not fear it among the Stoics, whom he did not refuse to engage when they wished to converse with him (Acts 17:16–31).

Dialectic itself acknowledges—and it is true—that no one is led through disputation consistently to a false conclusion unless he has first assented to falsehoods from which that conclusion follows, whether he wishes it or not.

Accordingly, anyone who takes care that falsehoods he does not want should not follow from his speech must willingly beware of the falsehoods that precede them. But if he has adhered to true premises, then whatever consequences he sees that he had thought false, or about which he had doubted, he should accept when admonished, if he is more friendly toward the most peaceful truth than toward the most contentious vanity.

## CHAPTER XXI

**26.** I shall have accomplished little unless I demonstrate what I am saying in this very conversation now taking place between us.

In that very question concerning Baptism, you proposed the question to me, asking where it is appropriate for you to be baptized: with us or in the party of Donatus. Since your intention is that a person ought to be baptized in the party of Donatus, you tried to prove this intention from the fact that we also do not deny that Baptism exists there.

You certainly see that you wished to proceed in such a way as to draw us from what we concede to what we do not concede: that is, because we concede that Baptism exists there, to compel us also to concede that a person ought to be baptized there.

## CHAPTER XXII

**27.** Consider carefully whether this follows, and answer yourself. Once this has been placed before your eyes, I think that, with the liveliness of your intelligence, you can see that you are treating non-consequences as consequences.

For we truly say that Baptism exists there as well; but we do not say that it is beneficial there. Indeed, we say that it is harmful there.

When the question is where someone ought to be baptized, I believe the question is asked because of what the Lord says: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). Therefore, since Baptism must be received for the sake of this benefit, when it is asked where it should be received, the question is not where it exists, but where it is beneficial for attaining the kingdom of heaven.

It would follow that Baptism should also be received there wherever it is known to exist, if it were taught that everyone who possesses something good also possesses it to his own good [Note: [Col. 0460] The printed editions read *docerentur* (“were taught,” plural). The manuscripts read *doceretur* (“were taught,” singular).]

But when so many people possess so many good things to their own harm, who does not see that, when it is asked where something should be received, the question is not where it exists, but where it benefits?

For example, if you conceded to me that gold is a good thing, you would also concede that thieves possess gold. But, I think, you would not want me to conclude from these two concessions that someone who wants to possess gold ought therefore to join the company of thieves.

Likewise, when I concede that Baptism is good, and also concede that Donatists possess Baptism, you should not conclude from these two concessions—as though the conclusion followed—that someone who wants to possess Baptism ought to belong to the company of the Donatists.

## Chapter XXIII

**28.** From this, too, I have no doubt that many considerations will occur to you yourself: although things may be good and established for some useful purpose, they are nevertheless not useful to everyone who possesses them, but only to those who use them well. For the same light pours upon healthy eyes and wounded eyes alike: to the former it is a help, to the latter a torment. The same food nourishes some bodily conditions and harms others; the same medicine cures some and weakens others; the same weapons protect some and hinder others; the same garment serves some as covering and entangles others. So also Baptism benefits some for the kingdom, but others for judgment.

## Chapter XXIV

**29.** Here I see what may move you. Perhaps you say that in all these examples I have mentioned nothing [Col. 0461] of a Sacrament: Baptism, however, is a holy Sacrament. Therefore it does not follow that, because it could be demonstrated in the case of gold, light, food, weapons, and clothing that things suitable for some of their possessors are unsuitable for others—even though they are good and established for some useful purpose—Baptism likewise immediately benefits some of its possessors and harms others.

It remains, then, to ask whether even those good things that belong to the law of God are beneficial to all who possess them. With this question proposed, our position is that not even all such things benefit everyone who possesses them. See how we prove this position from your own concessions. For you concede that the Apostle Paul must be believed in all things. I hold to one point. You also concede that the same Apostle said, “The law is good.” From these two statements it follows that the law is good, but good for those who use it lawfully (1 Tim. 1:8). If, therefore, someone does not use it lawfully, the law itself does not become evil; but certainly it will harm the evil.

## Chapter XXV

**30.** Perhaps you will say that no one can both be in the law and use the law wrongly: by the very fact that he lives contrary to the law, he is shown not to be in the law. I reply that it is possible for someone both to be in the law and not to use it lawfully. I prove this likewise from your own concessions.

For you concede that the Apostle cited a testimony from the Psalms against those who gloried in the law while living contrary to the law. “As it is written,” he says, “There is no one righteous, no one who understands, no one who seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they acted deceitfully. The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes.” And lest they should think that these words were spoken against people who were not in the law, he immediately added: “But we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are in the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become guilty before God” (Rom. 3:10–19).

Again, elsewhere he says: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not. Yet I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But, taking occasion through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of covetousness.” A little later he says: “Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Thus the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good. Therefore, did what is good become death to me? Certainly not; but sin, so that it might appear to be sin, through what is good brought death to me” (Rom. 7:7–13).

Observe how, after praising the law, he accuses those who are in the law—those who, by using what is good wrongly, possessed evil.

The Apostle himself also says that a certain knowledge derived from the law—which he said both that he himself and others possessed—is useless and harmful without love. “Concerning the sacrifices of idols,” he says, “we know that we all possess knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1). Accordingly, this knowledge too, although it belongs to the [Col. 0462] law of God, if it exists in anyone without love, puffs up and does harm.

What of the very body and blood of the Lord, the one sacrifice for our salvation? Although the Lord himself says, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6:54), does not the same Apostle teach that even this becomes harmful to those who use it wrongly? For he says: “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

[Note: [Col. 0462] The older manuscripts of the best quality read, “since the Lord himself says.” The Cygirannian manuscript reads, “although the Lord himself says.”]

## Chapter XXVI

**31.** See, then, how divine and holy things harm those who use them wrongly. Why should this not also be the case with Baptism? Why should evil heretics not be in good Baptism in the same way that evil Jews were in the good law?

I have already proved—since you concede that Paul must be believed and that the testimonies I cited from the Scriptures were spoken by Paul—that certain good and lawful things nevertheless harm those who possess and use them unlawfully. Why, then, should the same not be true of Baptism, although it is good and lawful, so that it does not benefit everyone who possesses it?

You were drawing the conclusion as though it were absolutely certain and necessary: a person ought to be baptized in the party of Donatus because we concede that Baptism exists there too. You did not consider that we could say that the Baptism of Christ is indeed there—just, holy, and good—but punitive, contrary, and harmful to the enemies of Christ’s body, which is the Church that, according to the divine promises, is spread among all nations.

## Chapter XXVII

**32.** What answer will you find here, except to say that Baptism should not be counted among those good things pertaining to the law of God which people can possess without being good; rather, that the law itself, knowledge, and the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ are good things which people can possess and yet be evil, whereas Baptism is such a good that whoever possesses it must necessarily be good?

If you wish to say this, you will say what is false. Therefore observe what other falsehood follows from it. I do not mention it in order to lead you from that falsehood of yours to other falsehoods, but so that, when you recognize this consequence to be false, you may free yourself from it and correct what precedes it.

[Note: [Col. 0462] Erasmus, Lyon, and Louvain omit the particle *ut* (“so that”); the reading with it is preferable.]

What precedes? The assertion among you that everyone who possesses good Baptism is good—which is plainly false. What follows? Namely, that those who were creating schisms, saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Cephas,” and “I to Christ,” must have been good. Rebuking them, the Apostle says: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13).

But it is false that these people were good, except for those who said, “I belong to Christ”; and yet they had been baptized with the holy Baptism of Christ. Why, then, did this falsehood follow? Because the falsehood that preceded it was that everyone who possesses good Baptism is good.

Let both assertions therefore be rejected and both judgments corrected. Since it is clear that those who were [Col. 0463] creating schisms were not good, and yet had been baptized with good Baptism, it must also be clear that not everyone who possesses good Baptism is good. Consequently, we are not compelled to concede that someone ought to be baptized in the party of Donatus merely because we concede that the party of Donatus—which we call evil—possesses good Baptism.

## Chapter XXVIII

**33.** Again, in order to hold me through that agreement to something to which I do not agree, you cited the statement:

[Note: [Col. 0463] We have added from the old Cygirannian manuscript the negative particle before *consentio* (“I agree”), which the Louvain editors thought was needed there; it is absent from the other books.] “One God, one faith, one Baptism, one undefiled and true Catholic Church” (Eph. 4:5). I grant all these points, even though they are written somewhat differently. But what does that have to do with the matter, since, as I have said, I grant all these things?

What you are trying to establish from them does not follow: namely, that those who are not in the one Church cannot possess the one Baptism. That is altogether false. And this is shown even more clearly because you yourself supplied the basis from which I can remind you of what I wish.

You presented these statements among my concessions in order to lead me to your position: that there is one God, one faith, one Baptism, and one undefiled and Catholic Church. Since we agree on these points, you think that the point on which we disagree can be demonstrated from them—namely, that among those who are not in this one Church there cannot be this one Baptism.

I say that there can be, provided it is not changed and the same Baptism is preserved. It does not cease to be one Baptism merely because it is found among those who are not in the one Church.

I prove this from what you included in the same statement concerning one God and one faith. We find the same God worshiped outside the Church by those who do not know him; yet he does not thereby cease to be God. And we find even those who do not belong to the members of the Church confessing the faith by which it is believed that Christ is the Son of the living God; yet it does not thereby cease to be one faith.

Likewise, when we find the same Baptism observed by those outside the Church in baptizing people, we ought not for that reason to think that it is not the same Baptism.

## Chapter XXIX

**34.** Perhaps you will say that it is impossible for the same one God to be worshiped outside the Church, or for the same faith by which we confess Christ to be the Son of God—the confession by which Peter was called blessed—to be found among those who are not in the Church (Matt. 16:16–17).

This, then, remains for me to prove. In the very speech of blessed Paul that I mentioned above from the Acts of the Apostles, you have his words concerning God, when he had found an altar inscribed, “To an Unknown God”: “The one whom you worship without knowing,” he says, “I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23).

Did he say, “Because you worship him outside the Church, the one whom you worship is not God”? Rather, he said: “The one whom you worship without knowing, I proclaim to you.” What did he desire to provide for them except that they should worship in the Church, wisely and beneficially, the same God whom outside the Church they worshiped ignorantly and uselessly?

So we say to you: “The Baptism that you observe without knowing, we proclaim its peace to you”—not so that, when you come to us, you may receive another [Col. 0464] Baptism, but so that you may use beneficially the one that was already among you.

[Note: [Col. 0463] The printed editions read “its power” (*potestatem*); the manuscripts more correctly read “its peace” (*pacem*). For the question here concerns not Baptism’s force and effect, but its usefulness, which avails nothing except in Catholic peace and unity.]

James the Apostle likewise speaks concerning faith against those who thought that what they believed was sufficient for them and refused to do good works: “You believe,” he says, “that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and tremble” (James 2:19).

Certainly the demons are not in the unity of the Church; yet we cannot say that what they believe is something different, since they also said to the Lord Jesus Christ, “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” (Mark 1:24).

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). I do not think that anyone is so foolish as to believe that a person who does not have love belongs to the unity of the Church.

Therefore, just as the one God is worshiped ignorantly even outside the Church, and yet he is not thereby not the same God; and just as the one faith is held without love even outside the Church, and yet it is not thereby not the same faith; so also the one Baptism is possessed ignorantly and without love even outside the Church, and yet it is not thereby not the same Baptism.

There is one God, one faith, one Baptism, one undefiled Catholic Church—not a Church in which alone the one God is worshiped, but one in which alone the one God is worshiped devoutly; not one in which alone the one faith is retained, but one in which alone the one faith is retained with love; not one in which alone the one Baptism is possessed, but one in which alone the one Baptism is possessed for salvation.

## Chapter XXX

**35.** Thus, with our agreement, you proposed to us one God, one faith, one Baptism, and one undefiled and Catholic Church. But you not only failed to establish from these the conclusion you wanted; you also greatly assisted us in reminding you, from these same premises, of what we wanted to establish.

Consider, then, how reasonable is the position we follow. When schismatics or heretics come to us, we correct the things they have corrupted; but whatever they have preserved as they received it, we recognize and approve, lest, moved by human faults beyond the bounds of justice, we do injury to divine things. For we see that the Apostle, even on an altar of the Gentiles—among whom idols were worshiped—confirmed rather than denied the name of God that he found there.

Nor should a royal mark on a man be changed or rejected because he has obtained from the king pardon for his error and permission to serve, merely because a deserter had branded him with the same mark in order to gather followers for himself. Nor should marks be changed on sheep when they are joined to the master’s flock merely because a runaway slave had imprinted the master’s mark upon them.

## Chapter XXXI

**36.** But if you fear that these examples are deceptive because they are not ecclesiastical examples—although you know that comparisons drawn from sheep and soldiers are given in Scripture—I wish to say something from the prophetic Scriptures called the Old Testament, since no example of this matter is found in the books of the New Testament, either by us or by you.

Surely, I suppose, you do not dare deny that the circumcision of the foreskin was observed by the ancients as a figure [Col. 0465] of the future Baptism of Christ. If a Jew who had been circumcised among the Samaritans had then wished to come to the Jews, could he be circumcised again? Would not the error of that man be corrected, while the sign of faith was recognized and approved?

Even now there are certain heretics who call themselves Nazarenes, while some call them Symmachians. They possess both the circumcision of the Jews and the Baptism of Christians. Therefore, just as one of them could not be circumcised again if he came to the Jews, so, when he comes to us, he ought not to be baptized again.

You will still say: “Circumcision among the Jews is one thing; Baptism among Christians is another.” But since circumcision was a shadow of this truth, why could that circumcision be found among heretics who followed the Jews, whereas this Baptism cannot be found among heretics who follow Christians?

**37.** Produce, at least, someone from the canonical Scriptures—whose authority is common to us—who came from the heretics and was baptized again.

[Note: [Col. 0465] At this point the manuscripts omit the words “whose authority is common to us.”]

For the fact that the Apostles commanded certain people to be baptized in Christ after John’s Baptism has an entirely different explanation. John was not a heretic; he was that friend of the Bridegroom (John 3:29), than whom no greater had arisen among those born of women (Matt. 11:11).

The reason, therefore, is entirely different. Otherwise, if Paul baptized after John, although both were in the unity of Christ, how much more ought your bishops—who claim to be in the unity of Christ—to baptize after their colleagues, in whom they rightly reprove certain conduct, when Paul could criticize nothing in John?

[Note: [Col. 0465] The manuscripts read “because they claim to be” (*quia se*) rather than “who claim to be” (*qui se*).]

That, then, has another cause and another explanation, which it would take too long to discuss here; and in other works of ours we have already said much about it.

Therefore, prove from the canonical Scriptures that someone coming from the heretics was baptized again. We, for our part, cite the words spoken to Peter: “Whoever has been washed once does not need to wash again” (John 13:10).

But you also say: “Peter had not been baptized among the heretics.” Therefore, since you cannot produce from the Scriptures—whose authority is common to us—anyone coming from the heretics who was baptized again, nor can we produce anyone who was received without such baptism, so far as this matter is concerned, our case is equal.

## Chapter XXXII

**38.** Yet we have shown that many things belonging to the law of God exist among those who are not in the Church—things that none of you dares deny. But why you should not want Baptism also to be such a thing, I entirely fail to see, and I am confident that you cannot demonstrate it.

In this matter, too, we follow the most certain authority of the canonical Scriptures. It should not be regarded as insignificant that, when this question was being disputed among the bishops of an earlier age, before the party of Donatus began, and when differing opinions existed among colleagues while their unity remained intact, it pleased the whole Catholic Church, spread throughout the entire world, to observe the practice that we maintain.

You also produce the council of Cyprian, which either never took place or was rightly overcome by the other members of the unity from whom he was not divided.

[Note: [Col. 0465] See below, Book 2, section 39.]

Nor are we for that reason [Col. 0466] better than Bishop Cyprian—if indeed he judged that heretics should be baptized again—because we rightly do not do this. Just as we are not better than the Apostle Peter because we do not compel the Gentiles to Judaize, although he is shown to have done so, as the Apostle Paul attests and corrects (Gal. 2:14). In the same way, a question concerning circumcision once wavered among the Apostles with no little difficulty, just as the question concerning Baptism later did among the bishops.

## Chapter XXXIII

**39.** Therefore, although no certain example of this matter is produced from the canonical Scriptures, the truth of those same Scriptures is nevertheless maintained by us in this matter, since we do what has already pleased the universal Church, which the authority of those Scriptures themselves commends.

Since Holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever fears being deceived by the obscurity of this question should consult that same Church concerning it—the Church that Holy Scripture demonstrates without any ambiguity.

But if you doubt that Holy Scripture commends the Church that is spread among all nations in the greatest multitude—for if you did not doubt this, you would not still be in the party of Donatus—I will burden you with many most unmistakable testimonies drawn from that same authority, so that, if you are unwilling to be excessively stubborn, you may be brought by your own concessions to this conclusion also. First, however, I will show that in your reply to my letter—which you chose to oppose—you were unable to answer anything relevant to the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0466] Two manuscripts read *certum* (“certain”) instead of *certe* (“certainly”).]

## Chapter XXXIV

**40.** For the moment, let this suffice. Because of the excessive obstinacy of certain people, I have judged that many things must be said against those who, although they have the principal case against them, seek to turn judges away from examining it by means of a preliminary objection, saying that they ought in no way to speak with us.

I have proved both from the Holy Scriptures and by every clear argument available to me that defenders of the truth need not fear any amount of eloquence or any kind of dialectic, lest this prevent them, by disputing with and refuting defenders of falsehood, from convicting them. I have also shown that the point by which I said you were moved, apart from my letter, does not follow:

[Note: [Col. 0466] The same two manuscripts read “you said” (*dixisti*) instead of “I said” (*dixi*).] if we concede that Baptism exists in the party of Donatus, we do not thereby also concede that anyone ought to be baptized in that same society. For just as the rejected Jewish people could possess the good law, so a rejected society of heretics can possess a good Sacrament.

What is properly given in the Church, and is not given anywhere outside it, will be shown without difficulty in its proper place (below, Book 2, section 16). For we would not rightly act toward heretics, whom we confess to possess Baptism, by urging them in every way to come to the Catholic Church, unless, by coming, they received something that they could not receive elsewhere; and unless they received it, they would possess in vain and to their harm whatever other things—although good and belonging to the law of God—they may have been able to receive anywhere.

Whatever this is, which according to the Scriptures and the most certain reasoning can be found to be capable of being given or received only in the Holy Church, belongs to the sealed fountain, [Col. 0467] the well of living water, and the paradise with the fruit of trees. You were able to mention these, but you showed that you did not understand what they signify, since you suppose that this refers to visible Baptism. Although visible Baptism is holy and must in no way be omitted, because it excels in its most sacred symbolism, consider how many receive it—not only the good, who have been called according to the purpose to be conformed to the image of the Son of God [Col. 0468] (Rom. 8:29), but also those who will not possess the kingdom of God, among whom, as the Apostle says, are drunkards and the greedy (1 Cor. 6:10).

I think that, if you set aside your obstinacy and reflect, you will easily answer yourself that I am speaking the truth, so that you will not seek the sealed fountain and the well of living water except where those who displease God are not divinely permitted to approach.

I have compared the texts; read them.

# Book Two

Examines other statements in Cresconius’s letter. He willingly grants that the Donatists should be called *Donatiani* rather than *Donatistae*, after Donatus. He nevertheless argues that they are rightly called heretics by Augustine; yet when they return to the Church they should not be baptized, and even their clergy may be received in their clerical offices if this appears suitable for the Church’s benefit. He teaches further that those who return receive something in the Church that is not given anywhere outside it, namely the gift of love. He demonstrates that Cresconius has wrongly defended Petilianus’s statement, “The conscience of the one who gives holily is considered, and it cleanses the recipient.” He examines the passages of Scripture cited by Cresconius, especially the one beginning, “Whoever is baptized by a dead person,” and so forth. Finally, he replies to the authority of Cyprian concerning the rebaptizing of heretics.

[Col. 0467]

## Chapter I

**1.** In the excessively lengthy discourse of the preceding volume, I think we finally persuaded you that your bishops should neither be praised nor approved for refusing to converse with us concerning the cause of dissension that divides our communion.

By means of this preliminary objection, they think themselves extremely [Col. 0467] shrewd in a very bad case.

[Note: [Col. 0467] Some old codices read “thinking themselves most secure” (*putantes securissimos*). The editor judges that the reading should be “they think themselves most secure” (*putant esse tutissimos*).] Unless I am mistaken, I have completely removed that objection by true and certain arguments, and especially by examples from the divine Scriptures. Through these I taught with the utmost clarity that holy preachers and defenders of the truth held discussions not only against the present adversaries of the truth, and not only against those who belonged to the same people as they did, but also against foreigners and outsiders. Above all, they held discussions against those who especially professed dialectic—the very people from whom you chiefly instill vain fears into the uneducated.

Let the most contentious person not therefore be regarded as the most diligent preacher, and let an active disputant not be thought a litigator, when, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, he insists “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2), so that those who contradict sound doctrine may be refuted (Titus 1:9–11), the empty talkers may be rejected, the disorderly corrected, the fainthearted consoled, and the weak supported (1 Thess. 5:14), while the word of evangelical salvation is defended with patience and proclaimed without hesitation against all who resist.

I also showed why you should not think that someone ought to be baptized among you merely because we agree that Baptism can both be possessed and given by you. For we also say that it is possessed and given harmfully, since holy things that can be used even by the wicked are handled by them all the more uselessly and disastrously the holier they are. Therefore, when such people come to the Holy Church, they themselves must be corrected; we must not violate those things that have not been changed even by the wicked.

**2.** Listen, then, Cresconius, while I briefly demonstrate this also: throughout your entire letter you have said nothing by which you refuted mine—unless perhaps you taught me how to derive or decline names, so that I should say *Donatiani* rather than *Donatistae* after Donatus. You nevertheless concede that this is at least a Greek declension: namely, that *Donatistae* are named from Donatus just as *Evangelistae* are named from the Gospel. You say that you take pleasure in this, so that, because your people preach the Gospel, the form of the word has been changed by analogy.

[Note: [Col. 0468] Some older manuscripts read *mutuata sit* (“has been borrowed”) instead of *mutata sit* (“has been changed”).]

See, then, whether they themselves may perhaps have wished to be called this first because they regard Donatus as their Gospel. For these people are named from Donatus in the same way that all holy people refuse to depart from fellowship with the Gospel; and for that reason they take pleasure in being called *Donatistae*, like *Evangelistae*.

You, rather, do them an injury when you write—in the Latin language, approving only the Latin rule—that you would have them called *Donatiani* after Donatus, just as *Ariani* and *Novatiani* are derived from Arius and Novatus.

When I wrote, this name was already being used—I do not know by whom—and I did not take care to change it, since I thought that it was sufficient for the distinction I wanted. If Demosthenes, the most distinguished of orators, whose concern for words was as great as that of our authors for their subject matter, when Aeschines had nevertheless charged him with some unusual expression, denied that the fortunes of Greece depended on whether he had used one word or another, or extended his hand in one direction or the other (Oration *Against Aeschines on the Crown*), how much less ought we to concern ourselves with the rules for deriving names, when, whether we say this or that, what we mean is understood without ambiguity? Our chief concern is not the refinement of speech but the demonstration of truth.

If one of our people was the first to bend this name into its present form, it seems to me that he certainly did not have in mind the analogy by which *Evangelistae* are named from the Gospel. Rather, because through Donatus—not only the Donatus of Carthage, who is said to have strengthened this heresy especially, but also the greater Donatus of Casis-Nigris, who first raised altar against altar in that same city—a great scandal arose, perhaps he wished them to be called *Donatistae* from Donatus in the same way that people might be called *Scandalistae* from scandal.

## Chapter II

**3.** In this matter, which does not diminish our case in any way, I make myself entirely accommodating. When I am dealing with you, I now call them *Donatiani*; when I am dealing with others, I follow common usage, which properly governs these sounds.

Only remember that I, to whom you have attributed such eloquence, still do not know how to decline names, and announce to your people that they are safe, lest they now fear a dialectician when you see that he still needs a grammarian.

Whether you call the discipline of disputation dialectic or something else, it nevertheless teaches with sufficient sobriety that, when the matter is clear, one should not labor over the name. Just as I do not care whether that discipline itself is called dialectic, although I care, as far as I can, to know and be able to dispute—that is, to distinguish truth from falsehood in speech—because if I do not care about this, I will fall into the most harmful error, so I do not care whether you decline *Donatistae* or *Donatiani* more expertly and learnedly.

Nor do I care whether, when we speak, the name should be derived from Donatus—whether from the one who first sacrificed outside the Church or from the one who most strongly strengthened this dissension—or from Majorinus, who was the first bishop of your party to be ordained against Caecilianus. The name may be supplied for the sake of distinction.

Nevertheless, unless I take care to demonstrate that you are heretics and therefore must be avoided with the greatest caution lest you deceive people, I will incur no small blame of negligence in bearing the burden of my office.

## Chapter III

**4.** Although you think that what happened between us ought to be called a schism rather than a heresy, and although—something dialecticians rarely dare to do—you distinguish these matters even by definitions, I will not be able to show sufficiently how much you assist us unless I insert your own words from your letter.

“What does it mean,” you ask, “that you say the sacrilegious error of heretics?” (*Book I Against the Letter of Petilianus*, section 1). “Heresies ordinarily arise only among those who follow different things, and a heretic is a worshiper of a religion that is contrary or differently interpreted, such as the Manichaeans, Arians, Marcionites, Novatians, and the rest whose differing opinion stands opposed to the Christian faith. Among us, who have the same Christ, born, dead, and risen again, one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance, what has occurred is called a schism, not a heresy. For heresy is the sect of those who follow different things; schism, however, is the separation of those who follow the same things. Therefore, in this too, through your zeal for accusation, you see the error into which you have fallen: you call what is a schism a heresy.”

These are your words, which I have taken from your letter.

[Note: [Col. 0469] The printed editions read, “which you fall into, you do not see the error.” The manuscripts read, “which you have fallen into, you see,” omitting *non* (“not”).]

## Chapter IV

**5.** Now consider, if you are not obstinate, how easily and briefly you yourself have settled what was being disputed between us.

If the same Christ—born, dead, and risen again—is ours and yours, if there is one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance, is it not perverse to rebaptize?

For you have stated three things, any one of which would have been more than sufficient. But as though you were acting faithfully against the Donatists, lest anyone—however clever—try to interpret differently what you had stated once and briefly, you took care to drive your position into dull ears and hearts [Col. 0468] as well:

“One religion,” you say; “the same Sacraments; nothing different in Christian observance.”

And still we labor against one another? At last, restrain your dissension, end the dispute, love peace. What do you reject? What do you exsufflate? Why do you rebaptize? There is one religion, the same Sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance.

For if there is not one Baptism for you and for us, how is there one religion? But you said, “One religion.” Therefore there is also one Baptism.

How are the Sacraments the same? But you said, “The same Sacraments.” Therefore Baptism too is the same.

Again, if Baptism is different for us and for you, how is there nothing different in Christian observance? But you said, “Nothing different in Christian observance.” Therefore Baptism is not different either.

[Note: [Col. 0470] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read, “therefore Baptism is not different.” The Louvain edition reads, “therefore Baptism too is not different.”]

Since these things are so, we rightly neither reject, exsufflate, nor repeat what is one and the same and not different; rather, we recognize it, receive it, and accept it.

But you impiously refuse to acknowledge, receive, and accept what is one and the same and not different. Instead, you choose to reject it, dare to exsufflate it, and do not fear repeating it.

And since, in the very matter that has not been changed between us, we receive what you repel; and since, if these things were given by you, we judge them to have been given, whereas, if they were given by us, you repeat them as though they had not been given—since you follow such different practices, you disdain being called heretics.

**6.** Pay careful attention to what you say and what I say.

You defined and stated: “Heresy is the sect of those who follow different things; schism, however, is the separation of those who follow the same things.”

You also said that there is one religion for us and for you, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance.

Why, then, do you rebaptize a Christian, while I do not rebaptize him? Obviously we follow different things.

Why do you not want to be called a heretic?

[Note: [Col. 0470] Two manuscripts read: “Why, then, do you rebaptize a Christian? But if, in the fact that you rebaptize a Christian while I do not rebaptize him, we follow different things, why do you not want to be called a heretic?”]

I think that we recognize heretics by no small sign: although they confess that there is one religion for them and for us, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance, they refuse to recognize us as baptized.

Or do you resist the truth with such obstinacy and such dissension that you separate Baptism from religion, from the Sacraments, and from Christian observance?

If you do this, you are heretics in that you refuse to allow Baptism to belong to religion, to the Sacraments, and to Christian observance.

But if you do not do this, you are heretics in that, although you confess that those who share with you one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance also share Baptism as belonging to religion, to the Sacraments, and to Christian observance, you nevertheless rebaptize them.

Pay careful attention, then, to your definition, in which you said: “Heresy is the sect of those who follow different things.” See whether you do not follow something different—either by separating Baptism from the religious observance of the Christian Sacraments, with which we join it among the great things, or by rebaptizing those with whom Baptism too is one within the single religious observance of the Christian Sacraments, something that we abhor.

## CHAPTER V

**7.** Would that I could, whenever your impious snares seize one of our faithful for destruction—one already baptized among us, whom you say has not yet begun to be a Christian; whenever, as though he were a pagan, you exorcise him, and make him a catechumen in order thereafter to rebaptize—or rather, extinguish—him, suddenly appear from somewhere [Note: [Col. 0471] Lovaniensis: “suddenly appear from elsewhere.”], and, with this letter of yours in hand, present this very passage of it by reading it aloud in the midst of their proceedings and cry out:

“What are you doing? Look here: listen, see, read! We and you have one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance. First ask in whose name this man was previously baptized; then, if in your Baptism you name another name that is better, administer it.”

Then perhaps, if the very evidence of the matter did not make them tremble, they would immediately bring forward their great and penetrating argument and say:

“Who among us is this whose letter you are carrying?”

“He is one of our laymen.”

“He would have defeated us, but he is defeated by himself.”

Then, if I were present, I would turn to you and say:

“You, at least, I beg you, tell us what these men are doing. Look: they are preparing to rebaptize one baptized among us. Certainly, then, we and you have one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance?”

Or would you reply:

“But Christ’s Baptism is not a religion, not a Sacrament, not a Christian observance”?

May God turn such madness away from your mind! What, then, would you answer me as I pressed you and said:

“We and you have one religion. But those who do not have one Baptism do not have one religion; therefore, we and you have one Baptism.

“We and you have the same Sacraments. But those who do not have the same Baptism do not have the same Sacraments; therefore, we and you have the same Baptism.

“Nothing in Christian observance is different for us and for you. But where Baptism is different, there is certainly something different in Christian observance; therefore, Baptism is not different for us and for you.”

Why is what is one rejected? Why is what is the same exorcised? Why is what is not different repeated?

## CHAPTER VI

**8.** If I were acting and pressing the matter in your presence in this way, to what evasions would you resort? No doubt they would disparage grammarians in your letter, while you would accuse dialecticians in ours. Yet truth would prevail over the heretics through both disciplines, showing that the only thing different in them from us is what is acknowledged to be perverse. For we recognize our Sacraments and correct alien error; you, however, acknowledge the same Sacraments, yet repeat them as though they were nothing, rejecting with great dissent what you concede is not different.

## CHAPTER VII

**9.** Accordingly, although I approve more of that distinction between schism and heresy according to which schism is said to be a recent dissension of a congregation arising from some diversity of opinions—for those who make a schism cannot do so unless they follow something different—and heresy is an old schism, yet what need is there here to labor [Note: [Col. 0471] It seems that *ut laborem* should be read.] when your own definitions assist me so greatly that, if this were granted to me even by others of your party, I would more readily call you schismatics than heretics?

For if those make a schism who have one religion with those from whom they separate, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance, your rebaptizing is thereby all the more condemnable. For in one religion, with the same Sacraments, and with nothing different in Christian observance, Baptism cannot be other and different [Note: [Col. 0472] Several manuscripts: “Baptism cannot be other as a result of difference.”].

But since what you follow as different is neither nothing nor something insignificant—for, separated from the bond of unity, you also dissent from us concerning the repetition of Baptism—it follows, according to this very definition of yours, in which you said, “Heresy is the sect of those who follow something different,” that you are both shown to be heretics and shown to be defeated.

You are heretics because you follow something different not merely in being divided, but also in rebaptizing. You are defeated because you repeat the Baptism given through us as though it were not the same Baptism, or as though it were no Baptism at all, although you confess that it is one, the same, and not different.

For these are your own words: that we and you have one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance.

## CHAPTER VIII

**10.** Therefore, if a member of the party of Donatus subscribed to your writings and then considered without insane obstinacy or shamelessness what you and I have said, he would neither think nor say anything further against us.

But since it is you to whom I am replying, I think that you now see for yourself that I spoke not from a desire to accuse, but to refute the destructive fallacy, when I called the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics by that name.

Of these four words, or names—for this pleases either you or the art of grammar—I correct and alter the first, which is *Donatistarum*, and say *Donatianorum*. But the remaining three, since by now, as I think, you perceive that they have been spoken with complete truth, correct and change yourselves.

Change and correct, I say, “the sacrilegious error of the Donatians”—or whatever else you may wish to be called—yet [remain] heretics in sacrilegious error. For you are heretics either because you have remained in an old schism, or, according to your definition, because you follow something different concerning the Church, which is the body of Christ, or concerning the repetition of Christian Baptism.

And it is a sacrilegious error not only to separate from Christian unity but also to violate and sever the Sacraments which, according to your own confession, are one and the same.

But if you correct and alter these things, how do we receive you as you were? Thus you have spoken at length to no purpose; and although you possess such a keen intellect, you have been dulled by the habit of listening to vanity, so that it seems to you that when people pass over to us from your party, we receive them as they were.

For we approve in them the Christian tradition which neither those who had become alienated had alienated, nor those who had become perverse had perverted. You too, although you are not such as we are, were nevertheless unable to confess these Sacraments as anything other than what they are—not as though they were similar to others, but as altogether the same.

## CHAPTER IX

**11.** I beg you, tell me: how is someone “as he was” who venerates the Church that he used to blaspheme; who holds the unity that he did not hold; who possesses the charity that he did not possess; who accepts the peace that he rejected; who approves the Sacrament that he used to exorcise?

Or have all things been so perversely confused between false and true that those in whom what had been different is corrected in accordance with truth are not said to have been changed, while those in whom what had been similar and one and the same is repeated in vanity are said to have been changed?

Do not continue, in this matter, to think not only carnally but childishly, imagining that we receive from you people just as they were. Through a change of will, they pass from error to truth, from division to unity, from dissension to peace, from enmity to charity, and from human presumption to the authority of the divine Scriptures. They do not begin to be ours before they have ceased to be yours.

This change of will suddenly transformed not only the sinner at the tax booth (Matt. 9:9), but also the criminal on the cross. Unless you suppose that Christ would have wished a bloodstained and criminal man to be with him in paradise if that conversion of the heart had not immediately made him innocent, so that on that very day, from that place and from that tree, he might pass to the immortal reward of faith [Note: [Col. 0473] The Louvain editors write concerning this passage: “The blessedness of just souls, consisting in the vision of God—for that alone is the immortal reward of faith—is therefore not postponed until the final day of judgment.”], on which he had received the punishment of death for his iniquity (Luke 23:40–43).

Whether the mind is changed toward evil or toward good, the change takes place in a brief moment; but what it merits is not therefore something small. Even in bodily and temporal punishments and benefits, a single stroke kills an age that has been long sustained, and an illness of thirty-eight years was healed as soon as the Lord deigned to command it (John 5:5–9).

Believe in established realities [Note: [Col. 0473] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Believe certainly in realities.”], not in empty words. Your people pass over to us changed; God forbid that they should be the same as they were. Would that you too might do this, and believe in yourself how true this is.

## CHAPTER X

**12.** You seemed to yourself to be saying something important when you mentioned Candidus of Villaregia and Donatus of Macomades, who, although they had been bishops among your people, were also bishops among us and, with their lives approved, attained the more honorable merit of old age [Note: [Col. 0473] The printed editions have *honorabilis*; from the manuscripts we have substituted *honorabilius*.].

You speak as though the Sacraments and the invocation of God’s name performed among you were themselves hostile to us, although even among those who are outside the Church there is nothing that is not, in some sense, of the Church.

In this question, if I were struggling on the basis of my own words, I would be assisted by yours. For if you believed that nothing ecclesiastical could exist outside the Church, you would not yourself have said that we and you have one religion, the same Sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance.

I do not wholly agree with these words of yours. You lack the Christian Church, and you do not possess Christian charity. Yet I recognize Christian Sacraments among you, and in these I condemn and reject that other difference: that although you possess the same Sacraments even in schism, you exorcise those same Sacraments in Catholics.

The whole Church recognizes in you everything that belongs to her. Nor are these things therefore not hers because they are also found among you. Among you they are alien; but when the Church, whose they are, receives you after you have been corrected, those things which you perniciously possessed as alien become, beneficially, yours as well.

Discord possesses you under the title of peace. Therefore let discord be expelled and peace introduced. Why should the title be laid aside?

“He is a bishop,” you say; “you receive a bishop.” “He is a presbyter;” you receive a presbyter.

You could also say to me: “He is a human being; you receive a human being.” For I recognize Christian Sacraments in him just as I recognize human limbs; and I do not care through whom they were sown, but by whom they were created.

If he wishes to use them badly, he becomes evil precisely because he offends the Creator through His good gifts. But if he begins to use them well, he corrects himself; he does not change those gifts.

## CHAPTER XI

**13.** The reception of bishops and clergy is another question. Although, when they are ordained among you, the name of Donatus rather than God is not invoked over them, they are nevertheless received in whatever way seems to accord with the peace and usefulness of the Church [Note: [Col. 0474] See the Council of Carthage of the year 401, on September 13.].

For we are not bishops for our own sake, but for the sake of those to whom we administer the word and Sacrament of the Lord. Accordingly, as the necessity of governing them without scandal requires, so we ought either to be or not to be what we are—not for our own sake, but because we exist for others.

Finally, some men endowed with holy humility, because of certain obstacles in themselves that affected them piously and religiously, laid down the office of bishop not only without blame but even with praise.

Would they likewise lay down the Christian name and faith commendably rather than condemnably? Just as there may be just reasons for someone to decline becoming a bishop when accepting such offices, so there can be no similarly just reason for anyone to decline becoming a Christian.

Why is this so, unless it is because we can be saved without the episcopate or the clerical office, but cannot be saved without the Christian religion?

## CHAPTER XII

**14.** Therefore your bishops or any of your clergy, insofar as ecclesiastical offices themselves are concerned, were received into Catholic unity in whatever manner seemed expedient to those whose salvation was being served by the decision either to exercise or to omit their office [Note: [Col. 0474] Book 2 against Parmenianus, §§27–28.].

Nevertheless, concerning those who administered the same offices among us, can you say, as you did, “He is a bishop; you receive a bishop,” and then also say, “He is a heretic; you receive a heretic,” or “He is a schismatic; you receive a schismatic,” or “He is a Donatian; you receive a Donatian”?

These names distinguish not a rank of honor from plebeian status, but the guilt of error from Catholic truth.

Accordingly, those things which, as ecclesiastical offices, are found even among aliens are, when those who leave you and pass over to us become ours, either received or not received for the benefit of the peoples whom we serve through this administration [Note: [Col. 0474] The printed editions had omitted: “are either received or not received.” It is restored from the manuscripts.]. But those things that are vicious and properly yours are healed, corrected, and changed.

At the same time, those Sacraments without which a person cannot become a Christian are treated even among heretics in such a way that, when they come to the Church, what is lacking is added and what is recognized is approved. We must not, while being excessively offended by the evils they produced against the Church, also persecute the good things that they carried away when they departed from the Church.

For even if a broken branch is to be grafted in again, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:23), the root is restored to it; its form is not changed.

**45.** “But,” you say, “because you call our people heretics and sacrilegious, which is a wicked and inexpiable crime, surely such people ought not, and cannot, be forgiven without some expiation. Why, then,” you ask, “do you not purify the person who comes? Why do you not first wash and cleanse him, and then communicate with him?”

What if, from these very words of yours, someone else were to say much more appropriately that such people so greatly neither ought nor can be forgiven, and were to show that you have spoken in contradiction with yourself—namely, that you said that such people must be forgiven with some expiation because what is charged against them is an inexpiable crime?

How, then, is what is inexpiable expiated? How can I hope that you will listen to what I say, when, so close at hand, you do not yourself listen to what you say, since you immediately contradict yourself by judging that what you have called inexpiable must be expiated?

We, however, call your error heretical and sacrilegious without calling it inexpiable. Otherwise, it would be pointless for us to judge that we must deal with you, by whatever means we can, so that, abandoning it and being corrected, you may pass over to the Catholic Church.

Nor should you imagine, as you write, that we are using your word, as though we were saying that this evil is without forgiveness and without a physician. We say nothing of the kind, since those who repent of this evil deserve forgiveness, and the physician is almighty who says through the prophet: “If you turn back and groan, then you will be saved” (Ezek. 18).

Therefore, if perhaps you encountered someone who was less instructed in these matters or less attentive to what he was saying, although he seemed to belong to Catholic communion, and if he said this to you, let that person rather deserve forgiveness for this thoughtless expression.

So may you, who are so liberally educated and not moderately skilled in the art of words, deserve forgiveness because, although attentive to what you say less than you should be, you judge that what you called inexpiable must be expiated—and, more monstrous still, that it must be expiated because it is inexpiable.

It is not Catholic to urge people to be saved by correcting their error when we assert that they are erring inexpiably and incurably [Note: [Col. 0475] The printed editions have *asserimus errare*; the manuscripts have *asseremus errare*.].

But the reason you think that they are not cleansed when they pass over to us from your party is that they are not baptized again—as though people were cleansed from error by Baptism alone, although Baptism ought not to be repeated when it is one and the same.

They are cleansed also by the word of truth, by him who says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3).

They are cleansed also by the sacrifice of a contrite heart, by him of whom it is said: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19).

They are cleansed also by almsgiving, by him who says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

They are cleansed also by that charity which surpasses all things, by him who said through the Apostle Peter: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). When this alone is present, all those things are rightly done; but when it is absent, all are done in vain.

Now hear from the Apostle where this charity comes from: “The charity of God,” he says, “has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Hence those who have received the Church’s Baptism outside the Church are rightly believed not to possess the Holy Spirit unless they cling to the bond of peace with the Church itself through the connection of charity.

## CHAPTER XIII

**16.** Now the time has come to show what we had postponed in the first book [at the final section], namely, what can properly be received in the Church, which cannot be received outside her.

Concerning those who made schisms, the same Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Read the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and you will find this.

Baptism, therefore, is the Sacrament of new life and eternal salvation. Many possess it not for eternal life but for eternal punishment, because they do not use so great a good well.

But holy charity, which is the bond of perfection, no evil person can possess; and no one who possesses it can be either a schismatic or a heretic.

When someone comes to the unity of the Church and is truly joined to her members, he receives the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts. That same charity covers a multitude of sins, so that he may now deserve to possess for reward the Baptism that he previously possessed for judgment.

How, then, can you deny that he is cleansed, unless you are entirely ignorant of what spiritual cleansing is?

We do not, as you slanderously claim, receive your guilty people as though into Romulus’ asylum. The city of God makes them innocent by receiving them when they pass over to it with a truthful heart; its founder says of it: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14).

For it was not founded by the one who, in proud anger, killed his brother, but by the one who, having been killed, humbly redeemed his brothers.

The Holy Spirit cleanses and gladdens this city. Concerning him Christ cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7:37). He was not commending the visible water given in the Sacrament of Baptism, which both good and evil can possess, although without it the good cannot be saved.

Although this water belongs to the Church, it also flows outside, since it is found among those who went out from us but were not of us (1 John 2:19). Just as, in the case of one of those famous four rivers, it cannot be denied that the water is water from paradise, although it is not found in paradise alone—for it also flowed out from there.

## CHAPTER XIV

**17.** He was therefore commending not this water, but, under the name of water, the holy invisible gift of God, the Holy Spirit, when he said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink.” The Evangelist clearly confirms this by adding: “Now he said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37, 39).

Insofar as the Sacrament of visible washing is concerned, before he had been glorified by rising again, he had already baptized more people than John, as the Gospel itself states (John 4:1).

Therefore he says to his disciples: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also going to receive not many days from now,” at Pentecost (Acts 1:5).

When this Holy Spirit came upon them, he first gave such a sign that those who received him spoke in the languages of all nations (Acts 2:1–4), because he foretold that the Church would exist among all nations and that no one would receive the Holy Spirit except one who was joined to her unity.

By the broad and invisible river of this fountain God gladdens his city, concerning which the Prophet foretold: “The force of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45:5).

No outsider approaches this fountain, for no one approaches it except one worthy of eternal life. This is the fountain proper to the Church of Christ, concerning which it was prophesied long beforehand: “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you” (Prov. 5:17).

For concerning this Church and this fountain it is said also in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain, a well of living water” (Song 4:12).

## CHAPTER XV

**18.** Your people, taking these words as referring to the Sacrament of visible Baptism, are so greatly mistaken that they are forced, against their will, to admit the most absurd conclusions: namely, that Simon Magus, whom we read was baptized by Philip (Acts 8:13), could approach that fountain which belongs to the one dove, concerning which it was said, “Let no stranger share it with you”; and could approach the enclosed garden and sealed well [Note: [Col. 0477] The printed editions add *vivum*, “living,” here; but the manuscripts do not, nor do the scriptural passages in question, namely Proverbs 5 and Song of Songs 4, to which Augustine refers.].

So too could approach it all the hypocrites concerning whom Cyprian speaks with a groan: “Renouncing the world in words alone and not in deeds”; and all the greedy bishops concerning whom he likewise testifies: “Seizing estates by deceitful frauds, multiplying interest, and increasing usury” (*Letter or Sermon on the Lapsed*).

Such people are found among those who have been baptized and who baptize with visible Baptism [Note: [Col. 0477] Several manuscripts: “For these baptized people and those baptizing are found with visible baptism.”].

Yet no one among them approaches that proper fountain to which no stranger has access—that sealed fountain, namely the gift of the Holy Spirit through whom the charity of God is poured into our hearts—unless he has been changed. He must be cleansed altogether, so that he is no longer a stranger but a participant in heavenly peace, a companion of holy unity, full of undivided charity, and a citizen of the angelic city.

Whoever, therefore, turns toward this city after laying aside the error of heresy or schism, with his conduct corrected and his mind devout—if he already carried the Sacraments, which could flow outside even to the unworthy—has those Sacraments honored in him, because they do not appear alien even in aliens.

But he is now cleansed by that proper fountain to which no stranger has access, by that sealed fountain of the Holy Spirit. Among you, anyone who is otherwise praiseworthy in conduct is separated from it solely by the crime of schism or heresy.

## CHAPTER XVI

**19.** When your people therefore come to us, ceasing to be yours and beginning to be ours, they receive what they did not have, so that they may begin beneficially to possess what they had possessed all the more perniciously because they possessed it unworthily.

First they receive the Church herself, and in her peace, charity, and unity, through her proper fountain, the invisible Holy Spirit. Without these, they would unquestionably have perished, regardless of whatever else they had possessed among you that could be carried outside from the Church.

They receive what they had not yet possessed with an easier pardon than if they had possessed it and nevertheless abandoned it.

Among us this distinction is maintained, so that those who abandoned the Catholic Church are received differently from those who come to her for the first time. The former are more heavily burdened by the crime of desertion; the latter are relieved by the bond of unity—not a bond torn by them, but one recognized and retained.

Hence it can happen that those whom they rebaptized after seducing them may themselves pray to the Lord on behalf of these repentant people, if the latter have first been reconciled to the Church before the former are reconciled.

Likewise, it can happen that even worshipers of idols, if they have perhaps seduced Christians to idols and made them apostates, may—if the seducers first become Christians and acquire some great merit in the Church—be the means through which those whom they deceived return, are commended, and are reconciled to the Lord: through those by whom they had abandoned the Lord.

What rightly received Sacrament of Baptism accomplishes in cleansing the sacrileges of the Gentiles, truly grasped charity of unity accomplishes in cleansing the sacrileges of schismatics and heretics.

Therefore, just as seducers of Christian believers who come to Christ are placed before the seduced when the seduced return—so that the former can become bishops while the latter cannot [Note: [Col. 0478] See Letter 245, vol. 2]—so those deceived by heretics should not be surprised, when they return to the Catholic Church, that their deceivers are placed before them when the deceivers come to the Catholic Church.

The latter more excusably seek what was lacking to them; the former more humbly seek again what they once were. We summon the former more honorably to where they had not previously stood; the latter we recall with greater suspicion from where they had fallen.

**20.** Accordingly, as I think, you now clearly see that I did not say without reason “the sacrilegious error of the Donatist—or, as you prefer, Donatian—heretics” (*At the beginning of Book 1 against the Letters of Petilianus*, §1), since you dissent from the Catholic Church and sever the Sacraments that you confess to be one and the same.

Yet you are not without forgiveness, nor are you incurable before the mercy of God. For when you lay aside your discordant error and turn toward Catholic truth and peace, you will be able to be cleansed and healed through his proper gift, namely his Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts.

This does not mean that the Sacraments of the Church are destroyed in you—the Sacraments that, while alien, you perniciously possessed outside—but that you may now beneficially possess within the Church those same Sacraments as your own.

## CHAPTER XVII

**21.** Let us now see how you show that Petilianus, or anyone else, rightly said: “The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is considered, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient.”

I said: “But what if the conscience of the giver is hidden and perhaps stained? How can it cleanse the conscience of the recipient?” (*Ibid.*, §2).

In reply, you spoke at length—not about what you, as an intelligent man, say, but about what your people say. It can all be stated briefly as follows:

“The conscience of the giver is considered, not according to its sincerity, which cannot be seen in it, but according to the reputation that surrounds it, whether that reputation is true or false. For he is a person who, even if secretly wicked, is sufficient for the recipient because he enjoys a good reputation: he has not yet been known, judged, or separated from the Church.”

Consider, I beg you, into what precipice the anxiety of people unable to find a way out has driven them [Col. 0479]. Can a giver’s stained conscience cleanse the recipient’s conscience if the giver has a good reputation? And can it cleanse only to the extent that his reputation is good, if he acquired a good reputation through deception?

Do you pay attention to what is being said and wish us now to pass over this point, or shall I continue to turn it over so that you may be compelled to attend more carefully?

Petilianus said: “The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is considered, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient.”

I said: “But what if the conscience of the giver is hidden and perhaps stained? How can it cleanse the conscience of the recipient?”

You—or rather, your people—for you, as the man you are, would not have said such things—replied:

“Although he has a stained conscience, it is enough for me, who am baptized by him, that because it is hidden and I do not know it, I receive from one whose innocent conscience I suppose him to have because he is in the Church.

“For this reason,” you say, “I consider the conscience of the giver—not so that I may judge what cannot be judged, namely hidden things, but so that, if anything about him is present in public awareness, I may not be ignorant of it.”

For this reason the Almighty God said: “The things that are known are for you; the things that are hidden are for me” (Deut. 29:29).

Therefore I always consider the conscience of the giver. Since I do not see the conscience itself, I inquire what is publicly known about it. It is irrelevant if one thing exists in his secret conscience and another in the public reputation surrounding him. It is enough to know that the conscience of the one from whom I receive has not yet been condemned.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**22.** Here I have set out your own words, by which I showed that you say what I briefly and clearly summarized: that the conscience of the one who cleanses is considered so that what reputation surrounds it may be known.

The conscience itself, therefore, is not considered, my good man; it is not the conscience itself that is considered, since it cannot be seen. What is considered is the reputation, which can also be false, as you yourself confess and admit.

For you too have seen that a stained conscience cannot cleanse. Therefore it is not the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is considered and cleanses the recipient’s conscience; rather, it is the reputation by which even one who does not give in holiness is thought to give in holiness, and by which one who does not cleanse is thought to cleanse.

Thus the good reputation of an evil man cleanses the recipient, not the polluted conscience of the giver himself.

Why, then, was it said, “The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is considered, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient,” unless it is because the recipient is not cleansed if the conscience of the giver is not holy?

If it is stained and unclean, what, then, is considered? “The conscience itself,” you say, “is considered when his reputation is considered. And if his reputation is good, it makes no difference for cleansing the recipient even when the conscience is evil; his good reputation cleanses him.”

Tell me, I beg you: when his conscience is evil, is his good reputation true or false? Without doubt, it is false.

Therefore, when the giver’s conscience is not good and is hidden, however much you may seem to consider it according to this opinion, it does not cleanse the recipient—unless the giver possesses either a false reputation or a polluted conscience.

Both alternatives are insane. If such things delight you, choose which is the more insane.

Since truth does not permit either the giver’s false reputation or his polluted conscience to cleanse the recipient’s conscience, it remains for us to ask you what we asked there as well. For, as Petilianus—or anyone else with your agreement—says, when the conscience of the one who gives in holiness is present, that is, when it is good and clean, it cleanses the conscience of the recipient.

By whom, then, is the recipient cleansed when the giver’s stained conscience is hidden?

I do not think you will now repeat and say that his false good reputation supplies the place of a good conscience in cleansing. You asserted that your people, not you, say this. Let them be ashamed of it, not you as well.

It remains, then, that in such a case God or some holy angel cleanses.

If you say this, the dreadful absurdity follows that I mentioned in that letter of mine (*Book 1 against the Letters of Petilianus*, §7)—not that you were unwilling to see it, since you did not touch upon it at all, but that you saw it the more attentively and keenly because you feared to touch upon it.

For if you say that when a holy man baptizes, his holy conscience washes the recipient’s conscience, but when the giver’s conscience is secretly unclean, God or an angel washes it, take care lest those who believe you when you say these things should wish to find hidden wicked men from whom they may be baptized, so that they may be washed much more holily by God himself or by his angel.

When you saw this absurdity, either to be mocked or detested, following from Petilianus’ preceding words and consequently recalled by me in my letter [Note: [Col. 0480] Erasmus and Louvain read “with the preceding words”; *in* is superfluous and is absent from Amiens and the manuscripts.], you cautiously acted as though I had said none of these things and thought that so important a matter should be passed over in silence.

But you fled to something even more absurd: when the giver’s stained conscience is hidden and therefore cannot cleanse the recipient, the recipient is cleansed by the giver’s false reputation, so that falsity produces truth in him.

**23.** Now go and slanderously accuse the dialecticians, claiming that by the evasiveness of their speech they bring it about that, if something is false, it is true, and if it is true, it is false.

Look: you yourself introduce something of this sort into the Sacraments of Christian regeneration—indeed, something worse and more deserving of avoidance.

The dialecticians say of certain expressions—not in their own fraud or in the truth of things, but in the ambiguity of human speech—that they appear true when they are false and false when they are true. When such expressions arise in discussion, the mind distinguishes them, even if they cannot be dissolved by speech.

You, however, say that not just any word or any thing, but the very true cleansing of the conscience through which we are reborn to eternal life, can be effected in a person by the false reputation of another’s conscience.

And lest this be attributed to you because you have studied dialectic, you say that it is the opinion of your people. To this opinion you have agreed not as a dialectician, but plainly as a heretic.

Thus, whether through you or through your people, this magnificent doctrine has been discovered or demonstrated:

“When the conscience of the giver who gives in holiness is good, the one baptized is made good by it; then the good tree bears good fruit” (Matt. 7:17) [Note: [Col. 0480] All our manuscripts read: “then he is made good for it.” Perhaps this is better than “by it.”]. But when the giver’s conscience is evil and hidden, his good reputation—which is false—is consulted, so that a person receives true Baptism from one who deceives precisely when he has believed something false about that person.

And thus, lest there be no mother to bear the fruit of heretical error, falsity becomes the mother of truth.

All this is so detestable, so astonishingly perverse and insane, for the purpose of preventing what belongs to God from being said to belong to God. What is received from God must instead be attributed to human beings, lest the person who said, “The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is considered, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient,” appear to have erred.

## CHAPTER XIX

**24.** “Our people,” you say, “prove this from the Scriptures, since Judas the betrayer, before he was condemned, performed everything as an apostle.”

What does this have to do with Petilianus’ fixed and definite statement, “The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is considered, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient,” except that Judas himself is exceedingly much against you when you try to provide support for your position from words carelessly spoken by another?

When Judas baptized as an apostle—for he was evil, since he was a thief and took away what was placed in the money box entrusted to him—his conscience was certainly not considered. Rather, God and Christ were considered, in whom belief was placed.

Nor did that evil man’s falsely good reputation cleanse believing recipients [Note: [Col. 0481] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *falso* rather than *falsa*.] [Note: [Col. 0481] The printed editions read “cleanse believing and receiving persons”; *and* is to be deleted in accordance with the manuscripts.]; nor did human opinion’s falsity generate in a person the grace of divine truth.

### 25

And that testimony which you produced from the Scriptures—“The things that are manifest belong to you; but the things that are hidden belong to the Lord your God” (Deut. 29:29)—refutes and disproves this argument. For if what is hidden must be left to the Lord God, how is the conscience of the giver—when it is hidden—not only in the case of evil but also of good, taken into account so that it may cleanse the conscience of the recipient?
