Or, if it is not taken into account when it is hidden, what then do you command the recipient to take into account, from which his conscience may be cleansed?

## CHAPTER XX

Wake up at last; say now, at least, “Let him take God into account.” Why are you afraid that you will be humbled if you glory not in man but in the Lord? “There is something I should fear,” you say. “For if, when the giver’s conscience is hidden, I say that the recipient should take God into account, and confess that his conscience is then cleansed by Him, I am confronted by this dreadful absurdity: people would be cleansed more holily when they have wicked baptizers whose wickedness is hidden than when they have good baptizers whose goodness is manifest—if man cleanses when the giver’s conscience is good and manifest, but God cleanses when it is evil and hidden.”

Say, then, what we say, because this is true, sound, and catholic: Christ cleanses the consciences of the recipients, whether through good ministers of his Baptism or through evil ones, since it is written of him: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word” (Eph. 5:25–26).

### 26

“You,” you say, “answer how those whom the Church has condemned can baptize.” You have therefore now departed from Petilian’s words. For when he says, “The conscience of the holy giver is taken into account, and it cleanses the recipient,” and I asked who cleanses the recipient’s conscience when the giver’s polluted conscience is hidden, no answer could be given me. It is just as contrary to truth to say that the giver’s false reputation can cleanse as it would be to say that the evil conscience itself could do so.

## CHAPTER XXI

But if you ask, “How do those whom the Church has condemned baptize?” I answer that they baptize in the same way as those whom God has condemned baptize, before the Church had judged anything concerning them. Whoever appears inwardly to belong to the Church while actually remaining outside has already been judged by Christ himself. For he says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). The apostle Paul, however, says: “The Church is subject to Christ” (Eph. 5:24). Therefore the Church ought not to place itself above Christ, supposing that those judged by him can baptize, but those judged by the Church cannot—since he always judges truly, whereas ecclesiastical judges, being human, are often deceived.

Accordingly, insofar as the visible ministry is concerned, both good and evil men baptize; but invisibly, it is he who baptizes through them, whose are both the visible Baptism and the invisible grace. Good and evil men can therefore perform the washing, but no one except him who is always good can cleanse the conscience.

Thus, even though the Church does not know it, those condemned by Christ because of an evil and polluted conscience are no longer in the body of Christ, which is the Church, since Christ cannot have condemned members. Consequently, they too baptize outside the Church. Far be it altogether that all these monsters should be counted among the members of that one dove; far be it that they should be able to enter the boundaries of the enclosed garden, whose guardian is he who cannot be deceived.

Yet if they confess and are corrected, then they enter; then they are cleansed; then they are counted among the trees of the enclosed garden and among the members of the one dove—and nevertheless they are not baptized again. So also, when they come from heretics with the very Baptism which they possessed outside, but not with the cleansing itself which they receive within, what was lacking is supplied, while what had not been changed is approved.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 27

“Your conscience,” you say, “has been condemned through your predecessors on the charge of betrayal and incense-offering, and through yourselves on the charge of persecution.”

As for the betrayers and incense-offerers—whoever they were who committed this sacrilege—you trusted not the Holy Scriptures but human reputation. But if a false good reputation can arise concerning evil men, why could not an evil reputation also arise concerning good men?

As for persecution, I shall answer you briefly once more with what I answered Petilian—an answer which you were completely unable to refute (Book 1 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, §20).  
[Note: The printed editions read “you were able”; the manuscripts, “you were able” (singular).] In Holy Scripture, which deceives no one, the Church of God is called a threshing floor; and the Lord himself is said to come with a winnowing fork and cleanse his threshing floor, gathering the grain into the granary but burning the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12).

Either, then, you rightly suffered persecution; or, if there was excess beyond the Christian measure, our chaff caused it—the chaff because of which the Lord’s threshing floor ought not to have been abandoned, lest anyone, before the time of winnowing, flee from the chaff on the threshing floor and, separated from the grain, become chaff himself.

But when you attempted to refute not my testimony but that of Holy Scripture, you said that no persecution could ever be just. Here you must be forgiven because you do not know the Scriptures, from which you might have recalled how justly it is said: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. 101:5). And by the Lord Jesus Christ himself, in a most exalted prophecy: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are consumed” (Ps. 18:38).

There are many other divine testimonies, to pursue which would be lengthy—provided, of course, that you do not slander me because of this expression, so that, since I said “it would be lengthy to pursue,” you accuse me of persecuting the divine testimonies.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 28

You oppose me with scriptural words whose repeated demonstration has shown how little they help your case: “The oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head” (Ps. 141:5). Yet you cannot deny that there are at least hidden sinners among you, and that they nevertheless baptize; nor are such men excluded by these words. For it does not say, “The oil of a manifest sinner,” but simply, “The oil of a sinner.”

And also: “They have become for me like deceptive water that has no faith” (Jer. 15:18).  
[Note: The Amsterdam and Erfurt editions read, “like deceptive water of a hidden pretender, whose false reputation has no end.” The Louvain editors corrected “end” to “faith,” while retaining the gloss; this gloss has been rejected on manuscript authority.]

Here I marvel at your judgment: how can deceptive water fail to seem to you the water of a hidden pretender, whose false reputation you believed could contribute something to the cleansing of another’s conscience? Unless you thought that the following was available to assist you—the not dialectical but plainly sophistical argument which you unsuccessfully reproached me with as though it were dialectical: “If you lie, you speak the truth.”  
[Note: Concerning this and similar sophisms of Chrysippus, see Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book 4.]

For what else are you trying to assert when, attributing Baptism to a man, though you do not wish to acknowledge that it belongs to God, you say that an adulterer can give true Baptism because, by concealing himself, he falsely claims to be chaste? Thus he speaks the truth in Baptism when he lies in his crime; and his water is not deceptive—the water which you want to exist in the Church according to the promise of so many prophecies, spread throughout the whole world.

Yet Jeremiah called not Baptism “deceptive water,” but deceptive men, according to the meaning that is clear in the Apocalypse.  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “which has been made clear.”] There, when John asked what the waters shown in the vision represented, the answer was that they were peoples (Rev. 17:15).

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 29

But concerning that testimony which is written, “What benefit is there in the washing of one who is baptized by a dead man?” (Ecclus. 34:30), consider briefly how you failed to understand what I wrote in that letter, and how much you have assisted me by your own words.

You thought that by “dead man” I meant here a worshiper of idols, as though I had exempted only such people from being able to baptize. Then, repeating the testimony about the oil as much as you could, you chose to say that the one who declared, “The oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head,” intended that no sinner should baptize, without exempting any sinner. This places you under still greater pressure, as I showed shortly before.

For if no sinner is exempted, then rebaptize those baptized by hidden evil men when those men have been convicted. At this point you will try to exempt the hidden sinner whom Holy Scripture did not exempt. Thus your entire interpretation is proved false by the truth, since it is shown equally to contradict your own intention.

For the Psalm does not in fact speak here about Baptism, but about the flattery of a sycophant; the preceding words make this sufficiently clear. The whole sentence is connected as follows: “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and reprove me; but the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.” He therefore preferred that his head be bruised by one who truthfully rebuked him rather than anointed by one who deceitfully flattered him—the words “oil” and “anointing” being used metaphorically to signify the smoothness of a flatterer.

## CHAPTER XXV

### 30

What I thought in that letter concerning this testimony, where it says, “He who is baptized by a dead man,” I shall show sufficiently, I think, by repeating the very words from it.

When I was explaining what a catholic Christian ought to answer to this statement, I said: “When he hears, ‘He who is baptized by a dead man, his washing does not benefit him,’ he will answer: ‘Christ lives, and he no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him’ (Rom. 6:9); and of him it is said, ‘He is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’ (John 1:33).

“Those are baptized by the dead who are baptized in temples of idols. For they do not think that they receive from their priests the sanctification they imagine, but from their gods. Since these gods were human beings and died in such a way that they live neither upon earth nor in the rest of the saints, these people are truly baptized by the dead.”

Thus far I have transcribed the exact words from my letter. In them, as I think you now perceive—if you are at least attentive this time—I did not call the worshipers themselves dead, although they too are dead in another sense. Rather, I was speaking of the false gods whom they worship, because they were human beings, departed from the body as human beings do, neither rose again, nor possessed any merit of the life promised after this life.

They are therefore baptized by those very gods—truly baptized by the dead, as I said—that is, those who are baptized in their name. For they too think that they are sanctified not in the name of their priests but of the gods concerning whom they hold vain beliefs.

Christ, however, rose again and lives. Therefore whoever is baptized by him—even through a wicked minister of ruined morals—is not baptized by a dead man. He is baptized by the one who lives forever, of whom it is said in the Gospel, as I also mentioned there: “He is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 31

You did not understand this in my letter, as your words indicate. I do not wish to say that, through lack of understanding, you wished to deceive. But I am surprised that you did not notice the words of mine that followed there, or thought that you could disregard them.

A little later I added and said: “For if in this passage I understand ‘dead man’ as a sinful baptizer, the same absurdity will follow: whoever has been baptized even by a hidden ungodly man has been washed in vain, as though he had been baptized by a dead man. For it does not say, ‘He who is baptized by a manifest dead man,’ but simply, ‘by a dead man’” (Book 1 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, §10).

What exposure of my words there would not have awakened someone from sleep—or rather, from death itself? Yet it did not awaken you. Moreover, what I had said against Petilian, you confirmed even more forcefully as though you were saying it against me, just as people who do not know how to remove an arrow that has been shot at them often drive it deeper and more firmly into themselves.

You asserted that “dead man” must be understood only as a sinful baptizer, and that no sinner was to be excepted. Consequently, what I was saying is concluded against you: the hidden sinner cannot be excepted when no one is excepted.

Therefore rebaptize those whom it is established were baptized by hidden sinners, since help can be given to them while they are living and known; so that only those who are either unknown or have already died may be harmed, since, once the evil of their baptizers is subsequently exposed, they can no longer be baptized.

“Baptize,” I say, “those whose baptism by an adulterer while he was hidden has been established after he has been exposed and condemned.” For you have said that those baptized by a dead man are baptized by every sinner without exception, who cannot baptize, adding the testimony about the sinner’s oil. You said it; you wrote it. Listen to yourself; read yourself.

If every sinner, as a dead man, cannot baptize, neither can the hidden sinner. He is not alive merely because he is hidden, since he has been swallowed up even more deeply by the lie of his pretense. He would be called less dead if he at least confessed. But what is written elsewhere happens in him: “From a dead man, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26).

Those who are shown to have been baptized by this dead man, submerged in such a depth of death, you do not rebaptize. Yet you do not hesitate to rebaptize those baptized by people in the remotest lands who have never heard the name of Caecilianus, Majorinus, or Donatus, throwing at them the words, “What benefit is there in the washing of one who is baptized by a dead man?” You call dead those to whom no breath could have come from any African corpses, whoever they may have been, while you do not consider dead the one who can conceal his own crime—even though Scripture cries out, “From a dead man, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes.”

Is he not dead because he is pretending? Indeed, because of that very pretense, having been deprived of the spirit of life, he has expired completely, as Scripture says again: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the pretender” (Wis. 1:5). Continue defending these dead men and call them living, so that by this false defense you yourselves may die even more grievously.

### 32

“They are dead,” you say; “but what was the person seeking Baptism to do when he approached them unknowingly?”

Let him do so now, when, after the man has been exposed, he recognizes that he was baptized by a dead man. If his conscience could not be harmed because he did not know, it now begins to be harmed because he knows. It is like someone who unknowingly wore a garment obtained by robbery: from the moment he learns of it, that garment becomes a garment of iniquity, and he himself becomes wicked unless he casts it off. Likewise, one who unknowingly married another man’s wife becomes an adulterer from the moment he learns of it, unless he withdraws from her.

Let this man, then, cast off the Baptism which he has learned he received from a dead man. For he still has something he can do: he can be baptized again.

Finally, whether he knew or did not know, “Baptized by a dead man, what benefit is there in his washing?” “The sentence is strict,” as you yourself proclaim; “it exempts no one: ‘He was baptized by a dead man,’ I say; ‘his washing benefits him nothing.’”

Cleanse the man by baptizing him—you who are alive—or rather cleanse yourselves from this error, lest you perish by holding such opinions. For you contend as though against me that no one is excepted in what is written, “The oil of the sinner” (Ps. 141:5), and “He who is baptized by a dead man.” You do not realize that, by resisting, you are tightening the knot by which you are bound.

This is precisely what I am doing and pressing: from this point I am driving you urgently toward changing your vain and perverse opinion—that in the oil of the sinner and in the Baptism of the dead, no dead man and no sinner is excepted, just as you speak on my behalf while seeming to speak against me.

Thus the hidden sinner too is not excepted. By this, everything you say is overturned, and those who have taught you such things are compelled to rebaptize all whom they can find in this life to have been baptized by hidden evil men.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### 33

What are you doing? Where will you turn? Your own words are being recited to you. For not only did you fail to refute them when I stated them; without knowing that you had chosen words of mine, you yourself said the same thing in other words as though it were your own. And so that it might be heard and considered more carefully, you wrote it down, so that it could be recited to you as often as you wished.

Listen, then, to your own words. They are these:

“But if,” you say, “you are so determined to except only the worshiper of an idol, what of the statement, ‘I do not want the oil of the sinner to anoint my head’? Is the sinner here also only the one who worships an idol, or anyone who does what is unlawful? And if you think that only the worshiper of an idol is a sinner, then if a Christian does anything against the law, is he not called a sinner? But since nothing more foolish or absurd can be said, it has plainly been declared that not only the worshiper of an idol, but anyone who is a sinner among all human beings, must not claim for himself the right of Baptism.”

These words which I have inserted are certainly yours. I did not except the worshiper of an idol; I said that the gods themselves were dead, and that baptism received from them was of no benefit to anyone. For they seem to themselves to be baptized by those gods, in whose name they believe themselves to be cleansed. But you exempted no sinner.

If, then, “sinner” here must be understood as the mortal man who baptizes, and you exempted no sinner, clearly you did not exempt the hidden sinner either. “It has plainly been declared,” you say, “that not only the worshiper of an idol, but anyone who is a sinner among all human beings, must not claim for himself the right of Baptism.”

Listen to yourself: you said, “Anyone who is a sinner.” You exempted neither the manifest nor the hidden. With what face, then, do those who refuse to rebaptize after a hidden sinner compel rebaptism after a manifest one, when they assert that no one is excepted?

Flee, brother, from this mad interpretation to a sound one, so that in this testimony about the sinner’s oil you may understand, as the preceding words of the same Psalm prescribe, the flattering smoothness of a deceitful flatterer.  
[Note: Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “the deceitfulness of a flatterer.”]

In this way no one will be excepted, and the hidden evil baptizer will not run into insuperable difficulties.

Likewise, in the other testimony where it is said, “He who is baptized by a dead man, what benefit is there in his washing?” either examine the ancient manuscripts carefully, especially the Greek ones, lest the words themselves have been written differently and, from the preceding and following context, suggest another meaning; or else let us understand “the dead” as I said: those in whose name the worshipers of idols are baptized, so that you may understand each person to have been baptized by the one in whose name he believes himself to have been cleansed.

Thus there too no one is excepted, since no dead pagan god can cleanse those who believe in him.

But if in this passage you understand every sinful human being to be dead, such consequences will follow—consequences which you do not want—that you will be unable to discover how you yourself can live. For John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Thus you will find no human being by whom you can be baptized if you wish to avoid every sinner.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 34

Even if you understood “dead man” to mean nothing other than a heretic or schismatic, so that whoever is baptized among them is “baptized by a dead man; what benefit is there in his washing?”—you see how rashly this is accepted, as though it had been said, “Whoever is baptized by a heretic or schismatic.”  
[Note: The Louvain editors suspect that something is missing here, and propose approximately: “so that whoever is baptized among them is baptized by a dead man, of whom Scripture says: ‘He who is baptized by a dead man, what benefit is there …?’”]

Even so, it would not be against us, since we confess that Baptism conferred by Christ benefits a person nothing if he is baptized among heretics or schismatics, while attributing to those persons the Baptism with which he is baptized. It begins to benefit him only when he passes into the body of Christ, which is the Church of the living God.

Then, under the same Baptism—which was Christ’s even outside, though it benefited him nothing while he remained outside—it will benefit him once he has been cleansed by the one whose members he has entered.  
[Note: Two manuscripts read: “it will benefit the cleansed person, not through the one whose hands baptized him, but through the one whose members he has entered.”]

### 35

Nor will I fear that excessively severe statement of yours in which you said, “Anyone who is a sinner among all human beings must not claim for himself the right of Baptism”—unless it is because you cannot find anyone who can truthfully say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), without confessing that he is a sinner.

I should like to question individually those who baptize among you, to ask whether they are entirely without sin. Any one of them could answer me: “I am not a betrayer; I am not an incense-offerer; I am not an adulterer; I am not a murderer; I am not a worshiper of idols; finally, I am not a heretic or a schismatic.”

But “I am not a sinner”—I do not know whether anyone could be found, even with heretical pride, who would dare to say or dare to think this. I do not know whether anyone could be blinded by such a swelling of arrogance that he would not merely profess aloud, but even silently judge within himself, that he has no need of the prayer in which we say to God, “Forgive us our debts.”

For we do not ask that those debts be forgiven which we are confident were forgiven once in Baptism; rather, we ask forgiveness for those without which human frailty does not exist, however watchful we may be in observing the Lord’s commandments.

Finally, let whoever wishes assume the boldness of this shamelessness and say: “I am not a sinner; since everything was forgiven me in Baptism, no sin can be found in me.” I place far greater trust in John, and answer much more confidently: “You deceive yourself, and the truth is not in you.”

This rash and deceptive profession does not bring it about that no sins are found in you, but that the sins which are found are not forgiven.

If, then, you have already been baptized, I should like to know whom you found who, contrary to the apostle John, said, “I have no sin.” For if you were able to find such a person, how were you baptized by one who was deceiving himself and in whom the truth was not present?

But if, mindful of whatever humility he possessed, he said that he was a sinner, how did he, according to your judgment, claim for himself the right of Baptism? You said it; you were not even afraid to write it: “Anyone who is a sinner among all human beings must not claim for himself the right of Baptism.”

But if you have not yet been baptized, either correct this utterly worthless opinion or seek angels by whom you may be baptized.

### 36

But let us suppose that, having been convicted, you corrected yourself and said: “Anyone who is a sinner among all human beings in the crime which our people allege must not claim for himself the right of Baptism.”

This is not against us. For if such a person has claimed this right and has given Baptism, I say that he ought not to have claimed it for himself; I do not say that he did not give it. For the one who received it, if a good man received it from an evil man, a faithful man from an unfaithful man, a pious man from an impious man, the result will be harmful to the giver, not to the recipient.

That which is holy judges the one who uses it badly and sanctifies the one who uses it well.  
[Note: Thus all the manuscripts. The printed editions read “sanctifies the one who receives it well.”]

But if the recipient too received it wickedly, even then the Sacrament is not annulled. Once recognized and corrected, what had been harmful to the perverse person will benefit him.

[Note: The printed editions read, “what was harmful by itself.” This is incorrect, for the Sacrament is beneficial in itself. The reading of two manuscripts, the Cygirannensis and the Georgianus, “what was harmful to the perverse person,” is therefore more accurate.]

## CHAPTER XXIX

### 37

I shall therefore suppose that you meant to say not now, “Anyone who is a sinner”—for, unless I am mistaken, you can now see how rashly that was said—but: “Anyone among all human beings who is the kind of sinner our people describe must not claim for himself the right of Baptism.”

This is like what is written: “But to the sinner God says, ‘Why do you recite my ordinances and take up my covenant upon your mouth?’” And, to show what sort of sinner he was addressing, lest all human beings refrain from proclaiming his word—since they neither dare to think nor to say that they are not sinners—the text continues and describes him:

“But you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue embraced deceit. When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers. You sat and slandered your brother, and you laid a stumbling-block against the son of your mother” (Ps. 50:16–20).

To such a sinner, then, he says: “Why do you recite my ordinances and take up my covenant upon your mouth?” It is as though he said: “You do this in vain. As far as you are concerned, it benefits you nothing; it will serve you for the judgment of condemnation, not for the merit of salvation.”

Nevertheless, if, while such a sinner recites God’s ordinances and takes up his covenant in his mouth, those who hear from his mouth believe, act, and make progress, will they not be praised when he is rejected, justified when he is condemned, and crowned when he is damned? They took care to obey the Lord who says: “What they say, do; but what they do, do not do: for they speak and do not act” (Matt. 23:3).

Therefore, just as this sinner, if he claims for himself the right to preach the divine covenant, benefits himself nothing, while what he preaches benefits those who hear and do it—not he, but what he preaches—so also the man who ought not to have claimed for himself the right of Baptism harms himself because he has wrongly claimed what is good, but does not harm the one who rightly received what is good.

## CHAPTER XXX

### 38

You see that you were not only unable to refute what I said against Petilian, but that what you yourself said against me is refuted in every way by the full light of truth.

You continue and say that we make our case unacceptable, and in some way confess ourselves to be sinners, because when we are asked by what right we claim the right of Baptism, we do not discuss the merit of our actions or the innocence of our life, but say that it is permitted to everyone.

Consider carefully what has been said. We do not say that it is permitted to everyone, but that punishment falls upon the person who handles what is holy unlawfully. Such a person must be corrected; the holy thing which he handles unlawfully must not itself be unlawfully annulled.

This is like our wish to correct people who do not use the law lawfully, without declaring the law itself invalid; and like our reproving the one who takes up God’s covenant unlawfully in his mouth, without denying or tearing up the covenant itself.

Nor do we therefore confess that we have sinned because, in the sinner, we condemn what belongs to him while honoring what belongs to God. We do not want the person who believes in God to depend upon hidden human matters; rather, we admonish him to glory in the Lord, concerning whom he is secure.  
[Note: Several manuscripts read “upon hidden things of human conscience”; the printed editions, “upon hidden things of human beings’ conscience.”]

For the Apostle himself was not distrustful of his own evil conscience, but did not want the hope of the believer to be placed in man; he firmly established it in God when he said: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Therefore, when we say what is written, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 115:1), we are not accusing our own conscience. But because you want the hope of those who are baptized to be placed in the conduct of human beings, you do not recognize your own pride.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### 39

What of the fact that you also dare to mention blessed Cyprian, as though he were the author of your division—he who was so great a defender of catholic unity and peace?

First be in the Church which Cyprian is known to have held and proclaimed; then dare to name Cyprian as though he were the author of your position. First imitate Cyprian’s piety and humility; then produce Cyprian’s council.

We do Cyprian no wrong when we distinguish any of his writings from the canonical authority of the divine Scriptures. For it was not without reason, and with such salutary vigilance, that the ecclesiastical canon was established, assigning certain books of the Prophets and Apostles to it—books which we dare not judge at all, and according to which we freely judge other writings, whether of the faithful or of the unfaithful.

Accordingly, when the Apostle—whose Epistles possess canonical authority—says, “Let all of us who are perfect think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you” (Phil. 3:15), how long did Cyprian think differently, if the writings you believe ought to be produced on your behalf are truly his?  
[Note: Thus the Cygirannensis manuscript; the printed editions read, “has revealed.”] As long, therefore, as he thought differently on this matter from what a more careful consideration of the truth revealed—until God should reveal that also to him—he nevertheless, with inexpressible praise for his love, did not abandon catholic unity and peace even with colleagues who thought differently from him.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 40

You inserted in your writings his words from the letter to Jubaianus, by which you sought to show that he and his colleagues approved the view that those baptized in heresy or schism ought to be baptized in the Catholic Church. I am not bound by the authority of this letter. I do not regard Cyprian’s writings as canonical; rather, I examine them in light of the canonical writings. Whatever in them agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures, I accept with praise of Cyprian; whatever does not agree, I reject with respect for him.

Therefore, if you were quoting what you have recalled as having been written by him to Jubaianus from some canonical book of the Apostles or Prophets, I would have nothing at all to contradict. But since what you quote is not canonical, I use the freedom to which the Lord has called us. I do so concerning a man whose praise I cannot attain, whose many writings I do not compare with my own, whose genius I love, whose speech delights me, whose charity I admire, and whose martyrdom I revere: I do not accept what he thought differently on this matter.

I do not accept, I say, what blessed Cyprian thought concerning the baptism of heretics and schismatics, because the Church for which blessed Cyprian shed his blood does not accept it.

But since you say that he established this position by legal documents—although he could not establish the legal documents, but rather established whatever he rightly thought by means of them—leave aside Cyprian’s writings and recall those very legal documents which you say he used. If I do not show that they contribute nothing to your case, you have won.  
[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Most printed editions read “contribute to our case,” omitting “nothing.”]

Accordingly, I do not accept this position of Cyprian’s, although I am incomparably inferior to Cyprian, just as I neither accept nor practice that action of the apostle Peter by which he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2:14), although I am incomparably inferior to Peter.

But you who oppose Cyprian’s writings to us as foundations of canonical authority must yield concerning whatever we can produce from Cyprian against you. It is right that, once defeated, you should be silent and at last turn from the error of your most destructive dissension to catholic unity.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 41

Therefore, so as not to make this lengthy, consider what I shall bring forward from this very letter to Jubaianus, something that overturns and destroys your error.

When either blessed Cyprian or whoever wrote that letter was trying to persuade people that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized—because, evidently, the Baptism they had received outside among heretics was not to be counted as Baptism—he raised an objection against himself and said:

“But someone will say: What, then, will become of those who in the past, coming from heresy to the Church, were admitted without Baptism? The Lord is able in his mercy to grant pardon, and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, having been admitted simply into the Church, fell asleep within the Church.”

This simplicity is sufficient for us. Cyprian himself bears witness to it, understanding unity in the body of Christ to be so great a good that, in his pious reflection, he presumed that those who had been admitted into it simply—even those whom he thought were without Baptism—had obtained pardon through divine mercy and were not separated from the gifts of the Church.

This was the custom of the Church before Cyprian’s council. It could not be overcome or removed even by Cyprian’s council: those coming from heresy were admitted—not indeed without Baptism, as he says, because the same Baptism was present in them even outside, although it did not benefit them; nevertheless, being admitted simply, as he again says, they obtained pardon through God’s mercy and were not separated from the gifts of the Church.

This simplicity, rather than duplicity, pleased the whole Church spread throughout the entire world.

42. Hear what kind of testimony Cyprian himself bears to this, from the letter he composed on Unity [Note: [Col. 0491] It is also entitled *The Book on the Simplicity of Prelates*.]. “Take away,” he says, “a ray of the sun from its body: the unity of light does not admit division. Break a branch from a tree: once broken, it cannot put forth growth. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up.”

In these words of Cyprian, we understand “the unity of light does not admit division” only of the saints predestined for the kingdom of God, who can in no way be divided from the Church; and we take “the broken branch does not put forth growth” as referring to the shoot of eternal salvation. We recognize the dryness of the stream cut off from its spring in the fact that those who are separated from unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit—not in the sacrament of Baptism, which both good and evil may possess, openly outside the Church just as they may possess it inwardly while secretly separated from the Church’s holiness.

But observe what Cyprian thought about the fruitfulness of that very Church, spread throughout the whole world, in what he adds: “Thus also the Lord’s Church, flooded with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; yet there is one light, which is diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. She extends her branches over the whole earth through the abundance of her fruitfulness; she spreads her widely flowing streams ever farther; yet there is one head, one source, and one mother, rich in the succession of her offspring.”

Cyprian loved, held fast, and commended this Church, promised in the Holy Scriptures and made manifest throughout the entire world. The ruined schismatics and heretics, however, wishing as though to distinguish and separate themselves from the wicked, abandoned it through impious seditions. And lest they should attempt to cleanse their impious departures by empty excuses, Holy Scripture foretold: “A wicked son says that he is righteous, but does not cleanse his departure” (Prov. XXIV, after v. 22 according to the Septuagint). For the good who are truly within must not be abandoned because of the wicked who appear to be within.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

43. From the letter which blessed Cyprian wrote to the presbyter Maximus and the others, in which he congratulates those returning to the Church from schismatic and heretical error, learn what he thought. He says:

“For although tares appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought therefore to be hindered, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves depart from the Church. Our sole task must be to work so that we may be wheat, so that, when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord’s barns, we may receive the fruit corresponding to our work and labor. The Apostle says in his Letter: ‘But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some indeed are honored, others dishonored’ (II Tim. II, 20). Let us apply ourselves, and work as much as we can, so that we may be vessels of gold and silver. For the breaking of earthen vessels has been granted to the Lord alone, to whom an iron rod has been given (Ps. II, 9). ‘A servant cannot be greater than his master’ (John XIII, 16); nor may anyone claim for himself what the Father granted to the Son alone, imagining that he can already carry a winnowing shovel for threshing-floor and cleansing, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment [Note: [Col. 0492] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read this passage as follows: ‘and for cleansing the chaff, can already carry a winnowing shovel, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment.’ M.]. This obstinacy is proud, and this presumption sacrilegious—the madness of corruption assumes it for itself. And while certain people continually assume for themselves more than mild justice demands, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling, they lose the light of truth.”

You see, brother, that according to the divine Scriptures Cyprian taught this even because of the wicked: although they are spiritually separated from the good in life and conduct, they nevertheless appear bodily mingled with them in the Church until the day of judgment, when they will also be bodily separated for the punishments they deserve. The Church must not be abandoned because of the chaff or tares, like wheat; nor because of dishonored vessels, like a great house [Note: [Col. 0492] Thus the printed editions, erroneously; the grammatical construction requires the nominative case, *domus magna*, “a great house.” M.]. You see, hear, perceive, grasp, and understand how great a crime it is that, because of those who displease you—whether rightly or while you are deceived—you separate yourselves from the Church spread throughout the whole world, to which, according to the divine Scriptures, Cyprian bears testimony so great, so firm, so clear, and so radiant.

## CHAPTER XXXV

44. Therefore attend carefully to my brief reasoning concerning this entire question. If those who come from the heretics are rightly received into the Church, so that their error may be corrected in them, while the divine sacrament is not invalidated, we rejoice over those who live well there [Note: [Col. 0492] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “those living there.”] as the Lord’s wheat.

But if, as you suppose and loudly claim that Cyprian supports you in this opinion, they do not have Baptism, then certainly, having been admitted simply into the Church, according to that same Cyprian, they obtain God’s indulgence on account of the merit of unity itself [Note: [Col. 0493] The printed editions read, “on account, nevertheless, of the merit of unity itself.” *Nevertheless* is absent from the manuscripts.] and are not separated from the Church’s gifts. Whoever admits them simply according to the earlier custom—which Cyprian did not conceal—and lives rightly and peacefully is counted among the same wheat destined for the barn.

But those who either knowingly and contentiously fight against the truth in receiving them, or live by depraved and perverse conduct, are tolerated among the tares and chaff destined for the flames. Nevertheless, God commands that the Church, which is enlarged throughout the entire world through abundant increase—that is, the Lord’s wheat, which grows together until the harvest or is threshed together until the winnowing—must not be abandoned because of them. Cyprian bears witness to this.

Accordingly, if the wicked stain the good through communion in the sacraments, then when, in Cyprian’s time or before Cyprian, heretics were received without Baptism, as you suppose, say that the Church perished, and show from where you yourselves were born. But if, as the truth teaches even through Cyprian, when tares known to be present are tolerated for the sake of the Church’s peace, they do not stain the wheat, then “a wicked son says that he is righteous, but does not cleanse his departure,” because he ought not to have departed from the Church on account of the wicked.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

45. I say it again, and I do not allow you to evade this [Note: [Col. 0493] The printed editions read, “behold, from this.”] most invincible argument: if the wicked destroy the good, who do not share in the sins of the wicked, merely through communion in the sacraments, then when those coming from heresy were formerly admitted to the Church without Baptism, they certainly destroyed the good by their contagion. Therefore the Church did not then exist—the Church which Cyprian held and preached, and from which Donatus could later depart.

But if that contagion did not destroy the good, then the contagion of those whom you accuse could not destroy the Christian world either. Cease your calumnies, you who are separated, and return to the Church corrected.

You must accuse Caecilian and his associates, against whom Secundus of Tigisis then assembled and constituted a council; I do not need to defend them. Accuse them with all the force you can. If they were innocent, your blustering will harm them nothing, as they are wheat; if they were guilty, the wheat should not have been abandoned because of those tares, which did them no harm.

Accuse as much as you can. I win if you do not prove it; I win if you do prove it. I say, I win if you do not prove it, with you yourself as judge; I win if you do prove it, with Cyprian as witness.

What do you claim they were? If innocent, why do you, being tares, calumniate the Lord’s wheat? If guilty, why do you separate yourselves from the Lord’s wheat because of the tares?

The Church stands forth [Note: [Col. 0493] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read, “let the Church stand forth.”], clear and conspicuous to all—a city that cannot be hidden, set upon a mountain (Matt. V, 14)—through which Christ rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth (Ps. LXXI, 8), like the seed of Abraham multiplied as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea, in which all nations are blessed. [Col. 0494] Blessed Cyprian also commends this Church in such a way that he says she is flooded with the Lord’s light, extends her rays throughout the world, and spreads her branches throughout the whole earth through the abundance of her fruitfulness.

Either this Church [Note: [Col. 0494] At this point the printed editions changed “either” (*aut*) to “that” (*ut*), incorrectly.] was not to be accused in its wheat, or it was not to be abandoned because of the tares. Answer one of these alternatives yourselves; learn the other from Cyprian’s admonitions. For these are his own words, in which he testifies and says:

“For although tares appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought therefore to be hindered, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves depart from the Church.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII

46. You say that the Church perished from the world because of the contagion of wicked Africans, and that its remnants remained in the party of Donatus, as though wheat separated from tares and chaff. In this you plainly think contrary to Cyprian, who says both that the good do not perish in the Church through the mingling of the wicked and that the wicked cannot be separated from the mingling of the good before the appointed time of divine judgment.

According to your error—or rather, your madness—you are therefore compelled to accuse not only Caecilian and those who ordained him, but also those Churches which we read of together in the apostolic and canonical Scriptures: not only the Church of the Romans, for your few people in Africa you are customarily wont to ordain a bishop, but also the Churches of the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Thessalonians, Colossians, and Philippians, to which the apostle Paul writes most openly; the Church of Jerusalem, which the first apostle James governed by his episcopate; the Church of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts XI, 26); and the Churches of Smyrna, Thyatira, Sardis, Pergamum, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, to which the Apocalypse of the apostle John was addressed.

You are also compelled to accuse so many other Churches of Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, to which the apostle Peter writes (I Pet. I, 1), as well as everything else that Paul testifies he filled with the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Rom. XV, 19)—to say nothing of the other broad and immense regions of the earth into which the Church, extended from these apostolic labors and plantings, has grown and continues to grow.

You are compelled to accuse these Churches, which I have named from the divine and canonical Scriptures and which are situated so far from Africa, as though they had perished because of the sins of Africans, lest you correct the error that drives you by your wicked dissension into so great a crime [Note: [Col. 0494] The printed editions read, “and you do not correct.” The manuscripts read, “lest you correct.”].

47. But, in order more easily to refute this error of yours, we are not compelled to defend even the Africans themselves, whose falsely alleged crime you dare to spread over the other nations as well. They have fellowship with those transmarine Churches in the kingdom if they were innocent. But if they were guilty, then, like tares among wheat, they could not harm even in Africa those who refused to separate themselves from the unity of the Church because of them, even when their guilt was known.

To pass over the many who believed them innocent, although their crime—if they had committed any—could not in any case be proved; and to pass over the fact that you yourselves certainly cannot say that these people could be stained by unknown sins belonging to others: even those who knew or supposed them to be guilty, although established in the African Churches, saw that they could not be convicted before the transmarine Churches, nor could their crimes be demonstrated to the members of the Church spread far and wide.

If they had wished, because of those whom they knew to be wicked, to separate themselves from communion with so many nations to which they could not prove the charges against them, as though out of fear of a deadly contagion, it would have been Cyprian—not I, not you, not Donatus, not Caecilian—but the very man whom you dared to name, Cyprian, who would have held them back and spoken the words he wrote to Maximus.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

48. “For although tares appear to be in the Church,” he says, “neither our faith nor our charity ought therefore to be hindered, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves depart from the Church. Our sole task must be to work so that we may be wheat, so that, when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord’s barns, we may receive the fruit corresponding to our work and labor. The Apostle says in his Letter: ‘But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some indeed are honored, others dishonored’ (II Tim. II, 20). Let us apply ourselves, and work as much as we can, so that we may be vessels of gold and silver. For the breaking of earthen vessels has been granted to the Lord alone, to whom an iron rod has been given (Ps. II, 9). ‘A servant cannot be greater than his master’ (John XIII, 16); nor may anyone claim for himself what the Father granted to the Son alone, imagining that he can already carry a winnowing shovel for threshing-floor and cleansing, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment. This obstinacy is proud, and this presumption sacrilegious—the madness of corruption assumes it for itself. And while certain people continually assume for themselves more than mild justice demands, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling, they lose the light of truth.”

By these words of Cyprian, those who wished to separate themselves from the Church because of known wicked people would have been held within the Church, if they feared God. By these same words you are condemned, because, after separating yourselves, you accuse even the good.

By these words Cyprian holds us also in the house of God, whose beauty he loved—even if, something you have never been able to do, we could know the traditors whom you accuse and identify, or any other wicked people—lest we abandon that house because of vessels made for dishonor.

By these words, may he also bring you, once corrected, peacefully into catholic peace, so that, offended by whatever sins of others, whether true or false, you may not hurl such great evils against the Church of Christ, which throughout the world bears fruit and grows according to the Scriptures; so that you do not accuse the wheat because of the tares, abandon the wheat because of the chaff, or remain outside the great house because of dishonored vessels.

49. See how greatly blessed Cyprian, whom you cited against us, has helped us. If he held a different view concerning the repetition of Baptism, the Lord undoubtedly revealed to him that it required correction, in view of his immense merits and ardent charity. For he remained in the vine as a branch so rich in the fruit of peace and love that, even if something requiring cleansing were found in him, it would certainly have been cleansed, if by nothing else, then by the pruning knife of martyrdom.

Although, therefore, these arguments could have sufficed, and more than sufficed, to refute your error—and, if you are willing, to correct it—nevertheless, lest anyone think that you included something in your letter which I could not refute, or that I could not demonstrate that you offered no adequate response to our writings against Petilian, let us examine the rest in the following volume.

# BOOK III

He proceeds through the remaining portion of Cresconius’s letter, briefly refuting each point in order.

[Col. 0495]

## CHAPTER I

1. If I did not have to attend to the understanding of slow-witted people, who cannot grasp that in the two preceding books I answered in many ways the whole case contained in your letter, brother Cresconius, so that even those matters which remain there have already been dissolved and rendered void, I ought by now to have brought this work to an end.

But because there are many people whom it is fitting for us to serve, who do not think that everything has been disposed of unless each point is also dealt with in its proper place, I shall briefly proceed through the remaining parts of your discourse, refuting them in order.

2. Whatever you thought should be inserted concerning the writings of the venerable martyr Cyprian and of certain Eastern bishops—namely, that they approved the rejection of the sacrament of Baptism administered among heretics and schismatics [Note: [Col. 0495] This perhaps refers to the letters of Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, addressed to Cyprian and published among Cyprian’s works, in which the proceedings of the Council of Iconium concerning the baptism of heretics are recounted. The Council of Synnada, held at approximately the same time, adopted the same position concerning the Baptism of heretics. But [Col. 0496] the Eastern bishops later corrected this judgment, as is read below. See Eusebius, Book 7, chapters 3 and 4, and Nicephorus, Book 6, chapters 7, 8, and 9.]—does not harm our case, if we retain that Church which Cyprian did not abandon, even when many of his colleagues were unwilling to agree with this position.

For even in the council itself he said: “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion.” And he concluded the same letter to Jubianus as follows:

## CHAPTER II

“These things, dearest brother, we have answered you according to our limited ability, prescribing or prejudging no one, so as to prevent each bishop from doing what he thinks right, since he has free authority to exercise his own judgment,” and so forth.

Therefore count us for the present among those whom Cyprian could not persuade of that position, but from whom he did not in the least separate his communion, even though they held a different opinion on this matter.

Your predecessors, however, to whom you bore such testimony—that they separated themselves from communion with the Eastern bishops precisely because those bishops rescinded their judgment, by which they had approved the view that Cyprian and that African council ought to be followed on this question of Baptism—acted contrary to Cyprian. For they ought, together with their colleagues who held a different opinion on this question, to have maintained the unity of communion, which we read that Cyprian maintained in his letters.

They reply that he wished to speak in this way so that, perhaps deterred by fear of excommunication, they would not dare to state freely what they thought—not because he intended to remain in communion with them if they held a different opinion. In saying this, they plainly declare that Cyprian lied.

For if he said, “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion,” as the written records of the council indicate that he said [Note: [Col. 0497] See Book 3, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, paragraphs 4 and 5, and Book 6, paragraph 10.], yet if any one of those to whom he said this showed that he held a different opinion, and Cyprian would not have shared Christ’s sacraments with him, then he was unquestionably lying when he made such promises deceitfully rather than truthfully.

And what is worse in that lie, he was deceiving the simplicity of his brothers with a double heart, especially since the words spoken were also being written down. For whoever held a different opinion from that council—how could he have been condemned or excommunicated by Cyprian’s own mouth, when he could recite the council’s opening statement on his own behalf?

Who, then, has the more tolerable opinion of Cyprian: we, who say that he could have been mistaken as a man concerning the obscure question of Baptism; or you, who say that, in promising Christian communion, he wished to deceive as a bishop—not one individual brother, but the entire episcopal fellowship?

But if you too consider it wicked to believe this about him, then your predecessors acted against his judgment when they separated themselves from communion with the Eastern bishops because they held a different opinion on this matter.

## CHAPTER III

3. Therefore, if we are now to believe at all that fifty Eastern bishops held the same view as seventy Africans, or somewhat more, against the many thousands of bishops throughout the world who rejected this error, why should we not rather say that those few Eastern bishops corrected their judgment, rather than, as you put it, rescinded it?

For just as it is praiseworthy not to be moved from a true opinion, so it is blameworthy to persist in a false one. The first praise is never to hold a false position; the second is to change it, so that either the truth remains true from the beginning, or the false position, once changed, yields to the truth.

Nor does it now concern our question what position the greater part of the Christian world held together with the Eastern bishops [Note: [Col. 0497] The Cygirannus manuscript has *maxima*, “the greatest,” but that is not correctly said of Africa alone.]. For if that is true, and if that is what must be held and preserved, namely, what we hold and preserve concerning Baptism, then we charge you with two evils: one, that you are mistaken in the question of Baptism; the other, that you separate yourselves from those who hold the truth on this matter.

But if, speaking according to you, the truth in that question is what you yourselves hold, then you are certainly stained by this crime: that you departed from the Church, for whose peace you ought, as Cyprian both did and advised, to have endured even those who held a different opinion.

## CHAPTER IV

4. Now cry out that I said, “Make no distinction between the faithful and the faithless; let the pious and the impious appear the same to you”—which I did not say.

But I did plainly say the statement from which you wished to shout as though I had said this, and to claim that I said what I did not say: “Whether a person receives the sacrament from a faithful or from a faithless steward” (*Book I against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 6, paragraph 7).

In that statement I did make a distinction between the faithful and the faithless, nor did I command that the pious and the impious should appear the same to anyone. I said only that both the pious and the impious can possess the same sacrament. You yourself do not deny this, since at least you concede that Baptism ought not to be repeated after hidden impious ministers.

Therefore you join things together without cause and say, “It is of no benefit to live by good conduct, because whatever is permitted to the righteous can also be performed by the unrighteous.” For this is both false and not something I said.

Good conduct, of course, distinguishes the lives of the good and the wicked and leads them to different ends. Nor can whatever is permitted to the righteous also be performed by the unrighteous, because the righteous fulfill Christ’s law through love, from which the unrighteous are alien.

Nevertheless, the unrighteous can do something that the righteous also do: they can baptize, if nothing else, when their wickedness remains hidden. They can also proclaim God’s commandments just as the righteous do, though they cannot live according to them as the righteous do. Of such people it is said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3).

## CHAPTER V

5. But suppose that an unrighteous person, not hidden and known to some good people, cannot be separated from the Church through some seditious faction [Note: [Col. 0498] Several manuscripts read, “through a seditious faction or sedition.”]. Hear Cyprian: tolerate the tares; be wheat.

How well the words you repeatedly applied in different ways to one matter seemed to sound to you. “What,” you ask, “could be more unjustly said under this command: ‘Let the stained man purify another; let the filthy man wash him; let the unclean man cleanse him; let the faithless man give faith; let the criminal make the innocent’?”

I answer briefly: Christ is neither stained, nor filthy, nor unclean, nor faithless, nor criminal. He loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word (Eph. V, 25), making us certain of his good gifts, so that we would not be corrupted by the faults of others.

For behold: when the wicked minister is hidden, yet you do not invalidate the Baptism he administered, can all these words of yours not be repeated against you? The stained man purifies; the filthy man washes; the unclean man cleanses; the faithless man gives faith; the criminal makes the innocent.

“No,” you say, “he himself does not do this, but his good reputation does, even though that reputation is empty and false.”

Should this not make me cry out, “O crime! O monstrosity!”—not, as someone said, something to be carried off to the ends of the earth (Cicero, *First Speech against Verres*), but rather something to be driven, if possible, beyond every heaven and every land?

I am not speaking of you yourself, whom I wish to see corrected, but of this error, from which I desire you to be corrected.

Is it really the case that, when the true life of a good minister is lacking for cleansing a person, the false reputation of a wicked minister is sufficient to accomplish what a good life would accomplish, so that, when the minister’s wickedness is hidden in the sanctification of a person, falsehood serves God as minister [Note: [Col. 0498] We have restored these words from the Georgian and Cygirannus manuscripts: “when the true life of the good minister is lacking, then the false reputation of the wicked minister.”]?

All this is said so that you may not say what we say: whether someone receives the sacrament from a faithful or a faithless steward, it is God alone who sanctifies.

6. Next you recall my words, in which I said: “Christ must always give faith; Christ must be the source of the Christian; the Christian must fix his root in Christ; Christ must be the head of the Christian” (*Book II against the Letters of Petilian*, paragraph 11).

I certainly said this, and I still say it; nor have you been able to answer it at all. For you appear almost to have yielded beneath the great weight of the truth when you added, “This we too recommend; this we desire.”

## CHAPTER VI

You then once again place before us the human being in whom the recipient is to set his hope: “But we ask,” you say, “through whom this is better accomplished.”

Since we too do not say that a person can be baptized without a minister, you ask me whether the minister should preferably be unrighteous or righteous.

I answer that it is better for the minister to be righteous, because human weakness finds what God commands laborious and difficult without an example, and is more easily raised to a good life by imitating a good minister. Hence the apostle Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV, 16).

But if, for the baptizing and sanctifying of a person, what is received is better in proportion to the goodness of the one through whom it is administered, then there would be as much variety among Baptisms received as there is diversity in the merits of ministers.

For if Paul was unquestionably better than Apollos, then according to this empty and perverse opinion of yours he gave a better Baptism. And if he gave a better Baptism, he certainly envied those whom he rejoices were not baptized by him (ibid. I, 14).

Moreover, if, among good ministers, one is better than another, yet the Baptism given through the better minister is not better, then by no means is the Baptism given even through a wicked minister bad, when the same Baptism is given. Therefore, through unequal ministers, God’s gift is equal, because it belongs not to them but to him.

## CHAPTER VII

We do not therefore, as you idly attack us, make no distinction between the faithful and the faithless. We distinguish human merits, not divine sacraments. You too, compelled by the force of truth and forgetting your heretical intention, have said that the sacrament is not different for us and for you, but one and the same.

7. How can you say, “This we too recommend and desire: that Christ always give faith; that Christ be the source of the Christian; that the Christian fix his root in Christ; that Christ be the head of the Christian,” when you defend Petilian’s letter, in which he plainly tried to show, by commending the merit of the baptizer and emphasizing the power of human righteousness in administering Baptism:

“The conscience of the one who gives in holiness is taken into account, and this conscience cleanses the recipient. For whoever knowingly receives faith from a faithless person receives not faith but guilt” (*Book I against the Letters of Petilian*, paragraphs 2 and 3)?

And as though he were asked, “How do you prove this?” he immediately added: “For every matter consists in its origin and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing” (ibid., paragraph 5).

Why, I ask, because you have undertaken the defense of reckless falsehood, do you try to cast a cloud over matters that are perfectly clear?

The man plainly says that the origin, root, and head of the person regenerated through Baptism cannot be anyone except the one through whose ministry he is baptized. Yet you say: “This we too desire: that Christ be the origin, root, and head of the Christian; but we ask through whom this is better accomplished.”

What you say is one thing; what Petilian said is another. Even if what you say is true, it is not what he said.

## CHAPTER VIII

8. Therefore, if you too desire Christ to be the origin, root, and head of the Christian, resist Petilian, not me, since “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 7).

When I had included this passage from the Apostle in my writings, you wished to answer in such a way as to say: “It is indeed God’s work to give the growth; but just as, for planting and watering, only a faithful and diligent farmer is sought, so also in the sacrament of Baptism only a faithful and most righteous laborer is employed.”

As though what an unfaithful farmer planted would fail to sprout because of his unfaithfulness; as though the power of the seed, the fruitfulness of the earth, and the tempering of the heavens had not received from God the efficacy by which they produce fruits; as though they waited only for a planter or waterer to work for the propagation of fruits, without caring with what mind he worked or with what intention he labored—whether he faithfully loved the lord of the field or sought his own profit rather than that of his master.

You also add prophetic testimony, saying: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline” (Jer. III, 15).

I know that this has been fulfilled. Such were the Apostles, and such people still exist, although, given the breadth of the Church, they are very few. Nevertheless, you ought to have sought, read, and considered what is also said through the prophet Ezekiel against wicked shepherds. For there God says: “I will feed them, not the shepherds” (Ezek. XXXIV, 13).

## CHAPTER IX

9. Therefore, through good shepherds and wicked shepherds alike, when he administers his word and sacrament, it is he himself who feeds, because he said of himself: “That there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16).

“For it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Ps. CXVII, 8); and, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII, 5).

When I recalled this in that letter, you showed that you understood it to mean that you more particularly seek a righteous and faithful person through whom the sacrament may be celebrated because you have hope and confidence in God, not in man; yet you say that faith and righteousness belong to God, while you continually take account of them in his ministers.

You say this truly, because “we have nothing that we have not received” (I Cor. IV, 7), and therefore faith and righteousness come to us from God.

But when you say that God cannot give you these unless the man through whom you are baptized possesses them, you plainly place your hope in a man whose participation in righteousness you do not know. And if he does not possess it, you then attend to his reputation; when you discover a good reputation concerning a wicked man who remains hidden, you believe that reputation sufficient for your sanctification.

I ask you: if you have confidence in God, not in man, and therefore seek all the more that the person through whom this sacrament is celebrated should be righteous, good, and faithful, because faith and righteousness belong to God, does the false reputation also belong to God? If a wicked minister has a good reputation, do you say that this reputation is sufficient for your sanctification [Note: [Col. 0500] Some manuscripts read, “unto your sanctification” rather than “in your sanctification.”]?

I would rather have you trust in a man—something I was vehemently forbidding you to do—than in the falsehood of his reputation. For however a human being may be, insofar as he is human he is God’s creature; but no falsehood is God’s creature.

Moreover, if the one who places his hope in man is accursed, how much more is the one who places his hope in the falsehood of human opinion, so as to fall into what is written elsewhere: “He who trusts in falsehood feeds the winds” (Prov. X, 4)—that is, becomes food for evil spirits?

## CHAPTER X

10. “If Baptism,” you say, “once given by anyone and in any manner ought not to be invalidated, why did the Apostles baptize after John?”

How much more forcefully can this be put: If the Apostles baptized after John, why should not either a better or an equal person baptize after any holy man? This should compel you to understand, if only from this point, that John’s baptism has no bearing on the present question.

“And to the Jews,” you say, “who had been baptized by Moses, Peter said: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ’” (Acts II, 38).

If the Jews had already been baptized for the reason that Moses baptized their ancestors through the Red Sea so long before (Exod. XIV, 22), then those who are born of baptized Christians are baptized today without cause. Yet you say these things and write them; you are heard and read, and are thought to be answering our writings—as though being unwilling to remain silent were the same as being able to answer.

## CHAPTER XI

11. Nor did you refute at the beginning of this letter, as you imagine you did, that other point which you thought should be passed over: what I said, “If those who wished to belong to Paul were in error, what hope, then, is there for those who wish to belong to Donatus?” (*Book I against the Letters of Petilian*, paragraph 5).

For who does not see that this division arose from this very point, and that it persists even today in this plague, while hope is placed in human righteousness, so that Christ’s Baptism is acceptable only if a person is baptized by a righteous man?

Against this error, and against those who had already begun to create schisms because of differing human merits, Paul himself cries out: “I thank God that I baptized none of you, so that no one may say that I baptized in my name” (I Cor. I, 14–15).

What else was he indicating except that Christ’s Baptism belongs only to the one in whose name it is given, and that it does not become better when given through a better minister, nor worse when given through a worse one?

12. Therefore you exult in vain thereafter and say: “It follows that I may conclude that everything written by Saint Petilianus (or whoever the speaker is) was rightly said.” For the very words that you conclude were rightly said prove themselves not to have been rightly said, because the conscience of the one who gives in holiness is not what cleanses the recipient, when the giver’s defilement is hidden. Defeated there, when you ought to have yielded to the truth, you appealed to his false reputation as to an unhappy judge deceived by a lie: for his conscience is not considered when his reputation is considered, and no one can be cleansed by another’s false reputation any more than by another’s bad life. No one receives the Christian faith from a human being, whether perfidious or faithful, but from the one of whom it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9). If someone hears from a faithful person what he ought to believe, he certainly imitates that person, but he is not justified by him. For if a minister justifies the ungodly, it follows that one must also rightly believe in the minister: yet the clear and certain apostolic judgment is: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 5). Therefore, if the minister does not dare to say, “Believe in me,” let him not dare to say, “You are justified by me.”

**13.** Now as for what follows—“Everything consists in its origin and root; and if it has no head, it is nothing”—if the origin, root, and head of the baptized person is the minister who baptizes, then it is not Christ; if it is Christ, then it is not the minister. Finally, when the minister is secretly evil, what is the origin, what is the root, what is the head of the baptized person? Is it his false reputation? Cresconius says so, but the truth contradicts him. Therefore, if Christ was then the origin, root, and head, he is so also when the minister is good, lest—which is most absurd—the condition of one baptized by a secretly evil minister be better, when Christ is the head, than that of one baptized by an openly good minister, if in that case the minister is the head. I would say the same about the good seed. For what follows is: “And nothing regenerates well unless it is regenerated by good seed.”

[Note: [Col. 0502] Lovaniensis reads: “Therefore even then the origin …” Later, together with other editions, Am. and Er. read: “For he himself is [the origin] when the minister is good.” A little later they have: “if this minister is the head.” These readings are corrected from the manuscripts.]

**14.** The passages that follow, which you inserted from Petilianus’s letter, where he says (Book 1 *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §§8–9):

> “Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can there be in one who is guilty through his own crimes making another innocent, when it is written: ‘A good tree bears good fruits, and a bad tree bears bad fruits. Do people gather grapes from thorns?’ (Matt. VII, 17, 16); and again: ‘Every good person brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart, and an evil person brings forth evil things from the treasure of his heart’ (ibid. XII, 35).”

These words sufficiently and quite openly prove that Petilianus referred all these matters only to the person through whom Baptism is administered: so that he is understood, if innocent, to make innocent the person whom he baptizes; he is the good tree whose fruit is the person baptized; he is the good person from whose heart’s treasure the sanctification of the baptized proceeds.

And so, when this minister is secretly evil, tell me: by whom is that person made innocent? Tell me: whose tree’s fruit will he be? Tell me: from whose heart’s treasure will the baptized person be sanctified? Or, if at that time he deserves to have as the author of his innocence, and as the tree from which good fruit is born, not a human minister of Baptism but Christ, then he has more happily fallen into the hands of a hiddenly evil minister than if he had fallen into the hands of an openly good one.

If this is said—which would be utterly absurd and insane—then the fruit belongs to Christ, since the person sanctified by Christ’s Baptism is baptized through the work of any minister. Unless perhaps, when he encounters the minister’s stained and hidden conscience, he will have recourse to your counsel, so that you may show him as the tree from which he is born the falsely good reputation of an evil person. If you seek its root, you will find the cunning of one who deceives; and if good fruit can arise from it—which God forbid—then Christ lied when he said: “A bad tree cannot produce good fruits” (ibid. VII, 18).

But because Christ spoke the truth, let a good person, like a good tree, have good fruit, namely a good work; and an evil person, like an evil tree, evil fruit, namely an evil work. But let the person who is baptized be born not from any human being but from the Spirit of Christ, if he wishes to be fruit that is not spoiled by the wind and a tree that is not uprooted.

Since these things are so, when you said, “It follows that I may conclude that everything written by Saint Petilianus (or whoever the speaker is) was rightly said,” I think that I, rather, conclude that none of those things was rightly said.

**CHAPTER XII**

**15.** Let us now see what you subsequently wove into your letter, and how your teachers instructed you about the case of Optatus and the Maximianists—or rather, so that I may become more learned through you, the Maximianenses. As for Optatus, concerning whom I am unable to recite anything that has been written, I readily yield to whatever opinion you may hold. I know only this: if the things that were said about him—if I may not say “demonstrated,” at least asserted—are true, then he himself was not good and did not have a good reputation. Hence those baptized through him could have been cleansed neither by his conscience, according to Petilianus, nor by his reputation, according to you.

But if his alleged evils were spread, as often happens, by an envious reputation, see how rightly we do not readily believe what you have never been able to prove to us concerning the traditors whom you accuse: for even a bad reputation can lie about good people. Therefore, if it is not their innocence, nor—what is true and firm—the grace of God, and not our conscience, that makes Baptism valid for us, let your judgment at least make it valid.

[Note: [Col. 0503] The manuscripts read: “and our conscience,” omitting the negative particle.]

**CHAPTER XIII**
