**16.** For when you were speaking about Optatus, you said: “I neither acquit Optatus nor condemn him.” If I do this—or rather, if not I alone but the whole African Catholic Church, and still more the overseas Church spread so far and wide, says of Caecilianus and his ordainers, “We neither acquit nor condemn them”—do you think this too little for those whom they baptized, none of whom ever saw Caecilianus, when you think what you said about Optatus sufficient for those whom he himself baptized with his own hands?

Or is it because you recite the council of your parents concerning Caecilianus, while no council concerning Optatus is recited by us, that you think no one among us is permitted to say, “I neither acquit nor condemn Caecilianus,” although you were permitted to say this about Optatus?

But a later overseas judgment was made on behalf of Caecilianus, at the insistence of your people before the emperor Constantine.

[Note: [Col. 0503] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read: “a later judgment, by your people overseas.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503] Namely, the Roman and Arles councils.]

Or, if ecclesiastical judgments that were made earlier cannot now be overturned, what will you do about Primianus, your bishop of Carthage, against whom at first one hundred men—certainly more than had judged in the case of Caecilianus—passed judgment,

[Note: [Col. 0503] At the council of Cabarsussi.] and, after depriving him of the episcopate, appointed Maximianus in his place? Does Primianus not rely upon the later judgment made for him in the town of Bagai, according to which judgment he does not wish anyone to doubt him, but demands that all of you acquit him?

Therefore, in accordance with the later judgment concerning Caecilianus, we acquit him completely and without hesitation. Yet it is sufficient for the case if we say of him what you said of Optatus: “We neither acquit nor condemn Caecilianus.” Let them—whether your people or ours—see how they judged him; let them themselves give an account of their judgments; let them themselves bear the burden of their work, whether evil or good. At least permit us to doubt about the deeds of others, lest we be compelled to condemn in ourselves the Sacraments concerning which it is not permitted to doubt.

But, as I have already said, think of Optatus whatever you wish. For there is no basis on which we can convict one who did not commit his acts before the official records—although he committed them in such a way that he was considered, held, and died as a chief among the satellites of Gildo.

Are you likewise permitted to chatter whatever you wish about Felicianus and Praetextatus, the associates of Maximianus, whom three hundred and ten of your bishops, together with the others expressly named, condemned by one and the same sentence of the council of Bagai, and whom, after not a short time, they received as bishops together with all those whom the condemned men had baptized?

[Note: [Col. 0504] In the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* he says that almost three full years intervened.]

**CHAPTER XIV**

**17.** Accordingly, whatever you said against us or against our people, as though sparing us and passing over the matter—without names, without witnesses, and without any evidence whatever—partly blaming things that ought not to be blamed and partly failing to prove things that ought to be blamed, it is pointless to wish to excuse.

[Note: [Col. 0504] Printed editions read “you said”; two manuscripts read “you said” in the singular, referring to Cresconius.]

Look carefully at these men—these men, I say, once more:

[Note: [Col. 0504] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read: “to excuse these men. Look again.” Lov. reads: “to excuse. Look again at these men.” M. has a different division.] Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri. Examine their whole case somewhat more closely. In its proper place, if the Lord permits, I shall explain it in such a way (below, Book 4) that even if you wish to be an extreme enemy of the truth, you will not be able either to defend or to deny the falsehood of your people.

For the present, however, I am content to proceed according to what they told you. I am not yet examining how truthfully they spoke; I am not yet demonstrating with what astonishing blindness of shamelessness they lied. Certainly, when you read in my letter about those whom I called Maximianists—condemned by a council of your people and afterward received—you were, as you write, deeply disturbed, since, to use your own words, you were still unaware of what the truth contained.

Finally, as you relate, you immediately made a more careful inquiry among your bishops; and, while they instructed you, you learned both the decree of the council and the sentence pronounced against those who had been condemned, as well as the whole sequence of events. And because you thought that I, too, was unaware of what had happened, you urged me to learn what the truth was, and thereafter narrated everything in this way. See that here I set down your own words from your letter; for they are extremely necessary to me.

**CHAPTER XV**

**18.** “When Maximianus was trying to associate very many bishops with himself in error,” you say, “our people convened a council, and a sentence was issued against all who had persisted in his schism; you testify that you, too, have read it. Although this sentence was confirmed by the agreement of all, nevertheless, you say, it was decided by decree of the council that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be regarded as innocent.

Thus it happened, you say, that not only those two whom you mention,

[Note: [Col. 0505] Praetextatus and Felicianus.]

but also many others, having been cleared and declared innocent, returned themselves to the Church. Their Baptism therefore ought not to be annulled, because, having been restored within the appointed period, they were not held by the final sentence; and when they baptized, they had not been separated from the Church, since they had not yet been separated by the expiration of the fixed limit of time. But those who even after the aforesaid day persisted obstinately with Maximianus, being held by the sentence of condemnation, lost both Baptism and the Church.”

Surely, my Cresconius, you recognize these words as expressly drawn from the composition of your letter.

**CHAPTER XVI**

**19.** Therefore I ask you: If they had not yet been separated from the Church, how was a sentence issued against all who had persisted in the schism of Maximianus, a sentence which, although confirmed by the agreement of all, nevertheless led to the decision, by decree of the council, that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be regarded as innocent?

By these words you show that, if anyone among those who had persisted in the schism of Maximianus wished to be corrected within the period of delay, he would be regarded as innocent. He would therefore be corrected if he wished to be corrected from that schism in which he had persisted with Maximianus. Before he was corrected, then, he was in the schism in which he had persisted, although, because he was corrected within the appointed period, he had not persisted in it obstinately.

For shortly afterward, in your later words, you make the distinction in this way: “But those who even after the aforesaid day persisted obstinately with Maximianus, being held by the sentence of condemnation, lost both Baptism and the Church.” By saying “persisted obstinately,” you plainly show that those who were corrected had also persisted, but not obstinately.

That sentence was issued against all of them together,

[Note: [Col. 0505] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “against whom the sentence was issued by all together,” and so forth.]

and, you say, although it was confirmed by the agreement of all, it was nevertheless decided that the period of delay should be granted by decree of the council.

How, then, were they in the Church who, before they were corrected, were persisting with Maximianus in the schism? If they were not in the Church because they were in the schism, how did they baptize? Furthermore, how did it happen, as you say, that not only those whom I mentioned but also many others, having been cleared and declared innocent, returned themselves to the Church, if they had not been separated from the Church? To whom did they return, from whom they had not departed?

Or, if they had departed, tell me, I ask: before they returned themselves to the Church, by what right did they baptize? “Their Baptism therefore,” you say, “ought not to be annulled, because, having been restored within the appointed period, they were not held by the final sentence.”

Restored to what? Wake up, I beg you, and tell us: restored to what? You will surely say, “Into the Church,” to which you said they had returned themselves. Is anyone restored to the Church who has not been separated from the Church? Does anyone who has not been separated from the Church persist in schism for however few days? Does anyone who has not been separated from the Church return himself to the Church after however short a period?

**CHAPTER XVII**

**20.** I think, dearest brother, that you not only failed to consider the words you were going to write, but did not even read what you had written. Yet what could you do, when necessity in this work forced you to defend, as best you could, a sentence concerning Maximianus and his associates that was not your own but had been spoken by others?

[Note: [Col. 0506] Printed editions read “in whatever way”; the manuscripts read “how.”]

For even if you had not used these words, I would still recite the very decree of the council of Bagai, where it is written:

> “But those whom the plantings of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile—that is, those who with the modest reverence of faith withdrew their own hands from the head of Maximianus—we permitted to return to Mother Church.”

**CHAPTER XVIII**

**21.** Therefore, even if I had not found such words in your writing, I would certainly say here, and here cry out for the truth: How are those permitted to return to Mother Church who have not departed from Mother Church? Or, if they departed, by what right could they baptize before returning—unless, in repairing this schism, you forgot your own vanity, by which you maintain that, following bishops in an unbroken succession from the very seats of the Apostles down to the present time, not one person, not one household, not one city, not one nation, but the whole world must be baptized?

Or else it was because the horror of this deed has always shaken even the hearts of those who committed it: when so many peoples were returning to your communion from the communion of Maximianus, you were willing to restore so many, but were ashamed to rebaptize so many. Yet, however much you might detest and recoil from this, you would do it for the salvation of human beings; and the more widespread that salvation was, the less it ought to have been despised, if you had ever done this with regard for the truth rather than through the prejudice of error.

You surely see that in this return of the Maximianenses to your communion it has been revealed that what we say about Baptism is true. For if human beings have any understanding, either to say or to hear something, then whoever baptizes before returning to the Church certainly baptizes outside the Church. Yet Baptism is not to be annulled, just as you did not annul it in those people. Without alteration, each person baptizes in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, not in his own name, nor in anyone else’s.

Furthermore, beyond the Sacrament of Baptism—which remains entire either for the punishment of the perverse or for the salvation of the upright or corrected—I wish to say something about the expiation or cleansing of those who were corrected. For you remember what you said against us: that we receive those who come to us from your side out of the sacrilegious error of heretics without any expiation.

Now tell us about those returning to you from the schism of Maximianus, who were received even with their former honors: by what expiation, I ask, were they cleansed? Since they had shared in that enormous crime, were they not stained by such a nefarious association?

**CHAPTER XIX**

**22.** Pay attention to what that truthful mouth of your bishops sounds forth, what it denounces, and what it admits in that renowned council. “Maximianus,” it says, “a rival of the faith, an adulterer of the truth, an enemy of Mother Church, a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiron, was hurled from the bosom of peace by the thunderbolt of the sentence; and the fact that the gaping earth has not yet swallowed him (Num. XVI) has reserved him for greater punishment above. For by the short cut of death he had gained his punishment; now, while dead, he collects heavier interest on his debt among the living.”

So then, those who, as you yourself said, were persisting in his schism, before they had returned themselves to your Church within the period of delay—as you likewise said—had they drawn no stain, or only a slight stain, from association with him? But hear what follows; hear, I say, what the author or speaker of that sentence adds:

> “Nor does just death condemn this man alone for his crime; it also drags many into partnership in the crime by the chain of sacrilege. Of them it is written: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace’ (Ps. XIII, 3–4). We would not have wished them to be cut off as though from the joint of our own body; but since the pestilential decay of a festering wound has more relief in amputation than in the administration of a remedy, a healthier course was found, lest the poisonous virus creep through all the limbs, so that the wound, born amid brief pain, might fall away.

> “Therefore know that the following, guilty of a notorious crime, have been condemned by the truthful voice of the universal council, under the judgment of God who presides: Victorianus of Carchaba, Martianus of Sullectum, Baianus of Baia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabrata, Miggenus of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assuri, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzita, Felicianus of Musti, and Martialis of Pertusa, who by the deadly work of destruction glued together a filthy vessel with collected filth; and also certain clerics of the Church of Carthage, who, while attending upon the crime, offered their procuring assistance to an illicit incest.”

[Note: [Col. 0507] See below, the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus the Donatist*, §§10–11.]

What more serious things could you have said against them? What more serious things do you ordinarily say against us ourselves?

“But,” you say, “they were corrected from this very great evil within the period of delay.” I shall see whether they were corrected; for they truly would have been corrected if they had returned to the true Church. But if your Church is the true one, tell us how they were cleansed from such an enormous crime. If they were not cleansed, then according to your own sentence all of you are stained by their crime. But if they were cleansed, you concede that they could have been cleansed by their return alone, because of the love that covers a multitude of sins; and yet you accuse us with empty slanders concerning your people when, having been corrected, they come to us.

Unless perhaps, as the words of the council indicate, they had indeed already perpetrated the sacrilege of schism, but before the day granted for the delay they had not yet been polluted by that same sacrilege, and therefore were not thought to require expiation.

[Note: [Col. 0507] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “some persons.”]

**CHAPTER XX**

**23.** If this is so, who would not listen to you, since you have received such astonishing power over human beings? They sin whenever they wish, and they are defiled whenever you wish.

We are not reciting something obscure, or less known and widespread. It is that sentence which, by the merit of such eloquence, circulates in everyone’s hands and on everyone’s lips who are devoted to reading such things. You now at least see how truly I said that it ought not first to have rejoiced in being eloquent, lest afterward it grieve at being spread abroad (*Book 1 Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §11). Pay attention to what it contains; hear how loudly it resounds.

**CHAPTER XXI**

**24.** “Maximianus,” it says, “a rival of the faith, an adulterer of the truth, an enemy of Mother Church, a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiron, was hurled from the bosom of peace by the thunderbolt of the sentence.”

If, then, someone knowingly communicated with him in the Sacrament of the altar for one day, would that person, according to your vaunted severity, not be so polluted by such a great evil as to become his equal? What, then, were those men—or what did they become—who not only approached the altars with him but themselves, by raising altars, installed him as bishop in opposition to your Primianus?

But why should I question you about these men? Let the sentence itself speak, whose words shine so brightly that, if you wish to conceal it, its excessive brilliance will break through the darkness of any hiding place. Let us see with what thunderous force of condemnation it rises against the associates of Maximianus.

**CHAPTER XXII**

**25.** “Nor does just death condemn this man alone for his crime,” it says; “it also drags many into partnership in the crime by the chain of sacrilege, of whom it is written: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace.’”

Then, shortly afterward, having named all Maximianus’s ordainers individually—including these two about whom I am speaking, Felicianus and Praetextatus—it adds what they did, so that such things might deservedly be said against them:

> “They glued together a filthy vessel with collected filth by the deadly work of destruction.”

By this he wished it to be understood that they themselves were present and that they themselves ordained Maximianus by the imposition of hands. He adds also concerning the clerics of Carthage:

> “But also the clerics of the Church of Carthage, who, while attending upon the crime, offered their procuring assistance to an illicit incest.”

**CHAPTER XXIII**

**26.** I ask you, Cresconius: am I exaggerating this crime with any words of my own? If I had wished to do so, perhaps I would not have lacked words that, though not of this kind, would nevertheless have been adequate in some fashion.

I ask you, then: before these two men about whom I am presently speaking had returned to the concord of your communion, while they were held in that chain of sacrilege, with the poison of asps under their lips, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, and their feet swift to shed blood, how did they baptize? Was there in them the holy conscience of those who give, which cleansed those who receive? Did even a good reputation—however false—commend them, a reputation that, in your predicament, provided you not an escape route but a way to hurl yourself down, when so distinguished a council proclaims them guilty of a notorious crime?

Then, when they returned, as you believed your bishops who told falsehoods, before the day of delay, how were they received with their honors, together with those whom, while established outside the Church with Maximianus and held in the chain of sacrilegious schism, they had baptized?

[Note: [Col. 0509] Several manuscripts read: “they had baptized while held in the chain of schismatic sacrilege.”]

From what were they cleansed of so great a sacrilege? From what were they released from that chain? From where were their lips and mouths cleansed of the poison of asps?

[Note: [Col. 0509] The printed editions read: “their mouth, the poison of asps.” The manuscripts read: “their mouth from the poison of asps.”]

From where were they cleansed of cursing and bitterness? From where were their feet washed clean of the shedding of spiritual blood, toward which they had run swiftly? From where were their hands purified from the deadly work of destruction? From where was the inclination of their souls cleansed of illicit incest—not the limbs of their bodies?

[Note: [Col. 0509] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “their inclinations were cleansed.”]

**CHAPTER XXIV**

**27.** Whether you wish it or not, in order to defend this case you will be compelled to appeal to the patronage of the truth, which says that the Baptism of Christ, given not only through hidden but also through manifestly evil persons, and not only by the converted but also by the perverse, retains the unshaken firmness of its power; that such persons may indeed possess Baptism, but that it cannot benefit them unless they are corrected; and that those who are corrected may also be cleansed through the prayers of their brothers, by the love that covers a multitude of sins.

Before I show how shamelessly your bishops lied to you about the reception of the Maximianenses, I think that, according to their very lie and your account, you ought to see how your entire case has been overturned. You should no longer be seeking an answer but acknowledging the truth; you should no longer be preparing a contradiction but rather considering correction.

For now at least you see how truthfully I spoke those words to which you tried in vain to respond with a lie, and how rightly I said: “If no one rebaptizes those baptized in the sacrilegious schism for the unity of the party of Donatus, why is the true and complete law of that inheritance not acknowledged for the unity of Christ?” (*Book 1 Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §14).

You yourself admit that those who had persisted in the schism of Maximianus deserved a sentence by which they would not be bound if they returned themselves to the Church within the day of delay. Hence it is clear that, before they returned themselves, they baptized while in the schism in which they had persisted, and that they were received into your communion together with those whom they had baptized.

You see how the dead baptized: for concerning those who had persisted in the schism of Maximianus, before they returned to you, the sentence of the council of Bagai had said: “The shores are very full of the funerals of the Egyptians who are perishing.”

**CHAPTER XXV**

**28.** As for what I said—“When the decree was read out among them, they shouted with their mouths wide open; but now, when it has been read out by us, they fall silent” (ibid., §11)—they would already be falling silent much more appropriately under these penalties than they were becoming entangled when they spoke such things.

[Note: [Col. 0509] The Michaelinus codex reads: “what is worse?” The other manuscripts read: “under which they would be worse”; shortly afterward these same codices, together with the edition of Am., read: “when they were entangled while speaking such things,” omitting “how.”]

You see how true was what I said: “At last they ought to realize how much must be endured for peace, and, for the peace of Christ, return to the Church, which did not condemn what it did not know, if, for the peace of Donatus, it was decided to recall those who had been condemned” (*Book 1 Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §14).

For, according to your account, this is much more true: you said that even those were recalled after the period of delay had been granted, concerning whom it had already been stated in express terms: “Know that they have been condemned by the truthful voice of the universal council, under the judgment of God who presides.”

Since the period of delay was established after these words, how was it not decided to recall those who had been condemned? Or how can those things be unknown to us, who were born so much later, or even to the Christian world itself, which could not prove the charges brought against Caecilianus in the later judgment made overseas, when you, though an African—as you say—still did not know after so many years what had been done concerning the Maximianenses in Africa and in our own times? And, as we shall be able to show you, you still do not know it, because you believed your lying bishops.

**CHAPTER XXVI**

**29.** You say that I wished, as though by *anticategoria*—the Greek term for the rhetorical device—to turn back upon your ancestors the charge of traditio that had been made against mine, and you blame me for doing so, as though we were discussing types of cases or questions in a school of rhetoric rather than seeking the truth in the Church.

Would you say this to the prophet Elijah, who, when the most wicked king accused him of overthrowing Israel, replied: “I am not overthrowing Israel, but you and your father’s house are” (III Kings XVIII, 18)?

What does it matter to us that this kind of retorted objection is called by the Greeks *anticategoria* in the art of rhetoric, when we find it in prophetic authority? Whenever someone says, “I did not do it, but you did it,” it is necessary to speak the truth; one must not be afraid to say it.

And as for how you are to show that your ancestors did not do what they are shown to have done by reading their own confessions, you must consider this with the utmost vigilance, if you are capable of it, rather than frighten the inexperienced away from listening to us by means of a Greek word.

You have not proved that our ancestors were traditors. For merely saying that there are many documents by which this could be demonstrated does not mean that you have already demonstrated it.

But concerning your ancestors there exists the council of Secundus of Tigisis, held with very few participants at Cirta after the persecution involving the surrender of the books, so that a bishop might be ordained there in place of the deceased.

**CHAPTER XXVII**

**30.** Hear what took place there; for I have taken care to write below whatever was necessary.

In the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximianus for the seventh, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, at Cirta,

[Note: [Col. 0510] These proceedings of the council of Cirta were recorded in the copy more carefully examined at the time of the Carthage Conference as having occurred “after the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximianus for the eighth time, on the third day before the Ides of March”—that is, in the year of Christ 305, as Augustine attests below in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 3, §32. In Optatus, Book 1 *Against Parmenianus*, the same session at Cirta is noted as having been held “after the persecution, on the third day before the Ides of May.” From Augustine’s cited passage you will understand that “the persecution” was not that of Maxentius, as Albaspinaeus wished, but the persecution involving the surrender of the books. This persecution ceased in the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximianus for the eighth time.]

when Bishop Secundus of Tigisis had taken his seat in the first chair, in the house of Urbanus Donatus,

[Note: [Col. 0510] Optatus, Book 1, says: “Because the basilicas had not yet been restored, they took their seats in the house of Urbanus Carisius.”]

he said the following:

> “Let us first prove ourselves, and then we shall be able to ordain a bishop here.”

Secundus said to Donatus of Masculita:

> “It is said that you surrendered [the Scriptures].”

Donatus replied:

> “You know how Florus sought me out so that I might offer incense, and God did not deliver me into his hands, brother. But since God has forgiven me, you too preserve me for God.”

Secundus said:

> “What, then, shall we do concerning the martyrs? Since they did not surrender, they were crowned.”

Donatus said:

> “Send me to God; there I shall give an account.”

Secundus said:

> “Stand aside.”

Secundus said to Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae:

> “It is also said that you surrendered.”

Marinus replied:

> “I gave the little books to Pollus; for my books are safe.”

Secundus said:

> “Stand aside.”

Secundus said to Donatus of Calama:

> “It is said that you surrendered.”

Donatus replied:

> “I gave up medical books.”

Secundus said:

> “Stand aside.”

And elsewhere:

Secundus said to Victor of Rusucade:

> “It is said that you surrendered the four Gospels.”

Victor replied:

> “Valentianus was the curator; he himself forced me to throw them into the fire. I knew that they were destined for destruction.”

[Note: [Col. 0511] The manuscripts read: *delititia fuisse*.]

> “Forgive me this offense, and God also forgives me.”

[Note: [Col. 0511] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “and God will forgive me.”]

Secundus said:

> “Stand aside.”

And elsewhere:

Secundus said to Purpurius of Limata:

[Note: [Col. 0511] The Corbeiensis manuscript, of excellent quality, reads “of Liniata.” In some manuscripts of Augustine’s Letter 43, the reading is “of Liniacensis,” instead of “of Limatensis.”]

> “It is said that you killed the two sons of your sister at Milevis.”

Purpurius replied:

> “Do you think that I am frightened by you, as by another man? What did you do, when you were detained by the curator and the magistracy so that you would surrender the Scriptures? How did you free yourself from them, unless because you gave, or ordered to be given, something or other? For they did not let you go freely. I have killed, and I kill, those who act against me. Therefore do not provoke me to say more. You know that I make accusations concerning no one.”

Secundus the younger said to his uncle Secundus:

> “Do you hear what he says against you? He is ready to withdraw and make a schism, not only he himself but also all those whom you accuse. I know that they intend to leave you, pass judgment against you, and that you will remain alone as a heretic. Therefore, what does it matter to you who did what? He must give an account to God.”

Secundus said to Felix of Rotaria Centurion and to Victor of Garba:

[Note: [Col. 0511] The same Corbeiensis manuscript reads “of Rotoria Centurionis.” Other manuscripts likewise have the genitive form *Centurionis*. Optatus read the passage quite differently; speaking of the same session at Cirta, he says in Book 1: “Those who remained were consulted, namely Centurio, Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarius, and Nabor of Centurion,” and so forth.]

> “What do you think?”

They replied:

> “They have God, to whom they must give an account.”

Secundus said:

> “You know, and God knows. Sit down.”

And they all replied:

> “Thanks be to God.”

### 31

You defend these traditors, who, together with others at Carthage, pronounced sentences against Caecilian and his associates—among whom was also Silvanus of Cirta—in a remarkably “excellent” manner. Concerning this traditor’s case I shall shortly insert the records. For you are evidently going to say more about these men, and you thought that something important had to be said about the one Silvanus: you therefore supposed that you could clearly demonstrate the falsity of the charge of traditio brought against him because you inserted the sentence which he pronounced in the council, together with the other bishops, against Caecilian and the others who shared his communion—as though it were impossible for a traditor to condemn a traditor.

You see these matters more wisely than the apostle Paul. For he brought certain absurd charges against some people and did not consider that what he said could be impossible:

> “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?”  
> And especially: “In judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things that you judge.” (Rom. 2:21–22, 1)

These traditors, then, whom Secundus, terrified by their confessions, pardoned, he had with him at the council of Carthage. They pronounced sentences against those who were absent and had not confessed, although those who were present were not condemned on the basis of their own confession. This council would not have survived, nor continued in the memory of posterity, unless it had been recorded by others and preserved by those who were preparing to defend themselves by means of it, if anyone later accused them of the same crimes after those crimes had been released there.

[Note: Optatus, book 1: “Not long afterward, those same men”—who had taken part in the council at Cirta—“went to Carthage, traditors, conspirators, murderers, and ordained Majorinus after Caecilian’s ordination, creating a schism.” This happened in the year of Christ 311, and not earlier. The same Optatus places Caecilian’s ordination after the pardon sent by Maxentius to Africa, by which freedom was restored to Christians. But Maxentius began to gain control of Africa after defeating the tyrant Alexander; Alexander, according to Zosimus, was defeated after the death of Maximianus Herculius himself, which occurred in 310.]

[Note: Silvanus was ordained bishop of Cirta by Secundus of Tigisis in the council cited above. Compare Augustine’s Letter 53, §4.]

### Chapter 28

#### 32

It was also in the interest of Secundus himself that it should appear that, so as to prevent a schism—as peaceful men customarily do above all others—he had left all those matters to divine judgment. He ought to have done this much more at the council of Carthage, where nothing had been established against the absent, had not Lucilla, then a woman of immense power and wealth, inflamed by furious hatred, pressed on with great determination that another bishop should be ordained against Caecilian, as though Caecilian had been condemned.

[Note: Majorinus, whom Donatus succeeded.]

This was later recalled in the trial before the proconsul Zenophilus by a certain Nundinarius, at that time the deacon of Silvanus of Cirta, your bishop. Nundinarius had suffered hostility from his said bishop and was unable to reconcile himself with him as he wished. He had in fact dealt with this matter before Silvanus’s colleagues, more threateningly so that he would not reveal everything than submissively so that he might deserve pardon.

### Chapter 29

#### 33

From the records of that trial I have inserted the following brief excerpts. When Victor the grammarian had been brought forward from the entire district of Mociacus and placed before Constantine Maximus Augustus and Constantine the Younger, most noble Caesar, who were consuls, on the Ides of December, and when the deacon Nundinarius was also present, the proconsul Zenophilus said:

> “What is your name?”

He replied:

> “Victor.”

A little later, in another passage:

> Nundinarius replied: “Let the records be read.”  
> The proconsul Zenophilus said: “Let them be read.”

And Nundinius the court secretary read:

> “In the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximianus for the seventh time, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, from the records of Munatius Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the colony of Cirta:
>
> “When they had come to the house in which the Christians assembled, Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Paul the bishop: ‘Bring out the Scriptures of the law, and whatever else you have here, so that you may obey both the order and the command.’
>
> “The bishop Paul said: ‘The readers have the Scriptures, but we give what we have here.’
>
> “Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Paul: ‘Show me the readers, or send for them.’
>
> “The bishop Paul said: ‘You all know them.’
>
> “Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said: ‘We do not know them.’
>
> “The bishop Paul said: ‘The public office knows them—that is, the court secretaries Aedesius and Junius.’
>
> “Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said: ‘While the matter concerning the readers whom the public office will show remains pending, give also what you have here.’”

The bishop Paul was seated, together with the presbyters Montanus, Victor of Castellum, and Memorius. Mars was present with Aelius, as was Mars the deacon. Marcuclius, Catulinus, Silvanus, and Carosus the subdeacons brought out the items, together with Januarius, Marculius, Fructuosus, Miggene, Saturninus, Victor of Samsuricus, and the other gravediggers. Victor of Aufidius recorded the following inventory:

> “Two golden chalices; likewise six silver chalices,” and so forth.

And elsewhere:

> “After they had reached the library, empty cabinets were found there. There Silvanus brought out a silver *capitulata* and a silver lamp, saying that he had found them behind the chest.”

Victor of Aufidius said to Silvanus:

> “You would have been dead if you had not found them.”

Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Silvanus:

> “Search more carefully, lest anything remain here.”

Silvanus said:

> “Nothing remains here; we removed everything,” and so forth.

And elsewhere:

> “Copy of the written statement delivered to the bishops by the deacon Nundinarius:

> “Christ and his angels are witnesses that you have shared communion with traditors”—that is, that Silvanus of Cirta is a traditor and a thief of the property of the poor, as all of you bishops, presbyters, deacons, and elders know; and that, concerning the four hundred folles of the most illustrious woman Lucilla, on whose account you conspired among yourselves so that Majorinus might become bishop, a schism consequently arose. For Victor, your fuller, also gave twenty folles in the presence of yourselves and the people so that he might be made a presbyter, as Christ and his angels know,” and so forth.

And elsewhere:

> “After these things had been read, the proconsul Zenophilus said: ‘It is established by both the records and the letters that Silvanus is a traditor.’”

Again, elsewhere:

> The proconsul Zenophilus said: “What office did Silvanus then hold among the clergy?”  
> Victor replied: “Under the bishop Paul, persecution arose, and Silvanus was a subdeacon.”

[Note: The judicial records against Silvanus are found in the Appendix to this volume; they read “on the December Ides, with Sextus of Thamugadi brought forward.”]

[Note: Here the reading was “Constantius Maximus Augustus.” Baronius thinks that Constantius Chlorus, Constantine’s father, who died in A.D. 306, is meant, and that “Constantine the Younger” means his son Constantine. But in no consular lists are Constantius and Constantine the Younger joined together; the title *Maximus* was not assigned to Constantius Chlorus; nor was his son Constantine—who had no older namesake—called “the Younger.” And if Constantine had been consul with Constantius that year, then in the following year, when he held the consulship with Maximianus Herculius, he ought in the lists to have been called consul for the second time; this is nowhere found. We correct the error from an old copy of these same Records, in which the heading reads, “With Constantine Maximus,” etc.; this is A.D. 320. You have these Records in the Appendix below, and in them many passages from which you may understand that these events could not have occurred in the consulship of Constantius Chlorus, that is, in A.D. 306. For there the citizens of Cirta are called Constantinians, and the city itself is called Constantina, a name given it from Constantine, its restorer, only after Maxentius’ death. Moreover, it is there read that the innocence of Bishop Caecilian had already then been established by many judgments. “Why, therefore, passing over the man whose innocence has been proved, do you communicate with Silvanus?” Clerics questioned by Zenophilus also answered that they had received from their elders that Silvanus was a traditor, because in the persecution involving the surrender of the codices, which belongs to A.D. 303, he had handed over sacred property; they thus indicate that Silvanus committed the crime of traditio long before that time. Add that in the time of Constantius Chlorus Silvanus could not have been brought before the public court of Zenophilus, a consular official, by the deacon Nundinarius on the charge of traditio, nor finally have been driven into exile under the persecution of Ursacius and Zenophilus (as Cresconius later alleges here, §31).]

[Note: The same records have “Victor of Deusatelum and the presbyters Memorius.”]

[Note: The published editions have *Carioso*. All the manuscripts, however, have *Caroso*.]

[Note: It should be read *Victore Samsurici*, as is clear from the judicial records against Silvanus, where that Victor is repeatedly called “Victor of Samsuricus.”]

[Note: The published editions read *apertum est*, “it was opened.” The text is corrected from the following book, book 4, section 66, and from the judicial records against Silvanus.]

[Note: The records against Silvanus consistently have *orcam*, “chest.”]

[Note: The same records read *tradiderunt quibus communicastis*, “you shared communion with those to whom you handed them over.”]

[Note: *Follis* is a type of coin. Compare book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8, section 9, and Sermon 389.]

[Note: The published editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “Who was administering? Then Silvanus, in the clerical order, replied.” The text is corrected with some assistance from the manuscripts of this work, but especially from the copy of the Records against Silvanus.]

[Note: In the editions, *nulli*, “to no accusers.” The manuscripts have *nulla*, “nothing,” so that the reference is more likely to the charges brought than to the accusers.]

[Note: The passage is mutilated. It might be restored by adding the four words *baptizare me vis, debes*, “you wish to baptize me; you must,” so that the text would continue: “you must baptize those who unknowingly received [baptism] from adulterers whom you have now exposed.” Since *baptizare* occurs again immediately afterward, a copyist’s error is easy to understand.]

[Note: Most manuscripts omit *turbatae*, “of disturbed [peace].”]

[Note: The two same manuscripts read *in hac sententia ventilari*, “to be tossed about in this opinion.” Other manuscripts have *ventilare*, “to toss about.”]

[Note: The published editions read *dicuntur*, “are said.” The manuscripts have *dicit*, “he says”; and one manuscript, the Georgian, has *hortamento esse*, “to be an encouragement,” as in Cyprian.]

[Note: Am. and Er. and several manuscripts read *fraudibus parare*, “acquire by deceit.”]

[Note: Am. and Er. read: “For the bishops did not establish this Church.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts read *displicent*, “they displease.”]

[Note: Am. and Er. read: “Nor, if you showed me in it that I myself was a traditor,” etc.]

[Note: The published editions have *constitutis*, “having been established.” The manuscripts have *constitutos*, “those established,” governed by the following verb *macularent*, “would stain.”]

[Note: Am. and several manuscripts read *Militiadis*.]

[Note: Am. reads *in campo facundiae sepositos*, “set aside in the field of your eloquence.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *in campo facundiae sepositus*, “set aside in the field of your eloquence.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

### Chapter 30

#### 34

Do you have anything to say to these things, brother Cresconius? I think that shame has not so entirely disappeared from human affairs that you still suppose that, for Silvanus’s acquittal, the sentence he pronounced against Caecilian and his colleagues as traditors ought to be read aloud—lest you compel us even more to quote something similar from the apostle’s Letter, as I recalled shortly before:

> “You who preach that one must not hand things over, do you hand them over?”  
> And: “In judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things that you judge.”

“But afterward,” you say, “when he was unwilling to share communion with Ursacius and Zenophilus, who were persecuting him, he was sent into exile.”

[Note: The editions read, “But after Ursacius.” Some manuscripts read more correctly, “But afterward, you say,” etc.; Cresconius himself makes this reproach.]

On the contrary: he who was already a traditor also wanted to remain a heretic, so that he might possess in the party of Donatus the false honor which he could not possess in the Catholic Church, now that the records of his traditio had been exposed in a public trial with such manifest evidence.

You will surely say that these things are false and, on behalf of your ancestors, will produce whatever you can against ours. Perhaps you will not be able to do so, because you will find nothing to produce. But suppose that you found something; suppose that you produced it. Is your shamelessness so great that you insist that what you produce should be believed more readily than what we produce?

Either traditors existed on both sides, if you also read something concerning the confession of our people; or, if you think that something has been fabricated by our people against yours, why do you not allow us to suppose that your people likewise fabricated something against ours?

Therefore, in view of human actions—whether they have been made manifest on both sides or remain uncertain on both sides—let us not quarrel, we who believe in one God, but let us agree in the grace of Christ, which is a certain and divine gift. For when the records of our ancestors and yours are read to us, born so long afterward, with opposing accounts from both sides, what could be more unjust than to forbid us even to doubt? But if doubt is permitted, what could be more sufficient?

For just as it is uncertain from whom the evil of traditio arose, so it is not uncertain from whom the good of restoring disturbed peace is commanded.

[Note: Most manuscripts omit *turbatae*, “of disturbed [peace].”]

### Chapter 31

#### 35

Accordingly, whoever rejects the peace of Christ on account of another person’s uncertain evil is certainly evil himself. Cyprian, after all, did not abandon the peace of the wheat on account of the certain wickedness of the mixed tares. Writing to Maximus, he said:

> “Even if tares appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity must nevertheless not be hindered, so that, because we see that there are tares in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church.”

He did not say, “We suspect,” “we suppose,” “we imagine,” “we infer,” or “we believe”; he said, “We see.” O word by which every doubt would be removed, so that the body of Christ would not be divided!

If you desire wheat alone, groan in the labor of the field, rejoice in the hope of the granary, and endure the wicked in communion with Christ’s Sacraments, lest, before the time of the shore, you break the nets and produce what you were unwilling to endure.

I would say these things if you had proved anything concerning the traditors whom you accuse. Indeed, at the present time I would not even say these things; for I am not commanded to tolerate those with whom I am no longer compelled to live.

But if a traditor were now demonstrated to me, with what conscience would I abandon so many Christian peoples to whom no traditor has been demonstrated? Moreover, if I myself now learn what I did not know shortly before, why do you revoke in me what I did know? I knew that I had received Christ’s Baptism; and you yourselves grant that another person’s crime, when unknown, harms no one.

### Chapter 32

#### 36

Why, then, do you rebaptize today someone who was baptized yesterday, when today you teach him of another person’s crime, which I did not know yesterday? When he did not know from whom he had received it, he was not guilty regarding the Baptism he had received. Now that he has learned this from you, why is he made guilty of having his Baptism annulled?

For whether he agrees with your documents or does not agree with them, the person who received Christ’s Baptism through the ministry of a traditor cannot, according to your own position, be rightly baptized unless you prove that he knew from whom he received it.

Now turn your mind away from partisan zeal and consider how innumerable is the multitude of Christians in Africa itself who do not know who the traditors were—how much more so throughout the rest of the world. Unless you prove that they knew this when they were baptized, you will either not dare to call them persons who ought to be baptized, or you will dare to judge what is hidden in the heart.

And where is the divine statement that pleases you, which you yourself inserted:

> “The things that are manifest belong to you; but the things that are hidden belong to the Lord your God.” (Deut. 29:29)

Believe the Christian world when it says to you: “I know Christ’s Baptism; but who the traditors were in Africa, or anywhere else, I do not know.” Why do you judge hidden human matters in me in order to revoke manifest divine things in me?

Suppose that you now prove to me the other person’s crime of which you speak. I did not know it when I received Baptism. If, because of those whom you now expose, you wish to baptize me, you must baptize those who unknowingly received [Baptism] from adulterers whom you have now exposed. What do you say to this except:

> “Nothing is holy, nothing is clean, except what I want and in whatever manner I want”?

[Note: The passage is mutilated. It may perhaps be restored by adding the four words *baptizare me vis, debes*, “you wish to baptize me; you must,” so that the text then continues, “baptize those who unknowingly received [Baptism] from adulterers whom you have now exposed.” A copyist could easily have slipped at the word *baptizare*, which recurs immediately afterward.]

[Note: The manuscripts have *et quando voluero*, “and whenever I want.”]

### Chapter 33

#### 37

“In this matter,” you say, “the conscience of nearly the whole world is a witness.”

You are answered: In this matter the whole world has absolutely no common knowledge.

“This,” you say, “our ancestors received from their parents.”

You are answered: They received it from people who were mistaken or who were making accusations. The ancestors of the Jews, too, received from their ancestors the story that Christ’s body had been stolen from the tomb.

“Those who knew by whom and in what places this crime of traditio was committed,” you say, “did not die long ago.”

You are answered: Our people say the same on behalf of their own side.

“There are also books,” you say, “in which the sequence of events has been faithfully and carefully recorded; there are records, there are letters, and the manifest confession of many is also preserved.”

You are answered: Our people likewise have these things on behalf of their own side.

Either, then, let us believe those who were able to persuade of their cause those Churches which we read about in the divine and canonical Books; or, as you said concerning Optatus, let us neither acquit what is doubtful nor condemn it, and let us hold fast, in brotherly love, to the peace of Christ, whose goodness is not doubtful.

[Note: Some manuscripts have *pro suis parentibus*, “on behalf of their parents.”]

### Chapter 34

#### 38

“But you admit,” you say, “that the Easterners, whom you now concede to be ours, were not unaware of this crime.”

To prove this, you insert the beginning of the letter of the Council of Sardica, where the name of Donatus, your bishop of Carthage, is found written. You think and affirm that this happened because the Easterners, who sent these writings from their council, disapproved of the crime of the traditors, withdrew from communion with them, and therefore shared communion with your Donatus.

Learn, then, what you do not know: the Council of Sardica was an Arian council. This has long been entirely clear, as we have it in our hands: it was chiefly assembled against Athanasius, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, who vigorously argued against and refuted their error, which had arisen in that very city, more than anyone else.

It is therefore not surprising if those heretics attempted to enlist Donatus among themselves, since the Catholic Church condemned them throughout the whole world.

Yet we possess these letters without the names of the cities of the bishops to whom they were sent. Either there was some Donatus who was not a bishop in Africa, and the name “Carthage” was added to him by your people; or, as I said, an Eastern heresy attempted to attach the African heresy to itself.

The latter is especially credible because an Eastern Catholic would never have written to the bishop of Carthage while passing over the Roman bishop. At the very least, your bishop ought to have been named—the one whom you customarily send from Africa to Rome with a few of your own people.

But thanks be to God that, even if it began, that conspiracy of the Eastern heretics with the African heretics was unable to prevail.

In your letter you placed the Arians among the heretics detested by both you and us. Thus, I have no need to dispute with you about this question as well.

For you posed to yourself a question as though it had been raised by us:

> “If these things are so, how did the Easterners later separate from communion with your people?”

And you replied that they could not remain consistent when receiving our people again, whose case had been condemned.

Is it surprising that your bishops, from such distant lands, can safely tell you whatever they wish? And if the matter were altogether as you say, what did the many peoples do who, although they did not know these things, are nevertheless judged by you to require rebaptism?

Is it not plausible that these peoples could have been unaware of such matters, when you—being somewhat more diligent in these affairs—would not have asked what your Africans did with the Maximianists in Africa unless you wished to answer my letters?

[Note: The published editions read *si*, “if.” The text is corrected from the Corbeiensis manuscript.]

[Note: The manuscripts consistently write *Serdicensis* here, rather than *Sardicensis*; the earliest editions do likewise.]

[Note: See below, book 4, §52.]

[Note: This Sardican council is believed to be the same as the council of Philippopolis, which the Arian Easterners held separately after leaving Sardica.]

[Note: This is the reading of Am., Er., and all the manuscripts. Only the Lovaniensis edition has *quod notum jam diu est*, “which has long been known.”]

### Chapter 35

#### 39

As for what I said—“Even if the traditio of some of the deceased in our communion were proved, which we reject and disapprove, it would not stain us in any respect” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 1, section 19)—you thought it ridiculous and unworthy of my prudence.

I now wish to know how your prudence refuted it. Is it because you say that you do not see how or to what extent we reject and disapprove of it, since, placed in their schism, we never condemned it after recognizing the error?

Consider instead how briefly I shall answer you.

I am in the Church whose members are all those Churches which we know, from the canonical Scriptures, to have been born and strengthened through the labors of the apostles. With the help of the Lord, I will not abandon their communion, whether in Africa or anywhere else.

If there were traditors in this communion whom I do not know, when you demonstrate them I shall detest them as dead in body and heart. Nevertheless, I will not be separated on account of the dead from the living who remain in the holy unity of that same Church.

For those men did not establish this Church; rather, in it they were wheat if they were good, and chaff if they were evil.

But you—whose manifest Church could not be stained by tares or chaff—what caused your division except the desire for sacrilegious schism?

“If you are displeased,” you say, “with wicked men, flee and leave the Church of the traditors. Do not follow the footsteps of your erring ancestors.”

I reply: If they were not traditors, they are my ancestors; if they were traditors—which I am not—they are not my ancestors.

I hold fast to the Church, full of wheat and chaff. I do not say merely that, if you showed me others carrying their own burden; but even if you showed me that I myself was a traditor in it, where I am permitted to change for the better, I would have no need to separate from it.

If I come to know of such people in communion with its Sacraments, I correct those whom I can by the word and discipline of the Lord, and I tolerate those whom I cannot correct. I flee the chaff, lest I myself become chaff; I do not flee the threshing floor, lest I become nothing.

### Chapter 36

#### 40

Therefore do not needlessly toss me about with this statement. Rather, the apostolic command that you yourself quoted reminds me how I should act:

> “Do not share in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.” (1 Tim. 5:22)

For, to show how one does not share in the sins of others, he added: “Keep yourself pure.” The person who keeps himself pure does not share in the sins of others, even though he shares with them in the Sacraments of God—not their sins, but those divine Sacraments which they turn to their own judgment, whereas he has made himself separate from them by keeping himself pure.

Otherwise Cyprian too—God forbid—would have shared in the sins of his colleagues who were kidnappers and usurers, with whom nevertheless he remained in communion in the divine Sacraments. Concerning them he says:

> “Many bishops, who ought to have been an ornament and example to the rest, neglecting the administration of divine things, became administrators of worldly affairs. Abandoning their chairs and deserting their people, they wandered through foreign provinces, seeking the markets of profitable business. While the brothers in the Church were hungry, they wanted to possess abundant silver; they seized estates by treacherous frauds and increased loans through multiplying interest.”  
> (*Letter, or Sermon, on the Fallen*)

Did he share in the sins of such men? Did he follow their sect? Yet he remained with them in communion in those same Sacraments, because those Sacraments had not been established by their conduct; rather, by their evil conduct they made the Sacraments serve as a punishment for themselves.

[Note: The published editions read *dicuntur*, “are said.” The manuscripts have *dicit*, “he says.” The Georgian manuscript has *hortamento esse*, “to be an encouragement,” as in Cyprian.]

[Note: Am. and Er. and several manuscripts read *fraudibus parare*, “to acquire by fraud.”]

### Chapter 37

#### 41

What is the meaning of what you say when, speaking in my person, you proposed that I had never handed over the divine Testament? You add:

> “But the one who handed it over created you.”

Then you weave together statements that seemed to sound well to you:

> “The stream is drawn from its source, and the members follow the head. When the head is sound, the whole body is sound; and if there is any disease or defect in it, it weakens all the members. Whatever has developed in the stock looks back to its origin.”

After this, as though drawing your final conclusion, you say:

> “The person who does not follow the sect of the innocent cannot be innocent.”

In all these words of yours, you made my creator and my head nothing other than a traditor—whom you were able only to accuse, not to convict.

I do not, however, make his innocence my creator, source, or head. Rather, you return to the very error in which Petilian was mistaken: you do not want Christ to be the source and head of each person who is born in the sanctification of Baptism.

You do not want to fall under the curse of which it is written:

> “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being.” (Jer. 17:5)

Yet you cannot escape this by any other route, lest, when you recoil from one thing, you fall into another.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *nec cum resilieris*, “nor when you recoil.”]

### Chapter 38

#### 42

You also admonish me by testimony from the Scriptures concerning what I should still answer to these matters. For you say that this was written for this reason:

> “Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers.” (Ezek. 20:18)

You do not notice that this was said to the Jews so that they would not imitate the evil deeds of their fathers, not so that they would be cut off from that people of God.

If, therefore, King David, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, and the other holy men and prophets of God were permitted to keep God’s commandments among despisers of God’s law, and to hurl many fitting and true words against those very transgressors of the commandment; if they were permitted not to imitate or follow the sins of their fathers—sins by which, under Moses, they so offended God that none of them was worthy to enter the promised land—but to detest and flee them, and to rebuke those who committed such deeds by comparing them to such fathers; and if they nevertheless did not establish for themselves another people, as though purified and refined by a sacrilegious separation, how is it not permitted to us neither to imitate deeds—of people whom I do not know—which you accuse more than you prove, nor to separate from the holy Church which, as the apostle says, “bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world”? (Col. 1:6)

Did traditors institute any Sacraments in which I might be baptized? Did they compose books for posterity concerning the practice or imitation of traditio, whose teaching we hold and follow?

If they had done so, and refused to share communion with anyone except those who read and approved those books, they themselves would have separated from the unity of the Church. If you saw me in their division, then you ought to say that I was in the Church of the traditors.

But if they wrote their wicked instructions concerning the practice of traditio and nevertheless did not gather outside the Church in their own congregation and communion, they would on that account be counted as tares, on whose account the wheat ought not rightly to be abandoned.

[Note: The manuscripts read *et illis qui ea committerent; similitudinem talium patrum increpare*, “and to rebuke those who committed such deeds by the likeness of such fathers.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts read *et eliquatum*, “and refined.”]

### Chapter 39

#### 43

Look, I say again what prevents you from saying more to me:

> “You accuse before me those who died long ago, whom my knowledge has not judged.”  
> (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 1, section 19)

You reply:

> “It is permitted for you to judge even today, and judgment can be passed not only on the living but also on the dead. For although the one who sinned is dead, what he committed never dies.”

What if, while he was alive, he corrected himself and reconciled himself to God? Has what he committed not died and been erased? Thus Felicianus and Praetextatus, the ordainers of Maximianus, when—according to what you say—time had been granted them, corrected themselves from so great a crime.

It is astonishing if people’s own sins do not harm those who have corrected the deeds they committed, but do harm others who have not committed them at all. If this concerns us, add: “who have not even known of the deeds.”

But you say that I am permitted to judge even today because judgment can be passed not only on the living but also on the dead.

Very well: I want to judge, but you do not want to bring the case itself to trial. Rather, although we demonstrate that it was then brought to trial and without doubt then settled, you do not want to acknowledge it.

But let us instead grant you something that you can teach. Why do you insist that those whom you have not yet taught must already be rebaptized, since, once you have taught them that they were baptized by traditors whom they did not know, you ought not to baptize them—just as you do not baptize those who were unknowingly baptized by adulterers after those adulterers have been exposed and convicted?

### Chapter 40

#### 44

Perhaps you will say here:

> “But judgment has already been passed concerning Caecilian.”

You are answered: Judgment had already been passed concerning Primianus as well, by one hundred of your bishops, whom Maximianus had persuaded that he was most unjust, before you held the council of Bagai.

In the first judgment he was condemned while absent; in the second he was acquitted while present. If those whom he baptized cannot be rebaptized after the first judgment, how much more is this true after the second?

Likewise, Caecilian was condemned at Carthage in the first judgment of Secundus of Tigisis while absent, but in the second judgment of Miltiades of Rome he was acquitted while present.

You do not want us to be certain about him; at least allow us to doubt. For not only does the person who knows Caecilian to be innocent defeat you, but so does the person who does not know him to be guilty.

Yet you judge that both must be rebaptized: both those who say, “We know,” and those who say, “We do not know what kind of man Caecilian was.”

Are those whom Primianus baptized after the first judgment, in which he was condemned while absent, not to be baptized, while those whom Caecilian baptized after the second judgment, in which he was acquitted while present, are to be baptized?

It was not permitted to condemn the one who had been condemned; at least let it be permitted to doubt concerning the one who had been acquitted.

Even if his crimes were certain to us, since we are established in the Church which the Holy Spirit foretold as a threshing floor containing chaff, the sins of others, which we have not imitated, would in no way stain us.

And yet, even when these things are said to be uncertain to us, we are not merely declared guilty; we are also judged to require baptism.

Is this how you act? Is this how you overturn everything? Do you really think that you have so much license that whatever you want is holy and whatever you want is unclean?

Restrain yourselves. Do not advance in evil, lest you perish from what is good.

[Note: Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *Militiadis*.]

[Note: The published editions have *constitutis*, “having been established.” The manuscripts have *constitutos*, “those established,” governed by the following verb *macularent*, “would stain.”]

### Chapter 41

#### 45

As for what I said—“If you are speaking about persecutions, I answer quickly: if you have suffered anything unjustly, it does not pertain to those by whom the people who do such things against you, although they do them wickedly, are nevertheless commendably tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 1, section 20)—you attempted to refute this deceitfully, without considering at all that your letter would have a reader with a sound head.

For you answer as though I had said that persecution ought to be inflicted upon you for the sake of the peace of unity. I did not say that in that passage. Rather, I said:

> “If you have suffered anything unjustly, it does not pertain to those by whom the people who commit such things against you, although they do them wickedly, are commendably tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity.”

Since this was stated with complete clarity, let at least those whom you wished to deceive attend to its explanation.

I do not think that you failed to understand something so clear. Rather, you easily thought that the brevity of my statement could be cast into darkness, so that, by saying something else, you might appear to have answered it.

Why, then, did I say that the wicked members of our communion—that is, the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor—are commendably tolerated by our good people for the sake of peace when they act unjustly toward you? Why should I myself point this out and defend it, when the blessed Cyprian, speaking openly and candidly on my behalf, says that even when wicked people are seen in the Church, the Church must not be abandoned on their account?

This is what I said: that they must be tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity.

For those who unjustly persecute you do not persecute you more than they persecute us. By unjustly persecuting you, they give you—though it is a false likeness of glory—to deceive the inexperienced; but to us they give a great wound of grief.

### Chapter 42

#### 46

Then, recalling certain dead people whom you say were killed by our people, you enlarge the passage at great length, as though you had been placed in the field of your eloquence, in which you think yourselves like martyrs.

Meanwhile, every day we suffer unbelievable deeds from your clerics and Circumcellions, much worse than those of any robbers or bandits.

Armed with terrifying weapons of every kind and wandering about menacingly, they disturb not merely ecclesiastical quiet and peace but human quiet and peace itself. In nightly attacks they invade the houses of Catholic clerics and leave them stripped and empty. They seize the clerics themselves, beat them with clubs, cut them with iron, and throw them aside half alive.

Moreover, in a new and previously unheard-of form of crime, they pour and force lime mixed with vinegar into their eyes. Although they could have blinded them quickly by tearing out their eyes, they choose to torture them more severely rather than blind them at once.

At first they used only lime for this crime; but after they learned that those to whom they had done this quickly recovered their sight, they added vinegar.

## CHAPTER XLIII

**47.** I pass over how much they previously committed—acts that compelled the establishment of these laws against your error, laws tempered more by Christian gentleness than enforced with the strength of vigor appropriate to such great crimes.

The Catholic bishop Servus of Thubursicum, when he was reclaiming a place invaded by your people and the representatives of both parties were awaiting the proconsular hearing, suddenly had your armed men rush upon him in that very town and barely escaped alive. His father, a presbyter grave in age and character, died a few days later from the slaughter in which he had been grievously afflicted.

Maximian, the Catholic bishop of Bagai, after a judicial sentence had been pronounced between the parties, had recovered the basilica of the Calvian estate [Note: Thus in all the manuscripts. But the printed editions read *Calmanensis*.], which your people had once illegally usurped. When he was retaining it by an indisputable right, your men attacked him there beneath the altar where he had taken refuge; breaking the altar above him, they brutally beat him with its timbers and other clubs, and also with swords, until he filled the entire place with blood.

He had also received a great wound in the groin, from which he would have died immediately because of the abundant flow of blood, had not their greater cruelty, through God’s hidden mercy, proved beneficial. For when he was being dragged half alive and face down, with the limbs on that side exposed, dust secretly blocked the gushing veins [Note: The printed editions read *obstruxit*, “blocked.” All the manuscripts read *obstrusit*. And in Letter 185 to Boniface, where the slaughter of this same Maximian is described, §27 reads: “dust blocked the overflowing vein.”].

Then, while he was being carried away in the hands of our people, they again rushed upon him, violently snatched him away, punished him more severely, and threw him at night from a high tower. Below, he lay gently received upon a bed of dung and ashes, deprived of consciousness and scarcely retaining his last breath [Note: The Michaelinus manuscript reads *trahens*, “drawing” or “dragging.”].

There a passing pauper found him, having turned aside to that place for the purpose of relieving himself. He recognized him, and, frightened, summoned his wife, whom he had kept at a distance out of modesty because she was carrying a lamp. Then the two of them carried him home, either out of pity or also in hope of gaining some small reward, since, whether alive or dead, he would at least be shown to our people after being recovered.

What more need I say? He was healed by a wondrous recovery and is alive; more scars are counted on his body than limbs. News had reached the lands across the sea that he had been killed by your people, and the enormity of that crime and its grievous outrage had stirred everything with dreadful sorrow wherever it could be heard. When he himself later followed there, his still-fresh scars defended that false report: those who then looked at him and scarcely believed him alive could not seem to have rashly asserted that he was dead.

There he found the fellow bishop of Thubursicum whom I mentioned shortly before, as well as several others who had endured similar or scarcely lesser sufferings. Since no opportunity seemed open to them for returning to their own places, and since the notorious frenzy of your Circumcellions—providing a dreadful bodyguard for your clerics—had become universally and most odiously known, immense hatred against you was kindled. From this it came about that all the earlier laws against you were revived and these new ones enacted [Note: The laws of Honorius. See the note above, vol. I, cols. 445–446].

Yet if the severity of all these laws is compared with the disordered savagery of your people, which rages without any law at all, it must be called remarkable leniency. For these laws commend Catholic gentleness, invested with such great authority, more than they punish heretical brutality. Indeed, against us that brutality rages all the more boldly and madly, devising, threatening, and carrying out murders, robberies, arsons, and mutilations.

## CHAPTER XLIV

**48.** I wished to recall these events because they caused these imperial statutes to be enacted in our own times against you—or rather against your error [Note: Compare Augustine, Letter 185, §26]. For what could be more beneficial, if you have any understanding? [Note: The editions of Erasmus and Louvain read: “For what now, if you have any understanding, could be more plausible?” The manuscript reading is restored.]

As for all the savage acts of your people that I have either learned from the writings of earlier generations or witnessed myself—acts by which, from the beginning of your division down to the present time, they have persecuted the Catholic Church—if I wished to recount them, what tongue, what writing, what amount of time and leisure would suffice?

## CHAPTER XLV

**49.** When I was dealing with Optatus, and you preferred to excuse this matter rather than clear it, you said that your people could not be held guilty here because no one had brought them forward for punishment. The many formal complaints of our people concerning the frenzied violence of yours filled the public archives more quickly than those acts ever deserved any punishment from you.

But perhaps here too it may be said that the complaints were indeed filed, but no case was brought to your people for them to punish [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The editions read: “but no complaint was brought for punishing them,” incorrectly]. Listen, then, to some events that I myself experienced.

When we had investigated the case of the Maximianists received by your people, whom they had condemned, and had publicized it everywhere with all the fervor at our command, those men, unable to find any answer to matters so recent and so clearly established, began with their customary violence and even greater boldness to deter us, through the furious assaults and riots of the Circumcellions, from proclaiming the Catholic truth and refuting their falsehood.

And because many who were entangled in the snares of their error—people with whom we were laboring to free them from it—answered us that we ought to deal with their bishops, and that they greatly desired our conference, where they could see by whose assertions the truth would prevail over falsehood, we decided at the council of all Africa at Carthage that, with the testimony of public records also introduced, we should show those who demanded this that we had not failed to fulfill their wish. Your bishops were therefore to be summoned peacefully, each by that one of our bishops who occupied the same place as he did [Note: See Augustine, Letter 88].

Our purpose was that, once error had been removed through our conference, we might enjoy Christian and fraternal fellowship, unity, charity, and peace. We considered that, if they were willing for this to happen, then, with God’s mercy assisting, whatever the truth might be in our case could very easily be recognized; but if they refused, at least their distrust would become apparent, and not without reason, to those who had requested this of us.

It happened: they were summoned, and they refused. To demonstrate the words they used—their deceit, cursing, and bitterness—would now take too long.

## CHAPTER XLVI

**50.** Meanwhile Crispinus, your bishop of Calama, when summoned by my fellow bishop Possidius in that same city before the official record, at first deferred the matter to your council, promising that there, together with his colleagues, he would consider what answer he ought to give.

Then, after a considerable interval, when the summons was renewed, he answered again before the official record: “Do not fear the words of a sinful man” (1 Maccabees 2:62). And again: “Beware of saying anything in the ears of a fool, lest, when he hears, he mock your sensible words” (Proverbs 23:9).

Finally, I define his answer in patriarchal language: “Let the impious depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways.”

When learned and unlearned alike laughed at this answer—for the man said that he did not fear the words of a sinful man to whom he did not dare reply, and that he did not wish to say anything in the ears of a fool, as though some secret were about to be rashly entrusted to a fool’s ears, although many sensible people could hear what he was saying, and although Christ the Lord spoke at such length to the Pharisees, foolish though they were, for the sake of people of that kind; and for saying that he did not wish to know the ways of the impious, as though those whom he considered impious wished to teach him their ways, rather than that he himself, if he held to the ways of God, ought to teach even the impious, as it is written: “I will teach the unjust your ways, and the impious will turn to you” (Psalm 50:15)—when, therefore, many understood this answer and many others demonstrated how empty it was as far as the case was concerned, but how bitter and abusive it was in what did not pertain to the case; and when it was thus shown and mocked that his learned old age, as you regard it, could prove nothing against the truth when confronted by a young recruit of yesterday [Note: He called the young man “yesterday’s recruit.”]—suddenly, a few days later, while Possidius was traveling, another Crispinus, his presbyter and, as is reported, his relative, laid an ambush of armed men.
