Our fellow bishop had almost fallen into it when, having seen and been warned of them, he fled and turned aside to a certain estate [Col. 0524], where that man would either not dare to do anything, or would not be strong enough, or, if he did anything, could not deny it.

When he learned this, he immediately followed with such blind madness that he now considered it disgraceful to remain concealed. Then he surrounded with armed men the house in which Possidius had shut himself in with his companions, battered it with stones, encircled it with flames, and sought access from every side.

The crowd of inhabitants who happened to be there, remembering the danger they would face if such a crime were carried out in that place, partly begged him to spare the man, whom they did not dare to oppose by resisting, and partly extinguished the fires that had been set. But when he, no less fiercely, fervently, and relentlessly, pressed on with what he had begun, the door eventually yielded to the blows.

They entered, wounded the beasts they found in the lower part of the house, and brought the bishop down from the upper rooms, inflicting blows and insults upon him. Crispinus himself intervened to prevent them from raging more violently—apparently yielding to the requests of others, though he seemed less concerned to heed their entreaty in his anger than afraid of having witnesses to his crime.

## CHAPTER XLVII

**51.** When these events became known in the town of Calama, people awaited Crispinus, your bishop, to see how he would punish his presbyter. An official complaint, recorded in the municipal proceedings, was also submitted; fear or shame of it ought to have compelled him to exercise ecclesiastical punishment.

When he utterly disregarded this, and such a tumult arose among your people [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read: “and such a tumult arose among our people.”], that they were thought likely to close the roads against the proclamation of the truth to which they could not reply [Note: Louvain reads: “so that, because they could not reply to the truth being proclaimed, they…” *Because* should be deleted, and the reading should be: “to which they could not reply.”]—indeed, they were already visibly doing so—the laws that were available but seemed not to be available lay inactive in our hands. They were brought to bear against Crispinus, your bishop, more to demonstrate our gentleness than to punish their boldness.

For there was no other way to make known what the Catholic Church, with Christ’s help, could and would do against her enemies: not according to the heretical presumption of private fury, with Circumcellions raging, but according to prophetic truth, with kings subjected to the yoke of the Lord God.

Crispinus was therefore brought before the authorities and, although he had denied to the proconsul who questioned him that he was a heretic, was very easily convicted. Nevertheless, because Possidius intervened, he was not compelled to pay the ten pounds of gold that the elder emperor Theodosius had established as the penalty for all heretics [Note: See Augustine, Letter 88, §7].

Not content with this exceedingly mild sentence, he decided, for reasons I do not know—though it was said that all your people disapproved of the decision—to appeal to the sons of that same Theodosius. The appeal was accepted and the rescript issued.

What else could this mean except that the party of Donatus already knew that it belonged, along with the other heretics, under that golden penalty? With those others, because of their communion in such persecution, it must either reckon that it shares a common justice, or, if it does not reckon this, it must not boast that it is just merely because it is restrained by the same penalty by which it sees those heresies restrained that it admits to be unjust.

And finally, it should understand that it is not punishment but cause that makes a martyr of Christ.

Let it accuse us of being such savage persecutors that even after the imperial rescript Crispinus did not pay that gold into the treasury, because Catholic bishops obtained a pardon for him; and that now, even amid the most recent laws [Note: See the note above, vol. I, cols. 445–446], which threaten confiscation to your bishops, he sits secure amid his own property, while Catholic clerics, in the hands of your Circumcellions and clerics, stake their homes, food, safety, and bodily sight.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**52.** What shall I call those who do such things—robbers, pirates, or some savage tribe of barbarians—when they cannot even be compared with the devil himself, the master of every cruelty?

He stripped the holy man Job of all his possessions and struck him with a grievous wound from head to foot; yet even there, while his entire body had been handed over to the devil’s power, a place remained for his eyes intact and unharmed, and he did not extinguish them.

But evidently these matters are not brought before your people [Note: Erasmus, Louvain, and Venice read: “are not reported.” M.], since Crispinus preferred to go to Carthage and be overcome by his own stubbornness, to reject the very mild sentence pronounced against him through the intervention of an episcopal gentleness, and to appeal to the sons of the man whose law he saw had caught him, thereby stirring up the entire party of Donatus over something which he neither wished nor was compelled to endure alone, rather than punish the exceedingly bold and hateful crime of one of his presbyters by simple deposition.

**53.** A certain Restitutus was your presbyter in the region of Hippo. When, moved by the reason of truth, he had openly and willingly passed over to Catholic peace before these imperial laws commanded it, he was dragged from his house by your clerics and Circumcellions, led openly in daylight to a nearby fortified town, and, while a crowd watched and no one dared resist, beaten with clubs according to the will of madmen, rolled in a muddy pool, and dishonored with a covering of reeds.

After he had sufficiently tormented the eyes of those who grieved and satisfied those who laughed [Note: Several manuscripts read “after he had been sufficiently tormented”], he was led from there to another place, where none of our people dared to approach, and was released only on the twelfth day.

I myself complained about this to your bishop Proculianus of Hippo, submitting an official municipal record, so that, if action proved necessary, he could not deny that the matter had been brought before him. What he answered, how he evaded investigating the case, and how afterward he attempted more deceitfully to elude our purpose by refusing to answer are sufficiently attested by those same proceedings [Note: See Augustine, Letter 88, §6, and Letter 105, §3].

But now, how much do the clerics who have crossed over to us from your side suffer at the hands of your people? When would we have enough time to tell it? In short, it is not only those who come to us from there who abandon the truth because of persecution; many do not come to us from there because they fear enduring persecution from your people for the sake of truth.

## CHAPTER XLIX

**54.** Remove, then, from consideration the needless resentments concerning the troubles that you suffer under royal commands because of your error. They are very small, almost nothing [Col. 0526], when compared with the great frenzy of your people. You even charge us with acts that are performed by the earthly authorities themselves, out of necessity rather than willingness, to drive your people’s assaults away from their own salvation.

If those forty men who had conspired to kill the apostle Paul had attacked the armed men escorting him and inflicted punishment upon them (Acts 23:12, 31), this could not have been charged to Paul.

I pass over the fact that you also transfer to us, by lying, the voluntary deaths that they themselves inflict upon themselves. For I have heard that Marculus threw himself down [Note: The *Passion of Marculus*, written by a certain Donatian, was published not long ago in volume 4 of the *Veterum Analectorum*. The manuscripts preface it with “the third” or “eighth day before the Kalends of December.” There Marculus is called a presbyter only, not a bishop—the title “bishop” was given to him by the Louvain annotators in *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 2, chapter 20.

According to those Acts of his Passion, he was first bound by order of Macarius, whom the emperor Constans had sent to Africa with Paulus, at the estate of Vaegessela, where Macarius encountered him with several bishops sent to him by the Donatian party. Soon afterward he was beaten with blows from ropes together with his companions, led through several cities of Numidia under extremely strict military guard to the fortified town of Nova Petra, and finally, after four days had passed, thrown by a soldier from the summit of a rock.

Although those Acts openly identify their author as a schismatic strongly hostile to Catholics, Marculus’s name was nevertheless transferred from them into the martyrologies. The same man is clearly intended by the entry that Molanus, in his additions to Usuard, reports for the sixth day before the Kalends of December from the spurious martyrology of Bede: “At Nicomedia” (for “in Numidia”), “the blessed Marculus, priest and martyr, who endured the greatest persecutions in the time of the tyrant Constans and was finally thrown from a high cliff.”

The Roman martyrology has a similar entry for the same day: “At Nicomedia” (for “in Numidia”), “Saint Marcellus” (read “Marculus”), “a presbyter who, in the time of Constantius” (more accurately, Constans), “was thrown from a cliff by the Arians” (for “by the Macarian party”) “and died a martyr.”

In the first Carthaginian Conference, chapter 187, Dativus, the Donatist bishop of Nova Petra, says: “I have no adversary, because the lord Marculus is there, whose blood God will demand on the day of judgment.” Compare Optatus, book 3, beginning with the words: “Thus Donatus of Bagai found the means by which he could lead a furious mob against Macarius,” and so forth.

Concerning this same Marculus, see also above, book 2 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapters 14 and 20, as well as *Tractate 11 on the Gospel of John*, §15.]

This is certainly more believable than that some Roman authority could have ordered such a thing, which is utterly foreign to Roman laws, since this evil is peculiar to your heresy among all the heresies wandering under the Christian name.

What benefit is it, then, that your bishops boast that they prohibited and condemned this practice in their councils, as you yourself recalled, when so many cliffs and sheer rocky precipices are daily made deadly by that Marculian teaching?

I have therefore said what I heard about Marculus and why this may appear more credible. But what the truth is, God knows.

As for the other three whose deaths you likewise brought forward, I confess that I did not ask those whom I think know what happened to them, or how it happened.

## CHAPTER L

**55.** Nevertheless, no good people in the Catholic Church approve this, if anyone is savagely treated even unto death, though he be a heretic.

Nor, if far short of death the desire for revenge returns evil for evil through the infliction of various troubles, do we approve that. We detest it even more if, under the pretext of striving for unity, anyone seizes what belongs to another—not those possessions which heretics ought not to hold under the name of the Church, but private property of whatever kind.

All these things displease good people. They prohibit and restrain them as far as they can; what they cannot prevent, they endure. And, as I have said, for the sake of peace they tolerate them in a praiseworthy manner—not judging them praiseworthy, but condemnable.

They do not abandon Christ’s field because of the weeds, Christ’s threshing floor because of the chaff, Christ’s great house because of the dishonorable vessels, or Christ’s nets because of the bad fish.

## CHAPTER LI

**56.** When kings are in error, they enact laws against the truth on behalf of that error; when they are in the truth, they likewise decree against error on behalf of the truth. Thus the good are tested by bad laws, and the bad are corrected by good laws [Note: Erasmus and all the manuscripts read *emundantur*, “are cleansed.”].

The wicked king Nebuchadnezzar issued a cruel law that an image should be worshiped; once corrected, he issued a severe law that the true God should not be blasphemed (Daniel 3:5, 6, 96).

For kings serve God in this respect, as they are divinely commanded, insofar as they are kings (Psalm 2:10): if in their kingdom they command what is good and prohibit what is evil—not only what pertains to human society, but also what pertains to divine religion.

**57.** You say in vain, “I am to be left to free choice.” Why do you not similarly proclaim that you ought to be left to free choice in murders, adulteries, and every other crime and disgrace? Yet it is most useful and salutary that all these things be restrained by just laws.

God indeed gave human beings free will, but he did not wish either a good will to be fruitless or an evil will to remain unpunished.

“You say,” you object, “that whoever persecutes a Christian is an enemy of Christ.” You speak truly, if he persecutes in that person what is an enemy of Christ [Note: Erasmus reads: “but does not persecute in that person what is an enemy of Christ.” Erasmus and Louvain read: “but persecutes in that person what is an enemy of Christ.” The manuscripts provide the corrected reading.]

For when both are Christians, a master, in his servant, a father, in his son, and a husband, in his wife, ought to persecute vices contrary to Christian truth.

Or, if they do not persecute them, will they not rightly be held guilty of negligence? Yet moderation appropriate to humanity and suited to charity must be observed in all things: the full extent of one’s power must not be exercised, and in what is exercised, love must not be lost; while in what is not exercised, gentleness must be shown.

Where no authority is granted by either divine or human laws, however, nothing should be undertaken rashly or recklessly.

## CHAPTER LII

**58.** Now hear about the Maximianists, a matter I had postponed, so that you may recognize that your bishops have lied to you. And recognize not only that this concerns the question of Baptism or the toleration of others’ sins in the Church without personal contamination, but also that it concerns the resentment surrounding persecution. In that matter your people have surpassed all Roman laws and protections against us; yet in this one case of the Maximianists, you will see the issue brought to an end.

If you did not shrink from reading the memorable sentence of the council of Bagai, composed of three hundred and ten of your bishops—a sentence of which I inserted above as much as seemed sufficient—then the words “condemned together with Maximian” clearly show that the twelve were condemned along with Maximian, those by whose hands he had been ordained.

The postponement of returning to your communion, however, was granted to those who had been in communion with Maximian and had condemned Primian, but had not been present when Maximian was ordained. For not all could have been present, nor ought all to have been present according to custom.

I am exceedingly surprised that you allowed yourself to be deceived—by whoever lied to you—when you could have recited the very words, which are not obscure and require neither a sharp intellect to analyze them nor anything except attention in order to understand them, so that you would not be deceived.

But since it is possible that you did not read the sentence and readily believed in simplicity whatever your bishop or bishops suggested to you, receive it, read it, and attend to the fact that I am telling you the truth.

For they cannot, merely to conceal their lie, alter or falsify it at will—the sentence that they cited in a public judgment before the proconsul and repeatedly had inserted into the municipal proceedings as the needs of their case required, when they were acting against those men so that they might be expelled from the basilicas.

## CHAPTER LIII

**59.** The sentence certainly begins as follows:

“When, by the will of almighty God and of his Christ, we were holding a council in the church at Bagai [Note: Louvain reads: “in the holy church at Bagai.” The word *holy* is absent from the manuscripts and from Erasmus.], Gamalius, Primianus, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarius [Note: Several manuscripts read *Januarianus*.], Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatianus, and the remaining three hundred and ten: it pleased the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish perpetual peace and cut away sacrilegious schisms.”

Then, after vomiting forth many horrors against them, it says shortly afterward:

“Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of the truth, enemy of the mother Church, minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, has been struck from the bosom of peace by the thunderbolt of the sentence.”

You see, I think, that Maximian was condemned without any uncertainty.

Then, after a few words—though words of the greatest gravity—with which it chose to declaim against him, it adds his ordainers and condemns them together with him without delay:

“Nor does just death condemn this man alone for his crime,” it says; “the chain of sacrilege also drags many into participation in the crime.”

Then, after pouring out whatever declamation it thought appropriate to magnify their own crime, it named them and concluded by condemning them:

“Therefore,” it says, “the following men are guilty of a notorious crime: Victorianus of Carcaba, Martianus of Sullectum, Beianus of Baiana [Note: Several other manuscripts also read *Beianensis*.], Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabrata, Miggenus of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assura, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzita [Note: Here all the manuscripts read *Velitanus*.], Felicianus of Musti, and Martialis of Pertusa, who, in the disastrous work of destruction, joined together a filthy vessel with the collected dregs; and also the clerics who once belonged to the Church of Carthage, who, while participating in the crime, provided assistance to unlawful incest. Know that they have been condemned by the judgment of the presiding God and by the truthful voice of the universal council.”

What could be said more plainly, more clearly, or more explicitly?

## CHAPTER LIV

**60.** Now hear to whom the postponement of time was granted, so that you may see that they were those who were not present when hands were laid upon Maximian at his ordination.

“But those,” it says, “whose nurseries the sacrilegious shoot did not pollute—that is, those who, with the reverent modesty of faith, withdrew their own hands from Maximian’s head—we have permitted to return to the mother Church.”

You see how they do not say that these men were condemned, but that they were to be held under the same sentence of condemnation if, after the appointed day had passed, they were unwilling to return.

They appoint the day as follows:

“And lest,” it says, “the pressure of a shortened day deprive those who return of the hope of salvation because the time is too brief, we open the door of recognition to all, insofar as it is permitted, while the preceding statutes remain in force, until the eighth day before the Kalends of the coming January, so that those who return with their honor and faith intact may have a foundation. But if anyone, through sluggish negligence, is unable to enter through it, let him know that by his own will the way to every avenue of pardon has been withdrawn from him.

For the sentence pronounced will remain against them, and fixed penance will await those who return after the appointed day.”

## CHAPTER LV

**61.** Surely now, most eloquent man, you see that you ought to turn against those from whom you heard the lie everything that you thought should be said against us, as though we had lied about this matter.

Surely you see that the two men under discussion belong to the number of those who were condemned without postponement together with Maximian and not to the number of those who were granted time to return.

Surely it is evident, clear, and visible—nor can it in any way be obscured or concealed [Note: In the better and in most manuscripts: “it is clear, it stands out” (or perhaps “it shines forth”), “it is perceived, it is obscured,” and so on.]—with what eloquence the man who pronounced that sentence distinguished, illuminated, and expressed the matter.

Why are words still being spent? Why is a manifest error defended against the clearest truth? Why do people deceive themselves?

If they tighten, entangle, and wrap more firmly the devil’s snares, which they ought to loosen and break, then receive further evidence by which they may blush more intensely—and, God grant, with some fruit of correction.

## CHAPTER LVI

**62.** In the council of Bagai, the day and the consul were recorded not only for the enactment of the council’s decree but also for the postponement itself.

Thus, from the eighth day before the Kalends of May, after the third consulship of Theodosius Augustus, and during the consulship of the Augusti Arcadius for the third time and Honorius for the second time [Note: All the manuscripts omit the words “during the consulship of the Augusti Arcadius for the third time and Honorius for the second time,” and instead have “and more abundantly.”], which was the date of the council of Bagai, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, which was the date of the postponement, nearly eight months are counted.

A petition is also found before the proconsul Herodes, made considerably later, against Felicianus and Praetextatus, concerning their expulsion from the places of Musti and Assura. I append a small portion of it.

“After the consulship of our lords Arcadius Augustus for the third time and Honorius Augustus for the second time [Note: A.D. 394], on the sixth day before the Nones of March, at Carthage in the secretariat of the praetorium, Titianus said:

‘Peregrinus the presbyter and the elders of the region of the Church of Musti [Note: Two manuscripts read: “of the Church of Musti and the region of Assura.”] pursue the following petition:

“When Donatus, a man worthy of revered memory, was defending the holiness of the Catholic Church against the error of Donatian perfidy, observance of the whole world, nourished in his name and worship, grew together into unity. But when the praiseworthy and admirable purpose of that religion was polluted by the poisons of a certain Maximian, a gathering of many bishops, brought together into one by God’s will, condemned the man—or rather the pestilence—which had displeased the majesty above, by the proper correction of a pure mind.

Those also whom the error of another’s presumption had drawn along, it restrained with a warning of equal force, first offering them a harbor of repentance if they wished to return within the time to the abandoned path of religion [Note: The printed reading is *destitutum*, “abandoned”; perhaps *praestitutum*, “appointed.”].

But iniquity delights in its own institutions and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For that same Maximian nourishes the boldness he has begun and joins others to himself in madness.

Among them is a certain Felicianus, who at first followed the right path but, darkened by contact with this corruption, believed, while residing in the city of Musti, that he could retain, as though under siege, walls consecrated to almighty God and the venerable Church.

Praetextatus likewise imitates him in the territory of Assura. But when the association of the priests became known to the authority of your equity, you ordered—as the records attest [Note: The proceedings against Salvius, below, book 4, §5]—that, every effect of opposition having been removed, the churches recovered from profane minds should be restored to the most sacred priests.’

You see, then, that by the date of this petition, nearly three months of the postponement established by that decree had elapsed.

The dispute was prolonged, as far as we have been able to investigate from the proconsular and municipal proceedings, until the time of the proconsul Theodorus—that is, until the eleventh day before the Kalends of January of the following year.

On that day, the clerics and elders acting under Bishop Rogatus, who had been appointed in place of the condemned Praetextatus of Assura, cited the order of the aforesaid proconsul: when Felicianus and Praetextatus were outside your communion, they were accused in the public courts as enemies of that communion and were sought for expulsion, as sacrilegious persons, from places consecrated to the supreme God.

## CHAPTER LVII

**63.** Whatever their number may have been—although it is sufficiently clear from what group they came—those who did not restore themselves to your communion within the appointed period of postponement: how did they return without being cleansed by another Baptism, together with those whom they had baptized outside your communion? [Note: Two manuscripts add here: “How were they able to baptize throughout that entire period while separated from you?”]

In this matter we do not criticize you: you recognized that the Baptism of Christ was not sacrilegious even within a sacrilegious schism; you approved what had been right even in the perverse once their human perversity had been corrected; you did not confuse human vices with divine seals; and you judged that the gifts of the Church—which could also be possessed and bestowed outside the Church, to the punishment of those who possessed and received them—were neither to be condemned in those who had been condemned nor changed in those who had been received.

## CHAPTER LVIII

**64.** Nor do we blame you for having judged that those same men, who were notorious criminals, should nevertheless be gathered and purified by the abundance of charity, both after the sentence of their condemnation and after the expiration of the period of postponement established for others, because of the weak people who had joined themselves to them—remembering, I suppose, the householder’s concern that the wheat not be uprooted together with the weeds—without any diminution.

[Note: In the old Corbie manuscript, *detraditione* appears instead of *detractione*. Perhaps *destructione* should be read, as below, Book 4, §§25 and 82, namely, the destruction of Baptism or Ordination. Shortly afterward, all the manuscripts read *famoso* rather than *fam os i* [the printed reading is corrected contextually].]

Nor do we blame you for having persecuted them, while they were still held by the sacrilege of their notorious schism, even through earthly authorities. For, as the outcome itself showed, this was done out of a desire to correct, not to harm: so that, harassed by those troubles, they might be compelled to reflect upon their crime and, after their fits of passionate hostility had been restrained, to amend it.

But because we do not blame these things, therefore we rightly accuse you of the crime of your schism, deservedly detest it, and convict you of it by every argument: for by bringing such charges against us, you separate yourselves from us—or rather from the Catholic communion of the whole world—in circumstances which, I think, you cannot deny were likewise present in your treatment of the Maximianists.

For if the Baptism of Christ is truly Baptism, and therefore in no way to be destroyed—the Baptism given through Felicianus and Praetextatus when they joined Maximianus after separating from you, although they had been condemned by you together with him for the crime of their impious schism—how is that Baptism not the Baptism of Christ, or how is it to be destroyed, which is given in the Church that, to use Cyprian’s words, “extends its branches throughout the whole earth in the abundance of its fruitfulness” (*On the Simplicity of Prelates, or On the Unity of the Church*)?

Finally, how is that Baptism not the Baptism of Christ which is given in those Churches whom you never cease citing in the apostolic writings and whom you have never condemned?

[Note: Two manuscripts add: “never in any council, as you condemned Felicianus and Praetextatus.”]

If you were pleased to restore those who had been condemned in their entirety, in order to repair Donatus’s portion, what offends you in the unity of Christ spread throughout the whole world? That unity either could not condemn those who had not been heard, or altogether neither condemned nor absolved those whom it did not know, or believed innocent those whom it learned had been acquitted.

If you expelled the Maximianists, who had been torn away from you, from their seats by persecuting them through judicial commands, what grounds have you for complaining that you suffer indignities at the hands of emperors who send those same judges, when you have torn yourselves away by an impious schism from the Church of the one of whom it is written: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him,” and “He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:11)?

## CHAPTER LIX

**65.** Behold, I do not now say, “If it is not permissible to persecute, Optatus did so”; nor should you continue to say that whatever Optatus did to them without their knowledge has nothing to do with your people, since they themselves do not allow that lands most remote from Africa should be brought into the discussion.

What the traditors in Africa were, or what evil the African bishops did, we do not know. But I say plainly: if it is not permissible to persecute, your people unquestionably persecuted the Maximianists, in such a way that you cannot deny it.

If those who suffer persecution are innocent, the Maximianists suffered persecution. Will you now say that the people destroyed Maximianus’s basilica or cave without any of our people being responsible? Even if it is investigated to what communion that crowd belonged—and your people should not be believed when they say that they sent them—perhaps they themselves will be found to have been your people, or at least to have been mixed with your people while assisting them.

But what does that have to do with us? You answer: “We did not do it; we did not send them; we do not know who those men were.” Nevertheless, the fact remains that he whom you acknowledge to be unjust—since the matter is clear—suffered persecution at the hands of some people; and the things you suffer cannot prove that you are just.

[Note: Thus two manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read *feceris* (“you have made”) instead of *fateris* (“you acknowledge”).]

But the proconsular records testify by whom the Maximianists also suffered persecution. Advocates were prepared, courts were approached, and proceedings were set in motion against them as though against heretics.

[Note: The printed editions read *ad ista judicia* (“to those courts”); this is corrected from the manuscripts.]

They were asking for protection of their possessions. Your people cited the council of Bagai and demanded that the condemned men be expelled from the sacred buildings.

[Note: Here Amerbach adds *iri Bagaiensi*. Erasmus and Louvain, with several manuscripts, read *in Bagaiensi*. We have deleted this on the authority of certain other manuscripts, which subsequently read *sacris sedibus* (“from the sacred seats”) in place of *sacris aedibus* (“from the sacred buildings”).]

The case was pressed and heard; with Salvius of Membressa present, you showed him to be a heretic, prevailed, and expelled him.

[Note: Some manuscripts and the edition of Amerbach read: “When, in the presence of Salvius of Membressa, you showed him to be a heretic,” and so forth. Others read: “When, with Salvius of Membressa present, you showed him to be a heretic,” and so forth.]

I therefore see that they suffered persecution and that you carried it out. I ask who is just; you claim that you are. I conclude: the one who suffers persecution is therefore not necessarily just, nor is the one who carries it out necessarily unjust.

## CHAPTER LX

**66.** Once again you will accuse me of dialectical devices; nevertheless, at least silently, you will approve that I am speaking the truth. You will choose instead to correct your own statement—that no persecution can be just—rather than call unjust those who persecuted the Maximianists, whom the proconsular records have finally acknowledged to have been your people.

Certainly, you did not persecute the error of your schismatics without result. For by the same conflict and troubles you corrected Felicianus and Praetextatus. Optatus the Gildonian, moreover, is said to have threatened Mustitani and Assuritani with still greater dangers; as I have also heard from them in person, they were afraid and compelled their bishops to return to Primianus’s communion.

But since Optatus did not enforce this through any public records, what am I to do with such people against you, who are ready to deny whatever you can deny? Proconsular and municipal records exist. When we read them out, we show how forcefully the men mentioned above were pressed by your people to withdraw from their places.

[Note: The printed editions read *gerebantur*; the manuscripts, more correctly, read *urgebantur*.]

We do not blame you, nor do we begrudge you what you achieved. Your labor was not pointless; you did not frighten them without result; you did not act in vain. Their hostility displeased them when they had been afflicted; they were broken, amended, corrected, and received—after their own condemnation, after the postponement imposed on others, and after your persecution.

They were received, however, as they had been: honored, without being either purified or degraded through any harsher humiliation of penance—neither they themselves nor those with whom they were received, whom they had separated with themselves against you, baptized outside you, and perhaps rebaptized after joining you.

## CHAPTER LXI

**67.** You now have nothing by which to thrust your shadowy lies about events of the distant past upon ignorant people. The public records proclaim that your people accused Caecilianus before Constantine, then emperor; that the case was heard and brought to its proper conclusion, even to the acquittal of Felix of Aptunga, Caecilianus’s ordainer, whom they had called the source of all evils in the council of Carthage and whom they repeatedly accused before that same Constantine, as he himself indicates in his writings. The proconsular archives bear witness to this.

You resist, protest, and oppose the clearest truth. You say that the judges overseas were bribed by Caecilianus and that the Emperor himself was corrupted by some unknown favor. The defeated accuser is all the more shameless because he also becomes a slanderer of the judge.

Nevertheless, amid all those lies of yours by which you slander the judges overseas, we at least establish this: your first ancestors brought this case before the Emperor; your first people accused Caecilianus and his ordainer before the Emperor; your first people persecuted Caecilianus and his associates before the Emperor. From this you stir up against us, as it seems to you, the greatest hatred, because, having been defeated, you suffer what you would certainly have done as victors—as though Daniel’s accusers had wished to charge him with wrongdoing because, when he had been delivered innocent, they themselves were devoured by the lions by which they had wished to have him devoured through their false accusation (Daniel 6).

We establish this also: whatever one may think about the judges, Caecilianus was acquitted in the overseas judgment before which he was present;

[Note: Perhaps this is a gloss originating in the margin; or *by whom* should be added here.]

whatever one may think about the man before whom your ancestors accused Caecilianus, they finally chose that man’s judgment over an episcopal judgment, even if you believe—or pretend—that Constantine the Emperor was corrupted by favor.

All the Catholic Christians who then existed, scattered far and wide throughout nearby and distant lands, to whom reports of Caecilianus and his colleagues could have reached, nevertheless ought to have trusted not defeated accusers but ecclesiastical judges. For where we cannot all be judges, we more rightly trust those judges who were able to be present than, by trusting defeated litigants whom we could not judge, dare to judge the judges themselves.

## CHAPTER LXII

**68.** Therefore, since those before whom Caecilianus was acquitted in the presence of his accusers attempted, with the most audacious wickedness, to smear not only those by whom he was acquitted

[Note: We restore these words here from some manuscripts. In several later editions *not only us* had been substituted before *but also*.]

but also all Catholic Christians established in every nation—those who either knew nothing at all of that African dispute or preferred to trust the judges, whatever danger they believed those judges incurred in pronouncing judgment, rather than defeated accusers—they eventually sent you the case of the Maximianists.

In that case, you yourselves condemned them, you yourselves persecuted those whom you had condemned, you yourselves received those whom you had persecuted in the same rank, and you yourselves accepted the Baptism of the condemned. Thus those who had dared to accuse the innocent were compelled to absolve the innocent—not those whom they had believed to be innocent, but those whom, as they say, by the judgment of God presiding over them, they had condemned with the truthful voice of their plenary council.

Has anyone ever said to anyone else: “Because you trusted the judge who acquitted me rather than me, who accused me, you are guilty together with those whom I accused”? And yet this is said to the Christian world. If it were said to one man, it would appear not merely most unjust but utterly insane.

What an astonishingly outrageous situation! They accused the Africans of the crime of handing over the Scriptures; the judges overseas acquitted the accused; and the peoples of the nations became traditors because they trusted the acquitting judges rather than the accusers who brought the charge!

## CHAPTER LXIII

**69.** The case of the Maximianists has deservedly been served to you, Donatist party. Drink the cup from the hand of the Lord who reproves and admonishes. If you understand and submit, this is the mercy of one who corrects, lest you fall under the judgment of one who punishes.

To you it is said: “Proud and stiff-necked people, be reconciled to the Christian peoples everywhere whom you unjustly accused—at least now that you have been reconciled to your own condemned people.”

[Note: The printed editions have *reconciliare*; incorrectly.]

Why do you destroy Christ’s Baptism in those Churches—or in those arising from those Churches—which the Apostles founded? You have already received the Baptism which your condemned men gave before they were reconciled to you.

Why do you glory in the persecution you suffer? If it is a sign of justice, the Maximianist party is more just. For it both suffered at your hands and continues to suffer. And together with it hear the divine Psalm: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

You call us your persecutors, although, because we desire your salvation, we medicinally attack the wounds in you that we want to be healed. For this reason we are grievously afflicted by your clerics and Circumcellions, as though by your teeth and hooves, while we are treating you.

Do not be ungrateful for such medicine, which you yourselves have imitated. You also corrected Felicianus and Praetextatus through persecutions. If only you had corrected them entirely; and if, just as they returned to you, you and they might return to the Catholic mother!

**70.** Against her, brother Cresconius, you were carried away with such audacity that you even attempted to refute those divine testimonies which I had cited and to contradict the words of God.

For in that letter against which you argue (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 1, §25), I set down what is contained in the Holy Book concerning the seed of Abraham, when God said to that father of ours: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

The Apostle calls this a testament when he says: “Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a humanly confirmed testament no one annuls or adds a provision to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3:15–16).

The fruitfulness of this seed was promised to be so abundant that it was said to him: “So shall your seed be as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered” (Genesis 22:17).

You dare to place the party of Donatus before this multiplication and fruitfulness of the Church

[Note: The editions and manuscripts read *libertati* (“freedom”); here *ubertati* (“fruitfulness”) must undoubtedly be read. A little later, where they read *you remit alone*, *you customarily send* must be read.]

which is spread throughout the whole world, which is believed in accordance with prophecy, and which is displayed before the eyes even of all unbelievers in such a way as to silence the mouths of the pagans who remain opposed to it in very small numbers.

You say that, apart from Africa, you have some people whose existence nevertheless does not become apparent; and you do not deny that you customarily send bishops from Africa to them—one, or two, or at most three. You then argue pointlessly against the most evident truth that the whole world does not share our communion because either many barbarian nations still exist that have not yet believed in Christ, or many heresies exist under Christ’s name that are alienated from communion with our fellowship.

## CHAPTER LXIV

**71.** You neither consider nor even ask those who know how many of the barbarian nations you mentioned have already been devoted to Christ’s name, and how the Gospel continues to bear fruit as it grows among the rest, until, when it has been preached among all, the end comes.

For the Lord says: “This Gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

Unless perhaps insane pride drives you so far that you think what was foretold must begin with the party of Donatus, rather than with those Churches which the Apostles planted and with which the party of Donatus does not share communion. Or will it attempt to rebaptize those Churches as well, so that it may fill the world, while the Catholic Church grows everywhere and that party diminishes daily even in Africa itself?

O the mad perversity of human beings! You believe that you are praised for believing in Christ whom you do not see, and you do not believe that you are condemned for denying the Church which you do see, although the one is the head in heaven and the other the body on earth.

**72.** You recognize Christ in what is written: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God”; and you do not recognize the Church in what follows: “And your glory above all the earth” (Psalm 107:6)?

You recognize Christ in what is written: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves and cast lots for my clothing”; and you do not recognize the Church in what follows shortly afterward: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Psalm 21:17–19, 28)?

[Note: Some manuscripts add here: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”]

You recognize Christ in what is written: “Give the king your judgment, O God, and your justice to the king’s son”; and you do not recognize the Church in what the same Psalm testifies: “He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents; and all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:2, 8, 9, 10–11)?

You recognize Christ in what is said to the Jews: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands”—for Christ’s coming certainly removed all those Jewish sacrifices—and you do not recognize the Church in what follows: “For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, says the Lord Almighty” (Malachi 1:10–11)?

[Note: The same manuscripts add here: “And in every place incense shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty.”]

You recognize Christ in what the prophet says: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7), together with the other things there that are read about him as though in the Gospel; and you do not recognize the Church in what he says shortly afterward:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said: Enlarge the place of your tent and stretch out the curtains of your dwellings; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes, extending farther and farther to the right and to the left. For your seed shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit cities that had been deserted. Do not fear, for you shall prevail; do not be ashamed because you have been abominable. For you shall forget your confusion forever and shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood, because I am the Lord who made you; the Lord is his name. He who delivers you, the very God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:1–5).

## CHAPTER LXV

**73.** In these very Holy Scriptures Cyprian speaks of the Church when he says:

“Thus the Church of the Lord, flooded with light, extended her rays throughout the whole world and spread her branches throughout the whole earth in the abundance of her fruitfulness” (*On the Simplicity of Prelates, or On the Unity of the Church*).

Against this great manifestation of the divine utterances, Cresconius, you bring accusations by looking at the remaining nations which the Church has not yet occupied, while you pay no attention to how much territory she has occupied and from what extent she is daily spreading in order to possess what remains.

How can you not deny the future fulfillment of these prophecies, when you do not hesitate to deny such progress as is itself responsible for that fulfillment—not merely against the divine words, but now even against your own words? For the force of that very truth expressed itself through you, so that, without knowing or attending to what you said, you declared that “the whole world is daily being converted to the Christian name.”

Why, then, does the party of Donatus not share communion with this Church, which is enlarged by growing throughout the whole world? Clearly, so that it may not be polluted by sinners.

And where is the fact that Cyprian was unwilling to abandon—not this church of yours, which remains in Africa and slanders the whole world, or which migrates from Africa among a few hidden people, but that Church which extends her branches throughout the whole earth in the abundance of her fruitfulness—even though sinners are not merely in its communion but visibly present in it?

He says:

“For although weeds appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity ought not on that account to be hindered, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (*Letter to Maximus*).

## CHAPTER LXVI

**74.** Here you too should answer, if you are willing to answer anything truthful: how will what is written be fulfilled, “The wicked son declares himself righteous, but does not cleanse his way” (Proverbs 24, according to the Septuagint)?

Give us, then, the wicked son who condemns and persecutes the Maximianists, becomes reconciled to those whom he has condemned and persecuted, and is either thereby convicted, thereby confounded, or thereby corrected.

[Note: Amerbach and all the manuscripts read: “Give, then, to the wicked son.” Perhaps the text should read *da* [“give”] again, in place of *ad* [“to”]. Shortly afterward, nearly all printed editions read: “whether he is convicted, whether he is confounded, or whether he is corrected.” Some manuscripts more correctly read: “or thus.”]

“How,” you ask, “is the whole world filled with your communion, when there are so many heresies, none of which shares communion with you?”

Indeed, the world is filled not only with heretics but also with other evil people; and the world is filled with holy and faithful servants of God. For the sea is full of bitter waves, but it is also full of sweet fish.

**75.** “Truth,” you say, “is often found among the few; it is the many who err.” And, lest you seem to contradict with your words the great fruitfulness of that barren woman to whom it was said, “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband,” you added a testimony from the Gospel: “For few are those who are saved” (Luke 13:23).

Solve, then, the question of how the Lord himself says: “How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matthew 7:14), while elsewhere that same Lord says: “Many shall come from the east and from the west and shall recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11).

How is it also shown in the Apocalypse that there is a multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, and tongue, clothed in white robes and carrying palm branches—those who had endured tribulations for the faith of Christ (Revelation 7:9)? How can the same people be few and many?

Neither statement can be true while the other is false, since both have been spoken by divine Truth. The explanation is that those same good and true Christians, who are many in themselves, are few in comparison with the evil and false, who are likewise many.

Thus we call the many grains with which great storehouses are filled few in comparison with the chaff. Likewise, to speak of the very testament of God made to Abraham concerning his seed, which is Christ, there are many stars that we cannot count, by which the great heaven shines on every side; yet we call them few in comparison with the sand of the sea.

Perhaps the stars signified spiritual Christians, while the sand of the sea signified carnal Christians, through whom and from whom heresies and schisms also arise. Nevertheless, the world is full of both kinds, because the same Lord says: “This field is the world.” And you yourself, compelled by the truth, said: “The whole world is daily being converted to the Christian name.”

Therefore, throughout the whole field—that is, throughout the whole world—there is wheat, and throughout it there are weeds, because the one who cannot be deceived said of both: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matthew 13:38, 30).

## CHAPTER LXVII

**76.** Let the impious deserters, then, restrain themselves from boasting of the small number of certain weeds separated from them, while the wheat grows throughout the whole world with such abundant fruitfulness.

But if they do boast, the same Maximianists oppose them even in this matter. By divine judgment they have been placed before them to confound them in every respect and, if they have wisdom, to correct them. Your people persecuted them, trusting in the multitude of their own party, although they were much fewer; and by persecuting them they converted some of them again to their communion, thus leaving the others as supremely just because they were extremely few.

[Note: The printed editions read “in the judgment”; *in* is redundant and is absent from all the manuscripts.]

**77.** “The East,” you say, “does not share communion with Africa, nor Africa with the East.”

Certainly not—but only in the case of the heretical chaff separated from the Lord’s threshing floor. In the Catholic wheat, however, and in the chaff that remains within it, the East unquestionably shares communion with Africa, and Africa with the East.

In one place heretics contend with the Catholic unity spread everywhere; in another place, and elsewhere again, other heretics do so. For that Church is everywhere—the Church from which those people went out who could by no means be everywhere, saying, in accordance with what had been foretold about them: “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there” (Matthew 24:23).

Some display their own little portions here, others elsewhere, portions formed from various presumptions—or rather, amputations—and in impious pride deny the root from which they were broken.

Your ancestors ought therefore to have proved whatever true evidence they possessed concerning the traditors against this Church which, as it expands throughout the whole world in abundant success, brings forth from every nation, tribe, and tongue a multitude of those clothed in white and carrying palms, as it is written in the Apocalypse—a multitude which no one can count.

I mean this Church, with which it is evident that the party of Donatus does not share communion. If your ancestors had presented their evidence to that Church, they themselves would have been within it, while those whom they accused would have been outside it.

But now, when we see that the accused remained within it, what good opinion ought we to form of their accusers, whom we see outside it?

Accordingly, in that fourfold division which I proposed when documents concerning the traditors are produced from both sides—either both sets are true, or both false, or ours are true and yours false, or ours are false and yours true (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 1, §23)—when you saw that you were easily defeated in the first three alternatives, you foolishly chose this last one as though it were an escape.

Although you should recognize how shamelessly it is stated, nevertheless, if you possessed any human evidence that was truly yours, that evidence ought to have been proved against that Church which is proved by divine evidence.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

**78.** Tell me, I beg you—but do not spread clouds before the ignorant, so that, because you cannot convict the traditors whom you accuse, you may continually wish to accuse dialectical devices. Tell me, I ask you: was this case of yours, together with your true evidence, brought to judgment before the overseas Churches founded through apostolic labor, or was it not?

If it was brought, did you prevail in that judgment, or were you defeated? If you say that you prevailed, why do you not share communion with those Churches in whose judgment you prevailed?

But if—as the fact that your communion is alienated from them sufficiently indicates—you were defeated, why do you continue to litigate with us over a case lost either for good or for evil, bearing this greatest crime: that you pour out upon the Christian world the accusation of the traditors whom you were utterly unable to convict even when presenting true evidence in the judgment of the overseas Churches, because, in a case in which it could not participate, the Christian world chose to trust judges rather than defeated accusers?

You are not guilty, then, merely because you lost a good case, to speak according to your own position, in an overseas judgment. You are guilty because you do not hesitate to bring against so many innocent Christian peoples, spread far and wide among so many nations, the crime of the accused and—even if we concede far too much to you—the crime of the judges.

By clinging to the communion of these peoples as to the Lord’s wheat, you ought, in accordance with the evangelical Scriptures and with Cyprian’s admonition, to have tolerated until the time of winnowing both those men whom you call traditors and those whom you consider evil judges, as chaff within the threshing floor, lest by abandoning the threshing floor you perish.

But if your case, together with the true evidence which you have chosen, was not brought before the judgment of the overseas Churches, how could so many bishops established in their own congregations have been justly condemned by them when the case was unknown and had not been brought before them at all?

Or how ought African Christians to have separated themselves from the wheat growing so far and wide—whether those Christians thought the men innocent or whether any of them knew them to be traditors—because they saw weeds in the Church, so clearly and manifestly that, on account of another’s crime, which they would not have been stained by tolerating for the sake of unity, they would instead be condemned for the crime of violating that very unity?

## CHAPTER LXIX

**79.** What, then, does it profit your case that, from those four alternatives, you chose this one: that your documents should be considered true, while those we produce against your people should be judged false?

Behold, here too you are defeated. For the traditors could not be convicted, where they ought to have been, by the documents which you consider true—whether those same documents were concealed by your people, whether the traditors themselves hid from the judges by some stratagem, or whether they were concealed by the corrupt judges themselves.

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and all our manuscripts read: “or were not concealed.”]

Look at the seed of Abraham, which in the testament of God grows among all nations like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea (Genesis 22:17). Dare to say, dare to believe, dare—if there is any fear of God in you—to consider whether such an abundant harvest throughout the field of the world could have perished because of certain African weeds hidden for reasons unknown to me.

**80.** You exaggerate the persecutions which you claim to suffer, although, while you rebel against the peace of the holy Church with such sacrilegious and manifest obstinacy, you are spared with astonishing gentleness.

At the beginning of your letter you say that, when Caecilianus’s crime was being made evident to the Emperor Constantine, Constantine himself condemned him by his own sentence, so that he might live in exile at Brixia.

[Note: The manuscripts consistently read *Brixae* (“at Brixia”); so also Amerbach and Erasmus.]

Who could doubt that you are either mistaken or attempting to deceive, since you also mentioned Felix of Aptunga as having been convicted of handing over the Scriptures before the proconsul by some Vincentius or other?

## CHAPTER LXX

Behold, I insert the sentence of Aelianus the proconsul, by which Felix was cleared and acquitted. If you wish to read the entire record, obtain it from the proconsul’s archive.

Aelianus the proconsul said:

“From the deposition of Caecilianus, who says that the records are false and that very much was added to the letter, it is evident with what intention Ingentius did these things; and therefore he shall be taken back into custody, for he is necessary for a stricter interrogation.

“But it is evident that Felix, the religious bishop, is free from the burning of the divine documents (*Instrumenta deifica*), since no one has been able to prove against him that he handed over or burned the sacred Scriptures.

[Note: The booklet of the proconsular proceedings reads *falsata* (“falsified”) rather than *falsa* (“false”).] For the entire interrogation written above makes it clear that no divine Scriptures were either found, falsified, or burned.

“This is contained in the records: that Felix, the religious bishop, was neither present at those times, nor lent his knowledge or consent, nor ordered anything of the kind to be done.”

I also insert the rescript of the Emperor Constantine, which testifies to the same matter and shows how importunately your ancestors, the accusers of innocent men, acted.

The Emperors Caesar Flavius Constantine, and Maximianus,

[Note: The manuscripts read *Maximinus*. Shortly afterward they read either “when the most defective men were present” or “when the most perfect men were present.” Amerbach and Erasmus have “when the most perfect men were present.” Lovaniensis, drawing on Augustine’s Letter 88, reads “the most perfect man Verus.” Concerning the title *perfectissimus*, see the Theodosian Code, Book 6, final law.]

and Valerius Licinianus Licinius, to Probianus, proconsul of Africa:

“Your predecessor Aelianus, rightly, since the most perfect man Verus, vicarius of the prefects then throughout our Africa, was confined by serious illness, performed his duties and, among other matters, judged that the dispute—or the resentment—which appeared to have arisen concerning Caecilianus the bishop and the Catholic Church should be referred to his examination and command.

“For after he had caused Superius the centurion,

[Note: The manuscripts read *cum tam Superium centurionem*; Louvain alone reads *Superium Saturianum*, corruptly.]

Caecilianus the magistrate of the Aptungitani, Saturninus the excurator, Calibius the younger

[Note: Thus Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts; Louvain reads *Callidium*.]

curator of the same city, and Solon

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *Solum*.]

the public slave of the aforesaid city to be present, he granted a proper hearing. Thus, when it had been objected to Caecilianus that the episcopate seemed to have been conferred upon him by Felix, against whom the betrayal and burning of the divine Scriptures appeared to have been alleged, Felix’s innocence in that matter was established.

“Finally, when Maximus, a decurion of the city of Ziqua, maintained that Ingentius had falsified Caecilianus’s letter as one of the two magistrates, we examined Ingentius himself, who had been held under suspension, in light of the records that were available. We therefore did not subject him to torture, because he asserted that he was a decurion of the city of Ziqua.

“Therefore we wish you to send this same Ingentius under a suitable escort to my court, that of Constantine Augustus, so that, in the hearing of those who are acting at the present time and who do not cease to make repeated appeals for many days,

[Note: All the manuscripts, together with Amerbach and Erasmus, read here and below *diurnis diebus*, “for daily days” or “for successive days,” rather than the printed *diuturnis diebus*, “for prolonged days.”]

it may be shown and made clear, with those who are now present hearing and attending in person, that they have attempted in vain to stir up resentment against Caecilianus the bishop and to rise violently against him.

“For thus it will come about that, once such disputes have been dismissed, as is proper, the people may serve their own religion with due reverence and without any dissension.”

## CHAPTER LXXI

**82.** I insert still further Constantine’s words from his letter to Eumalius the vicarius, where he testifies that he himself investigated the matter between the parties and found Caecilianus innocent.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read “to another”; the manuscripts read “to Eumalius.”]

After recounting in what he had said above how the parties had been brought before his judgment after the episcopal judgments, he says:

“In this matter I examined Caecilianus, a man endowed with complete innocence, observing the duties required by his religion and serving it as he ought. It became evident that no crime could be found in him, just as the allegations of his opponents had been fabricated against him while he was absent.”

83. Why did you not insert the sentence of Constantine by which you say that he was condemned and placed in exile at Brixia, most eloquent of men? How much more appropriately would you have inserted this than I know not what about the Council of Sardica, which is shown to have no relevance at all either to you or to the case between us and you! Why Caecilian was at Brixia—which you most maliciously call exile—since he preferred that the Church lack his presence rather than lack peace, what need is there for me to say, when meanwhile you quote no sentence of the emperor condemning him, yet so rashly think that Caecilian, condemned by the emperor, should not merely be heard or mentioned but even written about?

Nevertheless, in accordance with your own words, behold: I see Caecilian in exile, with the emperor condemning him. At least answer: who was accusing him? And now ask me the question which, after much else, you similarly inserted in vain in your letter [Note: [Col. 0541] The printed editions read *inaniter* (“in vain repeatedly”); the manuscripts read *inane* (“in vain”). It refers to “which”]: “Who is less in agreement with the testament once it has been produced: the one who suffers persecution, or the one who inflicts it?” These are certainly your words. Look, then, at Caecilian suffering persecution and, as you yourself said, placed in exile. Look also at your own people, who, as the emperor himself testifies in his very words, did not cease for many days to bring accusations against Caecilian. And answer me with those same words of yours when I ask: “Who is less in agreement with the testament once it has been produced: the one who suffers persecution, or the one who inflicts it?” But when you read everything through carefully, you will find that Caecilian suffered persecution from your people even before the emperor; you will not find that he was condemned by the emperor. Rather, you will find that he was acquitted.

## CHAPTER LXXII

84. Moreover, if you have chosen as something of great importance this position—that the documents you produce concerning the crimes of the *traditores* [Note: [Col. 0541] In the manuscripts, *traditionum* (“traditions”).] are true, whereas those we produce are false—even in this respect the truth of God surpasses you. Just as he foretold, so he makes the Church fruitful and growing throughout the whole world. For even true documents concerning the crimes of others do not prejudice it, although such documents, among neighboring overseas bishops through whom the report of such matters either passes into more distant regions or does not pass, may either not have been presented as they ought to have been, or may not have been believed by those to whom they could have been presented, or, though believed and concealed, may never have reached others. Nor can any one person—much less so great a number of Christians [Col. 0542] established among so many nations—be guilty of sharing in another’s crime, whether he has learned nothing of the genuine evidence concerning it or whether someone has deceived him by a pretended innocence supported by false documents. [Note: [Col. 0542] The printed editions read *refellerit* (“has refuted”). This has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

If, then, as I had begun to say, in this matter which you have chosen as something of great importance—that the evidence you produce against the *traditores* is true, whereas what is produced against you is false—you are powerless against the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, and against the providence of God by which, to use your own words, the whole world is daily being turned toward the Christian name, how much more do you fail in your accusations when we bring against you this very tradition—for those who caused this schism, as though they shuddered at the name, separated themselves from the body of Christ and handed themselves over to the devil—much more plausibly, as I said in that letter and now say again, than you bring it against us! (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 1, no. 23.) From you we hear only the names and crimes of the *traditores*; but we produce both the ecclesiastical records in which they confessed against themselves [Note: The records of the Council of Cirta, above, no. 30.] and the municipal records in which they are read to have committed these acts. [Note: The records before Zenophilus, chapter 29.]

## CHAPTER LXXIII

85. But you, a clever examiner and weigher of words, teach us what the comparative degree signifies, and, as though victorious, rejoice because I could not say, “We bring the tradition against you more plausibly,” unless I admitted that you brought it against us plausibly. “For,” you say, “if you bring it against us more plausibly, then we bring it against you plausibly.” You teach this because *plausibly* and *more plausibly* function like *truly* and *more truly*: the comparative degree increases what has been stated earlier, rather than disproving what was said earlier.

You add other words by which we may understand this more clearly, saying: “So it is with *well* and *better*, *badly* and *worse*, *horribly* and *more horribly*”—thereby showing that the same applies to *plausibly* and *more plausibly*. From this you think it follows that if I bring against you what is false “more plausibly,” it remains that you have brought against us what is true “plausibly.”

Here, surely, I am not saying that in an ecclesiastical question or dispute you are trying to teach us the grammatical technicalities concerning the force of the comparative degree: that it increases what has been stated before rather than disproving what was said before. I see how ineptly I would be objecting this to you—something you refused to see when you thought that a counter-accusation, as though drawn from rhetorical art, should be brought against me. I demonstrated this type of question, in which one says, “I did not do it, but you did,” even from prophetic authority. (Above, no. 29.)

## CHAPTER LXXIV

86. Consider more carefully, however, whether you may perhaps find in the authors of Latin speech, for whom the technicalities of grammarians serve, that this degree does not always increase what has been stated before but is sometimes placed over against it in the contrary sense.

For the moment an example of this usage occurs to me from the Epistle which the Apostle wrote to the Hebrews. When he was speaking of the earth which, after receiving rain, produces fruit, he then added: “But when it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse; its end is for burning.” [Hebrews 6:7–8.] And lest he should seem to have wished this for those to whom he was speaking, he immediately says: “But we are confident concerning you, beloved brothers, of better things and things accompanying salvation.” [Note: The manuscripts read *confisi sumus* (“we have been confident”); the printed editions read *confidimus* (“we are confident”).] (Hebrews 6:9.)

You certainly observe how he says here, “better things”: not because the things he had mentioned above—producing thorns and thistles and deserving burning—were good, but rather because they were bad, so that, avoiding those things, they might choose and desire better things, that is, good things opposed to such evils.

But perhaps you think that the Apostle should be heard as he describes himself—as a human being, “even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.” (2 Corinthians 11:6.) And therefore you maintain that in him we should follow not the authority of words but of matters and meanings, arguing that he ought to have written “good things” where he himself wrote “better things.”

What if I too, now accustomed to these letters and having forgotten what I learned as a boy, said, “You bring the tradition against us; we bring this same tradition against you much more plausibly,” as though I were using the comparative in place of the positive—not because you brought it against us plausibly, but rather because you brought it implausibly, just as he said “better things” not because those things were good, but rather because they were bad? Why, then, do you so rashly conclude from this that I confirmed that you brought it against us plausibly, simply because I said that we brought it against you more plausibly?

## CHAPTER LXXV

87. Indeed, even according to the grammarians you would not have reproached me for having erred in the word, if only you had been willing either to read attentively or to recall from memory the very authors of those words. For school literature contains the following—not spoken by an ignorant boy:

> “May the gods grant better things to the pious, and grant that error to their enemies!”
>
> They were tearing the severed limbs with their bare teeth.”

(Virgil, *Georgics* 3.513–514.)

How, then, could he wish “better things” for the pious, as though those things were good for the others, and not rather great evils for those who were tearing the severed limbs with their bare teeth? You now surely see that just as he could wish better things for the pious, although the things in comparison with which he wished them were not good, so I too could say, “We bring the tradition against you more plausibly,” although you did not bring it against us plausibly.

I omit the fact that when something is called *plausible*, it does not consequently follow that it is true. The term may be used of things that can and usually do happen, and which are therefore approved and believed, even if they have not happened. But what is true, when it is demonstrated, is necessarily plausible, and certainly more plausible than that. Recall the books in which you learned these words: you will surely find that I am not deceiving you.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

Therefore, even if I granted that your people brought the tradition against us plausibly, I would not for that reason contend that they brought something true against us; and I would rightly say that we bring it against you more plausibly. For from you we are accustomed to hear only that certain people were *traditores*, while no ecclesiastical or public records are recited or demonstrated in which they confessed this. From us, however, public records are produced in which your people committed *traditio* (handing over), and ecclesiastical records in which, having been left to God as judge, they confessed.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

88. But I do not pass over so evident an assistance from you, by which, even without knowing it, you greatly favor us when you teach the rules of the comparative degree: “It increases what has been stated before; it does not disprove what was said before.”

According to this rule of yours, and according to certain words of yours in your letter, we have won our case without any difficulty. For at the beginning of your letter, as though accusing our obstinacy, you said that so many legal documents—“which is better and truer”—could not persuade us.

From this I conclude, according to your grammatical technicalities, that we already possess what is true and good, if what is truer and better cannot persuade us. Since, then, we do not invalidate your Baptism, which according to you is truer and better, why do you invalidate what is true and good in us?

Again, after you had said, “We too want Christ to be the origin, root, and head of the Christian,” you immediately added, “But we are asking through whom this is done better.” By saying this you certainly conceded that it is done well through a bad minister, but better through a good one.

Since, then, we do not invalidate the Baptism which you say is given through your minister as through a good minister, why do you invalidate the Baptism which you maintain was given through ours as through a bad minister? You said, “We are asking through whom it is done better.” And your rule is: “The comparative degree increases what has been stated before.” Therefore, if it is done better through your minister, as you think, it is also done well through ours. Consequently, when you rebaptize someone baptized by us, you invalidate with sacrilegious presumption what, according to this rule of yours, you concede was done well.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

89. I fear that I may press your embarrassment too far if I show how lightly and clownishly you thought that certain words of mine, which I used figuratively, should be mocked: “forehead” for shame, “mouth” for speech, “trident weapon” for a three-part argument, and “three-headed beast” for an error raging through three accusations against the innocence of so many peoples. (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 1, no. 29.) Preserve such childish matters for children.

For I am not troubled by your saying that a Neptunian weapon, on account of its trident, is unbecoming for a bishop, since it is also a fishing weapon [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read “of fishermen.” Manuscript M reads “of a fisherman.”] and therefore an apostolic one: for the Lord made his Apostles fishers of human beings. (Matthew 4:19.) Scripture likewise says that our God has wings (Psalms 16:8; 35:8) and arrows (Psalm 17:15); yet we do not worship Cupid.

90. You also reproach me for not having kept the gentleness promised at the beginning, because, when mention was made of the Manichaeans, I was moved to say: “Just as what the Lord says cannot happen—that Satan should cast out Satan” (Matthew 12:26), “so the error of the Manichaeans cannot overthrow the error of the Donatists.” (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 1, no. 28.) You take this as though I had compared Petilianus with Satan, rather than the error from whose snares I desire him to be released.

It is well that the Apostle fortified us against such accusations in the very passage where he admonishes us to be gentle, patient, and modest when we correct someone who dissents. For after saying, “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with modesty,” he immediately added: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance for recognizing the truth, and they may recover from the devil’s snares, having been captured by him to do his will.” (2 Timothy 2:24–26.)

Behold the apostolic gentleness: the very people with whom he commanded that one should act calmly, patiently, and modestly, he says have been captured by the devil; yet he did not lose the gentleness he commended, because he did not refuse to speak the truth which he taught. [Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts omit “gentleness,” since “gentleness” occurs shortly before.]

## CHAPTER LXXIX

91. But you yourself must see whose side you are taking, since, by accusing my words as abusive and savage, you try to incite to litigation those whom you do not wish to meet for discussion. I will not say that you yourself take pleasure in quarrelling.

For you bring against me, more sparingly and modestly, but as though indirectly, charges that have absolutely nothing to do with me.
