What judgment could I pass on the most pestilential and, for all Christians, anathema-worthy vanity of the Manichaeans if I merely used to speak of it, and did not also bear witness in many extensive books that I have written? Even then there would be no ground for your accusation against me.

For the Catholic Church would not be surprised to be falsely accused by you, since by you the whole Christian world, together with all those Churches propagated by apostolic labor from the earliest times, is accused by false charges. But when anyone who wishes can read my many writings against the Manichaeans, who once deceived me in my youth, he is not so foolish as to believe what you say about me rather than his own eyes and understanding.

## CHAPTER LXXX

92. “But,” you say, “many of our people possess a letter from your leader, in which he wrote something about you when he did not want you to be ordained.”

I would scarcely care about that letter even if a plainly favorable judgment of the person said to have written it were read, condemning that accusation and falsehood. How much less does the Catholic Church care about it—the Church whose cause we are defending against you, and which, presiding over so many divine testimonies, cannot be deprived of the truth it possesses by any human testimony concerning anyone, whether true or false!

Stop such arguments. I am only one man; it is the cause of the Church between us, not my own. It is the cause of the Church which learned from its Redeemer to place its hope in no human being.

Even concerning me personally, you could not rightly be believed by us, even if you knew my manner of life, since you are my enemies. For human reputation has an abundance of witnesses who know me; but before God’s sight there is only conscience. Although I maintain that conscience undaunted against your accusations, I nevertheless do not dare to justify myself under the eyes of the Almighty. Rather, I await from him an abundant gift of mercy than the full severity of judgment, thinking of what is written: “When the just king sits upon the throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?” (Proverbs 20:8–9.)

## CHAPTER LXXXI

93. But what does it matter what sort of person I am in the question at issue between us? In the Lord’s threshing floor I am straw if I am bad, grain if I am good.

If you were grain, however, you would not reject the chaff mixed with it before the time of winnowing, as Cyprian himself also teaches. Thus, if we find among you a known bad person, we rightly bring him against you. For this is the entire basis of your defense: that you separated yourselves for this reason, lest you perish through contact with the sins of others.

Hence you boast that you have made a new kind of threshing floor—one which contains only wheat, or on which only wheat appears—which does not need a winnower but an examiner. Your Parmenianus, too, contrasting your celebrated purity with our impurity as its opposite, dared to introduce the statement of the prophet Jeremiah: “What has straw in common with wheat?” (Jeremiah 23:28.) (*Against the Third Letter of Parmenianus*, Book 3, no. 17.) He said this, as the passage itself indicates, against those who equated their dreams with divine oracles.

Yet your arrogance and dreadful pride are revealed in Parmenianus’s writings, where, contrary to the divine Scriptures and to Cyprian’s admonitions, he proclaimed you to be wheat cleansed of chaff before the final winnowing for which the world waits.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

94. What, then, could have been brought forward more suitably against this most deceitful presumption than the case of the Maximianists? Whatever you habitually say against us as though we were *traditores*, you said more seriously against the Maximianists, whom you received as condemned, when you condemned them.

You seek to bring odium upon us on account of emperors as persecutors; yet you persecuted the Maximianists before judges whom the emperors themselves sent. You maintain that the Baptism of the Church cannot be given outside the Church; yet you did not invalidate the Baptism which the Maximianists had given in the crime of schism when you received those to whom they had given it.

If these things ought to have been done for the sake of peace and unity, you find no basis on which to accuse us. But if they ought not to have been done, do not accuse us unless you condemn yourselves. [Note: These words are now restored from the manuscripts: “you find no basis on which to accuse us; but if they ought not to have been done, do not accuse us.”]

I do not want you to draw the matter out at length. I too could briefly recall what has been said against you. But consider only this: place the case of the Maximianists before your eyes. If you can answer us concerning it, proceed to the other matters; but if you cannot, it is better for you to keep silent than to kick against the goad.

# BOOK FOUR

He again answers all parts of Cresconius’s letter, refuting his objections and accusations one by one solely from the case of the Maximianists.

[Col. 0547]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. Although I have already answered your letter, Cresconius, in three volumes—not small ones—with sufficient care, since you thought that Petilianus’s letter should be defended against my writings by which it had been refuted, nevertheless in this shorter work I have also decided to deal with you solely concerning the case of the Maximianists, and from this one case to show how vainly and pointlessly you made all the statements contained in that letter.

For the benefit of God must not be disregarded: he has graciously provided it both for shortening our labor and, if you are wise, for assisting your correction. Without your knowledge, and without our intending it, he so ruled the minds of your bishops that those who accused the Christian world of being stained by the sins of others—even by false and unproved accusations—were compelled, in the case of the Maximianists, to admit that those who remained in one communion of the Sacraments had not been stained by the sins of those whom they had condemned: namely, those to whom they gave time to return as though innocent, if not the ordainers of Maximianus, at least those who stood on his side as condemnors of Primianus.

Those who were unwilling to acknowledge Christ’s Baptism, refusing to recognize it even in those Churches which the labor of the Apostles propagated and founded, and insisting that Baptism could not be given outside the one Church, while blaming us for not invalidating the Baptism given by those whom we denied to be in the true Church, received people baptized in the sacrilegious schism of Maximianus and did not dare to invalidate the Baptism in them.

Those who accuse us of persecuting them on account of the laws of the Christian emperors, by which their perversity is ordered to be corrected, approached judges sent by those very emperors; before them they brought grave accusations against Maximianus and his associates; they cited the council by which they had condemned them through proconsular records; and they secured highly effective orders by which those men were expelled from their sees.

After all these actions of their own, they still try to spread a fog before the ignorant—not only despite the holy Scriptures and the many sure documents concerning their earlier actions, by which they separated themselves from unity, but also despite the clearest evidence of their own most recent acts and examples.

## CHAPTER II

2. From this point, then, I shall proceed; from this point I shall answer all parts of your letter, insofar as the Lord assists me, without any difficulty, indeed with great ease.

First, there is the matter in which you, contradicting yourself, eloquently wished to disparage eloquence, as though it were an enemy of truth and rather a patron of falsehood, so that in this way you might show the ignorant that I, as an eloquent man, should be avoided and shunned. If my eloquence were truly as great as you attribute to me, although as an accuser, would you not be compelled to praise my eloquence after the decree of the Council of Bagai had been read? [Col. 0548] That decree, as it is written there, hurled from the embrace of peace by the thunderbolt of its sentence Maximianus, “an adversary of the faith, an adulterer of truth, an enemy of Mother Church, a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram.”

Moreover, if that material had been placed before me, when would I have been able to say:

> “Although the cavity of a poisoned womb may for a long time have concealed the harmful offspring of a viperous seed, and although the moist coagulations of conceived crime may with slow heat have formed themselves into the limbs of asps, nevertheless the conceived poison could not remain hidden when its sheltering shadow vanished. For, though late, the pregnant vows of crimes have brought forth their public crime and parricide.”

When would I have constrained myself to search out such words? When would I have rolled them forth in expression? When would I have stirred the mind of a reader or hearer so violently, with such force and resonance, toward hatred of the guilty?

Does this mean that the words spoken against those to whom they were directed were any less truthful? Is the authority or credibility of so great a council diminished or weakened by this eloquence? Surely the wording that seemed the more eloquent was selected precisely because everyone wanted it to be his own, so that with this one utterance the silent mouths of three hundred and ten men might resound.

Behold the eloquence you disparaged, which you warned us to detest and avoid as seditious and, even by a Greek term, maliciously artificial. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and by a Greek term also malicious and artificial.”] It so pleased all those bishops of yours that, in their plenary council, each one did not wish to express his own judgment; rather, they all made their own the single judgment which one man had been able to state more eloquently and elegantly.

Let us therefore be permitted, without incurring ill will, to dispute with reasonable polish against human errors, if so many and such great bishops of yours were permitted to condemn the men themselves so eloquently and elegantly.

## CHAPTER III

3. You also criticize, under the vicious name of contention and hostility, our zeal for striving on behalf of the truth, because we have often wished to confer with your people so that, once error had been removed, fraternal love might be joined by the bond of peace. [Note: All the manuscripts read “might rejoice.” The same reading occurs in Augustine’s Letter 88, no. 7.]

I ask you: would it not be better for the cause of truth and unity to be conducted among bishops in peaceful words and more peaceful places than for bishops to litigate in the courtroom through advocates? This is what was done by the party of your bishop Primianus of Carthage against Maximianus and against those who were condemned with him by the Council of Bagai, before the legate of Carthage and before four or more proconsuls.

Certainly, in a disputation conducted by conference, one must take care not to break out into litigation; and modest and gentle people can and usually do take such care. But when a dispute is conducted in court, with advocates struggling on both sides, then without question there is litigation.

I do not criticize your people for this, if they were compelled to it not by a love of litigation but by the necessity of seeking a remedy. Nevertheless, I urge you, a man endowed with good sense, to notice, perceive, and understand that those who did not avoid but undertook and carried out the noise of the courtroom and the judicial quarrels by which they would convict and expel people whom they had already condemned in council could have conferred peaceably with us much more easily—unless they preferred to cover a bad case with an excuse rather than bring it to an end by discussion.

## CHAPTER IV

4. But before you come to my discussion in which I criticized Petilianus, you ask me by whom it is appropriate for you to be baptized: whether rather by one whom I too affirm to possess Baptism, or by one whom your side maintains does not possess it.

This question too has been removed by the case of Maximianus from the empty talk of the ignorant, at least insofar as you are concerned; among the Maximianists themselves it still remains.

For when your people had condemned Maximianus for the sacrilege of schism—Maximianus whom Primianus had condemned as his deacon, and through whom Primianus had been condemned when many of his fellow bishops conspired against him—twelve ordainers of that same Maximianus were immediately condemned with him by the same sentence.

Two of these, Praetextatus of Assur and Felicianus, were accused by your people before the proconsular court. Your advocates demonstrated by the sentence of the Council of Bagai that they had been condemned with Maximianus. When your people tried, at the proconsul’s command, to expel them from the places they occupied and utterly failed, they later received them in such a way that they remained in communion with them while they retained their full ecclesiastical honors, and, after restoring their peoples to peace with them, they did not rebaptize any of those whom they had baptized in schism.

5. The decree of the Council of Bagai exists; it was cited before the proconsul by the advocate Nummasius when he was acting to have the church of Membressa handed over to the communion of Primianus, with Salvius expelled—Salvius who had long held it and had obtained the episcopate in the party of Donatus.

He was sought for expulsion because Nummasius cited him as condemned by the Council of Bagai among the twelve ordainers of Maximianus, although the same Nummasius, making a numerical mistake, calls them eleven.

Titianus later recited this petition of Nummasius, expressly and by name acting before the same proconsul against Praetextatus and Felicianus. The words of his advocate are these:

> “But iniquity delights in its own institutions and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For that same Maximianus nourishes the audacity he began and joins others to himself for madness. Among them is also a certain Felicianus, who at first followed what was right but is darkened by the stain of this corruption. Established in the city of Musti, he has believed that the walls consecrated to Almighty God, the venerable church, should be retained as though under a kind of siege. Praetextatus likewise imitates him in the region of Assur.
>
> “But when the association of priests became known to the authority of your justice, you ordered—as the records testify—that, with every effect of opposition expelled, the churches rescued from profane minds should be restored to the most sacred priests.”

Then, a little later, to show what had been ordered, the same advocate recites the petition of Nummasius mentioned above. In it, after the proconsul had said to Nummasius, “Read the episcopal judgment,” [Note: Some manuscripts read: “in which, after Nummasius had demanded that the episcopal judgment be read.”] the judgment of Bagai was recited. In it Maximianus was condemned in these words:

> “It hurled Maximianus, an adversary of the faith, an adulterer of truth, an enemy of Mother Church, a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, from the embrace of peace by the thunderbolt of its sentence. And because the earth, gaping open, has not yet swallowed him (Numbers 16), it has reserved him above for a greater punishment. For, snatched away, he had gained a shortened punishment by death; now, while dead, he collects heavier interest on his debt among the living.”

Then the judgment of Bagai proceeds against his twelve ordainers:

> “Nor does a just death condemn this man alone for his crime,” they say. “It also drags many into partnership in the crime by a chain of sacrilege. Of them it is written: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes.’” (Psalm 13:3.)
>
> “We would not indeed wish them to be cut away as though from the joint of our own body. But since the pestilence of a festering wound has more relief in amputation than in the application of medicine, a healthier course has been found: lest the poisonous infection spread through all the limbs, the wound born of it should be cut away through a brief pain.
>
> “Know, therefore, that the following men, guilty of a notorious crime—Victorianus of Carcabia, Martianus of Sullectum, Beianus of Baiana, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula [Note: The manuscripts read “of Musula.”], Donatus of Sabrata, Miggenus of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assur, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzita, Felicianus of Musti, and Martialis of Pertusa—who, through the deadly work of destruction, joined a filthy vessel to the accumulated dregs, and also the clerics once belonging to the Church of Carthage, who, while participating in the crime, furnished assistance to an unlawful incest, have been condemned by the judgment of God presiding and by the truthful voice of the universal council.”

After the condemnation of these men, among whom Praetextatus of Assur and Felicianus of Musti are read to have been included, and with whom, as I said earlier, your people agreed after securing the proconsul’s order against them [Note: The printed editions read: “the proconsular orders obtained against them agreed.”], they granted to the others remaining in the same schism of Maximianus—including the condemnors of Primianus—a period of delay in the same Council of Bagai, defined by a fixed date, solely because they had not participated in Maximianus’s ordination. It is contained in these words:

> “But those,” they say, “whom the offshoots of that sacrilegious age did not pollute—that is, those who, through the modest shame of faith, held back their own hands from the head of Maximianus—we have permitted to return to Mother Church.
>
> “For as much as we are cleansed by the death of the guilty, so much do we rejoice in the return of the innocent. And lest the pressure of a shortened day take away the hope of salvation from those returning, while the preceding statutes remain in force, we open to all until the eighth day before the coming Kalends of January the door for acknowledging their error, so that those who return may possess the foundations of undiminished honor and faith. If anyone through sluggish negligence is unable to enter, let him know that by his own will the way to all access to pardon has been removed from him. For the sentence pronounced against them will remain, and repentance will be fixed for those who return after the appointed day.”

## CHAPTER V

6. From all these facts, then—since you yourselves do not deny that some returned to your communion, and since, in so recent a memory, while the people concerned are still alive, the matter is famous and clearly known [Note: The printed editions read “of celebrated renown,” omitting *agitur*, “the matter concerned,” which has been added here from the manuscripts]—both those who were granted a delay (for, as the words of that council sufficiently indicate, they invite them to return to Mother Church and rejoice in their return as though they were innocent) and those whom they condemned together with Maximianus without granting any delay baptized outside your Church throughout that entire period:

whether until the day of the delay, when they were in communion with Maximianus and remained in his schism, or even after the day of the delay had passed, when the advocate Titianus expressly demanded that Praetextatus and Felicianus be expelled from the basilicas, with whom Primianus later reconciled while they retained their full honors—how do you now dare to say that the one Baptism cannot be given except in the one Church, when you have unquestionably recognized and received the Baptism given by these men in sacrilegious schism, and have not dared to invalidate it?

Nor can you say that you conferred nothing upon those whom you received in the same Baptism. [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “already.”] If I ask what you conferred, you will undoubtedly answer:

“We provided that they should not perish through the sacrilege of schism; that they should not possess Christ’s Baptism for judgment rather than reward, for destruction rather than salvation, as the mark of military service remains upon deserters. We provided peace; we provided unity; we provided fellowship with the Church, so that they might deserve to receive the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts, without whom no one reaches the kingdom of heaven, even if he has been instructed in all the lawful Sacraments.”

You would answer this truthfully if you held the true Church. Nevertheless, it is enough for your admonition that you understand that in the true Church you will receive what you believed those who were baptized in the sacrilegious schism of Maximianus received in your communion when they returned from there to you with those who had baptized them.

And thus you should understand that you too will be punished, even after receiving Christ’s Baptism, if you do not hold the unity of the Catholic Church—just as you would undoubtedly consider those baptized in the schism of Maximianus liable to punishment if they were not joined to your communion, since, in the case of those who came to you from there, you judged that their Baptism should not be invalidated.

You see, therefore, that even the matter which troubled you concerning the Sacrament of Baptism has already been resolved by the case of the Maximianists.

## CHAPTER VI

**7.** Let us now examine those points by which you thought you had refuted my letter. First, you ask why I call your people Donatists, adding that Donatus was not the founder and originator of a Church that had not previously existed, but one of the bishops of an ancient Church derived from Christ. [Col. 0552] Do you not notice that Maximian says this very thing about himself, although you call his entire communion by his name? Nor do you distinguish the schism he created from yourselves or from other sects by any designation except by calling them Maximianists, Maximianenses, or some other name derived from Maximian’s name—or, more simply and without fear of grammatical rods, by calling them “the party of Maximian.”

Will you say that Maximian created a schism from your communion, but that Donatus did not create one from the Catholic communion? Yet Maximian does not say this. Rather, he maintains that Primian and all of you created a schism from the party of Donatus, in which he himself remained, and he recites the decrees of the councils: first, the one held at Carthage by forty-three men, by which Primian was condemned in advance; and second, the one which a hundred or more of your bishops at that time composed at Cebarsussi, by which he was condemned more fully and completely.

When someone produces such documents, what will you answer him except that the Council of Bagai has greater authority—the council in which three hundred and ten condemned that same Maximian and his associates? Primian did not plead his case before them as one who needed to be cleared, but sat among them as the completely innocent judge; he pronounced sentence against Maximian and his twelve associates, in whose presence Maximian had been ordained, and, granting a delay, recalled the many others—by whom he himself had been condemned—to their own peace as though they were innocent.

## CHAPTER VII

**8.** In this conflict of yours, what do you want us, who belong neither to Maximian’s communion nor to yours, to judge as neutral parties? What, I ask, do you want us to judge here except that, against the two councils by which Primian was condemned, the later Council of Bagai ought to prevail on his behalf, just as the council by which Maximian was condemned prevailed against him? We judge that the later council is all the more authoritative because, being later, it was able to judge the earlier proceedings.

See, in this respect we favor you. We have another case with the Maximianenses, if they dare to complain. [Note: The Am. edition and the manuscripts read *aliena* (“another”), rather than *alia*.] I say that we favor the third, Bagai, judgment, which was made for Primian against Maximian and his colleagues, and by which the later judgment could rightly annul the earlier ones.

Nevertheless, we neither read nor hear of any appeal by Primian from the first two judgments to the third, except that he was condemned in advance in the first and condemned in the second while absent. But that famous Bagaitan sentence was also pronounced against Maximian and his associates while they were absent.

And those forty-three men at Carthage testified that they had acted more moderately, cautiously, and diligently toward that same Primian because they had sent envoys to him not once but twice and three times, asking that, if he did not wish to come to them, he should allow them to come to him. Since he refused both alternatives and, as they write, treated those who had been sent with an insulting rejection, they assert that necessity was laid upon them to provide for the Church. Even then they did not dare to precipitate the final [Col. 0553] judgment; rather, they acted with a kind of preliminary judgment, taking care that, if he trusted his case, an opportunity should remain for him to answer and clear himself at the next and more distinguished council. When he refused to come to that council, they finally thought that he necessarily had to be condemned, without any further suspension of sentence.

In the decree of the Council of Bagai, however, we read not only that no envoys sent by Maximian were mistreated, but that no envoys were even sent to summon him. Yet we see altar raised against altar and a bishop ordained against the bishop who sat in the very chair in which he had been ordained, sitting there in such a way that he neither abandoned the assembly of his people nor had his communion severed by the many other bishops. So great was the indignation aroused by the perpetration of sacrilegious schism that the condemnation of Maximian himself and of those who had ordained him could no longer be postponed.

**9.** Although these things are so, they do not move you in the case of Caecilian. While Caecilian remained and presided over the people, with altar raised against altar, Majorinus was ordained against him. Against Caecilian, not two judgments—as Maximian’s adherents brought against Primian—but one judgment was produced, accelerated by a horrifyingly rash haste.

Caecilian did not, like Primian, refuse to allow his colleagues to come to him; rather, he invited them to come. Even this they could not suppress in the decree of their council which they composed against him. [Note: The manuscripts read *Januarianus* for *Januarius*.] On Caecilian’s behalf not one later judgment, as on Primian’s behalf, but four are cited. [Note: Caecilian, condemned by one Carthaginian council of schismatics, was acquitted by four later judgments: two episcopal judgments, at Rome and Arles; a third judgment by Emperor Constantine; and a fourth by the proconsul Aelianus, by which Felix, his ordainer, was cleared. See below in the Appendix.]

His opponents, unlike Primian’s opponents, were not absent but present when they were refuted: before judges whom they had agreed would judge; before the emperor Constantine himself, before whom they first accused Caecilian; before whom they later complained about the episcopal judges by whom Caecilian had wanted the case itself to be heard, alleging that they had not judged rightly; and before whom they again appealed from another episcopal judgment, so that, when Constantine himself examined the case between the parties after one and another episcopal judgment, they might be defeated. Their fourth defeat was not lacking either.

For when the slanderers had been found guilty in their own crimes, and they had raised against him the question of the *traditio* of Felix of Aptunga, his ordainer, Felix himself was also cleared by the proconsular judgment. Constantine had ordered that his case be investigated, since they were wearying him with continual appeals. [Note: The printed editions read, “to whom they again appealed a second episcopal judgment,” and, a little later, “whose fourth conviction of Caecilian was also not lacking. For when the slanderers had been found guilty in their own crimes, and they had raised against him the question of *traditio* concerning his ordainers at Aptunga (or, his ordainer at Aptunga).” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

The Maximianenses did not inflict such injuries upon Primian; they were not defeated so many times; they were not defeated while present; nor were they defeated before judges whom they themselves had chosen. Yet, as is clear, they themselves created a schism from your communion. You do not wish to observe that your people have created a schism from the Catholic communion. With what shameless and utterly empty animosity [Col. 0554] you do this, I simply do not know.

For if you want everything you say about Caecilian and Felix, his ordainer, to be true because nearly seventy bishops judged the matter, why do you not want what is said about Primian to be true, when first forty-three and later a hundred bishops judged that matter also, and confirmed the earlier preliminary judgment by a later judgment?

But if you think Primian’s crimes were false because the later Council of Bagai is cited on his behalf against his enemies, why do you not confess that the crimes brought against Caecilian were utterly false, on whose behalf so many later judgments are cited?

If Caecilian, against whom those seventy men had once judged, ought not thereafter to have found an opportunity for clearance before other judges, then neither ought Primian to have found one, whom a much larger number than seventy condemned in a second examination, confirming the first. [Note: Perhaps read *primam* (“the first [examination]”).]

But if, after a man has been condemned twice, the third judgment now made on his behalf is fully sufficient, why do you argue, with some brazen lack of shame, that for a man condemned once a second, third, fourth, and fifth judgment should not suffice for acquittal?

If the number troubles you, so that you think the Council of Bagai should prevail against the hundred by whom Primian was condemned because three hundred and ten participated in it, why do you refuse to consent to the whole world in the far greater number of bishops? [Note: The word *tanto* (“so much”) has been added from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VIII

**10.** As for what you bring against Caecilian—that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit of which the Lord says, “It shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:32)—we could also say that you charged Felicianus of Musti, whom you now have as a bishop together with Primian, one of the ordainers of Maximian and of those who condemned Primian—and from whom you did not rebaptize those baptized even in sacrilegious schism—that you charged him with the sin committed against the Holy Spirit, since you charge him with the sacrilege of schism, just as the sentence of the Council of Bagai proclaimed.

For just as you think those whom you accuse of handing the divine Scriptures over to persecutors to be burned sinned by that unforgivable offense against the Holy Spirit because men of God spoke those same Scriptures while moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21), so we could charge this same crime not only against your own traditors—whom the official records convict—but, as I have said, against Felicianus, and show that you charged him with this crime in his sacrilegious schism. For the unity of love and peace is preserved in the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3). Whoever commits schism plainly violates this unity.

But we do not charge you with this guilt—the insoluble and eternal sin committed against the Holy Spirit—because we do not despair that you can be healed if you are corrected while you live. Nor do we charge it against your people who handed the holy books over to be burned, unless [Col. 0555] they remained separated from unity to the end of this life with an unrepentant heart.

Nor do you show that you charged this against Felicianus and Praetextatus, with whom you later communicated—men who, having been drawn with Maximian into partnership in the crime by the chain of sacrilege, are recorded as having been condemned by the truthful voice of your plenary council, yet are shown to have been received after the day of delay had passed—not as men already condemned, but as though they were innocent.

## CHAPTER IX

**11.** As for your displeasure with the derivation of the name, so that Donatists are called from Donatus, and your opinion that the word ought rather to be declined according to the rule of Latin usage, I do not reject your admonition. [Note: The manuscripts read *declinandam*, referring to *derivationem* (“derivation”).] Nevertheless, seek out grammatical judges before whom you can dispute this art with the Maximianenses and convict them.

For I no longer even want to call them Maximianists, lest I offend your highly educated ears. Those judges, at least as I suppose, will not yield to you as easily as I did by allowing you to call them Claudianenses, or something else, whom they called Claudianists. [Note: Claudianists, concerning whom see *Expositions on the Psalms* 36, sermon 2, section 20.]

They counted Primian’s reception of them into communion among the charges by which they both condemned him in advance and condemned him. At the same time, recognize that this rule of declension did not please me alone, as you reproach me for it; perhaps I alone yielded to you so readily in a matter that has nothing to do with the case.

## CHAPTER X

**12.** You thought I ought to be attacked more vigorously because, although I called the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics a heresy—a term which you want regarded rather as “schism”—we nevertheless receive into communion those who have not been cleansed from sacrilege.

You, who attack us so seriously in this matter, answer how your people cleansed the sacrilege of Felicianus and Praetextatus, with whom they later communicated, joining them to themselves and restoring them as bishops just as they had previously been, without rebaptizing any of those whom they had baptized in the sacrilege of schism.

Or perhaps they were not stained by sacrilege, as some of your people foolishly say, claiming that they sinned not against God but against a human being? Yet sacrilege is a sin all the more serious because it can be committed only against God.

This is why you thought I should be attacked in your argument: not for any other reason, but because I called your error sacrilegious. Read the Council of Bagai. Surely its opening words are these:

> “Since, by the will of almighty God and of Christ his Savior, we had gathered from all the provinces of Africa and were holding a council in the holy church of Bagai, Gamalius, Primianus, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarius, Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatianus, and the remaining three hundred and ten, it pleased the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish perpetual peace and to cut off sacrilegious schisms.”

[Note: Several manuscripts read *Januarianus* instead of *Januarius*.]

Do you hear? Do you understand? Do you pay attention? “To cut off,” they say, “sacrilegious schisms.” Therefore, when this sentence was pronounced, it was not against a human being but against God that, by criminal perversity, Maximian alone in that schism was held guilty of sacrilege.

Read a little farther what they say about his associates, among whom are written the names of those under discussion:

> “Nor does a just death condemn this man alone for his crime; the chain of sacrilege also drags many others into partnership in the crime.”

## CHAPTER XI

**13.** What is this, most eloquent man? What do you have to say to me? Read what follows. Among the many whom that chain of sacrilege drags into partnership in the crime, see Praetextatus and Felicianus.

I read: sacrilegious men. I see: bishops.

[Note: The Ambrosian and Erfurt manuscripts read, “Praetextatus and Felicianus, sacrilegious envoys; I see bishops.” The Louvain edition reads, “Praetextatus and Felicianus, bound men. I see sacrilegious bishops.” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.]

What will you do if you cannot prove that they were cleansed? Surely you are forced to yield to the truth, when we say that, when your people come to us, their sins are covered by the very bond of fraternal peace and love, as it is written: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

What of those whom they baptized after they had been separated from your communion and bound to Maximian in partnership with the sacrilegious chain of his schism—those whom you received together with them into peace and concord in the same Baptism?

Will you answer anything except that you rightly approved in them the same Sacraments which we also approve in you? You will be more consistent if you answer this and will not contradict the words of your letter.

In that letter, when you attempted to show that what had been committed between us and you was not heresy but rather schism, you said that we and your people have one religion, the same Sacraments, and no difference in Christian observance.

You could not have more seriously condemned the repetition of Baptism than by these words, when those led astray by us are rebaptized by your people, among whom you both believe, say, and write that the same Sacraments exist.

By what shameless criminality, then, is not preserved in those whom the Christian world baptizes in holy unity what was preserved in those whom Praetextatus and Felicianus baptized in sacrilegious schism?

You therefore settled our case with you by your own judgment when you received into the harmony of the altar, without any degradation and without repeating Baptism, those who had been struck by your condemnation, who had earnestly warned the peoples not to come over to you, who even held that baptism was to be administered after yours, together with those whom they baptized while outside your communion and established in sacrilegious schism.

You believed that they had been cleansed from that sacrilegious crime by nothing other than the holy fire of love.

And this would truly have happened if you held that same love in true unity.

## CHAPTER XII

**14.** Let us also examine the words of Petilianus’s letter, which you wanted to defend against me, and see how you can extricate yourself in this case of the Maximianenses, which alone I have now decided to pursue against your [Col. 0557] writings.

He certainly wrote these words:

> “The conscience,” he says, “of the holy giver is taken into account; it cleanses the conscience of the recipient.”

I replied to him:

> “But what if the giver’s conscience is hidden and perhaps stained? How will it be able to cleanse the recipient’s conscience?”

Because this unavoidable question is not answered at all in Petilianus’s words, you attempted to answer it in your own words. You said this not against me but against the man whom you wanted to defend.

He said, “The conscience of the giver is taken into account, and it cleanses the conscience of the recipient.” You, however, acknowledged that a hidden conscience cannot be seen and said that it is taken into account in such a way that the conscience itself is not seen, but rather what is known about it through public reputation.

[Note: The printed editions read, “acknowledging that you say the hidden conscience of a certain person cannot be seen.” The manuscripts do not contain “of a certain person,” nor do they contain the verb “you say.”]

From this it follows that it is no longer true that the giver’s conscience cleanses the recipient’s conscience. According to you, his reputation cleanses it—a reputation that certainly deceives the observer when it speaks good things about a very wicked man, chaste things about an adulterer, or religious things about a sacrilegious man.

It cleanses only when it lies. For if a reputation speaks truthfully about a secret criminal, it does not cleanse but stains the person who receives Baptism from him.

Therefore consider what sort of patron you wanted to bring forward for so bad a case: a reputation that, when lying, cleanses, and when truthful, pollutes—so that, by your marvelous argument, water is not false in its presence when that reputation itself is false.

[Note: The manuscripts read “in its presence”; the printed editions read “in your presence.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

**15.** But why should we speak longer about this, when Felicianus now sits among your bishops? While he was separated from them and clung to Maximian in the chain of sacrilege, no one rebaptized those whom he baptized.

I ask Petilianus what sort of conscience Felicianus had at that time. I read to him the decree of the Council of Bagai, where it is written:

> “Nor does a just death condemn this man alone for his crime; the chain of sacrilege also drags many others into partnership in the crime, concerning whom it is written: ‘The venom of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’” (Psalm 13:3).

Among these many, then, Felicianus too is numbered. With such lips and such a mouth he baptized. You did not reject any one of these people; you did not cut them off; you did not destroy what they had done. And because the water was consecrated by the evangelical words, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” through whatever tongue and whatever conscience, you recognized and received it as true, not false.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “and you did not reject water—or some water—from such a mouth.” A little later they read, “it was consecrated, not false,” omitting the word “water.” Perhaps the text should read: “With such a mouth he baptized, and you did not reject the water from the mouth of such a baptizer.”]

But I ask you concerning this Felicianus: when he baptized in the chain of sacrilege and his conscience was so evil, what was his public reputation at that time?

I again recite the council itself, where it is written:

> “Know, therefore, that the notorious criminals Victorianus of Carcabia and, among the others whom it is wearisome to repeat, Praetextatus of Assuri and Felicianus of Musti, who by a fatal work of destruction joined together a filthy vessel with the collected sediment, were shortly afterward condemned by the truthful voice of the plenary council.”

## CHAPTER XIV

**16.** What do you answer to these things?

If [Col. 0558] a person separated from your communion does not baptize, I read that Felicianus baptized after being drawn with Maximian into partnership in the crime.

If one who sins against God does not baptize, I read that Felicianus baptized while bound in the chain of sacrilege.

If the conscience of the holy giver is taken into account because it cleanses the recipient, I read that he baptized while poisoned by the bites of asps.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript and other manuscripts read “with the behavior of asps,” rather than “with the bites of asps.”]

If the giver’s conscience is taken into account so that it can cleanse, and his public reputation is what matters, I read that he baptized as one guilty of a notorious crime.

Felicianus remains in the body; with him are all those whom he baptized in sacrilegious schism and whom you received into your communion without anyone rebaptizing them.

Against Petilianus, a man stained by a sacrilegious conscience baptized. Against you, a man guilty of a notorious crime baptized.

How do you defend yourselves, I ask, except by eventually saying—convicted by your own actions of what we also say—that neither the giver’s conscience nor his reputation cleanses the recipient’s conscience, but rather the recipient’s own faith and the grace of God, who gives, not the human being?

If, however, the recipient does not possess an answer of a good conscience, and if faith itself wavers either wholly or in some part, then human behavior must be corrected, not the Sacraments destroyed. You yourself confess that these Sacraments are not different or similar, but entirely the same.

Thus you judged that the life and will of those whom Felicianus and Praetextatus baptized in sacrilegious schism had to be corrected, so that they would not remain in that sacrilegious schism.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “so that they would not remain in that sacrilege of schism.”]

You did not violate Baptism, although it had been administered to the most unworthy by the most unworthy ministers.

## CHAPTER XV

**17.** Therefore you tried in vain, with a slanderous mouth, to accuse our conscience as though it had been publicly exposed and condemned for the crimes of burning incense, *traditio*, and persecution, in order to prove from this that we cannot give Baptism.

You do this although you make false accusations, and although, whatever the truth of the matter may be, a conscience condemned for the sacrilege of the Maximianenses could certainly give Baptism—a Baptism which you were afraid to annul and which, through your own actions, you teach can even be given by persecutors.

For you not only baptize those same Maximianenses, whom you persecuted most fiercely, but insist that you alone ought to baptize.

[Note: The printed editions read “those who persecuted.” Several manuscripts, and more correctly, read “those whom you persecuted.”]

## CHAPTER XVI

**18.** You say that it is written in the Law: “I do not want the oil of the sinner to anoint my head” (Psalm 140:5). But that is neither how it is written nor how it is to be understood, as you think.

Yet surely the oil of sinners is the oil of the sacrilegious Praetextatus and Felicianus.

You likewise say that it is written: “What does his washing profit the one who is baptized by a dead man?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:30). But you neither pay careful attention to this nor understand its meaning from the context of the passage itself.

Nevertheless, attend to what that most eloquent Bagaitan sentence says:

> “The desired brotherhood of peace and concord is indeed joined together, as it is written: ‘Justice and peace have kissed one another’ (Psalm 84:11). But the members, shipwrecked by the truthful wave and dashed upon the harsh rocks of some, have been cast away; the shores are full of the corpses of those perishing in the very likeness of the Egyptians. [Col. 0559] Their punishment is greater even in death, because after their life has been torn from them by avenging waters, they do not find burial even for themselves.”

[Note: The manuscripts read *invicta* (“unconquered”), or *injuncta* (“joined”), for *juncta* (“joined”).]

How, then, could these men baptize, who were not only dead but also, what is more serious, unburied? How did the washing profit those who were baptized by these dead men—those whom you received in the same washing but did not wash again—if that passage is to be understood as you think?

As for your belief that in my letter—which you think you have answered—I merely excepted an idolater as one guilty of a very grave sin (*Against Petilianus’s Letters*, book 1, section 10), and your vigorous insistence that you may prove that no sinner is excepted in the statement you say is written, “I do not want the oil of the sinner to anoint my head,” consider Felicianus and Praetextatus.

Were they not sinners when they were said to be dragged with Maximian by the chain of sacrilege before so great a council? Dare to assert it; dare to maintain it; dare at least to say that they were indeed sinners, but hidden ones, whereas I read there that they were guilty of a notorious crime.

Even if they had sinned lightly, even if they had remained hidden, you are trying in this proposal, by the testimony you cite about the sinner’s oil, to extract the conclusion that no sinner is excepted.

Where will you be if this is so? Where will you flee? In what hiding places will you be able to conceal yourselves with your sacrilegious men, with those guilty of notorious crimes, with your unburied corpses?

**19.** You say that when it is objected to us by what right we claim the power of Baptism, we do not deal with the merit of our actions or the innocence of our lives, but say that anyone may baptize; and that, as though we were guilty through crimes already adjudged, by wanting to show that sinners possess the ability to baptize, we openly admit that we have sinned. [Note: Two manuscripts read, “and as though guilty through crimes already adjudged.”]

You speak as though we had to speak against God on the basis of our merits, so that Baptism might be as just as we are, although no human being ought to presume upon his own righteousness. We prove above all from this that Baptism belongs to Christ, not to human beings, because it does not vary according to the variation of human merits.

I would discuss this more fully if I were not making greater use of the shortcut you have provided. For by accepting Baptism—and not destroying the Baptism given by the Maximianenses—you yourselves have sufficiently judged that the asps, vipers, parricides, Egyptian corpses, and whatever else was proclaimed against them in the grandiloquent language of the Council of Bagai, so as to make our case exceedingly easy, do not establish Baptism by the merits either of those by whom it is administered or of those to whom it is administered.

Rather, Baptism rests upon its own holiness and truth, because of the one by whom it was instituted. It becomes destruction for those who use it badly and salvation for those who use it well.

## CHAPTER XVII

**20.** I am astonished that you could also be persuaded to mention Cyprian in your argument, since the very letters which you claim are his, concerning the destruction of Baptism given among heretics or schismatics, completely overturn your entire case.

We ought to bring this argument against the Maximianenses, or against others who refuse to accept Baptism given either among us or among you. But you have already ended this case with remarkable ease. You have already received in their communities the Baptism given in Maximian’s sacrilegious schism by Praetextatus [Col. 0560] and Felicianus. Against the letters of Cyprian, as you call them, and against anyone else who has held this opinion, you have acted without hesitation.

As for your claim that the Easterners were separated from your communion because, later agreeing with us, they preferred to revoke their judgment concerning Baptism, if this was done by some few Easterners—which indeed depends on whether it can be demonstrated—they corrected their own judgment.

You, however, after receiving the Baptism given in Maximian’s schism, revoked your former judgment, yet you remain with yourselves and do not wish to be with the Easterners.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**21.** Apparently you thought you had found an opportunity to display your eloquence when, in response to what I wrote in my letter—“Whether a person receives the Sacrament of Baptism from a faithful or an unfaithful steward, let all his hope be in Christ” (*Against Petilianus’s Letters*, book 1, section 7)—you exclaimed:

> “O splendid command of a priest! O praiseworthy instructions of a good father concerning justice!”

Then you said:

> “You make no distinction between the faithful and the unfaithful; let the devout and the impious seem the same to you. It is of no benefit to live with good morals, since whatever is permitted to the just can also be accomplished by the unjust. What more unjust instruction could be given than this: Let the stained purify another; let the filthy wash another; let the unclean cleanse another; let the faithless give faith; let the criminal make an innocent person?”

These are certainly your words, by which you criticize my position. Yet I did not agree to or write anything of the kind.

There is indeed a very great difference between the faithful and the faithless—not with respect to the Sacrament, if both possess it, but with respect to merit, because one possesses it for salvation and the other for punishment.

Nor can whatever the just person may do also be done by the unjust. For even if an unjust person can baptize, an unjust person cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.

Nor does the person who administers Baptism purify, wash, or cleanse anyone, nor make anyone innocent. This is done by the grace of God who gives it and by the good conscience of the recipient.

But consider whether there was no difference between Primian and Felicianus when Primian sat among the three hundred and ten who were saying of Felicianus that the venom of asps was under his lips, that his feet were swift to shed blood, that ruin and misery were in his paths, that he did not know the way of peace, and that there was no fear of God before his eyes (Psalm 13:3).

Was he not then stained, unclean, and filthy—the man who had joined a filthy vessel with collected sediment? Was he not faithless, with the venom of asps under his lips? Was he not criminal, guilty of a notorious crime?

And yet he too now sits as your bishop together with Primian. Those whom he baptized then are now with you and have nowhere afterward been washed again.

## CHAPTER XIX

**22.** You still fight against the truth and refuse to concede that Christ always gives faith, that Christ is the source of the Christian, that the Christian fixes his root in Christ, and that Christ is the head of the Christian (*Against Petilianus’s Letters*, book 1, section 6).

After I had placed these words in my letter against Petilianus, you added your own words and said:

> “This is what we also teach; this is what we want. But we ask through whom this may better be accomplished.”

You do not notice that Petilianus does not teach this—the very Petilianus to whom I then replied and whose letter you are trying to defend [Col. 0561] and affirm against my response.

He plainly said:

> “The conscience of the holy giver is taken into account; it cleanses the conscience of the recipient. For whoever receives faith from a faithless man does not receive faith but guilt.”

Tell me what place he left for Christ to cleanse the baptized person’s conscience, or from whom the baptized person receives faith, when you say that the giver’s conscience is taken into account because it cleanses, and that the person who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt.

You seem, indeed, to yield to the great weight of truth, and you say that this is what you teach and want: that Christ should give faith and that Christ should wash the Christian in order that he may enter upon a new life. But you ask through whom this is better accomplished, since it ought not to be accomplished without a minister.

Petilianus, however, did not say, “The conscience of the minister is taken into account, through which Christ cleanses the recipient,” or “through which Christ gives faith.” Rather, he wanted the recipient’s conscience itself to be cleansed by the conscience of the giver.

He did not say, “Whoever receives faith through the faithless does not receive faith but guilt,” so that he might appear to receive it from Christ, though through another. He said plainly, “Whoever receives it from the faithless.”

[Note: The printed editions read, “whoever receives faith through Christ.” The manuscripts, however, support the reading translated above.]

To this, as though to prove it, he added:

> “For every thing consists in its source and root; and if something has no head, it is nothing.”

He thus made the minister himself—the one whose conscience he said must be taken into account—not a means through which Christ cleanses, but the minister whose conscience cleanses the recipient. He made that minister entirely the source, root, and head of the baptized person.

## CHAPTER XX

**23.** Therefore, at this point I am answering not Petilianus, whose words you have not defended, but you, who have said something different on behalf of your own position.

As you write, you want and teach that it is not the conscience of the holy giver which cleanses the recipient or gives faith to the recipient, as Petilianus said; nor is that conscience the source, root, and head of the believer.

Rather, through that conscience Christ cleanses; through it Christ gives faith; through it Christ is the source of the Christian; through it the Christian fixes his root in Christ; through it Christ is the head of the Christian.

For this is why you ask through whom that which you concede is done by Christ may be better accomplished. Here, as I see, you do not deny that this can also be done through a bad minister, but you say that it can be done better through a good one.

For what else do you mean when you say, “This is what we also teach; this is what we want, but we ask through whom it may better be accomplished”?

Accordingly, Christ cleanses through the stained conscience of one who does not give in holiness, but better through the clean conscience of one who gives in holiness.

Christ gives faith through a bad minister, but better through a good one.

Christ becomes the source of the Christian through an unfaithful steward, but better through a faithful one.

The Christian fixes his root in Christ even through a rejected cultivator, but better through an approved one.

Christ can be the head of the Christian even through Felicianus, but you think he is better so through Primian.

**24.** Thus, in this matter there is little disagreement between us, or perhaps none at all. I too say that the divine Sacraments are administered better through a good minister than through a bad steward.

But this is better on account of the minister himself, so that his life and conduct [Col. 0562] may correspond to the things he administers—not on account of the person who receives them. Even if that person should encounter a bad minister administering the truth, he receives security from his Lord, who warns and says: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they preach, but do not practice” (Matthew 23:3).

I also add that it is better for the person to whom the Sacrament is administered, because by loving the goodness and holiness of a good minister, he more easily imitates him.

But the things administered are not therefore truer and holier because they are administered through a better minister. They are true and holy in themselves because of the true and holy God to whom they belong.

Therefore it can happen that someone approaching the fellowship of God’s people finds one person from whom he can easily receive Baptism and chooses another whom he may imitate to his salvation.

For it is certain that Christ’s Sacrament is holy even when it has been administered through a person who is less holy or not holy at all. But the recipient is punished by the holiness of that same Sacrament if he receives it unworthily, if he uses it badly, or if he does not live in a manner suitable and fitting to it.

## CHAPTER XXI

**25.** For I ask you: Suppose that someone whom Primian baptized in your communion lives most wickedly, while someone whom Felician baptized in the schism of Maximian lives most uprightly. To which of them do you think the kingdom of God is open: to the one whom, according to you, the good man baptized while he was evil, or to the one whom, according to the Council of Bagai, the sacrilegious man baptized while he was religious?

But perhaps you say—and you say what is true—“A person established in schism cannot be religious.” I agree. Nevertheless, someone baptized by Primian, whom you believe to be religious, can be sacrilegious or secretly so within your communion.

Furthermore, if the person whom Felician baptized while bound by sacrilege’s chain were corrected by abandoning the sacrilege of schism and restored to ecclesiastical communion, would you dare say that his Baptism thereby became better, although you cannot deny that the man himself could have become better? You yourselves judged this by the deed itself, since you received all those whom Felician and Praetextatus baptized in the schism’s sacrilege, which you condemn and detest, when they returned with them to you, without destroying or repeating their Baptism.

But if, when you said, “We are seeking through whom it is made better,” you used the comparative degree instead of the positive—speaking as though you had said, “We are seeking through whom it is made well,” intending it to be understood that through a bad minister it is made badly—I do not press you on the word, but rather warn you that you ought to have said, “We are seeking through whom it is made,” rather than, “We are seeking through whom it is made well.” For could it happen that Christ does not well give faith, that Christ is not well the source and head of the Christian, that the root is not well planted in Christ? Either it does not happen, or, if it happens, it unquestionably happens well.

**26.** Nevertheless, we are discussing these matters so that, on account of evil dispensers—not of their own sacraments, but of the Lord’s Sacraments, whom it is necessary to keep mingled until the time when the Lord’s threshing-floor is winnowed—the unity of the wheat itself may not be abandoned.

But to make a schism from the unity of Christ, or to be in schism, is plainly evil, and a great evil. Nor can it possibly happen that Christ gives a schismatic not faith but sacrilegious error; or that a schismatic has fixed his root in Christ; or that Christ is the source and head of a schismatic.

And yet, if he gives Christ’s Baptism, it will have been given; if he receives it, it will have been received—not for eternal life, but for eternal punishment if he persists in that sacrilege. This is not because the good that he possesses is turned into evil, but because, so long as an evil man possesses it, he possesses the good to his own harm.

## CHAPTER XXII

**27.** You may ask how I prove this. What else can I say to you except what I have undertaken in this work? Read the decree of Bagai; look at Felician and Praetextatus. Schismatics gave Baptism, and both men were received and gathered in by you; neither was degraded, and neither was rebaptized.

Surely you are no longer asking whether it is made better through a just minister or through an unjust one, since the Baptism given by Primian—whom you consider just—is not therefore better than the Baptism given by Felician, whom you consider unjust.

Surely you are now compelled to understand how the Apostle said, “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3:7). And you recall that you said in vain: “Just as, in the case of one who plants and waters, only a diligent and faithful farmer is sought, so also in the Sacrament of Baptism only the most righteous worker is approved.”

Behold: Felician was neither diligent, faithful, nor most righteous, but rather negligent of his own salvation, unfaithful, and most unjust, when, joined to Maximian and—just as your three hundred and ten repeatedly proclaim with one most eloquent voice—established in the chain of sacrilege, he administered the Baptism which you did not dare to annul.

**28.** Surely you see that the testimony you quoted from the prophet does not pertain to this case: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding with discipline” (Jer. 3:15).

For Felician was neither a sacrilegious man according to the heart of God, nor did he feed God’s sheep with discipline in sacrilegious schism. Yet he baptized those among whom, when they were received, you recognized that what he gave belonged not to him but to God.

Surely you see how I recalled from Holy Scripture, “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Ps. 117:8). And, as far as this case is concerned, you answered uselessly that you therefore seek for the person through whom this Sacrament is celebrated to be more just and faithful, because you have hope and trust in God, not in man; yet you always look for God’s faith and righteousness in His ministers.

Behold: in Felician, when he was guilty of a notorious crime, there was neither righteousness nor faith; and yet there was Baptism. And those to whom he gave it, when they were gathered in by you, you say that righteousness came to them; you do not say that Baptism was lacking.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**29.** Therefore, regarding what you ask me next—“If Baptism given by anyone and in any manner ought not to be annulled, why did the Apostles baptize after John?”—you must now solve this question: If, as you say, the Apostles baptized after John, why did your people not baptize those whom Felician had baptized in sacrilegious schism?

From this at least learn that whatever is read or discussed concerning John’s Baptism is entirely unrelated to this case.

I do not know what you were thinking when you said that the Jews to whom Peter said, “Let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38), had already been baptized by Moses—although they were born many generations after that servant of God led their ancestors through the Red Sea (Exod. 14:22).

*[Note: The American and Erasmian editions and the manuscripts read “led across.”]*

Or, if they possessed Moses’ Baptism for the reason that they were descended from those whom the Apostle says were baptized into Moses (1 Cor. 10:2), dare to say that all who are born of faithful Christians already possess Christian Baptism. You see, I suppose, how absurdly this would be said.

But whatever the truth may be concerning that matter, even if the Apostles had not baptized after Moses, the servant of God, I would still compel you to explain why your people did not baptize after Felician, the sacrilegious Maximianist.

**30.** As for what I wrote: “If those who wished to belong to Paul were in error” (ibid. 1:12), what hope, then, is there for those who wish to belong to Donatus? (Book 1 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, no. 5.) I think you did not refute me in the earlier parts of your letter because you yourself also consider what we have sufficiently discussed above.

Therefore, contrary to your own impression, and as though you were exulting as one certain of victory, you cannot conclude that everything said by Petilian or anyone else was rightly said.

Following precisely the order in which you briefly rehearsed these matters, as though recalling them, I instead conclude in this case concerning the Maximianists that they were not rightly said. For Felician did not possess the conscience of one who gives holy things when, joined to Maximian, he was being dragged along in the chain of sacrilege; and those whom he baptized were baptized by one guilty of a notorious crime, and therefore by an openly faithless man.

Nor was that sacrilegious man their source, root, and head unto salvation; nor was he a good tree, condemned in the fellowship of sacrilegious schism and still established in that same sacrilege; nor was he good who brought forth good things from the good treasure of his heart (Matt. 12:35), when it was said of him and of his other associates, “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness” (Ps. 13:3).

And yet, when your people agreed with him, they were compelled by the force of truth to recognize that the Baptism such a man had given belonged not to him but to Christ.

*[Note: For “refuted,” American and Erasmian editions and all manuscripts read “defended.”]*

*[Note: Perhaps “victorious,” as above, book 3, no. 85.]*

*[Note: In the manuscripts: “in which you briefly rehearsed them, as though recalling or remembering them.”]*

## CHAPTER XXIV

**31.** Come, let us now see, at the proper point in your letter, how you extricate yourself from the case of the Maximianists. All who read these letters are surely waiting to learn either what you have said about this, and where you said it, or what answer I have made.

Accordingly, I do not wish to examine what you replied concerning Optatus of Gildonianus; I do not wish to linger longer over the case of a man whose condemnation by your people is not my concern.

I am certainly sacrificing this charge, and perhaps future generations will consider it insignificant once his memory has been obliterated. But as long as there are people who know his life and character, they will complain that I said too little about him rather than that I said something false.

For they do not read our letters as you do. You ask me whom I called “a swift wave,” and what it swallowed, although you have Praetextatus and Felician there.

My words there are as follows:

> “Thus, indeed,” I said, “these men insult their own schismatics, calling them both dead and unburied. But surely they ought to have wished to be buried, lest, from the multitude of unburied corpses lying on the shore, Gildonianus Optatus, advancing with a military column like a swift wave surging farther forward, should later swallow Felician and Praetextatus farther within” (Book 1 *Against the Letters of Petilian*, no. 11).

When you read these words of mine there, why did you not quote the whole passage? Why do you accuse me as though I had not said what that swift wave swallowed, when you see written there that it would later swallow Felician and Praetextatus farther within?

*[Note: The manuscripts read “a rabid wave”; and below they consistently read “a rabid wave.”]*

*[Note: Two manuscripts here add: “when you attempted to answer them.”]*

## CHAPTER XXV

**32.** For what else do your people usually reply, as though in their great defense, when the reception of Praetextatus and Felician, who had been condemned, is brought against them, except: “Optatus wanted this; Optatus did this”?

The cities of Mustitana and Assuritana themselves testify to this. They say that, fearing the Gildonian soldier because of Optatus’s threat, they compelled their bishops to return to Primian’s communion.

But because you saw that it could be impudently denied that this had been done by him, you denied that I had written it—perhaps thinking that my writings could more easily be made unknown than the event itself.

Yet your bishops may, by some Donatist or Numidian privilege, have been permitted to remain ignorant about their own colleague of what all Africa was proclaiming, while they do not allow charges alleged by Africans against Africans—never proved, repeatedly acquitted—to remain unknown in the eastern and western bounds of the world.

Let the Baptism given by Optatus avail among you—a man whom you were unwilling so to condemn that you nevertheless did not dare to acquit him—while Baptism given in the Churches founded through apostolic labor, those of the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, Thessalonians, and the other Churches recorded in the Holy Scriptures, which you too read, does not avail, though there not even Caecilian’s false charge, perhaps not even his true name, was heard.

Let Optatus have had the conscience of one who gives holy things in that life which, as your writings indicate, you were ashamed to condemn for our sake but feared to acquit before God; let it have been considered even in that public reputation, in which you thought a hidden conscience could be observed.

And yet shall the conscience of so many and such great Christian peoples be accused because they did not know the quarrels of Africans in the most distant regions? Could they likewise have been ignorant of the crimes of Felician and Praetextatus, whom three hundred and ten men condemned in a plenary council?

## CHAPTER XXVI

**33.** And still you bring against Catholic unity certain alleged deeds of our people, which are either false or are not sins; or, even if they are true and sins, cannot defile the fellowship of the good.

For the good do not share in the sins of others, since they certainly do not consent to those sins being committed. Yet, together with those who commit them, until they are separated from the Lord’s threshing-floor like chaff by the final winnowing (Matt. 3:12), they share not in their sins but in God’s Sacraments.

Within the same net, like good fish among bad until the separation that will occur on the shore—that is, at the end of the age, as at the end of the sea (ibid. 13:47–50)—they are separated from the wicked not by bodily segregation but by difference in life and conduct.

The eleven Apostles, for example, did not share in Judas’s thefts. Yet they remained visibly joined with the same Lord as he did; they listened to the same Teacher, received the same Gospel to be believed, and partook of the same Sacraments (John 12:4–6; 13:26).

*[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “the Gospel believed from the same [one].”]* They were mingled with him in bodily assembly but separated from him by spiritual difference.

Likewise, the Apostle Paul did not share in the insolence and envy—that is, in the devilish vices—of those who proclaimed Christ without purity. Yet he preached the same Christ with them and partook of the Sacraments of the same Christ. Concerning them he said, “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:17–18).

For the martyr Cyprian, who loved unity most deeply, both understood and wrote that these men were not separated by any schism or heresy but were mingled with their brothers in bodily assembly (*Letter to Maximus*).

The same Cyprian did not share in the greed, thefts, and usury of his colleagues. He said that, while brothers in the Church were hungry, they wished to possess money in abundance, seized estates through treacherous frauds, and increased interest through multiplying usury. He compared this evil even with idolatry (*On the Lapsed*).

Yet he did not avoid their bodily assembly. He stood at the same altars and partook of the same most holy food and drink. For they were eating and drinking judgment upon themselves (1 Cor. 11:29), whereas he, together with such men, shared not in their sins but in Christ’s mysteries—most closely joined to them in assembly, most widely separated from them in conduct.

The comparisons in Scripture and the examples cited above were given for this reason: so that we might learn to be wheat and not abandon the Lord’s threshing-floor because of the mingling of chaff (Matt. 3:12); to be good fish and not go outside because the nets have been torn apart on account of the mingling of bad fish (ibid. 13:47–48); to be vessels of mercy, made and cleansed for honor, and not flee from the great house because of vessels of destruction and dishonor (2 Tim. 2:20–21).

For there is no reason why the wicked are commendably tolerated in the temporal assembly and mingling of both groups except that the good may not be damnably abandoned.

Since you too act from the same necessity amid your many and obvious evils, you can easily perceive, if you wish, that it is only through sacrilegious hostility that you separate yourselves from so many Christian peoples.

*[Note: The printed editions unnecessarily add “if”; it is absent from the manuscripts.]*

*[Note: “Good fish” would more correctly be read as “good ones.”]*

## CHAPTER XXVII

**34.** Therefore, if not only Optatus, so notorious among you in that Gildonian association, but also some obscure person among you does something evil with your knowledge, and you cannot separate him from your communion because either no one believes you as accuser or you dare not accuse him lest you be unable to prove the charge, then you must either abandon Donatus’s party or become like the man whose sin you know, even though you live differently.

This is said to you with complete correctness—not according to the true judgment, but according to your own judgment.

For who does not know that you are separate from his evil if, by consenting to his sin, you do not share in it? But from this you are compelled to recognize how impiously you bring against the Christian world crimes of Africans that are either false or at least unknown, while you do not want it brought against you that you belong to another, because you cannot persuade those whose fellowship you do not want to leave.

Thus, so that you may not abandon those whom you consider good, you are compelled to tolerate those whom you know to be evil.

Consequently, truth convicts all as evil who, because of the crimes of others—whether true or false, but unknown to the rest and incapable of harming them—have abandoned the good by breaking the unity of so many peoples.

To prevent you from being able in any way to excuse this great sacrilege of Donatus’s party, the case of the Maximianists has been provided for you. In it, as in a mirror, you may see your perversity and correct it, if you wish. If you do not wish to, I do not want to say anything harsher, since I know that you have a heart.

For what will you say against these things?

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**35.** It is good that you yourself write that, when you had read everything I inserted in my letter concerning the Maximianists who had been condemned and received, you were greatly disturbed. I entirely believe it; I clearly see the reason that ought greatly to have disturbed you.

Let us therefore see by what explanation this disturbance of yours was calmed.

You say that you immediately made more careful inquiries of your bishops and that, with them instructing you, you learned both the council’s decree, the judgment pronounced against those who had been condemned, and the whole order of events.

Then, believing that I still did not know what had happened and urging me to learn what the truth contained, you plainly narrated not what the truth contains but what your people, incautious and negligent, put forward in place of the truth.

For you say that, when Maximian’s error was striving to attach very many bishops to itself, your people assembled a council and pronounced against all who had persisted in his schism the sentence which, you remind me, I too had read.

Although this sentence was confirmed by the agreement of all, you say that it was nevertheless resolved by the council’s decree that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent.

You say that this was done so that not only the two whom I mention, but also many others, might be cleansed and restored as innocent to the Church.

*[Note: Praetextatus and Felician.]*

You think that their Baptism therefore ought not to be annulled, because they were restored within the appointed period and were not held by the final sentence; nor, you say, had they been separated from the Church when they baptized, since the limit of the appointed period had not yet passed and they had not yet been separated.
