Here, in the very falsehood of your account—since I have quoted not only your sentences but your very words—I marvel at your ingenuity; I marvel at your spirit resisting your ingenuity.

Never has the power of the prejudice of human presumption appeared so clearly, whether in refusing to perceive the most obvious truth or in asserting the most shameless falsehood.

Do you not perceive that you have set down contradictions so openly that it is scarcely credible that one man could have said both things?

You say that a sentence was pronounced against all who had persisted in Maximian’s schism, and that it was resolved that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent.

How, then, can you yourself also say that they did not baptize outside the Church before they corrected themselves from that schism, if, when they were with Maximian, they were not outside the Church?

Do you notice what you are saying? Have you found a way out, a refuge, a place in which to hide?

*[Note: One manuscript, the Michaeline, omits the negative particle.]*

## CHAPTER XXIX

**36.** You certainly see that, while trying to defend the obvious errors of others, you accomplish nothing except adding your own more obvious errors.

Behold, read your words; I quote them exactly as you wrote them:

> “When Maximian’s error was striving to attach very many bishops to itself,” you say, “a council having been assembled by our people, a sentence was pronounced against all who had persisted in his schism, which you also testify that you have read. Although this sentence was confirmed by the agreement of all, it was nevertheless resolved by the council’s decree that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent.”

In saying this, do you so close your mind against yourself that you do not notice that all those who deserved to have the council’s sentence pronounced against them because they were joined to Maximian remained in that same schism until they corrected themselves within the period of delay?

There, therefore, they also baptized.

I beg you: why do you cast empty darkness over matters that are clear, when you again disperse it with no less clarity through your own words?

For I say that Praetextatus and Felician, the ordainers of Maximian, baptized in the sacrilegious schism in which they committed their offense; and that those whom they baptized were received together with them, without the Baptism that they had given in schism being annulled—the Baptism they had administered sacrilegiously, the Baptism they had consecrated with a mouth full of cursing and lips bearing the venom of asps.

Such things are said against them, and that is the sentence which you do not deny was pronounced against all of them.

*[Note: The manuscripts read “sacrilegiously”; the printed editions read “with sacrilege.”]*

## CHAPTER XXX

**37.** Here you reply that not only the two whom I mention, but also many others, cleansed and innocent, returned to the Church within the period of delay.

By this statement you assist me; by this statement you affirm the truth with me and dispel the darkness you were trying to spread.

For when you say that they returned themselves to the Church, you unquestionably admit that they had been outside the Church.

Wherever they were before returning themselves to the Church, there they baptized. Therefore they gave Baptism outside the Church.

While trying to escape from this inexplicable entanglement, you become entangled again. For you say that their Baptism ought not to be annulled because, having been restored within the appointed period, they were not held by the final sentence.

How, then, can you say that those who, as you admit, were restored to the Church before the day of the delay were not separated from the Church before the day of restoration?

If we are human beings, if we possess any reason, if we have human understanding, if we do not speak like beasts to beasts, or like wood and stones to wood and stones, it is evident—not merely from my words but also from your own—that your people did not dare to annul the Baptism given in Maximian’s sacrilegious schism.

Yet they do not hesitate to call Christians, to exsufflate, and to rebaptize people baptized in Churches which the Apostles propagated by their own labor through the grace of the Lord.

You say it; you write it. Listen to yourself; read yourself.

You, I say, say it; you write it: a sentence was pronounced by your people against all who had persisted in Maximian’s schism.

You say it; you write it: after this sentence had been confirmed by the agreement of all, it was nevertheless resolved that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent.

You say it; you write it: not only the two whom I mention, but many others, cleansed and innocent, returned themselves to your Church.

You say it; you write it: their Baptism therefore ought not to be annulled because, having been restored within the appointed period, they were not held by the final sentence.

## CHAPTER XXXI

**38.** What can so bad a cause accomplish against such a good intellect, clear-minded and educated man?

Those against whom that sentence was pronounced because, as you yourself say, they persisted in Maximian’s schism, before they were restored—as you say—were celebrating the Sacraments wherever they were, and there they were baptizing.

To use more fully the words of the plenary council:

> “There they were heating, with lingering warmth, the poisonous offspring of the viper’s seed; there they were giving birth to the criminal desires of their crimes, pregnant with public wrongdoing and their own parricide; there they conceived labor and gave birth to iniquity; there, no longer a confused forest of crimes, their names were marked out for punishment; there, while the cord of indulgence was being released to them by the line of mercy, the case had already found those whom it would punish; there, like wreckage against rugged cliffs, the truthful wave had cast their shipwrecked limbs; there the shores of those perishing were full of funerals after the example of the Egyptians, who did not find even burial” (Exod. 14:31).

> “There not only had the thunderbolt of the sentence cast Maximian—rival of the faith, adulterer of the truth, enemy of Mother Church, minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiron—from the bosom of peace, and not only did a just death condemn him for his crime; it also dragged many into fellowship in the crime by the chain of sacrilege.

> “There was the venom of asps beneath their lips; there their mouth was full of cursing and bitterness; there their feet were swift to shed blood; there were ruin and misery in their ways, and they did not know the way of peace; there was no fear of God before their eyes (Ps. 13:3).

> “There lay severed limbs, which pestilential decay had so corrupted that they possessed more relief in amputation than in the application of medicine.

> “There were Victorianus of Carcabia, guilty of a notorious crime, and the other twelve with him, among whom were Praetextatus of Assur and Felician of Musti, whose reception we are discussing—men who had ordained that same Maximian while present. That is, by the deadly work of destruction they had glued together a filthy vessel with the collected dregs, where the clerics of Carthage furnished *lenocinium* (“pandering”) to so great a crime, as to an illicit incest.”

Such ministers of the Sacraments, not yet corrected and not yet returned and restored to you, baptized in Maximian’s schism. After such ministers of the Sacraments had been corrected, returned, and restored, your people did not rebaptize those whom they had baptized.

*[Note: The manuscripts read “while the cord of indulgence was being released.” Compare the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*.]*

*[Note: The manuscripts read “nor finding burial itself”; the printed editions read “nor finding burial itself” with a different grammatical form.]*

## CHAPTER XXXII

**39.** What does hostility alone accomplish among you? Let truth at last be considered; let it at last be heard.

Why are the utterly empty clouds of the granted period of delay thrown up?

*[Note: The printed editions read “utterly insane”; the manuscripts more aptly read “utterly empty.”]*

That period was not granted to those of whom it was said, “Know that they have been condemned”; concerning them it was also declared what they had been, what they had done, and why they ought already to be condemned without delay—namely, because they had ordained Maximian while present, laying hands upon him.

For this is what they signified when they said that, by the deadly work of destruction, they had glued together a filthy vessel with the collected dregs.

The period of delay, however, was granted to those who had not participated in Maximian’s ordination, although they were established in his fellowship and schism. Because they had not laid hands upon him, since they had been absent, they were distinguished from the condemned ordainers by the same council’s sentence.

For after they had said of those whose names they also recorded, “Know that they have been condemned,” they continued:

> “But those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile—that is, those who, with the modesty of a reverent faith, withdrew their own hands from the head of Maximian—we permitted to return to Mother Church.”

What could be plainer, more distinct, more open?

They say that those guilty of notorious crime, who by the deadly work of destruction glued together a filthy vessel with the collected dregs, were condemned.

But they say that those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile—that is, those who with the modesty of a reverent faith withdrew their own hands from the head of Maximian—they permitted to return to Mother Church.

And because two of those condemned were later received with their honor intact, this cannot be defended except by saying that the period of delay was granted to everyone.

*[Note: The manuscripts read: “For they are distinguished from the condemned ordainers in this way.”]*

*[Note: The printed editions read “guilty of an insane crime”; the manuscripts more appropriately read “guilty of a notorious crime.”]*

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**40.** But let it have been granted to everyone. Certainly, all who returned to you from that schism were there before they returned; there they baptized. Returning from there to you without the destruction of their dignity or Baptism, they have closed your mouths—if you have any shame.

For when we ask where they were before they had returned themselves, as you yourself said, to the Church and had been restored before the appointed day, what else does the fact itself compel you to answer except: “In Maximian’s schism, on account of which that sentence was pronounced against all”?

There, therefore, they baptized those whom, when they came from there to you together with them, you did not dare to deprive of Christ’s Baptism, because you were compelled to recognize it.

Thus, by your own deed, your own work, and your own judgment, the conclusion is rightly and deservedly drawn against you that Christ’s Baptism must be recognized even when it has been given outside the Church—and therefore that we piously recognize this in your people, while you impiously annul it in ours.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**41.** But perhaps you regret having written such words, since they pressed this truth too forcefully. You said: “It happened that they returned themselves to the Church and, having been restored before the appointed day, were not held by the final sentence.”

You could therefore be answered: “How did they return themselves to the Church? How were they restored to it if they had not been separated from it? Or, if they had been separated, how were they baptizing?”

But what else could you have said except what you had heard from those whom you consulted when you were greatly disturbed by my letters concerning this matter?

And yet perhaps they criticize and reproach you for having carelessly used such words.

There is something that especially protects you against them and consoles your sorrow. For they themselves also used such words in the decree of the same council.

Therefore, if they wish to reply to this little work of ours after reading it, saying that the words of their layman do not prejudice them, we will immediately recite their own words:

> “But those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile—that is, those who, with the modesty of a reverent faith, withdrew their own hands from the head of Maximian—we permitted to return to Mother Church.”

When they are asked, “These whom you permitted to return to Mother Church—where were they before they returned?” they are pressed in the same way that you were pressed a little earlier by the words you yourself wrote.

For where will they answer that those people were except in Maximian’s schism?

But let them insist that they were wherever they wish. Certainly, those who were permitted to return to the Church were not in the Church.

Therefore they baptized outside the Church. And when both the baptizers and the baptized returned to the Church, neither did the former lose the honors they had held outside, nor did the latter lose the Baptism they had received outside.

## CHAPTER XXXV

**42.** As far as you could in a bad cause, you spoke cautiously, saying: “It was nevertheless resolved by the council’s decree that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent.”

They, however, did not say that those to whom the period of delay was granted needed to be corrected. Rather, they speak of them as though they had been entirely undefiled and innocent in Maximian’s fellowship, when they extend the period of delay itself.

For what else do they mean when they say:

> “But those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile, we permitted to return to Mother Church”?

And, as though this were not enough, see what they add:

> “For in proportion as we are cleansed by the death of the guilty, we rejoice in the return of the innocent.”

Why, then, do you say that it was resolved that a period of delay should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be considered innocent, when you see that it was granted to the undefiled and innocent?

But evidently you feared that you would be asked, “Why was a period of delay granted to those whom Maximian had not defiled?” Therefore you judged that they needed to be corrected during that period.

They feared being asked, “Why did you wish to receive those who had been defiled while retaining their honors?” Therefore they said that they had given a period of delay to the undefiled.

*[Note: Two manuscripts add here: “unless we say that those whom Maximian’s fellowship did not defile were permitted to return to Mother Church.”]*

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**43.** Therefore each of you feared something different, but each is attacked by what the other has said.

You are asked: “How do you consider those in need of correction whom your people proclaim undefiled?”

They are asked: “How do you assert that they were undefiled, even though they did not lay hands upon Maximian’s head, yet were defiled by fellowship in his schism?”

Whose mind, whose strength, whose tongue would suffice to express such intolerable grief?

To repair the division of Donatus’s party, Maximian does not defile his African associates in Africa; but, so that broken branches may not be permitted to return to the very root of unity, Caecilianus defiles so many distant peoples from Africa!

### CHAPTER XXXVII

**44.** From the day of the Council of Bagai—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of May—until the day on which that period of respite was granted, namely, the eighth day before the Kalends of January, eight months are counted. During this very long interval, were those to whom the respite was granted being defiled by association with the condemned Maximian, or were they not being defiled?

If they were being defiled, how can it be said: “Those, however, whom the plantings of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile, we permitted to return to Mother Church”? If they were not being defiled, how could the unknown—indeed, I will not say false—contagion of others’ sins have defiled us and all the Christian peoples everywhere?

“But,” he says, “the respite was granted for this reason: if it elapsed and they did not return, then they would be defiled and incur the penalty of condemnation.” Therefore it was not the sin of that association, but the appointed day, that defiled them. If no day had been appointed, then they would certainly have remained undefiled.

What evil had the whole world committed against you? Why do you declare it defiled by others’ sins, when you appointed no period of respite for it, although your power is so great that people become associated with sinners whenever you wish, and become polluted whenever you wish?

They were innocent and undefiled [Note: [Col. 0572] The printed editions read: “whenever you wish they become associated with sinners, and whenever you wish the innocent are polluted. And they were already polluted.” The manuscripts correct this.], those to whom, while they were in Maximian’s party, a respite was granted, within whose period, if they returned to you, they would retain the foundations of unimpaired honor and faith. But if that day passed without their returning, then they would be polluted, then criminal, then lost; they would incur the punishment of condemnation, and then be humbled through repentance.

What a remarkable degradation on the part of men who proclaim such things [Note: [Col. 0572] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “through repentance—a remarkable degradation on the part of men who proclaim such things.” Morel, *Éléments Critiques*, p. 162, conjectures that the reading should be: “through repentance. O remarkable gradation of men who speak piously!”]; no longer, as the old proverb is said to have it, “What we will is holy,” but even, “When we will it, and for as long as we will it”!

Let one of you happen to pray with us in a boat: he is immediately called polluted, immediately called a traditor. Those who condemned Primian share altars with Maximian, the adulterer of truth, the enemy of Mother Church, the minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram; yet for eight months they remain innocent and undefiled.

Accordingly, if some of these restored themselves to your communion on the ninth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0572] The printed editions read “the fifth day before the Kalends.” More correctly, however, the Corbie manuscript reads “the ninth day before the Kalends.”], you rejoiced at the return of the innocent—namely, of those whom the plantings of the sacrilegious shoot had not defiled.

What service did all the days of those eight months render you, from the eighth day before the Kalends of May until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, which you so sanctified that, throughout them, whoever clung to the communion of the sacrilegious and condemned Maximian was not polluted and was not made guilty?

And what offense did that most holy birthday of our Lord himself commit against you, that by its coming and passing alone it polluted the innocent; that in those who baptized within that schism the Baptism of Christ remained holy throughout all those days, yet became unclean through Christ’s birthday?

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

**45.** What will human recklessness not dare, when it is driven into the judgment of a wicked error—an error which it is ashamed to abandon because of its absurdity, yet is not ashamed to defend against the truth?

But why say more about this, when even the most obstinate person, hardened against every voice of reason, must admit the point concerning those of whom it is said: “If they had restored themselves to the Church and had been restored before the appointed day”—words that you yourself set down—and concerning whom it is said: “We permitted them to return to Mother Church”; “We rejoice at the return of the innocent”?

“And lest the shortness of the time withdraw the hope of salvation from those returning, pressed by the constraint of the shortened day, we open the door of recognition until that day, so that those who return may possess the foundations of unimpaired honor and faith. But if anyone through sluggish negligence is unable to enter it, let him know that the way to every avenue of pardon has been withdrawn from him. And for those returning after the appointed day, repentance has been fixed” [Note: [Col. 0573] The Louvain edition alone reads “fixed repentance,” referring the phrase to the word “let him know.”].

These words, which the three hundred and ten repeated so many times in their sentence, make it necessary, I say, for any opponent to admit that those to whom these things are said—before they restored themselves to you, before they were restored to you, before they returned to you, before they entered, after returning, through the door of the respite—were not with you; that they baptized outside your communion, in that schism by which they had separated themselves from you.

From there they were restored and returned to you—from the place where they had been alienated from you, from the place outside where they had been away from you. Yet they retained their honors undiminished and brought in with them their baptized people, who were not to be rebaptized.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

**46.** Why do you still offer such obstinate patronage to such a wretched cause? Yield at last—not to me, but to the truth itself by which you are convicted. See how true was what I said, which you attempted in vain to undermine: how much must be endured for the sake of peace.

And, to use again the very words I used in that letter: “For the peace of Christ, return to the Church, which did not condemn what was unknown, if, for the peace of Donatus, it pleased you to recall those who had been condemned” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §14).

For if, from among the twelve whom they had condemned together with Maximian without granting a respite, they later received Felician and Praetextatus, how is it false that they recalled those who had been condemned?

But if a respite was also granted to those concerning whom they said, “Recognize that they are condemned,” it nevertheless pleased them to recall the condemned; even if none of them had subsequently returned, this was so because, after the sentence in which it was said, “Recognize that they are condemned,” a respite was granted during which they were permitted to return with their condemnation annulled.

These statements would suffice even if what you say were true—namely, that, when you were greatly stirred by this affair of the Maximianists, you learned it from your bishops. But what are you to do, since that too is false? Search for, or, if you have it, examine the date of the proconsular proceedings [Col. 0574] in which Titian made his petition against Felician and Praetextatus, so that they might be expelled from their sees [Note: [Col. 0574] See above, Book 3, §62], and observe how long after the day of that respite this took place.

The day of the Council of Bagai fell during the consulship of the emperors Arcadius for the third time and Honorius for the second time, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. The period of respite extended from that date until the eighth day before the Kalends of January. But this petition of Titian’s was delivered after that consulship, on the sixth day before the Nones of March.

### CHAPTER XL

**47.** It therefore appears that the third month was nearly underway when the proconsul was asked to expel Felician and Praetextatus from their places as associates of Maximian, whom they had joined in his madness.

For when the aforesaid advocate had said in that same petition what seemed sufficient concerning Maximian, he added:

“He also restrained those whom the error of another’s presumption had drawn along, first proposing a harbor of repentance and, if they wished to return, assigning a period for the path of religion, by an admonition of equal force [Note: [Col. 0574] Perhaps “a predetermined period.”]. But,” he says, “iniquity delights in its own institutions and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For that same Maximian nourishes the audacity he has begun and joins others to himself in his madness.

“Among these is a certain Felician, who, having initially followed what was right, was darkened by contact with this depravity. Residing in the city of Musti, he believed that the walls consecrated to Almighty God—the venerable church—were to be retained as though under siege. Praetextatus likewise imitates him in the region of Assuras.”

Do you hear the advocate’s clear and unmistakable words, in which he says that these men of whom we are speaking, because they despised the proposed harbor of repentance while iniquity delighted in its own institutions after falling headlong, were to be expelled from their ecclesiastical places?

Even if the date of the proceedings could be concealed, it would be sufficiently clear to anyone utterly dull that proconsular authority would not have been brought against them unless either they had been condemned at that council, as is there more plainly shown, without any respite being granted, or, if the respite had been granted to everyone [Note: [Col. 0574] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “if it had been granted to everyone.”], they had refused to be restored to you within the period of respite.

But when even the date of the proceedings strikes the eyes and ears of any obstinate person with such force—showing that they were not in your communion even after the period of respite had elapsed and that they had remained associated with Maximian, so that for this reason the authority of such a terrible judicial order was obtained against them—what can be said in response?

Why is there still a struggle against such evident truth with this astonishing blindness of shamelessness? Why do those who, along with the unity of Donatus’s party, wished to retain even the concord of sacrilegious condemned persons still rebel with such madness against the unity of Christ?

Why is the Baptism of Christ, recognized with due reverence even in a sacrilegious schism, still rejected through impious presumption and violated by sacrilegious repetition throughout so many Catholic peoples?

### CHAPTER XLI

**48.** I do not wish to ask how long after this petition—by which Felician and Praetextatus were so severely accused in the words of Titian’s advocate [Col. 0575]—they were received into your communion.

It is enough that this same petition proves them to have been separated from your communion and to have been in Maximian’s schism long after the end of the appointed respite. You later received them; you diminished their honors in no respect; and you were afraid to annul the Baptism they had administered, even though it had been given in a sacrilegious schism, as you truly had reason to fear doing.

Would the tongue of any obstinate person now be stirred against us in this matter, if he perceived that the tongue was moving in a human mouth and beneath a human brow?

I plainly erred, I confess, because in that letter I wrote concerning the sentence of the Council of Bagai: “When it was read out before them, they shouted with the broadest acclaim; but now, when it has been read out by us, they are silent” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §11).

What you said is true: “Behold, they are not silent.” For in matters so manifest, shame—or even shamelessness itself—can be silenced; madness cannot.

Do not take this statement as referring to you, since you believed your lying bishops; nor to all of them, for you could not have consulted all of them about this matter. It refers to those who, knowing how much had been done against Praetextatus and Felician before the judges, and when it had been done, dared to tell you what you inserted into your letter: that Felician and Praetextatus, having been restored to your communion before the appointed day of respite, were not held bound by the peremptory sentence.

But if they too perhaps did not know these things, then, now that you read this, let shame be silent, and let whatever human shamelessness there may be also be silent. Certainly let only the madness that cries out against such evident truth be left—and perhaps it will be curable if it is restrained by sane people.

### CHAPTER XLII

**49.** Now consider how you spoke about me: “A lying witness will not go unpunished,” since you thought that I had lied in this affair of the Maximianists.

I do not return this charge upon you. Perhaps you spoke what you believed through careless friendship, not what you fabricated with a deceitful heart. We are human beings: by what vigilance can we ensure that, whether in thought or in speech, we do not make some mistake? But we must not become deaf to the remedy of correction.

### CHAPTER XLIII

**50.** Now observe how greatly this affair of the Maximianists gives me an easy opportunity to respond also to the other parts of your letter.

Whatever you thought ought to be said about the traditores as though they were ours—although it has been shown that your people rather committed this offense, as I demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently in that work of three books—consider nevertheless, and answer if you can, whether this crime, whoever committed it, could have polluted Christians throughout the unity of so many peoples, whether those far removed or those living long afterward.

The crime of the sacrilegious shoot Maximian could not pollute even the African associates whom your three hundred and ten bishops, when granting them a respite, said were “those whom the plantings of the sacrilegious shoot had not polluted”; nor could it pollute you yourselves, who received with such complete concord not only those whom you called innocent but even those already condemned in that sacrilege.

**51.** You say that the crimes of the traditores were known to the Easterners, although you, an African, were unaware of the Maximianist schism committed in the heart of Africa until, after reading my letter, you were greatly stirred and consulted your bishops; and even after consulting them, you could not hear the truth from them.

If you defend them so as not to call them liars, you admit that they were ignorant. Yet you do not permit us—or all the many peoples of East and West—to be ignorant of Caecilian’s case, even though these men did not know the case of Praetextatus and Felician, whom three hundred and ten bishops of the African party of Donatus—that is, either all or nearly all of them—condemned as Africans in Africa and received as Africans in Africa.

### CHAPTER XLIV

**52.** You insert the beginning of the Council of Sardica, from which you attempt to prove that the Eastern bishops, after learning of the crime of the traditores, communicated with Donatus’s party. Your one great piece of evidence, apparently, is that the name Donatus is found among the bishops to whom they write.

Yet nowhere there is anything stating that they learned about the African traditores. Moreover, lest this council escape your notice, it belongs to the Arians, whom you have already named among the other heretics. The names of the cities are not usually added when bishops write letters to bishops, since that is not the ecclesiastical custom.

Therefore I do not know who this Donatus was. I wonder whether he was not made Carthaginian in your own letters. Still, those men, separated from Africa by such distant lands, may have been able, at the very time when they wished to write, to inquire who the bishop of Carthage was.

I omit saying that perhaps the Easterners had attempted in some way to associate themselves with heretics [Note: [Col. 0576] Some manuscripts read “heretics” instead of “with heretics.” Either reading seems necessary for the complete sense here.].

But you, a prudent man, when you wished to resolve the question—when you could have been told, “If these things are so, and the Easterners wrote to your Donatus, how were the Easterners later separated from communion with your people?”—answered and said: “Because, in receiving your people again, they were unable to maintain consistency in a condemned case.”

And it is written: “He who is joined to a prostitute is one body” (1 Corinthians 6:16).

Here you have bitterly accused your own people: in the affair of the Maximianists, they could not maintain consistency, since they condemned the sacrilegious with execration but honorably received the condemned.

You prove nothing of the former claim concerning the Easterners. But of the latter you hear, read, see, and judge concerning your own people.

### CHAPTER XLV

**53.** You order me to leave the Church of the traditores, whom neither you before us nor your ancestors before our ancestors were able to convict and demonstrate. If you had demonstrated them now, I would condemn their crime and offense; but I would not abandon the Catholic fellowship of so many peoples to whom they are unknown because of them.

Consider, however, why you do not wish the memory of those dead people to be mentioned in our communion—people whose deeds we do not know, whose good reputation among their own people we have learned through the succession of later generations—while in your communion those whose evils you experienced and whose sacrileges you condemned live without any degradation.

**54.** You dare to say to me, prudent man: “The one who betrayed created you,” not knowing that he is our creator in the respect in which we are Christians, just as he is our creator in the respect in which we are human beings. Yet you have not even convicted the man whom you suppose to be my creator of traditio.

I do not repay this insult to you. I do not call Felician your creator—or the creator of your sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons, if they belong to Donatus’s party. I merely warn you, since you permit it, lest your creator find you a deserter, running after a man’s name with impious vanity [Note: [Col. 0577] The printed editions read *currentis* (“of one running”); the manuscripts more appropriately read *currentem* (“one running”).].

Then you seem to add, plausibly:

“A stream is drawn from its spring, and the members follow the head. When the head is sound, the whole body is sound; and if there is any disease or defect in it, all the members are weakened. Whatever has arisen in the stock looks back to its origin. He cannot be innocent who does not follow the sect of the innocent one, especially since it is written: ‘Do not walk in the ordinances of your fathers’” (Ezekiel 20:18).

In all these words of yours, I pass over the fact that what you compared to the human body is not analogous. It can happen that the foot hurts while the head is sound, and that the head hurts while the foot is sound.

I also pass over the fact that you forgot what you had said shortly before [Note: [Col. 0577] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian and Louvain editions read: “what you had said shortly before.”]: “This is what we too want; this is what we urge: let Christ be the head of Christians.” Yet now I do not know what traditor you wish to make the head of unknown Christian peoples, among whom you refuse to acknowledge the Baptism of Christ as given and received—as though those baptized had been created only by that traditor.

I also pass over how greatly it helps me that you yourself quoted the scriptural testimony addressed to the Jews: “Do not walk in the ordinances of your fathers.” For anyone who then wished to observe this command—such as the holy prophets and the seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal—did not separate themselves from their own people or from the common sacraments.

This is what I say; whether you wish it or not, I repeat and press it upon you, however burdensome I may seem: do not make Caecilian, absolved so many times, a head for us who come after him [Note: [Col. 0577] The printed editions read “our descendants.” The manuscripts more correctly read “descendants for us”]; whereas I, though Primian was condemned by Felician and Felician by Primian, nevertheless do not make either of them a head for your descendants.

### CHAPTER XLVI

**55.** As for the resentment concerning persecution, which you glory in enduring from earthly authorities on behalf of Donatus’s party, although I answered you sufficiently and abundantly in that work of three books, I will not now be silent about what can be answered briefly from this affair of the Maximianists.

You commend yourselves in this way to ignorant and uninstructed peoples. Maximian himself does the same, as do his associates, who were unable to yield even under the persecutions of your people in order to return to their communion [Note: [Col. 0577] The Louvain edition alone reads “were unwilling.”].

But those who think soberly understand that, in the case of people who suffer some hardship, one must consider not their punishments but their causes. They understand that the Maximianists deservedly and justly suffered even the disturbances of secular judgments because of the crime of sacrilegious schism, in which they had been deservedly and justly condemned by you.

I do not even mention what you wrote in your letter: that it was not Optatus but the people who overthrew Maximian’s basilica—or rather, cave. Although even there, while it is uncertain whether your people did it, it is nevertheless certain that he suffered persecution, though he was not just but impious.

Thus you are already compelled to admit that one must attend not to what someone suffers, but why he suffers it.

**56.** But it is not enough for me, for the moment, to demonstrate from Maximian’s example that someone is not immediately just merely because he suffers persecution under the pretext and appearance of Christ’s name, since the sacrilegious Maximian also suffered. I must compel you to admit that the religious persecute the sacrilegious, and the just persecute the impious—not, indeed, from a desire to harm, but rather from the necessity of providing correction.

I do not produce examples from the Old Testament, although you said that you wished to be instructed even by prophetic examples [Note: [Col. 0578] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “although you said that you wished to teach those things.”]. I do not, I say, produce those very ancient examples, for they belonged to another dispensation and another period.

After gentleness had been revealed and commended at the proper time, your bishops persecuted your schismatics. We do not call this just; but as long as you remain there and defend such a cause, you are compelled to say this.

### CHAPTER XLVII

**57.** I will therefore no longer say, “Maximian suffered persecution; Optatus inflicted it,” since you answer that you do not know this and that he acted in such a way that I cannot cite any official proceedings from it—although, given how recent the memory is, the cities themselves cannot deny it if questioned.

I will not say this. Rather, I say: “Maximian suffered persecution; Primian inflicted it.”

I shall read out the proceedings in which I will show that Primian, acting under a commission and in the name of the ecclesiastical exorcist’s office, with the support of the priest delegated to him [Note: [Col. 0578] The Louvain scholars observe in their annotations that this is the same man who above, §3, is called the delegate of Carthage], took away the house which Maximian was defending as his own.

I do not deny or refute that the judge may have acted from justice rather than favor. Why, then, did Primian, in the records of the magistrate of Carthage, among the other insults he ordered to be brought against us, say: “They take away what belongs to others; we leave alone what has been taken,” when he himself had taken what belonged to another, if the house belonged to Maximian? And if Maximian had rather usurped it, why had Primian not left alone what had been taken?

But if you do not wish even this to count as persecution, I say that your bishops and clerics persecuted the Maximianists while they remained in the sees in which they had formerly been ordained. They accused them before proconsuls, obtained orders against them, and secured the assistance of official staffs and of the cities for carrying out those orders.

Thus those who had already been condemned with the severity of the judgment of Bagai, and who had been cut away from the body of your communion by a swift painful act lest the pestilential poison creep through all its members—those who no longer posed any danger to you through the diseased contagion of their communion—were, together with the congregations cut away with them, frequenting their own conventicles and retaining in perpetual possession the places and basilicas they had not invaded, along with the peoples attached to them. Yet they were terrified, driven out, expelled, and produced under guard.

### CHAPTER XLVIII

**58.** Read what was said concerning them or against them by the advocates who prosecuted them; read what crimes of sacrilege were alleged and with what force the authorities were stirred by the accusations.

Ask what was done to Salvius of Membresa, because the agitation of that persecution could not extort from him a return to partnership in the crime. He preferred to submit himself to examination and to answer his persecutors in the proconsular court. I believe he acted with the confidence that his adversaries could not use the laws promulgated against heretics before the judge without entangling themselves in the same laws.

But this expectation deceived him. For before Seranus, then proconsul, either favor proved stronger, or perhaps the Council of Bagai proved stronger still, since it too was read out there against that same Salvius.

In one of his interlocutions the proconsul plainly showed what was being done: namely, that Salvius was either to be restored to the choir of Primian’s communion of bishops or driven from his see, so that Restitutus, whom Primian had ordained against him, might possess without opposition all the places held by Salvius.

Yet in the same interlocution he expressly stated that Salvius was suffering persecution. For the proceedings read as follows:

“Seranus the proconsul said: ‘According to the law, the dispute of bishops must be heard by bishops; the bishops have judged. Why do you not either return to the choir of your former standing under an undertaking of satisfaction, or, as it is written, turn your back to your persecutors?’”

What do you think of this? Is it acceptable to call Salvius just, when the proconsul before whom he was accused by Restitutus, your bishop, who was opposing him, even gave him counsel from Holy Scripture to turn his back to his persecutors, since it is written in the Gospel: “If they persecute you, flee” (Matthew 10:23)?

You certainly see what appearance Salvius presents among his own people, whether as a martyr or as a confessor, since, while Restitutus was persecuting him, he deserved to hear these words from the proconsul. Yet, not only according to us but also according to you, he is judged impious and sacrilegious.

### CHAPTER XLIX

**59.** Later, after the proconsul’s sentence had been presented to the people of Abitina, by which your people had deserved to have the neighboring city enforce the judgment [Note: [Col. 0579] Some manuscripts read “to be enforced”], since nearly all the people of Membresa loved Salvius, I am reluctant to say what those same people of Abitina did to a man already advanced in age.

Because they did not do it in the official proceedings, but because the testimony of the cities, together with all the evidence, makes the matter clearer in such recent memory, I shall briefly mention what I learned there while traveling.

For since Salvius, trusting in the support of the crowd that favored him, had attempted to resist them in defense of his see, however much of it remained to him even after the proconsul’s judgment, he was eventually overcome and seized—not now to be led before the judge, where the sentence had been delivered between the parties, but to be paraded in a pitiful spectacle of triumph.

After seizing the old man, they tied dead dogs around his neck and danced with him for as long as they pleased.

If I wished to heighten the account by my wording, would I not perhaps show that this punishment should be compared only with the tortures of the Etruscan kings, who joined dead bodies to the living [Note: [Col. 0580] Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.483–488]?

Would not an old man who wished to be regarded as a bishop deserve, by everyone’s judgment, to be expelled from the fellowship of the living and the dead, if, when two punishments were set before him and one had to be endured, he chose not to cling to human corpses but to dance with canine ones?

### CHAPTER L

**60.** Now consider those words of mine which you thought you had refuted—or rather, no longer those exact words, but what I will say in their place.

For I do not say, “If it is not permitted to persecute, Optatus did so”; rather, I say, “If it is not permitted to persecute, Restitutus did so.”

Nor do I say, “If the one who suffers persecution must be regarded as innocent, Maximian suffered it”; rather, I say, “If the one who suffers persecution must be regarded as innocent, Salvius suffered it.”

I read out the proceedings; I repeat the words you do not wish to hear: “Restitutus did it; Salvius suffered it.”

Which of these two will you answer is a Christian, if not Restitutus? Which a sacrilegious man, if not Salvius?

Therefore what you said must collapse and be rejected as disproved: that no persecution is just; and what you said, “Who does not wish to agree with the evidence presented? The one who suffers persecution, or the one who inflicts it?”

For the persecution that Salvius endured was just, and Restitutus inflicted it. Salvius suffered it, and Restitutus is praiseworthy to you, while Salvius is condemnable.

You will not say that this was done secretly. Could Primian have been unaware of what happened in that city where he himself presided as bishop, and in so large a city, before so important a judge, that it could not have remained hidden from the other cities as well?

Or if this too must be counted among hidden matters, why do you wish the whole world to be ignorant if Caecilian did anything evil during the persecution—which, of course, may it be far from him that he did—when Primian could be unaware of the persecution suffered by Salvius from the man whom Primian himself ordained against him, in the city where Primian held primacy over his colleagues?

You will therefore admit, whether you wish it or not, lest you be compelled to condemn Restitutus, Primian, and Donatus’s party, that not only can the unjust suffer persecution, but the just can also inflict persecution.

Or if you think that what is done justly should not be called persecution, you will not be able to prove that either we suffered persecution from you or your people from ours. Rather, we shall demonstrate that we suffer it from your clerics and Circumcellions, who, hard-hearted and senseless, neither understand nor endure what we advise for their salvation, and rage against us with such fury that I am not capable of numbering, recalling, or adequately expressing in words all that they do to us.

### CHAPTER LI

**61.** Thus, when a madman harasses a physician and the physician binds the madman, either both are persecuting each other, or, if persecution is only what is done wrongly [Note: [Col. 0580] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “if what is done wrongly is not persecution,” omitting “only”], then it is not the physician who persecutes the madman, but the madman who persecutes the physician.

Your savagery and most violent audacity, made known to everyone through your Circumcellions [Col. 0581], the satellites of your clerics, had therefore to be restrained by the laws enacted against you and, in a certain sense, bound.

This was done so that, warned at least by the terror itself, you might wish to consider and correct the error in which you were found and the sacrilege by which you appeared to be divided against the unity and peace of Christ [Note: [Col. 0581] Perhaps “by which you were divided.”].

In the same way, driven by the terrors produced through the orders of secular authorities, Felician and Praetextatus—unlike Salvius, who refused through excessive and most perverse hardness of heart—corrected the schism they had made from you and returned to your communion and fellowship [Note: [Col. 0581] The printed editions read: “and Praetextatus, through excessive and most perverse hardness of heart, corrected the schism they had made from you.” The manuscripts correct this reading.].

Everything would be corrected if all of you returned from your side to the Catholic root.

Whatever was done against you that exceeded the moderation of Christian love must no more be imputed to the Catholic Church than I would impute to Primian or Restitutus what the people of Abitina did to Salvius.

### CHAPTER LII

**62.** After exaggerating the persecutions which you said Donatus’s party had endured, while saying nothing about all that had preceded them at the hands of your people and recounting many things that are not proved against ours, you added a testimony from the Psalms and said:

“Is it not said of those who do such things: ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood, and they have not known the way of peace’?” (Psalm 13:3).

At that Council of Bagai, your bishops said these very things, and others much more serious, against Felician and Praetextatus.

Certainly those men had shed no one’s physical blood and had made no bodily attack upon you. But those who said these things against them judged that, through the sacrilege of schism, they were shedding spiritual blood much more criminally.

Therefore, if after such grave statements had been made against them you made peace with them without disgracing their honors and without annulling their Baptism, there is no reason to despair that you can also agree with us.

The entire Christian world ought to delight you much more in making peace than Praetextatus and Felician. For if those whom you condemned with such savage accusations did not defile you, the unity of so many Christian peoples defiles you much less—peoples to whom you demonstrated the crimes of certain Africans [Note: [Col. 0581] Perhaps “did not demonstrate.”].

What greatly defiles you is the crime by which you separated your fellowship from the fellowship of that Church for which so many and such great divine testimonies are recited. You dared to contradict those divine testimonies with human recklessness, although you yourself, somehow compelled by the force of the truth, were forced to confess the same thing: that the whole world is daily being turned toward the Christian name.

### CHAPTER LIII

**63.** You dared, I say, to resist God’s testament, although the Apostle says:

“No one annuls or adds a supplementary provision to a confirmed human testament. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring” (Galatians 3:15–16).

You were not afraid to annul this testament and to add Donatus’s party as a supplementary provision to it. For when God says in that same testament to Abraham, “So shall your offspring be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea” (Genesis 22:17), you annul this statement and add Donatus’s party, for which you recite no testimony, saying: “Truth is often found among the few; it is the many who err.”

You do not understand how the Lord said that few enter through the narrow gate (Matthew 7:14), while he also said that many would recline from east and west with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11). Moreover, in the Apocalypse, thousands from every nation, tribe, and language are shown—so many that no one can number them—clothed in white (Revelation 7:9).

They are indeed many in themselves, and yet those same people are few in comparison with the far greater number who will be punished with the devil.

Nevertheless, these grains of wheat, destined for the divine granaries forever, joined throughout the world by the unity of love, endure the heat and threshing of this age, to be cleansed by the final winnowing—whether from the scandals and violence of heretics or from the interior chaff of the many who do not live rightly.

But in every matter the affair of the Maximianists answers you most readily. If truth is often found among the few and it is the many who err, allow the Maximianists, in proportion as they are fewer than you, to surpass you in truth.

You certainly do not do so. Therefore do not boast of your small number in comparison with the multitude of Catholic peoples, just as you do not want the Maximianists to boast of their small number in comparison with your multitude.

## CHAPTER LIV

**64.** As for what you report about the African traditors, you either do not understand—or, whatever may be in your heart, do not perceive in the conflict in which truth is sought—how empty and foolish such a report is when no proof follows it. I would not spend time refuting it, even if I did not have, in the case of the Maximianists, such an easy and unambiguous short answer.

The sacred Scriptures say: “The Lord, God of gods, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; from Zion comes the splendor of his beauty” (Ps. 49:1–2). The Gospel agrees with this prophetic testimony, where the same Lord says of himself: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

What is said there—“He summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting”—is said here as “among all nations.” And what is said there—“From Zion comes the splendor of his beauty”—is said here as “beginning from Jerusalem.”

For Christ not only suffered there, but also rose there; from there he ascended into heaven; there, on the day of Pentecost, he filled the one hundred and twenty people gathered together with the Holy Spirit sent from heaven; there, on one day, he received three thousand believers, and on another five thousand, converted into his own body. From there the Church spread and continues to spread, bearing fruit, throughout all Judea and Samaria and the remaining nations of the world.

Foretelling this to his disciples as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

This Church, therefore, beginning from Jerusalem and spreading among all nations [Col. 0583] with such evident fruitfulness that it compels you yourself to confess that, through God’s providence, the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name—this Church, I say, which, when the Lord God of gods speaks, is summoned from the rising of the sun to its setting, could in no way have been polluted by African traditors whom it did not know at all.

The sacrilegious shoots of Maximian did not pollute so many of his colleagues’ plantations merely because they had not laid hands on him in ordination—although they praised him after Primian had condemned him, and condemned Primian; although, while established in his schism, they received a delay within which they might return.

## CHAPTER LV

**65.** Moreover, because I said, “We bring the charge of traditio against you with much greater probability” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §23), you reply that I thereby confessed that you bring this charge against us “with probability.” You even teach the rule of usage by which the comparative degree increases what was previously stated, rather than condemning what was previously done, adding that just as there are *well* and *better*, *badly* and *worse*, *horribly* and *more horribly*, so there are *with probability* and *with greater probability*.

Thus you think you can conclude, and you say: “If you say ‘with greater probability,’ then we say ‘with probability.’”

In that longer work of three books I answered you sufficiently—or perhaps more than sufficiently—in its proper place. I showed from those writings in which we learned the uses of words how the comparative degree does not always increase what it compares, but sometimes condemns that with which it is compared.

Hence the expression, “May the gods grant something better to the righteous” (Virgil, *Georgics* 3.513). Hence also, “I pray for better auspices” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.498–499). Read carefully; you will find many more examples yourself.

But do you not marvel, I ask you, that in this case of the Maximianists—which I have now determined to use in answering you on every point—I have not lacked an example of this very usage?

For in the splendid and eloquent judgment of the Council of Bagai they say: “A more salutary course was found, so that the pestilential poison might not creep through all the limbs: by a brief pain, the wound that had arisen should be cut away.”

Certainly, according to your rule, they ought to have said *salutary*, not *more salutary*. For it was not salutary but destructive that the pestilential poison should creep through all the limbs. The course was therefore more salutary—that the wound which had arisen should be cut away by a brief pain—even though it was not salutary but, on the contrary, fatal for the pestilential poison to creep through all the limbs.

In the same way, we bring the charge of traditio against you “with greater probability,” although you do not bring it against us “with probability.”

## CHAPTER LVI

**66.** As for my statement that Silvanus, your bishop of Cirta, was a traditor, the municipal records testify to it. They were drawn up there at Cirta by Munatius Felix, curator of the commonwealth.

For, as we read written there [Note: The manuscripts read, at [Col. 0583], “it was opened”]:

> “After they had reached the library, empty cupboards were found there. Silvanus then brought out a silver *capitulata* and a silver lamp, saying that he had found them behind the chest.”

[Note: The printed editions read *capsulam*, “a casket”; all our manuscripts read *capitulatam*.]

Victor Aufidius said to him:

> “You would have been dead if you had not found them.”

When Felix the curator said to him, “Search more carefully, in case anything has remained here,” Silvanus replied:

> “Nothing has remained here; we threw everything out.”

When these records were read before the proceedings of Zenophilus, the governor, and inserted among the many other pieces of evidence supplied by the witnesses, the governor asked:

> “What office was Silvanus then exercising in the clergy?”

Victor replied:

> “A persecution arose under the bishop Paul; Silvanus was a subdeacon.”

You think you set against this most evident public documentary proof, so as to make it less credible, something of great importance, because you recall a sentence he pronounced against Caecilian, as though punishing traditors. You argue that it could not have happened that he was a traditor, since he had been so severe an avenger of traditio.

It is as though anything could appear more severe to those wicked elders when they raged so fiercely to put Susanna to death, while their own consciences were being pierced by the very crime for which they pretended they wished to punish her (Dan. 13) [Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “appeared”].

But let us leave such examples aside. What of Felicianus? Does he not now condemn, together with Primian, what he himself committed with Maximian—but with a better judgment because he has been corrected, not with greater shamelessness?

If Silvanus had wished to do the same, he would have condemned not a false traditio in Caecilian but the true traditio in himself. By a salutary correction he would have both acknowledged Caecilian’s innocence and, even if he were not a bishop, passed over to Caecilian through the correction of his own perversity.

So, if Felicianus could pass over to Primian—whom, just as Silvanus had condemned Caecilian, he had likewise condemned as innocent—without stain either to Primian or to himself, and even with episcopal honor, Silvanus could likewise have passed over to Caecilian’s innocence. [Note: The manuscripts read “if Felicianus.”]

**67.** Nor should you understand my statement that certain traditors, whom your ancestors accused—if they accused them truthfully—ought to have been convicted, as though I meant that they should have done this among themselves.

You reply that they did so, and that for this reason they judged our people to have lost Baptism.

First read carefully what you are writing against. Either understand what is being said, or do not turn what you understand into something else.

I said that they ought to have been convicted not before your people, but before the churches overseas, to whom those men who were accused appeared innocent.

The Maximianists, too, seem to themselves to have convicted and condemned Primian—but not before those who, being farther away and more removed from either favor or hostility, could have delivered such a judgment concerning him as would easily have been accepted by the whole party of Donatus.

Instead, they condemned him before one hundred and more than three hundred bishops, leaving him to be acquitted by those before whom they themselves would have incurred the danger of condemnation.

They ought to have persuaded so many of their colleagues of their judgment that they themselves would have remained inside with them, while Primian would have been outside, if he had refused repentance after being condemned.

But if they could not persuade this much larger number of colleagues, and all the churches of their communion spread throughout Africa, then either they ought to have rescinded their judgment through wiser counsel—for, being human, they could have been mistaken about a human being—or, if they had learned beyond doubt that he was truly guilty, yet could not persuade so many others of it, they ought more wisely and patiently to have tolerated a guilty man than to separate themselves through an impious schism from so many innocent people who did not know these things. [Note: Lov. reads “this charge [*crimen*] to a larger number”; the manuscripts read “so large a number [*tam*] of colleagues.”]

They would then have retained that most complete judgment of blessed Cyprian in charity and devotion, in which he says:

> “For even if tares appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity ought not to be hindered, so that, because we see that there are tares in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (*Letter to Maximinus*).

This would indeed have benefited them if, purified in the bosom of the Catholic Church, they had tolerated the refuse which they could not separate before the proper time. [Note: The printed editions read “if, amid the refuse of the Catholic Church, they tolerated refuse”; the manuscripts read “purified in the bosom,” or “in the purified bosom,” in place of “amid the refuse.”]

But when we say that they ought to have acted in this way within the fellowship of your error, which you imagine to be the true Church, your ancestors ought plainly to have acted in this way within that manifestly true Church in whose unity they were, lest they separate from it.

For just as someone among your people who knows nothing at all about Primian’s case nevertheless simply believes him innocent, although one hundred Maximianists condemned him, because he proved himself before a much larger number, so also in the Catholic communion, whoever is unaware of Caecilian’s case reasonably persuades himself that the man was innocent who was able to be known as innocent—or to remain hidden as guilty—not only throughout Africa but also throughout the lands of so many Christian nations, before so many other bishops.

Before those bishops he either deserved acquittal from one who recognized his innocence, did not deserve condemnation from one who was ignorant of it, or, having been acquitted by a corrupt judge contrary to what he deserved, could not be shown to others who had not judged the case.

You, therefore, are convicted by evident truth as guilty of schism, since we see that you have separated yourselves from us, your brothers, on account of crimes belonging to others which were not demonstrated to our ancestors when they ought to have been.

If this is what the congregations and clergy of those places will rightly say—those places from which the three hundred and ten bishops who established the Council of Bagai against the Maximianists came—if, I say, this is what Africans will rightly say to Africans, the very many Numidians and Moors to the few Byzacenes and Provincials, how much more rightly will the whole world say this to the Africans [Note: The better manuscripts read “Africans to Africans, Numidians to Numidians, Moors to Moors, the very many to the few,” rather than the printed text.] concerning the crimes of certain African traditors, even if those crimes were true—especially since the Catholic Church in Africa itself is so closely joined by the bond of unity to the other nations?

Nevertheless, even the evidence of the crimes of others that you are now trying to show me does not make the peoples of the nations guilty—peoples to whom these things were not demonstrated when they ought to have been, whether because you did not take care to demonstrate them. If I separate myself from those peoples, who are innocent in this case, I cannot remain innocent of the sacrilegious crime of schism on account of crimes belonging to others.

Therefore, so that you may prevail as much as possible and now demonstrate to me that these things are true, we condemn traditors who are dead, but do not abandon the living who are innocent.

## CHAPTER LVII

**68.** From this it is shown how easily you are defeated even in the final point which you chose from my fourfold division—for you could choose no other.

I said that if evidence of the crime of traditio had been brought forward by both sides, then either both sets of evidence were true or both were false; or ours were true and yours false; or ours were false and yours true.

After demonstrating our easiest victory in the first three alternatives (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §23), you either understood less clearly that you are defeated in the fourth, or—what I believe more strongly—tried to conceal it from others beneath certain shadows and thought that you should discuss the type of argument involved.

We may perhaps deal with this elsewhere too, if necessary [Note: Several manuscripts read *unde etiam alias*; the printed editions read *unde et cum aliis*], so that we do not now spend time on matters that are unnecessary.

## CHAPTER LVIII

**69.** Pay attention, then, to whether I can demonstrate this also in that clear mirror of yours—that is, in the case of the Maximianists.

For after all the people among whom these events occurred have died, it may someday happen that a question concerning communion will be debated between your descendants and theirs. They will say that Primian was condemned by nearly one hundred or more bishops from among their ancestors, and they will produce first the judgment written against him at Carthage and then the other written against him at Cebarsussi. In opposition, your people will recite the Council of Bagai.

They will demand that the crimes of Primian, contained in the judgment of their ancestors, be shown to have been disproved.

Will not your people much more justly say:

> “These crimes that you bring against him, even now that he is dead—if they are true, prove it by showing that you brought them before our ancestors and demonstrated to them that these things were true. But if you tried to do this and could not accomplish it, could crimes belonging to others, even if true, have polluted our ancestors, when those crimes had not been demonstrated to them? How much less so if you did not even try to demonstrate them? How, then, could the guilt of that case pass over to us, when it did not involve even those who were living with Primian at the time, except insofar as the matter was unknown and unproved to them?”

Thus, with evident truth, we convict you of schism, since you have separated yourselves from us, your brothers, on account of crimes belonging to others that were not demonstrated to our ancestors at the time when they ought to have been.

If the congregations and clergy of those places from which the three hundred and ten bishops came who established the Council of Bagai against the Maximianists will rightly say this—if, I say, Africans will rightly say this to Africans, Numidians and Moors to the very numerous few Byzaceni and Provincials—how much more rightly will the whole world say this to Africa concerning the crimes of certain African traditors, even if those crimes were true, particularly since the Catholic Church in Africa itself is so great and joined to the other nations by the bond of unity? [Note: The manuscripts read “so great”; the printed editions, “so greatly.”]

These documents concerning the crimes of others that you are now attempting to show me do not, nevertheless, make the peoples of the nations guilty—peoples to whom they were not demonstrated when they ought to have been, or because you did not take care to demonstrate them. If I separate myself from those peoples, who are innocent in this matter, I cannot be innocent of the sacrilegious crime of schism on account of the crimes of others.

Therefore, to prevail as much as possible, and now to demonstrate to me that these things are true, we condemn dead traditors but do not abandon living innocents.

**70.** When I said, “But if any of your evidence were true, you ought to have proved it before the Churches—that is, before the Catholic Church—so that you would remain inside while those whom you convicted would be driven outside” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §24), what did you intend to answer when you said that the separation occurred because we had been driven outside, while your people remained in the complete and Catholic Church?

If the Maximianists say exactly the same words to you, what will you answer except that they deserve not refutation but ridicule? For they dare to assert that their Church is complete while they have fewer than one hundred bishops, in opposition to so great a number and multitude governed by more than three hundred bishops.

Throughout all the regions of Africa where the Maximianists are found, the communion of Primian is also present; but throughout the other, much more numerous and extensive regions of Africa, no one finds a single Maximianist, except perhaps one traveling through.

With what face, then, in opposition to the Church promised and restored from the rising of the sun to its setting by the voice of Truth, do you dare to call the party of Donatus the complete Church, when it is confined to Africa, whereas that Church includes both all the nations and Africa?

But perhaps this Church drove that one outside? Please do not send this expression outside yourself: the forehead is on a person’s face, not beneath the shoulder.

Did this Church, then, drive that one outside? Do you not see that if the Church is driven outside—the Church of which the Lord says to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18); of which it is foretold, “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest, and all nations shall come to it” (Isa. 2:2); of which it is sung, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence” (Ps. 22:28); of which it is proclaimed that it bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world (Col. 1:6); which the Lord himself says is to spread among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47)—do you not see, I say, that if this Church is sent outside, it is sent outside together with the Law of God, the Prophets, the Psalms, the Apostles, the Gospel itself, and finally the whole Testament and the heir himself?

## CHAPTER LIX

If you attend to this abomination, if you shudder at it, if you tremble, see where you are and come back inside. For you did not send that Church outside; rather, you yourselves have gone outside.

See what bold blindness does [Note: Two manuscripts read *animositas, caecitas*, “passionate obstinacy, blindness”]. It is said that Maximian sent Primian outside, and people laugh; it is said that the party of Donatus sent outside the labors of the Apostles, bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, and no one shudders!

**71.** To prevent you from being deceived—or from deceiving others—since you either failed to notice, or pretend to have noticed, what I have so frequently recalled, you claim that I said that the Lord’s wheat is not what I maintained the Catholic Church to be, as divine Scripture itself now maintains it. [Note: Two manuscripts read “which Scripture does not maintain,” while the other manuscripts and printed editions read “which Scripture now maintains.”]

Only the wheat will be stored in the granary; for now the Church is threshed as a threshing floor together with the chaff. This is what presses and constrains you, and unless you correct yourselves, it will destroy you. You said that you could not tolerate the chaff of this threshing floor, which you have shown yourselves to be; you shamelessly pretended that you were the purified wheat. Thus, by empty and turbulent accusations, like the lightest dust of the threshing floor lifted into the air, you have gone out from that very threshing floor before the time of the final winnowing. [Note: Some manuscripts read *turbulenti*, “turbulent,” in place of *turbulentis*, “turbulent [accusations].”]

That most arrogant and false statement is yours, not ours: “What has straw in common with grain?” (Jer. 23:28). Jeremiah said this concerning the dreams of vain men and the revelations of prophets [Note: *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, Book 3, §§17–19]. Parmenianus writes as though it had been said about us and you.

Ask Maximian as well: he says nothing else about himself. For among all who tear themselves away from the unity of Christ, there is no other swelling of impious pride than to boast that they alone are Christians and to condemn everyone else—not only those who know them, but even those who have never heard their name. [Note: The manuscripts read “no other swelling of that very pride”; the printed editions read “no other swelling of his pride.”]

## CHAPTER LX

**72.** How elegantly you seemed to yourself to speak when, after I had said concerning the Testament of God, “Let it be read wherever it has been produced” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §25), you thought you should reply that this already amounted to a confession of the crime, and that I had therefore said, “Let it be read wherever it has been produced,” because it was established in my mind that it had been burned by our people but preserved and produced by yours.

Suppose, then, that, trusting in the truth, you wish a copy of the Law to be produced by Maximian, from which you might read about Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, who were swallowed alive when the earth opened (Num. 16:31), and whom the judgment of Bagai compared to him. It will not be read against him with greater force merely because it is found in his copy.

What I said—“Let the Testament be read wherever it has been produced”—is not a confession of crime but confidence in the truth. What could be more advantageous or more admirable than that, if possible, what is read against you should be produced by you?

This is not because I lack evidence on my side. But conviction is easier and more certain when you possess against yourself what, if you are corrected, will become evidence on your behalf.

**73.** Since you have wished to repeat empty arguments against the universality of the Church, I answer you here as well.

In Africa, you are the party of Donatus, and it is evident that the party of Maximian formed a schism from you, because they are not found throughout Africa wherever you are, whereas you are not absent even from the regions in which they are found. Other schisms, too, arose from you, such as the Rogatists in Caesarean Mauretania, the Urbanists in a certain part of Numidia, and several others. But wherever they were cut off, there they remained.

This also shows that they came out from you, not that you came out from them, because you are present even in those lands where they are; whereas they are found throughout the regions where you are only if they happen to be traveling.

So the Catholic Church, which, as Cyprian says, “extends its branches throughout the whole earth by the abundance of its fruitfulness” (*On the Simplicity of Prelates*, or *On the Unity of the Church*), everywhere endures the scandals of those who are cut off from it chiefly through the fault of pride—some here, others there, and others elsewhere.

Displaying their own parties, they say, “Here is Christ,” or, “There he is”; and the Lord himself warned that they should not be believed (Matt. 24:23).

They do not point out the way concerning which it was prophesied in the Psalms: “That we may know your way upon the earth, your salvation among all nations” (Ps. 67:3). Instead, each one points to the regions of his own communion: “Here,” “There.”

For where they fall, there they remain; where they are separated, there they wither. The Church from which they are cut off extends even into those lands where the various fragments lie, each in its own region. [Note: Some manuscripts here lack the particle “even” (*in*).] But those fragments are not present wherever that Church itself extends, although occasionally the wind of pride scatters a few very rare leaves from their dryness into foreign lands.

## CHAPTER LXI

**74.** This Church, then, which—as I repeat the words of the same writer—“extends its branches throughout the whole earth by the abundance of its fruitfulness,” will, by growing, reach many barbarian nations beyond the Roman world as well.

I believe that you both inquired into and discovered this, when you said:

> “I leave aside the native territories of barbarian nations, the rites of the Persians, the stars of the Chaldaeans, the superstitions of the Egyptians, and the gods of the Magians, so that all these things may cease to exist, since through God’s providence the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name.”

You spoke the truth in this, and thus the promise made to Abraham is fulfilled: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).
