He says, “All nations”; he did not say, “All people of all nations.” Therefore the whole world must necessarily be filled, up to the end of the judicial separation, not only by the fruitfulness of the growing Church but also by the mingled multitude of its enemies, through whom its devotion may be exercised and tested.

This testament was likewise recalled to his son Isaac when the Lord said:

> “I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father; I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give you and your seed all this land, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 26:3–4).

And likewise to his grandson Jacob:

> “Your seed shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall spread over the sea, toward the southwest, toward the north, and toward the east; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you” (Gen. 28:14).

When Scripture says “over the sea,” it generally signifies the western region; anyone who reads knows this.

If you had been willing to agree with this testament when it was produced, you would not have remained in Africa alone [Note: The printed editions read “not in Africa alone.” The manuscripts read “not in the southwest alone.” The allusion is to the cited passage in Genesis, where the reading is “toward the southwest” rather than “toward the south”].

**75.** Therefore the Novatians, Arians, Patripassians, Valentinians, Patricians, Apellites [Note: All manuscripts read *Anthropians, Apellians* instead of *Patricians, Apellites*], Marcionites, Ophites, and the rest—the sacrilegious names of what you call “ungodly plagues, not sects”—do not share communion with us, as you say.

Nevertheless, wherever these people are, the Catholic Church is also present, just as in Africa, where you are. But wherever the Catholic Church is, neither you nor any one of those heresies is necessarily present.

Thus it is evident which is the tree extending its branches throughout the whole earth in the abundance of its fruitfulness, and which are the broken branches that do not possess the life of the root, lying and withering in their respective places [Note: The printed editions read “and growing in their respective places.” The manuscript reading is adopted here].

But if they do not remain in unbelief, as the Apostle says concerning the Israelites, they will be grafted in again. “For God is powerful enough to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:23). This does not mean that they should again receive the sacrament of Baptism, which, once taken from the tree, they did not change; rather, they should revive from the root of charity and unity, from which, having been separated, they wither through the barrenness of their obstinacy.

You yourselves thought Praetextatus and Felicianus should be grafted in again, although Maximian had cut them off along with himself, and you did not reject the Baptism of those who had been cut off.

You would truly have done something beneficial for them if you had restored both yourselves and them not to your fragment but to the Catholic root [Note: The printed editions read “to your grain,” an ironic expression, as the Louvain editors observed. Certain of our manuscripts more suitably read “to your fragment”].

## CHAPTER LXII

**76.** Now what am I to answer concerning the point on which you thought I had spoken in your favor—namely, that when I said Baptism does not benefit those who depart from unity, yet remains in them, this is proved by the fact that it is not restored to those who return?

You affirmed that you too say that the Baptism received by our ancestors in the Church did not benefit them when they did not return to the Church [Note: Here the negative particle is supported by the authority of certain manuscripts].

If you said this, there would be no dispute between us except over which Church is the one in which Baptism benefits.

But you do not say that Baptism exists among us yet does not benefit. You say that it does not exist at all—that what we received came from those who had lost it by departing.

Therefore you neither could nor can answer what I stated: that the fact that Baptism remains in those who depart is proved by its not being restored to those who return.

For if Felicianus had lost Baptism by departing from you, why was he not baptized again when he returned, so that what he had lost might be restored to him?

Finally, if Maximian himself returns to you, he is not baptized. He certainly ought to be, if he had lost Baptism. For your own words are that, after being held under a sentence of condemnation in his schism, they lost both Baptism and the Church.

Therefore, just as the Church is restored to them when they return, so let Baptism be restored. I say: let them be baptized when they return, if they lost Baptism by departing.

Because you do not do this, you too admit that Baptism remains in those who depart from the Church, although it does not benefit them. They therefore give as they have received—that is, Baptism remains even in those who receive it from them outside the Church, although it does not benefit them.

Thus, just as what they did not lose is not restored to them when they return, so what they received should not be given again to them. Rather, they should be dealt with so that, through the Church, what could exist outside the Church without benefiting them may benefit both parties.

Accordingly, I said nothing in support of your error, and you have not answered what I said.

## CHAPTER LXIII

**77.** You also add something about the enclosed garden and the sealed fountain, although you do not understand at all what it means.

“If the garden is enclosed,” you say, “and the fountain sealed, how can someone who is outside, separated from the garden—that is, the Church—and from its fountain—that is, Baptism—give what he does not have?”

Ask Felicianus whether he had been in the enclosed garden when the door of delay was opened to him, as though he were returning to that same enclosed garden.

Or did he perhaps steal the fountain from there so that he could baptize his laypeople in Maximian’s schism? If so, where were your people washing themselves at that time? Or did they postpone them likewise during that delay, until those thieves returned to the garden with the fountain?

Were these men not false prophets when, by lying about Primian’s crimes, they led the deceived over to their sacrilege? Were they not ravenous wolves when they dragged those seduced from Primian’s flock toward the fragments of their own cutting-off?

You deny the tyrannical domination and drunken revelry of your people on others’ estates, which I mentioned (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §26). Deny it as much as you can. I am not afraid that, on account of this, you will be reluctant to agree with us.

I did not say of you anything like what the Maximianists condemned by you deserved to hear.

You deny the madness of the Circumcellions and the sacrilegious and profane cult of those who voluntarily threw themselves from heights and died. Yet you do not deny that, when the shores were filled with the funerals of those who perished in a manner very much like the Egyptians, and whose punishment was greater even in death because they did not find burial, you clung to those unburied corpses.

For Praetextatus and Felicianus were lying there. Or, if they came back to life among you, what are you doing about the Baptism which they, being dead, had then administered?

## CHAPTER LXIV

**78.** You say that I did not preserve the peace and gentleness which I had promised at the beginning of my letters, because I called Petilian Satan.

I compared neither Petilian nor any human being in the party of Donatus to Satan. I compared the error of the party of Donatus itself to Satan, from whose snares I desire the people whom I love to be liberated.

For if you read more carefully, you will find this.

Even if I said something somewhat harsh, read what you yourselves said—not against the error of the Maximianists, but against the men themselves.

Let Petilianus therefore imitate Felicianus and not become angry with me, who desire peace [Note: The printed editions read “let them not become angry”; the manuscripts read “let him not become angry”].

**79.** I certainly do not resent you yourself for thinking that the Manichaeans should be indirectly brought against me because of the error of my youth.

For this reason I do not grieve so much over my former unhappiness as I rejoice, trusting in the perpetual glory of my Liberator. [Note: Two manuscripts preserve this full reading; subsequently the other manuscripts also read, “and yet, if you please, I remind you.”]

And yet, if you please, I remind you to seek out and read what, how much, and in what manner I have written against the extremely deadly Manichaean heresy. There you will see with what faith I defended Christian truth against them and with what clarity I demolished their deceptions.

Do not be incredulous toward me when you believe that Felicianus faithfully adhered to Primian, although in his condemnatory sentence for Maximian he had spoken such grave charges against him; and when you suppose that, after separating from that same Maximian, he may perhaps have written something against him.

For Felicianus had not encountered Maximian as I, when young, a layman, and a catechumen, had fallen among the Manichaeans. Rather, an old man had made an old man—him to whom he is now joined—his adversary; a bishop had made a bishop his opponent.

Therefore, when, with the same urbane indirectness, I mention the letter of our primate which you mentioned—a letter which he wrote angrily about me when he was pressed in a council of bishops to prove what he had alleged—I read that it was condemned by the judgment of that very man when he corrected himself and asked pardon in this matter [Note: The printed editions read “because he had done it” or “to have done it.” Two manuscripts more suitably read “which you mentioned”].

You, then, inquire whether you can find a place where Felicianus, after being corrected, condemned what he had said against Primian—not as an accuser, but as one passing judgment—or at least where Primian himself annulled what he had said in condemning Felicianus.

Even if you find such a thing, the cases will still not be equal. He had initiated an accusation which, recognizing to be false, he condemned by asking pardon. He did not disdain the humility of correction because of the dignity of his primacy; rather, he wisely remembered what is written: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find favor before God” (Ecclus. 3:20).

These men, however, had not accused one another before others; they had sat as judges against one another. Therefore they condemned one another, and, once condemned, they were reconciled.

We do not begrudge the condemned their peace within the party of Donatus, provided they do not reject the peace of Christ throughout the world.

## CHAPTER LXV

**80.** You now see, I think, how emptily you said that you had answered everything contained in my letter [Note: At Louvain, “contained in my letter”; Erasmus and Lyons, “contained in it”].

If you replied merely because you did not wish to remain silent, then you did not indeed answer everything, but you did reply.

If, however, you replied in order to nullify what I had said, I see that you replied to many points, but I see that you refuted nothing.

Considering everything I said, I think you will very easily understand that you refuse to discuss the matter with us not because you wish to avoid contention—for there is no contention when truth is sought, or when there is no disputing for empty glory—but because you distrust your bad case.

For, to bring forward this one case of the Maximianists, you perhaps now recognize that nothing can be said against it.

Therefore I did not, as you believe or maliciously allege, wish to commend it as though it possessed an invincible eloquence. Rather, I wished readers to see that the case is of such a kind that, in defending it—or, more properly, demonstrating it—it requires the patronage of no eloquence.

**81.** I will no longer call your error a three-headed beast, since you are a most agreeable corrector of words [Note: Two manuscripts restore this passage in this form. The printed editions read, “as though you were the most agreeable correctors of words”]. Instead, I call it a threefold calumny.

I will no longer say that we ought to resist it with a trident-like weapon drawn from this case of the Maximianists. I say instead: with a threefold defense.

I will no longer say, “Fix it upon their forehead,” or, “Hem it in at their mouth” (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book 1, §29). I say instead: “Restrain their shamelessness and suppress their speech.”

Has the case of the Maximianists changed merely because the words have been changed, and expressions that were transferred have been made literal? It is by the concise force of this case that you are so thoroughly defeated that, if you ever come to your senses, nothing remains for you except to end your obstinate hostility and make peace.

## CHAPTER LXVI

**82.** If the issue is communion—not communion with other people’s sins, but with divine Sacraments—then you communed with the condemned, and it was said of those other sacrilegious men who communed with the condemned Maximianus that those sacrilegious branches did not defile the nurseries. If the issue is persecution, you persecuted the condemned and corrected the emboldened through persecutions. If the issue is Baptism, you received Baptism conferred in a sacrilegious schism. Why, then, are divine testimonies still brought forward uselessly, so that the truth may not be recognized and error abandoned, because they are not understood?

It is written: “If anyone thinks that he is contentious, we have no such custom” (1 Cor. 12:16). But Restitutus too, who fought with Salvianus of Membressa through the noise and litigation of the courts over cottages and little fields, [Col. 0593] in order to drive him from those properties, was not regarded by you as contentious. How much less ought one to be considered contentious who argues faithfully, not for seizing or taking away an inheritance, but for sharing the inheritance of heaven [Note: The printed editions read, “with those”; “with” is absent from the manuscripts.] with those who think differently?

“It is written,” you say, “Do not say anything in the ears of a fool, lest he mock your wise words” (Prov. 23:9). Do not speak into our ears as though it were a secret, if you consider us not wise; nor did Christ speak into the ears of the Pharisees what he nevertheless brought forward in their hearing in order to refute them. Show us openly how, if we are not corrected, we may be convicted; and show us how the Christian world, if you come to unity, defiles you, whom the condemned [Note: The printed editions read *quos damnatos* (“whom [as] condemned”); this is corrected to *quos damnatus* (“whom the condemned [Felicianus]”) from the two manuscripts cited above.] Felicianus does not defile.

It is written: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him.” Does it not continue there: “But answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (Prov. 26:4–5)? Do this also: do not, by your answer, consent to what you regard as our folly, but answer in such a way that it may be refuted. Answer, I say, how you received without any destruction the Baptism which the Maximianists administered in a sacrilegious schism, while you destroy the Baptism conferred in the Churches which Christ propagated through the Apostles.

**83.** Therefore, since at the end of your letter you thought that everything you had said above at greater length ought to be reviewed briefly, so as to refresh the reader’s memory, accept it in the same order—for you ought not to deceive either yourself or others.

It is not arrogance either to seek or to assert the truth. What you think could never have been settled was not only settled by prudent and God-fearing men, but you yourselves also brought to an end everything that you thought endless by receiving the Maximianists.

We summon you not to contention but to conference, you who struck down the Maximianists even by lawsuits. In those who were baptized in Maximianus’s schism, although they certainly ought not to have been baptized there, you nevertheless recognized the Baptism of Christ.

You demonstrated that the fountain of the Church must be understood differently—the fountain to which no one but the good approaches—by accepting the Baptism which sacrilegious men had conferred outside it. [Note: The manuscripts read *acceptato* (“having accepted”); the printed editions read *accepto* (“having received”).]

You are compelled to confess that neither our ancestors nor the holy Church which we hold could be defiled by the crimes of others—namely, by incense-offering and handing over the Scriptures—even though you never proved those charges against us. For you said that the sacrilegious branch of that same Maximianus did not defile the nurseries of Maximianus’s associates, to whom you allowed a delay for returning. Therefore we, born so much later, can much less belong to the same origin of traditors and incense-offerers, if the fellowship of those of our ancestors who were living at that time could not be defiled by it.

Although you habitually inflict persecutions upon us, savage persecutions directed against the truth, nevertheless you corrected the Maximianists in some measure through persecutions. And you received them after the term of that delay, although that delay had not been granted to them when they were already condemned. And although those to whom you opened the door for returning had conferred outside your communion the Baptism which they had conferred, you did not annul that Baptism after the same delay, even though you recognized and approved it.

Therefore, since you see that nothing can be said by you which this one case of the Maximianists does not refute and expose, pardon me if I have offended you by some word perhaps uttered too harshly. And if, as an African in Africa, you so late sought out the great case of the Maximianists, which arose in the capital of Africa after you had been warned by my letters, and, as you now see, could not find it once you had sought it because your people reported falsehoods—fear God. Do not drench so many Christian peoples, spread so widely throughout the world in Christian unity, with the unknown crimes of unknown Africans. Return, for the peace of Christ, to the Church which did not condemn the unknown, if, for the peace of Donatus, it pleased you to recall the condemned.

[Col. 0593] At this point the following three short works ought to have been added, if they could have been found: *A Book of Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists*, which Augustine mentions in *Retractations* 2.27; *A Book against Some Donatist or Other*, concerning which he speaks in *Retractations* 2.28; and *An Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists*, one book, which is listed in *Retractations* 2.29.

## [ON THE ONE BAPTISM, AGAINST PETILIAN.]

[Col. 0593]

## IN THE FOLLOWING WORK, BOOK II OF THE *RETRACTATIONS*, CHAPTER XXXIV

At that time a certain friend of mine received from some Donatist presbyter or other a book *On the One Baptism*, the presbyter indicating that Petilianus, their bishop of Constantinople, had written it. My friend brought it to me and earnestly asked me to answer it; and this was done. I also wished my own book, in which I replied, to bear the same title, namely, *On the One Baptism*.

In that book I said that the emperor Constantine, when the Donatists accused Felix of Aptunga, the ordainer of Caecilianus, had not denied that there was grounds for the accusation, although he had found them to be slanderers in the fabricated charges against Caecilianus (chapter 16, no. 28). Later, however, when the sequence of events was examined, this was found to be otherwise. [Note: From this it is clear that the subsequent book *On the One Baptism* was published before the year 412. For in the *Short Account of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 24—which Augustine composed around the end of 411—he indicates that by then, from an examination of the official records, he had discovered that error. Moreover, this entire book says nothing about the Carthaginian Conference held with the Donatists in 411, on June 1, with Petilianus himself present, although the book was written against him.]

For the emperor mentioned earlier first had Felix’s case heard by the proconsul [Note: “Aelianus.” See below in the Appendix.], where Felix is recorded as having been acquitted. Afterwards Constantine himself heard Caecilianus and his accusers and found Caecilianus innocent; there he discovered that they were slanderers in their charges against him.

This sequence of events, established by the consuls, convicts the Donatists’ slanders in that case far more forcefully and completely overturns them; we have shown this elsewhere (*Book after the Conference*, chapter 33). This book begins as follows: “To answer those who hold opposing views.”

[Col. 0595]

**THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE ONE BAPTISM, AGAINST PETILIANUS, TO CONSTANTINE** [Note: Written around the year of Christ 410.] [Note: In editing the book *On the One Baptism*, we collated the earlier editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain scholars with ancient manuscripts: one Vatican manuscript and ten Gallican manuscripts, namely the Georgian, Victorine, Dominican of the Paris convent in the Rue Saint-Jacques, Laon Cathedral, Cygirannus, Corbie, Fleury, Michaelian, Bec, and Pratelles manuscripts. We also used the various readings of Belgian codices found in the Louvain edition.] [Note: In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

Augustine refutes Petilianus’s book *On the One Baptism*, in which Petilianus contended that the one Baptism existed only in the true Church, or rather only in Donatus’s party. He teaches that the truth of the one Baptism, even when found among heretics, must be approved, not violated. He answers the authority of the martyr Cyprian and of other African bishops who are alleged to have held a different opinion with Cyprian. Against the Donatist schism, he proves from Cyprian’s own conduct that no one in the unity of the Church is defiled by the sins of others. Finally, he repels the slanders which Petilianus directed against Melchiades and certain other Catholic bishops.

[Col. 0595] **CHAPTER ONE.—1.** To answer those who hold opposing views and deviate from the rule of truth, brother Constantine, we are very often compelled to speak, even about matters which we have treated repeatedly in various sermons. I consider this useful, both because of the slower understanding of those who think that something different is being said when they read it expressed differently, and because of the abundance of discussions themselves: thus something rare may reach not only the diligent, but something [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read, “in any manner”; Louvain, “something in a manner.” But the manuscripts read “something,” omitting “in a manner.”] from among many treatments may also fall into the hands of someone less attentive.

Accordingly, see with what ease, aided by the Lord, I refute the discourse *On the One Baptism* composed by those who repeat Baptism. You gave it to me when we were together in the countryside, after receiving it from some Donatist presbyter or other, and you earnestly asked me to answer it. It is inflated with nothing but a din of words and bristling with slanderous accusations.

**2.** The first point of resentment there is that a private matter is being made public. Let those who think this ought not to be done keep silent, then. Or if they say that they are compelled to speak in order to answer those who hold opposing views, this is our reason as well for answering—not only those who hold opposing views, but also those who act accordingly.

What harms in secret ought to be openly reproved, because something is also openly defended when, in secret, what is harmful is urged and then carried out [Note: In the manuscripts: “when it is urged so that it may harm in secret when it is carried out.”]. For who baptizes anyone in the presence of the profane? Yet no profane person is unaware that Christians are baptized, since he hears publicly what he may receive secretly if he believes.

## CHAPTER TWO.—3.

Let us therefore see what those who are ashamed to say openly say about the repetition of Baptism—though I wish they were ashamed to admit it openly. “The question is where the true Baptism is,” he says. Then he adds: “It is so much mine that what I have given as the one Baptism is not repeated even by the sacrilegious themselves.”

We answer him: A sacrilegious person is not someone who dares not repeat the one Baptism—not yours, but Christ’s. For the one consecration of a human being in Baptism belongs to Christ; the repetition of the one Baptism belongs to you. I correct what is yours in you; I recognize what is Christ’s. This is just: when we reject the evil things belonging to human beings, we should approve whatever good things of God we find in them.

This, I say, is just: even in a sacrilegious person I must not violate the true Sacrament which I find; nor should I correct a sacrilegious person in such a way that I commit sacrilege in him. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “nor should I thus correct.”]

## CHAPTER THREE.—4.

For these people are evil in relation to a good Baptism just as the Jews are evil in relation to a good law. Thus, just as the Jews will be judged by the very law which their wickedness did not make evil, so these people will be judged by the very Baptism which evil people possessed as something good.

Therefore, just as, when a Jew comes to us to become a Christian, we do not destroy God’s good things in him but his own evil things—for we correct his error in not believing that Christ has already come, that he was born, suffered, and rose again; and, having destroyed that unbelief, we establish the faith by which these things are believed; and because he errs by clinging to the shadows of the ancient Sacraments, we dissuade him from this and demonstrate that the time has already come which the Prophets foretold, when these things would be removed and changed—but we praise, approve, and acknowledge that he believes in the worship of the one God who made heaven and earth, detests all the idols and sacrileges of the Gentiles, awaits the coming judgment, hopes for eternal life, and does not doubt the resurrection of the flesh; and just as he believed what ought to be believed, [Col. 0597] so we strengthen him in what ought to be held—

so also, when a schismatic or heretic comes to us to become Catholic, we cut away his schism and heresy by dissuading him from and destroying them. But if we find the Christian Sacraments in him unchanged, and whatever else he holds that is true, far be it from us to violate it; far be it from us to repeat what we know was given once [Note: The printed editions read, “if it ought to be given once.” Most manuscripts more correctly read, “if it was given once.”], lest, while treating human vices, we condemn divine remedies, or, by seeking to heal what has not been wounded [Note: Amerbach and the Louvain edition read, “what has been wounded,” omitting the negative particle found here in Erasmus and in our manuscripts.], wound a person who is injured in one place where he is healthy.

Accordingly, if I find a heretic dissenting from some matter belonging to Christian and Catholic faith, indeed even from the unity of the Trinity itself, and yet baptized according to the evangelical and ecclesiastical rule, I correct the human understanding; I do not violate God’s Sacrament. I am speaking of Jews, schismatics, or heretics who err under Christ’s name, in whatever manner.

## CHAPTER FOUR.—5.

Concerning the Gentiles and worshipers of idols, who differ from us in so many respects, the Apostle shows us nothing other than that we should correct whatever is perverse in them in such a way that we approve whatever may happen to be right.

For he was certainly reproving idolaters—and, what is more serious, not merely worshipers but also makers of images—when he said: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise [Note: The printed editions read, “For claiming to be wise.” The word “for” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.], they became fools; and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of serpents.”

We know that such images belonged to the Egyptians, among whom idolatry is said to have been established in greater abundance and with much greater disgrace. Did he nevertheless deny that they possessed knowledge of God? Did he not rather affirm it when he said, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God”?

If, then, he had tried to reject and destroy this knowledge as a lie because he had found it among sacrilegious people, would he not—far be it from us—have become an enemy of the truth? Therefore he condemns, detests, and overturns what they exchanged for their lie. For here too he said: “They exchanged the glory of God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man,” fabricating God, that is, as God is not, and handing on to human beings not the God whom they knew.

A little later he says of such people: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.” For the truth of the creature comes from God; it is not God. They turned that truth into a lie, worshiping as gods the sun, moon, and whatever heavenly and earthly things there are.

Thus what they exchanged for their lie he censures, detests, and overthrows; but what they preserved as true in their teaching, although mixed and confused with many falsehoods, he approves, attests, and confirms. For he also began that same passage in this way: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:18–25), not denying the truth, although it was held in unrighteousness.

**6.** Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, when he was teaching the Athenians about the one true God—that “in him we live and move and are”—he immediately added: “As some according to you have said” (Acts 17:28).

Therefore this statement, that we live and move and are in God, comes from the truth which those impious worshipers of images also held in unrighteousness, although they knew God and did not glorify him as God. Yet, as we see, the Apostle does not destroy this truth when he finds it among impious and sacrilegious people; he confirms it and uses its testimony to teach those who did not know these things.

Bishop Cyprian, a follower of this apostolic rule, argued about the one true God against worshipers of many false gods and brought forward many testimonies from the books of authors whom they regarded as distinguished (*On the Vanity of Idols*). These testimonies came from that truth which they held in unrighteousness.

Still more remarkably, the Apostle, while passing around their shrines, found among the altars of demons an altar on which was written, “To an unknown god.” He did not destroy this inscription by denying and refuting it; rather, by confirming it, he found in it the most suitable beginning for his argument, saying: “What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23).

## CHAPTER FIVE.—7.

Following this apostolic rule, handed down to us through our ancestors, we too, whenever we find something right even among perverse people, correct their perversity but do not violate what is right. Thus, in one person, false things are corrected on the basis of the truths he holds, rather than true things being destroyed because false things have been refuted.

In the time of the Apostles, those who said, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas,” were making impious schisms, although not under the names of impious people but of saints. This was their own distinctive and detestable vice. But their knowledge that Christ had been crucified for them and that they had been baptized in his name was not an error of theirs but a divine gift among them. They held this truth of God in the unrighteousness of their schisms.

Blessed Paul took hold of this truth. He did not destroy it along with the destruction of their vices; rather, by confirming it, he proved that those vices had to be corrected. “Was Paul crucified for you?” he asks, “or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13). Through the true thing belonging to God which they held, he made them ashamed of the false thing they were doing.

Thus one says to a Jew: “Hold to the faith in the resurrection of the dead, as you held it; but now believe that Christ has risen from the dead, which you did not believe.” For you hold God’s truth concerning the resurrection of the dead in your unrighteousness because you do not believe that Christ has risen.

To a worshiper of idols one says: “Hold to the belief that the world was created by the one true God, as you held it; but do not believe that pieces of wood and stone, or whatever parts of the world you worshiped, are gods.” For you hold God’s truth—that the world was created by him—in your unrighteousness, by which you wish to be a worshiper of false gods.

So too one says to a heretic who has not altered the Christian Sacraments as they are transmitted in the Catholic Church through any falsehood of his own: “Hold the Christian Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, as you held it; but acknowledge Christ’s Church growing throughout the whole world, as it was prophesied, the Church which you were cursing with sacrilegious speech.” For you hold God’s truth concerning the unity of Baptism in the unrighteousness of your division.

Correct the unrighteousness of the heretical fabrication, lest it destroy you; and do not take pride in the truth of the Christian Sacrament, which is there in order to judge you. For my part, far be it from me to detest your unrighteousness in such a way that I deny Christ’s truth which I find in you for your condemnation. Far be it from me to correct you in such a way that I destroy the very thing by which I correct you—unless, perhaps, I ought to destroy the truth which I find in the souls of heretics, when the Apostle did not destroy the truth which he found in the stone of the pagans.

**8.** One God is greater than one Baptism. Baptism is not God; it is something great because it is God’s Sacrament. Yet the one God was worshiped even outside the Church by people who did not know him. Thus the one Baptism too is given outside the Church by people who do not understand it.

Let the person who says that the one true God could not have been worshiped by ignorant people outside the Church consider how he can answer—not me, but the Apostle himself, who says: “What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.”

## CHAPTER SIX

Therefore, just as it did nothing for the salvation of those who, while ignorant of the true God, nevertheless worshiped him—and indeed harmed them toward perdition because, while worshiping false gods alongside him, they inflicted sacrilegious injury upon that same true God—so it does nothing for the salvation of heretics that, through ignorance, they both confer and possess the true Baptism outside the Church.

Indeed, it harms them toward condemnation that, in the sacrilegious unrighteousness of human error, they hold the truth of the divine Sacrament—not as something by which they may be cleansed, but as something by which they may be judged more severely.

And just as the Apostle, when correcting those sacrilegious people, acknowledged rather than denied the true God whom they worshiped in ignorance outside the Church, so we too, when correcting the errors of the sacrilegious separation of heretics [Note: Some manuscripts read, “when correcting sacrilegious separations from error.” Others read, “when correcting sacrilegious separations and errors.”], must acknowledge, not deny, the true Baptism which they confer in ignorance outside the Church.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.—9.

“But Paul,” they say, “when he came to Ephesus, ordered certain people who said that they had been baptized with John’s baptism to be baptized in Christ” (Acts 19:1–5).

Whoever thinks that this example proves that schismatics and heretics ought to be baptized should dare to say, if he can, that John was a heretic or schismatic. If it is impious to say this, then clearly what those people lacked was given to them; what they already possessed was not condemned.

Either they had lied when they said that they possessed John’s baptism, as some think, or John’s baptism was not the Baptism of Christ, although it served Christ, just as the ancient Sacraments of the Law served a kind of preliminary and prefigurative purpose.

“If people were baptized after John, the friend of the Bridegroom,” they say, “how much more ought people to be baptized after a heretic?” Another person, moved by a similar and seemingly justified indignation, could say: “If people were baptized after John, who drank no wine at all, how much more justly should someone be baptized after a drunkard?”

Let these people do this, then, if they can: let them baptize after their drunkards, if the Apostles baptized after the sober John. What can they answer here [Note: Amerbach and the manuscripts read, “What can they answer from this?” Others read, “What do they answer from this?”] except that they do not baptize after these people because, through those who were baptized, they received not their baptism but Christ’s Baptism?

Let them believe [Note: The printed editions read, “They believe.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “Let them believe.”], therefore, that people were baptized after John either because they possessed no baptism at all or because they did not yet possess Christ’s Baptism.

**10.** The man to whom we are replying himself raised this objection, but did not resolve it. For he says:

“Perhaps someone will say: ‘But those whom Paul baptized again had been washed with John’s baptism, not with the Baptism of Jesus Christ. Therefore I say that those who are known to have been baptized in the name of Christ by traditors ought not to be rebaptized.’”

Having proposed this objection to himself, observe how he tried in vain to answer it. “The Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “answered this matter in these words: ‘Whoever does not gather with me scatters’” (Matt. 12:30). And again: “‘Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven. For many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” And then I will say to them, “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity”’” (Matt. 7:21–23).

“It is therefore beyond doubt,” he says, “that one who has dared to act sacrilegiously, even in the name of Jesus Christ, has lost his own false work.” Whether they wish it or not, then, traditors offend Christ more through sacrilegious Sacraments. If they also dare to say, “In your name we prophesied,” he will say to them, as to the others, “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you.”

He will rightly say this to them, since, among the unworthy, the cases are not different: baptizing, casting out demons, and performing other marvelous works. See how much he has said, and how he was entirely unable to resolve the objection he had raised against himself—not only did he fail to resolve it [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and not only did he fail to resolve this.”], but he even instructed us about what we ought to say against them. For these evangelical testimonies not only do nothing to help him; they also strongly support our case.

**11.** The matter concerned John’s baptism. If the Apostle baptized certain people who had been baptized by John, he did not give John’s baptism again to people who already possessed it; rather, he ordered those who did not possess Christ’s Baptism to be baptized in Christ. Thus he destroyed neither baptism but distinguished the two.

The man against whom we are arguing also saw this. For, when he had put forward to himself, as though from the opposing side, the objection that those whom they call traditors baptize and are baptized with Christ’s Baptism, not John’s, and that therefore Baptism ought neither to be annulled nor repeated after them, he says that Christ answered this question when he said, “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

It is as though Christ had said: “Among those who do not gather with me, even whatever is found to be true and mine must be denied, rejected, and destroyed.”

He also says that Christ would answer certain people who said, “Lord, Lord, in your name we prophesied, and in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we performed many mighty works,” by saying, “I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.”

Did he also say here: “Because of your iniquity I will deny even my truth, which is held in your iniquity”? For he will not admit into his kingdom everyone in whom he finds some truth, but those in whom he finds love corresponding to the truth. If love is absent, there will be iniquity.

Yet the truth held within that iniquity must not be denied; rather, the iniquity itself must be condemned without destroying the truth. Hence the Apostle also says: “Even if I know all the Sacraments and all knowledge, and if I have all prophecy and all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2).

He said that he was nothing if he did not have love—not that the Sacraments, knowledge, prophecy, and faith were nothing. Those things are great, even if the person who possesses them without love is nothing and holds their truth in his own iniquity.

We say the same to these heretics: “We do not destroy the truth of Baptism which you hold in your iniquity. When we correct you, we destroy and overturn that iniquity; but we acknowledge and retain the truth.”

The numerous evangelical testimonies therefore do nothing to help this man.

**12.** Observe how they greatly support us. Listen to his very words. “It is beyond doubt,” he says, “that one who has dared to act sacrilegiously, although in the name of Jesus Christ, has lost his own false work.”

This is entirely true, since sacrilegious people who dared to act in the name of Jesus Christ lost their own false work. But does that mean that the name of Jesus Christ itself is sacrilegious, even when sacrilegious people perform something through it? Who, however insane, would dare to say this? Who, at this time, even among pagans, would dare to assert it?

Accordingly, although Jesus Christ himself most truly said, “Whoever does not gather with me scatters,” when the disciples told him that they had found someone casting out demons in his name and had forbidden him because he did not follow the Lord with them, he answered: “Do not forbid him, for no one performs mighty works in my name and can speak evil of me” (Mark 9:37–38).

That man’s own iniquity consisted in this: he was not gathering with the Lord and was not following the Shepherd with the disciples within the unity of his flock. Yet in that iniquity he held another’s truth: he cast out demons in Jesus Christ’s name and did not speak evil of him.

The Lord therefore condemns his iniquity in the words: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Yet he does not deny or disapprove his truth when he says: “Do not forbid him, for no one performs mighty works in my name and can speak evil of me.”

Following this example of the Lord, we too, to the extent of our ability, cannot deny the truth of Baptism or whatever else heretics hold that is true; we do not dare to disapprove or destroy it. But we rightly detest their iniquity, by which they do not gather with Christ but scatter, and, while leaving the truth in them inviolate, we condemn that iniquity or correct it insofar as we are permitted.

## CHAPTER EIGHT.—13.

Let this man therefore consider under what error he said what he added next: “Whether they wish it or not, traditors therefore offend Christ more through sacrilegious Sacraments.”

There is one matter that is rash and, in some fashion, tolerable: he calls people traditors, although he does not prove them to be so. But who can endure his saying that the Sacraments of Christ are sacrilegious, even if, as he slanderously claims, they were truly held by traditors, when they are celebrated in the evangelical rite in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit?

Perhaps here he will say that what is given by sacrilegious people is no longer Christ’s Sacrament. Why, then, does he not also say that the name of Christ is no longer the name of Christ when it is spoken by sacrilegious people? He did not dare to say this at all. For he says: “It is therefore beyond doubt that one who has dared to act sacrilegiously, although in the name of Jesus Christ, has lost his own false work.”

“Although in the name of Jesus Christ,” he says. Did he say that it was not the name of Jesus Christ? Therefore, just as it benefits sacrilegious people nothing that they act in the name of Jesus Christ, so it benefits heretics nothing that they baptize or are baptized in the Baptism of Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, just as that is the name of Jesus Christ, so this is the Baptism of Jesus Christ.

Both must be acknowledged and approved, not denied and destroyed, lest injury be done to such great gifts of God when the life of sacrilegious people who misuse those same gifts is corrected.

**14.** He says that the Lord will say to sacrilegious people who baptize outside the Church, cast out demons, or perform any mighty works in the name of Jesus Christ: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.”

But we say—and the Truth itself says—that God will say this to all the evil fish who swim within the very nets of unity together with the good until the shore. For when the good have been gathered into vessels and the evil have been separated and cast away, what else will be said to them but, “Depart from me, you who work iniquity”?

Yet we do not destroy Christ’s Sacraments in them when we recognize such people, whether baptizing or baptized, within those same nets of unity.

I do not think that they themselves are so shameless as to dare to say that the Lord will not say to the many evil and wicked people who are plainly lost and polluted by crimes and offenses in their party—greedy people and robbers, savage usurers, or bloodstained Circumcellions—“Depart from me, you who work iniquity.”

Yet they know, see, and maintain that many such people baptize and many are baptized by such people; and those who disapprove their crimes do not violate Christ’s Sacrament in them.

Thus, when he brought forward these evangelical testimonies, he not only said nothing against us; he also instructed us about what we should say against them.

## CHAPTER NINE.—15.

Accordingly, when he next says, exultantly [Col. 0603]—“I have briefly resolved the question” [Note: The printed editions read, “Having exultantly said, ‘I have resolved the question briefly,’” omitting the word “and,” which is restored from the manuscripts]—he truly resolved it, but in our favor.

For by saying that, among the unworthy, the cases are not different—baptizing, casting out demons, and performing other similar mighty works—and by saying that to those who claimed, “We did these things in your name,” he would say, “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity,” he demonstrated that it is just as true that those separated from the Church baptize with Christ’s Baptism as it is true that they cast out demons in the name of Jesus Christ. Yet neither of these things brings them to eternal life or delivers them from eternal punishments [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition add here, “it can.” M.].

Accordingly, if someone came to the Church from among those from whom the man whom the disciples saw, separated from Christ’s flock, cast out demons in Jesus Christ’s name, the power manifested in that man would not be denied; rather, what the newcomer lacked would be added. So too, whoever has been consecrated outside the Church by heretics or schismatics in Christ’s Baptism, when he comes to the Church, must not have the Sacrament of truth with which he was imbued denied; rather, the piety of unity from which he has been separated must be added. Without that unity, the Sacrament could exist in him, but it could not benefit him.

This is what we do; this is what we received as handed down by our ancestors; this is what we preserve in the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, against every cloud of falsehood.

What more, then, should we debate about this matter, when he himself has briefly resolved the question by recalling the evangelical testimonies—testimonies which, if he did not wish to be contentious, would surely lead him both to condemn his own error and to recognize the truth of Baptism?

**16.** Why, then, is it necessary to go through all his words, by which he thinks he speaks cleverly and turns many things over with great verbosity, claiming that the true Baptism is with him because it is also acknowledged and not denied by us?

Whoever firmly and immovably holds what the most true and inviolable rule of truth reveals—that in each person whatever is false and defective must be rejected or corrected, while whatever is true and right must be acknowledged and accepted—has at once seen both what we detest in the Donatist heresy and what we must not violate in any way.

For while they hold the truth of Baptism in the iniquity of their separation, we blame their iniquity, but the truth of Baptism is acknowledged and approved everywhere.

## CHAPTER X

**17.** For whoever says that Christ’s Baptism must be destroyed when heretics baptize with it [Note: In the manuscripts, *baptizantur* (“are baptized”).], must consequently say that Christ himself must also be denied when demons confess him. Hence Peter was praised when he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16–17), while the demons, when expelled, said the very same thing: “We know who you are, the Son of God” (Mark 1:24–25). Thus this confession was beneficial to Peter and harmful to the demons, yet in both it was not false but true; [Col. 0603] it must not be denied but acknowledged, not detested but approved.

So too the truth of Baptism is given by upright Catholics, as that confession was given by Peter; it is given [Col. 0604] by perverse heretics, as that same confession was given by demons: it helps the former and condemns the latter; yet in both cases it must be acknowledged and approved, and in neither case denied and violated.

For this reason the apostle James, when he rebuked certain people who said that faith alone was sufficient for a person [Note: The manuscripts read, “true faith was sufficient for a person.”] and did not join works of charity to it, convicted them by this comparison with the demons, so that they would not think themselves to belong to God merely because they believed something true about God, even if they did not take care to add good works to their faith. “You believe,” he says, “that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe, and tremble” (James 2:19). Thus he compared those who believe what is true about God but live wickedly to the demons; yet he did not destroy, out of hatred for the demons, that very truth which the demons believe about God.

Therefore, since this very man against whom we are arguing proposed that the Apostle said, “One God, one faith, one Baptism” (Eph. 4:5), behold, we find the same God worshiped outside the Church by those who are ignorant; behold, we find the same faith concerning the one God confessed outside the Church, not only by certain human beings but also by demons. Yet both were confirmed by the Apostles rather than denied. Why, then, when we find one Baptism among those who are outside the Church, should we not likewise confirm it rather than deny it, so that we do not corrupt what is right because of what is wrong in them, but instead correct in them what is wrong on account of what they hold rightly?

## CHAPTER XI

**18.** What, then, does he mean when he says that true Baptism exists where there is true faith? It is entirely possible for some to possess true Baptism and not possess true faith, just as it is possible for them to possess the true Gospel and, by not understanding it rightly, to believe something false about God. Shall we therefore consider the Gospel, which is found as something true among them, detestable or in need of correction merely because of the falsity of their faith?

Nor do I think that those Corinthians whom he rebuked for having split into schisms possessed true faith in saying, “I am of Paul”; for this was false. Nevertheless, they possessed Baptism, and from the truth of that Baptism they heard from the Apostle, so that they might correct this falsehood: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13).

There were also some there who did not believe that the dead would rise, and in that respect they neither held nor possessed true faith. Yet because they held what was true [Note: The editions of Erasmus and Louvain alone read, “because they held true faith.”]—because they believed that Christ had risen, in whom they had been baptized—the Apostle took care to heal also that point in which their faith was unsound, saying, “If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised” (1 Cor. 15:16). Since they had believed that Christ had risen, and this belief in them was sound, what they falsely and most perniciously believed about the resurrection of the dead might also be healed.

Therefore, since in the canonical sacred Scriptures neither do they find heretics coming to the Catholic Church being baptized again, nor do we find those who had received that Baptism in heresy being received in that same Baptism, in this matter alone [Col. 0605] our case is equal: neither do they have an explicit example from apostolic times for what they do when they baptize heretics—or those whom they consider heretics—again, nor do we have an explicit example from apostolic times for what we do when we receive Christ’s Baptism as having been given even among heretics.

But because we find that the Apostles, in people who were in error of whatever kind or sacrilegious through whatever impiety, confirmed whatever truth they recognized rather than denied it, while correcting or condemning the error and impiety of those people without destroying what was true in them, we follow this same rule concerning the truth of Baptism. Wherever we find it retained and preserved in the manner in which it is retained and preserved in the Catholic Church, we neither deny nor destroy it; rather, while it remains, we take care to correct, reform, or amend whatever is defective, perverse, or false in each person—or, if we cannot do so, we avoid it as something detested and condemned.

**19.** Therefore, when we receive them, we do not receive their iniquity, by which they sacrilegiously separated themselves from Christ’s Church; by which they attack the Christian world, to which God bears so many testimonies through the Law, the Prophets, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Apostles, with calumnious and abusive accusations. Nor do we receive that error of theirs by which they refuse to acknowledge Christ’s Baptism, guarded by ecclesiastical rule even among heretics; by which they dare to destroy it and do not hesitate to repeat it. Indeed, if they can draw over to themselves anyone—not only laypeople but also clerics, and not just any clerics but priests and bishops—even if they were baptized in those Churches which the Apostles founded through their own labor, they make them catechumens if they can in any way seduce them into coming over.

We by no means receive these detestable evils of theirs, since they cannot pass over to us unless they have been corrected.

## CHAPTER XII

**20.** Nor do we pass over without distinction the fact that those who have already become believers and then deserted the Catholic Church undertake a more humble penance than those who have never belonged to it. Nor are they admitted to the clergy, whether they have been rebaptized by heretics, or, having previously been received by us, have returned to them, or have been clerics or laypeople among them.

And those of our own people who carelessly disregard these rules and perhaps make such persons clerics in the Catholic Church or allow them to remain clerics—although they are rightly censured in a brotherly manner by the more diligent—nevertheless do not themselves think that clerical office should be granted to such persons unless they either know or believe that they have been corrected of those evils.

Accordingly, all who are separated from the Catholic Church’s unity by a wicked crime make their accusations against it in vain. To use the Apostle’s words more fully: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:18). If they do not correct themselves, this wrath will also find those men who suppress the truth of Christian Baptism in the unrighteousness of their sacrilegious separation [Note: Erasmus and Louvain, together with some manuscripts, read, “this wrath will find these unrighteous men.”].

## CHAPTER XIII

**21.** The Catholic Church, however, which—as was foretold concerning it—spreads throughout all nations with abundant fruitfulness, does not correct anyone’s iniquity [Col. 0606] in such a way that it destroys in that person not his own truth but the truth of his Lord.

What, then, does this man mean when he cries out as though with license and confidence: “I baptized securely the one whom you, sacrilegious man, polluted; I baptized, I say, and did what the Apostle Paul did”? Let him read where the Apostle Paul did this. If he wishes this to be understood of those at Ephesus, then let him dare to say that John polluted them as a sacrilegious man. If he does not dare to say this, since it is manifestly impious, let him finally stop raising clouds of false resemblance concerning a matter that is altogether different.

**22.** For as to what he adds about Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, about the illustrious martyr Cyprian, and about Cyprian’s seventy predecessors—that they did this and ordered it to be done [Note: He is speaking of the council of African and Numidian bishops under Agrippinus, which Cyprian frequently mentions in his letters to Quintus, Jubaianus, and Januarius. See above, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book 3, no. 17.]—O how detestable is the error of people who think that they are laudably imitating certain things wrongly done by illustrious men, while they are strangers to those men’s virtues!

Thus some also wish to compare themselves with the Apostle Peter if they have denied Christ; and if they have compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, they aspire to be called his genuine fellows. These things were blameworthy in that great man; but such abundant apostolic grace shone forth in him that they were immediately erased. No Christian of our own times, not even a bishop, who has neither denied Christ nor compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, could be preferred to him—or, I do not say preferred, but even equaled or closely compared with him [Note: This passage was restored with the aid of the Floriacensis manuscript. In the printed editions it had previously read: “they aspire to be called his genuine fellows, so that they may immediately be declared by apostolic grace; since they cannot, I do not say be preferred to him…”.].

So too with the most glorious martyr Cyprian: if he did not wish to acknowledge Christ’s Baptism given among heretics or schismatics, while he detested too intensely those whom he grieved to see separated from the Catholic unity that he loved so greatly, his merits nevertheless continued all the way to the triumph of martyrdom. Thus the shadow cast by this matter was dispelled by the light of the charity in which he excelled; and, so that he might become a more fruitful branch, whatever in him required purification was removed—if by nothing else, certainly by the final pruning knife of his suffering.

Nor, because we acknowledge rather than deny the truth of Baptism even amid the iniquity of heretics, are we therefore better than Cyprian—just as we are not better than Peter because we do not compel the Gentiles to Judaize.

This is what I would answer concerning Agrippinus and the other bishops who are said to have held those councils. They held different opinions, yet remained in unity with those against whom they held those opinions, where charity covers a multitude of sins. For while they were walking in the truth of the Church [Note: Louvain reads, “in the unity of the Church.” Some manuscripts read, “in that truth.” The others, together with the older editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, read, “in the truth of the Church.”] into which they had come, God was able, as the Apostle says, to reveal to them also that they held a different opinion (Phil. 3:15).

For at that time it was a new question how heretics should be received. Its novelty disturbed certain brothers who rightly and vehemently detested the destruction caused by heresy, so that they believed that what those people held to their own harm—the good itself—must also be condemned. [Col. 0607]

But to state briefly what I think about this matter: to rebaptize heretics, which they are said to have done, was then an error of human beings; but to rebaptize Catholics, which these people still do, is always an act of diabolical presumption [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “of diabolical deception and presumption.”].

## CHAPTER XIV

**23.** But I want this man to answer a question for me. When he listed in succession the bishops of the Roman Church, he also listed Stephen among them and acknowledged that they had held the episcopate unimpaired.

Since Stephen not only did not rebaptize heretics but also judged that those who did this, or decreed that it should be done, ought to be excommunicated, as the letters of the other bishops and of Cyprian himself show, Cyprian nevertheless remained with him in the peace of unity.

What will these men say to this? Let them exert their ingenuity as much as they can and consider whether they are able to answer. Behold, at one and the same time there were two men—leaving others aside—who held different opinions: two bishops of the most eminent Churches, namely the Roman and Carthaginian Churches, Stephen and Cyprian, both established in Catholic unity. Stephen held that Christ’s Baptism must never be repeated and was gravely angered with those who did so; Cyprian, however, thought that those baptized in heresy or schism should be baptized in the Catholic Church, as though they did not possess Christ’s Baptism.

Many agreed with him, some also with Stephen, and both remained in unity with those who shared their respective opinions [Note: Amerbach and all the manuscripts read, *sistentes* (“remaining”).].

If, then, what these people say is true—the basis on which they try to assert or excuse the cause of their separation: “In one communion of the Sacraments the wicked stain the good, and therefore one must withdraw bodily from contact with the wicked, lest all perish together”—then it must be admitted that the Church perished already in the days of Stephen and Cyprian, and that nothing was left for later generations where Donatus himself might be spiritually born.

But if they judge it impious to say this—and it truly is impious—then, just as the Church remained from those times until the time of Caecilian and Majorinus, or Donatus, and those who, according to their own view, were admitted into it without Baptism could not destroy it by staining it with all their sins and crimes, and just as Cyprian and those who held the same opinion about Baptism made no separation from their communion, because they did not think that they could be stained by the evils of others while remaining in the unity and communion of Christ’s Sacraments, so the Church could continue thereafter.

The Church, growing throughout the whole world, as had been foretold concerning it, could in no way be stained [Col. 0608] by the alien crimes of whatever traditors and criminals there might be—just as, in one threshing floor, the grain cannot be stained by the chaff until the time of winnowing; and just as, in one net, the good fish are not destroyed by swimming together with the bad fish until the time when they reach the shore.

**24.** There was therefore no rational basis for this, but only the greatest madness, by which these people, as though avoiding communion with the wicked, separated themselves from the unity of Christ, which is spread throughout the whole world.

Unless perhaps they distinguish crimes from crimes by some marvelous art, producing rules of distinction not from the Scriptures but from their own hearts, and saying that within the unity of sacramental communion other people’s crimes may be tolerated without contamination, whereas through the crime of betrayal all who have shared the Sacraments with such people are held guilty.

But it is unnecessary to argue this point at greater length, especially since they very rarely dare to say it, being themselves ashamed and aware that they are speaking nonsense; and when they do say it, they do not attempt to support it with any divine testimony.

For when they accuse some people on account of the sins of others, in order to excuse the wickedness of their separation, they are more accustomed to have these passages in their mouths: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Ps. 49:18); “Do not share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. 5:22); “Depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52:11); “Whoever touches a polluted person is polluted” (Lev. 22:4–6); and “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6); along with other passages of this kind.

These passages do not distinguish the crime of betrayal from other crimes by any particular feature; rather, they prohibit every association with sin.

If Cyprian had understood these divine testimonies or commands in the way these men do, he would certainly have separated himself from Stephen and would not have remained with him in the communion of Catholic unity. For according to the opinion which these men think must be held concerning Baptism, Stephen, by admitting heretics and schismatics—who, as they suppose, did not possess Baptism—was sharing in the sins of others, since the sins of those who had not been washed with true Baptism certainly remained in them.

Cyprian therefore ought to have withdrawn from this man’s communion [Note: The editions read *hujusmodi* (“such a one”). The manuscripts read *hujus*, that is, “of this man”—namely, Stephen.], lest he run with a thief, lest he share in the sins of others, lest he be defiled by contact with the unclean, lest he become polluted by touching what is polluted, and lest he be corrupted by another’s leaven.

Since he did not do this, but remained with them in unity, the whole lump of that unity was then corrupted, and the Church did not continue—the Church that later gave birth to the saints Majorinus and Donatus.

Because they dare not say this in any way, it remains for them to acknowledge that the good remained in the communion of Christian Sacraments with the wicked without any stain of their own, and that the Church of Christ continued until the time of Caecilian—not as though it had already been stored in a granary without any wicked people, but as though it still stood in a threshing floor with the chaff mixed in.

Thus it could continue thereafter as well, and so it continues, until it is cleansed by winnowing on the final day of judgment.

## CHAPTER XV

**25.** What, then, does this great madness of their separation from the unity of Christ’s body mean? That unity, as we read it prophesied and now see fulfilled, is being extended throughout the whole world and among all nations.

Here, certainly, as it is written, “The wicked son declares himself righteous, but does not wash his departure” (Prov. 24, according to the Septuagint); that is, he neither excuses, dissolves, nor defends his going out from the house of God into the plague of heresy, which in schismatic madness he did not fear to undertake. [Col. 0609]

For if he were truly righteous, then, just as the Apostle Paul remained with the false brothers about whom he laments in his Epistles, and just as Cyprian remained with those whom he considered to be without Baptism and full of their former sins, and whom he knew were admitted to the Church by Stephen, so he too would remain in the Church of Christ, without any contamination of his own, with those whom he either knew or supposed to be unjust. He would not abandon the good because of the wicked, but would rather tolerate the wicked for the sake of the good, like grain enduring the threshing under the weight of charity together with the chaff, not like the lightest dust yielding to the blasts before the winnowing.

For in this way also, while remaining in Catholic unity with the wicked whom these nets must necessarily contain until the shore, he would not run with a thief, would not share in the sins of others, would not be stained by touching anyone’s uncleanness [Note: Some codices read, “any unclean person.”], would not be polluted by touching what is polluted, and would not be corrupted by anyone’s leaven.

These things happen through consent to sins, by which the serpent, through the woman, deceived the first human being even in the happiness of paradise; they do not happen through communion in the Sacraments, in which the unclean Judas could not contaminate his fellow disciples, who were clean.

Even now, in the threshing floor rather than the granary, the good separate themselves from the wicked with whom they share God’s Sacraments. They separate themselves through dissimilarity of conduct, not through bodily segregation; by living differently, not by going to different gatherings. Thus they neither become one with the wicked nor depart from the Church’s unity.

**26.** Why, then, do they exaggerate for us the crime of certain traditors, whom they have never been able to convict either? But if we defend them against these people’s calumnies, we will seem to be pleading the case of certain individuals rather than that of the Church.

Whatever they were, and wherever they were, all those who were traditors—and not only the sin of the traditors but also that of those who compelled them to betray, and that of all criminals, scandalous persons, and sacrilegious people—were admitted by Stephen into the Church, according to these men. For if such people did not possess Baptism, then whatever grave and horrifying sins they had committed were in them and held them guilty without any remission.

Stephen admitted such people; Cyprian was in Catholic unity with such people. Yet the Church did not perish but continued. Other people’s sins therefore do not stain anyone within its unity.

In vain did the wicked son hurry to leave his father’s household; in vain does he call himself righteous, but does not cleanse his way.

Or will they perhaps say that those whom Stephen admitted were cleansed by participation in that very unity, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8)? Would that they say so! For this is also what we say when we urge or admonish them to return to unity.

But in that case no question about Baptism would remain between us. For if those baptized among heretics are cleansed by the charity of unity itself when they come to the Church, then they are rebaptized without cause.

[Col. 0610]

## CHAPTER XVI

**27.** You see, then, in this speech to which you wanted me to reply, how much that man has said on our behalf. Why, then, is it now necessary for us to dispel the crimes he has brought against the bishops of the Roman Church, whom he has attacked with unbelievable calumnies?

Marcellinus and his presbyters Melchiades, Marcellus, and Silvester are accused by him of the crime of handing over the divine books and of burning incense. But are they thereby also convicted, or are they shown to have been convicted by the strength of any evidence?

He says that they were wicked and sacrilegious; I reply that they were innocent. Why should I labor to prove my defense when he has not even made a slight attempt to prove his accusation?

If there is any humanity in human affairs, I think we may more justly be blamed if, concerning unknown people whom their enemies accuse without demonstrating their crime by any testimony, we believe them guilty rather than innocent. For if the truth should happen to be otherwise, at least the debt owed to human decency is paid when one person rashly suspects nothing evil of another and readily believes no accuser, especially when the one making the accusation without a witness or any evidence has proved himself an abusive slanderer rather than a truthful accuser.

**28.** In addition, when Melchiades was presiding as bishop of the Roman Church, by order of the Emperor Constantine—to whom the accusers of Caecilian, bishop of the Carthaginian Church, had brought the whole case through the proconsul Anulinus—the same Caecilian was declared innocent.

When the ancestors of these people complained to the emperor about that judgment with most importunate obstinacy, saying that it had not been fully or properly examined and decided, they said nothing about Melchiades’ alleged betrayal or incense-burning.

They certainly ought not even to have come before his tribunal without first bringing this matter to the emperor’s attention, or insisting that it be brought forward: namely, that they ought not to conduct their case before a betrayer of the divine books and one polluted by sacrifices to idols.

Since they did not bring this forward beforehand, nor, after judgment had been given against them in favor of Caecilian, even in defeat and anger think it worth raising, why do they now, so late, piece together these empty calumnies—as though Caecilian’s innocence were darkened by the discrediting of the judge Melchiades, and as though the Roman Church itself were stained?

There they had been unable, by any judgment of whatever kind, to condemn anyone or to put one of their own forward as a substitute in the place of one condemned. Against that Church, for the very few Africans of their party, they initially sent in secretly and from afar imported administrators [Note: *Interventores*, or *intercessores*, were those who administered a Church while its see was vacant. Compare Augustine’s Letter 44, no. 8, and the fifth Council of Carthage, canon 8.], whom this man was not ashamed to name individually, until they ordained them as supposedly their own bishops among the deceived little populace.

Indeed, after Caecilian’s acquittal before the emperor, they accused Felix, bishop of Abthungi [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read, “of Abtugnensium.”], alleging that he was an unmistakable traditor and that Caecilian therefore could not be bishop because he had been ordained by that traditor.

Constantine did not reject their accusation as inadmissible, although he had found them to be calumniators in the fictitious charges brought against Caecilian; and therefore he ordered Felix’s case to be examined [Note: See *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 34.].

In Africa it was examined by the proconsul Aelianus. Felix too was declared innocent. The proconsular proceedings still exist [Note: See below in the Appendix.]; whoever wishes may take them up and read them.

This not only contributes to the fullness of the demonstration of Caecilian’s innocence, to Felix’s most evident acquittal, and to the exposure of the calumnies of those who had called him the source of all evils in their council; it also contributes to consideration of Melchiades’ wholly unblemished life in the face of their accusations.

Unless someone is so foolish as to believe that, when they did not spare Felix, by whom Caecilian had been ordained, they could have spared Melchiades, by whom Caecilian had been acquitted, if they had been able to reproach that bishop’s life—although no wound of conscience had destroyed him—with at least some kind of unfavorable reputation.

Or was what had been fabricated about the forum of Abthungi brought forward by these people as an accusation, while what had happened in the Roman Capitol was kept silent? [Note: The printed editions read “what had happened”; the Floriacensis manuscript more suitably reads “what had been fabricated.”]

**29.** What should I answer concerning Mensurius, when during his time, until the day of his death, no member of the unity’s people was divided, and the very letters of Secundus of Tigisis—by which he is said to have been censured—confirm that they wrote to one another peacefully and remained in fellowship as a college?

As for what he also wished to say about the Church of Cirta, and how he attacked its Catholic bishops with whatever insults he chose, what else did he accomplish than to show, by reviling holy men who lived in our own times and were well known to us, what we ought also to think about the unknown people whom he reviles in the same way?

Therefore, Profuturus, who died a very few years ago, and Fortunatus, who is still alive and succeeded him as bishop, were traditors only in the same sense in which they were Manichaeans; so too were those traditors whom these people do not cease to accuse, though they are utterly unknown and far removed from our times. Their blameless life, however, is well known to us, despite the reproaches of these people [Note: So read the manuscripts. Louvain reads, “their obscure life because of the reproaches of these people,” and so forth.].

**30.** It is certainly no small or inglorious consolation for any of us if the enemies of the Church accuse us together with the Church. Yet the Church’s defense does not consist in defending those individuals whom these people attack by name with false accusations.

Whatever Marcellinus, Marcellus, Silvester, Melchiades, Mensurius, Caecilian, and the others whom they accuse on behalf of their dissension may have been, nothing prejudices the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. We are in no way crowned by their innocence, nor are we in any way condemned by their iniquity.
