If they were good, they were cleansed like grain in the threshing of the Catholic threshing floor; if they were evil, they were crushed like straw in the threshing of the Catholic threshing floor. Good and evil can exist within that threshing floor; outside it, there can be no good.

Whoever is separated from this unity by the wind of pride, like mere chaff, what accusation does he bring against the Lord’s threshing floor because of the chaff mixed within it?

## CHAPTER XVII

**31.** We too make this claim, and not only make it: we also establish it by ecclesiastical and public written records. Secundus of Tigisis, at whose council they say Caecilian was condemned, granted peace to confessed traditors so that schism would not occur, even though the crime of betrayal had itself been brought against him by Purpurius of Limata [Note: The manuscripts read, “of Liniata.”].

We say that Victor of Rusiccade, Donatus of Calama, Donatus of Mascula, Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae, and Silvanus of Cirta were traditors, and that these same men were as though the strictest condemners of traditors.

We prove this from ecclesiastical, municipal, and judicial records.

But it does not follow that everyone in the party of Donatus is a traditor because these men were traditors in it; nor is the party of Donatus therefore innocent if these men are shown to have been innocent of the iniquity of betrayal.

For we heed Holy Scripture rather than either slander anyone concerning other people’s sins or fear a similar slander from anyone.

“For the soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18:4); “Each person shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5); and “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment, not to another but to himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

Both are allowed to grow until the harvest, lest, when the weeds are gathered before the proper time, the wheat also be uprooted with them (Matt. 13:29–30). Goats and lambs feed together in the finest pastures until they are separated by the shepherd who cannot err (Matt. 25:32–33). The nets of unity are filled with fish of every kind until they are brought to the shore for judgment (Matt. 13:47–48) [Note: The Floriacensis codex reads, “they draw together.”].

Except that these people, by their perverse and false opinion, bring judgment upon themselves when they say that they have rightly separated themselves from communion with the Christian world on account of other people’s sins. Through this absurd and insane opinion they themselves ensure that the sins of certain members of their own group are imputed to everyone.

If they consider this just, then all are guilty of the most manifest crime found in one person among them; but if, as is just, they recognize this to be unjust, then all are guilty of the most unjust separation.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**32.** Since, then, the question in this discussion concerns one Baptism in particular, let us bring our argument to its conclusion. Just as, in the unity of the Lord’s threshing floor, the wicked are not to be praised because of the good, nor the good abandoned because of the wicked, so, in one person, neither should his perversity be accepted on account of what is sound in him, nor should his integrity be denied on account of what is perverse in him [Note: The editions read *ut* (“so that”). The reading has been corrected according to the Floriacensis manuscript.].

For in the iniquity of the Jews the truth of the resurrection of the dead is retained; in the iniquity of the Gentiles the truth of the one God who created the world is retained; in the iniquity of those who, because they do not gather with Christ, scatter, the truth is retained by which they drive out an unclean spirit in his name [Note: The editions read *quia* (“because”). The manuscripts more suitably read *qua* (“by which”).]; in the iniquity of sacrilegious temples the truth was found by which they worshiped an unknown God; and in the iniquity of demons the truth was found by which they confessed Christ.

So too, in the iniquity of heretics, the truth by which the sacrament of Baptism is retained must not be denied.

[Col. 0613]

There is no book *Against the Maximianists against the Donatists*, which is placed after the work *On One Baptism* in book 2, chapter 35 of the *Retractions*.

# A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE CONFERENCE WITH THE DONATISTS

[Col. 0613]

## FROM THE SUBSEQUENT WORK, BOOK II OF THE *RETRACTIONS*, CHAPTER XXXIX (C)

After our Conference with the Donatists had taken place [Note: The Conference took place in June of the year 411. This Brief Account of the Conference was therefore written toward the end of the same year, 411. Concerning the same Brief Account, see Letter 139 to Marcellinus, no. 3: “The abridgment of the proceedings of our Conference was sufficiently laborious for me, since I saw that no one wished to commit himself to reading so great a mass of writing; as was also my letter to the Donatist laypeople themselves concerning this same Conference, which I have just completed after several nights of work.” Again, in Letter 185 to Boniface, no. 6: “As for how they were defeated in every respect in the Conference itself, since the proceedings are exceedingly lengthy and it is too much for you, occupied with other matters necessary to the peace of Rome, to read them, perhaps their Brief Account can be read to you. I believe that my brother and fellow bishop Optatus has a copy; or, if he does not, he can very easily obtain one from the Church of Sitifis.”], I briefly recorded and set down in writing what had taken place, according to the three days on which we conferred with them.

I considered this work useful, so that anyone who was informed by it might either learn without effort what had been done, or, by consulting the numbers that I marked beside each matter, read in the same proceedings whatever passage he wished. For those proceedings weary the reader by their excessive length.

The title of this work is *A Brief Account of the Conference*. It begins as follows: “When the Catholic bishops and those of the party of Donatus…”

[Col. 0613]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE CONFERENCE WITH THE DONATISTS

[Note: Written toward the end of the year 411.]  
[Note: The *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists* has here been newly collated with the older editions, since manuscript codices were unavailable to us.]  
[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions*, volume 1. M.]

## Conference of the First Day

[Col. 0613]

### PREFACE

When the Catholic bishops and those of the party of Donatus, by order of the Emperor [Note: Honorius.], had conferred with one another by disputing in proceedings held before the tribune and notary Marcellinus, the adjudicator, a very lengthy written record of those same proceedings was produced, although the entire matter could have been conducted much more briefly.

But those who knew that they did not have a good case first did everything they could to prevent the Conference from taking place and to prevent the case itself from being heard at all. Since they could not achieve this, they accomplished through the multiplicity of the proceedings that what had been done would not easily be read.

It therefore seemed appropriate to encompass everything in this Brief Account, so that, by means of the numbered markers noted both in this Brief Account and in the proceedings themselves, anyone could easily find whatever he wished.

### CHAPTER I

When both parties had entered, first the imperial rescript was read [Note: It is set out below in the Appendix.], by which the Emperor ordered the Conference to take place among the bishops mentioned [Col. 0614], so that manifest reason might refute superstition.

### CHAPTER II

Second, the edict of the judge himself was read [Note: Below in the Appendix.]. He had sent it throughout the province so that the bishops of both parties would be summoned and assembled at Carthage by the first day of June for the purpose of conferring.

In that edict he returned the basilicas to the Donatists without the Emperor’s command, provided that they promised to come, thereby inviting them to confer even by means of benefits.

In the same edict he also offered them the opportunity to appoint another judge of their choosing together with him. He swore that he would judge whatever truth persuaded him to judge, along with the other matters contained in that edict for the purpose of encouraging their assembly.

## CHAPTER III

Third, an additional edict of the Presiding Officer was read [Note: [Col. 0614] Ibid.]. It had been issued when the bishops of both parties were already present at Carthage, specifying what place and what procedure the Conference would have, on the same day mentioned and fixed above [Col. 0615]. He also directed that each party reply to him whether they approved the provisions contained in the edict.

## CHAPTER IV

Fourth, when the bishops of the Donatist party demanded that their opponents explain why they had been assembled, the Presiding Officer deferred the matter, so that everything enacted before the day of the Conference might first be read in sequence.

The Donatists’ memorandum was then read [Note: [Col. 0615] It is sometimes written *notoria*. This Donatist letter is reproduced in the Appendix to this volume]. In it they said that they did not approve the provision in his edict that only those bishops should come to the place of the Conference whom the others had selected to conduct the case itself. These numbered thirty-six in all, eighteen from each side: that is, seven who would dispute with one another, another seven who could be added to the council if necessary, and four pairs who would be responsible for preserving and recording the proceedings. Instead, they asked that all who had come should be present, so that their number might be evident; for they said that their opponents had falsely claimed that they were few.

There they said that all of them had come, even the very old men, and that the only ones absent were those whom ill health had prevented from coming. Such were the other matters contained in the memorandum itself.

## CHAPTER V

Fifth, the Catholics’ letter to the Presiding Officer was read [Note: Letter 128 among Augustine’s letters], which they had sent in reply, as he had directed in his edict. They indicated that they agreed to everything arranged in that edict.

In the same letter they also bound themselves and promised that, if the truth of the Church were demonstrated to them on the side of Donatus, they would not seek episcopal rank there, but would follow their counsel for the sake of Christian salvation. If, however, the truth were shown to reside rather in their own communion, they would not deny them episcopal honors. They said that they were doing this for the sake of peace, so that those to whom this concession was made might understand that the Catholics detested in them not Christian ordination but human error.

If the congregations could not tolerate two bishops in one Church, then, with both men withdrawing, individual bishops would be appointed, to be ordained by those bishops who were each found in their own congregations.

The same letter also recalled the case of the Maximianists. Some of those whom the Donatists had condemned for the sake of peace within the Donatist party they had accepted with their honors intact; nor had they annulled the baptism administered by them in their sacrilegious schism. Such were the other matters contained in the aforesaid letter.

## CHAPTER VI

Sixth, the edict of the Presiding Officer himself was also read [Note: In the Appendix]. He had issued it together with the Donatists’ aforesaid memorandum and the Catholics’ aforesaid letter, informing the people what each party had written back to him.

## CHAPTER VII

Seventh, the Catholics’ letter to the Presiding Officer was read [Note: Letter 129 among Augustine’s letters]. In it they replied to the Donatists’ memorandum, granting what the Donatists had requested: that all who had come should be present [Col. 0616] in the place where the Conference was to take place. Nevertheless, only those Catholic bishops whom the Presiding Officer had specified in his edict would be present there, so that, if any disturbance arose—which the Catholics greatly feared—it would not be attributed to those who were present in very small numbers, but rather to those who had wished their multitude to be present.

The entire case was also included in the same letter, so that it might be shown that the Catholic Church was not the party of Donatus, but rather that Church which bore fruit and increased throughout the whole world, beginning from Jerusalem according to Holy Scripture (Luke 24:47). It was also shown that none of the wicked within it could prejudice it, since they were to be separated at the final divine judgment.

It was further shown that the Donatist elders had been unable to prove anything even against Caecilianus, who had been found and declared innocent in ecclesiastical judgments [Note: The Roman and Arles judgments], and especially before the Emperor [Note: Constantine], before whom he had been accused by them.

And because they habitually sought to arouse hatred against the imperial commands issued on behalf of the Catholic Church, the letter also recalled from Holy Scripture that kings had decreed, in their kingdom, the gravest penalties for those who blasphemed God (Dan. 3:96).

The case of the Maximianists was also recalled. The Donatists had themselves pursued them through public courts; yet, from among those they had condemned, they accepted some with their honors intact and did not destroy the baptism administered by them in the schism. They had said that those whom they had allowed a delay, while communicating with Maximianus, had not been polluted by his contagion. Such were the other matters contained in the same letter.

All these matters were recalled there so that perhaps, if the Donatists had reflected on them together and seen how bad the case of Donatus’s party was, they might have wished all who had come to enter the place of the Conference in order to bring about peace and unity.

## CHAPTER VIII

Eighth, when the Presiding Officer asked whether, as he saw had already been done by the Catholics, the Donatist party too had selected those who would conduct the case they had undertaken, the Donatist party replied that the Catholics had already conducted the case before the persons of the disputants had been determined—on account of the Catholics’ letter, which briefly contained the entire case.

Then they began insisting that the matter of the date, the authorization, the persons, and the case itself should be dealt with first, and only afterward should they proceed to the merits of the dispute.

When the Presiding Officer stated that nothing concerning the case had been omitted, and again asked whether they had complied with his edict concerning the establishment of the number of disputants—for everything that needed to be done would have to be conducted through them—the Donatists began arguing about the date. They claimed that the case itself could not be heard because the date had passed.

For by the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, four months had elapsed from the date of the Presiding Officer’s edict, which he had sent to the province, as the Office replied when questioned. Since the Emperor had ordered that the case be heard within four months, they therefore said that the date had already passed and demanded that a judgment be issued against the Catholics as though they were contumacious—just as though the Catholics had been absent, or as though the Donatists had ever entered to conduct the case while the Catholics were absent, or as though the Catholics, after being warned or summoned, had failed to appear.

They made these accusations, therefore, in a slanderous and evasive manner—arguments that would not even have been made lawfully in a courtroom—because they did not want anything to be done.

The Presiding Officer replied that both parties had agreed to the Kalends of June. Moreover, even if either party had still not appeared, two additional months could have remained, since the Emperor had added them in three edicts and ordered that they be observed.

## CHAPTER IX

Ninth, since the Presiding Officer had said above that the objection concerning the date—namely, that the case should not be heard—was more a forensic than an episcopal objection, the Donatist party found an opportunity to say that nothing, therefore, ought to be conducted against them according to public law, but only according to the divine Scriptures.

Accordingly, when the Presiding Officer asked what each party thought about this, the Catholics replied that he should order the authorization of the Catholic council to be read. In it, the method of proceeding had been assigned to the bishops selected as disputants; there, it could be seen more clearly that the case was being conducted not through forensic evasions but rather through divine testimonies.

The dispute continued for some time. The Catholics insisted that the authorization be read, while the Donatists refused. But afterward, once all delaying disputes had been set aside, the Presiding Officer ordered that the authorization be read.

## CHAPTER X

Tenth, the authorization of the Catholic council was read [Note: It is preserved in the Appendix]. In it, the bishops selected for the dispute were charged with defending the Catholic Church against the accusations of the Donatists.

As in the preceding letters, this authorization again contained the entire case in brief. First, it distinguished the case of the Church—which, as promised, is spread throughout the whole world—from the case of Caecilianus, whatever that case may have been. It showed that the wicked within the Church, whether tolerated in ignorance or for the sake of the peace of unity, cannot harm the good, provided that the good do not consent to their wickedness. This was demonstrated by Gospel comparisons, by the example of the Prophets, by that of the Lord Christ himself and the Apostles, by that of the bishops, and even by the judgment of the Donatists themselves in the case of the Maximianists.

Next, it demonstrated by certain proofs that Caecilianus’s case was not a bad one. These proofs showed that both Caecilianus himself and his ordainer, Felix of Aptunga—whom they had accused with particular criminality in their own council—had been cleared.

Such were the other matters contained in the same authorization, whether concerning baptism or the persecution that the Donatist party habitually charged against the Catholics. For the case of the Maximianists was again recalled there, as in the preceding letters, demonstrating that the Donatists had, by their own judgment, completely dissolved every objection they habitually raised against the Catholics, whether concerning baptism, persecution, or contamination through communion.

It was also added that, if they should even now wish to bring accusations against the Catholic bishops in order to create delays, the hearing and examination of those accusations should be postponed until later, for the sake of bringing to an end the case that was already pressing.

The Catholics did this—namely, included the entire case both in the preceding letters [Col. 0618] and in this authorization—in order to prevent the Donatists from attempting, as rumor had spread, to introduce some delaying objections. If they were perhaps barred from the Conference itself, they might withdraw. Even though the case of the Catholic Church had been recorded only briefly, it would remain to be read in the written record of the proceedings; the Donatists were understood to have feared this and therefore to have been unwilling to confer.

## CHAPTER XI

Eleventh, when the Presiding Officer stated that the Catholics’ authorization contained divine testimonies rather than forensic bonds, and ordered that the signatures of all the signatories also be read, a dispute arose and continued for some time.

The Donatists demanded the presence of those who had signed the authorization. They objected that, if men who were not bishops had been substituted for them, they might have deceived the Presiding Officer, in whose presence they were recorded as having signed. They also alleged that the Catholics had added other bishops to ancient sees in order to increase their number.

The Catholics resisted having their own bishops brought forward, fearing that the Donatists were preparing some disturbance by which the Conference itself would be completely broken off. The Donatists plainly seemed altogether unwilling for the Conference to take place, especially when they had tried to raise the objection concerning the date, as though the case had already lapsed and could no longer be heard.

They were thought not to have caused such a disturbance earlier because, if one occurred, they saw that it could not be attributed to the Catholics, who were present in very small numbers, but rather to themselves, whose multitude was present.

When the Catholics yielded to their demand that all who had signed should enter, it later became clear that the Donatists had wanted this because they thought that as many Catholics had not come to Carthage as the signatures appeared to indicate. They were thought to have formed this opinion because the Catholics had not entered Carthage with the same display that the Donatists had made, and for that reason they suspected that the Catholics had come in small numbers.

## CHAPTER XII

Twelfth, when the Catholic bishops whose presence had been demanded entered, they were all read out individually and, coming forward into the middle, were recognized by the Donatists, either by their neighbors or by those with whom they were staying in the same place.

Whenever Catholic bishops were read out from places where the Donatist party did not exist, the Donatists themselves knew well enough that they had no colleagues or communion there, and that Catholics were present there—whether men whom they knew or men about whom they had heard in the neighborhood of their own region.

Thus it happened that no Catholic’s signature was read concerning whose presence they had any doubt.

When they came to the name of Victorianus, the Catholic bishop of Mustitana, and he came forward and replied that he had two opponents—Felicianus in the city of Mustitana and Donatus in the place called Turris—the Catholics demanded that the record state that Felicianus was in communion with Primianus.

For they had condemned Felicianus, together with Maximianus, among the others: Felicianus had condemned Primianus and ordained Maximianus, whom they later received with his honor intact and whose baptism they did not destroy in those whom he had baptized in Maximianus’s schism.

But when the Catholics questioned them, they refused to answer, saying that this should not be demanded of them. When the demand was repeated more insistently, they said that the matter belonged to the internal proceedings. The Presiding Officer ruled in accordance with them that what had been begun should be continued, and that the other question could be investigated later if necessary.

In the diocese of Mustitana itself it also became clear that they too had added another bishop to an ancient see—something they had falsely charged the Catholics with doing out of empty spite. It was later shown that they had done this in other places as well.

## CHAPTER XIII

Thirteenth, after the Catholic bishops who had signed had been listed and recognized as present, the Presiding Officer offered them seats, asking that they conduct the proceedings seated rather than standing.

The Donatists nevertheless refused, although they expressed thanks that he had offered seats to such old men. In refusing, they said many things in their own praise and in praise of the Presiding Officer himself. Whoever wishes may read these remarks in the written record of the proceedings.

For the matter is relevant: although they praised him in such terms as honorable, just, respectful, and kind, they did not want the case—which had brought so many people together—to be conducted before him.

## CHAPTER XIV

Fourteenth, the Donatists’ authorization was also produced and read [Note: It is reproduced below in the Appendix]. It had been drawn up briefly so that those whom they had selected might act as though against their own betrayers and persecutors.

Their names were also read, at the Catholics’ request, so that it might be established whether they had signed while present at Carthage. But the Donatists pressed the Presiding Officer much more insistently to have this done, so that their number too might become apparent; they showed that they desired this very strongly.

During this reading, some men were found on whose behalf, because they were absent, others had signed. One man was also found who did not answer when his name was read. They said that he had died while traveling.

When the Catholics asked how he could have signed at Carthage if he had died while traveling, the Donatists wavered for a long time, disturbed and unsure what to answer. At first they said that the statement had been made not about that man but about another.

When the Catholics thought they meant another man—namely, a cleric who could have signed for the deceased—it was asked whether the cleric had signed in his own name or in the name of the deceased. But afterward they replied that the man himself had signed while present, when the authorization was drawn up on the eighth day before the Kalends of June; because he had signed while ill, however, he had collapsed on his journey home.

When the Catholics heard this, they asked that the Donatists’ earlier statements be read out, so that the contradiction itself might be exposed. When this had been done and the contradiction was apparent, the Presiding Officer asked whether they would at least affirm under God’s testimony that the man had been at Carthage when those who were present had instructed the persons present [Note: Thus the Am edition. But Lov., “when those who were present had instructed him, who was present”; this wrongly corrects the older reading, which is confirmed by the Carthaginian Conference, Part One, chap. 87 and following].

At this they were even more confused and replied, “What if someone else was substituted for him?” Leaving their detected falsehood to God’s judgment, the Presiding Officer ordered the remaining names to be read [Col. 0620].

When these had been read, he asked about the number of bishops belonging to each party.

The Office replied that the names of the Donatist bishops totaled 279, including those on whose behalf others had signed because they were absent, and including the man who had died. The names of all the Catholic bishops present, however, totaled 286.

Twenty had not signed, but they nevertheless demonstrated their presence by coming forward. Except for those whom bodily illness had kept there at Carthage, they professed, through the proceedings recorded in the presence of all, that they had authorized and approved them.

Therefore, at the place of the Conference—that is, at the Gargilian Baths, since that location was later agreed upon—the only Catholic bishops who had signed the authorization or had authorized the proceedings while present who were absent were those who were being kept at Carthage by ill health.

Among those whose names were contained in the Donatist signatures, not only were those whom they said were ill at Carthage absent, but also those on whose behalf others had signed because they were absent—that is, because they had not been present at Carthage.

Since the Donatists were boasting about their numbers, although it had been established that more Catholics had come to Carthage, the Catholics said that another 120 bishops had not come to Carthage. Some had been prevented by old age, some by illness, and some by various necessities [Note: Perhaps, “had been prevented”].

When the Donatists heard this, they replied that many more of their own had also not come to Carthage and that they had many sees among them vacant of bishops. Yet in the memorandum they had given to the Presiding Officer they had stated most explicitly that all of them had come to Carthage, to such an extent that neither age nor exertion had been able to deter even the very old men; the only ones who had not come, they said, were those whom ill health had kept in their own seats or on the journey.

Regarding the sees that they said were vacant among them, the Catholics also replied that there were sixty such sees for which successor bishops had not yet been ordained.

Thus, in the signatures of both parties, it became clear that falsehoods had been detected among the Donatists and that their number of bishops was smaller. For they claimed that only the sick had not come to Carthage, although others had signed on behalf of those who were ill while traveling; and the signatures contained 279 names, including even those on whose behalf others had signed.

Nor is it credible in any way that far more than 120—namely, a third of all their bishops—could have been ill in their own places [Note: Perhaps, “could be ill”] and therefore not have come to Carthage.

## CHAPTER XV

Fifteenth, after all those whose presence was now unnecessary had departed, and those whom both parties had selected as necessary had remained, the Conference was postponed by mutual agreement until the day after the next, since the present day already seemed to have elapsed.

# The Conference on the Second Day

[Col. 0621]

## CHAPTER I

First, when, after a day’s interruption, they assembled at the aforesaid place, as had been agreed and arranged, the Presiding Officer again offered them seats, asking that they use them.

The Catholics immediately sat down. The Donatists, however, refused. Among other things, in refusing they said that it was written for them not to sit with such men (Ps. 25:4).

The Catholics did not reply to this at the time, so as not to cause delay, but reserved their response for a more suitable place in the Conference on the third day.

The Presiding Officer himself then replied that he would conduct the examination while standing.

## CHAPTER II

Second, the memorandum that they had given the previous day was read. In it they had asked that the Catholics’ authorization be handed over to them, so that, after examining it, they could come prepared on the appointed day, since the clerks could not arrive with the written record of the proceedings. The Presiding Officer’s reply was contained in the same memorandum [Note: Perhaps, “to the same memorandum”], and he ordered that what they requested be done.

## CHAPTER III

Third, when the Presiding Officer asked what they also replied concerning the signatures—that is, whether they approved the provision he had made in the edict that each person should sign his own statements—and the Catholics replied that they had already expressed their agreement to this in writing, the Donatists said that they were greatly troubled because this was not customary.

When the Presiding Officer asked whether they were satisfied with the custodians who had been appointed from both parties to write out the proceedings [Note: Perhaps, “whether those appointed were sufficient”], they began asking for a postponement, so that the written proceedings might be given to them and they could then reply.

A lengthy dispute arose with them. Their agreement that the matter should be conducted on that day was repeatedly read from the records. When they said that they did not know the shorthand notes and asked that the written proceedings first be given to them, the Presiding Officer ordered that what their own notaries had recorded should be read to them, once the sealed codices [Col. 0622] in which they were kept had been brought forward, so that they would not contradict their own agreement.

When they repeatedly complained that the written proceedings had not been produced because the clerks had not arrived [Note: Perhaps, “had not been able”] to write them down, they were also reminded that they had said they requested that the Catholics’ authorization be delivered to them precisely so that they could arrive prepared for the present day, because the clerks could not arrive with the written proceedings.

Finding nothing to say, they again wished to reopen their objection concerning the date, to which they had already received a sufficient and more than sufficient answer, and from which the proceedings had already moved on during the first day.

The Catholics then replied that not only was the day of the Kalends of June established in the Presiding Officer’s edict, but that they themselves had written their authorization on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, after the day on which they claimed the case ought to have been heard had already passed—namely, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

It was also said that Primianus himself had promised to appear by the Kalends of June.

The Catholics said all this because they had heard that the Donatists had also spoken about the matter in this way among their own people, with the intention of stirring resentment. Nevertheless, amid all these arguments, the Donatists persisted most vehemently in requesting a postponement.

When the Catholics saw that their request continued to be refused for this purpose, so that the proceedings might be burdened with many words, they asked the Presiding Officer to grant them the postponement they were seeking.

A postponement of six days was granted. The clerks replied when the production of the proceedings could take place, and the Donatists promised that, once the proceedings had been produced, they would sign their own statements.

# The Conference on the Third Day

[Col. 0621]

## CHAPTER I

1. On the third day of the Conference—that is, on the sixth day before the Ides of June—when the parties had entered, the Presiding Officer first asked whether the written proceedings had been delivered to them.

The Office replied that they had delivered them before the day they had promised, as was proved by the acknowledgments of both parties. The acknowledgments were then read, establishing that the Catholics had received the proceedings on the eighth day before the Ides of June at the fifth hour of the day, while the Donatists had received them on the same day at the third hour.

## CHAPTER II

2. Second, when the Presiding Officer ordered that the principal case now be presented, the Catholics said that they had long wished to address the principal case, and that this was it: namely, that the accusations which the Donatists habitually made against the Church spread throughout the whole world should be proved, if they could prove them.

The Donatists replied that it should first be determined who the persons were who would conduct the case, so that delays could be introduced concerning the examination of the persons.

The dispute over this matter continued for a long time. The Catholics refused, insisting vehemently that, once these unnecessary delaying evasions had been removed, the proceedings should come to the case itself.

The Donatists, however, resisted with the utmost determination, demanding that the persons be examined and insisting that it be stated who had asked the Emperor for this Conference.

They wanted it established that the Catholics were the petitioners, so that, according to forensic law, they could examine the persons of the petitioners. Yet in the first proceeding the Catholics’ authorization had already been read, in which they showed that they were not petitioners but defenders against the accusations that the Donatists habitually brought against their communion.

The Donatists themselves had previously insisted that the case of the Church should be conducted not through forensic forms but rather through the testimonies of the divine Scriptures. After the Catholics’ authorization had been read, they had acknowledged that the Catholics wished to establish the Church’s case through the Holy Scriptures, and had promised that they too would proceed in turn from the authority of the same divine law.

Now, as though they had forgotten both what they had demanded and what they themselves had promised [Col. 0623], when the Catholics had proposed that the accusation and vindication of the Church should be addressed, they began [Note: Am. and Er. read *coeperant*, “they had begun”] asking about the persons of the petitioners, so that they could examine them according to forensic law.

The Catholics therefore resisted them. To cut short the delays which they had heard the Donatists were preparing and which they already saw them introducing, they persisted in demanding that the Church’s case be addressed instead.

The dispute reached the point at which the Emperor’s order that the Conference be held was read, so that the identity of the petitioners might thereby be established. The Presiding Officer also seemed to think that, lest anything be denied to the Donatists even in terms of forensic law, as though they were requesting something just, the persons of the petitioners should first be determined.

After the imperial order had been read, it was declared that the Catholics had requested the Conference and that it had been granted to them.

The Donatists then began asking that the petitions by which they had requested the Conference also be produced. When the Presiding Officer replied that petitions were not ordinarily included in a pragmatic rescript, they turned to demanding that the Catholics’ authorization—by which they had instructed that a Conference be requested from the Emperor—and the same legates whom they had sent to obtain it should be delivered and disclosed to them.

They asserted that they ought to examine what had been authorized and that they could find there the Catholics’ instructions concerning what they had said to the Emperor.

The Catholics understood that this inquiry was being made in order to find opportunities for prolonged delays and postponements. They maintained that what the Donatists were requesting had absolutely nothing to do with the case, since the Emperor himself had made it perfectly clear that they had requested a Conference, and had appointed the Presiding Officer so that manifest reason might refute superstition.

The Donatists were strongly pressed to remove all interposed delays and inquiries intended to introduce further delays, and instead to address the matter which the Emperor had ordered to be addressed in that Conference—for it was clear that it had been requested from him and granted by him.

## CHAPTER III

3. In the course of this, the two parties exchanged a few remarks and objections concerning the name “Catholic,” and it was ordered that the matter be reserved for the principal case.

After some further exchanges, whenever the name “Catholic” was mentioned, the Donatists said that the Catholic Church was rather on their side.

The Presiding Officer ruled that, for the time being and without prejudicing anyone, he could not call the Catholics anything other than what the Emperor had called them—the Emperor who had appointed him. As for the Donatists, he said, the more strongly they claimed to be Catholics, the more they ought now to conduct the case itself, once all delaying devices had been removed, in which case they could prove that they were the Catholics.

After so many delays and so many rulings by the Presiding Officer against them—rulings that demanded that the case itself be addressed and declared that neither the persons of the legates nor the authorization given to them had anything to do with the case, and that he had received no instruction to investigate anything on that account—the Donatists said that, if the Catholics were unwilling to obey the rulings by producing the authorization given to the legates, they should at least answer whether they stood in the position of petitioners.

The Catholics were greatly astonished that the Donatists should say they were disobeying rulings by not producing the legates’ authorization, since the Presiding Officer had rather ruled against the Donatists themselves on this point in so many decisions.

The Catholics therefore asked: “Which rulings have we disobeyed?”

When the Donatists gave no answer, the Presiding Officer ruled that the Catholics should answer the Donatists’ question about the position of petitioners.

They replied that their proposal was this: that the accusations which the Donatists habitually brought against their communion should either be proved or refuted, so that the Donatist separation might either be defended or corrected.

When the Presiding Officer then demanded an answer from the Donatists, they replied that the Africans who called themselves Catholics wished to defend another’s case—namely, that of the Church of the whole world. Nothing concerning this case, they said, ought to prejudice them, since the dispute was being conducted among Africans. Instead, the overseas Church should be awaited, so that whoever won would appear to belong to it and would possess the name “Catholic.”

But at the end of their statement they again asked that they be answered concerning the person of the petitioner.

The Catholics briefly replied to both points. First, they said that the question concerning the persons had already been settled in the first and second proceedings. Second, they said that they themselves, not the Donatists, were in communion with the Church spread throughout the whole world, to which divine Scripture bears witness; therefore they were rightly both Catholic and called Catholic.

The Donatists replied that the name “Catholic” had not been established from the universality of the nations but from the fullness of the Sacraments. They demanded that the Catholics prove that all nations were in communion with them [Note: Compare Augustine, Letter 93, §23].

The Catholics gladly accepted this challenge and asked to be allowed to prove it. But the Donatists again began reopening the question concerning the authorization given to the legates, which they had demanded should be produced for them. They again withdrew from the Church’s case, which had now reached the point of being examined publicly—at one moment demanding the aforesaid authorization, at another insisting that the identity of the petitioner be established, and at another demanding that the Presiding Officer rule on these very matters they had requested, concerning which he had already ruled so many times and declared that they were seeking them in vain.

## CHAPTER IV

4. Although the Presiding Officer saw that they did not properly request that the authorization given to the legates be produced—for it was sufficient for the case that the Conference had been requested and granted—he nevertheless did not think it unjust for them to ask that the identity of the petitioner be established.

The Catholics, however, saw what had already been announced to them earlier, and they understood clearly from the Donatists’ intention that the Donatists were asking about the persons of the petitioners for no other reason than to make it possible, through an examination of persons, to introduce extremely long delays and postponements. For they were vehemently unwilling to reach the case, in which they knew perfectly well that they had nothing to say, as the matter itself eventually, though only later, made completely clear.

Seeing this, therefore, the Catholics refused to accept the position of petitioners. They asserted that they were not bringing accusations but defending themselves against accusations already brought. Once they had defended those accusations and demonstrated them to be false, it would consequently become clear who the Donatists were and with what injustice they had separated themselves from unity [Col. 0625].

The Donatists maintained that, in whatever manner the Catholics wished to refute the very accusations at issue, the Catholics were voluntarily compelling them to respond as adversaries and thereby showed that they occupied the position of petitioners.

The Catholics replied that they had requested the Conference not as a place where they would bring accusations to be refuted, but as a place where they would refute accusations already brought. For the Donatists’ authorization had been composed against betrayers and persecutors, and Primianus’s own words, when the Catholics had earlier invited him to a Conference, testified that he had brought an accusation against them. He had said: “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of betrayers should come together” [Note: See below, Book after the Conference, §§1–2].

Although Primianus had not wished to confer at that time, he later said that he wished to be heard and examined in the court of the prefects. Holding to this agreement of theirs concerning the Conference, the Catholics had asked the Emperor that it be held.

5. Then the Cognitor ordered them to prove the crimes they had alleged, and declared that, if both parties were proved to have requested the Collation, the person of the petitioner could not be established merely from the fact that a Collation had been requested. At this point the Donatists repeatedly began demanding that he pronounce judgment concerning the petitioner’s status. The Cognitor then pronounced that, if both parties had requested a Collation, the petitioner was the one who brought accusations. The Donatists demanded that the Catholics prove whether both parties had requested a Collation. When the Cognitor said, “The Catholics will have to prove this,” another delaying dispute arose concerning the term “Catholic,” as opposed to “Donatist” and “Caecilianist.”

The Catholics then produced the records made in the prefectural court, by which they could prove that the Donatists too had requested a Collation. When the Cognitor ordered these records to be read, the Donatists again returned to matters already passed over and began demanding that the Cognitor pronounce judgment on points about which he had pronounced so many times: namely, the question of the petitioner’s status and the mandate given to the envoys, which they had so often and unnecessarily requested to have published. They were doing this, as could be understood, because they feared that the prefectural records would be read, in which they had injured their own case through certain ill-considered and reckless statements.

Thus they carried on a long dispute, especially with the Cognitor himself. They demanded that the mandate entrusted to the envoys be published, or that he pronounce that they had requested it unnecessarily. He, however, said both that he had already pronounced on this matter and that it had absolutely no bearing on the present trial, where the imperial letters would show what had been requested and what had been granted. At last, by his order, the prefectural records began to be read. When the date and the consuls had been read out [Note: [Col. 0625] In the Collation, book 3, chapter 141, the exceptor Martialis began reading: “Copy of the proceedings on the third day before the Kalends of February, in Ravenna, when Our Lord Arcadius, Perpetual Augustus, and Probus were consuls for the fourth time,” that is, in the year of Christ 406.], the Donatists immediately interrupted again and began demanding those same earlier matters. But when the Cognitor stated that the records had to be read so that the status of the petitioner might be established, they began by saying that there were earlier records which ought rather to be read. The Catholics replied [Col. 0626] that the reason the Donatists did not want the prefectural records read was that they feared the statements they themselves had made in them.

## CHAPTER V.—6.

The Donatists therefore produced the records of the proconsular and vicariate prefectural courts [Note: [Col. 0626] These are exhibited below in the Appendix.], where the Catholics had requested that the Donatists be summoned before the municipal records, so that, after a Collation between both parties, the error might be removed. This had occurred long before they had requested the Collation itself from the Emperor. By these records they wanted to show that the Catholics occupied the position of petitioners, because in those proceedings the Catholics had called the Donatists heretics and said that they committed many offenses against divine and human laws.

The Catholics replied that they had demanded a Collation even then for the purpose of answering their accusations on behalf of the Church. Accordingly, they repeatedly requested that, if records were to be read, those which were demonstrably earlier should rather be read—namely, those in which the Donatists had first sent an accusation against Caecilianus to the Emperor Constantine through the proconsul Anulinus. After the records produced by the Donatists had been read, however, the earlier records, which had already begun to be read before the prefects, were not read.

A dispute then arose: if the records produced by the Donatists had been given precedence over those produced by the Catholics because they had been found to be earlier and therefore were to be read first, then at least, after those records had been read, the much earlier records should also be read—those in which it would become clear that, throughout the entire case then under consideration, the Donatists had first appeared as accusers before the Emperor through the proconsul.

The Donatists therefore resisted vehemently to prevent these records from being read, opposing them through many and varied statements, just as they had resisted and compelled the authorities not to read the prefectural records. During this resistance they often repeated the now-worn-out point, already rejected in so many rulings by the Cognitor, concerning the publication of the mandate given to the envoys. They also repeated a question that had already been settled: whether the Catholics preferred to proceed by the testimonies of the Law or by public records.

They said that, if the Catholics chose the testimonies of divine Law, they would suffer the loss of all public laws and records; but if they preferred to proceed by public laws and records, they would be abandoning the divine testimonies. Yet if the Catholics chose to proceed by the evidence of public records, the Donatists said that they would not even permit the records offered by the Catholics to be read, on the grounds that they possessed a valid limitation of time—namely, the one about which both the Catholics and the Cognitor had given them an adequate answer. They claimed that the case had lapsed and could no longer be heard because the date had passed by which the four months would have been completed.

It was plainly evident that they were exceedingly afraid that the records would be read which would show that their ancestors had first accused Caecilianus before the Emperor, and that he had subsequently been acquitted and cleared both by ecclesiastical and imperial judgments. In other words, they feared that the very case which had brought everyone there would be heard, where they felt they could be defeated most clearly. They were so unwilling and afraid of this that they were even forced to admit it, saying that they were being led into the case gradually—that is, little by little—and being brought to the inner substance of the case. They ought certainly to have desired this if they trusted not in empty and delaying procedural objections but in the truth of the case itself.

## CHAPTER VI.—7.

The Catholics therefore made every effort to reach the case itself, to which they clearly saw that the Donatists were wholly unwilling to proceed. Nevertheless, they repeatedly answered the very points that the Donatists kept bringing back after they had already been settled. Since two matters had come before the court—one concerning the publication of the mandate entrusted to the envoys, and the other concerning whether the Catholics preferred to proceed by divine testimonies or by public records—the Catholics replied concerning publication of the mandate that it did not concern them and had absolutely no relevance to the present case.

The Cognitor himself again pronounced what he had often pronounced before: that he could not examine the status of the envoys or the mandate they had received, and that he ought not to depart from what had been entrusted to him. For it was sufficiently clear from the imperial letters by which the judge had been appointed to this case that the Emperor had granted a Collation.

As for the other matter, in which they asked what the Catholics would choose—divine documents or public records—the Catholics repeatedly replied that, if the Donatists did not bring accusations against human beings, such as they were accustomed to bring against traditors, but only sought to determine what or where the Church was, they would proceed by no public records at all, but solely by the testimonies of divine Scripture. But if the Donatists persisted in accusing and indicting human beings, since they themselves could demonstrate such matters only through records of that kind, then without doubt the Catholics too would defend themselves against such accusations through public records; for otherwise these matters could neither be accused nor defended.

These points were repeated and pressed upon them many times, both by the Catholics and by the Cognitor himself, in many different ways. The Donatists repeatedly returned to the same matters and repeated them, so that the case would not be heard and the records—which they saw were already in the hands of the court—would not be read. At last, however, the Cognitor overcame their prolonged obstinacy and ordered the documents submitted by the Catholics to be read. Finally the case began to be heard, the case for which so many bishops of both parties had assembled.

This happened remarkably: the Donatists had sought to establish the identity of the petitioner precisely to prevent the case from being reached, yet the very inquiry into the petitioner’s status suddenly brought the case itself into consideration.

## CHAPTER VII.—8.

These proceedings therefore took place at the third stage. The report of Anulinus, proconsul, to the Emperor Constantine was read. When the Donatists asked where it had been produced from, the Catholics replied that, if they doubted it, they should inquire in the proconsul’s archive.

That report most clearly states that the Donatists themselves had first sent to the Emperor Constantine, through the aforementioned proconsul, an accusation concerning the crimes they alleged against Caecilianus. After it had been read through, the Donatists began asking whom the Catholics called their father. When they were answered from the Gospel, where it is written, “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, God” (Matthew 23:9), they nevertheless, even after hearing this, began asking whether Caecilianus was their father or their mother.

The Catholics had already stated that he was neither their father nor their mother, but their brother—whether a good one, if he was good, or an evil one, if he was evil—because even an evil man was their brother on account of their common sacraments. At this point they disputed for somewhat longer, the Donatists repeating the same questions and the Catholics giving the same answers.

The Donatists also raised the objection: How could the Apostle say, “Though you have countless tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for I became your father in Christ Jesus through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15)? The Catholics replied that this had been said as an honorific expression, on account of the evangelical ministry administered by the Apostle. For the only father of faith and eternal salvation was God.

The Apostle could not have spoken contrary to Christ, so that, when Christ said, “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, God,” the Apostle, as though resisting Christ’s words, would call himself the father of those to whom he had proclaimed the Gospel. Therefore it was necessary to distinguish what was said on account of divine grace from what was said as an honorific expression.

9. They also asked who had ordained Augustine, preparing, as was being alleged, certain accusations. When he fearlessly replied that he had been ordained by Megalius, who at that time was the primate of the bishops of the Catholic Church in Numidia, and insistently urged them to produce what they had prepared, so that they might also be shown there to be making false accusations, they diverted the inquiry to something else and returned to the person of Caecilianus.

They said that Caecilianus did not harm the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0628] According to Morel, the reading should be quam dicebant Catholici, “which the Catholics said.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 254. M.], even if his alleged crimes were proved true; yet they also said that these crimes themselves could not be proved true.

## CHAPTER VIII.—10.

The Donatists then produced letters which they said they had received from their entire council [Note: [Col. 0628] They appear below in the Appendix.], in which an answer was made to the Catholics’ mandate, which had been cited on the first day of the proceedings. On the following day, before they came to the second session on the third day, the Donatists had requested that the notice delivered to them be supplied to them, so that they could come prepared for the hearing. Perhaps it was also because these letters had to be carefully written that they requested a postponement during the second session; a postponement of six days was granted to them.

These proceedings therefore took place at the fourth stage. The aforementioned letters of the Donatists were read, in which they attempted to answer the Catholics’ mandate inserted in the records of the first stage. Anyone who wishes to read and consider both documents will discover that they were unable to answer that mandate [Note: Here we restore *plimum* from the Am. edition, for which the Lov. edition mistakenly substituted *comperiet*.].

First, they did not wish even to discuss or touch the testimonies drawn from the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the apostolic and evangelical writings, by which it is shown that the Catholic Church is spread throughout the whole world, beginning from Jerusalem and growing into near and distant regions, reaching even Africa and the other places and cities through which it was first extended. In those places many churches belonging to that one Church were founded through apostolic labor, and it is evident that the Donatists do not share communion with them.

They not only refused to examine these matters; they did not touch them at all. Nor did they dare to produce any testimony from the sacred Scriptures in their lengthy letter by which they could assert that the Church of Donatus’s party had been foretold and announced, as the Catholics had produced so many testimonies on behalf of the Church with which they shared communion—a Church that begins from Jerusalem and spreads throughout the entire world.

Since they had entirely avoided these many testimonies, passing them over as though they had not been stated in the Catholics’ mandate to which they appeared to be responding, they attempted instead, by producing many testimonies from divine Scripture, to show that the Church of God had not been foretold as one that would exist amid a mixture of evil people.

Yet later, when they came to the Gospel parable which the Catholics had included in their mandate concerning the nets cast into the sea—nets in which, the Lord said, every kind of fish would be gathered, and the good would be separated from the bad on the shore, that is, at the end of the age—they themselves admitted that at least hidden evil people were mixed within the Church.

They said, however, that the weeds were mixed with the wheat not in the Church but in the world itself, because the Lord said, “The field is this world” (Matthew 13:47–50, 38). As for the threshing floor, to which the Catholics had said that chaff remains mixed until the time of winnowing, they did not even attempt to explain this parable, as though nothing of the kind had been written in the Gospel. Instead, as if the Catholics had invented the point themselves, they merely criticized it, appealing as though to the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah: “What has straw in common with wheat?” (Jeremiah 23:28). They did not attend to the context in which he had said this. For he was not speaking about the Church, but about the divine visions of the prophets and human dreams, so that they should not be compared in any way.

Nor did they wish to touch at all upon the other parable of the sheep and the goats that graze together and will be separated at the end of the age, which the Catholics had also included among their Gospel testimonies (Matthew 25:32–33). For there they could not say that the goats too were unknown to the shepherds in the common pastures, as they had said that the bad fish in the sea were unseen by the fishermen among the nets.

11. Likewise, when the Catholics, wishing to show that evil people are tolerated by the good within the Church and that the good are not polluted by the contagion of the evil, had recalled examples from the Prophets, from the Lord Christ himself, and from the Apostles, and afterward also from good bishops, as well as the judgment of the Donatists themselves—who denied that some of their own people involved in the Maximianist schism had been polluted by Maximian’s contagion—the Donatists attempted in their letter to respond to these points.

They said whatever they wished about the Prophets, the Lord Christ, and the Apostles, but they remained silent about the bishops and the Maximianists. In the matter of the bishops they were constrained by the authority of Cyprian, whose words from one of his letters the Catholics had included in their mandate. Those words most clearly showed that Cyprian had commanded that evil people be tolerated in the Church for the sake of unity and that the Church should not be abandoned on their account (*Letter to Maximus*). They also showed that he himself had tolerated in the Church certain colleagues whose evil conduct he strongly detested and whose very wicked deeds he did not conceal (*Sermon on the Fallen*).

Thus, overcome by this authority, the Donatists said something about the Prophets, the Lord Christ, and the Apostles, but, in order to show that evil people mixed within the Church were not to be tolerated [Note: [Col. 0630] Perhaps: “in order to show that evil people mixed within the Church were not to be tolerated,” etc.], they were entirely unwilling to say anything about the bishops.

Cyprian himself also understood and wrote about Judas the betrayer and those whom Paul tolerated—those who preached Christ out of envy—in the very way the Catholics had presented it in their mandate: the Lord endured Judas as an example of evil people to be tolerated in the Church (John 6:71–72), and Paul endured those of whom he spoke in this way not outside but within the Church (Philippians 1:15–18).

What could they say about the Maximianists, while the people by whom they could be convicted most plainly and easily were still alive? Accordingly, the Catholics had stated in their mandate that the Donatists had driven those same Maximianists from the basilicas by public legal proceedings. The Donatists attempted somehow to answer this by saying that they had not accused them criminally or compelled anyone unwillingly to join their communion, but had reclaimed civilly their own property or that of their people. They forgot what Primianus had once ordered to be entered in the records [Note: [Col. 0630] Augustine frequently cites those records and reports Primianus’s words from them: *Exposition on Psalm 36*, Sermon 2, no. 18; *Against Cresconius*, book 4, chapter 47, no. 57; and *The Book after the Collation*, chapters 16 and 31, nos. 1, 20, 53.]: “They take away what belongs to others; we leave what has been taken away.”

But concerning what the Catholics had said in their mandate about the Maximianists—that the Donatists had received into full honor those whom they had condemned; that they had denied that the associates of Maximian were polluted by him; and that they had preferred to approve rather than rescind and repeat the baptism given by them in schism—they did not even attempt a superficial response. Instead, they passed over all these points in a remarkable silence, as though they had never been said.

12. Concerning Baptism itself, the Catholics had stated in their mandate that the Apostle said of certain people, “They suppress the truth in iniquity” (Romans 1:18), to show that it is possible for the truth not to be destroyed when iniquity is destroyed. The Donatists either did not understand this or attempted to obscure by their words what they themselves had understood, saying that the Apostle had spoken about the error of the Gentiles.

But it is irrelevant whose error he was discussing, since he showed that truth can be held in iniquity. Thus, when these two things are found in one person, the truth may be approved while the iniquity is corrected. This is what the Catholic Church does when it recognizes and embraces the truth of the Sacrament in the Donatists, while detesting and correcting the heretical iniquity found among them.

The Catholics had also stated in their mandate that Christ’s Baptism should not be destroyed merely because heretics also administer it, just as Christ should not be denied merely because demons also confess him. The Donatists either did not understand this point or attempted to obscure it, saying that the Catholics had spoken against the martyrs, though they did not specify which martyrs they meant. They also said that the Catholics wished to share communion with demons [Col. 0631], as though one shared communion with heretics when one anathematized their iniquity, even though one did not destroy the Baptism found in their consecration—just as one anathematizes the iniquity of demons without denying the Lord’s name heard in their confession.

13. They also included much in their letter about the persecutions they claimed to suffer. Yet they did not dare to answer what had been stated in the Catholics’ mandate: that they themselves had first accused Caecilianus before the Emperor Constantine. They complained about the emperors’ laws, stirring up hatred against the Catholics and exaggerating either the deaths that their Circumcellions inflicted upon themselves or all the punishments they suffered under public laws and disciplines—not on account of the communion of Donatus, but on account of the crimes through which they acted with violent savagery and lived impiously.

They even dared to mention the town of Vagaitanum [Note: [Col. 0631] For *Bagaitanum*.], where it was demonstrated how many evils they had committed and how much lesser were the sufferings they themselves had endured.

14. Nor did they wish to respond at all, in their lengthy letter, to what the Catholics’ mandate had said about the clearing and acquittal of Caecilianus and Felix of Aptunga, whose alleged crimes they were accustomed to use among the uninformed to stir up great hatred against the Catholics. The entire case for which they had come was at issue in that matter.

For in what they said and appeared to support with divine testimonies—that evil people should not be tolerated in the Church, but that one should withdraw from them because of the contagion of sins—they presented their position in such a way that they nevertheless admitted that no one could be defiled by the sins of others when those sins were unknown. They had said the same about the bad fish: just as fishermen do not see those fish lying hidden beneath the waves, although they are already within the nets, so priests do not know the evil people who lie hidden in the Church and therefore are not polluted by them.

Yet in a letter so lengthy and written after so long a postponement, they did not even slightly or faintly attempt to prove what the Catholics had especially emphasized in their mandate: not merely that Caecilianus’s crimes were true—for that would not be enough—but also that those crimes could have been proved and made known to the Church spread among all nations to the ends of the earth, so that, consequently, at least according to their own position, the Church could have been polluted by the contagion of known sins.

## CHAPTER IX.—15.

When the Donatists’ letters had therefore been read, the Cognitor wanted the documents which the Catholics had submitted for reading to be read as well. But the Donatists began demanding that a response be made to what they had written. The Catholics too preferred this, so that the letters would not remain as though no answer could have been made to them.

When the Catholics began to respond, the Donatists began interrupting and shouting objections, so that the speaker’s uninterrupted discourse would not proceed as their letter had been read without interruption. The Catholics wished to show how the divine testimonies they themselves had presented and those the Donatists had cited [Note: [Col. 0632] Am., Er., and Lov. read *illic*. The reading should be *illi*, so that it refers to the Donatists.] were to be understood, so that they would not be found contradictory, since both were divine and therefore ought to be harmonious rather than opposed.

They began first with the parable of the threshing floor. The Donatists interrupted and said that nothing about a threshing floor was written in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0632] Compare *Against Gaudentius*, book 2, chapter 4, no. 4.]. When the Catholics cited the Gospel passage more explicitly, the Donatists again interrupted and said that hidden evil people were meant by the chaff to be winnowed later.

Amid their shouting and interruptions, a dispute then arose about the weeds and the wheat, because of the word “world.” The Donatists did not want the Church to be understood by that term, since it is written, “The field is this world.” They produced many testimonies by which they claimed that Holy Scripture mentioned the world only in reference to evil people, such as: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15), and other passages of the same kind. They did this as though thereby showing that the Church could in no way be signified by the word “world.”

The Catholics, on the other hand, produced other testimonies showing that the word “world” can be used in a good sense, such as: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19), and other passages of this kind, where it was shown that the Church was meant, since it is certainly through Christ that the Church is reconciled to God.

These proceedings took place while the Catholics tried to continue their speech without interruption, whereas the Donatists kept shouting so that this would not happen. They did not reserve their response, as the Catholics had done when their letter was read; instead, by repeatedly interjecting objections, they prevented the Catholics’ statement from proceeding without disturbance.

16. The Catholics therefore demanded that the Donatists exercise patience and, through many rulings by the Cognitor, scarcely obtained it. They answered their letters, showing by many testimonies and examples from the Holy Scriptures that evil people are now so mixed within the Church that, although ecclesiastical discipline must remain vigilant and correct them not only by words but also through excommunications and degradations, such people are not merely unknown when they lie hidden; often, for the sake of the peace of unity, even those who are known are tolerated.

Thus they showed that the divine testimonies are harmonious: those that commend the Church as existing amid a mixture of evil people signify the present time, when the Church is as it is in this present age; while those testimonies that commend the Church as having no evil people mixed within it signify the time when it will exist forever in the age to come.

Now the Church is mortal, that is, it consists of mortal human beings; then it will be immortal, when no one in it will die. In the same way, Christ himself was mortal for the Church in this present time, but after the resurrection he no longer dies, and death no longer rules over him (Romans 6:9). The same gift he will grant to his Church at the end of the age.

These two periods of the Church—what it is now and what it will then be—were also signified by two miraculous catches of fish. The first occurred before Christ’s resurrection, when he ordered the nets to be cast without naming either the left or the right side (Luke 5:4–10), thereby teaching that neither only evil people nor only good people, but evil people mixed with the good, would be within the nets of his Sacraments.

After the resurrection he ordered the nets to be cast on the right side (John 21:6–11), so that we might understand that after our resurrection only the good would remain in the Church. There will then be no heresies or schisms by which the nets are now torn. The Gospel did not fail to mention that the nets were torn in the first catch; but concerning the final catch it says, “Although there were so many fish, the net was not torn.”

It was said of such a Church that “the uncircumcised and the unclean would not pass through it” (Isaiah 52:1). Schismatic divisions belong to the unclean; they will not exist then, because the nets will not be torn. This was also signified by the fact that the raven, an unclean bird, went out from the ark and did not return.

Yet when the raven went out, the ark was certainly not without all unclean animals. Both clean and unclean animals were in it until the Flood (Genesis 7–8), just as good and evil people remain in the Church until the end of the age. But just as Noah offered sacrifice not from the unclean animals but from the clean, so it is not those who are evil in the Church but those who are good who reach God.

17. Since the Donatists had said in their letters that they did not share communion with those against whom the Prophets had spoken such grave evils, the Catholics replied that there had been one temple used by all, and that none of the Prophets who had spoken so strongly against evil people had established another temple, sacrifices, or priests for himself.

The Donatists had also included in their letter testimonies from Scripture intended to show that the children too were implicated in the sins of their parents. This has never been rightly understood except of those children who imitate their parents’ iniquities. The Catholics therefore replied that, although the divine utterances contained so many harsh and bitter statements against that people—statements which the Donatists themselves had cited—so that it might appear that no good person remained there, nevertheless not only had those same holy Prophets been present among them, but people had also arisen from that very nation whom the Lord himself found worthy of praise at the coming in his flesh. Such were Zechariah and Elizabeth, their son John, and the aged Simeon and the widow Anna (Luke 1–2).

From this it is clear how impiously and calumniously the crimes of Caecilianus were charged against the Catholics spread throughout the world. The crimes of that people in which Simeon, Anna, and others like them had been born could not be charged against them, even though they had been consecrated through the sacraments of that same people and the crimes of that people had been denounced not by human opinion but by the divine word.

A prophetic testimony was also recalled in which those who lamented the crimes committed in their midst were marked so that they would not perish with the evil people (Ezekiel 9:4); yet they were not separated from them bodily.

18. The discussion then recalled what kind of separation the good ought to make from the impious and evil in the present time [Col. 0634], so that they might not share in the sins of others: namely, a separation of heart, life, and conduct. The words, “Go out from their midst, withdraw from there, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isaiah 52:11), were not to be understood otherwise than as meaning: distinguish yourselves by living differently, and do not consent to uncleanness.

At a very appropriate point the Catholics also answered the Donatists’ statement that, when the Cognitor had asked them to sit down, they had written for themselves that they should not sit with such people (above, Collation, day 2, chapter 1). When responding to their letter, the Catholics said that separation from evil people in the present age was not to be understood in the way the Donatists had understood it when they refused to sit with them as though they were impious, because it is written, “I have not sat in the council of the impious.”

For if they considered those people impious, they ought not to have done what the same psalm immediately goes on to forbid: “And I will not enter in with those who commit iniquity” (Psalm 25:4). Since they had entered with those whom they considered impious, why had they not also sat with them? In that way they might have appeared to avoid in both cases not a bodily but a spiritual sitting and entering.

The case of the Maximianists, which had so often been brought against them, was also recalled: the Donatists had said that both they themselves and those whom they had granted a postponement, although placed in the schism of Maximian and associates of Primianus in his condemnation, were nevertheless not polluted by Maximian’s contagion. Yet they had insisted that the Christian world had perished because of Caecilianus’s crimes, even to the ends of the earth.

## CHAPTER X.—19.

Since the Donatists were unable to answer these points with the strongest testimonies of Scripture and with their own example concerning the Maximianists, they returned to what had already been dealt with. They said that the word “world” could not properly be understood as the Church, in which the wheat and the weeds had been commanded to grow together.

This was despite the fact that the Catholics had already cited so many divine testimonies showing that “world” could also be used in a good sense and could in that sense signify only the Church. Moreover, however “world” was understood, since both seeds grew throughout the world, the wheat ought not to be abandoned because of the weeds throughout the world.

These matters had already been stated, and the question itself appeared to have been settled. Nevertheless, in the greatest poverty of argument they returned to it, repeating the same things through the same things and asking how the devil could have sown weeds in the Church. They then accused the Catholics of saying that there were two Churches: one that now contains evil people mixed with the good, and another that would not contain them after the resurrection. They spoke as though the saints who would reign with Christ in the future were not the very same people who now endure evil people while living justly for his name.
