20. The Catholics replied that the Donatists themselves had already admitted that there were hidden evil people in the Church. They in turn asked how the devil had sown them in the Church; for the Donatists were asking about the weeds as though such a thing could not happen.

The Catholics also repeated the testimony of Cyprian, who understood the same Gospel parable in no other way than by saying that there were weeds in the Church—not hidden, but visible (Letter to Maximus). The Donatists had dared to answer absolutely nothing to this testimony, even though they held Cyprian’s authority in such high regard that they attempted to defend through it their mistaken belief and practice concerning the repetition of Baptism.

The Catholics also refuted their accusation concerning two Churches. They repeatedly and more explicitly showed what they had said: they had not said that the Church which now contains evil people mixed with the good was alien to the kingdom of God, where evil people will not be mixed with the good. Rather, they had said that the same one and holy Church exists now in one condition and will exist then in another: now it has evil people mixed within it; then it will not have them.

It is like its being mortal now because it consists of mortal human beings, but immortal then because no one in it will die bodily. In the same way, there are not two Christs merely because the one who first died will not die afterward [Note: [Col. 0635] Perhaps the reading should be: “because he first died.”].

The distinction between the external and the internal human being was also mentioned. Although these are different, we do not therefore say that there are two human beings. How much less should we speak of two Churches, since the very same people who now tolerate evil people mixed with the good and die in order to be resurrected will then neither contain evil people mixed with them nor die at all?

The question of number was also raised. The Donatists had commended one Church by the testimony of Scripture, as though this were contrary to the two Churches which they falsely claimed that the Catholics had asserted. The Catholics replied that Scripture also speaks of many churches, including the seven to which John writes (Revelation 1). Nevertheless, these are understood as members of that one Church. This showed that the Catholics should much less be accused of asserting two Churches, since they had said that the same one Church is not now what it will be in the resurrection; and the apostolic writings do not object to the many churches from which that one Church consists.

The Donatists continued to repeat the same points. They also added, with malicious emphasis, that the Catholics had called the Church mortal. They therefore denied that it was mortal because the Trinity, by whose grace the Church is consecrated, is immortal, and because Christ died for it precisely in order to make it immortal.

The Catholics replied that they had not denied that the Church would be made immortal by God’s grace and by the blood poured out for it by the Savior. Rather, they said that the times must be distinguished: the present time, in which all the saints die just as Christ himself died, and the future time, in which they will rise and live without anyone dying, together with him who has already risen.

## CHAPTER XI

**21.** While these matters were being discussed among them, and although the Donatists’ contentious repetition of things clear and plain was superfluous, the Presiding Judge promised that he would pronounce a final judgment on the matters he had heard sufficiently, and ordered that the matter from which the original cause of the division had arisen should rather be taken up. Then the Donatists began pressing him to judge first the matters he had heard. When the Catholics also demanded this, and he remained firm in what he had said, ordering instead that the cause of the original division be demonstrated, the Catholics asked that the documents they were offering be read aloud.

When he ordered this to be done, the Donatists began resisting more vigorously and tried to compel him to judge matters already heard, repeating what had been completed and adding that he ought not to judge that cause at all, which he wished to have dealt with by reading what the Catholics had submitted for reading. They said that Christ ought to be the judge of this case; they stirred up resentment against the Catholics because they had sought a human judge; and they also repeated their customary complaints about the persecutions they claimed to be suffering.

The Catholics replied that they ought not to stir up resentment over the request for a human judge, since they too had judged the case of the Maximianists and had not reserved it for Christ the Judge. They had also first brought Caecilian’s own case before a human being—that is, before the Emperor Constantine—by accusing him and sending the case to him. Nor should they complain about persecutions, since the Catholics were asking the emperors for something on behalf of the Catholic Church while their Circumcellions, under clerical leaders, were committing such appalling crimes.

When the Donatists replied—vainly—that this had nothing to do with priests, the Catholics maintained that the acts had been committed under clerical leaders.

**22.** At that point it was also stated that they had attacked human eyes with lime and vinegar, surpassing the devil in cruelty in that crime, since the devil had not done this to the flesh of the holy man whom he had received power to afflict (Job 2). The Donatists then asked whether those who inflicted these things or those who suffered them were the devil’s sons—as though the Catholics had been referring to anything other than their own most savage sufferings at the hands of their clergy and Circumcellions.

Nevertheless, on this occasion too the Catholics did not fail to take the opportunity to bring up the Maximianists against them. They said that, according to the Donatists’ own judgment, the Maximianists were better men—those whom the Donatists had persecuted before three or more proconsuls. For the Maximianists suffered persecution, whereas the Donatists inflicted it.

[Note: **[Col. 0636]** Perhaps it should read: “For they suffered persecution, whereas these inflicted it.”]

The Catholics continued pressing them to answer whether they had not received Felicianus from among those whom they had condemned and persecuted, and whether they did not have him in their own fellowship.

At this charge they became, as always, completely silent and turned to another matter, accusing the Catholics of having defended the devil because they had said that the devil spared the eyes of the holy Job, and that the Donatists had therefore surpassed him in cruelty. They proceeded to accuse the devil, as though the Catholics had defended him, saying that he had spared Job’s eyes with still greater cruelty so that they would remain to witness the wound he had inflicted upon the whole body.

It is very surprising why they wanted to say this as though it were a great achievement, unless perhaps so that those who had attacked men’s eyes might be understood to have acted piously, lest the victims suffer by seeing the wounds they had received from them over their entire bodies.

**23.** But when the Donatists again exaggerated the persecutions they claimed to endure and recalled the deaths of some of their people in the town of Bagai, the Catholics replied that they had suffered these things while resistance was being offered to their violence, which they had also attempted to inflict upon the judge.

The Catholics recalled that the Donatists had committed appalling acts in that town: even a basilica had been burned, and sacred books had been thrown into the fire. As for their deaths, the Catholics said that they arose more from the Donatists’ own customary practice of throwing themselves to their deaths.

When the Donatists replied to these charges, repeatedly exaggerating them as persecutions they were suffering, loudly proclaiming from these “fruits” that their opponents were a bad tree, and repeatedly demanding judgment concerning the field, the tares, and the one immortal Church, while the Catholics in turn recalled the Donatists’ schisms, rebaptisms, and the fact that the Donatists themselves had first accused their predecessors before the Emperor—and when the dispute continued for a long time amid such mutual accusations—the Presiding Judge preferred to restrain all these matters, promising to give judgment on them in a later decision.

He ordered that the document submitted by the Catholics, whose reading had already begun and then been interrupted, should be read aloud. Thus the case of the Church was concluded, a case which the Catholics had taken great care to distinguish from Caecilian’s case, since no one’s crimes could prejudice it, when it had earned so many divine testimonies against every human accusation.

From that point the case of Caecilian also began to be heard.

## CHAPTER XII

**24.** These proceedings therefore took place as the fifth stage. Two reports by Anulinus, the proconsul, to the Emperor Constantine were read aloud. One had already been read earlier (above, §8); in it he showed that the Donatists’ predecessors—that is, those belonging to the party of Majorinus—had given him documents containing accusations against Caecilian and had requested that they be sent to Constantine, and that he had sent them to the aforementioned emperor.

The other report showed that, at the emperor’s command, he had summoned ten men from each party to conduct the case, and that they had promised to do so.

Next, a letter of the aforementioned emperor to the bishops was also read. In it he had charged them to hear Caecilian’s case.

[Note: **[Col. 0637]** See below in the Appendix.]

From there, in due order, the episcopal judgment of Melchiades, bishop of Rome, and the other Gallic and Italian bishops who were with him began to be read. It had been issued in the same city of Rome.

The first part of that judgment—that is, the proceedings of the first day—was read. The accusers of Caecilian who had been sent had denied that they had anything to say against him. Donatus of Casis-Nigris had also been convicted in their presence of having caused a schism at Carthage while Caecilian was still a deacon. For it was from the schism at Carthage that the party of Donatus had arisen against the Catholic Church.

The same opponents of Caecilian had also promised that on another day they would produce those whom they were accused of having withheld as necessary to the case. Yet this too was a lie: they refused to proceed further to judgment.

When this portion of the judgment had been read, and the reading began to recount what had happened on another day, the Donatists interrupted and urgently demanded that what they were offering should first be read. They asserted that it was not procedurally proper for the acquittal of Caecilian, whom they had not yet accused, to be read first.

They disputed this at considerable length. The Catholics said that what had already begun to be read ought not to be interrupted until everything recorded in that same judgment had been completed. The Donatists, on the contrary, maintained that the material being interrupted ought never to have been begun, since it was not appropriate for a man to be defended before he had been accused.

The Catholics replied that, when the Presiding Judge was asking about the cause of the schism, they had requested that the documents submitted for reading be read, since the person of the petitioner was being considered.

They had therefore wanted these matters read for two reasons: first, so that it might become clear that the Donatists had themselves initially sought a human judge in this case, while accusing the Catholics because a human judge was presiding over the Conference; and second, so that the identity of the petitioner might be established.

Since the reading had already begun, they said it ought not to be interrupted, but should be carried through to the end.

Meanwhile, although the Presiding Judge had initially favored the Catholics’ request that the reading already begun be completed, the Donatists later prevailed upon him to permit the documents they were offering to be read first, with the other material postponed.

## CHAPTER XIII

**25.** The Donatists then prefaced their presentation by saying that Mensurius, who had been bishop of the Church of Carthage before Caecilian, had handed over the sacred Scriptures to the persecutors during the persecution.

To prove this, they read his letter to Secundus of Tigisis, who at that time held primacy among the bishops of Numidia.

In that letter Mensurius seemed to confess his own crime. Yet he had not written that he had handed over the sacred books; rather, he had removed and preserved them so that the persecutors would not find them. In the Basilica Novorum [designation uncertain], however, he had left whatever reprehensible writings of heretics there were. When the persecutors found and removed these, they demanded nothing further from him.

He added that certain men of the Carthaginian order had later suggested to the proconsul that those sent to remove and burn the Christians’ Scriptures had been deceived, since they had found nothing except certain writings that did not belong to them. The sacred books themselves, they said, were being kept in the bishop’s house and ought to be brought out and burned. The proconsul, however, refused to agree to this.

The same letter also stated that Mensurius disapproved of those who, without having been apprehended in the persecution, voluntarily presented themselves and said that they possessed Scriptures which they would not hand over, although no one had asked them for them. He prevented Christians from honoring such men.

Certain criminals and debtors of the treasury were also accused in the same letter. They wished either to escape a life burdened by many debts by taking advantage of the persecution, or thought they could cleanse themselves and, as it were, wash away their crimes, or else acquire money and enjoy luxuries in custody through the services of Christians.

The Donatists, however, brought no accusation against Mensurius except concerning the books allegedly handed over. They said that he had lied when he claimed that those were not sacred books, and that he had wished to conceal his sin—although they also accused him of the very deception itself.

They also read aloud the peaceful reply of Secundus of Tigisis to the same Mensurius. In it Secundus himself described what the persecutors had done in Numidia, including how some people had been arrested, refused to hand over the sacred Scriptures, suffered many evils, been tortured with the most severe punishments, and killed. He commended them as worthy of honor for the merit of their martyrdom, praising them for not handing over the sacred Scriptures, after the example of the woman who refused to hand over to the persecutors the two spies in Jericho, who represented the two Testaments, the Old and the New (Joshua 2).

If that example is to be understood in accordance with this symbolism, it actually supported Mensurius. In his letter Mensurius criticized those who, although they did not hand over the sacred Scriptures, nevertheless admitted that they possessed them. The woman had not done this: she did not admit that the spies being sought were with her, but denied it.

Secundus also wrote that a centurion and a beneficiarius had been sent to him by the curator and the council to demand that the divine books be burned. He said that he had replied to them, “I am a Christian and a bishop, not a traditor.” When they wished to receive from him some *ecbola* or whatever else, he had not given them this either, following the example of Eleazar Maccabaeus, who refused even to pretend that he was eating swine’s flesh, lest he provide others with an example of apostasy (2 Maccabees 6:21–28).

[Note: **[Col. 0639]** Here *ecbola* means refuse, or things of no use. The statement of Silvanus in the Acts cited above, *Against Cresconius*, book 3, §33, is relevant: “Nothing has remained here; we have thrown it all out.”]

The Catholics listened patiently until these letters of Mensurius and Secundus had been completely read, although they declared that they were private letters and had no bearing on the case of the Church.

## CHAPTER XIV

**26.** The Presiding Judge therefore reminded the Donatists that they should return the favor of patience and ordered that the documents submitted by the Catholics, of which part had already been read, be read through.

The Donatists then requested that what they were offering concerning Caecilian’s case also be read first. The Catholics permitted this without difficulty, commending the patience with which they allowed it so that the Donatists might return the same favor to them. The Presiding Judge ordered the submitted material to be read.

The Donatists’ reading consisted of a council of nearly seventy bishops held against Caecilian at Carthage. They condemned him in his absence because he had refused to come to them, alleging that he had been ordained by traditores and that, when he was a deacon, he had forbidden food to be brought to martyrs confined in prison.

Certain colleagues of Caecilian were also named as traditores in official proceedings, although those proceedings themselves were not read.

[Note: **[Col. 0639]** Among Caecilian’s colleagues there named under the accusation of traditio were Novellus of Thysica and Faustinus of Thuburbo, according to the book addressed to the Donatists after the Conference, §38.]

Among these, Felix of Abthugni was accused most bitterly, so that he was called the source of all evils.

Then each bishop pronounced his sentence, beginning with Secundus of Tigisis, who was their leader, and followed by the others. They declared that they did not maintain communion with Caecilian and his colleagues.

After this council had been read, the Catholics replied that the letters exchanged between Mensurius and Secundus had sufficiently shown that they were at peace with one another, and that no accusation or judgment concerning Mensurius’s conduct had subsequently been made.

As for the council that had been read against Caecilian, although it did not contain the name of the consul or the date, the Catholics said that they raised no accusation on that account, since this could have resulted from negligence rather than fraud.

## CHAPTER XV

**27.** The same Catholics then produced another council held under Secundus of Tigisis in the city of Cirta.

[Note: **[Col. 0639]** See book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, §30, and Optatus, book 1.]

When its consulship and date were read, the Donatists said that councils of this sort customarily contained neither the consul nor the date.

The Catholics replied that this might perhaps be the Donatists’ custom, since they did not want their councils to be exposed as false, whereas Catholic councils had always included consuls and dates.

The council produced by the Catholics then began to be read repeatedly. In it Secundus questioned individually certain men whose traditio he had heard about, and removed those who confessed from the assembly.

The text was read in such a way that, after the confession of a traditor had been read from the council of Cirta, that person’s name was also read from the council of Carthage as that of a traditor condemned in Caecilian’s case.

Next, the accusation made by Purpurius of Limata against Secundus of Tigisis himself was reached. Secundus had accused Purpurius of killing his sister’s sons in the prison at Milevis. Purpurius, in turn, accused Secundus of traditio, saying that Secundus had been detained by the curator and the council so that he would hand over the Scriptures, and that he could not have been released unless he had handed something over.

Secundus himself almost confessed this charge made against him by Purpurius—that he had been detained by the curator and the council so that he would hand over the Scriptures—in the letter he had written in reply to Mensurius. There he said that a centurion and a beneficiarius had been sent to him by the curator and the council, and that they had demanded the Scriptures or any *ecbola* from him. He said that he had not handed them over.

But since Secundus himself mentioned there so many martyrs who, when they refused to hand over the Scriptures, had been tortured and killed, how could he, after being detained and convicted and refusing to hand over anything, have suffered nothing and been released? He neither wrote this to Mensurius nor replied to Purpurius concerning it.

He did not tell the centurion and the beneficiarius that he did not possess the Scriptures; rather, he replied that he absolutely would not hand them over.

How those men could report what they had heard after releasing him without bringing about their own death is not apparent—especially since Secundus said that not merely obscure persons but even heads of households had been killed by the most savage deaths when they had given the same reply to the persecutors.

The Catholics, however, brought no accusation against Secundus on this matter. They wished only that what Purpurius had accused him of, and on account of which Secundus had set aside everything for the sake of peace and, lest a schism arise, entered into communion with traditores, should be read aloud, so that it might become clear what sort of men had pronounced sentences against the absent Caecilian.

## CHAPTER XVI

**28.** After this had been read, the Catholics requested that the material previously postponed also be read—the material concerning the council of Carthage in which it had been read that Caecilian had been condemned by many bishops.

The Catholics had read the reports of Anulinus, the proconsul.

[Note: **[Col. 0640]** The passage is corrupt and mutilated. It should probably be restored, on the basis of the *Index of the Conference*, chapters 369–370, approximately as follows: “so that the material previously postponed might also be read, since they asserted that from it it could be shown what had been done concerning Caecilian and what ought to be thought about the council of Carthage, in which it had been read that Caecilian had been condemned by many bishops. The Donatists, on the other hand, pressed the Catholics to admit that that council was genuine, because the Catholics had read the reports of Anulinus, the proconsul.”]

Those reports showed that the documents containing the accusations against Caecilian had been sent to the Emperor Constantine. By doing this, the Donatists had plainly confirmed that their predecessors had accused Caecilian before the emperor.

The Catholics replied that the council of Carthage did not prejudice the absent Caecilian, just as the Donatists’ council did not prejudice the absent Primianus—the council by which Primianus had been condemned in the case of Maximianus. The Donatist party had given greater weight to what was done afterward on behalf of Primianus than to the authority of the council by which he had previously been condemned.

So, too, in Caecilian’s case, attention ought to be given to what happened later.

Pressed by the case of Maximianus, the Donatists then said that one case did not prejudice another case, nor one person another person.

All Catholics customarily have this principle on their lips when the Donatists, accusing some people’s crimes by attributing them to others, defended their separation and accused the Christian world on the basis of certain crimes committed by Africans.

Indeed, throughout this Conference the Catholics’ entire effort to distinguish the cause of the Church from Caecilian’s cause—by asserting that wicked people mingled within the Church do not harm the good, nor stain them with their own sins—was directed precisely toward showing that one case should not prejudice another, nor one person another.

The adversaries themselves, while pursuing another matter, confirmed this in the clearest possible terms.

But when the Presiding Judge asked what the Catholics’ response was to the council of Carthage, they again replied that the similarity of Primianus’s case should not be disregarded, since the Lord Christ himself, when convicting the Jews of their deeds, led them toward the truth.

**29.** The Donatists then argued at length that Caecilian’s condemnation should be confirmed on the authority of that council of Carthage, because he had refused to come before so many priests.

They spoke as though Primianus had not likewise refused to come to those by whom he had been condemned, since he knew their faction and acted with the same resolve.

They also argued that Caecilian had not waited for a leader to be ordained by a leader, although Catholic Church custom was otherwise: the bishop of the Church of Carthage was ordained not by bishops of Numidia but by neighboring bishops, just as no metropolitan bishop ordains the bishop of the Roman Church; rather, the bishop of Ostia, as the nearest bishop, performs the ordination.

[Note: **[Col. 0641]** In the *Am.* manuscript: “had.”]

By saying this about their own custom—a custom whose origin I do not know—they attempted to prejudice the Catholic Church. If that custom were ancient, they should have brought it against Caecilian when they condemned him in his absence.

They also said that Optatus had written that Caecilian declared: “If those who ordained me are traditores, let them come and ordain me.”

[Note: **[Col. 0641]** See Optatus, book 1.]

If he did say this, it could have been said in mockery of those who were alleged to have imposed this demand upon him, since he was certain that his ordainers were not traditores.

For he did not say, “They are traditores,” but, “If they are traditores,” so that their innocence might remain to be established where it could rightly be proved.

**30.** To this, and to whatever else the Donatists had said in their lengthy argument, the Catholics replied briefly that the council of Carthage was insufficient for Caecilian’s case. The Donatists themselves had judged the matter when they accused Caecilian before the emperor and sent the case to him.

They therefore showed that what ought rather to be awaited was the outcome of the case before the emperor, to whom they had decided that the same case should be sent.

The Catholics kept insisting that, with all the shadows of delay removed, the documents should instead be read which, once read, would make it shine more clearly than daylight that the case had long ago been concluded and Caecilian’s innocence established.

The Donatists absolutely refused to have these documents read, obstructing them by inserting one matter or another.

When the Presiding Judge asked whether the council of Carthage had occurred first and Caecilian’s case had afterward been sent to the emperor, the Catholics replied that, since the council did not contain the consul or the date, they had an answer for either possibility.

If the case had first been sent to the emperor, then its outcome ought to be awaited. If the council had occurred afterward, then what ought to be sought was still not the judgment of those men, but the judgment of the emperor to whom they had thought the case should be sent after their own judgment.

The Donatists inserted many arguments about the consul and the date, asking why these were not recorded in the council of their predecessors, lest they thereby be accused of falsity. They maintained that it was an ecclesiastical custom not to record dates and consuls in episcopal decrees.

They even wanted the council of Cyprian to be read in order to prove this, since they were seeking nothing but delay. For the Catholics had not based their case on this matter when they had answered that, whether the council held at Carthage against Caecilian had occurred earlier or later, the same answer applied.

The Presiding Judge, at the Catholics’ insistence, ordered that the material previously postponed should instead be read.

## CHAPTER XVII

**31.** The Donatists then introduced another question full of delays. In truth, they wished to work in their own favor through it, if they could establish what they wanted—namely, that the council of Cirta was false. In that council the confessions of traditores who had forgiven one another so that a schism would not arise had been read, while those same men were read as having pronounced sentences against the absent Caecilian.

Attempting therefore to prove it false, they said many things. But, judging the other points themselves to be trivial, they strongly emphasized two matters and lingered over them at length.

First, the council of Cirta, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, contained a date and consul. Second, a council could not have been assembled during a time of persecution.

The Donatists therefore demanded that the Catholics either produce other ancient councils of bishops in which consuls and dates were also recorded, or read something of this kind from the sacred Scriptures themselves.

The Catholics saw that astonishing and interminable delays were being introduced over a most empty matter. Who would believe that they would accuse a document of falsity because a chronological notice had been written at the beginning with greater care, so that the truth might perhaps at some future time be investigated through it? Who, then, would believe that they would make this objection in order to force the production of ancient councils demonstrating such a custom? Or who would at that moment go and search through the ancient ecclesiastical archives?

The Catholics, seeing this, pointed out that the date and consul were recorded in the council of Melchiades. They also recalled from the sacred Scriptures themselves that the Prophets had marked out the most ancient periods in their writings, stating in what year, in which month of the year, and on what day of the month the word of the Lord came to them.

The Presiding Judge considered the objection concerning the date and consul unworthy of consideration and ordered the remaining proceedings held before Melchiades to be read. They were read.

It became clear from the judgments of all the bishops who had then assembled, and from that of Melchiades himself, that Caecilian had been acquitted and cleared, while Donatus had been condemned—the Donatus who had been present and convicted in the first hearing, namely, Donatus of Casis-Nigris, whose presence there was then established.

**32.** After this had been read, the Donatists were asked what they had to say about the council of Cirta. They returned to that subject, attempting to show that it was false.

They then said that a council could not have been assembled during a time of persecution.

The Presiding Judge did not disregard this point. Considering it substantial, he asked the Catholics for a response. Meanwhile, he asked how it could be proved that the period in question had been a time of persecution.

The Donatists then produced the proceedings of the martyrs, in which they had been heard and had suffered for their confession.

The Presiding Judge also ordered the Office to calculate the dates and report back, taking into consideration the consuls and dates both of the council of Cirta and of the proceedings of the martyrs.

[Note: **[Col. 0643]** *Am.*: “both consuls.”]

The Catholics had said that, after the suffering of those martyrs—which established that the period was one of persecution—nearly a year elapsed before the consulship and date of the council of Cirta.

The Office’s calculation, however, reported that only a month separated the events.

The Catholics therefore wanted what they had said removed from the records, so that the proceedings would retain only what the Office had reported, since they believed that to be more accurate.

The Donatists, however, refused to allow the Catholics’ statement to be removed from the records. The Catholics therefore did not press the matter, so that the Donatists’ malicious spirit might become apparent.

In fact, what the Catholics had said was more accurate. The Office, making an error in its calculation, had given a false report, as the proceedings written down later and examined more carefully demonstrated—as anyone may establish who wishes to read them and is not too lazy to calculate.

The proceedings of the martyrs, which established the period of persecution, took place in the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian, on the day before the Ides of February. The episcopal proceedings of the decree of Cirta took place after that consulship, on the third day before the Nones of March.

Thus thirteen months are found to have intervened—certainly more than the eleven months which the Catholics had earlier stated after calculating less carefully.

The Office, however, in order to be deceived and report that only a month intervened, assumed the same consulship and failed to notice the phrase “after the consulship,” at which point another year was already in progress.

Consequently, relying as though upon the Office’s true report, the Catholics were forced to maintain that those eleven or twelve bishops could have assembled in a private house during the time of persecution.

The Donatists insisted that the Catholics should demonstrate this from other councils, if they could find any councils of bishops held during a period of persecution.

Since the Catholics could not at that moment investigate the matter or search through old documents in the ecclesiastical archives, they replied that twelve men could much more easily have assembled in a private house at a time when gatherings of the common people also regularly took place, even while the persecution was raging—as the very proceedings of the martyrs showed. In their sufferings they confessed that they had held an assembly and celebrated the Lord’s service.

The Catholics had said this even before the Office calculated and gave its report.

They also stated that those episcopal proceedings from Cirta, which the diligence of their predecessors had preserved and made available down to the present time, ought to be treated in the same way as the letters of Mensurius and Secundus that the Donatists had read.

The council of Carthage, at which seventy bishops condemned Caecilian in his absence, was also mentioned by Melchiades as having been held—

[Note: **[Col. 0644]** Perhaps: “in the judgment that was held.”]

—in the judgment where Caecilian was acquitted.

The letters of Mensurius and Secundus, on the other hand, were said to be mentioned nowhere else. Consequently, their truth was supported by no other testimony; nevertheless, the Catholics did not on that account say that they were false.

The Catholics also said that the Donatists should produce, if they could, evidence that bishops had written to one another during the persecution in the same way that they claimed Mensurius and Secundus had written.

They did not say this in order to prove that the letters of Mensurius and Secundus were false—for whether those letters were genuine or false, they contributed nothing to the case—but so that the Donatists might understand how empty their evasion was in forcing the Catholics to produce other councils assembled during the persecution.

For if the Donatists were addressed with a similar obstinacy—“Produce other letters written and sent in this way during the persecution”—then, if such letters were discovered, the hidden books could be demanded, and the council, curator, centurion, and beneficiarius who were alleged to have released Secundus, although he refused to hand anything over, could be brought into danger of death.

There would be no way of finding, at that moment, other letters similarly sent by bishops to bishops over such long distances during the persecution.

**33.** A lengthy dispute therefore arose over this matter. The Donatists repeatedly maintained that, during the persecution, a council could not have been assembled to ordain a bishop, because the world was in apostasy and there was no one for whom bishops could be ordained, along with other arguments of the same kind.

The Catholics replied that even bishops could easily assemble in such a small number that the gathering ought not even to be called a council, at a time when the common people were assembling, as the proceedings of the martyrs testified. There were certainly people for whom bishops could be ordained: the very crowds whom the proceedings of the martyrs said were accustomed to assemble at that time.

These points were stated and answered continually, in many different ways. It was also established that a private house had been made available for Christians to assemble during the persecution, as was read in some of the proceedings of the martyrs. For the Donatists had said that it could not have happened that anyone offered his house at that time.

It was recalled that it was not at all incredible that those few bishops had assembled in a private house during the persecution. Indeed, while the persecution was raging, martyrs are even said to have been baptized in prison and the Sacraments celebrated there by Christians—in the very place where Christians were confined because of those same Sacraments.

## CHAPTER XVIII

At length, after the Presiding Judge had often also intervened, he declared that the bishops could have held that gathering when it had been established that the common people too had assembled. He compelled the Donatists to say whether they had anything to offer against the council and judgment of Melchiades, in which Caecilian was read to have been cleared and acquitted, since the case rested there rather than in the council of Cirta.

**34.** The Donatists then began accusing Melchiades himself of the crime of traditio. They said that their predecessors had refused his judgment for that reason, because he was a traditor—as though they had not already appeared before his judgment.

[Note: **[Col. 0645]** Something seems to be missing. Perhaps after “had appeared before his judgment” one should read: “when witnesses introduced by them themselves replied that they had nothing to say against Caecilian.” Optatus, book 1, says concerning this matter: “The witnesses introduced by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilian.” Shortly afterward he gives Melchiades’s judgment in these words: “Since it has been established that Caecilian was not accused by those who came with Donatus, in accordance with their own admission, nor convicted by Donatus in any respect, I rightly judge that he should be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired.”]

Nevertheless, when the judge pressed them as to whether any public or ecclesiastical judgment concerning Melchiades’ alleged crime of traditio could be produced, and the Catholics themselves waited and insisted that they prove it, the Donatists read some extremely long proceedings before a prefect.

Neither the identity of the prefect nor the place where these events occurred was apparent from the text. The proceedings themselves resounded with a very long recital of numerous people handing over numerous ecclesiastical objects; yet Melchiades’ name was not mentioned at all.

When this had been completed, the Presiding Judge expressed surprise that one thing had been promised and another read. The Donatists, still asking for his patience, read other proceedings. In them it was recorded that Melchiades had sent deacons, together with letters from the Emperor Maxentius and a letter from the prefect of the praetorium, to the prefect of the city, so that they might receive back the ecclesiastical buildings that the aforementioned emperor had ordered restored to Christians after they had been seized during the persecution.

When neither the Presiding Judge nor the Catholic advocates saw any crime of Melchiades in these proceedings either, the Donatists said that the deacon Straton, whom Melchiades had sent with other deacons to recover the ecclesiastical buildings, had been identified as a traditor in the proceedings read earlier. They therefore wished to implicate Melchiades also in the crime of traditio because he had employed that deacon without degrading him.

In their argument they said that Melchiades had been the third bishop after the man who was bishop at the time when that traditio had occurred.

The Presiding Judge then asked whether those proceedings concerning the alleged traditio at least explicitly stated that Straton had been a deacon.

It was read that he had been called “an encourager of the most vain superstition”—a title applied not only to him but also to the others who were handing things over.

The Donatists replied that the pagan persecutors had used this term insultingly against the religion, calling both deacons and presbyters by that name.

35. Therefore the Catholics replied that it was not surprising, and was extremely common in human affairs, for not merely two but even several people to be called by one name. It was quite possible that the traditor Strato had been a presbyter, while this other Strato was a deacon [Col. 0646], since the Donatists had said that the Gentiles called both deacons and presbyters “promoters of the most worthless superstition.” Indeed, the Gentiles might have called all clerics by this insulting name, and it would have been much more uncertain to which clerical rank that traditor belonged. Nevertheless, even if it could be shown that he had been a deacon, this would neither be incredible nor surprising, since shortly before, in the city of Rome itself, there had been two deacons named Peter.

The Catholics added this as well: even if it were demonstrated—which was not demonstrated at all—that the deacon Strato who had committed the traditio was the same person whom Melchiades later sent, together with other deacons, to recover the ecclesiastical properties, Melchiades would not thereby immediately be implicated in this crime. Persecution might have kept him far away, so that he knew nothing whatever of the matter and might have considered innocent the man whom no accuser had shown to be guilty. Against this, the Donatists repeatedly shouted the same things for a very long time, but to no avail.

36. After the Conference, they also slandered Melchiades concerning Cassianus, because this name too is found both among the deacons whom Melchiades sent to the prefect and in those records where the traditio was reported. If they had raised this point at the Conference, the Catholics could easily have replied that, among such a large crowd of Roman clerics, it was not at all surprising if there were two or more men not only named Strato but also named Cassianus—just as among the twelve Apostles we read of not only two Judases but also two Jameses. Unless, perhaps, the Donatists were permitted to distinguish Casensis from Donatus of Carthage, when they feared that their more authoritative Donatus of Carthage might be thought to have been condemned in Melchiades’ judgment, while the Catholics were not permitted, among such a multitude of Roman clerics, to have several persons bearing similar names.

For it was false that the Donatists had said that the persons, places, and regions corresponded. The records of both cases showed no correspondence of places, regions, or even the expressly stated ranks of the persons, but only a coincidence of names—a coincidence that the custom of the human race constantly produces among different individuals.

## CHAPTER XIX

37. The Judge therefore, rejecting the most uncertain suspicions, ordered that something definite be brought forward against those records, or at least that Constantine’s judgment, which had already been mentioned, be read. Constantine’s judgment was read: he had written to Eumalius, the vicar of Africa, explaining how he had heard the case of Caecilianus between the parties. He testified that, with all arbiters removed, he had found Caecilianus innocent and the others most calumnious. He also recalled the episcopal judgment delivered at Arles on behalf of Caecilianus, a judgment to which many had already assented after their disagreement, while the rest still resisted and remained at variance; hence he himself had been compelled to judge the whole matter between the parties.

After these imperial letters had been read, the Judge asked the Donatists what they had to say in reply. Thereupon the Donatists again tried to return to their calumnious accusation against Melchiades. When they were driven from this by the Judge’s ruling, and were urged to read out anything they possessed against Melchiades’ judgment or the imperial sentence, they replied that even imperial ears had been filled with evil suggestions.

The Judge then answered that he had carefully observed that judgment had been rendered between the parties. But they began demanding that it be read whether the Emperor had judged between the parties. When this was read by order of the Judge, and they found nothing to say, they began to slander the imperial letters just mentioned on the ground that they had been read without the consul’s name.

A dispute then arose. The Donatists maliciously said that the episcopal council had been read with the consul’s name, whereas the Emperor’s letters did not contain the consul’s name. The Catholics replied that the issue did not turn on this. The Judge also ruled that the matter was settled by the clearest laws: imperial enactments were not thrown into doubt even if the consuls were not named.

The Catholics then pressed them to state openly that what had been read was false; for the archives could be searched.

## CHAPTER XX

38. Repulsed on this point, they asked that Optatus be read, as they had also requested earlier, intending thereby, they said, to prove that Caecilianus had been condemned by the Emperor. This had been promised them but postponed.

The Judge therefore first wanted them to state whether they dared accuse the imperial letters of falsity. They certainly did not dare do so; nevertheless, they most maliciously kept complaining that the consul’s name was absent, while insisting much more urgently that Optatus be read.

While this was being debated for some time, the consul’s name was found on another sheet of those imperial letters. When this was pointed out, the Donatists said, “Certainly it ought not to have a consul’s name,” as though anyone had ever said that it ought not to have one—and as though, even if the consul’s name had been absent, this would prevent the truth of the imperial enactment.

After the Judge had repeatedly given them this reply, Optatus too was read. The Donatists read the passage in which he says:

“At the same time, the same Donatus requested that he be permitted to return and not go to Carthage” [Note: [Col. 0647] In earlier editions: “and go to Carthage,” with the particle *nec* omitted; we have restored it on the authority of the Germanensis manuscript. For no one will readily believe that that Donatus, already condemned, dared request permission to return to Carthage, where he had created the schism—and that this man was not bishop of Carthage but of Casæ Nigræ.]; “then, at the suggestion of his adviser Philomenus” [Note: [Col. 0647] Thus the ancient editions. But Optatus, and the Louvain editions following him, substitute *hic*, “here,” for *suffragatore*, “supporter” or “adviser.]; “it was suggested to the Emperor that, for the sake of peace, Caecilianus should be detained at Brixia” [Note: [Col. 0647] In Am. it is consistently written *Brixae*.]; “and this was done” (Optatus, Book I).

Since these words of Optatus contained no condemnation of Caecilianus whatever, although the Donatists had promised that they would demonstrate one, the Judge ordered the entire page to be read, so that the intention of the writer might be understood from the preceding and following words. The official record then read:

“Caecilianus was pronounced innocent by the judgments of all those mentioned above.”

When this was read, the Donatists said that they had not requested this passage to be read. They grew angry at those who had been unable to restrain their laughter when they heard how openly the page they had produced had spoken against themselves.

Then, when they said that by the words they themselves had read, Optatus had minimized Caecilianus’ condemnation [Col. 0648] and had not wished to state it explicitly, they were challenged to read elsewhere something manifest which, they claimed, he had minimized. When they were entirely unable to do so, and after further empty delays and perplexities—including their dispute over the name Donatus, since it was not Donatus of Carthage but Donatus of Casæ who had appeared in Melchiades’ judgment against Caecilianus, a point the Catholics also conceded—the matter was eventually passed over [Note: [Col. 0648] See below, Book II after the Conference, §54.].

## CHAPTER XXI

39. Since it was established from Constantine’s letters that he had heard the case between the parties and judged in favor of Caecilianus, the Judge compelled the Donatists to reply if they had anything to say. They requested that their own written petition be read, which they said had been submitted to Constantine by their predecessors.

In this petition they showed clearly enough how falsely they had spoken about Caecilianus’ condemnation at Brixia. For the petition itself showed how Constantine had decided against them. They said there that they would in no way communicate with “that scoundrel, his bishop,” and that they were prepared to endure whatever he wished to do to them. By “that scoundrel, Constantine’s bishop,” they clearly intended Caecilianus.

How, then, could they call Caecilianus Constantine’s bishop, while affirming in their speech against Constantine that they would not communicate with him, if they had defeated him before Constantine and knew that he had been condemned by Constantine at Brixia?

## CHAPTER XXII

40. When the Catholics therefore said that the Donatists had read this against themselves—and the Judge himself had made the same ruling—they added another powerful confirmation of the Donatists’ falsehood by reading Constantine’s own letter to Verinus, the vicar, in which he ordered that they be released to their own discretion and indicated that he had commanded them to return from exile [Note: [Col. 0648] See the same work, §§53–56.].

In this letter Constantine denounced them in such terms that nothing more disgraceful could be found in that act of clemency. He certainly would not have censured them in this way, but rather praised them, if Caecilianus had been defeated by them before him and condemned by him at Brixia and exiled.

Thus, by producing and reading these statements against themselves, they showed most clearly that they had been defeated by Caecilianus in the judgment of the Emperor mentioned above. They also most plainly refuted their own falsehood that he had been condemned. And because they boasted that the Catholics were persecutors while they themselves were sufferers, they nevertheless wished falsely to boast that Caecilianus had been condemned by the Emperor on account of their accusations.

After these passages had been read, the Catholics pointed out—and the Judge briefly acknowledged the same thing, as he himself clearly saw—that the passages had been read in their own favor, that is, in defense of Caecilianus’ innocence against them. The Donatists replied: “Your authority says nothing about freedom of choice.” They thought that, on the basis of Constantine’s letters, this freedom might be granted to them by the Judge then present, and therefore considered that the letters should be read against themselves in Caecilianus’ case as well.

When the Judge answered that he had received a different instruction from the Emperor of the present time, they turned to another matter [Col. 0649] which, even more remarkably, they repeatedly produced against themselves.

## CHAPTER XXIII

41. They also read another letter of the same Emperor Constantine, addressed to Probianus, the proconsul [Note: [Col. 0649] It is preserved above, in Book III against Cresconius, §80.]. This letter indeed did not contain the consuls’ names, but the Catholics did not wish to make an issue of this mutual objection, although here too the Donatists convicted themselves of how maliciously they had raised the matter against the Catholics. For the earlier document from which Constantine’s judgment had been read—the judgment by which Caecilianus was acquitted—did not contain the consuls’ names, although they were soon found in another document.

This letter sent to Probianus, the proconsul, contains the Emperor’s order that Ingentius be sent to him. Through Ingentius’ testimony, Felix of Abtugni, the ordainer of Caecilianus, had been acquitted of the charge of traditio in the hearing before the proconsul Aelianus.

The Donatists said that they were reading this imperial order in order to suggest that Caecilianus’ case had still been pending even after the judgment in which Constantine had already written that, hearing the case between the parties, he had brought everything to a conclusion. Yet in the very letter to Probianus that they read—as though it showed that the judgment was still pending, since the Emperor had ordered Ingentius to be sent to him—they read so much against themselves that it is altogether astonishing with what eyes they could have looked at those words or with what mouth they could have pronounced them.

For Constantine said there that the proconsul Aelianus had granted a proper hearing and that Felix had been found innocent of the burning of the divine books. He added that those who would not cease troubling Felix for many days were to be refuted in the present proceedings, so that it might become entirely clear to them that they were trying in vain to bring odium upon Caecilianus and to rise up violently against him.

By these letters, therefore, they showed that not only Caecilianus but also Felix had been cleared, and that they themselves had appeared before the Emperor as persecutors of the innocent.

## CHAPTER XXIV

42. Taking advantage of this opportunity, the Catholics also produced for reading the report of Aelianus himself, then proconsul, which had been sent to Constantine concerning this matter. In it Aelianus recalled that he had heard and concluded Felix’s case. They also produced the proconsular records [Note: [Col. 0649] They are preserved below in the Appendix.], in which Felix was acquitted and, on the testimony of all the necessary persons, proved innocent of the charge of traditio.

After these documents had been read, the Judge asked what could be said against them. The Donatists then repeatedly returned to what they had already begun saying earlier. They asked whether Ingentius had been sent to the court at the Emperor’s command and what had subsequently been done, demanding that the Catholics produce this evidence. They tried, insofar as they could, to refute the proconsular records by which Felix had been acquitted, alleging favoritism by the judge, the substitution of persons, and the other charges that people habitually throw out in suspicious complaint against records by which they have been defeated.

They also said that Felix had not been properly acquitted in his absence.

The Catholics replied that everything read plainly concerned the acquittal of Caecilianus and Felix [Col. 0650]. If the Donatists thought that, when Ingentius was sent to the court, a judgment had been rendered in their favor and that the judgment had been changed—the judgment by which Constantine, hearing the case between the parties, had found Caecilianus cleared and had condemned them as most calumnious—they themselves ought to produce the evidence.

When the Catholics said this, the consuls could not be examined within that brief period. Anyone who considers their sequence in the records themselves will find that Caecilianus was acquitted by the Emperor Constantine later than Felix’s case was examined and cleared by the proconsul Aelianus [Note: [Col. 0650] See below, Book after the Conference, §56.]. He will also find that several years later Constantine wrote to the vicar Verinus—the letters which the Donatists themselves read—where they claimed that the Emperor had granted them freedom of choice, while in those letters he portrayed them as utterly wicked and hostile to Christian peace.

He certainly would not have done this if, when Ingentius was sent to the court, he had judged anything in their favor against Caecilianus.

The Judge therefore ruled that records supported by such great antiquity could not be set aside unless later records to the contrary were read. The Catholics also said that Felix’s absence had served rather to establish his innocence, since suspicion of favoritism would more likely have arisen had he been present.

## CHAPTER XXV

43. The Judge then began pressing the Donatists to produce at once any later records they had against the acquittal of Caecilianus or Felix. At this point they tried once again to return, as though from the beginning, to matters they had already mentioned repeatedly and to which the Catholics had repeatedly replied and which had already been concluded.

The Judge ruled that they ought now to be ashamed of repeating the same things, and repeatedly compelled them to produce anything they had that should be read against the exceedingly clear acquittals of Caecilianus and Felix. But they produced absolutely nothing against those documents and nevertheless did not cease repeating the same matters, demanding that judgment be given on what they had said.

The Judge, on the contrary, insisted that they should read anything they had that could be read against the imperial and proconsular judgments, so that judgment might be rendered concerning everything, since the laws forbid the delivery of a half-complete sentence.

The Catholics also urged that, since everything had been made clear to the Judge and the Donatists could find no reply but continued repeating themselves, the case should at last be brought to an end.

Finally, the Judge said: “If you have nothing to read in opposition, please withdraw, so that a complete judgment concerning everything may be written.”

When both parties had withdrawn, he wrote his judgment [Note: [Col. 0650] The judgment is preserved in the Appendix.]. He then had the parties brought back in and read it aloud. In it he included everything he could remember from the lengthy proceedings of the three days. Although he did not recall every matter in the order in which it had occurred, he nevertheless stated everything truthfully, declaring that the Donatists had been refuted by the disclosure of all the evidence.

## [AFTER THE CONFERENCE, TO THE DONATISTS]

[Col. 0651]

## In the Subsequent Work, Book II of the *Retractationes*, Chapter XL (C)

I also wrote a sufficiently large book, as I think, and composed it with adequate care for the Donatists themselves [Note: [Col. 0651] He means the laypeople of Donatus’ party, to whom Letter 141 was also addressed; he mentions it below. Concerning this Letter 141, or perhaps concerning the subsequent book to the Donatists, Augustine wrote to Marcellinus in 412, in Letter 139, §3: “As I also had an arduous letter to the Donatist laypeople themselves concerning this same Conference of ours, which I have just completed after several nights of labor.”], after the Conference we held with their bishops, so that they would not be deceived by them any longer.

In it I also answered some of their foolish claims that had reached us, which, after being defeated, they broadcast wherever and however they could. I included these in addition to what I had said about the records of the Conference, so that people might briefly understand what had taken place.

I dealt with the matter much more briefly in another letter to those same people. But because, at the council of Numidia, all of us who were present agreed that this should be done, it is not among my letters [Note: [Col. 0651] It is now Letter 141, in its present order.]. It begins as follows:

“Silvanus the elder, Valentinus, Innocentius, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus, and the other bishops of the council of Certa to the Donatists.”

This book begins as follows: “Why, Donatists, are you still being deceived?”

[Col. 0651]

## One Book of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, to the Donatists after the Conference

[Note: [Col. 0651] Written in the year 412.]  
[Note: [Col. 0651] The book *To the Donatists after the Conference* was corrected with the assistance of the exceptionally elegant and ancient Corbie manuscript, the Michaelinus and Beccensis manuscripts, and also with the various readings of the Belgian manuscripts used by the Louvain editors, as well as the earliest and most authoritative editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]  
[Note: [Col. 0651] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractationes* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

Augustine warns the laypeople of the Donatist party not to be deceived any longer by their bishops. The Records show that, at the Conference held at Carthage, these bishops had been refuted by their own words, judgments, and documents produced by them themselves. Augustine dispels their empty slanders against the judgment of that Conference, briefly examining and refuting certain writings which they circulated publicly after the Conference.

[Col. 0651] ## CHAPTER I

1. Why, Donatists, are you still being deceived by your bishops, whose deceitful darkness has been dispelled by the clear light; whose error has been exposed; whose obstinacy has been overcome? Why do they still parade their empty lies before you? Why do you still believe defeated men?

When they tell you that the judge was corrupted by a bribe, what new thing are they doing? What else have all defeated people accustomed to do when they refuse to agree with the truth except lie about the judge’s injustice?

Ask them—and let them first answer you this, if they can: why did they dare to come to Carthage and meet with us in one place for the sake of the Conference?

Several years earlier we had publicly summoned them to meet us, so that the truth might become clear through our conference and the disagreement dividing us might be removed. But, refusing to face the truth itself, they replied in the records: “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditores should meet together.”

Why, then, did they now agree to meet with us? I think they would not have done what they considered unworthy unless they knew that we were not the offspring of traditores.

Or let them answer you themselves: why did they say, “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditores should meet together,” and afterward meet with us in one place? What compelled them to do what was unworthy? They were not brought there in chains; they came entirely free.

If they say that the Emperor had ordered it, then do they do what is unworthy whenever the Emperor orders it? Why, then, are they angry at certain traditores who have nothing to do with our case? To hand the Lord’s books over to persecutors is certainly unworthy. Yet, when a traditor did this, according to them he bears no guilt, because the Emperor had ordered it.

We say this not according to the truth but according to their perversity. For they themselves said it; the public records proclaim it; they said it in the official proceedings. It was not some unknown person but their own bishop of Carthage, Primianus, who said this.

Primianus gave this written statement to the magistrate of Carthage and instructed his deacon to have it declared in the official proceedings:

“It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditores should meet together.”

Here we are, meeting together in one place. What do they reply to this?

If they say, “It is not unworthy,” why did they lie when they said that it was unworthy? If they say, “It is unworthy,” why did they do what was unworthy?

They can maintain in only one way that they did not do what was unworthy and that Primianus’ words did not contain a lie: by saying, “It is indeed unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditores should meet together, but we met with you in one place because we discovered that you are not the offspring of traditores.”

But if that is so, why, when they were already meeting with us in one place, did they bring those very accusations against us? Was it perhaps so that we too might discover that they were not the sons of martyrs?

Martyrs are called witnesses; and the witnesses of Christ are true witnesses. But these men proved to be false witnesses, accusing others of the crimes of traditio and being unable to prove even those accusations.

## CHAPTER II

2. Why do you still heed human lies and not heed divine testimonies? Why do you still believe defeated human beings and not believe the truth, which has never been defeated?

The truth of God, as we also established in the Conference itself, bore witness to its Church through many documents of the holy Scriptures, through the prophetic and evangelical writings. The place from which Christ’s Church was to begin was identified, as were the ends of the earth to which it was to extend.

The Lord says that his Church will exist among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). The divine reading is recited, showing how it began from Jerusalem, where, after the faithful had first gathered, the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven (Acts 2). The divine readings are recited, showing how it spread from Jerusalem through neighboring and distant regions.

The names of places have been explicitly stated; the names of cities have been made known, cities in which the Church of Christ was founded through apostolic labor. These places and cities also deserved to receive letters from the Apostles. The Donatists themselves read those letters in their assemblies, yet they do not communicate with the Churches of those places and cities that deserved to receive the letters. Instead, they charge them with certain crimes of Africans, claiming that those Churches perished through contact with the Africans, even though the Donatists themselves said in the very Conference we recently held at Carthage that neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person (Conference 3, chapter 372).

## CHAPTER III

3. They said this when we told them:

“The council you produce against Caecilianus does not harm the absent Caecilianus any more than the council held in the case of Maximianus, in which Primianus was condemned, harms the absent Primianus.”

For there they produced more than seventy bishops who condemned Caecilianus in his absence [Note: [Col. 0653] The Belgian and Gallican manuscripts all read: “For there they produced a council in which seventy or more bishops had condemned Caecilianus in his absence.” The sense is: “They produced a council in which seventy or more bishops had condemned Caecilianus in his absence.”], while approximately one hundred bishops [Note: [Col. 0653] The printed editions read “not fewer than one hundred.” All the manuscripts, however, read “approximately one hundred” [Col. 0654]. This reading is more like the other passage, §52, where we find “nearly one hundred.”] of their own party are produced who had condemned Primianus in his absence.

When we therefore told them that the former did not harm Caecilianus just as the latter did not harm Primianus, since both councils had been held against absent persons, they immediately found nothing to reply and, suffering dreadful embarrassment, said:

“Neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person.”

This is what the Catholic Church has in its mouth against all human slanders. But now it has done so with much greater force and much greater freedom, since the confession of its enemies has confirmed what the truth has always maintained.

Who, then, could endure this without sorrow? Who could restrain a groan? Who would not break into tears and a cry of anguish if he considered it properly?

Behold: so that Primianus, condemned by the bishops of Donatus’ party, does not lose his episcopate; so that Primianus, though condemned, does not disturb Donatus’ party—neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person. Yet so that Caecilianus, whom his enemies likewise condemned in his absence, may not be regarded as a bishop and may contaminate all Christian peoples to the ends of the earth, one case does prejudice another case and one person another person.

## CHAPTER IV

4. But let the Churches of Pontus, Bithynia, Asia, Cappadocia, and the other eastern regions, to which the blessed Apostle Peter writes (1 Peter 1:1), cry out with the voice [Note: [Col. 0654] The manuscripts read, “if with the voice.”] of that very unity:

“O party of Donatus, we do not understand what you are saying. Why do you not communicate with us? If Caecilianus did something evil which was neither proved nor demonstrated to us, nevertheless, if he did something evil, why does it prejudice us? If you do not wish to listen to us, listen to yourselves saying, ‘Neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person.’ Can your perversity go so far that these words are effective to prevent Primianus from prejudicing you, while these words are ineffective to prevent Caecilianus from prejudicing us?”

Let the seven eastern Churches to which the Apostle John writes likewise cry out—Ephesus, Smyrna, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea, and Pergamum (Revelation 1:11)—and say:

“What have we done to you, brothers, that you preferred to belong to Donatus rather than to our communion? If Caecilianus sinned—even though you were unable to demonstrate his crime, since he too was condemned in his absence, just as your Primianus was—whatever he may have been, what have we done to you? Why do you refuse to have peace with Christians, as Christians? Why do you sever the common Sacraments among us? What have we done to you?

“Why does Primianus’ case not prejudice Donatus’ party, unless what you said is true: ‘Neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person’? Why, then, does Caecilianus’ case prejudice Christ’s inheritance, in which we have been planted through the labor of the Apostles?

“The Apostle John writes to one of us that there are in Sardis a few names of those who have not defiled their garments (ibid. 3:4). Yet the garments of those few were not polluted by those who were unclean in that same Church, because what you said is true: neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person.

“How, then, can Caecilianus’ case and person prejudice us? Or if they do not prejudice us, why do you separate yourselves from us?

“Let the Churches to which the Apostle Paul writes also speak—the Churches of the Romans, Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. For Galatia and Ephesus have already been mentioned above. Let these Churches also say:

“‘Brothers, you read every day the letters sent to us, you who still wish to belong to Donatus’ party. In those very letters the Apostle greeted us with the name of peace, saying, “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Why did you learn peace by reading our letters, yet refuse to maintain it with us?

“‘To us, who live in lands so distant and beyond the sea, you bring forward against us the African Caecilianus. Surely what you said is true: neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person. What is this private and peculiar sanctification by which you allow the case of the African Primianus not to prejudice the African party of Donatus, and the person of Primianus of Carthage not to prejudice the person of Felicianus of Mustitana, while African prejudices are sent so far away that Caecilianus’ case prejudices us?’”

5. Let the Catholic Church established in Africa itself also speak, joined to all those Churches in the peace and unity of Christ. Let it say:

“Caecilianus’ case does not prejudice me, since a sentence was issued against him in his absence by seventy bishops. It does not prejudice the Church spread throughout the whole world, in whose communion I remain.

“Or rather, let Primianus’ case prejudice Donatus’ party, since his fellow bishops condemned him in his absence by an even larger council. But if it does not prejudice that party because neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person, then this justice must be observed all the more toward the catholic unity of Christ, if Donatus’ party demands that it be observed toward itself.

“This is what the Catholic Church established in Africa proclaims:

“‘O party of Donatus, you spoke these words; you recognized these words as your own; you even subscribed to these words: “Neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person.”

“‘I count Caecilianus among the spirits of those who have long since come to rest; you still see Felicianus living with you in the body, the man by whom Primianus was condemned. In Primianus’ own case you condemned Felicianus, and afterward you joined him to Primianus and to yourself as bishop, just as he was.

“‘If the principle that neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person has such force that Felicianus’ communion with you today does not prejudice you, how can the memory of Caecilianus, who died long ago, prejudice me?’”

6. What answer do those give who still parade empty claims before you—lies that will harm their own salvation if they do not correct themselves? Why do they still say that we corrupted the Judge so that a sentence might be issued in our favor?

Did we perhaps also corrupt that bishop, a man of such distinguished standing among you and such a celebrated defender, so that he would say such things on our behalf [Note: [Col. 0655] He seems to mean Emeritus.]?

For this was what we were striving for with all our strength; this was what we insisted upon: to show that Caecilianus’ case and person, whatever he may have been, did not pertain to the case and person of the Church, which God has strengthened by his holy testimonies.

We also pursued this through evangelical comparisons: the case and person of the weeds should not prejudice the case and person of the wheat, although both grow together in the same field under the same rain until the harvest, when they must be separated; the person of the chaff should not prejudice the person of the grain, although both are threshed together on the same threshing floor until they are separated by the final winnowing; the case and person of the goats should not prejudice the case and person of the sheep, although both kinds of animals are kept mixed together in common pastures until the supreme Shepherd, at the final judgment, separates some to the left and others to the right; the case and person of the bad fish should not prejudice the case and person of the good fish, although they are caught within the same nets and are to be separated at the shore at the end—that is, at the end of the sea, which signifies the end of the age (Matthew 13 and 25).

Through these parables and figures the Church was foretold as possessing good and evil together until the end of the age, in such a way that the evil cannot harm the good, whether the evil are unknown or are tolerated for the sake of the peace and tranquility of the Church, when it is not necessary to expose or accuse them, or when they cannot be demonstrated to other good people.

Nevertheless, vigilance in correction must not cease: reproving, degrading, excommunicating, and using the other lawful and permitted forms of discipline that take place daily in the Church while the peace of unity is preserved, according to the Apostle’s command and with charity maintained. He said:

“If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed; and do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

Thus discipline preserves patience, and patience moderates discipline; and both are directed toward charity, lest undisciplined patience foster iniquity or impatient discipline destroy unity.

## CHAPTER V

7. When these things are done by the good, they are not defiled by the wicked. For they do not share in the wicked’s sins by consenting to them, and they withdraw from the wicked—if not by bodily separation, then by the spiritual difference of their lives and the dissimilarity of their conduct—in obedience to the Lord’s command:

“Depart from there, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isaiah 52:11).

Those who think this must be observed only physically, and not spiritually, fall through the arrogance of their vanity into what the Lord condemns through the same prophet, saying:

“Those who say, ‘Do not touch me, for I am pure’—this man is the smoke of my indignation” [Note: [Col. 0656] The printed editions have *hi*, in the plural. But the manuscripts have *hic*, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, *houtos*.] (ibid. 65:5).

Your bishops thought this was what they had to do when, after the Judge offered both sides seats, they refused to sit with us. They said that it had been written for them not to sit with such people, understanding in a carnal rather than a spiritual way what is stated in the Psalm:

“I will not sit with the ungodly.”

Yet they did what is prohibited in that very passage of the Psalm as well. For there the Prophet says:

“I will not enter in with those who do iniquity” (Psalm 25:5, 4).

If, then, they refused to sit with us because they knew or supposed that we were wicked, why did they enter with us, something that is likewise prohibited, being partly holy and partly polluted? Was it not because, by failing to understand the holy Scriptures and by thinking in a carnal manner, they shattered unity itself?

8. Therefore the wicked do not defile the good when they are situated in the same field, on the same threshing floor, in the same pastures, and in the same nets; for the good do not share communion with them, but with the altar and the Sacraments of God. They do, however, share communion with the wicked if they consent to the deeds of the wicked. For it is written: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who approve of those who do them” (Rom. 1:32).

## CHAPTER VI

When, however, the wicked are tolerated out of the necessity of preserving peace, they are not sought as partners in sharing iniquity. Thus, although the wheat drinks the gentle rain together with the weeds, it nevertheless preserves its own fertility and is not changed into the weeds’ barrenness; rather, both grow together until the harvest, lest, when the weeds are gathered, the wheat too should perhaps be uprooted with them. The wicked have no share with the good in salvation or in destruction. For what fellowship has righteousness with iniquity? The wicked have no partnership with the good in the kingdom or in eternal fire. For what fellowship has light with darkness? The wicked have no harmony with the good in life or will.
