For what harmony has Christ with Belial? The good have no portion with the wicked, neither in the punishment of crime nor in the reward of piety. For what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever? (2 Cor. 6:14–15).

And although, within the same nets until they reach the shore, they receive the divine Sacraments together, the former are joined together and the latter are separated; the former are in harmony and the latter discordant; the former have a portion with mercy and the latter with judgment—for the Church sings mercy and judgment to the Lord (Ps. 101:1)—and whoever eats unworthily eats judgment, not to another but to himself (1 Cor. 11:29). For from that very bread, and from that very hand of the Lord, Judas too received a portion, and Peter likewise; and yet what fellowship, what harmony, what portion did Peter have with Judas? For neither does one cause prejudice to another cause, nor one person to another person.

9. Whether, then, the wicked go out—of whom it is written, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19)—or whether they appear to be within, concerning whom the blessed Cyprian speaks with complete clarity, saying: “For even if weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that, because we see weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (*Letter to Maximus*)—your bishops dared not answer these words at all, although for a long time they argued unsuccessfully that the aforesaid weeds would not be in the Church, because the Lord said, “The field is this world” (Matt. 13:38), and did not say, “The field is the Church.”

We, however, said that “world” was used to signify the Church, just as Cyprian also understood it, because the future Church was prefigured throughout the whole world. Hence they said that “world” was always used in a bad sense, and they produced testimonies from Scripture, since it is written, “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15), and other passages of this kind. We, on the other hand, replied that in Scripture “world” is used not only in a bad sense but also in a good one, and among other passages we recalled this: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19)—and surely he reconciles to himself none other than the Church.

## CHAPTER VII

Whether, then, the wicked go out, or whether they remain within, either unknown or visible, the mercy and justice of God bring this about: the wicked do not harm the good who do not consent to their evils, but each carries his own burden. Thus a son does not receive the sins of his father unless he has imitated him in his evils; rather, “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4).

When someone consents to the wicked in evil, he already has one cause with them and becomes one person with the whole fellowship of the wicked. Consequently, when they perish and are condemned together, each person’s own cause and own person prejudice him, not someone else’s. But when the good and the wicked hear the same word of God together and receive the Sacraments of God together, yet have different causes for their actions and bear different persons through the diversity of their wills, some eating the same holy food worthily and others unworthily, neither does one cause prejudice another cause nor one person another person.

10. Accordingly, whatever testimonies of the divine Scriptures your bishops were able to recall, by which the Church was foretold as pure from every mixture with wicked people, those testimonies did not foretell it as it is now, but as it will be after this mortality, in eternal life. And whatever testimonies of Scripture they produced concerning sons whom they wished, because they imitated their parents’ wickedness deservedly, to have one cause with them—because they did not understand them, they forced the divine testimonies to fight among themselves. They did not distinguish and reconcile both statements of God according to the differences of times, causes, and persons; rather, just as they wanted the divine documents to fight against us, so they wanted them to fight among themselves. Nor is it surprising that they did not understand the peace of God’s Scripture, since they did not have peace with his Church.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. We, however, accepting both sets of testimonies, demonstrated their agreement. For we accepted both what they recalled as having been said to the Church in their letters: “The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you” (Isa. 52:1), and what is written: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matt. 13:30). The latter is in the field; the former will be in the granary.

Finally, those very men who argued for a long time that the weeds permitted to grow together with the wheat until the harvest were not in the Church but in the world—contrary to the understanding of the martyr Cyprian, who said, “And even if weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that, because we see weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church”—and who refused to agree that “world” could signify the Church, contrary to the Apostle’s words, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” and contrary to the words of the Lord himself, “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17)—for the world cannot be reconciled to God and saved through him unless “world” is understood as signifying the Church, which alone is reconciled to God and saved through him—nevertheless, in that parable which we recalled from the Gospel, namely, that good and bad fish are held mixed together in the same nets until they are separated on the shore, that is, at the end of the age (Matt. 13:47–50), overcome by the evidence of truth, they confessed that the wicked remain mixed in the Church until the end of the age. But they said that these wicked are hidden, since they are unknown to the priests in the same way that fish within the nets, while still in the sea, are unseen by the fishermen.

How, then, can the prophetic testimony that they included in their reply—the statement spoken to the Church, “The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you”—be understood as applying to the present time, when the Church is compared to nets, in which, while they are still in the sea, they confessed that bad fish are mixed with the good or hidden among them? Hence it is clear that only in the future age, after the judgment, will no uncircumcised or unclean person pass through the Church. O violence of truth, which torments its enemies—not in the flesh but in the heart—so that they confess it unwillingly!

## CHAPTER IX

12. Behold, what we were saying has been made clear: the times of the Church must be distinguished. It is not now as it will be after the resurrection; now it has the wicked mixed within it, whereas then it will have them not at all. Those divine testimonies by which God foretold that the Church would be wholly free from any mixture with the wicked refer to that purity of hers, not to the mixture of the present time.

Behold, even those who said that hidden wicked people are now mixed within the Church have been compelled by evangelical truth to confess no other conclusion. Behold, now an unclean person passes through her, even if hidden. Therefore this is not the time foretold when the Prophet says, “The uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you.” Thus they pass through now, even if hidden. For the very words “shall no longer” show that they were previously accustomed to pass through, but will not pass through thereafter.

And they maliciously demanded of us how the devil could have sown weeds in the Church of Christ, although they themselves admitted that at least hidden wicked people are mixed within the Church, and were unwilling to consider that they must have been sown by the devil.

## CHAPTER X

13. Even what they thought they had discovered as a clever argument was actually brought forward against themselves. If the Lord compared the Church to nets that gather good and bad fish together because he wished the wicked in the Church to be understood as not manifest but hidden—people whom the priests do not know, just as fishermen do not know what the nets have caught beneath the waves—then for this very reason he also compared it to a threshing floor, so that manifest wicked people too might be foretold as being mixed with the good there.

For the chaff that is mixed with the grain on the threshing floor does not itself lie hidden beneath the waves. It is so visible to everyone that rather the grain within it is hidden, while the chaff itself is manifest. Concerning this likeness of the threshing floor, since we had also included it among the other Gospel images, they could write nothing against us in their letters except that the prophet Jeremiah had said, “What has straw in common with wheat?” (Jer. 23:28). He said this because they are not alike, not because they cannot be mixed; because they will not be together in the granary, not because they are not threshed together on the threshing floor.

Although, when Jeremiah said this, he was not speaking about the people of God but about the dreams of men and the visions of prophets, since these two things cannot be compared by any likeness, just as the emptiness of straw cannot be compared with the fullness of wheat.

14. Your bishops did indeed attempt to deny that the Gospel says that the Church is compared to a threshing floor. But, soon convicted by the Gospel words, they turned to saying that there too hidden wicked people, not manifest ones, were signified. Of these it is written: “He will come with a winnowing shovel in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12).

You, therefore, judge for yourselves: open your eyes and lend your ears to the truth. If, as they themselves said, the Lord compared the Church to nets because he wanted the wicked in it to be understood as not manifest but hidden, people whom the priests do not see just as fishermen do not see the fish beneath the waves within the nets, is the threshing floor also threshed under water or under the earth? Or, at least, is it beaten during the night rather than in the sunlight? Does a blind farmer work upon it?

How much better it would be for them to correct themselves than to distort the holy Gospels and attempt to twist the Lord’s words toward the empty error of their own minds! Either the likeness of the fish was placed by the Lord not because of hidden wicked people, but only because of the wicked mixed within the Church; or else distinct likenesses were assigned to distinct things: the fish signify hidden wicked people, and the threshing floor manifest wicked people. The former are mixed with the good in the Church until the shore, and the latter until the winnowing shovel.

They themselves admonish us to understand the chaff on the threshing floor as manifest wicked people in the Church, since they want the rejected fish within the swimming nets to be understood as hidden wicked people: just as the fishermen do not know the former, so the priests do not know the latter. Why should we not therefore say that the chaff signifies manifest wicked people because the threshers see it openly? But just as the fish cannot be separated before they reach the shore, so the chaff cannot be winnowed before the appointed end.

God, however, guards the innocence of his saints and faithful people, like the good fish and the rich grain, so that within these nets the mixed kinds destined for rejection do not harm them, and within this threshing floor the mixed chaff destined for winnowing does not harm them. For, as they themselves said, reread, and subscribed: “Neither will one cause be able to prejudice another cause, nor one person another person.”

## CHAPTER XI

15. Perhaps they would deny that they had said these words if they could not be convicted by their own subscription. Behold how carefully action was taken for your salvation, so that they might subscribe to our words: something they absolutely did not want to do, and which shame eventually compelled them to do. Their words remain on record where they refused to do this, and again other words where they agreed to do what they had first denied. Everything was written down, and everyone subscribed.

They therefore appeared unwilling to subscribe so that they might be able to deny having said what they had said and accuse the judge of having falsified the proceedings. Since they cannot do this now, they say that the proceedings themselves were falsified—although they themselves made the judge rule against them, by saying so much against themselves on our behalf. And so that they could not deny it, even though compelled and unwilling, they subscribed to their own statements.

They were unwilling to subscribe so that, by alleging that the proceedings had been falsified, they might be permitted to deny what they had said. Later, when the judge insisted, they agreed because they realized that everyone could see that their unwillingness to subscribe indicated nothing else except that they feared their words would be read back to them.

[Note: “Am.” and “Er.” read, “that nothing else was being adjudicated against them.” “Lov.” reads, “that they were claiming nothing else.” This is corrected with the aid of the Beccensis manuscript.]

For they preferred to defend their own statements later by whatever clouds of obfuscation they could summon rather than condemn them so quickly.

## CHAPTER XII

16. But observe, we beg you, how by their very defense they entangle themselves still more deeply, advance our case, and utterly destroy their own. After the Conference, when they had been defeated and wished to appeal, these words were brought against them. They attempt to defend them by becoming even more deeply entangled, whenever you ask them what they had done.

They think you have no understanding, so that you do not realize that they have been defeated in every respect, when they tell you things they certainly would not say if they could find anything useful to say. For who could tolerate defeated men complaining that the sentence was pronounced against them at night—as though judges were not often held by the necessity of hearing cases, so that they are compelled to sit until a late part of the night? Or is what is said not true because it is said at night?

They do not listen to Scripture crying out, “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. 42:8); and again, “To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth throughout the night” (Ps. 92:2). Or, when they said that the persecutors came at night to seize the Lord, did they fail to consider that during those very nighttime hours the Lord also preached the truth to his disciples? Nor did they wish to notice that it is written that the Apostle Paul prolonged his discourse until midnight (Acts 20:7).

If they had anything true to say, the night could not have hindered them. But they were suffering a very dark night in their minds when they brought forward so much against themselves and did not correct their perverse spirit in the light of truth. It was still day, moreover, when, in forensic fashion, they raised a procedural objection concerning the time, saying that the case had lapsed and could no longer be heard at all. They did not understand that they had shown people nothing except how greatly they feared that the case should be heard, in which their perversity and Catholic truth would be exposed.

## CHAPTER XIII

17. It was still day when, wishing to destroy the judgment of Melchiades, bishop of Rome, by which Caecilian had been cleared and acquitted, they also declared Melchiades himself to have been a traditor. When proof of this accusation was demanded from them, they read out very extensive proceedings in which the name of Melchiades did not appear as having handed anything over.

They also read out other proceedings in which it was recorded that Melchiades had sent deacons, with letters from the emperor Maxentius and the praetorian prefect, to the prefect of the city, so that they might recover the places that had been taken from Christians during the persecution. Since no crime of Melchiades appeared there at all, they said that in the earlier proceedings concerning the handing-over, a traditor named Strato had been mentioned. They insisted, without demonstrating it, that he was the same man as one of the deacons whom Melchiades had sent to recover the places.

For they did not even show that Strato, who had handed things over, had been a deacon. We replied that even if he had been, two deacons named Peter had belonged to the same clergy of the Roman Church a short time earlier.

Thus, blind in mind, they wove together dark calumnies, adding an utterly obvious falsehood: that not only the name but also the places, regions, and persons corresponded, so that Strato could be shown to have been no one other than the same man. Yet in those proceedings nothing corresponding was read except the similarity of the name; and human custom is full of such cases, since not merely two but even more people are often called by one name.

For they themselves too loudly insisted that their Carthaginian Donatus must be distinguished from Donatus of Casa, lest he be thought to be the one condemned in the judgment of Melchiades. Many hold him in high esteem.

[Note: The Corbeiensis and Michaelinus manuscripts read, “whom they hold in very high esteem.” The Beccensis reads, “and whom they do not hold in very high esteem.”]

They insisted that Donatus of Carthage must be distinguished because he had been sent against Caecilian to the episcopal judgment of Melchiades. They carried such a thick night in their hearts that they did not want their own Donatus to be disgraced by the similarity of his name, yet wanted to stain Melchiades by the similarity of someone else’s name.

Now, moreover, they are said to add the name Cassianus to Strato, although they kept silent about it at the Conference—as if Strato alone could have had a namesake, and Cassianus could not.

Prevented by their inner night, they could not consider that there were not only two Johns, one the Baptist and the other the Evangelist, but also two Simons, one Peter and the other Magus; and finally, even among that very small number of Apostles, not only two Jameses, one of Alphaeus and the other of Zebedee, but also two Judases, one holy and the other the devil. Anyone similarly blind in mind who were to slander that holy apostle Judas on account of the crime of Judas the betrayer would be imitating these men.

For it is not surprising if, after so long a time, the reputation of Melchiades can endure such calumniators concerning two Cassians or two Stratos, when evangelical truth endures them concerning two Herods. Since it has not been expressly stated which Herod died immediately after the killing of the infants for Christ’s sake, and which Herod persecuted the Lord with Pilate, they suppose that there was only one and bring a charge of falsehood against the Gospel. In the same way, these men suppose that there was only one Strato or one Cassianus and bring against Melchiades the stain of handing things over.

Yet those others err more tolerably, because not only the name but also the dignity corresponds: both are read of as King Herod. These men, however, falsely claimed that the dignity corresponded, since they could in no way read that both men had been deacons.

[Col. 0663] ## CHAPTER XIV

18. It was still day when, concerning the council at Cirta—if it should even be called a council, since scarcely eleven or twelve bishops were present—we read out that certain traditores were among those who, together with Secundus of Tigisis, issued judgments against Caecilian. Wishing to show this to be false, they said that during the time of persecution those eleven or twelve bishops could not have gathered in any house.

To prove that it had been a time of persecution, they produced the proceedings of the martyrs, so that, by considering the days and consuls, it might become clear what period it had been. They were convicted of having brought forward those proceedings of the martyrs against themselves. For in those proceedings it was made clear that at that time Christian communities were accustomed to gather.

It therefore became clear that it was not incredible that those bishops too, as they were read to have done, had gathered in a private house, so that, just as the proceedings of the martyrs showed that the people could gather even during persecution, a bishop might be secretly ordained for the people who were able to assemble. He could then secretly ordain clergy for himself in such great necessity, when the previous bishop, together with his clergy, had lapsed, as was shown by the letter of Secundus himself, which they cited.

Admonished by the proceedings of the martyrs that they themselves had produced, we were led to examine other proceedings of the martyrs as well. We found—and stated—that while the persecution was raging, a private house had been granted to an assembly of Christians, something they had denied could happen, and that martyrs had been baptized in prison. Thus they could see how far from incredible it was for a few bishops to gather in a private house during persecution, when even in the prison the Sacraments of Christ were celebrated, though people were confined there for the faith of Christ.

Who, then, would not see how much the proceedings of the martyrs assisted us when they produced them—unless he has the same kind of night in his heart as those men had, who failed to see this?

## CHAPTER XV

19. They also slandered the very proceedings at Cirta on this point: that days and consuls were recorded there. They demanded that we produce some ecclesiastical councils in which the day and consuls were recorded. They themselves produced the Council of Carthage without a day or consul. For they said that Cyprian’s council also had no consuls, although the day is recorded there; whereas in their own Council of Carthage not even the day is recorded.

We, however, demonstrated from what was at hand—the Roman council of Melchiades—that, like the proceedings at Cirta, it contained both the day and the consuls. At that time we did not need to search through the ancient ecclesiastical archives to establish that this custom had also belonged to earlier times.

Nor did we wish to make empty accusations against them, asking why a day could be found in Cyprian’s council but not in their own. They wanted to introduce pointless delays, whereas we were trying to remove them. They even demanded that we show from the holy Scriptures that days and consuls are recorded somewhere—as though the councils of bishops had ever been compared with the canonical Scriptures, or as though they themselves could produce from the holy Scriptures a council at which the Apostles sat as judges and either condemned or acquitted someone who had been accused.

Yet we replied that the Prophets too prefaced and situated their books within specified times: stating in what year, under which king, in which month of the year, and on which day of the month the word of the Lord had come to them. We did this to show how empty and calumnious were the utterly trivial questions they raised about the days and consuls of episcopal councils.

It is possible that there is a variation among the manuscripts: some record the days and consuls with greater care, while others omit them as superfluous. Thus, the manuscript from which we first read the judgment of Constantine—which declared Caecilian innocent and them most calumnious between the parties—did not contain the day or consul; another manuscript, which we later produced against their calumnies, did.

For there too they had most maliciously protested that we had read out the emperor’s letters without a day or consul. Yet they themselves read out other letters of the same emperor in the case of Felix, Caecilian’s ordainer—letters which, with astonishing blindness, they produced against themselves—without a day or consul. We made no accusation against them on that account, lest, like them, we should waste necessary time in superfluous words.

We say these things now so that you, at least, may open your eyes and be rid of the dark night that your bishops carried in their hearts. They objected to the judge’s consideration that the sentence had been delivered at night, while they themselves, during the day, enveloped in inner darkness and astonishing blindness, said so much against themselves.

## CHAPTER XVI

20. The recorded proceedings before the magistrate of Carthage contain the explicit words of Primianus, where he says that their parents had harassed our elders with various exiles. In the Conference they attempt to prove that their predecessors had accused Caecilian and that the emperor had condemned him to exile.

In their letters they say that their communion is the Church of truth, which suffers persecution, not the Church that inflicts it (*In the Mandate of the Donatists*, below in the Appendix). They attempt to show that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor’s judgment while their predecessors were persecuting him. They say that this was done not by Donatus of Casa, but by the man whom they praise above all others, Donatus of Carthage.

This is what they are now said to boast in their writings through their followers, accusing the judge after being defeated, because the truth that emerged at night refuted the night of their hearts. They wanted to commend that Donatus—that Donatus, I say, whom they called the ornament of the Church of Carthage and a man of martyrial glory—in such a way as to say that, at the inquiry conducted by the emperor Constantine, he both asserted that Caecilian was guilty and convicted him (In the *Collation*, part 2, chapter 10).

That man, then, a man of martyrial glory, presented Caecilian as guilty at the emperor’s inquiry and maintained the charge against him; and Caecilian’s condemnation followed that inquiry. Caecilian was condemned by the emperor while that man of martyrial glory accused and pressed his case.

We proved this false by reading out from the public archive the emperor’s own letters, in which he testifies that he had heard and judged between the parties and, after acquitting and clearing Caecilian, expressed his abhorrence of their calumnies. They could find no answer at all to these letters; indeed, in order to confirm them, they produced other documents against themselves.

Thus it was established that Caecilian had been accused before the emperor by their predecessors; it was not established that he had been condemned. Rather, it was established that he had been acquitted. But even so, consider how greatly your bishops assisted our case when they wished to glory in that falsehood.

If that Donatus, the man of martyrial glory, asserted Caecilian’s guilt at the emperor’s inquiry, and if Caecilian was condemned by the emperor while that man of martyrial glory accused and pressed his case, let them answer you this: when these things were happening, which of them was the martyr—Donatus, who persecuted a man before the emperor, or Caecilian, who was condemned by the emperor while Donatus persecuted him?

Where is now their definitive rule that the communion of Donatus is the Church of truth, which suffers persecution and does not inflict it? Behold: Caecilian suffers, and Donatus inflicts it. Which of them is the man of martyrial glory?

## CHAPTER XVII

21. Pay attention, take heed, and do not allow yourselves to be led any longer into a destructive error. God has deigned to reveal the truth that was hidden from you; God has deigned to refute the falsehood that was imposed upon you. Why, after so great a benefit from him, are you still ungrateful?

This is precisely what they often said to you, by which cunning deception clouded the eyes of your hearts. Even now, after being convicted, they boast of this and attack us because we inflict persecution while they suffer it. This is all that remains to them after being defeated in every respect, from which they can still cast mists before the inexperienced, presenting themselves as though they were the Church of truth, which suffers persecution and does not inflict it.

Do not therefore allow them to deceive you any longer. We do to them what they boast that their predecessors, and that very man whom they praise as a man of martyrial glory, did to Caecilian. He acted before the emperor so that Caecilian, having been convicted, might be condemned by the emperor’s judgment; and we too acted so that these men, having been convicted, might suffer similar consequences.

If it was wrong for him to do this, why did that Donatus do it? But if he did it rightly, why should the Catholic party not do the same to Donatus? Indeed, even those who loudly praise their predecessors do not doubt that it was right for them to do this. Nor do we doubt that it ought to be done to them: those who are not corrected by words should, without the shedding of blood, be restrained by some very mild punishment under the laws. And if perhaps the emperor, moved by their sacrilegious obstinacy, should determine that it must be punished with a harsher penalty, the judges may act more mildly; they have always been permitted to soften and mitigate a sentence.

[Note: See Augustine’s Letter 139, section 2.]

For the present, then, although it cannot be shown that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor Constantine, that error has nevertheless been removed from you—the error by which you thought that the true Church was the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it. Donatus inflicted it; Caecilian suffered it.

And if the party of Donatus suffers persecution, the party of Maximian suffers it with them as well, although they themselves affirm that this party is not the Church of Christ. Consequently, inflicting persecution is not a sign of iniquity, since the good inflict it upon the wicked, and the wicked upon the good. Nor is suffering persecution proof of righteousness, since not only the good suffer it for piety, but the wicked also suffer it for iniquity.

22. Once this error has been driven away, it remains for you to see and hold the Catholic Church of Christ, not to choose it because it suffers persecution. For when the Lord had said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” lest heretics boast on that account, he added, “for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10).

You too know how many evils the frenzied clerics and Circumcellions of the party of Donatus inflicted upon our people. Churches were burned, holy books were cast into the flames, private houses too were burned, and people were dragged from their homes. After everything they possessed had been taken away or destroyed, the people themselves were beaten, mangled, and blinded. Even murder could not be avoided—although it is milder for one to die to this light than to take this light away from someone who is alive.

They came upon people not in order to detain them and lead them away somewhere, but merely to make them suffer these things. Yet we do not justify our people merely because they endured such things, but because they endured them for Christian truth, for the peace of Christ, and for the unity of the Church.

Under so many and such severe laws, and under the great authority over the Catholic Church that the Lord has granted it, what similar suffering do they endure? For whenever they are punished with death, either they kill themselves, or they are killed while their bloody violence is being resisted—not for the communion of the party of Donatus, nor for the error of sacrilegious schism, but for their most manifest crimes and offenses, which they commit with the savage fury and cruelty of brigands.

For the party of Donatus they scarcely suffer anything comparable to what they said Caecilian suffered when Donatus pressed his case against him.

23. Either, then, not every persecution is unjust, or persecution should not be called persecution when it is just. Therefore, either the party of Donatus suffers a just persecution, or it does not suffer persecution, because it suffers justly.

Caecilian, however, did not suffer justly, because he was proved innocent and acquitted. They denied this and instead said that he had been condemned by the emperor; and so they confessed that their predecessors, especially Donatus—the man whom they themselves praise so highly—had persecuted Caecilian.

But they could not prove that Caecilian had been convicted and condemned. Rather, by reading many passages against themselves, they too confirmed what we were saying: that he had been acquitted and cleared. Yet they boast that the emperor granted them freedom of choice. Defeated and confounded, they were even now demanding that the same freedom be granted to them which their predecessors had not granted to Caecilian.

They accused him before the emperor in such a way that, by those accusations—or, perhaps, those accusers—the emperor condemned him; this is what they too wished to assert falsely. If free choice must be granted to every person, it should first have been granted to Caecilian. If these matters should not be entrusted to a human judge but rather left to God, then Caecilian should not first have been accused before the emperor.

## CHAPTER XVIII

24. Awake at last. Do not allow yourselves to be bound by a Tartarean sleep; do not let impious habit plunge you still deeper into sacrilegious error. Already harmonize with peace, cling to unity, yield to charity, and submit to truth. Recognize that the Catholic Church, beginning from Jerusalem, is spread everywhere; the party of Donatus does not share communion with it, and Caecilian’s cause does not prejudice it.

For even though he had been cleared and acquitted so many times, and even if he had not been innocent, neither does one cause prejudice another cause nor one person another person. This is what the universal Church throughout the world proclaims; a member of that Church in Africa also cries out:

“I know the testimony of God; I do not know the case of Caecilian. I believe that he was innocent and persecuted by your predecessors; I read that he was acquitted so many times. But whatever his cause may be, it prejudices nothing in my cause; whatever his person may be, it prejudices nothing in my person.”

You said this; you subscribed to this: “Neither does one cause prejudice another cause, nor one person another person.”

Behold, the Lord says, “Among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47). Let us hold the divine truth in the one Church, and at last bring human quarrels to an end.

## CHAPTER XIX

**25.** For when they said that neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person, were they in any way able to defend these words after the Conference, or did they not rather entangle themselves much more perplexingly? For this is how they spoke in some of their writings:

“It has been recalled that we said, ‘One case does not prejudice another case, nor one person another person’; but we maintain that we are not prejudiced by those whom we have either rejected or condemned. But how can those who descend from Caecilian’s ordination—whom their origin from their predecessor counts as liable to guilt—not be bound by their ordainer’s crimes, since a chain of sins stretched out in succession must make all whom it binds by the bond of communion partners in sin?”

[Note: Col. 0667. All manuscripts read: “but at the place for us” (sed ad locum nobis; the reading is materially uncertain).]

O marvelous defense! The place where their feet have become stuck is so dense and so narrow that, as they try to pull themselves out, they plant both hands and head in vain, and, remaining stuck in the same mud, become more tightly entangled.

For among those whom they recall having either rejected or condemned—that is, among the Maximianists—they have with them Felicianus, both the condemner of Primianus and one condemned by them in the case of Primianus. Why do they strive to stretch so long a rope from Caecilian all the way to the present time of the Catholic Church, and fail to notice their own chain lying so near at hand?

For that celebrated sentence of Bagai concerning Maximianus and his associates says: “The chain of sacrilege drags many into partnership in the crime.” Felicianus, therefore, was dragged along by this chain. If Felicianus does not prejudice them, why does Caecilian prejudice us? Or does a case prejudice them wherever they wish it to, while wherever they do not wish it to, one case does not prejudice another—and, according to their pleasure, is the ancient rope stronger than the new chain?

Maximianus does not prejudice Felicianus, by whom he was condemned; Maximianus and Felicianus do not prejudice Primianus, by whom they were condemned; Maximianus does not prejudice those who received a postponement and with whom he was associated in one schism; Felicianus does not prejudice the party of Donatus, by which he was received in the same rank, nor was the baptism he administered in the sacrilegious schism destroyed there. Yet Caecilian prejudices so many Christian nations, though he was once condemned while absent, as Primianus was, and acquitted three times while present, unlike Primianus.

[Note: By the judgments of the Roman Council, the Council of Arles, and the emperor Constantine.]

An unknown man long ago dead prejudices us; yet the living man does not prejudice them, although he is read to have been condemned shortly before by those same people and is now seen associated with them. Caecilian’s rope is wound around us by people who do not know him; yet Felicianus’s chain is not wound around them, although the sentence they pronounced against him is recited, in which that very chain is condemned.

They are permitted to say: “For the sake of Donatus’s peace, we received those whom we condemned, because neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person.” Yet we are not permitted to say: “Because of those whom you condemned, we do not abandon Christ’s peace, because neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person.”

O brazen forehead! O darkness of madness! They bring a nocturnal sentence against the judge, grope about in the night of their own hearts, stumble, fall, contend furiously against us, and, in our defense, say so much!

## CHAPTER XX

**26.** Furthermore, even now they dare to recall the prophetic and apostolic testimonies to which we gave a universal answer in that Conference, showing that the holy Prophets themselves lived among the wicked in one temple, under the same priests, amid the same sacraments, and yet were not polluted by the evil. For they knew how to distinguish between the holy and the unclean—not as these people think, by bodily separation of the populace, but by judging rightly and living rightly.

They did this without interruption, so that in that great house where, as the Apostle says, there were “some vessels for honor and others for dishonor,” they might cleanse themselves from such people by the diversity of their conduct and be “vessels for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (II Tim. 2:21).

It is well, then, that they themselves have now recalled, after the Conference, as though it were their chief testimony, the passage from the prophet Haggai—one of the many testimonies which they inserted into their writings without understanding them, and which they brought forward and read at the Conference (Haggai 2). In this prophet, therefore, we demonstrate much more clearly what we maintain: it is not bodily contact but spiritual contact, which occurs through agreement, that pollutes people, because that agreement itself makes their case one.

**27.** For when the Lord wished to destroy the wicked even by a visible punishment, he separated the righteous from them by warning: Noah and his household from those whom he was about to destroy by the Flood (Gen. 6–8); Lot from those whom he was about to consume by fire (ibid. 19); and his people from the synagogue of Abiram, which he was soon to destroy (Num. 16).

For this reason, too, the Lord of the banquet himself—not those who had invited the guests—ordered the man who did not have a wedding garment to be bound and thrown out. He was not, like a fish beneath the waves, invisible to those who had invited him, as a fish is to fishermen. Therefore, lest anyone should think—as these people do—that he had slipped secretly into the crowd as a single person unknown to the others, the Lord immediately made clear, through that one man whom he ordered to be thrown from the banquet into the outer darkness with hands and feet bound, that a great multitude of wicked people is to be understood among whom fewer good people live at the Lord’s banquet.

For after saying, “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he immediately added, “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:1–14). How is this true, when rather one person among many was thrown into the outer darkness, unless that one person symbolized the great body of all the wicked mingled with the Lord’s banquet before the Lord’s judgment?

Meanwhile the good separate themselves from these people in heart and conduct, eating and drinking the Lord’s body and blood together with them, but with a great distinction: the former are clothed in the wedding garment in honor of the bridegroom, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ; the latter do not have the wedding garment—that is, the bridegroom’s most faithful love—but seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ.

Accordingly, although they are at one and the same banquet, the former eat mercy, while the latter eat judgment, because the song of that banquet is the one I mentioned above: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

**28.** Nevertheless, ecclesiastical discipline is not asleep, so that it may correct the restless. We do not separate from the people of God those whom, by degrading or excommunicating them, we reduce to a humbler place of repentance. And when we are not permitted to do this for the sake of the Church’s peace and tranquility, we do not therefore neglect the Church.

[Note: The Beccensis manuscript reads, “we reject the Church’s discipline.” Other manuscripts read, “we reject the Church,” omitting the word “discipline.”]

Rather, we tolerate what we do not want in order to reach what we do want, using the caution prescribed by the Lord’s command, lest, when we wish to gather the weeds before the proper time, we uproot the wheat at the same time (Matt. 13).

We also follow the example and command of the blessed Cyprian, who, out of consideration for peace, tolerated his fellow bishops as usurers, defrauders, and robbers, without becoming like them through their contagion (Sermon on the Lapsed). Hence, if we are wheat, we confidently repeat the words of that blessed martyr: even if weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our love should be hindered, so that, because we see weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church (Letter to Maximus).

Our predecessors would have spoken these words most justly and piously even if they had seen Caecilian and some of his fellow bishops to be evil, yet could not separate them from the Church because of those to whom their evil could not be demonstrated and who thought them good and innocent. They would have spoken and thought precisely this, lest, when they rashly wished to separate the weeds, they uproot the wheat as well.

**29.** Therefore, when a certain prophet was ordered neither to eat bread nor drink water in Samaria, where he had been sent to rebuke those who had set up calves to be worshiped in the manner of Egyptian idols (III Kings 13), he had to do exactly what the Lord had commanded. At that time the Lord was pleased that he rebuke them in this way, so that the prophet he had sent would touch none of the food there.

For this also happens daily in the Church: when we rebuke those whom we correct more sharply, even if we are in possession of their property, we take nothing there from them, so that they may realize how deeply we grieve over their sins.

Does this mean, however, that the people must also be divided, so that, like tender grass, the weak—who cannot judge what lies in human hearts and in unknown deeds, even when those deeds are known to us—may be uprooted indiscriminately?

For in Samaria itself there were Elijah and Elisha. If they were in the wilderness, this was not to avoid the sacraments, but because they were suffering persecution from wicked kings. For there were there, though not in the wilderness, a separate body unknown to Elijah himself: seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal (III Kings 19).

Finally, Samuel, regarded among the chief saints, severely rebuked Saul and nevertheless went with him without excuse to offer sacrifice to the Lord (I Kings 15). He was not polluted by Saul’s contagion, but remained entirely clean by preserving his own merits.

**30.** But although this question has been clearly settled both in the Conference and now, let Haggai settle it even more clearly. They chose his testimony above all others so that they might still boast of it as their sole support.

Through the prophet Haggai, the Lord rebukes the people who remained from Babylonia, where they had been held captive, because they neglected the Lord’s house while cultivating their own houses; and he says that for this reason he had struck their land with the plague of infertility.

Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, and all that people, divinely inspired, began to work on the house of the Lord their God. For the same Scripture says:

“And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and the spirit of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people; and they entered and worked on the house of the Lord Almighty, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year under King Darius.”

[Note: Col. 0670. The manuscripts omit “and the month and the year.”]

Here the day, month, and year are specified when they entered to work on the house of God.

I believe that those men and that people, working on the house of God, were not unclean—especially since the Lord had said to them, “I am with you,” and had stirred up their spirit to work well in his house.

Finally, see what follows. The same Scripture continues:

“On the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the Lord spoke by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, saying: Who is there among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, as though it were not before your eyes? And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Jesus son of Jehozadak, high priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord Almighty; and my spirit presides in your midst. Take courage, for thus says the Lord Almighty: Yet once more I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and I will shake all the nations, and all the chosen things of the nations will come, and I will fill this house, says the Lord Almighty.”

And so forth—what he added while also prophesying future events, which are more rightly understood as referring to the times of our Lord Jesus Christ. His people are the truest and holiest temple of God—not those who are tolerated while mingled with them, but only those who meanwhile separate themselves spiritually from such people by living well and afterward will also be separated bodily.

Nevertheless, it is very easy to see from the words of the Prophet, which we have inserted exactly as they were spoken, how the Lord exhorted and commended that people to whom this prophecy was announced and who were then working on the house of God, where those two men also were, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jesus son of Jehozadak.

Can we call this people unclean, then, if anyone who approaches it will be polluted, when the Lord says to that people: “And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Jesus son of Jehozadak, high priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord Almighty; and my spirit is present in your midst”? What madman would say that this is a people which pollutes anyone who approaches it?

**31.** Now consider what Scripture goes on to say after that prophecy, which announced the times of Christ to this people.

“On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year under King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man takes sanctified flesh in the edge of his garment, and the edge of his garment touches bread, or stew, or wine, or any food, will it be sanctified? The priests answered and said, No. And Haggai said: If one who is unclean in soul touches any of these things, will it become unclean? The priests answered and said, It will become unclean. And Haggai answered and said: So is this people, and so is this nation before me, says the Lord, and so are the works of their hands; and whoever approaches them will be polluted, because of their presumptions in the morning before their labors, and because you hated those who reproved you at the gates.”

[Note: Printed editions read, “and just as.” The manuscripts read, “and so.”]

What people are so unclean that whoever approaches them is polluted? Is it the people to whom it was said, “Be strong, and my spirit presides in your midst”? Far be it from us to say that it is they.

There were therefore two peoples: one unclean, and another forbidden to approach the unclean, which was exhorted to be strong because the Spirit of God was in its midst. If there were two peoples, then let two temples be shown—one into which the former entered and another into which the latter entered. Let two altars be shown—one on which the former offered victims and another on which the latter did so. Let priests be shown, some belonging to the former and others to the latter, each offering sacrifices separately for his own people.

But if anyone attempts to affirm this, he is insane. These were two peoples within one people, entering one temple under one high priest, just as under one Moses there were some who offended God and some who pleased God. Of them the Apostle says, “God was not pleased with all of them” (I Cor. 10:5).

He does not say, “God was pleased with none of them,” as though all had displeased God; rather, he says, “God was not pleased with all of them”—therefore, with some but not with all.

All of them were under the same priests, offering sacrifices in one and the same tabernacle and at one and the same altar. Yet they were distinguished by their deeds, not by their locations; by their disposition, not by their temple; by their conduct, not by their altars.

Thus some did not approach the others, lest they be polluted by them—that is, they did not consent to their evil deeds, lest they be condemned together with them. For did that great prophet Moses not know those evil people, whose impious murmuring and terrible bitterness he endured daily?

But let us suppose that Moses did not know them. Did Samuel not know Saul, whom God had condemned through Samuel’s mouth with an eternal sentence? Yet Samuel saw Saul and holy David entering the one tabernacle of God and participating in the same sacrifices. He saw them distinctly, of course, because he saw them as distinct: he loved one of them eternally, while tolerating the other for a time.

So Haggai knew that within one people there were two peoples entering one temple and living under one high priest. He showed one to be unclean and forbade the other to approach the unclean; yet he did not separate either them or himself from that same temple and those same altars.

He therefore forbade spiritual approach and agreement in deeds. The very words cry this out, if there are ears which furious hostility does not close and the uproar of varied contention does not obstruct.

For the Prophet says, “Everyone who approaches him will be polluted.” He identified the vice by which he prohibited approach; he did not exclude people from people by bodily separation. One approaches the vice of corruption through the vice of agreement.

**32.** And lest anyone should say that the people to whom it was first said, “Be strong, because my spirit is present in your midst,” had changed for the worse after a few intervening days and become so bad that they deserved to hear, “So is this people and this nation; everyone who approaches them will be polluted,” nearly ninety days are counted between the words spoken for the good of the people and those by which their uncleanness is to be avoided.

Therefore, lest anyone should suppose that this good people had become so evil within that short interval, observe what follows and attend to what is said on that very day—that is, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the day on which it was said, “So is this people and this nation; everyone who approaches them will be polluted.”

After saying this and recalling their evil deeds, by which they were shown to be unclean—adding also, “You hated those who reproved you at the gates”—he immediately continued:

“And now set your hearts on this day and on the time before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. You were those who, when you put twenty measures of barley into the bin, found ten measures; and when you entered the winepress to draw fifty jars, found twenty. I struck you with barrenness, with blight and mildew; all the works of your hands suffered hail, yet you did not turn to me, says the Lord. Therefore set your hearts on this day and from now on, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, and from the day on which the temple of the Lord was founded. Set your hearts on this: whether seed is still in the barn, or whether the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet produced fruit. From this day I will bless” (Haggai 1–2).

Behold, on that very day they also deserved to be blessed. I therefore think that this blessing does not apply to those whom he forbids anyone to approach because of their uncleanness, but to those good people who are forbidden to approach them.

Thus they were both mingled and separated within one people: mingled by bodily contact, but separated by the withdrawal of the will. Scripture speaks in its customary manner, rebuking the wicked as though all in that people were wicked, and consoling the good as though all there were such.

Your bishops therefore inserted Haggai’s prophecy for us—even in what they are said to have written after being defeated at the Conference—in order that they might remind us to prove more clearly what we maintain: that in one people, in one temple, under the same priests, amid the same sacraments, people living with different intentions, different conduct, and differing ways of life, neither one case can prejudice another case nor one person another person.

[Note: Printed editions read “subscribed”; shortly afterward, “from which they recall,” and below, “separating by different conduct.” The manuscripts correct these readings.]

## CHAPTER XXI

**33.** There is also the passage from the Apostle’s Letter which they now recall in their writings: “Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has light with darkness?” (II Cor. 6:14), along with the other passages we mentioned above and explained how they should rightly be understood.

What else are they doing by this except reminding us to whom the Apostle wrote these words?

For we demonstrate what we are saying in that very people of Corinth, lest they suppose that it was merely the custom of the Prophets, and that it belonged not to the practice of the New Testament but to that of the Old, to rebuke reprehensible people as though everyone in the people were being rebuked, and to address those worthy of praise as though everyone there were being praised.

Behold, the Apostle also speaks in this manner to the Corinthians:

“Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the Church of God that is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

“I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge. Thus the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace.”

Who, hearing these words, would believe that there were any reprobates in the Church of the Corinthians, since this praise sounds as though it were addressed to everyone?

Yet shortly afterward he says: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you.”

Again, as though rebuking and reproving everyone for this dreadful vice, he says: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. 1:1–13).

I suppose that those among that people who said, “I belong to Christ” did not share the yoke with those who said, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” or “I to Cephas.” Yet all approached one altar and shared the same sacraments, although they did not share the same vices.

To these Corinthians was also said: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (ibid. 11:29). What else was the Apostle thinking of but these vain talkers, so that it was not enough for him to say, “He eats and drinks judgment,” unless he added, “upon himself”—lest this also apply to those who ate together with them, but did not eat judgment?

**34.** Among the Corinthians themselves there were also people who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, a doctrine that is the distinctive faith of Christians. The Apostle says to them:

“But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?”

He did not say, “In this land” or “in this world,” but “among you.” For he could not be arguing from Christ’s resurrection except with Christians, to whom he says concerning Christ’s resurrection itself, “This is how we preach, and this is how you believed” (ibid. 15:12, 11).

Now let us consider those words with which, at the beginning of the Letter, he praises the Church of the Corinthians, saying:

“I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, so that the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, and you lack nothing in any grace.”

Behold, they had been enriched in Christ in every word and in all knowledge, lacking nothing in any grace, and yet there were among them people who still did not believe in the resurrection of the dead.

I suppose that those who lacked nothing in any grace did not share the yoke with those who did not believe that the dead would rise. Behold how they do not share the yoke with unbelievers, although they are mingled with them within the same people and instructed under the same priests and by the same sacraments.

**35.** Finally, lest those whose faith already held the resurrection of the dead should consent to this unbelief, the Apostle did not command them to separate bodily from the others. There were many of them—not like the one man who had his father’s wife, whom he judged worthy of a more direct correction and excommunication (ibid. 5:1–5).

A multitude infected with vice must be treated and healed in one way, and that one man in another, lest, if one people is separated from another, the wheat also be uprooted through the sacrilege of schism.

The Apostle therefore does not separate bodily those who already believed in the resurrection of the dead from those who did not believe it within the same people. Yet he does not cease to separate them spiritually, saying: “Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals” (ibid. 15:33).

He fears not their gathering but their agreement, lest they give their assent to evil conversations, which corrupt good morals. He admonishes them to be separated by conduct, not by altars.

Finally, before the Apostle wrote these things to them, there were already in that same Church people who did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, while there were also those who lacked nothing in any grace. The former did not pollute the latter through their unbelief, because the latter did not consent to the former in that same unbelief.

Behold how one does not approach it, lest whoever approaches it be polluted. Behold how there is no partnership between light and darkness. Behold how, although both kinds of fish swim within the same nets, neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person.

**36.** Since this is so, what crude stupidity, what sleep of an iron heart, could fail to be shaken awake and at last understand that Caecilian’s case cannot prejudice the Catholic world, with which the party of Donatus does not communicate, if the case of Maximianus—or rather the case of Felicianus and Primianus, now joined together though shortly before condemned by one another—does not prejudice the party of Donatus?

Certainly, if we speak according to their own argument, it is enough for our case that bad fish lurking beneath the waves do not pollute fishermen who are unaware of them. Although the question is not really about fishermen, whom the Lord may perhaps have intended to be understood as angels in that comparison.

What must be considered more carefully is that within the nets themselves the good fish cannot be stained by the bad. For they themselves also see one another swimming together, just as they are not seen by the fishermen while inside the water.

But, as I have said, it is enough for our case that the wicked do not pollute those whose evil deeds are unknown.

## CHAPTER XXII

**37.** There were, in the time of Caecilian, certain blessed lovers of peace who, even if he had not been innocent, would have tolerated him for the sake of Catholic unity. They saw him joined in communion for the sharing of the sacraments with so many unknown nations through which that unity is spread, and they knew that he could not be shown to those nations as the kind of man they themselves knew him to be.

They would defend themselves against these slanders with the words of the blessed and peace-loving Cyprian, confidently proclaiming and saying: “For this reason we do not abandon unity because of Caecilian: even if weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our love should be hindered, so that, because we see weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (Letter to Maximus).

To the peaceful patience of these people would belong that outstanding praise with which the angel of the Church at Ephesus is praised—no one who understands correctly doubts that this angel represents the Church itself. In the Apocalypse the Spirit says to him:

“I know your works, your labor, and your patience, and that you cannot tolerate the wicked. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them to be liars. You have patience, and you have endured for my name’s sake, and you have not grown weary” (Rev. 2:2–3).

[Note: The manuscripts read “may they be praised”; printed editions read “they are praised.”]

So let those who lived in the time of Caecilian be praised—those who, for the sake of the Lord’s name, which already spread throughout the whole world like poured-out perfume through innumerable nations, did not grow weary but endured with the greatest patience even one whom they knew to be evil, if that man was evil, yet could not be shown to others according to their judgment or removed and separated from them.

Our situation is different; we ought not to claim for ourselves the praise of such patience. We cannot say that we tolerated for the sake of peace what could not possibly have come to our knowledge.

Caecilian’s case was hidden beneath the waves from us. Our voice is like that of the other Christian nations, against whom these people found absolutely nothing to say.

Nevertheless, we rightly believe Caecilian’s unknown case to have been good: we read that he was once condemned by the faction of his enemies but was acquitted three times when they themselves were accusing him.

Let them believe the nearly one hundred bishops of the party of Donatus concerning Primianus’s crimes; then let them compel us to believe the seventy elders of their own party concerning Caecilian’s crimes.

As for their claim that Caecilian confirmed the charges brought against him at that council by remaining silent because he was absent: Primianus therefore also confirmed the charges that one hundred bishops brought against him, since he is not even afterward shown to have cleared himself of them.

**38.** But of course neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person—lest the party of Donatus be diminished. Yet it does prejudice, so that Christ’s inheritance may be divided.

Does Caecilian’s case not prejudice the Catholic unity which we hold and whose fellowship we rejoice in, because Caecilian was bishop of Carthage, while the case of Novellus of Tizicus and Faustinus of Tuburbis does prejudice it—men whom they did not even think worthy of being accused afterward as they thought Caecilian and Felix worthy?

The names of these men—or rather, even the names of the cities in which they were—are not known throughout Africa, perhaps not even throughout the province of Proconsular Africa.

Behold: they wish the case of these little fish, even if they were wicked and hidden in such deep waters, to prejudice the case of so great a catch, whose full nets are spread throughout the whole world—fish who could scarcely have been known even to those swimming beside them.

Why should we not also believe these men to have been innocent, since, as I have said, they were not afterward considered worthy of being accused by their opponents, and since the man whom their elders declared in the hostile conspiracy of that council to be the source of all evil was able to be cleared?

## CHAPTER XXIII

**39.** But whatever sort of men these were, what does it have to do with us? Surely they do not truly deny us the right to say that the case and person of these unknown men do not prejudice the case and person of the Catholic Church, if neither one case prejudices another case nor one person another person.

And yet they object to us—still trying to deceive you—that we gave gold to the judge so that he would pronounce a sentence against them in our favor.

You tell us, if you can, how much we should have paid your chosen defending bishops so that they would say or produce so much against themselves and on our behalf, so that they would conduct our case in such a way and destroy their own in such a way.

How much should we have paid so that, after Primianus had said, “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditors should come together in one place,” they would nevertheless come and meet together with us in the very gathering they had declared unworthy?

How much should we have paid so that, in the manner of forensic advocates, they would try to bar us by appeals to times and dates, and even to persons, and would thus show clearly enough to everyone—even to those unable to understand our debates—how bad their case was, how afraid they were to present and conduct it before the judge whose kindness and justice toward them they had praised with such great fanfare, and whose hostility toward them they had not yet experienced at all?

How much should we have paid so that afterward they themselves would insist that the matter should not be handled with forensic formulas but rather with divine testimonies, and would promise that they too would answer from the sacred Scriptures? Then, when the mandate of the Catholic council which we had offered was read, and it became clear—with their own acknowledgment—that we had wished to conduct the Catholic Church’s case by the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, they returned once more, as though they had forgotten what they had said they approved, to the same forensic objections with perplexing and offensive arguments.

[Note: Perhaps “the case” should be added here.]

**40.** How much should we have paid so that, moved by the number of our subscriptions displayed in that same mandate, they would demand the presence of our entire council, when, according to the Cognitor’s edict, only eighteen of us were present from that council, and would raise a charge of forgery on the ground that some people could subscribe on behalf of others?

Thus matters proceeded until their number also had to be counted, and they themselves were caught in the very forgery whose suspicion they had tried to cast upon us.

Not only were certain men found, according to their mandate, to have subscribed for absent persons who had not even come to Carthage; it was also said that one particular man, whose name had been read but who did not answer, had died on the journey. When they were asked how a man who had already died on the journey could have subscribed at Carthage, after great confusion caused by their embarrassed, inconsistent, and contradictory answers, they asserted that he had not died on the way while coming, but while returning home after he had subscribed.

Then, when they were questioned under divine attestation whether it was certain that he had been at Carthage, they became even more confused and said: “What if someone else signed in his place?”

[Note: The manuscripts read, “substituted himself for him.”]

Thus, by their own words, they confirmed that the forgery which they had charged against us had appeared in their own mandate, had been exposed, and had been proved.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 41

How much should we have had to pay for this—that, when they wished to boast of their numbers, they should also expose their lies in this matter? For when a somewhat larger number of our people had appeared, and we had said that nearly one hundred other Catholic bishops had not come to Carthage, some prevented by old age, some by ill health, and some by various necessities, they, upon hearing this, said that many more of their own had not come.

Likewise, even now, while boasting that they numbered more than four hundred throughout Africa, they forgot what they had written in their *notoria* [Note: [Col. 0677] The printed editions have *notaria*. The manuscripts, consistently throughout this entire book, have *notoria*.]—namely, that all of them had come to Carthage to such an extent that, apart only from those whom bodily illness had detained either in their own sees or on the journey, not even the most aged men could have been prevented by old age and the hardship of a long journey. Their subscriptions were also read aloud from their mandate; and, when the Office had made the calculation, it replied that there were two hundred and seventy-nine [Note: [Col. 0677] The *Am.* and all the manuscripts have “two hundred and seventy-three.” But in the *Collation*, part 1, chapter 213, and in the *Brief Account of the Collation*, first day, no. 26, “two hundred and seventy-nine” is read.], counting even those in whose case falsification had been detected, and those who had subscribed for absentees who had been unable to come to Carthage because they were detained by illness.

How, then, is it true that they number more than four hundred, when they said that only those had failed to come to Carthage whom bodily illness had prevented—especially since, in the case of some of those very men, others had subscribed on their behalf? We will not even say that this was done for all who were ill. Or had an epidemic perhaps attacked them so violently that it suddenly struck down a third of them?

They had been summoned by their primate through a *tractoria* [Note: [Col. 0678] The *Am.* and all the manuscripts have “by their primacy” (*a primatu suo*).], so that, setting everything aside, they might hasten to assemble at Carthage; and thus they knew that they had forfeited whatever was best in their case, whoever had been unwilling to come. This, evidently, was the best point in their case: that their number should appear immense—as though a greater multitude of blind searchers made something easier to find!

### 42

How much should we have had to pay for this—that, when the hearing had been postponed by mutual agreement to the day after the next, they should on the preceding day request through a *notoria* that our mandate be issued to them by the Office, so that, equipped with it, they might be able to attend? They alleged that the Office could not, in so short a time, keep up with the recording of the proceedings.

Thus it happened that, on the following day of the hearing, although they were making an unjust request [Note: [Col. 0678] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “although they were unjustly requesting it.”], they obtained a postponement. For, when they considered the case, which was contained in its entirety in our mandate, they were suffering great distress; nevertheless, they were convicted of coming against their own agreement [Note: [Col. 0678] Lov. has “when they were convicted.” We delete “when,” because it is absent from the manuscripts.].

For what could be more just than to grant a postponement to men thrown into confusion by such a force of truth? Would that this had benefited them, so that, after considering our mandate—which they could in no way answer—they might have preferred to correct their perversity rather than increase it for the worse.

They were therefore right to request a postponement. But on the preceding day they ought not to have said in their *notoria* that our mandate had to be issued to them so that they might come prepared on the appointed day, on the ground that the shorthand writers could not keep up with recording the proceedings; and then, on the very day of the proceedings, they ought not again to have wished to complain about those same shorthand writers because they had not kept up.

What compelled them to do this, except intense confusion, when they saw that we had conducted the case in the written mandate in such a way that they could find no answer? For how much should we have had to pay for this—that they should request the postponement itself and receive six days, so that no one could say that, hindered by lack of time, they had been unable to answer our mandate?

## CHAPTER XXV

### 43

On the third day of our *Collation* itself, how much should we have had to pay for this—that, by inserting the most empty and superfluous delays, they showed in every way that they did not wish to reach the case, and by their very fear proclaimed how bad their case was!

Their fear also burst forth as unmistakable testimony when they said, “We are gradually being led into the case”; and elsewhere: “Your Authority clearly sees that we are gradually being led into the interior of the case.”

O violence of truth, stronger than any rack [Note: [Col. 0679] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “than any goad.”], stronger than any claws, for extracting a confession!

So many bishops assembled from all Africa. They entered Carthage with such a splendid display of a grand procession that they drew the eyes and attention of so great a city upon themselves. Men were chosen by everyone to speak for everyone. A place worthy of so important a matter was also secured in the middle of the city. Both sides came together; the judge was present; the tablets lay open; everyone’s anxious hearts awaited the outcome of so great a *Collation*.

Then, by the most distinguished and eloquent men, something that ought to have been conducted with all the force at their command was conducted with such force that nothing was done. In the manner of a court, they sought to examine the persons involved—a question over which litigants customarily wear away many years.

By this very procedure they confessed that the Catholics had composed their mandate from divine testimonies rather than from legal formulas, and they likewise promised that they would answer from the Scriptures. And because God, by a marvelous aid, wished that, while they were seeking to examine the petitioner’s status in order to avoid coming to the case, the very investigation of the petitioner should suddenly bring the case into the midst of them, those distinguished men who seemed to have been chosen to conduct the proceedings began to shout—and testified that they had rather been chosen not to conduct them. They complained resentfully to the judge that they were gradually being led into the interior of the case, as though, after everything else had been set aside, something other than that which they did not wish to address until much later—or, indeed, ever—ought to have been undertaken. For they never wished the case to be addressed at all where they feared being defeated!

Who could have forced this most open expression of fear from their closed hearts—not to mention if we had enriched them with the most lavish gifts, but even if we had tortured them with the most savage punishments?

### 44

For when they were seeking the identity of the petitioners through forensic examination, wishing to show that we were the petitioners so that they might be permitted to examine our persons legally and discover delays lasting for many years, they read a petition once given by us to the proconsul. In it we had requested that they be summoned, so that the *Collation* between us might then take place. We had now obtained from the Emperor that it should take place. They used this petition to show that we were supposedly the petitioners.

We replied that we had always wished the *Collation* to take place—not where we would bring charges against them, but where we would clear ourselves of the charges they usually bring. For it is precisely on this account that heretics, separated from the unity of the Church, bring charges which they cannot prove.
