Then, because the Examiner seemed to be following the chronological order and therefore preferred the petition of ours that they themselves had produced—since the proceedings before the prefects in which they too had requested a *Collation* preceded it in time—we very easily and most justly took advantage of this opportunity to obtain from the Examiner that, if he was going to prefer what was demonstrably earlier in time, he should instead order that the document be read in which they themselves, before the Emperor Constantine, through the proconsul Anulinus, accused Caecilian. They bring Caecilian’s alleged crimes against our communion, and we wished to clear them away in that *Collation*.

Accordingly, after it began to be read—for there they were being defeated most openly in every respect—they began to shout, “We are being gradually led into the case”; and again: “Your Authority clearly sees that we are gradually being led into the interior of the case.”

O great confusion—but not surprising! When would a demon ever have feared an exorcist in this way? Yet they feared that those documents would be read in which it appeared that Caecilian had been accused before the Emperor by their own predecessors and had been acquitted in so many judgments, not only episcopal but also imperial.

### 45

For what price, or at what cost, could we have purchased this—that, thrown into confusion by that very fear, they dared to return even to the limitation of time concerning that period, when they had said that the case had already lapsed and could not be heard at all after four months had elapsed?

What is this? What judge so suitable for their state of mind could be found as this fear, expressed and exposed in such a way that, although fear usually deprives one of freedom, they feared so freely that they did not even conceal their judgment about their bad case in silence, but revealed it in the clearest words?

O violent agitation, sufficient to extort a confession! Fear sprang so forcefully from their mouths that, under its assault, shame fled from their faces.

If the documents showing that Caecilian had been accused and acquitted were not read [Note: [Col. 0680] The printed editions have “but when they were read.” The manuscripts are corrected here.], the petitioners were being sought in order to conduct the case, and the persons involved were being examined. Although delaying devices were being intricately woven, in a deliberately evasive fashion, to prevent the case itself from being reached, these matters nevertheless seemed to be demanded as though by right for the conduct of the case.

After the excellent case of Caecilian had been produced for reading, the limitation of time—which had been rejected and refuted—was recalled, and they cried out that the day for conducting the case had already passed.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 46

What are you still waiting for the Examiner to have pronounced in our favor, when you see what the fear of your bishops pronounced against themselves?

The Examiner had certainly granted them the power to appoint another judge together with whichever judge they wished. They refused this, because, if they had chosen someone, they could not have lied to you by saying that he too had been corrupted by us.

But they did what they had refused: they appointed another judge together with him—not just any outsider, but their most intimate companion.

Behold, their very fear was another judge. Certainly it had received nothing from us, and it judged freely in our favor. It did not indulge the persons to whom it was inwardly attached, and from whose secret chamber it proceeded. Before the case was pleaded, it judged first, because it had first come to know the case in their hearts.

In the end, the one judge came forward to learn the case, while this one came forward already knowing it. The former judged by standing, listening, and speaking; the latter merely by coming forward. I think they would have put it better [Note: [Col. 0680] The manuscripts have “they were saying.”] if they had said that the case should no longer be heard.

For how much more quickly did the litigants’ fear finish the case than the Examiner’s labor? He was asking what was being read from their documents; this one revealed what was taking place in their hearts.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### 47

How had they come to this point? Terrified by the documents that had been produced for reading, they said that the case had already lapsed through the passage of time and could no longer be heard.

They set before us what had already been dealt with earlier: if we conducted the case from the Holy Scriptures, those documents should not be read at all; but if we read the documents that were to be read, they had a valid limitation of time, so that they would not allow the case, having lapsed through time, to be heard at all.

Yet they themselves had not kept what they had previously promised: that, since they had confessed that we had conducted the Church’s case in our mandate by testimonies from the Scriptures, they too would answer with testimonies from the Scriptures. They had insisted that the persons of the petitioners should be examined, not in the manner of disputants, but in the manner of litigants.

We therefore replied to them that, if they wished nothing else to be done except to investigate which Church was Catholic and where it was, we would conduct its case only by those divine testimonies by which it had been foretold. But if they brought certain crimes against human beings, since they themselves could not demonstrate those crimes by divine testimonies but only by other documents of that sort, we too would clear ourselves by documents of that sort.

While they kept repeatedly repeating their empty claims, these points were repeatedly brought forward by us with the greatest persistence. Thus truth conquered them and, after they had been refuted and defeated, compelled them to listen to the documents we had produced.

For they saw that, if they brought no crimes of Caecilian against our communion, which is spread throughout all nations, they had nothing left with which to excuse their separation from unity in any way. But if they brought Caecilian’s crimes, they could assert them only by documents of that sort, and we could defend ourselves only by documents of that sort.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 48

Among all the uproar of their most contentious disputes, how much should we have had to pay for this as well? When we said that our proposal was that they should prove, if they could, the crimes which they habitually bring against our communion, which is spread throughout all nations, so that it might be known from this whether their separation had been just, they replied that we wished to conduct another person’s case—that is, the case of the transmarine Churches—against which they did not bring these charges, since the dispute was among Africans.

They said that those Churches ought rather to wait until they could unite to themselves those who had won in this *Collation*, and that they themselves might possess the Catholic name with them.

What, then, are you still asking, or what do you doubt, concerning which Church you ought to hold? Behold, you have the Church against which your bishops confessed that they had no case, the Church to which our communion is joined and from which their communion is separated.

For if they have just now said that it ought to wait until those of us who win might be joined to it and hold the Catholic name with it, then surely our predecessors had already defeated their predecessors; and for that reason, joined to that Church, they held the Catholic name within its unity.

But if these men were already defeated by our predecessors in the persons of their own predecessors, why do they still contend with us? If they were not defeated, why do they not communicate with that Church which, since they cannot deny that it is Catholic, they have confessed they have no case against?

Behold, the transmarine Catholic Church, spread among so many nations—whom they said it ought to await: how ought it to wait to join to itself those who have won, unless it is separate from the crimes at issue between us? For if it is not separate from them, how will it, itself defeated as guilty together with the defeated, join the victors to itself?

But if, as they confess, it is separate from these crimes, then so are we, who are joined to it in communion. For if the foreign crime contaminates us because of this communion, then our crime contaminates the Church to which we communicate.

Yet they themselves confessed that the Church was not polluted by the crime of the Africans, although they are joined to it through communion in the Sacraments. They were therefore convicted there that we too could not have been polluted by the crime of those with whom we are joined through communion in the Sacraments, since we are entangled by no bond of consent.

Moreover, the victorious case of Caecilian himself can very easily be demonstrated to them in accordance with these same words of theirs. For if the transmarine Church, being separate from these crimes, ought to wait while we struggle, so that it might join to itself those who have won and add them to the Catholic name, then it was waiting at the time when their predecessors were fiercely struggling against Caecilian.

Therefore, the one whom that Church—which had been waiting for this—joined to itself after the struggle was the one who won at that time. Or, if it could join to itself someone polluted through communion in the Sacraments and, as they have now confessed, remain unpolluted by these crimes, then we have won all the more by showing that each person bears his own burden, and that neither case prejudices case nor person prejudices person.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### 49

How much should we have had to pay for this as well—that, when they thought they ought to answer our mandate, in which we had embraced the entire case, not with spontaneous words but with written letters, it should have become clear that they could not answer all the matters contained in our mandate, which they did not even attempt to address in their own letters?

No one can say that they were unable to retain our argument from memory and therefore did not wish to answer all the necessary points. Our mandate was issued to them at their request through a *notoria*, and they themselves alleged that they had requested it so that, equipped with it, they could answer everything.

And when seven had already been chosen by the others to conduct the entire case on behalf of everyone, they nevertheless produced the very letters by which they had tried to answer our mandate in the name of their entire council, as though they were a letter given by all of them to the Examiner.

If we had refused to admit it, we would have acted with the greatest justice. For it was not procedurally proper that, after the case had been entrusted to seven men, anything should now be done except through those who had been chosen.

But so that we would not appear to have feared their letters, we admitted them to be read without any hesitation. Indeed, it was to be desired—and, as I have said, worth paying for—that, after the postponement of so many days which we had granted at their request, they should bring forth a laboriously prepared work in which it would be clear to everyone reading both letters that they had not answered our mandate, and that it would be evident that we had immediately answered them through those same letters of theirs without any postponement.

For if people are so slow-witted that they think they have said something in those places where they did not wish to remain silent in our mandate, I do not think anyone is so foolish as to suppose that they answered anything in those places where they were completely silent.

For these are not minor matters or matters to be treated with contempt; rather, the entire case depends upon them.

### 50

The testimonies of the Scriptures by which we asserted that the Church to which we communicate began from Jerusalem and spread throughout the whole world—they passed over them entirely, crushed, as it were, beneath the great weight of divine authority, as though they had never been uttered at all.

Likewise, what was contained in our mandate concerning the blessed Cyprian—who both admonished that the wicked should rather be tolerated within the Church than that the Church should be abandoned on their account, and confirmed this by his own example—they did not dare to address at all.

I suppose they did not understand that, if they attempted to weaken Cyprian’s authority in any of his writings, they would also be admitting that we rightly do not yield to his authority concerning what they customarily produce as his opinions or decrees about repeating Baptism.

They did not even wish to mention openly Cyprian’s own opinion concerning Baptism, knowing that, if they did so there too, they would come to grief—as though upon a shipwreck—because Cyprian did not abandon unity, and remained in it together with those who held a different view on this matter.

From this it would follow either that the Church must then be said to have perished, so that there was no Church from which their Donatus could be born; or, if—as is true—the Church remained, that the wicked do not contaminate the good within it, as Cyprian also judged, since he remained in the same Church amid disagreement with those who held a different opinion.

Accordingly, these men clothed themselves in the detestable sacrilege of schism, who, because of the unproven crimes of certain people—even if those crimes had been true—ought in no way to have separated themselves from the unity spread throughout the whole world.

Foreseeing this, as far as can be understood, they passed over in complete silence that testimony of Cyprian which had been mentioned in our mandate [Note: [Col. 0683] The printed editions have “that testimony.” The manuscripts have “from that testimony,” and so forth.].

### 51

They also passed over in silence, rather than revive with any contradiction, the point which they themselves had established by their own judgment in the case of the Maximianists: that unity should not be abandoned on account of the wicked. They had said that the associates of Maximian had not been polluted by Maximian, and they received in unimpaired honor those among them whom they had condemned.

They had also shown that Christ’s Baptism, even when given outside the Church, ought rather to be recognized than destroyed, since they did not dare to baptize again those who had been baptized by Felicianus in schism and later received back with him.

When they read this too in our mandate, they judged that it should rather be kept silent and passed over than touched upon by any contradiction.

They also did not address at all, in their response, the distinction made in our mandate between Caecilian’s case and the case of the Church, although Caecilian’s case itself had also been defended in every respect.

Who, then, would think that they answered our mandate when they did not say a word against all these points, or even attempt to conceal them under any kind of response?

But as for what they appeared to answer, let whoever wishes read it and judge, comparing their letters with that same mandate of ours, apart from the response which we immediately gave and by which all their contrivances of vanity were overturned [Note: [Col. 0683] See below in the Appendix.].

## CHAPTER XXX

### 52

If we were to give mountains of gold, when could we purchase this? When the case of Maximian was brought against them, so that they might understand that the council in which seventy bishops pronounced whatever they wished against the absent Caecilian had not harmed him, just as it had not harmed Primianus when nearly a hundred bishops similarly condemned him in favor of Maximian while he too was absent, they were thrown into the greatest confusion and driven into dreadful straits.

They replied that neither case prejudices case nor person prejudices person. In these very few words they confirmed that our entire case—the case over which we had been contending with them above—was altogether unconquered.

For what else were we doing through so many testimonies of the sacred writings, through such great authority of the Prophets, Apostles, bishops, and even their own opponents, than demonstrating that the good are not polluted by the wicked through communion in the Sacraments, provided that they have different cases in heart, will, conduct, and actions, and represent different persons?

What else were we laboring to make evident except that neither case prejudices case nor person prejudices person?

They themselves, compelled by the greatest necessity, said this briefly, because [Note: [Col. 0684] Perhaps “who,” rather than “because.”], after we had long been saying it, they refused to yield to the truth.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### 53

With what treasures, what riches, what heaps of precious stones should we have had to purchase this—that they did not hesitate merely to confess that their predecessors had persecuted Caecilian before the Emperor Constantine, but even to proclaim and boast of it, and to attempt, by lying, to assert that he had been condemned by the Emperor?

Where is that claim with which they customarily deceive you, stirring up hatred against us because we conduct the Church’s case before the Emperor?

Where are Primianus’s words recorded in the proceedings of the Carthaginian magistrate: “They carry the sacred documents of many emperors [Note: [Col. 0684] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and Venice edition have “sacred document” (*sacra*). M. has the plural.]; we offer only the Gospels”?

Where is that celebrated praise by which they exalt their separation, saying that the Church of truth is the one which suffers persecution, not the one which inflicts it?

It has certainly been shattered; it has certainly been overthrown. Their persecutions are read aloud; they cannot deny them, because their subscriptions are also read aloud.

We have them confessing, proclaiming, and boasting that their predecessors severely persecuted Caecilian before the Emperor. We also have them asserting that Caecilian was condemned by the Emperor while they were persecuting him.

Let them therefore no longer cry out that their separation is the Church of truth because it does not inflict persecution but suffers it. Or let them admit that it was not the Church of truth when Caecilian was suffering at the hands of their predecessors.

For if those who suffer persecution are immediately good, then Caecilian was good when he suffered. But if it can indeed happen that the wicked suffer persecution, while those who inflict it cannot be good, then their predecessors were not good when they persecuted Caecilian.

Furthermore, if it can happen that both the good inflict persecution and the wicked suffer it, then we are not to be blamed for this reason, nor are they to be praised because they suffer something like what they boast Caecilian suffered when their predecessors inflicted it upon him.

And yet it was not established at all that Caecilian was condemned by the Emperor. Rather, in his acquittal and exoneration, which were established by the reading of the episcopal and imperial judgments, nothing subsequently could be shown to have been altered.

Thus, once Caecilian’s condemnation—which they had falsely alleged—was removed, there remained the persecution which they had confessed their predecessors had carried out.

### 54

It was not enough that they dared both to boast, by lying, that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor and were unable to prove it by their assertions. They also produced proof—and more powerfully supported our own documents on the matter—that Caecilian’s acquittal had remained entirely firm, and had not, as they had lied, been changed in the opposite direction by a later judgment of the Emperor.

First, they thought that the Catholic bishop Optatus of the Church of Milevis should be read aloud, promising that from him they would prove that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor.

When this passage was read, it turned out rather to be against them, and no one could restrain his laughter. That laughter, however, could not have been added to the written record of the proceedings and would have remained entirely hidden, unless they themselves had prevented even it from remaining hidden by saying, “Let those who laughed listen.” This, at least, is written down and subscribed.

What they wished to have read in their favor was ambiguous. Therefore, when the Examiner had quite properly ordered a passage somewhat earlier to be read, so that, if possible, those words might thereby be clarified, what they did not wish was read: namely, that Caecilian had been cleared, the man whom they had earlier submitted for reading—not, as they boasted, condemned, but retained at Brixia for the sake of peace.

When he had said that, in those words, Optatus wished to weaken Caecilian’s condemnation, they were told to produce from elsewhere a clear condemnation of Caecilian, so that it might be shown that Optatus had weakened it, since he had written most plainly that Caecilian had been cleared.

When they were completely unable to do this, after all the superfluous delays and finished evasive circumlocutions, they began most openly to assist us.

As though instructed by us, or as though chosen together with us to defend and demonstrate Caecilian’s innocence, when they were asked to show, if they could, what they were claiming—that Caecilian had been condemned by a later judgment of the Emperor whose letters we had read and which had shown him acquitted—they produced a petition of their predecessors addressed to that same Emperor Constantine. By it they most clearly demonstrated that, rather, they themselves had been condemned by his judgment.

For what happened to them before the imperial authority was the same as what happened to the enemies of the holy Daniel, who suffered from the lions what they had wished an innocent man to suffer (Dan. 6:24).

When we briefly reminded them that this petition had been read aloud more in our favor and against them, they added something else. They produced letters of that same Emperor addressed to the vicar Verinus, in which he severely condemns them and, leaving them to the judgment of the Lord, who had already begun to avenge himself upon them, released them from exile by an utterly dishonorable pardon.

Thus it was most clearly established not only that no condemnation of Caecilian had subsequently occurred, but also that his acquittal and exoneration, as well as their punishment, had been confirmed by that detestable pardon.

We did not have these outstanding documents of the case in our hands, as must be admitted. But perhaps, if we heard that they existed somewhere and could not obtain them from there for nothing, we would have procured them by whatever reward was necessary so that they might be permitted to be copied for us.

How much would we have given, if they had been offered for sale, so that they might also be read in our favor by the adversaries themselves?

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 55

What more could they seemingly have added to help us even more abundantly? And yet they added more.

For they recalled the case of Felix of Aptunga [Note: [Col. 0686] The old Corbie codex has *Aptucensis*. Two other Callican manuscripts have *Aptugensis*.], by whom Caecilian had been ordained and against whom they had brought the charge of handing over the Scriptures.

After Caecilian had been acquitted and pressure was being applied to complete the unity, they had raised a question concerning this Felix, thinking that Caecilian, already cleared, could thereby be entangled in the crimes of another.

This case of Felix too was therefore examined in a proconsular judgment [Note: [Col. 0686] See below in the Appendix.], where Felix’s innocence appeared with complete clarity.

But because a certain Ingentius, who confessed in that same trial that he had committed a falsehood against Felix, could neither easily be punished when the bishop’s case was at issue nor easily be dismissed by the proconsul as guilty of so great a crime without consulting the Emperor—for all these proceedings were taking place at the Emperor’s insistence—the proconsul referred the matter, and the Emperor replied that Ingentius should be sent to his court.

He wished their predecessors, by whom he was daily being petitioned, to be refuted in person. Yet he had no doubt about Felix’s exoneration; indeed, he confirmed it even by the explicit wording of his own reply, as the rescript shows.

We had all these documents concerning Felix’s case in our hands and had decided to hand them over for reading. In this matter they anticipated us and were the first to produce those same imperial letters ordering Ingentius to be sent to the Emperor.

They read them aloud, perhaps because they thought that we would no longer read them, since we considered it sufficient that Caecilian’s case had been dealt with in such a way that nothing further seemed necessary.

But when our adversaries were working to make the persecution which their predecessors had carried out against our predecessors before the Emperors, and the defeat of their slanders, appear all the more completely, what could we do except gladly accept what was offered and give thanks to the Lord in all things?

They themselves therefore produced Constantine’s letters; they themselves read them aloud.

What I am saying seems incredible, but the proceedings bear witness: their arguments have been written down, and their subscriptions are preserved.

They themselves, I say, read aloud that Constantine had written that the proconsul Aelianus had granted a proper hearing in Felix’s case and that Felix had been found innocent of the charge of handing over the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0686] Erasmus and the manuscripts have “had subscribed.”].

But Constantine said that he wished Ingentius to be sent to his court so that, as he says, “it might become apparent and be made known to those who are now active in the matter and do not cease petitioning day after day, when they are present and standing by, that they have vainly brought odium upon Caecilian and wished to rise violently against him.”

They themselves read this aloud.

Who among us would dare hope for this—that those whom iniquity had made our accusers, truth would make our defenders [Note: [Col. 0687] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “those whom iniquity had made our opponents, equity would make our defenders.”]?

So also truth compelled Balaam, whom iniquity had hired in ancient times to curse God’s people, to bless them (Num. 23).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 56

The chronological order of the consuls demonstrates this, although the constraints of time did not then permit us to examine it. For the documents called consular records were not at hand, and no one would have thought that they would bring forward so empty a matter as to ask us to answer what had happened after Ingentius was sent, or whether Ingentius had been sent at all, since the proconsular judgment had declared Felix’s innocence, and the Emperor’s reply—produced and read aloud by them—had confirmed that same judgment.

Indeed, they themselves would surely have produced anything that had been done in their favor after Ingentius was sent, if they had trusted in such a thing.

Thus, as the consular chronology shows, first Caecilian was acquitted in the episcopal judgment of Miltiades [Note: [Col. 0687] See the Appendix.]; then, not long afterward, Felix was established as innocent in the proconsular judgment; and thereafter Caecilian was also cleared by the Emperor, who examined the matter between the parties.

Then, after four years, his adversaries were released by that disgraceful pardon.

Miltiades gave judgment when Constantine was consul for the third time and Licinius for the second time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October. The proconsul Aelianus heard Felix’s case when Volusianus and Annianus were consuls, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March—that is, approximately four months later.

Constantine wrote to the vicar Eumalius concerning Caecilian’s exoneration [Note: [Col. 0687] *Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 82.] when Sabinus and Rufinus were consuls, on the fourth day before the Ides of November—that is, after nearly two years and eight months.

The same Emperor also sent letters to the vicar Valerius concerning the release of those men from exile and their abandonment to God, the avenger, who was to punish their madness. He did so when Crispus and Constantine, the latter for the second time, were consuls, on the third day before the Nones of May—that is, after four years and nearly six months.

Therefore, without any circumlocution, it is perfectly clear that, whether Ingentius was sent to the imperial court or not, nothing was subsequently judged against Caecilian. Rather, even by the imperial judgments, he was later shown to have been victorious over his adversaries and persecutors.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**57.** Let the party of Donatus now go on—so often discredited, so often slanderous, so often lying, so often refuted, so often overcome and confounded in every way—and continue to boast that the judge was bribed by us, as though the defeated were accustomed to utter any other cry. Surely the judge had to be bribed, so that his authority might invalidate what they themselves had done well. Yet I would not say that they acted badly; indeed, they acted extremely well by saying so much in defense of the truth against their own errors. For if their case is considered, it was truly against them; but if their pleadings are read, he judged more in accordance with their own position.

Could the man who stood between the parties have opposed us in a case in which those standing on the opposite side said, produced, and read out so much in our favor? What would we have needed to buy from the judge, when we did not buy from our opponents the very things that would have compelled the judge—even if he had accepted money from them—to pronounce judgment in our favor?

Even if we did not know him to be a man who feared God, loved justice, and was estranged from every such sordid practice, we ought to direct such a suspicion against him: for, with excessive patience, when he saw them overwhelmed by the truth and did not wish to appear hostile to them, he endured with extraordinary patience men wandering through emptiness, saying so many superfluous things, and returning so often to matters already refuted—so that almost everyone became reluctant to unfold the proceedings, burdened as they were by such extensive volumes, and to discover by reading how the case had been conducted. Whether they did this more from lack of truth or from the calculated skill of cunning, I do not know.

Nevertheless, this was the only way in which they were able, however inadequately, to assist so bad a case—a case which they ought rather to have abandoned. Finally, if the others should turn their accusation against those who conducted the case, and should assert instead that these men had been bribed by us, so that through so many pleadings and readings brought forward by themselves they would thus help our case and destroy their own, I do not know how they could defend themselves and clear themselves of this suspicion—unless perhaps they should say:

“If we had been bribed, we would quickly have brought such a bad case, already refuted both by us and by them, to an end. But now you may infer from this that we were present wholeheartedly and wished to be of some benefit: we spoke at length so that what had been done might not easily be read and so that it might not quickly become known that we had been defeated.”

If they did not say this, perhaps no one—neither they nor we, even under oath—would believe that they had freely provided us with all the things they said and read out against themselves and in our favor. Yet we give thanks for this not to them, but rather to God. In bringing forward and making public all those things, whether by speaking or reading, it was the truth that wrung them out, not charity that invited them.

## CHAPTER XXXV

**58.** Therefore, brothers—if indeed you are not angry that we call you brothers. For when they heard this from us, they said in the record that an injury had been done to them. Yet, when reminded by our instruction where this testimony from the prophet had been set down, they could not recall that God had commanded:

“Say to those who hate you and detest you: You are our brothers, so that the name of the Lord may be honored and may appear to them in joy, while they themselves are put to shame” (Isaiah 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore now, brothers, may the name of the Lord—which has been invoked over us and whose Sacraments both parties bear—appear to you in joy; and rightly are we called brothers. Love peace now; abandon at last the habit of slander and litigation [Note: [Col. 0688] Beccensis MS: *consuetudinem et litigiosam calumniam* (“the habit and contentious slander”). Other MSS: *consuetudinem, et litigiosam, calumniosam* (“the habit, and contentious, slanderous [practice]”).], already convicted and confounded. Do not hate them when, having been corrected, they pass over to us; hate them when, remaining in their wicked error, they continue to lead you astray.

Nor should they consider themselves great because we confer upon them in unity the honor which they possess in order to be liberated. For, possessing this honor outside unity, they are rather to be condemned on that account. Military standards, after all, are more dangerously held by usurpers than if they were not held at all. Yet when the usurpers have been corrected and brought back into the emperor’s camp, the standards are neither broken nor abolished; rather, they begin to adorn and protect those whom previously they had exposed and punished.

Why do you continue to heed their insane complaints and empty lies? The case was brought to an end at night—but so that the night of error might come to an end. The judgment was pronounced at night—but it shone with the light of truth. They complained that they had been shut up as though in a prison. We were there also: either an injury was done to both parties, or diligence was exercised toward both.

But how can we call it an injury, when we remember that we were in such a spacious, bright, and cool place? Or how could it have been a prison when the judge was there as well? Finally, we did not know that we had been shut in, since we were inside together with them. How do they know it, unless perhaps they wished to flee?

But who would not see that they would not have said these empty and laughable things—things more deserving of ridicule than refutation—about such a Judge, if they had been able to find anything substantial to say in defense of their case?

We know how many of you—and perhaps all or nearly all of you—are accustomed to say: “If only they would come together in one place! If only they would at some time engage with one another, so that, while they debated, the truth might become evident!”

Behold, it has happened. Behold, falsehood has been convicted. Behold, the truth has appeared. Why is unity still avoided? Why is charity still despised? Why are we divided by the names of men? The God who created us is one; the Christ who redeemed us is one; the Spirit who ought to unite us is one.

Let the name of the Lord now be honored and appear to you in joy, so that you may recognize your brothers in his unity. In the pleadings of your bishops, the error that separated us has already been defeated. Let the devil at last be defeated in your hearts as well, and may Christ, who commands this, be merciful to his gathered and pacified flock.

[Col. 0689]

## SERMON OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, DELIVERED TO THE PEOPLE OF THE CHURCH OF CAESAREA IN THE PRESENCE OF EMERITUS

[Note: [Col. 0689] The sermon to the people of the Church of Caesarea, the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, and the two books *Against Gaudentius* are absent from Gallican manuscripts; here again, however, they are corrected through comparison with the ancient editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0689] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

**(C)**

**1.** You recognize with what joy we receive the eagerness of your Charity. For we rejoice in the Lord our God, of whom the Apostle says: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). We therefore give thanks to that same Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ.

He has granted us that, even before we know the will of our brother Emeritus, we have already learned how much he loves unity. But hear how God has willed that we should hear the beginning of this matter from his own mouth.

As soon as he entered this church, standing in the place where we first began our conversation with him, he said to us—under the inspiration of the Lord, who both instructs the heart and governs the tongue:

“I cannot be unwilling to do what you want, but I can will what I want.”

Consider what he promised when he said that he could not be unwilling to do what we want. If he cannot be unwilling to do what we want, he knows what we want. For we want what you also want. We all want what the Lord wants.

And what the Lord wants is not hidden. His Testament is read—the Testament of him who made us his coheirs. In it we read: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Therefore, whether soon or late, he cannot be unwilling to do what we want.

But his second statement delays us somewhat: “I can will what I want.” For this is what he said: “I cannot be unwilling to do what you want, but I can will what I want.” He can will what he wants, but he cannot be unwilling to do what we want.

We see the thing he says he can do. For now he wills what he wills; but God does not will the very thing that he wills. What does he now will? To remain in disagreement with the Catholic Church; to remain in communion with the party of Donatus; to remain in schism; to remain among those who say, “I belong to Paul,” “But I to Apollos,” “But I to Cephas.”

But God does not will this, when the Apostle reproves it by saying: “Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:12–13). He can therefore will what he wills—but temporarily, for the moment, from embarrassment rather than from sound reasoning. For this is what he now wills, and he can will what he wills.

But because he cannot be unwilling to do what we want, may God not will what he wills [Note: [Col. 0689] Perhaps: “may he finally not will what he wills”] and do what we want.

Therefore, brothers, do not be disturbed by some delay while he wills what he wills. Pray that he may do what he has promised, so that he may not be able to be unwilling to do what we want.

And all cried out: “Either here or nowhere!” You have expressed your hearts in your voices; help us also with your prayers. The Lord, who commands unity, is powerful enough to change a will for the better.

As for what your Charity cried out—“Either here or nowhere”—we recognize and love in it the voice of your Charity directed toward him. We too have thought and desired this, not only now but always. The mind of our brother and fellow bishop, your bishop Deuterius, is the same; and this is especially necessary.

His mind has long been known to us. Together with the council he poured out prayers to the Lord about this matter, when we promised and offered this to those who are outside. Our signatures concerning this matter are already retained. We never cherish our own honor so jealously that we begrudge unity. We are lesser in honor [Note: [Col. 0691] Perhaps: “let us be lesser”], though we are greater in love. We know how weakness must be invited so that unity may be perfected.

**2.** We do not say these things, brothers, as though those who remain under schism have any hope before the Lord. Many argue without understanding what they are saying, and ask: “If they are schismatics, if they are heretics, why do they receive them in this way?”

Listen, my brothers. If we were receiving them, we would already be receiving this man, our brother Emeritus—whether good or bad, nevertheless our brother. I say this because he too knows that what was spoken to us through the prophet was also said to them at the Conference:

“Say to those who hate you: You are our brothers” (Isaiah 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

We believe that what they hate must be brought to an end; nevertheless, for as long as he hates, he is called “brother.” Until the hatred is ended, the name remains as a testimony.

We do not therefore receive them as they are. Far be it from us. For they are heretics. Rather, we receive Catholics: they are changed, and then they are received.

But because of the evil they possess, we cannot persecute the good things that we recognize in them. The evil of disagreement, schism, and heresy is their own evil; but the good things that we recognize in them are not theirs. They possess the good things of our Lord; they possess the good things of the Church.

Baptism is not theirs but Christ’s. The invocation of God’s name over their head when they are ordained bishops—that invocation belongs to God, not to Donatus. I would not receive him as a bishop if, when he was ordained, Donatus had been invoked over his head.

In the case of a soldier who has gone astray and deserted, the crime belongs to the deserter, but the mark does not belong to the deserter; it belongs to the emperor. But our brother did not desert from a place where he had never yet been. Rather, the deserter’s error arose in him when he was marked by the deserter.

The one who first created the schism, who separated himself from the Catholic Church together with those whom he drew after him, was a deserter. The others were marked by deserters, but not with the mark of a deserter—with the mark of the emperor.

For the deserter did not imprint his own mark. What do I mean by saying that the deserter did not imprint his own mark? Donatus did not baptize in the name of Donatus. For if Donatus, when he created the schism, had baptized in the name of Donatus, he would have imprinted the mark of a deserter. When I called such a person to unity, if I found the deserter’s mark, I would expel it, erase it, abolish it, cast it away. I would not approve it; I would reject it, anathematize it, and condemn it.

But now the deserter himself imprinted the mark of his emperor. God and our Lord Jesus Christ seeks the deserter, erases the crime of error, but does not destroy his own mark.

When I come to my brother and gather my erring brother, I look for faith in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is the mark of my emperor.

Concerning this mark, the Lord commanded his soldiers—or rather, his companions—to imprint it upon those whom they gathered into his camp, saying: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Because Paul knew that this mark, prescribed by the Lord, was to be imprinted upon all believers, he is alarmed at those who wished to belong to Paul, and says to them: “Was Paul crucified for you? Why do you want to be mine, and not rather my Lord’s? Why do you want to be mine, and not rather belong to him whose I am? Recognize and consider your mark. Were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

Thus we gather them, so that those whom we do not gather may not flatter themselves. Let them too be gathered, not puffed up; let them come and be received.

We do not hate in them what belongs to God. We do not hate them themselves, because they belong to God. What they possess belongs to God; and they belong to God because they are human beings, and every human being is God’s creature.

The fact that they bear the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit belongs to God. The baptism of the Trinity belongs to God. The Gospel they possess belongs to God. The faith they possess belongs to God.

**3.** “And what do they not possess,” someone might say to me, “if they possess these things?”

You say, “They possess Christ’s Baptism.” I say, “Yes.”

You say, “They possess Christ’s faith.” I say, “Yes.”

If they possess these things, then what do they not possess?

What is Baptism? A sacrament. Hear the Apostle: “If I know all mysteries”—that is, all sacraments. It is a great thing to know all God’s sacraments. However many sacraments we may know, who knows all God’s sacraments?

What does the Apostle say? “If I know all mysteries, if I possess all prophecy”—add still more—“and all knowledge.” But you had spoken of faith. Hear further: “If I have all faith.”

It is difficult to possess all faith, just as it is difficult to know all the sacraments. And what does he mean by “all”? “So that I may move mountains; but if I do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

Pay attention, brothers; I beg you, pay attention to the Apostle’s voice, and see why we seek our brothers with such labors and dangers. Charity seeks them from our hearts.

“For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors,” says the Psalm, “I was speaking peace concerning you” (Psalm 122:8), addressing holy Jerusalem.

See, then, my brothers, what the Apostle said: “If I possess all the sacraments, all knowledge, prophecy, faith”—what kind of faith?—“so that I may move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.”

He did not say, “Those things are nothing,” but, “If I do not have charity, I am nothing.” For what madman would say, “God’s sacraments are nothing”? What madman would say, “Prophecy is nothing, knowledge is nothing, faith is nothing”?

Those things are not nothing. But although they are great, and although I possess great things, if I do not have charity, I am nothing. They are great, and I possess great things; yet I am nothing if I do not have charity, through which the great things benefit me.

For if I do not have charity, those things may be present in me, but they cannot benefit me.

**4.** Consider, then, brother; consider, I beg you. You say to me, “Why are you seeking me?”

I answer: “Because you are my brother.”

You reply and say: “If I am lost, why are you seeking me?”

And I answer: “If you had not been lost, I would not be seeking you.”

“You seek me,” you say to me, “but if I am lost, why do you seek me?”

And I answer: “I seek you because you have been lost.”

And why do I seek you? For what benefit do I seek you? So that one day it may be said to me: “Your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

You reply and say to me: “But I possess the Sacrament.”

You do; I acknowledge it. That is why I seek you. You have added a great reason why I should seek you more diligently.

You are a sheep from my Lord’s flock; you have gone astray bearing the mark. That is why I seek you more earnestly: because you possess the very mark.

Why do we not possess one Church? We have one mark; why are we not in one sheepfold? I seek you so that this Sacrament may be an aid to your salvation, not a testimony to your condemnation.

Do you not know that a deserter is condemned because of the mark by which a serving soldier is honored? I seek you so that you may not perish with the mark.

For the mark is a mark of salvation if you possess salvation, if you possess charity. For this sign of salvation can be present in you outside [the Church], but it cannot benefit you.

Come, so that what you possessed may benefit you—not so that you may receive what you possessed, but so that what you possessed may begin to benefit you, and so that you may receive what you did not possess.

You possessed the mark of peace, but you did not possess peace itself. In that house—that is, in you—discord lived, while at the threshold it displayed the inscription of peace.

I recognize the inscription, but I seek the one who dwells there. I read the inscription of peace: “Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” It is an inscription of peace; I read it. But I ask who dwells there. I look for my brother; I recognize the inscription of peace.

I too possess it; I wish to enter.

What does “I wish to enter” mean? Receive me as a brother, so that together we may pray to the Father.

I do not pray with you. These are inscriptions of peace, and discord contradicts me? I will certainly labor, with the Lord’s help, to cast out discord, which wrongly possesses the house, and to bring in peace as its rightful owner.

Therefore, when I exclude discord and bring in peace, why should I remove the inscriptions of peace?

I say plainly to my Lord: “O Christ, who are our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14), make us one, so that we may rightly sing: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1).

Bring in concord; drive out discord. Bring yourself into your own inscriptions. Remain yourself; let no other possess them and deceive others through your inscriptions.

Change this contradictor, you who changed the thief on the cross in a single hour (Luke 23:40–43).

**5.** And certainly, let us see what you possess.

“I possess,” he says, “the Sacrament; I possess Baptism.”

If I say to you, “Prove it,” you show me what you received; you tell me what you confessed; you tell me what you hold.

I recognize it. I do not change it; I do not blow upon it. Far be it from me, when I seek the deserter’s salvation, to injure the emperor.

You have therefore proved to me that you possess the Sacrament by explaining the Sacrament [Note: [Col. 0693] Perhaps, instead of *exponendo Sacramentum*, one should read: *ego non do* (“I do not grant it”).]

[Col. 0694] You have proved to me that you possess faith. Prove to me that you possess charity; hold fast to unity.

I do not want you to say to me, “I possess charity.” Prove it.

We have one Father; let us pray together. What do you say when you pray, I ask you?

“Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9).

Thanks be to God. Following the teaching of our Lord, you added, “who are in heaven.” For on earth we each had individual fathers; together we have found one in heaven.

“Our Father, who are in heaven”: you invoke him as Father. Our Father wished to have one wife. Therefore, if we worship one Father, why do we not acknowledge one mother?

If you say that you were born from another, it was she who bore you from another womb [Note: [Col. 0694] *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, book 1, §§23–25.]

Not all of you could understand what I said. We know that through legitimate wives it came about that even those who were not born from legitimate wives were joined to the same inheritance. The wife’s will accomplished this.

For Ishmael was disinherited. Sarah herself had borne him, although from another womb. Sarah bore him from another womb by her own desire. She said: “For I want you to have children by her” (Genesis 16:2–4). And for this reason Abraham did so.

“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Corinthians 7:4).

For he would have been a son if he had not become proud. Ishmael was disinherited because of his pride. The slave woman raised her neck, so that [Sarah] said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Genesis 21:10).

Do you wish to know the power of peace, the power of concord, the power of humility, and what pride obstructs?

Sarah disinherited Ishmael, but Jacob’s sons born of slave women were called into one inheritance, because those women too wished to bear children through lawful marriages. We know that the sons of the slave women born to Jacob were called into one inheritance.

All twelve patriarchs were counted together. Difference of womb did not separate one from another, because charity united them all.

What difference, then, does it make where you received Baptism?

“Baptism is mine,” Sarah says to you.

“Baptism is mine,” Rachel says to you.

Do not be proud; come to the inheritance—especially since our inheritance is not that land which was given to Jacob’s sons.

The land was given to the sons of Israel; the more numerous its possessors became, the more constricted it was. Our inheritance is called peace.

I read the Testament: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Let us hold together what cannot be divided.

Its multitude of possessors does not constrict it, however many may come, just as it was promised: “So shall your offspring be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore. In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:17–18).

“And I saw,” he says in the Apocalypse, “many in white robes and with palm branches, whom no one could number, coming from every nation” (Revelation 7:9).

Let them come; let them hold peace. Let our possession not be constricted [Note: [Col. 0694] Perhaps: “let it not become constricted.”] Nothing causes constriction except disagreement.

Behold, my brothers, disagreement on the part of our brother causes us still to suffer constriction. Let him consent to peace, and spaciousness has been created.

**6.** But what can we do except bear with our brother’s weakness and not grow weary? We believe that this sweat of mine will be fruitful.

The Lord our God, who willed that we should come to you, who commanded us to seek him, who caused us meanwhile to find him face to face, will—helped by your prayers—make us find his heart, rejoice in his concord, and give thanks to God for his salvation, which he cannot possess except in the Catholic Church.

Outside the Catholic Church he can possess everything except salvation. He can possess honor; he can possess the Sacrament; he can sing “Alleluia”; he can respond “Amen”; he can hold the Gospel; he can possess and proclaim faith in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But nowhere except in the Catholic Church will he be able to find salvation.

All these things pass away, my brothers. At present he thinks that he will be great among his own people if he does not consent and is called a martyr of the party of Donatus. Far be it from us; may this swelling pride be removed from his heart in the name of the Lord.

He knows it himself; he reads it himself: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

I am not saying that if he boasts of having suffered some injuries or worldly losses for the party of Donatus, this profits him nothing. I say more: even if he suffers outside from an enemy of Christ—not from a Catholic brother seeking his salvation, but from an enemy of Christ—and, while suffering outside, the enemy of Christ says to him, “Away from the Church of Christ! Offer incense to idols; worship my gods,” and he is killed by that enemy of Christ because he refuses to worship, he may shed blood, but he cannot receive a crown.

**7.** They themselves know, from the time they were present at our Conference held at Carthage, how they confessed that their fathers had persecuted Bishop Caecilian.

At that time, disagreeing with the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0695] Am.: “with a Catholic.”], they created a schism. Their fathers—that is, the first men who created the party of Donatus—persecuted Caecilian. By persecuting him, they brought him before the emperor.

They sent charges against him to the emperor, although those charges were not true. The emperor ordered the case to be heard. It was heard before bishops, and those false charges were found to be false; Caecilian was acquitted.

Nor did they cease persecuting him. Rather, they repeatedly appealed to the emperor, before whom they later established the judge of the case. He too heard and investigated the matter between the parties.

The emperor investigated it and judged Caecilian innocent.

When we brought this against them, they disputed with us and said that the emperor had condemned Caecilian to exile—which is false. But observe what they did say: “Caecilian was brought before the emperor because he had been pursued by our elders, and he was sent into exile.”

We have read the proceedings. His pleadings are extant; his own subscribing hand is preserved with his own words.

Pay attention, I beg you; now judge our case. Certainly their elders persecuted Caecilian; certainly they brought him before the emperor; certainly they caused him to be condemned.

I do not wish to say that he was not condemned; I do not wish to say that he was declared innocent. But let us accept what they say.

When they persecuted him, when they caused him to be condemned, what was Caecilian then? When he was suffering persecution from the elders of these men, what was he? Let them tell me: what was he?

Was he a Christian? Was he a Catholic? What was he?

They do not say, “He was not a Catholic,” but “He was criminal.”

Therefore, criminal men can suffer persecution from saints. Let us accept this. Caecilian was a criminal man who suffered persecution. I do not say, “They were lying”; I say, “They were mistaken,” so that we may agree with them that he was criminal.

What were the men who carried it out? Choose whichever answer you wish. If they were wicked, abandon the wicked and come to us. But if they were holy, then it can happen that holy men persecute an unjust man.

Do not be angry with us if we persecute you. Do not say, “You are unjust because you persecute us.” For you have already shown that it can happen that the just persecute the unjust.

Can it happen, or can it not? Let one of the two answers be given to me. If it cannot happen, why did your people persecute Caecilian? But if it can happen, why are you surprised? Why praise the punishment without demonstrating the cause?

“Blessed,” says the Lord, “are those who suffer persecution.” Add: “for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10). By adding this, you have excluded robbers, criminals, adulterers, impious persons, sacrilegious persons, and heretics. Such people suffer persecution, but not for righteousness’ sake.

**8.** And yet what sort of persecution does our brother suffer, he who has been brought to us? It is the more glorious kind of persecution. I openly profess that I engage in this persecution. Let whoever wishes reproach me; I profess such persecution.

I read the Psalm: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 100:5).

If I rightly persecute the man who secretly slanders his neighbor, do I not more rightly persecute the man who publicly blasphemes the Church of God—when he says, “That is not the Church”; when he says, “Our Church is the one belonging to our party”; when he says, “That woman is a prostitute”?

Shall I not persecute one who blasphemes the Church? Certainly I shall, because I am a member of the Church; certainly I shall, because I am a son of the Church.

I use the voice of the Church herself. The Church herself speaks through me in the Psalm: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are destroyed” (Psalm 17:38).

Let them be destroyed in evil and advance in good.

Brothers, do not think that anything new has happened to our brother. When the party of Donatus held power at Constantina, they seized our layman Petilianus, born of Catholic parents and still a catechumen [Note: [Col. 0696] Earlier editions read: “Petilianus seized him,” and shortly afterward: “That man carried him away to death.” We do not hesitate to correct this as a scribal error, considering the second book *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §239, where Augustine says to him: “May God distinguish you from the party of Donatus and recall you to the Catholic Church, from which they seized you as a catechumen and bound you with the deadly bond of honor.”]

They used force against him unwillingly; they searched for him as he fled; they found him while he was hiding; they dragged him out while he trembled; they baptized him while he shook with fear; they ordained him against his will.

Behold the violence they used against one of ours. That party carried him away to death; are we not drawing him toward salvation?

**9.** I have said these things to your Charity because of what you said: “Either here or nowhere.”

This is what we too want: “Here, here”—but in unity, in peace; “here, here”—but in the fellowship of charity. Then it is good that he be here. For it would be better for him to be nowhere than here. But may the Lord grant that he be here rather than nowhere.

If not here, far be it from us that he should not be elsewhere. Let it be “here or elsewhere.” You have heard; he has heard. What God has done in his heart, he himself knows.

We strike his ear outwardly; he knows how to speak within. He inwardly proclaims peace and does not cease proclaiming it, if only he is heard.

[Col. 0698] His mercy will be present, and with the help of your prayers he will make our labor fruitful.

Nevertheless, if today he does not wish to communicate with us, although we ought not to grow weary but ought to persist as much as we can, even so we must not become weary. We may be delayed; we neither can nor ought to remove our persistence.

May he who brought him here to us be present, so that he may cause us to rejoice with him, together with you, in unity and in his peace.

[Note: [Col. 0697] At this point, if it should ever be found, one book *To Emeritus, Bishop of the Donatists, after the Conference* ought to be added; Augustine mentions this book in book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 46.]

[Col. 0697]

[Note: [Col. 0697] “On the Proceedings with Emeritus.” See book 2, chapter 51, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, column 650, from the words “Some time after the Conference” through the word “consuls.” M.]

## ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE PROCEEDINGS WITH EMERITUS, BISHOP OF THE DONATISTS AT CAESAREA

**(C)**

**1.** In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time [Note: [Col. 0697] In the year of Christ 418], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, at Caesarea in the Major Church, when Deuterius, the metropolitan bishop of Caesarea, together with Alypius of Thagaste, Augustine of Hippo, Possidius of Calama, Rusticus of Cartenna, Palladius of Tigaba, and the other bishops had come forward into the apse, with the priests and deacons, the entire clergy, and a very large crowd of people present—and when Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, was also present—Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said:

Dearest brothers, you who were Catholics from the beginning, and all of you who came over to the Catholic Church from the error of the Donatists, who came to know the peace of this holy Catholic Church and held fast to it with a truthful heart, and you who perhaps still doubt the truth of Catholic unity: hear us, who are concerned for you with pure love.

When our brother Emeritus, still a bishop of the Donatists, came to this city the day before yesterday, word suddenly reached us that he was present. And because, with the charity that God sees, we desired his presence, we immediately hurried to see him. We found him standing in the street.

After exchanging greetings, we urged him that it would be harsh and disgraceful for him to remain in the street, and that he should come with us to the church. He agreed to this without any refusal. We therefore thought that he would not refuse Catholic communion, just as he had offered his arrival voluntarily and had not hesitated to come to the church.

But while he remained longer in his heretical perversity, although inside the Catholic Church, I addressed your Charity, as you graciously remember. I said many things that you heard and that, without doubt, you remember as well as you can: many things about peace, many about charity, and many about the unity of the holy Catholic Church, which God promised and brought about.

In that sermon I was addressing you and exhorting him. And insofar as the entrails of charity within me could do so, in that sermon I was giving birth to all who were placed in danger concerning their souls, and I desired that they should be born for the Lord.

For the blessed Apostle Paul also said to some people: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

But even after our sermon, while he continued in that obstinacy of his, we did not think that hope should therefore be abandoned. Nor do we think that anyone should be despaired of as long as he lives in this body.

For I did not say the day before yesterday that I had not despaired of him in such a way that today I would dare to despair.

## 2.

But the matter has been brought to this point so that, since he has come—and, as far as we have learned, has come voluntarily—his arrival may not be fruitless for this Church. For either—and this is what we most hope and desire—we shall rejoice with you in Catholic peace over his salvation as well; or, if—as we abhor and detest—he persists in that obstinacy, you ought, from his presence, to understand more clearly what difference there is between Catholic peace and heretical dissension.

He is indeed a bishop of the party of Donatus [Col. 0699], but he was ordained by the Donatists of this city. [Note: The Louvain edition reads, “but by the Donatists,” adding the preposition *a*, which was absent from the first Amerbach edition. We judge that the reading should be, “and by the Donatists.”] We have already received a large part of these Donatists into the Catholic fold in the name of Christ, so that we rejoice that nearly all have been joined to Catholic communion. Yet since even among those who have already entered communion, not all but some appear—as I said shortly before—to doubt the Catholic truth itself, while others not only do not doubt but, still inwardly attached to the party of Donatus, offer us their bodily presence—whether men or women, physically within and spiritually without—we think it good to question their bishop.

If he has anything further to say on behalf of that party, now that the universally known Conference at Carthage has taken place, let him say it without prejudice to the party of Donatus, but in a way which he nevertheless believes may benefit you, in whose city he considers himself to have been ordained for your salvation in Christ. We, for our part, shall answer without prejudice to the Catholic Church, since no one has now imposed upon us the role of defending either party; yet we shall answer in a way which, as we think and desire, may benefit you who are present, confronting him who is present.

Thus, if he has been deceived, he may not deceive; but if we were deceiving you, let us be exposed, refuted, convicted, and instructed in the presence of one who perhaps makes many boasts outside. I have said this so that he may not refuse to speak on the ground that he can say, “My party has imposed no defense upon me at present.” For he did not remain silent after the Conference; he did not fail to come to this city after that Conference; he did not at some point depart from this province; nor do we believe that, after that Conference, he said nothing at all to anyone on behalf of the party of Donatus.

I know what was being said to you. I address you who came from that party: I know what was being said to you—that we had bought the verdict of the Examiner. I know that you were told that he had belonged to our communion and therefore had by no means permitted these men to say whatever they wished, but had suppressed them by authority rather than by truth, refusing to accept what they were saying. [Note: The Amerbach edition has, “rather than by integrity.” Perhaps it should be read, “because he did not accept as truth what they were saying,” or, “because he did not accept what they were saying.”]

All these claims were circulated after the Conference, whether by him himself or by members of that communion. What difference does it make from whom you are disturbed, when we want you to be tranquil in Catholic peace? If he were absent, I would say to you about him: “But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians 5:10). These are the words of blessed Paul against absent persons by whom the simple were being disturbed. But now he is present. Let him deign to tell us why he has come.

## 3.

Brother Emeritus, you are present. You attended the Conferences. [Note: The same Amerbach edition reads, “When you attended the Conferences.” Perhaps it should be read, “You attended the Conference with us.”] If you were defeated, why have you come? But if you do not think that you were defeated, explain on what grounds you appear to yourself to be victorious. You were defeated, then, if you were defeated by truth. But if you seem to have been defeated by authority and to have conquered by truth, this is not the authority by which you appear to have been defeated. Let your [Col. 0700] fellow citizens [Note: See Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 14.] hear on what grounds you presume to be victorious.

But if you know that truth was victorious against you, why do you still reject unity?

Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said: “The proceedings show whether I was defeated or victorious, whether I was defeated by truth or overwhelmed by authority.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Why, then, have you come?”

Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said: “To say what you are asking.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I am asking why you came. I would not be asking this if you had not come.”

Emeritus, bishop of the party of Donatus, said to the notary who was recording the proceedings: “Do it.”

## 4.

When he remained silent, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If, then, you kept silent because of the truth, you did not come without a reason—unless you wished to deceive these people.”

When he remained silent for a long time, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “You see, brothers, how long he has been silent. I urge you to pray that he may recover his senses; I beg you not to follow one who is perishing.

“Nevertheless, since he has mentioned the proceedings of our Conference, at which he said it could be shown whether he had been defeated by truth or overwhelmed by authority, there are indeed many passages in which they filled the proceedings with superfluous and delaying speeches, accomplishing nothing with all their strength except that nothing should be accomplished. But, with the Lord presiding and conducting his own cause, we reached the point they did not want to reach. The case was argued and decided.

“If we wished to read the entire proceedings to you—although, in your presence, I bind my brother and fellow bishop Deuterium to ensure that, just as is done at Carthage, at Thagaste, at Constantina, at Hippo, and among all Churches that are devoted to their duty, he does not shrink from doing the same thereafter, so that every year during the days of fasting—that is, during Lent before Easter, when you have more leisure to listen because you are fasting—the entire proceedings of the Conference may be recited each year, in order, from beginning to end—we nevertheless cannot read everything to you now.

“As I was beginning to say, deign first to hear, before the Conference, what letter we sent to the Examiner. In it we promised either how we would wish to be received if we were defeated, or how we would receive them if we conquered, so that it might be evident that the victory lay not in contention but in humility.”

## 5.

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, read the letter: [Note: Here Alypius passed over in silence certain matters wholly unnecessary to the purpose. We have included this entire letter, restored from the acts of the Conference, among Augustine’s letters as no. 128.]

“To the honorable and most beloved son, the most distinguished and eminent man, Tribune and Notary Marcellinus, Aurelius, Silvanus, and all the Catholic bishops.

“By this letter we inform you that we agree in every respect with the edict of Your Eminence, by which provision has been made for preserving the tranquility and peace of our Conference and for making the truth manifest and safeguarding it, just as you deigned to admonish us.

“Trusting in the truth, we also bind ourselves by the bond of a condition: if those with whom we are treating should be able to demonstrate to us that, although the Christian people, in accordance with God’s promises, had already spread by continual growth through all regions, filled a large part of the world, and were expanding to fill what remained, nevertheless the Church of Christ had suddenly perished through the contagion of the sins of certain persons whom these men accuse and had remained only in the party of Donatus—if they can demonstrate this, as stated, we shall seek no episcopal honors among them, but shall follow the counsel of those whose concern is solely for eternal salvation, to whom, once the truth has been recognized, we shall owe gratitude for so great a benefit.

“But if we are rather able to show that the Church of Christ, now occupying [Col. 0701] lands abundantly fruitful in their multitude of people, throughout all provinces—not only African but also overseas—and among very many nations, and, as it is written, bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, could not have perished through the sins of any persons mingled with it; if, moreover, we show that the case of those whom they then preferred to accuse rather than were able to convict has been settled [Note: In Letter 128: “we shall show the question to have been settled.”]—although the cause of the Church does not rest upon them—and that Caecilian was judged innocent, while they were judged violent and calumnious, by the emperor to whose tribunal they voluntarily sent their accusations by accusing them; and finally, if, by human documents or divine proofs, we prove whatever they may say about the sins of any persons, either that their innocence was assailed by false accusations or that the Church of Christ, to whose communion we adhere, has not been destroyed by any of their offenses: then let them preserve unity with us in such a way that they may not only find the way of salvation but also not lose the honor of the episcopate.

“For we do not reject in them the divine sacraments of truth, but the inventions of human error, which we detest. When these are removed, we shall embrace as a brother the heart united to us by Christian love, which we now grieve to see separated by diabolical dissension.

“Indeed, each of us may sit in a more prominent place in turn, joined to his colleague in honor, just as a visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. When this is granted alternately in the basilicas of both sides, each anticipating the other with mutual honor [Note: In the same letter: “each is anticipated in honor by the other.”], then, wherever the commandment of love has enlarged hearts, the possession of peace does not become confined. Thus, when one of them dies, thereafter each may succeed individually to the other in the customary manner.

“Nothing new will be done. From the very beginning of the separation, Catholic love has preserved this arrangement among those who, after the condemnation of the wicked error of schism, came—however late—to savor the sweetness of unity.

“Or, if the Christian peoples prefer to have individual bishops and cannot tolerate the association of two because of the unusual character of the situation, let us both withdraw from office. Let the individual churches, once the cause of schism has been condemned and they have been established in peaceful unity, have individual bishops appointed in the places where they are needed, from among those who are found individually in the individual churches once unity has been achieved.” [Note: See above, *Abridgment of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 5.]

## 6.

While he was reading, Augustine, bishop, said:

“I shall tell Your Charity and recall a most delightful and pleasing event that, with the Lord’s help, we experienced. Before the Conference, when some of our brothers were discussing this matter among ourselves—because, for the sake of Christ’s peace, bishops ought either to be willing to do this or ought not to be bishops—we must confess to you that, as we looked around at all [Col. 0702] our brothers and fellow bishops, we could not easily think of anyone who would be willing to undertake this and offer such humility to the Lord.

“As usually happens, we would say, ‘That man can do it; this one cannot. That one agrees to it; this one cannot tolerate it,’ speaking more from our suspicions, since we could not see their hearts.

“But when the time came for this to be made public, in the council of all the bishops—a gathering of almost three hundred—everyone was so pleased and all were so inflamed with zeal that they were ready to lay down the episcopate for Christ’s unity, not to lose it but to entrust it more securely to God.

“Only two were scarcely found who disliked the proposal. One was an aged old man, who ventured to express this more freely; another indicated his will by a silent expression. But after the brethren’s correction overwhelmed that old man when he spoke so freely, and he changed his opinion, he also changed his expression.

“Hear, then, in what ways the exhortation itself was given, for the sake of the one who says, ‘The one who humbles himself will be exalted’ (Luke 18:14).”

## 7.

He also read:

“Why should we hesitate to offer our Redeemer the sacrifice of this humility? Did he descend from heaven into human members so that we might be his members, while we fear to descend from our chairs lest those very members of his be torn apart by cruel division?

“For our own sake, nothing is more sufficient than that we be faithful and obedient Christians. Let us always be this. We are ordained bishops for the sake of Christian peoples. Therefore, let us do with our episcopate whatever benefits Christian peoples for Christian peace.”

Augustine, bishop, said:

“For your sake we ought to be what you are. What ought you to be, whoever among you I am addressing? A Christian, faithful, obedient: this you must be for your own sake, and I must be this for my own sake. Therefore, what you must always be for your own sake, and what I must always be for my own sake, we must always be.

“But what I am for your sake, let me be if it benefits you; let me not be if it harms you. Here is what has been said: pay attention.”

He also read:

“If we are useful servants, why do we begrudge our Lord’s eternal gains on account of our temporal dignities? The dignity of the episcopate will be more fruitful for us if, once laid down, it gathers Christ’s flock rather than, when retained, scatters it.”

While he was reading, Augustine, bishop, said:

“My brothers, if we are thinking of the Lord, this higher place is the watchtower of a vine-grower, not the summit of one who is proud. If, when I wish to retain my episcopate, I scatter Christ’s flock, how can the loss be the flock’s and the honor the shepherd’s?”
