He also read:

“For with what confidence shall we hope for the honor promised by Christ in the future age if, in this age, our honor hinders Christian unity?

“For this reason we have taken care to write these things to Your Excellence, and we ask that through you they become known to everyone. With the assistance of our Lord God—by whose admonition we make these promises and with whose help we trust that we can fulfill them—may pious love, even before the Conference if possible, either heal or soften human hearts that are weak or hard. Thus, with minds already at peace, let us not resist the most evident truth; let us either precede our discussion with harmony or follow it with harmony.

“For we must not despair if they remember that the peacemakers are blessed, because they will be called the children of God (Matthew 5:9). It is far more fitting and easier for them to wish the party of Donatus to be reconciled with the entire [Col. 0703] Christian world than for the entire Christian world to be rebaptized by the party of Donatus.

“This is especially so since, when those coming from the sacrilegious and condemned schism of Maximianus—whom they had also tried to correct by persecuting them with the commands of earthly authorities—were sought with such diligence, they did not dare to invalidate the Baptism conferred by them and received some of them, though condemned, without any diminution of their honor, while judging others to have remained unpolluted in the association of that division.

“We do not begrudge the harmony they have among themselves. But they ought to observe how piously the Catholic root seeks with such zeal the branch broken from it, if that branch in turn labored so earnestly to gather a small fragment cut off from itself.”

And in another hand:

“I wish you, my son, health and well-being in the Lord.”

## 8.

After this had been read, Augustine, bishop, said:

“Listen, you who do not know; listen, I beg you. Thanks be to God, because I am speaking in his presence.

“The case of the Maximianists, which I now wish to explain to you—the case in which they broke their ship, as it were, against all their calumnies, like a vessel carrying bad merchandise—when we brought it up so many times in our Conference, they were unable to say anything against it. That is, against our objection, so often inserted, so often repeated, and so often hurled against their faces, they could make no reply at all, because they found nothing to answer.

“Listen to it carefully, then. Here he is; he is hearing me. If I am lying, let him refute me and compel me to prove what I say. The proceedings themselves are not here, but let the case be presented there. Let us endure whatever delays may be necessary until we come to the relevant documents, provided I prove what I am saying.

“If he nevertheless doubts it—or, God forbid, pretends to doubt it—let him not join communion if I do not prove it; I say this with due regard for his peace. But if he already knows that I am speaking the truth and understands that he did not wish to answer because he could find nothing to say, I ask you to judge for yourselves what is more tolerable for him to accept as part of his honor: to receive those whom he condemned, or to acknowledge as a brother one whom he never defeated.

“Pay attention, I beg you; listen to the account.”

## 9.

A certain Maximianus was a Carthaginian deacon belonging to the party of Donatus. Whether because of the merit of his arrogance, or—as they themselves think—because of the merit of his justice, he offended his bishop, namely Primianus of Carthage: unjustly, if he was arrogant and Primianus the better man; justly, if he was upright and Primianus the worse.

Primianus excommunicated him. He went to the neighboring bishops, aroused hostility against Primianus, and accused him before them. The matter came to Carthage. The many Donatist bishops who had come wanted Primianus to come to them, just as the leaders of these men wanted Caecilian to come to them.

When Primianus learned of the faction, he refused to come to them, just as Caecilian had refused to come to those men. Primianus was condemned in his absence by these men, just as Caecilian had been condemned in his absence by the others.

God wished to place before our eyes, in recent times, an image of these events, because excessively ancient forgetfulness was already erasing them. He was condemned in his absence. Primianus was restored to communion by the other bishops of the party of Donatus; indeed, since they did not depose him, he was confirmed in his own see.

The Maximianists were condemned, just as Donatus deserved to be condemned by the visiting and overseas [Col. 0704] bishops who acquitted Caecilian. Maximianus was condemned together with his twelve ordainers. The faction itself contained very many members—perhaps there were a hundred bishops. But to avoid a more extensive amputation, these men wished to impose discipline on the many by overthrowing a few.

They condemned only those who had taken part in Maximianus’s ordination, when he was unlawfully elevated as bishop against his own bishop. The others who belonged to the faction were to be allowed to retain their honors if they wished to return to the Church. In their own words they showed that these men were outside the Church: for the one whom you urge to enter is outside.

A day was therefore fixed, within which, if they returned, the things said against Primianus would do them no harm; this they confirmed by the decree of Bagai. Maximianus was condemned together with the twelve.

Action was then begun to expel the condemned men from the basilicas. Judges were petitioned; proconsuls were petitioned; the episcopal council of Bagai was cited in court; they were called heretics and shown to be condemned; orders were obtained; forces were assembled; people came to expel from the basilicas men who had been condemned and remained in their obstinacy.

When those men were condemned, the people who supported them resisted. Wherever they could not prevail, they were defeated; in the place of those who had been defeated and expelled, others were ordained. Of these, to say nothing of the rest, we know two: Felicianus and Praetextatus of Assuri.

After two or three years, through Optatus Gildonianus, and after many persecutions had been inflicted upon them through judicial proceedings and with the full severity of the authorities, they received them back in their positions of honor. After their condemnation, after their expulsion, after the persecutions, they received them back in their honors and joined them to themselves as associates and colleagues.

For in the place of one of them, Praetextatus of Assuri, they had already ordained another named Rogatus, who is now a Catholic. The army of these men—that is, the band of the Circumcellions—cut out his tongue and hand.

Those who during the time when the condemned men were outside—nearly three years—were baptized by them, baptized outside the Church of these men, were nevertheless received in this way. No one said, “You do not have Baptism, because you were baptized outside.” Yet a person coming from Ephesus, Smyrna, Thessalonica, and the other Churches planted by the Apostles through their labor—Churches to which we read that the Apostles’ Letters were sent, and in which we hear them read—was rebaptized.

## 10.

The judgment is preserved; and, as we have heard from our own brother—may God make our brother Emeritus peaceful—it was the judgment he delivered when those men were condemned. Let the judgment under which they were condemned be read, and let the judgment under which the leaders of these men condemned Caecilian be read. Let us see which defendants were treated more harshly, which were punished by the more severe judgment, and which were condemned amid the greater uproar.

There he said:

“Although the poisonous womb’s cavity long concealed the harmful offspring of a viperous seed, and the moist clots of conceived crime slowly steamed into the limbs of asps by delayed heat, nevertheless the conceived poison could not remain hidden beneath its vanishing screen.

“For although late, the public crime nevertheless gave birth to its own parricide, as a brood of crimes brought forth its purpose. As was said beforehand [Col. 0705]: ‘He conceived injustice, was pregnant with trouble, and gave birth to wickedness’ (Psalm 7:15).

“But since the sky now shines clear after the clouds, and the forest of crimes is no longer confused once the names have been marked out for punishment—the cause had previously been granted indulgence, while we allowed the line of clemency to continue—it has found those whom it should punish.

“And among other things:

“‘Let us speak, beloved brothers, of the causes of the schism, since we can no longer remain silent about the persons: Maximianus, a rival of the faith, an adulterer of truth, an enemy of the mother Church, a servant of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram.’

“These are the words of the party of Donatus against the Maximianists, spoken, as we have heard, at his dictation.

“You know who Dathan, Korah, and Abiram were. They were the first to make a schism; the customary punishment was not enough for them, and the opened earth swallowed them alive (Numbers 16:32). ‘A servant of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram’: these are his own words. From the bosom of peace he hurled the thunderbolt of judgment.

“Listen further:

“‘And because the gaping earth has not yet swallowed him,’ he says, ‘it has reserved him for a greater judgment above. For, having been snatched away, he had gained the punishment he deserved by the brevity of his death; now he exacts the interest of a heavier debt, though dead he remains a concern to the living.’

“These are the words of the man condemning Maximianus—or rather, as he himself says, striking him with thunder from a truthful mouth.

“And yet the asps, vipers, and parricides were gathered back, and the Baptism given by the asp, the viper, and the parricide was not rejected.

“You have heard how great a fire of eloquence blazed when he found hay that he could burn.

“Brother Emeritus, you embraced your brother Felicianus, condemned by the thunderbolt of your own mouth. Acknowledge your brother Deuterium, who is also related to you by family.”

## 11.

“Whenever, my brothers, we brought this case of the Maximianists—which I have explained to you as best I could—against them while we were dealing with it at the Conference, he was more silent about it than he is now silent about everything. Let them not hide behind evasive maneuvers—not by defense but by flight.

“For they say that they granted those men a period of delay and received their own people within that period. This is false. Twelve were condemned together with Maximianus; the others, however, were not present at his ordination when hands were laid upon him. It was to those others that they granted a delay.

“For these are his own words:

“‘Not only does a just death condemn this man for his crime,’ he says; ‘the chain of sacrilege also drags many into partnership in the crime. Of them it is written: “The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 8:3).”

“‘We would not wish to cut apart the union of what is, as it were, one body. But since the pestilential decay of a festering wound provides greater relief through amputation than through the application of medicine, a healthier course has been found: lest the poisonous infection creep through every member, the wound that has arisen should be removed through a brief pain.’

“Thus he names the defendants in the notorious crime. Here [Col. 0706] he names twelve, including Felicianus and Praetextatus, although I do not recall all the names. He continues:

“‘Know that those who by their deadly work of destruction joined together a filthy vessel with collected filth, and also the clerics of the Church of Carthage who, by participating in the crime, lent their services to illicit incest, have been condemned by the judgment of God who presides and by the truthful voice of the universal council.

“‘But those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not pollute—that is, those who, through the modesty of a bashful faith, withdrew their hands from the head of Maximianus—we have permitted to return to the mother Church.’”

[Note: See Book 4 against Cresconius, sections 2, 4, 5, and 38.]

“They wished to cleanse their own face, because they forgave sacrilegious men and openly granted schismatics a way to return.

“What does this mean? I ask him now to deign to explain to me how the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not pollute those men. Why do you grant them a delay if they could have had no share in Maximianus’s schism? But if they are associates of the faction, although they were not present at the ordination, how is Maximianus unable to pollute them, while Caecilianus—once condemned in his absence by the whole world, and acquitted a third time while present—pollutes the whole world?

“Does an African not pollute Africans, a living man the living, a known man those who know him, a participant his associates, while Caecilianus pollutes people overseas, people far away, people who were not condemned? Felicianus sat with you, condemned by you, and does not pollute you?

“I did not see that man; you know this one. I believe that man innocent; you condemned this one as guilty. Or, if you admit that you received an innocent man, you admit that you condemned an innocent man.”

## 12.

“And yet, my brothers, we do not begrudge their harmony. They have ended the diabolical hatreds that had arisen among them; somehow, they have returned to peace.

“But this is what I say: if a broken branch sought the small shoot broken from it, with what diligence ought the tree itself to seek the branch broken from it?

“This is why we sweat; this is why we labor; this is why we have been endangered amid their weapons and the bloody frenzies of the Circumcellions; and this is why we still endure the remnants of those men with whatever patience God has granted us—while the tree seeks the branch, while the flock seeks the lost sheep from Christ’s sheepfold.

“If we are endowed with pastoral compassion, we must force our way through hedges and thorns. With our limbs torn, let us seek the sheep and bring it back with joy to the Shepherd and Ruler of all (Luke 15:4–6).

“We have said much, even though we are weary; yet our brother, for whose sake we say these things to you, to whom we say them together, and for whom we undertake so much, still remains obstinate.

“He thinks that a cruel strength is constancy. Let him no longer boast of a vain and false strength. Let him hear the Apostle saying, ‘Power is made perfect in weakness’ (1 Corinthians 12:9).

“Let us pray for him. How do we know what God may will? ‘There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever’ (Proverbs 19:21).”

---

[Col. 0707]

[Note: [Col. 0705] **ON THE BOOKS AGAINST GAUDENTIUS.** See Book 2, chapter 59, of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 654, from the words “At the same time” to the words “the bishop of Thamugadi.” [Note: That is, approximately the year of Christ 420. For the books of Augustine listed immediately before this belong approximately to that period: *On the Soul and Its Origin*, *On Adulterous Marriages*, and *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*. On the same occasion Letter 204 was written to the tribune Dulcitius. M.]]

# TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST GAUDENTIUS, BISHOP OF THE DONATISTS [Col. 0707]

[Note: Written approximately in the year 420.]

## BOOK ONE

In which two letters of Gaudentius to Dulcitius are refuted.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1.

Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, had threatened to set fire to himself in the church together with certain condemned persons associated with him. Dulcitius, the distinguished tribune and notary to whom the most pious Emperor had entrusted the execution of his laws for the completion of unity, was dealing with the furious man as he ought—with gentleness—and had first sent Gaudentius a peaceful letter. Gaudentius replied with two letters: one shorter, written in haste for the bearers, who—as he indicates—were hurrying; the other longer, in which he thinks he has answered more carefully according to the Scriptures.

Thus, with the Lord’s help, I have undertaken to refute his writings, so that even those who are slower in understanding may have no doubt that I have answered every point. First I shall set down his words, and then I shall append my own—not in the manner I used when answering Petilianus’s letter. There, whenever his words were inserted in their respective places, the text read, “Petilianus said”; when my words followed, it read, “Augustine replied.”

For this reason he slandered me as though I had lied, saying that he had never debated with me face to face—as though he had not said what he wrote merely because I had not heard it from his mouth but had read it in his letter, or as though I had not replied because I had not spoken in his presence but had answered his writing by writing in turn.

What are we to do with people who have such a heart, or who suppose that those to whom they wish their writings to become known have such a heart? Let us satisfy even such people in this way. When we quote Gaudentius’s words, let us not say, “Gaudentius said,” but, “Words of the Letter”; and when we answer, let us not say, “Augustine replied,” but, “Response to this.”

Let us therefore begin to refute Gaudentius’s first and shorter letter.

### 2.

**Words of the Letter:** “To the honorable Dulcitius, tribune and notary, whom—if you so wish—you may regard as especially desirable to us, Gaudentius, bishop.”

**Response to this:** We ought not to examine even these words, lest we linger almost needlessly over matters when there are important passages that compel us to speak at somewhat greater length.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3.

**Words of the Letter:** “I received the writings of Your Religion through those whom it is manifest that everyone loves, both for their character and for their manner of life.”

**Response to this:** I shall not examine how you said, “Your Religion,” of a man whom you rather consider irreligious. You returned the honorific expression as you thought it should be returned, because he had treated you more honorably in the letter he sent you than a Catholic ought to treat a heretic, thinking that your mind might be healed by such language.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 4.

**Words of the Letter:** “In them,” he says, “you said many things on behalf of Your Dignity, which for the moment I pass over in silence; but since the sharpness of your intellect did not perceive it, in that same writing you were unable to assert us either completely innocent or guilty.” [Col. 0708]

**Response to this:** How did he not assert the guilt of those whom he said had been wrongly gathered together? How did he not assert the guilt of a man when he said that, under your leadership, the souls of the wretched would perish in a wicked death, adding that you ought to understand how much envy could remain for you both in this world and despair at the final judgment?

[Note: The edition of Amerbach has, “how much punishment could remain in despair.” The Louvain editors think it should be read, “how much punishment could remain in despair.”]

How did he not assert the guilt of the man whom he exhorted, as best he could, to follow the example of others to be imitated, abandon the error of his former heresy, and bring himself to the one true faith of God?

Nevertheless, we undertook not to defend the words of the Tribune but to refute the heretic. If this man of ours, as a military layman, said something too incautiously, who would not forgive him? Who would insist that the Catholic Church should be prejudiced by his words?

Consider more carefully what you say, since the party of Donatus presented you at our Conference held at Carthage, together with six others, as a defender of its division.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 5.

**Words of the Letter:** “But if,” he says, “you consider us criminals, you must flee and condemn our association.”

**Response to this:** Certainly the association of criminals must be avoided, but the association of those who have been corrected must not be rejected. We therefore avoid the one in a salutary manner, while mercifully willing, desiring, and striving for the other.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 6.

**Words of the Letter:** “But if,” he says, “you consider us innocent—which you yourself also said—we rejoice to endure persecutors established in the faith of Christ.”

**Response to this:** I examined the letter of the Tribune addressed to you, and nowhere in it did I read that he called you innocent; rather, he said that he had heard or learned from others that you were prudent. In the Holy Scriptures, however, not only good but also evil persons are customarily called by this name. Indeed, even the serpent who deceived the man received this designation there.

For what some translators rendered “the wisest of all the beasts” (Genesis 3:1), the Greek manuscripts have rather “the most prudent” (*Phronimetatos*) [Note: [Col. 0709] *Phronimetatos*.]; from there that passage was translated into the Latin language.

But if we are to suppose that the Tribune called innocent those whom he said you were holding against their will for destruction, what is surprising if he believed that the same thing was happening there which he had learned was happening elsewhere?

You therefore have no reason to rejoice that you are suffering persecution, since you cannot find a way to assert that you are innocent. Yet far be it from us to call this a persecution by human beings, since it is rather a persecution of vices for the liberation of human beings, of the kind exercised by the diligence of physicians even toward the sick.

Moreover, even if you were innocent, you would thereby become guilty, because you desire to kill innocent people. For those who strive to assert that they are innocent and nevertheless refuse to spare their own lives—what else are they shown to be doing than killing innocent people?

## CHAPTER VI

**7. Words of the Letter:** “In this church,” he says, “in which, as you yourself also said, the name of God and of His Christ has always been invoked in truth, we either remain alive for as long as it shall please God, or, as befits God’s household, we end our life within the Lord’s camp—that is, on the condition that, if force is brought to bear, this may then happen. For no one is so insane as to hasten toward death when no one is driving him to it.”

**Reply:** Nor is it stated in the Tribune’s letter that you invoked the name of God in truth, although he did say that it was invoked. Yet even if he had said this, it could be understood not as referring to your glory but to your punishment. For the Apostle also said of the impious Gentiles, “who suppress the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:18), as you do when you suppress the truth of divine Baptism in the unrighteousness of human error. Therefore, when we correct your unrighteousness, we certainly ought not to destroy the truth of that Sacrament.

You openly profess, though in other words, that you and your companions will perish with the church. For when you say “in the church,” what else do you wish to be understood than “with the church,” since you are preparing to bring this about by fire? Such is the innocence of the party of Donatus: you do, with your own deaths added, what you are said to have done at Carthage, as far as you could and with whomever you could, to bring discredit upon us concerning the basilicas that had belonged to you, but without your own deaths. Who, then, would not believe that you did this out of zeal [Note: [Col. 0709] In the Ambrosian manuscript, “under cover,” perhaps in place of “out of zeal”]—which you are now preparing to do even by dying?

But if you did not do that, then what you are preparing to do is certainly more insane. Yet you said, “if force is brought to bear,” and you added, “For no one is so insane as to hasten toward death when no one is driving him to it.” How much more insane, then, is the one who, while being driven toward life, hastens toward death?

[Col. 0710]

## CHAPTER VII

**8. Words of the Letter:** “As for those who are with us,” he says, “I call God and all His Sacraments to witness that I have urged them and earnestly persuaded them that whoever wished to leave should declare this publicly without fear. For we cannot retain unwilling people either, since we have learned that no one is to be compelled to embrace the faith of God.”

**Reply:** Why do you not also openly acknowledge that you are an exhorter to a good work, even if not a retainer of unwilling people, if what you are about to do is good? Or do you yourself perhaps understand how evil it is, and threaten to do it more to frighten than to carry it out—either unfaithful because you are lying, or cruel because you are telling the truth?

## CHAPTER VIII

**9. Words of the Letter:** **IN ANOTHER HAND:** “I wish you safety, prosperity in the affairs of the state, and withdrawal from the disturbance caused by the Christians.”

**Reply:** We too can wish him safety and prosperity in the affairs of the state, but not that he cease from correcting heretics.

## CHAPTER IX

**10. Words of the second Letter:** “To Dulcitius, honorable and worthy of every affection, Gaudentius the bishop.”

**Reply:** If you desire the man with every affection, why do you refuse to maintain with him the unity of Christ? Do you wish, by returning evil as though for evil, to rebaptize the man whom you regard as your persecutor?

## CHAPTER X

**11. Words of the Letter:** “People who are known to one another only by reputation,” he says, “are accustomed either to wish to see one another, or to exchange words upon an uncertain meeting [Note: [Col. 0710] An old Parcensis manuscript reads “infecto,” perhaps for “inserto.”], or at least not to shrink from the presence of someone previously unknown. Yet in your letter you informed me that, when you found me absent, you rejoiced, but that when I returned, you were saddened.”

**Reply:** Not everyone who is known to another only by reputation wishes to see that person, but only those whom reputation itself commends as worthy. Yet it is truly remarkable what has happened to you: you say that you long for the man from whom you complain of suffering persecution, while the man who persecutes you prefers that you be absent and does not wish to find the one whom he persecutes. But why is this, unless he wished you rather to be understood as the persecutor of those whose salvation in Christ he believed your presence to obstruct?

## CHAPTER XI

**12. Words of the Letter:** “But since the other day,” he says, “so that I might not remain silent in my reply because of the delay of the bearers, I briefly and cursorily communicated certain matters. Now I must respond to the writings of Your Dignity with the words of the most sacred divine Law. The Lord said: ‘You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous, and you shall not acquit the guilty by a purge’ [that is, by clearing him] (Exod. 23:7). It is therefore certain that, in God’s judgment, those who absolve the guilty and those who kill the innocent are bound by an equal crime and equal guilt. If, before communion, the Gabinus whom you named [Note: [Col. 0710] The same manuscript reads here and below “Gabinius”], or the other faith-breakers, were guilty and partners in that evil fall according to God’s words, they certainly ought not to have been absolved. But if they were received as innocent or holy, why do you kill the innocent while they remain in the faith in which you receive them as though they were holy?”

**Reply:** You speak maliciously and falsely. The man to whom [Col. 0711] you are speaking did not receive such an order that you should be killed, but that you should be corrected; and, if you should refuse, you would be sent into exile so that you would not obstruct the correction of others. But if the just ought not to do this to the unjust, why did you also wish falsely to boast at our Conference about Caecilian’s exile, saying that he had been sent into exile by the emperor Constantine at the insistence of your predecessors? [Note: [Col. 0711] The same Parcensis codex reads “laws enacted for the sake of unity”; the printed editions read “promulgated laws,” omitting “for the sake of unity.”]

This Tribune to whom you are writing, who has been entrusted with responsibility for the laws enacted for the sake of unity, wants you to live so greatly that he fears you may kill yourself. Behold, I have set before your eyes him himself and yourself [Note: [Col. 0711] The same codex reads “I set”]. He wants you to live in the peace of Christ; you seek to kill yourself within the party of Donatus. Recognize which of you is your persecutor.

## CHAPTER XII

**13.** Gabinus, now one of our number, who was once one of yours, and very many others who have crossed over from you to us after considering the Catholic truth, should not seem to you to have remained unpurified from your contagion merely because they were not rebaptized by us. Those who have not yet been baptized are washed from all sins in the Catholic Church by the laver of regeneration. But in those who receive this Sacrament outside the Church not for help but for judgment, since we do not violate the royal seal even in a deserter, what is written comes about: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

See, then, how those who ought not to be baptized can be cleansed by the love of Catholic unity itself: what was already present outside them does not begin to be present within them, but what was harmful to them outside begins to benefit them within. We do not therefore receive them from you as though they were holy; by crossing over to us they are sanctified, for while remaining among you they cannot be holy at all. Nor do we kill innocent people when we wish even the guilty among you to live.

## CHAPTER XIII

**14.** But you, who rightly remember the testimony of the divine word and reproach us with God’s saying, “You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous”: if you are innocent and righteous, why do you kill yourself? We do not call you innocent and righteous, and yet we do not want you to be killed. You consider yourself innocent and righteous, yet you do not spare the innocent and righteous.

It is certain, then—as you yourself said—that in God’s judgment those who absolve the guilty and those who kill the innocent are bound by an equal crime and equal guilt. Why, then, did you absolve Felicianus, the guilty Maximianist? Why do you kill the innocent—and yourself?

We do not even absolve the guilty; rather, we first wish them to be corrected so that they may deserve to be absolved. Nor do we judge you innocent, whether you spare yourself or kill yourself, if you remain in the party of Donatus. For however greatly you may glory in your innocence, by killing yourself, an innocent person, you cannot remain innocent—unless you perhaps answer me by saying: “When I kill myself, I do not kill an innocent person, since by the very will with which I decide to kill myself I become guilty in mind before I have killed the body.”

If you say this, you speak the truth, and in wondrous fashion you defend yourself by accusing yourself. For when you show that, by killing yourself, you first become guilty through your intention, no one will convict you [Col. 0712] of having killed an innocent person once the deed has been committed.

By this reasoning, therefore, it follows that although many innocent people are killed by others, no innocent person is killed by himself. For by the very thought with which he attempts to kill himself, he is first stripped of his innocence, so that when he kills himself, he does not die innocent.

This would happen to you if you had been innocent before preparing to kill yourself. But now, because even previously, as a heretic, you were not innocent, your killing yourself would not be the beginning of your iniquity but its increase.

## CHAPTER XIV

**15. Words of the Letter:** “For,” he says, “a false report certainly reached you concerning the holy Emeritus of Caesarea. If this were so [Note: [Col. 0712] Perhaps “hear” (*audi*) should be read in place of “with” (*apud*)], it would accord with the Apostle’s saying: ‘If some of them fell away from the faith, does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not’ (Rom. 3:3).”

**Reply:** What you were afraid to say about Emeritus of Caesarea must be said. A false report was indeed spread about him, namely, that he had become a Catholic. But just as you heard this, so you could also have learned the whole truth of what happened. Why, then, did you wish to remain silent about the praise due to your fellow bishop, whose name was put before you as an example? Surely, if he did anything worthy of praise in so grave a crisis, you ought not to have concealed it. But since you do not want us to believe that you could have begrudged his praise, why did you remain silent unless you were afraid to be ashamed of him?

Emeritus therefore came to Caesarea, where we were present. He came neither seized by anyone’s cleverness nor brought by another’s authority, but, moved by his own will, he wished to see us. We saw him; we went together to the Catholic church; a very large crowd was present. He was unable to say anything in defense either of himself or of you. He refused to communicate; he persisted in postponement; when convicted, he fell silent; he departed unharmed.

What could have been gentler on our part, in view of our mildness? What could have been more invincible on behalf of Catholic truth [Note: [Col. 0712] The Louvain editors think “for the truth of the Catholic Church” should perhaps be read]? What could have been more salutary for your correction, if you have any wisdom?

Since he had come to us voluntarily, and could not have come for any reason except to say something on your behalf against us, he would certainly have spoken if he had found something to say. Whatever he had prepared to say in order to come was refuted beforehand, with the Lord’s mercy assisting us, before it could be brought forth by his attempt to circumvent us.

And certainly, if you think that he could have answered but did not wish to, read what was done with him, and answer for yourself. If Emeritus had crossed over into Catholic peace, you would have said that he had not consented to the light of truth through divine mercy, but had yielded to the burden of persecution through human weakness. Finally, if he had been captured and brought unwillingly, you would have claimed, according to your preference, that he had fallen silent not because he lacked an answer but because he had planned to escape.

But now, since he came of his own accord, what failed him was not his tongue but his cause. And because he did not wish to cross over into Catholic unity, confusion made his proud soul utterly obstinate. Yet this contributed as much to the destruction and punishment of himself as to the confirmation and salvation of others.

For if they had seen Emeritus [Col. 0713] communicating with us, they would have suspected that he was afraid. But when they saw him remaining in the party of Donatus and yet keeping silent against the Catholic Church, it appeared to them more clearly that by his silence he was crying out against his own people. Indeed, while he stood there with a sound and free voice and mouth, was that Emeritus—Emeritus, I say, both hostile and mute—not a competent witness against us on behalf of your cause?

## CHAPTER XV

**16.** Yet you thought you had rightly consoled your people with apostolic authority—not on account of Emeritus, who could not do more for you than, finding nothing to say on your behalf, nevertheless did not depart from you, but on account of the others who, abandoning your error and being changed into the Catholic fellowship, are incorporated into something better. You recalled that the Apostle had said: “If some of them fell away from the faith, does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not.”

In truth, what remains is that those who believed in God should be said to have fallen away from the faith, while those who believe human beings should be said to retain the faith. God said, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Behold whom those who cross over from you to us believe.

Human beings said that the nations across the sea perished through Caecilian’s sin. Behold whom those who persist in your fellowship believe. You say that those who followed the faith of God have fallen away from the faith, while those who remained in human words possess the faith of God.

Where, then, is what the Apostle immediately adds to this statement that you have quoted: “But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Rom. 3:3–4)? If those who believe what the truthful God said have fallen away from the faith, while those who believe what a lying human being said remain in the faith?

## CHAPTER XVI

**17. Words of the Letter:** “You persuade me to flee,” he says, “as though this were a command of the Law. But only the doer of the Law ought to be obeyed, because the Apostle Paul says: ‘It is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified’ (Rom. 2:13). For hear also the Lord saying: ‘Because the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, but the hired man, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters them’ (John 10:11–12).”

**Reply:** See how the party of Donatus understands the Gospel. Was the Apostle, then, not a shepherd but a hired man when he was lowered through a wall in a basket and fled the hands of the man who wanted to seize him (Acts 9:25)? And are you a shepherd, who wish to destroy with yourself those whom you call the Lord’s sheep [Note: [Col. 0713] Perhaps: “those whom you say are the Lord’s sheep among you”]—so that they may perish in mind through error and destroy their bodies through madness—and who seek to kill them along with yourself, while refusing to hear the Shepherd and Prince of shepherds saying, “The thief comes only to kill and destroy” (John 10:10)?

Did you come back for this, after you had departed? Did you return for this, after you had fled? This is the work of a thief and robber, not of a shepherd and guardian.

Nevertheless, even without our forcing you, consider how you wanted all your colleagues who fled to be understood as hired men, not shepherds. But if the Lord’s sheep were with you, they would either come with you, so that, once corrected, they might have you as their shepherd, or, leaving you behind, they would flee to the shepherd.

The hired man whom the Lord signifies flees at the sight of the wolf, not in body but in mind, when through fear he abandons righteousness. So your own Secundus of Tigisis fled when he feared Purpurius of Limata, who had confessed to homicide and was all the more terrifying, lest he lose either the primacy or the episcopate.

But in body even the good shepherds, the Apostles, fled during persecution; nevertheless, they did not abandon Christ’s sheep in care and spirit.

If you were therefore a shepherd [Col. 0714], first [Note: [Col. 0714] The old Parcensis codex reads “first”; the printed editions, “earlier,” less well.] you would not be on the wolf’s side. Then you would obediently have listened, through the mouth of anyone—even a sinner—to the command of your Lord, who ordered His servants to flee during persecutions. You would not argue against your Lord and say, “Only the doer of the Law ought to be obeyed,” because the Apostle Paul says, “It is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified.”

## CHAPTER XVII

**18.** Why do you twist clear words into another meaning? He denied that hearers of the Law, and not doers, are righteous before God; he did not forbid their being heard by human beings when they speak the truth. Otherwise, as you do, he would have been speaking against his Lord, who said of certain people, “Do what they say; but do not do what they do, for they speak and do not do” (Matt. 23:3).

You see how Christ commanded others to hear and practice the Law even through people who hear and preach the Law but do not practice it. Yet you say, “Only the doer of the Law ought to be obeyed,” and, wishing to rebuke someone as your persecutor, you speak against your Creator.

God indeed says to the sinner, “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Ps. 49:16). But this is because it benefits him nothing when he says what he does not do. It benefits the person who hears what is good even through an evil person and does what he hears.

“Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9), but it is fitting in the life and conduct of one who practices what is good, even if he heard that praise from the mouth of a sinner.

However sinful you may consider the Tribune to be, and however much you may regard him as not practicing the Law, obey—not him, but the One who speaks even through him and says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23).

Why are you standing still? Hear and flee. Christ commands this, not the Tribune.

Unless perhaps you answer and say: “Christ did say, ‘If they persecute you in this city, flee into another’; but why should I leave this city, when neither is this man my persecutor nor am I a hearer of Christ?” And so, if you remain, you are a raging wolf; if you flee, you are a fearful wolf.

And since the Bridegroom says, “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth in the footsteps of the flocks and pasture your kids beside the shepherds’ tents” (Song 1:7), even if you boast that you are a shepherd, nevertheless, because you have gone out from the Lord’s fold, you pasture your kids, not Christ’s sheep.

[Col. 0715]

## CHAPTER XVIII

**19. Words of the Letter:** “Then,” he says, “what places will receive the priests to keep them safe, as into a harbor, when, amid this storm of persecution, the calm has been disturbed on every side [Note: [Col. 0715] The Parcensis manuscript reads, ‘places that have been disturbed on every side and are to be preserved for tranquility’], when the Lord has said, ‘When they begin to persecute you in this city, flee into another’?

“Then the Apostles fled because no emperor had ordered anyone to be proscribed on their account. But now those who receive Christians, frightened by proscriptions [Note: [Col. 0715] The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions read ‘dragged away’] and fearing danger, not only do not receive them but even fear seeing those whom they silently venerate.”

**Reply:** I certainly praise this: that you acknowledge yourselves. But I grieve that you do not correct yourselves. For what could be clearer than this profession of yours, by which you sufficiently declare that you do not belong to the company of those to whom the Lord said, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another”?

This is precisely what I said shortly before: you could answer me with complete truth if you said, “Neither is this man my persecutor, nor am I a hearer of Christ.” Behold, you say this most plainly.

For how are you a hearer of Christ, when He promises His hearers—that is, His followers—that until the end of the age there will always be cities to which they may flee whenever they suffer persecution, saying, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another. Truly I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes”?

Yet in this persecution, which you complain of suffering, you now say that places are lacking for you to flee to and where, as in a harbor, you might rest from this storm. In doing so, you speak against Christ’s promise: He says that there will always be cities to which His people who suffer persecution may flee until He comes—that is, until the consummation of the age.

Since He promised this to His people, but you do not find it, He must be lying if you are His. But since He does not lie, you are not His.

Accordingly, neither is the Tribune to whom you write your persecutor. Rather, he is the persecutor of your persecutor—that is, of your error, by which you are compelled to do such things that you belong to the class of those of whom it is written that they suffered persecution from their own deeds (Wis. 11:21).

Therefore, if you understand what those who love you are persecuting within you, you will undoubtedly flee from the evil deeds themselves through which you suffer persecution, and you will join those who, in order to free you, persecute your persecutors. For they persecute nothing except your errors.

## CHAPTER XIX

**20. Words of the Letter:** “Through the Maker of all things, the Lord Christ,” he says, “almighty God fashioned human beings to be like God and left them to free choice. For it is written: ‘God made human beings and left them in the power of their own will’ (Ecclus. 15:14). What is now being taken from me by human authority, when God granted it?”

“Consider, most distinguished man, how great sacrileges are being committed against God, so that human presumption may take away what He granted and vainly boast that it is doing this on God’s behalf. It is a great injury to God if He is defended by human beings. What does the person who wishes to defend Him by force think about God, except that God is unable to avenge His own injuries?”

[Col. 0716]

**Reply:** According to these most deceitful and empty arguments of yours, let all sins be left unpunished to human license, with the reins loosened and cast aside; let no barriers of law be set up to restrain the audacity of doing harm and the lust for wantonness. Let no king restrain his kingdom, no commander his soldier, no provincial governor his subject, no master his slave, no husband his wife, or father his son from the freedom and pleasure of sinning by any threats or punishments.

Take away what sound teaching wisely says through the Apostle for the health of the whole world, and, in order to strengthen the children of perdition in a will all the worse because it is freer, erase what the chosen Vessel says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God. Those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. For it is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Rom. 13:1–4).

Erase these words, if you can; or, if you cannot erase them, despise them as you do. Form the worst possible judgment about all these matters, so that you do not lose your free choice.

Or, since you blush before human beings as human beings do, cry out, if you dare: “Let murders be punished, adulteries be punished, and all other crimes and disgraces, however great, whether of wickedness or lust, be punished; only sacrileges we wish to remain unpunished by the laws of rulers.”

Do you say anything else when you say, “It is a great injury to God if He is defended by human beings. What does the person who wishes to defend Him by force think about God, except that God is unable to avenge His own injuries?”

When you say these things, what else are you saying but this: “Let no human authority oppose or obstruct our free choice when we injure God”? O grief! Earlier ages were deprived of instruction of this kind, since you had not yet been born when holy Moses bore his own injuries with the utmost gentleness [Note: [Col. 0716] So the Parcensis codex. The printed editions read “very lightly”], but avenged God’s injuries with the utmost severity.

But you, a teacher through the most malicious presumption of heresy, cry out, “God made human beings and left them in the power of their own will. What is now being taken from me by human authority, when God granted it?” You are obviously demanding that, in order to inflict injuries upon God—who made human beings with free choice—free choice should be left to you by human beings.

Yet those who, by decree of King Nebuchadnezzar, with the penalty of death and the destruction of their homes set before them, were terrifyingly forbidden to blaspheme God—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—and were severely punished if they disobeyed (Dan. 3:96), could have said what you said: “It is a great injury to God if He is defended by human beings. What does the person who wishes to defend Him by force think about God, except that God is unable to avenge His own injuries?” They too could have said these words to him, and perhaps they did; and if not with the same freedom, at least with no different emptiness.

**21.** Free choice was therefore given to human beings when they were created, but so that, if they did evil, they might become [Col. 0717] subject to suffering. Indeed, when the first human beings had sinned, they were condemned to death; and before bodily death finally overtook them, they were sent into exile from paradise.

The Emperor has imposed milder measures upon you, out of Christian gentleness: he wished to inflict exile upon you, not death. But you, learned men, considering what is deserved and what is the lesser punishment, add death—not on the basis of his judgment but on the basis of your own.

Do not perish eternally while you wish human beings to grant you free choice at this time for offending God. Hear the Apostle, and you will have a great shortcut by which royal authority cannot harm you: “Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it.” From this authority, the righteous before our time received praise—not only those who faithfully obeyed religious kings, but also those who endured impious kings as adversaries for the sake of God’s truth. The former received praise for obedience [Note: [Col. 0717] Something may be missing here: “the latter, praise for suffering”]. Both received praise from authority, but by doing what was good, not by resisting authorities.

What you do, however, is not merely not good; it is a great evil: to tear apart the unity and peace of Christ, to rebel against the promises of the Gospel, and, against Him of whom it was said, “He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8)—that is, against the true and supreme King of Christians—to carry Christian standards as though in civil war.

Let it therefore suffice for your opportunity to be corrected that, for such great evils of yours, you have received punishments far milder and lighter, provided you do not voluntarily inflict upon yourselves what the Emperor did not decree. Do not wish free choice to be granted to you by human beings for licentious impunity, lest you fall even more disastrously into the hands of God Himself.

For your predecessors too judged that, in injuries of this kind against God, human free choice ought not to be left unpunished by kings. Although they had a bad case, they nevertheless pursued Bishop Caecilian all the way to the judgment of the emperor Constantine.

## CHAPTER XX

**22. Words of the Letter:** “Our faith,” he says, “which the Lord Christ left to the Apostles, is made most grievous for us by these persecutions alone. ‘Blessed,’ He says, ‘will you be when people persecute you, curse you, and speak every evil thing against you for the sake of the Son of Man. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you, their fathers’ (Matt. 5:11–12). If this was said only to the Apostles, faith had its rewards only until them; and what benefit was there for those who would believe afterward? It is therefore clear that it was said to everyone.

“Then the Apostle Paul says: ‘All who wish to live holy lives in Christ must suffer persecution’ (2 Tim. 3:12). The Lord also said this in the Gospel: ‘The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering a sacrifice to God. But they will do these things because they have not known the Father or me’ (John 16:2–3).”

**Reply:** You would rightly say these things while seeking the glory of martyrs if you possessed the martyrs’ cause. For the Lord did not call those blessed who suffer these evils, but those who suffer them for the sake of the Son of Man [Col. 0718], who is Christ Jesus. You suffer not for His sake but against Him. You suffer because you do not believe in Him, and you endure these things so that you may not believe.

How, then, do you boast that you hold the faith which the Lord Christ left to the Apostles? Do you wish people to be so blind and deaf that they neither read nor hear the Gospel, where they may learn what faith concerning His Church the Lord Christ left to the Apostles? Separated and divided from that Church, you do nothing except rebel against the words of the head and the body, and yet you boast that you suffer persecution for the sake of the Son of Man and the faith He left to the Apostles.

Let us set aside everything else and listen to His final words on earth, where we may see what faith concerning the Church He left to the Apostles and what kind of testament He made, so to speak—not as one who was about to end His life, but as one who would live without end; not as one who was to be placed in a tomb, but as one who was to ascend into heaven.

After rising from the dead, He appeared to His disciples so that they could look upon Him and touch Him with their hands. “It was necessary,” He said, “that what is written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me should be fulfilled.” Then He opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in His name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:44–47).

Likewise, on the Mount of Olives, after saying nothing further while He was present on earth, He entrusted what was most necessary as His final charge. For there were to be many people throughout every part of the earth claiming the name of the Church for themselves and barking from the corners of their own ruins against the whole household that throughout the earth sings the new song of which it is written, “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1).

The Apostles wanted to hear something else and did not ask what was most necessary for them. “Tell us,” they said, “whether you will be present at this time, and when—the kingdom of Israel?” [The supplied wording is defective.] But He said: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in His own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” After He had said these things, a cloud received Him (Acts 1:6–9).

He added nothing further in words. With all the greater firmness, because it came last, He fixed this in the minds of those who heard Him. As the Bridegroom departed, He entrusted this Bride to His friends. He therefore left this faith concerning the holy Church to His disciples [Note: “faith” appears to be missing here].

Donatists, you resist this faith, and you claim to suffer persecution for the faith which the Lord Christ left to the Apostles. With astonishingly blind impudence you oppose this Son of Man, who entrusted His Church—beginning at Jerusalem and bearing fruit, spreading, and growing among all nations—with such care; and you cry out that you suffer evil for the sake of the Son of Man.

Or do you say this perhaps because you have found another son of man for yourselves, whose name you bear and whose party you are said to belong to? [Col. 0719] You are mistaken; it is not he. When He said that it was blessed to suffer persecution for the sake of the Son of Man, that Bridegroom was proclaiming Himself, not an adulterer.

**23.** We too admit, as you say, that the words “Blessed will you be when people persecute you” were not spoken only to the Apostles. For this applies to everyone—not to all who suffered, suffer, or will suffer any kind of persecution after the Apostles, but to those who suffer for the sake of righteousness, as the Apostles themselves did.

For shortly before this He had said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). Then He added the words that you wished to recall and claim for yourselves, though in vain (Matt. 5:11, 10 [as printed]).

You vainly think that this blessedness applies to you, since you do not demonstrate in yourselves the righteousness to which the reward is owed. Indeed, on the contrary, you suffer for iniquity—less from others and more from yourselves—so that, even before God’s future judgment, you may in some measure repay yourselves what you deserve.

Therefore, since you yourself said that this was spoken not only to the Apostles but to everyone, just as it was spoken not only to the Apostles but to all who would afterward suffer any evils for the sake of righteousness, so too was it spoken to everyone: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23).

Why do you not do this, if you belong to the company of those to whom these words were spoken? Even if you do it, you will not belong to them for that reason, since robbers too can do this—robbers whom the public laws have ordered to be sought.

Nevertheless, because you do not wish to do it, you demonstrate by this shortcut that you do not belong to those to whom these words were spoken. And so that your very excuse may show much more clearly that you are alien to the number of true Christians, you now say that the places to which you may flee—places which He promised would not be lacking until the end of the age—are lacking for you.

In no way do you thereby prove that He made a false promise; rather, you show that you do not belong to the company of those to whom He made the promise, and therefore that you are not true martyrs but deceitful heretics.

What more can we say to you, when your own tongue defeats you?

# CHAPTER XXI

## 24

For as to what you added—that the Apostle said, “All who wish to live piously in Christ must suffer persecutions”—he did not in fact say “must”; rather, he said, “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (II Tim. V, 12). But who doubts that you do not belong among these? For if you are indeed among those of whom the Apostle said this, why do you not do what the Apostle himself did? If the gates were closed against you, you ought to have been lowered down over the wall, so that you might escape the hands of your persecutors. The gates stand open, and you do not wish to leave. What persecution do you suffer except from yourselves? Your persecutor loves you, while your fury persecutes you. The former wants you to flee; the latter drives you to destruction.

You understand the Apostle’s statement, “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution,” in such a way that you must confess that your ancestors did not live piously under the apostate emperor Julian. For whoever became a Donatist at that time did not live piously—since he did not suffer persecution—if he died before the devout care of the Christian emperors again rose up against your error.

But if the Apostle said this because, as it is written elsewhere, “Man’s life upon earth is a trial” (Job VII, 1), and because true and devout Christians are continually tested not only by the assault of adversity but also by the seduction of prosperity, so that the human spirit may either succumb through affliction or vanish through pride, then certainly, as long as one lives here, “all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution”: either, once defeated, they are seized by the devil, or, having been tested, they conquer the devil. Those whom he already possesses as seized and captive he does not persecute in order to gain possession of them, but because he possesses them, he uses them.

## 25

Moreover, if only the one who torments someone with pain, or wishes to hold someone in order to torment him, is to be called a persecutor, do not suppose that the tormentor of the heart is less severe than the tormentor of the body. Consider what sort of persecution was suffered by the one who said in the Psalm, “I saw the senseless, and I wasted away” (Ps. CXVIII, 158).

The righteous Lot suffered this persecution in Sodom even before the Sodomites sought to violate the angels who were lodging in his house, while they thought the angels were human beings (Gen. XIX). The righteous man could not see people so publicly disgraceful, even before the outrage committed at his own house [Note: [Col. 0720] Perhaps, “door”], without suffering great anguish of heart.

# CHAPTER XXII

Thus the Apostle Paul also counts such things among his persecutions, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (II Cor. XI, 29).

Therefore, the greater Christ’s love is in us, the greater is the anguish of heart with which we see you possessing the sacraments of Christ, yet separated from the members of Christ and rebelling against the peace of Christ. But as long as you live in this body, we retain some hope for you; when, however, you die in that division, we grieve for you much more bitterly.

And when you kill yourselves—whether by rushing upon other people’s weapons, or by plunging from heights, drowning yourselves, or using your own fires—it cannot be adequately expressed how greatly you torment us with grief. For the impious Absalom afflicted his holy father David more by his death than by his rebellion (II Sam. XVIII). David wanted him captured alive, so that the man who had been advancing through wickedness might be healed through repentance. Absalom was therefore his father’s persecutor not only by dividing God’s people, and not only by bearing arms and waging war against God’s law and his father’s legitimate kingdom; he persecuted his father’s heart far more by dying in that impiety.

Finally, the best of fathers mourned his worst son, whom he had not mourned while alive because he had not despaired of him, once he was dead because hope had come to an end. Learn, then, what the Apostle means when he says, “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.”

If the Donatists had not plundered Catholic homes, if they had not burned Catholic churches, if they had not cast the sacred books of Catholics into those very fires, if they had not afflicted Catholic bodies with the most savage massacres, if they had not cut off Catholic limbs [Col. 0721], if they had not put out their eyes, and finally, if they had not cruelly killed Catholics, we would most truly say that we suffer this one very grievous persecution from you: because we see you as senseless and waste away; because you are weakened, and we are weakened; because you are scandalized, and we burn; because you are lost, and we mourn.

These evils of yours, which send you into eternal destruction, persecute us more bitterly than those which you inflict upon our bodies, possessions, homes, or basilicas. You persecute us less when you rage against us than when you perish yourselves. Indeed, in that persecution in which you rage against us, we rejoice with praise; but in this one, in which you perish, if we rejoice, we perish with you.

Yet as long as you live in this flesh, we cannot despair of you. When, however, you die in this impiety—especially when you kill yourselves through the horrible blindness of fury—only one thing consoles our most bitter sorrow: that which consoled holy David, namely, that God’s people, which had been divided by the tyranny of its wicked son, was gathered together in unity.

For it is far more tolerable that your much smaller number of the most obstinate should perish through their own plunges, drownings, or fires than that innumerable peoples, prevented by those men from attaining salvation, should burn with them in the fire of eternity. Therefore the Church of Christ has never lacked, nor will lack, grounds on which, according to the Apostle, those who wish to live piously in Christ may suffer persecution: either by enduring the malice of the impious while they themselves live innocently, or by grieving over them when they perish. We must strive with great effort and prayer that all may live with Christ; but if this cannot be accomplished because of the fury of some, at least we must labor so that not all may perish with the devil.

# CHAPTER XXIII

## 26

Do not therefore be deceived by the statement made to you: “The hour will come when whoever kills you will think that he is offering service to God”; or, as you quoted here as testimony, “will think that he is offering a sacrifice to God.”

It is plainly evident that this was not said of the persecutions which the Gentiles inflicted upon the Church. When the Gentiles did this to the one God, they considered themselves to be offering service to their many gods—who of course do not exist. Thus what the Lord foretold to his own was either fulfilled by the Jews, who killed holy Stephen and many others while thinking that they were offering service to God, because they seemed to worship the one true God; or it was said to us—that is, to Catholics—about the various heretics raging everywhere, who, whenever and wherever and however they can, think that they are offering service to God by killing Catholics. It was said above all about you, who have made yourselves pre-eminent in Africa for such sacrifices.

For if this had been said to you, you would certainly not kill yourselves; rather, you would wait to be killed by us, who, as you say, think that by doing this we are offering service to God. But now, when you hurry toward death lest you be held by our people, you fear living, not being killed, because you are ashamed to be corrected or refuted on your own ground [Note: [Col. 0721] So in the earliest editions. In later editions, without necessity, this was emended to “to be convicted of your fault”].

Or perhaps you are the ones to whom both parts apply: when you are killed, and killed by yourselves, you think that you are offering service to God and presenting him with these sacrifices from yourselves. What follows, therefore, applies to you, and you yourself cited it. For immediately the Lord added and said: “But they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me” (John XVI, 2–3).

When, then, you kill yourselves while thinking that you are offering service to God, you have not known the Father, whom you have not heard saying, “Flee” [Note: [Col. 0722] The second member is missing here. Perhaps it should read: “You have not known the Father, whom you have not heard forbidding it with the words, ‘You shall not kill’; nor have you known the Son, whom you have not heard saying, ‘Flee.’”].

# CHAPTER XXIV

## 27. Words of the Letter

“But,” he says, “they boast that they are inhabitants of a warlike peace and a bloody unity.”

Let them hear the Lord saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace. Not as the world gives do I give to you” (John XIV, 27). For the peace of the world is joined together among the minds of peoples divided by arms through the outcome of war; the peace of the Lord Christ, tranquil in salutary gentleness, invites those who are willing but does not compel the unwilling.

### Response

You indeed wish to create a warlike peace and a bloody unity, either through our violent deaths or through your voluntary deaths—refusing to count against yourselves what you do to us, while counting against us what you do to yourselves. But we are compelled both to endure what you do to us and to grieve over what you do to yourselves, provided that the peace and unity of Christ may be established for the salvation of many, as it is established among very many, even if it is not established among all because of the fury of a few.

If you were willing to look with a faithful rather than an envious eye, you would see how many great peoples who have come from you to us rejoice in the true peace and unity of Christ. Even if some of them are still disturbed by the novelty of the change, they too are gradually healed of this weakness.

And if some hypocrites persist, that certainly does not mean that those whom we see to be sincere should not have been gathered in with them. Some of these sincere people have appeared in your regions, even greater in number than some of our own, when, although the liberty of destruction had been granted to you, they refused to return to you.

Therefore, so that we might not lose these people, we ought to gather in the hypocrites as well, because the Gospel says that the servants gathered guests to their lord’s wedding feast, both good and bad. This is especially so because the spirit of pride, like a wicked wind, has shaken you from the Lord’s threshing floor before the time of winnowing; and from there we are trying, with God’s help as far as we can, to call you back.

You certainly know how, when grain is brought back to the threshing floor, the broom of diligence draws along with it not only the grain but also the earth.

# CHAPTER XXV

## 28

As for your view that the unwilling should not be compelled to the truth, you are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God, who makes people willing even while they are being compelled against their will.

Did the Ninevites repent unwillingly because they did so at the command of their king? The prophet had already foretold God’s anger to the whole city, walking through it for three days (Jonah III). What need, then, was there for the king’s command that they should humbly plead with God, who does not look upon faces but hearts, unless there were among them some who would neither have cared about nor believed the divine prediction unless they had been terrified by earthly authority?

Therefore, by this command of royal power—against which your voluntary destruction is directed—an opportunity for salvation in Christ is provided to many. Even if they are forcibly brought to the banquet of so great a master of the household and compelled to enter, once inside they find reason to rejoice that they entered.

The Lord himself foretold both things, and fulfilled both. For after rejecting certain people—understood, of course, as the Jews, because they had previously been invited through the Prophets but preferred to make excuses when the hour came—the Lord said to his servant: “Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame.” And the servant said to his lord: “It has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.” And the lord said to the servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Matt. XXII, 9–10; Luke XIV, 21–23).

We understand the roads as heresies and the hedges as schisms. For in this passage the roads signify diverse opinions, while the hedges signify perverse opinions.

Why, then, are you surprised if anyone who enters this banquet neither willingly brought in nor forcibly driven into it dies—not from bodily hunger, but from spiritual hunger?

# CHAPTER XXVI

## 29. Words of the Letter

“But,” he says, “we rejoice in hatred of the world; we do not succumb to its pressures but rejoice in them. This world cannot love Christ’s servants, since it is known not to have loved Christ, the Lord himself saying: ‘If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you.’”

### Response

How do you rejoice in hatred of the world and not succumb to its pressures but rejoice in them, when you wish to kill yourselves so as not to suffer any kind of trouble, and choose to die—not killed by others for Christ’s truth, but by yourselves for Donatus’s party? This is the madness of the Circumcellions, not the glory of martyrs.

Since your deeds are evident, why do you appropriate words that belong to others? “This world,” he says, “cannot love Christ’s servants, since it is known not to have loved Christ.” We therefore do not belong to this world, because we love you. But you are not Christ’s servants, since, repaying evil for good, and turning your malice back upon yourselves when you cannot exercise it against us, you neither love us nor kill yourselves.

When the Lord said, “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you; if they persecuted me, they will persecute you” (John XV, 18, 20), he did not say this to you but to those whom he commanded that, if they were persecuted in one city, they should flee to another. You do not do this.

He said it to those for whom cities to which they could flee would not be lacking until the end of the age (Matt. X, 23)—cities which you complain are now lacking for you, while you refuse to admit that you are not those to whom these things were said.

# CHAPTER XXVII

## 30. Words of the Letter

“But even if persecution should cease,” he says, “how would the number of martyrs be completed? John says: ‘I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain, crying out and saying, “How long, Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” And white robes were given to each of them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their brothers is completed—those who are going to be killed just as they were’” (Rev. VI, 9–11) [Note: [Col. 0723] Lyons edition, “of those men.” The Greek likewise has αὐτῶν, autōn, “of them.” M.].

### Response

If you wished to be martyrs beneath Christ’s altar [Col. 0724], you would not make yourselves a sacrifice to the devil by setting yourselves on fire. Who rejoices in this fury of yours except the devil, who inspires it in you, and those who belong to him?

It was he who once drove the boy of whom we read in the Gospel sometimes into the water and sometimes into the fire (Matt. XVII, 14). It was he who plunged that herd of pigs headlong into the waves and drowned them (ibid. VIII, 32). It was he who, in the boldest temptation, suggested even to the Lord himself that he throw himself down from the pinnacle of the Temple (ibid. IV, 5–6).

You unquestionably belong to the devil when you repeatedly employ three kinds of death—water, fire, and plunging from heights—in your own deaths. If madness had not destroyed your minds, the very words you quoted from the holy book ought to recall you from the destruction you inflict upon yourselves.

For what do the souls of the martyrs beneath God’s altar say? “How long, Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” They ask that their blood be avenged upon those by whom it was shed. Surely not upon others? Accordingly, your blood will be avenged upon you.

## 31

What could be more foolish than your belief that this prophecy concerning the martyrs who were foretold as future has been fulfilled only among the Donatists—as though, after blessed John wrote these words, no martyrs had been killed until Donatus’s party arose, whose members, whenever they cannot kill others, kill themselves; who perform the deeds of robbers and demons, yet claim for themselves the glory of martyrs?

Even if, during that long interval—from John down to these people—no true martyrs had been killed; even if we said nothing else except that martyrs would arise in the time of Antichrist, when that number of martyrs would be completed; still we would not believe that these people, guilty of the blood either of others or of themselves, should be added to the number of the true martyrs. Those martyrs were told to rest for a short time until the number of their brothers was completed—those who would begin to be killed as they had been, by others certainly, not by themselves as these people do; and therefore these people are not like them.

We may also say, with complete truth, that the Catholics whom the Donatists kill belong to the fulfillment of that number. But since, after the Apostle John, who wrote down those future events, such a great slaughter of martyrs has taken place at the hands of the impious everywhere, among so many nations, what do these extorters of their own souls and torturers of others want when they boast that what they read was foretold of the holy martyrs has been fulfilled in themselves?

Prepare yourselves instead so that your blood may be avenged—not upon those who wish to capture you or drive you to flight so that you may live, but upon yourselves. Or is it perhaps to prevent this that you do not shed it, but either dash yourselves to pieces by a fall, suffocate yourselves in water, or turn yourselves into ashes? You are mistaken: however you are killed by yourselves, your blood will be avenged upon you.

It would be avenged upon you even if it were shed by others, not in the Church of Christ but in Donatus’s party. Will you cry out to God to avenge your blood, and will he hear you unless he condemns you? For how could it be avenged unless the one who dared to slaughter it were condemned?

In this cry, therefore, you are nothing but your own accusers, because you are guilty of your own blood [Col. 0725]. God will avenge it only by condemning you, when your blood—whether you have dashed yourselves to pieces, suffocated yourselves, burned yourselves, or slaughtered yourselves by any other means, or, if you choose this, shed it—is avenged upon you.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

## 32. Words of the Letter

“Is this not persecution,” he says, “which drove many thousands of innocent martyrs to death? For Christians, ready in spirit but weak in the flesh (Matt. XXVI, 41), found a shortcut by which to snatch away their souls from the sacrilegious contamination of the furnaces, imitating the example of the presbyter Razias in the books of the Maccabees (II Macc. XIV, 41) [Note: [Col. 0725] Razias is consistently called Razius in Letter 204, §§ 6–7]. Nor were they afraid without reason: whoever fell into their hands did not escape.”

Do as much as you wish; what is certain is that those who act against God cannot belong to God.

### Response

You confess with complete clarity, and most truthfully, what persecution you suffer. It is the very persecution I have already mentioned, which is expressed clearly enough in the holy Scriptures concerning certain impious people, of whom it is said that “they suffer persecution from their own deeds” (Wis. XI, 21). This can most appropriately be said of you, even if other people’s hands were to slaughter you because of your sacrileges.

For robbers and any other people guilty of capital crimes, when they are punished under just laws, should not be said to suffer persecution except from their own deeds.
