But now, when Christian gentleness spares you, and your madness rages against you to such an extent that, as you say, you snatch away your souls by discovering a shortcut through the furnaces, it is extreme shamelessness to deny that in every way you suffer persecution from yourselves, since you accomplish both things: the means by which you justly perish and the fact that you perish.

You speak of many thousands who do this as though this were not also a substantial reason why Africa should be freed from such a teaching of yours. For these are people of the sort to whom you have been able to persuade this evil—people who were accustomed to do such things even earlier, especially when the license of idolatry was raging everywhere, at the time when they rushed upon the Pagans who were celebrating their festivals with weapons.

The Pagan youths used to vow to their idols how many people each of them would kill. These men, however, streaming together in groups from every direction, thrust themselves forward like wild beasts in an amphitheater, presenting themselves to the hunters’ spears; raging, they died; rotting, they were buried; deceiving others, they were venerated.

Besides these there are enormous rocks and the terrifying precipices of mountains, made famous by the frequent deaths of your volunteers. They did this more rarely with water and fire; vast groups were consumed by plunges from heights.

I am speaking of matters perfectly well known to people of our own age. For who does not know this kind of person—restless in horrible crimes, idle in useful works, most savage in the deaths of others, most contemptible in their own; terrifying the countryside, while absent from the fields; going around the rural cottages to obtain their food, from which they also received the name “Circumcellions”; notorious throughout almost the whole world as Africa’s most infamous reproach and error?

# CHAPTER XXIX

## 33

Who, then, does not know how many of this kind formerly went toward death and perished through various forms of death, and how few now burn themselves by comparison with them?

But if you think we ought to be moved because so many thousands die in this way, how much consolation do you suppose we have in the fact that vastly and incomparably more thousands are being freed from the madness of Donatus’s party—a party in which not only the error of an impious division but also this fury has been made into law?

Those who perish do not even equal the number of those from that same class who are now held under an orderly discipline and, having abandoned both the work and the name of the Circumcellions, serve by cultivating the fields, preserve chastity, and maintain unity. How much less do these lost people equal the number of both sexes—not only boys and girls, young men and virgins, but also married people and the elderly—innumerable numbers of whom are passing from the wicked division of the Donatists into the true and catholic peace of Christ?

Those who burn themselves are not even as numerous as the places filled with peoples that are being rescued from the deadly plague of that error and fury through this determined effort to accomplish unity.

I ask you: can it be a sound counsel of mercy that all these people should be preserved together with them for the eternal punishments of Gehenna, lest those few, in comparison with these, be burned by the fires of their own furnaces?

We must strive with great effort and prayer that all may live with Christ; but if this cannot be achieved because of the fury of some, at least we must labor so that not all may perish with the devil.

# CHAPTER XXX

## 34

You search the holy Scriptures with great ingenuity for something that might support this insane judgment in favor of voluntary death, and you think you have found it because it is written in the Gospel: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 41)—as though for this reason everyone ought to kill himself.

When it came to enduring suffering at the hands of persecutors, you could more appropriately have said that your false martyrs belong among those of whom it is written, “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. II, 16), and that they certainly do not belong among those to whom the Lord says, “By your endurance you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

Those of whom it is written, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak,” were overcome by involuntary sleep; they were not killed through voluntary destruction. Read carefully and pay attention to what you are saying.

What of the Apostle’s statement: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear; but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (I Cor. X, 13)? Are we not to believe this apostolic truth, and must we make ourselves our own enemies because we cannot endure other enemies? Far be this from Christian hearts.

Let Catholics believe the faithful Apostle—or rather, the faithful God himself, who does not allow his own to be tested beyond what they can bear, but with the testing also provides a way out so that they may endure. Let Donatists not believe it; and so that they may not always refuse to believe these things, let them cease to be Donatists.

For when, in various sufferings, people despair of obtaining wisdom from the Lord and therefore seek the shortcut of the furnaces, where they expose themselves—not to wild beasts, as the most blessed Cyprian says (Book on the Praise of Martyrdom, addressed to Moses and Maximus) [Col. 0727]—but nevertheless to flames, though no one has condemned them, this is not counsel but fury; it is not wisdom but madness.

Let those who do not say of the Lord’s help, “My patience comes from him” (Ps. LXI, 6), keep their fires.

## 35

Certainly, when the holy Job was rotting from head to foot under an intolerable wound and was tortured by immense pains, he had this shortcut of yours readily available. Through it he could have freed himself from such a life, full of horrible calamities, in which he undoubtedly remained. Power was available, but justice did not permit it [Note: [Col. 0727] Ambrose: “did not cease.” Erasmus: “did not abandon.”].

For in this sense he says, “Would that I could kill myself, or ask someone else to do this for me!” (Job XXX, according to the Septuagint). That righteous man denied that he could do what could not be done justly. In the same manner the Apostle says to the Galatians, “I testify to you that, if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me” (Gal. IV, 15). Why could this not be possible except because it could in no way be done justly?

So too, when the Lord was urging righteous Lot through his angels to hurry as he left Sodom for Zoar, he said: “I cannot do the thing until you enter there” (Gen. XIX, 22). He said that he could not do what, without doubt, he could do by power but could not do by justice.

The most patient Job could, if nothing else, refrain from taking food or drink and thus bring that wretched and horrible life to an end; but he could not justly do so, because no one is permitted to kill himself, especially when, in order to live, he is able to flee.

Could anyone doubt that the holy man, who spoke at such length amid his sufferings, could have asked someone to do this for him? His suffering and rotting body did not lack hands with which to kill him, nor did his tongue lack the ability to ask. Certainly he could have asked his own wife to do it. Yet she did not suggest that it be done, although she desired him to die by provoking God through blasphemy; and although she offered him a wicked counsel against God (Job II, 9), she did not dare tell him to kill himself.

The devil has greater power over you, since he so easily persuades you of what he could not persuade that foolish woman to do, even though he had preserved her as his instrument for deceiving her husband after taking everything from him.

That righteous man therefore said that he could not ask anyone to kill him, thereby also showing that this was not permitted. For what cannot be done justly cannot be done by a righteous person, since by deciding to do it he first loses his righteousness, so that what a righteous person cannot do, an unrighteous person may do.

Thus he said, “Would that I could kill myself!”—as though he were saying, “Would that it were just”; for then it could be done by a righteous person. He would not wish injustice upon himself merely so that he might do what only an unrighteous person can do. But if it could be done, he would want this to be justice. Since it could not be done so that it would be justice, the righteous man could not do what only injustice could accomplish.

Accordingly, it is not unjust for a righteous person to desire death when life is exceedingly bitter [Col. 0728]. But if God does not grant the death desired, then the only just course is to endure that exceedingly bitter life.

Similarly, it is not foreign to a righteous person to desire life when a bitter death threatens. But when he sees that he cannot obtain it, he says what the Lord, transforming us into himself, said: “Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

These things must be said to those whom persecutors seek to make do evil, not to those who seek to share in good things and are loved. They must be said, I repeat, to those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, not to those who inflict persecution upon themselves because of unrighteousness.

# CHAPTER XXXI

## 36

Therefore even the elder Razias, whom these people—deprived of examples for their crime—boast that they have found in the books of the Maccabees as someone to imitate (II Macc. XIX, 41), ought to have done what those same Scriptures say that the seven brothers did, with their mother exhorting them (ibid. VII): once captured, and not turned away from the law of their Lord, he should have accepted everything inflicted upon him, endured it in pain, and maintained patience in his humility.

Accordingly, unable to endure humility at the hands of his enemies, he provided an example not of wisdom but of folly, to be imitated not by Christ’s martyrs but by Donatus’s Circumcellions [Note: [Col. 0728] Compare Augustine’s Letter 204, §§ 6–7].

Nevertheless, if we consider the matter more carefully, it also becomes clear that you are unlike him. When Razias was already being captured by his enemies, he had no open avenue of escape. Therefore he struck himself with a sword; and when he could not kill himself by that means, he threw himself from the wall. Then, though he could no longer live, he was still breathing and moving his body forcefully; he reached a steep rock by running, though drained of blood. There, stretching out both hands, he tore out and scattered his intestines and died. He was surrounded by a crowd in such a way that he could not escape, even if he had been able to live.

You, therefore, who neither listen to the Lord saying, “Flee,” nor imitate Razias, who wished to flee but could not, plainly have neither the former as a command nor the latter as an example.

Besides, according to your reasoning, Razias must unquestionably be condemned. You said, on the basis of the Gospel saying in which the Lord declares, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak,” that you fled to the shortcut of the furnaces because you are too weak to endure the hands of enemies if they capture you.

Can it then be said of the man who severely wounded himself with a sword, who, wounded, made for the wall, who threw himself headlong from it onto his neck, who afterward was able to run to the rock, stand upon the rock, draw out his intestines, tear them apart, and scatter them, that “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak”? His spirit not only appeared so willing, but his flesh also so strong, that it is scarcely credible that he wished and was able to do what he did.

Therefore this man ought to displease you, since his strength disturbs the rationale of your weakness. Moreover, if, while able to flee but unwilling to do so, he had piled up wood in his house and, when his enemies rushed in to capture him, had set fire to it and burned himself together with his buildings, he would indeed have furnished you with an example, but he would have incurred a great punishment for himself.

As it is, since he was unable to flee, he is perhaps somewhat less guilty of his own blood because he inflicted death upon himself than he would have been if an enemy had already been about to inflict it upon him after capturing him.

## 37

But, you say, Razias was praised by the authority of the holy Scriptures. How was he praised? Because he was a lover of his city. This could have been understood in a carnal sense: he loved that earthly city, earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children, not the city above, which is the free mother of us all.

He was praised because he preserved continence within Judaism. Yet the Apostle says that, in comparison with Christian righteousness, these things were losses and refuse to him (Phil. III, 8).

He was praised because he was called the father of the Jews. This was even more the reason why impatience with humility slipped into him, as into a human being, so that he preferred to die rather than be subjected to his enemies.

It is said that he chose to die nobly. He ought rather to have chosen to die humbly; that would have been beneficial. The historians of the nations customarily praise such words and deeds, but they praise the brave men of this world, not Christ’s martyrs.

It is said that he threw himself manfully from the wall into the crowds. We do not say that he did this womanishly. Indeed, you who have made great progress through this example have taught even your women to do the same. We admit that they too do this not womanishly but manfully; nevertheless, they do not do it profitably, because they do not do it faithfully.

Finally, it is said that he called upon the Lord of life and spirit to restore these things to him again—that is, life and spirit. Even then he asked for nothing by which the good are distinguished from the wicked. For God will restore these things even to those who have done evil—not in the resurrection of eternal life, but in the resurrection of eternal judgment.

Thus Razias was praised as a lover of his city, as a man of excellent reputation—that is, of good fame—because he was called the father of the Jews, and because he had maintained continence within Judaism. Scripture narrated how his death occurred, more remarkable than prudent; it did not praise it as something that ought to be done.

Our task, however, as the Apostle admonishes us, is “to test everything, to hold fast what is good, and to abstain from every appearance of evil” (I Thess. V, 21–22).

### 38

The Jews do not possess this Scripture, which is called *Maccabees*, in the same way as they possess the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, to which the Lord bears witness as to his own witnesses, saying: “Everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Nevertheless, it has been received by the Church, not without benefit, provided that it is read or heard soberly—especially on account of those Maccabees who, for the law of God, endured from their persecutors sufferings so shameful and dreadful, as true martyrs did. [Note: [Col. 0729] See *City of God* 18.36; *On Christian Doctrine* 2.5; *On the Care of the Dead* 1.] Thus the Christian people might also learn from this that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18), for which Christ suffered, if they endured so patiently such things for the law that God gave through his servant to those people, for whom he had not yet handed over his Son.

Yet this Razias too [Col. 0730] has something useful for readers—not only so that the mind may be exercised in judging correctly what it reads, but also so that the human mind, indeed the Christian mind, may observe how much must be endured from enemies in the ardor of charity, since this man, through fear of humiliation, endured so much from himself. But the ardor of charity descends from the exaltation of divine grace, whereas fear of humiliation arises from love of human praise; and therefore the former contends through patience, while the latter sins through impatience.

We must not therefore approve by consenting to everything we read that people praised even with God’s testimony as having done in Scripture. Rather, we must distinguish by careful consideration, applying the judgment not, to be sure, of our own authority, but of the divine and holy Scriptures. They do not permit us either to imitate or to praise all the deeds of those people to whom they there give a good and distinguished testimony, if some things were not rightly done by them or are no longer appropriate to the present age. But why should we discuss in this inquiry those things that were once right but are not right now, when the matter under discussion—someone inflicting death upon himself, especially someone who is permitted, or rather compelled, to live—belongs among those actions that could never be right, nor ever could have been, as we have already demonstrated sufficiently? [Note: [Col. 0730] Perhaps “will be able to be.”]

### 39

Therefore, however you may understand the praise given to this Razias’s life, his death does not possess wisdom worthy of praise, because it does not possess the patience worthy of God’s servants. Rather, that saying of Wisdom, which expresses not praise but abhorrence, applies to him: “Woe to them who have lost endurance!” (Sir. 2:16).

For if you believe that all the deeds of those who are praised are to be imitated, was Razias better than David? Why, then, does no good person propose to himself David’s deed of desiring another man’s wife and killing her husband (2 Sam. 11), but instead regard it as something to be guarded against and avoided?

Was Razias better than Solomon? Do you therefore wish us to propose as an example for imitation his licentiousness toward women, by whose seductions he was led even to the construction of temples for idols (1 Kings 11)?

Was Razias better than the apostle Peter? When Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he was called blessed by the Lord and deserved to receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Yet that does not mean that he is to be imitated when, immediately and at that very moment, he was rebuked and heard: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings” (Matt. 16:17–23). [Note: [Col. 0730] Perhaps “in this respect.”]

And, to leave aside those things that the holy Church’s Scripture condemned in the clearest terms, let me speak of matters merely narrated and recorded there, concerning which no judgment of praise or blame has been issued in either direction, but which have been left for us to judge: was Razias better than Noah? Who, while sober, would praise that man for lying drunk (Gen. 9:21)?

Was Razias better than the patriarch Judah? Yet who would approve him, who would not rightly be displeased with him, in that act of fornication, since he entered not upon his daughter-in-law—for he did not know her as such—but upon a woman whom he thought to be a prostitute [Col. 0731] (Gen. 38)?

Was Razias better than Samson? Dare, then, if you can, to say that the great and divine secret of strength that he possessed in his hair ought to have been disclosed to a flattering little woman. As for the fact that he killed his enemies together with himself when he brought the house down upon himself and them, he wished to share with them the death that he was soon to suffer at their hands, since he could not escape. He did not do this of his own accord; it must instead be attributed to the Spirit of God, who used him to do, when that Spirit was present with him, what he could not do when the same Spirit was absent. Likewise, when Abraham wished to sacrifice his son, the act was obedience because God commanded it (Gen. 22); without God’s command, what would it have been except madness?

### 40

The blessed Cyprian, instructed in these sacred Scriptures, said in his *Confession*: “Discipline forbids anyone to offer himself.” [Note: In the *Acts of the Passion of Cyprian the Martyr*, whose opening words are “Under the emperor Valerian.”]

See how great an evil you commit when you wish to kill yourselves, although you are undisciplined—even if you wished to offer yourselves to others who desire to do this to you.

The one whom you call the Savior commands flight; the persecutor permits flight. What, then, do you follow, so that you perish in your own fires, except your own madness?

And yet you say: “Is this not persecution, which has driven so many thousands of innocent people to death?” Show how you are innocent, when you divide Christ and kill yourselves. Show how you are driven to death, when flight is commanded to you by divine authority and permitted to you by human authority.

Show how, by the shortcut of furnaces, you snatch your souls away from defilement, when rather, through the sacrilege of furnaces, you make them utterly defiled, as though by a diabolical sacrifice.

Ask Christ: he commands you to flee. Ask the governor: he permits you to flee. If you could also ask Razias himself, he would answer you: “I was unable to flee.” You therefore have neither Christ the Savior, nor the governor the persecutor, nor Razias as your authority.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 41

You said that it was not without reason that your people killed themselves, since whoever fell into our hands or the hands of our people [Col. 0732] did not escape. What, I ask, did he escape? If death, why do you inflict it upon yourselves with your own hands, if you fear it from ours?

But it is clear that you are not speaking about death. For you yourselves know how much we desire you to live; that is why you frighten us with your death.

Therefore, if by “our communion” you mean that none of you who fell into our hands escaped, I wish you had spoken the truth. For they would not escape the communion offered by Catholics with very great benefit, if by escaping it they were to escape the condemnation prepared for heretics.

But you could have recognized that what you say is false from your own Emeritus. When he came to us, he was more easily convicted by the truth than compelled to communicate with us.

There are others, less distinguished in reputation but equal in folly. For whoever was so like-minded in vanity that, through a most perverse shame, he became stubborn against the clearest truth—being ashamed to be thought inconsistent—departed from us without receiving Catholic communion.

But you said, “Whoever falls into their hands did not escape,” because you supposed that very few who had steadfastly resisted the clearest truth and departed were concealed from view.

Yet you inflicted, according to your own standards, a very grave injury upon Emeritus, who lost in your eyes the praise of his obstinacy, as though he had wished in vain to be among the few who did not consent to the truth, because he deserved to be counted among those who were hiding.

Who among us would not believe that you envy your colleague? Or, if you do not envy him, imitate him. Come to us as he did; hear what we say as he did; answer, if you can, what he could not answer. But if you wish neither to answer nor to communicate with us, depart as he did.

There he is: he departed unharmed from our hands. Why, then, do you say, “Whoever falls into their hands does not escape”? There he is: he did not believe that places where he could hide would fail him. Why, then, do you arrange to burn?

Do you still not see that it is rather you who do not belong to God and who act against God—not only through the common plague by which you resist Christ’s unity, but especially because you hasten to add your own deaths to this great crime of yours?

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 42

**Words of the Letter:** “But since,” he says, “the duty of an executor did not suit your prudence, I ask you to attend briefly. There is, as I believe, solid truth, and there is an image of truth; for truth stands established by its own strength, whereas an idol or image is what human presumption has made apparently similar to truth in order to inflict injury. Yet deception can never prejudice the truth. I call those worshipers of images who do not hold the truth; I consider a person who makes for himself something to worship, under another name, a pagan. Hence it is publicly and openly apparent that, through threats, terror, and persecutions, they are known to have lifted Gabinus and others like him from the freedom of their nature and fabricated for themselves faithless objects of veneration, to whose worship they are compelled against their will.”

**Response:** You add words of blasphemy to your madness and dare to say that the Catholic Church is a human fabrication, although God says to her: “For I am the Lord who make you; the Lord is his name.” And so that we may know that she is herself the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, he continues and adds: “And your redeemer, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:5).

You call this most evident work of God a human fabrication. Yet you do not consider that you could in no way have separated yourselves from this Church, which God promised to establish throughout the whole earth, unless you were following a human being.

We follow the one who said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). We follow the one who said to that very Church, as I have just recalled: “I am the Lord who make you; the Lord is his name; and your redeemer, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth.”

Therefore, by holding to the Church that is spread and grows among all nations and throughout the whole earth, we certainly do not follow a human fabrication, but a divine promise that has been fulfilled.

What do you follow, then, when, separated from communion with this divine promise and divine work, you wish to belong to the party of Donatus? Did a human being or God tell you that the promises of God perished from the whole world because of Caecilian’s sin and remained in the party of Donatus?

If God said this, read it to us from the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the apostolic and evangelical Scriptures. Read it, if you [Col. 0733] can—something you were entirely unable to do in our Conference.

But if human beings said these things, of those concerning whom it is written, “They have strengthened for themselves an evil word” (Ps. 63:6), then there is the human fabrication; there is what you worship; there is whom you serve; there is the reason why you rebel, rage, and burn.

### 43

Gabinus and the others, however, who recognized, chose, and held to this Church, wished to possess with the faithful not a human fabrication but the divine promise that had been foretold and fulfilled. They no longer wished to endure human hardships for a human fabrication.

Whoever has lost not merely his possessions but even this life for the truth and unity of Christ, provided that others take it away and kill him, truly has faith, truly has hope, truly has charity, and truly has God.

But whoever has lost even the fringe of his garment for the party of Donatus has no heart.

Why, then, is it surprising that wise people, when they saw that losses and exiles had been set before them in opposition to the most stubborn antiquity of an entrenched custom, considered whether they ought to endure these things for the party of Donatus against the Catholic Church—that is, for a human fabrication against a divine work? They saw clearly that they ought not, and they recognized that what you call persecution was for them an opportunity for correction. They did what is written: “Give an opportunity to the wise, and he will become wiser” (Prov. 9:9).

You see, then, how pointlessly you said to a man who, at the command of his most devout emperor, is seeking your correction that the duty of an executor did not suit his prudence. For what is more fitting for a religious soldier than, in a cause in which he considers for whom you wish there to be deception [the text is uncertain], to become himself the salvation of many who must be corrected? [Note: [Col. 0733] Perhaps “that you are exiled for the sake of certain fools.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### 44

**Words of the Letter:** “To instruct the people of Israel,” he says, “almighty God gave proclamation to the prophets; he did not command it to kings. The Lord Christ, Savior of souls, sent fishermen, not soldiers, to introduce the faith.”

**Response:** Hear, then, the holy Prophets and the holy Fishermen, and you will not find religious kings burdensome. I have already shown above that it belonged to the king’s responsibility to ensure that the Ninevites appeased God, whose anger the Prophet had announced.

Therefore, as long as you do not hold the Church that the Prophets foretold and the apostolic fishermen planted [Note: [Col. 0733] Perhaps “the Church which the Prophets foretold.”], kings who hold it rightly judge that it belongs to their responsibility to prevent you from rebelling against it with impunity. For God also had kings among the Prophets: the holy David, as you cannot fail to know, was a king.

Hear, then, the prophesying king, and you will not fear any religious king when he is angry. Hear, I say, the prophetic king speaking about Christ: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8). You will not fear a Christian king who is angered when you blaspheme this Church, which, as it was prophesied by a king, is displayed to the ends of the earth.

For [Col. 0734] King Nebuchadnezzar, although he was not a prophet, nevertheless restrained with religious severity those who blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Dan. 3:96).

## CHAPTER XXXV

### 45

**Words of the Letter:** “God,” he says, “has never awaited the assistance of worldly military power, since he alone can judge the living and the dead.”

**Response:** God does not await the assistance of worldly military power when he rather grants kings the benefit of inspiring them to see that their Lord’s command is carried out in their kingdom.

Those to whom it was said, “Now therefore, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord with fear” (Ps. 2:10–11), understand that their power must serve the Lord in such a way that those who refuse to serve his will are punished by that power.

But in making an accusation against soldiers, if this responsibility, as we have already shown, is demonstrated in the holy Scriptures to belong to kings, through whom will they act against the rebellious Circumcellions and their mad followers or leaders except through subordinate soldiers?

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### 46

**Words of the Letter:** “But they do not know this,” he says, “those who lie in wait for other people’s possessions, who neither heed God saying, ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s property’ (Exod. 20:17), nor the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon:

“‘Then the righteous shall stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. Seeing this, they shall be shaken with terrible fear and shall marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation, saying among themselves with repentance and groaning in anguish of spirit:

“‘These are they whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We senseless people regarded their life as madness and their end as without honor. How have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us. We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have walked through difficult deserts; but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All things passed away like a shadow’” (Wis. 5:1–9).

“This faith therefore urges us willingly to die for God in this persecution.”

**Response:** Acknowledge your crime and do not usurp a name that belongs to others. Scripture said: “Then the righteous shall stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors.” It did not say, “All who suffered evil shall stand,” but “the righteous shall stand.”

Likewise, when the Lord said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” unless he had added, “for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10), he would have included not only those who are crowned for their patience in the Lord but also those who are punished under just laws.

Therefore, if you think that these words of the righteous apply to you, first show that you are righteous. For you possess great matters that you parade among your claims to righteousness: the division of Christ, the destruction of Christ’s sacraments, the abandonment of Christ’s peace, war against Christ’s members, accusations against Christ’s spouse, and denial of Christ’s promises.

These are your “righteousnesses,” for which, evidently, you will stand with great [Col. 0735] confidence against those who afflicted you and took away your labors.

But when you begin to boast among your righteousnesses that you kill yourselves, who will be equal to you in righteousness? Then you will appear especially to require vindication.

But see from whom you are to be vindicated: from those, certainly, who killed you. Therefore, in order to be vindicated, you will be punished—and will you stand against yourselves?

You will stand especially firmly, since, with the furnaces closed, you confine yourselves in cruel straits, so that anyone who wishes to help cannot enter and anyone who wishes to escape cannot get out. Far be it, far be it, that they should stand with great confidence when they will stand with such an evil conscience.

Unless perhaps you think that God will then be able to spare you for your crimes because you do not spare yourselves now.

For this reason some of your consecrated women, being pregnant, threw themselves among the rocks, and, their wombs being torn open, revealed the crimes of homicide and the crimes of sexual violation. They thought that if they had thus taken vengeance upon themselves, God would in no way thereafter take vengeance.

In the same way, you think that the things that you have been able to commit through the sacrilege of schism and heresy—plundering, mutilating, blinding, killing Catholics, and finally even rebaptizing them, as well as whatever other abominations you have been able to commit—can somehow be expiated because you kill yourselves.

But you are mistaken. Judas thought the same thing. Do you wish to add this further evidence, by which we may know with greater certainty that your ancestors were rather traditors, because you imitate the death of the traditor?

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### 47

Thus, in this matter also, you confirm the truth of what you contentiously wished to deny at the Conference.

Among those confessed traditors, Secundus of Tigisis, who was then bishop of the first see in Numidia, granted pardon; he released, in the presence of those there, the men whose crimes of *traditio* were manifest and confessed at Cirta. Yet he punished them at Carthage as traditors who had neither been convicted nor present.

Secundus himself could not clear himself of this charge when Purpurius of Limata brought it against him and said: “What did you do when you were detained by the curator and the officials so that you might hand over the Scriptures? How did you free yourself from them, unless you handed over—or ordered to be handed over—something? For they were not releasing you without reason.”

Secundus also confessed this without ambiguity in his letter to Mensurius, which you yourselves produced and read aloud: he said that he had not handed anything over, but that persecutors sent by the curator and the officials had come to him, as Purpurius of Limata charged against him, in order that he might hand over the Scriptures.

When they asked him for them, he said that he had replied, “I am a Christian and a bishop, not a traditor,” and that he had been entirely unwilling to hand anything over to him. [Note: [Col. 0735] Perhaps “and to them.”]

You want us to believe this, although you yourselves can see how incredible it is that, during that persecution when it was raging, a bishop—or an assembly—detained so that he might hand over the divine Scriptures was released after handing over nothing.

You were always insisting that bishops could not assemble in the city of Cirta to ordain a bishop during the time of persecution. How, then, was that persecution raging, if a bishop could be detained for handing over the Scriptures and then, after handing over nothing, be released with impunity?

And yet you shouted while describing the savagery of that persecution, saying that not even twelve bishops [Col. 0736] could assemble in council to ordain a bishop and draw up those proceedings in which they mutually forgave the crimes of *traditio* and left the judgment of the Church’s peace to the Lord.

At the same time, you have claimed that you are now suffering a persecution such as never existed: namely, that places are lacking for you to flee to and hide in—even though you hold councils, ordain bishops, and appoint others in the place of those who perished in their own fires, men who are likewise prepared to perish in their own fires.

Yet during the council held in the midst of the persecution which, as you think and proclaim, was so great, you were able to assemble more than thirty people, including Petilianus, who was loudly claiming that during the persecution not even twelve could have assembled.

### 48

Furthermore, in that very council you decreed that those who had communicated with us unwillingly—bishops or presbyters—should be admitted to pardon and restored to their offices, provided only that they had not offered sacrifice or addressed the people.

Thus, by this decree of yours, you entirely cut away the force of all your accusations.

For where is the claim that, through communion with us, even those who were not [traditors] become traditors, because, as you slanderously say, those who handed over the ecclesiastical books under pressure from the impious authorities defiled us? [Note: [Col. 0736] Am. and Er. read “when the authorities were arising.”]

Why, then, do you now absolve from the crime those whom you know to have communicated with us unwillingly, provided that they did not offer sacrifice or preach to the people—as though those first traditors, under the terror and horror of monstrous punishments such as no one at all has inflicted upon you now, had not handed over the sacred books unwillingly, or had offered sacrifice there, or had preached to the people?

You see, therefore, that just as you were able to forgive those whom you most foolishly accuse of becoming traditors through our communion if they did something unwillingly, so your ancestors too could pardon genuine traditors, under a much harsher necessity, according to the same rule. [Note: The Louvain editors ordered the reading *traditoribus veris* (“genuine traditors”), although their editions, together with the older witnesses, read *traditoriis veris* (“genuine traitorous [men]”).]

But they were compelled by the faction hostile to Caecilian to condemn others who were absent and unheard, doing what the Apostle says about such people: “For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2:1).

### 49

Therefore, since the Donatists have always loved killing themselves and were themselves traditors from the beginning, what wonder is it if they taught their descendants also to love the death of the traditor (Matt. 27:5)?

To avoid this resemblance, they have killed themselves by the noose either never or only with great difficulty. Entirely in vain: for the one who compelled Judas the traditor to do this was the same one who often threw the boy whom the Lord healed into water and fire (Matt. 17:14), who cast the herd of swine into the sea (Matt. 8:32), and who, with bold presumption, suggested to the Lord himself that he throw himself from the pinnacle of the temple (Matt. 4:5–6).

Although, therefore, you cast yourselves voluntarily into death by various methods [Col. 0737], nevertheless, by the prompting of the same devil, you imitate the traditor by killing yourselves.

Even if you are not yourselves those people, you learned through the wicked instruction of those who were and who created the schism in which you willingly remain to do in yourselves what the traditor did to himself.

With what righteousness will you stand against those who afflicted you? If your deaths are avenged, they will be avenged most justly only upon yourselves.

### 50

What are these labors of yours that you boast have been taken away from you? Is it unjust that churches which were yours, when they pass into Catholic peace, should pass over with their possessions?

When they pass over to us, if you wish to retain their possessions, you undoubtedly wish to take away what belongs to others.

But the Catholic Mother says to you what the blessed Apostle said to certain people: “For I do not seek what is yours, but you” (2 Cor. 12:14).

Nevertheless, how are you not contradicting yourselves when you bring both accusations against us—that we desire to possess your property and that we violently compel you to be with us? You do not see how contradictory these two claims are.

If we seek and retain you unwillingly in our communion, how do we desire your possessions, which we cannot possess while you are communicating with us?

But if we desire to obtain those possessions, how do we seek you in order to lose them when you communicate with us?

We confess to you, however, that our desire is called charity. This charity seeks you in us; it desires to find you, correct you, and join you to Christ’s unity, so that we need not fear that you will burn in your furnaces. [Note: [Col. 0737] Perhaps “so that.”]

We burn with the fire of this charity. It inflames us so that we not only do not covet your possessions but also wish you to possess ours with us.

Recognize this, come, and do not perish. Or, if you are ashamed to come of your own accord, we accommodate your weakness, so that nothing may be lost to charity.

There: we wish to hold you. Why do you hasten to burn? We hold you for life, for salvation, for the unity, truth, and sweetness of Christ. And to the banquet of so great a master of the household, if you do not wish to enter voluntarily, we compel you to enter.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### 51

This is a contest over justice, not money. Beware, therefore, lest, while you think that what is written applies to you—“Then the righteous shall stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors”—the opposite should happen to you concerning your labors, namely, what is written elsewhere: “The righteous shall eat the labors of the ungodly” (Wis. 10:19).

For the Maximianists will not stand against you, whose basilicas you took away when you were able; nor will the Pagans stand against you, whose temples, wherever you could, you overturned and whose basilicas you built. [Note: [Col. 0737] The Parcensis manuscript reads “destroyed.”] We did the same.

Nor will the musicians of demons stand against you, whose pipes and stools you broke; we did the same. In the same way, you will not stand against us.

For in all such actions it is not plunder that is coveted, but error that is overturned.

Thus the Canaanites will not stand against the Israelites, although the Israelites took away their labors; but Naboth [Col. 0738] will stand against Ahab, because what occurred was a crime, not a command, when the unjust man took away the labors of the righteous (1 Kings 21).

So heretics will not stand against Catholics when the commands of the Christian empire are carried out in matters concerning heretics’ property. Their possessions are not taken away by Catholics; rather, they are sought out and kept so that, after the heretics have been corrected as far as possible, the possessions may be restored to them.

But Catholics will stand not only against the Gentiles, by whom the true martyrs were despoiled, but also against the Circumcellions of the Donatists, because they too took away their labors.

Yet the case concerning these material labors is easier. Every day, if someone passes over to us—and even those to whom the possessions belonged pass over into Catholic peace—we return your money, clothing, produce, vessels, fields, and houses. [Note: The words enclosed in parentheses may perhaps belong earlier, immediately after “the case is easier.”] How will you return to us the members of our people?

### 52

At last, wake up and see that neither are you among those of whom it is said, nor are we among those about whom it is said: “These are they whom we once held in derision”—whereas we hold you in tears.

You will not be counted among the sons of God unless, departing from the party of Donatus, you hold to this Church, which the Son of God, as he foretold, displays.

Your lot is not among the saints but among the heretics.

As for what you think others will say about you—“We senseless people regarded their life as madness”—I am amazed that you are so senseless that you do not say such things to yourselves now. [Note: [Col. 0738] The African edition reads, “so that you say nothing of the kind to yourselves.”]

The impure and faithless will indeed say these things then to the true and faithful saints—namely, to those whom they now think mad because they refuse to enjoy the luxuries they see, while believing what they do not see.

But if you do not consider your life madness, then at least consider this death, which you wish to inflict upon yourselves, madness; otherwise you are mad in a more desperate fashion.

As for those words, “Therefore we went astray from the way of truth,” and so forth, they will not be yours alone, but especially yours.

You clearly go astray from the way of truth; the light of righteousness does not shine for you; you grow weary in the way of iniquity and destruction; and you walk through difficult deserts, while you do not know the way of the Lord.

As for what follows—“What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All those things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:1–9)—I do not know whether anyone among the others could say it more aptly and appropriately than your predecessor Optatus.

Do not, then, suppose yourselves to be what you are not, and perish as what you are. [Note: [Col. 0738] The African and Erasmus editions read, “and perish as such,” omitting “what you are.”] For it is not this faith that urges you, but your evil error: not, as you say, to die willingly for God in this persecution, but to suffer persecution wickedly for Donatus because of your deeds.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### 53

**Words of the Letter:** “And in another hand: ‘I wish you,’ he says, ‘safe and sound, once the truth has been discerned, to soften your disposition and refrain from the deaths of the innocent.’”

**Response:** Rather, having discerned the truth, soften your own disposition, lest it rage in such a way that it spares not even you [Col. 0739]. [Note: Am., “we are gentle.”]

For what could more easily be found to be gentle than the man to whom you wrote this, who both invited you to life and, if you did not wish to live it with us, released you to flight?

You are harsh toward yourselves; you are unmerciful; you are cruel without any consideration for humanity. [Note: Am., Er., and the Parcensis manuscript read “inhumanity.”] You do to yourselves what lovers of error and persecutors of human beings have been accustomed to do to their enemies, so that those who persecute error and love human beings may have something over which to grieve most bitterly. [Note: The African and Erasmus editions read, “what the unmerciful have been accustomed to do.”]

What do you wish to be restrained from the deaths of the innocent? You are not innocent. Nevertheless, he gave you a way out, while you yourselves wish to give yourselves destruction.

I think that ignorance of the word deceived you, so that, intending to be understood as speaking of “destructions” (*exitia*), you said “ways out” (*exitus*).

Thus, when you urge the executor of the imperial laws, by way of a wish, to restrain himself from the destructions of the innocent, you are asking him to spare deceivers and to permit the innocent to be deceived with impunity.

What else does this amount to except asking the man whom you think you are benevolently addressing to keep faith neither with God nor with his emperor? For according to your justice—not true justice—such matters ought not to belong to the emperor’s responsibility so that a slanderous division might be healed; they ought to belong to it only so that, once established, the division might be confirmed.

If this teaching, which you learned not from the holy Scriptures but I know not from where, seems just to you—that such matters do not pertain to imperial authority—then this idea ought to have occurred to your ancestors when they sent Caecilian’s case to the judgment of the emperor Constantine by bringing accusations against him.

But now, because the lions did not harm Daniel on account of his innocence (Dan. 6:22), you want him to spare those who cast Daniel to the lions by accusing him.

Yet God does not judge as a human being judges. In his hand is the heart of the king, and he inclines it wherever he wishes (Prov. 21:1).

When the heart of a king is faithless, the good are either tested or proved; when it is faithful, the wicked are either corrected or punished.

Which of these two applies to your case, we have already said sufficiently, and we have responded sufficiently to your letters, leaving no passage untouched. By God’s mercy, we trust that this may benefit not only you but at least some among you.

54. But if you are preparing to answer these points, read also what was done with Emeritus, to which he was unable to reply—perhaps you may be able to do so, as I advised above, so that you might make the attempt (above, no. 41). We also dealt with him concerning the case of the Maximianists, which we repeatedly brought against you in the Conference, and to which you made no reply, because you could find nothing to say about a matter so perfectly clear and so recent [Note: [Col. 0739] In the Erfurt, Lyons, and Venice editions: “responderetis.” M.]: how Maximianus, whom you struck with a much more severe sentence than Caecilian—so severe that you said he was a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram (in the sentence of the Council of Bagai), whom the earth swallowed alive on account of the crime of schism (Num. 16)—did not defile his fellow-schismatics, to whom you granted a delay so that they might return to your communion; how “the African did not defile Africans, the living the living, the known the known, the participant his associates,” while Caecilian did defile those overseas, those far away, those unknown, and those not yet born.

Find, if you can, what you will say: how did you receive into their office Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras, whom you condemned without any delay along with Maximianus and ten others, and against whom you litigated before two—or, if I am not mistaken, three—proconsuls in order to expel them from the basilicas; and how, after you had already appointed another in Praetextatus’s place, you received them back into their offices after so long a time?

By what justice, by what reasoning, with what face is a condemned Maximianist received into his office, while the Catholic world, unheard, is condemned? By what justice, by what reasoning, with what face do you say that care must be taken lest Caecilianus defile you—now long dead and wholly unknown to you, once condemned by your elders when they judged him, yet acquitted three times when your elders accused him—while you did not think care had to be taken lest Felicianus defile you, although he had been condemned by the voice of your universal council and received by all of you, especially through the favor of your predecessor?

[Note: [Col. 0740] Optatus Gildonianus.]

By what justice, by what reasoning, with what face do you rescind the Baptism given by Churches which the Apostles planted through their labors, when you accepted the Baptism which Felicianus and Praetextatus administered outside your Church for so long a time, while you were litigating against them after their condemnation? For if, as you habitually misunderstand and allege against us, the statement “What benefit does one baptized by the dead derive from his washing?” (Ecclus. 34:30) is to be understood in this way, these men were lying among those who baptized when your sentence at Bagai resounded with such great tumult:

“The shores are filled, after the Egyptian example, with the funerals of those who perish; and in death itself their punishment is greater, because, after their life has been torn from them by the avenging waters, they do not even find burial.”

What will you say to this? Behold, the dead baptize those whom you receive, and you do not die; yet you slander us as though we were dead, so that, refusing to communicate with Catholic unity, you may truly die in your own fires. Answer these points. You have time to consider what you should say. At least let us confer this benefit on you: while you consider how to answer, you will not be considering how to burn.

But we do not want you, through lack of anything to answer, to think that you must still say that tired and battered phrase you are accustomed to use: “If we are such people, why do you seek us?” We answer: The Catholic Church ought rather to seek you, because you have perished, if you, having perished, sought the perished Maximianists. For you say to us from your heart, “Why do you seek people guilty of so many and such great crimes?” But we answer you from the Book of God: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

# BOOK TWO

Gaudentius’s reply to the preceding book is refuted.

[Col. 0741]

## CHAPTER I

1. I have received your reply, Gaudentius—if this is properly called a reply—which you wished to return to me for this reason: so that, if you had remained silent, we would not say that you had been refuted. But replying is not the same as not remaining silent. For if that is all that replying means, then you have certainly replied—but only so that even those who might have hoped for something from you may know that you did not discover what you ought to answer, and yet answered so as not to remain silent.

Thus, while you were taking care not to be called defeated, you acted in such a way as to show that you were defeated. Your own writings are sufficient to demonstrate this, if they are read by intelligent people and compared with mine through careful examination. But in order to demonstrate it through other writings as well, so that even those of slower understanding may be satisfied, a somewhat longer discussion is necessary. I shall undertake it if necessity and the Lord’s will require.

## CHAPTER II

2. In the meantime, since you attempted rather to assert that you are Catholics by the testimony of blessed Cyprian, consider for a little while what Church he called Catholic when he was defending its unity.

“The Church,” he says, “of the Lord, flooded with light, extends its rays throughout the whole world; yet there is one light, which is diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. It extends its branches over the whole earth in the abundance of its fruitfulness and spreads its abundantly flowing streams ever farther; yet there is one head, one origin, and one mother, rich in the succession of her fruitfulness” (*On the Simplicity of Prelates*, or *On the Unity of the Church*).

Why, then, do you deceive yourselves and wish to deceive others with shameless lies? If your Church is Catholic according to the testimony of this martyr, show that it extends its rays throughout the whole world; show that it extends its branches over the whole earth in the abundance of its fruitfulness.

Indeed, this is why it is called *Catholic* by a Greek word. For what is said in Greek as *holon* (ὅλον) is interpreted in Latin as “whole” or “universal.” Thus *throughout the whole* or *according to the whole* is *kath’ holon* (καθ’ ὅλον), from which it is called Catholic.

If you know this, why do you pretend not to know it? But if you do not know it, why, before speaking what you do not know, do you not first ask those who know? If this displeases you, find some language—not Greek—in which you can show that *kath’ holon* does not mean “throughout the whole,” “according to the whole,” or “according to the universal,” and then withdraw from Cyprian’s testimony.

For he speaks against you, as you can see. He says that the Catholic Church extends and spreads throughout the whole world and over the entire earth, agreeing with the Greek name and definition. You are found to hold, think, and say something else; and while you rely on Cyprian as your witness, you lie by the testimony of Cyprian.

## CHAPTER III

3. Accordingly, when you are questioned about the cause that led you to leave this true and genuine Catholic Church, which, flooded with the Lord’s light, extends its rays throughout the whole world and spreads its branches throughout the entire earth in the abundance of its fruitfulness, you find nothing just to say. You cannot cleanse your departure from this Church by any plausible excuse.

For what do you say except, “Necessity compelled us to leave the unjust, since we were just”? Divine Scripture answers you: “The wicked son declares himself just, but he does not cleanse his departure” (Prov. 24, according to the Septuagint). “He does not cleanse his departure,” it says—plainly the departure of which the apostle John says, “They went out from us” (1 John 2:19). It does not defend, excuse, or purify that departure at all.

For it belongs to the just within the Catholic Church to tolerate with the greatest patience the wicked whom they cannot correct or condemn. They must not leave the Lord’s field because of the weeds, the Lord’s threshing floor because of the chaff, the Lord’s house because of the dishonorable vessels, or the Lord’s nets because of the bad fish before the proper time, lest they attempt in vain to cleanse their departure.

If you try by any argument to turn these Gospel statements into another meaning, you contradict that same blessed Cyprian whose testimony you cite, just as you did in our Conference. For these are the words of the aforementioned martyr on this question, in a letter he wrote to Maximus and his companions in confession:

“Even if weeds appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity must not on that account be impeded, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church. We must labor only to be able to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord’s barns, we may receive fruit for our work and labor. The Apostle says in his Epistle: ‘In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honorable use, others for dishonorable use’ (2 Tim. 2:20). Let us apply ourselves and labor as much as we can to be a vessel of gold or silver. For the rest, it belongs to the Lord alone to shatter the earthen vessels, to whom the iron rod has also been given (Ps. 2:9). A servant cannot be greater than his master, lest anyone claim for himself what the Father granted to the Son alone, imagining that he can already bring the winnowing shovel to the threshing floor to winnow and cleanse it, or separate all the weeds from the wheat by human judgment. This is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which perverse rage assumes for itself. While certain people always take for themselves more than mild justice demands, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling, they lose the light of truth.”

## CHAPTER IV

4. Surely by now you see that, in our Conference, you shouted against holy Cyprian and resisted him with arguments by which you maintained that Christ’s field—which he says is “the world” (Matt. 13:38)—was not the Church but the world outside the Church, so that it could contain the weeds that were seen. For you said that manifest weeds could not exist in the Church.

How often did we set Cyprian’s testimony before you on this point, while you neither dared openly to resist him nor were willing to agree with him? Surely by now you are at last awakening, hearing, and perceiving that “even if weeds appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity must not on that account be impeded, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church.”

Why, then, do you depart from the unity of this Church through wicked schism and persist in that division with heretical presumption? Here is Cyprian before you: agree with him or answer him. You see how these words—by which he says that weeds exist and are seen in the Church, yet that one must not therefore withdraw from her—destroy all the slanders in your writings.

You advanced even to such a precipice, and threw yourself headlong in your customary manner [Note: [Col. 0743] The printed editions read, erroneously, “and threw yourself headlong with your swelling” instead of “and, in your customary manner, threw yourself headlong.” The allusion is to the Donatists’ custom of casting themselves headlong to destruction, criticized above in Book 1, no. 30.], that you said Christians throughout the world, without knowing who had sinned, could perish through the sins of others. For it is read in the holy Scriptures that one person stole something under the ban, and that on account of this alien sin an uninformed people was punished (Josh. 7). You failed to understand that those punishments of mortal bodies—that is, the deaths of those who were to die—served as a useful warning to the people, but that the sins of others, especially sins of which the dead were unaware, did not harm those dead with respect to the future life.

Did you really dare to believe and say that, because of the sins of others, even unknown sins, someone could perish before God? And did you not even fear your own colleagues, who, while you remained silent in our Conference—and perhaps, although you already held this opinion, lacked the courage to say it—fought with such massive arguments that bad fish in the Lord’s nets are unknown to the fishermen, lest they perish through the fish’s contagion if they knew of them?

Did it not occur to you that, when Emeritus was being pressed, you denied and said, “Do you not read about the threshing floor?” (Conference 3, chap. 262), while we were arguing [Note: [Col. 0743] Perhaps: “while we were arguing.”] that the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor—that is, of the Church—must be tolerated in one mixture until the time of winnowing? When he was reminded more privately by his own people and more openly by us, who recalled from the Gospel that the Lord would come bearing a winnowing shovel in his hand, cleanse his threshing floor, gather the wheat into his barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12), he immediately corrected the error of forgetfulness by which he had denied that this was written.

Yet he did not abandon the heretical or schismatic perversity by which he denied that the wicked ought to be tolerated with the good for the sake of the Church’s unity. He immediately said that, by the name “chaff,” hidden wicked people were meant, so that you might preserve with particular care this principal point of your case: that unknown wicked people cannot defile any of the good.

Behold, the distinguished advocate of your party has lost his labors because of your opposition. To safeguard the salvation of the good, he says that wicked people who remain in the Church are wholly unknown to the good, lest, if they are known and tolerated, they destroy them. But you said that the good perish even through the contagion of unknown wickedness.

Nor did you fear the many hidden criminals, evildoers, and impious people who have existed among your people from the beginning and who, according to your opinion, certainly destroyed you and all your people without your knowledge. Even now you did not tremble with fear lest one of your own might sin without your knowledge and destroy you while you were saying these things.

Or is it that, since you understand that you have perished when your deeds became known, you do not fear perishing because of unknown sins committed by others?

## CHAPTER V

5. What should I wish for you except that we may be permitted to find you, lest you wish to perish? For what hope will remain—not only for us, who agree with the Lord Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles, and holy Cyprian that even known wicked people must be tolerated for the bond of unity if we can neither correct nor punish them, but also for you, who approve of bodily separation from the wicked before the time of harvest, winnowing, and the shore—if your opinion is true, according to which each person perishes both through his own sins and through the sins of others, even when he does not know whether they have been committed?

For if this is so, then your ancestors too, who, as you think, separated themselves from known wicked people, perished through unknown ones.

This applies not only to you, who, when you say that a person perishes through another’s crimes whether he knows them or not, plainly allow no innocent person to remain; it applies also to Emeritus, who, holding a far more tolerable opinion, binds people in communion with the sins of others only when those sins are known and releases them from sins that are unknown. To him venerable Cyprian responds in a much truer voice: the wheat does not perish as it grows together with the weeds—not with weeds outside the Church, but with weeds established within the Church; not with hidden and unknown weeds, but with those plainly known and visible.

For I think that someone who argues that what is seen is hidden is blinded not in the flesh but in the mind. When that most blessed man warns us not to withdraw from the Church because of the weeds that are in her, he is not warning us on account of weeds that are hidden, but rather on account of those that are seen. These are what can disturb those who see them, unless wisdom makes them patient.

For how would we learn that we ought not to withdraw because of hidden things, of whose existence we are entirely unaware? “Even if weeds appear to be in the Church,” he says. He says “appear,” not “are believed to exist on the basis of suspicion.” And lest anyone think that “appear to exist” was said as though they did not exist but only seemed to exist, he explains what he meant in the words that follow:

“Our faith or charity must not,” he says, “on that account be impeded, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church.”

He does not say, “We suspect,” “we suppose,” “we believe,” or “we think,” but “we see.” For those people too did not believe that the weeds were covered over; they saw them openly—the people who said to the master of the household, “Do you want us to go and gather them?” These were the weeds of which it had been said, “When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared.” He answered them, “No, lest while you gather the weeds you also uproot the wheat. Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13:26–30).

And yet you say—whereby you contradict the Lord in every respect—that only weeds have grown throughout the world, while the wheat has diminished and perished throughout almost the whole world, even though the Church has not yet reached certain peoples as she grows. Yet she must reach them, and “the Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end will come.” The Lord predicted without any ambiguity that this would happen.

## CHAPTER VI

6. You see that, according to Cyprian’s testimony, the Church is called Catholic because of the whole world and is not without manifest wicked people, on account of whom he nevertheless warns that she must not be abandoned.

Within her there are many good people in themselves; but in comparison with the weeds or chaff, they are certainly few. For it is not outside her but within her that what the Lord himself says takes place: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

But there too is the people spread everywhere, to whom it is said: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). Those who have faith like a grain of mustard seed, by which even mountains may be moved (Matt. 17:19), are exceedingly rare. For it was concerning such faith that the Lord said: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8)—not concerning the apostasy of the whole world, as you most perversely understand it.

## CHAPTER VII

7. As for Baptism, which you think exists only in the Church, and for which you accuse us because, when people come from heresies, we judge that those who have already been baptized should not be baptized again, it is enough that you were entirely unable to answer how Felicianus, once condemned and established outside your Church, could baptize. You tried in vain to place him among those to whom you granted a delay.

Read the sentence of your council at Bagai. After many extremely bitter statements made against them—statements far more severe than those made against Caecilianus, whom your ancestors condemned in his absence although he was innocent—their manifest and unquestionable condemnation is set down as follows:

“Know that Victorianus of Carcabia, Martianus of Sullectum, Baianus of Baiana, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabrata, Miggenus of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membresa, Valerius of Melzita, Felicianus of Musti, and Martialis of Pertusa, guilty of notorious crime, who by the fatal work of perdition glued together a filthy vessel with collected filth; and also the clerics of the Church of Carthage, who, by taking part in the crime, provided encouragement for unlawful incest—know that they have been condemned by the judgment of God, who presides, and by the truthful voice of the universal council.”

Then the extension of a delay to the others begins in these words:

“But those whom the plantations of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile—that is, those who with the modest shame of faith withdrew their hands from Maximianus, their head—we have permitted to return to Mother Church.”

What had to be said about these matters has already been said sufficiently in my earlier letters to you. Anyone who reads this passage and pays even a little attention cannot doubt that you were wholly unable to answer it.

## CHAPTER VIII

8. It therefore seems pointless to you that the councils of Agrippinus and Cyprian should be followed in this question, since you yourselves disregarded them when you accepted, without any repetition of Baptism, people baptized outside your communion by those whom you had condemned and against whom you were litigating in order to expel them from the basilicas.

As for the opinion of Cyprian and his colleagues, who at that time thought that those coming from the heretics ought to be baptized, it would take too long to discuss it at the length it deserves. But answer this brief question for me, if you can:

When Cyprian, bishop of the Church of Carthage, was rebaptizing those who came from the heretics, Stephen, then bishop of the Church of Rome, was receiving heretics in the very Baptism they had received outside. While the two of them acted differently in this matter, they remained in Catholic unity.

Tell me: at that time, did the Church perish through the contagion of the wicked, when, according to you, through Stephen and his innumerable colleagues throughout the world who shared his opinion, she received without Baptism people guilty of every crime—or did she not perish?

For you will not be able to call these wicked people hidden, although you assert that even hidden people harm and kill. Therefore, whenever a murderer, or even a parricide, an adulterer, an incestuous person, an idolater, or finally someone who did not timidly hand over the holy books, but cruelly tortured and violently coerced people into handing them over, and finally burned them either by command or with his own hand, came to Stephen and his associates after being baptized among the heretics, he was received, according to you, without Baptism.

Do you therefore see that, if what you think about Baptism is true, all the crimes of these people were then assembled in the Church without Baptism? Answer whether Cyprian was defiled by these crimes in that same unity. Answer whether the Church perished or did not perish. Choose whichever you think.

If she had already perished, what did she give birth to Donatus? But if she could not perish when so many people were gathered into her without Baptism, please answer: what madness persuaded the party of Donatus to separate from her as though avoiding communion with the wicked?

9. But far be it from us to place ourselves above the most blessed Cyprian because he held a different opinion about Baptism from what truth—first through custom and later through more carefully considered reasoning—has shown. His many other great merits, and his spirit filled with exceptional charity, through which he remained at peace with colleagues who held different opinions, together with his glorious suffering in the unity of the Church, sufficiently demonstrated that he was a fruitful branch in Christ the root. The Father would even cleanse him of this fault, so that he might bear greater fruit.

For Jesus himself says: “Every branch in me that bears fruit, my Father purifies it, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). He thus shows that, even in those who bear fruit, the heavenly husbandman finds something to cleanse.

For who among us can be compared with the apostle Peter, although we have never compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, as he did when he was not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel? He was corrected by his later fellow apostle Paul through a salutary admonition (Gal. 2:11–14), and thereby offered posterity a more useful example of humility than he would have offered if there had been nothing in him requiring correction.

## CHAPTER IX

10. Established, then, in this Church—which neither could nor can perish through the contagion of the wicked, whether hidden or even manifest—we fear no slanders concerning any people.

For if they are wicked, the good either certainly do not know them, or, once they have been revealed through ecclesiastical proceedings, they condemn them according to the laws of the Church. Or, if they know them but cannot condemn them because they have not been accused and convicted before them, they tolerate them for the peace of the Church—not merely without blame but even commendably. They do not damnably separate themselves before the proper time from the bad fish by breaking the Lord’s nets.

For if they wish to do this, apart from the innumerable testimonies of the divine Scriptures that forbid them to do so, they are certainly restrained by the very witness whom you cited, the most blessed Cyprian, who cries out and testifies:

“Even if weeds appear to be in the Church, our faith or charity must not on that account be impeded, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church.”

He admonishes us not only by his words but also by his example. He endured, for the bond of unity (*On the Lapsed*), colleagues who seized estates through treacherous frauds and increased their loans through multiplying interest; he understood, according to the Apostle, that their greed was not some minor fault but idolatry (Col. 3:5). Yet he did not become like them through their contagion. He separated himself from them by the difference of his conduct, not by division of the Sacraments; he did not touch what was unclean, but recoiled from their deeds without gathering separate peoples.

But you, while understanding carnally what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah—“Depart, go out from their midst, and be separate, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52:11)—and similar statements in the Scriptures, appear entirely to be like those whose masters, as the same Prophet declares, say, “Do not touch me, for I am clean” (Isa. 65:5). You understand these things carnally, not spiritually.

Finally, when you perversely judged that the sins of others had to be avoided, you made other sins your own: sacrilegious schism by dividing peoples, and sacrilegious heresy by holding, with a wicked spirit, opinions against God’s manifest promises concerning the Church spread throughout the whole world and their fulfillment.

For if, as you think and reproach us in your statement, one and the same fellowship of the perished consisted simultaneously of schism and heresy, blessed Cyprian would not have said in this very letter—from which I quoted his testimony about the weeds established in the Church—to those confessors whom he rejoiced had been freed from the division of the Novatians:

“I was deeply grieved and greatly distressed that I could not communicate with those whom I had once begun to love, after schismatic error received you when you came out of prison” (*Letter to Maximus*).

Do not therefore evade either of these two truths deceitfully, or choose for yourself whichever one seems milder, in opposition to the clearest truth. You are both a schismatic through sacrilegious separation and a heretic through sacrilegious doctrine.

## CHAPTER X

11. Do not flatter yourselves that we do not rescind your Baptism. It is not yours but that of the Catholic Church which we hold; when you departed, you took it with you—not for your salvation but for your destruction.

For the Lord’s vessels remained holy even among foreigners. Hence the king who dared to use them insultingly was punished when God grew angry (Dan. 5). And the Ark of the Covenant, captured by enemies, did not in any way lose the power of its sanctification (1 Sam. 4–6).

If, then, those holy things, when they were among foreigners and therefore ceased to be among their own people, nevertheless could not in any way lose the force of their holiness, how much more do Christian Sacraments not lose it when they pass to heretics while still remaining among us?

This is what I wrote to you above (Book 1, no. 7), and what we also said to you in the Conference. You thought it better to evade this point [Note: [Col. 0748] See the Donatists’ Mandate in the Appendix.]—because you could not dissolve it—just as the Apostle says of certain people, “They hold the truth in iniquity” (Rom. 1:18).
