In the same way, you hold the truth of divine Baptism in the iniquity of human error.

We certainly ought not to rescind that truth, which is not yours, on account of your iniquity. And because the Apostle is understood to have said of the idolatrous Gentiles, “They hold the truth in iniquity,” you, as though replying to me, demanded that I prove what the Apostle does not rescind concerning the sacrilege of the Gentiles and what he does not condemn concerning their profane ritual. It was as though he could fail to rescind and condemn what is sacrilegious and profane, just as we do your schism and your heresy.

Nevertheless, the Apostle did not destroy certain statements of truth held by some Gentile philosophers concerning the unknown God [Note: [Col. 0748] The Parcensis manuscript reads “the known God.”]; indeed, when necessary, he used them as testimony. Speaking to the Athenians about God, he says: “In him we live and move and have our being, as even some of your own people have said” (Acts 17:28).

They suppressed in the iniquity of their idolatry this truth of wisdom, which blessed Paul not only did not destroy but also used to instruct them; and apostolic teaching overturned their idolatry through apostolic means.

In the same way, we do not rescind what your ancestors received as true in the Catholic Church and handed down to you; we acknowledge it. But we either rescind your sacrilege when you convert, or detest it when you persist in it.

## CHAPTER XI

12. Indeed, by explaining the whole question and everything at issue between us in a single statement by Dulcitius, you have entirely resolved the matter.

When I had said, “Nor is this found in Dulcitius’s letter—that the name of God was invoked by you in truth,” because I had simply not read that exact phrase there [Note: [Col. 0748] Namely, “in truth”], you replied, “You are mistaken, or rather you are deceiving.”

For Dulcitius’s words are: “And let it not be said that so great a work of the house of the Lord, where you have so often invoked the name of God and his Christ, has been burned through the religion established there by you. Understand that religion is the term used for truth, while superstition is the name given to falsehood.”

When would I have noticed this? When would I have reasoned in that way? When would I have proved one thing from another in that manner? I confess that this escaped the limited acuity of my intellect; therefore believe me: I could have been mistaken there, but I did not, as you said, wish to deceive in the wording.

Thus Dulcitius, as a military man, made a mistake when he said to someone whom he knew or believed to be a heretic, “through your religion,” since heresy is not religion but superstition, whereas religion, properly speaking, is not in falsehood but in truth. Accordingly, according to your explanation, the true worship of God is called religion, while false worship is called superstition.

Listen, then, to yourself; obey yourself, and you will not refuse to follow us. For in writing to that same Dulcitius, at the very beginning of your first letter, you wrote:

“To Dulcitius, an honorable tribune and notary, greatly dear to us and, if you wish it, greatly desired by us, Gaudentius the bishop.”

Immediately you added: “I have received the writings of your religion.”

Why, then, do you still hesitate to come to us? Behold, although Dulcitius the tribune is a man of our communion, according to your testimony he is not superstitious but religious; and therefore, according to your explanation, he holds not false but true worship of God.

He is therefore in the Catholic Church rather than you, since in this statement you did not err to such an extent that you even explained religion as differing from superstition as truth differs from falsehood.

But that man, as I have said, was a military man and less educated in the precise use of words; he did not know what religion was. Far be it from me to say that he deceived you by flattery.

But you, who accuse those against whom you argue from the prophet and cry out, “Woe to those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter, who call light darkness and darkness light” (Isa. 5:20), if what Dulcitius holds with us is superstition, why did you call it religion? But if you spoke truly, why, while holding heretical superstition, do you reject Catholic religion?

Follow your own testimony, especially since your own people, once they understand it, may perhaps not communicate with you, because through this statement you have communicated with the tribune Dulcitius.

Come, brother Gaudentius, do not lose the opportunity that the Lord has given you even through your own tongue. Or are you angry because I call you “brother”? You rejected this name from us also in our Conference [Note: [Col. 0749] In Conference 2, chap. 49, when Augustine had said, “It was not our doing that our brothers who stand opposed to us wish to charge us with this,” Bishop Petilianus said, “You insult us.”], where you showed that we are those to whom the Lord commanded through the prophet, “Say to those who hate you and detest you, ‘You are our brothers’” (Isa. 66:5, according to the Septuagint), while you are among those who hate and detest the people to whom the Lord says this.

Certainly you cannot deny that you called it religion in which the tribune Dulcitius stands. For this reason he sent you that letter: specifically so that you would not kill yourself but would communicate with the Church in which he himself stands.

If, then, his is religion, yours is superstition. Although you have both said this to one another, you nevertheless choose that he should have spoken falsely rather than yourself.

## CHAPTER XII

**13.** Therefore, according to this very truthful testimony of yours and your very truthful explanation, since what the tribune Dulcitius professes is religion, it follows that the religion by which the emperor’s command urges you toward our communion is also religion. Hence it follows that it is also a religious duty by which a Christian emperor judges it to belong to his responsibility to prevent divine matters from being sinned against with impunity—whereas you do not wish him to concern himself except with matters contained within the earthly commonwealth.

[Col. 0750]

Hence, forgetting what you have read, you said that the king of the Ninevites did not command his people to undertake repentance. For these are your words to me:

> “Why,” you ask, “are you deceiving the wretched? The God of Jonah commanded it; the Lord sent the prophet to the people; he commanded nothing of this kind to the king.”

Observe, then, what is written, and do not become angry with yourself [Note: [Col. 0750] Perhaps: “unless you become angry with yourself”], since you either do not remember the divine writings—or rather, since you are deceiving the wretched.

> “Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a great city, a three-days’ journey. Jonah began to enter the city, going about a day’s journey, and he preached and said: ‘In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown.’ And the men of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. When the word reached the king of the city of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, removed his garments, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and sat in ashes. And proclamation was made by the king and his nobles, saying: ‘Let neither human beings nor animals, sheep nor cattle, taste anything, nor feed, nor drink water. And humans and animals put on sackcloth, and cried out fervently to the Lord; and each person turned away from his evil way and from the iniquity that was in his hands’” (Jonah 3:3–8).

Do you finally hear that the king took care of something which you dislike being considered the responsibility of kings? Certainly, he ensured that what was being done insufficiently was done with earnestness.

Therefore the Ninevites were not driven by the king’s command to repentance through confiscations, proscriptions, or the terror of soldiers, because they obediently carried out the orders. We are not, then, presenting a people who suffered such things, since you too do not present a king who was despised.

Accordingly, when anyone obeys kings who command what belongs to God with reverent fear—a fear that begins the process and advances toward love—he receives peace from the Lord; not the kind of peace the world gives. The world gives peace for temporal advantage, but the Lord gives it for eternal salvation.

Therefore, since that is a religion in which the tribune Dulcitius stands—for you will surely not deny your own words—the party of Donatus is a superstition, from which this religion wishes to rescue you. It is a superstition that you seek to kill yourself, something this religion strongly forbids. It is a superstition that you criticize the emperor’s concern for these matters, a concern which this religion undertook to carry out.

## CHAPTER XIII

**14.** Therefore, since your own word has brought the case to an end, I beseech you by the God of religion and the God of truth: may your error also come at last to an end.

This is the Church of Christ, brother, which in the present age is being extended throughout the whole world by continual growth, containing both the wicked and the good, who will be separated at the final winnowing. And, to address you at last in the words of the man whom you wished to summon as a witness to the Catholic name:

> “This is she who, suffused with the Lord’s light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; this is she who stretches her branches over the whole earth through the abundance of her fruitfulness” (Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*).

Accordingly, even if tares appear to be in her, neither our faith nor our love ought to be hindered, so that, because we see that there are tares in the Church, we ourselves should withdraw from the Church.

Our only task must be to strive to become wheat, so that, when the wheat begins to be gathered into the Lord’s granaries, we may receive fruit in accordance with our work and labor.

The Apostle says in his Letter:

> “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some indeed are honorable, but others dishonorable” (2 Timothy 2:20).

Let us apply ourselves and labor as much as we can to be a vessel of gold or silver. But to break the earthen vessels belongs to the Lord alone, to whom also an iron rod has been given (Psalm 2:9).

A servant cannot be greater than his master. No one should claim for himself what the Father granted to the Son alone, imagining that he can already bring the winnowing shovel to the threshing floor to winnow and cleanse it, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment.

That obstinacy is proud, and that presumption sacrilegious—an evil madness lays claim to it. And while certain people continually assume more than gentle justice demands, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling pride, they lose the light of truth (*Letter to Maximus*).

These are the words of the most blessed Cyprian, not mine. They are the words, of course, of the man whom you placed at the beginning of your writings as a highly esteemed witness to the Catholic name and commended at great length; indeed, through him—for the words are true and divine—they are God’s words.

Behold what you must hear; behold what you must beware of: with the help of [Col. 0752] the Savior’s mercy, let us hold together the Catholic love, let us together cherish Catholic peace, let us together grow everywhere with its wheat, let us together tolerate the tares until the end, and let us together live forever in the granary.

You see, surely, that without any defense of Caecilianus, or of whatever persons you think should be accused, the Catholic Church stands secure through its own strength and firmness.

Moreover, the case of Caecilianus has been cleared by our Conference; and concerning the others whom you slander, the accusation is either doubtful or the condemnation unjust. But it is extremely foolish to place the case of the Church—which is supported and fortified by divine testimonies—upon human cases by straying from reason. Even if we saw those people to be manifestly wicked, and were no longer able to separate them from the Church’s sacraments, our faith or our love still ought not to be hindered, so that, because we would see that these people too were among the tares in the Church, we ourselves should withdraw from the Church.

If you intend to reply, do not abandon the case and wander into irrelevancies. Consider what has been said; respond to what has been said, not by deceitfully evading it, but by arguing rationally. If it should prove necessary, and the Lord grant it, I will demonstrate more carefully in another work what you accomplished—or rather, how you accomplished nothing—by that lengthy reply.

## [CONCERNING RUSTICIANUS THE SUBDEACON]

[Col. 0751]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING SERMON

Hieronymus Vignierius retrieved this sermon from the Cellensis manuscript and included it in the second volume of the Augustinian Supplement that he compiled. He had no doubt that it was genuinely preached by Augustine, and indeed that it was the first of those sermons which the blessed Bishop delivered to the people after the death of his predecessor Valerius.

But, without lingering here over an examination of its style—which seems to possess neither sufficient gravity and dignity nor a wholly Augustinian mode of expression—it is certain that the sermon mixes and confuses two histories which, by their chronology and other circumstances, are proved to be quite different: one concerning a certain deacon of Mutugenna, the other concerning Rusticianus.

For, in the first place, that Rusticianus who is called in this sermon the deacon of Mutugena, and who is said to have defected from the Catholic Church to the Donatists, to have been rebaptized by Macrobius, and to have been made a deacon—he, I say—is indicated by many signs to be precisely the same person as that rebaptized deacon of Mutugenna on whose account Augustine wrote Letter 23 to Maximinus, without mentioning the deacon’s name, around the year of Christ 392.

Yet several details found here do not fit him at all. For at the time when that deacon was received by the Donatists, Augustine was still a presbyter, as is clear from the same Letter 23. But the author of the sermon, in section 3, testifies that at the very beginning of his own office he had worked to place on level ground someone rushing headlong into a precipice.

Nor can “office” here be understood to mean Augustine’s presbyterate, since the preacher says in the same passage that he did not want the man to be taken away from him at the very beginning of his office—someone whom he had for quite a long time seen falling like a flash of lightning from heaven. Augustine had not lived at Hippo for a long time before his presbyterate.

The author not only assumes that this deacon had fallen only from the time of Augustine’s episcopate—which Augustine had indeed undertaken while Valerius was still alive—but also says in this sermon, although it was delivered after Valerius’s death, regarding the deacon’s pitiable fall as though it were an entirely recent event:

> “While we mourn the pastor who has been taken away,” he says, “an occasion for grieving over a lost brother arises.”

In section 6 he mentions Felicianus and Praetextatus, whom the Donatists had already received along with those whom they had baptized. This did not happen until the year 397.

There is also the fact that in section 5 he relates, concerning the same matter, words from Letter 107 written to Augustine by Theodorus and Maximus. These words in fact concern another case, namely that of Rusticianus the subdeacon, who likewise defected from Augustine in order to be rebaptized by Macrobius. On that occasion Augustine wrote him Letter 108, around the year 409.

Indeed, it is understood from the same Letter 108 that the case of this subdeacon Rusticianus occurred only after Honorius’s laws against the Donatists—that is, after the year 405. Yet, as we believe, no one would extend Valerius’s life that far, when he sees that from the beginning of his episcopate Augustine never mentions Valerius except in Letters 31 and 33, which were undoubtedly written around the year 396. It is scarcely plausible, moreover, that this deacon—if he is the man who had already been wavering from the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate—would not have fallen until ten years later.

Furthermore, the preacher presents certain statements as though they came from Augustine’s letter to Macrobius, although they are not found in that letter itself but are explicitly found in Letter 23 to Maximinus.

We pass over in silence other features that make this sermon doubtful: for example, the preacher calls the same man whom, in section 4, he describes as dissolute and ruined, “a soldier of the Lord” and “a vessel of honor” in section 3. He considers it more grievous because of the repetition of Baptism that this deserter from the Church was also made a deacon by the Donatists. He presses the same heretics who rebaptize with the example of Primianus’s Baptism. Moreover, he names Maximus and Theodorus—whom Augustine calls “sons” and “honorable men” in Letter 108—without any expression of honor.

In section 1 he uses the word *omen*, which Augustine rejects in *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 1. Finally, in section 4 he speaks of Primianus’s action as though it were known to everyone, although up to that point in the sermon he had said nothing about it to the people.

[Col. 0753]

## SERMON ATTRIBUTED TO AUGUSTINE CONCERNING RUSTICIANUS THE SUBDEACON, REBAPTIZED BY THE DONATISTS AND ORDAINED A DEACON (C, G, S)*

### 1

Still mourning and grieving, brothers, I present myself before your Holiness; for I have not been able to digest the grief of the recent event—shall I call it mine, or yours?

Three times I have attempted to supply you with the word which I owe you; as many times, the tears of both you and me, as I tried to speak, have silenced my voice. Nor could I better express the anxieties weighing upon me than through an abundance of tears.

What, then, will happen? Will no limit ever be set to my mourning, or to yours? Whenever you see me entering, will you never cease beating your breasts and uttering groans? Whenever I see you gathered together, shall I break into tears and sighs?

The divine words have prescribed for both me and you a time for mourning (Ecclesiastes 3:4). I did not grieve when I saw you weeping—for the Lord Jesus Christ also wept at the memory of Lazarus, and the Jews who saw him weeping said, “See how he loved him!” (John 11:35–36). Rather, if anything pleasant or welcome can be found in tears, I gathered it from yours.

For I said within myself: “See how they loved him! Those who followed their father with such affection will show the same affection to the son who has become their father. They will make the heir of the burden the heir of their love. The one who succeeds to the honor will also succeed to their affection.”

“It is a good omen for one who is entering upon his office” [Note: [Col. 0753] *Retractions* 1.1.3] to see in the sheep signs of their ancient love for the shepherd. Love will be transferred to the one to whom the responsibility has been handed over. Although the shepherd has changed, they will not cease loving the man who must feed the sheep, whose voice they will hear [Note: [Col. 0753] Perhaps: “and whose voice they will hear”], and who, with God as witness and his conscience as witness, is ready, with the Lord’s help, to spend and expend his life for the least of the little sheep.

### 2

If there is any reason for grieving or weeping, it belongs entirely to me, not to you, and not to him whose loss we mourn.

He has been released; I am bound. He has completed the race; I am running. He is in his homeland, while I am an exile. The responsibilities he laid down he placed again in my embrace.

He held the helm well; what will become of me, I do not know. He has reached the shore; I am tossed about.

From the shore he sees the raging [Col. 0754] sea and the furious storms. I cry out amid the waves, “Save us, we are perishing!” (Matthew 8:25). And truly we are perishing; truly danger presses upon us; truly it strikes my head—not merely my danger, but yours as well. For I cannot be safe without you. The loss of your souls is mine.

Whatever is lost from you before my Lord is lost at my peril. I shall have to give an account: “Skin for skin” (Job 2:4).

I have a merciful Lord, but a strict accountant. Every day he counts his little sheep; he has them listed in his hands. He demands the number, and if I do not return it, great danger is created for my head.

Consider, brothers, whether I can refrain from tears when I contemplate my burden; whether I should not grieve over my heavy responsibility.

Lighten my burden. Your love will make what is monstrous more bearable. With the Lord’s help, both the shepherd and the little sheep will find pasture; and after they have lain down at midday, they will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), where there will be neither sun nor any heat (Revelation 7:16), but peace and refreshment in the Lord’s shadow, when our mourning will be turned into a lyre and the voices of those who weep into songs of rejoicing.

### 3

But, beloved, while we mourn the shepherd who has been taken away, an occasion for grieving over a lost brother arises.

A member has been cut off from us; a part of us has become part of the party of Donatus. A soldier of the Lord has passed over to the camp of the Philistines, and from a vessel of honor has become a vessel of dishonor.

You understand what I mean. That wretched man, Rusticianus, the deacon of Mutugena, rejected the Sacrament which he owed to the Church and polluted his order by unfaithful participation.

What did I not do? What efforts did I not employ, in order to place on level ground a man rushing into a precipice, and rescue from danger one who loved the danger in which he perished?

That was my first and most urgent concern; it is now my grief. I did not want him taken away from me at the very beginning of my office—him whom for quite a long time I had seen falling like a flash of lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18).

And although, because of his sins, he deserved to be abandoned by the Lord, [Col. 0755] I nevertheless grieve that I cannot say concerning him to my Lord: “Here am I and the children whom you have given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

### 4

I know that all of you are aware of this, and I know it so well because I know that many of your people were displeased with the delays he caused here.

How often our venerable Valerius, in my presence and with paternal feeling, said to him:

> “What are you doing here? Why are you abandoning your station? Why do you not work together with your presbyter? Why do you prefer Hippo to Mutugena, to which you are bound?”

And when he replied that he had undertaken clerical service, not monastic life, because he was wholly unsuited to solitude, and that he had no one in Mutugena with whom he could associate, the holy old man would answer:

> “You are bound to your wife; do not seek release” (1 Corinthians 7:27). “The church of Mutugena is yours, not ours. You gave your name to it, not to Hippo. Did you not renounce the world? Did you not renounce friends, and blood relations?”

He heard the man speaking, but he heard badly, since he did not obey the speaker.

What happened? Since he was considered quite convivial and inclined by temperament toward buffoonery, amid the world’s frivolities, banquets, and daily drinking parties—often also nightly ones—he eventually defected.

The spirit of the fear of the Lord was extinguished. He rolled from mud into mud, alternately inviting others and being invited by others, both guest and host. Unable to pay the debts he had incurred, pressed by creditors, entangling himself in daily errors, and creating scandal for many, he was finally excommunicated by his presbyter.

He fled to the Donatists and was received by their bishop—not merely received, which is contrary to the law of the Churches; not merely rebaptized, which is impious; but, what is most grievous of all, made a deacon.

### 5

When I first received this news, our venerable old man Valerius was away. But my inmost feelings could not tolerate delay. I groaned and grieved, and poured out my soul for him in the presence of my Lord.

Since many had reported to me that Macrobius, the Donatist bishop to whom he had fled, was a peaceful man, not far from the kingdom of God and from concord with the brethren, and that if he rebaptized anyone he did so unwillingly, I decided to approach him by letter.

Through friends I intended to urge him with the most earnest prayers not to destroy Christ’s Baptism in our subdeacon, nor baptize again one whom he knew had been baptized and sealed in the name of God.

He received our letter reluctantly. But at last, compelled by the prayers of Maximus and Theodorus, to whom we had entrusted the matter, he allowed it to be read and himself read it as well. He replied nothing other than:

> “I can do nothing except receive those who come to me and give them the faith which they request” [Note: [Col. 0755] See Letter 107 among the Augustinian letters].

When they pressed him concerning Primianus’s action, he said that a son ought not to investigate his father.

In the letter which I sent to Macrobius, I had asked him to give a reply that could be read before our people; but if he refused, I would read our letter when the soldiers were first absent [Note: [Col. 0755] Compare Augustine, Letter 23, sections 6–7].

Today, brothers, I am fulfilling my pledge. No one is present who could [Col. 0756] stir up disturbances. I know that all of you are more ready for concord and for embracing outsiders than to be provoked by me. I produce the letter to Macrobius, so that nothing in the proceedings may be hidden from your conscience, but so that it may become known before God and human beings with how sincere a heart and peaceful an intention, under the Lord’s inspiration, I have handled the matter.

If our brother perishes afterward, he will perish in his own conscience, not in ours.

The Lord will come, who will judge both them and me. He will surely come to vindicate the wheat and scatter the chaff.

He himself will examine our waters, which they fear so greatly, and before everyone will judge most plainly whether he too regards as polluted the waters which they have judged polluted.

Surely they will see the one whom they pierced (John 19:37). For what else is it to rebaptize a Christian than to pierce the Lord again?

He received the King’s sign; he accepted the cross; he was immersed in Christ’s death. What else are you doing when you baptize such a person twice, when you blow away the King’s sign, when you erase the cross, than to make the Lord’s death empty and void, and to hold the whole dispensation of our salvation up to ridicule?

### 6

Our water is not alien. It is virgin and holy. The Spirit descended into our font; those whom it sprinkles are holy. Let them see with what audacity they assert to be polluted those whom they know to have been sprinkled with such waters.

O sacrilegious novelty! O impious utterance!

God sanctified the waters at the beginning of the world through the hovering of the Spirit. From them so many and such great miracles proceeded—miracles that would teach us about the holiness of our waters, instruct us concerning the truth of which those things were shadows, and assure us about the regeneration which we receive in the waters.

Yet they call those waters alien, abstain from them, call them deceitful, and deprive them entirely of credibility!

Then Primianus’s water will be truthful—the water of Primianus whom you struck with so monstrous an anathema and judged guilty of so many crimes in your assembly. Yet you did not baptize again those whom he baptized.

And the waters of the Catholic Church—our dove, our immaculate bride—will be unfaithful, impure, and deceitful among them?

Perhaps they will say: “Those who condemned the innocent Primianus were deceitful, and therefore his waters were not deceitful.”

But what will they say about Felicianus and Praetextatus, who condemned Primianus and had withdrawn from him in that great schism? Did they produce for their own Church, by a new and recent immersion, those whom they had baptized?

Certainly not. The waters of Felicianus and Praetextatus were faithful—though Felicianus and Praetextatus later joined together and conspired against the Catholic Church in a mad alliance—while our waters are unfaithful and profane?

O mad and perverse thought!

### 7

They add as well:

> “He who is baptized by one who is dead—what is his washing worth?” (Sirach 34:30).

You are mistaken, wretched people, because you do not understand the Scriptures.

We are not saying that the Baptism with which those whom we separate from the communion of the living as though they were dead baptize is nothing; we say that it is of no benefit so long as one lives among the dead.

Remove what harms, and it already benefits. What you received outside will become effective when you are within.

Correct the baptized person; that is enough. The power hidden in the seed will grow. He will put on the Spirit of God from above. And he who had been buried with Christ through Baptism, although outside, after he has been admitted into the bosom of the Church [Col. 0757] and has left the dead to bury their own dead, will experience faithful water, undefiled by the contagions of heretics.

He will hear the fatherly voice in his heart:

> “This son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:24, 32).

“My son, whom I had brought forth through waters serving as midwives, was dead because he was not living from my spirit; and he came to life again because, having rejected the company of the dead, he returned to the place of life.

“He was lost because he had been swept away in the same [Col. 0758] shipwreck as the impious; he has been found because, through the saving plank—that is, repentance—he was at last restored to the harbor—that is, the Church.”

Brothers, let us ask the Lord as earnestly as we can that this may happen to them: that, just as there is one Baptism, one water, and one faith, so also there may be one profession of love, and that no other rivalry may henceforth be heard among us than the striving after the better gifts.

## INDEX OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE AGAINST THE DONATISTS CONTAINED IN THE PRECEDING VOLUMES

[Note: [Col. 0757] This index refers to the works of Augustine of Hippo against the Donatists in PL 36–40.]

### IN THE SECOND VOLUME: LETTERS

**XXIII**, to Maximinus, a Donatist bishop, who was said to have rebaptized a Catholic deacon.

**XXXIII**, to Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop of Hippo, inviting him to a mutual conference.

**XXXIV**, to Eusebius, concerning a young man who had passed over to the Donatists and had been rebaptized by them.

**XXXV**, to the same man, urging him to see through Proculeianus the bishop that the license of Donatist clergy be restrained.

**XLIII**, to Glorius, Eleusius, and others, concerning the great impudence with which the Donatists persist in a schism after being convicted by so many judgments.

**XLIV**, to the same men, concerning what had begun to be done in the conference with Fortunius the bishop.

**XLIX**, to Honoratus, a Donatist bishop, concerning the Church spread throughout the whole world.

**LI**, to Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, pressing him on the case of the Maximianists.

**LII**, to Severinus, his kinsman, recalling him from the schism of the Donatists to the Catholic Church.

**LIII**, to Generosus, refuting a letter written to him by a certain Donatist presbyter and bringing against the Donatists ancient proceedings contrary to them, as well as the case of the Maximianists.

**LVI**, to Celer, briefly dissuading him from the error of the Donatists.

**LVII**, to the same man.

**LVIII**, to Pammachius, congratulating him because he had brought his Donatist tenants in Numidia from the schism to the Church.

**LXI**, to Theodorus, concerning the reception into their offices of clergy coming from the party of Donatus.

**LXVI**, a letter of rebuke to Crispinus of Calama, because he had rebaptized the Mappalians after subduing them by fear.

**LXX**, to Naucellio, concerning the case of Felicianus, who had first been solemnly condemned by the Donatists and afterward received back into his office.

**LXXVI**, to the Donatists, urging them to return to the Catholic Church.

**LXXXVI**, to Caecilianus, urging him by his edict to restrain the Donatists of the region of Hippo.

**LXXXVII**, to Emeritus the Donatist, proving that the schism had arisen without any just cause and asking him to respond to the arguments.

**LXXXVIII**, to Januarius or Januarianus, written in the name of the clergy of Hippo, protesting against the violence of the Circumcellions after the emperors’ laws against the Donatists.

**LXXXIX**, to Festus, teaching that the Donatists are rightly restrained by the laws and arguing against those who rebaptize.

**XCIII**, to Vincentius the Rogatist, refuting his letter and explaining that Augustine had once thought that one should proceed against heretics not by force but by the word of God and reason; but, overcome by the judgments and examples of others, had changed his view and now believed that the laws of the rulers were rightly invoked against enemies of the faith. He also adds much else against the Donatists’ obstinacy and their rebaptism.

**XCVII**, to Olympius, urging him to uphold the laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics.

**C**, to Donatus the proconsul, urging him to restrain the Donatists, not kill them.

**CV**, to the Donatists, urging them to come to unity. It shows that the emperors had enacted laws against them justly and necessarily; that the holiness of Baptism does not depend on the merit of the human minister; that the Catholic Church is recognized in the Scriptures; and finally, that the wicked found within it ought to be tolerated.

[Col. 0758]

**CVI**, to Macrobius, urging him not to rebaptize a Catholic subdeacon.

**CVII**, in which Theodorus and Maximus report to Augustine what Macrobius had answered them in person concerning Augustine’s letter.

**CVIII**, to Macrobius, concerning the non-repetition of Baptism. It refutes the Donatists’ obstinacy on this matter, since they had acknowledged the Baptism of the Maximianists as valid; and it subsequently proves that they had no just cause for producing a schism.

**CXI**, to the presbyter Victorianus, concerning the brigandage and cruelty of the Circumcellions.

**CXII**, to Donatus the former proconsul, urging him to attract his people to communion with the Catholic Church.

**CXXVIII**, written to Marcellinus in the name of the Catholic bishops, replying to his edict prescribing the conditions for the conference to be held at Carthage.

**CXXIX**, to the same man, in which the Catholic bishops reply to the Donatists’ *Notoria*.

**CXXXIII**, to the same man, urging him to punish the Donatists who had confessed atrocious crimes in the inquiry, but without capital punishment, as accords with the Church’s gentleness.

**CXXXIV**, to Apringius the proconsul, making the same request and warning him to punish more mildly the Circumcellions who had confessed atrocious crimes.

**CXXXIX**, to Marcellinus, urging that the proceedings conducted against the Donatists be published and that those convicted be punished more mildly and without the penalty of death.

**CXLI**, to lay Donatists, explaining how their bishops had been convicted at the Conference of Carthage.

**CXLII**, to Saturninus and Eufratus, presbyters, and other clergy, congratulating them on their return to the Church.

**CXLIV**, congratulating the people of Cirta who had been converted to fellowship with the Catholic Church.

**CLXXIII**, to Donatus of Mutugena, a Donatist presbyter who, after being ordered to be seized and brought to the Church, attempted to do violence to himself; urging him to come to his senses.

**CLXXXV**, to Boniface the count, concerning the correction of the Donatists.

**CCIV**, to Dulcitius the tribune and notary, executor of the imperial orders against the Donatists, showing the madness of the schismatics who, rather than be corrected by the laws, voluntarily inflicted death upon themselves.

## APPENDIX TO THE NINTH VOLUME OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, IN WHICH IS PRESENTED A BOOK AGAINST FULGENTIUS THE DONATIST BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR, TOGETHER WITH EXCERPTS AND ANCIENT WRITINGS RELATING TO THE HISTORY OF THE DONATISTS, WHOSE READING SHEDS LIGHT ON AUGUSTINE’S EARLIER BOOKS AGAINST THESE SAME HERETICS

[Note: [Col. 0759] We compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

[Col. 0759]

## CENSURE OF THE LOUVAIN THEOLOGIANS AND BERNARD VINDINGIUS ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK

It is absolutely certain that this book is not Augustine’s. To pass over the fact that it receives no mention in the *Retractions*, it certainly bears no trace whatsoever of Augustine’s intellect, learning, or eloquence.

In the first place, shortly after its beginning, it says that the whole argument of the opponent is divided into three parts, which it proposes to treat and refute in order: concerning one Baptism; concerning the sealed fountain of the one garden; and concerning the one oil which dying flies destroy.

This is plainly a most inept division, unworthy of Augustine, as though something both remained and were lacking in a matter governed by the laws of dialectic.

For those three matters ought to have been reduced to the single heading of the one Baptism. Yet this division says nothing about the contagion of the wicked, the mingling of the good and wicked in the Church, persecution, the handing over of the sacred books, the case of Caecilianus, or, finally, the complaint about the imperial edicts—although all these matters are discussed in this book of Fulgentius and are the very subjects of the Donatist controversy, which Augustine repeatedly treated.

But how variously and confusedly it handles those first two subjects, which it discusses through twenty entire chapters!

At the end of chapter 10, while discussing Baptism, it suddenly introduces, by way of anticipation, a discussion of the contagion of the wicked; then, immediately abandoning it, returns to Baptism. From there it again goes back to the second argument, only to fall once more into the question of Baptism, and so on.

Moreover, how entirely the composition and structure of the work lack solid substance! How entirely they lack sap and blood! How entirely they lack life and spirit! Certainly, nothing is worthy of Augustine’s doctrine, genius, or abundance.

[Col. 0761] What of the fact that, in citing and discussing the Scriptures, he differs and varies from Augustine in more than one place? First, in chapter 16 (unless our manuscript is defective), he adduces a passage from Isaiah 65 according to the Vulgate reading, although Augustine always uses the edition of the Seventy, even in that very passage, and so forth. Moreover, in Jeremiah 17, “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth,” he seems in chapter 3 to have read, “Those who depart from you shall be written in the book of death”—a reading which, I think, no one among the ancients besides Blessed Augustine ever cited. Those are indeed the Donatist’s words, but he should at least have briefly warned us, as he does in chapter 2, that the Prophet did not speak in that way. Augustine certainly always does this. Similar is the fact that, when the Donatist in chapter 5 names Ezekiel instead of Isaiah, this author does not correct him even with a word—something which, as I think, Augustine would never, here as elsewhere, have passed over in silence. Finally, in chapter 18 two testimonies of David are brought forward with the number of the Psalm added, an example of which I do not know whether it can be found in Augustine.

Nor does he entirely agree with Augustine in expounding the Scriptures. In chapter 9, when preparing to answer the passage from Psalm 140, “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head,” as though he were still uncertain about its true meaning, he says that he would prefer to hear the interpreters from above [Note: [Col. 0761] See the note attached to this passage for how, according to Morel, it should be read. M.]. But Augustine, in *Against Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 103; book 3, chapter 33; and *Against Cresconius*, book 2, chapter 24, says that the meaning is perfectly plain and clear. In chapter 12, regarding the passage once cited by Cyprian too, in book 1, letter 12, “Keep away from foreign water,” he says—not incorrectly—that it was spoken about conjugal chastity, but nevertheless differently from Augustine, who here understands it as a doctrine of the evil spirit, in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 26, and *Against the Donatists*, book 6, chapter 12. In chapter 2, wishing to prove that the circumcision of the Samaritans prefigured the Baptism administered among the Donatists, he twists to this purpose the passage in Colossians 2, which unquestionably speaks of circumcision and Baptism in general, and of their legitimate reception; Augustine interprets it in the same way in *Against Julian*, book 6, chapter 7. Finally, in chapter 4, when the Donatist had cited Jeremiah 15 concerning deceitful water, which has no faith, this author gives no answer at all. Augustine, however, does not act in this way: whenever such statements occur among the words of his opponents, he never allows them to pass without an answer, as in *Against the Donatists*, book 3, chapter 15; *Against Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 103; *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 23; and elsewhere.

There are also certain features foreign to Augustine’s custom and manner of speaking. First, in chapter 1, while indicating rather clearly that he regards this Fulgentius with suspicion, as though he doubted that he was the author of the transmitted pamphlet, he nevertheless in that same place attributes religion to him—something Augustine notes in Gaudentius, in book 1, chapter 2, and book 2, chapters 11 and 12. In the same place he attributes to him praise for the expansiveness of his intellect, although certainly none of that appears here. He recognizes such strength and power in his arguments that, he says, truth itself might seem to be overcome by them; yet in his own books Augustine often laughs at and despises those arguments as empty and feeble. In chapter 3 he says that many baptize contrary to the rule of the law that was given, whereas Augustine, in *Against the Donatists*, book 6, chapter 25, says that it is easier to find heretics who do not baptize at all than those who do not use the words prescribed by Christ. Indeed, in chapter 4 he seems to contradict himself: “Although all heretics disagree among themselves in their disputation, they nevertheless agree in the solemn wording of the administration of Baptism.” In chapter 2 he calls it the Donatists’ Baptism, something Augustine says should not be called that—among other places, in *Against Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 37. He never calls it so without immediately adding this or a similar correction: “rather, not yours but Christ’s.” In chapter 10 he says, “It is certain that God rejects and despises the holocausts of priest and people if a good conscience is not present.” I do not know whether this can be found anywhere in Augustine, who teaches that one must carefully distinguish between the sacrifice as a sacred thing and the fault of those who offer it. In chapter 1 he says, “Let us condemn the obstinate with an anathema, so that we may be able to remain victorious to this point.” When does Augustine ever speak so harshly? In chapter 17, in answer to the Donatists’ accusations, he sets his own conscience against them and says that it is fortified. Augustine sometimes does this too, as in *Against Petilianus*, book 3, chapters 2 and 10, and *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 80; but with what modesty and reverence! In chapter 22 he cites the *Acts* of Marcellinus. Augustine, however, always says of these: “In our conference, which we held with you or with them,” as in *The Book after the Conference*, *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, *Against Gaudentius*, and elsewhere more than a hundred times.

As for style, although in some places, where he has imitated Augustine, he may appear to agree with him, the work itself loudly proclaims that it is far removed from the elegance of Augustine’s diction. To mention only a few examples: in chapter 1 he uses the verb *admiror* in the sense of “I understand,” “I grasp,” or “I comprehend.” In the same place he says, “You have taken up so strong a barrier.” Again, “Let us compel them to take refuge in the house.” In chapter 2 he says, “You resemble him in every respect,” where he should have said, “Be likened to him.” In chapter 9 he says, “I prefer the interpreters from above,” instead of what should have been said: “I would prefer here to hear the interpretation of others” [Note: [Col. 0761] See the note attached to this passage for the reading that Morel considers preferable. M.]. In chapter 16 he uses *pessimatur* for “becomes utterly bad.” In chapter 24 he says, “so that you had driven them from their basilicas,” where he should have said, “so that you might drive them out.” When did Augustine ever stammer in this way?

From what we have said, therefore, I think it is abundantly clear that this book is not Augustine’s, but is altogether unworthy of him. Nevertheless, whoever its author was, he must have been ancient, since he saw that Council of Carthage held against Caecilianus and, in the final chapter, cited from it the judgment of Marcianus, which nowhere appears in Augustine. For that reason alone, I consider the book worthy of retaining its place. He also appears to have been an African, for he delights in the *homoeteleuton*—the repetition of similar word-endings—customary among that people, as in chapter 9: “A merciful rebuke is better than gentle flattery”; and again, “The oil of the sinner is the flatterer’s blandishment.” In chapter 12: “Who would not see that the prophet commended chastity to married couples, and that you have wandered far from the truth?” He also uses infinitives in place of nouns, as in chapter 13: “O to prove! O to err! O to rave!”—a usage not unfamiliar either to Optatus or to Augustine. The whole speech of the Donatist, or Fulgentius, has the flavor of African Latin and seems redolent of Augustine’s age; it is not very far removed from Petilianus’s style. Thus far the Louvain scholars.

Bernard Vindingus confirms the preceding judgment in his *Augustinian Critic* and adds the following signs of spuriousness (*νοθείας*) that he himself observed. In chapter 2, the author says that the Donatists fear God and observe the divine law. In chapter 12, he says that Silvanus of Cirta handed over the Sacraments to Felix the curator. Yet Silvanus had handed over only a silver vessel and a silver lamp, as is read in *Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 29, and book 4, chapter 56, and below in the proceedings before Zenophilus the consul. In chapter 23, he says that Ananias and Sapphira were killed by Peter. Augustine, however, writes in letter 44, section 10, that it cannot be shown from the New Testament that any righteous person killed anyone. What he adds about Simon Magus having been killed he drew from apocryphal books; Augustine would not have wished to rely on their authority against an opponent, as is clear from *Against Faustus*, book 13, chapter 9. Moreover, in chapter 26 he reproaches the Donatists for transgressing the commandment of the elders by establishing their own traditions. Augustine would instead have opposed to them the very words of Christ, Matthew 15:3: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” Finally, Vindingus places this book among the minor works believed to have been fabricated by Vigilius of Thapsus.

[Col. 0763]

# A BOOK AGAINST FULGENTIUS THE DONATIST, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER ONE

I did not disdain to receive the little book that your Religiousness, brother Fulgentius, sent to me. Whether you yourself composed it, or sought it elsewhere, I do not sufficiently understand. For it is also a duty of our religion not to fix attention on persons, but to seek the truth in all things, to acknowledge it when found, and to preserve it once acknowledged. Thus the Apostle Paul says: “Test everything; hold fast what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil” (1 Thess. 5:21–22).

I shall therefore briefly say what you have elaborated at greater length in writing. You said that there is one Baptism, which the Samaritan—that is, the heretic—was not worthy to possess; one enclosed garden, which is the Church, possessing a sealed fountain from which no outsider draws; one oil, which is the most holy chrism, which dying flies corrupt and which sinners will not impart at all.

Against these claims I must prepare an answer with the Lord’s help, drawing it from nowhere except divine reading. Let us therefore now take up the beginning of the Word—or rather, let us hold fast the Word himself as the beginning, Jesus the Lord, the leader and commander of the heavenly army. Let us wage war and, with his consecrated hand, sound the trumpet against the strongest walls of the impious city of Jericho. That is, let us surround the height of worldly wisdom with the Lord’s Testaments and resound with voices of truth and freedom. Let us compel our adversaries to take refuge in the house of Rahab—that is, in the Church, which received his messengers—because of the destruction of the world. Let us condemn the obstinate with an anathema, so that we may be able to remain victorious to this point.

Thus, against the Law from the Law, against God’s Testament from God’s Testament, and against the fountain of truth from the fountain of truth, you have at the outset taken up such a strong barrier, as though truth could be overcome by itself or the glory of light be darkened by its own radiance.

## CHAPTER TWO

**THE DONATIST SAID:** The Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, teacher and guardian of the one Baptism, proclaimed in his Gospel that there are perpetual draughts for thirsty souls, lest error lead them away through the dry channels of the mind, and testified as follows: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink; the one who believes in me, as Isaiah says.”

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** It does not say, “as Isaiah says,” but, “as Scripture says.” But I shall disregard these obstacles, lest by a lengthy speech I exclude the reader’s benefit.

**THE DONATIST SAID:** “The one who believes in me, as Isaiah says, from his belly will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:37–38). And lest it be said that one could drink everywhere and indiscriminately, he himself distinguished the qualities of the waters when he condemned the origin of Samaria’s apostasy in its own fountain. “The one who drinks from this water,” he says, “will thirst again; but the one who drinks from the water that I shall give will never thirst, but it will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** You certainly set these things down in order to show that we Catholics are, as it were, Samaritans and without Baptism. Begin, then, to discern the Donatists in the Samaritans. The teaching of the Samaritans, as the Third Book of Kings relates, was this: “They feared God and at the same time worshiped idols; they observed the divine law and did not at all abandon the errors of their fathers; they possessed the sign of circumcision and did not maintain fellowship with the Israelites” (3 Kings 12 and 13).

This is what you also do: you fear God and at the same time worship the earthen image of Donatus. For he too was fashioned from the dust of the earth. You observe the divine law and do not abandon the error of your fathers; you possess the sacrament of Baptism and do not wish to have fellowship with Catholics. Behold, you resemble them in every respect.

Therefore, just as the circumcision of the Samaritans could not then be given a second time, so now the Baptism of the Donatists ought not to be repeated, since the Lord Christ says: “The one who has been washed once has no need to wash again” (John 13:10).

The circumcision of the Samaritans signifies the Baptism of the Donatists, as the Apostle says: “You were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in Baptism” (Col. 2:11–12).

But when the Lord says, “The one who drinks from this water will thirst again,” he was speaking not of Baptism but of an earthly element. For if he wished to indicate Baptism here, he would in no way have asked it of the Samaritan woman. Finally, that well was called not the well of Samaria but Jacob’s; and Jacob certainly was not a heretic, but beloved of God, always dear to him. He himself drank from it, as did his sons and his cattle.

## CHAPTER THREE

**THE DONATIST SAID:** The spirit of the Church never permits things to be joined which, by divine utterance, deserved to be publicly condemned, since the proclamation of the Law gives prior warning: “Two against two, one against one” (Sirach 33:15). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one left; two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left” (Matt. 24:40–41).

You see, therefore, that there are two kinds of Baptism and two rewards corresponding to merit: one, which the ardor of a deadly disposition burns up and the perpetual draughts of thirsty longing boil dry; the other, which by the channels through which it is drunk once establishes the perpetuity of life, and which, in excavated pools, displays perpetual dryness, and, while piously closing its merit, opens the entrance to death. Jeremiah says: “This people has committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

And again: “All who abandon you will be confounded; those who depart from you will be written in the book of death, because they have abandoned you, the fountain of life” (Jer. 17:13).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** You assert one against one; I assert many Baptisms against one. For the pagan baptizes, and the Jew baptizes, and the Sadducee baptizes, and many do not cease baptizing contrary to the rule of the law that was given. But that is the one Baptism which is true; that is true which belongs to Christ; and that belongs to Christ which is of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is the true and saving Baptism, and none can be compared with it. Whoever does not receive it has closed for himself the reward of life and opened the entrance to death.

## CHAPTER FOUR

**THE DONATIST SAID:** But if, as you assert, one faith exists in both, why did the Lord distinguish faithful water from faithless water by a just separation, testifying through Isaiah:

“Who told you that the fire burns? Who told you of that eternal place? The one who walks in righteousness, proclaims the straight way, hates crime and injustice, abstains from accepting gifts, and makes his ear heavy so that he does not hear a judgment of bloodshed, and closes his eyes so that they do not see iniquity—this one will dwell in a lofty hope. Strong bread will be given to him, and his water will be faithful” (Isa. 33:14–16).

Separating faithlessness from its faith, as Jeremiah testifies, he says:

“Why do those who wrong me prevail? My wound has become solid; from where shall I be healed? It has become for me like deceitful water that has no faith” (Jer. 15:18).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Although all heretics disagree among themselves in their disputation, they nevertheless agree in the solemn wording of the administration of Baptism, just as one circumcision, though with differing faith, existed among the Jews and the ancient Samaritans.

Therefore, just as then, so now it is necessary that the converted should receive what they ought to receive: what is sought through disputation alone must likewise be resolved through disputation alone, so that they may hear from the Lord: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you; remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:3).

For all these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11).

## CHAPTER FIVE

**THE DONATIST SAID:** Ezekiel also said:

“And they will see that there are many who have turned away from the water of the ancient pool and have not looked toward the one who made it from the beginning, and they have not seen the one who founded it” (Isa. 22, according to the Seventy).

The madness of the faithless is unheard-of: they neither wish to believe the divine utterances nor to preserve the Apostle’s simple teaching within the jaws of their error.

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Far be it, far be it from us to assign the water of the ancient pool to a faction, as you do, or not to believe the divine utterances. What we read, we believe; and what we believe, we preach.

Hear what our origin is and where its water has been spread. In Zechariah you find this:

“Living waters will go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the western sea”—that is, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth—“in summer and winter they will be”—that is, they will exist at every time. “And the Lord will be king over all the earth” (Zech. 14:8–9).

That is, Christ will rule over the whole earth, not Donatus. This is Christ’s possession; this is his inheritance, which is honored by the saints and watered by an everlasting fountain. Of it he was told: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

Whoever is in it is enrolled as an heir; whoever is not in it is already condemned and destined for death, since Scripture says: “Whoever goes outside the doors of your house will be guilty before himself” (Exod. 12).

## CHAPTER SIX

**THE DONATIST SAID:** Hence God proclaims that there is one Baptism; hence the Apostle confirms that he has said one to all, with God proving it through Solomon:

“An enclosed garden, my sister, my bride, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apple trees” (Song 4:12–13).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Remember, read everything, pay close attention, and see that from this paradise, from this enclosed garden, from this sealed fountain, even outside salvation’s water flows—water that goes against the Assyrians, that is, against you Donatists.

For those Samaritans who are compared with you arise from the Assyrians. “It is the river,” says Scripture, “that goes against the Assyrians” (Gen. 2:14)—against the people hostile to God; it does not go for them but against them.

“For some we are an odor of death unto death, but for others an odor of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:16). Just as the one who eats and drinks the Lord’s blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11:29), so the one who receives Baptism unworthily receives judgment, not salvation.

For Judas the traitor received the good body, and Simon Magus received Christ’s good Baptism; but because they did not use good things well, they were destroyed by using them badly. Baptism is good, the blood and body of Christ are good, and the law is good—provided that someone uses them lawfully (1 Tim. 1:8).

Nor, because something is outside, is it therefore not divine; nor, because it is held by outsiders, will it be considered alien; nor, because it is handled unjustly by the wicked, will it be justly condemned by us.

The water of paradise is the water of the Trinity. When we recognize it as paradise’s water, we do not deny it; when we do not discern it there, we do not call it paradise’s water at all. Whatever has arisen outside cannot in any way be called paradise’s water. For example, the Manichaean, because he was never in paradise and did not go out of the Church as you did, must be judged not to have paradise’s water, since he arose outside [Note: [Col. 0766] According to Morel, this should read *putandus est* (“must be judged”), rather than *potandus est* (“must be given to drink”). See *Elementa Critica*, pp. 167–168. M.].

He needs this water in order to live and not die eternally; but in order to live lawfully, he must live within it, lest he eat and drink judgment.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** On the contrary, the Apostle testifies that he said: “One God, one faith, one Baptism” (Eph. 4:5). In every respect the servant follows the Lord; the disciple differs in nothing from the Master. Whom do you follow? Whom do you imitate? Whom do you consider the author of this crime?

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Show me one of the saints rebaptizing after the Trinity—the very thing you do. Read to me, not those Scriptures whose authority does not bind me, but the New and Old Testaments, to which both of us are subject.

If there is one Baptism, why do you duplicate the one? For you do not repeat anything other than what you find to be true. Since, therefore, you rebuild the things that you destroyed, you show yourselves to be transgressors.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

**THE DONATIST SAID:** Or if you think that the sacrament of Baptism is joined by some mixture to the guilty, hear the Prophets, by whom it was rightly administered. Solomon says: “The fountain of life is in the hand of the righteous” (Prov. 10, according to the Seventy).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** The Lord spoke well of you, foreseeing your error: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16:15).

If you are righteous and the fountain of life is in your hand, then you are not a man but God. Let people flee to you, believe in you, and place every hope of life in you; let Baptism itself be administered in your name, and let us say nothing about the Lord.

Do you wish to know where you should seek this fountain of life? You find it in the Psalm: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10).

Have you not read: “The evil son has proud eyes; the evil son calls himself righteous, but he will not wash away his own deeds” (Prov. 24, according to the Seventy)?

Unless you recognize yourself as guilty like any human being, unless you call yourself a sinner with a truthful heart, you cannot be justified at all, since the Prophet says: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

And the Apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

[Col. 0767]

## CHAPTER NINE

**THE DONATIST SAID:** David also says: “But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.”

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Then name for me one of your people whom you can prove not to be a sinner, so that your oil cannot be the oil of a sinner, since it is written: “There is no human being who does not sin” (Eccl. 7:21).

“I prefer the interpreters from above.” Read, so that you may be able to receive the meaning [Note: [Col. 0767] According to Morel, this should be read: “The interpreter is wrong; read above, so that you may be able to receive the meaning.” See *Elementa Critica*, pp. 164–165. Ms.].

He says: “The righteous will rebuke me in mercy and will correct me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5). That is: “A merciful rebuke is better than gentle flattery,” just as it is said: “The wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 17:6).

The oil of the sinner is the flatterer’s blandishment, of which he says elsewhere: “His words are smoother than oil, yet they are arrows” (Ps. 54:22).

The oil of the righteous is the Spirit of God, as Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38).

Therefore, stop calling the Holy Spirit the oil of a sinner, lest you begin to assert that God is a sinner.

## CHAPTER TEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** An open confession of the faithless is shown in this passage: what is touched by the hostile presumption of a criminal priest is polluted, and his sacrifice is rejected by the divine voice as though it were oil. “The criminal who sacrifices to me,” he says, “is like one who kills a dog; and the one who offers fine flour is like one who offers swine’s blood; and the one who offers incense as a memorial is like a blasphemer” (Isa. 66:3).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** It is certain that God rejects and despises the holocausts of priest and people if a good conscience is not present.

Or if you wish this to be understood as spoken only about priests, how is the consecration performed by criminal priests not polluted among you? You say: “As long as the wicked remain hidden, they cannot pollute,” on account of what is written: “The hidden things belong to me; the manifest things belong to you” (Deut. 29:29).

If, therefore, as long as the wicked remain hidden they cannot pollute, why are you not afraid to rebaptize distant nations for whom the names of Donatus and Caecilianus are unknown? Which of you has ever brought the sins of any of them to their knowledge? And even if he had brought them to their knowledge and had not proved them, it would have done no harm at all, in accordance with the saying: “The hidden things belong to me; the manifest things belong to you.”

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** The Prophet further reveals, by the Spirit, that his waters are turbid: “You placed your horses in the sea,” he says, “disturbing many waters” (Hab. 3:15). “The city of Gilead despised me, which practices foolishness and troubles the waters; and your strength is like that of a pirate” (Hos. 6:8–9).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Recognize that your own weapons have been turned against you, as it is written: “Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bows be broken” (Ps. 36:15).

Your strength, Donatist, is like that of a pirate: by force you rebaptize, by force you fight in the water, and by force you kill in the water. While carrying on these pirate deeds, you will be captured and killed unless you turn and repent, and serve as a soldier under Christ the King in the Catholic Church.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

**THE DONATIST SAID:** If, therefore, the Church boasts of one fountain, it is surely the den of traitors, which is exalted in the multitude of waters and, confused by the drunkenness of its Baptism, fornicates with kings. John says:

“Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute who sits upon many waters, and all those dwelling on earth became drunk from the wine of her fornication” (Rev. 17:1).

I ask: what are the many waters if not multiple Baptisms? What is the fornicating woman if not the den of traitors, which submits itself to the pleasures of kings, drinking from them the cup of persecutions, mixing it for the peoples in drunken blindness, and leading those whom it has watered into madness?

The most wise Solomon forbade access to her:

“Keep away from foreign water,” he says, “and do not drink from a foreign fountain, so that you may live for a long time and the years of your life may be increased” (Prov. 9, according to the Seventy). “Let the fountain of your water be private to you, and let no stranger share it with you” (Prov. 5:16–17).

Therefore, only the one who possesses the multitude of the prostitute’s waters does not have a private fountain. The Apostle John also condemns the multitude of waters, saying:

“And the angel said to me, ‘The waters that you saw, upon which the prostitute sits, are peoples, crowds, and nations’” (Rev. 17:15).

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** As I see it, wherever water is mentioned negatively, you have believed that Baptism is meant positively [Note: [Col. 0768] Perhaps: “or positively.”]. But you wished to assign it positively to yourselves and negatively to me, so that what the Apostle Paul said might be fulfilled concerning you: “Understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1:7).

Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these people resist the truth (2 Tim. 3:8). The angel says: “The waters that you saw are peoples, crowds, and nations.” Yet you resist the angel explaining the matter and say: “I ask: what are the many waters if not multiple Baptisms? What is the fornicating woman if not the den of traitors?”

If you wish to learn the names of the traitors, you have your own men: Silvanus of Cirta handing over the Sacraments to Felix the curator; Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae offering three codices to the curator Romanus; Victor of Rusiccade burning four Gospels as though they had been erased. These men dared to condemn the absent and innocent Caecilianus.

This is the den of robbers; this is the offspring of traitors; this is the fornicating woman who, having abandoned Christ, prostitutes brothels to Donatus. Her house, according to Solomon, is a retreat of death, and her ways lead to the underworld (Prov. 7:27). She calls herself clean though she is full of filth; she proclaims herself innocent though she is entangled in crimes; she commits shameful deeds and attributes her own acts to another, lest she first hear what she herself has committed.

For you defame Catholics on account of your own deeds, so that you may separate peoples from the Lord. Therefore, when you urge your people—as though they were your own—to abstain from our water, saying, “Keep away from foreign water, and do not drink from a foreign fountain; let the fountain of your water be private to you, and let no stranger share it,” who would not see that the Prophet commended chastity to married couples, and that you have wandered far from the truth?

Or if no stranger ought to share your fountain, why do you seek strangers? Why do you rebaptize Catholics?

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** It is therefore clear that among the traitors there is a multitude of waters: there are the various seeds of schisms, the manifold plagues of heretics, the detestable filth and dregs of the Manichaeans; or, having been carried away into the abyss of a muddy whirlpool, the whirlpool of destruction saw them in eternal death and set the oil of destruction aflame with devouring fires [Note: [Col. 0768] Perhaps: “where.”] [Note: [Col. 0768] Perhaps: “having been carried away.”].

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** O proving! O erring! O raving!

It is therefore clear that among the traitors there is a multitude of waters: there are the various seeds of schisms, the manifold plagues of heretics, and the detestable filth and dregs of the Manichaeans. How do you prove that the manifold plagues of schismatics are with us? If they were with us, they would not be heretics but Catholics.

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** Solomon teaches this when he says: “Dying flies destroy the sweetness of the perfume” (Eccl. 10:1). The oil therefore possesses an innate sweetness which, if violated by an improper touch, becomes polluted by an offensive admixture. And rightly you equate the traitors with unclean birds, because they fall improperly upon another’s table and defile the sweetness of the oil with unclean touches.

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Who violates it by an improper touch—the one who preserves what he found, or the one who shamelessly destroys what has been prepared? When did we touch your oil? When did we drive away the Holy Spirit by insulting him? Show that one of our people improperly fell upon the oil of the divinity, or unlawfully violated the Baptism of the Trinity, as you do.

The dying flies, the Donatists, fly around the members of the whole body. Wherever they find something wounded, they sting what is healthy, lick what is diseased, and pour worms of sins into their sores [Note: [Col. 0768] Perhaps: “infuse.”]—worms that bite the conscience, destroy the soul, nourish corruption, and spare not even corpses after death [Col. 0769].

When dying flies destroy the oil, they are themselves killed by the oil. For you are not alive, since you breathe out the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** The most holy David, supplying the rule of our faith, teaches this explicitly: the sinner’s oil brings no salvation and ought to touch no one’s head. “Let not the oil of the sinner,” he says, “anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5).

Therefore the person of the sinner must be sought out by careful examination, if the Lord did not speak about a sacrilegious priest, as the profane assert.

**THE CATHOLIC REPLIED:** Although you are conscious of sin, you dare to say, “The person of the sinner must be sought out.” Hear what this person of the sinner is.

The Apostle said: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Solomon said: “There is no human being who does not sin” (Eccl. 7:21). Job said: “He found perversity even in his angels; how much more in the sons of men, who have an earthly dwelling” (Job 4:18–19)?

This is the person of the sinner: every human being is a sinner. If you are a priest, you are a human being; and if you are a human being, you are a sinner. What are you making yourself?

You said that you alone are holy, alone righteous, alone without sin, alone without stain. You said that the Baptism is yours, that the holy oil is yours, that the Lord’s table is yours, and that all those things divinely bestowed upon the faithful are yours. What remains except for you wickedly and impiously to declare that you are God?

But hear what the head of pride deserved to hear:

“How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn, who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: ‘I will ascend above heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of God; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will be like the Most High.’ Nevertheless, you will descend into hell and into the depth of the pit” (Isa. 14:12–15).

Unless you repent, unless you turn back, unless you lay aside your pride and ask forgiveness for your sins, you will hear what he heard, because although you are a human being, you make yourself God.

## CHAPTER SIXTEEN

**THE DONATIST SAID:** Likewise, the Lord, through the prophet Haggai, showed by a salutary interpretation that unclean touches confer pollution and that no polluted person can sanctify another, if by unlawful presumption he tries to touch what he sees to contain something holy. He presented the Prophet as a warning for our sake.

“The Lord says,” he says, “ask the priests: If a man binds holy flesh in the fold of a garment, and the edge of the garment touches any food, or wine, or oil, is it sanctified?” The priests answered and said: “No.” And the Lord said: “If one polluted in soul touches any of these things, will it be polluted?” And the priests said: “It will be polluted.” And the Lord said: “So is this people, and so is this nation: everyone who approaches it will be polluted” (Hag. 2:12–15).

CATHOLIC replied: You have used this testimony against yourself, since you place God’s gift under your own control. For if contact with what is holy does not remove the defilements of the unclean, then what you perform, what you consecrate, and what you wash are futile. “If,” he says, “it touches what is holy—the substance of bread, wine, or oil—will it be sanctified?” And the priests answered and said: “No.” Where, then, is what you boast of, what you claim that your holiness confers as purity? Or, if you are moved by what he says, “So is this people, and so is this nation: everyone who approaches it will be defiled,” teach Haggai, who said these things, to have gone out from the midst of that same people, lest he himself also be defiled among them.

That contact signifies works. “If,” he says, “one who is holy touches the unclean, he will not be sanctified; if one who is unclean touches what is holy, he will be defiled.” That is: a holy person joined to this most wicked nation is more easily corrupted than this nation is changed for the better, because the mind runs more readily toward imitating the wicked than it is stirred toward the virtues of the good. It is like a small amount of wormwood thrown into a great quantity of honey: it quickly takes on bitterness; but even if twice as much honey is added, its sweetness cannot be recovered.

Therefore we must depart from the midst of the wicked in mind, not in flesh; in works, [Col. 0770] not in bodies. “Do not,” says the Apostle, “participate in the unfruitful works of darkness” (Eph. V, 11): he says “works,” not “altars.” For it is written in Isaiah: “Those who say, ‘Withdraw from me; do not come near me, for you are unclean,’ these shall be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day long” (Isa. LXV, 5). If human words do not frighten you, at least let the anger of God who threatens turn you back.

## CHAPTER XVII

DONATIST said: No robber ever brought his plunder into the light; the workers of night have always, and repeatedly, dreaded the light that is pleasing to all good people. The traitor alone is not broken even by God’s threats, and in another’s garment he glories. Against him the Lord cries out through Zephaniah, though he is not heard: “It shall be on the day of the Lord’s sacrifice: I will punish the princes and all those clothed in a foreign garment” (Zeph. I, 8).

CATHOLIC replied: I do not fear your accusations, because my conscience is fortified. Show the name and place of the traitor whom you say betrayed. You will never be able to show it, just as previously you were unable. But even if you produce someone, he cannot harm me, since the Lord says: “The soul of the father is mine; the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall die alone” (Ezek. XVIII, 4).

Yet I do not rejoice in another’s garment, for I always rejoice in the Catholic faith. That is the garment I possess, in which the merciful and kind Father clothed me in splendor on the day of redemption. “Bring,” he says, “the first robe and clothe him in it, because this son of mine was dead and came to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 22, 24). It is that robe of which the Apostle Paul said: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27). I possess this robe; in it I rejoice; in it I shall always appear more glorious. This is the robe which you have either carried off like robbers or, wretched men, soiled.

## CHAPTER XVIII
