DONATIST said: Since wickedness, insofar as it desires to support deviant errors by means of the possessions of others and attempts to cover falsehood with the clouds of a lying “Catholic” name, proceeds along winding hills, the Lord met it through Jeremiah as an opponent: “Do not trust,” he says, “in yourselves, in lying words, for they will in no way profit you when you say, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord’” (Jer. VII, 4). And the Lord says in Deuteronomy: “Take heed lest you offer burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe, there you shall offer burnt offerings, and there you shall do everything that I command you today” (Deut. XII, 13–14).

CATHOLIC replied: You have brought forward a testimony that is excellent and highly appropriate to your salvation: “Take heed lest you offer burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe, there you shall offer burnt offerings, and there you shall do everything that he will command you.” Hear, then, what place was chosen and which tribe of the Lord was proclaimed.

In Psalm 131 you have: “For the Lord chose Zion; he chose it as his dwelling. This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I chose it.” Likewise in Psalm 121: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city. For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel.”

This is the chosen place; this is the sanctified mountain; this is the city set upon a mountain, so that it cannot be hidden; this is the Catholic root; this is the fruitful vine spread far and wide, which cries out and says in Ecclesiasticus: “I was founded in Zion, and my power is in Jerusalem” (Ecclus. XXIV, 15).

For “it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV, 46–47).

You would rightly accuse me if you remained in this inheritance. But since you do not remain in this inheritance of God the Father, and do not serve in this tribe of Christ the King, why does a deserter rebuke a soldier? Why does a guilty man reproach the innocent?

And I say to you: “Take heed lest you offer in every place”—that is, in every heresy—and say, “God is here, and God is there.” Rather, in the place which the Lord your God will choose in your tribe—that is, in his tribe—[Col. 0771] there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do everything that has been commanded you. Do this, and you shall live.

## CHAPTER XIX

DONATIST said: What was scattered by a multitude of waters, what wickedness separated from the fountain of the Church, what a barren stream dried up, cannot in any way be called baptism. It neither saw an angel nor found a prophet who could heal it, just as in the Fourth Book of Kings the most holy Elisha dispelled death from deadly waters and healed them, and by a life-giving word allowed them to flow forth into abundant fertility.

“And the men of the city said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the dwelling-place of the city is good, as you yourself, lord, see; but the waters here are many and barren.’ And Elisha said: ‘Bring me one earthenware vessel, and put salt into it.’ And they took it. He came to the outlets of the waters, threw in the salt, and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.’ And the waters were healed to this day” (2 Kings II, 19–22).

CATHOLIC replied: Thanks be to God the Father, who faithfully fulfilled in us what he showed would take place. Thanks, I say, to God the Father, who sent us not only angels and prophets, as formerly to Jericho—that is, into this world—but his own Son, namely the Lord of angels and Prince of prophets. He dispelled the barrenness of the waters—that is, the fruitlessness of the nations—and healed it by destroying death.

He took an earthenware vessel, that is, the body of human frailty; he put in salt, that is, he filled it with divine wisdom; he threw it into the water, that is, he descended into the Jordan; he healed the waters by his descent, that is, he redeemed the nations by his coming; and by his life-giving word he gathered the Church from the nations and spread her far and wide into abundant fruitfulness.

Whoever does not see this fulfilled in us is blind; whoever does not believe is insane. Consider the abundant fruits: tell me where this Church is not found; tell me where yours is found, except that it has been collected badly in a corner of Africa, like a useless branch. From the point where it was cut off it remained there; it could not extend farther, because, cut off from the root, it immediately withered.

## CHAPTER XX

DONATIST said: One city received the substance of saving water; and a widow with her children received the gifts of oil. The prophet did not indiscriminately entrust the divine beneficence, but only to her whom he knew to possess a single vessel of oil, as the truth of the Book of Kings proves:

“And one woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out to Elisha, saying: ‘Your servant, my husband, is dead; and you know that your servant feared the Lord. And behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons as his slaves.’ And Elisha said: ‘What shall I do for you? Tell me: what do you have in your house?’ She said: ‘Your handmaid has nothing in the house except one vessel of oil.’ And Elisha said: ‘Go, ask vessels from outside, from all your neighbors—many vessels. Then go in, shut the door upon yourself and your sons, pour oil into all the vessels, and repay the debt’” (2 Kings IV, 1–4).

For Elisha worked through the anointing of true baptism. Since I do not approve yours, I therefore blow away your faithful.

CATHOLIC replied: Everyone does what you do: all blow away the faithful while claiming the sacrament of baptism exclusively for themselves. When you find such a person, you do not seize him, hold him, or bind him with this bond; but, recognizing the pirate’s signal, you allow him to depart safely so that he may practice his craft with you.

## CHAPTER XXI

FULGENTIUS said: Far be it from me to allow him to depart, since God said: “Compel everyone to come in, so that my house may be filled” (Luke XIV, 23). When he said “everyone,” he excluded no one.

AUGUSTINE replied: What, then, will you do?

FULGENTIUS said: I shall teach him that my church is the most certain one.

AUGUSTINE replied: On what grounds? Will you show that Christ, who received all the nations from the Father, remained only in a small part of Africa?

FULGENTIUS said: I shall say that it consists of a few.

AUGUSTINE replied: What if his church too has only a few? All have few in comparison with the Catholic Church.

FULGENTIUS said: I shall show that this is the true church which suffers persecution, not the one which inflicts it.

AUGUSTINE replied: What if it has inflicted no persecution at all?

FULGENTIUS said: I shall point out, according to the Apostle, that my church alone has neither wrinkle nor stain (Eph. V, 27).

AUGUSTINE replied: It will immediately be proved to have them. For it is written: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life upon the earth is but one day” (Job XIV, 4–5).

But why say more? By whatever stratagem you can, you will seize and hold the one who perhaps restrained your faithful, who extinguished the Holy Spirit in the heart of the believer.

## CHAPTER XXII

FULGENTIUS said: I punish him, blow him away, and baptize him with true water for the remission of sins.

AUGUSTINE replied: How do you forgive his sins, when it is written that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot be forgiven forever (Matt. XII, 32)?

But let us leave this man aside and consider another. Say also to the Maximianist, your rival, what you said to me: “How can another possess it, if it has been granted to me alone?” Or, if you assert that it has been entrusted to your authority, why do you approve what belongs to another?

This Maximianist will reply: “How can another not possess it, when you yourself have shown that it was granted to me just as to you?” For you received my Christians and clergy, baptized or ordained outside your church, without any alteration of their baptism or dignity, preserving them intact. When this was brought against you in the acts of Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0772] Namely, in the Conference.], you were entirely unable to refute it.

Again AUGUSTINE replied: If you are just, why is your judgment different? Why do you receive the Maximianists but blow away my faithful?

FULGENTIUS said: Because he was mine.

AUGUSTINE replied: And you were mine. Why are you merciful toward your schismatic and impious and implacable toward the Catholic?

## CHAPTER XXIII

FULGENTIUS said: You sinned more, and therefore a different punishment is inflicted upon you.

AUGUSTINE replied: What, then? Do you make baptism a punishment, and grant as a penalty what is promised for salvation? If in baptism you do not forgive sins but punish them; if in the water you do not liberate but scourge, you openly show yourself to be a pirate. And yet, what more did I sin? What did I do?

FULGENTIUS said: You handed over the books and sacrificed to idols.

AUGUSTINE replied: Prove it. I did not do so; you attribute your deeds to me.

FULGENTIUS said: Your father did it.

AUGUSTINE replied: I know no father except God. For it is written: “Do not call anyone your father upon earth, for one is your heavenly Father” (Matt. XXIII, 9).

FULGENTIUS said: I mean your father Caecilianus: he himself betrayed, he himself offered incense, he himself committed every evil.

AUGUSTINE replied: Read who accused him, who convicted him, and who condemned him after he had been brought before the court. Let us suppose he did what he did not do: shall a son be condemned for his father, when it is written: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall die alone” (Ezek. XVIII, 4)?

FULGENTIUS said: You are his son. You did not indeed betray, but you persecuted us.

AUGUSTINE replied: I certainly did not do so, although I believe that my people may have done it. Ask why. What if you deserved it? For it is not a sin to persecute the wicked. We read that the wicked persecuted both the saints and the Lord, the Holy One of holy ones. For the demons, unable to endure the Lord’s persecution, cried out: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come to destroy us?” (Mark I, 24).

Paul also avenged himself upon Elymas the magician with blindness (Acts XIII, 11), and handed a blasphemous man over to Satan (1 Tim. I, 20). Peter killed Ananias and his wife Sapphira for lying (Acts V, 1–10), and pursued Simon Magus until he destroyed him in death.

David, too, speaking in the person of Christ, cries out and says: “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them; I shall not turn back until they fail. I shall afflict them, and they will not be able to stand” (Ps. XVII, 38–39).

Therefore not everyone who has suffered persecution should immediately be considered righteous; rather, the one who has suffered on account of righteousness is surely blessed, as Peter says: “What glory is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, when you do good and suffer, you endure it patiently, this is grace with God” (1 Pet. II, 20).

## CHAPTER XXIV

FULGENTIUS said: The saints whom you mention did not deserve the edicts of secular judges, which your people did.

AUGUSTINE replied: Is it permitted or not? If it is permitted, it is not fitting to complain about what is permitted; if it is not permitted, correct your crime while it is permitted.

For, as the acts reveal, you persecuted your schismatic Maximianists by the authority of secular judges, with the assistance of various ranks of men [Note: [Col. 0773] Perhaps *variorum*, “of various men.”], and through the execution of different soldiers, appointing defenders of the church so that you might drive them from their basilicas.

You who rebuke me—why do you not first correct yourself?

## CHAPTER XXV

FULGENTIUS said: We took the basilicas from our schismatics so that we might return them to the true Church.

AUGUSTINE replied: Our people did the same to you: they took them from you, their schismatics, and returned them to the Catholic mother. What your people did for the peace of Donatus, our people did for the peace of the body of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVI

FULGENTIUS said: You are the schismatics, who both offered incense and handed over the books.

AUGUSTINE replied: “Let us become weak to the weak, so that we may win the weak.” I see what cannot be done: the party of Donatus has conquered the whole body of Christ; an African corner has excluded the whole world; one nation has brought all nations under condemnation [Note: [Col. 0773] Perhaps *addixit*, that is, “condemned.”]; it has cut off a branch from the vine and severed the little branches from the trees.

At least observe the laws established by your predecessors concerning us. Do not rebaptize, but, through repentance, free the souls of those who have gone astray, as you suppose.

Read again the decisions of your fathers and see what they decreed should be done with traitors, those who offered incense, and schismatics, when they had conspired against Caecilianus at Carthage.

Your Marcianus, among the others, issued the following judgment, which the seventy who were present certainly did not reject. He said:

“In his Gospel the Lord says: ‘I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will cut off and cast away; and every branch that remains in me and bears fruit, he cleanses it’” (John XV, 1–2).

Therefore, just as fruitless branches are cut off and cast away, so those who offered incense, traitors, and those ordained in schism by traitors cannot remain in the Church of God unless, having recognized their own wailing, they are reconciled through repentance.

Accordingly, one ought not to communicate with Caecilianus, who was ordained in schism by traitors. This is the fixed judgment of your fathers.

Behold—God forbid—we have betrayed, we have offered incense, we have committed schisms. Why do you transgress the command of your elders in order to establish your own traditions? “Just as,” he says, “fruitless branches are cut off and cast away, so those who offered incense, traitors, and those ordained in schism by traitors cannot remain in the Church of God unless, having recognized their own wailing, they are reconciled through repentance”: through repentance, not through immersion.

If you are willing, let your own leaders overcome you, or affirm their decrees and abandon your fabrications. Or, if you want your own statutes to prevail, declare that they were mistaken.

Among us truth reigns. Why does your tradition disagree? The Savior says in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand, but will be laid waste” (Matt. XII, 25).

[Col. 0773]

# EXCERPTS AND OLD WRITINGS PERTAINING TO THE HISTORY OF THE DONATISTS, THE READING OF WHICH SHEDS LIGHT ON AUGUSTINE’S EARLIER BOOKS AGAINST THE SAME HERETICS

## ORIGIN OF THE DONATIAN SCHISM

[Note: [Col. 0773] From Optatus, Book 1, collated and corrected against the old Germanensis manuscript.]

First, hear who the traitors were, and learn more fully the authors of the schism. It is agreed that two evil and most wicked deeds were committed in Africa: one in the betrayal, the other in the schism. Yet both evils appear to have been committed at the same time and by the same authors.

Therefore, brother Parmenianus, you must learn what you are understood to be ignorant of. For nearly sixty years ago and more, a storm of persecution spread throughout Africa. It made some martyrs, others confessors; it struck some down in a fatal death [Note: [Col. 0773] The old Germanensis manuscript reads: “it struck down a deadly [thing] unto death.”], and left those who were hiding unharmed.

Why should I mention the laypeople, who at that time held no office supported by any dignity [Note: [Col. 0773] The word “supported” is absent from the Germanensis manuscript]? Why mention the many ministers? Why the deacons in the third rank? Why the presbyters established in the second priestly office?

The very highest and leaders of all, certain bishops of that time, in order to purchase, at the cost of eternal life, the very brief delays of this uncertain light, wickedly handed over the instruments of the divine law.

Among them were Donatus of Masculiana, Victor of Rusiccade, Marinus of Aquae-Tibilitanae, Donatus of Calama, and the murderous Purpurius of Limata [Note: [Col. 0773] The same manuscript reads “of Liniata.”]. When questioned about his sister’s sons, whom he was said to have killed in the prison at Milevis, he confessed, saying: “I both killed them and kill them—not only them, but anyone who acts against me.”

There was also Menalus [Col. 0774] [Note: [Col. 0774] The Germanensis manuscript reads “Menalius.” See below the letter of Constantine to Celsus.], who, lest it be proved by his fellow citizens that he had offered incense, pretended to suffer from an eye ailment and hesitated to appear before his colleagues.

These men and the others whom we shall shortly show to have been your leaders, after the persecution, gathered in the city of Cirta—since the basilicas had not yet been restored—in the house of Urbanus Carisius on the third day before the Ides of May, as the written testimony of Nundinarius, then a deacon, records [Note: [Col. 0774] See below, “The Acts before Zenophilus the governor.”], and as the antiquity of the parchments bears witness. We shall be able to produce these parchments for those who doubt.

For we have appended the fullness of them [Note: [Col. 0774] The printed editions add *rerum*, “of the matters.” It is absent from the Germanensis manuscript, though the sense is understood: “the fullness of the parchments.”] in the final part of these little books, to complete the proof.

When questioned by Secundus of Tigisis, these bishops confessed that they had betrayed. And when Secundus himself was rebuked by Purpurius because he too had spent a long time among the stationaries [Note: [Col. 0774] The Germanensis manuscript reads *apud Stationarium*, singular: “among the Stationary.”] and had not fled but had been released—and could not have been released without reason except because he had betrayed—all of them had already risen and begun to murmur [Note: [Col. 0774] The printed editions read “all the heretics.” This is corrected from the Germanensis manuscript.].

Secundus, fearing their spirit, took counsel from his nephew Secundus the Younger, who advised him to reserve such a case for God. Those who had remained were consulted: Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotaria, and Nabor of Centurion [Note: [Col. 0775] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “Victor of Gabra, Felix of Rotaria, and Nabor of Centurionis.”].

They said that such a case ought to be reserved for God. Secundus said: “Sit down, all of you.” Then everyone said: “Thanks be to God.” And they sat down.

You therefore have, brother Parmenianus, those who were manifestly traitors.

Then, not long afterward, these same men—so many and of such a kind—went to Carthage. They were traitors who had offered incense and murderers, and they ordained Majorinus, whose chair you occupy, after the ordination of Caecilianus, thereby making a schism.

Since it has been shown that your leaders were guilty of betrayal, it will follow that they were also the authors of the schism. So that this matter may be clear and manifest to everyone, it must be shown from what root the branches of error have extended themselves to the present day, and from what source this little stream of wicked liquid, secretly creeping along, has flowed down to our own times.

It must be stated whence, where, and by whom this second evil arose; what causes came together and what persons brought them about; who were the authors of this evil and who nourished it; by whom judgments from the Emperor were requested between the parties; who sat as judges; where the council was held; and what judgments were issued.

The issue is division. In Africa, as in the other provinces, there was one Church before it was divided by the ordainers of Majorinus, whose hereditary chair you occupy.

It must be seen who remained at the root with the whole world; who went out; who occupied another chair that had not previously existed; who raised altar against altar; who performed an ordination while the other ordained man remained in office; and who lies under the sentence of the apostle John, who said that many antichrists would go out:

“They were not of us,” he says; “for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (1 John II, 18–19).

Therefore the one who did not wish to remain as one with his brothers, following heretics, went out like an antichrist.

No one is unaware that this happened at Carthage after the ordination of Caecilianus. It happened through a certain Lucilla, a factious woman, who, before the peace shaken by the storms of persecution, while the Church was still tranquil, could not endure the correction of the archdeacon Caecilianus.

Before the spiritual food and drink, she was said to have venerated the bone of some martyr—if indeed he was a martyr. And when she preferred to the saving cup the bone of some dead man, even if he was a martyr but had not yet been vindicated, she was corrected and withdrew in anger and confusion.

When she was angry and grieving, lest she submit to discipline, the storm of persecution, naturally arising, suddenly came to her aid.

At that time a certain deacon named Felix, who was summoned because of some notorious letter said then to have been written concerning the tyrant Emperor, is said to have hidden himself with Bishop Mensurius, fearing danger.

When Mensurius publicly denied that Felix had been demanded, a report was sent. A rescript came ordering that, if Mensurius did not return the deacon Felix, he should be sent to the palace.

Mensurius was subjected to no slight anxieties. For the Church possessed many ornaments of gold and silver, which he could neither bury in the earth nor carry away with him. He entrusted these, as it were, to faithful elders, having drawn up a memorandum which he is said to have given to a certain old woman. Thus, if he did not return, once peace had been restored to the Christians, that old woman would return them to the person whom she found sitting in the episcopal chair.

He set out and stated his case. He was ordered to return, but he could not reach Carthage.

The storm of persecution was completed and ended. By God’s command, when Maxentius sent clemency, freedom was restored to the Christians.

Botrus and Celesius [Note: [Col. 0775] The old Germanensis manuscript consistently reads “Caelestius.” Augustine likewise uses this form in the alphabetical Psalm against the Donatists.], wishing, as is said, to be ordained at Carthage, arranged that, since the Numidian bishops were absent, only the neighboring bishops should be requested to celebrate the ordination at Carthage.

Then, by the vote of the entire people, Caecilianus was chosen, and Bishop Felix of Autumnita ordained him by laying hands upon him.

Botrus and Celesius were cast down from their hope. Then a brief concerning the gold and silver [Note: [Col. 0776] Something appears to be missing here. M.] was handed over to Caecilianus while he was seated, just as it had been entrusted by Mensurius, with witnesses present.

The elders mentioned above were summoned. They had swallowed down the booty entrusted to them at the throat of greed; when they were compelled to return it, they withdrew from communion [Note: [Col. 0776] Thus the Germanensis manuscript. The printed editions read “they withdrew the people from communion,” which is less correct, since he is about to say that the entire civic multitude had gathered with Caecilianus against the schismatic Donatists.].

Likewise, the ambitious men who had failed to be ordained, and Lucilla, who for some time had been unable to endure discipline, a powerful and factious woman, refused to join the communion, together with all her followers.

Thus, when three causes and groups of persons came together, wickedness achieved its effect. The schism, therefore, was born at that time from the anger of the disgruntled woman, nourished by ambition, and strengthened by greed.

From these three groups accusations were fabricated against Caecilianus, so that his ordination might be called invalid.

A message was sent to Secundus of Tigisis [Note: [Col. 0776] The Germanensis manuscript reads “it was written”], asking that he come to Carthage.

All the traitors mentioned above set out. They were received as guests by the greedy, the ambitious, and the angry—not by the Catholics, at whose request Caecilianus had been ordained.

Meanwhile, none of those mentioned above came to the basilica where the entire civic multitude was with Caecilianus [Note: [Col. 0776] Thus the Germanensis manuscript. The printed editions read: “the whole city was present in a multitude.”].

Then Caecilianus sent word: “If there is anything that can be proved against me, let the accuser come out and prove it.”

At that time nothing could be fabricated against him by so many enemies. But because of his ordainer, whom they falsely called a traitor, he came to be branded with infamy.

Again Caecilianus sent word that, if Felix had contributed nothing to his case, as they supposed, they themselves should ordain Caecilianus as though he were still a deacon.

Then Purpurius, relying on his customary wickedness, as though Caecilianus were also his sister’s son, said: “Let him come out here, so that hands may be laid upon him for the episcopate and his head may be broken over penance.”

When the matter became known, the entire Church supported Caecilianus, so that he would not hand himself over to robbers.

At that time either the guilty man ought to be expelled, or the innocent man ought to be joined in communion. The church was crowded with people; the episcopal chair was occupied; the altar stood in its proper place, at which the peaceful bishops of earlier times had offered: Cyprianus, Carpophorus [Note: [Col. 0776] “Carpophorus” is added from the Germanensis manuscript; it had been omitted from the printed editions.], Lucianus, and the others.

Thus they went outside, altar was raised against altar, and an unlawful ordination was celebrated. Majorinus, who had been Caecilianus’s lector in the diaconate and Lucilla’s household dependent, was ordained bishop with her support by the traitors who, in the council of Numidia, as we said above, had confessed their crimes to one another and granted one another pardon.

It is therefore manifest that the ordainers who betrayed and Majorinus who was ordained went out from the Church.

Meanwhile, from the source of their own crimes, which had overflowed among them through the channels of many outrages, they thought that one accusation of betrayal should be diverted against Caecilianus’s ordainer.

They realized that fame could not speak of two similar matters at the same time. Thus, in order to silence their own crimes, they attempted to defame another’s life; and, although they themselves could have been accused by the innocent, they strove to accuse the innocent.

They sent letters everywhere, written at the prompting of envy, which we possess among the other acts for later consideration.

While still at Carthage, they anticipated one another with their letters, so that they might insert the lie into everyone’s ears through false rumors, spreading the report among the people. While falsehood was celebrated about one man, the utterly true crimes of those mentioned above remained hidden in silence.

People are often ashamed of a crime, but at that time there was no one before whom they could be ashamed, because all except a few Catholics had sinned; and it was as though innocence had been represented amid the many crimes [Note: [Col. 0776] The printed editions read “and since the image….” The reading is corrected according to the Germanensis manuscript.].

The crime of betrayal, which was clearly committed by Donatus of Masculiana and the others named above, was not enough: they joined the enormous crime of schism to the betrayal.

You see, therefore, Parmenianus, that these two crimes—so evil and so grave, betrayal and schism—belong to your leaders.

## Example of a letter to Caecilianus in which Constantine grants money to the churches

[Note: [Col. 0777] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 10.]

CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS TO CAECILIANUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

Since it has pleased us that, throughout all the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and both Mauretanias, something should be provided for necessary expenses to certain ministers of the legitimate and most holy Catholic religion, I have given a letter to Ursus, the most perfect rationalis of Africa, and have instructed him to arrange that three thousand folles be paid to Your Eminence.

Therefore, when you have received the aforesaid amount of money, you shall arrange for it to be distributed among all those mentioned above according to the schedule sent to you by Hosius.

If you should happen to discover that something is lacking for the fulfillment of my concern for all of you in this matter, you must without delay request whatever seems necessary to you from Heraclides, the procurator of our estates. For I have also instructed him personally that, if Your Eminence should request any money from him, he should arrange to have it counted out to you without any hesitation.

And since I have learned that certain men of insufficiently balanced mind are acting to corrupt the people of the most holy and Catholic Church by wicked and adulterous falsehood, know that I personally gave these instructions to Anulinus the proconsul and to Patricius, the deputy of the prefects: among their other duties, they are to take appropriate care of this matter and are not to tolerate neglecting or overlooking anything of this kind if it occurs.

Therefore, if you observe any such men persisting in this madness, you shall approach the judges mentioned above without hesitation and report the matter to them, so that they may take action against them, as I instructed them personally.

May the divinity of the supreme God preserve you for many years.

## That the clergy of the Catholic Church, presided over by Caecilianus, should be exempt from all public duties

[Note: [Col. 0777] Same source.]

CONSTANTINE MAXIMUS AUGUSTUS TO ANULINUS

Greetings, Anulinus, dearest to us.

Since it is established by many considerations that the religion in which the highest reverence for the divine majesty is preserved, when despised, has brought the greatest dangers upon the state, but, when rightly embraced and maintained, has brought the greatest prosperity to the Roman name and, by the beneficence of God, exceptional happiness to all human affairs, it has pleased us that those men who, with the proper holiness and constant observance of this law, offer their service to the worship of the divine religion should receive the reward of their labors, Anulinus, dearest to us.

Therefore, concerning those men within the province entrusted to you who serve this most holy religion in the Catholic Church presided over by Caecilianus—men whom they customarily call clergy—we wish them to be preserved as entirely exempt from all public duties, lest by any error or sacrilegious accident they be drawn away from the worship owed to the supreme divinity, but rather that, without any disturbance, they may serve their own law.

For it appears that, through these men’s offering the highest veneration to the divine power, the greatest benefit thereby accrues to the state.

Farewell, Anulinus, dearest and most desired by us.

## Report of Anulinus

[Note: [Col. 0777] It is extant in Augustine’s Letter 88, section 2, and in the Conference, third session, chapter 216.]

TO OUR AUGUSTI: ANULINUS, A MAN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK, PROCONSUL OF AFRICA.

[Col. 0778] After receiving and venerating the heavenly writings of Your Majesty, my devotion took care to report to Caecilianus and those who serve under him, who are called Clerics, in the official records of my humble office, and urged them that, with unity established by the agreement of all, they might appear to have been freed from every public obligation by the indulgence of Your Majesty, and that, with the Catholic faith preserved and the reverence due to the holiness of the law maintained, they should serve divine things.

But after a few days certain men appeared, having gathered a crowd of the populace around them, who thought that Caecilianus ought to be opposed. They presented to my jurisdiction a packet sealed in a leather case and a petition without a seal, and earnestly demanded that I send them to the sacred and venerable court of Your Divinity. Since Caecilianus remained in his position, my humble office took care to send these documents, with their proceedings appended, so that Your Majesty might be able to discern everything.

I transmitted two petitions: one, superscribed on a leather case, as follows:

“Petition of the Catholic Church concerning the crimes of Caecilianus, delivered by the party of Majorinus.”

Also another, unsealed and attached to the same leather case:

“Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the third consulship of Our Lord Constantine Augustus.”  
[Note: [Col. 0778] Perhaps this is the very petition of the following prayers, which the bishops of the party of Majorinus sent to Constantine.]

## Prayers of the bishops of the party of Majorinus to Constantine

[Note: [Col. 0778] From Optatus, book 1. Concerning these prayers, see Augustine, Letter 53, §5, and Letter 76, §2.]

“We appeal to you, excellent Emperor Constantine, because you are of a just lineage: your father did not carry out persecution among the other emperors, and Gaul is free from this crime. For in Africa there are disputes between us and the other bishops. We ask that Your Piety order judges to be given to us from Gaul.”

“Submitted by Lucianus, Dignus, Nassutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the other bishops of the party of Donatus.”

[Note: [Col. 0778] Henricus Valesius thinks that one should read “by the party of Majorinus,” since the party of Donatus was not so called until later. Augustine testifies in Letter 88, §1: “The party of Donatus was first called the party of Majorinus at Carthage.”]

## That a council should be held at Rome for the unity and concord of the Churches

[Note: [Col. 0778] Eusebius, book 10 of the Ecclesiastical History.]

CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, to MILTIADES, bishop of the city of Rome, and to MARCUS.

[Note: [Col. 0778] Namely, that petition concerning the crimes of Caecilianus delivered by the party of Majorinus, mentioned above in Anulinus’s report.]

“Since several documents of this kind have been sent to me by Anulinus, a man of clarissimus rank and proconsul of Africa—documents in which it is stated that Caecilianus, bishop of the city of Carthage, is accused by certain colleagues of his established throughout Africa on many charges—this seems exceedingly troubling to me. In these provinces, which divine providence has entrusted to my devotion by their voluntary submission, and in which there is an immense multitude of people, the populace is being led toward worse things as though divided into two parties, and the bishops are disagreeing among themselves.

“It has pleased me that Caecilianus should sail to Rome together with ten bishops who appear to accuse him and ten others whom he himself judges necessary for his case, so that he may be heard there before you and before your colleagues Rheticius, Maternus, and Marinus, whom I have ordered to hasten to Rome for this matter, in the manner that you know best accords with the most sacred law.

“Moreover, so that you may be able to obtain the fullest knowledge of the entire affair, I have sent to the aforesaid colleagues of yours copies of the petitions transmitted to me by Anulinus, appended to my letter. After reading them, Your Gravity will consider how the aforementioned controversy ought to be judged with the greatest accuracy and brought to an end according to the prescriptions of justice.

“For you are not unaware that I show such reverence to the most holy Catholic Church that I wish no schism or division to be left anywhere by you. May the Divinity of the Most High God preserve you for many years, dearest friend.”

## Concerning the Roman council under Miltiades

[Note: [Col. 0779] From Optatus, book 1.]

Judges were appointed: Maternus from the city of Agrippina, Rheticius from the city of Augustodunum, and Marinus of Arelate.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] In the Germanensis manuscript, “princes” is read in place of “judges.”]

These three Gauls and fifteen other Italians came to the city of Rome. They assembled in the house of Fausta in the Lateran, in the third consulship of Constantine and the third of Licinius, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, on a Friday.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] In the Germanensis manuscript: “in the fourth consulship of Constantine and the consulship of Licinius, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.” In Augustine, in the book after the Conference, §56: “When Constantine was consul for the third time and Licinius consul for the second time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0779] In the year of Christ 313.]

When Miltiades, bishop of the city of Rome, and the Gallican bishops Rheticius, Maternus, and Marinus had taken their seats, together with Merocles from Milan, Florianus from Caesena, Zoticus from Quintianum, Stemnius from Ariminum,  
[Note: [Col. 0779] Germanensis manuscript: “Florianus from Sinna, Zonticus from Quintianum, Stennius from Ariminum.”]

Felix from Florence in Tuscany, Gaudentius from Pisa, Constantius from Faventia, Proterius from Capua, Theophilus from Beneventum, Sabinus from Terracina, Secundus from Praeneste, Felix from Tres Tabernae, Maximus from Ostia, Evandrus from Ursinum, and Donatianus from Forum Claudii—nineteen bishops seated in all—the case of Donatus and Caecilianus was brought forward.

Each one gave his judgment against Donatus  
[Note: [Col. 0779] Donatus of Casas Nigrae, according to Augustine, Brief Account of the Conference 3, chapters 12 and 17.]

that he had confessed to rebaptizing and to laying hands upon bishops who had lapsed, which is foreign to the Church. The witnesses brought forward by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilianus. Caecilianus was pronounced innocent by the judgments of all those mentioned above, including the judgment of Miltiades, by which the proceedings were closed  
[Note: [Col. 0779] The same manuscript reads, “were made firm.”]

in these words as well:

“Since it has been established that Caecilianus is not accused, according to their own statement, by those who came with Donatus, and since it has not been established that he has been convicted by Donatus in any respect, I rightly judge that he must be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired.”

“It is therefore enough that Donatus has been struck down by so many judgments and Caecilianus has been cleared by so great a judgment.”

And yet Donatus thought that an appeal ought to be made from the bishops.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] The same manuscript omits “from the bishops.”]

To this appeal the Emperor Constantine responded as follows:

“O the rabid audacity of madness! As is customary in cases involving pagans, they lodged an appeal.”

[Note: [Col. 0779] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “Donatus thought that the bishop ought to be appealed against,” and so forth.]  
[Note: [Col. 0779] These words of Constantine are found in a letter written to the bishops after the Council of Arles. They were therefore spoken by Constantine when the Donatists appealed to him from the judgment at Arles. Compare Augustine, Letter 43, §20.]

## The bishops Eunomius and Olympius, sent to Africa, declare to the Carthaginians against the party of Donatus where the Catholic Church is, and reinforce the judgment delivered by the Roman council in favor of Caecilianus

[Note: [Col. 0779] From Optatus, book 1.]

At the same time, that same Donatus asked that he be permitted to return and not approach Carthage.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] We have restored this passage on the authority of the Germanensis manuscript. In the printed editions of Optatus it read: “that he might happen to return to Carthage.” No one will readily believe that that already-condemned Donatus, and specifically this bishop not of Carthage but of Casas Nigrae, dared to request permission to return to Carthage, where he had caused the schism, as we have already observed above, in the Brief Account of the Conference, day 3, chapter 20.]

Then, at the suggestion of his supporter Filuminus, it was proposed to the Emperor that, for the sake of peace, Caecilianus should be detained at Brixia.  
[Note: [Col. 0780] In the Germanensis manuscript, “Erixia.”]

And it was done. Then two bishops were sent to Africa, Eunomius and Olympius.  
[Note: [Col. 0780] The editions of Optatus add after “and Olympius”: “so that, after removing the two, they might appoint one.” From these words Albaspinaeus incorrectly conjectured that Donatus and Caecilianus occupied the same see. That this Donatus was bishop of the see of Casas is clear from the Index to the Conference, 3, chapter 540; from Augustine’s Brief Account of the Conference, day 3, chapter 20; and from his book after the Conference, §17. Those words, however, are entirely absent from our Germanensis manuscript. In fact, Eunomius and Olympius were sent so that they might rather establish Caecilianus in his own see, announcing to the Carthaginians that the party of Donatus was separated from the Catholic Church, while the innocence of Caecilianus had been confirmed by the judgment of the Roman council.]

They came and remained at Carthage for forty days  
[Note: [Col. 0780] In the Germanensis manuscript, “fifty.”]  
to declare where the Catholic Church was. The seditious party of Donatus did not allow this to happen.  
[Note: [Col. 0780] In the same manuscript, “zealous,” that is, attached to Donatus.]

Daily disturbances arose from the zeal of the parties. The final judgment of those same bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, is recorded as follows: they said that the Catholic Church was the one spread throughout the whole world, and that the judgment previously delivered by the nineteen bishops could not be annulled. Thus they entered into communion with the clergy of Caecilianus and returned.

Concerning these matters we have volumes of official records. Anyone who wishes may read them in the final sections. Meanwhile Donatus himself returned first, of his own accord, to Carthage. When Caecilianus heard this, he hastened to his own people. In this way the parties were again stirred up. Nevertheless, it is established both that Donatus was struck down by so many judgments and that Caecilianus was pronounced innocent by the same number of judgments.

## After Caecilianus has been cleared in the City, Felix is ordered to be cleared in Africa

[Note: [Col. 0780] From Optatus, book 1.]

But since, in this very case, two persons seemed long to have been under suspicion among the Catholics—the ordained man and the ordainer—after the ordained man had been cleared in the City, the ordainer still remained to be cleared. Then Constantine wrote to Aelianus the proconsul  
[Note: [Col. 0780] The same manuscript has “to Helianus.”]  
that, with public duties set aside, an official inquiry should be made into the life of Felix of Autumnum.

The one to whom the matter had been entrusted presided.  
[Note: [Col. 0780] We have restored these five words, “the one to whom it had been entrusted presided,” from the Germanensis manuscript.]

The following were called as witnesses: Claudius Saturianus, curator of the commonwealth who had held office during the persecution in Felix’s city; Callidius Gratianus, curator at the time when the case was being demanded; and Alfius Caecilianus, a magistrate. Superius the stationarius was also brought in,  
[Note: [Col. 0780] The editions of Optatus have “Superstationarius.” But the Germanensis manuscript has “Superius (or Exsuperius), the stationarius,” a reading reached by conjecture by Henricus Valesius.]  
and Ingentius, a public clerk, was suspended under the threat of impending tortures.

From the answers of all of them nothing was found that could sully the life of Felix the bishop. A volume of the official records is preserved, containing the names of those present who took part in the case: Claudius Saturianus the curator, Caecilianus the magistrate, Superius the stationarius, Ingentius the clerk, and Solon the public official of that period. After their answers, the following portion of the judgment was delivered by the aforementioned proconsul:

“As for Felix, the devout bishop, etc.”

## Proceedings of the proconsular court by which Felix was acquitted

[Note: [Col. 0780] Augustine calls them this in the Brief Account of the Conference, day 3, §42.]

Much is missing [lacuna] in the municipality of the Autumnitani. Gallienus the duumvir said:

“Since you are present, Caecilianus, hear the letter of my master, Aelius Paulinus, a man of eminent rank, acting in place of the prefect, stating what he has deigned to order according to the letter sent to us—a letter which compels you to produce yourself, the clerk whom you had at that time in your administration, and the archivist. But since the archivist of that period has died, and according to the testimony of the letter of that same master of mine you must bring with you all the records of your administration, it is necessary for you to proceed to the colony of Carthage with your clerk. The curator is present, under whose authority we compel you to appear. What do you answer to this?”

Caecilianus said:

“As soon as you brought me the letter of Aelius Paulinus, a man of eminent rank acting in place of the prefect, I immediately sent to the clerk Miccius, ordering him to come and bring me the records drawn up at that time. He is still making inquiries, since it is not a short time ago that I administered the duumvirate: it has been eleven years. Therefore, when he finds them, I shall obey so great a command.”

Gallienus the duumvir said:

“It is your concern to obey the order; for you see that the order is sacred.”

Caecilianus said:

“I am devoted to so great a command.”

Then, shortly afterward, when the clerk Miccius arrived, Fuscius the duumvir said:

“You too have heard, Miccius, that you are also required to go with Caecilianus to the office of the eminent-ranking deputy, so that you may bring with you the records of that period. What do you say to this?”

Miccius replied:

“After completing his year, the magistrate took all his records home with him. I am investigating whether any of mine can be found on wax tablets.”

While he was searching, Quintus Sisenna the duumvir said:

“He has answered what the office knew.”

Apronianus said:

“If the magistrate had taken all his records with him, where did the records that had then been issued or prepared over so long a period come from?”

And when he said this, the proconsul Aelianus said:

“Both my interrogation and the answer of each individual are contained in the official records.”

Agesilaus said:

“There are also other letters necessary to this matter. It is important that they be read.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Read them in the hearing of Caecilianus, so that he may acknowledge whether he himself dictated them.”

Agesilaus recited [lacuna] and in the consulship of Annianus, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in a legal proceeding before Aurelius Didymus, Speretius, priest of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and duumvir, he recited [lacuna].  
[Note: [Col. 0781] Perhaps “Volusianus” is missing.]  
[Note: [Col. 0781] Compare the book To the Donatists after the Conference, §56, where Augustine has “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0781] The verb “he recited” is either superfluous or indicates that something else is missing here.]

Maximus of the splendid colony of the Carthaginians said:

“I speak in the name of the elders of the Christian people of the Catholic faith. Before the greatest Emperors, a case will have to be brought against Caecilianus and Felix, who is striving to seize the leadership of the whole of that faith. Evidence of his crimes is being collected against them.

“For when persecution was decreed against Christians—that is, that they should sacrifice or surrender to be burned whatever Scriptures they possessed—Felix, who was then bishop at Autumnum, had consented that the Scriptures be handed over by the hand of Galatius so that they might be burned in the fire. At that time Alfius Caecilianus was magistrate, whom Your Power deigns to see present.

“And since it was the duty of his office at that time to see that everyone sacrificed by order of the proconsul, and that, according to the sacred law, they handed over whatever Scriptures they possessed, I ask—[the passage is corrupt]—and you see that he is an old man and cannot proceed to the sacred court: let him give evidence in the official records as to whether he has already issued letters concerning the agreement made with him by the aforesaid party, and whether what he communicated in the letters is true, so that the actions and credibility of these men may be exposed in the sacred court.”

[Note: [Col. 0781] The passage is corrupt.]

With Caecilianus standing there, Speretius the duumvir said:

“You hear what has been deposited in the official records.”

Alfius Caecilianus said:

“I was at Zama with Saturninus to purchase tiles. When we came there, the Christians themselves sent to me at the praetorium to ask: ‘Has the sacred order reached you?’ I said: ‘No, but I have already seen copies.’ I saw the basilicas being demolished at Zama and Furni, and I saw the Scriptures being burned. Therefore, bring forward any Scriptures you have, so that the sacred order may be obeyed.

“Then they sent to the house of Felix the bishop to remove the Scriptures from there so that they could be burned according to the sacred order. Thus Galatius went with us to the place where they had been accustomed to celebrate prayers. From there we removed the chair and the letters of greeting, and all the doors were burned  
[Note: [Col. 0782] Below, with a symbol.]  
according to the sacred order.

“And when we sent to the house of that same Felix the bishop, the public officials reported that he was absent. For when Ingentius, the clerk of Augentius, arrived later—under whom I administered the aedileship—I dictated a letter to that same colleague, which I composed for that same bishop Felix.”

Maximus said:

“He is present. Let the same letter be offered to him, so that he may recognize it.”

He replied:

“It is the letter.”

Maximus said:

“Since he has recognized his letter, I shall read it, and I ask that it be inserted in full into the official records.”

And he recited:

“Caecilianus sends greetings to his kinsman Felix.

“When Ingentius met my colleague Augentius, his friend, and asked whether, in the year of my duumvirate, any Scriptures of your law had been burned according to the sacred law [lacuna]—that Galatius, one of your faith, had publicly brought letters of greeting from the basilica.

“I wish you good health.”

This is the sign  
[Note: [Col. 0782] Add: “according to the agreement,” and “we burned them.” See below.]  
which the Christians had sent to me as a petition, and he himself  
[Note: [Col. 0782] Perhaps, “and you yourself, whose petition it is.”]  
whose petition it is. And you said:

“‘Take the key, and whatever books you find in the chair and codices upon the stone, take them. Be sure that the officials do not take the oil and grain.’

“And I said to you:

“‘Do you not know that wherever Scriptures are found, the house itself is demolished?’

“And you said:

“‘What, then, shall we do?’

“And I said to you:

“‘Let one of your people take them from the courtyard where you hold your prayers and place them there; then I shall come with the officials and remove them.’

“And we came there and took everything, according to the sacred order.”

Maximus said:

“Since the reading of his letter has been recited in the official records, and he himself acknowledged that he had sent it, we ask that it remain attached to the records.”

Speretius the duumvir said:

“What you said has been written down.”

Agesilaus said:

“He acknowledged the present letter; he says that the remaining portion, which he has now read, is false.”

Caecilianus said:

“My lord, I dictated it only as far as it reads: ‘I wish you, dearest kinsman, good health.’”

Apronianus said:

“This is how they have always acted—falsely, through intimidation, theatrics, and an irreligious mind—those who refused to agree with the Catholic Church.

“For while Paulinus was administering the prefects’ powers here, a certain private individual was suborned, one who had the capacity of a courier, to come to the Catholic unity and lead and frighten them. Thus the faction was exposed.

“For a falsehood was being prepared against Felix, the most devout bishop, so that he might appear to have betrayed and burned the Scriptures. Ingentius, since everything he was doing was harmful to the holiness and religion of Caecilianus, was suborned to come with a letter supposedly from Felix the bishop to Caecilianus the duumvir, and to pretend that he had been commissioned by Felix.

“Let him state the very words by which this was fabricated.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“State them.”

Apronianus said:

“He said: ‘Tell my friend Caecilianus that I have received eleven precious, godlike codices, and that he now approaches me so that I may return them. Say that you burned them in the year of your magistracy, so that I may not have to return them.’

“Therefore, Ingentius must be questioned as to how far these things were contrived and fabricated, and how far he wished to deceive the master  
[Note: [Col. 0782] Perhaps, “the magistrate.”]  
into a falsehood in order to besmirch Felix with infamy. Let him say by whom he was sent—yet let him also disclose this plot against Felix’s conscience, by which he intended to detract from Caecilianus’s honor and standing.

“For there is someone who has been sent as an envoy through Mauretania and Numidia from the opposing party.”  
[Note: [Col. 0782] Elsewhere, “the different party.”]

With Ingentius standing there, the proconsul Aelianus said:

“On whose order did you undertake the actions with which you are charged?”

Ingentius said:

“Where?”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Since you pretend not to understand what you are being asked, I shall put it more plainly: who sent you to Caecilianus’s magistracy?”

Ingentius said:

“No one sent me.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“How, then, did you come to Caecilianus’s magistracy?”

[Col. 0783] Ingentius said:

“When we had come and the case of Maurus, the bishop of Utica, who had bought his episcopate, was being heard, the bishop Felix of Autumnum went up to the city to discuss it and said: ‘Let no one enter into communion,’ because Maurus had committed a falsehood. And I replied to him: ‘Neither with you nor with that man, who is a traditor.’ For I was grieved over the case of Maurus, my host, because I had been in communion with him abroad, since I had escaped the persecution.

“After this I went to Felix’s homeland, taking three elders with me, to see whether he had truly betrayed or not.”

Apronianus said:

“He did not come to Caecilianus in order to ask about Caecilianus.”  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Perhaps: “Deign to ask about Caecilianus.”]

The proconsul Aelianus said to Caecilianus:

“How did Ingentius come to you?”

Caecilianus replied:

“He came to me at home. I was dining with the workmen; he came there and stood at the door. He said: ‘Where is Caecilianus?’ I replied: ‘Here.’ I said to him: ‘What is it? Is everything all right?’ He said: ‘Everything.’ I replied to him: ‘If you do not disdain dining, come and dine.’ He said to me: ‘I am returning here.’

“He came there alone and began to say to me: ‘Look, I have been charged to investigate whether the Scripture was burned in the year of my duumvirate.’ I said to him: ‘You are troubling me; you are a planted agent. Get away from me.’ And I rejected him.

“Then he came there again with my colleague, with whom I had been an aedile. My colleague said to me: ‘Our bishop Felix sent this man here so that you would write him a letter, because he received precious codices and did not wish to return them. Write to him that they were burned in the year of your duumvirate.’

“And I said: ‘Is this the faith of Christians?’”

Ingentius said:

“My lord, let Augentius come as well. I am an honorable man, and may my honor perish, and we have this man’s sides.”  
[The passage is uncertain.]

The proconsul Aelianus said to Ingentius:

“You are refuted under another heading.”

The proconsul Aelianus said to the court officers:

“Prepare him.”

When he was being prepared, the proconsul Aelianus said:

“Let him be suspended.”

While he was being suspended, the proconsul Aelianus said to Caecilianus:

“How did Ingentius come to you?”

He replied:

“Felix, our bishop, sent me here and said: ‘Write to him  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Perhaps, “to that man.”]  
because there is some utterly corrupt fellow—I do not know who—who has precious codices in my possession, and I do not wish to return them. Therefore, write a letter, because they have been burned, so that I may not return them.’

“And I said: ‘Is this the faith of Christians?’ And I began to rebuke him. My colleague said: ‘Write to our Felix.’ Thus I dictated the letter that appears up to the point where I dictated.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Listen without fear to the reading of your letter. Acknowledge how far you dictated it.”

Agesilaus recited:

“‘I wish you, dearest kinsman, to enjoy good health for many years.’”

The proconsul Aelianus said to Caecilianus:

“Did you dictate up to this point?”

He replied:

“Up to this point; the rest is false.”

Agesilaus recited:

“‘This sign, which you sent to me as a petition, unless I and you and the person whose petition it is  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Perhaps: “the Christians sent it; therefore, ‘you yourself, whose petition it is,’ and so forth.” See above.]  
and you said: “Take the key, and whatever books you find in the chair and codices upon the stone, take them. Be sure that the officials do not take the oil and grain.”

“‘And I said to you: “Do you not know that wherever Scriptures are found, the house itself is demolished?”

“‘And you said: “What, then, shall we do?”

“‘And I said to you: “Let one of you take them from the courtyards  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Above, “from the courtyard.”]  
where you hold your prayers and place them there; then I shall come with the officials and remove them.”

“‘And we came there and took everything according to the agreement, and burned it according to the sacred order.’”

Maximus said:

“Since the substance of his letter has also been recited in the official records, and he has said that he himself acknowledged and sent it, we ask that this remain attached to your records.”

Speretius said:

“What you said has been written down.”

Caecilianus replied:

“From that point onward  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Perhaps, “from that point.”]  
it is false—the letter is mine only as far as it says, ‘Good health to you, dearest kinsman.’”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Whom do you say added to the letter?”

Caecilianus said:

“Ingentius.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Your statement is attached to the records.”

The proconsul Aelianus said to Ingentius:

“You are being tortured; do not lie.”

Ingentius said:

“I was wrong. I added to this letter, out of grief over the case of my host Maurus.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Constantine the Great, ever Augustus, and Licinius the Caesars deign to show such piety toward Christians that they do not wish discipline to be corrupted, but rather wish this religion to be observed and honored. Therefore do not flatter yourself by saying to me that you are a decurion and therefore cannot be tortured. You are being tortured so that you will not lie, which appears foreign to Christians. Therefore speak plainly, so that you may not be tortured.”

Ingentius said:

“I have already confessed without torture.”

Apronianus said:

“Deign to question him about the authority, deceit, and madness by which he has gone around all the Mauretanias and Numidias, and by what means he has stirred up sedition against the Catholic Church.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Have you been to the Numidias?”

He replied:

“No, my lord. Let there be someone who can prove it.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Nor in Mauretania?”

He replied:

“I went there to conduct business.”

Apronianus said:

“And in this too he is lying, my lord. For one reaches the territory of Mauretania only through Numidia; yet he says that he was in Mauretania and was not in Numidia.”

The proconsul Aelianus said to Ingentius:

“What is your status?”

Ingentius replied:

“I am a decurion of the Ziquenses.”

The proconsul Aelianus said to the court officers:

“Lower him.”

After he had been lowered, the proconsul Aelianus said to Caecilianus:

“Are the things you said false?”

Caecilianus replied:

“No, my lord. Order the man who wrote the letter to come. He is his friend. He himself will say how far I dictated the letter.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Who is the man whom you wish to come?”

Caecilianus said:

“Augentius, with whom I was an aedile. I can prove it only through Augentius himself, who wrote the letter and to whom I dictated it up to a certain point. He can state it himself.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Is it therefore established that the letter is false?”  
[Note: [Col. 0784] Perhaps, “falsified.”]

Caecilianus replied:

“It is established, my lord. I am not lying at the cost of my blood.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Since you held the duumvirate in your homeland, credibility ought to be given to your words.”

Apronianus said:

“It is not new for them to do this. Besides, they added to the records whatever they wished. It is already their technique.”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“From the statement of Caecilianus, who says that the records were falsified and that much was added to the letter, it is clear with what intention Ingentius did these things. Therefore let him be taken into custody. He is needed for stricter interrogation.

“As for Felix, the devout bishop, it is clear that he is free from burning the sacred instruments, since no one has been able to prove anything against him—that he handed over or burned the most sacred Scriptures. For the interrogation of everyone recorded above makes clear that no sacred Scriptures were found, corrupted, or burned.

“This is contained in the records: that Felix the devout bishop was neither present at those times, nor gave his consent, nor ordered anything of the kind to be done.”

Agesilaus said:

“What does Your Power command concerning those who came to instruct Your Power?”

The proconsul Aelianus said:

“Let them return to their sees.”

## That Ingentius should be sent to the Emperor’s court

The Flavian Emperors and Caesars, CONSTANTINE THE GREAT and VALERIUS LICINIANUS LICINIUS, to PROBIANUS, proconsul of Africa.

“Your predecessor Aelianus, rightly, while Verus, a man of perfectissimus rank and deputy of the prefects throughout our Africa, was confined by serious illness and Aelianus was performing his duties, judged that, among other matters, that affair—or odium—which appears to have been stirred up concerning Caecilianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, should be referred to his examination and command [Note: [Col. 0784] Perhaps, “and jurisdiction,” or “without a command,”] etc.”

The remainder is to be taken from Against Cresconius, book 3, §81, and from Augustine’s Letter 88, §4.

## To the Vicar of Africa, ordering the parties between whom the controversy existed to go to Arles for a council

[Col. 0785] CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS to ABLAVIUS.  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “Aelafius.”]

“Previously, when it had been brought to my knowledge that in our Africa several people had begun, in an unspeakably mad fury, to withdraw from one another through empty accusations concerning the observance of the most sacred Catholic law  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “faith,”]  
and to disagree  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “to dissent,”]  
with one another, I had decided that, in order to settle this disagreement, both Caecilianus, bishop of Carthage, against whom nearly all of them had repeatedly come before me, and some of those who believed that certain charges ought to be brought against him, should present themselves at Rome.

“For I had also ordered certain bishops from Gaul to go to the aforesaid city of Rome, so that they, on account of the integrity of their lives and their praiseworthy discipline, together with seven bishops of the same communion and of the city of Rome  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “the bishop of the city of Rome,”]  
and those who would investigate the matter with them, might bring the affair that appeared to have been stirred up to its proper conclusion.

“They reported everything that had been done in their presence to my knowledge, with official records also taken, affirming in addition by word that their judgment had been delivered in accordance with the fairness of the facts. They said that those who had thought to stir up certain charges against Caecilianus were rather liable in the case, to such an extent that, after the judgment had been held, they prohibited them from returning to Africa  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “reported that they had prohibited them.”]

“From all this I had reasonably hoped that a proper end had been imposed upon all the disturbances and disputes which appeared suddenly to have been stirred up by those men. But when I read the written report of your administration, which Your Gravity had judged should be sent to Nicasius and the others concerning these same pretenses, I clearly recognized that they are willing to place neither regard for their own salvation nor—what is more important—the veneration of Almighty God before their eyes.

“For they persist in doing things that not only concern their own disgrace and infamy but also give an opportunity to those people who are known to turn their minds far away from this most sacred observance to disparage them.

“You should also know that some of these men came asserting that Caecilianus himself was considered less worthy of the worship of the most sincere religion. When I replied to them that they were making this claim in vain, since the matter had been settled at Rome by suitable and highly approved men, bishops, they judged that they ought to respond vigorously and obstinately that their entire case had not been heard, but rather that those same bishops had shut themselves up somewhere and had judged as it suited them.

“Therefore, when I saw that such numerous and serious disagreements were being prolonged with excessive obstinacy, so that no end to them appeared possible unless Caecilianus himself and three of those who disagree with him came to the town of Arles for judgment by those who think differently from Caecilianus  
[Note: [Col. 0785] Elsewhere, “with Caecilianus,”]  
and owe him their agreement, I considered it necessary to instruct your diligence that, as soon as you receive this letter of mine, you should arrange for the aforementioned Caecilianus, together with some of those whom he chooses—and also for men from Byzacena, Tripolitania, Numidia, and the individual provinces of Mauretania, each of whom must bring along some of his own people whom he considers suitable for selection—and likewise some of those who dissent from the same Caecilianus, once public transport has been provided, to sail across Africa and Mauretania and from there to Spain by the shortest route.

“From there, moreover, you shall grant each of these bishops an individual travel warrant, so that they may arrive at the aforesaid place by the first day of August. You shall promptly inform them that, before they depart, they must arrange matters so that, in their absence, proper discipline may be maintained and no disturbance or quarrel by anyone may arise that would bring the greatest disgrace. Thereafter, once full investigation has been undertaken, let an end be imposed.

“For when all those who are now known to be engaged in dispute have presented themselves—disputes which ought not unjustly to be brought to a timely end—they can immediately be terminated and settled.

“Since it is certain to me that you too are a worshiper of the Most High God, I confess to Your Gravity that I shall in no way consider it permissible for such disputes and quarrels to be ignored by us, since through them the supreme Divinity might perhaps be provoked—not only against the human race but also against me myself, to whose care, by His heavenly will, He has entrusted the governance of all earthly things—and might decree something contrary to what has hitherto been urged.”  
[Note: [Col. 0786] Elsewhere, “might decree,” and likewise immediately below.]

“Then indeed I shall be able to be completely and fully secure, and always to hope for everything most prosperous and best from the prompt benevolence of Almighty God, when I perceive that all men venerate the most holy God with the worship due to Catholic religion, in the fellowship of harmonious observance.”  
[Note: [Col. 0786] Elsewhere, “in the observance of fellowship.”]

### The Emperor commands Syracusanus, bishop of Syracuse, to proceed to the Council of Arles

[Note: Col. 0786; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 10.]

**CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, to Chrestus, bishop of the Syracusans.**

Previously, when certain men had begun, with a depraved and perverse mind, to dissent from the holy religion and heavenly virtue, and from the judgment of the Catholic Church, wishing to cut short such a dispute of theirs, I had determined that, after certain bishops had been sent from Gaul and those from Africa had also been summoned who, divided into two parties, were contending with one another stubbornly and obstinately, and with the bishop of the city of Rome also present, the matter that appeared to have been thrown into confusion might, in their presence, be settled by the most careful examination.

But since some men, as usually happens, have not ceased prolonging their private animosities, having forgotten both their own salvation and the veneration owed to the most holy faith, refusing to acquiesce in the judgment already pronounced and asserting that only a very few bishops had delivered a decision—and that they had hastened to pronounce judgment without carefully examining all the matters that ought previously to have been investigated—it has come about that those who ought to have been united among themselves in concord and fraternal spirit are divided by a shameful, or rather detestable, secession, and that an opportunity is offered for mockery to men whose minds are alien to the most holy religion.

Therefore I had to take diligent care that these matters, which ought already to have been finished by voluntary assent after the judgment had been delivered, might at last be brought to an end through the intervention of many. Since, then, we have ordered very many bishops from different and almost innumerable places to assemble in the city of Arles before the Kalends of August, we have likewise judged that you should be written to: having received a public vehicle from the most distinguished man Latronianus, corrector of Sicily, and taking with you two persons of the second rank whom you may deem suitable for selection, together also with three servants who can attend to you on the journey, you are to meet at the aforesaid place on the same day. Thus, both through Your Gravity and through the unanimous and harmonious diligence of the others gathered together, this controversy—which, through the most disgraceful altercation, has continued down to the present time—may at last be recalled to the proper observance of religion and faith and to fraternal concord, after the allegations of all those who are now divided among themselves, and whom we have also ordered to be present, have been heard.

May almighty God preserve you safe for the longest possible time.

## Concerning the proceedings at the Council of Arles

To the most beloved Pope Silvester: Marinus, Acratius [Note: Alternatively, Agroecius.], [Col. 0787] Natalis, Theodorus, Proterius, Vocius, Verus, Probatianus [Note: Alternatively, Probatius.], Caecilianus, Faustinus, Surgentius, Gregorius, Reticius, Ambitausus, Terminatius [Note: Alternatively, Termatius.], Merocles, Pardus, Adelfius, Hibernius, Fortunatus, Aristasius, Lampadius, Vitalis, Maternus, Liberius, Gregorius, Crescens, Avitianus, Dafnus, Orientalis, Quintasius, Victor, and Epictetus send eternal greetings in the Lord.

Clinging together through the common bond of charity and through the unity of the mother, the Catholic Church, and brought to the city of Arles by the will of our most pious Emperor, we greet you from there, most religious [Note: Alternatively, most glorious.] Pope, with the reverence that is your due.

There we encountered men of unbridled mind, grievous and harmful to our law and tradition. The present authority of our God, together with the tradition and rule of truth, rejects them so completely that in them there was neither any sound method of speaking, nor any proper manner of accusation, nor any suitable proof. Therefore, with God and the mother Church—which knows and approves her own—as judge, they were either condemned or rejected.

Would that, dearest brother, you had considered it worthwhile to be present at so great a spectacle! We firmly believe that a more severe sentence would have been pronounced against them, and that, with you judging together with us, our assembly would have rejoiced with greater gladness.

But since you could not depart from those regions in which the Apostles sit daily and their blood unceasingly bears witness to the glory of God, these were not the only matters that seemed to us worth treating, dearest brother, although they were the matters for which we had been invited. We also judged that we ought to consult for ourselves. Since the provinces from which we have come are different, various matters also arise which we think must be observed.

[It pleased us, therefore, in the presence of the Holy Spirit and his angels, that we should also bring forward for judgment concerning the present peace those matters that he admonished each person individually [Note: Alternatively, moved each person.]. It also pleased us that, before all things were made known through you, who hold the greater dioceses, this should be communicated above all through you [Note: The passages enclosed in brackets seem full of corruptions, so difficult is it to elicit a meaning consistent with reason. M.].]

What our judgment has been, we have appended in writing according to our humble capacity.

First of all, however, the matter of our life and welfare had to be addressed: since one died for many and rose again, all should observe this very time with a religious mind, so that divisions or dissensions may not arise in so great an act of devotion.

We therefore decree that the Lord’s Pascha is to be observed throughout the world on one and the same day.

Concerning those who have been ordained as ministers in whatever places: let them remain in those places.

Concerning those who cast down their weapons in time of peace: it was decided that they should abstain from communion.

Concerning charioteers who are believers: it was decided that, for as long as they drive, they should be separated from communion.

Concerning theatrical performers: it was decided that, for as long as they perform, they should be separated from communion.

Concerning those who are in a condition of illness and wish to depart [Note: Alternatively, believe.]: it was decided that hands should be laid upon them.

Concerning governors who are believers and who seek public office: it was decided that, when they have been promoted, they should indeed receive ecclesiastical letters of communion, but in such a way that, in whatever places they hold office, the bishops of those places are to exercise care over them; and if they begin to act against discipline, only then are they to be excluded from communion. The same was decided concerning those who wish to serve in public administration.

Concerning the Africans, who use their own law by rebaptizing: it was decided that, if any heretic comes to the Church, they should question him concerning the Creed. If they find that he has been baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands alone should be laid upon him. But if, when questioned about the Creed, he does not acknowledge the Trinity, then he should rightly be baptized; and so forth.

[Then Taediansus ordered all to return to their seats [Note: This seems to belong to the title of the following letter.].]

## Constantine, detesting the obstinacy of the Donatists, orders the Catholic bishops who attended the Council of Arles to return to their provinces

[Col. 0788]

**CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, to the most beloved Catholic bishops, his dear brothers, greetings.**

The eternal, religious, and incomprehensible mercy of our God by no means permits the human condition to wander longer in darkness, nor does it allow the hateful wills of certain people to advance so far that, by again opening a saving path through his most splendid lights, he does not bring them back to the rule of justice.

I have learned this through many examples; indeed, I measure it from my own experience. At first there were things within me that seemed to lack justice, and I thought that the heavenly power saw nothing of what I carried hidden in the secrets of my heart. These things, as I have said, ought to have received an equal fate—one overflowing with every evil. But almighty God, who dwells in heaven through the ages, granted me what I did not deserve.

Certainly, the things that his heavenly benevolence granted to me, his servant, cannot now be spoken of or counted, most holy bishops of Christ the Savior, dearest brothers. I therefore rejoice—indeed, I rejoice especially—that, after the most just judgment had been made, you have recalled to a better hope and fortune those whom the devil’s malignity seemed, through its wretched persuasion, to have turned away from the most splendid light of Catholic law.

O truly victorious providence of Christ the Savior, which also took thought for those who, already falling away from the truth and in a certain manner taking up arms against it [Note: Alternatively, putting on arms against it.], joined themselves to the nations!
