If they now wish to offer the most holy law the service of true faith, they will be able to understand how much has been provided for them by God’s will.

This, most holy brothers, I had also hoped might be recognized in those whose natural hardness of spirit is extreme [Note: Perhaps, “detected.”]. But the right judgment did not benefit them, nor did the gracious divinity enter their understanding.

Indeed, Christ’s clemency has not unjustly withdrawn far from those in whom it is clear, in the plainest light, that they are such that we see them hated even by heavenly providence. Such madness persists in them [Note: Perhaps, “because in them.”], while with incredible arrogance they persuade themselves of things that may neither be said nor heard, falling away from the right judgment that was given, by which, through heavenly providence, I discovered that they had demanded my judgment. Such is the force of malignity that persists in their hearts.

How often have they already been crushed by an answer worthy of their outrageous petitions, addressed to me personally? If only they had been willing to keep this before their eyes, they would never have introduced this very matter.

They demand my judgment, although I myself await the judgment of Christ. For I say, as the truth stands: the judgment of priests must be regarded as though the Lord himself were sitting in judgment. They are permitted to think or judge nothing other than what they have been taught by Christ’s instruction.

What, then, do these wicked men—the servants, as you truly said [Note: Perhaps, “I said.”], of the devil—think? They seek earthly matters while abandoning heavenly ones. O the mad audacity of fury! Just as is customary in the cases of the nations, they have lodged an appeal.

The nations, when at times avoiding lesser judgments, customarily resort to higher judgments by lodging an appeal where justice can be found [Note: Perhaps, “be reproved.”]. What, then, are these detractors of the law to think concerning Christ the Savior, when they reject heavenly judgment and suppose that mine should be demanded?

Behold the traitors! Behold, without any more searching inquiry, they have themselves exposed their crimes. What humanity is found in those who have savagely attacked God himself [Note: Perhaps, “attacked God”?]

Indeed, dearest brothers, [Col. 0789] although these things seem to have been detected in them, nevertheless, you who follow the way of the Lord and Savior, exercise patience. Grant them still the choice of what they think should be chosen. But if you see them persisting in these same things, depart at once with those whom the Lord has judged worthy of his worship, and return to your own sees. Remember me, so that our Savior may always have mercy on me.

For the rest, I have dispatched my men to bring those unspeakable deceivers of religion immediately to my court, so that they may live there and there foresee their death. I have also given suitable letters to the man who governs the vicariate prefecture of Africa, ordering him, whenever he finds others like them in this madness, to send them immediately to my court, lest under so great a clarity of our God they should continue to do things that might provoke the greatest anger of heavenly providence.

May almighty God grant that you remain safe for all ages, in accordance with my wishes and yours, dearest brothers.

## He orders the bishops of the party of Donatus to be present to bring Caecilianus’s case to an end

**CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, to the bishops.**

A few days ago, in accordance with your request, I had decided that you should return to Africa, so that there the entire case which you appear to have against Caecilianus might be investigated by friends whom I would choose and might receive its proper conclusion.

But after long reflection and after turning the matter over in my mind, it seemed especially appropriate that, since I know that certain men among you are sufficiently turbulent and obstinate in spirit, and have no regard for a right judgment or the standard of complete truth, it might happen that, if the case were investigated there, it would not receive an ending as propriety and the rule of truth require. Something might occur through your excessive obstinacy that would displease the heavenly divinity and greatly damage my reputation, which I always desire to remain unsullied.

Therefore, as I have said, it pleased me that Caecilianus should instead come here, in accordance with the previous arrangement. I believe that he will soon be present in accordance with my letters.

I promise you that, if, in his presence, you yourselves prove anything concerning even one crime or offense of his, it will have the same standing with me as though everything that you allege against him had been proved.

May almighty God grant perpetual security.

## Constantine promises to come to Africa to judge between Caecilianus and Donatus concerning the schism that arose in Africa

**TO CELSUS, vicar of Africa.**

Your most recent letters have also testified that Menalius [Note: Optatus, book 1, identifies him as accused of offering incense. See above, cols. 773–774.] [Note: Perhaps, “in that which.”] has persisted in the madness that he had undertaken long ago, together with the others who have departed from God’s truth and surrendered themselves to the most perverse error. You have stated, dearest brother, that you, in accordance with our command, were prevented from acting because of the merit [Note: Perhaps, “temerity.”] of their sedition and the tumult they were preparing.

From this it became clear that they had conceived impious plans: for indeed [Note: Perhaps, “also,” or “plainly.”], when I had determined to investigate most fully the various allegations between them and Caecilianus, they tried to escape my presence by fleeing. Through this very disgraceful act they confessed that they were hastening back to the things they had done before and continue to do now.

But [Note: Perhaps, “and.”], since it is clear that no one completely profits from his own offenses, even if their punishment has been delayed for a little while, I judged that I should command Your Gravity for the time being to leave them alone and understand that they are to be disregarded.

However, when you have read this letter, make it known publicly both to Caecilianus and to those same men that, when I come to Africa with the favor of divine piety, I shall demonstrate fully to all—both to Caecilianus and to those who appear to be acting against him—what and how great a veneration is to be offered to the supreme divinity, and with what kind of worship he appears to be pleased.

After applying a diligent examination, I shall also discover fully and bring to light the things that some of them now think they can conceal in the hiding places of ignorance and the mind. I shall destroy and investigate the very persons who stir up such matters and cause the supreme God not to be worshiped with the veneration that is required.

Since it is sufficiently clear that no one can seek the blessedness of martyrdom by a method that appears alien to the truth of religion and inappropriate, those whom I recognize as acting against law and religion itself, and whom I find guilty of violating [Note: Perhaps, “who have violated.”] the veneration that is due, shall without any hesitation pay the appropriate penalties for their madness, obstinacy, and rashness.

Know for certain, therefore, what they ought to have, so that I may establish the fullest truth, calling even my safety as witness: I shall investigate most diligently both the common people and the leading clergy, and I shall judge that which is manifestly most true and most religious. I shall also demonstrate to those same men what kind and what sort of worship ought to be offered to the divinity.

For I believe that I cannot otherwise escape the greatest guilt than by refusing to consider this wrongdoing something that may be disregarded. Nothing ought to be done by me, in accordance with my office and the duty of the ruler himself, more than this: after all errors have been investigated and every rash act cut off, to bring it about that all may exhibit true religion, harmonious simplicity, and the worship due to almighty God.

## Copy of the letter of the prefects of the praetorium to Celsus

**PETRONIUS, ANNIANUS, and JULIANUS, to DOMITIUS CELSUS, vicar of Africa.**

Since His Dignity has ordered the bishops Lucianus, Capito, Fidentius, and Nasutius, and the presbyter Mammarius, who, in accordance with the heavenly command of the Lord Constantine Maximus, ever victorious Augustus, had come to Gaul with other men of his law, to return to their own homes, we have provided them, brother, with transport and the appropriate grain allowance as far as the port of Arles, in accordance with the command of that most clement prince of eternity, so that from there they may sail to Africa.

It is appropriate that Your Diligence should know this through our letter.

We wish you, brother, to remain in the best possible health and happiness.

Hilarius the chief official presented this on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, at Trier.

## Concerning the judgment held by Constantine at Milan, where Caecilianus was again acquitted

In the index of the Carthaginian Conference, book 3, chapter 516, there is a passage entitled “Reading of Constantine’s judgment,” in which the Emperor indicates that Caecilianus had also been cleared before him after the Council of Arles. In the same work, chapter 521, there is “The interlocutory judgment by which the Emperor pronounced sentence between the parties.” Chapter 523: “An interlocutory judgment signifying this same thing from the imperial rescript recited above.”

Augustine cites this rescript, addressed to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, in the *Breviculus of the Conference*, book 3, no. 37, and in the book *After the Conference*, no. 56, where he says that it was issued under the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [Note: 10 November of the year 316].

He also gives Constantine’s very judgment in favor of Caecilianus from the same rescript in book 3 *Against Cresconius*, no. 82:

“I still insert,” he says, “the words of Constantine from his letter to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, where he testifies that he investigated the case between the parties and found Caecilianus innocent. For after he had related, in the matters mentioned above, how the parties had been brought before his judgment after the episcopal judgments:

‘In that inquiry,’ he says, ‘I saw Caecilianus to be a man endowed with complete innocence, observing the duties required by his religion and serving it as was proper; and it became evident that no crime could be found in him, just as the simulation of his adversaries had contrived it in his absence.’”

See Letter 43, no. 20, volume 2.

Some time after that judgment he issued an extremely severe law against the party of Donatus, as Augustine testifies in Letter 105, no. 9. He was the first to establish many measures against their error and ordered their basilicas to be taken away, according to book 2 *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, no. 205; and he ordered that the places of their assemblies be claimed for the treasury, according to Augustine’s Letter 88, no. 3.

Gratian mentions Constantine’s law against the Donatists in book 2 of the Theodosian Code, under the title “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated.”

## Copy of Constantine’s letter to the Catholic Church

**CONSTANTINE AUGUSTUS, to all the bishops throughout Africa and to the people of the Catholic Church.**

You know very well that, insofar as faith required, prudence permitted, and purity allowed, I have attempted everything through all the duties of humanity and moderation, so that, in accordance with the teachings of our law, that most holy peace of brotherhood—which the supreme God has infused into the hearts of his servants—might be established and maintained throughout complete concord.

But since the force of the crime that has been implanted, although it clings stubbornly to the minds of a few, could not be subdued by the purpose of our intention, because this wickedness still finds support in itself and refuses to have wrested from it the thing in which it rejoices to have sinned, we must wait until almighty God’s mercy mitigates this entire matter, which through a few has spread to the people.

For from there we must hope for a remedy whither [Note: Perhaps, “where.”] all good wishes and deeds are referred.

While the heavenly medicine is taking effect, our plans must be moderated in this way: we must cultivate patience and endure with the strength of tranquility everything that their insolence, in accordance with its habitual intemperance, attempts or does.

Let no injury be repaid with a corresponding injury. It is the mark of a fool to seize with human hands the vengeance that we ought to reserve for God—especially since our faith ought to trust that whatever it suffers from the fury of such men will have the value of martyrdom before God.

For what else is it to conquer in this world in the name of God than to endure with steadfast heart the uncontrolled assaults of men who harass the people of the peaceful law?

If your sincerity observes this, you will soon see, through the grace of the supreme divinity, that, as the institutions and morals of those who present themselves as standard-bearers of the most wretched contention grow weak, all may understand that they ought not, through the persuasion of a few, to consign themselves to eternal death, since, once their errors have been corrected, they may always be restored through the grace of repentance to eternal life.

Fare well through the common prayer, throughout the ages, at the command of God [Note: Perhaps, “with God living.”], dearest brothers.

## Copy of Constantine’s letter, together with the written petition of the bishops of Numidia, after the heretics had taken their basilicas, asking that a place or house be given to them for constructing another basilica

[Note: Perhaps from the year 317 or 318, before the law by which Constantine deprived the Donatists of their basilicas.]

**CONSTANTINE, the Victorious, the Great and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to Zeuzius, Gallicus, Victorinus, Sperantius, Januarius, Felix, Crescentius, Pantius, Victor, Babbutius, Donatus, bishops.**

Since it is clear that the will of the supreme God—the author and father of this world, by whose gift we enjoy life, look up to heaven, and rejoice in human society—is that the whole human race should agree together and be joined by a certain affection of fellowship, as though by mutual embraces, there can be no doubt that heresies and schisms have proceeded from the devil, who is the head of wickedness.

Therefore there is no doubt that whatever is done by heretics is done at his instigation, since he possesses their understanding, minds, and thoughts. For once he has brought such men under his power, he dominates them completely.

What good can a mad, faithless, irreligious, profane man, opposed to God and hostile to the holy Church, accomplish? He has departed from the holy, true, just, supreme God and Lord of all, who established us and brought us forth into this light, who gave us the spirit for the life we enjoy, and who, having willed that we should be his, accomplished everything by his will; yet this man runs headlong into the devil’s party through perverse error.

But once the mind has been possessed by evil, it must necessarily persist in the works of its teacher and accomplish what appears contrary to equity and justice. Therefore those who are possessed by the devil obey his falsehood and wickedness.

It is not surprising [Note: Perhaps, “It is not strange.”] that the wicked withdraw from the good. For the proverb rightly expresses it: “Like join with like.” Those who are infected with the evil of an impious mind must necessarily dissent from our fellowship.

For, as Scripture says, “The evil man brings evil things out of his evil treasure, but the good man brings good things out of his good treasure” (Matthew 12:35).

But since, as has been said, heretics and schismatics—who abandon what is good, pursue what is evil, and accomplish things displeasing to God—are approved by the devil, who is their father, Your Gravity acts most rightly and wisely: first, by restraining yourselves from their perverse disputes in accordance with the holy command of faith; and then by yielding to them what they themselves strive to usurp as though it were owed to them and belonged to them.

Otherwise, in accordance with their wicked and treacherous perversity, they might break out into sedition and stir up disturbances among crowds and gatherings like themselves, so that something might arise that would be impossible to quiet.

Their criminal purpose always seeks to perform the works of the devil. Therefore you overcome him, through patience, together with his own father, by the priests of God [Note: The passage is corrupt.]. Thus those who worship the supreme God obtain glory, while the others obtain condemnation and deserved punishments.

From this the just judgment of the supreme God is made still greater: he tolerates them with an even temper and condemns them through patience, enduring everything that has proceeded from them. For God has promised that he himself will avenge all things. Therefore, when vengeance is entrusted to God, punishment is inflicted more severely upon enemies.

I have learned that you, now, servants and priests of God, have willingly acted in this manner, and I have been greatly pleased that you seek no vengeance against the impious and criminal, sacrilegious and profane, faithless and irreligious, ungrateful to God and hostile to the Church, but rather ask that those same men be granted pardon.

This is truly and completely to know God; this is to adhere to his commands; this is to believe happily; this is to think rightly; this is to know that greater vengeance is summoned against the enemies of the Church when they are spared in this world.

Having therefore received the letter of Your Wisdom and Gravity, I learned that the heretics or schismatics had, with their customary wickedness, attempted to seize that basilica of the Catholic Church which I had ordered to be built in the city of Constantina. Although they had frequently been warned, both by us and by judges acting on our command, to return what did not belong to them, they had refused.

But you, imitators of the patience of the supreme God, peacefully relinquishing to their wickedness what belongs to you and instead asking one another for another place, namely, a property of the imperial treasury, made this request.

In accordance with my customary practice, I willingly embraced the petition. I immediately issued suitable orders to the financial administrator, so that he should transfer a house belonging to our property, with all its legal rights, into the ownership of the Catholic Church, which I have given with ready generosity; and I immediately ordered it to be handed over to you.

At that place, however, I ordered a basilica to be erected at the expense of the treasury. I also ordered the governor of Numidia to be written to, so that he himself might assist Your Holiness in every respect in the construction of that church.

Readers of the Catholic Church, subdeacons, and the others, at the instigation of those mentioned above, had also been summoned, according to their occupations, to public services or to the decurionate. In accordance with the provision of my law, I have ordered that they be summoned to no public service.

[Col. 0793] We have also ordered that those who were led into such duties at the instigation of the heretics be immediately released from these burdensome obligations.

For the rest, I have ordered that my law concerning Catholic clergy be observed. All these matters have been set down in writing, by the testimony of this letter, so that they might be made known to Your Patience.

Would that the heretics or schismatics would someday take thought for their salvation, wipe away the darkness from them, open their eyes to the vision of the true light, withdraw from the devil, and—even at the last—flee to God, who is one and true and the judge of all.

But since it is clear that they wish to remain in their wickedness and die in their crimes, our warning and the continual exhortation already given are sufficient for them.

If they had been willing to obey our commands, they would have been freed from every evil. Nevertheless, brothers, let us follow what belongs to us; let us adhere to the commands; let us guard the divine precepts; and, with the mercy of God favoring us, let us direct our life along the straight path, rescuing it from errors through good works.

## Proceedings before Zenophilus, the governor

[Note: Augustine cites this and calls it “The proceedings before Zenophilus the governor” in Letter 43, no. 17, and Letter 53, no. 4; “The judgment of Zenophilus the governor” in book 3 *Against Cresconius*, no. 32; and “The acts of Zenophilus the governor” in book 4 against the same opponent, no. 66.]

These proceedings establish that Silvanus was a traditor, and that, together with the others, he ordained Majorinus, whom Donatus succeeded.

Under the consulship of Constantine Maximus Augustus and Constantine the younger, most noble Caesar, on the Ides of December [Note: In the year of Christ 320], after Sextus Thaniugadiensis had been brought in and Victor the grammarian had been summoned, with Nundinarius the deacon also assisting, Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said:

“What is your name?”

He replied: “Victor.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “What is your status?”

Victor said: “I am a teacher of Roman letters, a Latin grammarian.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “What is your rank?”

Victor said: “My father was a decurion of the Constantinians; my grandfather was a soldier. He had served in the imperial retinue. Our origin descends from Moorish blood.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “Mindful of your faith and honesty, state plainly what the cause of the dissension among the Christians was.”

Victor said: “I do not know the origin of the dissension. I am one of the Christian people. When I was at Carthage, Bishop Secundus eventually came to Carthage, and they are said to have found Bishop Caecilianus improperly constituted in some respect; they appointed another in opposition to him. From that point the dissension began there at Carthage. I cannot fully know the origin of the dissension from that point, since our city has always had one Church; and if it had a dissension, we know absolutely nothing about it.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “Are you in communion with Silvanus?”

Victor replied: “I am.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “Why, then, setting aside [Caecilianus] [Note: Caecilianus is meant, whose case Victor had just mentioned and whose innocence had already been proved by many judgments.], whose innocence has been established [Note: Perhaps, “proved”]?”

And he added: “Moreover, it is asserted that you know with complete certainty another matter: that Silvanus is a traditor. Confess concerning him.”

Victor replied: “I do not know this.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said to Nundinarius the deacon: “Victor denies knowing that Silvanus is a traditor.”

Nundinarius the deacon said: “He himself knows whether [Note: An old manuscript reads, ‘not.’ Perhaps it should be read: ‘He himself knows, if he did not hand over the books’; or: ‘He himself knows, for he handed them over.’] he handed over the books.”

Victor replied: “I had fled this storm—and, if I am lying, may I perish. When we were struck by a sudden persecution, we fled to Mount Bellona. I was sitting with Mars the deacon, and Victor the presbyter. When they asked that same Mars for all the books, he denied having any. Then Victor gave the names of all the readers.

“They came to my house. Since I was absent, the officials went up into it, and my books were taken away. When I arrived, I found that my books had been taken.”

Nundinarius [Col. 0794] the deacon said: “So you stated in the proceedings [Note: Perhaps, ‘Why, then?’] that you had handed over the books. Why are these things denied, when they can be disclosed?”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said to Victor: “Confess frankly, so that you may not be questioned more strictly.”

Nundinarius the deacon said: “Let the proceedings be read.”

Zenophilus, the most distinguished governor, said: “Let them be read.”

And Nundinarius produced them, and the recording secretary read them aloud.

Diocletian being consul for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0794] A.D. 303.], from the records of Munatius Felix, perpetual Flamen and curator of the colony of the Cirtensians.

When they had arrived at the house where the Christians assembled, Felix F. pp., curator, said to Bishop Paulus: “Produce the Scriptures of the Law, and anything else you have here, so that you may obey the order and command.”

Bishop Paulus said: “The readers have the Scriptures; but whatever we have here, we shall hand over.”

Felix F. pp., curator, said to Bishop Paulus: “Identify the readers, or send me to them.”

Bishop Paulus said: “You all know them.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said: “We do not know them.”

Bishop Paulus said: “The public office knows them—that is, Edusius and Junius, the recorders.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said: “While the matter of the readers remains for the Office to identify, hand over what you have.”

While Bishop Paulus was seated with the presbyters Montanus and Victor, and the presbyters Densatelius and Memorius; while Mars was standing with the deacons Helias and Mars; and with the subdeacons Marcuclius, Catullinus, Silvanus, and Carosus; with Januarius, Meraclus, Fructuosus, Migginus, Saturninus, Victor Samsurici, and the other gravediggers present; Victor, son of Aufidius, making a written inventory as follows:

Two golden cups; likewise six silver cups, six silver jugs, and a silver little vessel; seven silver lamps, two candle-holders, seven short bronze candlesticks with their lamps; likewise eleven bronze lamps with their chains; eighty-two women’s tunics, thirty-eight mafortea [mantles], sixteen men’s tunics, thirteen pairs of men’s shoes, forty-seven pairs of women’s shoes, and nineteen rustic coplae [items of footwear].

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to the gravediggers Marcuclius, Silvanus, and Carosus: “Produce what you have.”

Silvanus and Carosus said: “Everything that was here, we have removed.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Marcuclius, Silvanus, and Carosus: “Your response is entered in the records.”

Afterward, when they came to the libraries, empty cupboards were found there. There Silvanus produced a silver dish and a silver lamp, saying that he had found them behind a storage jar.

Victor, son of Aufidius, said to Silvanus: “You would have been dead if you had not found them.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Silvanus: “Search more carefully, so that nothing remains here.”

Silvanus said: “Nothing remains; we have removed everything.”

When the dining room had been opened, four large jars and six storage chests were found there.

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said: “Produce the Scriptures you have, so that you may obey the emperors’ commands and order.”

Catullinus produced one extremely large codex.

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Marcuclius and Silvanus: “Why have you produced only one codex? Produce the Scriptures you have.”

Catullinus and Marcuclius said: “We have no more, because we are subdeacons; but the readers have codices.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Marcuclius and Catullinus: “Identify the readers for us.”

Marcuclius and Catullinus said: “We do not know where they live.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Catullinus and Marcuclius: “If you do not know where they live, tell us their names.”

Catullinus and Marcuclius said: “We are not traitors: here we are; order us to be killed.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said: “Let them be admitted.”

When they had arrived at the house of Eugenius, Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Eugenius: “Produce the Scriptures you have, so that you may obey the order.”

And he produced four codices.

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Silvanus and Carosus: “Identify the remaining readers.”

Silvanus and Carosus said: “The bishop has already said that the record-keepers Edusius and Junius know them all. Let them identify them for you by taking you to their houses.”

The record-keepers Edusius and Junius said: “We shall identify them for you, sir.”

When they had come to the house of Felix Sarsor, he produced five codices.

[Col. 0795] When they had come to the house of Victorinus, he produced eight codices.

When they had come to the house of Projectus, he produced five larger codices and two smaller ones.

When they had come to the house of Grammaticus, Felix F. pp., curator, said to Victor Grammaticus: “Produce the Scriptures you have, so that you may obey the order.”

Victor Grammaticus offered two codices and four quinions.

Felix F. pp., curator, said to Victor: “Produce the Scriptures; you have more.”

Victor Grammaticus said: “If I had had more, I would have handed them over.”

When they had come to the house of Euticius Caesarianensis, Felix F. pp., curator, said to Euticius: “Produce the Scriptures you have, so that you may obey the order.”

Euticius said: “I have none.”

Felix F. pp., curator, said to Euticius: “Your declaration is entered in the records.”

When they had come to the house of Coddeus, his wife produced six codices.

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said: “Search, in case you have more; produce them.”

The woman replied: “I have none.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Bovis, a public slave: “Go in and search, in case she has more.”

The public slave said: “I searched and found nothing.”

Felix F. pp., curator of the commonwealth, said to Victorinus, Silvanus, and Carosus: “If anything has been done improperly, the danger will affect you.”

After these things had been read, Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Confess straightforwardly.”

Victor replied: “I was not present.”

The deacon Nundinarius said: “We have read letters written by the bishops by Fortis [Note: [Col. 0795] It seems necessary to add, ‘and others.’].”

And he read a copy of the petition handed to the bishops by the deacon Nundinarius:

“Christ and his angels are witnesses that those with whom you have communicated have handed things over—that is, that Silvanus of Cirta is a traitor and a thief of the property of the poor. All of you—bishops, presbyters, deacons, and elders—know about the four hundred folles belonging to Lucilla, a most distinguished woman, on account of which you conspired that Majorinus should become bishop; and from this the schism arose. For Victor the fuller, in your presence and that of the people, gave twenty folles so that he might be made a presbyter; Christ and his angels know this.”

A copy of the letter was read.

“Purpurius, bishop, to Silvanus, fellow bishop: greeting in the Lord.

“Nundinarius, our son, the deacon, came to me and asked me to send you this supplicatory letter from me, most holy brother, so that, if it could be done, there might be peace between you and him. I want this to happen without anyone knowing what is taking place between us. If you wish, write to me [lacuna] so that I alone may come there in person and cut off this disagreement between you. For he handed me, in his own hand, a petition concerning what happened, on account of which he was stoned by your command. It is not right [Note: [Col. 0795] That is, ‘just.’] for a father to punish a son contrary to the truth; and I know that the things written in the petition he handed me are true.

“Seek a remedy by which this wickedness may be extinguished there before the flame rises—a flame which afterward cannot be extinguished without spiritual blood. Bring with you the clergy [Note: [Col. 0795] Elsewhere: ‘Bring your fellow clergy.’] and the elders of the people, ecclesiastical men, and let them carefully investigate what these disagreements are, so that what accords with the precepts of faith may be done. You shall not turn to the right or to the left. Do not willingly lend an ear to evil advisers who do not want peace. You are killing us all.

“‘And in another hand’: Farewell.”

Likewise, another copy of a letter:

“Purpurius, bishop, to the clergy and elders of the Cirtensians: eternal greeting in the Lord.

“Moses cried out to the entire council of the children of Israel and told them what the Lord commanded should be done; nothing was done without the counsel of the elders. Therefore, dearest brothers, whom I know to possess all heavenly and spiritual wisdom, recognize with all your strength what this disagreement is, and bring it to peace. For the deacon Nundinarius says that nothing is hidden from you concerning the origin of this disagreement between our dearest Silvanus and himself. He handed me a petition in which everything is written. He also said that it is not hidden from you. I know [Note: [Col. 0795] Perhaps: ‘I am silent.’] that there is no ear.

“Seek a good remedy by which this matter may be extinguished without danger to your souls, lest suddenly, when you take the role of a party in judgment, you fall [Note: [Col. 0795] Elsewhere: ‘come.’]. Judge a just judgment between the parties according to your gravity and justice.

[Col. 0796] “Take care that you do not turn to the right or to the left. This is God’s affair; he searches the thoughts of each person. Work diligently, so that no one may know what this conspiracy is. The things contained in the petition are yours [Note: [Col. 0796] Perhaps: ‘true’]; that is not good. For the Lord says: ‘By your own mouth you will be condemned, and by your own mouth you will be justified’ (Matthew 12:37).

“Another letter was read.”

“To Silvanus, our dearest brother: Fortis, eternal greeting in the Lord.

“Our son Nundinarius the deacon came to me and reported what happened between you and him through the intervention of an evil man who wants to turn the souls of the righteous away from the way of truth. When I heard this, I was overwhelmed, because such a disagreement had arisen between you. May it not happen that a priest of God should come to a point that is not expedient for us.

“Now therefore ask him that, insofar as possible, the peace of the Lord Christ the Savior may be with him. Let us not come before the public authorities and be condemned by the Gentiles. For it is written: ‘See that, while you bite and quarrel with one another, you are not consumed by one another’ (Galatians 5:15).

“Therefore I ask the Lord that this stumbling-block may be removed from our midst, so that God’s work may be celebrated with thanksgiving, the Lord saying: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you my peace’ (John 14:27). What peace can there be where disagreement and rivalries exist?

“For when I was separated from the soldier [lacuna] and came into that situation, suffering such an insult, I commended my soul to God and forgave you, because God sees the minds of human beings and their [lacuna] whether I was brought by you to them; but God delivered us, and we serve with you. Therefore, just as it has been forgiven us, be reconciled also to peace, so that in Christ’s name we may celebrate the peace [Note: [Col. 0796] Perhaps: ‘Passover.’] with joy. Let no one know … [Note: [Col. 0796] Perhaps something is missing: ‘another letter was read.’].”

“To the brothers, sons, clergy, and elders: Fortis, eternal greeting in the Lord.

“My son Nundinarius, your deacon, came to me and reported what has been done against you; indeed, it ought to have been settled by you, so that matters would not reach the point at which, after suffering such madness, they would be stoned for the truth—a fact known both to you and to us, just as you reported to us and as it is written: ‘Is there no wise person among you who can judge between brothers? Instead, brother goes to judgment against brother, and this before unbelievers’ (1 Corinthians 6:5–6)!

“Just so you are now contending in court. Matters have been driven to this point so that we give the Gentiles such an example that those who believed in God through us may themselves curse us when we come before the public authorities. Therefore, lest this occur, you who are spiritual must see that no one knows, so that we may celebrate Easter in peace. Encourage them to be reconciled to peace, and let there be no disagreement; otherwise, when the matter reaches the public authorities, you too will begin to be endangered if this happens, and afterward you will blame yourselves.

“Do your utmost, Possessor, Donatus the presbyter, each of you Valerii, and Victor, all of whom know everything; work so that peace may be with you.

“Another letter was read.”

“To Silvanus, brother: Sabinus [lacuna], eternal greeting in the Lord.

“Nundinarius, your son, has come to us—not only to me but also to our brother Fortis—bringing a serious and grievous complaint. I am astonished at Your Gravity, that you have acted in this way toward your son, whom you raised and ordained. For if an earthly structure has been built, nothing heavenly is added to it, though it is built by the hand of a priest.

“But you should not be surprised, since Scripture says: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent’ (1 Corinthians 1:19). And again it says: ‘People loved darkness more than light’ (John 3:19)—as you also do.

“It is enough for you to know everything; moreover, our brother Fortis has written to you about this. Now I ask of your charity, most kind brother, that you fulfill the saying of the prophet Isaiah: ‘Drive wickedness from your souls, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord’; and again: ‘Cast evil from your midst’ (Isaiah 1:16–18).

“Do this also: subdue and turn away the seditions that have refused to allow peace between you and your son. Let your son Nundinarius celebrate Easter with you in peace, lest this matter come before the public authorities, since it is already known to all of us. I ask you, most kind brother, to fulfill the petition of my humility: let no one know.

“Another letter was read …”

[Col. 0797] “To brother Fortis: Sabinus, eternal greeting in the Lord.

“I am particularly certain of the affection you enjoy among all your colleagues; nevertheless, in accordance with God’s will, who said, ‘Some I love more than my own soul,’ I am certain that you have esteemed Silvanus. Therefore I did not hesitate to give you this writing, because I arranged for your letter to him to be delivered on account of Nundinarius; and when someone acts diligently, God’s affairs always advance vigorously.

“Do not offer an excuse. For business presses us in these days and moves us without delay concerning this matter up to the most solemn day of Easter, so that through you the richest peace may be established, and we may be found worthy co-heirs of Christ, who said: ‘I give you my peace; I leave you my peace.’ Again I ask you to do this.

“‘And in another hand’: I wish you well in the Lord, and that you remember us. Farewell. But I ask you: let no one know.”

After these documents had been read, Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “From both the records and the letters that have been read, it is established that Silvanus is a traitor.”

And he said to Victor: “Confess straightforwardly whether you know that he handed anything over.”

Victor said: “He handed something over, but not in my presence.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What office was Silvanus holding in the clergy at that time?”

Victor replied: “Persecution arose under Bishop Paulus, and Silvanus was a subdeacon.”

The deacon Nundinarius replied: “When it came to the point of his being made bishop, the people replied, ‘Let another be made; hear us, God.’”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Did the people say, ‘Silvanus is a traitor’?”

Victor said: “I myself struggled [Note: [Col. 0797] Perhaps: ‘I myself struggled so that he would not be bishop.’] against his becoming bishop.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Then you knew that he was a traitor? Confess this.”

Victor replied: “He was a traitor.”

The deacon Nundinarius said: “You elders were shouting, ‘Hear us, God; we want our fellow citizen—he is a traitor.’”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Then you shouted with the people that Silvanus was a traitor and should not be made bishop?”

Victor said: “I shouted too, and so did the people. For we were asking for our fellow citizen, an upright man.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “For what reason did you think he was unworthy?”

Victor said: “We were asking for an upright man, and for our fellow citizen. For I knew that the emperors’ case would bring us to this point; for when such matters are entrusted …”

Then Victor Samsurici and Saturninus the gravediggers were brought in and presented.

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What is your name?”

He replied: “Saturninus.”

Zenophilus V. C. said: “What is your status?”

Saturninus replied: “I am a gravedigger.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Do you know that Silvanus is a traitor?”

Saturninus said: “I know that he handed over a silver lamp.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “What else?”

Saturninus replied: “I know nothing else, except that he removed it from behind the storage chest.”

After Saturninus had been removed, Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to the man standing there: “And you, what is your name?”

He replied: “Victor Samsurici.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What is your status?”

Victor said: “I am a craftsman.”

Zenophilus V. C. said: “Who handed over the silver dish?”

Victor replied: “I did not see. I will say what I know.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Although it has already been established from the replies of those questioned above, nevertheless you must confess whether Silvanus is a traitor.”

Victor said: “When asked a second time how he had allowed this, so that we should be led to Carthage, I heard it from the bishop’s own mouth. I was given a silver lamp and a silver dish, and I handed them over.”

Zenophilus V. C. said to Victor Samsurici: “From whom did you hear this?”

Victor said: “From Bishop Silvanus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Victor: “Did you hear from him that he had handed them over?”

Victor said: “I heard from him himself that he had handed them over with his own hands.”

Zenophilus V. C. said: “Where did you hear this?”

Victor said: “In the basilica.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “At Constantina’s?”

Victor said: “There he began addressing the people, saying, ‘What do they say makes me a traitor? The lamp and the dish?’”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “What else do you think should be investigated from these matters?”

Nundinarius said: “The treasury’s casks: who took them?”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Which cups?”

Nundinarius said: “They were in the temple of Serapis, and Bishop Purpurius took them. Bishop Silvanus, the presbyter Dontius, and Lucianus took the vinegar-vessel [Note: [Col. 0798] Or, ‘vinegar vessel.’] that was there.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Do those standing here know that this happened?”

Nundinarius replied: “They know.”

The deacon Saturninus said: “Our elders used to say that they had been taken.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “By whom are they said to have been taken?”

Saturninus said: “By Bishop Purpurius; and the vinegar by Silvanus and the presbyter Dontius, and by the deacon Lucianus.”

Nundinarius said: “He gave twenty folles, and Victor was made a presbyter.”

Saturninus said this, and as he was speaking, Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “To whom did he give them?”

Saturninus said: “To Bishop Silvanus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “So, in order to become a presbyter, did he give Bishop Silvanus twenty folles as a payment?”

Saturninus said: “He did.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “Were they placed before Silvanus?”

Saturninus said: “Before the bishops’ chair.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “From whom was the money taken?”

Nundinarius said: “The bishops themselves divided it among themselves.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Do you wish Donatus to be brought in?”

Nundinarius said: “Certainly. Let him come—the one about whom the people shouted two days after the parade, ‘Hear us, God; we want our fellow citizen.’”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Certainly the people shouted this?”

He replied: “They shouted it.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “Did they shout that Silvanus was a traitor?”

Saturninus said: “Certainly.”

Nundinarius said: “When he was made bishop, we did not communicate with him, because he was said to be a traitor.”

Saturninus said: “What he says is true.”

Nundinarius said: “I saw that Mutus the arena-worker carried him on his shoulders.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “Did it happen in this way?”

Saturninus said: “In this way.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Is everything Nundinarius says true—that Silvanus was made bishop by arena-workers?”

Saturninus said: “They are true.”

Nundinarius said: “There were prostitutes there.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus: “Did the sand-workers carry him?”

Saturninus said: “They themselves carried him, together with the people. For the citizens were shut up in the martyrs’ court.”

The deacon Nundinarius said: “Was the people of God there?”

Saturninus said: “They were shut up in the larger house.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Certainly everything Nundinarius says is true?”

Saturninus said: “It is true.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What do you say?”

Victor said: “Everything is true, sir.”

Nundinarius said: “Bishop Purpurius took one hundred folles.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Of the four hundred folles, whom do you think should be questioned?”

Nundinarius said: “Let the deacon Lucianus be brought in, because he knows everything.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “Do these men know?”

Nundinarius said: “They do not know.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Let Lucianus be brought in.”

Nundinarius said: “They know that the four hundred folles were received; but because the bishops divided them, they do not know.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus and Victor: “Do you know that the folles were received from Lucilla?”

Saturninus and Victor said: “We know.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Did the poor receive nothing?”

They said: “No one received anything.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Saturninus and Victor: “Was nothing taken from the shrine of Serapis?”

Saturninus and Victor said: “Purpurius took the cups; and Bishop Silvanus, Dontius, and Superius the presbyters, and Lucianus the deacon, took the vinegar.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “From the answers of Victor Grammaticus, Victor Samsurici, and Saturninus, it has become clear that everything Nundinarius alleged is true. Let them be removed and depart.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Whom else do you think should be questioned?”

Nundinarius said: “The deacon Castus, so that he may say whether he is not a traitor. He himself ordained him.”

Castus the deacon was brought in and presented.

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What is your name?”

He replied: “Castus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “What is your status?”

Castus said: “I hold no rank.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Although Victor Grammaticus, and also Victor Samsurici and Saturninus, have now come to acknowledge the charges made by Nundinarius, you too must confess whether Silvanus is a traitor.”

Castus replied: “He said that he had found the lamp behind the storage chest.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Confess also concerning the cups taken from the shrine of Serapis and the vinegar.”

Castus replied: “Bishop Purpurius took the cups.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Who took the vinegar?”

Castus replied that Bishop Silvanus, Dontius and Superius the presbyters, had taken the vinegar from there.

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Confess: how many folles did Victor give in order to become a presbyter?”

Castus said: “He offered, sir, a small shrine; but I do not know what it contained.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “To whom was the shrine given?”

Castus said: “That man carried it into the larger house.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Was the money distributed to the people?”

Castus replied: “It was not given, and I did not see it.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Of the folles that Lucilla gave, did the common people receive nothing?”

Castus said: “I did not see anyone receive anything.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Castus: “Where, then, did they go?”

Castus said: “I do not know.”

Nundinarius said: “Surely you either heard or saw, if it was said to the poor, ‘Lucilla gives you something from her property’?”

Castus said: “I did not see anyone receive anything.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Castus’s confession is clear: he did not know that the folles Lucilla donated had been distributed to the people; therefore let him be removed.”

And Crescentianus the subdeacon was brought in and presented.

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What is your name?”

He replied: “Crescentianus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Confess straightforwardly, like the others, whether you know that Silvanus is a traitor.”

Crescentianus said: “The earlier clerics who were here reported each matter.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “What did they report?”

Crescentianus said: “They reported that he was a traitor.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Did they say that he was a traitor?” And he added: “Who said this?”

Crescentianus said: “Those who associated with him among the people said that he had at some time handed something over.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Were they speaking about Silvanus?”

Crescentianus said: “Certainly.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “When he became bishop, were you present?”

Crescentianus said: “I was present with the people, shut up in the larger house.”

The deacon Nundinarius said: “The country people and the arena-workers made him bishop.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Certainly Mutus the arena-worker carried him?”

He said: “Clearly.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Do you know that the cups were taken from the shrine of Serapis?”

Crescentianus said: “Many said that Bishop Purpurius himself had taken the cups, and that the vinegar had come to our elder Silvanus; the sons of Aelionis said this.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “What did you hear?”

Crescentianus said: “That the vinegar was taken by the elder Silvanus, Dontius and Superius the presbyters, and Lucianus the deacon.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “Of the four hundred folles that Lucilla donated, did the people receive anything?”

Crescentianus said: “No one received anything from them; I do not know, nor do I know who distributed them.”

Nundinarius said: “Did the old women never receive anything from them?”

Crescentianus said: “Nothing.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Certainly, whenever anything of this sort is donated, all the local people publicly receive something from it.”

Crescentianus said: “I neither heard nor saw him give anything to anyone.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “So nothing was given to the people from the four hundred folles?”

Crescentianus said: “Nothing. Surely some small portion would have reached us.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Where, then, were they taken?”

Crescentianus said: “I do not know; no one received anything.”

Nundinarius said: “How many folles did Victor give in order to become a presbyter?”

Crescentianus said: “I saw baskets brought with money.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Crescentianus: “To whom were the baskets given?”

Crescentianus said: “To Bishop Silvanus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Were they given to Silvanus?”

Crescentianus said: “[Col. 0800] To Silvanus.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Was nothing given to the people?”

He replied: “Nothing. We too necessarily would have received something if it had been distributed, as is customary.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said to Nundinarius: “What else do you think should be asked of Crescentianus?”

Nundinarius said: “That is all.”

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “Since the subdeacon Crescentianus has confessed straightforwardly concerning everything, let him be removed.”

Then Januarius the subdeacon was brought in and presented.

Zenophilus V. C., the consular, said: “What is your name?”

He replied: …

The rest is missing.

Afterward, when Ursacius and Zenophilus were persecuting him, as Cresconius objects in book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, section 34, and when Silvanus had refused to communicate, he was sent into exile.

## On the indulgence and freedom of choice granted to the Donatists by Constantine

[Note: [Col. 0800] A.D. 321.]

In the index of the Third Conference, chapter 544, it reads:

“Statement of the Donatists, in which they assert that their elders handed a petition to the emperor Constantine, and that, moved by it, the emperor granted them permission to proceed.”

In the same work, chapter 549:

“Constantine’s letter to the vicar Verinus is read, by which he grants the Donatists freedom to proceed.”

In the same work, chapter 550:

“Statement of the Catholics, which says that Constantine’s letter supports their case more strongly, because nothing was judged concerning Caecilianus, but they were simply left to their own fury.”

In the same work, chapter 552:

“The Donatists ask that the judge, Marcellinus, pronounce concerning the freedom of choice granted to them by Constantine.”

Augustine, in the book written after the Conference, section 56, testifies that letters were sent to Valerius, or Verinus, the vicar, concerning the lifting of their exile and the abandonment of their fury to God the avenger. They were sent when Crispus and Constantine were consuls for the second time, on the third day before the Nones of May—that is, after nearly four years and six months had elapsed from the time of the rescript addressed to Eumalius. Compare the *Brief Account of the Third Conference*, section 40, and Letter 141, section 9.

## On the persecution by Paulus and Macarius, brought about by the unjust demand of the Donatists

[Note: [Col. 0800] From Optatus, book 3.]

“Many harsh things were indeed done by the agents of unity; but why do you attribute them to Leontius, Macarius, or Taurinus? Attribute them to your elders, and so forth—to those, first, who divided the people of God and made basilicas that were unnecessary.

“Second, attribute them to Donatus of Carthage, who provoked an attempt to establish unity in the near future.

“Third, attribute them to Donatus of Bagai, who had gathered a mad multitude and, so that Macarius would not suffer violence from it, requested the assistance of armed soldiers to protect himself and the things he carried. Then armed men came with quivers; every city was filled with shouting. When unity was announced, you all fled, and so forth.

“All the bishops therefore fled with their clergy. Some died; those who were stronger were captured and sent far away into exile. Yet none of all this was done with our wish, our counsel, our knowledge, or our action, and so forth.”

Who can deny what all Carthage principally witnessed: that the emperor Constans sent Paulus and Macarius at first not to establish unity, but with alms by which poverty, relieved throughout the individual churches, might recover its breath, be clothed, fed, and rejoice? [Note: [Col. 0800] Constans ruled Italy, Africa, and certain other parts of the empire from A.D. 337, when his father Constantine died, until A.D. 350. The event discussed here is assigned to A.D. 347 or thereabouts.]

When they came to Donatus, your father, and explained why they had come, he, inflamed by his customary fury, burst out with these words: “What has the emperor to do with the Church?” And from the spring of his levity he poured forth many insults, no fewer than those he once directed against Gregorius, to whom he did not hesitate to write: “Gregorius, stain of the senate, disgrace of the prefects,” and other such things.

To Donatus the Prefect replied with episcopal patience, and so forth. For the Emperor had sent ornaments [Col. 0801] for the houses of God and had sent alms for the poor—nothing for Donatus. Why, then, did he rage? Why was he angry? Why did he reject what had been sent? When those who had been sent said that they were going through each province and would give to those who wished to receive, he said that he had sent letters everywhere so that what had been brought would not be distributed to the poor anywhere, and so forth.

Paulus and Macarius were coming to distribute to the poor everywhere and to exhort individuals to unity. When they were approaching the city of Bagai, the other Donatus, as we have said above, the bishop of that city, wishing to place an obstacle and impediment to unity before the men mentioned above, sent heralds through the neighboring places and throughout all the markets. Calling the Circumcellions “Agonistici,” he invited them to assemble at the aforesaid place.

At that time, the assembly of men whose madness shortly before had seemed to have been impiously inflamed by the bishops themselves was demanded. For when this sort of people had wandered through various places before unity, and when Maxido and Fasir were called “leaders of the saints” by those very madmen [Note: [Col. 0801] The German manuscript has: “with Axido and Fasirab, those very madmen.”], no one was allowed to be safe on his own property. The written acknowledgments of debt had lost their force; at that time no creditor had the power to demand payment. Everyone was terrified by letters from those who boasted that they were leaders of the saints, and so forth.

Therefore, when envy was being stirred up by the bishops of your party, they are said to have written to Taurinus, who was count at that time, and instructed that such men could not be corrected within the Church, so that they might receive discipline from the count mentioned above.

Then, in response to their letters, Taurinus ordered armed soldiers to proceed through the markets, wherever the fury of the Circumcellions was accustomed to roam. At the place of Octavus [Note: [Col. 0801] The same manuscript has “Octavius.”] very many were killed, and many were mutilated. Their bodies could still be counted down to the present day at the whitewashed altars or tables.

When some of their number began to be buried in the basilicas, Clarus the presbyter at the place of Subbula [Note: [Col. 0801] The same manuscript has: “Clarus the presbyter at the place of Subbula.”] was compelled by his bishop to make the burial unburied. Thus it was revealed that an order had been given for what was done, since permission was not even granted for burial to be provided in the house of God.

Afterward their multitude grew strong. Thus Donatus of Bagai found from where he could lead a furious crowd against Macarius. Some of this same group were those who, out of a desire for false martyrdom, brought assassins upon themselves to their own destruction. From them also came those who, throwing away their worthless lives from the summits of high mountains, cast themselves headlong.

Behold from what sort of people the other bishop Donatus had formed his cohorts.

Terrified by this, those who were carrying treasures to distribute to the poor found, in such great danger, the expedient of requesting armed soldiers from Count Silvester [Note: [Col. 0801] The German manuscript has “Silvestre.” The man whom he previously calls Taurinus he now calls Count Silvester, perhaps in order to soften the insulting word. For Leontius, Ursacius, and Taurinus appear to be names imposed by the judges or commanders who corrected the Donatists, when they compared their punishments with the persecutions of the martyrs: “the first,” says Optatus in this same third book, “was like a lion, the second like a bear.”]—not so that they might inflict violence on anyone, but so that they might prevent the violence arranged by the bishop Donatus mentioned above, and so forth.

You bring forward a complaint in due order: that under Leontius and Ursacius very many were injured; that under Paulus and Macarius some were killed; and that under their successors certain persons were temporarily proscribed. What does this have to do with us? What does it have to do with the Catholic Church? Whatever you allege, you yourselves did it, because you were unwilling willingly to accept the peace commended by God, etc.

Some judge that unity should be accused or avoided because Marculus and Donatus are said to have been killed or to have died—as though, altogether, no one could deserve to be killed in the vengeance of God, etc. For we read in the prophet Ezekiel of a whitewashed wall, against which God threatened a storm, rain, hailstones, and accusations (Ezekiel 13:13), etc. These four things could not have occurred at one time.

First there was a storm under Ursacius [Note: On the authority of the Germanensis manuscript we restore here “under Ursacius,” and below “under Gregory,” as well as shortly afterward “under the Operatives of unity”; these expressions are entirely missing from the printed editions. Optatus lists three persecutions in order, of which those men complained: the first under Ursacius, also discussed in book 3 against Cresconius, no. 34; the second under the prefect Gregory, mentioned above; and the third under Paulus and Macarius. Here he passes over Leontius, whom at the beginning of book 3 he joined with Macarius, and whom later he either joined to Ursacius or placed before him.]: the wall was shaken, but did not fall, so that the rain would have a surface on which to work. Rain followed under Gregory: the wall was wetted, but did not become soaked, so that the stones would have a surface on which to work. After the rain came the stones under the Operatives [Note: Namely, Paulus and Macarius.] of unity: the wall was scattered, but repaired itself again upon its foundations. Three things have now been accomplished, etc.

## From the First Council of Carthage [Note: Approximately in the year of Christ 348.]

The bishop Gratus said:

Thanks be to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who brought an end to wicked schisms and looked upon His Church, so as to raise all its scattered members into her bosom; who commanded the most religious emperor Constans to undertake the cause of unity and to send the servants of God, Paulus and Macarius, ministers of this holy work.

Two canons of this same council are directed against the Donatists:

1. That baptism received in the Trinity should not be repeated.
2. Concerning the tombs and honor of the martyrs.

## Donatist bishops living in exile obtain permission to return from Julian [Note: From book 2 of Optatus.]

From your beginning your frenzy must be called rabid; your impiety must now be exposed, and your folly demonstrated. The first thing is to show that your joy ought to be blushed for, and your rejoicing is criminal, because you happened to return to the freedom of your former error [Note: The latest edition of Optatus reads, “that you happened to return from the freedom of your former error.” The text is corrected according to the Germanensis manuscript.].

Review the times; examine the sequence of events; consider the different vows and the different persons. Let the emperor Constans return to your memory [Note: Elsewhere, “the Christian emperor.” The word “Christian” is absent from the Germanensis manuscript. It seems that we should read “the emperor Constans,” to whom the things praised here more truly apply.], and consider what service he rendered to God and what vows he made, so that, when schisms had been removed and all dissension extinguished, the holy mother Church might joyfully see her children united under the whole heaven.

He had restored wives to their husbands, children to their parents, and brothers to brothers through a single communion. By such things God testifies that He rejoices, when He says, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1)! For when one peace united the African peoples, the peoples of the East, and the other overseas peoples, and unity itself, with all the members restored, joined together the body of the Church, the devil grieved—he who is always tormented by the peace of brothers.

At that time, under a Christian emperor, abandoned in the idols, he lay hidden in the temples as though confined there. At that same time your leaders and princes had been deservedly banished by their own deeds [Note: Some Donatist bishops had formerly been banished under Constantine but were recalled by his indulgence in the year 321. Others were later banished under Constans, in the time of Macarius, according to book 3 of Optatus, above, col. 800.]. There were no schisms in the Church, nor were the pagans permitted to perform their sacrilegious rites. A peace pleasing to God dwelt among all Christian peoples; the devil mourned in the temples, while you were in foreign regions.

Then another emperor followed, as is known to all, conceiving evil vows together with you. From being a servant of God he became a minister of the enemy, and by his edicts everywhere declared himself an apostate. You petitioned him [Col. 0803] so that you might be allowed to return. If you deny that you sent these petitions [Note: In book 3, where he mentions the same petitions, he says: “In them it is written below, ‘Given by Cassianus, Rogatianus, Pontius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party.’ So it is in the Germanensis manuscript. In the printed editions the names of the bishops have been omitted. See book 2 against the Letter of Petilianus, no. 224.”], we have read them. Nor was there any difficulty for the one whom you petitioned: he ordered those whom he understood to be coming in fury to disturb the peace to go, in accordance with his own desire.

Be ashamed, if you possess any sense of shame. The same voice restored your freedom by which the temples of idols were ordered to be opened. At almost the same moment your frenzy returned to Africa at which the devil was released from his prisons. And you are not ashamed, although at one and the same time you possess common rejoicing with the enemy.

## The atrocious crimes of the Donatist bishops after Julian restored their freedom [Note: From the book of Optatus.]

You came rabid; you came enraged, tearing the members of the Church, subtle in seductions, savage in killings, provoking the sons of peace to war. You drove many from their own seats. Coming with a hired band, you invaded basilicas. Many of your number, throughout numerous places whose names it would take too long to list, carried out bloody massacres—so atrocious that the judges of that time sent a report concerning such deeds.

But the judgment of God intervened and came to pass: the emperor who had long before ordered you to return—an impious and sacrilegious emperor, who had already sent, or was preparing to send, persecution at your instigation—died. A slaughter of Catholics was carried out in the places mentioned above. Recall your movements in each place.

Were not Felix of Zaba [Note: In the printed editions, with *za* changed to *dja*, as often happened through similarity of sound, the name was written “Djabensis”; an erudite man thought that “Djanensis” should be written instead. But in the old Germanensis codex it reads “Zabensis,” that is, the bishop of Zaba in Numidia or in Sitifis. Hence Lucius, bishop of Zaba, in the Carthaginian Collation 1, chapter 198.], Januarius of Flumenpiscis [Note: The printed editions read “Januarius Flamen Pistensis.” The text is corrected from the Germanensis manuscript, supported by the codex of the Carthaginian Collation 1, chapter 206, where Restitutus, bishop of Flumenpiscis, is named.], and the others who ran with all speed to the fortress of Lemella [Note: The Germanensis manuscript reads “Lemellensi”], where, when they saw that the basilica had been closed against their violence, they ordered their companions who were present to climb onto the roof, strip it, and throw down the tiles?

Their orders were carried out without delay. When Catholic deacons defended the altar, many were bloodied by the tiles and two were killed: Primus, the son of Januarius, and Donatus, the son of Ninus. Your fellow bishops mentioned above were urging and present, so that without doubt what is said in the Thirteenth Psalm might be applied to you: “Their feet are swift to shed blood.”

For this matter Primosus, the Catholic bishop of the place mentioned above, complained in your council at the city of Theveste, and you listened to his complaints with deliberate indifference, etc.

In the cities of Mauretania, at your urging, the people were subjected to violence; those who were destined to be born died in their mothers’ wombs, etc. What such thing was committed by us? We await God, the avenger. And you cast blame upon Macarius, who, even if he did something harsh for the sake of unity, might seem mild when you have done such great, bitter, bloody, and hostile things for the sake of dissension.

Why should I mention Tipasa, a city of Caesarean Mauretania, to which Urbanus of Forma and Felix of Idicra, two torches inflamed with rancor, ran from Numidia, disturbing the minds of peaceful people who were living in peace [Note: The editions of Optatus read “who and their minds.” The text is corrected according to the Germanensis codex.]? With certain officials assisting through favor and fury, and with the governor Athenio present with the standards, the Catholic congregation was expelled, bloodied, and driven from its seats: [Col. 0804] men were torn apart, matrons were dragged away [Note: So the Germanensis codex. The printed editions read “mothers.”], infants were killed, and unborn children were torn from the womb, etc.

And although it seems slight to you, a monstrous crime was committed. So that your bishops mentioned above might violate every sacred thing, they ordered the Eucharist to be poured out for dogs—not without a sign of divine judgment. For those same dogs, inflamed with madness, tore apart their own masters with avenging teeth, as though they were thieves guilty of profaning the holy body, treating them as strangers and enemies.

They also threw the chrism vessel through a window so that it would break. Although its being cast down assisted its fall, an angelic hand was not lacking: by spiritual support it brought the vessel down. When it was thrown, it could not suffer the impact; protected by God, it came to rest unharmed among the rocks, etc.

What could have been done by the Operatives [Note: Namely, Paulus and Macarius, mentioned above.] of unity from which you wished to manufacture empty blame against us Catholics? Returning from there, Urbanus of Forma and Felix of Icosium found mothers whom they had turned from consecrated women into ordinary women.

See what sort of bishops you defend, brother Parmenianus; and although you ought to blush for your own people, you accuse innocent Catholics.

Meanwhile the aforementioned Felix, amid his crimes and wicked deeds, did not hesitate to commit incest with a girl whom he had seized and upon whom he himself had placed the veil, and from whom shortly before he had been called “father.” And, as though he would become holier through sin, he hurried quickly to Tysedis [Note: The old Germanensis codex reads “Tysedi.” The name of the place was changed by the editors of Optatus into the particle “inde” (“from there”). In the Carthaginian Collation 1, chapter 135, Lampadius, bishop of the people of Tisedis, is named among the Catholics; and in chapter 198, Donatus, bishop of Tissedis, among the Donatists.]. There he dared to strip Donatus, a seventy-year-old bishop and an innocent man, of his episcopal name, office, and honor, etc.

It is therefore clear that you arranged everything with a certain malignity, so that in one outward form of your action you might fulfill other forms as well: so that, while a priest or bishop was deposed, the people might likewise be captured. When could a crowd of people stand firm if it saw that the ruler chosen by you had been removed? It is no different from wolves raging wherever a shepherd has been killed.

You exorcised the faithful [Note: The word “faithful” is omitted in the printed editions and is restored here from the Germanensis manuscript.] and washed the walls for no reason, so that by this form of wickedness you might undermine the minds of simple people, etc.

What is more unjust than to exorcise the Holy Spirit, break altars, and throw the Eucharist to animals? And, so that your own people may lead you into error, by praising you they call you fortunate; and rightly they name you so. They swear by you and are known already to regard your persons as God, etc.

Show us where you were commanded to shave the heads of priests [Note: That is, by imposing penance], when, on the contrary, so many examples have been set forth showing that this ought not to be done, etc.

For you stretched out your hand and spread deadly coverings over every head. Since, as I said above, there are four kinds of heads in the Church—bishops, priests, deacons, and the faithful—you were unwilling to spare even one of them; you overturned the souls of men, etc.

You found children and wounded them with penance, so that some might be prevented from being ordained. Recognize that you overturned souls [Note: Here the Germanensis codex adds: “You found new faithful and made them catechumens. Recognize that you overturned minds.”].

You found long-standing members of the faithful and made them penitents. Recognize that you overturned souls.

You found deacons, priests, and bishops and made them laymen. Recognize that you overturned souls, etc.

For what greater misfortune could there be than for God’s priests to live and yet not be what they had been? Matrons, children, and virgins alike, compelled by you, learned under your instruction to perform penance, although no sin had intervened and their innocence and chastity remained intact. Is this not a lesser misfortune?

You crushed the sexes and harassed the ages [Note: So the Germanensis manuscript. The printed editions read: “Having crushed the sex, you harassed the ages.”], etc. You imposed penance upon whole congregations. It was not undertaken by anyone voluntarily but exacted by you; nor did you act according to full periods of time, but according to persons. One performed penance for an entire year, another for a month, another scarcely for a full day, because you ordered penance [Note: The same Germanensis codex reads: “Another scarcely performed penance for a full day under you.”].

If consenting to unity, as you claim, is a sin, and if the guilt is similar, why is the penance not equal for the same offense?

## Donatist migrants residing in Rome have a schismatic bishop sent from Africa and, in place of a basilica, a cave outside the city for their gatherings [Note: From Optatus, book 2.]

Give the origin of your chair, you who wish to claim the holy Church for yourselves. But you also say that you possess some part in the city of Rome. It is a branch of your error, extended from falsehood and not from the root of truth.

Finally, if Macrobius were asked where he sits there, could he say, “In the chair of Peter”? I do not know whether he has even seen it with his eyes; and he does not approach the place commemorating him, behaving like a schismatic and acting against the Apostle, who says, “Sharing in the memorials of the saints” (Romans 12:13).

Behold, there are present there the memorials of two Apostles. Say whether he could enter these places or offer there [Note: So the Germanensis manuscript. The editions of Optatus read: “so that he might offer there.”] where it is established that the memorials of the saints are located.

It remains, therefore, that your associate Macrobius must admit that he sits where Encolpius once sat [Note: The Germanensis manuscript consistently reads “Enclopius.”]. If Encolpius himself could be questioned, he would say that he sits where Boniface of Bellita sat [Note: The same manuscript reads “Bellitanus.”]. Then, if he too could have been questioned, he would say where Victor of Garba sat, whom your people long ago sent from Africa to a few wandering individuals.

What is this, that your party in the city of Rome could not have a native bishop? What is this, that all the Africans and migrants in that city are known to have succeeded one another? Is the fraud not apparent? Is the faction, which is the mother of schism, not apparent?

Meanwhile, when Victor of Garba was to be sent here first, I do not say that he was a stone thrown into a fountain—for he was not strong enough to disturb the purity of the Catholic multitude—but because certain Africans had found residence in Rome pleasing and appeared to have gone out from you, they themselves requested that someone be sent from here to gather them.

Victor was therefore sent. There was there a son without a father, a recruit without a commander, a disciple without a teacher, a follower without a predecessor, a tenant without a house, a guest without hospitality, a shepherd without a flock, a bishop without a people. For the few who were there could not be called a flock or a people: among the forty—and however many more there were—basilicas, they had no place where they could gather.

Thus they enclosed a kind of cave outside the city with lattices [Note: The printed editions read “with barriers.” The Germanensis manuscript reads “with lattices,” which better suits the following verb, “enclosed.”], where at that time they might hold their assembly. From this they were called Montenses.
