Therefore, since Claudianus seems to have succeeded Lucianus, Lucianus Macrobius, Macrobius Encolpius, Encolpius Boniface, and Boniface Victor, if Victor were asked where he sat, he could show that no one had been there before him, nor point to any chair except one of pestilence.

## Constitution of Valentinian the Elder against those who rebaptize, in the year 373 [Note: See Augustine, Letter 105, no. 9.]

The emperors Valentinian and Valens, Augusti, to Julianus, proconsul of Africa:

We judge that a bishop who has doubled the holiness of baptism by an unlawful usurpation, and who has polluted that grace by repeating it contrary to the institutions of all, is unworthy of the priesthood. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of March at Trier, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian and Valens, Augusti.

## Constitution of Gratian against those who rebaptize, in the year 377

The emperors Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian, Augusti, to Flavianus, vicar of Africa [Note: Augustine mentions Flavianus, vicar of Africa, in Letter 87, no. 8.]:

We condemn the error of those who, trampling upon the commands of the Apostles, do not purify those who have received the sacraments of the Christian name by another baptism, but rather defile them, polluting them under the name of a washing. Your authority shall therefore order them to desist from their wretched errors, and shall restore to the Catholic Church the churches which they hold contrary to the faith.

For the institutions of those who have maintained the apostolic faith without alteration of baptism are to be followed. We wish nothing else to be commanded than what the faith and uncorrupted tradition of the Gospels and the Apostles have preserved, just as was also decreed by the divine laws of our parents Constantine, Constantius [Note: It may be necessary to substitute “Constans,” to whom Africa fell, or to add that name. See Augustine, Letter 105, nos. 9 and 12.], and Valentinian.

But many who have been expelled from the churches nevertheless rage with hidden fury, unlawfully frequenting the places of great houses or estates. Fiscal confiscation shall seize them if they provide secret places for impious doctrine, so that our sanction diminishes nothing from that rule which was established by the instruction formerly given to Nitentius.

If they love their error, let them, by their own misfortune and in domestic secrecy, nourish alone the men of impious discipline. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November at Constantinople, in the fourth consulship of Gratian Augustus and Merobaudes.

## Constitution of Theodosius the Elder against heretics, in the year 392, imposing a fine of ten pounds of gold; a later rescript of Arcadius and Honorius declared that the Donatists also, together with the other heretics, were included [Note: See book 3 against Cresconius, no. 51, and Letter 185, no. 25.]

The emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, Augusti, to Tatianus, praetorian prefect:

We decree that all persons who are found either to have ordained clerics among heretical sects or to have undertaken clerical office shall be fined individually ten pounds of gold. The place where forbidden practices are attempted shall likewise be added to the resources of our treasury if the owner’s connivance is established.

But if it is established that the owner was unaware of the matter, since it was carried on secretly, we order the tenant of that estate, if he is freeborn, to pay ten pounds of gold into our treasury. If he is descended from servile dregs and, despising the penalty because of his poverty, regards the loss as insignificant, he shall be beaten with clubs and condemned to deportation.

We further specifically provide that, if it was a landlord’s estate or one belonging to any public authority, and the tenant and manager allowed gatherings to be held, they shall be fined ten pounds of gold under the prescribed condemnation.

But if it is now revealed that any persons have assisted such rites and usurped for themselves the names of clerics, we order that ten pounds of gold be exacted from each of them and paid into the treasury. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July at Constantinople, in the third consulship of Arcadius and the consulship of Rufinus.

## Decree of the Council of Hippo, in the year 393, concerning the reception of Donatist clerics among the laypeople, confirmed at Carthage in 397

It was also decided that, since it was established in earlier councils that none of the Donatists should be received by us with his honor, but only among the number of the laity, this rule should indeed be maintained in their case for the sake of the salvation that must be denied to no one. The churches of Africa suffer such a shortage of clerics to be ordained that some places are entirely deserted [Note: Elsewhere, “has been handed down.”].

Nevertheless, an exception shall be made for those who are found not to have rebaptized, or for those who wish to cross over with their congregations into Catholic communion. For it is written that if two Christians agree, whatever they ask will be granted to them (Matthew 18:19).

There ought to be no doubt that, once the scandal of dissension among the whole people has been removed, those things which they committed by following the authority of their ancestors and repeating baptism may be abolished through the compensation of invited peace and the sacrifice of charity.

But it was decided that this matter should not be confirmed before the overseas Church had been consulted.

## Letter of the Council of Cabarsus, issued by the Donatist Maximianists against Primianus, the Donatist bishop of Carthage [Note: In the year of Christ 393.]

To the most holy brothers and colleagues throughout Africa, etc., Victorinus, Fortunatus, Victorianus, etc., and the others who were present with us in the council at Cabarsus: eternal salvation in the Lord.

No one, dearly beloved brothers, can be unaware that, concerning the priests of God, driven not by private will but by divine law, it is their duty both to pronounce judgment upon the guilty and rightly and justly to remove from the innocent a sentence inflicted upon them.

For whoever either spares the guilty or attempts to destroy the innocent will be subject to no slight danger, etc.

The remainder is to be sought from Sermon 2 on Psalm 36, no. 20.

## Judgment of the Council of Bagai, held by 310 Donatist bishops in favor of Primianus, pronounced against Maximianus, his ordainers, and his associates

When, by the will of almighty God and of Christ His Savior, we had come from all the provinces of Africa and were holding a council in the holy Church at Bagai, Gamalius, Primianus, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarius, Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatianus, and the others—three hundred and ten in number—it pleased the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish perpetual peace and cut away sacrilegious schisms.

A brotherhood united by the desires of peace and concord, etc.

The remaining portions are to be collected from books 3 and 4 against Cresconius and from the book on the Proceedings with Emeritus. Moreover, in book 4 against Cresconius, no. 46, the date of the Council of Bagai is noted as “during the consulship of the Augusti Arcadius III and Honorius for the second time, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May” [Note: In the year 394, on April 24.]

## Canon 48 of the Council of Carthage, held on September 1 or August 28, 397, concerning children baptized among the Donatists

Concerning the Donatists it was decided that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests Siricius [Note: The bishop of Rome.] and Simplicianus [Note: The bishop of Milan.] concerning only the infants baptized among them, so that, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a salutary purpose, the error of their parents—which they did not commit by their own judgment—might not prevent them from being advanced to become ministers of the sacred altar.

## Law of Honorius concerning incursions into churches [Note: From the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 2, “On Bishops, Churches, and Clerics,” etc.]

The emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Theodorus, praetorian prefect:

If anyone bursts into this kind of sacrilege, so that, rushing into Catholic churches, he inflicts any injury upon the priests and ministers, or upon the worship itself and the place, the matter shall be brought to the attention of the authorities through written reports from the officials, magistrates, curators, and the official notifications of the apparitors whom they call stationarii [Col. 0808], etc.

Thus the governor of the province shall know that the injury inflicted upon the priests and ministers of the Catholic Church, and upon the place itself and divine worship, is to be punished by a capital sentence against those convicted or confessing their guilt, etc.

But if a violent crowd cannot be brought before the authorities through the execution of the civil officials and the assistance of the officials or owners, because it protects itself with weapons or by the difficulty of the terrain, the African judges shall request an armed escort from the comes of Africa, a man of rank, by letters presenting the substance of this law, so that the perpetrators of such crimes may not escape.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May at Milan, in the third consulship of Honorius and the consulship of Eutychianus [Note: April 25, in the year 398.]

## Concerning the rescript obtained by the Donatists from Julian through flattering and deceptive petitions [Note: From the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 5, “On Heretics.”]

The same Augusti to Hadrianus, praetorian prefect:

We wish the rescript which the Donatists are said to have obtained from Julian, then emperor, to be posted before the most frequented places, together with the public notice, and the proceedings into which such an allegation has been inserted to be appended, so that it may become known to all both that the steadfastness of Catholic confidence has been established and that the Donatists’ despair is deceptive perfidy.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho and Aurelianus.

## Embassy of the Council of Carthage to consult Anastasius and Venerius concerning children baptized among the Donatists, so that they may be ordained clerics in the Catholic Church

After the consulship of Flavius Stilicho, a man of the highest rank, on the fourteenth—or sixteenth—day before the Kalends of July [Note: In the year of Christ 401, on June 18 or 16], at Carthage in the secretariat of the Basilica of Restituta, when Bishop Aurelius had taken his seat together with his fellow bishops and the deacons were standing by, Bishop Aurelius said:

Your Charity, most holy brothers, knows very well, together with me, the needs of the Churches established throughout Africa. Since the Lord has granted that the judgment of your holy assembly should be gathered here in some measure, it seems to me that we should bring before you these same needs, which our concern has enabled us to investigate.

When your sincerity has approved them, it follows that one of our number, a fellow priest, should be chosen who, with the Lord’s help and through your prayers, can undertake these very needs and diligently bring them to completion. He will proceed to the regions of Italy overseas, so that he may make known both to our holy brothers and fellow priests, the venerable holy brother Anastasius, bishop of the Apostolic See, and also the holy brother Venerius, priest of the Church of Milan, this very need, grief, and poverty of ours—for it was from these sees that the matter had been prohibited.

Let them know that provision must be made against a common danger, especially since there is such a great shortage of clerics that many Churches are so deserted that they cannot be found to possess even a single deacon, however unlearned. I think I should say nothing about the other, higher grades and offices, because, as I said, if a ministry of deacons is not easily found, it is absolutely certain that the higher dignities will be found even less easily.

We can no longer endure the daily lamentations of nearly lifeless congregations. Unless assistance is given them at some point, a grave and inexcusable responsibility before God for countless souls who are perishing will remain with us.

Therefore, since your unanimity acknowledges with me that it was established at the previous council that those who were baptized as infants among the Donatists, not yet able to know the destruction involved in their error, and who, after reaching an age capable of reason, recognized the truth, rejected their falsehood, and were received into the Catholic Church of God spread throughout the whole world, according to the ancient order, through the laying on of hands [Col. 0809], should not be prevented by the name of their former error from receiving the office of the clergy, etc.

Although some clerics of the same sect desire to cross over to us with their congregations and honors—men who, through love of honor, either persuade others toward life or retain them for salvation—I think this should be left to the more serious consideration of the brothers mentioned above. After weighing the substance of our petition with their wiser counsel, may they deign to inform us what they think should be done in this matter.

We are concerned only with those who were baptized as infants, so that, if it pleases you, your will may agree with ours concerning their ordination, etc.

## On reconciling the Donatists: the universal African Council of Carthage

In the consulship of Vincentius and Flavius, men of the highest rank, on the ides of September [Note: In the year 401, September 12], at Carthage in the secretariat of the Basilica of Restituta, when we bishops from all the provinces of Africa had assembled in council and taken our seats in the Church of Carthage—that is, Aurelius, bishop of that see, together with his colleagues, as their subscription makes clear—after the letters of our most blessed brother and fellow priest Anastasius, bishop of the Roman Church, had been read, in which he exhorted us with the concern and sincerity of paternal and fraternal charity not at all to disregard the plots and wickedness of the heretical and schismatic Donatists, by which they seriously harass the Catholic Church in Africa, we give thanks to our Lord because He was pleased to inspire that excellent and holy bishop with such pious care for the members of Christ, although they are situated in different lands but joined in one structure of the body.

Then, after everything that seemed relevant to the Church’s welfare had been considered and discussed, with the Spirit of God consenting and admonishing, we chose to deal gently and peacefully with the aforementioned people, although they had been cut off through restless dissension from the unity of the Lord’s body.

Thus, insofar as it lay within us, it might become thoroughly known throughout all the provinces of Africa to all who were entangled in their communion and association how wretched an error bound them—lest, as the Apostle says, while we correct those who think differently with gentleness, God might grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they might recover from the devil’s snares, having been taken captive by him for his will (2 Timothy 2:25–26).

Accordingly, it was decided that letters should be sent from our council to the African judges, from whom it seemed appropriate to request assistance, so that by their authority they might help the common mother, the Catholic Church, in whatever episcopal authority can be strengthened in the cities.

That is, by judicial power and diligence, in accordance with the Christian faith, they should investigate what was done in all the places where the Maximianists had obtained basilicas—the Maximianists who had formed a schism from them—and should have the matter entered in the public records, for the sake of firm knowledge necessary to all.

Then it was decided that letters should be sent to our brothers and fellow bishops, and especially to the Apostolic See, over which our aforementioned venerable brother and colleague Anastasius presides, so that he might know that Africa has a great need, for the peace and welfare of the Church, that any clerics among the Donatists who, having corrected their judgment, wish to cross over to Catholic unity should, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop governing the Church in that place, be received in their honors if this should seem beneficial to Christian peace.

This is just as it is manifest that it was done in the earlier periods of the same division, as the examples of many, indeed almost all, African Churches in which such an error arose testify.

This is not intended to dissolve the council that was held overseas concerning this matter, but to leave it in force for those who wish to cross over [Col. 0810] to the Catholic Church in such a way that no restoration of unity is brought about through them [Note: Elsewhere, “no cutting off.”].

But wherever Catholic unity appears capable of being either fully achieved or assisted through them, with the evident gain of their brothers’ souls, it should not harm them that the overseas council decreed something against their honors—although salvation has been closed to no one. That is, according to the overseas council, those who were ordained in Donatus’s party, if they wished to cross over to the Catholic Church after correcting themselves, were not to be received in their honors; but this should not apply to those through whom Catholic unity is being advanced.

Then it was decided that, after these matters had been completed, envoys for proclaiming the peace and unity without which Christian salvation cannot be obtained should be sent from our number to the Donatists themselves—both to those whom they have as bishops and to their congregations.

Through these envoys it should be made known to all what grounds they have, and how little, for speaking justly against the Catholic Church. Above all, it should become clear to everyone, even through the municipal records, for the sake of the reliability of the documentation, what they themselves did against their own schismatic Maximianists.

There, if they are willing to pay attention, God demonstrates to them that the Maximianists were then cut off from the unity of the Church just as unjustly as they now proclaim that the Maximianists formed a schism from them.

Yet from their number they later received again, in their former honors, those whom they had already condemned by the authority of their plenary council [Note: The Council of Bagai]; they accepted the baptism administered by those whom they had condemned and expelled.

Let them see, then, with what foolish hearts they resist the peace of the Church spread throughout the whole world, when they do such things for Donatus’s party. They do not say that they are contaminated by the communion of those whom they received in this way for the sake of peace; yet they contend that we—that is, the Catholic Church established even in the remotest regions of the earth—are polluted through communion with those whom they were then unable to convict when they accused them [Note: Elsewhere, “condemn” or “despise.”].

## Decree of the Council of Carthage, held by all Africa under the consulship of Theodosius Augustus and Rumoridus, a man of the highest rank, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [Note: In the year 403, August 25.]

Aurelius, bishop, said: “What has come under discussion at Your Charity’s initiative, I think ought to be confirmed by ecclesiastical records. For the declaration of all of you has brought out that each one of us should, in his own city, personally summon the leaders of the Donatists, or join to himself a neighboring colleague, so that together they may summon them in each and every city or place through the magistrates or the elders of the localities. If this pleases everyone, let it be proclaimed.” All the bishops said: “It pleases everyone, and we have all confirmed this by our signatures. We also request that Your Holiness subscribe on behalf of all to the letters sent from the council to the judges.”

Aurelius, bishop, said: “If it seems good to Your Charity, let the form of their summons be read aloud, so that, if it pleases, we may all adhere to this wording of the proceeding.” All the bishops said: “Let it be read.” Laetus, the notary, read it aloud.

### Form of the Summons of the Donatists

That bishop of the Catholic Church said: “What we have obtained from the authority of that most exalted see [Note: [Col. 0810] By the designation ‘most exalted see,’ Baronius, under the year 403, understands ‘the Apostolic See of the city of Rome,’ and believes that ‘letters sent from it’ are requested to be read here, ‘by which what had been obtained from it might be made known.’ In fact, the matter here concerns the authority itself which was soon requested through the petitions of this same Council of Carthage and obtained from Septiminus, the proconsul—or from the seat of the vicariate prefecture—the authority to draw up the records. Hence it is said, ‘When the order had been read aloud,’ namely, that of the ‘most exalted see’; by that order the magistrates were instructed to grant the Catholic bishops the power to summon the Donatists through public documents. This is also called the ‘most illustrious see’ and the ‘see of illustrious authorities’ in the Carthaginian Conference, 3, chapters 167 and 170.] we request that Your Eminence have read aloud, attached to the records, and carried into effect.”

When the order had been read aloud and attached to the acts, that bishop of the Catholic Church said: “May it please Your Eminence to hear the mandate to be conveyed to the Donatists through you, insert it in the records, convey it to them, and again make their response known to us in your records.

“We have come, sent by the authority of our Catholic council, desiring to rejoice in your correction, mindful of the charity of the Lord, who said, ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God’ (Matthew 5:9), and who admonished us through the prophet that we ought to say even to those who say that they are not our brothers, ‘You are our brothers’ (Isaiah 66:5, according to the Septuagint). Therefore you ought not to despise this peaceful admonition of ours, which proceeds from charity. If you think that you possess any truth, do not hesitate to assert it—that is, assemble your council and choose from among yourselves those to whom you may entrust the defense of your position. We too will be able to do this, so that from our council there may likewise be chosen men who, together with those whom you have chosen, at a place and time fixed by agreement, may peacefully discuss whatever issue separates your communion from ours. Then, at last, with the help of the Lord our God, may this long-standing error come to an end, lest, on account of human animosity, weak souls and ignorant peoples perish in sacrilegious dissension.

“For if you accept this in a brotherly spirit, the truth will easily become clear. But if you are unwilling to do this, your distrust will easily become apparent.”

### Petition Presented by the Same Council of Carthage, Representing All Africa, to Septiminus the Proconsul

“We request your equity, Septiminus, most illustrious man and most exalted of proconsuls. The Catholic Church suffers many things from the heretics of the party of Donatus, contrary to divine and human laws. If we wished to request that these things be prohibited and abolished by earlier or more recent imperial orders, they ought by no means to dare complain about our actions, knowing that, although they were aided by no such law, they nevertheless arranged through the orders of judges that their schismatic Maximianists be driven and expelled from their places and seats.

“Nevertheless, peacefully providing for their salvation and for our own reputation, and on account of the charity by which we are Christians, we wish gently to admonish them not to neglect, by considering and acknowledging it, their error; or, if they think that they possess some truth, not to defend it through the frenzied violence of the Circumcellions against the public peace, but through a calm presentation of reason.

“Therefore we request Your Sublimity that, when we wish to admonish them about this matter through the magistrates, whether in the cities or in the territories belonging to them, you order that the records be made available to us and that they be honorably summoned on the basis of our allegation. Having obtained this, we shall render abundant thanks to Your Excellency before God.

“Given by all the Catholic bishops from the Council of Carthage, in the consulship of Our Lord Theodosius, Most Pious and August, and Rumoridus, most illustrious man, on the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0811] In the year 403, on September 13], at Carthage.”

Septiminus, most illustrious man and proconsul, said: “In every place the bishops of the venerable law are granted, by the authority of public order, the power to draw up records; this power is also limited by the wording of this instruction, so that they may understand that they are to require the teachers of the misguided people [Note: [Col. 0811] Perhaps *magistri*, that is, the bishops of the Donatists, at the request of the Catholics, etc.] to give a reasoned account of their own persuasion, in order that the friendly moderation of the law may be preserved when the matters at issue have been brought into the open and superstition has been suppressed.”

### Embassy of the Council of Carthage against the Donatists to the Emperor Honorius, and the Memorandum Given to the Envoys

In the sixth consulship of the most glorious Emperor Honorius Augustus, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0811] In the year of Christ 404], at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district. At this council Theasius and Evodius undertook an embassy against the Donatists. The memorandum inserted in the council reads as follows.

### Memorandum for the Brothers Theasius and Evodius, Envoys Sent from the Council of Carthage to the Most Glorious and Most Religious Princes

“When, with the Lord’s help, they have approached the most pious emperors, let them inform them how, with full confidence and in accordance with the council of the preceding year, the leaders of the Donatists were summoned through municipal records, so that, if they trusted in their assertions, they might select from their number suitable men to confer peacefully with us and, with Christian gentleness, not hesitate to demonstrate whatever truth they held. In this way the sincerity of the Catholic position, which had long ago been made clear in earlier times, might now also become known to those who resist through ignorance or obstinacy.

“But because they were oppressed by distrust, they scarcely dared to make any response. Therefore, since the episcopal and peaceful duty toward them has been fulfilled, and since those who were unable to answer the truth have turned to savage violence—so that they have overwhelmed many bishops and many clergy, to say nothing of laypeople, by ambushes, and have also invaded some churches and attempted to invade others—it is now for their clemency to take measures so that the Catholic Church, which religiously bore them in Christ in her womb and nourished them with the firmness of faith, may also be protected through their foresight, lest reckless men prevail by terrifying weak peoples in religious times, since they cannot corrupt them by seduction.

“For the detestable hand of the Circumcellions, in whose fury they rage, is well known and has often been denounced by the laws; it has also been condemned by the frequent sanctions of those most religious emperors themselves. Against their fury we could obtain protections that are neither unfamiliar nor alien to the Holy Scriptures, since the apostle Paul, as is known to the faithful from the Acts of the Apostles, also removed the conspiracy of factional men with military assistance (Acts 23:12–33).

“But we request that protection be provided without any concealment to the Catholic orders of the churches [Note: [Col. 0812] Elsewhere: ‘to the Catholic churches of the orders’] throughout the individual cities and to the owners of neighboring estates in their various localities.

“At the same time, it should be requested that the law promulgated by their father of revered memory, Theodosius, concerning ten pounds of gold imposed upon those who ordain or are ordained as heretics, and also upon owners wherever their assembly is discovered, be henceforth confirmed in such a way that it may apply to those against whom Catholics, provoked by their ambushes, have lodged a formal complaint. Thus, at least through this terror, may those desist from schismatic or heretical depravity who, by consideration of eternal punishment, refuse to be corrected and reformed.

“It should also be requested that the law which denies heretics the power to receive or leave anything by gifts or wills be renewed by their piety to this extent: that it deprive of the right to leave or receive property those who, blinded by the madness of obstinacy, wish to persist in the error of the Donatists.

“Nevertheless, for those who wish to correct themselves out of consideration for unity and peace, the way to receive an inheritance should remain open, without the prohibition of this law, if anything came to them by gift or inheritance while they were still established in heretical error. Those, however, should be excepted who, having been brought before a court, have thought that they ought to pass over to the Catholic Church; for it is credible of such people that they preferred Catholic unity not through fear of heavenly judgment but rather from desire for earthly advantage.

“For all these matters, the protection of whatever authorities belong to the provinces is necessary. We decree that, for the interests of the Church, the embassy be given free authority to undertake and order whatever they understand to be beneficial.

“Moreover, it has pleased all of us that letters from our assembly be directed to the most glorious emperors and the most eminent authorities, informing them that, with the unanimous consent of all of us, envoys have been sent by us to the most blessed imperial court. But since it takes an extremely long time for all to subscribe to the same letters, and lest the letters be burdened by the signatures of individuals, we request you, brother Aurelius, that Your Charity deign to subscribe in the name of all of us.”

And they subscribed.

“Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, have agreed to this decree and subscribed.” Likewise, the remaining bishops subscribed.

Letters are also to be sent to the judges, so that, until the Lord permits the envoys to return to us, they may provide protection through the civic authorities and the owners of the estates of the Catholic Church.

### Law of Honorius against Those Who Rebaptize

[Note: [Col. 0813] The Theodosian Code, book 4, *Concerning Holy Baptism*.]

The Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augustuses, to Hadrianus, Praetorian Prefect.

“We have taken care, by the authority of this decree, to eradicate the adversaries of the Catholic faith. Therefore, by a new constitution, we have judged that the sect should be specifically destroyed which, lest it be called a heresy, preferred the designation of schism.

“For those whom they call Donatists are said to have advanced so far in wickedness that, trampling upon the sacred mysteries, they repeat holy Baptism with harmful presumption and infect, by the profane contagion of repetition, people once washed, as tradition records, by the gift of divinity.

“Thus it has happened that heresy was born from schism. From this point, a flattering error invites credulous minds to hope for a second pardon. For it is easy to persuade sinners that forgiveness once granted can be granted again; and if it can be granted again in the same manner, we do not understand why it should be denied a third time.

“These people also pollute slaves and persons subject to their own legal authority with the sacrilege of repeated Baptism. Therefore we enact by this law that anyone henceforth discovered to have rebaptized someone be brought before the judge who presides over the province, so that, punished by the publication of all his property, he may suffer the penalty of poverty, to be inflicted upon him permanently.

“Yet their property is not to perish for their children if the children dissent from the depravity of their father’s association. If the children themselves have perhaps become entangled in the savagery of their father’s depravity and now prefer to return to the Catholic religion, access to the acquisition of these goods is not to be denied them.

“Moreover, those places or estates which are subsequently found to have provided concealment for such deadly sacrileges are to be applied to the imperial treasury, provided that the master or mistress is proved either to have been present or to have given consent. These persons are also to be marked by infamy, branded upon them by sentence.

“But if it is proved that such a crime was committed in the house by their tenant or agent without the knowledge of the owners, the decision to confiscate the estates is to be suspended, while the perpetrators of the crime are to be punished with exile to the lead mines, in which they shall remain for their whole lives.

“And lest it perhaps be possible to conceal in silence, within domestic walls, the knowledge of a crime committed under religious obligation, those who may be compelled to rebaptize shall have the opportunity of fleeing to the Catholic Church, so that, under its protection, they may be defended against the authors of this crime and association by the protection of the liberty granted to them. They shall be permitted under this condition to preserve the faith which their masters attempted to extort from them against their will.

“Nor ought defenders of Catholic doctrine to be compelled by law, in the manner in which those placed under another’s authority are compelled, to commit the offense; and it is especially fitting that all people, without any distinction of condition or status, be guardians of the holiness infused from heaven.

“Let those who have not feared to repeat Baptism at the hands of the persons mentioned above, or who by consenting to this crime have condemned themselves by their own participation in this association, know that they are permanently denied not only the right to make a will, but also the ability to acquire anything under the appearance of a gift or through the execution of contracts, unless by returning to the true faith they correct the error of their depraved mind through a change of purpose.

“Let the same penalty likewise constrain those who have shown compliance with the forbidden assemblies or ministries of the persons mentioned, so that the governors of the provinces, if they have thought that consent should be extended in contempt of this sanction, may know that they are to be fined twenty pounds of gold [Col. 0814]. Their offices, too, are to be subjected to a similar condemnation.

“Let the leading men or defenders of the cities know that, unless they have carried out what we command, or unless violence has been inflicted upon the Catholic Church in their presence, they too are to be subject to the same fine.”

Given on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, in the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius [Note: [Col. 0814] In the year 405, on February 12].

Other laws of Honorius against the Donatists, issued in the same year, are found above, before the books against Cresconius, columns 445–446.

### Decree of the Council Held under the Consulship of Stilicho for the Second Time and Anthemius, Most Illustrious Men, on the Tenth Day before the Kalends of September

[Note: [Col. 0814] In the year 405, on August 23], at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district.

“Since unity has been achieved only at Carthage, let letters also be sent to the judges, so that they may order efforts toward unity to be undertaken in the other provinces and cities as well.

“Let thanksgiving on behalf of the Church of Carthage for all Africa, concerning the exclusion of the Donatists, be sent to the imperial court together with the letters of the bishops.

“The letter of Pope Innocent was read aloud: bishops should not readily travel overseas; this is also confirmed by the decisions of the bishops themselves.

“On account of thanksgiving and the exclusion of the Donatists, let two clerics of the Church of Carthage be sent to the imperial court.”

### Decree of the Council Held in the Consulship of the Emperors Honorius VII and Theodosius II, on the Ides of June

[Note: [Col. 0814] In the year 407, on June 13], at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district.

“Those peoples who have been converted from the Donatists and have had bishops are unquestionably to be allowed to have them, without consultation of the council. But if a people has had a bishop and, after his death, wishes not to have a bishop of its own but to belong to the diocese of some other bishop, this is not to be denied them.

“Moreover, it was brought forward that, before the law of the emperors concerning unity was enacted [Note: [Col. 0814] The Edict of Unity, above, before the work against Cresconius, columns 445–446], whichever bishops converted peoples to the Catholic Church should themselves retain them.

“Yet from the law of unity onward, all the churches ought to claim for themselves the Catholic bishops of those places to which the places had belonged under the heretics, whether of those converted to the Catholic Church or of the heretics who were not converted; and likewise the dioceses and, if there happen to be any, the church documents or property belonging to its right. But whoever has usurped anything after the law shall restore what was usurped when summoned to do so.”

At the Council held at Carthage in the following year, 408, on June 16, Bishop Fortunatianus again undertook an embassy against the pagans and heretics. At another council of the same year, 408, held at Carthage on October 13, Bishops Restitutus and Florentius undertook an embassy against the pagans and heretics, at the time when Severus and Macarius were killed; and on their account Bishops Evodius, Theasius, and Victor were slain.

The purpose of the embassy may be learned from Augustine’s Letter 97 to Olympius, section 2: namely, that by a new imperial edict the enemies of the Church might learn that those laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics which had been sent while Stilicho was alive had been established by the will of the most pious emperor. Whether they claim that these laws were made without his knowledge or against his will, deceitfully or in earnest, they thereby make the minds of the ignorant exceedingly turbulent and dangerously and vehemently hostile to the Catholics. Hence the occasion for the subsequent laws.

### Law of Honorius Confirming the Earlier Constitutions against Heretics

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augustuses, to Curtius, Praetorian Prefect.

[Col. 0815] “Everything that we have decreed by the authority of general laws against the Donatists, who are also called Montenses, the Manichaeans, the Priscillianists, or the Gentiles, we determine not only to remain in force but also to be carried into full execution and effect. Thus even the buildings belonging to these groups, or to the Caelicolists, who hold gatherings of some new and unknown doctrine, are to be claimed for the churches.

“The penalty established by the law must be imposed upon those who confess themselves to be Donatists or who refuse communion with the Catholics under the pretext of an evil religion, although they pretend to be Christians, and so forth.”

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of December at Rome, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus [Note: [Col. 0815] On November 15 of the year 408].

The same Augustuses. “Hail, Donatus” [Note: [Col. 0815] Augustine’s Letter 100 to Donatus, proconsul of Africa, is extant]. “K. NB.” [Note: [Col. 0815] “K. NB.” means “dearest to us.” See Morel, *Elementa Critica*, p. 139. M.]

“The new and unprecedented audacity of the Donatist heretics and of the Jews has been exposed: they wish to disturb the sacraments of the Catholic faith, and this plague and contagion spreads and flows ever more widely. Therefore we order that the punishment of just retribution be inflicted upon those who attempt anything contrary and opposed to the Catholic sect” [Note: [Col. 0815] The Theodosian Code, book 44, *Concerning Heretics*].

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December at Ravenna, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus [Note: [Col. 0815] In the year 408, on November 24].

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augustuses, to Theodorus, Praetorian Prefect.

“Lest the Donatists, or the vanity of the remaining heretics and other groups whose reverence for Catholic communion cannot be persuaded, and the Jews and Gentiles whom the common people call pagans, suppose that the provisions of the laws previously issued against them have grown weak, let all judges know that they must obey those commands with faithful devotion. Above all, they must not doubt that whatever we have decreed against them is to be carried out.

“If any judge, out of a spirit of connivance, should omit the execution of this present law, let him know that, having lost his dignity, he will undergo a more severe punishment at the hands of Our Clemency. His staff, too, which has failed to serve his own safety through a sufficient report, is to be punished by a condemnation of twenty pounds of gold, after three chief officials have been punished [Note: [Col. 0815] The Theodosian Code, book 46, *Concerning Heretics*].

“Let the men of the municipal order also know that, if they have kept silent about such a matter being committed in their own cities or territories to favor the guilty, they will suffer the penalty of deportation and the loss of their own property.”

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February at Ravenna, in the consulship of the emperors Honorius VII and Theodosius III [Note: [Col. 0815] January 16 of the year 409].

At the council held at Carthage on June 14 of the year 410, Bishops Florentius, Possidius, Praesidius, and Benenatus undertook an embassy against the Donatists, at the time when the law was issued providing that each person should freely choose to embrace Christian worship. On that occasion Honorius issued the following edict.

### Edict of Honorius Abrogating the Law by Which Freedom of Choice Had Been Granted to Heretics

[Note: [Col. 0815] The Theodosian Code, book 51, *Concerning Heretics*.]

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Heraclianus, Count of Africa.

“With the oracle wholly removed by which heretical superstitions had crept into their rites, let all enemies of the holy law know that they will be punished by the penalties of confiscation and blood if, with the detestable audacity of their crime, they attempt thereafter to assemble publicly.”

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Varane, most illustrious man [Note: [Col. 0815] August 25 of the year 410].

## First Day of the Carthaginian Conference

[Note: [Col. 0815] June 1 of the year of Christ 411.]

### Beginning

After the consulship of Varane, most illustrious man, on the Kalends of June, at Carthage [Col. 0816], in the record office of the Gargilian Baths, with Sebastianus, Maximianus, and Petrus, most devoted men and imperial bodyguards, present; with Ursus, Petronius, and Libosus, officers of the rank of two hundred thousand sesterces; Bonifatius and Evasius, attendants of the illustrious and eminent authorities; Filetus, attendant of the illustrious imperial household; Exitiosus, assistant to the chief clerk; Possidius, Quodvultdeus, and Colonicus, assistants to the record office of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished proconsul; Navigius, assistant to the numerical office of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished vicar; Nampius, secretary of the office of the most illustrious man, the envoy of sacred Carthage; Rufinianus, secretary of the most illustrious man, curator of exalted Carthage; with Hilarius and Praetextatus, recorders of Our Lord’s Most Victorious and Most Glorious Emperor and of the distinguished proconsul; Fabius, recorder of Our Lord’s Most Victorious and Most Glorious Emperor and of the distinguished vicar; and Romulus, recorder of the most illustrious man, envoy of sacred Carthage; with Januarius and Vitalis, notaries of the Catholic Church; and Victor and Cresconius, notaries of the Donatist Church—Ursus, officer of the rank of two hundred thousand sesterces of the illustrious and eminent authorities, said:

“Some time ago Your Sublimity, in accordance with the imperial command, dispatched both us and the others who have been assigned to the official duties of Your Sublimity, whether from the most sacred imperial household or from the African offices, to the individual provinces. You also sent edicts throughout all Africa, so that all Catholic and Donatist bishops were required to be present at the Conference within four months. That period appears to expire today.

“And since everyone is present, from all the African provinces—namely, from the proconsular province, the province of Byzacena, Numidia, the Mauritanias Sitifensis and Caesariensis, and also the province of Tripolitana—if Your Nobility so orders, let these same venerable men appear, so that everything may proceed in its proper order.”

Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the venerable men whom you report to be present appear.”

All the bishops of the party of Donatus entered. Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, and Possidius, bishops of the Catholic Church, also entered, together with their fellow bishops Novatus, Florentius, Maurentius, Bonifatius, Priscus, Serenianus, and Scyllacius, and Deuterius, Leo, Asterius, and Restitutus, likewise bishops and custodians of the records.

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said:

“I would certainly wish that the holiness of so great a multitude, which is reckoned under the one religion of Christ God, be separated by no disagreement among its members. But since it is certain that God now wishes what the error of the ancient enemy once introduced to be corrected, lest the true religion should for a longer time make itself a spectacle to the Gentiles through its contention, although I recognize that this judgment exceeds my merit, since I appear to judge those by whom it would rather have been fitting for me to be judged, nevertheless, because it is certain that this case is to be conducted with God looking on and the angels as witnesses, and that, under the examination of heavenly faith, it will bring either a reward if approved or judgment if violated, so that at last the truth may shine forth more clearly through the disputations of the bishops present, let the imperial sanction first be read aloud, so that everyone may understand in what manner and form the inquiry is to be received, although it is sufficiently clear that it is already known to all.”

### Command of Honorius Concerning the Holding of the Conference, Read on the First Day of the Conference

The Emperors, Caesars, Flavii, Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, victorious, triumphing, ever Augustuses, to their Flavius Marcellinus, greetings.

“Among the greatest concerns of our empire, reverence for the Catholic law is always either first or alone. For we undertake nothing through the labors of war or arrange anything through counsels of peace except that the devoted people of our world may preserve the true worship of God. It was also fitting that the Donatists be brought to this by fear or admonition, since through vain error and needless dissension they discolor Africa—that is, the greatest part of our realm, which faithfully serves its secular offices.

“Nevertheless, we do not hesitate to repeat frequently what the devoted authority of all emperors before us has determined in regard to God [Col. 0817], lest posterity, by a just judgment, be able to charge us with anything that may have arisen in our time to the injury of the Catholic law.

“Nor is the saying of the heavenly oracle hidden from our conscience [Note: [Col. 0817] That is, the law repealed by the law of the year 410, above, column 815], which the evil interpretation of the Donatists professes can contribute to their error. Although it invited depraved minds more gently to correction, we nevertheless ordered it abolished even earlier, lest it provide any opportunity for superstitions.

“Now also, by a similar authority, we judge that this surreptitious measure must be excluded, and we rightly declare that we willingly remove what had been established, lest anyone suppose that, with us as its authors, he can sin against divine worship.

“And although there is one clear judgment shared by all, namely, that the full truth of the Catholic law has been approved by the proper worship of human beings and by heavenly judgment, we have gladly accepted, out of zeal for peace and favor toward the venerable bishops, the embassy which desires that the Donatist bishops be assembled at the gathering of the most renowned city, so that, after priests chosen by both sides have been selected and discussions have been held, manifest reason may refute superstition.

“We order that this matter be explained within four months, so that our clemency may also more quickly recognize, as it desires, the conversion of the minds of the peoples.

“But if the Donatist bishops deliberately avoid assembling within the prescribed time, let the period of the contumacious be brought to a close by the summons of three edicts. When these have been issued and their periods completed, if they disdain to be present after being summoned, let the people, together with their churches, yield—those people who have learned in silence that their teachers have been defeated—and let them at last rejoice that they have been conquered, and know that, if not our commands, they must obey the true mandates of the Catholic law.

“Over this disputation we wish you to sit as judge in the principal place; whatever you previously received in your instructions, you remember fully. We wish you to undertake all responsibility both for assembling the bishops and for summoning them if they refuse to appear, so that you may be able to fulfill with approved diligence both what was commanded earlier and what you now recognize has been established.

“Above all, you are to preserve intact and inviolate whatever antiquity once ordered concerning the Catholic law, whatever the religious authority of our fathers established, or whatever Our Serenity strengthened, after removing the novel surreptitious measure [Note: [Col. 0817] In the Theodosian Code, book 3, *Concerning Religious Matters*, the reading is ‘superstition.’ Nevertheless, ‘surreptitious measure’ is not inappropriate here, that is, a law issued through a kind of surreptitious maneuver by which freedom of choice was granted to heretics. This is what they call the ‘heavenly oracle’ shortly before, and also ‘the surreptitious measure must be excluded.’ See above, the law of the year 410].

“Indeed, lest suitable assistance be lacking for your official duties, Our Serenity has admonished the distinguished Proconsul and Vicar that, if they wish to retain the status of their own dignities and to avoid the extreme penalties imposed upon their staff, they should arrange for a sufficient number of necessary men to be assigned both from their own offices and from the staffs of all the judges.

“It will now be your concern to report, by sending reports, anything that you discover to be delayed by any device, so that fitting correction may punish the negligent.

“You should report everything, whether the disputation completed by the bishops gathered together has confirmed it, or whether, if they perhaps withdraw, a decision has been issued concerning the contumacious, so that we may more quickly recognize what benefit our command has produced for the confirmation of the Catholic faith.

“And by the divine hand: Farewell, Marcellinus, dearest to us.

“Given on the day before the Ides of October at Ravenna, in the consulship of Varane, most illustrious man [Note: [Col. 0817] On October 14 of the year 410].”

### First Edict of Marcellinus, Sent through the Provinces to Summon the Bishops of Both Parties
What the most merciful emperor, our lord Honorius, decreed for the confirmation of the Catholic faith is shown by the tenor of the foregoing documents. For, gladly receiving the embassy of the venerable bishops, he did not permit Africa, always devoted to his empire, to be disturbed and disfigured any longer by its various kinds [Col. 0818] of religious division. In his zeal for peace and faith, he wished the dissensions of so many peoples, arising from an ancient persuasion, to be quieted by the manifestation of the truth, so that, after he had perceived that they could not be quieted by the imperial sanctions previously issued by him and drawn toward one judgment of faith, he might recall them after a hearing of both parties. For he wished all the bishops, both of the Catholic and of the Donatist party, to be assembled together, so that, after more experienced men had been chosen from each side and the truth of the faith had been examined, clear reason might refute superstition. Thus whatever each person thought could properly be advanced on behalf of his party would be brought into the open, and so the light of the true faith, even if late, might shine forth.

Indeed, the concordant petition of both parties appealed to this imperial decision. For just as a Collation had recently been requested by the Catholics, so it is beyond doubt that, shortly before, the Donatist bishops had requested a Collation before the judgment of illustrious authorities. And since the imperial clemency readily granted its assent and decreed that a universal council should be held within Africa, he wished me, at the just request of both parties, to sit as judge in the first place over this dispute.

Accordingly, by the tenor of this edict I admonish all the bishops throughout Africa, both of the Catholic party and of the Donatist party, not to delay assembling in the splendid city of Carthage for the holding of the council within the period prescribed by law, namely within four months—a period that will undoubtedly end on the day before the Kalends of June—lest the party whose absence is established appear to have judged the merits of its own faith [Note: [Col. 0818] Perhaps, “to have doubted.”]. I likewise summon, with the same admonition, all the administrators of the provinces, magistrates, and members of the municipal orders, as well as the agents, procurators, and elders of the individual places, under penalty of their own reputation and dignity and at the peril of their safety, to hasten to cause the bishops of both parties to assemble in the cities and places where they reside, either by the drafting of official records or by some surviving written document.

And if they cannot be found in the cities at that very time, let them also be sought through the countryside, and let both the form of the imperial command and the tenor of this edict be made known to them, so that within these four months I may learn, through reports from the municipal orders, the will of each party.

I also wish the bishops of the Donatist party to know that, if any one of them replies that he will attend, the church with all its rights—which may happen to be held by the Catholics in accordance with the imperial command—is to be handed over to him without any delay by men of the municipal order. If, however, all of them, or each one [Note: [Col. 0818] Perhaps, “each individually.”] in his own place, reply that they will attend, then the churches and those places that are established to have belonged to them or to have been held by them are to be restored to their right and possession through the intervention of the aforesaid orders, so that, after their status has first been restored to them, the beginning of the discussion may be made.

And since the most august Emperor wished to entrust me with the substance of so great a matter, I also freely acknowledge that, if any hesitation is raised concerning my person, I shall not refuse to have another judge sit with me, chosen by the Donatists themselves from their party and faith [Note: [Col. 0818] Perhaps, “of the Donatist party.”], of either higher or equal rank. Whether I shall be present as the judge in this matter with another or alone, I promise, by the admirable mystery of the Trinity, by the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation, and by the safety of the aforementioned Emperors, that I shall judge nothing other than what the examined arguments of the parties are able to demonstrate and what faith discovers to be true.

Nor could I leave unsaid this point, so that they may know that, whether judgment is given in favor of the Donatists or of the Catholics, the bishops of the Donatists will suffer no trouble at all, but will return to their own homes free and removed from every kind of injury. I promise that I shall act in this way, both by the dread of the day of judgment and by the sacraments mentioned above [Col. 0819].

All those who had been assigned to the individual provinces should know that from now on they must in no way summon or otherwise trouble any of the Donatists, or cause them any difficulty through the previous enforcement [Note: That is, the law of the year 410], unless they prefer, for their contempt of the more recent command, to be subjected to punishment.

It shall nevertheless be permitted to all the people of the Donatist party to complain about the extortions and plunderings of those who were sent, if they know that any such things have been committed, so that, once the character of the crimes has been established, a fitting vengeance may proceed against the offenders.

And in another hand: Let it be posted.

## Marcellinus’s second edict, posted in the presence of the bishops at Carthage, concerning the place and procedure of the Collation

The magnitude of this matter, undertaken for the recognition of truth and religion, even if it were assessed with too little consideration of its importance, nevertheless ought to be weighed by the very seriousness and authority of those conducting the dispute. For no one is unaware how weighty is the case that is to be discussed among persons who are bishops.

But since the august dignity has entrusted me with the hearing of this dispute and has given me as judge to those whom, out of reverence for so great a name, I recognize to be superior to me, I have taken thought for the concern of my faith in this respect: I wished to be judged by my own judgment. Therefore, on the authority of this posting, I have decided that all the bishops of both parties must be warned first of all that they should know that no more than seven bishops from each party will have a mutual conference with one another; these are the men whom the choice of their respective parties will have substituted for the duty of disputing.

For imperial authority has ordered a fixed number to be chosen from each party. There will also be another seven from each side, selected by the judgment of the bishops of their respective parties. Having maintained throughout the entire conference the restraint of silence, they are to understand that they are present only for this purpose: if any one of the seven disputants from either side wishes to confer with one of his colleagues, he may withdraw there with him to one side, and, after patiently discussing the matter through shared deliberation, return to his proper place, preserving the dignity of his office. In this way, the one who needs the advice may silently commend what he must hear, while the one whose duty it is may confirm by speaking what he has undertaken.

The most suitable place for the Collation will be the Baths of Gargilianus. On the Kalends of June, only those bishops who have been designated are to assemble there. From this it is entirely clear that no gathering of the people at all should take place there, since even all the bishops themselves are not permitted to assemble. For when the patience required for disputation, which is friendly only to silence, dreads every uproar of a crowd gathered in ranks, it makes no difference whether it is hindered by a mass of people or by a throng of bishops.

Therefore, let only the bishops mentioned assemble at the place and time prescribed. Yet all the remaining bishops of both parties, before the day appointed for the examination, must declare by letters sent to my office that they will regard as valid whatever has been done by their seven fellow bishops on either side. In these letters, moreover, let them all add before me the testimony of their own signatures. For it is entirely just that the whole Collation should be promised as valid by all those who are chosen by all.

Therefore, let no layperson or bishop attempt to enter that most peaceful place of the council beyond the prescribed number, contrary to the prohibition. Rather, let them also admonish their own congregations with a pious exhortation to quiet and modesty, first treating the matter throughout their own churches, so that the whole multitude may keep away from the day and place of the disputation and may prepare the people, softened by the religious discipline of patience, for Christian peace [Note: Compare Augustine, Sermon 358, no. 6, vol. 5].

For not only the bishops but also the rational people agree with this judgment: while the aforesaid men are disputing and seeking the truth, with the mind fixed upon a matter of greater importance, nothing disorderly, nothing tumultuous, and finally nothing [Col. 0820] untimely should make a disturbance. For in order that what will benefit the salvation of all may afterward be made public, those examining the truth must first be granted privacy.

As for me, my judgment must be promulgated in every respect in such a way that, once released into public knowledge, it may be weighed with the entire population of splendid Carthage as judge. In this way the whole course of the completed dispute will be laid open to the eyes not only of this city but also of the entire province, so that both the arguments of the disputing bishops and the sequence of my pronouncements may be set forth in volumes arranged and published for the public. For this is the security of faith in a judge: that he does not fear being judged concerning himself.

Therefore, so that no slanderous suspicion may intrude in any way upon the examination by which truth is elicited, and so that the clear light which the faith of evident proofs will cleanse for the minds of the public may not be covered by any clouds of accusation from either party, let all know that, against the disguises of suspicion and the devices of deception, it has necessarily been provided not only that this procedure ought to be observed but also that it is advantageous: namely, that, while I first subscribe in every respect to my own statements, all the disputing bishops likewise subscribe, without any excuse whatever, to all their arguments on the sheet.

For the merit of faith requires that, against one who might perhaps attempt by his assertions to withdraw assent from the truth and to deny what he has said, the authority of his own testimony should also stand, wherever victory benefits truth alone.

Those who perform the duty of recording the proceedings, apart from those who wait upon my office in the public duties, must also be accompanied by four ecclesiastical notaries from each party in alternating order. So that their trustworthiness may not waver through any ambiguity, four bishops chosen from each party by the judgment of their fellows are to be placed over them, in order that they may guard the same recorders and notaries with vigilant and careful supervision.

Thus, leaving with those recorders and notaries in turn, they are to ensure that what has been said is subsequently made clear in an orderly written record, so that, while the aforesaid bishops are still engaged in the dispute, some portion of the question that has been settled may nevertheless pass into clear written documents, and may immediately give prompt information to the public expectation, with the subscription of the seven bishops appended.

After the first day of the Collation, the following day shall be assigned for the recording and subscription of the proceedings, since the hearing will have been postponed. If anything should remain from the preceding Collation, the examination shall continue into the third day. Thus every interval of one day will distinguish the successive periods of conference, so that the proceedings may meanwhile be written down and subsequently subscribed, while the aforesaid guardians wait upon them. Their duty is measured out for this purpose: not to say anything, but to preserve what has been said.

Until, after the questions have been brought to their conclusion, truth has disentangled all the difficulties, the sheets written and subscribed from time to time shall be sealed both by the impression of my seal and by that of the eight custodians.

The authority of this edict shall also be made known to the Maximianists. They are to understand that they must refrain from that council by which the religious command of the merciful Emperors has established that the entire conflict between Catholics and Donatists is to be distinguished [Note: [Col. 0820] Perhaps, *diccingi*, that is, “be dissolved.”] and judged [Note: [Col. 0820] Perhaps, “by which”]. Nor can it help them in any way that they flatter themselves with the name of Donatists, since they are said to have been condemned by the Donatists.

If any one of them, having embraced the tenor of this posting—carefully devised against the many snares of suspicion, faithfully established, and diligently ordered—should refuse to observe any of its provisions, he not only confesses what he thinks about his own case but also reveals what he is attempting.

For the time being, it is sufficient as a prerogative of justice for the Examiner that, by this admonition concerning all the bishops, he has made the people of Carthage his witness—a people whom he will soon have as his judge.

It remains that, before the day of the council, the bishops of both parties, without any delay whatever, promise in letters sent to my office that they will fulfill the whole tenor of this arrangement. This must be accomplished especially promptly, so that the same letters, in which they will profess that they have agreed to all the provisions [Col. 0821] of this edict, may be authenticated only by the subscription of the bishops of first rank.

For it is enough that those letters should have, so to speak, the universal subscription of all the bishops attached to them, since they have promised that they will regard as valid the entire order of the dispute conducted by the seven representatives.

## Notice of the Donatists, responding to Marcellinus’s edict

After the consulship of the most illustrious Varanius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. To Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished man, tribune and notary: Januarius, Primianus, and the other bishops of sincere Christianity and Catholic truth.

We make known to Your Sincerity that, summoned by your edict, we came flying together from the various regions of Africa and entered Carthage on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. Both all the witnesses whom Carthage contains and Your Sincerity yourself are not unaware of this arrival of ours.

For such was the force of the oath expressed in your edict that, except for those whom bodily illness keeps in their homes or whom sickness seized on the road, neither the most venerable old men nor the hardship of the long journey could prevent us.

Although the first edict alone would have been sufficient before the case, you also deigned to issue a second, in which, though many things disturb us, this above all causes us great concern: that you judged that we ourselves ought to support your edict by our letters, although neither public custom nor the practice of judges requires this.

On this matter we earnestly exhort Your Sincerity to preserve the force of the first edict and order all of us to come to you, so that it may become clear as soon as possible how many we are—those whom our adversaries have often falsely claimed to be few—and so that, once everything properly required by our party has been arranged, the dispute may follow. Otherwise your edicts may appear to oppose one another, or something may prejudice us, so that, although you ordered all to come, you now appear to wish only a few to be present.

For it is fitting and advantageous that, while all are present, a few should speak concerning a matter common to all.

We have retained a copy of this Notice with us.

And in another hand: I, Januarianus, bishop, have subscribed.

And in another hand: I, Primianus, bishop, have subscribed.

## Letter of the Catholics responding to Marcellinus’s edict

To the honorable and beloved son, the most illustrious and distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary: Aurelius, Silvanus, and all the Catholic bishops.

By this letter we inform Your Distinction that we agree in every respect with your edict, by which provision has been made for preserving the tranquility and quiet of our Collation and for securing and bringing to light the truth, as you have deigned to admonish us, etc.

This letter is extant among Augustine’s Letters, volume 2, letter 128.

## Letter of the Catholics to Marcellinus responding to the Donatists’ Notice

To the honorable and beloved son, the most illustrious and distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary: Aurelius, Silvanus, and all the Catholic bishops.

The Notice, or letter, of our brothers, whom we desire to convert from their destructive dissension to Catholic peace, has made us very anxious, because they refused to agree with your edict of Nobility, by which you provided for the tranquility and quiet of our own dispute, etc.

This letter is extant in volume 2, letter 229.

## Mandate of the Catholics, in which the entire case is contained and the defense of the Catholic Church is entrusted to seven bishops chosen for the disputation

After the consulship of the most illustrious Varanius, on the third day before the Kalends of June. A Mandate made in the Church of Carthage by the entire council of the Catholic bishops [Col. 0822], with Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, presiding, and Silvanus, primate of Numidia.

### 1

Although the case of the Catholic Church is sufficiently and abundantly defended by divine testimonies against all the false accusations with which, throughout the world, schismatics and heretics harass it in their various regions, provinces, divisions, and separations through their empty and sacrilegious errors—and although in Africa the matter against the Donatists has also been settled by ecclesiastical and imperial judgment, as was proper or necessary—nevertheless, because this very fact must be manifested and explained more insistently to people who do not know these things, so that we may win them to eternal salvation through Christian charity [Note: Elsewhere, “through Christian love”], it has pleased us, by the will of God the Lord, to assemble in this church of the city of Carthage and to choose suitable brothers and fellow bishops of ours to undertake the defense of this case. They are to refute the utterly false charges brought by the party of Donatus against the Catholic Church, which, as the divine utterances concerning it testify, is spread throughout the whole world.

### 2

For the Church of Christ was promised by the divine and truthful voice to our holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to all peoples who would be their descendants and children through imitation of their faith, in such a way that no human and accursed voice can disprove it.

For God spoke thus to Abraham:

> “By myself I have sworn,” says the Lord, “because you have done this thing and have not spared your beloved son for my sake: surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is along the shore of the sea; and your offspring shall possess the cities of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22:16–18).

To Isaac also the Lord spoke these words concerning this matter:

> “I will establish my oath which I swore to Abraham your father, and I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven, and I will give to you and to your offspring all this land; and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your name, because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my commands, my ordinances, and my laws” (ibid. 26:3–5).

Speaking also to Jacob, he makes the same promise in an especially clear testimony:

> “Your offspring shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall multiply over the sea and toward the southwest, the north, and the east; and all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in you and in your offspring” (ibid. 28:14).

Therefore the prophet Isaiah, echoing these words and foreseeing in the Holy Spirit that this Church would come to be, addresses it as follows:

> “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said: Enlarge the place of your tent and your courts; drive in your stakes, do not spare; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. You shall yet extend to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall possess the nations, and you shall inhabit desolate cities. Do not fear, for you shall prevail; do not be afraid that you have been detested, for you shall forget your shame forever and shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood, because I am the Lord who made you—the Lord is his name—and he who delivered you, the God of Israel, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:1–5).

Likewise, in another place:

> “The Lord shall uncover his holy arm before all the nations, and all the nations shall see, even to the ends of the earth, the salvation that comes from God” (ibid. 52:10).

Again he says:

> “I have appointed you as a covenant of the race, as a light to the nations, so that salvation may reach to the ends of the earth” (ibid. 49:6).

The prophet Malachi, foreseeing that the sacrifice of the first people would cease and that throughout the whole world—from the rising of the sun to its setting—an eternal sacrifice would be celebrated among the nations when the name of the Lord had been glorified, speaks thus to the Jews:

> “I have no pleasure in you,” says the Lord Almighty, “and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name [Col. 0823] is great among the nations,” says the Lord Almighty (Mal. 1:10–11).

Jeremiah likewise foretells that the nations will come to the Lord from the end of the earth, their superstitions concerning idols having been condemned:

> “Lord, my strength and my help and my refuge in the day of troubles: to you the nations shall come from the end of the earth, and they shall say: How false were the idols that our fathers possessed, and there is no benefit in them” (Jer. 16:19).

But since it was foretold not that the nations would come to God from other places into one particular location on earth, but that they would worship him in their own places, where they had believed in idols that had been condemned, the prophet Zephaniah testifies as follows:

> “The Lord will prevail against them and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and each person shall worship him from his own place—all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2:11).

With these and many other testimonies of the Law and the Prophets asserting that the Church is spread throughout the whole world, the divine Psalms also sing in harmony:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:7–8).

Again, in another psalm concerning the Lord Christ under the figure of Solomon:

> “He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents; and all the kings of the earth shall worship him, all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:8–11).

Again, in another psalm:

> “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting: from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor” (Ps. 49:1–2).

### 3

For this reason the Lord Jesus himself, who had previously spoken through the mouths of the Prophets, after he rose from the dead, now promised the Church through his own mouth:

> “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled.” Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:44–47).

It was as though he were explaining in other words the testimony of the Psalm that we placed most recently. For where the Psalm says, “He summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting,” the Lord says, “among all nations”; and where it says, “from Zion comes the beauty of his splendor,” the Lord says, “beginning from Jerusalem.” For who does not know that Zion and Jerusalem are one city, from which the passion and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ began to be proclaimed through the world by a most renowned announcement, for the cleansing and salvation of the peoples?

Therefore, as he was about to ascend into heaven, foreseeing from where carnal people would quarrel on account of their divisions and separations, when the disciples had asked to hear from him something concerning the end of the age, he said:
