> “It is not for you to know the times that the Father has placed in his own authority; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth” (Acts 1:7–8).

Following this authority of heavenly teaching, the Apostles commend the Church as bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world (Col. 1:6). And so that they would not divide the members of Christ into factions by human names, the Apostle addresses the carnal people who had already begun to do this:

> “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment. For it has been reported to me, my brothers, by those of Chloe, that there are contentions among you, and that each one of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ.’ Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:10–13).

Therefore, we acknowledge as our brothers in the sacraments of Christ even these men against whose error and for whose salvation we have chosen our colleagues to answer their false and empty accusations in the name of Christ. We do not detest their perversity, but [Col. 0824] we approve in them the sacraments of Christ themselves, and we do not dare to invalidate them.

For we remember that it was commanded through the Prophet:

> “Hear, you who fear the word of the Lord. Say to those who hate you and detest you: ‘You are our brothers,’ so that the name of the Lord may be honored and he may appear to them in joy” (Isa. 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

What follows they should say beneficially to themselves, or rather hear from the Prophet rather than from us. We say what is milder, so that we may have peace with those who are corrected rather than litigation with the perverse. We call them our brothers so that the name of the Lord may be honored; yet they hate and detest us and deny that we are their brothers because they honor the name of human beings more than the name of the Lord.

### 4

And so our brothers and fellow bishops, whom we have chosen to refute their accusations, must defend the holy Church against their charges in the Collation that is to be held with them.

For they say that this Church—which we have received as foretold in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; expressed through the works [Note: Perhaps “through the mouth”] of the Savior; redeemed by his blood; disseminated and planted through the labors of the Apostles, beginning from Jerusalem, where the Holy Spirit came upon one hundred and twenty souls gathered together and, causing those upon whom he came to speak in all the languages [Note: Perhaps “the languages of all”] of the nations, taught by the most evident sign that the Church would exist among all nations and speak in the languages of all nations; this Church, therefore, which in this manner, as foretold and fulfilled, took its beginning from Jerusalem and from there spread through the preaching of the Apostles into Judea, Samaria, and the other regions of the world, and in whose Letters and Acts we find cities and provinces spread far and wide, into which they brought it on their beautiful feet, so that it might also grow in Africa—this Church, as we have said, they claim, these men against whose error we entrust our colleagues with the Collation and its defense, was polluted and destroyed through certain sins of Caecilianus, once bishop of the Church of Carthage, and of his associates, and that its remnants remained in the party of Donatus.

Those to whom we entrust this task should refute and reject this vain and sacrilegious accusation in such a way that they first distinguish and separate the case of the Church from the case of certain human beings.

For it was foretold that the Church would have the wicked mixed within it until, at the time of the harvest, the weeds were separated from the wheat; or until the chaff was winnowed away from the grain; or until the sheep on the right and the goats on the left—who are now mixed together in the same pastures—were separated; or until the bad fish were divided from the good fish, which are now drawn together within the same nets to the shore and are separated on that same shore, that is, at the end of the age.

Any human beings in the Church, if they are good, are its wheat or grain, its sheep, its good fish. But if they are wicked, they are its weeds, chaff, goats, and bad fish. Therefore, the whole harvest, the whole threshing floor, the whole flock, and the whole catch were not condemned on their account. Otherwise, if before the proper time we rashly dare to judge concerning the wicked and to charge some people with the sins of others, we might abandon the good on account of the wicked through a sacrilegious separation, when instead we ought to tolerate the wicked for the sake of the good in pious unity.

These men, therefore, enemies of the evangelical parables and of such manifest truth, must be pressed to explain what they intend and first to show, if they can, how the Church—which we have received and hold in the Holy Scriptures as beginning from Jerusalem and bearing fruit and growing through near and distant lands—could have perished through the contagion of any persons whom they accuse and could have remained in the party of Donatus.

For if they show that this could have happened, then the question will certainly concern the case of the Church, and perhaps another question will have to be taken up and examined: whether Caecilianus and his colleagues were such [Note: According to Morel, *Elementa Critica*, pp. 227–228, one should read “whether they were such”] as these men say they were, and whether this could have become known [Note: Perhaps “or whether this could have become known”] to the Christian unity, which already [Col. 0825] at that time was spread everywhere, in such a way that they could stain and destroy it through the contagion of that knowledge all the way to the farthest lands.

For they themselves admit that no one can be stained by sins committed by others if he is unaware of them. Therefore, if they wish to demonstrate that so extensive a communion of Christian peoples, spread through so many lands, could have been contaminated and destroyed by the sins of Caecilianus and his associates, it is not enough for them to show that these men were such as they accuse them of being. They must also show that their true crimes became known to everyone whom they claim to have perished through that contagion.

But if they cannot demonstrate that the Catholic Church among all the nations commended to it by the divine utterances could have been destroyed by the sins of others, then, setting aside for a little while the case of Caecilianus and of those whom they thought ought to be accused along with him—a case that has no bearing at all upon the case of the Church, since, even if it had been evil, it could not have contaminated the Church—what we assert for the rejection of their accusations should be demonstrated by those to whom we entrust the duty of defense, with the utmost clarity and with an abundance of examples.

That is: the Church of Christ cannot be polluted or destroyed by the corrupting influence of any wicked people mixed within it until the end, not only people unknown but even people known. This should first be shown by prophetic examples. The Prophets severely rebuked the sinful people who offended God with many detestable abominations and, through the scourges of correction, stirred hard and stubborn hearts even to dreadful hostility against themselves. Yet they did not separate themselves bodily from that people, among whom there were certainly also good people among the wicked. They judged it better to endure the wicked through patience than to abandon the good through accusation.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself provides a singular example of patience. He not only endured his betrayer, who was certainly exceedingly wicked, although known as one of the disciples [Note: Perhaps “of the disciples”], but even knowingly admitted him into the number of the disciples.

He also said to his disciples, “And you are clean, but not all” (John 13:10), so that they might know by this that their purity could not be soiled by another’s impurity.

The Apostle Paul is a witness to this in the times of the Apostles: he groans among false brothers (2 Cor. 11:26), and in his Epistle he notes that some were proclaiming Christ out of envy—a vice that is certainly diabolical (Phil. 1:15). Thus the good tolerated the wicked in communion in the sacraments, out of an earnest concern to preserve the unity of Christ, without suffering their own destruction, although they were far removed from the wickedness of those people.

After the Apostles, good bishops likewise tolerated wicked people—not only various laypeople but also fellow bishops—for the sake of the unity of Christ. The letters of the martyr Cyprian bear witness to this. In them he laments the avarice of certain colleagues, extending even to the cruelty of usury and to the seizure of estates. Yet he did not become like them through their contagion; rather, through love of the good he endured such people. He not only admonished by example but also instructed by precept. For in one of his letters he says:

> “And if weeds appear to be in the Church, nevertheless neither our faith nor our charity should be hindered, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (*Letter to Maximus*, now 54).

The judgment of the very people who oppose this truth must also be used to prove how true it is. When they had rightly condemned Maximianus for sacrilegious schism, they granted his associates, who had gone out with him and separated themselves from their communion, a delay for returning, saying that they had not been polluted by the plantations of that sacrilegious offshoot [Note: The decision of the Council of Bagai].

Although the partnership of one schism held them all bound together, we cannot see how this could rightly have been said. Nevertheless, let them be compelled, even if late, to understand from this that, within Catholic unity, the wicked cannot harm the good any more than chaff harms grain. For in the schismatic division, where there is only chaff, Maximianus was judged not to have been able to pollute the associates of his own division, merely because they had not been present at his ordination [Col. 0826].

Let them therefore see how thoughtlessly they say that Caecilianus, whatever his character may have been, and whatever his colleagues may have been, could have destroyed Christian unity among so many distant nations, when they think that Maximianus did not destroy even the Africans who shared in his schism.

Thus it will be apparent that the case of Caecilianus, whatever question it may contain, does not belong to the case of the Church whose defense we have entrusted.

### 5

As for their accusation of our Baptism—or rather, of Christ’s Baptism, which we possess and administer—and their attempt to destroy it among those whom they have deceived through lamentable error, it must be endured [Note: [Col. 0826] Perhaps, “defended.”] in the same way as the Church itself, whose gift it is. For they will no longer dare to accuse the Baptism we administer if the Church we hold is cleansed of their accusations.

But if they think they should raise, as they usually do, the objection that we acknowledge Christ’s Baptism as having been administered even outside communion with us, rather than rejecting it, and that we do not dare to annul it, they should be answered with whatever arguments and testimonies can be brought to bear: the divine gifts of the Church, even when found among thieves, usurpers, or even robbers, must be acknowledged rather than denied. For just as the Apostle says of certain people, “They suppress the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom. 1:18), so all who possess or administer Christ’s Baptism outside the Church of Christ suppress the truth of the divine Sacrament in the unrighteousness of human error. Therefore, once human unrighteousness has been corrected, the divine truth must not be violated.

Those who think that Christ’s Baptism must be denied because heretics also administer it may likewise think that Christ himself must be denied because demons also confess him. Therefore those who possess his Baptism outside communion with the Church ought to come to the Church—not so that what was lacking may be supplied, but so that what was already present may become beneficial.

Nor should it be thought that they will maintain this conflict for long, since in this matter too they can be admonished by their own judgment and example. For they preferred to acknowledge rather than annul Christ’s Baptism administered outside their communion, in the schism of Maximian, among those whom they received together with the men whom they had condemned. Accordingly, they are compelled to consider, in those people, how the saying which they habitually repeat—“Do not share in another’s sins” (1 Tim. 5:22)—is to be understood when they have said that those who shared the sacraments with the condemned Maximian remained undefiled. For this saying must not be applied by bodily separation, but by dissimilarity of conduct.

Likewise, concerning Baptism they commonly take the saying, “He who is baptized by a dead man” (Sir. 34:30), and other passages of this kind. They are compelled to recognize in those very people how such passages are to be understood, since they did not dare to reject or repeat the Baptism administered in the schism by those whom, when they condemned them, they declared to be dead.

They must also be compelled to approve in the case of the Maximianists the objection they habitually make against us: that, for the sake of correcting them in the unity of Christ, we are compelled to take some action with the earthly authorities. For when they accused the Maximianists before earthly judges as their own schismatics or heretics, in order to drive them from the basilicas, they repeatedly cited the Council of Bagai, by which they had condemned them.

All this must be said so that they may be reminded by their own judgment to lay aside their dissension at last; so that, having exhausted or cast away the animosity of false and empty accusations, they may love Catholic peace and embrace undivided charity, without which no human being can be good, whatever other good he may possess.

### 6

After these matters have been dealt with, we do not want them to abandon the case of Caecilianus himself. But they should take it up not as the case of the mother Church, but as the case of a brother bishop; and not so that it may be investigated again as though it were still awaiting completion, but so that it may be shown to have long ago been concluded by ecclesiastical and public documents.

Some of these documents will suffice, if they are willing to believe them when they are produced by us. The matter could also be demonstrated by the testimony of the archives [Col. 0827] [Note: Perhaps the text should read: “if they are willing to believe; but if they are unwilling, they can also be demonstrated by the corroborating testimony of the archives.”], which would show both that they sent Caecilianus’ case to the emperor by the proconsul Anulinus, accusing him, and that the same emperor, after the ecclesiastical judgments by which Caecilianus had been acquitted, examined the entire case in the presence of the parties and judged Caecilianus innocent but them most calumnious.

The innocence of Felix of Aptunga, Caecilianus’ ordainer, also became clear when the proconsul Aelianus investigated the matter by order of that same emperor—the man whom they themselves called, in their council, the source of evils.

Whatever accusations they may think ought to be brought against any of our fellow bishops—not now in the manner of people exchanging arguments or disputing, but in the manner of slanderers and litigants—we must answer that their cases do not belong to the case of the Church whose defense has now been entrusted to us. Nevertheless, those cases are not being taken away from them for investigation; they are merely being deferred because of the necessity imposed by the present time.

Once the case of the Church—which the most merciful Emperor has recently ordered to be investigated and demonstrated—has been concluded, whatever accusations they think should be brought against any of our people may be presented before whatever judges they wish, whether ours or theirs, once they have been joined to Catholic unity. There they may either be shown to have been cleared or be punished after conviction.

### 7

We command our brothers and fellow bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, and Possidius to carry out these matters in the manner in which they have been written, and also anything more extensive or more firmly supported that the Lord may grant them.

They testify by their subscriptions that they have undertaken this commission, just as we testify by our subscriptions that we have issued it. We shall regard as ratified whatever, with the Lord’s help, they accomplish in this defense.

We also add the following men, with whom they may take counsel whenever necessary: Novatus, Florentius, Maurentius, Priscus, Serenianus, Bonifacius, and Scillatius. For preserving the written record of the proceedings: Deuterius, Leo, Asterius, and Restitutus.

“I, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, established at Carthage in the presence of the distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary, have accepted and subscribed this Commission.”

In another hand: “I, Silvanus, of the first see of the province of Numidia, established at Carthage in the presence of the distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary, have agreed to and subscribed the Commission issued by us.”

In another hand: “I, Valentinus, bishop of the Church of Vaiana, established at Carthage in the presence of the distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary, have issued and subscribed this,” and so forth.

## SECOND DAY OF THE CONFERENCE

### Opening

After the consulship of Varanes, distinguished man, on the third day before the Nones of June, in the secretariat of the Gargilian Baths at Carthage, with Sebastianus, Maximianus, and others standing by, Libosus, ducenarius of the distinguished authorities, said:

“Since the hearing has been adjourned until today, and the bishops of both parties are present, if Your Sublimity orders it, they will be admitted.”

Flavius Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“Let them come in.”

After Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, and the others had entered, Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“It is quite certain that I repeatedly offered myself at the preceding hearing, and now I ask you to deign to sit. When the Catholic bishops had taken their seats, Bishop Petilianus said:

“What was not done at the earlier hearing, we do not dare to do now,” and so forth.

Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“Although I remember that I offered myself at the preceding hearing as well, I think that it was not done then for a sufficient reason, because, with so many priests assembled, there could not have been room for them to sit. Since I now see that the appointed persons have assembled, I ask you to deign to sit at least now.”

Bishop Petilianus said:

“We do not sit in the absence of our fathers, especially since divine law [Col. 0828] forbids our sitting together, lest we wish to sit with adversaries of this kind.”

Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“If Your Holiness has neglected to hear my request that you deign to sit, this cannot be forced upon me so as to prevent me from conducting the hearing while standing,” and so forth.

## THE DONATIST STATEMENT

### Read at the second hearing

After the consulship of Varanes, distinguished man, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, Januarianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Prothasius, Montanus, Gaudentius, and Adeodatus, bishops and defenders of ecclesiastical truth, say the following in their Formal Statement to Flavius Marcellinus, distinguished and eminent man, tribune and notary:

“Yesterday, on the Kalends of June, Your Eminence deigned to hear the case between us and our adversaries. Since, after almost the whole day had passed while you patiently allowed the parties to speak, you deigned to hear certain matters that formed the beginnings of the case, and since it is necessary for the case that the Commission submitted by our adversaries be brought to our attention, whereas the sequence of the proceedings cannot be explained because of its length, order that the Commission which our adversaries handed over to be read be supplied to us today, that is, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in copies, so that we may not appear to come to judgment unprepared, but may be able to attend instructed in the case entrusted to us.”

In another hand: “I, Primianus, bishop, have subscribed this Formal Statement on the fourth day before the Nones of June at Carthage.”

## Certain Submissions of Augustine

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

“Let this alone be clear: they themselves want to postpone the matter. We ask you to grant this, Your Sublimity. They wish to consider the matter; they wish to examine it; they wish to come better prepared. It is human. Let us not, by unwillingly postponing the matter, produce longer proceedings, and let the length of the proceedings themselves impose still greater delays upon us.”

Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“Although I am already becoming greatly uncertain about their declarations, let each party now specify once again whether the principal case is to be heard on the sixth day before the Ides of June, with all evasions cut short.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

“We want it today, and, if it were possible, we would have wanted it today. Nevertheless, because it was humane to grant our brothers what they did not seem to have requested unjustly, we promise that, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, with the help of our Lord God, we shall be present to carry out the principal case.”

## THIRD DAY OF THE CONFERENCE

### Opening

After the consulship of Varanes, distinguished man, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the Gargilian Baths, with Sebastianus, Maximianus, and Petrus, most devoted men, standing by, Ursus, ducenarius of the distinguished authorities, said:

“At the preceding hearing the bishops of the Donatist party requested an adjournment until today, so that in the meantime, having been instructed by the production of the proceedings, they might respond at Your Sublimity’s hearing. Now both parties are outside. If you order it, they will be admitted.”

Flavius Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“Let them come in.”

After the bishops had entered, and so forth, Marcellinus, distinguished man, tribune and notary, said:

“It is certain that the case was postponed so that today, once the proceedings had been produced, the principal action might be heard,” and so forth.

## Submissions of Augustine

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

“We have long desired that the principal case be concluded. Therefore, if permission is granted, even at this late hour, let them prove the accusations repeatedly brought from the opposing side against the holy Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world—accusations never proved.”

[Col. 0829] When the Donatists demanded that the persons who had requested that the Conference be held should first be identified, wishing it to be established that the Catholics were the petitioners, so that they could examine the petitioners’ standing according to forensic law, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

“If you judge that this is relevant to the case, it is for your prudence to consider it. The tenor of the imperial rescript shows that a Conference was granted to Catholic bishops or to representatives of Catholic bishops. We have come; both parties are here. God commanded us to be disputants and conferrers rather than litigants, and the most merciful Emperor, fearing God and serving God, wanted nothing else.

“Your Sublimity judged on the first day of our dispute that the proper persons had appeared and that their commissions had been confirmed. Let matters that are not necessary to the case not be introduced.

“It is the Church that we assert by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures—a Church known to all, established upon the highest mountain, as it is written, to which all nations come (Isa. 2:2–3; Matt. 5:14). If there is anything to be said against this Church, let it now be said, and let no delays be introduced. If there is nothing to be said, let him yield to the truth who cannot affirm, display, and prove his accusation before human beings.

“How long will this great expectation of the people remain suspended? Everyone is thinking about his soul, and we introduce procedural delays for the purpose of never arriving at the end of the investigation of truth.”

Again, after several submissions by the Donatists and statements by the judge, Augustine said:

“Let Your Nobility consider how much is being done so that nothing may be done,” and so forth.

Augustine said:

“Both parties are present; we have assembled here; this place is almost filled with bishops; the Commissions have been read and confirmed. Our party does not deny that the Conference was requested so that, in this Conference, they might at last either prove—or be shown to have been unable to prove—the accusations which they habitually bring not against us, not against any one of us individually, but against the entire Christian world. That Christian world has been both promised and fulfilled not by human opinion, but by divine testimonies.

“What further delaying evasions of some kind are being introduced by those who want to be called bishops of Christ? The expectation not merely of this city but of almost the entire human race is suspended; it wishes to hear something about the Church, while we continue to examine forensic formulas and engage in the most wretched litigation. Let Your Nobility now take note of what is happening. Deign at last, with God’s help, to free us from this case by cutting short all delays.”

Again, after several submissions by the parties and statements by the judge, Augustine said:

“The Conference was requested by our representatives. The law itself, which was delivered to Your Nobility, contains this,” and so forth.

“We all admit that we requested the Conference, because you were refusing it, so that at least in this way we might come to this place or to this time for the sake of a Conference, disputation, and demonstration of the truth. It has happened: we have come, and you do not want our coming to accomplish anything. We admit that we requested the Conference. The Emperor himself expressed in his own words nothing other than that we had requested the Conference.

“Let the Conference itself now take place. Let us see what is said against the Church spread throughout the whole world, which we demonstrate to have been both promised by the divine testimonies and now displayed in such a way that it strikes the eyes of the blind and breaks into the ears of the deaf.

“Our brothers do not want to reach the point of demonstrating this, so that what cannot remain hidden may be demonstrated. Let them state the accusations. Let us see by what accusations that which was promised to Abraham has perished: ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed’ (Gen. 22:18). Let us hear, learn, and know what accusations could erase this promise of the God who swore it. If there is nothing that can be said against it, either pronounce judgment or remove all delays, and let the case at last be concluded.”

Again, after further submissions by the parties and statements by the judge, Augustine said:

“The Church—which you do not want to hear about, but must hear about, since it is proclaimed by so many testimonies and divine utterances as spread throughout the whole world, and whose communion we appear to hold—has been attacked by you with false accusations, and from this your separation arose, which we grieve.

“Today we want to hear those accusations with which you habitually attack the Church spread throughout the whole world, as it was promised, and to know whether they are true. For if the accusations which you habitually bring against the aforementioned Church are true—if you are able to show that it has been polluted, defiled, overturned, destroyed, and extinguished by I know not what crimes of ours—then it will remain for us to ask whether what you proclaim to have perished everywhere has remained among you.

“But if that Church could not perish, it remains for you to acknowledge it and at last conclude the dispute.”

Again, after several submissions and statements, Augustine said:

“The confirmation of the persons on the first day of the hearing was also made clear by the form of your statement on the following day. But since he says [Note: [Col. 0830] The Donatist Emeritus.] that he has no dealings with Christians from abroad, and that everything being done here concerns Africans, this is the declaration of African Catholic Christians:

“‘We are joined in communion with the entire Christian world. We have chosen to retain that Church which we find in those Scriptures,’ and so forth.

“We retain the Church which we find in those Scriptures in which we also recognized Christ. For our Scriptures, to whose authority both parties submit, commend Christ and the Church as a holy marriage: Christ as the bridegroom, and the Church as the bride. Wherever we recognize him, there we must also find her.

“Therefore, if we had only now arisen and were considering in Africa to which communion of Christians we ought to be joined, without doubt we would have to hold the one we found in the Scriptures and reject the accusatory opinions of human beings, holding only to the divine utterances that cannot lie.

“This is what the African Christians did; they are called Catholics, and rightly so, bearing witness to the name by their very communion. For καθ’ ὅλον—‘according to the whole’—is the meaning of the word. Whoever is separated from the whole and defends a portion cut off from the universal body must not arrogate this name to himself, but should hold the truth with us.”

Gaudentius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0830] Donatist.], said:

“They think that the name ‘Catholic’ must be referred to provinces or nations, whereas ‘Catholic’ is the name of that which is full of the sacraments, which is perfect and undefiled—not a name referring to nations,” and so forth.

Again, after certain submissions and statements, Augustine said:

“They habitually bring against the Church we hold the accusation of betrayal, and contend that it was destroyed and extinguished by the sins of certain people. Through these accusations they deceive the hearts of the simple, whose salvation is our concern.

“Moved by these matters, we met with them so that they might confer with us and show whether they could prove what they allege against the Church against which they direct their attack. When they had refused our meeting, certain of them recently came to the imperial court and said in the official records that they wanted to be heard and examined.

“Embracing at last their agreement to the Conference, we thought that we should ask the Emperor for a Conference, so that the accusations which they habitually bring against the universal Church might either be proved, so that the truth would become apparent, or not proved, so that the truth would nevertheless become apparent.

“Let these accusations be brought forward and demonstrated if they wish or are able to display them. But if they cannot or will not, it is now for Your Sublimity to judge the whole matter, as reason itself indicates.”

Again, after certain submissions and statements, Augustine said:

“We requested the Conference in order to refute the accusations brought forward, not in order to bring forward accusations to be refuted. For once they have been unable to prove what has been alleged, what it is and what remains of it will be clear to everyone without our having to say anything, and Your Sublimity will judge it.

“We have now entered upon the task of refuting the accusations which they habitually bring against the Church we hold. Their own Commission also contains this: ‘Against our betrayers and persecutors.’

“Once, however, Primianus—our brother, if he deigns to accept the designation—was summoned concerning the Conference and replied: ‘It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of betrayers should meet together.’

“We undertook to refute these accusations; for the sake of refuting these accusations, we requested this Conference. It has been granted: let them either prove them or clear themselves of them.”

When the Donatists asked whether the Catholics preferred to proceed by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures or by public records, and said that if they chose the Scriptural testimonies they would have to abandon all public laws and records, but that if they preferred to proceed by public laws and records they would have to set aside the Scriptural testimonies, Augustine said:

“Let Your Sublimity give brief attention to what the opposing party has just argued. We show that we retain the Catholic Church by the testimony of our own communion. If they permit it, we have come to prove this Church not by human rumor or wandering opinions, but as it is declared by the divine utterances.

“But as for offering laws, records, or whatever documents are produced from the archives to be read at this Conference, those who proceed by such means themselves compel us to do so. For if, after removing all such documents, they wanted the Church to be considered only in the Scriptures, we would want and desire nothing else.

“They bring accusations of betrayal. Either they do not prove these accusations of betrayal from the archives, in which case they say nothing, or they prove them, in which case they compel us in turn to proceed by the archives.

“Thus Your Eminence clearly sees that the cases must be distinguished: when we are compelled to proceed by public laws, and when we wish and desire the Church’s case to be settled solely by the divine utterances.”

When the Donatists insisted that the Catholics should produce the Commission which had been entrusted to the representatives sent to request a Conference from the Emperor, Augustine said:

“We have proclaimed this so many times. They demand that the Commission entrusted by the bishops to the representatives of the bishops be read aloud. This is a demand for someone else’s documents, irrelevant to the case.

“The Commission entrusted to us for the Conference to be held with them has been read; let this suffice for them. What if the representatives were given certain instructions that are not relevant to this case but that we do not want them to know? It is enough that the Emperor has declared by his own testimony that we requested a Conference.

“This Conference was granted; for this we have come; let it at last take place. The ears of human beings are open to the truth.”

Adeodatus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0831] Donatist.], said:

“You have admitted what you once kept silent about. You have shown that you gave many instructions against us which we ought not easily to know,” and so forth.

Augustine said:

“I did not say that. You have not understood, or you pretend not to have heard, what I said. Listen: I shall put it more clearly, lest perhaps, because I expressed myself somewhat obscurely for the sake of brevity, you failed through my fault to understand it.

“It is known to everyone that the Church has many cases: its own cases and those of private persons entrusted to it. It can happen that many matters belong to the intercession of bishops. Secrets concerning the affairs and cases of others are entrusted to us; our intervention is often requested in them, and assistance is sought from the Church on their account. These matters must not be disclosed, lest we be found to be betrayers.

“It is enough for you that the most merciful Emperor himself bears witness that I requested a Conference in your case. Ask nothing further if you are not asking about other people’s affairs. For your case, it is enough that what was read from the Emperor’s law has been read, and that it has been confirmed by our Commission and subscriptions.”

When the Donatists again insisted that the Catholics choose whether they wished to proceed by public laws or by divine testimonies, and that, if they wished to use the latter, they should abandon the former, Augustine said:

“As everyone knows, and as they themselves have declared in the wording of their Commission, they habitually bring accusations of betrayal against the Church we hold—the Church whose enemies habitually agitate their minds with their accusations.

“If they abandon these accusations, we shall produce nothing from public documents. But if they persist in the same accusations, we shall use public documents to show that this case was concluded long ago, and yet that they have not ceased to bring such accusations.

“Therefore we have now requested this Conference, not in order to take up again for conclusion the case of betrayal which they brought against Caecilianus and his colleagues, but to demonstrate that it was concluded long ago. Thus the peoples who do not know these things and are still stirred up by their accusations may finally learn in which Church they should seek the path of Christian salvation.

“If, then, the question concerns the Church—what it is, how great it is, and what kind it is—the divine testimonies alone are sufficient to demonstrate it. If they appeal to human beings, if they bring accusations against human beings, although the Church’s case must be distinguished from the case of human beings, and although one must not place the Church’s hope in human beings if they are good, nor judge the Church of God to have perished if they are evil, nevertheless we also take up their case as that of our brothers.

“If they can be shown to us as criminals, we shall anathematize them today. Yet on their account we do not abandon or forsake the Church promised and manifested by God.

“Let them therefore choose what they wish. Let them not bring accusations against human beings, and the documents will cease; only divine authority will speak, only the Scripture of God—to which both parties submit—will be brought forward.”

After several further submissions and statements, when Petilianus had said, “Who is this man conducting the case? Is he Caecilianus’ son, or is he not?”, Augustine said:

“We have heard together, read together, and preach together to the peoples: ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth’ (Matt. 23:9). Why do you ask me whether I am Caecilianus’ son?

“If Caecilianus was innocent, let him rejoice in his innocence, with me rejoicing alongside him, not placing my hope in his innocence. But if he was guilty—which the examination of the case may perhaps establish in one way or another—the Church which I hold tolerated him, to use the Lord’s comparisons: as chaff on the threshing floor, as kids in the same pastures, and as bad fish in the same nets.

“Yet on account of the wicked we must not abandon either the Lord’s threshing floor [Note: [Col. 0832] The text appears to be missing ‘or the Lord’s pastures.’], the Lord’s pastures, or the Lord’s nets through criminally contentious dissension, nor leap prematurely from the shore into the sea.”

Again, after several submissions by the Donatists and statements by the judge, Augustine said:

“They habitually bring the case of Caecilianus or of his colleagues against the Catholic Church itself—or, to speak without ambiguity, against the Church we hold. Therefore, as I see it, they wish to offer us a great shortcut: if they do not bring this case against the Church we hold, let them say what they do bring against it.

“For if nothing, why are we separated? If something besides the case of Caecilianus, let them present and demonstrate that very thing.”

Petilianus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0832] Donatist.], said:

“Who are you? Are you Caecilianus’ son, or are you not? Does Caecilianus’ crime attach to you or not, if he was guilty?”

Augustine said:

“I am in the Church in which Caecilianus was.”

Petilianus, bishop, said:

“Where did you begin? Whom do you have as your father? Otherwise, if you condemn your father, you confess yourself to be a heretic, since you wish to have neither an origin nor a father.”

Augustine said:

“We are in the Church in which Caecilianus held the episcopate and died. We recite his name at the altar and share in his memory, as in the memory of a brother, not as in that of a father or mother.

“But you ask me where my communion takes its beginning. The Lord Christ himself asserts the beginning of my communion when he says: ‘It was necessary that the Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem’ (Luke 24:46–47).

“This preaching began from Jerusalem. From that most illustrious beginning it spread abroad, spreading the Church which we hold, first through the neighboring regions and then through distant lands; it also came to Africa.

“We open our eyes to this Church; in the divine utterances and testimonies we find it, just as we find the Lord Christ himself and our Redeemer. No human being’s crimes and no one’s calumny will separate me from that God as Father and this Church as Mother.”

Again, after certain other submissions and statements, Augustine said:

“Look, I say it—as often as they wish, I say it: Caecilianus is not my father, because I hear my Lord saying, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth; one is your Father, God.’

“I call Caecilianus a brother: a good brother if he is good, an evil brother if he is evil, because he is my brother through our common sacraments.

“But if you wish to hear my judgment about him, I also believe him innocent and think that he was attacked by false accusations. Yet I say this as a human being forming an opinion about another human being, not as one believing something certain.

“If you bring Caecilianus’ crimes against the Church, I stand by and defend him as a brother, showing that those crimes do not belong to the Church, do not belong to its case, and cannot prejudice it. In this way I demonstrate that you have brought no accusation against the Catholic Church, even if Caecilianus’ crimes were perhaps true—which you will in no way be able to demonstrate.

“But if you cannot demonstrate that they are even true, then, even by your own judgment, you see where you have been left and what you ought to choose once the animosity of error has finally been rejected: hold the truth with us and embrace charity with us, after error has been condemned.”

When the Donatists argued that Caecilianus was the root or head of the Catholics, Augustine said:

“I have a head, but it is Christ, whose Apostle I hear saying: ‘All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s’ (1 Cor. 3:22–23).

“For even when the Apostle called himself a father, lest we think that this fatherhood had a human basis in him, he added: ‘Through the Gospel I begot you’ (1 Cor. 4:15). Therefore the seed and the channel of my seed are derived from the Gospel.

“We call those who preceded us in time or merit ‘fathers’ as a matter of honor. But it is one thing to ask whom we have as a father for the faith, whom we have as a father for eternal salvation, and whom we have as a father for retaining the Church and receiving God’s promises.

“The former is a matter of honor, as when we say ‘Father’ daily to old men. We also say ‘Brother’ daily to certain people who are neither with us in one Church nor participants in the same sacraments. Lot even said to the Sodomites, ‘Brothers’—in order to soften their hostility, certainly, not because he recognized them as brothers or as sharing with him, so to speak, in a single inheritance [Note: [Col. 0833] Perhaps, ‘of the inheritance.’].

“Let these matters therefore be set aside. Let us distinguish the terms owed to human beings as a matter of honor from the term we require for salvation.

“For eternal salvation, let me say it in the peace of the Apostle—or rather, let me say it at the Apostle’s command: the Apostle Paul is not my father for eternal salvation, though he says to me, ‘I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Cor. 3:6–7).

“Regarding this, the Lord said, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth.’ Certainly he knew that the Apostle would say, ‘Through the Gospel I begot you.’ The Apostle was not going to contradict the Lord, who said, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth,’ by saying, ‘Though you have many fathers, through the Gospel I begot you.’

“But because the Lord distinguished the purpose for which he established a father for us, and the honorable sense in which we could also regard the Apostle as a father, he spoke in such a way that the Apostle’s statement would not contradict the Lord’s truth.

“Therefore, whatever fathers I acknowledge on earth, I acknowledge as a matter of honor. I recognize no father of my salvation except God, concerning whom the Lord said to me, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth,’ and to whom we say daily, ‘Our Father, who art in heaven’ (Matt. 6:9).”

When the Donatists asked who had ordained Augustine, Augustine said:

“I see that our brothers who stand opposite us are asking unnecessary questions. I do not refuse to answer even these unnecessary questions, provided that the case of the Church, to which no answer can be given, is placed upon the safest foundation.

“I am the man whose ordainer you ask about: I am a Christian, a believer, and—God is my witness—a Catholic. Thus we are still debating who deserves to be called by this name.

“I defend and assert that Church, with whatever voice I can, in which Church I am, whatever I may be. I see where you are heading: you are pursuing human calumnies. What you habitually boast and say is not unfamiliar to our ears or hearts.

“Megalius, primate of the Catholic Church of Numidia, ordained me, at the time when he had the power to ordain me. There: I have answered. Continue your case; produce what you are preparing. There too you will appear calumnious.

“There—I have named my ordainer. Now produce your calumnies.”

## Letter of the Donatists

### Produced on the third day, in which they attempt to answer the Commission of the Catholics cited on the first day of the Conference

“To Flavius Marcellinus, distinguished and eminent man, tribune and notary, Januarianus and the other bishops of the Catholic truth which suffers persecution, not of the truth which inflicts it.

1. Since we entrusted our defense to our brothers and colleagues in the records before Your Nobility, it is a great indication of a just judge that he should grant one party’s request while not denying it to the other, lest he appear to favor one party and oppress the other.

“Your prudence and far-sightedness, and even more your foresight, ought especially to guard against this, since by your edicts you invite the peoples to judge the fairness of your hearing.

“Accordingly, when our adversaries, our betrayers and persecutors, were introducing into the proceedings the laboriously prepared volume of their Commission, long conceived and set forth, you willingly heard it without prejudice to us. We earnestly request that you grant the same privilege to this letter of ours.

“We do not ask this because their depraved and perverse doctrine frightens us, but lest our defenders be burdened by having to contend against their lengthy book and against their submissions, since neither the entire day is sufficient for the case, nor voice or bodily strength sufficient for a defense in which book must contend with book and defense with defense.

“Therefore we ask you to accept this letter of ours and order that it be inserted in the record; then deign to hear the case.”

## 2.

For after running through the testimonies by which the Church is everywhere spread abroad with praise of its own excellence, our adversaries first instruct their advocates to carry out this argument against us, who defend the Church’s purity: they say that the same Church was foretold as having the good and the wicked mingled within it until the end of the age. For this reason we show all the more clearly that the Lord’s Church is everywhere proclaimed in the divine Scriptures as holy and spotless.

Through Isaiah:

> “Arise, Sion; put on your strength, Jerusalem, holy city; the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you” (Isaiah 52:1).

And again:

> “Say to the daughter of Sion, ‘Behold, your Savior will come to you, having his reward and his work before his face,’ and he will call that people holy, redeemed by the Lord. But you shall be called ‘the desired city,’ and ‘not forsaken’” (ibid. 62:11–12).

And again:

> “Strengthen yourselves, slack hands; and strengthen yourselves, weak knees. You who are fainthearted, do not fear. Our Lord will render judgment, and he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; the tongue of the mute shall be made plain, and the lame shall leap like a deer. For water has burst forth in the desert, and a spring in thirsty ground.”

And he added:

> “There shall be a clean way there, and it shall be called the holy way; the unclean shall not pass along it, nor shall there be an unclean way there. There shall be no lion there, nor shall any of the evil beasts ascend upon it, nor shall they be found there; but the redeemed and the chosen shall walk there” (ibid. 35:3–10).

Concerning this, it is written in the Song of Songs, in the person of the Lord:

> “You are wholly beautiful, my sister, and there is no reproach in you” (Song of Songs 4:7).

The apostle Paul demonstrated this most clearly when he said:

> “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word,” [Col. 0835] “and joining to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and immaculate” (Ephesians 5:25–27).

And again:

> “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present a holy virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

## 3.

Having therefore rejected and despised so many and such great testimonies concerning the purity of the Church, which was being promised through the Spirit, they incompetently affirm that the wicked will remain among the good within it, using the likeness of the weeds. Yet the Lord himself interpreted that likeness to his Apostles, saying:

> “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field, however, is this world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; the weeds are the children of the evil one; the enemy who sows them is the devil; the harvest is the consummation of the age; and the reapers are angels” (Matthew 13:37–39),

and so forth.

He says, “The field is the world.” Therefore it is not the Church but the world in which the good and the wicked are preserved together until the harvest, that is, until the divine judgment. For not even a man can corrupt what has been interpreted by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0835] Perhaps *homo*, “man.”].

For if the Apostles, the companions of the Lord himself, had learned that weeds in the Church—that is, the offspring of the devil—were to be left growing among the communion of the saints, they would never have expelled Simon, Erastus, Philetus, Alexander, Demas, Hermogenes, and the others like them from the Church’s threshold.

Indeed, if this were so, the whole proclamation of the divine Scriptures would be void, since they command that the polluted be separated from the midst of the saints through the diligence of the priests. The Lord says through Moses:

> “This is an everlasting statute throughout your generations: to divide between the holy and the profane, between the clean and the unclean” (Leviticus 10:9–10).

Elsewhere the Spirit rebukes this neglect in the person of the priests, saying:

> “Her priests rejected my law; they profaned my holy things; they did not distinguish between the clean and the unclean, and they did not separate between the holy and the polluted” (Ezekiel 22:26).

To this parable our adversaries also add that the chaff must remain together with the wheat in the Church. Jeremiah refutes this, saying:

> “What has chaff to do with wheat?” (Jeremiah 23:28).

And the apostle Paul says:

> “What partnership has a believer with an unbeliever? Or what communion has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:15, 14).

And Solomon:

> “If a wolf will ever share with a lamb, so will the sinner with the righteous” (Ecclesiasticus 13:21).

They also affirm that good and bad fish are held and drawn together in one net until the shore—that is, that the righteous and the unrighteous remain together until the end of the age—without observing that this was said about hidden offenders. For the fishermen, that is, the priests, do not know what the net cast into the sea contains until, after it has been drawn to shore, the good or the bad are revealed for separation.

Thus those who are hidden, established in the Church, and unknown to the priests are revealed in the divine judgment and separated from the company of the saints like bad fish. The Lord speaks figuratively in the Gospel concerning the hidden offender who had deceived the priests by stealth:

> “When the King entered to see those reclining at table, he saw there a man who did not have a wedding garment, and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here?’ But he was silent. Then the King said to his servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth’” (Matthew 22:11–13).

Accordingly, on this understanding they have said in vain that the good are not abandoned because of the wicked through a sacrilegious separation, but that the wicked are tolerated because of the good through a pious unity. For elsewhere the Lord, angered by such a profane mixture, shows that he is stirred up and calls for the greatest separation. He says:

> “Because the whole house of Israel has become a mixture for me, all bronze, silver, iron, tin, and lead, mixed together in the middle of a burning furnace; therefore he says: ‘Thus says the Lord: Because you have all become one mixture, therefore I shall gather you into the midst of Jerusalem, just as bronze, silver, iron, tin, and lead are gathered into the middle of a furnace, to blow upon them with fire so that they may be melted. So I shall gather you in my anger, and I shall burn you and blow upon you with the breath of the fire of my anger; and you shall be melted in its midst,” [Col. 0836] “and you shall know that I am the Lord, who have poured out my wrath upon you’” (Ezekiel 22:18–22).

## 4.

Against these and similar arguments, by which the Church of God is defended from the pollution of mingled unclean persons, it is clear with what conscience our adversaries, acting as patrons of error, refuse to have the wicked distinguished from the communion of the good.

For they proceed most openly in blasphemy, saying that the Church cannot be stained even by the offenses of manifestly wicked persons. They bring forward as examples the Prophets, who, although they rebuked such people for their offenses, nevertheless did not separate themselves from them bodily. Yet we show that the period in question was very different, since people were permitted to approach baptism repeatedly, as often as they sinned.

Even so, those same Prophets are found to have abstained from communion with the wicked. When the prophet Zephaniah was sent to Jeroboam, who was involved in schism, he was commanded to accept neither bread nor water; and when he was deceived and violated the command, he was killed by a lion.

Elijah and Elisha likewise never shared in the schismatic altars of Samaria, nor did they approve them [Note: [Col. 0836] Perhaps, “they shared in them, nor did they approve them.” *M.*]; rather, they lived mostly in solitude.

The prophet Hosea too is shown not to have participated in the rites of those whose sacrifices he detested and condemned, saying:

> “Their sacrifices shall be like bread of mourning; everyone who touches any of them shall be defiled” (Hosea 9:4).

Finally, when could Amos have mixed with the rites of Samaria? Concerning him the false prophet arouses the king’s resentment in this way:

> “Amos is forming conspiracies against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear his words” (Amos 7:10).

For this reason he is also expelled.

But in Jerusalem itself, how could the Prophets share in the sacrifices of sinful people, which they condemned while filled with the divine Spirit? Isaiah says:

> “Of what use is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? I am full. I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, or the blood of bulls and goats; nor should you come into my presence in this way. For who has required these things from your hands? You shall no longer trample my court. If you bring fine flour, it is in vain; incense is an abomination to me. I do not endure your new moons, Sabbaths, or great day. Your fasting, festivals, and feast days my soul hates. For you have become a great burden to me. I shall no longer spare your sins. When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply your prayers, I shall not hear you. For your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1:11–15).

And again:

> “The criminal who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog; and he who offers fine flour is like one who offers swine’s blood; and he who burns incense in remembrance is like a blasphemer” (ibid. 66:3).

Haggai too utterly curses not only their sacrifices but the sinful people themselves, saying:

> “So is this people, and so is this nation; and if anyone approaches it, he shall be defiled” (Haggai 2:15).

And Malachi:

> “You, O priests, who profane my name, and say, ‘In what have we profaned your name?’ By placing polluted bread upon my altar; and you say, ‘In what have we polluted it?’ In this: that you say, ‘The table of the Lord is blessed,’ while you have annulled the things that were placed upon it” (Malachi 1:6–7).

And so you will find throughout all the Prophets that, if they had shared with those whom they condemned in such powerful words, they would have incurred the crime of transgression. Thus the fact that they were among them was a matter of residence, not of communion.

## 5.

Next, in defense of their crime, they assume for themselves the authority of the example of the betrayer Judas. They say that Judas was taken up by the Lord, foreknown by him, and tolerated by him. Certainly, without prejudice to his foreknowledge, the Lord Christ took Judas into the number of the Apostles; and because he was known to the Lord but not to human beings, he tolerated him for the same reason by which he appears even today to tolerate those who are hidden.

For it is written:

> “The hidden things belong to me; the manifest things belong to you and your children” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

In the Psalms:

> “Will God not inquire into these things? For he himself knows the hidden things of the heart” (Psalm 43:22).

In the First Book of Kings:

> “Man looks at the face, but God looks at the heart” (1 Kings 16:7).

And in the Apocalypse:

> “All the churches shall know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and the heart” (Revelation 2:23).

Finally, while the Lord was reclining with his disciples and saying, “One of you will betray me,” and the same Judas replied, “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” and [Note: [Col. 0837] The sense is defective here. Perhaps *cum* should be read instead of *et*. *M.*] heard from the same Lord, “You have said it” (Matthew 26:21, 25), he immediately withdrew in confusion when he saw that he had been exposed. But afterward he came with the very crowd to betray the Lord.

Let the enemies of the Lord’s truth therefore go off with their patron Judas—those who, according to their custom, labor to defend manifestly guilty persons.

## 6.

Likewise, in defense of their polluted mixture, they bring forward the Apostle’s words:

> “Whether through pretense or through truth” (Philippians 1:18) [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0837] Some material is missing here.]

> “I shall have mercy, because they are children of fornication, for their mother has fornicated; she who bore them has dishonored them” (Hosea 2:4–5).

And in Isaiah:

> “As a garment spattered with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and killed my people. You shall not remain forever, wicked offspring. Prepare your children to be killed for the sins of their father, so that they may not arise” (Isaiah 14:20, according to the Septuagint).

And in the Third Book of Kings:

> “Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood of the Lord, so that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled which he spoke concerning the house of Eli at Shiloh” (Third Book of Kings 2:27).

## 7.

As for their claim that the baptism of Christ is to be defended in the same way as the Catholic Church itself is defended—as existing everywhere and among all people—that claim is briefly excluded by the decrees of our most blessed fathers and martyrs.

But how recklessly, forgetful of themselves, these enemies of the truth attack the proposition that baptism administered by any outsiders who are thieves and robbers must be accepted! They employ for this purpose an inappropriate testimony of the apostle Paul, which says:

> “Those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness”—

and here they have attempted to defend one theft by means of a stolen testimony.

For the Apostle was speaking about the Gentiles and rebuking unbelievers when he said:

> “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; his eternal power and divinity likewise, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks; instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools; and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents. Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness” (Romans 1:18–24).

Accordingly, by this interpretation they also profess that they accept the polluted rites of the Gentiles.

Then they followed their error by piling up the clearest blasphemies, saying that those who reject the baptism of heretics can reject Christ, even though the demons confessed him. Here they not only insult the decrees of the holy martyrs, but are more ready to mingle with the communion of demons because those demons confessed Christ.

Moreover, when they stated with subtle brevity that one who has been baptized outside must be accepted—not so that what is lacking may be supplied [Note: [Col. 0837] We emend this in accordance with the *Mandate of the Catholics*, above, col. 826, near the middle.], but so that what is present may be beneficial—they are shown to have ensnared themselves in both respects.

For all these matters, as has been said above, are nullified by the judgments of the holy martyrs. How can it happen, if there is one Church and Christ is undivided, that someone situated outside should obtain baptism?

## 8.

As for what they say we allege against them:

> “Do not lay hands quickly on anyone, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22),

and as though replying to us they answer that people ought to be separated by their conduct rather than bodily: we demonstrate by very many testimonies from the Law that the wicked must be separated not only in conduct but also bodily.

In Numbers:

> “Depart from the tents of these most hardened men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you perish together with them in all their sins” (Numbers 16:26).

Likewise Isaiah:

> “Depart, depart; go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean. Depart from the midst of them, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11).

Likewise the Apostle:

> “For you are the temple of the living God. He himself says: ‘I shall dwell in them and walk among them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people.’ Therefore, depart from the midst of them and separate yourselves, and do not touch what is unclean; and I shall receive you, and I shall be your father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty” (2 Corinthians 6:16–18).

## 9.

What sort of argument is this? When we charge them with the persecutions and savage cruelties by which they and their forebears afflicted and harassed us and our fathers continuously for a hundred years or more, they are not ashamed to use as a refuge the claim that some of our people, the Maximianists, inflicted persecutions.

Certainly, it is one thing to have wished to reclaim by civil means the usurped property of the Church and of fellow poor people, without compelling anyone unwilling or reluctant to join our communion; and quite another to exercise every kind of evil with open fury and cruelty throughout the entire Christian people.

For who does not know that these traitors and persecutors of ours, from the very beginning of their condemned betrayal, repeatedly petitioned all the rulers of this world, through fabricated prayers, for our destruction, and against God’s commands constrained people by threats and proscriptions to join their communion?

To say nothing of how much Christian blood was shed through Leontius, Ursacius, Macarius, Paulus, Taurinus, Romanus, and the other agents whom they obtained from the rulers of this world for the slaughter of the saints—when many venerable priests were killed, others banished into exile, Christianity widely harassed, consecrated virgins violated, the wealthy proscribed, the poor stripped, basilicas seized, and priests driven into flight as refugees—no one is unaware of how much they have committed in our own time.

They thrust bishops into exile; they drove fleeing Christians over precipices; they oppressed the people; they plundered the clergy; they invaded basilicas; they inflicted blows on those unwilling to consent; finally, in the single town of Bagai, the blood of many Christians was shed on their account. Not even then satisfied, they are content to continue without ceasing to this day.

Since it would therefore be superfluous to append testimonies from the divine Scriptures against such savage crimes of theirs, by which these offenses are prohibited—especially since such things are not even permitted by secular laws—it is enough that we have answered their error and washed away with divine testimonies what they offered needlessly in response.

And in another hand:

> May the Lord preserve you safe and sound; this is our wish.

# Augustine’s Responses to the Letter of the Donatists

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

Let us, illustrious sir, not linger any longer over superfluities in the Church’s case. If only our brothers standing on the other side had presented this letter before all their delaying speeches, so that we could now address something concerning the Church, which is the matter at issue.

Your Nobility has therefore observed in this letter two kinds of inserted material, whether objections or arguments, to which we must respond: one concerning the divine Scriptures and the words of the holy Law; the other concerning human accusations, which I do not know who thought should be brought forward more for the sake of provoking hatred than of speaking truth.

With the Lord’s help, we shall answer these two matters briefly, so that we do not respond to such lengthy material with an equally lengthy speech.

The question concerns the Church: whether it was foretold that it would have wicked persons mingled within it until the end, or whether, in this present age, it would have absolutely all good, all holy, and all immaculate persons until the final end of the age. [Col. 0839] Both testimonies are divine, and certainly ought not to be contradictory; indeed, they cannot be, if they find someone capable of understanding them.

I did not say, nor did any of us say, that the Church is the threshing floor. The Gospel speaks of this, where it is written that the one who is to come will have a winnowing fork in his hand and will cleanse his threshing floor, gathering the wheat into his barn.

Emeritus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0839] Donatist.], said:

You do not read “threshing floor.”

Augustine said:

John said, “He will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn” (Matthew 3:12).

Petilianus said:

The Evangelist said this concerning hidden offenders, not concerning manifest ones, whom you wish to have mingled with you.

Augustine said:

Let our statement be treated as their letter. He began to read; no disturbance was raised by us, no confusion, no interruption. Let him permit me to finish what I began to say, and then let him answer. Why is there no return to us of what we granted first? Your Nobility observed our patience while such a long letter was being read.

Emeritus said:

We are burdened when he says that he is patient; and he ought not to pass judgment about himself, since another person judges him.

Augustine said:

If only you too were patient until I finished what I am saying!

Therefore, as I began to say, the divine testimonies concerning the weeds and the wheat are those which they have tried to understand [Note: [Col. 0839] The passage is corrupt.]. Yet at some point they confessed, concerning the nets, that the Church would contain wicked and good people; but they said that these were unknown to the priests, and therefore did not prejudice the good, since they were not known.

I, however, could demonstrate, with whatever arguments my limited ability permits, that the more truthful understanding is that the Church has both good and wicked people—namely, weeds and wheat—and that the world itself has been called by the name of the Church, since the Lord himself says:

> “Not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17).

Yet we know that the Lord saves no one except the Church.

Emeritus said:

> “The world did not know you” (ibid. 17:25).

Therefore the Church did not know God, if the Church is the world. And again he said:

> “So that the whole world may become guilty before God” (Romans 3:19).

And again he said:

> “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates and persecutes you” (John 15:19).

And again:

> “They are of the world, and the world obeys them” (1 John 4:5).

And again:

> “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (ibid. 2:15).

Augustine said:

We too could say all these things and, as though they were contradictory to what was first proposed, resolve them. Therefore they are interrupting with this disturbance without cause; for we could have used such arguments from their letter to prevent it from being read. Let them listen patiently. Let Your Sublimity admonish them to do what they ought to have done voluntarily.

Let them listen patiently: the matter we are treating is not trivial. Today we have undertaken, with God’s help, to answer their lengthy letter. Nor are we asking them to give it to us so that we may examine it and answer later, as they themselves did with our *Mandate*. Let them grant us some patience, for the sake of your safety.

*(After several further exchanges.)*

Augustine said:

When the letter was being read, we conducted ourselves as though they themselves were presenting their case. We gave silence to their presentation—I do not wish to call it patience, because they make that a charge against us—so let them also grant us silence.

Montanus, bishop [Note: [Col. 0839] Donatist.], said:

How can we keep everything in mind if we do not answer each point?

Augustine said:

That is why those matters were written down and these are being recorded. If anything escapes my memory, I too can ask that it be read to me from the letter; and they can likewise ask that it be read to them from their copies. Let silence be granted, and let us accomplish something.

As I was therefore beginning to say, prompted by their own arguments, we find in the Scriptures the name “world” used in an evil sense and the name “world” used in a good sense.

The name “world” in an evil sense occurs, as they said:

> “The world did not know him” (John 1:10);

and:

> “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15);

and so forth.

The name “world” in a good sense occurs:

> “That the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

For believing is not the action of the wicked.

The name “world” in a good sense also occurs:

> “He did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (ibid. 3:17).

Only the Church in the world will be saved.

Since, then, “world” occurs both in a good sense and in an evil sense, where is the quarrel among these Scriptures if there is no interpreter? Apply the light of understanding. See in the evil sense of “world” all lovers of temporal things throughout all nations; see in the good sense of “world” all the faithful and those who hope for eternal life throughout all nations.

> “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

If that hated world can be reconciled to God—the world of which it was said that the love of Christ is not in the one who loves the world—let those who speak judge the matter.

Let Your Nobility therefore listen patiently. I see that Holy Scripture, through the good and wicked mingled together, has prefigured the Church, just as they themselves have already admitted concerning the nets.

Petilianus said:

What the world is and what the Church is has been defined most clearly by the very author and maker of the world, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. For the Lord himself said:

> “The world is this field” (Matthew 13:38).

He could have said, “The world is the Church.” Who among human beings therefore dares to define what the world is, when the very maker and creator of the world has already deigned to define it?

Marcellinus, illustrious man, tribune and notary, said:

Clearly show which world is said to be saved.

Petilianus said:

Human beings are called “the world” where he said, “Reconciling the world to himself.” For God did not wish to reconcile beasts to himself, but human beings.

Augustine said:

The world, then—for we could not understand it otherwise—is understood to mean human beings. We are certainly not so foolish as to say that beasts and whatever irrational animals there are belong to the salvation promised by Christ.

We say precisely this: “The world is placed in the evil one” (1 John 5:19)—these are human beings; “that the world may believe that you sent me”—these are human beings; “reconciling the world to himself”—these are human beings; and all the other expressions spoken in the evil sense refer to those human beings, those human beings.

For throughout the whole world both groups exist, the wicked mingled with the good.

So too the Church, which they have admitted is shown under the name of the net to contain wicked people, although they said that these were hidden from the fishermen: it is already established that it contains both good and wicked people. The question concerns whether they are hidden or not; that is, whether it belonged to the piety of the good to tolerate even known wicked people so that they would not abandon the good, or whether, because of the wicked, they wished to abandon everything. The question is what kind of wicked people appeared in the Church. This is what we are proving.

For we say that ecclesiastical discipline must certainly not be neglected, and that wherever wicked people are exposed, they must be restrained so that they may be corrected—not only by a word of correction, but also by excommunications and degradations, so that they may seek a humble place of salvation in the Church. This is done for their healing, not out of hatred, but out of concern for their brothers’ salvation, just as the Apostle himself most clearly declares in one place, saying:

> “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him” (2 Thessalonians 3:14) [lacuna].

The remaining chapters of the third day are missing.

# Judgment of the Examiner

Flavius Marcellinus, illustrious man, tribune and notary, said:

I would certainly wish—and this is what I now desire with the whole intention of my hopes—that, just as great joy arose from the demonstration of the truth and the final exposure of error, so a congratulation might arise from the conversion of the ancient superstition and the change of opinion for the better.

For who could doubt that there are great joys when an unexpected cure comes to a longstanding illness? In such circumstances, the restoration of health makes the cause for rejoicing greater than health that has always been retained.

But because the obstinacy of ruined minds, which the bonds of a simultaneously perverse persuasion had tied together, either pretends not to return to the path of salvation that has been shown to them or—what is worse—shrinks from it through shamelessness, the force of the laws must now be brought forth and the sentence enforced. Those whom milder medicines, after the truth had been openly confronted, do not recall to sound health, a harsher course of treatment must restore.

For what person of sound judgment could fail to declare clearly—just as the sequence of the proceedings set out below demonstrates, and as the examples contained in the divine books also testify—that one person cannot be made guilty of the guilt of another, even if that guilt could have been proved; that the condition of the universal Church ought not to be overthrown through the accusation of Caecilianus, concerning whom nothing blameworthy could be established; and that a sentence pronounced against him in his absence by those who separated themselves from the body of the Church could not have prejudiced him?
