[Note: [Col. 0840] Elsewhere, “nor even the absent person.” Perhaps it should read, “nor could the sentence passed against the absent person.”]

Nor did the condemnation recently pronounced by the Maximianists against the absent Primianus prevail to harm him.

What should also be sufficient, at least in part, for the purpose of correction is the proof, disclosed by so many judgments, of Donatus as the originator of the schism; the vindication and acquittal of Caecilianus; and the final judgment of the three, recorded by Constantine, by which the innocence of Caecilianus and the calumnious accusation of Donatus and his associates were demonstrated with the greatest clarity, together with the exoneration of Felix of Aptunga, his ordainer, shown by the documents of the proconsular judgment? [Col. 0841]

Therefore, if these matters, so clear and manifest, cannot cure an illness of long standing, the putrefaction of the wound must be restrained, so that, with its freedom obstructed, it may begin to harm only itself, since it has chosen this course. Through this it will eventually become willing to be healed.

Let falsehood, therefore, once exposed, bow its neck to the truth that has been declared.

Accordingly, by the authority of this edict I admonish all men of the various orders, as well as owners of estates, agents, tenants both of imperial and of private property, and the elders of every place, to remember the laws, their dignity, their reputation, and their own salvation, and to strive to prohibit the assemblies of the Donatists in every city and place.

They must hasten, without any delay, to hand over to the Catholics the churches which, through my clemency and without an imperial command, are known to have been granted to them up to the day of the sentence, unless they prefer to be caught in the snares of so many decrees. If they wish to consent to Catholic unity, it is certainly established that these churches belong to them.

But after unity has been exposed in every way and the superstition has been convicted, they must be driven away from the intention of their own crime with even greater force and diligence.

Those who, after the laws have forbidden it, mingle with their assemblies must understand without doubt that they can no longer escape the penalty established by imperial authority. It is sufficiently clear that, after the reverence due to the Catholic law had been acknowledged, they returned in the foremost place to their profane assemblies and communion.

I had previously delayed action to some extent solely out of consideration for patience and hope of correction, so that this might not happen.

Let it therefore suffice that the enemies of the Christian faith have insulted the laws up to this point. Since their persons are known, what need is there to subject them to the bonds of so many decrees, when no correction has followed?

Let the Donatists know that even after the victory of the truth the decision of the Catholic bishops remains: after the hearings have been completed—hearings that public knowledge remembers were previously offered to them, and that it is now sufficiently certain are being offered again without hesitation—they may be received.

It is certain that the force of the earlier edict is preserved in every respect.

Therefore every bishop of Donatus’s communion ought to return to his own place without any disturbance or harassment, so that, once established in his own place, he may either return to the one true Church or not delay in fulfilling the laws without concealment.

Those who know that they have crowds of Circumcellions on their estates should understand that, unless they earnestly desire to suppress and restrain their insolence in every way, those estates will soon be seized by the treasury.

In this way provision is being made both for the Catholic law and for the public peace, so that their madness may cease.

A rereading of the proceedings, in which it is shown that the error of schism previously mentioned arose among the Donatists, and that Caecilianus and the others whom they wickedly believed should be accused were exonerated, will be able to instruct Your Holiness fully.

Let it be published.

*(Given at Carthage, after the consulship of Varanes, illustrious man, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.)* [Note: [Col. 0841] In the year of Christ 411, on June 26.]

# Laws of the Emperor Honorius against the Donatists, issued after the Conference

[Note: [Col. 0841] See the Theodosian Code, law 52, *On Heretics*.]

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Seleucus, Praetorian Prefect.

After annulling whatever might be obtained through a pragmatic sanction or through a note written by our hand, and while those provisions remain which were established long ago concerning this matter and preserved by the enactments of the former emperors: unless, from the day on which this law is issued, all Donatists—priests, clerics, and laypeople alike—restore themselves to the Catholic Church, from which they sacrilegiously withdrew, the following persons shall individually be compelled to pay into our treasury, as a penalty:

- Illustrious men, fifty pounds of gold;
- Spectable men, forty pounds of gold;
- Senators, thirty pounds of gold;
- Clarissimi, twenty pounds of gold;
- Men of priestly rank, thirty pounds of gold;
- Principales, twenty pounds of gold;
- Decurions, five pounds of gold;
- Merchants, five pounds of gold;
- Commoners, five pounds of gold;
- Circumcellions, ten pounds of silver.

If they are not presented for the exactor by the tenants under whom they live or by the procurators, those persons themselves shall be held liable to the penalty, so that not even the people of our own household shall be considered exempt from such a judgment.

Their wives too shall separately be bound by the fine appropriate to their husbands’ rank.

For those whom the damages inflicted do not correct at all shall next suffer the confiscation of all their property.

The warning of masters shall recall slaves from the wicked religion; and colonists shall be recalled by the more frequent blows of the whip. If they prefer it, they themselves, even if Catholics, shall be held liable for the aforesaid losses. [Col. 0842]

Their clerics and ministers, and their most pernicious priests, having been removed from the African sun—which they polluted by their sacrilegious rite—shall be sent individually into exile in the various regions under a suitable escort.

Their churches, meeting places, and estates—if any wrongful generosity has transferred property to their churches—shall be vindicated for the ownership and authority of the Catholic Church, as we established long ago.

*Given on the third day before the Kalends of February at Ravenna, in the consulship of Honorius, ninth time, and Theodosius, fifth time, Augusti.* [Note: [Col. 0842] January 30, 412.]

The same Augusti to Julian, proconsul of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0842] See the Theodosian Code, law 54, *On Heretics*.]

The Donatists and heretics whom the patience of Our Clemency has hitherto spared, We have determined should be struck down by appropriate authority, so that by an unequivocal command they may recognize that they are both legally incapacitated and possess no power to enter into any contract, but are to be burdened with perpetual infamy and excluded from respectable gatherings and public assemblies. Those places in which dreadful superstition has until now been maintained are to be joined to the venerable Catholic Church. Thus their bishops, presbyters, and all their other leaders and ministers, stripped of all their possessions, are to be sent into exile, each to a separate island or province.

Whoever receives these fugitives in order to conceal them from the punishment prescribed shall know that his patrimony is to be added to the profits of Our treasury and that he himself will be subjected to the punishment imposed upon them. We also clearly impose losses of patrimony and pecuniary penalties upon men, women, individuals, and persons of rank, to be inflicted according to each one’s status.

Therefore, whoever is invested with proconsular, vicariate, or first-rank *comitiva* [official rank], unless he turns his mind and purpose toward the observance of Catholicism, shall be compelled to pay two hundred pounds of silver, to be added to the benefit of Our treasury. And lest this alone be thought sufficient to cut short his resolve, whenever he is convicted of having joined such a communion, the fine shall be exacted each time. If it is established that he has done so five times and has not been recalled from his error even by these losses, then the matter shall be referred to Our Clemency, so that We may judge more harshly concerning his entire property and status.

We bind the remaining persons of rank by similar conditions: namely, that a senator who, without being protected externally by any privilege of rank, is found in the flock of the Donatists shall pay one hundred pounds of silver; members of the priestly order shall likewise be compelled to pay the same sum; the ten leading members of the municipal council shall be condemned to fifty pounds of silver; and the remaining decurions shall pay ten pounds of silver, if they choose to remain in heresy.

Our tenants, if they allow these practices to take place on the estates belonging to Our venerable property, shall be compelled, as a penalty, to pay as much rent as they have been accustomed to pay under their lease. The same authority of this sacred decree shall also bind the *emphyteuticarii* [long-term hereditary lessees].

Tenants of private owners, if they allow assemblies to be held on these same estates, or if through their tolerance the sacred mystery is polluted, shall be reported by the judge to the knowledge of the owners. It will be their responsibility, if they wish to escape the penalty of the sacred command, either to correct those who resist or to replace those who persist, and to provide their estates with such administrators as will observe the divine commands.

If they neglect to arrange this, they too shall, by the authority of the promulgated order, be fined in the amount of the rents they have been accustomed to receive, so that whatever could have accrued to their profit may be joined to the sacred treasury.

Officials of various judges, if they are found involved in this error, shall be liable, by way of penalty, to the payment of thirty pounds of silver. If, after being condemned five times, they refuse to abstain, they shall be restrained by flogging and committed to exile.

The strictest coercion shall punish slaves and tenants for such attempts. If tenants, even when compelled by flogging, persist in their resolve, they shall then be fined one third of their personal property; and everything that can be collected from such classes of persons and places shall immediately be directed to the sacred distributions.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July at Ravenna, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans. [Note: [Col. 0842] 22 June 414.]

The same Augusti to Julian, proconsul of Africa. [Note: [Col. 0842] See the Theodosian Code, law 55, *Concerning Heretics*.]

Through the knowledge and diligence of Marcellinus, a man of illustrious memory, the proceedings conducted against the Donatists were undertaken; and We wish the records transferred into the public archives to possess perpetual validity. For the public faith ought not to perish with the death of the judge.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September at Ravenna, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans. [Note: [Col. 0842] 30 August 414.]

[Col. 0841] The Donatists are also concerned by a law issued by the same emperors to Heraclianus, count of Africa, on 25 August 415, in the Theodosian Code, law 56, *Concerning Heretics*. Likewise, a law of Valentinian III issued to Georgius, proconsul of Africa, on 4 August 425, in the Theodosian Code, law 63, *Concerning Heretics*. They are also named among other heretics in a law of Theodosius the Younger issued to Florentius, perpetual Flamen, on 30 May 428, in the Theodosian Code, law 65, *Concerning Heretics*. Yet the Donatist schism could not be abolished by these exceedingly severe imperial constitutions. Indeed, it still flourished throughout Africa in the time of Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff, as we learn from Gregory himself: book 1, Letter 75, to the bishops of Numidia; book 2, Letter 35; book 3, Letters 32 and 35; and book 5, Letters 36 and 61.

[Col. 0843]

# INDEX OF THE SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THIS NINTH VOLUME

[Col. 0843] **Preface to Volume Nine.** 9–10.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Psalm against the Party of Donatus.** 23–24.

**Admonition concerning the Books against the Letter of Parmenianus.** 31–32.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Three Books against the Letter of Parmenianus.** 33–34.

**Book One.** — He answers the accusations and unjust complaints that Parmenianus brought against the Catholics; and he shows that Christian rulers rightly establish penalties, in accordance with their office and legal authority, for restraining heretics and schismatics. Ibid.

**Book Two.** — The testimonies of Scripture are examined, by the perverse interpretation of which the Donatists attempted to deceive the inexperienced. 49–50.

**Book Three.** — The remaining passages of Scripture that Parmenianus had alleged are treated. 81–82.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Seven Books on Baptism against the Donatists.** 107–108.

**Book One.** — He proves that Baptism can be conferred outside the Catholic communion by heretics or schismatics, but that it ought not nevertheless to be received from them and that it is of no benefit within heresy or schism. Ibid.

**Book Two.** — Augustine proves that the authority of Cyprian, bishop and martyr, is wrongly brought forward by the Donatists, since it is more opposed to them than to the Catholics. For Cyprian did not judge that the opinion of his predecessor Agrippinus—that heretics should be baptized in the Catholic Church when they come to it—ought to be accepted, except on the condition that peace should always be maintained with those who thought differently and that the unity of the Church should never be broken by any schism. 125–126.

**Book Three.** — He undertakes to refute the points in Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus that seem to prove that the Baptism of Christ cannot be conferred through heretics. 139–140.

**Book Four.** — He treats the passages that follow in the same letter of Cyprian to Jubaianus. 153–154.

**Book Five.** — He examines the final part of Cyprian’s letter to Jubaianus, as well as his letter to Quintus, his synodical letter to the bishops of Numidia, and his letter to Pompeius. 175–176.

**Book Six.** — The Council of Carthage concerning the Baptism of heretics, held under the direction and authority of Cyprian, is examined. 197–198.

**Book Seven.** — The remaining decisions of the Council of Carthage are treated. 223–224.

**Admonition concerning the Books against the Letters of Petilianus.** 243–244.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Three Books against the Letters of Petilianus the Donatist, Bishop of Cirta.** 245–246.

**Book One.** — Written in the form of a letter addressed to the Catholics, in which the first parts of Petilianus’s letter—which he himself had written to his own people—are refuted. Ibid.

**Book Two.** — Augustine responds to each and every word of Petilianus’s letter as though he were conversing with an opponent present before him. 259–260.

**Book Three.** — Augustine refutes the second letter that Petilianus wrote against him after seeing the first of the preceding books, a letter full of curses. Setting aside his own defense, he shows that Petilianus has failed in the case and has been unable to respond to the matter at issue. 345–346.

**Admonition concerning the Book on the Unity of the Church.** 389–390.

**Letter against the Donatists to the Catholics, commonly called One Book on the Unity of the Church.** — The question is proposed whether the Church of Christ is among the Catholics or among the Donatists; this is to be determined here only from clear and certain passages of sacred Scripture. First, very many testimonies from the Old and New Instrument are brought forward, by which it is shown clearly and certainly that the true Church of Christ is the one spread throughout the whole world. Then, the few passages from the same canonical Scriptures that the schismatics commonly allege on behalf of the Party of Donatus are shown to be ambiguous and uncertain and, since they can be explained by contrary reasoning, to possess no force for defending their cause. The Donatists’ accusations against the Catholics concerning tradition, persecution, and other matters are also refuted when the occasion arises. 391–392.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Four Books against Cresconius the Grammarian of the Party of Donatus.** 445–446.

**Book One.** — Augustine begins to refute the letter of Cresconius, published in defense of Petilianus and addressed to Augustine himself. He proves that neither eloquence nor any kind of dialectic should be feared by defenders of the truth, lest they refute its adversaries by disputing with them; nor should a person who has undertaken [Col. 0844] a contentious verbal exchange with harsh and resistant speakers in order to refute them be considered quarrelsome. Afterwards he shows that it does not follow that, if Baptism is conceded to exist in the Party of Donatus, it must also be conceded that it ought to be received there. For outside the Catholic Church it is held—futilely and perniciously, yet truly and wholly—as the same Baptism. 445–446.

**Book Two.** — He examines other statements in Cresconius’s letter. He willingly grants Cresconius’s preference that Donatists be called *Donatiani* rather than *Donatistae*, after Donatus. He contends, however, that he was right to call them heretics; nevertheless, they are not to be baptized when they return to the Church. Indeed, their clergy may be received in their offices if this seems beneficial to the Church. He teaches, moreover, that something is given in the Church to those who return which is not given outside it at all, namely the gift of charity. He demonstrates that Cresconius has poorly defended Petilianus’s statement, “The conscience of the one who gives holily is considered; it cleanses the one who receives.” He examines the passages of Scripture cited by Cresconius, especially the one beginning, “He who is baptized by a dead man,” and so forth. Finally, he responds to the authority of Cyprian concerning the rebaptism of heretics. 467–468.

**Book Three.** — He runs through the remaining part of Cresconius’s letter, briefly refuting each point in sequence. 495–496.

**Book Four.** — He responds again to all the parts of Cresconius’s letter, refuting his objections and accusations one by one solely from the case of the Maximianists. 547–548.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, One Book on the One Baptism against Petilianus, addressed to Consentius.** — Augustine refutes Petilianus’s book on the one Baptism, in which Petilianus contended that it exists only in the true Church, indeed only in the Party of Donatus. He teaches that the truth of the one Baptism, even when found among heretics, should be approved, not violated. He responds to the authority of the martyr Cyprian and of other African bishops who are alleged to have held a different opinion with him. From Cyprian’s own conduct he proves, against the Donatist schism, that no one is stained within the unity of the Church by the sins of others. Finally, he repels the accusations that Petilianus brought against Melchiades and certain other Catholic bishops. 595–596.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists.** 613–614.

**Conference of the First Day.** Ibid.

**Conference of the Second Day.** 621–622.

**Conference of the Third Day.** Ibid.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, One Book to the Donatists after the Conference.** — Augustine warns the laypeople of the Party of Donatus not to be led astray any further by their bishops. The proceedings demonstrate that, at the conference held at Carthage, those bishops were refuted by their own words, opinions, and documents produced by those very men. He dispels their empty accusations against the judgment of that conference, briefly examining and refuting certain writings that they circulated publicly after the conference. 651–652.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea, delivered in the presence of Emeritus.** 689–690.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, One Book on the Proceedings with Emeritus, Donatist Bishop of Caesarea.** 697–698.

**Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Two Books against Gaudentius, Bishop of the Donatists.** 707–708.

**Book One.** — Gaudentius’s two letters to Dulcitius are refuted. Ibid.

**Book Two.** — Gaudentius’s reply to the preceding book is dispelled. 741–742.

**Admonition concerning the Sermon on Rusticianus the Subdeacon.** 751–752.

**Sermon—attributed to Augustine—on Rusticianus the Subdeacon, rebaptized by the Donatists and ordained deacon.** 753–754.

**Index of the Short Works of Saint Augustine against the Donatists contained in the preceding volumes.** 757–758.

**Appendix to Volume Nine of the Works of Saint Augustine.** 759–760.

**Censure of the Louvain Theologians and Bernard Vindingus on the Book against Fulgentius.** Ibid.

**One Book against Fulgentius the Donatist, by an uncertain author.** 763–764.

**Excerpts and Ancient Writings Relating to the History of the Donatists**, the reading of which sheds light on Augustine’s preceding books against these same heretics. 773–774.

[Col. 0843] **END OF VOLUME NINE**
